# Volume Front Matter

## Series Title Page

**Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, and Economical Library of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who Flourished from the Apostolic Age to the Time of Innocent III**

A chronological reissue of all the surviving monuments of Catholic tradition from the first twelve centuries of the Church, based on the most accurate editions, diligently corrected by comparison both with one another and with certain manuscripts; continually illustrated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by all works discovered after the extensive editions produced during the last three centuries; furnished with separate analytical indexes following each volume and each author of some importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject matter below; expanded by works both doubtful and apocryphal, and also by works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: the first, of subjects, by consulting which everything written by each Father on any topic may be surveyed at a glance; the second, of Sacred Scripture, from which the reader may readily discover which Fathers commented on the individual texts of each book of Scripture, and in which places of their works they did so.

The most accurate edition, and one easily to be preferred to all others, if the following are properly weighed: the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the works reprinted, the extremely convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the entire work, the low price, and, above all, the fact that this collection—single, methodical, and chronological—is the first in our library to assemble six hundred fragments and little works previously scattered here and there, gathered from works concerning every age, place, language, and form.

**Second Series**, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the universal library of the clergy, or of complete courses in the several branches of ecclesiastical learning.

Patrology was printed in two editions, one Latin and the other Greek-Latin. The Latin edition comprises 1,200 volumes and is sold for 1,000 francs; the Greek-Latin edition comprises 1,300 volumes and is sold for 800 francs. The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the Eastern authors, however, are presented in it only in Latin translation.

# In the Year of the Lord 980

## Wigo, Dean of the Monastery of Phyuhtwang

[Col. 0009]

# Letters of Wigo

*(Pez, Diplomatic Codex, p. 110.)*

## I. To the Empress Adelheid

*He earnestly commends himself and his flock.*

[Col. 0009A]

To the most exalted mistress, most noble nurturer of kings and kingdoms, A., Augusta, ever unconquered, the brothers newly gathered for the service of the Church of Phyuhtwang send the title of highest greeting in Christ the Savior.

Since we know that all the assemblies of the faithful are continually present to the memory of your piety, we have thought it right to make known to you also our humble name as the Church of the great God and Savior, and our monastic purpose, which we have only recently begun to pursue in that place, so that henceforth, protected by the shadow of your dominion, we may be able safely to endure the disturbances caused by worldly assaults.

We therefore believe that the Church would be exceedingly blessed if in our time we were deemed worthy to have you as its mother. We judge the communities of monks happy who, under such a protectress, devote themselves to the discipline of spiritual warfare, whose very intellect is enriched with such wisdom that it has subjected the whole empire to itself. Strengthened by the security of this great hope, we do not cease day and night to beseech God for the continuance and stability of your reign. Moreover, by continual prayer we ask Christ to grant the blessed spirits of our emperors the delights of the heavenly Elysium. Farewell.

## II. To Theodoric the Hermit in the Forest of the East

*He writes of the many duties and cares with which he is overwhelmed in providing for his monastery, and asks that Brother Adalgoz be sent to him as an assistant.*

[Col. 0009C]

To T., most devoted cultivator of the hermit’s way of life, W., unworthy provider of the monastery of the Lord Savior, with the color of pretense wiped away, offers the devoted submission of obedience.

We cannot conceal from your Fatherhood the condition of all the affairs that laboriously press upon us from every side, since, as we hope, you will in no way withhold the comfort of your customary compassion from those who ask for it. We recently visited the brothers of our monastery and brought back Brother Helperic, who had been granted as an assistant. Because he refused to grant this request with us, we had lodged with our abbot a complaint concerning all those matters with which we know you to be thoroughly acquainted through your experience of labors.

We have no relief through the comfort of any brother from the burdens of many kinds that continually weigh heavily upon us: one is ill, another is occupied with a different ministry, so that there is no one to grant even for a short time a respite to one who labors alone. I myself carry all the keys of the monastery, hung on a jingling belt all around me. In addition, I must provide with the greatest care for the observance of the rule, now oversee the provisions, now preside over the cooks, sometimes attend to the refectory [or: *refectorium*, “refectory”], and always serve all the members of the household who live within, as well as all the guests who arrive from outside.

We ask, with your permission, that Brother Adalgoz, recently restored to the monastery after the death of his father, be granted to us as an assistant. Since we have obediently complied in everything with the instructions we received from you concerning him, and have not compelled him to do anything unwillingly, the common petition of our brothers asks that, in accordance with the obedience he owes you, he be granted to us, to be appointed to a monastic office—not as though he had been removed from your guardianship, since none of us withdraws from your command, but because, if we dare say so, it is fitting that you return a good deed in charitable reciprocity. We ask that you frequently remind Brother Engilpert by letter to advance from good things to better ones. Farewell.

## III. To Dietrich

*He asks that Dietrich send him a book of canons, which he will need in the case of a cleric badly treated by laymen.*

[Col. 0010C]

To Lord Dietrich, Wigo, a fellow brother in the supreme God, sends greetings.

Just as through a shepherd’s negligence the sheep often suffer losses, so through the dullness of our inexperience [so the manuscript] the servants of our neighbors, gathered together, mangled one of our clerics limb by limb. And behold, various conflicts among many people follow. To annul these and destroy them by canonical reasoning, we ask that, if you have any book of precedents with you, you lend it to us and send it through the present messenger. Farewell.

## IV. To Liutold, Bishop of Augsburg

*He asks him to bring aid to the grievous circumstances of his monastery.*

[Col. 0011A]

To L., clothed from heaven with the pallium of the highest priesthood, W., the unarmed shepherd charged with gathering the flock, sends the joy of heavenly happiness in Christ.

First we hymn the supreme God because the course of our effective embassy has prospered toward our monastery. He always directs by a straight step and a road-guiding course those who turn their hearts toward him. We rightly ascribe the increase of our fraternal escort to your piety, because you sent us on our way the fur-bearing man whom our ignorance had not sufficiently instructed, and the lukewarm words of the writing, strengthened by the living flame of your wit.

We endure that inconvenience with great difficulty while we are gathered for the service of God in the Church: we cannot overcome by singing the chattering of the clustered birds, which are carried in from every side through the wide-open windows on winged flight; and whenever we lie prostrate on the snowy pavement, blown upon by snow from every direction, we roll about in the mud. Yet we would endure these things suitably while living together if only we could defend the Lord’s altar from the snow. The lighted candles, disturbed by the force of the winds, are extinguished amid abundant tears. If you provide some linen cloths for closing the windows, you can easily remedy this complaint. We ask, bending our neck, that whatever iron tools need repairing and are necessary for us may be sent to our Vulcan.

## V. To Gozpert, Abbot of Tegernsee

*He explains the difficulty caused by the construction of his new monastery and asks that Weicher be sent to him for assistance and Sigihard for the sake of study.*

[Col. 0011C]

To Abbot G., who in monastic steadfastness imitates the ancient Fathers in the place of the Saints, Wigo, together with his little brother assigned with him to the ministry, sends whatever a tender child owes to a mature parent.

It is remarkable that you wish to propagate the shoots of a new plantation in winter, according to the novelty of your writing, since snowy winter is accustomed not to make crops grow green but rather to freeze them white and hard like stones. Yet, if we wish to lay foundations suitable in every way for the adornment of Solomon’s house, of a structure like that, glorious Solomon was not so much supported by all the abundance of David’s preparations as our heart’s dwelling is gladdened by a beautiful building. It is not to be established with stony material, destined one day to fall, but by your highness’s help it must be stabilized for our bishop through the cultivation of a foundation that will endure.

We rejoice that we have been sent according to the pattern of the Lord’s ordinance, by which he sent twelve disciples to preach to the peoples; and we grieve that we cannot imitate the work of their ministry. For they, divided into thirty-six pairs, could have made up for the accomplishment of the command entrusted to them, if not by holiness, then—so to speak poetically—by the number of their fulfillment. We have no helpers with us except two very old men, decrepit with age, whom no kind of work suits at all. The heavenly citizens smile at them only insofar as they wish them daily to become divine [the manuscript has *deficare*, apparently for *deificare*] among those above.

Therefore we ask your Fatherhood’s kindness to help us by the assistance of our brother Weicher, so that the root of some good fruit may be increased in the place entrusted to us through the outpouring of greater irrigation, so that the Lord Savior may repay you with an accumulation of heavenly reward. We also ask that our brother Sigihard, whom you decided to send during the green season of the year for the sake of learning, be sent now as well, if he wishes and if you deem it fitting. Farewell.

## VI. To Liutold, Bishop of Augsburg

*He asks him to receive kindly the brothers whom he obtained from Gozpert, abbot of Tegernsee, for the benefit of his monastery, and to send them to him provided with the necessities.*

[Col. 0012B]

To Bishop L., who watches over the care of Christ’s sheep with prudent pastoral guardianship, W., together with his brother, an unworthy novice of God the Savior, sends continual prayer for heavenly salvation in Christ.

By the authority of your holiness, supreme shepherd, charmingly persuaded and compelled by the singularity of our communal life, we have sailed by messenger toward the firmest shore against the blows of stagnant waters, and toward the anchor of the truest hope—namely, the safest harbor of our abbot—so that he may deign, by the pious increase of brothers, to calm by some consoling support the waves inflicted upon us by the scarcity of our brethren.

If God’s predestination directs them toward the city of Augsburg, we ask that, aided by companions for the journey, by the support of horses, and by the horses’ drivers, you order them to be received humanely; and, once received, we ask that you deign to send them to us.

Vuillihard the cleric, returning from you, came to us on the Thursday before Epiphany. He told us that you were surprised that we had not made known through a messenger or letter what we were doing or how we might proceed. May the health of your holiness prosper in the Lord! Through your favor, everything concerning us is proceeding well. To make you certain about every uncertainty of our life together, we are making everything known in writing in due order.

On Friday, the day immediately following the Nativity of the infants, we sent a letter by messenger so that, once it had been seen by your eyes, if you were in Augsburg it might be sealed with the impression of your seal. Here is a copy of the letter.

## VII. Copy of the Foregoing Letter

*Wigo commends two young monks to F., a teacher at Augsburg, and asks that he be allowed access to Priscian the Elder.*

To F., numbered by heavenly will among the apostolic ranks in hereditary order, worthy of the degrees of those who judge the heavenly promise exceedingly precious.

Nourished by the formation of Benedictine life, we are compelled to submit in mind to the obedience of spiritual warfare, and, having swiftly accomplished the commands of our superiors, we are ordered to be ready for everything.

G. [Gozpert, abbot of Tegernsee], a lover of the highest perfection and a most devout shepherd of faithful monks, entrusted to me a brother flourishing in vigorous youth to be taught, hoping that I had tasted with a discerning mind a drop from some little stream. For the reputation of all teachers declares that the city of your see abounds especially in the teachability of all the liberal arts. Strengthened by the security of this hope, and supported by your persuasive petition, he had also willingly admitted another brother.

We can in no way fulfill his command and desire concerning them unless we have the support of your consolation. We ask that you order the larger book of Priscian to be lent to us for a little while, so that we may have the opportunity to read at least two small books, as we have been ordered, lest we incur the guilt of disobedience by neglecting what has been assigned to us as though we despised it; or lest we presumptuously appear to accuse the inexhaustible abundance of your Church’s library of poverty if we are compelled, for such a need, to bow our knee foolishly before some outsider. Farewell.

## VIII. In the Name of His Brothers, to Henry, Duke of Bavaria

*He asks that fish be sent to them so that they may celebrate Easter more festively.*

[Col. 0013B]

To H., most excellent leader of the Christian people, the brothers gathered in the monastery of Phyuhtwang send the most devoted offices of prayer in Christ.

Called monks merely by the addition of the name, servants of your distinguished power, and little brothers of the monastery of Saint Quirinus, we remain in the coenobium of Phyuhtwang by the command of our father Gozpert, while the others remain elsewhere, serving, as we are able, the custom of monastic discipline.

Happy is the Church that rejoices most worthily, supported by such a prince! Your celebrated name, continually flying here and there in conversation from a loving heart and spreading everywhere with the highest renown, has announced to our lowliness that you are present in a neighborhood exceedingly convenient for us.

Therefore, as though from the harshness of a hermitage where the earth does not know how to produce the inlets of ponds and, so to speak, has no idea at all what a fish is, we send this request to your noble highness: if your spacious fishponds yield a proper abundance and, as they rightly should, continue to overflow with abundant and customary fertility of fish, order our Easter to be gladdened by a fish-bearing gift, bestowing that customary mercy, which you have made a pious advocate for yourselves before God, always showing compassion to the needy. Farewell.

## IX. To G., Archpriest

*He asks him to defer for a while the punishment to be inflicted on the priest Ortwin.*

[Col. 0013D]

To G., venerable archpriest, W., unworthy provider of the Church of Phyuhtwang, sends greetings in Christ.

We have heard that the priest Ortwin, subject to your discipline, has been guilty toward you. We were deeply grieved, since he cannot have us at peace if he has offended you. But because he has been convicted by synodal judgment and found guilty, we ask your piety to defer the measure of penance deservedly imposed upon him, at the request of our most humble petition, until we can see him and speak with him face to face.

We do not ask this in order to excuse him from your service, while we ourselves offer devoted service with all our people, but because we also have many other matters to discuss with you, if you are willing. Farewell.

## X. To Count E.

*He wishes E. to be the defender of a saltworks recently granted to him and of the entire monastery of Saint Savior of Phyuhtwang.*

[Col. 0014A]

To E., who ennobles the glorious stem of either line of nobility through his comital office and renowned cultivation of virtues, W., appointed guardian at the place called Phiuhtwanc, together with the brotherhood, sends a devoted greeting in Christ.

The conscience of every good person rejoices in the fruitful dispositions by which the possessions of many faithful people are transferred to holy places, for they do not doubt that heavenly things can be acquired through an earthly inheritance.

Moved by love of this blessed hope, as we have heard from those who report it, your parents transferred to the monastery of our Savior a portion of a spring that produces salt in a vigorous flow. We know that you are well acquainted with what was given and under what condition the serfs granted for this purpose were to serve.

For this reason we have determined that it would be ratified, with the harmonious consent of our advocate, to commend to your protection such properties as were assigned to the monastery through the benefit of your predecessors. For it is reported that outsiders who have been brought in pursue their own profits with an unjust rivalry.

Since we desire, if you are willing, to have your support in all matters pertaining to us, we send this brother to your kindness. We had appointed him to administer these same affairs, so that through him we might always have a means of complaint, according to the law established for that family, as you know: namely, that no one should oppress them with unjust service, or neglect to collect and return from them the census owed to the house of God and to be rendered to it.

Although some people, excessively attached to human and perishable things, may regret that such patrimonial gifts have been entirely taken away from them, nevertheless the clear and distinguished reward of that inheritance will not be extinguished for pious descendants if the same devotion of their predecessors accompanies them in cultivating it and devoting themselves faithfully to God’s service, so that what a man owed by nature his soul may possess in the future as an inherited reward. Farewell.

## XI. To Liutold, Bishop of Augsburg

*Concerning the injuries inflicted upon him by Rihhard’s son.*

[Col. 0014D]

To L., distinguished by the office of bishop through heavenly grace presiding over the episcopate, Brother W., appointed to the monastery of Phyuhtwang, offers whatever a servant of the most devoted prayer or service may perpetually owe to the Lord as an inheritance.

With every occasion for murmuring wiped away, we frequently turn over in our hearts the mournful lamentations by which the Hebrew bands grieved greatly that Moses and Aaron had made themselves stink before Pharaoh and the Egyptians, while they themselves are daily pressed by the reproach of burdens of many kinds, and even harsher ones.

Wounded by bloody injuries, we had lodged a complaint about the many insults repeatedly and arrogantly inflicted upon us by Rihhard’s son, but we felt no correction whatsoever. Instead, because we brought the matter before you, we have become hateful to all the inhabitants of that region. No one loves us, no one reveres us, because no one, whether shaven on top or shaven all around, fears either God or man.

All pursue us like enemies, and most of all the aforesaid man. After we returned home from you, inflated with still greater boldness because he had found no civic assistance, he gathered as many Swabians as he could and grazed our meadows for the most part with their horses. He does not cease, secretly and openly, to fish in that water—apart from which we have no other—and which we have often forbidden him to use.

In all these matters we have no defender! For the business of various affairs is continually brought to you, while our advocate is held and torn apart on every side by the ambushes of enemies. Thus, defended by neither party, we are pitifully battered here and there by such a little man [the manuscript reads *homullo*, apparently a diminutive or corrupt form]. Nevertheless, we confidently hope to be defended by the Royal Head. Farewell.

## XII. To the Same

*He hopes that the extreme scarcity of provisions will be relieved by his beneficence.*

[Col. 0015C]

To Bishop L. [the manuscript reads J., but apparently in error], guardian of God’s Church and Catholic shepherd, W., a humble little man, sends the devoted offices of diligent prayers in Christ.

With our customary persistence in excessive and foolish talk, we press upon you with a great petition, and we ask for very great things, because until now we have felt that you grant great things.

We now have no silk tunics, which until this time we had in sufficient number through your almsgiving, except one for each brother, and those themselves are almost worn out by age. For no woman assigned to us under your authority performs wool-working, because, as the inhabitants of the region contend, they are in no way bound by such a law.

We recently reported to you in vain about the shortage of grain, because last year the infertility of the soil, the irregularity of the weather—as we also see happening today—the destruction by the harshness of winter and the biting frost of the crops of richer places from which we receive our food, destroyed on both sides more than sixty yokes of land.

We do not know what should be done for that little household, which is scattered here and there through various places, wandering about without sufficient provision of its proper food and necessities.

Leaving these and other matters aside, we speak with compassion about the members of our household who trouble us daily by shouting, demanding food and clothing in exorbitant quantities: tailors, namely, and restorers of the Church and of the other buildings; also two cooks, one collecting wood and the other vegetables; two bakers; a herdsman and a swineherd; a goatherd; a keeper of horses; shoemakers; launderers; and brewers [or: *braxatores*], who now remain idle every day.

For we cannot receive any guest or refresh him with drink, because those whom you ordered to do so have not supplied us with malt. For we have received you as an almsgiver to the poor, and we do not dare deny assistance to those who stream here and there to us.

With the money which both our lords have given us, we will have to buy a not inconsiderable amount of wine to be mixed for the brothers every Saturday after the *Mandatum* and to be used on the other great festivals for the sake of charity.

We hope that the many remaining matters of this kind that are lacking will be remedied by the father of the monastery, whom we confess you to be. Farewell.

## XIII. The Same, Apparently, to G. and E.

*He asks for more frequent letters and their affection.*

[Col. 0016C]

To our most beloved father G. and worthy mother E., the elder W. and his brother younger in age, greetings in the Lord.

Because we have been deprived of your conversation for a long time, we are repeatedly saddened with no little grief. Yet, trusting greatly in your kindness, we ask nothing else except the fullness of charity and compassion that we have always found in you. We have no other service at hand.

Know this without doubt: we continually pray before the supreme God for your blessedness here and in heaven. Farewell.

# In the Year of the Lord 980

## Helperic, Monk of Saint Gall

[Col. 0015]

# Historical Notice Concerning Helperic

*(From Fabricius, Library of Medieval and Later Latin Authors.)*

[Col. 0015D]

Helpricus, Elpricus, Hulpricus, Helpericus, Helphericus, Chilpericus, Hilphericus, and Hilpericus, monk of Saint Gall of the Order of Saint Benedict, wrote around the year 980 a book *On Ecclesiastical Computation*, which Bernard Pez published in volume II, part II, of the *Anecdota*, pages 182–222.

The same book is the one entitled *On the Art of Calculation* in other manuscripts. Mabillon published the preface addressed to Asper, abbot or dean of the monastery of Saint Germanus near Auxerre, in volume I of the *Analecta*, page 113 (new edition, page 431), from a manuscript of the library of Saint Germanus of the Meadows, in which this Helperic appears under the title of abbot.

Sigebert, in chapter 145 of *On Ecclesiastical Writers* and in his *Chronicle*, refers to him under the year 1005. The words of the example that he cites, however, are absent from the manuscript examined by Mabillon and appear to have been added by the scribe of the codex used by Sigebert. For I do not find them in Pez’s edition either.

William of Conches, in book III of the *Secondary Work*, or *Dialogue on Substances*, page 89, says: “If you seek the causes of the names of those signs”—in the zodiac—“read Helperic.”

But the letter of the monk Elpricus, explaining why we celebrate the birthdays of the saints with joy but Good Friday with sorrow, which is read appended to chapter 18 of Alcuin’s *On the Divine Offices*, either was added after Alcuin’s time or, if it was written to Alcuin, has a different and earlier author named Helperic.

Trithemius, in book *On Illustrious Men of Germany*, chapter 42, testifies that Helperic, a monk of Saint Gall whom he calls a most celebrated philosopher, astronomer, and poet, also wrote a book *On Music* and certain poems. There he assigns his lifetime to the year 1040; but in book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 325, to the year 1096. So also in II, 76, of the *Illustrious Benedictines*.

# Book on Computation by Helperic, Monk of Saint Gall

[Col. 0017]

*(From Pez, Newest Treasury of Anecdotes II, II, 182.)*

## Preface of Helperic

[Note: [Col. 0017C] John Trithemius reports in book II, chapter 76, *On Illustrious Men of the Order of Saint Benedict*, that Helperic, soon to be praised as the author of the book, was a monk of the monastery of Saint Gall. We possess this book in our copy from the library of Saint-Germain, but under the name Hericus and without the earlier preface printed here; we transcribed that preface from a parchment codex of the monastery of Vicoigne near Valenciennes. In that codex Helperic is given the title of abbot in the title of the work, which reads: “Helperic the Abbot, on Computation.”

Asper, to whom the preface is addressed, was abbot, or at least dean under a secular abbot, of the monastery of Saint Germanus near Auxerre. Hilperic was sent there for certain business from the monastery of Grandval, then of the Order of Saint Benedict in the diocese of Basel, which long ago changed over to secular canons.

Trithemius, in the place already cited, writes that Helperic flourished in the year 1020. But Helperic himself, at the end of his book, indicating the time at which he was laboring to write it, notes the year 880, as it is read in our copy, which was written during the reign of Henry, the first Frankish king of that name.

I note this because Sigebert, in his *Chronicle*, establishes that this book was composed by its author in the year 1005. Yet the words of the example that he cites do not appear in our copy and seem to have been added by the scribe of the codex used by Sigebert. Both in the *Chronicle* under the year mentioned and in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 145, he calls the author Chilperic, the person whom we are discussing here.

I would believe that he is the same Hilpric whose letter is reported in Alcuin’s *On the Divine Offices*, chapter 18.]

*(From Mabillon, *Analecta*, p. 431.)*

[Col. 0017B]

To the most holy Lord Father Asper in name, but in character most gentle, Helperic, a humble little servant, sends the means of eternal prosperity.

While I willingly obey the commands of your Fatherhood, I expose myself to be torn apart by many people for my ridiculousness. Therefore, submitting myself, I beg your Fatherhood to excuse my rashness in this matter.

You demand that the little work on the art of Computation which I recently composed in rustic speech at the request of our younger brothers, and which I had given only to them to read—especially to one of them, who had driven me to undertake it by his persistent importunity, and to whom I had sent it while he was staying at Grandval—you demand, I say, that, when last year I was serving at Auxerre as the representative of our brothers living at Grandval, I send it transcribed to your Fatherhood for examination, so that, having done this, like a shrew, I might submit to my miserable judgment.

For I had resolved to hide the foolishness of my trifles in suitable hiding places, lest, once they began to emerge, they should stir up the gall of many against me, who would justly complain that I was occupying parchment with utterly worthless nonsense.

But who would not obey your commands, even to his own harm? I above all, who have so devoted myself to your service that, whenever I know something to be approved by you, I do not doubt that I must undertake it, however difficult it may be.

Therefore I ask one thing of your Fatherhood: that, compelled by your command to undertake what I am undertaking, I may emerge unharmed under the protection of your support. This can happen if the reading of this work is withheld from all the fastidious people who are capable only of criticizing others, and if it is offered for examination to you and those like you who look upon everything without envy, with—so to speak—the eye of a dove.

But let every heretic take these matters in whatever way he wishes: I am convinced that your judgment is sufficiently reliable, to which the supreme [Truth] has deigned this year clearly to reveal how useless it is to resist the most holy commands of your fatherhood. It also most justly tends to happen that whoever has scorned a father’s salutary counsels eventually pays the penalty owed for his stubbornness. I can confess this all the more truly because this year, more frequently and more bitterly—and indeed more justly—I have continually experienced it.

And not without reason. For when divine mercy had restored me to that place where it had long ago chosen me to serve it, and from which I, unhappy man, had departed solely because of instability, although there I abounded in every good thing and—what I value above all—was cherished by the holiest love of the holy Fathers; when, I say, heavenly clemency had recalled me there after my long wandering, and your fatherhood, as usual ardent toward me, had wished to keep me with it, I did not submit, as is evident, when adverse fortune drove me on; instead, reverting to my former frivolity, I returned to the place where I remembered having endured much and knew that I would endure worse.

By doing so I also learned how powerful prayers are with God—prayers that you had poured out to him from the depths of your heart, obtaining by one and the same lightly uttered prayer so much against me. For I remember that, when you could not retain me, you prayed that I might find someone who would beat me most severely in the place to which I was hastening so eagerly; and the result immediately followed that prayer. No tongue can express how many insulting words, how many derisive attacks upon my good name, and what tortures of mockery I have since endured from those especially who were once my peacemakers, and whom I praised to you with the highest commendation.

Since I recognize that this has justly befallen me as punishment for my fickleness, I praise God’s justice in it all. And so that I may finally be rescued from them, I earnestly request the support of your prayers: though I am unwilling, may you, by praying, relieve me of so great a baleful burden of severity by extending the hand of your more favorable prayer. But these matters will be dealt with more fully in living speech, if the Lord grants the conversation I desire. May your merciful prayer, through frequent petitions, obtain that this may happen more quickly.

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0019]

[Col. 0019C] When I had begun explaining certain rudiments of the art of computation to our younger brothers in ordinary speech, so that I might impart to them some knowledge of this science as well—which many consider not unworthy of regard—and had introduced them to some extent into grammatical studies, insofar as divine generosity had assisted me, I do not know by what desire they were inflamed, but they began insistently and urgently to ask that I publish in some kind of writing what I had set forth orally, since it would benefit many. Thus, if these matters should at some time slip from memory—as the human mind, occupied with various concerns, is accustomed to forget many things—they would be able somehow to recover them with the help of written letters.

Although I resisted them earnestly [the manuscript reads *obnoxius*, perhaps for *obnixius*], pleading what was in fact the case—namely, that books on this same subject already existed, works published both clearly and elegantly in the time of our predecessors, especially those of the venerable man, Lord Bede the priest, who labored greatly for the benefit of holy Church in many matters, including this one—I urged them to press on to read those works, to strive to master them through prolonged reflection, to turn their attention away from me, and not to compel me to undertake a work exposed to everyone’s spitting and worthy of universal ridicule, particularly since I am dull in intellect, impeded in speech, and incapable even of stammering in rustic eloquence, let alone presuming to devise anything concerning the truth.

When I offered these and many other such excuses as a pretext [sic in the manuscript: *obtentu*], they persisted even more stubbornly and said: “We are not asking you to forge something new, as though we thought that nothing could now be found that had not been stated by others. Rather, from the matters that you say others have treated abundantly and in scattered form, we ask that you select what is most useful and necessary for us through your study, gather it together, and assemble it like a kind of garland from different flowers.

“In this work we do not demand the trappings of pompous language or the charms of urbanity, which one may find in the commentaries of the ancients. Rather, we ask that what others have expressed more obscurely be made clearer through your exposition.”

Overcome by their persistence, trusting in the lavish generosity of God, and nevertheless stirred by the devoted affection of the brothers, whose request I perceived to be humble, I dared to attempt this work on the condition that they promise never to show it for reading to anyone except themselves, nor to make the author of the work known.

But if this should offend the ears of any learned men, let them not brand me with the epithet of rashness. Let them know instead that I obeyed the command of charity and served the benefit of the brothers as far as study made possible. I have therefore gathered together the more widely known daily and annual principles of the Computus—principles that even a layman, let alone a cleric, cannot safely remain ignorant of—collecting them from various sources and presenting them in plainer language than that used by others. I have added nothing of my own; rather, I have explained more clearly, in rustic speech, those matters that others have expressed more obscurely in proportion as they expressed them more elegantly. Thus, if anyone should be so free from every serious occupation as to deign to read this, he may more easily investigate the loftier teachings of the learned.

## HERE BEGINS THE COMPUTUS OF HELPERICUS THE MONK

[Col. 0021]

### CHAPTER ONE. From what the solar year is composed, and concerning the nature of the leap year

[Col. 0021C]

The solar year, as the diligence of our predecessors has established through investigation, consists of 365 days and a quarter. If you wish to know clearly what a quarter is, understand that whatever you divide into four equal parts, each one is called a quarter, while the remaining three are called three-quarters. Since it is clear that a complete day—that is, together with its night—consists of twenty-four hours, and since this number is formed by four times six, because it contains four sets of six hours, those six hours are properly called a quarter of a day.

If, then, you wish to understand clearly from where these days are counted, know first that a solar year is so called because the sun passes through the entire zodiac, that is, the twelve signs of the zodiac. As our predecessors discovered through careful inquiry, it traverses each of them in thirty days, ten hours, and half an hour. Since there are twelve signs, and the sun remains in each of them for thirty days, multiply thirty by twelve and you have 360 days. Then multiply the ten hours remaining in each sign by twelve, and the total is 120 hours. Distributing these equally into periods of twenty-four hours, you will undoubtedly find five days, each of twenty-four hours. Add these to the preceding total, and you have the 365 days of the entire solar year.

There still remains in each sign half an hour. When this too is multiplied by twelve—that is, when the halves from each sign are collected into one total—it plainly makes six complete hours; and this is the quarter, that is, the fourth part of a day, as was demonstrated above with complete clarity. Since these cannot be counted in each individual year, it has been decreed that they should always be passed over without calculation for three years, until in the fourth year, gathered together, they can produce one complete day of twenty-four hours.

This is the day that we call the leap day in the fourth year, because it is pronounced on the sixth day before the Kalends of March; and that entire year is called a leap year, consisting of 366 days. If this day is neglected, it will happen after some years that the summer months will occur in winter, and conversely the winter months in summer. For over 364 years the calculation will fall so far backward that the solstices will occur at the Kalends of the equinoxes, and conversely the equinoxes at the solstices. That is, when you pronounce the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, which ought to be the spring equinox, the winter solstice will appear, namely the twelfth day before the Kalends of January. And when you pronounce the twelfth day before the Kalends of July, which is the summer solstice, the spring equinox will occur, though it ought to be on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April. The same will happen on the other days of the year.

To avoid this error, the leap day is always intercalated every fourth year. With this as a kind of foundation laid in advance for discovering the following principles, let us now proceed to explain the principles derived from it.

### CHAPTER TWO. The physical account of the signs, and concerning the solstices and equinoxes

But since we have undertaken to compose this little work for the unlearned—that is, for people like ourselves—it does not seem fruitless to touch briefly upon the account of the signs, insofar as the capacity of our small intellect has been able to retain it from the statements of our predecessors.

First, it must be understood that the signs are nothing other than certain regions of the heavens, determined by the position and arrangement of the stars and marked out by the skill of calculators with certain boundaries, so to speak. The divine [the manuscript has *ut divinae*, but a verb is then lacking] and human writings testify that the Egyptians, whom they show to have excelled all other peoples in knowledge of this art, measured the sun’s path—through whose annual course it completes its circle—into twelve parts, as Macrobius relates. Anyone who wishes to know more fully by what ingenuity they did this should undertake to read Macrobius’s commentary on *The Dream of Scipio*.

Posterity, following them, first generally called those parts “signs.” Hence that same sphere was given the Greek name *zōdiakos*, and in Latin the name *signifer*, “sign-bearing.” Then it assigned particular names to the individual signs. The poets invented these names absurdly, to be sure; but those called philosophers attempted to embellish them with certain physical allegories.

But let us [so the manuscript], setting aside poetic fictions—which contain no solid truth—insert a few natural explanations that we have been able to extract from the commentaries of the ancients. This should not seem burdensome.

They therefore assigned the beginning of the zodiac itself to the place where the sun, once made, is known to have been positioned: namely, from the sign which it is said to enter on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April. Since this was the first day of the world, and since the sun itself testifies that it was created on the fourth day thereafter, at the equinoctial day, they called this principal sign by the name of the Ram, or Aries. The name was drawn from the nature of the animal, by analogy with the sun’s activity: either because that animal is especially strong in its horns, just as from that time the sun begins to exercise the force of its rays to loosen the earth, which had until then been congealed by the cold of winter; or because from that equinox through the whole summer, until the next equinox, it traverses the right-hand hemisphere, just as that animal is said throughout this period to lie upon its right side. During the remaining half of the year, the sun completes its circuit on the left, and the ram rests upon its left side.

I think they placed the Bull second because, when the sun approaches those regions, the labors of oxen—that is, the crops—tend toward ripeness, and in certain warmer lands are even harvested.

Concerning the allegorical meaning of the Twins I have so far been able to find only a little, though even that is not far removed from a fabulous fiction. For it is said in that mythological image that, among the twins whom they call Castor and Pollux, one was born immortal and the other mortal. But the one who was mortal, by offering his own death, acquired immortality for his brother. They attempt to prove this from the stars themselves, because when one rises the other sets. They also adapt this to the sun in this way: one and the same sun sometimes descends to the lowest depths of the world and sometimes rises again to the greatest height.

The meaning of Cancer is obvious: just as this kind of animal walks backward with reversed steps, so the sun, when it reaches this sign and is no longer able to climb higher, returns to lower regions. At the fourth part of this sign it celebrates the solstice, namely on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July, from which it is also called a turning point. For there are three principal risings and settings of the sun: the winter, equinoctial, and northern risings. This rising of which we speak is called *therinos tropicos* in Greek [the printed wording is uncertain]; θέρος (*theros*) means “summer,” the compound name deriving from the character of the season and the sun’s turning.

The following sign is called Leo because of the hottest period of that month, namely August, since the lion is believed to surpass other animals in heat, and because Leo is vigorous in its first part but declines in its latter part. In the same way, once the sun has reached the middle of that sign, around the month of September it begins to moderate the heat of its force for us.

They assigned Virgo to September itself because in that month the exhausted earth produces no more fruits.

By Libra, which they form in the image of a balance, they indicate the equality of day and night at the equinoctial point, which the sun completes in the fourth part of that sign in autumn, namely on the twelfth day before the Kalends of October, just as it does in spring in the fourth part of Aries, that is, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April. These are the risings or settings, each of which is called *isemerinos*, that is, “equinoctial.”

Scorpion with its sting and Sagittarius were placed to express the hailstorms and storms of that season. In addition, Sagittarius, degenerating in its latter part into animal limbs, signifies the sun’s being driven down at that time from the heights to the depths.

The significance of Capricorn is also very easy to recognize with one’s eyes. No one is unaware that a goat, while feeding, always seeks the heights from the lowlands. In the same way, this sign sends the sun back to us from the lower regions toward the higher ones, after it has completed, in the fourth part of the sign—namely on the twelfth day before the Kalends of January—the winter solstice, just as it does the summer solstice in Cancer. Hence this sign, like the other, is called *tropicon*, that is, “turning” or “convertible.”

For this reason philosophers called these signs the gates of the sun: in each of them, when the solstice confronts it, the sun is prevented from ascending farther. The solstice is not so called because it should be believed that the sun ever literally stands still, but because the very brief intervals in which it reaches the highest or lowest part of the zodiac are designated by this name [the manuscript has singular *censetur*]; and no one doubts that this occurs in an indivisible instant.

It must also be understood that at the winter solstice the day becomes shortest and the night longest, while conversely at the summer solstice the night becomes shortest and the day longest. It is plainly evident that this occurs because of the circles and the globular form of the earth. The celestial sphere through which the zodiacal line is drawn extends very high above the earth toward the north, concealing its shorter part beneath the earth from us. Conversely, toward the south it rises only a little above the earth but extends beneath it to an immense distance.

Since the zodiac is not drawn straight like a circle but, in the manner of a belt, inclines from the northern region toward the southern—that is, from Arcturus toward the south—it bears one of the tropics, Cancer, near the northern pole, and the other, Capricorn, near the southern pole. Thus, according to the position of the celestial sphere in which the signs are fixed, Cancer is farther from the earth above than the other signs, while Capricorn is nearer; below, conversely, Cancer is nearer the earth and Capricorn farther away.

Although the sun is not fixed in heaven, because it is carried along with the zodiac it must, according to the curvature of the zodiac, either approach the earth or recede from it. Thus, when it is positioned in Cancer, because it completes the greatest distance above the earth from rising to setting, advancing as it does at the greatest height, while beneath the earth it travels the shortest distance, hastening toward its rising after traversing only the circumference of the earth, it prolongs the day for us by its slower course and shortens the night by its quicker rising.

It is evident that all this occurs conversely in Capricorn, because as much as the sun is raised above the earth in the one sign, so much is it submerged beneath the earth in the other; and again, as much as it travels beneath the earth in the one, so much does it travel above the earth in the other. Hence the summer days correspond in length or brevity with the winter nights, and the winter nights in turn with the summer days.

The individual signs do not have an oblique course, so that those which are in the north might at some time turn toward the south, as certain people think when they assert that, while the sun is in Cancer, it traverses the northern regions by day and the southern regions by night, and conversely, when positioned in Capricorn, the southern regions by day and the northern regions by night. Rather, each sign circles the earth in a straight course; whatever region the sun traverses above the earth by day, that same region it always traverses beneath the earth by night.

The equinoxes, however, do not vary the night and day as the solstices do. At either equinox, day and night are divided by equal measures of time. Anyone who takes care to observe properly what was said above concerning the solstices can very easily see the reason for this.

For the equinoctial signs, unlike the solstitial signs, are not one higher or lower than the other. Rather, situated as though in a kind of midpoint and placed opposite one another, they divide the zodiac equally like a diameter. When either rises, the other sets; when one occupies the upper center, the other occupies the lower, and each has an equal portion of the zodiac on either side.

For as much ascent as there is from Capricorn, the lowest of all the signs, to Aries, the equinoctial sign, there is just as much from Aries itself to Cancer, the highest of all the signs. Likewise, as much descent as there is from Cancer to Libra, the other equinoctial sign, there is just as much from Libra to Capricorn. Since Cancer is therefore higher than all the others and Capricorn lower, it is perfectly clear that Libra, positioned between them, is at the same altitude as Aries.

Consequently, when the sun approaches either of these signs, because it is carried through the middle of the sphere, it measures out day and night in equal spans for the entire world, both above and below.

Since reason, from both sides—namely, the diurnal and the nocturnal—nevertheless compelled that day to be called by the same term because of its equality, and since, as I think, neither of these languages, Greek or Latin, could conveniently devise one euphonious word from all three concepts—equality, day, and night—it came about that in one language it was named from the better part, namely day, and in the other from the inferior part, namely night, with the addition in both languages of the notion of equality. Thus in Latin it is called *aequinoctium*, “equinox,” from *aequitas*, “equality,” and *nox*, “night”; in Greek it is called *isemeria*. If absurdity allowed it, it could have been called *aequidies*, “equal day.”

The two final signs of the zodiac, Aquarius and Pisces, were named on account of the rainy months.

Concerning the solstices and equinoxes we shall, if the Lord grants it, give a clearer exposition below, in chapter 31. [Col. 0026C]

### CHAPTER THREE. How the sun is said to be in some sign, although the signs are in heaven while the sun moves through the ether

I think it should also be added by what reasoning, since the zodiac together with its signs is said to be fixed in heaven, while the sun moves far below it through the expanse of the ether, the sun is nevertheless asserted to move through its signs.

The explanation requires no laborious argument. We say that the sun is in a particular sign when it moves through the region of its own circle that lies beneath that sign, so that the sign travels above while the sun moves beneath it. The same should be understood of the other planets.

### CHAPTER FOUR. Against those who say that the seven planets are carried counter to the universe

[Col. 0026D]

I am not a little troubled by the fact that many people—and nearly all who treat this art—assert that the sun, moon, and other planets strive against the universe. For I cannot see who leads them toward the setting if their natural motion is always directed toward the rising. Their claim that they are driven by the force of the celestial sphere is plainly frivolous, since none of them touches that sphere, but all move at a very great distance beneath it.

The argument by which they attempt to prove this is easy to weaken. They say that, since the signs are arranged so that Taurus follows Aries, Gemini follows Taurus, and the others follow in order, the sun withdraws from Aries not into the preceding sign but into the following one, namely Taurus, and from Taurus into Gemini, and so through the rest—as though it could not happen that, while the heaven above moves more rapidly and the sun below more slowly, a sign fixed in the heavens passes along with the heavens, while the sun, left behind because of its slower progress, is found beneath another sign as that sign follows on.

I say this without prejudging the learning of others, simply setting forth what seems to me to be the case. Having briefly touched upon these matters concerning the sun’s course through the zodiac—ineptly, perhaps, but not, as I think, altogether unprofitably—for those ignorant of them, let us now complete, as far as we can, the task we have undertaken.

### CHAPTER FIVE. From what source the regular numbers for finding the weekday of the Kalends arise

[Col. 0027B]

Let us first see from where the regular numbers of the months arise. Since the solar year, as stated above, consists of 365 days, and since the sun spends thirty days in each of the twelve signs in completing this course, the number must necessarily be measured by one of these quantities. Multiply either by the other and you will find 360: twelve times thirty and thirty times twelve produce the same total.

Pronounce the five days that remain as the regular number assigned to March: March has five. For the other months proceed as follows. Always take the days of the preceding month and add its regular number; divide the resulting number by seven, because the regular numbers do not exceed that number. Give the remainder to the following month.

For example: March has 31 days and a regular number of five, making 36 altogether. Seven times five is 35; give the one that remains to April, and proceed in the same way thereafter. If, after the entire total has been divided by seven, nothing remains, know that seven is to be given as the regular number to that month.

### CHAPTER SIX. From what source the concurrent numbers arise

To discover the origin of the concurrent numbers—which they call epacts, that is, “additions of the sun,” and which accompany the aforesaid regular numbers—distribute the days of the solar year by seven, since the concurrent numbers too do not exceed seven. Say fifty-two times seven is 364; place the one day that remains at the head of the concurrent numbers, and add one in each year, without exceeding seven. But every fourth year, because of the leap year, skip one number, and in this way run through twenty-eight lines.

### CHAPTER SEVEN. How to find on which weekday the Kalends fall, and the weekday of each day of the month or year

If you happen to ask what either these concurrent numbers or the preceding regular numbers are useful for, know that they were established for finding the weekday of any Kalends.

If you wish to know on which weekday the Kalends of any month fall, take the regular number of that month and add the concurrent number belonging to that year; we shall explain later how to find the latter. If the sum exceeds seven, subtract sevens from it; whatever remains tells you the weekday on which the Kalends you seek fall. If the sum is exactly seven or less, know that number itself to be the weekday of the Kalends.

### CHAPTER EIGHT. How to find the weekday each day

If thereafter you wish to find the weekday of any day throughout a month, take the preceding days of that same month up to the day you are investigating, add to them the number of the weekday that occurred on the Kalends, and first subtract one day for the Kalends, since it has been counted twice. Divide the remainder by seven; however many remain, know that to be the weekday you seek. If nothing remains, it will be the seventh day, that is, Saturday.

If you wish to calculate the same thing through the days of the year, likewise gather all the days of the year that have elapsed—that is, from the Kalends of January up to the day about which you have begun to inquire—and, if it is a leap year, count the leap day as well once it has elapsed. Then add to this number the weekday on which the Kalends of January fell, and, as above, first remove one day for the Kalends; divide the remaining days by seven and retain whatever remains.

### CHAPTER NINE. Why the aforesaid regular numbers take their beginning from March

If, as a student eager for this art, you also happen to ask why the aforesaid regular numbers begin from March, or why the concurrent numbers change there, know that this month was the first month of the year established by Romulus, the founder of the Romans. He arranged the first Latin year in ten months and ordered that this arrangement should continue to be observed in memory of that first institution.

He named this month after Mars, whom he believed to be his father, and, as has been said, established it as the beginning of the year. Some of the months that follow testify to this: they received names based on the order in which they stand after March and on the season’s weather. Thus September is so called because it is the seventh month after March, and because more abundant rains usually begin to flow by then. The same applies to October, November, and December, as well as to July and August, one of which subsequently changed its name after Julius Caesar and the other after Octavian Augustus. Previously they had been called Quintilis and Sextilis for a similar reason.

The fact that we now begin the year from January was established by Numa Pompilius, Romulus’s successor. He added two months to Romulus’s ten, and, considering Janus—whom pagan error regards as the beginning of things—he named the first of them January and made it the beginning of the year. He named the other February after Pluto, whom they both believed and called *Februm*, that is, “the purifier.”

I have passed over the reason for the names assigned to the individual months because it has been treated sufficiently in the *Dialogue* of a certain Praetextatus and subsequently excerpted by Lord Bede in the second book of his work *On Times*, where it has nevertheless been arranged with great abundance. In that work, through a lengthy though not barren discussion, it is fully explained how the year was first divided by Romulus into ten months, by Numa into twelve, and how, even after that, it was finally polished to the exactness of its modern arrangement, long afterward, by Julius Caesar, a man of shrewd intelligence and memorable learning.

That dialogue is read in the books of Macrobius under the title *Saturnalia*.

### CHAPTER TEN. From what source the other regular numbers proceed for finding the moon on the Kalends

Here you will find the other regular numbers of the months, which are assigned for finding the moon on the Kalends. Since the solar year consists of 365 days, divided as above by the numbers twelve and thirty, give the five remaining days to September as its regular number.

You will find the others in this order. Always take the days of the preceding month and add its regular number. If that month bears a thirtieth-day moon, subtract thirty and assign whatever remains to the following month. But if the month does not count beyond a twenty-ninth-day moon, subtract that number and regard the remainder as the regular number of the following month.

We shall give an example from two months, so that you may proceed in the same way with the others. September has thirty days and a regular number of five, making thirty-five. Set aside thirty and give the remaining five to October. October has thirty-one days and a regular number of five, making thirty-six altogether. Subtract twenty-nine, because a complete lunar cycle is twenty-nine days; give the seven that remain to November.

Why one lunar age is counted as thirty days and another as twenty-nine, we shall explain shortly. (Below, chapter 26.)

### CHAPTER ELEVEN. From what source the epacts arise

The epacts, which are added to these regular numbers, arise from the inequality between two years, namely the solar and the lunar. Concerning this inequality, if the Lord grants it, we shall speak later.

The solar year, which runs through 365 days, exceeds the lunar year of 354 days by eleven days. Because the moon has eleven fewer days in its year, these eleven days are taken each year as epacts for finding the moon of the Kalends. Eleven is added to the number of the epacts every year, because the same inequality exists in every year.

Therefore place eleven at the head of the epacts, and, as stated, add eleven to it each year. If the total exceeds thirty—the number which the lunar age never surpasses—subtract thirty and retain the remainder as the epacts.

For example: add eleven to eleven and the result is twenty-two. This is the next epact. Then add eleven to twenty-two and the result is thirty-three. Subtract thirty and retain three as the epact for the following years. Proceed in the same way with the rest.

### CHAPTER TWELVE. What purpose the epacts serve

[Col. 0029D] The epacts, added to the preceding regular numbers, show the age of the moon at each Kalends in the following way. Take the regular number of each month and add to it the epacts belonging to that year, whose annual calculation we shall explain later. Whatever number the sum reaches is the age of the moon at the Kalends. If it exceeds thirty, subtract thirty; the remainder is the lunar age.

### CHAPTER THIRTEEN. Why they begin from September

These epacts, together with their regular numbers, begin from September because Egypt, the teacher of the other peoples in this art, began its year from that month. Thus, just as the regular numbers previously mentioned begin with their concurrent numbers from March by the authority of Roman antiquity, so, out of reverence for this Egyptian mastery, the Latins appear to begin this calculation from September.

### CHAPTER FOURTEEN. Why no epact is pronounced in the middle

It seems necessary to explain why no epact is pronounced at the beginning of the epacts.

First, it must be understood that this order of the epacts returns upon itself in the manner of a circle. Since each year receives an increase of eleven, in the nineteenth year—the last year of the nineteen-year cycle—when there are eighteen epacts, we add not eleven as in the other years but twelve, on account of the one day by which the lunar year is then reduced. This is called the lunar leap. Subtracted from the preceding lunar age, it compels the entire following lunar age always to be counted as one day greater.

We shall explain this more clearly when we have set forth the calculation of the leap itself. Thus, when twelve is added to eighteen, the result is thirty. These are the epacts of the first year of the nineteen-year cycle. If they were added to the regular numbers of the months, since the moon does not exceed this number, it would be necessary to subtract the same number in every month and to calculate the moon at each Kalends according to the regular number.

For example, to make the matter clearer: September has the regular number five. Add the epact thirty, and the result is thirty-five. October likewise has the regular number five; add the epact thirty, and the result is thirty-five. Subtract thirty and five remain; the same applies to the other months.

What need, then, is there to add thirty and subtract it again so many times, when in that year the lunar age at every Kalends is simply the month’s regular number? For this reason no epacts are pronounced in that year.

After the Kalends, you will find the moon’s age on the following days in this way. Take the preceding days of the same month and add to them the lunar age that occurred at the Kalends. First subtract one day for the Kalends. If the remainder is less than thirty, it is the lunar age. If it exceeds thirty, subtract thirty; whatever remains will reveal the lunar age.

Take care only that, if the month bears a thirty-day moon, you subtract thirty from the total, but if it bears a twenty-nine-day moon, you likewise subtract twenty-nine.

### CHAPTER FIFTEEN. How the moon is pronounced each day

If you wish to investigate the same matter through the days of the year, take all the days of the year that have elapsed—that is, from the Kalends of January up to the day for which you are asking—and add the lunar age that occurred at the Kalends of January. First subtract one day for the Kalends.

If the total has reached this point, divide the remainder by fifty-nine, which is the number of days in two lunar cycles. The remainder reveals the lunar age of the day in question. If, after the entire number has been divided by fifty-nine, nothing remains, or if the remainder exceeds thirty but has not reached fifty-nine, subtract thirty; whatever remains is the lunar age.

In this calculation you will not count the leap day.

### CHAPTER SIXTEEN. Why sometimes the moon is pronounced thirtieth and sometimes twenty-ninth [Col. 0030D]

It is time to explain what we promised above: why, that is, the moon is now reckoned as thirty days and now as twenty-nine. For this to be examined more clearly, one must understand that lunar months are not reckoned uniformly, but that one kind is the month in which the moon traverses the zodiac, while the other is the month in which the moon catches up with the sun. To make all this clearer, we must first state how much time it spends in each sign, and then how much in traversing the entire zodiac.

As has been established by more diligent investigators with no small care, the moon passes through each of the twelve signs in two days and six hours, together with two-thirds of an hour. Multiply two days by twelve, therefore, and the result is twenty-four. Likewise, multiply the six hours remaining in each sign by twelve, and you have seventy-two hours, which make three days of twenty-four hours each. Add these three days to the preceding twenty-four, and the result is twenty-seven. There still remains in each sign two-thirds of an hour.

If you ask what *bissis* means, know that *bissis* is said of two parts of anything after the third has been removed. For whatever you divide into three equal parts [another hand: “or portions”], each of those parts is called a *triens* or *trien*. When one of these has been removed, the two remaining thirds are together called a *bissis*. A *bissis*, therefore, consists of two parts of an hour. Thus twelve *bisses* make eight hours, since they are reckoned in groups of three *bisses*. It is therefore clear that the moon traverses the entire zodiac in twenty-seven days and eight hours; and this is one kind of lunar month.

But since the natural lunar month is reckoned from the conjunction, and the moon itself does not catch up with the sun during this entire interval so as to be rekindled by it, unless two days and four hours are added, when these are joined to the preceding amount we acknowledge the lunar month to be twenty-nine days and twelve hours. Since, however, twelve hours cannot be reckoned as a complete day, and it is difficult to [find or supply one complete day], especially since the moon is said to be rekindled alternately at midday and at midnight, for ease of calculation the twelve hours are omitted on one occasion, while on another the twelve hours collected together from both lunations are reckoned as a complete day; then the moon is pronounced to be thirty days.

Moreover, those two days and four hours that remain for the moon, after completing the zodiac, in order to catch up with the sun, when collected together over twelve lunations produce twenty-six days—the moon’s single traversal of the zodiac—although one day is lacking. This is what the lord Bede says: that the moon traverses the zodiac thirteen times in its twelve months.

All these days, reduced to a single total, make a lunar year of 354 days. Twelve times twenty-nine is 348. Twelve hours multiplied by twelve is 144, making six days; when these are added to the preceding number, they produce 354, which are, as we have said, the days of the lunar year. This year was evidently always observed in the past with the twelve months mentioned above alternating in such a way that one had thirty days and the other twenty-nine, until, through the skill of Julius Caesar, the solar year was discovered, because the lunar year fluctuated in many respects and did not correspond at all with the course of the sun.

## CHAPTER XVII. That the ancients observed only a lunar year, and why we now speak of a common and an embolismic year

Thus it was observed by the ancient Greeks and Romans: after twelve complete lunations, they began the following year with the thirteenth lunation. But since, on account of the eleven days that we have said are lacking from the lunar year, it often happened that the winter months fell in the summer season and the summer months likewise in winter—for every eight years they moved backward through three months—it was decided that ninety days should be intercalated in the eighth year. These days had accumulated over that number of years from the eleven-day differences and the two leap days.

For our part, because of the observance of Easter, which may lawfully be celebrated only on the fourteenth day of the moon after the equinox, we began to distinguish common and embolismic years by the moon in the following way. If, after twelve complete lunations, the following lunation happens to reach its fourteenth day either on the equinox itself or after the equinox has passed, we immediately take the beginning of the following year from that lunation’s conjunction, the preceding year—having been a common year—ending with twelve lunations and 354 days.

But if, after twelve complete lunations, the fourteenth day has already passed, we join that lunation to the preceding year, assigning to the preceding year thirteen lunations and 384 days. This year is called embolismic, that is, “increased” or “intercalary.” The preceding years are called common because normally two equal common years precede it, except in the eighth-year and eleventh-year cycles, each of which is preceded by only one common year.

These points concerning the difference between solar and lunar years, and between common and embolismic years, have now been stated briefly. If anything remains, we shall explain it, as far as possible, when we come to the exposition of the date of Easter itself. For the present, in calculating the sequence of time, we use the computation of the solar year, which is regarded as more reliable.

## CHAPTER XVIII. How the lunar *saltus* is produced, and where it is more properly omitted

At this point it seems appropriate to explain what we can about the lunar *saltus*, and I think we should begin from its very origin. Above we said that, from the day on which the moon withdraws from the sun, after nineteen days and twelve hours it again catches up with that same sun, and that this is the month by which a common lunar year is completed with twelve months and an embolismic year with thirteen.

But it has been discovered that in each month, before the seventh hour has been completed, the sun catches up with the moon and the moon is again rekindled by the sun, while from that same twelfth hour there remain in each month four moments, one-twelfth of a moment, and one atom. These four moments increase in each month to such an extent that over nineteen years they complete one entire day. The diminution of that day always compels it to be skipped in the nineteenth year, so that neither the lunar calculation nor the entire arrangement of the observance of Easter may be thrown into confusion.

For if that day is neglected, it will happen that after fifteen nineteen-year cycles—that is, after 285 years—when one ought to reckon the first day of the moon, the fifteenth day, that is, the full moon, will occur; and conversely, when the fifteenth day is reckoned, the first will appear.

But so that it may be plainly clear how that day gradually diminishes until it disappears entirely, since the nineteen-year cycle is said to lose four moments, one-twelfth of a moment, and one atom in each month, let us first see how many months there are in all nineteen years. We shall gather the number of the aforesaid moments, twelfths, and atoms, and then convert them again into hours, to determine whether they can produce a complete day of twenty-four hours.

It follows that the nineteen-year cycle has 235 months, because it is established that it contains twelve common years of twelve months each and seven embolismic years of thirteen months each. Twelve times twelve is 144, and thirteen times seven is 91; these added together produce 235. Multiplied by four, this number gives 940, as follows: four times 200 is 800, and four times thirty is 120; together these make 920, and the remaining four times twenty completes the stated number, 940. This is the total of the four moments collected from each month of the nineteen years.

Since these moments can make hours, let us consider them in the following manner. Because an hour consists of four points, and each point of ten moments, let us measure each hour by forty moments. We shall find in the number of moments written above twenty-three and a half hours, as follows: forty times twenty, together with three times forty, makes 920; the remaining twenty moments make half an hour. Thus, as stated, there are twenty-three and a half hours.

But to complete a whole day of twenty-four hours, we must supply the other half of this hour from the twelfths and atoms that have been added to the four moments in each month. A *uncia* is a twelfth part of anything. Twelve *unciae*, therefore, make one moment.

Accordingly, 235 *unciae* make nineteen moments, with seven remaining. Twelve times nineteen is 228, leaving, as stated, seven *unciae* out of the 235. To these seven *unciae*, in order to complete one moment, five more must be added; and we shall supply these five from the 235 atoms that still remain, assigning forty-seven atoms to each *uncia*: forty-seven times five is 235.

Add these five *unciae* to the preceding seven, and they make twelve, that is, one complete moment. Add this moment to the preceding nineteen, and you have twenty moments, that is, half an hour. Joining this to the twenty-three and a half hours mentioned above, you obtain twenty-four hours, or one complete day.

The calculation explained above therefore compels this day always to be skipped in the nineteenth year; for this reason it is called the lunar *saltus*. Thus, in the remaining years, the moon is reckoned alternately as thirty and twenty-nine days, and then three twenty-nine-day months proceed without any intervening thirty-day month.

When this day is subtracted from the preceding age of the moon, it causes the following lunation to be reckoned a whole day greater, in this way: if yesterday you pronounced the moon to be on its twenty-ninth day, today you must reckon it as on its thirtieth, tomorrow as on its first, and the day after tomorrow as on its second. But if, after pronouncing the moon to be on its twenty-ninth day yesterday, you skip the thirtieth day today and call it the first, you must reckon tomorrow as the second and the day after tomorrow as the third.

This is what the lord Bede says in his shorter work: the lunar *saltus* removes a night but adds to the moon’s age.

They intercalate this day in different places. But it seems to me that, since we begin the Egyptian epacts in September, we ought, according to their system, to skip that day in the month of July, so that the lunar calculation of the following Kalends may not be disturbed. For if you postpone it until November, as many do, and the moon occurs according to the rule of the epacts from the Kalends of September, it will remain out of sequence for three months, that is, until the Kalends of December. But if, at the place mentioned—namely, in July, on the third day before the Kalends of August—you skip this day, the moon differs from the reading of the epacts on only one Kalends of August.

## CHAPTER XIX. How many hours the moon shines on each night

Calculate the number of hours during which the moon shines on each night as follows. First know that, from the time when it withdraws from the sun and is called the first day of the moon until the fifteenth day, when it can withdraw no farther from the sun, it adds four points of light to each night as it increases, and thereafter, as it approaches the sun again from the other side of the circle, it diminishes by the same amount until the thirtieth day.

Therefore, while it is increasing—that is, up to the fifteenth day—multiply its age by four for the purpose of determining how long it shines, and from the points you obtain make each hour consist of five points. For the time during which it does not shine, likewise multiply the number from its age up to the fifteenth day, and again turn the resulting points into hours and add them together. If in the total you find twelve hours, you may know that you have calculated correctly.

Once it has begun to decrease, that is, from the fifteenth day onward, multiply for the time during which it shines the number from its age up to the thirtieth day; for the time during which it does not shine, use the number from the fifteenth day up to its age, and proceed in every respect as stated above.

The fifteenth day, because it is full, shines throughout the entire night. Four times fifteen is sixty points, and these make twelve hours. Conversely, the thirtieth day shines not at all, since it is placed beneath the sun and obscured by its greater light. The Greeks call this hour *synodos*; the Latins call it *coitus*, because at that time the two come together equally.

## CHAPTER XX. At what hour an eclipse of the sun and moon occurs

At what time does an eclipse—that is, a failure—of the sun usually occur? First, when the moon happens to travel along the same line as the sun. The breadth of the zodiac extends over twelve parts, of which the sun traverses only the middle one. The moon, however, traverses its entire breadth. The earth, being the center of the whole spherical universe and placed at the center of the world, lies beneath that middle part in particular. Hence it is always surrounded by the sun.
