When, therefore, the sun is carried above, the moon below, and the earth lies beneath both, if the sun and moon come together on the middle line, the solar light must be removed from the earth, which lies beneath that same line, by the moon’s interposition.

But when the thirtieth-day moon opposes the sun in any other part of the twelve parts of the zodiac, since the earth does not lie beneath that line and the moon is not between the earth and the sun, the moon cannot conceal the sun’s light from us who are situated on the earth. This is why we suffer a solar eclipse in every month.

A lunar eclipse, which usually occurs around the full moon—that is, on the fourteenth, fifteenth, or sixteenth day of the moon—although it likewise occurs because of the middle line, is nevertheless produced differently. For it is established that the moon has no light of its own, but shines by reflecting light received from the sun in the manner of a mirror. It can therefore never shine unless it has been penetrated by the sun’s rays.

But because the sun, as careful investigation has established, is eight times larger than the earth, it can never be entirely covered or concealed by the earth, so that it does not send its rays back upward on every side even when it is beneath the earth. The earth’s shadow penetrates upward toward the middle line of the zodiac, beneath which the earth lies and along which the sun travels.

When, therefore, the full moon, situated in the opposite hemisphere from the sun, travels along this same middle line, because the sun penetrates into the lower regions, the moon must ascend into the upper regions; and conversely, when the sun is above the earth in the upper region, the moon is beneath the earth in the lower region. It must therefore suffer eclipse, whether below or above, since it travels through the earth’s shadow and the sun does not look upon it in the usual manner.

But if the moon travels along either of the other lines, which are set apart from the middle one, and from which the earth, because of its smallness, can never remove the sun’s light, the moon can escape the loss of its light by deviating from the shadow-bearing line—that is, if it travels either higher toward the north or lower toward the south than the sun.

This is likewise the reason why the moon does not fail at every full moon, although some assert that both the sun and the moon more rarely fail above and more frequently below. For this reason the aforesaid middle line is called the *ecliptic*, because it is the cause of both eclipses, solar and lunar.

It is therefore clear that in its eclipse the sun suffers no diminution, but is deprived of being seen. The moon, however, is entirely deprived of light during an eclipse. Virgil seems to touch upon this when he says:

> “The varying eclipses of the sun, and the moon’s labors.”

By “labors” he calls the losses of light that the moon itself suffers.

## CHAPTER XXI. In which sign the moon is found on each day

You will investigate in which sign the moon remains each day, or how many degrees it moves away from the sun on each successive day, in the following manner. Always take the moon’s age, whatever it may be, multiply it by four, and then multiply that number again by three. The number you find in the total tells you by how many degrees it is separated from the sun; that is, in what place it remains toward which the sun will come after that same number of days.

For we say that these degrees are nothing other than the sun’s daily progress through the zodiac.

If you also wish to determine by this method in which sign the moon is situated on a given day, first see in which sign the sun is staying on that day and in which degree of that sign—that is, how many days it has completed there. Since the sun passes through each sign in thirty days, next see how many days remain from that point up to thirty, that is, until the sign is complete.

This is very easy to discover, since the sun enters not only each sign in definite months but also on definite days of those months, especially on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of each month. On the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April, it enters the first sign of the zodiac, Aries.

Once you have discovered how many days the sun has so far remained in the sign in which it is situated, take the number of degrees in which you found the moon to be separated from the sun. Assign to that same sign as many degrees as are needed to complete the sun’s course through it; distribute the remaining degrees through the following signs in order, thirty to each.

When a sign lacks thirty degrees, know that the moon is in that sign, in the entire portion represented by however many degrees from the aforesaid total have fallen to it.

But if in the total you find only as many degrees as the sun still has days remaining in the sign in which it is located, or fewer, know that the moon is in the same sign as the sun. This usually occurs on the first or second day of the moon, when the sun is situated in the earlier degrees of each sign.

But if the number of degrees has grown so large that, after the sign in which the sun is situated has been completed, and after all the remaining signs have each received thirty degrees, degrees extend through each sign up to the one in which the sun is known to be, with some still left over, it is likewise clear that the moon is in that same sign.

This usually occurs on the twenty-eighth or twenty-ninth day of the moon, when the sun is situated in the final degrees of its sign.

The former situation occurs when the moon is withdrawing from the sun; the latter when the moon is approaching the sun again. For as many degrees as it moves away from the sun each day while withdrawing along one side of the circle, up to the opposite hemisphere, which is the fifteenth day, so many it thereafter occupies while approaching the same sun along the other side, until it comes to the sign—or rather, to the same part of that sign—where it had left the sun, having traversed the whole zodiac. As was stated above, it completes this in twenty-seven days and seven hours.

But because it no longer finds the sun there, since the sun has moved away from it by the twenty-seven degrees through which the moon itself had traversed the zodiac, after completing the circuit of the zodiac in two days and four hours—the time in which the sun had completed its course in the aforesaid twenty-seven days and eight hours—the moon catches up with it again. Coming together with the sun, it is entirely obscured and becomes the thirtieth day. This day is also usually called *interlunium*, because it lies between the moon’s disappearance and its rebirth.

## CHAPTER XXII. At what hour the moon is rekindled, or at what point in its rekindling it changes its age

If you wish to know at what hour of the day the moon is rekindled by the sun, that is, changes its age, see which year of the cycle it is—of the cycle properly called lunar, whose calculation we shall explain later—and multiply that number by five. To this add the days of the year already elapsed from the Kalends of January up to the day about which you are asking.

When these have been reduced to one total, if the number remains below sixty, know that it represents the points of the hours of that day. Reckoning each hour by five points, you will know that the moon is rekindled in the hour lacking as many points from the complete five points of that hour as the other hours have left over in groups of five.

But if the aforesaid number exceeds sixty, divide it by sixty, which is the number of points in each day, that is, in the twelve hours. Remember that the points remaining belong to that day. Turning them into hours as has been shown, you will discover in which hour and at which point of that hour the moon of that day is rekindled.

If the number is exactly sixty, or if, after repeated division by sixty, nothing remains, know that the moon is rekindled at the twelfth hour of the day and at the fifth, that is, the final point of that hour. You may regard this as certain: it is never rekindled at night, but always during the day.

But if you wish to determine by the day’s calculation at what point in its rekindling the moon changes its age, multiply the aforesaid cycle by six. For every group of sixty that you find in the preceding number, add one *monas*, together also with the points left over after the groups of sixty. If these exceed thirty, remove as many as exceed thirty; the number remaining will reveal the age into which the moon entered at the hour of its rekindling.

Up to this point the calculations have been called daily calculations, because they change on each individual day. From here let us proceed to the annual calculations.

## CHAPTER XXIII. How the years from the Incarnation of the Lord are found

Let us first see how the years from the Incarnation of the Lord are to be found, so that through them we may discover the remaining calculations.

To find how many years have elapsed from the Incarnation of the Lord, take the series of indictions that have run from the Incarnation itself until now, namely seventy-one, since each indiction proceeds through a cycle of fifteen years. Multiply this number by fifteen, and the result is 1,065. To this add twelve, because when the Incarnation occurred, three years of that indiction had passed and twelve remained. Add those twelve that remained to the aforesaid number, and the result is 1,077.

Always add the indiction of the year about which you are asking—thirteen in the present year—and the result will be 1,090. These are the years from the Incarnation of the Lord.

Proceed in the same way each year, and you will find the years of the Lord without error. Remember only that, when fifteen indiction-years have passed and the first has returned again, you must always add one to the aforesaid number: that is, instead of multiplying seventy-one, as at present, multiply seventy-two, and observe the rest as stated.

## CHAPTER XXIV. The origin of the indictions, and how they are found for each year

If you wish to find the indiction of any year, take the years of the Lord that have elapsed in the present period and add to them the regular number three, namely the three years that had passed in the indiction in which the Lord was born. Divide the entire sum by fifteen, and the number that remains is the indiction of the present year. If nothing remains, it is the fifteenth indiction.

It is pleasant to disclose the origin of the indictions in a few words. The term is said to derive from *indicere*, “to proclaim” or “to impose.” When the Romans ruled almost all peoples, they imposed tributes on everyone, which were always paid in the fifth year. In the first five-year period bronze was paid, in the second silver, and in the third gold. In the fourth, the sequence was begun again from the beginning, that is, with bronze. Thus, by joining the five-year periods together, indictions of fifteen years each were established, and it was decreed that no law should be considered valid and no imperial edict authoritative unless it displayed the indiction.

After each five-year assessment had been made, it was customary to purify the City by making a circuit of it, as though for its cleansing. Hence a five-year period is called a *lustrum* [the reading seems intended], and we very frequently use *lustrare* in the sense of “to purify.”

This was done in the month of February, which they therefore named from *Februus*, that is, Pluto, whom they believed to be the purifier. For *februare* is said to mean “to purify”; indeed, they dedicated the entire month to the spirits of the dead.

## CHAPTER XXV. How the epacts are found

To find the epacts of any year, neither adding anything to nor subtracting anything from the years of the Lord, first divide them by nineteen. Multiply the number that remains by eleven. If that number remains below thirty, know that it is the epact of that year.

But if it exceeds thirty, after subtracting as many thirties as you find, you will take the remainder as the epact [manuscript: *remanserint*; it seems that the text should be altered thus: “after subtracting thirty, whatever you find …”].

If nothing remains, there is no epact, because the cycle of the epacts revolves through nineteen years. For this reason we divide the years of the Lord by that number and multiply the remainder by eleven, since that many epact-days are added each year. We then measure that number again by thirty, which the epacts do not exceed.

We neither add anything to nor subtract anything from the years of the Lord, because when the Lord was born there were eleven epacts, at the point where the cycle of the epacts began.

## CHAPTER XXVI. How the solar cycle is found, and why it recurs after twenty-eight years

To find the concurrent days, that is, the solar epacts, you must first find the solar cycle itself, through which they run. It revolves over twenty-eight years so that each set of concurrent days may fall in a leap year. This cannot happen in fewer years, since the concurrent days advance up to the number seven and a leap year occurs only every fourth year. Four times seven is twenty-eight.

Therefore, if you wish to find the solar cycle, always add nine to the number of the years of the Lord, because nine years of that same number had elapsed before the Incarnation. Then divide this sum by seventeen [as printed; the context appears to require twenty-eight], and the number that remains is the year of the cycle. If nothing remains, it is the twenty-eighth year.

## CHAPTER XXVII. How to find the concurrent days of any year

If you wish to find the concurrent days of a particular year, again take the aforesaid years of the Lord. Since one day is always skipped in every fourth year on account of the leap year, add a quarter of the entire number. Add also the regular number four, because four concurrent days had elapsed before the year of the Lord’s birth. Divide the entire number by seven, and retain the number that remains as the concurrent days of that year. If nothing remains, know that the number is seven.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Which year it is from the leap year

It is very easy to find whether a year is a leap year or how many years it is from one. Divide however many years of the Lord have elapsed by four, neither adding nor subtracting anything. The number that remains is the year from the leap year; if nothing remains, it is a leap year.

This can also be found through the solar cycle. Whatever the cycle-year may be, subtract one and divide the remainder by four. As above, through the years of the Lord, you will discover whether the year is a leap year or how many years it is from one.

## CHAPTER XXIX. How the lunar cycle is found, what difference there is between it and the nineteen-year cycle, and how it is found through the zodiac

To find the lunar cycle, subtract two from the number of the years of the Lord—those two years being the years remaining from the same cycle when God became human—and divide the remainder by nineteen, through which the cycle revolves. The remainder reveals the lunar cycle. If nothing remains, it is the nineteenth year.

You should know that this cycle is proper to the Romans, just as the nineteen-year cycle is recognized as proper to the Hebrews and, from the time of the Lord’s resurrection, also to Christians. This cycle is observed in the January moon, which is the first month of the Romans, just as the other is observed in the Paschal moon. The Lord himself testifies that this was the first month of the Hebrews’ nineteen-year cycle when, having instituted the Paschal sacrament, he said: “This month shall be for you the beginning of months; it shall be the first among the months of the year.”

For just as that cycle begins with the rekindling of the Paschal moon and extends until the same point, so this one, beginning with the first moon of January, is brought back to that same point and ends there. It too has common years, namely twelve months and 354 days, as well as embolismic years of thirteen months and 374 days. Except that the Paschal celebration is now conducted according to the latter, it is in every respect equivalent to it, as the Venerable Bede discusses at length. Both are established by a cycle of nineteen years and by lunar reckoning.

For the sake of distinction alone, one is called the lunar cycle and the other the nineteen-year cycle. The latter name is formed from three corrupted words, namely from “nineteen” and “year,” just as among the Greeks it is called, using the same words in their complete forms, **ἔννεα καὶ δεκαθέρηκα**—“nine and ten-year” [the Greek form is textually uncertain].

Here it should be noted that in the Latin compound the word *annus*, “year,” is sounded, whereas in the Greek the word for year is not present, but is understood from the season of summer; for *théros* means “summer.”

It should also be noted that the nineteen-year cycle always precedes the lunar cycle by three years: the lunar cycle, beginning in the nineteenth cycle’s fourth year, ends in its third year. This happens because at that point the moon is completed at the Kalends of January, since the year of both cycles is embolismic.

The knowledge of this lunar cycle seems to provide us with only this benefit: through it, as we stated above, we find each day the hour of the moon’s rekindling. Therefore, leaving this aside at last, let us proceed to investigate the nineteen-year cycle, which is more useful because of the various calculations concerning Easter.

If you wish to find which year of this cycle it is, always add one to the number of the years of the Lord, because the Lord is said to have been born in its second year, and proceed with the rest as we explained for the lunar cycle. Through this cycle you should know that the sequence of the epacts, the date of Easter, and many other calculations are determined, as well as the figures called the *Computus*.

## CHAPTER XXX. What the date of Easter is, and when it is observed

By the date of Easter we mean nothing other than the fourteenth day of the moon that first occurs after the spring equinox. At that time the Jews were formerly commanded to celebrate Passover by the sacrifice of a lamb. On that same night our Lord was delivered according to the pattern of that first Passover, although on the following day, that is, the fifteenth, he was sacrificed for the salvation of us all.

It was shown above that the equinox occurs on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April. Therefore, on whatever day of the week the fourteenth day of the moon occurs, whether on the equinox itself or after it has passed, we call that the date of Easter.

We defer the celebration itself to the Sunday on which the Lord rose. If that date should happen to fall on a Sunday, nevertheless we await the following Sunday for our Easter, as many say, so that we may not appear to observe the Jewish Passover by beginning the same solemnities with them and likewise ending them with them. For they, like us, celebrate the same feast for eight days, and there is no difference between our celebration and theirs except, as has been said, that they do not begin them at the same time.

But if the fourteenth day of the moon falls on a Saturday, and either that day is the equinox or the equinox has already passed, we celebrate Easter immediately on the following Sunday.

The date of Easter is contained in the nineteen-year cycle for this reason: only after that many years have been completed does the fourteenth day of the moon return to the same day of the Kalends. When these years have been completed, it returns indeed to the same day of the Kalends, but the days of the week now return by the same sequence because of the solar concurrent days, which vary through twenty-eight years.

This circumstance compels both the date and the festival itself to wander much farther, and causes the great Easter cycle to extend through twenty-eight nineteen-year cycles, that is, 532 years. For even if, within this number of years, either the date or the festival returns to the same day of the Kalends or to the same day of the week, it does not do so for a succession of several years. But once the great cycle has been completed, everything returns to the same days and along the same lines.

By the universal tradition of the Church we are forbidden to celebrate this date of Easter before the spring equinox. Concerning the equinox itself there is disagreement not only among the ancients but also among modern authorities: some assert that it occurs on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, others on the seventh day before the Kalends.

It does not seem inappropriate to show how we have seen our teachers investigate this even by physical observation. If anyone is so devoted to inquiry that he would rather trust what he sees with his own eyes than what he reads in books, here he may find a model by which he can successfully investigate what he seeks. First, the days of the solstices—which in a certain sense surround the equinox on either side—must be marked, so that afterward the equinox, lying between them, may more easily be found once the boundaries on both sides have been indicated.

## CHAPTER XXXI. Concerning the equinoxes and solstices: how they may also be ascertained by direct observation, and concerning the sun’s ascent and descent.

First, then, choose [the manuscript has *diligetur*, read *deligatur*, “be chosen”] a dining room facing east [Col. 0041A] and mark in it an opening through which the sun may cast its rays at each of its 182 risings. Then, for each rising, mark the places on the western wall of the aforementioned room that this ray illuminates. It is certain that at the winter solstice the ray is directed toward Caurus [*corum*], but at the summer solstice toward Africus. At the equinox, since the sun rises from the midpoint of the east, it plainly seeks the midpoint of the west in a straight line; for the sun always directs its rays toward the side opposite it.

Therefore, to detect the winter solstice, when the sun is in Capricorn, proceed as follows. Beginning on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of January, when the sun enters the aforesaid sign, mark each morning the individual places toward which the rising sun first directs its ray, making points on the wall up to the twelfth day before the Kalends [Col. 0041B]. You will see that at each successive rising the ray continually advances farther toward Caurus, since the sun is still moving toward the lower regions. Then, on the twelfth day before the Kalends, observing the sun’s rising with the utmost care, mark most attentively the place where the ray from the aforesaid opening first appears.

Again, on the following day—that is, the eleventh day before the Kalends—having observed the sun’s rising with the greatest diligence, note whether the ray proceeds farther forward than usual, or whether, however slightly, it returns backward. If you see it return even a little, as will certainly happen, know with complete certainty that the sun, having completed the solstice on the preceding day—that is, the twelfth day before the Kalends—has begun to retrace its course toward the higher regions.

Then, if you wish to mark at every rising the places it reaches later and later, you will see it proceed daily toward Africus up to the twelfth day before the Kalends of July. If you carefully mark that day, you will see on the following day [Col. 0041C]—that is, the twelfth day before the Kalends—how it turns back, since the solstice has been completed and the sun is returning toward the lower regions.

If you examine the matter again, you will find that each day the ray returns to Caurus along the same lines by which it had previously come toward Africus; that is, as the sun descends through the same risings from the summer solstice to the winter solstice through which it had descended from the winter solstice to the summer solstice. This is what we stated above: that there are only 182 risings of the sun, although it completes 365 days in a year.

For it completes its year by ascending from the winter solstice to the northern solstice and then descending again to the winter solstice; and, as was said, while descending it follows the same risings that it had observed while ascending. This does not mean that it retraces the same signs—for otherwise it would traverse only half the zodiac—but rather that the zodiac itself is stretched obliquely across the heavens from pole to pole, so that the two signs always placed opposite one another have the same risings and settings. Only the two tropics are excepted, since they have distinct risings and settings: Cancer and Capricorn, one of which is evidently placed higher and the other lower.

To make what we have said perfectly clear: Cancer, being higher and more elevated than all the others, rises and sets above them all, as the summer rising in July most clearly reveals. The remaining signs, however, according to the order in which they are placed, preserve—as was said—the same risings and settings, and indeed the same course: one through the signs preceding it, the other through those following it.

For example, before [Col. 0042A] Cancer are Gemini, and after Cancer is Leo. These are placed opposite one another in such a way that they appear to rise and set at the same point; and the sun, when situated in either of them, is carried along the same lines. Yet in Gemini it ascends, whereas in Leo it descends.

Likewise, before Gemini is Taurus, and after Leo is Virgo; the same statements apply to them. Before Taurus, moreover, is Aries, and after Virgo is Libra. Their corresponding placement is attested by the equinoxes, which occur annually in both of them. The same is true of the remaining signs up to Capricorn, which, being lower than all the others, has its own rising and setting and its entire course.

Since, then, the sun completes the year by ascending through 182 risings or lines and descending through the same number, double the aforesaid number and you have 364 days of the solar year. Let us now see how the one remaining day, together with its quarter, is composed from the minutes of the hours.

The sun remains in each sign for 30 days and 10½ hours. Take first the six signs through which the sun ascends to the solstice, and assign to each sign 30 days and 10½ hours. You will have 182 days and, in addition, 15 hours—that is, 150 minutes. From these 300 minutes, therefore, the 365th day and its quarter are formed from the minutes of the hours that the sun spends in each sign beyond the 30 days; it completes this day both in its ascent and in its descent.

But since, during its ascent, the day has not yet been completed, it cannot be counted as a whole; it is counted instead during the descent. Hence, from the summer solstice to the winter solstice, one day—that is, the 183rd—is counted, although, as was said, the sun always descends along the same lines along which it had ascended. In this way, when in the fourth year a complete day has been produced from the quarters and added to the sun’s ascent, both ascent and descent are reckoned with an equal number of days, namely 183; taken together, these make the 366 days of a leap year.

But enough has been said briefly about these excesses. Let us return to demonstrating the sun’s annual course, from which we digressed in order to establish the dates of the equinoxes—dates that are plainly discoverable if what has been said about the solstices is accepted as correct.

If, at the winter solstice, when it produces the shortest day and the longest night, the sun thereafter contracts the night daily and lengthens the day until the summer solstice, when the night is shortest and the day longest [Col. 0042D], it is perfectly clear that, after half the intervening span of days has elapsed, the night has been reduced and the day increased until they are measured by equal lengths. The day still retains its usual increase, *αὔξησις* [the text has *αὐξθόην*; corrected in the margin as *augmentum*, “increase”; another reading is suggested], and the night its *ἔλυξις* [apparently *αὔξησιν*, “increase”], until they reach the length or narrowness beyond which neither can go; this occurs again at the other solstice.

Since one solstice is known to fall on the twelfth day before the Kalends of January and the other on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July, and since there are 182 days from one [read: *ad*, “to”] to the other, if you wish to know which day lies in the middle, divide the aforesaid number into equal portions, and you have 91 on either side. On the ninety-first [the codex reads *Nogesimo*] day after the winter solstice, therefore, know that the spring equinox occurs; this day falls on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April. This occurs during the sun’s ascent.

If you wish to detect the other equinox, the autumnal one, do the same during the descent. Observe that the sun descends from the summer solstice to the winter solstice in 183 days, and know that the autumnal equinox falls in the middle of these—that is, on the ninety-second day. This is the day called the twelfth day before the Kalends of October.

For it is entirely certain that, just as during the sun’s ascent from south to north the night is shortened and the day lengthened, so during its descent from north to south the day is diminished and the night increased in equal measure each day.

If you desire to detect this with your own eyes as well, it can be done very easily. After marking on the wall of the dining room, as stated above, the points made by each ray at the successive risings of the sun from one solstice to the other, you will see that at both equinoxes the ray of the rising sun reaches the midpoint of those points.

I have spoken at excessive length and with foolish loquacity about the investigation of the solstices and equinoxes for the sake of slower learners; I ask that this not be tedious to those more knowledgeable. Let us now explain briefly how the Paschal date is found, the subject from which we digressed.

## CHAPTER XXXII. A repetition concerning the Paschal date, and why the feast itself is celebrated only on Sunday

By the Paschal date, as we have stated above, we mean nothing other than the fourteenth moon after the spring equinox, when the Jews were commanded each year to sacrifice a lamb at evening in memory of their deliverance and exodus from Egypt, accomplished on that same night. Whenever the aforesaid moon occurs on any day of the week, they immediately celebrate their Passover, and on the following day—that is, on the fifteenth day of the moon—they begin the feast of Unleavened Bread, which they celebrate for seven days.

We, however, both await the fourteenth moon after the equinox and, when it arrives, nevertheless defer our Passover to Sunday, out of memory and reverence for the Lord’s resurrection, which took place on that day. For the Paschal feast does not wander indiscriminately through all the days of the week like the other feasts, because this feast is unique. As blessed Gregory says, it is the solemnity of solemnities. Blessed Augustine likewise says:

> In the other feasts we merely recall to memory what has been done; in this one, however, we not only recall past events to memory, but also proclaim beforehand what is to come in us.

It is therefore lawful to celebrate the joys of the Lord’s resurrection only on Sunday, both on the first day and on the eighth in the sequence of time. On the first day, certainly, because we read that on it God’s first creature was made, namely light. On the eighth, because it follows the seventh: the same resurrection both preceded our Head for the first time on that day and is to be accomplished for all of us who are his members, after the completion of the six ages of labor and the seventh age of the souls’ rest, in the eighth age—when all who are in the tombs will hear the voice of that same Head and come forth.

If the date—that is, the fourteenth moon—falls on a Sunday, we transfer the joy of the Paschal feast to another Sunday, as some say, so that we may never celebrate Passover with the Jews, nor appear to serve with them the legal shadow. But, as Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, writes, this is also done so that, if the thirteenth moon falls on a Saturday, we are not forced to end our fast while acting contrary to the law, since the moon has not yet displayed the full circle of its light; nor, if the fourteenth moon occurs on Sunday, are we forced by the authority of the law—which commands the lamb to be sacrificed at evening on that day—to fast contrary to the tradition of the Church, according to which it is not lawful to fast on Sunday.

For this reason the Paschal date occurs between the twelfth day before the Kalends of April and the thirteenth day before the Kalends of May. If the date itself—that is, the fourteenth moon—falls on the equinox, the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, and that day is a Saturday, we celebrate the sacred vigils that night and the Lord’s resurrection on the following day, the eleventh day before the Kalends. But if the date falls on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May, beyond which it cannot be later, and that day is a Sunday, we defer the Sunday feast to the following Sunday, as stated above; that day is the seventh day before the Kalends of May.

At the feast itself, the moon’s age can be neither less than fifteen nor greater than twenty-one. If the fourteenth moon, which is the date, falls on Saturday, the following day, Easter, will be the fifteenth. But if the date, that is, the fourteenth moon, falls on Sunday, it occurs on the twenty-first in the other Sunday on which the feast is celebrated.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. How the Paschal date is found for each year

If you wish to know on which day of the Kalends any date will occur, you must learn this verse by heart. It is composed in a versified form and is chanted as follows:

> The Nones of April know the fives.

This verse teaches, for each of the nineteen years of the cycle, on which day of the Kalends the date will occur—that is, the fourteenth moon after the equinox. You will also find the weekday, that is, the day of the week on which it falls, by joining the regulars assigned to each date—for this one, the five—with the concurrents of the year, in the manner in which we taught you to find the Kalends of the months.

If the aforesaid verse has slipped from your memory, we shall teach you how it may be recovered even without the help of letters.

To find the Paschal date of any year, take the date of the preceding year at the first joint of the thumb of your left hand. Then count, in order, the individual days of the Kalends through the joints and fingertips of all the fingers of that hand. Whichever day of the Kalends comes again at the same joint after the others have been counted, know that this is the date.

Remember only this when seeking all the dates: when, in counting, you reach the Kalends, thereafter always proceed by calculating toward the Kalends of April; or, after the Kalends of April, always proceed through the Nones of the year, and after the Ides count backward from the eighteenth day before the Kalends to the date.

If the date itself falls on the Kalends or on any day of the Nones or Ides, know that it belongs to April. But if it falls on the twelfth day before the Kalends or earlier—that is, on the eleventh or tenth—or later, then know that it belongs backward, that is, to March, and you will pronounce the Kalends themselves as the Kalends of April.

If, however, it falls backward—that is, on the fourteenth or thirteenth—or later on the fifteenth day before the Kalends, since these days are in March before the equinox, you will calculate the date in April and pronounce the Kalends themselves as the Kalends of May. This happens only three times in the nineteen-year cycle: in the eighth year, when the date is the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May; in the eleventh year of the same cycle, when the date is the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May; and in the nineteenth year, the last year of the cycle, when the date is the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May.

Perhaps, however, you will say that you do not even know the date of the preceding year. We also provide for this ignorance. Even if you are extremely dull, you can nevertheless retain the date of the first year of the nineteen-year cycle once you have heard it: the Nones of April.

If you have forgotten the others, first calculate which year of the nineteen-year cycle it is, using the method we explained above. When you have found it, count as many dates from the Nones of April as the year of the cycle. Whichever date you find in that order, know that it is the one you seek.

To make what we are saying clearer, suppose, for example, that it is the fifth year of the often-mentioned cycle. Count the individual dates in the manner we described, beginning with the Nones of April; and whenever the fifth date occurs, know that it belongs to the fifth year of the aforesaid cycle. Proceeding in the same way for the other years, you will very easily find the date of each year.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. How the regulars of the date are found

To find the regular of any date, always place the Kalends of April on the first weekday, and count each day of the Kalends through the successive weekdays up to the date. On whichever weekday you find each date, assign that number of regulars to it.

For example, place the Kalends of April on the first weekday, and the Nones of April fall on the fifth weekday. Therefore say:

> The Nones of April know the fives.

Proceed in this way for the others, and you will find the regulars of each without error.

Observe this point carefully: if the date is before the Kalends, count both the Kalends and the weekdays backward. For example, with the Kalends placed on the first weekday, the day before the Kalends is immediately on the seventh weekday backward, the third day before the Kalends on the sixth weekday, and so forth, always counting backward to the date.

If it is after the Kalends of April, count everything forward. Having found the regulars, join them, as stated, to the concurrents of the year. When you find the weekday on which the date falls, we celebrate the Lord’s Passover as it arrives.

It remains now to show how the other dates are found from this one.

## CHAPTER XXXV. How the other dates are found from the Paschal date

If you wish to find the date of Septuagesima, first see how many days the Paschal date is distant from the Kalends of April, whether backward or forward, and count the same number of days from the fifth day before the Kalends of February. Proceed in the same way, either forward or backward, and you will find the date of the seventieth day without difficulty.

The date of the seventieth day is the tenth moon, which is the moon of February—that is, the moon that ends in that month. We call the moon of each month the moon that ends in that month.

Seek the date of Lent from the twelfth day before the Kalends of March. Beginning in every respect, proceed as we said concerning the seventieth day. It is the second moon of March.

Observe this concerning these two dates: in a leap year you must begin the search one day later—that is, for the seventieth day, on the fourth day before the Kalends of February, and for the fortieth day, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of March. Do not do this with the other dates.

With the seventieth day, observe this in every leap year. With the fortieth day, do so only when the date itself falls before the leap day. If it is to occur after the leap day, seek it in a leap year just as in other years, on the twenty-second day before the Kalends of March.

In the date of the seventieth day, the eleventh moon sometimes occurs in a leap year. I have noted this so that, when it occurs, it may not confuse the calculator.

The date of the Rogations is always sought from II Nones of May; everything is calculated as above. It is the twentieth moon, which is the moon of May.

The date of Pentecost is always sought from the thirteenth day before the Kalends of June, in every respect as with the preceding dates. It is the fourth moon of that month.

All the dates will fall on the same weekday, and just as Passover, so also these other feasts, will be extended to Sunday. Understand this concerning the other feasts as concerning Passover: if the date falls on a Sunday, defer the feast to another Sunday.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. The three years of the nineteen-year cycle in which the epacts do not follow their order, and how the Paschal moon is observed

Concerning the intercalary moon, I thought that only this should be added: it never conflicts with the course of the epacts except in three years of the nineteen-year cycle—namely, the eighth year, which in Greek is called the *ogdoas*; the eleventh; and the nineteenth, which is the last and is called the *endecas* in Greek, because it is the eleventh after the *ogdoas*.

In these years it occurs, contrary to the usual order of the epacts, on certain Kalends. We must show where it gives the ordering.

In the eighth year, therefore, when the epacts are seventeen, the intercalary moon begins on the second day before the Nones of March and ends on the first day before the Nones of April, being counted as the thirtieth moon, although it ends in April, which never has thirty days. This moon is neither April’s nor any other month’s, but the intercalary moon, which is never assigned to a month and is always counted as the thirtieth.

The April moon follows; it is also the Paschal moon. It begins on the Nones of April and ends on the fifth day before the Nones of May. It is not counted as the thirtieth moon, although it ends in May, since May always has a thirty-day moon; for this moon, as stated, belongs not to May but to April.

On the Kalends of May it is the twenty-seventh moon, although according to the reckoning of the epacts and regulars it ought to have been [lacuna]. The May moon begins on the fourth day before its Nones and ends on the fourth day before the Nones of June, being counted as the thirtieth moon because it belongs not to June but to May.

The June moon begins on the third day before its Nones and ends on the Kalends of July themselves. It is counted as the twenty-ninth moon, as the moon of June always is, although according to the epacts and regulars it is counted as the thirtieth.

The July moon begins on the sixth day before its Nones and ends within that same month as the thirtieth moon, on the second day before the Kalends of August. The dispute concerning it is then settled.

The verse of the epacts, however, differs in this year on the third day before the Kalends of May and July.

In the eleventh year of the nineteen-year cycle, which has epacts of twenty, the intercalary moon begins on the second day before the Nones of December and ends on the fourth day before the Nones of January. The January moon begins on the third day before its Nones and ends on the Kalends of February as the thirtieth moon, as the verse of the epacts also shows.

The February moon follows, beginning on the fourth day before its Nones and ending on the sixth day before the Nones of March. Since it is February’s moon, although it ends in March, it is counted as the twenty-ninth—unless this occurs in a leap year, which always compels the February moon to be counted as the thirtieth.

In this year the moon on the Kalends of March ought, according to the sequence of the epacts, to be the twenty-ninth, but because of the intercalation it occurs as the twenty-eighth, except in a leap year. If this year is a leap year, then on the Kalends of March it will occur as the twenty-ninth according to the verse and according to the calculation of that year, and, as stated, on the sixth day before the Nones of March it will be the thirtieth.

The moon of March then begins on the fifth day before its Nones and ends on the Kalends of April, occurring as the thirtieth according both to the epacts and to the preceding calculation.

The moon of April begins on the fourth day before the Nones of April. It is also the Paschal moon, and ends on the Kalends of May as the twenty-ninth, as it always does. Thus the dispute concerning that year is again settled.

The nineteenth year, however, which has epacts of eighteen, begins the intercalary moon on the third day before the Nones of March; nevertheless it ends it on the third day before the Nones of April. The following moon is April’s, and it is also the Paschal moon. It begins, as it always does, on the second day before its Nones and ends on the sixth day before the Nones of May. Since this moon belongs not to May but to April, it ends as the twenty-ninth.

Although according to the epacts it occurs as the twenty-ninth on the Kalends of May, it is counted as the twenty-eighth for the reason stated above.

The May moon begins on the fifth day before its Nones and is completed on the Kalends of June, being counted as the thirtieth in every respect. Thereafter it will preserve its usual course up to the Kalends of September.

For from the Kalends of September in this year, until you pass over the leap day—a day that many insert in November—you will find the moon on none of the Kalends according to the regulars. On the Kalends of September and likewise on those of October it occurs as the fourth, although according to the regulars it ought to be the fifth in both cases. On the Kalends of November it is the sixth, although according to the regulars it ought to be the seventh. Once the leap has been made in November, it will thereafter preserve its course without alteration.

You can avoid this entire dispute if, as we said above, you choose to pass over the leap day according to the Egyptians in the month of July. The sole exception is the Kalends of August, on which you will count the moon as the third, although according to the epacts it is pronounced the second.

Wherever you insert the leap, observe this rule: count three successive lunations as twenty-nine days, without inserting a thirtieth among them.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. A brief remembrance of the other intercalations

Concerning the other intercalations, which [so the codex] do not conflict with the epacts, I thought that only this should be said: if, according to the verse, two thirtieth lunations occur together, one of them is called intercalary and is assigned to no month, except when it is a leap year.

Then three thirtieth lunations occur together, none of which is intercalary. January, as always, has thirty days; February likewise then has thirty because of the leap year; and the following March moon is also thirty, as it always is.

If it is the *ogdoas* or the *endecas*, a fourth thirtieth moon follows together with the leap year; this is the intercalary moon of that year, as was stated above.

Whoever desires fuller knowledge concerning the intercalations and common years, the *ogdoas* and the *endecas*, or everything pertaining to the calculation of Easter, should diligently read the book of the venerable Bede, elegantly composed on these subjects. There, without doubt, he will find in the greatest abundance whatever he seeks concerning all these matters.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. Epilogue of the little book

At the request of our students, we have gathered and compiled from various sources, according to the capacity of our small intellect, those matters that we judged necessary for boys being introduced to this art.

If, in gathering them, we have wandered somewhat more verbosely, whoever reads them should understand that we did so with the aim of making what was said clearer to readers. For this reason we avoided the display of more obscure [or: more polished] words, although perhaps these too were available to us.

For, as blessed Augustine says, one who speaks elegantly but does not instruct his hearer speaks only for himself and not for the person whom he has undertaken to teach.

We ask whoever deigns to read these things that, if he finds anything in them useful for his own benefit, he give thanks to the Giver of all good things. If the opposite should occur, let him not immediately complain that our labor is worthless, since it often happens that one person is instructed precisely where another suspects nothing useful.

Even though a golden cup is more precious, a little Samnian vessel is not for that reason devoid of every usefulness. Indeed, earthen vessels are sometimes as much more useful as they are less valuable, because slaves make great use of them, whereas the gems lying in a treasury and used only by kings are for the most part unavailable for servants’ use.

If anyone despises using this work, let him understand that it was not published for him, but only for those who are not yet able to penetrate greater matters, so that, first introduced by these as by certain letters of the alphabet, they may afterward attain the greater things more easily.

**In the year of the Lord 982. Bernerus, abbot of Humolières.**

## HISTORICAL NOTICE

(From Fabricius, *Bibliotheca medii et infimi Latini*.)

Bernerus, formerly a monk of Saint Remigius at Rheims and abbot of Humolières in Vermandois, Gaul, of the Order of Saint Benedict, wrote around the year 964 a *Life of Saint Hunegundis*, who died in 650. The work is found in Surius under 25 August and in a more genuine form in Mabillon, *Acta Benedictina*, Second Age, p. 1018, together with the history of the translation in the Fifth Age, p. 215.

## THE LIFE OF SAINT HUNEGUNDIS, VIRGIN OF HUMOLIÈRES, BY BERNERUS, ABBOT

(From Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum of the Order of Saint Benedict*, Second Age, p. 1018.)

## PRELIMINARY OBSERVATION

It has not been entirely established by which author or at what time the Life of Blessed Hunegundis was written. One might suspect that it was committed to writing by a contemporary author from these words of the prologue: “I undertake to describe a few of the deeds of her life, as I have learned them from the faithful who recount them.” Yet by this manner of speaking the author sufficiently suggests that he learned the history from the reports or tradition of others rather than from a written source.

Surius thought that the author was a bishop, and he was the first to publish this Life in a more polished style. Although in the prologue the biographer calls himself the last of priests—a title by which bishops are very often designated among the ancients—we nevertheless think that a presbyter is meant in that passage, and perhaps Bernerus, the first abbot of Humolières, is the likely person.

For Bernerus himself wrote the history of the translation of Blessed Hunegundis, which follows this Life in a manuscript codex of the monastery of Saint Thierry at Rheims—not in a continuous series, as in Surius, but as a distinct and more extended narrative. This is followed in the same codex by a *History of the Translation*, composed by another author, in which these words concerning Bernerus occur:

> “For those wishing to know the account both of the discovery and of the translation, as well as the notable miracles divinely revealed there, the abbot Bernerus, a lord of blessed memory, strove to set them forth in a clear style and radiant language. By God’s arrangement, he was the first to succeed to this little place after the nuns who had been there were expelled because of the shameful allurements of carnal pleasure.”

We shall state in its proper place that this occurred in the year 948.

The monastery of Humolières, commonly called Humblières, lies near the walls of Augusta Veromanduorum, on the Somme. Its origins and founders are unknown.

When we received two copies of this Life, one complete and the other mutilated, we initially thought that the first was the work of a different author. But after more careful consideration, they appeared to be not two works but one and the same composition. Accordingly, what we said in the preface to the First Age of the Benedictine series about two authors of the Life of Saint Hunegundis must be corrected.

## AUTHOR’S PREFACE

### 1

The memorable description of the blessed and venerable Fathers, who struck down the limbs and stratagems of the cunning enemy with the Gospel sword, breathes upon our inner man through divine discourse. No less does the renowned comparison of maternal and virginal women, affecting our outer and corruptible self with a weighty encomium, invigorate it.

From these there arose an outstanding kind of victory by which the devil, together with his weapons, lost all dominion, and through which the first parents experienced the loss of life; through the same means, the heavenly empire was again enlarged for their increase.

Thus the same nature that offered the man the taste of death also, through holy virgins, supplied all people with restraint from vice. The woman who first readily consented to fall and became the mother of calamity afterward, through Christ’s grace, resisted bravely so as to overthrow the devil, and was freely chosen, to her happiness, to become both sister and mother of the Lord and Savior.

Having obtained the portion of this divine grace, the glorious virgin Hunegundis emerged reborn from the immaculate womb of the divine font, brought up in the bosom of the Catholic mother Church. I undertake to describe a few deeds of her life, as I have learned them from the faithful who recount them.

I therefore ask you to support me, a chief among sinners and the least among priests, with your prayers, so that the Holy Spirit may deign to be present with me—he who may wipe away the stains of our crimes and make my tongue eloquent in recounting certain deeds of the virgin.

## THE LIFE BEGINS

### 2

When the supreme and incomprehensible providence of the Godhead was waging war against the prince of the world through its omnipotence and had resolved completely to uproot his stratagems, it not only overcame him powerfully and stripped away his weapons, but also mercifully bestowed such a splendid brilliance upon those very weapons that they drove away and destroyed the dominion of the most filthy prince. What had formerly been dark weapons became lights of Christ.

In this way the cruel scepters of the world are transformed, and every portion of darkness, together with its followers, is extinguished by such a radiance. A new light and joy arise through the new little page [*pagella*, perhaps corrupt]; necks are bowed before the King of kings, and little by little, from the rising of the sun to its setting, the dominion of Christ was proclaimed.

Among these peoples, the Frankish nation—renowned for many distinguished deeds and most famous for many triumphs—although it came more slowly to Christ in holy faith, nevertheless, once it perceived the Lord’s clemency, began everywhere to put forth new growth and beget a new and holy offspring for God the Father.

From its most sacred fellowship the holy mother and virgin Church of Christ has now been enlarged. Forgetting her father’s house and her former people, she offered the bosom of her heart to the unity of the Trinity, so that the immaculate Lord might consecrate for himself an undefiled household.

### 3

The land of France, namely the district of Vermandois, adorned with the intercession of the most powerful martyr Quintinus, longed with all its strength to offer the Lord a pleasing gift, a most fragrant offering.

In this district, in the village called Lembaidis, the holy virgin Hunegundis was born of noble lineage. She emerged like a little twig of smoke from the aromatics of myrrh, frankincense, and every kind of spice, since she was born to noble parents who worshiped Christ.

They say that she was lifted from the sacred font by Eligius, bishop of the Church of Noyon and Vermandois. There she received the pledge of the true Bridegroom, together with a precious garment, whitened as a sign of immortality and illumined by the triumph of suffering, as well as the mystical royal and priestly crown in the order of chaste love.

There also, in the seven stages of baptism, she received the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, confirmed by episcopal blessing and anointed with holy chrism. Strengthened by these gifts on every side, the young girl strove to live through seven cycles of days, so that, when seven were multiplied by seven and a unit was added, she might acquire in the present life the fruit of the jubilee; and, when this was doubled in body [Col. 0052B] and soul after the course of her life had been completed, she might gather the hundredfold fruit consecrated to the most holy virgins.

Because she was of glorious character and birth, she is said to have been betrothed from her earliest infancy to one of equal birth. But, because she was more beloved by the heavenly Bridegroom, the earthly bridegroom was thwarted and, by the hidden judgment of God, confined within the boundary of death.

### 4

When the holy virgin began to grow into adolescence, with a fair body, bright countenance, and blond complexion, she was again betrothed to a certain man named Eudaldus, of noble stock. He endowed her with various marriage gifts, including servants and small estates.

Although compelled by her parents, she endured all these things with a peaceful expression and chaste mind. For a long time she pondered in her heart how she might surrender herself and her possessions to Christ the Bridegroom, become a religious woman under the protection of the holy virgin Mother, and, adorned with the veil upon her head, be able to say with the young women of the true King:

> “I am black but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem; therefore the King loved me and brought me into his chamber” (Song of Songs 1);

and again:

> “Do not look upon me because I am dark, because the sun has discolored me” (ibid.).

Such an intention and so splendid an exercise occupied the girl’s heart continually. The flower of the virginal Mother gave off its fragrance in this holy virgin, and many graces of virtue shone forth from her virginal achievements.

### 5

Then, wishing to bring the holy purpose of her mind into active fulfillment, she used wise counsel. By whatever skill she could, she gently tried to soften her bridegroom and, by soothing him with the subtlety of her intelligence, draw him completely away from sexual embraces.

Addressing him in the sweetest words, she said:

> “O sweetest and most loving husband, since we were born of thoroughly Christian and orthodox parents, it is not fitting for us to defile ourselves and be polluted by lustful unions like the nations that do not know God, and like the horse and mule, which have no understanding.
>
> “May it please you, I beg and beseech you before the Lord, to accept my salutary counsel and conform yourself to my words. Let us seek together how our marriage may be made pleasing to God, so that from us an earthly offspring may not emerge, but a heavenly one.
>
> “For it is fitting, and greatly beneficial, for us to seek the prince of the apostles and visit the holy places, so that at least, once the apostolic blessing has been poured over us, we may receive a long life, continual health, prosperity in our possessions, fruitfulness in our descendants, and tranquility in enduring peace.”

O blessed virgin, O bride of the heavenly King, how devoted you are said to have been! You speak as though wishing the world to blossom for you, although in your heart you had already utterly despised it and rejected it like decaying dung that you had completely trampled underfoot.

What more need be said? Thus the anxiety surrounding the wedding was deceived, and the day of marriage was postponed. When the wedding preparations ought to have been made, the expenses and conveyances necessary for such a journey were prepared instead.

For since she was a very tender virgin and unmarried both in will and in age, and since the bridegroom himself was God-fearing and a worshiper of Christ, he calmly consented. When he learned that it was not lawful to resist, he too began to encourage the journey, hoping and praying that everything would happen for him as the girl had declared.

6. [Col. 0053B] When these matters had been duly completed, and everything suitable for the use and sustenance of all the travelers had been prepared, they gave thanks to God and proceeded along the public road. The bridegroom was cheerful and lively outwardly, in secular splendor; the virgin rejoiced far more greatly within. For Christ granted her every prosperity, to whom, already with true faith, perfect hope, and whole-hearted charity, she had devoted her soul always to serve. In silent prayers she asked Jesus Christ to preserve her heart and body undefiled, lest she be overcome by alluring pleasures. Her mind prayed in silence, and with the eyes of her heart she contemplated the Lord who protected her. In sweetest converse she summoned holy legions of angels to her aid, and with tears asked that the entire choir of the heavenly hosts be present to her. The handmaid of God was heard, and, as divine mercy accompanied her, she deserved greater consolations through the regard of heaven [Col. 0053C]. She soon perceived that sacred protections were present with her; defended by them from every harm, she was brought to Rome into the apostolic presence with complete integrity of faith and body.

While they were visiting the sites of the mistress of the world, and the bridegroom, surrounded everywhere by his companions in proud display, went about visiting various relics of the saints, she avoided the company of arrogance and went alone to the thresholds of the apostles. The bridegroom supposed that she was resting from the fatigue of the long journey; but she, as though renewed in spirit and made stronger, visited all the oratories both outside and within the city of Rome. He, therefore, gazed with bodily eyes in amazement upon the buildings of the city of Jericho, soon to fall; she, with the vision of her mind, contemplated the radiant walls of the heavenly Jerusalem, which shall endure forever [Col. 0053D]. Always for love of her heavenly homeland she lay prostrate in prayer, vigils, and fasts before the thresholds of the apostles, scarcely returning to the lodging.

7. Then, despising transitory things and leaving the bridegroom with all his company, she spent the night in prayer, mortifying her body with vigils and hunger, and distributing to the poor everything she possessed. Thus she became a nun, though she had been thought a bride; and the earthly union, with all its pomp, was cast down, while from above chastity, queen of the virtues, was poured upon her. She was certainly joyful, as though at last possessing what she had long desired; hence she could not for a moment leave what she had deserved to find with such splendor.

When the day of the apostolic station came again, she prostrated herself [Col. 0054A] at the feet of the prelate of the holy Catholic mother Church. She offered her protected virginity to Christ the Lord, after the example of the Virgin Mother, and requested that she be consecrated by the seal of chastity and the veil of her head under the protection and service of the incomparable Virgin Mary. The pious Father heard her most kindly intention and devotion, and understood that the Lord had enlightened her mind. Astonished at such wisdom in a girl, he is said to have spoken in a voice full of tears:

“Blessed are you, Lord God of all, who place your dwelling in the virginal bed of a chaste mind and body, and who work many wonders in the sex of fragile matter. Let the tongue of all therefore speak your praise universally, because in deeds such as these it is fitting to exalt you, Lord of all. Indeed, Lord, I shall praise you forever for these things and shall glorify your name throughout the ages” [Col. 0054B].

8. Then, turning to the chaste virgin of God, he began to speak as follows:

“Whose daughter are you, girl, or from what shores have you come? Tell me your name and also declare the faith of your people. For I judge that you were born from a most noble stock and that from the very cradle of infancy you were instructed in the letters of ecclesiastical discipline.”

At this she began to address him, her mind and face most serene, her head bowed:

“If you ask, Father and lord, about my people, I am of the Frankish nation. My name is Hunegundis, and I was born in the Vermand region, from which I was brought here. I was indeed raised by Christian parents, and, against my will but, as I believe, in accordance with God’s pleasure, I was given in marriage to a young man. Bound by the love of Christ, I have put him behind me and avoid him; under Christ’s guidance and favor I am whole in body and undefiled in mind [Col. 0054C].

“To him who created all things I devote myself, and I preserve intact the faith which you ask of me. If you wish to hear it clearly, I shall reveal it to you, excellent Father. Although I am barbarian by nation, nevertheless we profess this true and holy faith, which at the end of time has been brought to us from this holy apostolic see and Catholic mother Church.

“Behold: while your holiness demands the faith from us, you seem to us almost like Christ asking the Samaritan woman for water from the spring. By deigning to engage in such a conversation, he secretly indicates that no region can exclude anyone from the faith. Therefore, since we are not ashamed of our faith, we are in no way confounded by our province, since David commands all nations to clap their hands and shout to God with a voice of exultation, and so forth.

[Col. 0054D] “Nevertheless, since apostolic institutions instruct us to give to all who ask an account of the hope and charity that are in us, let us no longer delay in showing your blessedness, in a few words, the glory of our faith. We believe and confess that, without beginning in time and without end, the supreme and boundless Spirit is the one almighty God, according to what Moses said: ‘Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God’ (Deut. VI).

“One, I say, is God the Father, unbegotten; one is his only-begotten Son; one is the Holy Spirit, proceeding from both and coeternal with the Father and the Son. Yet always the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God: from whom are all things, through whom are all things, and in whom are all things, and without whom nothing was made [Col. 0055A].

“This threefold conjunction and conjoined division excludes union among the persons, yet preserves unity in the distinction of the persons. We do not believe that, just as there are three persons, so there are three gods; rather, in the three persons we confess one Godhead. We believe the holy Trinity in the subsistent persons, but unity in the nature, majesty, and substance of the Godhead.

“Thus we divide everything that exists into two. Apart from the Trinity alone, everything that exists or acts or moves in heaven, on earth, and in the sea we believe and confess to be a creature; God alone is the Creator.

“We also believe that the Son of God was conceived in the last times from the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary [Col. 0055B], and that he assumed flesh and a soul of human nature. In that flesh we believe and confess that he was crucified, buried, and raised from the dead; and in that same flesh, though in another glory, that after his resurrection he ascended into heaven. From there we await him as judge of the living and the dead.

“We confess also the complete and perfect resurrection of our flesh, in which we now live and move in the present life; and in that same flesh we shall either receive the rewards of good things for good deeds or endure the punishments of penalties for evil deeds.

“We profess repentance for sins with the fullest faith and receive it as a second grace, according to what the Apostle says to the Corinthians: ‘I wished to come to you, so that you might have a second grace’ (II Cor. I).

[Col. 0055C] “This is the treasure of our faith, which we preserve sealed in the ecclesiastical creed that we received in baptism. Thus we believe with the heart before God; thus we confess with the mouth before all human beings, so that knowledge of it may establish faith among human beings, and its image may give testimony to God.”

9. Repeating publicly before everyone these and countless other mysteries of the faith of the same kind, the most devoted virgin Hunegundis offered wholesome discourse to the ears of those standing by, and desirable silence to her virginal lips. Then the venerable pontiff of the supreme apostolic see, reflecting that it was not a human being who was speaking, but rather understanding that the Holy Spirit was resounding in a chaste breast, spoke before them all:

“Blessed are you, daughter, by the Lord God of hosts, for in your pure mind you have prepared a dwelling pleasing to God [Col. 0055D]. It is therefore not fitting to grieve the Holy Spirit, whose sanctuary a chaste mind is believed to be. For the Apostle says that those who live chastely are temples of the Holy Spirit (I Cor. XII); and therefore whoever violates the temple of God, God will destroy.

“Greatly to be revered in you is that supreme craftsman who works all things in all people, distributing to each as he wills. Come, chaste virgin; come, pure mind. Receive what may advance eternal love. You have cast away the little gifts offered to you by a corruptible man under the appearance of piety; receive now [Col. 0056A], through our blessing, the bridal gifts granted to you by the Lord, by which you may recognize yourself forever as Christ’s bride and, by despising transitory things, grasp everlasting joys.

“He looks ahead to what you will do in your mind and observes how becomingly you accompany his virgins. Therefore strive earnestly to be greatly loved by his young men, and hasten eagerly to run after the fragrance of his ointments, always giving thanks to the Lord for what has been granted and humbly praying for what is yet to be granted.

“I exhort you to keep in mind what you desire to possess in eternal life, so that, having confessed yourself his bride on earth, you may deserve to enjoy his embraces in everlasting glory.”

10. After these words, the holy pope placed upon the holy altar a head-veil and the other garments signifying, in humility, chastity of heart and body, and contempt for the world [Col. 0056B]. He blessed them, and, consecrating her according to holy custom with an outpouring of blessing, duly dedicated her to serve Christ, as she had requested.

Then, turning to the Lord and praying, he said:

“Look, Lord, upon this handmaid of yours, so that, under your guidance, she may preserve the purpose of holy virginity which she has undertaken through your inspiration. Let there be in her, Lord, through the gift of your Spirit, prudent modesty, grave gentleness, and chaste freedom. Let her burn with charity and love nothing outside you. Let her strive to live commendably and not desire to be praised. Let her love you above all things by fearing you, and fear you in all things by loving you.

“Be her joy, Lord; in sorrow, her consolation; in uncertainty, her counsel. In injury, be her defense; in poverty, her abundance; in fasting, her food; in sickness, her medicine [Col. 0056C].

“Preserve what she has professed, so that she may conquer the ancient enemy and cleanse away the filth of vices; so that, with a hundredfold fruit, adorned with virginal beauty and the lamps of the virtues, she may deserve to attain the company of the chosen virgins.”

When all had answered, “Amen,” the holy bishop kissed the head of the holy virgin Hunegundis and dismissed her in peace.

[Note: [Col. 0055D] In the fourth reading of the Breviary, the Church of Saint-Quentin identifies Martin I. This cannot stand unless Eligius had lifted Hunegundis from the sacred font before he became a bishop. For Eligius presided over the see of Noyon before Martin presided over the Roman see.]

11. [Col. 0056D] When Eudaldus heard this—he who had formerly been called her bridegroom—and learned that he had been rejected by the virgin, he was indignant in his heart and began to be tormented in every faculty, turning over in his mind, in extreme agitation, how he might pierce her through with a sword. But he feared incurring the danger of homicide, and was terrified by hearing the apostolic sentence that we have quoted: “It is not fitting to grieve the Holy Spirit, whose dwelling the holy virgin was”; likewise by Paul’s words, where he says that those who live chastely are temples of the Holy Spirit (I Cor. III). Therefore, moved to repentance, he no longer dared to touch her.

He then sent messengers and rejected the holy virgin from his company and from the retinue of his return, leaving her alone on the public road and withdrawing from her everything necessary for such a journey. Deprived of human assistance [Col. 0057A], the virgin began to act courageously and to strengthen herself in the Lord, reciting the psalmist’s songs:

“The Lord shepherds me, and I shall lack nothing; in a pasture of grazing he has placed me,” and so forth (Ps. XXII).

“For you have led me into the harbor of your will. May your mercy, Christ, I beg, go before me and follow me, so that I may deserve to reach the desired service of the holy virgin Mary. And so that I may be able to dwell in your tabernacle forever, I beg to be sheltered beneath the covering of your wings.”

12. When she had completed this prayer, she began to travel alone and to return to Gaul according to God’s will, surveying byways and highways and continually asking that the protections of the saints be present to her. She had indeed been abandoned by human support, but was sustained and protected by the accompanying grace of Christ.

[Col. 0057B] As she journeyed, she was like one already living under monastic discipline—or, to put it more profoundly, like a holy hermit serving Christ in the remote solitude of the desert. On feast days she took only bread and very little water; on other days she refreshed her weary little body with bread mixed with ashes and with the nourishment of herbs and trees. Therefore the miracle which the Lord deigned to work through the holy virgin must not be passed over in silence.

13. When the aforementioned Eudaldus, burning with excessive indignation, discovered that he had been utterly rejected, and wished but did not dare to attack the holy virgin with a sword, he took counsel with a certain traveling companion whom he had brought with him and hastily resolved to return to his paternal inheritance, selling and distributing his burdensome possessions so that he might reach his own land more quickly. [Col. 0057C] As he considered this, he turned over in his mind the plan to sell all the virgin’s patrimonies and hereditary rights, and to reduce to nothing whatever he could not sell; thus he would eradicate them completely, together with all their equipment and dependents.

Accordingly, with the swiftest horses [or: horsemen], he began to take the road at speed, declaring that he would fully accomplish the deed which he had formerly conceived in his deceitful heart. This could not remain hidden from the holy virgin, who had taken care to lodge in the chamber of her heart the Lord who knows all things.

Thus the handmaid of God, moved by divine impulse and strengthened by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, though on foot, became swifter than all the horsemen and wagons; indeed, traveling by another road, she outstripped them all and passed ahead of the swift wagons. Finally, she reached first the land of her birth and, according to her wish and will, at the place commonly called Humolarias, handed over all her possessions to the holy Mother of God, together with herself, so that she might serve Christ there for as long as she lived [Col. 0057D].

14. Not long afterward, the same Eudaldus followed and arrived to fulfill his purpose. He presented himself as possessor and master of all the virgin’s property, not knowing that everything had already passed into the service of God and the protection of the holy Mother of God.

[Col. 0058A] When he learned what had happened, and discovered by both hearing and sight the truth of the virgin’s deeds, he returned to himself and began silently to marvel and revere her, recalling what miracles, and how many, the Lord had worked through the holy virgin. Therefore he immediately offered God such praises and thanks as he could, because God had guarded him from evil action and contact, so that he would not sin against the holy virgin, and had not allowed him, raging on his return, deservedly to perish.

Performing worthy fruits of repentance for what he had done against the virgin, he could not find praises with which to exalt her or gifts with which to please her, so that he might deserve even to be seen by her, or that she herself might deign to pour out prayers to Christ for him. At last, having found a salutary plan, he offered himself in humility of heart and body; prostrating himself before the sacred altar of the Mother of God Mary, he begged forgiveness for his offenses. Then, turning his face toward the place where the unmarried virgin sat, he asked her to have mercy on him and earnestly begged her that he, whom he had formerly wished to have as her bridegroom, might at least then deign to receive him as a servant.

[Col. 0058B] “Because,” he said, “you did not put me before a corruptible lover as an insult to me, nor did you prefer to me any person, whether powerful or lowly, but instead placed before me the King of the ages and Creator of all things, and accepted a heavenly Bridegroom for yourself in the virginal bed, behold, I gladly offer myself and all that is mine to him. What I once gave you as bridal gifts, hand over to your true Bridegroom Jesus Christ for the support of needy sisters and brothers.

“I, I say, as long as I live and bear this body, shall take care to be your steward in external matters; and after my death, by this testament of authority, I perpetually hand over all my possessions, together with my goods and dependents, in honor of almighty God and of the holy Virgin Mother of God.”

Confirming the testament, he said publicly before everyone:

“Receive these things from me now, most chaste virgin, and command by your prayers that my corpse be buried in this place, so that when the heavenly King and Bridegroom has led you into the virginal bridal chamber, I may appear clothed in a wedding garment and girded with the snowy fleece of the Lamb, worthy, even as the last, to take part among the banqueters at the king’s table and in heavenly life” [Col. 0058C].

15. He therefore obtained what he sought and returned home unharmed with holy devotion of spirit. The Lord granted him the power to live well and brought his desire to the desired fulfillment. For, devoted to God, he took care to supply the holy virgin with more than was necessary, and likewise provided food and clothing in the established hospice.

Then, supported by manifold power from Christ and spending the time of his life in such work, he was stripped of the contagion of the present age. Having completed his course through transitory light, he heard from above a voice speaking these words to him:
