“Well done, good and faithful servant, because you have been faithful over a few things; I will set you over many things. You shall be ruler over ten cities.”

Then the blessed virgin Hunegundis offered his holy soul, together with the offering of sacrifice, through the hands of the priests to Christ, King of kings, praying and beseeching that the holy angels come to his aid and that his spirit be placed among the choirs of the heavenly hosts.

She ordered his body to be placed in a coffin and had it carried to her within the monastery; there she entrusted it to a fitting and desired place of burial [Col. 0058D].

16. [Col. 0059A] After his departure, she submitted herself to a stricter life and to the service of Christ, punishing and lamenting the thoughts and harmful deeds already performed. With frequent fasts and vigils she chastised her wearied body, remembering that it is not the one who has begun, but the one who has persevered, who will be saved.

Finally, in this holy meditation of spirit and devoted practice of faith, dying to the world and living for Christ, she is said to have passed the whole period of her life, so that she often seemed to lament and utter the prophetic words:

“Alas for me, because my sojourning has been prolonged,” and so forth (Ps. CXIX).

The heavenly mercy considered her holy and long-suffering pilgrimage and resolved to satisfy her most ardent petition, so that what she had hitherto seen “through a mirror and in a riddle” she might then begin to behold face to face.

[Col. 0059B] 17. One day, while lying alone and holding outstretched hands in prayer, she was struck by bodily heaviness and the great heat of physical illness. Yet she deserved consolation through the aid of the angels and the intercession of all the saints, whom she never ceased to invoke even in the prison of her afflicted body.

Meanwhile, as Christ’s servants of both sexes stood around her—having assembled from neighboring and distant regions for the departure of so great a mother and virgin—there was great pain, mourning, and sobbing among them all. For they saw themselves deprived of such great consolation, although they trusted that they would always be protected in heaven by her most devoted patronage.

Then she turned to the priests who were sitting beside her and asked for the oil of anointing and communion [Col. 0060A]. With all her strength she entreated the Lord to have mercy upon her.

At last, receiving the viaticum of the Lord’s body and blood, with a rosy countenance and beautiful face, as though she were about to be presented to the King of kings in the heavenly bridal chamber, she ordered everyone to sing sweet and hymn-like melodies of psalmody. Among other words, as though rising from sackcloth and ashes, she said:

“Here I am, Christ, your handmaid. Come, I beg you, most gracious King, and kindly receive me.”

As she continued in this utterance from the middle hour of the night until the third hour of the day, suddenly an exceedingly sweet fragrance struck the faces of those standing by together with an immense light. They could scarcely remain upright because of the light, although they were strengthened by the balsamic breath of perfumes.

[Col. 0060B] A voice also is said to have descended with the great light. Though it caused terror in everyone, it revealed itself clearly to no one; yet what else did it seem to proclaim than what is said to be spoken to every holy soul? For it began:

“Arise, hasten, my beloved, my dove, my beautiful one, and come.”

“Beloved,” that is, through love; “dove,” through simplicity; “beautiful,” through beauty of conduct; and so forth.

18. Sweetened by these and other consolations of this kind, the holy and blessed soul is believed to have departed to the Lord on the eighth day before the Kalends of September [Note: [Col. 0059C] Around the year 690, since Hunegundis was lifted from the sacred font by Blessed Eligius, who migrated to heaven around the year 660. Hunegundis is mentioned in the additions to Usuard and in the Benedictine [Col. 0060C] and Gallican martyrologies on the eighth day before the Kalends of September, although, because of the feast of Saint Louis, her office is transferred by the canons of Augusta Veromanduorum to the following day.]—the Lord who alone reigns without beginning, God perfect in unity and Trinity, now and forever and unto all ages of ages. To him be glory, praise, and jubilation, honor and dominion, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0059]

## The Translation of the Body of Saint Hunegundis the Virgin at Vermand, by Bernerus the Abbot

*(In Mabillon, Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict, Fifth Century, p. 213.)*

## Preliminary Observations

1. We presented the Life of Saint Hunegundis, virgin and nun of Humolarias, in the Second Benedictine Century, and attributed it to Bernerus the abbot as its author. This is confirmed by the following history of the translation, which shows that it is the work of one and the same writer. The following words in section 9 demonstrate this:

“Having first set forth these matters concerning the life and deeds of the frequently mentioned glorious virgin, we have judged it right to describe, by adding a few words, the notable miracles.”

Now Bernerus committed the translation to writing, as the Anonymous author testifies in the subsequent little book *On the Transfer of the Body of Saint Hunegundis*:

“Anyone wishing to learn the account of her discovery, and also of her translation, together with the notable miracles divinely revealed there, should know that the venerable abbot Bernerus, of blessed memory, who by God’s ordering was the first to succeed to her resting place, took pains to work it out in lucid style and abundant speech,” and so forth.

Indeed, the style and character are the same in both works, except that in the translation and miracles, which he wrote as an ear-witness or eyewitness, his authority is more reliable than in the Life, which he wrote three hundred years after Hunegundis. Before saying more about Bernerus himself, something must first be said about Berta of Humolarias, the first translator’s principal agent.

2. After her husband’s death, she was consecrated to the Lord at Reims “under the protection of the most blessed Mother of God, having assumed the veil.” This is said to have taken place in the nunnery of Saint Peter by a later monk of Humolarias, who composed the Life of Saint Hunegundis in the French language in 1681.

They say that she was then brought from there to govern the nuns of Humolarias, whose lapsing morals she struggled to restrain. This gave rise to the opportunity to investigate the body of Saint Hunegundis. That Berta labored earnestly to increase the resources of her monastery is proved by the charter of Transmarus, bishop of Noyon, which, as a genuine testimony to the completed translation, it is useful to reproduce here:

“I, Transmarus, in the name of God, unworthy bishop of the holy Church of Vermand and Noyon, make known to the faithful of the holy Church that the lady Berta, abbess of the monastery of Humolarias, has come into our presence, humbly asking that we grant to the congregation serving God there the altar of Saint Stephen’s church, which is in the same village of Humolarias, where the aforesaid abbey is situated, to the place of Saint Mary and Saint Hunegundis.

“Having presented her petition to Lord King Louis, and likewise to Lord Artoldus, archbishop of the Church of Reims, and to our fellow bishops, his suffragans, by command of the aforesaid king and with the counsel of the metropolitan lord and the other bishops, we have most willingly decided to comply with so humble a request.

“We have therefore given the aforesaid altar to the congregation of the same monastery, for the place of Saint Mary and Saint Hunegundis, to be held in perpetuity without any opposition, on the condition that every year it pay two solidi of denarii, as authority commands, for the honor of the episcopal see.

“And because the body of Saint Hunegundis, such a venerable virgin, has this year, God willing, been raised from the earth amid shining miracles, we have gladly given the aforesaid altar.

“We therefore order that, when one person has died, another be brought before the bishop, to whom the same bishop shall give the prescribed altar without payment and entrust the care of souls.

“And so that this gift may remain inviolable and unshaken, we have ordered this charter to be written and have marked it with the sign of the cross. By the authority of the holy Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, we have excommunicated, and excluded from the thresholds of the holy Church, all those who by force or deceit remove the aforesaid altar from the place of Saint Hunegundis.

“Signature of King Louis. Signature of Queen Gerberga and of her son Lotharius. Signature of Hugh, duke. Signature of Heribert, count. Signature of Arnulf, marquis. Signature of Adelelmus, knight. Signature of Rainaldus, knight. Signature of Theobaldus, knight. Signature of Helbertus, knight. Signature of Evrardus, knight. Signature of Gerbertus, knight. Signature of Artoldus, archbishop of Reims. Signature of Rodulfus, bishop of Laon. Signature of Transmarus, bishop of Noyon. Signature of Abo, bishop of Soissons. Signature of Stephen, bishop of Thérouanne. Signature of Gerald, bishop of Amiens. Signature of Ingram, bishop of Cambrai. Signature of Gildricus, bishop of Meaux. Signature of Evagrius, bishop of Tournai. Signature of Hincmar, abbot of Saint-Remi.

“Done at Laon, at Clavato, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 947, on the fourth day before the Ides of April, in the fifth indiction, with epact 26, while King Louis reigned in his thirteenth year. Odo the deacon wrote and reread it on behalf of and by order of Erchemboldus, chancellor of Lord Transmarus, bishop of Noyon.”

No one should be troubled by the fact that Bishop Transmarus states that in the year of the charter, that is, in the year of Christ 947, the body of the virgin Hunegundis was raised from the earth, although the acts of the translation themselves give the year 946. In these words the bishop is reckoning not by the Christian calendar year but by the year elapsed since the translation.

Two things are noteworthy in the subscriptions of this charter: first, that it was granted at a public assembly of bishops and nobles at Laon; second, that the subscriptions of the bishops are placed after those of all the nobles, contrary to customary practice. Perhaps the nobles themselves occupied one side of the document in an uninterrupted series after the king, while the clergy occupied the other side in the same order. I return to Berta.

3. The efforts of the most devout abbess Berta did not have either happy or lasting success. As the minds of the nuns inclined toward worse things, she withdrew from the position around that time, or perhaps died. For in the year 968 monks summoned from the monastery of Saint-Remi at Reims entered Humolarias, under the leadership of Bernerus, to restore the place’s better reputation. This is shown by the letters of Louis Transmarus, which were subsequently supported by John XII in the first year of his pontificate.

Placed in charge of the monastery of Humolarias, Bernerus brought it an astonishing degree of dignity and prosperity. For men of the highest rank eagerly desired to embrace the monastic life under him. Among them was Landebertus, governor of the town of Saint-Quentin, who there renounced the world together with neighboring soldiers.

The increase of Bernerus’s household resources is proved by the Humolarias charter collection, from which the catalogue of abbots is to be completed among the works of Sainte-Marthe. In the year 964 Bernerus was still alive and flourishing, when he sent his pupils to the monastery of the town of Saint-Quentin on the island. After expelling the disorderly clerics, they established monastic laws there.

Bernerus’s work on the translation of Saint Hunegundis ends with a description of miracles performed before the year 965.

4. Another translation of that virgin, or transfer of her body, was celebrated on the fourth day before the Ides of June in the year 1051 by Macarius of Humolarias, Gerard of the island monastery at Augusta Veromanduorum, Rainerus of Saint-Prejectus, and Walerannus of Saint-Quentin of the Mount near Péronne. The event is narrated at greater length by an anonymous writer of that period, who continued Bernerus’s history.

After these events—that is, in the year 1678—on the twelfth day before the Kalends of September, Peter, the second abbot of Humolarias by that name, had a reliquary of exceedingly fine workmanship made and arranged for the relics of Saint Hunegundis to be placed in it by the illustrious William Marafinius, bishop of Noyon. John, abbot of Saint-Quentin on the island; John of Saint-Prejectus; John of Arrouaise; John of Vermand; and other leading men, both from the clergy and from the military, stood beside him.

Then Peter, abbot of Humolarias, granted one of the holy virgin’s ribs to Louis XI, king of the Franks; another to William, bishop of Noyon; and a third to the dean and canons of the collegiate church of Saint-Quentin.

A document concerning this matter, made in the year 1679, was found in the same reliquary of Saint Hunegundis. In that year, on the sixth day before the Kalends of July, the illustrious Francis of Clermont, bishop of Noyon, opened the reliquary and discovered the relics of the holy virgin, which had been kept for a long time at Augusta Veromanduorum because of the storms of war, and had now been returned to the people of Humolarias. After delivering a solemn sermon and holding a procession, he displayed them to the people for veneration.

Let us now examine the history of the Translation.

## Prologue of the Author

[Col. 0061]

[Col. 0061A] 1. When the human mind searches with faithful devotion into the great works of divine goodness by which almighty God deigns to reveal the merits of the just, the spirit is raised from the sluggishness of its own torpor. And because it sees that those whom it admires were of the same condition as that in which it itself exists, and that no privilege of merits but only the grace of the divine gift enabled heavenly clemency to grant them such distinction in virtue, it is stirred to faith in order to merit these things, strengthened in hope [Col. 0062A], and, in the exercises of divine worship, stretches out its arms with vigorous effort toward good action.

It bursts forth with all the greater confidence toward courageous deeds when it sees the weaker sex shining more gloriously in the clear light of signs. Let us therefore undertake, in whatever ways we are able, to recount certain evident miracles which the Lord deigned to display in the translation of his most blessed virgin Hunegundis.

We have judged it useful to make the text of this account clearer by indicating the names of the persons involved in this work, the causes of the events, the number of years, and also the sequence of times. Thus the dignity of the persons casts away the mark of frivolity; the certainty of the account removes the stain of rashness [Col. 0064A]; the defined number of years suggests to us something mystical in that number; and the sequence of times likewise increases the glory of the miracles.

## The Translation Begins

[Col. 0063]

[Col. 0063A] 2. There was therefore a certain religious woman named Berta who, as they say, in her youth had been joined to a husband because her parents compelled her. When he had been taken away from this light, she resolved in her heart no longer to serve a mortal husband.

For many noble and very wealthy men were eager to marry her. Escaping only with difficulty from the hands of her friends, she fled to the city of Reims for protection under the most blessed Mother and ever-virgin Mary, and devoutly received the veil of her head [Note: [Col. 0063D] This veil was a token of the celibate life to be undertaken. Thus the woman Gundi is said to have been clothed in the garment and veil of the holy Mother of God Mary in a legal proceeding of the year 874, published in Book VI of *De re diplomatica*.]

Afterward, by God’s providence, it happened that she presided over this place, where in our own time she lived for a long period a life worthy of imitation by all. She was indeed a woman of remarkable abstinence, victorious patience, love of poverty, devoted humility, and dedication to works of mercy; she was suitably intent upon fasts, vigils, and prayers.

Moreover, certain religious women who were shamefully wallowing there in the allurements of miserable carnal desire, she invited to restrain themselves and imitate her, in accordance with the Apostle’s admonitions, by reproving, beseeching, and also rebuking them.

But just as the life of the just is always accustomed to be contrary to the morals of the reprobate, she became grievous to them even to look upon. Therefore, through the many insults, curses, and darts of ambush which they hurled against her, because she seemed to remain in that place out of love for the most holy virgin Hunegundis, some of them dared to invent false stories about the absence of her sacred body.

For this reason the faithful purpose was stirred to seek the most holy treasure of so great a body, saying that it was no longer fitting for her to remain there if that place had been deprived of such a holy and glorious mother.

3. Therefore, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 946, while Louis was reigning, on the fifth day, the day before the Nones of October, after very many fasts, frequent vigils, and many tears, she spent that same night sleepless with all those whom she had been able to summon to this purpose, through abundant and immeasurable showers of tears, humbly imploring the clemency of the almighty Lord that he might deign to reveal to her the most sacred body of his holy virgin. When morning came, after the solemn celebration of Mass, the faithful and God-devoted woman, intent on diligently seeking the precious jewel of the sacred body, seized a mattock. And it came to pass, with the assent of the omnipotence of the Godhead, which is accustomed to deny nothing to those who ask in truth, that she happily found what she had faithfully sought.

Rejoicing and exulting, she gave thanks to the almighty Lord, who had granted her what she had long sought with such great anxiety of spirit. She therefore went forth exceedingly cheerful and greatly exultant, and, as though swallowed up by an immeasurable vastness of joy, having formed the whole plan in the gravity of her counsel, she suddenly attempted to raise the heavenly pearl, that it might be forever inserted among the eternal ornaments of the heavenly King. But the disposition of the divine plan intervened and showed that nothing concerning the pledges of the blessed body should be done inconsiderately or lightly.

For immediately there arrived—not by chance but by God’s providence—the venerable priest Giso, a suitable guardian of the relics of the holy martyrs Quintinus and Victoricus. He scarcely brought an end to the aforesaid haste and restrained their efforts with the strongest reprimand. “It does not seem reasonable,” he said, “that the body of so blessed a virgin should be raised without the authority and consent of the bishop of this diocese; otherwise she, whose fame for virtues had long been renowned far and wide among many people, might be diminished by the report of this sudden and seemingly furtive translation.”

By this arrangement, then, he put an end to their efforts. For thirty-two days they kept open and untouched the chest in which the most blessed body lay, attending upon it day and night with sacred vigils while they awaited the bishop’s arrival. The almighty God certainly did not wish this delay to occur without cause, but so that the one whom he had glorified before the angels and all the spirits of the righteous already reigning with Christ in heaven, he might also designate as worthy of veneration on earth among human beings still burdened with corruptible flesh and the weight of sins.

4. At that time there was indeed such a great inundation of rain that, because of the excessive outpouring of water, the farmers could in no way cultivate the land or sow seed except in despair. At that very hour and moment, however, when the cover was lifted from the sarcophagus, an exceedingly bright ray of sunlight poured through the window situated beside the place of the holy tomb and shone wondrously over the body of the most blessed virgin. Thus, when all the density of the clouds had been driven away, clear weather returned with such speed that it seemed as though another sun had arisen upon the earth for the body of the life-giving virgin. It was as if that visible sun were proclaiming with its own voice that it could not fail to minister unstable light on earth to her for whom the light of eternity shines steadfastly in heaven.

[Col. 0065A] The place of the most holy body was so suffused with brightness that those looking on could not tell whether it shone materially by the ray of that sun or by the light of divine radiance. And throughout all the days during which the mausoleum lay opened, she was visibly present to those who piously sought her, so that the force of that great brilliance never entirely departed. From the breast upward, instead of the tiny particles and impurities of dust, shining fragments of pearls gleamed; and, as certain exceptionally bright sparks burst forth, they dazzled the eyes of those looking upon them.

Together with that light there was diffused such a fragrance of wondrous odor that the nostrils of all who stood nearby were filled with ineffable sweetness. Throughout the entire period during which she lay thus exposed, whenever she was revealed for viewing to those afflicted by various illnesses—for whoever could see her, no matter what illness held them, was immediately healed—the aforesaid exceedingly sweet odor, made still sweeter and ever renewed for the better, filled the sense of smell of those present.

At the discovery of so great a mother, therefore, immense joy arose throughout the entire neighboring region. The earth rejoiced that it had so long concealed so bright a star; the air exulted that, through the grace of so great a virgin, it had obtained clear skies instead of clouds; the sun’s ray rejoiced to offer service to the limbs of the sacred body; and the heavenly host of blessed spirits gave thanks because they saw being faithfully venerated, in the narrow cavern of the tomb, those most sacred members of the one whose soul they already enjoyed accompanying, members destined to be glorified according to their merits with ineffable joy on the day of the resurrection of all.

5. We believe that we are able to render praise to the Creator of all if the miracles which the Lord wished to work at the discovery of his most holy virgin Hunegundis are handed down to the knowledge of posterity. For a certain demoniac was brought by the hands of friends who, in firm faith, had placed their hope of curing the man whom they led in the holy virgin. Resisting and with all his strength obstructing his own progress, he was at last, with great difficulty and many pressing upon him, forced into the church of that blessed virgin. As he was dragged by hands and arms toward the altar, the nearer he came to it, the more violently was he inflamed with frenzy and the more he resisted the efforts of those driving him.

After struggling for a long time, they finally overcame the madman and set him before the altar. Then, bringing him forward to behold the tomb of the most holy body, they compelled him to turn his eyes toward it. Wishing to grant their request, the often-mentioned religious woman Berta opened the tomb and allowed them to see the veil which lay over the holy limbs. When he saw it, the man who was tormented was immediately restored to his senses and to all his former health. At once, with no one compelling him, he prostrated himself on the ground and implored the clemency of the almighty Lord through the merit of the blessed virgin, giving thanks for the health restored to him and praying for protection in the future. As a proof of perfect health, not long afterward he returned with lights and paid honor to the holy virgin. As testimony to his recovered health, he brought with him many of his neighbors and promised that every year, for as long as he lived, he would visit that place with lights and a company of friends.

6. During this same interval, a certain peasant named Lupus, who is still alive and lives in the stronghold called Parrona [Note: [Col. 0065D] Elsewhere Perona, a castle or royal estate on the river Somme, distinguished by an ancient palace; more concerning it in book IV of *De re diplomatica*.], came with his natural daughter, called Afflindis. Both sought the aid of this most holy virgin because of the affliction of their illness. The father had lost his hearing because his ears were dulled; the daughter had for a considerable time lost the light of her bodily eyes. Therefore, suppliant and weeping with excessive bitterness, they implored the mercy of the almighty Lord that, through the merit of the most blessed virgin, a remedy of health might come to them; and so it came to pass. From that day the father deserved to have his hearing, and the daughter her sight, restored more fully [Col. 0066B].

At the very hour of the discovery described above, a certain poor man in spirit named Adelbodus lay deprived of all use of his limbs. Since his end seemed near, when the day had passed he had been fortified with the sacraments of the Lord's body and blood, and everyone considered him close to death. But as soon as he heard the bells ringing out the clear vision of so great a body's appearance [Note: [Col. 0066D] This author, using a Greek expression, understands this as the uncovering of the body.], he rose from his bed, showing no sign of infirmity in the motion of his limbs. He ran to the church of the holy virgin, eagerly desiring to see the tomb; taking one of his own sheep, he offered it to the holy virgin as a gift. Recovering at once from his illness, he thereafter felt no harm from the affliction he had undergone.

7. While this rejoicing was still resounding, a widow named Wiburgis lay gravely ill. A little earlier, in expectation of her death, having received the divine sacraments, she had been reconciled by priests to the divine mercy through penitence and tearful confession [Col. 0066C]. Perceiving the voices of the exulting people full of joy, she asked what that commotion meant, or on whose account such joy in the people resounded in celebration. She immediately learned from those around her that such joy had arisen among the people at the discovery of the sacred body.

On hearing the name of the holy virgin, quicker than speech, she raised her head from the bed, composed her limbs, put on clothing, and hastened to the church. As she silently considered and wondered that, restored to herself by heavenly power, her illness had been banished and health suddenly returned to her, she gave thanks and praise to divine omnipotence. Immediately, before many witnesses, she gave one of her own slave women, named Isigildis, to the most blessed Hunegundis in return for the benefit of health received [Col. 0066D]. Thus she recovered from that illness and afterward lived for a long time.

After these things had been done, and not a few other miraculous signs by which the Lord wished the glory of his virgin to be made manifest—signs which, because of their multitude, I judge it unsuitable to insert fully into this little writing—

8. For, in order to show everyone how great a grace of healing he had granted his handmaid, almighty God caused at that same time such a disease of severe illness to rage in that very village that scarcely a house remained in which no sick person lay [Col. 0067A]. All of them were healed with such speed at the aforesaid solemnity that, when the most blessed virgin was raised from the tomb, none of them remained sick in bed.

Finally, Rodulf, archdeacon of the Church of Noyon and afterward its devout bishop, was summoned. From the congregation of the most blessed martyr of Christ Quintinus, Fathers Giso, Rotbertus, and many others filled with great devotion were called together, and the office, long delayed, was hastened to completion. When the solemn celebration of Mass had been performed, they approached the tomb with humble minds and devout hearts. The divinely infused light already mentioned was still shining so clearly around the blessed virgin's head and breast that, because of its intensity, it could not be fully looked upon. The most holy body was raised from the tomb on the seventh day before the Ides of November [Col. 0068A].

But we, dearest brothers, to whom these deeds of the blessed virgin and the many examples of other saints are shown for reading and set before us for imitation, must observe diligently and strive bravely, lest, lacking their works, we become strangers in that everlasting life to the common joy of all the saints. Let us therefore knock with the sighs of our inmost heart upon the ears of the most merciful Creator, so that, by his gift, we may be able effectively to fulfil what he commands and what he profitably counsels; so that, when he comes in that strict examination of judgment, our Lord Jesus Christ may find in us not what he condemns, but what he mercifully crowns with his redeemed, he who lives and is glorified as God with God the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

MIRACLES.

[Col. 0067]

[Col. 0067B] 9. We believe, therefore, that it is fitting to offer praise to the Creator of all if the miracles that the Lord wished to perform at the discovery of his most holy virgin Hunegundis are handed down to the knowledge of posterity. For what we have undertaken to describe we were scarcely able to learn from certain people of our own time who reported it; there were also innumerable deeds of power which, had they not been consigned through negligence to oblivion, might have been committed to writing with sufficient dignity.

One sign, however, which is known to have been wondrously performed must now be narrated in brief. At a certain time, wicked men, trusting in their superior power, entered the forest belonging to the holy virgin, situated beside the river Sambre in the village called Dediniacus, with audacious presumption. They allowed their pigs to consume it and refused in any way to agree that any rent or service should be rendered to the same holy virgin for that forest.

The blessed virgin herself took care to rebuke them and restrain them from such great audacity. While they were freely enjoying themselves in the abundance of the forest, suddenly that virgin of God appeared to the herdsmen in a terrifying form. She asked them why they were stealing the forest’s produce from her, struck them with the rod she carried in her hand, and so the entire herd of pigs, scattering in every direction, set off at a headlong run toward the monastery of Humolaria.

Thus it came about that those from whom the lady could not obtain the revenues of the forest were afterward possessed by her household under secure right. For when they entered the village with great force and scattered from one another through the streets and farmyards around the monastery, no one ever afterward sought them.

There are many witnesses to this event. Among them was a certain woman named Dodisma, recently taken from this life, who truthfully affirmed that she had been present at so great an event and had received her share from it.

10. At the same time there was a certain soldier of noble birth named Magenerus. Attracted by the beauty of a nun of that monastery, he could not at all refrain from her illicit embraces. One day, as he was going to the monastery as usual in order to satisfy the desire of his flesh and hers, the holy virgin Hunegundis visibly appeared to him in the courtyard of that monastery and, sharply rebuking him, asked where he was going.

At the voice of the rebuking woman he became exceedingly ashamed and, restraining himself from the abominable deed, withdrew for a time both from the approach and from the wicked act. But the aforesaid nun, unstable and wanton, thinking that the man had rejected her, lamented that she was despised by him, tormented by the sharpest grief. Armed by the snares of the ancient enemy, she tried by whatever cunning she could to call the same man back to her.

“Kind friend,” she said, “why did you think me worthy of contempt? Do not let the apparition you saw frighten you, for it was not the presence of Saint Hunegundis, but one of my rivals, wishing to turn you away from me.”

Having thus given the signal, and secretly prepared an entrance elsewhere, that most filthy man attempted to repeat the interrupted wickedness. Immediately the ever-watchful guardian, Saint Hunegundis, came to meet him and struck him in the groin with the staff she held in her hand. At once he became bloodless and collapsed; he was carried in the hands of others, while his thigh swelled, and he ended his life in that same agony. For a full year before his death, his thigh rotted away on the ground.

Nevertheless, in the hope of curing him, his friends prepared very large gifts to offer to the holy virgin, but these were rejected as though they were the filthiest dung. When they offered a great quantity of coins, a whirlwind from heaven suddenly arose and, blowing away and scattering the aforesaid offering with such violence, made nothing of it afterward visible to any mortal.

No one, however, ought to find it incredible that we have reported the holy virgin of God appearing visibly to her enemies, since Saint Pope Gregory relates something similar concerning blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, in the third book of the *Dialogues*, chapter twenty-four. For he says that the same venerable Peter appeared in a white stole to a certain Theodore, the doorkeeper of his church, who had risen earlier than usual and was standing on wooden steps tending the lamps; Peter stood below on the pavement and rebuked him for rising so early.

11. Having briefly touched upon these matters, let us return at last to what we had interrupted for the time being and narrate what remains. A certain man named Guntardus, deprived of the light of his eyes, went to the church of the holy virgin in order to hear Mass. But when, after the solemn celebration had been duly completed there, he found the church doors locked at midday, he threw himself down on the ground outside in the portico and prayed for a long time that God’s mercy might be present to him.

After many tears, he rose from prayer and began to wipe his eyes with his hand, the function of sight having been restored to him through the most gracious favor of the holy virgin. Therefore he said to the woman guiding his steps:

“Woman, let me go. I no longer need you to pull me, for, thanks be to God, having received the light, I see perfectly what the intercession of my most beloved lady, namely Saint Hunegundis, has mercifully obtained for me.”

Thus filled with immense joy, he returned to his own home, praising God.

12. There is also another miracle of great power, which I do not think should suitably be concealed in silence. Another man named Rotbertus, deprived of the use of his feet and supported on crutches, as is customary for such people, hastened as best he could to take part in the glorious solemnity of the same virgin of God.

After remaining for a long time at a distance in the church, he asked that the grace of healing be poured into his wretched limbs. At last, through God’s mercy, by the merits and intercession of the blessed virgin, he deserved to be restored openly to perfect health before everyone. Thus it came about that he who had arrived bent over with contracted sinews returned afterward in joy, his joints made sufficiently firm and properly aligned.

Let it suffice that we have narrated these few things. The pen of our account could say more if the permission of time allowed it, although many works of miracles have been carelessly omitted through the fault of negligence. Let us therefore give thanks to our God, who so glorified his holy virgin in the world. Through her merits and supplication, may the Lord bring us to the joys of the heavenly homeland, where she herself rejoices happily and sings a new song to the Lord with the choirs of virgins. To him be glory, honor, and power forever and ever.

13. In recounting the wonders of divine action, that man must certainly be praised with the whole strength of his mind to whom the prophet sings in thanksgiving: “Blessed is the Lord God of Israel, who alone works great wonders” (Psalm 134:4). Therefore let us praise and bless him with all our strength, for he does not allow the glory of the merits of those who faithfully serve him to perish. Just as he eternally makes them share in heavenly joys, so also, temporarily, through certain wonders, he recalls their merits to human memory.

Since we are about to relate a great miracle of divine power that we saw with our own eyes, we do not doubt that in the minds of some a scruple of doubt will arise—an evil thing, alas, and the worst kind of unbelief. Let the detractors of divine works beware lest they be condemned with those of whom Scripture speaks: “Their throat is an open tomb; with their tongues they dealt deceitfully; the poison of asps is under their lips” (Psalm 5:10).

When they saw the Lord Jesus performing innumerable wonders and could not conceal them from the knowledge of the people, they tried in their wickedness to slander them, saying: “He casts out demons by Beelzebub, the prince of demons” (Mark 1:15). But let us set aside the false speakers, unhappily occupied with their lies, whose foolish heart, according to the Apostle, was darkened and who became vain in their thoughts. Unless they correct themselves, they will receive the reward of their error. Let us return to our subject and faithfully relate to pious and believing minds what we saw with our own eyes.

14. In the year 964 from the Lord’s Incarnation, on the eighth day before the Kalends of September, that is, on the feast of the blessed virgin Hunegundis, the miracle of which we speak was accomplished by divine power.

In the territory of a certain village called Sasnulficurtis, reapers were cutting grain on the feast itself. Their priest, Lantfridus by name, had frequently rebuked them for this presumption, saying that he had attended a synod at which Rodulf, bishop of the Church of Noyon, had ordered this feast to be celebrated with the greatest devotion.

But they, following the error of their neighbors, said that they alone could not celebrate the feast while they saw all their neighbors attending to their own necessities by working. It therefore happened that a certain girl named Rotgildis—according to what the aforesaid priest himself reported, his niece through his sister—followed the reapers already mentioned. She gathered the ears of grain that escaped their hands.

When she bent down to collect the ears carefully, she picked up one from the ground and found it wet with fresh blood. Astonished and wondering where that blood came from, she threw it away. Then she picked up another, likewise wet with the same blood, and threw it away as well. So with a third, fourth, and fifth, and thereafter, until she was weary, she saw all the ears she could gather filled with blood.

Trembling and exceedingly frightened, she ran to her father, who happened at that moment to have come into the same field, and told him what had happened to her. Her father, as though she were relating the words of childish frivolity, rebuked her harshly and advised her to return to her work.

But when she continued trembling and affirming that the matter was as she had said, her father followed her through the field. Together they gathered many ears soaked by an outpouring of the same blood and investigated whether perhaps one of the reapers in that field had cut his hand or finger, from which the blood might be flowing.

When everyone expressed astonishment and denied this with strong assurances, they carried some of the ears to the church. Finding the priest standing before the altar, they gave him the ears full of blood and explained in order what had happened to them in the field.

But the priest, reluctant to become the author of so great a report, said: “If I do not see something more concerning what you say, I do not dare proclaim this incredible matter to the people.”

As he said this, drops of blood began to flow from the tips of the grains, larger, as it were, than tears, and to fall upon the ground before his feet. At the sight, the priest was struck with such trembling that, his strength failing, he could scarcely keep himself upright on his shaking knees. What he had previously feared to announce, he afterward feared even more might reach the knowledge of the people too late through his negligence.

Thus, after the signs had been touched, he summoned the people to the church, rebuked them for their disobedience, and revealed this divine miracle to them. An excessive fear seized them because of the extraordinary miracle and made them most ready to perform penance for their presumption.

Finally, they left the church and ran everywhere through the fields, countryside, cultivated lands, and the outlets of the roads, announcing to all their neighbors that they should no longer persist in the work they had begun, but should come to the church and behold the divine miracle. All were greatly terrified; as the report swiftly spread, they were driven from their work as though by roaring pagans and humbly prayed that the Lord’s wrath might not come upon them from heaven.

15. A certain peasant named Rotbertus was threshing grain with a rod in the threshing floor of the same village. When he heard this, he promised to abandon his own work and threw down his flail. But, foolishly thinking that this would be a lesser offense, he seized a broom and began sweeping around the threshing floor, gathering the grain together.

Divine vengeance immediately followed this madness. For at once his arm stiffened, and, struck by the divine blow, he fell to the ground, crying out that he was guilty, wretched, and about to die with the utmost speed.

This event increased the fear already described. Meanwhile the priest ran about everywhere, carrying the bloodstained ears in his hands, and announced what had happened to the priests of the neighboring churches.

All of them, disturbed by the sign of so great a novelty, summoned the people of their parishes. With crosses and candles, forming a single procession, they came barefoot with supplicatory vows—together with the man whose arm had stiffened and the girl carrying the bloodstained ears in her hands—to the monastery of Saint Mary and Saint Hunegundis.

Confessing their guilt and prostrating themselves on the ground, they humbly asked the brothers to pray for them; and this was done.

Let those who do not believe this sign go and slander the One who likewise caused something to happen in blood in Egypt under Pharaoh. But let us bless him who is wondrous among his saints, the God of Israel, who gives strength and power to his people. Blessed be God forever. Amen.

# Appendix to the Translation of the Body of Saint Hunegundis the Virgin among the Viromanduans

Here begins the account of the removal of the body of Saint Hunegundis, the life-giving virgin, and of the miracle divinely performed there in the year 1051.

1. Everyone should regard it as especially fitting, honorable, and necessary for the faithful to describe the miracles of the saints and to commit their distinguished deeds to writing on tablets for the knowledge of posterity. For when the mournful tales of fables are thrust, through recitation, into the ears of fools inclined toward evil, the beguiled spirit grows sluggish, the mind becomes dull, and, abandoning its own light, flows downward, desiring the destructive allurements of corruption and abandoning the path of virtue. Thus it happens that the heart of the foolish, proceeding downhill after hearing stupidities, binds a chain by which it may be dragged and finally plunged into Tartarus.

But when the merits of the saints, made public, are brought before the hearing of the people, and their virtues are proclaimed for the sake of spiritual progress, the faithful mind rises from the sleep of death to life and stretches its arms from the darkness of unbelief toward the pursuits of holiness. Rising toward prosperity, it burns for courageous deeds and, taking up the path of devout intention, avoids the precipices of wickedness. Thus freed from the bonds of destruction, it hastens with unhindered foot toward the joys of heavenly life, so that it may behold the God of gods in Zion—that is, in the watchtower of peaceful vision.

Therefore, brothers, may it not weary your charity to hear a certain miracle that our Lord Jesus Christ, by his gracious will, wished to display in the removal of the body of his most holy virgin Hunegundis. Since an opportunity to speak of this removal has presented itself to us from nearby, may it not be tedious to linger for a little while out of reverence, so that the faithful may learn through writing, however unskilled, how this removal itself was carried out and completed. For an earnest devoted intention possesses its own reward.

2. In the year 1051 of the Lord’s Incarnation, while the excellent prince Henry, father of King Philip, governed the monarchy of the Franks, and while Abbot Macarius administered the care of the monastery of Humolaria,

[Note: Macarius, its abbot, rendered many services to his monastery of Humolaria, which, God willing, we shall publish elsewhere from the charter archive of that place.]

it seemed to the brothers of blessed Benedict, who served the Lord under the Rule, that the body of their lady Hunegundis ought to be moved, if the opportunity were available. Since they did not doubt that her soul was honored among the choirs of virgins in the heavenly bridal chamber, they did not wish to fail to bury her glorious body on earth in an honorable mausoleum.

At that time the sacred pearl was enclosed only in a small wooden chest, which, to those looking from outside, presented a wretched dwelling, but within preserved a very precious treasure. The little structure itself had been so surrounded and closed off with iron plates, within which the most devout bones were enclosed, that it could scarcely be opened except through a very few devices of mechanical craftsmanship.

Another somewhat larger chest had also been placed over it. It too had been constructed with no less skill and carefully secured with iron bindings and very many nails, fortified on every side with shrewd care and industry, so that it would not easily be accessible to crafty or fraudulent contrivances. For the one who hides his treasure in concealed and very strong coverings plainly does not wish it to be plundered.

In this manner, then, we learned from those who had seen it and reported it to us that the body of the virgin Hunegundis, beloved of God, had been enclosed from the time of the discovery and translation of that virgin. That discovery and translation took place in the year 946 of the Lord’s Incarnation, while Louis was reigning and Berta, a woman consecrated to God, governed the abbey of Humolaria.

For those wishing to learn about the account of that discovery and translation, together with the distinguished miracles divinely manifested there, the abbot BERNERUS, of blessed memory, labored to set them forth in clear style and splendid language. By God’s providence, he was the first to succeed to this little place after the nuns who had been there were expelled because of the obscene allurements of carnal pleasure.

But for the present, setting these matters aside, let us pursue the little work we have begun as best we can.

[Col. 0073B] **3.** When, therefore, the monks, as we have related above, were deliberating together with their spiritual father whether they might somehow bring to completion what they greatly desired, yet did not dare to begin, and when the fortune of the place was smiling somewhat favorably—God’s providence foreseeing all things—it happened that a certain man from the borough of the glorious martyr Saint Quentin, who made his living by commerce and trading, named Baldwin, came to our monastery out of devotion and for the advancement of his soul, so that, in return for mutual affection, the brothers might deign to grant him their fellowship.

The brothers, together with their Father, gladly accepted this request because of the Lord’s commandment which says: “Give, and it will be given to you; and with the same measure with which you measure, it will be measured back to you” (Matt. 7:2); and: “Whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37). They therefore gratefully bestowed upon him the fellowship and benefits of the place, as is customary among monks.

For although that man was a layman, he was devoted to religion, applying himself to works of mercy and preserving the devotion of faith through the intention of his heart, as the outcome later made clear. For after taking the habit in that place, he subsequently proved himself a devout monk. Drawn, finally, by this intimacy, the man made a practice of frequenting the monastery cloisters, becoming, as it were, another Adam among the brothers. Consequently, whenever he came, he often noticed the brothers whispering more and more frequently about the matter mentioned above.

But because, as has been said, they were afraid to begin, lest, according to the Gospel, people should mock them, saying: “These men began to build, but they were unable to finish,” the aforesaid man, moved—as people commonly suppose—by divine inspiration (for he too desired to honor the limbs of the holy virgin), summoned the assembly of the elders and began his address in these words:

“Since, venerable Fathers,” he said, “I perceive that some of you are conversing among yourselves and wishing, if the means were available, to place the body of our lady, the most holy virgin Hunegundis, in a more splendid shrine, I rejoice in my heart and promise my assistance to the best of my ability. Only do not delay beginning the little work you desire. But if you do not dare to undertake such a task, I myself shall take the whole matter upon me, and, relying on the aid of almighty God, shall bring it to completion, provided only that the offering of the people be granted to me.”

When the monks heard this, they were exceedingly delighted, gave thanks to the Creator of all things, and blessed the man for his promise, revering the prerogative of the divine will amid such great, sudden, and unexpected joy.

What need is there for words? Once the man had undertaken the task, he had a shrine made in repoussé work. Its length was two half-cubits; its continuous height was one cubit at both ends, and half a cubit on either side, with the remaining structure rising most suitably in the manner of panels, worked in chased and sculpted craftsmanship. On its surface are seen representations of the holy apostles and prophets, with three rows of very beautiful and polished panels of gleaming gold and shining silver, and icons arranged in order on both sides.

On one end, moreover, an image of Saint Hunegundis and of Saint Eligius, bishop of Noyon and the virgin’s patron at baptism, is seen raised in a particularly fitting manner. On the other, the majesty of Christ our Lord is represented with considerable elegance; his kingdom and dominion endure without end throughout the ages.

What more? Once the work had been hastened and, as has been said, splendidly completed, the lord abbot Macarius, who at that time administered the affairs of the place of Humolaria, as has already been mentioned, took care to invite the lord bishop of Noyon and summoned the neighboring abbots: namely, the lord Gerard of the Island, the lord Rainer, vicar of Saint Praejectus [Note: That is, coadjutor, if I interpret it correctly. The abbot of the Island is the abbot of Saint Quentin on the Island, once beside the walls and now within the walls of Augusta Veromanduorum; the abbey of Saint Praejectus is near the city; the abbey of Mount Saint Quentin is near Péronne.], [Col. 0074B] and the lord Boniface Walerannus of Mount Saint Quentin, as well as many other noblemen and soldiers of the territory of Vermandois.

He also urged monks and clerics to be present at this undertaking, lest such a precious pledge should seem to be handled or secretly moved like something stolen or unknown, without the knowledge and testimony of honorable and religious persons.

When, therefore, the appointed day arrived on which these things were to be done, and the news had flown—no messenger being swifter—an assembly of the elders took place. Noblemen, countrymen, women, and a rejoicing crowd of children came together. Nor was this without reason: they believed that, out of reverence and due honor to be shown to so great a mother, and also through her intercession, they would receive protection and obtain forgiveness while seeking aid for their offenses.

Meanwhile, the entrance to the treasury of glory was opened. The iron bands fastened around it with careful skill were raised with the aid of hammers; the covers were torn away; and the cradle of the precious body was revealed.

[Col. 0074C] **4.** But almighty God, wishing to honor the limbs of his bride by the prerogative of his hidden purpose, caused the day for moving the blessed bones to be postponed until the third day, on the occasion that furnished the justification for this delay. For the bishop, in whose diocese the place called Humolaria is situated, was detained by royal service and business and did not come at all on the appointed day. For this reason they were compelled to await him for three days.

The venerable shrine, therefore, remaining open as it was, was placed upon two wooden bases inside the Holy of Holies, between the altar of Mary, the Mother of God and ever-virgin, and the altar dedicated in honor of Saint Hunegundis.

Among the many thousands of devout people who gathered for so distinguished a celebration, very many who were physically weak strove to take part in this holy action, each intending to ask the Lord’s mercy for his or her own affliction. Accordingly, by divine will, as we have said, it happened that a girl named Emelina, seized by the disease of epilepsy, was brought to the monastery with the assistance of friends, in hope of recovering her health. She had been born in a village called Herleius, situated on the bank of the Somme, midway between the fortress of Saint Quentin and the monastery of Humolaria.

The Greeks call epilepsy *appensio*—“a seizure”—of the mind and body. This condition produces *spasmos*, that is, contractions of the limbs; the disease arises from melancholic humor, that is, from an excess of bile spread through the limbs, and it occurs through the imagination.

When the little girl had been brought into the church to obtain a remedy for herself, she was placed before the altar of the incomparable virgin Saint Mary, so that through her intervention and through the intercession of Saint Hunegundis she might deserve to regain the former state of her health.

For the girl of whom we speak was so oppressed by epilepsy that she allowed no interval of rest, displaying through the movements of her body the force of her torment. She declared that, because of the excessive heaviness of her condition, she was approaching death and almost breathing out her spirit.

At this, the assembled people, overcome with astonishment and pierced at once by pity and compassion, poured out showers of tears. Beating their breasts with their fists, they implored the Almighty with devout hearts for the deliverance of the pitiable woman.

But the little girl, afflicted with an immeasurable torment, did not cease for a moment. She filled the oratory with dreadful cries, struck herself with her hands, and, with her head shaking, presented to everyone a spectacle of wonder for two days, no respite appearing.

The faithful people, therefore, inspired by the Spirit above, begged the abbots and brothers, in the name of charity, to grant the pitiable little woman an opportunity to see the bones of the nourishing virgin Hunegundis, in case, with Christ’s clemency favoring them, such a great affliction might somehow be eased.

They granted this request, themselves also moved by humanity. What then? Shall I speak or remain silent? Indeed, I shall reveal the evident manifestation of a virtue worthy of proclamation.

For as soon as her eye saw the bones, after she had thrust her head inside, the framework of her entire body recovered the health she desired. The pain died away, the sickness was put to sleep, the sorrow was torn away, and the former condition of her body returned.

When the people standing by saw this, they blessed the Lord God of all things and offered him thanks, for he makes his saints wondrous as he wills and when he wills. There were, in truth, as many witnesses of this divine deed—which Jesus Christ, our Lord and God, deigned to display through the merits of the glorious virgin Hunegundis, for his own praise and glory—as there happened then to be faithful people present.

**5.** Upon this event, the abbots and monks rejoiced together and discussed the matter among themselves. They agreed that the transfer should not be delayed any longer and that they should not await the bishop’s presence, especially after witnessing so great and worthy a miracle, lest the people, already wearied by the long delay and prolonged waiting, should seem to be feeding upon empty hopes.

By common counsel and decree, therefore, the blessed relics were carried into the crypt dedicated in honor of the holy and undivided Trinity, built behind and adjoining the tribunal of that same monastery.

They undertook this for two reasons: first, lest in any circumstance the holy gifts should be offended by the excessive tumult pressing upon them from both sexes; and second, lest people should handle fragments of pearls before ignorant and inexperienced persons who did not know how to value them, since it is said: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, and do not cast your pearls before swine” (Matt. 7:6). Hence Isaiah says: “My secret to myself, my secret to myself” (Isa. 24:16).

After firmly bolting the doors which, on the right and left sides of the screen, opened access to those seeking the crypt, they surrounded the blessed gifts with anxious hearts, out of reverence for what was being displayed. For they hesitated over which of them ought more worthily to touch such precious gifts granted by Christ.

At last, however, they customarily entrusted this care and administration to the lord Gerard, abbot of the Island, because he was older by birth, more advanced in age, more serious in conduct, more devoted in religion, and more inclined toward pious deeds.

Why do we prolong the delay? The aforesaid abbot, therefore, accepting with humble submission the commands of his brothers, bared his arms and prepared himself with particular solemnity for the duties he had vowed to perform.

The blessed bones were moved with the utmost reverence and placed in a more fitting cradle.

O happy virgin, who, because you dwell resplendent in glory in heaven, are thus venerated in the earthly court! O truly happy young virgin, to whom that heavenly bridegroom, smiling, spoke in Solomon’s wedding song:

“Come, my sister, into my garden,
that you may eat the fruit of my apples,
my bride, my dove, my undefiled one;
come from Lebanon, come,
you shall be crowned” (Song 4:16).

O happy virgin, I say, who, applauding with answering voice together with the choirs of virgins, deserved to respond to the bridegroom calling you:

“We shall run after you
in the fragrance of your perfumes” (Song 1:4),

that is, in the fragrance of your virtues.

**6.** The two military men who were present then performed solemn offerings. For they had earnestly requested that they be permitted to be present at the transfer and to see the holy bones with their own eyes.

One of them, named Godefrid the Elder, presented the holy virgin with a most fitting mantle as a gift. The other, named Rotbert and surnamed Anguillula, offered himself as a servant out of devotion by means of a deerskin thong [Note: Cangius properly distinguishes the various kinds of servitude in his *Glossary*, where the pious vows of nobles are praised. You will find instruments of conveyance frequently noted both in that work and in our treatise *On Diplomatic Practice*.], and, in the performance of his servitude, transferred by right of estate a garden in the village called Marceia.

The brothers, however, performed not earthly but divine services, sufficiently suitable, as was proper, to the veneration being shown.

At last, having carefully and skillfully closed the honored workshop, they emerged from the crypt with candles, censers, and crosses. The monks were dressed in white linen garments, that is, in white robes, and carried the bier according to the custom of the fathers, with hearts exceedingly joyful.

**7.** But the basilica was not large enough to receive the multitude of the assembled people. Indeed, the church was so full of the abundant gathering of both sexes, who had come to await the sanctity whose gifts they had come to see, that even those carrying the pledge of devotion could not leave through the little doors by which they had entered.

After conferring among themselves, therefore, they carried the shrine of veneration through a door arranged in the side of the crypt, a passageway for those going toward the chapel of Saint Nicholas, bishop and confessor of marvelous sanctity. They brought it out through a small cloister and then, by a little rear door made in the wall of that cloister, carried it out through the orchard and the brothers’ cemetery to another entrance, without the people’s knowledge.

But again, because the forecourt before the church doors was overflowing with country people, they scarcely managed, after great struggle, to draw it out through the gate beside the chapel of the holy archangel Michael.

Finally, after expending much and strenuous labor, and already exhausted, they carried it to a cultivated field lying near the monks’ hospice. There, by a certain providence, a wooden table had been spread out, and they hastened to place and set the holy treasure upon it, though with the reverence that was due, so that it could be approached and venerated without difficulty by all the waiting—and also longing—multitude.

For such a large crowd had sprung up that not even the capacity of the entire village was sufficient to contain it. People wandered uncertainly through the surrounding fields, not knowing by what means, in what manner, or from which side they might reach the church.

When the day had already begun to decline toward evening and the sun had grown mild after the heat of midday, the Fathers and brothers once more took up the candle-bearing poles and crosses. Dressed in white garments as before, they hastened to revisit the glorious shrine.

At the beginning they had returned because necessity compelled them to do so, leaving only a very few people there to watch over the bier and receive the blessings and offerings, since the crowd was causing great difficulty and inconvenience.

Taking up the precious bier with care, while the people were still pressing forward in fulfillment of their vows, they returned the holy relics to the holy Church of God with due honor and a hymn-filled procession, accompanied by a considerable crowd. They enthroned them within the sacred enclosure behind the altar of Saint Hunegundis, inside the pyramid which we call an oratory, arranging them with fitting service, in honor of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the coeternal Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages.

**In the Year of Our Lord 983. Ethelwold, Bishop of Winchester.**

[Col. 0077]

# HISTORICAL NOTICE ON ETHELWOLD

*(In Oudin, Ecclesiastical Writers, vol. II, p. 469.)*

[Col. 0077A] Saint Ethelwold, bishop of Winchester, an Englishman by nation and a native of Ventus or Winchester, is called by the *Chronicle* of John Bromton, abbot of Jervaulx, “Father of the monks” and “the star of the English,” col. 877.

This man was born at Winchester. He was educated and clothed in the monastic cowl at Glastonbury under Saint Dunstan; in the time of King Eadred, around the year 950, he became abbot of Abingdon; and then, in the time of King Edgar, in the year 961, he was elected bishop of Winchester.

For, as the *History of Ramsey*, chapter 13, says:

“At the same time in which Saint Dunstan was raised to the see of Canterbury”—that is, in the year 961—“at that same time also, by the will of the Lord, a man of marvelous sanctity, Ethelwold, abbot of Abingdon and disciple of Saint Dunstan, attained the dignity of that same see after Brithelm, bishop of Winchester, had been removed from human affairs.”

According to Symeon of Durham in his *Chronicle*, however, he became bishop in the year 963. He removed the clerics from that see because of the marriages to which they were rushing indiscriminately and substituted monks there by order of King Edgar.

The abbot of Jervaulx thus briefly summarizes his life at the place cited:

“He became bishop of Winchester, where he established a monastery of nuns and transferred the body of Saint Swithun. This man, therefore, having been made bishop of Winchester from a monk, used bread and water because of the lavish banquets then being displayed in England since the arrival of the Danes. He was devoted in all things to blessed Mary and Saint Cuthbert. After his death, no one could occupy his seat by sleeping there with impunity without springing back from dreadful visions, which reproached him for unworthily usurping the bishop’s seat.

“Once, when an anxious quarrel had arisen between that bishop and Earl Godwin, and they could not be reconciled on the day appointed for this purpose, the angry bishop, as he withdrew, said: ‘By my lady Mary, it will go badly with you.’ From that hour Godwin did not cease to suffer torture in his intestines until he received the bishop’s blessing.

“At last this man went to Durham, where, in an act that seemed very bold, he removed the lid of the tomb and spoke with Saint Cuthbert as with a friend. There he placed a gift of love and died, in the year of the Lord 984, the twenty-fourth year of his episcopate and the third of King Ethelred’s reign, having obtained the vision of the Lord which he had always desired.

“Saint Elphegus, then abbot of Bath, succeeded this Ethelwold.”

In manuscript codex 5164 of the Bodleian Library, among the manuscript codices of Francis Junius, codex 52, no. 2, there is:

“Ethelwold, bishop of Winchester, *On the Daily Custom of the Monks of the Order of Saint Benedict*, in Saxon, from a codex of the Cotton Library under the mark Tiberius A, 3.”

Likewise, among the manuscript codices of the University of Cambridge, no. 2427, there is in the public library at Cambridge, among the manuscript codices which Matthew Parker, archbishop of Canterbury, bequeathed to that library, codex 247, no. 8:

“Ethelwold, *On the Abbots of Lindisfarne*.
9. *On the Kings, Kingdoms, and Bishoprics of All England*.
10. *On the Time of the British Kings*.”

Because of these little works, Gerard John Vossius included this Ethelwold among the Latin historians, book II, chapter 41, p. 354 in my edition.

But those works do not concern that Ethelwold, the bishop of Winchester, who could never have written about the abbots of Lindisfarne, but rather correctly about the abbots of Glastonbury or Abingdon, where he had been abbot.

It is therefore correctly entitled, among the manuscript codices of the cathedrals and other celebrated libraries of England, codex 6115, and among the manuscript codices of Thomas Gale, codex 281:

“Ethelwold of Lindisfarne, *On the Lives of the Abbots of Lindisfarne*.”

Likewise, there, codex 6183, codex 349 of the same Gale:

“Works of Ethelwold, the so-called book.”

But that work unquestionably concerns another Aethelwulf, more than two hundred years older than this man, who was called Bernician and was famous around the year 750. He dedicated his work *On the Abbots of Lindisfarne and Illustrious Men* to his lord Egbert, archbishop of York, in the preface preserved in an old codex of the Bodleian Library, in the Bodleian manuscripts, letter B, 4, codex 10:

“To the most excellent and dearest of friends, the great priest Egbert, Aedilwulf, a presbyter by merit, sends the greeting of intimate charity.”

Gerard John Vossius made this error in book II, chapter 41 of *On Latin Historians*, although in chapter 29 of the same book he correctly attributes that work to Ethelwulf the Bernician, whom he says was famous in the year 750.

As far as I know, therefore, Ethelwold, bishop of Winchester, wrote nothing historical. But *On the Custom of the Monks*, by Aethelvold in Saxon, exists as a manuscript in the Cotton Library under the mark Tiberius A, codex 3, p. 171. It is an ancient and excellent-quality codex written by different hands before the occupation of England, containing images of Saint Benedict, King Eadgar, and Saint Scholastica.

Likewise, among the manuscript codices of Corpus Christi College, Cambridge, marked S, 6, at the end of the codex after page 263, there is the *Rule of Saint Benedict* in Latin and Saxon, by the author Aethelwulf.

Because of his translation into Saxon, as the *History of Ely* relates, King Eadgar and Alfreth or Aelfred permanently granted Saint Ethelwold the estate of Suthburn, together with its charter.

Concerning his work against the marriages of presbyters, see Vincent of Beauvais, *Speculum Historiale*, book XXIV, chapter 83; Antoninus, archbishop of Florence, *Summa Historialis*, part II, title 16, chapter 6, § 4.

John Leland discusses Ethelwold in the *Collectanea*, volume IV, no. 90, p. 127, preserved among the manuscript codices of the Bodleian Library in England, codex 5105; Gerard John Vossius, *On Latin Historians*, book II, chapter 41, p. 354 in my edition; and Humphrey Wanley, *Catalogue of Anglo-Saxon Manuscript Codices Found in the Libraries of England*, published at Oxford in folio in 1706, pp. 122 and 199.

[Col. 0079]

# LIFE OF SAINT ETHELWOLD, BISHOP OF WINCHESTER

**By WOLSTAN, a monk and his disciple, as it seems.**

*(In Mabillon, Acts of the Benedictine Saints, Fifth Century, p. 606.)*

# PRELIMINARY OBSERVATIONS

[Col. 0079A] **1.** The fact that the English Church in the tenth century attempted to restore the ancient discipline of ecclesiastical and monastic affairs is due above all to the piety and zeal of three distinguished bishops: Ethelwold, Oswald, and Dunstan. With the primary cooperation of King Eadgar, they removed abuses introduced into the Church and recalled monks of stricter life to their former seats.

“While these three men were active, as it were with a threefold light brightening the Church, the dense darkness of vices” vanished, says William of Malmesbury in book II, chapter 8 of *On the Kings*.

Many authors celebrated Ethelwold, also called Athelwold. The first seems to have been Alfric of Abingdon, who, in the twentieth year after Ethelwold’s death, briefly committed his deeds to writing. We found his work in a manuscript codex from Fécamp.

Immediately after him, another anonymous writer did the same; he is the author whom we publish here. His date is understood from the prologue and chapter 39. For he testifies that he is reporting what he himself saw as a contemporary and what he learned from the reliable account of elders.

This writing, without the author’s name, is preserved in the codex of Utica, or of Saint Evroul, written in that period. But its author seems to me to be none other than Wolstan, a monk of Winchester, about whom William of Malmesbury says the following in book II, chapter 8 of *On the Kings of the English*, where he is discussing Ethelwold:

“A certain Wlstan, a cantor of Winchester—his disciple and fosterling, that is—composed his Life in a modest style.”

The following considerations, among others, lead me to think that this is Wolstan’s work: its date agrees perfectly, and so does the author’s poetic genius, since he inserted several verses into this Life. Moreover, some things reported by William in book II of *On the Bishops of the English*, where he discusses Ethelwold, were not taken from Alfric—for Alfric omitted them, and I do not know whether William knew him as the first author of the Life of Saint Ethelwold—but from our author, undoubtedly Wolstan, whom he alone praises as the writer of Saint Ethelwold’s Life.

Furthermore, we have preferred Wolstan to Alfric because this author reports exactly the same things, often in the very same words, while adding certain details absent from Alfric and reported, as I have said, by William. We shall note this in its proper place.

It is useful to quote Alfric’s prologue here:

“Alfric, abbot and fosterling of Winchester, sends greetings in Christ to the honorable bishop Kenulf and the brothers of Winchester.

“Since I finally consider it fitting to entrust to memory something about the deeds of our father and magnificent teacher Athelwold, namely, twenty years having passed after his departure, I insert into this writing a brief and rustic account of what I learned from you or elsewhere from faithful people, lest, through lack of writers, these things should perhaps be handed over entirely to oblivion. Farewell.”

Pitseus praises Alfric, or Elfric, under the year 1016, where he says that he was first promoted to the bishopric of Wilton and later to the metropolitan see of Canterbury.

It is enough to mention the other authors who wrote about Ethelwold: Roger of Hoveden, Henry of Huntingdon, Matthew of Westminster, John Bromton, Harpsfield, and Thomas Mayhew. To these may be added the authors who wrote the deeds of Saints Oswald and Dunstan.

Bromton is mistaken in these matters, confusing the deeds of Ethelwolf with those of Alfwolf, bishop of Sherborne.

[Col. 0080A] **2.** What Ethelwold accomplished for monastic affairs is demonstrated by the monastery of Abingdon and especially by the two monasteries of Winchester, the old and the new. In one of these monks replaced expelled clerics; in the other they were established. This is related at greater length not only in the following Life but also in the acts of Oswald and Dunstan, in William of Malmesbury, in the *Anglican Monastic History*, and elsewhere.

William of Malmesbury should be heard on this subject, in book II, chapter 8 of *On the Kings of the English*:

“How effective was the holiness and goodness of his disciples”—namely, Dunstan—“is shown by Athelwold, a monk of Glastonbury, abbot of Abingdon, and thereafter bishop of Winchester, who established so many and such great monasteries that it now scarcely seems believable that a bishop of one city could have done what scarcely the king of all England could do.

“If I am mistaken, and sin through a hasty judgment, let what I say be openly disproved. How small are the monasteries of Ely, Peterborough, and Thorney, which he raised from their foundations and completed through his industry? Though they are continually harassed by the wickedness of tax collectors, they are nevertheless sufficient for their inhabitants.”

After praising Wolstan, the author of his Life, and then Oswald, who placed monks at Worcester in place of clerics, William adds:

“Previously, by royal command, Bishop Ethelwold had expelled the clerics from Winchester. When the king gave them the choice either to live according to the rule or to withdraw from the place, they had preferred a softer life.”

Orderic Vitalis supports William in book IV of his *History*, p. 517, where he says:

“Then the monastery of Medeshamstede, which Bishop Sexwulf had formerly built in the time of Wulfhere, king of the Mercians, Bishop Adelwold, under King Edgar, restored in the village called Peterborough and enriched at great expense the basilica erected in honor of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles.

“Afterward, the monastery of Thorney, that of Ely, and many others were built in various places; and communities of monks, clerics, or nuns were carefully established in them. An abundance of revenues was generously distributed to each monastery, from which sufficient food and clothing were provided for those devoted to the contemplative life, lest, weakened by lack of necessities, they should in any way falter in divine worship.

“Thus the monastic order was renewed in England,” and so forth.

What Ethelwold did in the old and new monasteries of Winchester was celebrated in verse by the aforementioned Wolstan in his letter to Elphegus, bishop of Winchester, prefixed to two metrical books written by Wolstan *On the Life and Miracles of Saint Swithun*, likewise bishop of Winchester.

We shall present this letter after this Life.

William does not praise this poem in the passage cited above. Besides the book on the Life of Ethelwold, he attributes another work, *On the Harmony of Tones*, to him in these words:

“He also produced another work, *On the Harmony of Tones*, very useful and an indication of an educated Englishman, a man of good life and polished eloquence.”

He seems to have neglected that eloquence in the *Life of Saint Ethelwold*, which is in fact written in a modest style.

Concerning the new monastery, read what we said above in the *Eulogy of Saint Grimbald*.

[Col. 0081A] **3.** William writes beautifully about the monastery of Thorney, cultivated by Ethelwold, at the end of book IV of *On the Bishops of the English*:

“A vast solitude was given to the monks for rest, so that they might cling more tenaciously to heavenly things the more strictly they observed mortal ones. If a woman is seen there, she is regarded as a monster; when men arrive, they are applauded as though they were angels. Moreover, no one remains there except momentarily.”

From the beginning of his episcopate, Ethelwold “began to practice an eremitical life there and, as he was able, tasted the first fruits of the future rest for forty days in the most remote church, which he himself had built, devoting himself there alone to God.

“For this reason he gathered there not so much land as elsewhere, but only as much as would be sufficient for himself and twelve monks. He brought there so many bodies of saints who had formerly dwelt in that wilderness, and of others from throughout England, that almost every corner of the church is filled.”

Passing over the others because of the harshness of their names, William mentions one Benedict, abbot of Wearmouth, the fosterer of the venerable Bede. Of him he says:

“Ethelwold purchased Benedict’s body at great price, brought it to Thorney, and introduced a light-giving radiance among the more obscure saints.”
