The island of Thorney, called Thornig here in chapter 24, lies near the city of Ely in the county of Cambridge. On this subject read the *Anglican Monastic History*, p. 242 onward, where it is said on p. 243 that the northern part of the church was dedicated to Saint Benedict.

**4.** From the time of his death, the English Church celebrated Ethelwold’s memory in sacred matters, as is especially attested by the Mass published here, in the form in which it is found in a very ancient manuscript codex from Utica.

Alfric assigns the day of his death to the third day before the Kalends of August—that is, 30 July—if our copy is not misleading; Wolstan and others after him assign it to the Kalends themselves, 1 August. For this is read not only in chapter 41 but also in the very title of his Life, which we shall soon reproduce.

**5.** Pitseus, in his book *On the Illustrious Writers of England*, commends our Ethelwold and attributes several little works to him, namely:

*On His Authority over Presbyters*, addressed to Pope John XIV, book I;

*Against Fornicating Presbyters and Their Concubines*, book I;

*On the Abbots of Lindisfarne*, book I;

*On the Kings, Kingdoms, and Bishoprics of All England*, book I;

*On the Time of the British Kings*, book I;

*On His Visitations*, book I;

*On the Planets and the Climates of the World*, book I;

and many others.

But it is not easy to determine whether these works are truly his, or which of them are, since the works themselves are not readily available.

Nevertheless, I would not doubt that the book *On the Abbots of Lindisfarne* is none other than the poem by Ethelwulf, a monk of Lindisfarne, on this subject, which we published in the preceding volume.

Pitseus adds that the book *On Visitations* is the work of Ethelwold, a monk of Winchester. The rest also seem foreign to him, perhaps with the exception of the first two.

# LIFE OF SAINT ETHELWOLD

[Col. 0081]

# HERE BEGINS THE PREFACE

**On the life of the glorious Father Athelwold, bishop, whose sacred memory is celebrated on the Kalends of August, the day on which he departed to the heavenly kingdoms.**

[Col. 0081C] After Christ, the Savior of the world, appeared incarnate to the human race through the court of the virginal womb, and, having completed the ineffable dispensation of his mercy and our salvation, returned in triumphal glory to the seat of the Father’s majesty, he spread throughout the whole world many lights of apostolic teachers.

Filled with the illumination of evangelical faith, these teachers drove the blind darkness of ignorance from human hearts; they inflamed the minds of believers with the fire of heavenly love; and, removing the prolonged hunger of enduring poverty, they satisfied the crowds of peoples with the banquets of eternal life.

From their fellowship the blessed Father and chosen pontiff of God, Adelwoldus, appeared in his own times, flashing like the morning star among the stars. Founder of many monasteries and instructor in ecclesiastical doctrines, he alone shone with singular brilliance among all the bishops of the English.

For those who desire to know about his birth, deeds, and death, we have judged it fitting to relate certain things. And lest the memory of so great a Father be handed over entirely to oblivion, we have briefly sketched in these pages what we ourselves saw as contemporaries and what we learned from the faithful account of elders.

Trusting in his holy intercessions, we have done this believing that it will benefit both us who have written and those who will read or hear it.

# HERE BEGIN THE CHAPTERS OF THE FOLLOWING LITTLE BOOK

[Col. 0081]

[Col. 0081D] I. On the origin and times of the blessed Bishop Adelwold. II. On the visions seen in dreams by his mother. III. On the interpretation of those same dreams. IV. How his mother perceived that the soul of the child yet to be born had come and entered into him. V. How the child, once born and reborn in Christ, was suddenly found one day in the church with his nurse. VI. How earnestly and diligently, already in childhood, he devoted his mind to the sacred studies of letters. VII. How the adolescent Adelwold became known to King Adelstan and attained the clerical office and priesthood. [Col. 0082D] VIII. On the prophecy that Saint Aelfegus, Bishop of Winchester, foretold concerning three priests. IX. How Adelwold reached Glastonbury, became a monk, and lived there. X. On the death of King Adelstan and the succession of his brothers to the kingship of the English people. XI. How, with King Eadred’s favor, the holy man took charge of the monastery at Abbandun and was appointed abbot of that place. XII. That King Eadred came to the monastery and the drink could not be exhausted, though the guests feasted all day. XIII. That, during the reign of Eadgar, the temple of the aforesaid monastery was built and dedicated. XIV. On the ordination of Dunstan, and on Abbot Adelwold’s sending the monk Osgar overseas; and on a certain brother, Aelstan, a simple man of great obedience. XV. How the ancient enemy attempted to destroy the holy man through the fall of a certain post. [Col. 0083B] XVI. That King Eadgar chose the holy man for the bishopric of the Church of Winchester. XVII. On the Communion chant sung by the clerics, when the monks coming from Abbandun stood at the church entrance. XVIII. On the expulsion of the clerics from the old monastery. XIX. How the holy man drank poison and, inflamed by the warmth of faith, extinguished the deadly drink. XX. On the expulsion of the clerics from the new monastery. XXI. That at Abbandun he appointed Osgar abbot. XXII. That he appointed nuns in the monasteries of women. XXIII. How, in the province of the East Angles, he established the monastery at Ely with monks living according to the rule. XXIV. That in the province of the Girvii as well he assigned two monasteries—Burgh and Thornig—to monks in the same manner. [Col. 0083C] XXV. On the holy man’s intimacy with King Eadgar. XXVI. On the revelation of the holy bishop Swithun, whom the holy Father Adelwold translated with every honor on the day of the Ides of July and then placed in the church. XXVII. That many other monasteries of monks and nuns were built and established throughout the English people through Dunstan and Adelwold. [Col. 0084A] XXVIII. How Saint Adelwold tempered the severity of discipline with the charm of gentleness. XXIX. How, in a time of famine, he rescued a multitude of poor people from the very jaws of death. XXX. That amid these events the holy man often suffered illnesses of the bowels and swelling of the legs. XXXI. That he always found it sweet to teach the young. XXXII. On the almost empty flask of chrism that was found full of oil during a journey. XXXIII. On the monk who committed a theft, and what he suffered from a single word of the man of God. XXXIV. On the monk who fell from the highest summit of the temple and, suffering no harm, rose unharmed. XXXV. On the monk who presumed to imitate the man of God in reading, and what he suffered. XXXVI. On the candle that, while the bishop slept, lay burning upon a leaf of a book, yet did not damage the page at all. [Col. 0084B] XXXVII. That not all the works of virtue performed by the holy man can be explained. XXXVIII. On a vision of the man of God in which a certain enormous ship appeared to him, full from bottom to top with fish and eels, who, when awakened, became human beings and were restored to their former reason. XL. On the new dedication of the old church, which took place on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of November. XLI. On the death of the holy Father on the Kalends of August, and his burial on the third day before the Nones of that same month. XLII. How, before he was raised from the tomb, the holy man revealed himself to a certain townsman named Ethelmo, afflicted with extensive blindness. XLIII. On the translation of the holy man, which took place on the fourth day before the Ides of September, and on the miracles performed at his tomb. [Col. 0084C] XLIV. On the sick girl who recovered her health there. XLV. On the blind boy who was himself enlightened there also. XLVI. On a certain bound thief, stretched out in the stocks, who was released by a single word of the man of God.

# THE LIFE OF SAINT ADELWOLD, BISHOP AND CONFESSOR OF WINCHESTER, BEGINS

[Col. 0083]

[Col. 0083D] CHAPTER I.—The parents of the holy bishop Adelwold were descended from a noble Christian lineage. They were townsmen of Winchester and flourished in the time of the elder King Eadward of the English, walking faithfully and blamelessly in the commandments and ordinances of the Lord. While they prospered daily in the increase of good works, they were adorned with an exceptional gift from God: they were deemed worthy to beget such offspring that, through his instruction and example, not only the people of the present age but also those of the future might come to know the true light, so that, stripped of the darkness of error, they might enjoy the glory of eternal brightness.

CHAPTER II.—Accordingly, while his fortunate mother was carrying him conceived in her womb, she saw in the dead of night a dream of this kind, which was a sure foretokening of what would come to pass. It seemed to her that she was sitting before the doors of her house and that a certain lofty standard stood before her eyes, whose summit appeared to touch heaven. Inclining itself honorably toward the earth, it surrounded the pregnant woman with the covering of its fringes; then, raised again to its great height and firm with unbending stability, it returned to the heaven from which it had inclined itself.

When the woman awoke, sleep again overcame her. And behold, suddenly she saw a golden eagle of astonishing size spring and fly from her mouth. As it flew over all the buildings of the city of Winchester, it cast the gilded pinions of its wings over them like a shadow, and, rising into the heights of heaven, disappeared.

When the woman awoke and, astonished, wondered to herself, silently turning the vision of her dream over in her mind, she could not herself guess its interpretation. She therefore went to a certain servant of Christ named Edeldrida, mature in character and age, who in the aforesaid city was nurse to virgins devoted to God. To her she related in order what had been shown to her in the nighttime vision. But Edeldrida, being exceedingly prudent and of a discerning mind—and at times, by the Lord’s revelation, knowing things to come—foretold many things concerning the child who was to be born, and the outcome of events showed these predictions to be true.

CHAPTER III.—We too may become interpreters of these same dreams, understanding in the lofty standard the holy man who was then carried in the womb and who would one day become the standard-bearer of God’s army—as indeed he did. We saw him engaging in many struggles against the ancient enemy in defense of holy Mother Church, and, while he fought—or rather, while God conquered through him, we saw the plots of the wicked reduced to nothing.

And because the eagle is so called from the sharpness of its eyes, and because, as sacred speech testifies, a desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise, the illustrious man is rightly represented by the golden eagle that was seen to overshadow the whole city with the shelter of its wings. Adorned with the treasure of all wisdom, he always flew through contemplation toward heavenly things, meditating upon divine matters with the keen and undazzled sight of his heart. Over the Church—the city of the great King—which hostile powers strove to attack, he spread far and wide the shelter of paternal protection. Having completed the course of the good contest, he reached the vision of God in the company of the saints, as the Lord’s voice says in the Gospel: “Wherever the body is, there the eagles will be gathered.”

For where our Redeemer is in bodily presence, there, without doubt, the souls of the elect are now gathered; and there too, in the glory of the future resurrection, their bodies will be gathered. We have said this briefly concerning the interpretation of the dreams; now let us return to the order of the narrative.

CHAPTER IV.—One day, while his mother was standing in the church surrounded by townspeople and wishing to attend the celebration of Holy Mass, she sensed that the soul of the child whom she carried in her womb had come and, by the will of God who governs all things, entered into him. The holy man himself, who was then to be born and later became a bishop, subsequently joyfully related this to us.

From this it is shown that he had been chosen by God even before he was born, and that the soul of a human being conceived does not, as some think, receive the beginning of its existence from father or mother, but—as is truly and without any doubt believed—is vivified with the living spirit by the Creator alone, and that this spirit is given individually to each person.

Thus the future bishop of God was born, and, reborn in Christ through the baptismal font, was named Adelwold by his parents. Confirmed by the anointing of sacred chrism, he was commended in all things to the grace of God.

CHAPTER V.—It happened on a certain feast day that, as his nurse had decided to go to the church as usual and devote herself to prayer, so violent a storm of driving rain broke out that she could not move her foot beyond the threshold of the place where she had been sitting, holding the infant in her lap.

As she wept most bitterly in sorrow because she could not fulfill her vow of pious devotion, she humbly bowed her head to pray to the Almighty Lord and immediately deserved to be consoled by divine mercy. For, feeling no hardship from the stormy weather, she was suddenly found sitting with the infant in the church she had intended to visit, where the priest was celebrating the solemn Masses.

She was profoundly terrified by what had happened, since she could not possibly have believed that such a thing could occur; and all who learned of the miracle were seized with great astonishment. Just as a prophet was once suddenly carried away from Judaea and set down in Chaldaea with his meal, so blessed young Adelwold was presented in the temple with his nurse in a moment, so that, just as that prophet at the proper time refreshed Daniel in the lions’ den, this child might one day feed thousands of peoples in the Church of the saints.

CHAPTER VI.—The boy of good character therefore grew through daily progress and was soon, in his very childhood, devoted to the sacred studies of letters. He who was to show others the way of salvation himself sat humbly with Mary at the Lord’s feet and listened profitably to the word from his mouth.

He was naturally active and sharp-witted, so that whatever he learned through the teaching of his elders he did not carelessly consign to oblivion but rather entrusted to a tenacious memory. He also strove to surpass the tender years of childhood in moral integrity and maturity of virtues, to dedicate all his limbs continually to divine service, and to direct the whole intention of his mind toward fulfilling God’s will. Thus, by living rightly according to Christ’s commands and gifts, he offered thanks, so that he might be found worthy to receive greater things.

CHAPTER VII.—When he reached the age of flourishing adolescence, the fame of his holy way of life was reported to King Adelstan, son of the aforesaid King Eadward. The king ordered that the young man be summoned without delay. When he had been brought and stood in the king’s presence, he found favor in the king’s sight and in the eyes of his nobles. Spending much time at the palace in the king’s constant company, he learned many useful and profitable things from the king’s wise men.

At last, by order of the king, he was first tonsured by Aelfegus, Bishop of Winchester, for the clerical office according to ecclesiastical custom; then, after a few years had passed, he was consecrated to the priestly rank.

CHAPTER VIII.—That Father Elfegus, of blessed memory, possessed the spirit of prophecy among the other gifts of spiritual graces bestowed upon him is shown by what happened. At that time he ordained Dunstan and Adelwold together, along with a certain man named Edelstan, who later abandoned the monastic habit and remained an apostate to the end.

After the celebration of Mass had been completed, the holy bishop Elfegus addressed those standing beside him: “Today, before God, I laid hands upon three men and consecrated them to the priestly order. Two of them will attain the episcopal summit: one first in the city of Worcester and then in Kent, which is the metropolitan church of the English people; the other will one day succeed me in the dignity of the episcopate; but the third, through the slippery allurements of pleasures, will waste away in a wretched end.”

Then Edelstan asked the holy bishop, his kinsman: “Will it happen that I shall be one of the two who are to be raised to the episcopal chair?” The bishop replied: “You will have neither part nor share in the order I have mentioned; nor will you remain in that holiness which you seemed, in the sight of men, to have begun.”

The outcome of events proved how truly the words of this prophecy had been spoken. For two of them—as Scripture says, “Let the righteous still be justified, and let the holy still be sanctified”—reached the honor of the episcopate. But the third, in accordance with the terrifying warning of the earlier sentence, which says, “Let the filthy still be filthy,” ended his life in the stench of lust.

CHAPTER IX.—Adelwold, the servant of Christ, benevolent in name, mind, and deed, walked by a straight path along the narrow way that leads to life. With God’s cooperation, he diligently strove to grow better day by day, devoting himself to the teachings and examples of Elfegus, his sponsor and ordainer.

By the king’s command he stayed with him for some time so that he might be more fully instructed. Later, reaching Glastonbury, he placed himself under the tutelage of the illustrious Dunstan, abbot of that monastery. Making great progress under his instruction, he eventually received the monastic habit from him and devoted himself humbly to his governance.

There he learned the liberal knowledge of the grammatical art and the honeyed sweetness of metrical composition. Like a most prudent bee, which by flying about seeks trees of good fragrance and settles upon herbs of pleasant taste, he gathered the flowers of the divine books. He also diligently read Catholic and distinguished authors, while persevering in vigils and prayers, subduing himself through abstinence, and continually exhorting the brothers to arduous endeavors.

Although he was loved by all because of the merit of his holiness and was appointed dean of the monastery by his abbot, he incurred no danger of pride. Rather, he offered those subject to him so great an example of humility that he labored daily with his hands, cultivating the garden, and prepared apples and various kinds of vegetables for the brothers’ meal. Thus, after providing spiritual nourishment for their souls, he also supplied what their bodies required, always keeping before his eyes the Lord’s saying: “Whoever wishes to become great among you shall be your servant; and whoever wishes to be first among you shall be your slave”; and also: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things, and you will find grace before God.”

Keeping these and other testimonies of Scripture in his memory, he guarded his subjects through discipline and himself through humility.

CHAPTER X.—Meanwhile it happened that the most victorious King Adelstan died in the fourth year after he had destroyed a hostile pagan army with a very great slaughter, and that his brother Eadmund assumed the governance of the kingdom in his place.

After six and a half years, when Eadmund had been cruelly killed, his brother Eadred succeeded him in the kingdom. Eadred was a particular lover and defender of the old monastery at Winchester, as is demonstrated by the ornaments made at his command: namely, a great golden cross, a golden altar, and other objects which, with generous hand, the benevolent king sent there in honor of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and ordered to be preserved there perpetually for the praise and glory of God. He also intended, if life should permit, to adorn the eastern portico of that Winchester church with gilded tiles.

During his reign, the man of God Adelwold, still desiring to be taught more fully in the knowledge of Scripture and more perfectly instructed in monastic religion, resolved to travel overseas. But the venerable Queen Eadgiw, mother of the aforementioned king, forestalled his efforts. She advised the king not to allow such a man to leave his kingdom, further asserting that there was in him so great a wisdom from God that it could suffice both for himself and for others, even though he did not travel for this reason to the borders of a foreign land.

CHAPTER XI.—Hearing this, the king was pleased and began to hold great affection for the servant of God. At his mother’s urging, he decided to give the holy man a certain place called Abbandun. It had once contained a small monastery, but at that time it was neglected and abandoned, consisting of poor buildings and possessing only forty hides. The remaining land of the aforesaid place, extending around it for a hundred “cassates” [cassati], was held by the king himself under royal ownership.

With the consent of Abbot Dunstan, it therefore came to pass, according to the king’s will, that the man of God Adelwold undertook the care of the aforesaid place, so that he might establish monks there serving God according to the rule.

> **[Note: [Col. 0087D]]** This Abbot of Abbandun subscribed, by Eadred’s privilege, for the monastery of Crowland in the year 948, in Ingulf. Yet in volume I, page 16, column 1, of the *Monasticon Anglicanum*, he is said to have been appointed abbot of Abbandun in 954; should 944 be read? Ethelwold is said by Harsfeld, *Saeculum X*, chapter 9, to have summoned from the monastery of Corbie in Gaul men exceptionally skilled in monastic discipline; see volume I, page 97, of the *Monasticon*.

The servant of God came to the place entrusted to him. Certain clerics from Glastonbury immediately followed him—namely, Osgar, Foldbirht, Friwegar, and Ordbirth from Winchester, and Eadric from London—submitting themselves to his tutelage.

Within a short time he gathered around himself a flock of monks, and by the king’s command he was appointed their abbot. The king also gave the abbot and the brothers the royal property he had possessed at Abbandun—that is, a hundred hides with excellent buildings—to increase their daily sustenance, and helped them generously with money from his royal treasury. His mother, however, sent them even more lavish assistance in the form of gifts.

The Lord bestowed such grace upon those serving him that all riches seemed to flow together into the aforesaid monastery, which had previously been extremely poor in resources. Everything proceeded with such prosperous success that the fulfillment of the Lord’s promise appeared openly manifest, the promise that says: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you.”

CHAPTER XII.—One day the king came to the monastery to supervise the construction of the buildings himself. He measured all the foundations of the monastery with his own hand, according to how he intended to raise the walls. The abbot then asked him to dine with his companions in the guesthouse.

The king immediately agreed. It happened that a considerable number of his nobles from the people of Northumbria were present, and they all went with the king to the feast. The king rejoiced and ordered abundant mead [or *medon*] to be poured for the guests. The doors were carefully closed, so that no one might appear to abandon the royal banquet by fleeing from the drinking.

What more need be said? The attendants drew drink throughout the entire day, to the full satisfaction of the feasters; yet the liquor could not be exhausted from the vessel except by a palm’s measure, while the Northumbrians, in their drunken fashion, departed joyfully in the evening.

CHAPTER XIII.—Nevertheless, Abbot Adelwold did not begin to build the work assigned to him during the days of King Eadred, because that king quickly departed this life on the ninth day before the Kalends of December.

But during the reign of the glorious King Eadgar, distinguished, most merciful, exceedingly powerful, and unconquered, son of King Eadmund, he built and completed on the same site an honored temple in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God and ever-virgin. To this day it is better displayed to the eye than described in words.

CHAPTER XIV.—About this time Dunstan was chosen for the bishopric of the Church of Worcester, in accordance with the prophecy of Saint Bishop Elfegus, as we mentioned above. After the passage of several years he became archbishop and remained in Kent for thirty-seven years, like an immovable column, outstanding in teaching and action, beautiful with an angelic countenance, and eminent in almsgiving and prophecy. We have heard that heavenly miracles often occurred at his tomb.

Adelwold, however, sent the monk Osgar overseas to the monastery of Saint Benedict at Fleury, so that he might learn there the customs of regular observance and teach them to the brothers at home. In this way, by following the norm of monastic religion and avoiding every deviation together with those subject to him, he might lead the flock entrusted to him to the promised homeland of the heavenly kingdom.

In that community there was a certain brother named Elfstan, a simple man of great obedience. The abbot ordered him to oversee food for the monastery’s workmen. Devoting himself most earnestly to this service, he cooked meat every day and diligently served the laborers, lighting the fire, bringing water, and voluntarily cleaning the vessels again, while the abbot assumed that he performed these tasks with the comfort and assistance of another servant.

One day, as the abbot was making his customary rounds of the monastery, he saw the brother beside a boiling cauldron in which he was preparing food for the workmen. Upon entering, he found all the vessels perfectly clean and the floor swept. With a cheerful expression he said to him: “My brother Elfstan, you have stolen this obedience from me—the one you practice without my knowledge. But if you are such a soldier of Christ as you show yourself to be, put your hand into the boiling water and quickly draw out for me one piece from the bottom.”

Immediately, without delay, he put his hand to the bottom of the cauldron and pulled out a piece of meat, feeling none of the heat of the boiling water. When he saw this, the abbot ordered that the piece be put aside and that no living person be told of it.

We later saw that brother appointed abbot. He was subsequently raised to episcopal honor and placed over the Church of Wilton; he completed his life in the Lord with a blessed end.

> **[Note: [Col. 0089D]]** William of Malmesbury reports the same event in exactly the same words, and no more, in book II of *On the Bishops of the English*, chapter 4.

CHAPTER XV.—Saint Adelwold was a great builder of churches and various works, both while he was abbot and while he was bishop. Therefore the common adversary set his customary snares of wickedness for him, so that, if he could in any way, he might destroy him.

One day, while the man of God was laboring on a construction, an enormous post fell upon him, threw him into a certain pit, and broke almost all the ribs on one side of his body, so that, had the pit not received him, he would have been completely crushed.

CHAPTER XVI.—Nevertheless, by the assistance of the grace of Almighty God, the holy man recovered from this injury. The most fortunate Eadgar, basileus of the English, then chose him for the bishopric of the Church of Winchester, before the church of the aforesaid monastery had been dedicated.

At the king’s command, Dunstan, archbishop of the Church of Canterbury, consecrated it in the year 963 of the Lord’s Incarnation, on the third day before the Kalends of December, on the vigil of Saint Andrew the Apostle, which at that time was observed on the First Sunday of Advent of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.

At that time, in the old monastery where the episcopal chair is located, there were canons entangled in the abominable practices of their crimes, overcome by pride, insolence, and luxury. Some of them even disdained to celebrate Mass in its proper order, repudiating wives whom they had illicitly taken and taking others instead; they were continually devoted to gluttony and drunkenness.

The holy man Adelwold could by no means endure this. Having received permission from King Eadgar, he immediately expelled the detestable blasphemers of God from the monastery. Bringing monks from Abbandun, he installed them there, and he himself became both their abbot and bishop.

CHAPTER XVII.—It happened on a Saturday at the beginning of Lent—

> **[Note: [Col. 0090D]]** You see that even then the beginning of Lent was reckoned from the First Sunday of Lent, on which this antiphon is sung at the Communion of the Mass.

—that the monks coming from Abbandun stood at the entrance of the church while the clerics were finishing Mass by singing the Communion:

“Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice in him with trembling; embrace discipline, lest you perish from the righteous way.”

They seemed to be saying: “We were unwilling to serve God or keep his discipline; you, at least, do so, lest, like us, you perish from the way that opens the heavenly kingdoms to those who guard righteousness.”

When the brothers heard this, they rejoiced, understanding that their journey had been made prosperous by the Lord and that, by God’s will, this psalm had been sung because of their presence. At once they applied to themselves the command of David, Osgar exhorting them and saying: “Why are we delaying outside? Let us do as the canons exhort us: let us enter, and, walking along the way of righteousness, let us serve the Lord our God with fear and rejoicing, so that when his anger soon burns forth, we may deserve to share the lot of those of whom it is added: ‘Blessed are all who trust in him.’”

[Col. 0091B] CHAPTER XVIII.—The king also sent there with the bishop one of his most renowned servants, named Vulfstan Aetdelham.

> **[Note: [Col. 0091D]]** Aelfric has: “The king also sent one of his most renowned servants, named Wolfstan, with the bishop, by royal authority,” and so forth.

By royal authority he ordered the canons to choose one of two alternatives: either to give place to the monks without delay or to assume the habit of the monastic order.

But they, overcome by excessive fear and detesting the monastic life, immediately departed when the monks entered. Later, however, three of them came to conversion: namely, Eadsin, Vulsin, and the priest Wilstan. Returning with humble hearts to the monastery they had left when expelled, they submitted their necks to the yoke of Christ.

For up to that time there were no monks in the English people, except those who lived at Glastonbury and Abbandun.

> **[Note: [Col. 0091D]]** Spelman, in volume I of the *Councils*, page 434, where he relates similar events, interprets this as referring to regular monks, not to secular monks or those of a looser way of life. It is clear that such men existed in other places and were regarded as secular canons, as we have observed elsewhere concerning the Gallican clergy in the monastery of Saint-Denis and the monastery of Saint Martin.

[Col. 0091C] CHAPTER XIX.—After the aforesaid brothers had begun to observe the rule of regular life in the old monastery, and many elderly men converted to the service of God, young men were brought, and little children were offered and came together there, the clerics, out of envy, arranged for the bishop to drink poison while dining in his hall with guests and showing them every courtesy. Their aim was that, once he had been killed, they might expel the servants of God and, gathering together again, freely enjoy their former vices.

It was his custom to drink a little immediately after three or four mouthfuls. Unwittingly, he therefore drank all the poison that had been brought to him in the cup. At once his face changed color and became pale, while his inward organs were tormented by the excessive force of the spreading poison.

He scarcely rose from the table and went out to his bed. The poison spread through all his limbs, threatening him with imminent death. At last, reflecting, he began to reproach himself and said to his soul: “Where is your faith now? Where are the thoughts of your understanding? Are not Christ’s words true and trustworthy, by which he promises in the Gospel, saying: ‘If believers drink anything deadly, it will not harm them’? Is not he who speaks these words present in divinity, even if absent in body? He himself, without doubt—he himself—can empty this poison’s venom from you, he who can always do all things.”

His faith, kindled by these and similar words, extinguished the entire deadly draught that he had drunk. When the pain of the raging poison had been driven away, he rose and went back to the hall with a cheerful face, showing those who looked at him no sign at all of pallor. He inflicted no harm on his poisoner but forgave him the offense he had committed.

Thus, by God’s power, the wicked plan of the clerics was dispersed. When they saw that their evil had accomplished nothing, they scattered for so long through the various provinces of the English people, here and there, until they ended their lives.

CHAPTER XX.—From that time Bishop Adelwold, the eagle of Christ, spread his golden wings. With King Eadgar’s approval, he expelled the canons from the New Monastery and introduced monks there who lived according to the rule.

He appointed his disciple Edelgar as their abbot. Edelgar later became bishop of the province of the South Saxons and, after Saint Dunstan had been translated to the heavenly kingdoms, became archbishop of Canterbury.

CHAPTER XXI.—At Abbandun, however, he appointed Osgar as abbot in his place. That place was enriched with six hundred hides and more and was further supported by privileges of perpetual freedom, written by both divine and royal authority. Sealed with golden plates, these privileges are preserved there to this day.

CHAPTER XXII.—In the third Winchester monastery also—

> **[Note: [Col. 0092D]]** The sacred body of Saint Eadburga, daughter of King Eadward, is said to rest there, according to volume I, page 32, of the *Monasticon Anglicanum*.

—which in English is called Nunnaminster, consecrated to God in honor of the ever-virgin Mary, he established communities [or “companies,” *mandrae*] of nuns. Over them he placed as mother Etheldrid, whom we mentioned briefly above. The rule of regular life is observed there to this day.

CHAPTER XXIII.—The holy bishop Adelwold took care to gather monks for the service of Almighty God not only within the borders of the West Saxons but also in the distant regions of Britain.

There is a famous region situated in the province of the East Angles, surrounded by marshes and waters in the manner of an island. From the abundance of eels caught in those same marshes, it received the name Ely. In that region there is a place worthy of every veneration, greatly distinguished by the relics and miracles of Saint Etheldrida, queen and perpetual virgin, and of her sisters.

At that time, however, the place was abandoned and assigned to the royal treasury. The servant of Christ therefore began to venerate this place most earnestly, out of love for so many virgins. Having paid a considerable sum of money, he bought it from King Eadgar and established there a substantial flock of monks.

He appointed his provost Brithnod as their abbot, most suitably renewed the site with monastic buildings, enriched it abundantly with landed possessions, confirmed it with the privilege of perpetual freedom, and commended it to Almighty God.

> **[Note: [Col. 0092D]]** We gave the acts of Saint Etheldrita in the second volume, under the year 679, where the monastery at Ely was discussed.

CHAPTER XXIV.—He also obtained from the king and the nobles of the land, for a price, another place in the region of the Girvii. It was situated on the bank of the river Nen, to which the English formerly gave the name Medeshamstede; it is now commonly called Burgh.

> **[Note: [Col. 0093D]]** Concerning this monastery in the territory of Huntingdon, read William of Malmesbury, book IV, *On the Bishops*, where he discusses the bishops of Dorchester, and the second Benedictine volume, page 756.

He consecrated the basilica of this place in honor of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, adorning it with suitable buildings and richly endowing it with the neighboring lands. There too he gathered together a company of monks in the same manner. He placed his monk Ealdulf over them as abbot.

> **[Note: [Col. 0093D]]** Concerning him, see the preliminary observations to the acts of Saint Oswald, bishop, below.

After the death of Lord Oswald, bishop of the Church of York, Ealdulf assumed the archbishopric.

He acquired for a price a third place as well, situated beside the bank of the aforesaid river. Because thorn thickets grew up all around it, it was commonly called Thornig in English. He assigned it to monks under the same conditions as the others. He also appointed Godemann as their ruler and abbot, dedicated the monastery he had built in honor of Mary, Mother of God and Virgin, and joyfully enriched it with possession of every good thing.

> **[Note: [Col. 0093D]]** The monastery at Thorney was discussed above in the preliminary observations.

CHAPTER XXV.—The man of God Adelwold was highly influential in the counsels of the illustrious King Eadgar, in word and deed. He dedicated churches in many places and preached the Gospel of Christ everywhere, in accordance with the exhortation of the prophet Isaiah, who says: “Cry out, do not cease; raise your voice like a trumpet, and announce to my people their crimes and to the house of Jacob their sins.”

CHAPTER XXVI.—His preaching was greatly aided by the holy bishop Suvithun, who at that same time was manifested by heavenly signs, then translated beneath the royal roof of the temple with the greatest glory and placed there with the utmost honor.

Thus two lights shone together in the house of God, set upon golden lampstands. For what Adelwold preached through the salutary exhortation of his words, Suvithun wonderfully adorned, for the praise of Christ’s name, through the glorious manifestation of his miracles.

[Col. 0093D] **CHAPTER XXVII.**—And so, with the king’s consent, it came about that, partly through Dunstan’s counsel and activity, and partly through Adelwold’s diligent cooperation, monasteries were established everywhere among the English people—some for monks, others for nuns—under abbots and abbesses living according to the rule. And Christ’s servant Adelwold went around each monastery, establishing its customs: exhorting the obedient with words so that they might advance in goodness, and sternly correcting the foolish with blows so that they might turn away from evil.

**CHAPTER XXVIII.**—For he was as terrifying as a lion to the disorderly and perverse; but to the humble and obedient he showed himself as gentle as a lamb, tempering the severity of serpent-like prudence in such a way that he did not lose the mildness of dove-like simplicity. Whenever zeal for righteousness compelled him to impose the laws of discipline upon his subjects, that anger proceeded not from cruelty but from love; and inwardly, with paternal affection, he loved those whom outwardly he chastised as though pursuing them.

He was the father and shepherd of the monks, the ever-watchful guardian of the nuns, and the protector of virgins; the consoler of widows, the receiver of pilgrims, the defender of churches, the corrector of those who wandered, the refresher of the poor, and the helper of the fatherless and orphans. In deed he accomplished more than our littleness can unfold in words.

[Note: [Col. 0093D] After this, Aelfric, omitting the following chapter, adds: “He was often ill in his bowels and legs, passing sleepless nights because of the pain; and during the day, although pale, he nevertheless walked as though he were well. Yet he made no use of the flesh of four-footed animals or birds except once,” and so forth, as below in chapter 30. But Willelmus of Malmesbury reports the substance of this chapter 29, and therefore used this author.]

**CHAPTER XXIX.**—For it happened at a certain time that a bitter famine pressed heavily upon the whole region of Britain, and the severity of the shortage destroyed many by a dreadful disaster. But the man of God, taking pity on the multitude perishing from severe hunger, spent all the money he possessed for the needs of the poor. When the money ran out, he ordered that every ornament and very many silver vessels be taken from the church’s treasures; and he commanded that they be broken into small pieces and converted into money.

With an inmost sigh of the heart he declared that he could not patiently endure lifeless metals remaining whole while a human being, created in the image of God and redeemed by the precious blood of Christ, perished through beggary and starvation. Thus, after purchasing food, he sustained an innumerable multitude of needy people who, wishing to escape the danger of famine, had fled to him from every direction. Those who lay half-dead in the streets and on the roads, deprived of every comfort, he revived and strengthened, snatching the wretched from the very jaws of death; and he provided daily provisions for each one, until God’s mercy looked down from heaven upon the earth and, coming to the aid of the human race with its customary kindness, lessened the evil of the scarcity.

In this work of compassion he followed the imitable example of blessed Laurence, deacon and martyr, who, when the time of persecution was approaching, dispersed the treasures and resources of the Church and gave them to the poor, “so that his righteousness might endure for ever and his horn be exalted in glory.”

**CHAPTER XXX.**—But because the Lord, as Scripture says, chastises the one whom he loves and scourges every son whom he receives, the man of God was frequently ill in his bowels and suffered a swelling disease in his legs. He usually passed sleepless nights because of the pain; and during the day, although pale, he nevertheless walked as though he were well and felt no discomfort, remembering the apostolic consolation which says, “Power is made perfect in weakness,” and again, “For when I am weak, then I am stronger and powerful,” and once more, “I will gladly glory in my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may dwell in me.”

And although he was afflicted by severe suffering, he nevertheless made no use of the flesh of four-footed animals or birds, except once, when compelled by a very serious illness lasting three months—and he did so at the command of Archbishop Dunstan—and again during the illness by which he died.

**CHAPTER XXXI.**—For it was sweet to him always to teach adolescents and young men, to explain Latin books to them in English, to teach them the rules of grammatical art and metrical composition, and to encourage them toward better things with pleasant conversation. Thus it came about that very many of his disciples became priests and abbots, and honorable bishops; some even became archbishops among the English people.

**CHAPTER XXXII.**—Meanwhile it pleased almighty God to show by a heavenly sign that it was pleasing to him for Adelwold to dwell in his holy place. For when the holy bishop was making a certain journey to sow the seed of God’s word in the Lord’s field, it happened [Note: [Col. 0095D] Aelfric says: “It once happened that a cleric of his, who had been assigned to carry his flask, took less oil, and so forth, which had not previously contained even half [of its contents].” It was once customary for bishops never to travel without chrism. The First Council of Orange, canon 2: “No minister who undertakes the office of baptizing may go anywhere without chrism.” See the preface to the First Century, no. 101.] that his cleric, to whom the holy chrism had been entrusted, took less oil than necessity required, and lost even that small amount during the journey.

When Christ’s servant reached the appointed place, after the celebration of Mass and after the sweet conversations of holy preaching, he ordered that oil be brought to him according to custom for confirming the children. But the cleric, who had thought that he was carrying the flask with him, suddenly realized that he had lost it. He therefore hurried back along the road by which he had come and, looking carefully here and there, found the flask of chrism lying on the road, full of oil, although a short while earlier only half of it had contained any liquid.

Taking it up, he returned with great fear and joy, presenting himself to the holy bishop and truthfully recounting the miracle of the heavenly outpouring. This is shown to have occurred by God’s will: he who was flooded with the grace of the Holy Spirit and by whose anointing gladdened the hearts and faces of many was himself rewarded not only inwardly but also outwardly with the oil of heavenly joy.

**CHAPTER XXXIII.**—[Note: [Col. 0096D] Aelfric: “A certain monk living under him, named Eadwinus, stole a certain man’s purse at demonic prompting,” etc.] A certain monk lived under his authority and, prompted by a demon, committed the crime of theft. Consequently great sorrow invaded the entire congregation, since each subordinate thought that another brother had done what he himself certainly knew he had not done. For this reason the holy bishop ordered a moderate correction to be announced in the assembly of the brothers: if anyone was conscious of that theft, he should return what he had taken as quickly as possible with God’s blessing, or throw it down in a place where it could be found.

But that brother hardened himself with an obstinate heart and neglected to obey the man of God’s command. After three days and three nights had passed, and the stolen object had still not been found, the holy man spoke in the chapter before the whole multitude of the brothers, saying with terrible indignation and threat:

“That sacrilegious man was unwilling to return the money he stole with a blessing, as we commanded. Let him now return it with the curse of almighty God, and by our authority let him be bound not only in soul but also in body. What more need be said?”

The brothers said, “Amen.”

And behold, as the monk sat there, he was invisibly bound, his arms clinging to one another beneath his cowl. He remained stupefied, wondering what he ought to do. All his other limbs remained mobile and fit for use, except his arms, which the holy man, by the authority granted him by God, bound and rendered useless.

At last, when the chapter was finished, the wretched man rose, still bound in this way. He went out after the holy bishop and secretly confessed to him that he was guilty and had committed the crime of theft, yet he said nothing about the binding by which he was held fast.

But the bishop, seeing that he was seized by immense terror—for it was his custom to forgive penitents and mourners mercifully and to sympathize with them from the depths of compassion—answered him in gentle speech:

“At least now you have done well, although late, by confessing your sin. Now have our blessing.”

Immediately his arms were released, without the bishop’s knowledge. The man went away exceedingly joyful and told a certain brother named Wlfgar [or Wlfaro], in due order, about his binding and release. Wlfgar advised him to keep the matter more carefully secret and to disclose it later at an appropriate time.

From this it may be understood what merit this man possessed before the Lord: by a mere word, though unaware of it, he displayed such power. Since he had faithfully and worthily guarded the pastoral care of holy governance in conduct and morals, he plainly obtained the authority of blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, to bind and loose.

**CHAPTER XXXIV.**—Therefore, when the man of God resolved with great effort to renew the old church, he ordered the brothers frequently to devote themselves to labor together with the craftsmen and workmen. As they labored zealously, the building gradually rose upward, supported here and there by numerous chapels in which the intercession of the saints is venerated and will benefit all who approach faithfully.

It happened one day, while the brothers were standing with the masons at the highest summit of the church, that one of them, named Godus, fell from the heights all the way to the ground. As soon as he touched the earth, he rose unharmed and stood, having suffered no injury from so great a fall. He blessed himself with the sign of the cross, wondering what he was doing there or how he had come there.

In the sight of all who were present, he climbed back to the place where he had previously stood; and, taking up his trowel, he applied himself even more diligently to the work he had begun. To whom, then, should this miracle be attributed except to the one at whose command he had gone forth to the work of obedience? He could not be injured because, in his fall, he carried the merit of the man of God, which protected him unharmed from the danger of the fall.

**CHAPTER XXXV.**—At a certain wintertime, when the brothers rose earlier for vigils in accordance with the command of the Rule (Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter II), and devoted the nighttime interval to psalmody and reading, a certain monk named Teodricus went to the man of God, wishing to inform him by signs about a certain matter. He found him holding a candle-holder in his hand and reading, sharpening his aged sight with the diligent movement of his eyelids.

Teodricus stood there for a long time, observing how intently he fixed his eyes upon the page. At last the holy man rose from his reading, and the brother, sitting down, took the candle and began to read, testing whether he too could sharpen his healthy eyes for reading as carefully as he had seen the bishop sharpen his failing eyes.

But this presumption did not go unpunished. On the following night, when he had given his limbs over to sleep, someone unknown in appearance appeared to him and said with a terrible threat:

“With what presumption did you dare to reproach the bishop in reading last night?”

When he trembled and denied having done this, the other looked at him with fierce eyes and said:

“You cannot deceive me and play with me as you imagine. But take this as the sign of your presumption.”

With these words he violently struck his eyes with his finger. Immediately severe pain followed in his eyes, afflicting him intensely for many days, until he wiped away by satisfaction the fault which he had carelessly committed against the holy man.

**CHAPTER XXXVI.**—It also happened that, while Christ’s servant was occupied with reading at night, he fell asleep because of excessive wakefulness, and the burning candle fell from the candle-holder onto the book in which he had been reading. It lay burning upon the page for a long time, until a certain brother named Leofredus arrived.

He quickly took the still-flaming candle from the book and looked closely. He saw the candle’s embers lying across many lines, and, blowing them away, found the page unharmed. In this event the merit of the holy man was revealed: the flame consumed the burning candle and lost so much of its force that it could not damage the page.

**CHAPTER XXXVII.**—By Christ’s generosity we have briefly related these things, so that we might arouse both present and future faithful people, with humble devotion, to love and reverence for so great a Father.

Moreover, it is not easy for us to explain how great or what kinds of dangers Saint Adelwold endured in defending the monks; how affectionately he loved zealous and obedient brothers; how much he labored in the construction of the monastery, repairing the church and building other houses; how watchful he was in prayer; how devotedly he urged the brothers toward the remedy of confession; or how many thousands of souls he withdrew from the devil and brought, restored to God, into heaven.

From these few examples, however, much can be understood that we are unable to recount.

[Note: [Col. 0097D] Willelmus of Malmesbury mentions this in Book II of *On the Bishops of the English*.]

**CHAPTER XXXVIII.**—For the dream that the glorious and angelic Dunstan, archbishop of the English people, had once said that he had seen concerning him had to be fulfilled.

When Dunstan was abbot of the monastery of Glastonbury and Adelwold, God’s servant, served under his governance, as we related above, he saw in a dream, outside the dormitory, what appeared to be a tree of extraordinary height. Its branches seemed to spread east and west, north and south, extending with vast length and breadth over the whole region of Britain.

The branches of this tree were laden with countless large and small cowls. At its highest summit the tree itself bore one enormous cowl, which, rising above the covering of its sleeves, protected the others; surpassing them all in immense height, it touched the sky.

The man of God, Dunstan, greatly astonished by such a vision, questioned a priest adorned with angelic white hair who had shown it to him:

“Please, venerable elder, what is this strong and lofty tree, whose branches, spread far and wide, are seen to support so innumerable a multitude of cowls?”

He replied:

“This tree which you see, Abbot Dunstan, signifies the position of this island. The great cowl raised at the top of this tree is that of your monk Adelwold, who serves Christ devoutly in this monastery. The other cowls with which these branches appear to be laden signify the multitude of monks who are to be instructed by his teaching and gathered from every direction in this region for the service of almighty God. Under his leadership they will reach the glory of the heavenly kingdom and the fellowship of the blessed spirits who reign with Christ.”

Having received this answer, the holy man awoke. He silently pondered the vision within himself and later disclosed it to the faithful in a faithful account. As time passed, it became known to many through widespread report, and at last it reached even the knowledge of our littleness.

[Note: [Col. 0097D] Aelfric, omitting the rest, briefly records the saint’s death as follows: “He died in the twenty-second year of his episcopate, on the third day before the Kalends of August, while Aelred was reigning as king of the English, and he was buried in the church of the blessed Peter and Paul,” and so forth.]

**CHAPTER XXXIX.**—Another dream also had to be fulfilled, which Saint Adelwold himself once related to us concerning himself, saying:

“I thought I was standing beside the seashore, where I saw what appeared to be a very large ship, in which a great multitude of fish, especially eels, was enclosed from bottom to top. As I silently considered what this dream that I was seeing might mean, suddenly I heard a voice calling me by name and saying to me:

‘Adelwold, Adelwold, this command has been sent to you from God out of heaven. Awaken these fish with which this ship you see is filled, and by your prayers make them human beings, as they formerly were.’

“I immediately obeyed his command. I stood in prayer for them and, drenched by a shower of tears, groaning, said:

‘Lord Jesus, for whom nothing is impossible, look mercifully upon the souls deceived by diabolical fraud, who have been alienated from the sense of human reason and, like beasts, are miserably entangled in the slippery mire of this age. I ask you, good Jesus, do not permit the enemy of the human race to triumph over them and glory in their destruction. Rather, by the omnipotence of your holy name, let them be restored to life, so that, escaping the sleep of eternal death, they may recognize you as the true and only Savior of the world. From then on, let them always flee to the tranquil harbor of your salvation and remain free from all the disturbances of the world, secure under your governance.

“‘For it is yours, O Christ, to give life to the dead and to restore to its former beauty the image you created. You came into this world to save sinners, and, having endured the terrible punishments of death upon the cross, you deigned to pour out your precious blood for the salvation of us all.’

“When I had poured out these and similar words of prayer with a contrite heart and a spirit of humility, behold, those fish whom I had previously seen entangled in the mud of filth and in the pit of misery I suddenly saw transformed into human beings and raised from death. A great multitude of people rose from the ship and hurried toward the land, many of whom I recognized individually.

“Among them, one fell backward and was changed again into an eel—namely Adelstan, who had once been ordained a priest together with me. I could in no way awaken him again or make him become human. All the others, however, raised their voices unanimously toward heaven, clapping their hands and giving thanks to almighty God, because through his ineffable mercy and through the arrival of my littleness they had deserved to be recalled from death to life and restored to the human reason they had lost.

“I, rejoicing in the Lord and sharing their joy, awoke. I relate this vision to you, my little sons, for this reason: so that you too may persevere in your holy purpose with the practice of good works, and by God’s grace may be counted among those who, though I am unworthy, have been entrusted to me, so that they may willingly be saved from the filthy abyss of this age and forever in eternal blessedness.

“These dreams that we have recorded were indeed seen at that time; but from then until today they have never ceased to be fulfilled, as people fervent in divine love hasten to leave the world and lead the coenobial life, and as the people of every rank strive to turn away from evil, do good, and humbly bow their necks to Christ, the King of kings. Thus both monks and laypeople, following the footsteps of Saint Father Adelwold, may deserve to attain the everlasting joys of the heavenly kingdom.”

**CHAPTER XL.**—In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 980, the church of the Old Monastery was renewed and constructed, and nine bishops solemnly dedicated it with great splendor. The first and chief of them were Dunstan the archbishop and Saint Adelwold himself, the bishop. The dedication took place on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of November, in the presence of King Aedelred and in the assembly of nearly all the dukes, abbots, earls, and leading nobles of the entire English people. They celebrated the dedication for two days with complete joy.

We too, rejoicing in the Lord over it, sang this poem:

Bishop Adelwold, filled with holy breath,  
Made many works pleasing to God, rejoicing.  
He restored the halls of this ancient temple  
With lofty walls and newly raised summits.

Strengthening it on the southern and northern sides,  
With solid porticoes and varied arches,  
He added many buildings to the sacred altars,  
Which make the entrance at the threshold uncertain.

Whoever walks through these halls with unfamiliar feet  
Does not know where he comes from or where to set his foot.  
For doors are seen standing open on every side,  
And no definite path or sure way is apparent.

Standing there, he turns his wandering eyes this way and that,  
And marvels at the Attic structures of Daedalian workmanship.  
Until a guide arrives to make his way certain  
And leads him to the threshold of the outer vestibule.

Here he wonders to himself, signs himself with the cross,  
And cannot discover with an astonished heart how to leave.  
So constructed it shines; so variously it flashes—  
The structure that sustains the ancient church.

That pious Father, filled with the highest devotion,  
Strengthened, roofed, endowed, and consecrated it  
For the praise of the name of the heaven-thundering Lord,  
And deserved to fulfill the vows of his temple,

With the face of the modest King Aedelred present,  
Who still presides today upon the throne of the kingdom.

There the bishops were present, three times three, rejoicing,  
Fulfilling the sacred ministry in due order.  
First among them was Dunstan, mature in face and conduct,  
Angel-like, his hair white with snow.

With him stood, rejoicing, the light of the English people,  
Lord Adelwold, kindly disposed in heart.  
After them came seven others, whose names are written here  
In a metrical poem with a dactylic foot:

Elfstan, Edelgarus, and again Elfstanus and Aeswig,  
Aelfeh, Edelsinus, and Athulfus also.

And finally the tenth, Bishop Poca, came there,  
Doing no work but drinking many cups.  
After them many more nobles and leaders were present,  
And the greater part of the English people’s earls,

Whom he had gathered together from that council  
Which had been held in the king’s village at Andover—  
That same rejoicing and often-to-be-sung shepherd, Adelwold,  
As the grace of the Lord had granted him.

And all celebrated the greatest solemnities of the church,  
Applauding the Lord with hearts pouring forth praise.  
That kindly man rejoiced above all in the good things  
Which the bishop had ordained to be generously given to all.

Dishes were added to the feasts; every kind of food abounded;  
No one was sad, and everyone was cheerful.  
There was no hunger, for provisions were plentiful for all,  
And the table remained filled with varied food.

The wandering cupbearers frequently visited the cellars  
And urged the guests to begin drinking.  
They set out mixing bowls and crowned the sweet wines,  
Mixing drink with countless other drinks.

And so one day and another passed amid hymns,  
And every heart blessed God.  
When at last all the hymns had been solemnly completed,  
Those which the people’s voice had sung in honor of God,

Each person happily returned to his own region,  
Rejoicing in the Lord in heart and singing with his lips.  
Never, I think, was there such a dedication of a church  
Performed throughout the whole English people,

As was powerfully celebrated in the city of Wenta,  
In the Old Monastery of Saint Peter.

May almighty God thus protect it undefiled,  
So that it may always be a dwelling worthy of him.  
And may all who enter this humble refuge  
Rejoice as full participants in forgiveness.

We have thought it appropriate to insert here these verses composed concerning the renovation and dedication of the Old Church. Thereafter heavenly mercy bestowed such grace upon the holy bishop that the exalted leaders of secular powers—dukes, tyrants, and judges—and everyone who had previously seemed opposed to him and resistant to the way of God were suddenly changed, as it were, from wolves into sheep. They revered him with extraordinary affection; bowing their necks to his knees and humbly kissing his right hand, they commended themselves in all things to the prayers of the man of God.

**CHAPTER XLI.**—At the time when the holy bishop Adelwold was about to depart from this mortal life and receive from God the rewards of his labors, he came to a village commonly called Beaddingtun, sixty miles distant from the city of Winchester.

While he remained there for some time, he began to be weighed down by a severe illness. After being anointed with the liquid of the sacred oil, he fortified his departure by receiving the body and blood of the Lord. Thus, bidding farewell and giving peace to his sons, he returned his spirit to heaven amid words of prayer on the Kalends of August, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 984, in the twenty-second year of his episcopate, while King Aedelred governed the English kingdom.

Those who were present there testified to us that the body of the holy man was suddenly transformed, renewed in appearance, suffused with a milky whiteness and adorned with a rosy flush, so that it seemed in some way to display the face of a seven-year-old boy. In it a certain glory of resurrection already appeared through the transformation of the flesh.

It cannot be said how great a multitude of people gathered for his funeral. From every direction, the rich and the poor streamed together from neighboring towns and fortified places, hastening to bid their shepherd a final farewell. All followed the bier with grief and bitter sorrow. It was precious beyond comparison, armed with the most holy Gospels and crosses, adorned with coverings of pallia, and surrounded on every side by burning lights, heavenly hymns, and the harmonies of psalms.

When they entered Winchester on the following day, the whole city came out together and unanimously went to meet the body. Here one could see the grieving crowds of monks; there the pale ranks of virgins; here one could hear the voices of clerics singing on high; there the groaning of weeping poor people and the wailing of crying needy ones. Unable to bear being deprived of the presence of their shepherd, they sent innumerable cries of tears toward heaven.

The man of God was therefore brought with heavenly funeral rites into the church of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, to his episcopal seat. After the solemn rites of vigils and Masses had been completed, he was buried in the crypt on the southern side of the holy altar, where he himself had formerly told them that it had been shown to him from heaven that he ought to rest.

**CHAPTER XLII.**—In the twelfth year after the death of the glorious bishop Adelwold, it pleased the heavenly dispensation that he should be revealed by heavenly signs and that his bones should be raised from the protection of the tomb, so that the lamp which had for a time been hidden beneath a bushel might be placed upon a candlestick and shine for all who are in the house.

There is a certain modest city, abundantly supplied with commerce, commonly called Weallingaford. A vigorous man lived there named Elehelmus, who, having accidentally lost the light of his eyes, suffered blindness for many years.

At cockcrow, Saint Bishop Adelwold appeared to him in a dream and urged him to go more quickly to Winchester and approach his tomb in order to receive the grace of sight. He said:

“For this reason I visit you as you lie in your present condition and announce beforehand what is to happen to you: so that through the sign of your healing it may be made manifest that I must be raised from the tomb in which I lie.”

When he heard this and recognized the voice speaking with him, the man gave thanks to the holy Father for deigning to visit him. Since he had no knowledge whatever of where the saint was buried, he carefully asked how he could learn of and approach his tomb. Immediately the man of God made known to him the name of his disciple and monk, of whom the man had until then been unaware, and said:

“When you have hastened to Winchester and entered the church of the Old Monastery, have a certain monk summoned to you, Wlesfanus by name, surnamed the Cantor. When he hears from your mouth the words of my message, he will immediately and without doubt lead you to my tomb. There you will recover the light of your eyes.”

What more need be said? Trusting the words and promises of the holy bishop, the man went quickly to Winchester, entered the church, summoned the aforementioned brother, and asked the one summoned to fulfill the message of the blessed Father, recounting to him and to all who stood nearby the sequence of his vision.

It was evening, the time when the nativity of the most holy Mother of God and perpetual Virgin Mary is solemnly and most honorably celebrated throughout the world. The brother, astonished, placed himself between hope and fear; then, with the foot of obedience close at hand, he humbly obeyed the commands of the holy bishop and led the blind man to the chamber of the sarcophagus.

The man remained there all night in prayer. When morning came, he no longer needed a guide, but returned joyfully to his own home, seeing and blessing the Lord in heart and spirit.

[Col. 0103B] **CHAPTER XLIII.**—This revelation, confirmed by so evident a miracle, was widely proclaimed. Thereafter Christ’s servant appeared in nocturnal visions to the aforementioned brother Wlfstanus and to many others, and through various signs made known to them that it was pleasing to the heavenly will for him to be transferred from the tomb and worthily placed in the church.

Therefore the venerable Bishop Elfagus, his successor, thoughtfully considering these things in his keen mind, gave the most humble thanks to almighty Christ with a joyful heart, because in his own time God deigned to glorify his saint by heavenly signs.

Without delay, after a multitude of the clergy, brothers, and people had assembled, he honorably transferred the relics of the holy bishop Adelwold on the fourth day of the Ides of September and placed them in the choir of the church. There they are held in great veneration to the present day. There also, before our eyes, heavenly miracles have been performed, of which we briefly mention two as evidence of their certainty.

**CHAPTER XLIV.**—At that time there was in the city of Wenta a small girl, the daughter of a certain household servant named Adelward. She was suffering from extreme illness and was tormented almost to death. Her mother brought her to the tomb of the man of God, where she fell asleep for a short while. Immediately she awoke, rose healthy, and returned home rejoicing with her mother.

**CHAPTER XLV.**—There was also a small boy, the son of a certain gentle and modest man named Aelffinus, who lost the light of his eyes in infancy and was carried in his mother’s arms to the tomb of the venerable Father Adelwold.

Wonderful to relate, immediately the darkness of blindness departed, and the returning splendor of light opened the boy’s eyes. All the people rejoiced with him and, in complete devotion, faithfully gave thanks to Christ, who can do all things.

**CHAPTER XLVI.**—Nor should it be passed over in silence that the aforementioned successor of the holy man, Bishop Elfagus, ordered a certain thief, who had been beaten with whips for multiple offenses, to be placed in the stocks and tormented with harsher punishments.

After he had lain condemned in such sufferings for a long time, Saint Bishop Adelwold appeared to him one night in a vision and said:

“Wretched man, why do you lie stretched out in this log for so long?”

Recognizing the holy man, whom he had often seen during his mortal life, the thief replied:

“I am enduring, my lord, deserved punishments, and by the bishop’s just judgment I am being tormented in this way, because I have often been caught in thefts and have not ceased from them. I repeatedly repeated the evil things I had done.”

Then the saint said:

“Cease, wretched man—cease from thefts even now—and be released from the bond of this fetter.”

Immediately the wretched man rose, freed. He went out from there, came before Bishop Aelfagus, and fell at his feet. He recounted to him in order what had happened to him, and, out of respect for so great a Father, the bishop allowed him to depart unharmed.

It is therefore evident that this saint, joined to eternal life by the power of his merits, can release us from the bonds of our sins and lead us to the heavenly kingdoms. Even while he was dwelling in the flesh, the power to bind and loose was granted to him from heaven. This is granted by our Lord Jesus Christ, who, with God the co-eternal Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns as God through endless ages of ages. Amen.

**Here begins a hymn in honor of Saint Adelwold the bishop, composed alphabetically in elegiac and paraeteric verse:**

The blessed lamp shines and supplies light to the people:  
Bishop Adelwold—the blessed lamp shines.

This warrior of God fought victorious battles:  
Swift into battle rushes this warrior of God.

From whose sacred mouth the teachings of life flowed:  
From whose sacred mouth we drank every good thing.

With pious heart let us resound sweet songs to the Father:  
Let us sing sweet verses with a pious heart.

[Col. 0104C] Behold, the pontifical crown shines abundantly for you:  
Here and there, behold, your crown shines.

As you sow words, the fountain and source of goodness flowed:  
In you the fountain and source of goodness poured forth.

Everlasting glory will now and throughout the ages be yours:  
How deservedly you retain everlasting glory.

For love of this flock you despised the darts of death:  
Driving away the strong ones, for love of this flock.

The renowned and mighty King Eadgar loved you:  
Under your guidance, renowned and mighty, he grew strong.

The camps of God resound when you establish the song:  
The Davidic melody resounds—the camps of God.

The monastic multitude applauds you with countless praises:  
It joins its jubilation to you with countless praises.

The lofty walls of this house were raised by your care:  
And rejoicing dedicated these lofty walls.

Night and day you celebrated the sacred hymn of the heart:  
Fulfilling the sacred office night and day.

Everywhere you scattered the seeds of light:  
Everywhere you drove away the darkness.

Be ever-watchful, we ask, as defender of your children:  
Be ever-watchful as protector of your servants.

Cut away whatever harms and grant whatever is beneficial:  
Recall the good things, and cut away whatever harms.

Happy ruler and doorkeeper of the apostolic hall,  
And ruler of this apostolic Church,

Release your servants in Peter’s place; release those who are bound:  
Release us, your servants, from sins.

[Col. 0105A] Under your leadership, may we climb to the star-bearing halls of heaven:  
Under your leadership, may we share the kingdom of the star-bearing one.

In hymnic verses we join together these songs, and you  
We honor as patron in hymnic verses.

Because you were accustomed to multiply Christ-loving souls,  
Calling Christ-loving souls back to the heavens.

The harmful hydra may flee, lest it mislead us through byways:

May your right hand protect us; may the harmful hydra flee.

Jealousy cannot harm when Christ conquers the Evil One:

Christ is present as victor; jealousy cannot harm.

Look upon, holy Father, the adversities that weary us:

Look upon the evils that tear us, holy Father.

Be gentle and present to your own pupils who serve you,

Who praise you together; be gentle and present to your own.

Rescue, shepherd, the sheep whom you have always loved in your heart,

And whom you had nourished; rescue them, shepherd.

[Col. 0105B] May Christ, in the citadel of heaven,

Record our names together with his saints. Amen.

## Evening Hymn

An evening hymn composed in Sapphic hendecasyllabic metre, containing an Adonius in the fourth place.

Illustrious shepherd and ruler of the people,

Whose triumph we honor as distinguished,

Now Adelwold, joyful without end,

Reigns among the stars.

He who was our Father and teacher,

Displaying the lessons of the sacred life,

And always striving to please God

With a kindly heart.

[Col. 0105C] O holy, celebrated, radiant day,

Which God’s mercy consecrated for us,

So that we might deserve to offer a worthy song

To so great a Father!

Now let us entreat him with every effort,

That the merciful one may wash away our guilt,

And by his holy prayer lead us

To high Olympus.

To God alone be glory and power,

Praise in the highest, honor everlasting,

Who governs and rules the whole world,

Directing it by his laws. Amen.

Illustrious senator of heaven, holy Father of the Church,

Adelwold, hear your suppliant little servants.

[Col. 0105D] Now a star among the stars, you shine above the heavens;

In your kindness obtain for us the gifts of the Paraclete.

With bowed minds we pray here before your relics;

Be present to our prayers, gracious and favorable.

So that, protected by your necessary patronage,

We may attain the everlasting joys of heaven.

May the Unbegotten and the Only-Begotten grant this to us,

The Holy Spirit of them both, the triune and one Lord.

Amen.

## Let us pray

God, who on this day have caused a new light to shine upon the peoples of the English through the illumination of the brilliant star of the holy bishop Adelwold: we humbly implore your mercy, that we may be instructed by the example of him through whose teaching we have learned the principles of the whole religious life, and aided by his patronage. Through.

## At Mass

God, who have made this day honorable for us through the passing of your blessed confessor, Adelwold the bishop: mercifully grant that, through the intercession of him whose instruction fills us with the light of your truth, we may attain the joys of heavenly life. Through.

## Secret

We ask you, Lord, to accept favorably the gifts of our service, commended to you by the annual solemnity of our holy Father Adelwold the bishop, so that, strengthened by his devout supplication, we may deserve to obtain remission of all our sins and a share in everlasting blessedness. [Col. 0106B] Through.

## Preface

It is truly fitting, eternal God, because the joyful and votive gladness of the present day is with us—a day which you have made sublime through the honor of the apostolic dignity and solemn through the rosy blood of martyrdom, and which you have consecrated by the modern celebration of the glorious bishop Adelwold—and because you have bestowed upon us the hope of so great a confidence, so that through his fatherly intercessions you may both free us from the bonds of our sins and lead us to the heavenly kingdom. Through Christ.

## Postcommunion

Having been refreshed, Lord, by the sacraments of life-giving nourishment, protect us through the glorious intercession of your holy confessor Adelwold, and grant that we may reach the everlasting banquet of the heavenly table. [Col. 0106C] Through.

## Another prayer

Govern your flock, eternal Shepherd, by the protection of our devout advocate, Father Adelwold, we ask, Lord, so that, moved by his goodwill, we may be nourished by the sweetness of heavenly love and, through his intervening patronage, be rescued from the disturbances of temporal life and admitted to the lasting joys of the citizens above. Through.

## 18 September, on the Translation of Saint Adelwold

God, who have given us your holy bishop Adelwold as a teacher of eternal salvation: mercifully grant that we may always be aided by the merits and prayers of him whose annual translation we celebrate. [Col. 0106D] Through.

## Over the Offering

We ask you, Lord, that the prayer of our holy Father Adelwold the bishop commend our sacrifice to you, so that through his intercession it may become an appeasement before your holy majesty for us, and the desired remission of our sins. Through.

## Preface
