Celebrating with devout reverence the votive translation of the blessed bishop Adelwold, and entreating you with bowed devotion that we may experience him as our patron before your mercy, whom by your gracious gift we have deserved to receive as a teacher of eternal salvation. Through Christ.

[Col. 0107A] ## Postcommunion

We ask, Lord, that the blessed Adelwold, our Father, may obtain through his devout intercession that this communion make us worthy of you. Through.

## On the Special Hours

Moreover, the blessed Father Adelwold instituted regular and special hours for his own distinctive service, which he arranged in three courses. With the greatest humility and diligence he admonished all his subjects to resist watchfully, through this secret service, the fiery temptations of Satan and, by resisting them through God’s grace, to overcome them; and so that the faith which shone more brightly than light itself through the incarnation of our Creator and most merciful Redeemer might not—when the time of the future persecution presses on, which is already imminent in the times near to Antichrist—waver in any way, God forbid, through hesitation, but, strengthened by these divine proclamations, might continually remain whole and inviolate.

The chant of the first psalmody was prepared in praise of the blessed Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary; the second, in honor of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and of all those who presently serve the humanity of our Savior; the third, to seek the intercessions of all the saints, so that, protected by their devout intercession, we may deserve to overcome the many-sided deceit of the cunning Antichrist and his members, and, with Christ as our rewarder, receive the palm of heavenly rewards. These hours are written down in many places and have therefore been omitted from this little book.

[Col. 0107] ## Tropes

The Father’s festal day is present; let us sing in triumph.  
He appointed him.

The bishop whom he consecrated for himself in this temple.  
And prince.

Among the apostolic hierarchs, with shining stole.  
That he may be for him.

Adelwold, defend us wretched ones with devout prayer.  
Forever.

Because Bishop Adelwold shone greatly in the episcopal order.  
He appointed him.

Establishing him today above the heavens.  
And prince.

Glory, splendor, honor, beauty, and perpetual veneration.  
Forever.

[Col. 0107]

# Letter of Wulfstan, Monk of Winchester, to Ælfheah, Bishop of Winchester

Prefixed to the Book on the Life of Saint Swithun, in which there is much about Saint Æthelwold.

The special letter begins to the lord Father,

Ælfheah, who sits as bishop in the city of Winchester,

Concerning the insignia of the holy Father Swithun, and concerning

The basilica of Peter, who opens the threshold of Olympus.

[Col. 0107B] To the lord bishop, prince of Winchester through Christ,

Who rules the Church, I shall sing all prosperity.

May he grant Ælfheah the honor of the heavenly kingdom,

Who gave this bishop to the whole people.

May he himself grant you unending, everlasting peace,

He who is the glory, peace, and honor of the saints.

This is what the last little servant of the English,

The hymn-singer—literally, “of the singers”—desires with pious mouth

And kindly heart.

Though my speech is feeble and lacks the fire of doctrine,

And I cannot write anything worthy of so great a man,

Yet this small gift of love which I bring

I have tried to commend to you, great Father:

In it I have briefly touched upon what the Ruler of Olympus accomplished,

The heavenly signs of the Father through Swithun’s merits:

[Col. 0107C] Through him he bestowed great miracles upon his English,

Offering up the bodies of thousands of sick persons.

These great deeds I have sung in poor song,

Presuming upon the goodness of the good God,

Who is accustomed to weigh great things from small ones,

Gladly accepting the widow’s two small coins.

[Col. 0108B] For it was not poverty but intention that was weighed,

Since she despised her livelihood and gave all that she had.

These little gifts, therefore, I commend to you, Father,

Which I vowed to return to the Lord with a devout heart,

So that your authority may deign to strengthen them,

And to protect them from hostile snares.

You, who sit as a worthy bishop in the apostolic hall,

Instructing the people in Catholic doctrine.

You adorn this monastery with varied ornaments,

Raising it everywhere, inside and out.

The bishop Adelwold once renewed it in triumph,

Whose concern night and day was

To increase the flocks of Christ’s people,

And with a father’s mouth to nourish them with milk,

With the milk of heaven.

He built all these dwellings with strong walls,

[Col. 0108C] And covered them themselves with new roofs.

He adorned the whole place with every honor in triumph,

And drew here the sweet streams of the fish-filled water.

The secluded channels of the lake enter the hidden parts of the buildings,

Cleansing the entire monastery with their murmuring.

[Col. 0109A] He also restored the halls of this ancient temple

With lofty walls and new roofs,

Strengthening it on the southern and northern sides

With solid porticoes and varied arches.

He added more buildings to the sacred altars,

Which leave the entrance of the doorway uncertain.

Anyone walking through its halls with unfamiliar feet

Would not know from where he came or where to turn his steps.

For doors appear open on every side,

And no definite path or route is evident.

Standing there, he turns his wandering eyes this way and that,

And marvels at the Attic structure of Daedalus:

Until a more certain guide comes to him

And leads him to the threshold of the farthest vestibule.

There, wondering to himself, he signs himself with the cross; and how

[Col. 0109B] He might get out, he cannot know with astonished heart.

Thus constructed it gleams, and thus varied it flashes—

The structure that supports this mother church—

Which that pious Father, filled with supreme devotion,

Founded, built, endowed, and then consecrated

To the praise of the high-thundering Lord,

And fulfilled the vows of his temple,

While King Æthelred, the modest king,

Watched; he who remains today upon the throne of the kingdom.

Many bishops followed him in procession,

Properly completing the sacred ministry.

Foremost among them was Dunstan, mature in face and conduct,

White with snowy age and angelic.

Following him in triumph was that same light of the English,

Bishop Adelwold, kindly of heart.

[Col. 0109C] After them were seven others, whom it is now easy to add—

Cwig,

In metrical verse with a dactylic foot:

Ælfstan, Æthelgar, and again Ælfstan, and Æs,

Ælfheah, Æthelsinus, and Adulfus were there.

Many other nobles and leaders were present,

And the greater part of the English people’s leading men,

Whom that same shepherd, the often-to-be-praised Adelwold,

Had gathered together from the council

That had taken place at the king’s settlement of Andover,

As the grace of the Lord had granted him.

And everyone celebrated the temple’s great solemnities,

Applauding the Lord with a heart flowing with praise.

The kindly bishop rejoiced above all in the good things

Which the Bishop had determined should generously be given to everyone.

Dishes were mingled among the feasts; every kind of food abounded.

[Col. 0109D] No one was sad; everyone was cheerful.

There was no hunger, since there were full provisions for all,

And the table remained laden with varied food.

The wandering cupbearers often visited the cellars,

And invited the guests to begin drinking.

They set out great mixing-bowls and crowned the wines,

Mixing drinks with countless other drinks.

The cups were fertile, when the tireless rustic drained

The foaming bowl, sweet with its honeyed flood;

And at last he drenched himself completely in the full gold,

Shaking his bristly chin.

Thus one day and another day passed in hymns,

[Col. 0110A] And every heart blessed God.

When all the hymns had finally been completed solemnly,

Those which the people’s voice had sung in God’s honor,

Each person cheerfully returned to his own region,

Rejoicing in the Lord in heart and singing with his mouth.

I believe that never was such a great and splendid dedication of a temple

Performed among the entire English people,

As was powerfully celebrated in the city of Winchester,

In the Old Monastery of Saint Peter.

May almighty God protect it undefiled,

And deign himself to dwell in it continually;

And may all who enter this humble refuge

Rejoice as full participants in forgiveness.

In addition to these things, the bishop, filled with holy inspiration,

Offered very many vows to his own Lord.

[Col. 0110B] For he joyfully laid their foundation from the hinge,

So that the portico might stand built for God.

He raised a new temple after laying the foundation. [Note: [Col. 0109] Wulfstan reports these matters concerning the construction of the new monastery at Winchester so clearly and unequivocally that they cannot be attributed to King Alfred.]

But before he could complete it, he was snatched from the world;

He was deservedly translated, for his merits, to the heavenly court,

Whose manifold riches cannot be counted.

With these he delighted the One enthroned on high from the beginning,

Until he himself gave his soul back to Christ.

Your authority immediately succeeded him in the citadel,

And with vigilant heart built up the work he had begun.

Moreover, you took pains to add hidden crypts,

Which ingenious craftsmanship had constructed like a labyrinth.

Anyone who entered them as a stranger

Would not know from where he came or where to turn his steps.

There are hidden recesses in which other hiding places lie concealed here and there;

Their roofs are open, while caves lie hidden within.

Their entrances stand open, as do their exits;

A person who does not know them might think they lacked light.

They appear to stand beneath the dark night and in shadow,

Yet they possess hidden lights of the sun.

When, at its rising, its first rays flash back,

The morning star enters and scatters its radiance everywhere;

It penetrates every cavern with the splendor of its light,

Until the sun falls into the western Ocean.

Their structure stands and supports the sacred altar,

And the holy relics of the saints in due order.

Their roof remains useful in many ways,

Bearing the outer parts and covering the inner ones.

You also increased organs here of such a kind as nowhere

Are seen, established on a double floor.

[Col. 0110D] Twelve bellows are joined above in a row,

And fourteen lie below.

With alternating blasts they produce the greatest breaths,

Driven by seventy strong men.

They turn the arms, wet with much sweat,

And each urges on his companions competitively:

To force the blasts upward with all their strength,

So that the case, filled to capacity within, may roar.

It alone supports four hundred Muses [i.e. pipes] in order,

Which the hand of the organ-player’s skill controls.

He opens these when closed and closes them again when open,

Demanding that the varied melody produce a definite sound.

[Col. 0111A] Two brothers sit there with harmonious hearts,

And each governs his own keyboard.

There are forty hidden openings for the tongues,

Each retaining ten in its own order.

Some run here, others run back there,

Preserving each pitch in its proper modulation.

And they strike the jubilation of seven divisions of voices,

With a half-tone mixed into the lyric song.

In the manner of thunder, an iron voice strikes the ears,

So that, apart from this single sound, it can contain nothing else.

The sound resounds so loudly, echoing from here and there,

That everyone closes his open ears with his hands,

Unable at all to endure the approaching roar

Produced by the clashing of the varied sounds.

The music of the pipes is heard everywhere through the city,

[Col. 0111B] And its fame, flying, traverses the whole country.

Your care vowed this adornment of the church to the Thunderer,

And built it in honor of holy Peter, the bearer of the keys.

Moreover, you caused a lofty temple to be added,

Where day continues without night.

A tower flashes from the place where the sun sparkles at its rising,

And scatters the first rays of its light.

It contains five sections, pierced with broad, eye-like windows,

And opens passages everywhere toward the four regions.

Lofty, beaked peaks of the tower stand above the domes,

And gleam, curved with various vaults.

Such was the skill that taught the craftsman to bend them,

Who is accustomed to add beauty to beautiful places.

A structure stands upon gilded knobs of the rod.

A golden brilliance adorns the whole work,

[Col. 0111C] And whenever the moon shines in its crowned rising,

Another radiance rises from the sacred building toward the stars.

If a traveler sees it at night while passing by,

He thinks that the earth possesses stars of its own.

As an additional ornament, a cock stands upon its summit,

Golden, great in adornment and appearance.

It looks down upon the whole earth and rises above all the fields,

Seeing the beautiful stars of the star-bearing sky and of the north.

He holds the scepter of empire in his proud feet,

And stands above the whole people of Winchester.

Raised into the air, he rules all the cocks,

And nobly governs the western empire.

Indefatigable, he receives from every side the rain-bearing winds,

And, turning, presents his face to them.

He bravely withstands the terrible blows of the whirlwind,

[Col. 0111D] Standing undaunted, enduring blasts and snows.

Alone he has seen the sun falling into the Ocean;

He also sees the first ray of dawn.

Coming from far away, he clings close to the eye,

And fixes the gaze across the intervening distance.

Toward him the weary traveler is drawn by his wondering sight,

Separated by his feet yet joined to him by light.

Why should I add more to these things? You labor with all your strength

To beautify the entire monastery on every side.

Its recent dedication was properly completed,

And celebrated in a sufficiently wondrous order,

When eight distinguished hierarchs consecrated it to the Lord,

Whom God’s piety caused to be present here together.

The first of them was Sigeric, with his beautiful name,

Powerful in victory, shining victoriously in the citadel,

Gleaming before and behind, venerable in bearing and conduct,

From whose eloquence sweet honey flows.

May God guard him everywhere in the heavenly realms,

And preserve him unharmed for the peoples of the English.

[Col. 0112A] Ælfstan followed him in triumph, and another Elfstan,

Both bishops, each filled with God.

Ælfheah was present, Ordbirht was present, Wilfsinus and Ælfric,

All shining by right of their priestly office.

They all began to sing with measured voices:

Peace be to this house, and peace also to its faith;

Peace to the one entering, and peace to the one departing;

Always in this place, may praise and honor be given to God.

Thus the new walls of the temple resound in God’s praise,

And every tongue joyfully echoes in the Lord.

[Col. 0112B] On one side stand nobles, on the other boys, young men, and old men,

And they celebrate the joys of the holy monastery.

Thus the long-desired day, now to be remembered throughout the ages,

Shone in the city, full of devout vows;

On it the Shepherd deserved to behold his joys

And to fulfill his vows to God through sacred service.

On one side bishops surround you, on the other ministers;

Honor encircled you on one side, favor on the other.

As the singing crown of the brothers came together,

Each sang your vow with whatever skill he possessed.

Cymbal-like voices were mingled with sharp pipes,

And the sweet music sounded with varied tropes.

Moreover, the whole people of the clergy, and every child, shouted for joy,

And the threefold instrument thundered the help of the Divinity.

For an increase of joy was heaped upon every part

[Col. 0112C] Of this ancient monastery.

Everyone rejoiced, refreshed with food and banquets,

And with various drinks and every good thing.

Thus the celebration of this holy temple shone forth,

Sanctified to God by the apostolic name.

This is the hall of the pious Peter, shining in name,

Who is accustomed to bind the lofty heavens with a key,

Who, by God’s gift, both loosens bonds for the world

And unlocks the heavenly kingdoms for all the devout.

This hall, Paul, is also entrusted to you for protection,

You who subdue all the peoples of the world with your mouth.

May you both exist here as its special patrons,

You for whom there is one summit, and equal glory in heaven.

Pray to God almighty that he may deign to hear

The vows and prayers of his people.

[Col. 0112D] Whoever seeks to ask benefits in this temple,

May he obtain from the devout Lord joys in full.

Here lies the blessed apostolic man Birinus,

Who washed these western peoples in the font.

The standard-bearing Swithun also rests there in demate [read: corpore, “body”],

Who by his prayers lifts up this entire people.

In the middle of the temple shine Byrnstan and Ælfheah,

Both worshipers of God by right of their priestly office.

The supreme bishop, the glory of his homeland, nourisher of the needy,

Hope of travelers, splendor and honor of the Fathers:

Our Adelwold, shepherd, father, and teacher,

Whose crown shines in eternal light.

His name gleams at every threshold among the English,

[Col. 0113A] And in many monasteries and many places

Which, by vow, he built for the Lord and consecrated to him,

Gathering in them flocks by the hundred.

He stands in no respect least among the bishops,

For the radiance of his teaching shines everywhere.

But among the apostolic hierarchs he shines in heaven;

Through him God now performs manifest signs,

Giving light to eyes submerged in dreadful darkness,

And restoring weakened limbs to their nerves.

Whoever comes to his holy tomb

Receives full forgiveness together with his prayers.

Those who, full of faith, seek the benefits of Christ

Find from heaven the gifts they desire.

A certain nobleman, Ælfhelm, recently learned this,

When he was ordered, sleepless, to approach the sacred tomb.

[Col. 0113B] His eyes were closed by excessive glaucoma,

And he could see neither the sun nor its ray.

As soon as he came here, the Saint commanded that he receive

The clear faculty of sight,

And, returning without a guide, marveled within himself

At what he had been when he came and what he was when he returned from here.

Likewise, a certain girl who had become extremely weak

Was led to the sacred tomb by her grieving mother.

Immediately she fell asleep; she awoke completely healthy,

And returned home unharmed with her mother.

What wonder, then, that such radiant signs shine through him,

And that after death he gleams brightly in heaven?

His life was everywhere full of virtues;

He continually strove to please God in his heart.

[Col. 0114A] In his own time he offered bright examples for those to come,

Always loving God, enthroned on high,

And rejoicing happily with manifold jubilation;

Therefore Christ’s noble Church exults.

For the Lord is wondrous and fearful,

He who performs astonishing signs in his saints.

There are also many others placed here and there,

Of whom the Church sings that it is written:

“The bodies of the saints are buried here in peace,

And their names live forever.”

Following their deeds and faithfully fulfilling their sayings,

You diligently perform the office entrusted to you.

Your tongue supplies the apostolic light to the peoples,

And, when you open it, the word of the Lord is revealed.

You give food to the poor and clothing to the naked,

[Col. 0114B] And, devoutly, you distribute generous gifts to the wretched,

So that, returning the talents entrusted to you doubled,

You may enter the true joys of your Lord.

Receive, I ask, Father, the gifts that I bring to you,

And accept what I repay as due for your merits.

May this life long provide you with every prosperity,

And may the future light bring you still greater things.

Here, for many years, may you fulfill devout vows to the Lord,

So that the sheep entrusted to you may multiply.

And may you enter the heavenly kingdom with your flock accompanying you,

Always joyful with the saints in the citadel of heaven.

May he grant this to you who governs all the elements,

The one powerful God everywhere in the Trinity. Amen.

# In the Year of the Lord 983. Widukind, Monk of Corvey

[Col. 0113]

# Historical Notice on Widukind

*(Fabricius, Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis.)*

[Col. 0113]

Witkind, also called Widukind, a Saxon by nationality, was a monk of Corvey. For the sake of study he went to the monastery of Hirsau; afterward he returned to Corvey, where he presided over the schools. Magnoald Ziegelbaur, in *Conspectus rei litterariae ordinis S. Benedicti*, part I, p. 99.

Around the year 980 he wrote three books *On the Deeds of the Saxons*, first published among Hervagius’s *German Writers*, Basel, 1532, folio; afterward by Reiner Reineccius, Frankfurt, 1580, folio; and by the elder Heinrich Meibom, Frankfurt, 1621, folio, with annotations which his grandson repeated in volume I of the *Collection of German Writers*. Finally Leibniz inserted the *Summary of the Chapters of Witichind* from an old Cassinese manuscript in volume I of the *Brunswick Historical Sources*, p. 208. There follow, in the same work, p. 211, variant readings from the manuscript of the Dresden archive, and, on p. 221, those of the Cassinese manuscript.

According to Sigebert, chapter 129, his poetry consists of the *Passion of the Virgin Thecla* and the *Life of Paul the Hermit*, which contained prose interspersed with verse; neither work has yet been published in print. Add Lyser’s *History of the Poets of the Middle Ages*, pp. 283–284, and Paulinus, *On the Illustrious Men of Saxon Corvey*, p. 96.

[Col. 0115]

# The Saxon Deeds of Widukind

Edited by D. Georg Waitz, Ph.D.

*(In Pertz, Monumenta Germaniae historica, Scriptores, vol. III.)*

[Col. 0115]

# To the Reader

[Col. 0115A] It is sufficiently certain that Widukind, the author of the book which we are now about to publish, was a Saxon and a monk of Corvey; he himself acknowledges this in his preface. He lived in the middle of the tenth century. According to the brief Corvey chronicle, he was received as a monk under Abbot Folkmar, who governed the monastery from 917 to 942. He is named next to last among forty-nine monks, so that he seems to have entered the monastery only during the final years of Folkmar.

He recalls Folkmar’s successor, Bovo, who governed the monastery of Corvey from 942 to 948, as having been shown by God but not granted to him [Note: [Col. 0115B] III, 2, manuscripts 2 and 3.]. During Bovo’s time, in 946, he saw the Bohemian hostages, presented to the people at Otto’s command [Note: [Col. 0115B] II, 40.]. Sigebert of Gembloux mentions him and the books he left both in his *Chronicle* under the year 973 and in his book *On the Ecclesiastical Writers* [Note: [Col. 0115B] Chapter 129, in Fabricius, *Bibliotheca ecclesiastica*, p. 108.]. Trithemius [Note: [Col. 0115B] *Annales Hirsaugienses*, p. 98.] says that he presided over the school at Corvey for more than forty years, and relates that he had been attracted by the reputation of Meginrad, the teacher at Hirsau, had visited him, and had stayed with him for several days.

Nothing else is known about Widukind’s life [Col. 0115B]; he recorded nothing about himself, nor do we know the year in which he died [Note: [Col. 0115B] Only the more recent Corvey annals, in Leibniz, *Scriptores*, I, 302, relate that in 1004 Hosed, abbot of the monastery, erected a monument to him. They add that he was called there a pious and learned master of the school and a historian dear to both king and queen; I do not wish to determine with certainty how much weight should be given to this.].

The works that have preserved Widukind’s memory have transmitted this information about him. Sigebert reports that, in addition to histories, he composed a *Life of Saint Paul the Hermit* and a *Passion of the Virgin Thecla* [Note: [Col. 0115B] Neither of these lives is mentioned in the *Acts of the Saints*; they therefore appear to have been lost.]. Trithemius likewise mentions this, but also lists several other writings of his. Thus he testifies that Widukind composed a book *On the Studies of the Ancient Monks*, from which he quotes the following words [Note: [Col. 0115B] *Annales Hirsaugienses*, loc. cit.]:

> “That most learned teacher of monks, Meginrad, like another Jerome, the profoundest interpreter of the divine Scriptures, turned us to amazement by his learning, so that he may truly be called a treasury of heavenly wisdom, since nothing in the disciplines escaped him.”

In his catalogue of illustrious men [Col. 0116A] he attributes to him *Sermons to the Brothers*, one book of letters to various persons, and one book of epigrams [Note: [Col. 0116B] *Opera*, Frankfurt, 1601, II, p. 129.]. He makes no mention of these elsewhere, and there seems good reason to doubt whether they were truly written by our author [Note: [Col. 0116B] I would altogether deny that the verses published by Letzner from a Corvey manuscript under Widukind’s name, in the *Life of Louis the Pious*, chapter 19, fol. 63, belong to him.]. Certainly all these works have either been lost or remain unknown to us. Far superior to them, however, are the works Widukind wrote on the history of the Saxon emperors and of the Saxons.

Sigebert reports that he wrote the history of the Saxons up to the death of Otto I and, in addition, a life of Otto. Apparently following Sigebert as his source, Trithemius repeated this [Note: [Col. 0116B] *Catalogue of Illustrious Men*, book I; *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 301, in Fabricius, p. 78.]. In the *Chronicle of Hirsau* [Note: [Col. 0116B] *Opera*, II, p. 32.] he attributes to him only a history arranged in three little books, concerning the deeds of Henry I, Otto I, and the origin of the Saxons. Finally, in the annals of that same monastery, he lists four historical works [Note: [Col. 0116B] *Annales Hirsaugienses*, p. 98.]:

> “Among other little works of his intellect, he wrote three books on the origin of the Saxons; he also wrote for Mathilda, daughter of Otto I, one book on the deeds of Henry I, the first king; for the same woman, a life and account of the deeds of Queen Mathilda, wife of that same Henry, the first king; and he also composed for her the deeds of Otto I.”

Three books of the *Deeds of the Saxons* survive, in which the author described both the origin of the people and the deeds performed by Henry and Otto. I would altogether deny that he composed any other work on the history of his people and its kings. Trithemius seems, through a gross error, sometimes to have entered the whole work and sometimes individual books into his catalogue; I do not know from where he derived what he added about the *Life of Mathilda* [Note: [Col. 0116B] Unless perhaps he indicated by that title a continuation of the third book.]. It is sufficiently clear that the published *Life* cannot in any way be attributed to our author. Its writer knew no other *Life*, but when the emperor Henry II, the queen’s grandson, desired such a work, he composed it. Sigebert, however, may perhaps have been led into error by Widukind’s own words.

For he begins the first book with these words:

> “After the beginnings of our works, in which I revealed the triumphs of the soldiers of the supreme emperor,”

and so forth. These words undoubtedly refer to the *Lives* of the martyrs, the soldiers of God, mentioned above. Sigebert, however, seems to have thought of the emperor Otto, and therefore concluded that Widukind’s deeds had already been separately described and published.

Widukind dedicated the books of the *Deeds of the Saxons* to Mathilda, daughter of King Otto. His chief purpose was to write the deeds of Henry and Otto, her grandfather and father; he prefaced them with only a brief account of the origin of the Saxons. He aimed at a concise, elegant, and lucid manner of narration and writing: “We write briefly and in sections,” he says, “so that the discourse may be clear and not tedious to readers.” He regrets that the book lacks clarity of intellect and language; but the fact that he regrets this shows that he aspired to those qualities. And indeed, in the apt and almost rounded construction of his words, and in his lucid and serious narrative, Widukind surpasses by far nearly all the writers of this century.

He himself saw a large part of what he described, and almost nowhere copied other books. For this reason he must be counted among the outstanding sources of medieval history. He testifies that, concerning the most ancient times, he wrote by following almost nothing but oral report [Note: [Col. 0117C] I, chapter 2.]. He had read, if I am not mistaken, Bede’s history of the Anglo-Saxons [Note: [Col. 0117C] I, chapter 8.], Paul the Deacon’s history of the Lombards [Note: [Col. 0117C] I, chapter 14.], Jordanes’ history of the Goths [Note: [Col. 0117C] I, chapter 18.], and the *Deeds of the Franks* [Note: [Col. 0117C] I, chapter 15.], but he inserted only a few things from these books into his own work. In describing the wars waged by the Franks against the Saxons [Note: [Col. 0117C] I, chapter 15.] and Otto’s appearance and character [Note: [Col. 0117D] II, chapter 36.], he seems to have had Einhard’s *Life of Charlemagne* before his eyes.

I would scarcely think that he used Rudolf’s *Translation of Saint Alexander* [Note: [Col. 0117D] *Monumenta Germaniae*, II, p. 673.]. It seems to me that both writers drew from the same source, an ancient tradition; for this reason they agree very closely with each other, though they do not entirely agree. Where he agrees with Liudprand in the narration of events [Note: [Col. 0117D] Compare I, chapter 19, concerning the Hungarians; I, chapter 22, concerning the death of Adalbert.], I would reach much the same conclusion: certainly he did not see Liudprand’s books.

Later as well he incorporated much into his history from popular rumor and from vernacular songs. He did reject as fabricated by popular rumor what was reported about Hatto’s treachery toward Adalbert [Note: [Col. 0117D] I, chapter 23.], but the account he gives of the deception devised against Henry scarcely deserves greater confidence. Here and elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0117D] I, 23; II, 23.] he seems to indicate that source by the word “it is said” and similar expressions. He himself also cites the songs of performers [Note: [Col. 0117D] I, 23.], and I do not think I am mistaken if I conclude that a large part of the first book must be traced to such material.

During the early years of Duke Henry, he himself was either not yet born or was a child of the earliest age; what he later wrote about those events he could have drawn only from tradition. He nowhere indicates that he used a written book in narrating these matters. It cannot be demonstrated that he drew from some Corvey chronicle, as several have maintained. The chronicle published under this name by the distinguished Wedekind in the last century was for the most part compiled from Widukind himself. He seems not to have seen the Corvey annals published above, and certainly not to have used them in writing his book [Note: [Col. 0117D] What is read under the years 963 and 964 agrees in some way with Widukind III, 63. The fact that news of Otto’s conquest of Calabria in 964 reached Corvey is shown by this: a certain monk—perhaps Widukind himself—reported the matter in the annals, and our author inserted it into his book.].

For he entirely neglected the reckoning of years, which those annals present with reasonable accuracy, and he omitted many other matters recorded in them. I am confident that it will be evident to anyone who reads through Widukind’s history that it was not composed from annals, but written from knowledge of events acquired elsewhere. He had a sound knowledge of the events of Henry’s final years and, especially, of Otto’s times. He was a contemporary of these events and himself connected with the royal household; therefore he was undoubtedly well informed through personal knowledge. He also committed errors in this part of his work, but he understood correctly what took place in Saxony itself, and in these matters we may rightly trust him.

The published books carry the history down to the death of Otto I; but it is easy to demonstrate that most of it had already been written earlier. For Widukind very often indicates that he was writing while Emperor Otto was still alive [Note: [Col. 0117D] “From this point the affairs of the Franks began to decline, while those of the Saxons grew, until, enlarged, they now suffer from their own size, as we see in the love of the world and the capital of the whole earth, your father;—let us have you as our advocate before the earthly king, namely your father and brother.” (I, ch. 34);—“although your father’s power now extends into Africa and Asia” (II, pref.);—“(Otto) knows how to speak Latin and Slavic, but it is rare for him to deign to use either of them . . . he enjoys board games, etc.” (II. 36);—“sons were born to the king—the third designated by the majesty of his father’s name, whom the whole world already hopes will be lord and emperor after his father.” (III, 12.)]; and the Dresden manuscript does not contain the whole of the third book, but ends at chapter 69 with these words: “That was the end for Wichmann and for nearly all who had taken up arms against the emperor, your father.”

[Col. 0118B] Up to this point, unless I am mistaken, Widukind wrote as the year 967 was drawing to a close. There are indeed indications that he had already brought the book to an end earlier. After Wichmann had been subdued and affairs, to use his own words, had been properly settled, he reports that Otto departed once more for Italy, but touches upon what was done there as briefly as possible. “It is not,” he says, “for our humble ability to announce these things; but, as I said at the beginning of the history, it is enough to have labored so far in faithful devotion. For the rest, toward your brilliance and serenity—great devotion should make a humble work magnificent. But let the end of the civil war be the end of the little book.” Everyone can see how closely these words fit an ending.

Our author does not even mention the events carried out either in Italy or in Germany from 964 to 967, except for the Slav wars. Up to the middle of 964, chapter 63 briefly summarizes events; at the beginning of 965 Otto returned to Germany; in June Gero died, and in October Bruno died. In the following year Mathildis, Otto’s daughter, was elected and installed as abbess of Quedlinburg [Col. 0118C] [Note: [Col. 0118D] Annals of Quedlinburg, under this year. For this reason Bouquet, VIII, 217, already thought that Widukind’s book had previously been dedicated to her.], while the emperor departed again for Italy. Widukind says nothing about any of these events.—Nevertheless, it cannot be maintained that his book was written as early as 964.

After the death of Archbishop Bruno [Note: [Col. 0118D] I, 31: “whom we saw performing the office of supreme pontiff and great leader.” Cf. II, 36. Of Gero, who died a few months later, he says in III, ch. 54: “Gero was,” etc.], while Emperor Otto was staying in Italy with his son Otto [Note: [Col. 0118D] III, 63: “whom [Mathildis] the greatness of her father and brother left to her country for every honor and to us for consolation.”], in the thirtieth year after the victory over the Hungarians won in Saxony in 938 [Note: [Col. 0118D] II, 4.], Widukind was occupied with writing his history.

Wichmann, whose death he discusses in the final chapters, appears to have died in September 967 [Note: [Col. 0118D] Sigebert, followed by the Saxon Annalist and the Chronicle of Saint Bavo, placed Wichmann’s death in the year 967. Although he nowhere deserves complete confidence in his dates, he is broadly correct here, as is established by the words of chapter 70, where the continuation begins. Meibomius, p. 701, and van Spaen, *Inleiding tot de Historie van Gelderland*, p. 53, thought that Wichmann had died before Gero, whereas Gero’s death is not reported until the continuation, III, ch. 75.]; at Christmas of the same year Otto II received the imperial crown [Col. 0119A]. Since this event is mentioned only in the continuation added later [Note: [Col. 0119D] The emperor himself reported this matter to the Saxons in a letter written on 18 January 968.], I think it correct to conclude that the book was completed in the final months of 967 or the first months of 968 [Note: [Col. 0119D] Before that letter had reached Saxony.].

But he wrote the events of Otto’s reign in these years in sections. Up to 958 he set out Saxon affairs at considerable length; afterward, when the emperor had departed for Italy and remained there for several years, he did not wish to commit to memory what had been done there [Note: [Col. 0119D] For he had undertaken to write books about Saxon affairs.], but described the end of the disturbances which Wichmann had stirred up in Saxony and Slavia. Finally, after the death of Emperor Otto the Great, he judged that only a few additions needed to be made to the history.

The emperor’s letter (968), the wars fought against the Greeks (969), the marriage of Otto II (972), the deaths of Queen Mathildis, Bishops Wilhelm and Bernhard (968), Duke Hermann, and finally the emperor himself (973) are reported here. In most manuscripts these passages are read in the closest connection with the earlier material; Thietmar already used them, and Sigebert, Ekkehard, and the Saxon Annalist likewise employed them. I therefore have no doubt that these additions too were made by Widukind himself, although I seem to detect a somewhat different manner of expression, and although Trithemius says that Widukind’s history was completed by someone else [Note: [Col. 0119D] *Chronicon Hirsaugiense*, preface, works II, p. 2.].

I could never concede that the passages which seem to come close to the *Life of Mathildis* were actually drawn from it. Without doubt they were written shortly after Otto’s death and added by Widukind himself, in order to complete the emperor’s deeds—those which he himself had witnessed in Germany. He did not compose a continuous history of these years, but committed to memory only a few things which seemed relevant here. If only he had set these out more carefully; if only another Widukind had written the history of Otto II and Otto III!

When he later enlarged the book with that continuation, he also seems to have added, in III, ch. 2, the material about Bovo of Corvey which is missing from the Dresden manuscript. But I think that the sparse and excessively cautious history of Hatto and Adalbert, as we read it in the same manuscript [Note: [Col. 0119D] I would not attribute to Widukind the account of the first recension concerning Hatto, which is certainly sparser than the facts required, nor, in the enumeration of the offenses of Archbishop Frithuric of Mainz, would I regard him as so timid—though the passage is richer where Cassel is mentioned. PERTZ.] [Col. 0119C] should be attributed not to Widukind but to some scribe of the Mainz diocese. 

Afterward, however, he seems to have revised the entire book. For in the Casinensis manuscript, the passages written about Adalbert’s death and about Bovo are omitted; some things are expressed differently, and words have been changed for other words. This manuscript alone divides the books into chapters and places a table of contents before each book. This appears to have been done when Widukind was putting the final hand to his work.

The following materials were available for preparing the new edition of Widukind:

**A.** A manuscript formerly belonging to the archive and now to the royal library of Dresden, parchment, 21 folios, formerly from the monastery of Old Cell, of the twelfth century, according to Pertz, who saw it. Ebert thought that it had been copied from a Corvey manuscript [Note: [Col. 0119D] *Archiv*, III, p. 605. But all Widukind manuscripts must doubtless be derived from Corvey books.]. It ends at chapter 69 with the words quoted above and lacks the continuation; I therefore judged that it should be given first place.

Otherwise it cannot be judged the best manuscript. The scribe does not appear to have been sufficiently accurate everywhere, sometimes changed names, and did not scrupulously preserve the ancient spelling; he seems to present an interpolated version of the history of Hatto. Fabricius used this manuscript in his books; Reineccius prepared his edition from it; afterward Leibnitz published various readings communicated to him by Tenzel [Note: [Col. 0119D] *SS.*, I, p. 211.]. Finally, the late Ebert compared the manuscript more carefully with Meibomius’s edition in 1821, and under his guidance I have recorded the complete variety of readings. Two of its folios are missing [Note: [Col. 0120D] II, ch. 11: “he made peace with the king”;—ch. 24: “with steadfastness and authority.”].

All the remaining manuscripts and editions carry the history down to the year 973:

**1.** The Casinensis manuscript of the monastery, no. 289, parchment, quarto, fols. 39–120, written toward the end of the eleventh or at the beginning of the twelfth century in Beneventan script [Note: [Col. 0120D] At the command of Wibald, abbot of Corvey and Monte Cassino? P.], whose readings Leibnitz published after they had been sent to him by L. Zaccagni, keeper of the Vatican Library [Note: [Col. 0120D] *SS.*, I, p. 221.]. Pertz again compared the manuscript with Frecht’s edition and described it more accurately [Note: [Col. 0120D] *Archiv*, V, p. 144.].

It is the oldest of all those surviving, and seems to have preserved Widukind’s books in the form in which he himself revised them in individual passages [Col. 0120B]. Yet it is not free from errors and defects. More often than the others it violates the rules of Latin grammar, though I strongly doubt that this should be attributed to Widukind. Its spelling frequently departs from ordinary usage, and many features indicate an Italian scribe [Note: [Col. 0120D] Thus it writes *judicabit*, *judicabimus* for *judicavit*, etc.; *ververibus* for *verberibus*; *vestucam* for *festucam*; *structio* for *strutio*; *joseppo* for *josepho*; *impuero*; *discendendi*, *oppungnare*, *hammaburgnensem*; *scissitare*; *progecit*, *agebat* for *aiebat*; *atho*, *omerus*, *erimannus*, *odiernum*, *reveunt*; *afinitas*, *afirmare*, *caliditas*, *conexerat*, *rarisumus*, *redidit*; *erumpando*, *difficele*, *palulum* for *paululum*; *odoni* for *odonis*, *generis* for *generi*, etc.].

**2.** C., formerly belonging to the monastery of Steinvelt [Note: [Col. 0120D] Cf. *Archiv*, VII, p. 364.], apparently written in the middle of the twelfth century, fols. 135–198, which I compared as carefully as possible myself. Twice [Note: [Col. 0120D] I, 22; III, 2.] it preserves passages omitted in the Casinensis manuscript, apparently later deleted by Widukind. Although the manuscript was not written with equal care throughout, it is highly valuable, and in the presentation of individual words is scarcely less authoritative than the Casinensis. The scribe seems generally to have followed his exemplar accurately, though he sometimes disturbed the order of words and suffers from various other errors.

**3.** Frecht prepared the first edition of Widukind, printed by the Hervagian press at Basel in 1532, folio. He used a manuscript from the monastery of Erbach (Eberbach) near the Rhine, whose age and condition he did not state. In the passages cited above it agrees with manuscript 2; nevertheless, it cannot have been copied from it. Many words absent from 2 are correctly read in 3; where the Steinvelt manuscript gives corrupt readings, Frecht prints sound ones; elsewhere he altered Widukind’s words, which remain intact in 2. When the two are carefully compared, their relationship to each other, greater than their relationship to the other manuscripts, is scarcely detectable except in the two passages mentioned.

For the rest, Frecht’s exemplar presents a very corrupt Widukind; nevertheless, I judged that all its readings should be recorded.

I have already said that Reineccius corrected this edition with the aid of the Dresden manuscript (Frankfurt, from the workshop of Wechel, 1577, folio). But, pursuing elegance of style, he often changed the author’s words—for example, *quia* always into *quod*—added some things, omitted others, and moreover badly disfigured the book with typographical errors. I therefore made no use of him, except that I attempted to fill from him the lacuna in the Dresden manuscript. For Reineccius read the two folios that had already been lost in Tenzel’s time; accordingly, for these chapters I have recorded all his readings, although doubtless not all were taken from the manuscript, and have marked them with the letter *a*.

**4.** The elder Meibomius published Widukind again at Frankfurt in 1621, folio, and illustrated it with annotations of no little value. His nephew reprinted this edition in the first volume of the *Scriptores rerum Germanicarum* (Helmstedt, 1688, folio). The elder states that he prepared his edition with the aid of a manuscript which, although incomplete, was mutilated in places, but that he generally followed Frecht’s exemplar.

He mentions the manuscript only twice [Note: [Col. 0121D] At the interpolated passage about Hatto’s treachery he notes (p. 675) that *iniquius* should be read instead of *aequius*, since no other manuscript supplies it; but at I, ch. 35, he says that some copies have *Rietni*, others *Kiesni* (p. 682). Reineccius published *Rietni* from the Dresden manuscript; it is now established that *Kietni* is read there.]. Otherwise he followed sometimes Frecht, sometimes Reineccius, without any consistent plan. In his notes, too, he compares only the readings of Reineccius and Urspergensis with Frecht’s edition. Although I would not deny that he saw a manuscript, perhaps the Dresden manuscript itself, it is sufficiently clear that he nowhere used it [Col. 0121B]. New errors were added to those of the editors, whether through typographical mistakes, the editor’s carelessness, or bold correction. I have recorded readings only in a few places.

Leibnitz, *SS. rerum Brunsvicensium*, I, p. 70, and Bouquet, *SS. rerum Gallicarum*, VIII, p. 217, also included fragments of Widukind, but without the aid of any manuscript.

Falke states that he possessed a manuscript of the monastery of Corvey [Note: [Col. 0121D] *Braunschweigische Anzeigen*, 1752, p. 1443.], and in his *Traditions of Corvey* gives several readings from it (pp. 159, 307, 401, 416, 456, 465, 471, 574, 584). I would certainly think that both the manuscript and the Corvey chronicle were fabricated, and that the readings were taken from those published by Leibnitz [Note: [Col. 0121D] After comparing the passage copied on p. 456 with Meibomius’s edition and the readings of the Casinensis manuscript, I still find this quite plausible.], unless Grupen, a man of the highest reliability, had professed that he himself had seen this manuscript [Note: [Col. 0121D] *Observationes*, I, p. 553.]. I would not readily say that he had been deceived by Falke. I found no trace of the manuscript, whether it has been lost or lies buried in darkness. So that nothing might be lacking from our edition, I have included the various readings noted by Falke [Col. 0121C] and marked them with β.

Ebert has shown that at the beginning of the sixteenth century a manuscript of Widukind was in the monastery of Neuwerk near Halle [Note: [Col. 0121D] *Archiv*, V, 526.]; unless it was the same as the Dresden manuscript, it must be regarded as lost.—No report of other manuscripts was made public for three centuries.

During the Middle Ages, however, there seem to have been several copies; for many chroniclers followed Widukind and copied him word for word in part. Thietmar must be named first: it is already sufficiently established that he drew a large portion of the first and second books from our author. Yet he almost nowhere retained Widukind’s actual words, but, in his customary manner, expressed the same events in altered language. He can therefore be used more to explain Widukind than to restore his wording.

**5.** The *Annals of Metz*, written in the tenth or eleventh century, took a very large amount from Widukind and reduced his narrative to an epitome. The manuscript edited by Chesne [Col. 0121D] ends with the words, I, ch. 36, “and having received the oath” [Note: [Col. 0121D] Cf. *Archiv*, VII, p. 385.], and generally agrees with the correct readings.

**6.** Ekkehard of Aura copied almost the whole of Widukind nearly word for word, using a manuscript which seems to come close to 2 [Col. 0122A] [Note: [Col. 0122D] Thus, on p. 143 of the 1609 edition, in recounting the deception devised by Hatto against Adalbert, it agrees entirely with 2.]. Through him Widukind’s narrative reached a great many medieval chroniclers: the monk of Hamersleben, the Saxon chronicler, the author of the Halberstadt chronicle, Albert of Stade, the writer of the Chronicle of Saint Pantaleon, Henry of Herford, Andrew of Regensburg, Trithemius, Staindel, and others [Note: [Col. 0122D] Thus the history entitled “How the Saxons first came to the land of Saxony,” published by Ludewig, *Reliquiae manuscriptorum*, VIII, p. 154, and what the anonymous author wrote about the origin of the Swabians (Goldast, *SS. rerum Suevicarum*, p. I) were taken from Ekkehard’s chronicle.]. All these, except Trithemius, seem not to have possessed Widukind’s book [Note: [Col. 0122D] The Saxon Chronicle seems to have taken from the Saxon Annalist what Ekkehard omitted.], but followed Ekkehard in narrating Saxon affairs.

Sigebert of Gembloux, however, used Widukind himself in writing his chronicles, but, aiming at a brief narrative, changed the wording almost everywhere, so that one can discern the manuscript’s reading scarcely once or twice; in these passages, however, he agrees generally with 1.

**7.** The Saxon Annalist used both Ekkehard and Widukind. He followed a manuscript of the same type as 2 (3) and 6, and reproduced it sufficiently accurately that he can often be useful in confirming the true reading.

[Col. 0122B] Several Saxon chroniclers of a later age may perhaps have possessed Widukind—for this is established in the case of Gobelinus Persona [Note: [Col. 0122D] Cf. VI, ch. 38.]—but no one copied the complete wording before Trithemius. Although he generally used Ekkehard, he certainly narrated the election and coronation of Otto with Widukind as his guide [Note: [Col. 0122D] *Annales Hirsaugienses*, I, p. 73.], while adding a great deal from his own invention.

With the aid of these materials I have attempted to restore Widukind’s books to integrity, following chiefly the Casinensis manuscript as the oldest, and correcting it with the help of the Dresden and Steinvelt manuscripts. None was copied directly from another; consequently, common errors and defects are scarcely to be detected, while I took care not to attribute the error of one manuscript to Widukind. Thus, where 1 often—but not always—has *urbs qui*, I refused to accept it; but where 1 and A have *fluvius quod*, I judged that it should be written so.

In presenting the wording I generally followed 1 and 2. Everywhere I wrote *namque*, *tamquam*, *umquam*, *aliquamdiu*, *dampno*, *tempto*, *sumptus*, *promptus*, etc.; *adm.*, *adn.*, *adp.*, *adq.*, *adt.*, *inb.*, *inm.*, and *inp.*, except in *imperio* and *imperatore*; *obp.*, *obt.*, *subc.*, *subp.*, which is what is usually found in both manuscripts and almost always in 2; moreover *heremitis*; from 1, *nothus*; from 2, *totiens*, and so forth.

Manuscripts 1 and 2 give *indutiae*, *contio*, *convicia*, *deliciae*, but in words of this kind they differ greatly from one another and are not always consistent with themselves. Manuscript 1 has *otium*, *pretium*, *nuntius*, *negotium*, *initium*, *audatia*, *tertius*, *vitium*, *palatium*, where 2 has *ocium*, etc.; it also has *amicitia*, *spacium*, *hospicium*, *sentencia*, but elsewhere *conditio*, *militia*, where 1 has *condicio*, *milicia*. In this variation I chiefly followed 1 and preferred *ti*.

Everywhere I also wrote *ae* and *ae*, although 2 very often gives *e* for *ae*, *et* for *ae*, and *ae*; but *ae* in these words—*paene*, *aelatus*, *aepiscopus*, *aequus*, *variae*, etc.—from 1; *aequus*, *laegatus* from 2—I refused to accept, nor did I record the manuscripts’ readings at every individual occurrence. Where certain peculiar forms occur in 1, such as *redidit*, *afirmare*, *neglego*, and so forth, I reported them in the critical notes [Col. 0122D].

In adding annotations, I chiefly aimed to correct the author’s errors, explain obscure passages, and illuminate geographical and chronological matters. Whatever Meibomius had already correctly observed, I thought should be credited to him, though I rejected most of his notes. What Leibnitz and Bouquet annotated seemed worthy of repetition scarcely once or twice. Throughout the preparation of this edition of Widukind, I gratefully acknowledge that I was aided by Pertz’s counsel and assistance to the greatest extent.

Hanover, 11 February 1839.  
G. WAITZ

# BOOK I

## TO LADY MAHTHILDIS [Note: [Col. 0123] *mathildam* in 1.], DAUGHTER OF THE EMPEROR. THE PREFACE TO THE FIRST BOOK BEGINS

[Note: [Col. 0123] Thus 1; these words are absent from 2 and A; 3 has “Widukind’s preface to Queen Mathildis.”]

[Col. 0123B] To Lady Mathildis, shining with maidenly bloom [Note: [Col. 0123] *mahthildi* in 2; here and usually *mathildae*, though once *mahtilda*; *mahtildi* in A.], imperial majesty, and singular wisdom: Widukind of Corvey [Note: [Col. 0123] *chorbeius* in 3.], the lowliest of the servants of Christ’s martyrs Stephen and Vitus [Note: [Col. 0123] *widikindus* in 2; *V.* in 3; *A.*], offers the most devoted [Note: [Col. 0123] *devotissimus* in 1.] service of all service and true salvation in the Savior. Although the singular glory of your paternal power magnifies you and your most illustrious wisdom adorns you [Note: [Col. 0123] A has “wisdom” for “power.”], our humility nevertheless presumes upon the ready clemency always associated with scepters, because our devotion may be received by your piety, even if it does not deserve to be.

For when you read, through our labor, the deeds of your most powerful father and most glorious grandfather committed to memory, you have material by which you may become better and more glorious than the best and most glorious of them. Yet we confess that we cannot comprehend all their deeds; we write briefly and in sections, so that our speech may be clear to readers and not wearisome.

I have also taken care to write a little about the origin and condition of the people over whom the lord of all things, King Heinricus [Note: [Col. 0123] *henricus* in 3 throughout; absent from A.], first ruled, so that by reading this you may refresh your mind, lighten your cares, and devote yourself to beautiful leisure. May Your Splendor therefore read this little book, mindful of us with the same piety with which it was written in devotion. Farewell [Note: [Col. 0123] Absent from 1.].

[Col. 0123] THE PREFACE ENDS [Note: [Col. 0123] Added from 1.].

## THE CHAPTERS BEGIN

[Col. 0123C]

1. Why he wrote other little books besides this one.  
2. He recounts the differing opinions of many concerning the origin of the Saxon people.  
3. That they came by ship to a place called Hadolaun.  
4. That the Thuringians were deeply angered by their arrival and fought with them.  
5. How a young man purchased land with gold.  
6. The Thuringians accuse the Saxons of breaking the treaty; but the Saxons emerge victorious.  
7. From where the Saxons are said to have received their name.  
8. The name of the Saxons becomes famous, and they are summoned by the Britons for assistance.  
9. Thiadricus [Note: [Col. 0123] *thriadricus* in c.] is chosen king and summons the Saxons for help against Hirminfridus.  
10. Iring [Note: [Col. 0123] *irring* in c.] incites Thiadricus [Note: [Col. 0123] *thadricus* in c.] against the Saxons.  
11. Hathagath challenges the Saxons to battle.  
12. After capturing the city, the Saxons take down the eagle.  
13. Thiadricus [Note: [Col. 0123] *thadricus* in c.] gives the land to the Saxons, and Hirminfridus is killed.  
14. How the Saxons divide the fields, and how they live according to a threefold class and law.  
15. How the great Charles made them Christians.  
16. Concerning Luthuvicus, Bruno, Oddo, and King Conrad.  
17. Concerning King Heinricus.  
18. Concerning the Hungarians, who are also called Avars.  
19. The Hungarians were confined by Charles the Great but released by Arnulf.  
20. How the Hungarians ravaged Saxony.  
21. Heinricus becomes duke of Saxony.  
22. Concerning Hinricus [Note: [Col. 0123] *hinricus* in c.], Bishop Hatto, and Count Adelberhtus.  
23. Concerning Conrad and his brother Evurhardus [Note: [Col. 0123] *euuthardus* in c.].  
24. Conrad besieged Heinricus.  
25. King Conrad’s speech before his death.  
26. Evurhardus [Note: [Col. 0123] *euuhardus* in c.] establishes Heinricus as king.  
27. After becoming king, Heinricus quickly gathers together the kingdom, which was in confusion.  
28. Concerning Luthuvicus and his sons.  
29. Concerning Charles, Oddo, and their descendants.  
30. How King Heinricus [Note: [Col. 0123] *regnus* in the manuscript.] obtained the kingdom of Lotharingia.  
31. Concerning the sons of King Heinricus and Queen Mathildis, and her genealogy.  
32. Concerning the Hungarians and their captive, and how peace was secured through him for nine years.  
33. Concerning the hand of Dionysius the martyr.  
34. Concerning Saint Vitus the martyr.  
35. How King Heinricus enjoyed nine years of peace.  
36. Concerning the Redarii and how they were defeated.  
37. Concerning the marriage of the king’s son.  
38. The king’s speech, and how he defeated the Hungarians in open battle.  
39. How he returned victorious and concerning his character.  
40. How he defeated the Danes.  
41. How he was weighed down by illness, died, and was buried.

[Col. 0125] THE CHAPTERS END.

## THE FIRST BOOK OF SAXON DEEDS BEGINS

[Note: [Col. 0125] These words are absent from 2 and 3.]

[Col. 0125B]

1. After the beginning of our works, in which I set forth the triumphs of the soldiers of the supreme Emperor, let no one wonder that I wish to commend the deeds of our princes to writing; for in that work I discharged, as best I could, what I owed to my profession, and now I do not avoid laboring, as I am able, for the devotion owed to my people and nation.

2. [Note: [Col. 0125] I supplied the number “2” here and corrected the subsequent numbers through chapter 8.] First, I shall briefly explain the origin and condition of the people, following in this matter almost nothing but popular report, since excessive antiquity has obscured nearly all certainty. For there is diverse opinion on this subject. Some think that the Saxons derived their origin from the Danes and Northmen [Note: [Col. 0125] *Nortmannisque* in 3 and A.]; others believe—as I myself heard someone proclaim when I was a young man—that the Saxons derived from the Greeks, because they themselves said that the Saxons were remnants of the Macedonian army which had followed Alexander the Great and, after his premature death, had been dispersed throughout the whole world [Note: [Col. 0125C] The fabulous origin of the Saxons, traced back even to the Macedonians, seems, as far as can be established, to have first been asserted by our Widukind. MEIBOM.].

In any case, there is no doubt that they were an ancient and noble people. A speech about them is also woven into Agrippa’s address to the Jews in Josephus [Note: [Col. 0125] *joseppo* in 1.]; and the judgment of the poet Lucan is cited in confirmation [Note: [Col. 0125D] In Lucan I, v. 423, the reading formerly stood:

> *Et Biturix, longisque leves Saxones in armis.*

But now, according to the judgment of Micylti and Turnebus, confirmed by the authority of the best manuscripts, the reading is *Suessones*.].

[Note: [Col. 0125D] Josephus’s passage occurs in *The Jewish War*, book II, chapter 16, where, however, there is no mention of the Saxons, but Germans are spoken of generally. MEIBOM. Others have observed that Hegesippus introduces Josephus delivering a speech about the Saxons in his history of the Jewish war; did our author perhaps have this passage in mind?]

3. But we know for certain that the Saxons came by ship to these regions [Note: [Col. 0126D] Cf. Rudolf concerning the translation of Saint Alexander, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, II, p. 674, who adds that the Saxons came forth from the Angles, inhabitants of Britain; our author does not seem to suggest this at all. Cf. Lappenberg, *History of England*, I, p. 87.—Our author, reporting that the Saxons came by ship to these regions—that is, to Saxony, which includes Nordalbingia—seems to regard them as having come from some distant region, as Rudolf thinks they came from Britain; I noted above that this agrees with the logic of the tradition. PERTZ.], and that they first landed at the place which to this day is called Hadolaun [Note: [Col. 0125] 2 has *vocatur* or *nuncupatur*; 1 has *hadolam*.] [Note: [Col. 0126D] It is sufficiently certain that Thuringians never settled in Haduloha (Hadeln).].

4. The inhabitants, who are said to have been Thuringians, were deeply angered by their arrival and took up arms against them; but the Saxons resisted fiercely and gained possession of the harbor. After they had fought among themselves for a long time, with many falling on both sides, both parties decided to negotiate peace and enter into a treaty. The treaty was concluded on these terms: the Saxons would have the opportunity to sell and buy, but would otherwise refrain from the fields, the killing of people, and robbery. The treaty stood inviolate for many days [Note: [Col. 0125] 3 has *ictumque*; A has *initumque*.]. But when the Saxons’ money ran out, so that they had nothing with which to sell or buy, they thought the peace useless to them [Note: [Col. 0125] 3 has *arbitrantur*.].

5. At that time, therefore, it happened that a certain young man [Note: [Col. 0125] 2 has *adolescentulum*, “a very young man.”] came out of the ships loaded with much gold [Note: [Col. 0125] 2 has “much gold” in the opposite order.], with a golden torque and golden bracelets as well. A certain Thuringian met him.

“Why,” he said, “is so much gold hanging around your hungry neck?”

“I am looking for a buyer,” he replied. “I carry this gold for nothing else; for I am dying of hunger—what pleasure can gold give me?” [Note: [Col. 0125] 1 has *delector*, “I am delighted.”]

The Thuringian asked about the quality and quantity of the price.

“There is no distinction in price for me, Saxon,” he replied; “whatever you give, I shall consider acceptable.” [Note: [Col. 0125] 2 and 6 have “there is no Saxon distinction for me,” an uncertain reading.]

The other, smiling at the young man, said: “What if I fill your lap with this dust?” For a great deal of earth had been dug up at the place.

The Saxon did not hesitate. He opened his lap, received the earth [Note: [Col. 0125] 3 has “received” in the past tense.], and immediately handed the gold to the Thuringian. Each returned happily to his own people.

The Thuringians praised the Thuringian to the skies because by a noble trick he had deceived the Saxon, and said that he was the luckiest of all mortals, since he had obtained so much gold for so low a price. For the rest, confident of victory, they were already, as it were, celebrating a triumph over the Saxons [Note: [Col. 0125] A has “the others.”].

Meanwhile the Saxon, deprived of gold but loaded with much earth, approached the ships. When his companions met him and wondered what he was doing, some of the friends began to mock him [Note: [Col. 0127] 3 has “some of the friends began to mock him.”], others to rebuke him; all alike thought him mad.

But he asked for silence and said: “Follow me, excellent Saxons, and I shall prove to you that my madness was useful.” Although doubtful, they nevertheless followed their leader [Note: [Col. 0127] A consistently has *secuntur*]. He took the earth and scattered it as finely as he could over the neighboring fields, then occupied the sites of the fortifications.

6. When the Thuringians saw the Saxons’ fortifications, they thought the matter intolerable [Note: [Col. 0127] 2 has “the matter seemed intolerable to them.”], and sent envoys to complain that the Saxons had broken the treaty and violated the agreement. The Saxons replied that they had hitherto preserved the treaty inviolate; they wished to retain the land purchased with their own gold in peace, or certainly to defend it by arms.

When they heard this, the inhabitants began to curse the Saxon gold; and the man whom shortly before they had proclaimed fortunate [Note: [Col. 0127] 2 has “they had proclaimed to be fortunate.”] they acknowledged as the author of their own destruction and that of their country [Note: [Col. 0127] Omitted in 3.].

Then, inflamed by anger, they rushed upon the camp in blind warfare, without order or plan. The Saxons, however, were ready to receive the enemy and struck them down; after affairs had gone well, they occupied the neighboring lands on every side by right of war.

After they had fought for a long time and repeatedly on both sides, and the Thuringians thought that the Saxons would prove superior to them, they asked through intermediaries that both parties meet unarmed and negotiate peace again, on a fixed day and at a fixed place. The Saxons replied that they would obey the request [Note: [Col. 0127] I have adopted this reading from 1.].

In those days the Saxons used large knives, of the kind still used by the English today, following the custom of their ancient people. Armed with these beneath their cloaks, the Saxons left the camp and met the Thuringians at the appointed place.

When they saw that the enemy were unarmed and that all the Thuringian leaders were present, they judged the time ripe for taking possession of the entire region. Drawing their knives, they rushed upon the unarmed and unsuspecting men and slaughtered them all, so that not one of them survived. The Saxons began to become famous and to inspire enormous terror in the neighboring peoples.

7. There were also those who report that their name was given to them because of this deed [Note: [Col. 0127] Omitted in A.]. For knives are called *sa[lacuna]s* in our language [Note: [Col. 0127D] Cf. Nennius, *History of the Britons*, ch. 48. Schaten, *History of Westphalia*, second edition, p. 119: “The use of this word,” he says, “still survives in Saterland among inhabitants who most faithfully preserve the ancient language; I heard them speaking there myself, and *sachs* means ‘knife.’”], and therefore they were called Saxons because they had slaughtered so great a multitude with knives.

### 8

While these things were happening among the Saxons [Note: [Col. 0127] 2 adds *quae*, “which.”]—or rather in the region now so called [Note: [Col. 0127] 2: *saxonicam*, “Saxon”—Britannia [Note: [Col. 0127] 3 consistently has *britannia*], long ago reduced to the status of a province by the emperor Vespasian [Col. 0128A] and for a long time living prosperously under the protection of the Romans, was attacked by neighboring nations, because it appeared to have been deprived of Roman assistance. For the Roman people, exhausted by serious foreign wars after the emperor Martialis had been killed by his soldiers [Note: [Col. 0127D] Is *Martiali* here the same as *bellicoso*, “warlike”—namely Maximus? Certainly no other mention of an emperor Martialis occurs elsewhere; nor is it likely that Widukind was thinking of the emperor Marcus, elected in Britain but shortly afterward killed (cf. Zosimus VI, 2). Since traditions are being discussed here, it is not surprising that the name of the emperor Marcianus, famous in the same fifth century, has been wrongly introduced. PERTZ.], was unable to provide its friends with the customary assistance.

Nevertheless, after constructing a massive work of defense for the protection of the region between the boundaries, from sea to sea, wherever the enemy’s attack seemed likely to come, the Romans abandoned the region. But against a fiercer enemy, ready for war, where a soft and indolent people resists warfare, there was no difficulty in destroying the work. Accordingly, when reports revealed the Saxons’ successful achievements, they sent a suppliant embassy to request their aid [Note: [Col. 0128D] Bede II, 15, also records that an embassy was sent; but our author alone gives this speech.].

The envoys came forward and said:

“Excellent Saxons, the wretched Britons [Note: [Col. 0127] A has *britti*, later *breiti*; 3 consistently *bracti*], worn out and utterly crushed by the enemy’s repeated incursions, have heard of the splendid victories you have won and have sent us to you, begging you not to withhold your aid from them [Note: [Col. 0127] 2 reverses the order: *auxilia vestra*, “your aid.”]. They place a broad, spacious land, richly supplied with every resource, under your authority. Until now we have lived freely under Roman protection and guardianship; after the Romans, we know of none better than you. Therefore we seek refuge beneath the wings of your valor. Through your valor and your arms may we be found so much superior to our enemies, and whatever service you impose upon us, we shall gladly endure.”

To this the fathers replied:

“Know that the Saxons are reliable friends of the Britons and will always assist their needs and interests equally.”

The envoys returned home rejoicing [Note: [Col. 0127] *in patriam redierunt*, “they returned to their homeland,” A.], making their allies even happier with the desired message. Then the promised army was sent to Britannia [Note: [Col. 0127] *brittaniam*, 1.], and, warmly received by its friends, soon freed the region from the raiders, restoring the homeland to its inhabitants. For there was not much labor involved in this task, since the enemy, already terrified by the fame of the Saxons heard long before, was panic-stricken as soon as their presence drove them away.

These peoples were hostile to the Britons: the Scots and the Picts [Note: [Col. 0127] *scothi et pechti* 1; later *scotti et pehti*; *scoti et pehiti* 2, later *scotti*; *scotti et pehtti* A; *schoti pehiti* 3.]. While fighting against them, the Saxons received from the Britons everything necessary for their use. They therefore remained in that region for some time, making good use of the Britons’ reciprocal friendship.

But when the leading men of the army saw a broad and fertile land, that the inhabitants’ hands were sluggish in warfare, and that they themselves, together with the greater part of the Saxons, lacked settled homes, they sent to recall a larger army [Note: [Col. 0129C] 2 reverses the order: *ad revocandum majorem exercitum mittunt*, “they send to recall a larger army”; cf. III, 54: “he recalled the entire army.”], and, after making peace with the Scots and Picts [Note: [Col. 0129] A: “after peace had been made with the Scots and Picts”; 3: “after a treaty had been established with the Scots and Picts.”] [Note: [Col. 0129C] Bede II, 15, says that a treaty with the Picts was entered into for a time; cf. Lappenberg, p. 70, n. 4.], rose together against the Britons, drove them from the region, and divided the region among themselves under their own authority.

And because that island lies in a certain corner of the sea [Note: [Col. 0129C] Cf. Jordanes, *On the Origin and Deeds of the Goths*, ch. 2: “Britannia, an island situated in the bay of the Ocean between the Spains, Gauls, and Germany.” It is strange that Widukind concealed the true origin of the name. Lappenberg has noted that Procopius and Pope Gregory were the first to call all the new inhabitants of Britain Angles, pp. 88, 118; but I have never found it stated when the name “Anglo-Saxons” became current.], they are called Anglo-Saxons (*Anglisaxones*) down to the present day.

If anyone wishes to know more fully about all these matters, let him read the history of that same people [Note: [Col. 0129C] I have no doubt that he means Bede’s *History*, where both the deeds of the Saxons and their conversion are related (II, 23).]; there he will find how, and under which leaders, all these events took place, and how they arrived at the name of Christianity through a man who was most holy in his own time—namely Pope Gregory [Note: [Col. 0129] *deest* in 3; perhaps also in 1.].

But let us return to the course of the history we have begun [Note: [Col. 0129] *recurramus*, corrected to *decurramus* in A, by a later hand.].

### 9

After this, Huga, king of the Franks [Note: [Col. 0129] *hugo*, 2, A.], died, leaving no other heir to the kingdom except his only daughter, named Amalberga, who had married Irminfrid [Note: [Col. 0129] Consistently *ermenfrido*; 1 sometimes *yrminfridus*.], king of the Thuringians.

The Frankish people, having been treated humanely and kindly by their elder, in return for giving thanks anointed as their king the son whom he had begotten from a concubine, named Thiadricus [Note: [Col. 0129] 2 consistently has *thiedericus*; 3 generally *thiadericus*; A consistently *theodericus*.] [Note: [Col. 0130C] No one can fail to see how greatly all this departs from the truth. King Theuderic of the Franks succeeded his father Chlodovech together with his three brothers; Gregory of Tours II, 28, also reports that he was born of a concubine. Concerning his father’s name Huga, cf. the *Quedlinburg Annals*. Amalberga, the wife of Irminfrid, was the granddaughter of Theoderic, king of the Goths: Jordanes, ch. 58. Cf. Procopius I, 14.].

Now Thiadricus, having been designated king, took care to send an embassy to Irminfrid in the interests of peace and harmony. The envoy entered Irminfrid’s presence and said:

“The best and greatest of mortals, my lord Thiadricus, has sent me to you, wishing you good health and long strength in a great and extensive reign. He commands me to say that he wishes to remain toward you not as a lord but as a friend, not as an emperor but as a kinsman, and to preserve inviolate toward you the rights of kinship to the very end. He asks only that you not dissent from the harmony of the Frankish people, for they follow him as their appointed king.”

To this Irminfrid, as befitted royal dignity, replied kindly that the wishes of the Frankish people pleased him [Note: [Col. 0129] 2: “that the wishes of the Frankish people pleased him.”], that he did not dissent from their harmony [Note: [Col. 0129] *ad*, 1.], and that he greatly needed peace [Note: [Col. 0129] *pacem*, 1.]. Regarding the matter of the kingdom, however, he wished to defer his answer until his friends were present. He treated the man honorably and made him remain with him for some time.

When the queen heard that her brother’s envoy had arrived and had spoken with the king about the matter of the kingdom, she urged Iring [Note: [Col. 0129] *hiringo*, 3.] that together they should persuade her husband that the kingdom had passed to her by hereditary right, since she was the daughter of a king and of a queen; whereas Thiadricus was her slave [Note: [Col. 0129] *deest*, 3.], born of a concubine, and it would therefore be disgraceful ever to place one’s hands in submission to one’s own slave [Note: [Col. 0129] A has *daret*, “should give.”].

Iring was a bold man, strong in hand, keen in intellect, sharp in judgment, persistent in carrying out undertakings, and skilled at persuading others to whatever he wished. Through these qualities he had bound Irminfrid’s mind to himself [Note: [Col. 0129] *conexerat*, 1; *connexuerat*, 3.].

Irminfrid summoned his leading men and close friends and laid the envoy’s words before them. They unanimously advised him to pursue what belonged to peace and harmony [Note: [Col. 0129] 2 has *et*; 2 also reads *consentire*, “to agree,” instead of *sentire*, “to judge,” or “to think.”], because he could not withstand the attack of the Franks, especially since he was being pressed from another side by more aggressive enemy forces.

But Iring, satisfying the wishes of the wanton woman, persuaded Irminfrid that he ought not to yield to the Franks, that he had the stronger claim in the matter of the kingdom, and that his extensive dominion, the hands and arms of his soldiers [Note: [Col. 0129] 2: “the hands of the soldiers,”] and his other resources for war were little different from those of Thiadricus [Note: [Col. 0130C] That is, they differed little between them. Cf. II, 10.].

In accordance with these words Irminfrid replied to the envoy that he did not deny Thiadricus his friendship and kinship, but that he could not help wondering [Note: [Col. 0129] *satis*, “quite,” added in 6; cf. ch. 13.] how he wished to seize an empire before possessing freedom: born a slave, how could he seek mastery over himself [Note: [Col. 0129] 1 has *dominum*—abbreviated *dñm*—“a lord”?]. He could not submit his hands to his own slave.

The envoy, greatly angered by this, replied:

“I would rather hand you this head of mine than hear such words from you [Note: [Col. 0129] 1: *audire a te*, “hear them from you.”], knowing that they must be washed away with much Frankish and Thuringian blood [Note: [Col. 0129] *diluenda*, 2, by a second hand, and 3.].”

After saying this, he returned to Thiadricus [Note: [Col. 0129] *deest* in A.] and concealed nothing of what he had heard.

Thiadricus, hiding excessive anger beneath a calm expression [Note: [Col. 0129] 2: *sereno celans*, “hiding it beneath a calm expression,”] said:

“We must hasten to serve Irminfrid [Note: [Col. 0129] 1 has *servitutem*, “servitude,”] so that, deprived of liberty, we may at least enjoy an empty life.”

As he approached the borders of the Thuringians with a powerful army, he found his brother-in-law [Note: [Col. 0130C] Widukind very often uses *gener* for “brother-in-law,” as Meibomius has already noted. Cf. I, 22; II, 18, and elsewhere. At times he uses the word in a broader sense. Cf. I, 39; II, 2.] waiting for him with a strong force at a place called Runibergun [Note: [Col. 0129] 2 has *runibergum*; 3 *rumbergum*.] [Note: [Col. 0130C] Now Ronneberg. MEIBOM. “Ronnenberg,” a village an hour and a half from Hanover toward the south and west, situated in the district of Marstem and famous for its ancient assembly; see above, *Quedlinburg Annals*, p. 32. PERTZ.].

A battle was joined, and the fighting continued with uncertain outcome for one day and a second. On the third day, Irminfrid was defeated and yielded to Thiadricus; fleeing, he finally withdrew with the rest of his retinue into the city called Scithingi [Note: [Col. 0131] A has *scidingi*; 3 *scithinge*; 2 *schidingin*; 6 *schidinga*.] [Note: [Col. 0131D] Now Burg-Scheidungen.
