Gregory of Tours III, 7, also relates that the Thuringians, defeated by King Theuderic, were driven as far as the river Unstrut.], situated on the river called Unstrode [Note: [Col. 0131] 1 has *unstredae*; 2 *unstrod*; 3 *unstruod*.].

Thiadricus then assembled his dukes and the leading men of the soldiers and asked the opinion of his army: did they think Irminfrid should be pursued, or should they return to their homeland?

Among them, Waldricus [Note: [Col. 0131] 2 and 3 have *waldericus*.], when consulted, said:

“I advise that we return home in order to bury the slain, tend the wounded, and gather a larger army. For I do not think that, after losing many thousands of your men, we shall be sufficient to complete the present war. If countless barbarian nations rise against us, while many of our men are disabled, through whom will you win [Note: [Col. 0131] 3 has *vinces*, “you will win,” instead of *vincis*, “you win.”]?”

Thiadricus had a sufficiently intelligent slave, whose sound judgment he had often tested and to whom he was consequently attached by a certain intimacy [Note: [Col. 0131] 2 has *quadam familiaritate propterea*, “for that reason by a certain intimacy.”]. When asked to give his opinion, he said:

“In honorable undertakings, I have always considered perseverance to be most beautiful. Our ancestors cultivated it so diligently that, once they had undertaken a task, they rarely or never abandoned it [Note: [Col. 0131] The reading *a ceptis* is uncertain.]. Yet I would not consider our exertions equal to those of men who, with small forces, overcame the immense forces of nations [Note: [Col. 0131] 1 has *superaverint*; 3 *superavere*.].

“Now the land is in our power, and by our withdrawal shall we provide the defeated with an opportunity to win? I too would embrace returning home and seeing my family and close relations, if I knew that our enemy was enjoying leisure during that interval. But perhaps our wounded men need this. Let the labor be that of the camp; for men with vigorous spirits, I think, it is the greatest pleasure.

“Thus the army has been severely weakened by the slaughter. Have all the enemies escaped? Certainly only very few [Note: [Col. 0131] 1 has the OCR-like form *rarisumus*, evidently for *rarissimus*]. The commander himself, like some little animal protected in its hiding place, is surrounded by the city’s defenses and does not dare safely to look upon the sky itself, compelled by fear of us. Yet he has no lack of money with which to hire barbarian nations, nor of soldiers, though they are weary. All these resources, however, are restored by our absence. It is disgraceful for victors to give the defeated an opportunity to win.

“Are we sufficient to provide garrisons for individual cities [Note: [Col. 0131] 1 has *sufficeremus*, “would suffice”]? We shall lose them all while going and returning.”

As he continued in this vein, Thiadricus and all who thirsted for the glory of victory decided to remain in the camp and send to the Saxons, who had long been the most bitter enemies of the Thuringians, so that they might come to his aid [Note: [Col. 0131] *deest* in 3.]. If they defeated Irminfrid and captured the city, he would hand over the land to them as an eternal possession.

The Saxons did not hesitate at all, but sent nine dukes, each with a thousand soldiers. The dukes entered the camp, each with a hundred soldiers, leaving the remaining multitude outside the camp, and greeted Thiadricus with peaceful words. When Thiadricus received them with an especially cheerful spirit, exchanged right hands with them, and granted the men permission to speak, they said:

“The Saxon people, devoted to you and obedient to your commands, have sent us to you. And here we are, ready for whatever your will may suggest [Note: [Col. 0131] 2 has *quod*, “whatever,” instead of *quodcumque*.]—ready either to defeat your enemies or, if fortune should command otherwise, to die for you. For you should know that the Saxons have no other purpose than the will to win, or at least the refusal to live [Note: [Col. 0131] A has *ni*, “if not,” instead of *nisi*, “unless”]; nor can we show our friends a greater favor than by despising death for them. And we wish you to learn this by experience.”

As they spoke, the Franks admired the men, outstanding in body and spirit. They also admired their unfamiliar dress, their weapons, their shoulders spread with flowing hair [Note: [Col. 0131] The first hand of 1 and the second hand of 3 read *diffusos scapulas caesarie*; the second hand of 1 and 2 have *diffusos scapulis caesarie*; A has *diffusam scapulis caesariem*.], and above all their immense firmness of spirit. For they were dressed in cloaks, armed with long spears, and stood supported by small shields, with large knives at their waists.

There were also those who said that the Franks had no need of friends so great and so formidable; that this was an untamed race of men and that, if they inhabited the present land, they would undoubtedly one day destroy Frankish rule.

Thiadricus, however, looking to his own interests [Col. 0132C], received the men into his allegiance and ordered them to prepare to attack the city [Note: [Col. 0131] 2 and A add *et*, “and.”]. Returning from the king, they pitched their camp on the southern side of the city, in meadows adjoining the river [Note: [Col. 0131] *deest* in 3.]. The next day, rising at first light and taking up their arms, they attacked and set fire to the town [Note: [Col. 0131] 1 has *oppungnant*, an erroneous form.].

After the town had been captured and burned, they drew up their battle line opposite the eastern gate [Note: [Col. 0131] A: “on the side opposite it.”]. The men shut inside the walls, seeing the battle line arranged and themselves placed in the extremity of their need [Note: [Col. 0131] 1 has “seeing the battle line arranged and themselves placed in the extremity of the multitude”], boldly burst through the gates and in blind fury rushed upon their opponents. Once missiles had been discharged, the fighting continued with swords.

As a fierce battle arose, many fell on one side and many on the other: the former fighting for their homeland, wives, and children, and finally for life itself; the Saxons fighting for glory and to acquire the land. The cries of men exhorting one another rose up, together with the clash of weapons and the groans of the dying, and the whole day passed in such a spectacle.

Since slaughter took place everywhere, with wailing everywhere, and neither army had yielded ground [Note: [Col. 0133] 2, 3, and 6 have *neutrum*, “neither one,” instead of *neuter*.], the late hour finally brought the battle to an end. On that day many Thuringians were killed and many wounded; of the Saxons, six thousand were counted among the slain [Note: [Col. 0133] 3 has *numerata*, “were counted,” and perhaps 1 also; 6 likewise.].

### 10

Iring was therefore sent by Irminfrid with a suppliant embassy and all his treasures to Thiadricus, seeking peace and voluntary surrender. Iring approached and said:

“Your kinsman, now your slave, has sent me to you, so that, if you do not pity him, you may at least pity your wretched sister [Note: [Col. 0133] 2 and 6 have “your sister”] and your nephews, who are placed in the greatest extremity.”

After he had said this weeping [Note: [Col. 0133] 1 has *lacrimis*, “with tears.”], the intervention of leading men corrupted by gold added that it would be fitting royal clemency not to reject such a supplication and not to forget the common laws of human nature. It would also be more advantageous to receive into his allegiance a man whom he already held defeated and so crushed that he could never rise against him, rather than that untamable race of men, enduring in every hardship, from whom the Frankish empire could expect nothing but danger.

After the war had been completed, he could also consider how hard and unconquerable the Saxons were [Note: [Col. 0133] 1 has *quandiu*, “for how long”; 3 *quam diu*, “how long”; A *superabiles*, “surmountable,” instead of “unconquerable.”]. It would therefore be better, once the Thuringians had been received, for them to drive the Saxons together from their own borders [Note: [Col. 0133] At this point 1 begins chapter 11, which does not agree with the preceding table of contents; it is evident that the scribe made a mistake, since chapter 17 was later numbered twice.].

Although unwilling, Thiadricus was nevertheless swayed by these words and promised that on the following day he would receive his brother-in-law and cast out the Saxons. When Iring heard this, he fell at the king’s feet, praised the decision as an act of imperial clemency, and, sending his lord the desired message, made him and the whole city more secure. He himself remained in the camp [Note: [Col. 0133] 3 has *in castris ipse*, “himself in the camp”], lest the night bring about some hostile action.

Meanwhile, now that the city had been made more secure by the promised peace, a certain man went out with a hawk, seeking food along the bank of the aforesaid river. When he released the bird [Note: [Col. 0133] *emissa*, “when it had been released,” feminine, referring to the bird], one of the Saxons on the farther bank immediately caught it [Note: [Col. 0133] 3 has *eam*, “it,” feminine]. When the man asked that it be returned [Note: [Col. 0133] In A, the words from *in ulteriore* through *Quo rogante* were written by a second hand after other writing had been erased.], the Saxon refused to give it back.

The man then said:

“Give it back, and I shall disclose a secret useful to you and your companions [Note: [Col. 0133] A adds *tuis*, “your.”].”

The Saxon replied:

“Speak, so that you may receive what you seek.”

“The kings,” he said, “having made peace with one another, have agreed that if you are found in the camp tomorrow, you will be captured or certainly killed.”

The Saxon replied:

“Are you saying this seriously [Note: [Col. 0133] A and 6 have *serio*, “seriously”] or in jest [Note: [Col. 0133] 2 reverses the order: “or are you saying this in jest”]?”

“The second hour of the following day will prove it,” he answered, “for you will have to act without jesting. Therefore look to your own interests and seek safety in flight.”

The Saxon immediately released the hawk and reported to his companions what he had heard [Note: [Col. 0133] 1 has *rettulit*, “reported back.”]. They were sufficiently disturbed and could not find at once what they ought to do about it [Note: [Col. 0133] 2 and A have *non inveniebant*, “they did not find.”].

### 11

At that time there was in the camp a certain man from among the veteran soldiers [Note: [Col. 0133] The words *de veteranis militibus*, “from among the veteran soldiers,” are omitted in 4.], already advanced in years but still vigorous in a green old age. He was rightly called the father of fathers among men of good qualities. His name was Hathagat [Note: [Col. 0133] Ruodolfus says that he was then the Saxons’ duke, *ibid.*].

He seized the standard that was held sacred among them, marked with the figures of a lion and a dragon, and above them a flying eagle [Note: [Col. 0133] 2 has *effige*, “figure.”]. In displaying the effectiveness of courage and prudence and declaring the steadfastness of his spirit by his bodily movement [Note: [Col. 0133] This phrase is absent from 2 and A.], he said:

“Thus far I have lived among the finest of the Saxons, and age has brought me to almost this final old age. I have never seen my Saxons flee [Note: [Col. 0133] 2 has *meos Saxones*, “my Saxons.”]. How am I now compelled to do what I have never learned [Note: [Col. 0133] Omitted in 2 and A.]? I know how to fight; I do not know how to flee, nor am I able to do so. If fate does not allow me to live longer, at least let me be permitted to fall with my friends, which is sweetest to me.

“The bodies of our friends lying prostrate around us are an example to me of ancestral valor [Note: [Col. 0133] 2, 3, and 6 have *virtutes*, “virtues,” instead of *virtutis*, “valor.”]. They preferred to die rather than be defeated, to lose their vigorous lives rather than yield their ground before their enemies.

“But why must I prolong an exhortation concerning contempt for death? Look: we shall go against men who are secure, for slaughter alone, not for battle. They suspect nothing because of the promised peace and our serious wound; fatigued by today’s battle, they remain without fear, without watchfulness, and without their customary guard.

“Let us therefore rush upon men taken unawares and buried in sleep; the labor will be slight! Follow me as your leader, and I offer you this old head of mine if what I say does not come to pass.”

Roused by these excellent words, they spent what remained of the day restoring their bodies. Then, when the signal was given during the first watch of the night, at the time when deeper sleep usually overtakes mortals, they took up their arms, their leader going before them, and rushed upon the walls. Finding neither watches nor guards, they entered the city with a mighty uproar.

Awakened by this, some of the enemy sought safety in flight; others wandered like drunken men through the streets and along the walls of the city; others fell upon the Saxons, thinking them their fellow citizens. The Saxons put all those of full age to death and preserved the underage as booty [Note: [Col. 0133] 3 has the contracted forms *quaesiere*, *erravere*, *incidere*, *tradidere*, and *servavere*.].

That night was full of shouting, slaughter, and plunder, and no place in the entire city was quiet until the glowing dawn arose and proclaimed the bloodless victory [Col. 0134D]. Since complete victory lay with the king—namely Irminfrid [Note: [Col. 0135C] That is, victory in capturing or killing King Irminfrid.]—he was sought out and found to have escaped with his wife, children, and a small retinue.

### 12

When morning came, they set up an eagle at the eastern gate. Building an altar of victory, they venerated their own sacred things with the worship proper to each, according to the error of their ancestors: in name they imitated Mars, in the figure of the columns Hercules [Note: [Col. 0135] 2 has *effigie*, “in figure,”] [Note: [Col. 0135] 4 has *innitentes*, “leaning upon,” instead of *imitantes*, “imitating”], and in the location the Sun [Note: [Col. 0135] The manuscripts punctuate the words as printed here; 3 has *solis*, “of the sun.”], whom the Greeks call Apollo [Note: [Col. 0135C] The Saxons venerated the god Hirmin after gaining the victory. Widukind thought that Hirmin was the same as Hermes; but when he calls Hermes—that is, Mercury—a god whom the Greeks call Mars, he is mistaken. I add here the words of the distinguished V. Grimm, communicated to me in a letter:

“Widukind therefore says that the Saxon Hirmin signifies by name Mars—that is, Mercury—by form Hercules, because he appears armed in heroic fashion, as Wuotan normally does not; and by the place where he was erected, the Sun. This can, as you yourself have already noted, refer only to the eastern gate.”

Concerning the god Hirmin, cf. his *Mythology*, p. 209, etc., where, however, he followed the earlier reading.

I would explain the passage, in accordance with Ruodolf’s opinion concerning the Irminsul cited above (*SS.* II, 676), as follows: in constructing the altar of Victory, they venerated their gods with the worship proper to each of them—Mars by placing his name, that is, Irmin, upon the altar; Hercules by imitating his form in the figure of the columns—a wooden column raised high, which in some fashion represented the sign of Hercules; and the Sun by choosing the site of the altar at the eastern gate. This is Widukind’s meaning: he therefore relates that, as a sign of victory, the Saxons erected an Irminsul altar at the eastern gate of Scheidingen. Hence light is also shed upon the passage in Tacitus, *Annals* I, 61: “Faces of men fixed upon tree trunks; barbarian altars in nearby groves, before which they had slaughtered tribunes and centurions of the first ranks.” PERTZ.].

From this it appears that the opinion of those who think that the Saxons derived their origin from the Greeks is in either case plausible, because Hirmin or Hermis [Note: [Col. 0135] 3 has *chermis*, “Chermis.”] is called Mars in Greek. We still use this word, whether in praise or blame, down to the present day, even when we do not know its meaning [Note: [Col. 0136C] “Do the final words mean: ‘We use the intensifying prefix *irmin*—without understanding its meaning—in words of good and bad significance?’ Thus, doubtless correctly, J. Grimm interpreted these words, *Mythology*, p. 210. Cf. ibid., p. 82ff.

It seems to me that the relative clause should refer to Mars: although the Saxons did not at all fail to understand *Hirmin*, they used the word in their own language for praise in *mari*, *mar*, “bright,” and for blame in *mara*, meaning “incubus,” and in compounds of those words. PERTZ.].

For three days, therefore, they celebrated the days of victory, divided the enemy’s spoils, and performed the funeral rites of the slain. They raised their commander to heaven with praises, proclaiming that he possessed a divine spirit and heavenly strength, and that by his steadfastness he had led them to accomplish so great a victory.

All these events occurred, as the memory of the ancestors has handed down, on the Kalends of October [Note: [Col. 0135] *deest* in 3]. Those days of error were later changed, by the decree of religious men, into fasts and prayers, together with the offerings of all the Christians who preceded us [Note: [Col. 0136D] Beginning on the Sunday immediately following the feast of Michael, that week known as *die gemeine Wochen*—“the common week”—begins. Traces of it are found down to the sixteenth century and later. The old chronicle of the dukes of Brunswick, Leibniz II, p. 16, also connected it with this Saxon victory. Halthaus collected further evidence for it in *Calendar of the Middle Ages*, p. 131. Grimm notes that during the same days the festival of the goddess Cisa of the Suevi was also celebrated, *Mythology*, p. 188.].

### 13

After all these events had been accomplished [Note: [Col. 0135] A, 2, and 3 have *peractis*, “completed.”], they returned to Thiadricus in the camp. He received them, praised them sufficiently, and granted them the present land as an eternal possession [Note: [Col. 0135] 3 adds *in*, “in.”]. They were also called allies and friends of the Franks, and they first inhabited the city which they had spared from the fire as though it were their own walls.

Since the fate that followed the kings is a memorable story, I do not neglect to relate it [Note: [Col. 0135] 1 has *neglego*, “neglect,” instead of *negligo*.]. Finally, Iring, sent to Thiadricus on the day the city was captured, was received by him on the following night and remained in the camp.

When it was learned that Irminfrid had escaped, Thiadricus arranged for him to be recalled by deceit, so that Iring might kill him, as though Iring were to receive splendid gifts from him and be honored with great power in the kingdom, while Thiadricus himself would appear unrelated to the murder.

Although Iring accepted this unwillingly, he was corrupted by false promises and eventually yielded, confessing that he would obey Thiadricus’s will [Note: [Col. 0135] *deest* in 1 and 3.].

Irminfrid was therefore recalled and threw himself at Thiadricus’s feet. Iring, standing beside him like a royal armor-bearer with drawn sword, slaughtered his prostrate lord [Note: [Col. 0135] 2 has *truncavit*, “cut down,” instead of *trucidavit*, “slaughtered.”].

Immediately the king said to him:

“Having made yourself hateful to all mortals by such a deed, by killing your lord, you have an open road for departing from us [Note: [Col. 0135] 1 has *discendendi*, an erroneous form]. We do not wish to share in the lot or portion of your wickedness.”

Iring replied:

“I have rightly become hateful to all mortals, because I obeyed your deceit. Before I leave, however, I shall cleanse this crime of mine by avenging my lord [Note: [Col. 0135] 1 and 3 have *vindicabo*, “I shall avenge,” instead of *vindicando*, “by avenging.”].”

With his sword drawn, he stood over him and cut down Thiadricus as well. Taking his lord’s body, he placed it upon Thiadricus’s corpse [Note: [Col. 0135] *deest* in 3], so that at least in death he might conquer—the man who had been conquered while alive—and, making a path with his sword, he departed.

Whether any credence should be given to these words is for the reader to decide [Note: [Col. 0135] 2: “whether credence should be given to the words.”]. Everyone understands that this narrative was drawn from ancient poems [Note: [Col. 0136D] The editor observes that the account clearly derives from ancient songs.].

Nevertheless, we cannot be sufficiently amazed [Note: [Col. 0135] 6 adds *satis*, “sufficiently”; cf. above, ch. 9.] that the story became so widely famous [Note: [Col. 0135] 1 has *tantam*, “so great,” instead of *in tantum*] that, after Iring’s name—as he is called—the Milky Way in the sky is still marked to the present day [Note: [Col. 0136D] Cf. Grimm, *Mythology*, p. 214ff.].

### 14

The Saxons, therefore, having taken possession of the land, rested in the greatest peace [Col. 0137A], enjoying alliance and friendship with the Franks. They also divided part of the fields among their allied helpers and freedmen, while condemning the remnants of the expelled people to tribute [Note: [Col. 0137] 3 has *condemnavere*, “they condemned.”]. Hence, down to the present day, the Saxon people is divided according to a threefold status and law, apart from the servile condition [Note: [Col. 0137] The words from *praeter* through *dividitur* are omitted in 2.] [Note: [Col. 0137D] Ruodolfus relates that, after the Saxons had been weakened by war, they handed over part of the land, especially the eastern part, to settlers, p. 675; afterward he lists four orders of the people, placing slaves fourth. I would scarcely think that our author wrote this passage from him.].

The duchy of the entire people was administered by three princes, who were content with the authority to assemble an army within fixed boundaries [Note: [Col. 0137] 2 has *contendendi*, “of striving,” instead of *congregandi*, “of assembling.”]. We know these districts by their proper locations and names: the Eastern peoples, the Angarii, and the Westphalians [Note: [Col. 0137] 3 has *westvalos*.].

If a general war broke out [Note: [Col. 0137] 2, by a second hand, and A have *ingruerit*, “should break out.”], a leader was chosen by lot, whom everyone was required to obey [Note: [Col. 0137] 2 has *oporteat*, “must obey,”] for the conduct of the impending war. Once it had been completed, each man lived under equal right and law, content with his own authority [Note: [Col. 0137D] Cf. Bede V, 11: “For these ancient Saxons do not have a king, but many rulers placed over their people. When a time of war arises, they cast lots equally, and whomever the lot indicates, all follow him as leader during the war and obey him. Once the war is finished, all the rulers again possess equal power.” These words do not seem inconsistent with Widukind; Frecht also maintained that our author derived his account from them.].

It is not for us to discuss the diversity of laws in this little book, since the Saxon law is found carefully described in several works.

The Trans-Badanian Suevi [Note: [Col. 0137] 1 has *suuavi*; 2 *suabi*; 3 *suevi*.] [Note: [Col. 0137D] That is, Suevi living beyond the Bode in the district of Suevego. Cf. Grupen, *Origins* II, p. 397ff.] invaded the region they inhabit at the time when the Saxons entered Italy with the Lombards [Note: [Col. 0137] 1 has *saxonis*; 3 *adiere*, “entered.”] [Note: [Col. 0137D] As their history relates, Paul the Deacon II, 6.], and therefore they use laws different from those of the Saxons [Note: [Col. 0137D] Traces of this distinction remained throughout the Middle Ages, as is shown by the work called the *Saxon Mirror*. Cf. Homeyer, *Index*, s.v. “Schwabe,” p. 372.].

Thus the Saxons, having experienced the varied loyalty of the Franks—about which it is not for us to speak, since it is found written in their deeds [Note: [Col. 0137D] Perhaps the works of Einhard, the *Life of Charlemagne* and the *Annals*, from which what follows may appear to have been taken.]—remained bound by their ancestral error down to the time of Charlemagne [Note: [Col. 0137] 1, 3, and A consistently have *carolus*.] [Note: [Col. 0137] A, 2, and 3 have *perdurabant*, “they remained,” instead of *perdur arunt*, “they endured.”]

15. But the great Charles, being the bravest of kings, watched over his realm with no less wisdom. Indeed, he considered that in his time there was no mortal wiser than himself, and that a neighboring and noble people ought not to be held back by a groundless error. He strove by every means to lead them onto the true path—[Note: “the true way” in A, 2, and 3]—sometimes compelling them by gentle persuasion, sometimes by the force of war. At last, in the thirtieth year of his reign, he succeeded; for, having been made emperor from a king, he did not cease his efforts over many years. Consequently, those who had once been allies and friends of the Franks have now become, through the Christian faith, brothers and, as it were, a single people, as we see today.

16. The last of the Carolingians to rule among the East Franks was Hluthowicus [Note: In Migne, the letter in square brackets is printed above the preceding letter. I have written it thus everywhere, following the Annals of Corvey and manuscript 1, where it is sometimes *hluthouicus* and *hluthuuicus*, but more often *luthuuicus* or *luthouicus*, and later *lu]dewicus*, followed by *ludewicus* in A and *ludowicus* in 2; 3 has almost always *Lothowicus*]. He was born from Arnulf [Note: 3 generally has *Arnulphus*], Charles’s cousin, the great-grandfather of this King Lothar [Note: Lothar was king of the West Franks from 954 onward; but Widukind confuses his great-grandfather—not his great-great-grandfather—Charles the Bald with Charles the Fat, the paternal uncle of Arnulf. See chapter 28]. After taking as his wife a woman named Liudgarda [Note: 2 alternates between *luidgarda* and *liudgarda*; A always has *ludgarda*], the sister of Bruno and of the great Duke Oddo [Note: 2 alternates between *otto* and *oddo*; A and 3 always have *otto*], he did not live many years thereafter.

Their father was Liudulfus [Note: 2 has both *luidolfus* and *liudolfus*; A always has *ludolfus*; 3 generally has *luidolphus*]. He went to Rome and brought back the relics of Blessed Pope Innocent [Note: On this translation, see Agius, *Life of Hathumod*, chapter 1; Hrotsvit, *On the Gandersheim Convent*, lines 118 ff.; Wedekind, *Notes* I, pp. 159 ff., demonstrates that it took place in 844]. Among these descendants, Bruno [Note: *Bruno* in 3], after administering the dukedom of all Saxony [Note: *administraret* in 3], led an army against the Danes. Surrounded by a sudden flood and having no place in which to fight, he perished with his entire army [Note: See the Annals of Fulda for 880. As for the site of the battle, see Grupen, *Germanic Origins* II, pp. 214 ff., and Wedekind, *Notes* I, pp. 295 ff. Wedekind likewise observed that, with Thietmar (p. 32), this should be understood as a flood of the river, not, as in the Annals of Saxony for 879, a flood of troops], leaving the dukedom to his younger brother [Note: *also* in A], who was far superior in every virtue, in 880.

King Hluthowicus, however, had no son, and the entire people of the Franks and Saxons [Note: See I, chapter 26; II, chapter 1] sought to place the diadem of the kingdom upon Oddo. But Oddo, as though already burdened by age [Note: His father Liudulfus had died forty-six years earlier, already in 866. See the Annals of Xanten for that year], declined the burden of rule. Nevertheless, at his advice, Conradus, formerly duke [Note: Absent in 2], of the Franks was anointed king [Note: *ungitur* in A, 2, and 3]; supreme authority, however, always and everywhere remained with Oddo [Note: 2 and 3 have *vigebat*].

[Col. 0139A] 17. A son was then born to him, necessary to the whole world, the greatest and best of kings: Heinricus, who was the first to rule Saxony with unrestricted authority [Note: Meibomius already understood that these words must be interpreted in light of another passage in Widukind (I, chapter 34): Heinricus governed Saxony in such a way that, with every other authority removed, he himself held the entire government of the land as both king and duke].

From his earliest youth he adorned his life with every kind of virtue, advancing day by day in outstanding prudence and in the glory of every good action [Note: “of the good arts” in A]. From adolescence, his greatest concern was to bring glory to his people and to establish peace throughout all his authority. His father, observing the young man’s prudence and the greatness of his judgment, entrusted him with the army and military command against the Dalamantians [Note: 2 always has *dalmatia*] [Note: This Slavic province, called Glomaci by the Slavs themselves, according to Thietmar (p. 4), lay near the Elbe in the territory of Meissen]. His father had himself campaigned against them for a long time. Unable to withstand his attack, the Dalamantians [Note: *dalanci* in 1; *dalamanti* in A; *dalmatii* in 2; *Dalmatae* in 3] brought the Avars against him, whom we now call Hungarians [Note: 3 always has *Ungaros*], a people most fierce in war [Note: Absent in 2] (906).

[Col. 0139B] 18. The Avars, as some believe, were remnants of the Huns [Note: *hunonum* in 1]. The Huns emerged from the Goths, and the Goths, as Jordanes relates [Note: Jordanes, chapter 3, who calls the island Scandza; what follows is taken from the same work, chapter 24], departed from an island named Sulza. The Goths were named after their own leader, called Gotha [Note: *Gotho* in 3].

When certain women in his army were accused of practicing magic, they were investigated and found guilty. Although their number was great, he refrained from inflicting the punishment they deserved; nevertheless, he expelled them all from the army. After their expulsion, they sought a nearby forest [Note: Absent in 2]. Since it was surrounded by the sea [Note: *cingerentur* in 2 and 3] and by the Maeotian marshes, no route of departure lay open to them. Some of them, already pregnant [Note: Absent in 1], gave birth there. As one generation after another was born from them, a strong people came into being. Living like wild beasts, uncultivated and untamed, they became exceedingly skilled hunters.

After many centuries, when they had no knowledge at all of the other part of the world where they dwelt, it happened that a hind was found while hunting and pursued until, with the animal leading the way, they crossed the Maeotian marshes by a route that had previously been impassable to all human beings. There they saw cities, fortified towns, and a previously unseen kind of human being. They returned by the same route and reported such things to their companions.

The others, out of curiosity, went in a multitude to test what they had heard. When the neighboring cities and fortified towns saw the unknown multitude and bodies frightful in appearance and dress, they believed them to be demons and fled. The newcomers, astonished at these strange sights, at first refrained from slaughter and plunder. But when no one resisted them, touched by human desire [Note: The words beginning “but … desire” are absent in 2], they carried out a great slaughter of human beings and thereafter spared nothing. After taking substantial booty, they returned to their settlements.

But when they saw that events were turning out differently for them, they came again with their wives, children, and all their rustic belongings [Note: *aggresti* in 1], ravaging the neighboring peoples on every side, and finally began to inhabit Pannonia.

19. After they had been defeated by the great Charles [Note: 2 reverses the order to “by the great Charles”] and [Note: Absent in A] driven beyond the Danube, they were enclosed by a huge rampart [Note: 3 has *circumfusi*] [Note: The belief that the Avars had been enclosed by a great rampart by Charles the Great was common in the tenth century. See Liudprand I, chapter 13] and prevented from continuing their customary devastation of peoples.

Under Arnulf, however, the work was destroyed, and a route by which they could inflict harm was opened to them, because the emperor was angry with King Centupulchus [Note: 3 has *Centupulchro*] of the Moravians [Note: 2 has *maurorum*; 3, *Moravorum*] [Note: Swatopluk, or Zwentibald, duke of the Moravians].

[Col. 0140B] Thereafter, how great a slaughter and how great an injury they inflicted upon the Frankish Empire is still testified by the cities and regions lying desolate. We have thought it worthwhile to speak of this people for this reason: so that your clarity may recognize with what kind of men your grandfather and father had to contend, and from what enemies nearly all Europe has now been liberated through the power of their foresight and the distinction of their arms [Note: *almost* is absent in 1].

20. Thus the aforesaid army of Hungarians, hired by the Slavs [Note: 1 generally has *slavi*, sometimes with the letter *c* written above it; 2 alternates between *slavi* and *sclavi*; A and 3 have *sclavi*], after inflicting great slaughter in Saxony and capturing immeasurable booty, returned to Dalamantia [Note: 3 has “into Dalmatia.”]. There they encountered another Hungarian army, which threatened to make war upon their allies because they had despised their assistance after leading them to such great plunder.

As a result, Saxony was ravaged a second time by the Hungarians [Note: 1 has “they ravaged Saxony”]. While the first army waited for the second in Dalamantia, that land itself was reduced to such miserable poverty that, leaving their native soil, its inhabitants served other nations for food that year.

21. (912.) When the father of his country and great duke Oddo had died, he left the dukedom of all Saxony to his illustrious and magnificent son Heinricus [Note: 3 adds *ipse*; 1 perhaps also]. He had other sons as well, Thancmarus [Note: *thangmarus* in A and 2] and Liudulfus, but they had died before their father.

King Conradus, having often tested the new duke’s valor, feared to entrust him with all his father’s authority [Note: Thietmar (p. 6): “He received by hereditary right and from the king’s free gift the inheritance and the greatest part of the benefice.” Conrad seems to have denied the new duke the Thuringian districts administered by his father Otto]. For this reason he incurred the indignation of the entire Saxon army [Note: 2 reverses the order to “of the Saxon army”].

Nevertheless, speaking at length in feigned praise and glorification of the excellent duke, he promised that he would give him greater things and honor him with great distinction [Note: The words “and honor him …” are absent in 1]. The Saxons paid no attention to such pretenses, but advised their duke that, if the king was unwilling voluntarily to honor him with his father’s honor, he could obtain whatever he wished even against the king’s will [Note: A has *regi*; 1 perhaps also].

When the king saw that the Saxons’ attitude toward him was more severe than usual, and that he could not crush their duke in open war, he proceeded—with the support of a force of brave soldiers [Note: Widukind’s *milites* are greater vassals. See chapter 22 and II, chapter 1] and with an army of countless numbers—to arrange for him to be killed by treachery, by whatever means.

22. [Note: On this passage, see the preface. Manuscripts 2, 3, and also 6 and 7 read the text as follows.]

At that time there was an archbishop of the see of Mainz named Hatho [Note: *hattho* in 1], sharp in counsel, fierce in intellect, and accustomed by his versatility to surpass many mortals. Wishing to please King Conrad and the Frankish people at the same time, he attacked by his customary art a man whom supreme clemency had specially granted to us, and had a golden torque made for him [Note: On this manner of death, see *Waltharius*, line 1059, ed. Grimm, p. 39; see also p. 72]. He then invited him to a banquet at which he was to be honored with great gifts from him.

Meanwhile, the bishop entered the goldsmith’s workshop to inspect the work. When he saw the torque, he is said to have sighed deeply. The goldsmith asked the reason for his sigh. He replied that the torque was destined to be dipped in the blood of the excellent and very dear Heinricus [Note: Absent in 1]. The goldsmith concealed what he had heard in silence [Note: 2, in the first hand, has “concealed”]. When the work had been completed and delivered, he asked for and received permission to depart [Note: 1 has “asked”]. Meeting the duke as he went to attend to these matters, he told him what he had heard.

The duke, greatly angered, summoned the bishop’s envoy, who had already arrived to invite him, and said: “Go and tell Hatho [Note: 1 has *athoni*; 3 always has *Hattoni*] that Heinricus does not have a harder neck than Adelberhtus [Note: 1 has *adelberthtus*, later *adelberhtus*; 2 and 3 always have *adelbertus*], and that we have judged it better to remain at home and discuss his service than now to burden him with the multitude of our retinue.”

That Adelberhtus, as they say, having once been received into the faith by the bishop himself, was deceived by his counsel—we do not approve this, and therefore never assert it, but believe it to have been fabricated more by popular rumor.

Then he immediately occupied everything that belonged to Hatho’s jurisdiction throughout Saxony or the land of the Thuringians [Note: “his own jurisdiction” in 2] [Note: That is, Hatho’s, as Thietmar also understands the passage]. He also afflicted Burghardus [Note: 2 has *Burchardus*] and Bardo [Note: Burghardus and Bardo seem correctly to have been judged by Wenck (*History of Hesse* II, p. 545 n. e.) to have been sons of Duke Burghardus, killed in 908; which of them was the king’s son-in-law—that is, his brother-in-law—is not known]—one of whom was the king’s son-in-law—to such an extent, and crushed them in frequent wars so completely, that they withdrew from the land [Note: It is probable that those counts possessed estates in southern Thuringia, and that Heinricus, having gained control of them, held all Thuringia from this time onward]. He divided all their property among his own soldiers [Note: “his soldiers” in 2 and 3].

But when Hatho saw that his cunning had been brought to an end, and that the affairs of the Saxons were flourishing, he was overcome by excessive grief and illness alike and died after not many days [Note: 4 has “justice” instead of “grief”]. There were also those who said that he had been struck by a thunderbolt from heaven and, shattered by the blow, had died the following day (913, May 15) [Note: According to Ekkehard, he was consumed by an Italian fever].

[Note: Manuscripts 2 and 3 give the following account.]

For this undertaking he had, as is reported, a man particularly suited: Hatho, bishop of the see of Mainz [Note: *Hattonem* in 3]. He was of obscure birth and sharp intellect, so that it was difficult to determine whether he was better or worse in counsel [Note: 3 reads *et* (“and”) for *ut* (“so that”)]. This can be inferred from one of his actions.

When there was a war between Cuonradus [Note: *Chuonrado* in β], the father of King Conrad [Note: *patre* in 2], and Adelbertus [Note: *Adalberto* in β], the king’s nephew through his sister [Note: *nepote* in β; the words “through his sister” are absent in 2], Adelbertus’s brother was killed first [Note: 3 and β read *primum* (“first”)]. Later [Note: *est*, perhaps in A and β], in revenge for his brother, Cuonradus too was killed by Adelbertus. No king could put an end to so great a war between eminent men [Note: 2 reads *ne* (“not”); β reads “could calm it”].

At last the supreme bishop was sent to settle so immense a discord. Entering Adelbertus’s city, he swore under oath either to make peace between him and the king or to restore him unharmed to his place [Note: 3 has “after he had made peace”]. Adelbertus agreed to these terms and, as a token of faith and friendship, asked him to taste something. When the bishop refused, he immediately left the city.

After he had crossed the town with his entire retinue, he is said to have cried out [Note: 3 has “proclaimed”]: “Alas,” he said, “the man who rejects what is offered asks too often. I am tired of the longer road and the later hour, for we cannot walk all day fasting.”

Adelbertus, delighted, bent his knees before the bishop and begged him to return to the city so that he might taste something. The bishop returned to the city with Adelbertus and, as it seemed to him, was released from the obligation of his oath because he had restored Adelbertus unharmed to his place.

Afterward Adelbertus was presented by the bishop to King Ludwicus and condemned; he received the death sentence. What is more wicked than such treachery [Note: The manuscript has “more unjust”]? Yet, when one head is cut off, the heads of many peoples are saved. And what counsel could be better than that by which discord was dissolved and peace restored?

Thus, because of such inconsistency, the man was, and so forth, as manuscript 1 has it [Note: The sentence is omitted]. “He, as they say, Adelberhtus … we believe,” through “had collapsed” after the third day [Note: Absent in 2].

[Note: Codex A has the following account.]

Finally, royal friends plotted an ambush for him [Note: *insidiare* in manuscript e]. The plot was nevertheless discovered by a goldsmith who was making a golden torque for the purposes of the deception.

One of those laying the ambush entered the goldsmith’s workshop in order to inspect the work and, after examining it, is said to have sighed more deeply. When the craftsman asked the reason for so great a sigh, he received this answer: that, before long, that torque would have to be soaked in the blood of the excellent Heinricus.

The goldsmith concealed what he had heard in silence, as though treating it as insignificant. When the work had been completed and delivered, he asked for and received permission to depart. Meeting the duke near a place called Cassala, he secretly asked where he was going. The duke replied that he had been invited to a banquet and an honorable gift, and that he intended to go there.

The goldsmith immediately revealed what he had heard and prevented the duke from making the journey. The duke summoned the envoy who had arrived at that hour to invite him and ordered him to thank his masters for their faithful invitation, but to say that he could not visit them at present because of the sudden incursions of barbarians; otherwise, he would remain without hesitation in their service.

Turning eastward with his retinue and gathering a force, he occupied everything belonging to Hatho, the bishop then presiding at Mainz, throughout Saxony or the land of the Thuringians. He also so harassed and crushed in frequent wars Burghardus and Bardo, one of whom was the king’s son-in-law, that they withdrew from the land, and he divided all their property among his soldiers.

When Hatho saw that his stratagems had been brought to an end and that the affairs of the Saxons were flourishing, he was consumed at once by excessive grief and illness. After not many days he died—a man of great prudence, who during the youth of Ludwicus had watched over the Frankish Empire with keen concern, reconciled many quarrels in the kingdom, and adorned the church at Mainz with noble construction.

[Note: On this passage, see the preface; manuscripts 2, 3, 6, and 7 read the text.]

23. (915.) The king sent his brother with an army to devastate Saxony. When he approached the city called Heresburg [Note: *heresburch* in 2 and A], they say that he spoke proudly [Col. 0143B], declaring that nothing concerned him more than the fact that the Saxons did not dare to show themselves before the walls, so that he could fight with them.

The words were still in his mouth [Note: Absent in 2], and behold, the Saxons met him one mile from the city. Battle was joined, and the Franks were punished with such slaughter [Note: 2 has the masculine “so many”] [Note: A has *multati*, 2 *multati*] that the jesters [Note: Joculators, actors, and buffoons are frequently mentioned in the ninth and tenth centuries; the same *mimi* are also named in a letter of Ermenricus of Reichenau] declaimed about where that enormous hell could be that was able to contain so great a multitude of the slain.

The king’s brother Evurhardus [Note: 2 and 3 always have *Everhardus*; A always has *Eberhardus*], freed from fear of the Saxons’ absence [Note: A has “of the absent”]—for he saw them present—and shamefully routed by them, withdrew.

24. When the king heard that his brother had fought unsuccessfully [Note: A has “shamefully”], he gathered all the strength of the Franks and marched to seek Heinricus. Finding him in the fortress of the city called Grona [Note: 6 and 7 have *Gruona*] [Note: Grona is most probably the village near Göttingen; others have thought of Grohnde and Gronau], he attempted to besiege the fortress.

He sent an embassy to request voluntary surrender and promised that, through this, he would become Heinricus’s friend rather than prove his enemy [Note: 1 has *ne*, “rather than”]. Thiadmarus [Note: 2, in the first hand, and 3 always have *thiatmarus*; 2, second hand, and later witnesses have *thietmarus*; A always has *diethmarus*], from the East [Note: Count of the district of North Thuringia, among the leading men of Saxony under King Heinricus; see chapter 36. What is reported of him here scarcely accords with history], a man highly skilled in military discipline, great and versatile in counsel, and one who by his innate cunning surpassed many mortals, came upon the king’s envoys while they were present.

He asked where they wanted the army to pitch camp [Note: 1 has *exercitus*; 2, in the first hand, has “to measure out a camp”]. The duke, already persuaded to surrender to the Franks, took confidence when he heard about the army, believing the report to be true. But Thiadmarus was speaking deceitfully: he had come with only five men [Note: Absent in A; the entire phrase “with only five … had come” is absent in 1].

When the duke inquired about the number of legions, Thiadmarus replied that they amounted to nearly thirty legions [Note: 3 and A add “that he could produce”; the words from “about the number … replied” are absent in 2]. Thus the envoys were deceived and returned to the king.

Thiadmarus overcame by his cunning those whom Heinricus himself could not overcome by force of arms [Note: A has “overcome by force”]. For, before dawn, the Franks abandoned their camp and each returned to his own [Note: 1 has “returns”].

25. The king then departed for Bavaria [Note: A and 2 have *bawariam*; 2 sometimes has *boioariam*; 3 has *Baioariam*], fought against Arnulfus [Note: The Annals of Alamannia report that Arnulf rebelled in 917; Conrad then marched against him for the second time and, according to Liudprand II, 19, drove him to the Hungarians], and there, as some report, was wounded. He returned to his homeland (918).

When he felt himself suffering from illness, together with the decline of his former good fortune, he summoned his brother, who had come to visit him [Note: 2, 3, 5, and 7 have “had approached”], and addressed him as follows:

“I feel, brother,” he said, “that I cannot hold on to this life any longer, since God, who has ordered things thus [Note: 2 has “has thus ordained”], commands it and severe illness compels it. Therefore, consider your own position, and provide for what chiefly concerns you: the entire kingdom of the Franks, attending to the counsel of your brother [Note: Absent in 3; 6 and 7 have “my counsel”].

“We have, brother, the resources to assemble and lead an army; we have cities and weapons, together with the royal insignia, and everything that royal dignity requires, except fortune and character. Fortune, brother, yields to Heinricus, together with the noblest character; among the Saxons, the governance of public affairs is supreme.

“Take, therefore, these insignia—the sacred lance [Note: 2 reverses the words], the golden bracelets with the cloak, the ancient sword of kings, and the diadem—and go to Heinricus. Make peace with him, so that you may have him as an ally forever. For what need is there that the Frankish people should fall with you before him? He will truly be king and emperor of many peoples.”

After these words, his brother replied through tears that he agreed. Soon afterward the king himself died, a brave and powerful man, excellent both at home and in war [Note: 3 has “in military affairs as well”], serene in generosity, and distinguished by the marks of every virtue [Note: A has “distinguished by every virtue”]. He was buried in his own city, Wilinaburg [Note: 2 has *wilinaburch*; 3, *Quidelingaburg*] [Note: Weilburg. The Continuation of Regino (I, p. 615) says that the king was buried in the monastery of Fulda; the Annals of Metz (5) seem to have taken this statement from it: “and he was buried in the monastery of Fulda”], amid the sorrow and tears of all the Franks [Note: Compare the recurring formulas: “with the tears and lamentation of many peoples,” I, 41; “with the groaning and tears of all the Saxons,” II, 37; “with the weeping and lamentation of all the Franks,” III, 47; “with the mourning and lamentation of many peoples,” III, 57].

26. As the king had commanded, Evurhardus [Note: 1 has *euuthardus*, and frequently so] approached Heinricus, surrendered himself and all his treasures to him, made peace, and earned his friendship, which he faithfully and familiarly retained to the end.

Then, after the Frankish princes and the senior leaders of the army had assembled (919) at the place called Fridisleri [Note: 2 has *fridislere*] [Note: Fritzlar], he designated Heinricus king before the entire Frankish and Saxon people.

When the supreme pontiff of that time, Hirigerus [Note: 2 has *hirisgerus*; 3, *Herigerus*] [Note: Archbishop of Mainz, Hatho’s successor], offered him anointing with the diadem, he neither rejected nor accepted it. “It is enough for me,” he said, “that, with God’s grace and your goodwill, I should be called and designated king before my elders [Note: A has “before my elder”]. Let the anointing and diadem remain with those better than we are; we consider ourselves unworthy of so great an honor [Note: 2 has “we consider”.”

This speech therefore pleased the entire multitude. Raising their right hands toward heaven, they repeatedly saluted the name of the new king with a loud shout.

27. Having thus become king, Heinricus marched with his entire retinue to fight against Burghardus [Note: 2 and A always have *burchardus*; 3 has *Burckhardus*], duke of Alamannia [Note: A has *alemannia*] (920).

Although he was an unconquerable warrior, he nevertheless understood, being very prudent, that he could not withstand the king’s assault. He surrendered himself to him together with all his cities and people [Note: Absent in 2].

After affairs had prospered, Heinricus went from there into Bavaria, over which Duke Arnulfus presided. When he learned that Arnulfus was in the fortress of the city called Raginesburg [Note: 1 has *raeginesburch*; A, *reginesburg*; 3, *ragenesburg*; 5, *Raginesburg*], he besieged him.

Seeing that he was not strong enough to resist the king, Arnulfus opened the gates and went out to the king, surrendering himself together with his entire realm [Note: 1 has *semed ipso*]. Heinricus received him honorably and called him the king’s friend.

The king, advancing and growing day by day [Note: 1 has “day”], became stronger, greater, and more renowned. Having gathered together, pacified, and united the kingdom, which under his predecessors had been confused on every side by civil and foreign wars [Note: 3 adds “and”], he moved his standards against Gaul and the kingdom of Lothar.

28. Lothar was the son of the Emperor Hluthowicus [Note: 1 has *luthouicus*], born from the great Charles. His brothers were Charles and Hluthowicus.

The regions of Aquitaine [Note: 2, in the first hand, has *equitaneae*; in the second hand, *aquitaneae*; A and 3 have *aquitaniae*] and of the Gascons [Note: A has *uuasconorum*] fell to Charles. His boundary extended in the west to Barcelona [Note: A has *barcilona*; 3, *Barcinona*], a city of Hispania [Note: A has *spanie*]; in the north to the British Sea; in the south to the ridges of the Alps; and in the east to the River Meuse [Note: 1 has *masan*; 3, *Mosam*].

Between the River Meuse [Note: 1 has *masan*; 3, *Mosam*] and the Rhine [Note: A and 3 always have *rhenum*], the kingdom fell to Lothar. From the Rhine to the borders of Illyricum [Note: A and 3 have *illyrici*] and Pannonia, and also to the River Oder [Note: A has “to the shore”; 2 has *odoram*], together with the Danish borders [Note: 3 has the singular “border”], belonged to Hluthowicus.

Under these brothers, a famous war was fought at Fontinith [Note: 3 has *Fontinith*], before this division of the kingdom took place. Afterward, the division remained inviolable until, by hereditary right, all these kingdoms fell to Charles [Note: This cannot refer to Charles the Bald, Lothar’s great-grandfather, but may refer to Charles the Fat, whom our author imagines to have been the father of Charles the Simple; Bouquet has already noted this. Our author, like Liudprand, *Antapodosis* I, 5 and 14, treated the two Charleses—Charles the Bald and Charles the Fat—as one, and regarded Charles the Simple, the posthumous son of Louis the Stammerer, as his son. Pertz], the great-grandfather of this Lothar [Note: “Louis” in 3], whom we mentioned above [Note: Chapter 16].

29. A certain man from the East Franks, named Oda, a brave and prudent man, approached this Charles and by his counsel arranged that the war against the Danes—who had already for many years been harassing Charles’s kingdom [Note: 2 reverses the order]—should be fought successfully, and that as many as one hundred thousand of them should be killed in a single day [Note: Our author may perhaps have had in mind the defense of the city of Paris against the attack of the Northmen; otherwise, what he reports about Odo and Charles the Simple is entirely false. Odo was the son of Count Robert and was made king by the West Franks after the deposition of Charles the Fat; Charles the Simple, the son of Louis the Stammerer, attempted to deprive him of that dignity. Richer also committed similar errors, so that Ekkehard, following both writers, could not discover the truth].

As a result, that Oda was regarded as illustrious and distinguished and was designated second to the king, since he had come to him content with only one servant as his companion [Note: 2 reverses the order].

When Charles was dying, he ordered Oda to remember his benefaction and not to deny mercy to his son, if one should be born. For he had no son at that time [Note: 2 has “there was no son”], but the queen was pregnant [Note: Louis the Stammerer’s wife Adelheidis gave birth to Charles only after her husband’s death; therefore Charles the Fat claimed the kingdom].

After the father’s death, when a son was born, Oda declared him both to the kingdom and under his father’s name [Note: 2 has “deprived him”]. But the Emperor Arnulfus, who had driven the elder Charles from Germany [Note: That is, Charles the Fat; but Widukind had already spoken of the same man earlier], after Charles’s death claimed his entire kingdom for himself [Note: The words “after his death” are absent in 1].

Oda offered him the diadem, scepter, and the other royal ornaments [Note: See the Annals of Vedastinus for 888], and obtained the empire through the favor of his lord, the Emperor Arnulfus [Note: 2 has “and obtained the empire as a favor for his lord”].

From this time to the present there has been a dispute between the royal descendants of Charles and the posterity of Oda over the kingdom; there is also contention between the kings of the Carolingians and of the East Franks over the kingdom of Lothar [Note: 1 and A have *odoni*, but shortly afterward *odonis*].

30. For this reason King Henry moved his camp against Charles and repeatedly routed his army [Note: [Col. 0147D] Widukind treats the matter far too briefly, and therefore it is impossible that he did not commit errors.], and fortune assisted the brave man. For Hugh [Note: [Col. 0147] *Hugo* in A.], whose father Robert [Note: [Col. 0147] *Robberhtus* 1; *Rodbertus* 2, 3; *Robertus* A.], (923), Odo’s son, had been killed by Charles’s army, sent [object unexpressed], and captured him by a stratagem [Col. 0147B] [Note: [Col. 0147D] It is established that it was not Hugh but Herbert who kept Charles captive.], and placed him in public custody until he died. But when King Henry heard of Charles’s misfortune [Note: [Col. 0147] *casu* (“by misfortune”) 2.], he grieved and marveled at the common lot of human mutability [Note: [Col. 0147] A. has *communemque* (“and common”)], since Charles had shone with no less religious devotion than military prowess. He judged that he should indeed abstain from arms, but hoped rather that he would overcome the Lotharians by strategy [Note: [Col. 0147D] Much the same is read below, chapter 39: “so that even while playing they would not believe that they were being released into any wantonness,”] because the people were changeable and accustomed to stratagems, ready for war and inclined toward novelties.

At that time there was a certain Lotharian named Christian [Note: [Col. 0147] *Christianus* in A. and 3.], who, seeing that everything was proceeding successfully for the king, asked how he might be honored with greater favor by the king; and [Note: [Col. 0147] A. omits *et* (“and”).], feigning illness, summoned Isilberht [Note: [Col. 0147] 2 and A. always have *Isilbertum*, *Isberthum*, or *Hisberhtum* 1; 3 usually has *Giselbertum*; β has *Isliberhtum*.] to him [Note: [Col. 0147D] The Saxons wrote this name without G or K, as all the manuscripts of Widukind and the Corvey Annals printed above show.], to whom the rule of the region had fallen by paternal succession [Note: [Col. 0148D] Giselbert was prince and duke of the Lotharians after the death of his father Reginar; but in what year he received this dignity is uncertain. Compare Richer below. Widukind alone records his captivity.]. He captured him by a stratagem and sent him under guard to King Henry [Col. 0147C].

Isilberht was born of noble lineage and an ancient family. The king received him with considerable joy, since he believed that through him alone he would possess the whole kingdom of Lothair. Then, seeing that the young man was very capable, distinguished by birth and power and also renowned for his wealth, he began to treat him generously; finally, after betrothing to him his daughter Gerberga [Note: [Col. 0148D] Giselbert seems not to have married Gerberga before 928.], he joined him to himself in kinship [Col. 0148A] [Note: [Col. 0147] *afinitate* in 1.], as well as in friendship [Note: [Col. 0147] 3 omits the word], assigning to him the whole kingdom of Lothair [Note: [Col. 0147] *sublegato* (“having been assigned”) in place of *legato* (“assigned”) 1.].

31. The famous and most noble queen of singular prudence, named Mathilda [Note: [Col. 0147] *Mahtilda* A.; *Mathilda* 1.], also bore him other children: first-born Odo, the darling of the world [Note: [Col. 0147] 2 has *amatorem* (“lover”)]; the second, Henry, distinguished by his father’s name, a brave and capable man; and the third, Bruno, whom we have seen performing the office of supreme bishop and great duke [Note: [Col. 0148D] See above, col. 118.]. And lest anyone should call him blameworthy on this account, let us remember that we read of the holy Samuel [Note: [Col. 0147] *Samuelem* A., 2, 3.] [Note: [Col. 0147] 2 omits *sanctum* (“holy”)] and many other priests who were likewise judges.

She also bore another daughter [Note: [Col. 0147] A., 2, and 3 read “she bore a daughter”] [Note: [Col. 0148D] Glaber Rudolphus, *History* I.4, calls her Hadwig. Meib.], who had married Duke Hugh. For she herself, the lady queen [Note: [Col. 0147] β has *domna* (“lady”); 1 omits *regina* (“queen”).], was the daughter of Theodoric [Note: [Col. 0147] *Thiaderici* 1.], whose brothers were Widukind, Immed, and Reginbern.

[Col. 0148B] Reginbern [Note: [Col. 0147] The readings are: *uuidukin. inmed et raeginberth* (corrected to *raeinbern*); *raeinbern autem* 1; *uuidikint i. et reinbern r. autem* 2; *widikind i. et reinbern. Reimbern autem* A.; *Widekind Immet Reginbern. Reginbern autem* 3; *W. Immed et Rainbern ex Raginbern. Rainbern autem* β. (In the collection of manuscripts by Dr. at Leibniz, *ex* is falsely read for *et*).] was the very man who fought against the Danes, who had long been devastating Saxony; he defeated them and freed his country from their incursions down to the present day [Note: [Col. 0147] *odiernum* 1; 3 omits the word]. These men were of the lineage of the great Duke Widukind, who waged a powerful war against the great Charles for nearly thirty years [Note: [Col. 0147] 2 omits *potens* (“powerful”)].

32. (924) When the civil wars had now ceased, the Hungarians again traversed the whole of Saxony, committed cities and strongholds to the flames, and everywhere inflicted such slaughter [Note: [Col. 0147] 3 has *egere* (“they inflicted”)] that they threatened a final devastation [Note: [Col. 0147] 3 has *commi­n­arentur* (“they threatened”)]. The king, however, was in the fortress of a town called Werlaon [Note: [Col. 0148D] A royal palace near Goslar; compare Grupen, *Observations* I, pp. 1 ff.—today Burgdorf near Goslar. P.]. For he did not trust the still inexperienced soldiery, unaccustomed to public war, against so savage a people.

But how great a slaughter they inflicted in those days [Note: [Col. 0147] A. has *fecerint stragem* (“inflicted slaughter”)], or how many monasteries they burned [Col. 0148C], we judged it better to leave unspoken [Note: [Col. 0147] 1 has *judicabimus* (“we shall judge”)], rather than repeat our calamities even in words [Note: [Col. 0147] 2 has *nostras calamitates* (“our calamities”)].

It happened that one of the Hungarian princes was captured, bound, and brought to the king. The Hungarians loved him so greatly [Note: [Col. 0147] 3 has *dilexere* (“they loved”)], that they offered immeasurable weights of gold and silver for his ransom [Note: [Col. 0147] 2 omits “for his ransom.”]. But the king, scorning gold, demanded peace and finally obtained it: after the captive had been returned together with other gifts, peace was established for nine years [Note: [Col. 0149] 3 has *confirmaretur* (“was confirmed”)].

33. When the king had crossed the Rhine in order to extend his power over the Lotharians, Charles’s envoy met him and, after greeting him [Note: [Col. 0149] 1 omits the phrase], said in the most humble words:

“My lord Charles, once endowed with royal power but now deprived of it, has sent me to you, asking that, although he is surrounded by enemies, nothing could be more pleasing or sweeter to him than to hear something of the glory of your magnificent success and to be comforted by news of your virtues. He has also sent you this token of faith and truth.”

Then he brought from his bosom a hand of the precious martyr Dionysius [Note: [Col. 0149] *Dionisii* elsewhere; 1 has *Dyonisii*; A. and 3 have *Dionysii*], enclosed in gold and gems.

“Keep this,” he said, “as a pledge of perpetual alliance and vicarious love. This part of the one consolation of the Franks who inhabit Gaul, after the renowned martyr Vitus left us to our destruction and visited Saxony for your perpetual peace, has preferred to share itself with you. For ever since his body was transferred [Note: [Col. 0149] 3 omits the phrase] from us, neither civil nor foreign wars have ceased; for in that same year the Danes and Northmen [Note: [Col. 0149] A. has *Nortmanni*; 3 has *Normandi*] invaded our region [Note: [Col. 0149D] The translation of Saint Vitus took place in 836; and from the years 834 and 836 onward, Northmen’s incursions in fact grew more frequent.].”

The king received the divine gift with every expression of thanksgiving, prostrated himself before the holy relics, kissed them, and venerated them with the utmost reverence.

34. The renowned martyr about whom Charles’s envoy spoke was born in the province of Lycia [Note: [Col. 0149] 2 has *Litia*; A. and 3 have *Lycia*] of a noble but pagan family [Note: [Col. 0149D] Widukind drew this account of the saint’s life from his *Passion*, written in the sixth or seventh century; see it in the *Acta Sanctorum* of the Bollandists, June, vol. II (15 June), pp. 1021 ff.]. His father presented him to Valerian, the governor of the province, and the governor himself [Note: [Col. 0149] 3 has *praeses ipse* (“the governor himself”).] compelled him to sacrifice to the images. But meanwhile the governor lost a hand and received it back healthy through the boy’s prayer. The torturers’ arms withered, but were restored to them through the martyr’s merits [Note: [Col. 0149] 1 has *restituti* (“restored,” masculine) rather than *restituta* (“restored,” neuter)].

When the father saw that the boy mocked the tortures, he took him home and shut him in a chamber overflowing with every luxury. There, when Hylas—so his father was called [Note: [Col. 0149] 1 has *Ylas*; 3, *Hilas*]—saw certain secret things, he became blind. Compelled by this, he renounced the idols and confessed Christ. But after being given sight through the merits of his son Vitus, he denied Christ and sought to kill his son.

At the command and guidance of an angel, Modestus, now an older tutor, took up the boy, sailed across the sea [Note: [Col. 0149] 1 has *navigavit* (“he sailed”)], and reached the river Siler. There, resting beneath a certain tree, they devoted themselves to prayer, while eagles supplied them with their daily food [Note: [Col. 0149] 2 has *cottidianum* (“daily”); 2 has *administrantibus* (“administering”)]. When the people visited him [Col. 0149D] [Note: [Col. 0149] 1 has *enim* (“for”) instead of *eum* (“him”)], the boy preached Christ, converted many, and caused many to receive baptism.

After this, summoned to Rome by the emperor Diocletian, he set out; after cleansing the emperor’s son from a demon through Vitus’s prayer [Note: [Col. 0149] 1, in a second hand, adds *beati* (“of the blessed [Vitus]”)], he was compelled to offer incense to the gods. But when he answered the emperor more harshly [Note: [Col. 0149] 2 has *diutius* (“for a longer time”) rather than *durius* (“more harshly”)], he was thrown to the beasts and was not harmed. Then he was cast into the middle of a burning furnace, but, while an angel subdued the flames [Note: [Col. 0149] 2 omits “and”], he emerged unharmed.

Loaded with the immense weight of iron chains, he was handed over to prison, but there he was visited by the Lord and a multitude of angels. Finally, he was fastened to the instrument of torture called the *catasta*, together with Modestus and a certain noble woman, Crescentia, and, when all movement of his limbs had been broken, he was comforted by Christ.

For after the torturers had been struck by a thunderbolt from heaven and terrified by mighty thunder [Note: [Col. 0149] 2 has *tonitruo* (“by thunder”)], they were driven away from him. Suddenly he was found in the place [Note: [Col. 0149] 2 omits this phrase; 1 omits “in the place”] where he had previously devoted himself to prayer, with the angel of the Lord restoring him there [Col. 0150B]. After the final prayer had been celebrated, they surrendered their souls to heaven.

A certain illustrious woman, Florentia, buried their bodies in the same place, which is called Marianus. I have taken care to report his final prayer to Your Glory, so that from it you may derive a reason to burn with love for him and, through the ardor of that love, merit his perpetual patronage [Note: [Col. 0149] 4 omits “so that from it you may derive…”]:

“Lord Jesus Christ [Note: [Col. 0149] 3 has “Jesus Christ, he said”], Son of the living God, fulfill the desire of their hearts [Note: [Col. 0149] 2 adds: “who wish to glory in your name in the passion of my martyrdom”], and free them from all the impediments of this age, and lead them to your glory—those who glorify you on my account and wish to glory in the passion of my martyrdom [Note: [Col. 0149] 2 omits the words from “and wish” to “passion”].”

This utterance was followed by the assurance of the divine promise [Note: [Col. 0149] 2 has the abbreviated reading “of the divine promise”], confirming that everything he had asked for would be valid and firm.

After a long time, a certain man named Fulradus [Note: [Col. 0149] A. has *Folradus*] came to Rome and, reading there the deeds of the precious martyr [Col. 0150C], noted the location of the tomb. He came, took up the holy relics, and placed them in the region of Paris [Note: [Col. 0149] 3 has *collocavitque* (“and placed”)]. From there, during the reign of the emperor Louis, they were transferred to Saxony. As Charles’s envoy acknowledged, from that time the affairs of the Franks began to decline and those of the Saxons to grow, until, having expanded, they now suffer from their own greatness, as we see in the love of the world and in the head of the whole earth, your father, whose majesty and power not only Germany, Italy, and Gaul but almost the whole of Europe cannot bear [Note: [Col. 0149] 2 omits “until”; A. has “their own greatness.”].

Therefore honor such a patron, through whose arrival Saxony was transformed from a slave into a free people and from a tributary into the mistress of many nations [Note: [Col. 0149] A. omits *tantum* (“such a”)]. For such and so great a friend of the supreme God does not need your favor [Note: [Col. 0149] 2 has “of the supreme God” rather than “of such and so great a friend”]; but we, his servants, do need it. Therefore, so that you may have him as an intercessor with the heavenly emperor, let us have you as an advocate with the earthly king [Col. 0151A]—namely, your father and brother [Note: [Col. 0151] 1 reads *habeat* (“may he have”) after erasure of the other readings; 3 has *advocatam* (“female advocate”), perhaps 1?].

35. Accordingly, after King Henry had obtained peace from the Hungarians for nine years, how prudently he kept watch over the fortification of his country and the subjugation of barbarian nations is beyond our ability to relate, although it must by no means be left unspoken [Note: [Col. 0151] 1 has *liceat* (“although it may be permitted”)].

First, selecting every ninth man from the agricultural population, he made him live in the cities [Note: [Col. 0151] 2 has “made him live” in the reverse order], so that he might build dwellings for his eight fellow householders and receive and store a third part of all the crops. The other eight were to sow and reap and gather the crops for the ninth and store them in their proper places.

He ordered councils, all assemblies, and banquets to be held in the cities [Col. 0151B]. In building these cities, the people worked day and night, so that in peacetime they might learn what they would have to do against enemies in time of need [Note: [Col. 0151] 2 has *deberent* (“they would have to”)]. Outside the cities there were either weak or no defensive walls [Note: [Col. 0151] Reineccius received *autem* (“however”) from an unknown source; Leibniz noted that in manuscript Dr. (A) *ola* was read, but Ebert expressly states that this is false. Thus this much-disturbed passage is sound and complete.].

When he had accustomed the citizens to this law and discipline, he suddenly attacked the Slavs called Heveldi [Note: [Col. 0151] 2, 3, and A. have *Hevelli*] [Note: [Col. 0151D] The Heveldi were Slavs whose settlements lay along the Havel; their city was Brandenburg.], and, wearing them down through many battles [Note: [Col. 0151] 2 has *fatigare* (“to wear down”)], finally, in the harshest winter, with his camp placed upon the ice, captured the city called Brennaburg [Note: [Col. 0151] 1 has *qui* (“which”) rather than *quae*; 2 has *Berneburch*; 5 has *Brinnaborg*] by hunger, iron, and cold.

After taking that city and the whole region [Note: [Col. 0151] 3 has “and the whole region”], he turned his standards against Daleminzia, against which his father had formerly left him a military command. Besieging the city called Gana [Note: [Col. 0151] 2 has *Grona*; 6 and 7 have *Grana*; A. has *Kietni*] [Note: [Col. 0151D] This seems to be Jahna, between Meissen and Lommatzsch. It is no longer permissible to read *Grona* or *Kietni* against the agreement of the best manuscripts.], he finally captured it on the twentieth day. After the city’s booty had been handed over to the soldiers, all the adults [Note: [Col. 0151] 2 omits the phrase] were killed, while the boys and girls were preserved for captivity [Col. 0151C] [Note: [Col. 0151] 1 has *reservatae* (“preserved”); 2 has *sunt servati* (“were preserved”)].

After this he went with his whole army to Prague [Note: [Col. 0151] 3 has *adito* (“having approached”)], the city of the Bohemians [Note: [Col. 0151] 3 always has *Bohemorum*], and accepted its king into submission. Certain marvelous things are reported about him; because we do not approve them, we judge that they should be covered in silence [Note: [Col. 0151D] Widukind indicates quite openly that this was Saint Wenceslaus, but he seems to have avoided naming the king.]. He was, however, the brother of Bolizlav [Note: [Col. 0151] 1 has *Boritlavi*; 2 *Borizlavi*; A. *Bolizlai*; 3 *Bolizlavi*; 6 *Bolizlawi*], and [Note: [Col. 0151D] That is, Wenceslaus.] as long as he lived he remained faithful and useful to the emperor. Thus the king made the Bohemians tributary [Note: [Col. 0151] 2 has “making the Bohemians tributary”; A. and 7 have “making the Bohemians tributary”] and returned to Saxony.

36. When the neighboring peoples had been made tributary by King Henry—the Apodriti [Note: [Col. 0151] 3 has *Abotriti*] (929), the Wilti [Note: [Col. 0151] 1 omits the word; 2 has *Uiulti*; 3 and 7 have *Vulzi*], the Heveldi [Note: [Col. 0151] 2 has *Hevelle*], the Daleminzi [Note: [Col. 0151] 2 has *Dalmaci*; 3 has *Dalmatae*], the Bohemians, and the Redarii [Note: [Col. 0151D] The distinguished Lisch most recently investigated with the greatest precision the settlements of the Redarii in the land of Strelitz, in the *Annals of the Historical Society of Mecklenburg*, vol. III, pp. 1 ff.]—and there was peace, the Redarii broke faith. Gathering a multitude, they attacked the city called Wallislevu [Note: [Col. 0151] 2 and 3 have *Uuallislevi*; A. *Wallisleu*; 5 *Wallisleheim*] [Note: [Col. 0152D] Walsleben near the Elbe, between Werben and Arneburg.], captured it, and seized and killed all its inhabitants, an innumerable multitude.

When this had been done, all the barbarian nations were emboldened and dared to rebel again. To suppress their ferocity, an army with a military force was entrusted to Bernhard, to whom the province of the Redarii itself had been assigned [Note: [Col. 0151] 5 and 7 have *subjugata* (“subjugated”)]. The envoy Thietmar was added as his colleague [Note: [Col. 0151] 1 corrects *legato* to *collega*], and they were ordered to besiege the city called Lunkini [Note: [Col. 0151] 2 has *Lunkani*] [Note: [Col. 0152D] The Quedlinburg Chronicle places this city on the Elbe; it would therefore be Leontium, or Lenzen. Meib.].

On the fifth day of the siege, the guards came, announcing that the barbarian army was not far away [Note: [Col. 0151] A. has *barbarum* (“barbarian,” singular); 2 has “saying or announcing”], and that they had decided to attack the camp on the following night. When several confirmed the same thing, the people gave credence to their equal reports. As the assembly [Note: [Col. 0151] 1 has *ventus*] of the people [Note: [Col. 0151] 2 omits *populi*] was gathered around the envoy’s tents [Note: [Col. 0151] 3 has “the tents, the envoy”], at that very moment, on the advice of his colleague, he ordered them to remain ready throughout the night, lest some sudden incursion of the barbarians into the camp occur [Note: [Col. 0151] 1 has *yrruptio*].

When the crowd had been dismissed, sorrow and joy alike varied throughout the camp: some feared war, while others desired it. According to their different dispositions, the warriors wavered between hope and fear [Note: [Col. 0151] 1 corrects *versabant* (“they wavered”) to *versantibus* (“waving”)]. Meanwhile the day passed, and night came, darker than usual, with a tremendous rain, by divine providence, so that the barbarians’ evil plan might be hindered [Note: [Col. 0151] 1 has *impeditur* (“is hindered”)].

As ordered, the Saxons remained armed throughout that night. At first light, when the signal had been given [Note: [Col. 0151] 1 omits the phrase], and after an oath had been taken [Col. 0152C] [Note: [Col. 0151] Manuscript 5 ends here], first the commanders and then each man promised under oath to give his assistance for the present war [Note: [Col. 0152D] Our author reports that the same thing was done in the battle fought against the Hungarians in 955, III.44.].

When the sun had risen—for after the rain clear serenity returns [Note: [Col. 0151] 3 and 7 have *rediit* (“returned”)], they advanced from the camp with standards raised [Note: [Col. 0151] 3 omits the phrase], with the envoy attacking the barbarians at the front. But when the few proved unable to prevail against the innumerable, he returned to the army, reporting that the barbarians had not many cavalry [Note: [Col. 0151] 1 has *equitates* (“cavalry forces”)], but an innumerable multitude of infantry [Col. 0153A], so hindered by the night’s rain that they scarcely advanced to battle even when compelled by the cavalry [Note: [Col. 0153] 3 omits “scarcely”].

As the sun sank upon the barbarians’ wet garments, it caused smoke to rise as far as heaven, giving God’s people hope and confidence [Note: [Col. 0153] 2 has “the people of God”], as the brightness and serenity of His countenance shone around them. Then, when the signal had been given and the envoy had encouraged the legions, they fell upon the enemy with a mighty shout.

Because the enemy’s extreme density left no passage through which they could advance, they broke out with the sword to right and left and killed everyone whom they separated from his companions [Note: [Col. 0153] 3 has *se sternebant* (“they laid low”)]. When the battle had now become severe [Note: [Col. 0153] 1? omits the words from “to right and left” through “had become severe”], and many were falling on both sides while the barbarians still held their ranks, the envoy called upon his colleague to bring assistance to the legions.

He sent a prefect with fifty armed men against the enemy’s flank [Note: [Col. 0153] 2 has *laetari* (“to rejoice”)], and threw their ranks into confusion.
