From that point the enemy was exposed to slaughter and flight throughout the day [Note: [Col. 0153] A. has *caede* (“slaughter”)]. As they were being slaughtered throughout the fields, they attempted to flee to a neighboring city.

But the colleague prevented them from doing this. They entered the nearest body of water [Note: [Col. 0153D] Near Lenzen there are two, though smaller, lakes], and it came about that the whole immense multitude was either destroyed by the sword or drowned in the water. Not one of the infantry survived; only a very few cavalrymen remained. The war was brought to an end with the fall of all the adversaries.

Meanwhile immense joy arose from the recent victory [Note: [Col. 0153] 1 has “increasing victory”], while everyone praised the commanders and each soldier praised another [Note: [Col. 0153] 3 adds *evangelium* (“gospel”)], including even the coward, as usually happens in such good fortune.

On the following day [Note: [Col. 0153] 1 has “afterward”] they moved their standards toward the aforesaid city. The townspeople laid down their arms, asking for and obtaining only their lives. They were therefore ordered to leave the city unarmed [Note: [Col. 0153] 1 has *degredi* (“to descend”)]. But a condition of servitude, together with all the barbarians’ money, wives, children, and every possession, underwent captivity under the barbarian king [Note: [Col. 0153] 1 places a full stop after *regis* and A. does the same].

Two Lotharians [Note: [Col. 0153] 2 has *Luitharii*; A. *Lutharii*] and several other noble men also fell in that battle [Note: [Col. 0154D] On these men, compare Thietmar I, p. 8.]. The envoy, his colleague, and the other princes returned victorious to Saxony and were honorably received and sufficiently praised by the king, because, with divine mercy favoring them, they had achieved a magnificent victory with small forces. For there were men who said that two hundred thousand barbarians had been killed.

All the captives were put to death on the following day [Note: [Col. 0153] 2 reverses the words: “on the following day, the captives”], as they had been promised [Note: [Col. 0153] 1 corrects *captivi* (“captives”) to *capiti* (“for the head”)].

37. Thus the joy of the recent victory was increased by a royal wedding, which was celebrated at that time with magnificent generosity [Note: [Col. 0153] A. and 3 have *celebrantur* (“are celebrated”)]. For the king gave his son Odo as wife the daughter of Edward, king of the English [Note: [Col. 0154D] Edith, daughter of King Edward.], and sister of Athelstan. She bore him a son named Liudolf [Col. 0154A], a great man and deservedly dear to all peoples, and also a daughter named Liudgard [Note: [Col. 0153] 1 and 2 have *Liutgardam*], who married Conrad, duke of the Franks.

38. Since the king now had cavalry tested in mounted battle, he ventured to engage his ancient enemies, namely the Hungarians. And (932), having summoned the whole people [Note: [Col. 0153] 1 has *vocato* (“having summoned”)], he addressed them in this speech [Note: [Col. 0153] A., 2, and 3 have *ratione* (“speech,” “account”) rather than *oratione*]:

“You yourselves know better than anyone from how many dangers your realm, formerly thrown into confusion on every side, is now free, since you were so often worn down by civil dissensions and foreign wars. But now, with the supreme divinity favorable to us [Note: [Col. 0153] 2 has *divina* (“divine”)], through our labor and your valor [Note: [Col. 0153] 3 adds *-que* (“and”)], you see it pacified and restored, the barbarians defeated and subjected to servitude.

“What remains is that we must rise together against our common enemies, the Avars. Until now I have stripped your sons and daughters and filled their treasury with it. Now I am compelled to strip the temples and the ministers of the temples, with no money left to us except their naked bodies. Therefore take counsel for yourselves and choose what should be done by us in this matter.

“Shall I take away the treasure sanctified for divine worship [Note: [Col. 0153] 2 has *tollam* (“shall I take away”) without the ending] and give it to the enemies of God for our ransom? Or should I add the honor of money to divine worship [Note: [Col. 0153] 1 has *pecuniam* (“money,” accusative); A. and 3 have *pecunia* (“money,” nominative), rather than *pecuniae*], so that we may instead be redeemed by him who truly is both our creator and [Note: [Col. 0153] 1 has *ac* (“and”) rather than *pariter et* (“equally and”)] our redeemer? [Note: [Col. 0153] 2 omits *ab* (“by”)].”

At this the people raised their voices to heaven, saying that they earnestly desired to be redeemed by the living and true God, because he is faithful and just in all his ways and holy in all his works. Then, promising their assistance to the king [Col. 0154C] [Note: [Col. 0153] 1 omits the words], against the fiercest people [Note: [Col. 0153] 2 has *asperrimam* (“very fierce”)], they raised their right hands to heaven and confirmed the agreement.

When this pact with the people had thus been completed, the king dismissed the multitude. Afterward the Hungarian envoys approached the king for the customary gifts; but, rejected by him, they returned empty-handed to their own land [Note: [Col. 0153] 1 has *reversi sunt* (“returned”)]. When the Avars heard this [Note: [Col. 0153] 2 omits the phrase], they delayed no longer [Note: [Col. 0153] A. adds *sunt* (“they were”)], but hastened with a heavy and hostile force to enter Saxony.

Traveling through Daleminzia [Note: [Col. 0153] 2 omits *per* (“through”)], they asked help from their old friends. But those men, knowing that they were hastening toward Saxony and that the Saxons [Note: [Col. 0153] A. has *Saxones*] were ready to fight them [Note: [Col. 0153] 2 adds *esse* (“to be”)], threw them a very fat dog as a gift [Note: [Col. 0153] A. has “throw them the dog as a gift”]. Since there was no opportunity to avenge the insult while they were hastening toward another battle, they pursued their friends farther with quite ridiculous shouting.

Thus, as suddenly as they could, (933) they entered the territory of the Thuringians, ravaging that whole land in a hostile manner [Note: [Col. 0153] 2 reverses the order: “ravaging that whole land in a hostile manner”]. There they divided their forces. Some went westward [Col. 0155A], seeking to enter Saxony from the west and south. But the Saxons, gathered together with the Thuringians, engaged them in battle and, after their commanders had been killed, made the rest of that western army [Note: [Col. 0155] 2 has “the western forces”] wander throughout the entire region.

Some of them, consumed by hunger; others, weakened by cold [Note: [Col. 0155] A. omits the phrase]; and still others, killed or captured as they deserved, perished miserably.

The army that remained in the east heard about the king’s sister, who had married Wido the Thuringian [Note: [Col. 0155D] Nothing certain is known about Wido, his wife, or his city; compare *Göttingische gelehrte Anzeigen*, 1838, no. 204, p. 2036.]—for she had been born of a concubine [Note: [Col. 0155] 1 omits the words]—and that she lived in a neighboring city [Note: [Col. 0155] 1 omits the words] and possessed much gold and silver. They therefore began to attack the city with such force that, unless night had hindered the combatants’ vision, they would have captured it.

That night, however, they heard of the fall of their companions and of the king’s approach against them with a powerful army—for the king had pitched his camp near the place called Riade [Note: [Col. 0155] A. has *Riede*; 3 *Riaede*; 7 *Riede*] [Note: [Col. 0155D] I do not dare to determine anything about the location of this place.]. Struck with fear [Note: [Col. 0155] 2 corrects the feminine *perculsae* to masculine *perculsi*], they abandoned their camp and, as was their custom, gathered their scattered troops together by means of immense fire and smoke.

On the following day the king led out his army and exhorted them to entrust their hope to divine mercy; they should have no doubt that divine assistance would be present for them, just as it had been in other battles. The Hungarians were the common enemies of all; they should think only of avenging their country and their parents. They would soon see the enemy turn their backs if they persisted in fighting bravely.

Raised up by these excellent words [Note: [Col. 0155] A. has *certi* (“made certain”)], and seeing the emperor moving among the foremost, the middle, and the rear troops, the soldiers gained great confidence and steadfastness. Before him there was an angel—for the standard was marked with this name and image, which was its chief distinguishing emblem [Note: [Col. 0155D] Compare III.44.].

The king, however, feared—as happened—that when the enemy saw the armed soldiers they would immediately give themselves to flight. He sent a legion of Thuringians with a small number of armed men to pursue the unarmed enemy and drive them as far as their army [Note: [Col. 0155] 1? omits the words from “and drive” to the end]. And so it was done. Nevertheless, when they saw the armed army, they fled [Note: [Col. 0155] 2 has *fugierunt* (“they fled”)], so that over eight miles scarcely any were killed or captured [Note: [Col. 0155] 3 has “after completing a mile”; 2 has *aut* (“or”) rather than *vel* (“or”)]. Their camp was stormed, and all the captives were freed.

39. After returning victorious, the king in every way paid thanksgiving to divine honor, as was fitting, for the victory divinely granted him over his enemies [Col. 0156A]. He devoted to divine worship the tribute that he had been accustomed to give the enemies and decided that it should be used for gifts to the poor [Note: [Col. 0155] A. and 7 have *tributum* (“tribute”) rather than *tributumque*].

Then, having been proclaimed by the army father of his country, lord of affairs, and emperor [Note: [Col. 0155D] The same is said of Odo in book I.], he spread the fame of his power and virtue far and wide among all peoples and kings [Note: [Col. 0155] 1 omits “and kings”]. Therefore the nobles of other kingdoms also approached him, seeking to find favor in his presence; having tested the faithfulness of such a great man, they loved him.

Among them, Herbert [Note: [Col. 0155] 2 has *Hiriberhtus*; 3 *Hiriberthus*; A. *Heribertus*], Hugh’s son-in-law [Note: [Col. 0155D] Hugh was the son of Beatrice, daughter of Herbert I, the father of this Herbert, and therefore Herbert’s sister. Thus “son-in-law” here means “uncle.” Bouquet. [Col. 0156D] Perhaps, however, Herbert had married Hugh’s sister; for his son is later called Hugh’s nephew, III.3.], when Rudolph opposed him and had been established as king against every law, human and divine, begged Henry to stand before his own lord as his protector [Note: [Col. 0155] 1 has *adverses Rothulfus*; A. *Rudolfus*; 3 *Ruodulfus*; 2 omits *ei* (“for him”)]. For he himself was a king of such a kind that he denied his friends nothing.

Accordingly, the king went to Gaul [Note: [Col. 0155] 3 adds *in* (“into”)], addressed the king, completed the business, and returned to Saxony. As he was exalting his people, there was scarcely any prominent man, or none at all, throughout Saxony whom he did not advance by a distinguished gift, an office, or some administrative position [Note: [Col. 0155] 2 omits the word “throughout”].

Although he excelled greatly in prudence and wisdom, bodily stature also accompanied him, adding every beauty to his royal dignity. In exercises and games [Note: [Col. 0155] 1 omits *ludi* (“of games”)], he surpassed everyone by such excellence that he displayed terror to the others.

In hunting [Note: [Col. 0155] 1 has *veneratione* (“in veneration”)], he was so ardent [Note: [Col. 0155] 2 and 6 have *acer* (“keen”) rather than *acerrimus* (“very keen”)], that on one occasion [Note: [Col. 0155] 2 omits the phrase] he captured forty or more wild beasts. Although he was quite cheerful at banquets, he diminished nothing of royal discipline. For he infused the soldiers with so much favor [Note: [Col. 0155] 3 has *fervorem* (“ardor”) rather than *favorem* (“favor”)], and at the same time with so much fear [Note: [Col. 0155] 2 omits the words from “so much” through “infused”], that even while he played they did not believe themselves free to give themselves over to any wantonness [Col. 0156C] [Note: [Col. 0155] 3 and 6 have *dissolvendos* (“to be released,” masculine plural)].

40. (934) When he had subjected all the surrounding nations, he attacked and defeated the Danes, who were harassing the Frisians by naval piracy. He made them tributary and caused their king, named Chnuba [Note: [Col. 0155] 1 has *Chonpam*, a reading to which Sigebert of Gembloux seems to conform; in his work the king’s name is written *Chuipia* or *Chinpa*; 2 has *Cnubam*; 3 and 7 *Nubam*; β *Chnutam*] [Note: [Col. 0156D] Widukind seems to have been thinking of Cnut, son of King Gorm, who ruled in the southern part of Denmark; see Thietmar I, p. 12. Nevertheless, he undoubtedly wrote the name with b or p. The Vienna manuscript of Adam of Bremen likewise gives *Kunt* for *Knut*. But the statement that he received baptism seems to be an error of our author.], to receive baptism.

After he had subdued all the surrounding peoples, he finally decided to set out for Rome, but, overcome by illness, he abandoned the journey.

41. When he felt that he was already being weighed down by illness [Note: [Col. 0155] 1 has *gravi* (“severe”); 2 has “being weighed down by severe illness”], he summoned the whole people and designated his son Odo as king [Col. 0157A], distributing estates and treasures among his other sons as well. Odo himself, who was the greatest and best, he placed over his brothers and over the entire Frankish empire (936, July 2).

After his will had been lawfully made and all his affairs properly arranged, the lord of all things and greatest of Europe’s kings died. In every virtue of mind and body he was second to none, leaving behind a son greater than himself [Note: [Col. 0157] 3 omits the phrase], and to his son a great and extensive empire [Col. 0158A], not left to him by his fathers [Note: [Col. 0157] In A., the words *non a* have been erased], but acquired by his own efforts and granted by God alone.

(936) The days of his reign were sixteen years [Note: [Col. 0157D] It is readily apparent that Henry held the kingdom from April 919 until July 2, 936—seventeen years and nearly three months.], while his life lasted approximately sixty years.

His sons transferred his body to the city called Quedlinburg [Note: [Col. 0157] 1 has *qui* (“which”) rather than *quae* (“which”); A. and 3 have *Quidelingeburg*], and buried it in the basilica of Saint Peter before the altar, amid the mourning and tears of many peoples.

[Col. 0157] **THE FIRST BOOK ENDS** [Note: [Col. 0157] 2 likewise; A. has “The first book ends.”]

**[BOOK II]**
# The Second Book of the Deeds of the Saxons Begins

## Preface to the Second Book, Addressed to Lady Mathilda, Daughter of the Emperor

[Col. 0157]

[Col. 0157B] As I undertake—or certainly resume—this immense work, since a large part of it has already been completed, may it be supported by your favor, you who are recognized as mistress by right of all Europe, although [Col. 0158B] your father’s power already extends into Africa and Asia. I hope, indeed, that whatever in it is less suitable may be upheld by the glorious gentleness of your clemency, and that it may remain dedicated with the same devotion with which it was written.

[Note: [Col. 0157] The preface heading stands thus in 1; A has “Prologue to Book Two”; 3, “Preface to the Queen.” Printed reading: ita 1; Prologus in librum secundum A. Praefatio ad Reginam 3.]

[Note: [Col. 0157] For *magna ex*, “from a large [part],” 2 reverses the order to *ex magna*. Printed reading: ex magna 2.]

[Note: [Col. 0157] For *dinosceris*, “you are recognized,” 2 has *dinoscetur*, “he/she will be recognized.” Printed reading: dinoscetur 2.]

[Note: [Col. 0157] For *Africam*, “Africa”: the spelling *affricam* in 2, *Aphricam* in 3. Printed reading: affricam 2. Aphricam 3.]

[Note: [Col. 0157] *Jam*, “already,” is absent from A; 2 has the order *potestas jam*, “power already.” Printed reading: deest A. potestas jam 2.]

[Note: [Col. 0157] For *conscripum*, “written,” A, 2, 3 have *inceptum*, “begun.” Printed reading: inceptum A. 2. 3.]

## The Second Book Begins

[Col. 0159]

### 1

[Col. 0159A] When the father of his country and the greatest and best of kings, Henry, had died (936), the entire people of the Franks and Saxons chose as their ruler his son Otto, whom his father had long before designated as king. Marking the place of the universal election, they ordered it to be at the palace of Aachen.

That place lies near Jülich, named after its founder, Julius Caesar.

When they had arrived there, the dukes and the leading men of the prefects, together with the remaining body of the princes and soldiers, gathered in the *xystus*—that is, the portico—adjoining the basilica of the great Charles.

They placed the new leader upon a throne constructed there, giving him their hands, promising loyalty, and pledging their service against all enemies; thus, according to their custom, they made him king.

While these things were being done by [Col. 0159B] the dukes and the rest of the magistracy, the chief bishop, with the entire priestly order and all the people, awaited below in the basilica the procession of the new king.

When he proceeded, the bishop went to meet him, touching the king’s right hand with his left. Carrying his staff in his right hand, clothed in linen and wearing the stole and chasuble, he advanced and stopped in the middle of the church. Then he turned back toward the people standing around him—for there were ambulatory passages arranged in a circle below and above in that basilica—

so that the king could be seen by all, and said:

“Behold, I bring before you Otto, chosen by God and formerly designated by the lord of all things, Henry, but now made king by all the princes. If this election pleases you, signify it by raising your right hands toward heaven.”

At this, [Col. 0159C] the entire people raised their right hands on high

and with a loud shout invoked prosperity for the new leader.

Then the bishop proceeded with the king, who was dressed in a close-fitting tunic according to Frankish custom,

behind the altar, upon which the royal insignia had been placed: the sword with its belt, the cloak with its armlets, the staff with the scepter, and the diadem.

At that time the chief bishop was named Hildebert,

a Frank by birth and a monk by profession. He had been raised or educated in the monastery of Fulda and had advanced through merit to the honor of being appointed father of that place; thereafter he had attained the dignity of the supreme episcopal see of Mainz.

[Col. 0160A] He was a man of remarkable holiness and, beyond his natural wisdom of mind, sufficiently distinguished in literary studies. Among his other gifts of grace, he is said to have received the spirit of prophecy.

When a dispute arose among the bishops concerning the consecration of the king—namely, between the bishop of Trier and that of Cologne—the former claimed the honor because his see was older and was regarded as founded by the blessed apostle Peter; the latter because the place belonged to his diocese. They therefore believed that this honor of consecration belonged to them. Nevertheless, both yielded to Hildebert’s universally acknowledged graciousness.

Hildebert himself approached the altar, took from it the sword with its belt, and said to the king:

“Receive this sword, with which, by the divine authority entrusted to you and with all the power of the entire empire of the Franks, you may drive out all the adversaries of Christ, [Col. 0160B] barbarians and evil Christians, for the firmest peace of all Christians.”

Then, taking the armlets and cloak, he clothed him and said:

“May these horns, lowered to the ground, remind you with what zeal you should burn for the faith and that you must persevere in maintaining peace to the end.”

Then, taking the scepter and staff, he said:

“Admonished by these signs, correct your subjects with paternal discipline; above all, extend the hand of mercy to God’s ministers, widows, and orphans. May the oil of compassion never fail from your head, so that in the present life and in the future you may be crowned with an everlasting reward.”

Immediately he was anointed with holy oil and crowned with a golden diadem by the bishops Hildebert and Wicfrid,

When the entire lawful consecration had been completed, [Col. 0160C] those same bishops led him to the throne, which was reached by stairways and had been constructed between two marble columns of extraordinary beauty. From there he could see everyone, and everyone could see him.

### 2

After divine praise had been offered and the sacrifice solemnly celebrated, the king descended to the palace. Approaching a marble table decorated with royal magnificence, he sat down with the bishops and the entire people; the dukes served.

Isbert, duke of the Lotharians, under whose authority that place lay, [Col. 0161A] arranged everything. Everhard presided over the table. Hermann the Frank presided over the cupbearers.

Arnulf was in charge of the cavalry and of selecting and placing the camps.

Siegfried,

the best of the Saxons and second to the king, formerly the king’s son-in-law and then related to him by marriage,

was at that time administering Saxony, lest any incursion of the enemy occur in the meantime, and he kept the younger Henry with him, bringing him up.

After this, the king honored each of the princes with an appropriate gift according to royal generosity and dismissed the multitude in complete good humor.

[Note: [Col. 0161] For *pincernis*, “over the cupbearers,” 2 has *pincerna*, “cupbearer.” Printed reading: pincerna 2.]

[Note: [Col. 0161] For *Sigifridus*, “Siegfried,” A and 3 have *sifridus*. Printed reading: sifridus A. 3.]

[Note: [Col. 0161] For *affinitate*, “by marriage relationship,” 1 has *afinitate*. Printed reading: afinitate 1.]

[Note: [Col. 0161D] Compare chapter 9.]

[Note: [Col. 0161D] That is, in the king’s absence he held authority in Saxony in his place. I have discussed Widukind’s words more fully elsewhere (*Yearbooks* I.1, p. 159); compare II.26, 34, III.23, and *to administer a city*, II.15.]

### 3

Meanwhile the barbarians grew violent in preparing new disturbances.

Boleslav struck down his brother,

a Christian man and, as they say, extremely devout in the worship of God. Fearing [Col. 0161B] the neighboring sub-king because he had obeyed the commands of the Saxons, he declared war against him.

The latter sent to Saxony to request assistance. Asic was sent to him with a legion of the Mesaburians and a strong force of the Hassigani.

An army of Thuringians was added to them.

That legion had been assembled from robbers. King Henry, although quite severe toward outsiders, was lenient toward his own people in every matter. Therefore, whenever he saw a thief or robber who was strong of hand and fit for war, he spared him the punishment he deserved, settled him in the suburb of Merseburg, gave him land and weapons, and ordered him to spare the citizens but to exercise robbery against the barbarians as far as they dared.

Thus a multitude collected from such men brought [Col. 0161C] a full legion on campaign.

When Boleslav heard about the Saxon army, and that the Saxons and Thuringians were advancing against him separately, he too divided his allies and, being extremely shrewd in counsel, planned to meet each army separately.

When the Thuringians saw the enemy unexpectedly approaching them, they avoided danger by flight.

Asic, however, with the Saxons and the other auxiliaries, rushed without hesitation against the enemy, [Col. 0162A] routed most of them by force of arms,

forced the rest to flee, and returned victorious to the camp.

Since he did not know about the army that had pursued the Thuringians, he made insufficiently cautious use of the victory he had won.

But when Boleslav saw our army scattered—some occupied in stripping the slain of their spoils, others in restoring their strength, and others in gathering straw for the horses—he reunited his army, including those who had fled and then returned, and suddenly attacked the unsuspecting men, secure in their recent victory.

He destroyed the commander and our entire army.

Then he proceeded to the city of the sub-king,

captured it at the first assault, and reduced it to a desolation that remains to this day.

That war continued until the king’s fourteenth year of rule.

From that time onward he remained [Col. 0162B] a faithful and useful servant of the king.

[Note: [Col. 0161D] Köpke has sufficiently demonstrated that the barbarians were pagan Slavs (compare II.19–20 and III.48), and that the Christian Bohemians are not meant by this designation. (*Yearbook* I.2, p. 85.) Yet not all Bohemians were Christians at that time. P.]

[Note: [Col. 0161] For *Bolizlav*, “Boleslav,” 2 and 3 consistently have *bolizlaf*. Printed reading: bolizlaf 2. 3. semper.]

[Note: [Col. 0161D] Many have convinced themselves that Wenceslaus was killed on September 28, 936. Compare Dobner on Hájek III, pp. 652–657; but it seems more correct to assign the event to 935.]

[Note: [Col. 0161] At *autem ei*, “however, to him,” 2 has the order *ei autem*. Printed reading: ei autem 2.]

### 4

When the king heard this report, he was not at all disturbed. Strengthened by divine power,

he entered the territory of the barbarians with his entire army to restrain their savagery.

His father had previously made war against them as well, because they had violated the envoys of his son Thankmar. We shall, as we believe, speak of this more fully below.

It therefore pleased the new king to appoint a new commander of the army. For this office he chose a noble, industrious, and sufficiently prudent man named Hermann.

By this honor he aroused the jealousy not only of the other princes but also of Hermann’s brother Wichmann.

For this reason Wichmann withdrew from the army, pretending illness.

Wichmann was a powerful and brave man, high-spirited, [Col. 0162C] experienced in war, and so knowledgeable that his subjects declared that he knew many things beyond human capacity.

Hermann, however, being in the front line, encountered the enemy in battle upon entering their territory, defeated them bravely, and thereby inflamed his enemies with even greater jealousy.

Among them was Eckard, the son of Liudolf.

He took Hermann’s success so badly that he promised either to accomplish greater things [Col. 0163A] or not to live.

Accordingly, after gathering the bravest men from the entire army, he violated the king’s prohibition and crossed with his companions the marsh that lay between the enemy city and the king’s camp. He immediately encountered the enemy and, surrounded by them, perished with all his men.

Of those who fell with him, eighteen had been chosen from the entire army.

After slaughtering a multitude of the enemy and making the rest tributary, the king returned to Saxony.

This occurred on the seventh day before the Kalends of October.

[Note: [Col. 0161] For *roboratus*, “strengthened,” 3 has *corroboratus*, also “strengthened.” Printed reading: corroboratus 3.]

[Note: [Col. 0162D] Contrary to the common view, Otto did not undertake this expedition against the Bohemians but against another Slavic people. He himself states that he went against the Riadri—that is, the Redarii—in this year. Compare the charter in Schannat, *History of Fulda*, *Collection of Documents*, p. 143.]

[Note: [Col. 0161] Before *plenius*, “more fully,” in 1, *nos*, “we,” is written above the line; 2 has the order *plenius nos*. Printed reading: ante plenius in 1 vocabulum nos superscriptum est; plenius nos 2.]

[Note: [Col. 0162D] Compare Wedekind, *Notes* II, p. 63.]

[Note: [Col. 0161] For “he inflamed his enemies with greater jealousy,” 2 has *maiorem invidiam accendit*, “he inflamed greater jealousy.” Printed reading: maiorem invidiam accendit 2.]

### 5

After this, the ancient enemies, the Hungarians, came to test the new king’s strength (937).

Entering Francia, they planned, if possible, to invade Saxony from the western region. But when the king heard of it, he delayed not at all. [Col. 0163B] He met them with a powerful army, put them to flight, and drove them from his borders.

[Note: [Col. 0163] For *venerunt*, “they came,” 3 has the equivalent shortened *venere*. Printed reading: venere 3.]

### 6

When foreign wars had ceased, civil conflicts began to arise. For the Saxons, having been made glorious through the king’s rule,

disdained to serve other nations and refused to hold the offices they had held by the favor of anyone but the king alone.

Therefore Everhard, angered against Bruning,

gathered a force and gave his city, called Elmeri, to the flames, killing all the inhabitants of that city.

When the king heard of this presumption, he condemned Everhard to pay one hundred talents, assessed in horses,

and imposed upon all the military leaders who had assisted him in this crime the dishonor of carrying dogs—which they bore as far as the royal city we call Magdeburg.

[Note: [Col. 0163] At *gloriosi facti*, “made glorious,” A, 2, 3 have the order *facti gloriosi*. Printed reading: facti gloriosi A 2, 3.]

[Note: [Col. 0163] For *habuerunt*, “they held,” 3 has the equivalent *habuere*. Printed reading: habuere 3.]

[Note: [Col. 0163] For *alii*, “of another” in this construction, 2 and 3 have *alius*, the standard genitive form. Printed reading: alius 2, 3.]

[Note: [Col. 0163] For *Bruningum*, “Bruning,” A has *brunignum*. Printed reading: brunignum A.]

[Note: [Col. 0163] For *succendio*, “burning,” 2 has *incendio*, “fire.” Printed reading: incendio 2.]

[Note: [Col. 0163] For *vocabulo Elmeri*, “named Elmeri,” 2 has *elmeri vocabulo*; 3, *v. Elveri*; β, *v. Helmeri* (“named Elveri,” “named Helmeri”). Printed reading: elmeri vocabulo 2, v. Elveri 3, v. Helmeri β.]

[Note: [Col. 0163D] It seems to have been Helmershausen on the lower Diemel, as Meibomius already proposed; alternatively, Elmershausen or Helmarshausen in the same region.]

[Note: [Col. 0163D] Compare Grimm, *Antiquities of Law*, p. 715, who found no earlier testimony to this punishment.]

[Note: [Col. 0163] For *Magathaburg*, “Magdeburg”: *magathaburch* 2; *magedeburg* A; *Magadaburg* 3. Printed reading: magathaburch 2, magedeburg A. Magadaburg 3.]

### 7

[Col. 0163C] At the same time the king transferred the relics of the martyr Innocent to the same city.

The king himself, being exceedingly merciful, immediately received with compassion those whom he had punished with deserved correction as disturbers of the peace. Honoring each of them with a royal gift, he dismissed them in peace.

Nevertheless, they continued to cling to their duke in every wickedness, because he was cheerful in spirit, approachable toward men of moderate means,

generous in giving, and by these qualities associated many of the Saxons with himself.

[Note: [Col. 0163] At Innocent’s relics, 1 adds *sancti*, “of Saint,” above the line. Printed reading: add. sancti 1, vocabulo superscripto.]

[Note: [Col. 0163D] King Rudolf of Burgundy sent these relics to him. Compare Otto’s charters for the church of Magdeburg, dated September 21 and 27, 937, in Meibomius I, p. 741.]

[Note: [Col. 0163] For *dimisit in pace*, “he dismissed in peace,” 2 has the order *in pace dimisit*. Printed reading: in pace dimisit 2.]

[Note: [Col. 0163] For *haerebant*, “they clung,” 2 and 7 have *adherebant*, “they adhered.” Printed reading: adherebant 2, 7.]

[Note: [Col. 0163] For *mediocribus*, “to men of moderate station,” 3 has *mediocris in rebus*, “moderate in affairs.” Printed reading: mediocris in rebus 3.]

### 8

[Col. 0164A] At that time Arnulf, duke of the Bavarians, died, and his sons, lifted up in pride, disregarded the king’s command to attend the royal court.

[Note: [Col. 0163] For *contempserunt*, “they disregarded,” 1 has *contemserant*, “they had disregarded.” Printed reading: contemserant 1.]

### 9

At that same time Count Siegfried died.

When Thankmar claimed his office,

and the king transferred it by royal gift to Count Gero,

Thankmar was afflicted with great sadness because he was related to Siegfried. For his mother was the daughter of Siegfried’s maternal aunt, and from her King Henry had fathered Thankmar.

The king then went to Bavaria, put matters there in proper order, and returned to Saxony (938).

[Note: [Col. 0163] For *Sigifridus*, “Siegfried,” 3 always has *Sisfridus* and A *sifridus*. Printed reading: 3 semper Sisfridus, A. sifridus.]

[Note: [Col. 0163] For *legationem*, “commission/office,” 3 has *ditionem*, “jurisdiction.” Printed reading: ditionem 3]

[Note: [Col. 0163D] The count’s *legatio* signifies the dignity of command over the borders; compare I.36.]

[Note: [Col. 0163] For *vendicasset*, “had claimed,” 3 has the spelling *vindicasset*. Printed reading: vindicasset 3.]

[Note: [Col. 0163] For *Thancmarus*, “Thankmar,” A has *thangmarus*. Printed reading: thangmarus A.]

[Note: [Col. 0163] For *ei esset*, “he was related to him,” 1 has *esset ei*; 2, A, 7 have *ejus esset*, “he was his [relative].” Printed reading: esset ei 1. ejus esset 2, A. 7.]

### 10

The discord that had arisen between Everhard and Bruning advanced to the point that [Col. 0164B] public killings took place, the countryside was ravaged, and they nowhere refrained from setting fires.

There was also a dispute concerning the diversity of laws. Some said that grandsons should not be counted among the sons, nor share a lawful inheritance with the sons if their fathers happened to die while their grandfathers were still alive.

Therefore the king issued an edict that a general assembly of the people should be held at the village called Stela.

It was decided that the case should be examined and judged by arbiters. But the king, following better counsel, did not wish noble and elderly men of the people to be treated dishonorably. Instead, he ordered the matter to be decided by champions.

The side that counted grandsons among the sons therefore won.

It was confirmed by an everlasting agreement that they should [Col. 0164C] divide the inheritance equally with their paternal uncles.

There too the disturbers of the peace were exposed—those who until then had denied having done anything against royal authority, claiming that they had merely avenged an injury against their associates.

When the king recognized that they had despised him—for they had not deigned to come to the appointed place as ordered—he delayed taking up arms and gave room for pardon, as he was always accustomed to do through his characteristic clemency.

But this delay drew many onward to greater ruin.

Moreover, the rebels committed many wicked acts: [Col. 0165A] murders, perjuries, ravaging, and arson. In those days little distinction was made between right and wrong, sacred obligation and perjury.

[Note: [Col. 0163] *Quae*, “which,” is absent from A. Printed reading: deest A.]

[Note: [Col. 0163] At *facta est*, “arose,” 2 has *erat* in place of *est*: “had arisen.” Printed reading: erat 2.]

[Note: [Col. 0163] For *fueruntque*, “and there were,” 3 has equivalent *fuereque*. Printed reading: fuereque 3.]

[Note: [Col. 0163] For *legitime cum filiis*, “lawfully with the sons,” 2 has the order *cum filiis legitime*. Printed reading: cum filiis legitime 2.]

[Note: [Col. 0164D] Opposite Werden on the Ruhr River, today Steil. Meibom. A charter shows that the king was there on May 18, 938; see Moser, *History of Osnabrück* I, Appendix, p. 4.]

[Note: [Col. 0163] For plural *computabant*, “they counted,” 1 has singular *computabat*, “it counted.” Printed reading: computabat 1.]

[Note: [Col. 0163] At *patruis*, “paternal uncles,” 1 has *patrius*, corrected to *patribus*, “fathers.” Printed reading: patrius corr. patribus 1.]

[Note: [Col. 0163] *Pacis*, “of the peace,” is absent from 2. Printed reading: deest 2.]

[Note: [Col. 0163] *Facti sunt*, “were made/became,” is absent from 1. Printed reading: facti sunt desunt 1.]

[Note: [Col. 0163] For *qui hactenus*, “who until then,” A has *quia actenus*, “because until then.” Printed reading: quia actenus A.]

[Note: [Col. 0163] For *vindicassent*, “they had avenged,” 2, A, 7 have infinitive *vindicasse*, “to have avenged.” Printed reading: vindicasse 2, A 7.]

### 11

Thankmar was also joined to Everhard. After gathering a strong force, he attacked the fortress called Badiliki,

where the younger Henry was staying. After giving the plunder of the city to his fellow soldiers, he departed, taking Henry with him like some worthless slave.

There Gevehard, son of Udo

(the brother of Duke Hermann), was killed. Because of his death, with God ordering all things, the Frankish dukes were divided among themselves.

Thankmar’s soldiers, enriched by such great spoils, were now prepared for every enterprise.

After this he captured the city called Heresburg,

and, gathering a strong multitude, [Col. 0165B] settled in it, carrying out many acts of robbery from there.

Everhard kept Henry with him.

At that same time Dedi was killed before the gates of the city called Larun,

where Everhard’s soldiers were stationed.

Wichmann, who had first alienated himself from the king, heard of the rebels’ great crime and turned back. He made peace with the king, for he was exceedingly prudent, useful, and faithful, and remained so to the end.

Thankmar, the son of King Henry, had been born of a noble mother.

He was quick-handed, sharp-minded, skilled in warfare, but amid arms he made less use of honorable chastity.

His mother possessed extensive property.

Although he had been enriched by his father with many other things,

he nevertheless bitterly resented being deprived of his maternal inheritance, and [Col. 0165C] for this reason took up arms against his lord the king, to his own destruction and that of his followers.

The king, although unwilling, saw the matter advancing toward such grave danger and went with a large retinue to Heresburg to subdue Thankmar’s insolence.

When the citizens of that city learned that the king was approaching them with a strong force, they opened the gates and admitted the army that had been besieging the city.

[Col. 0166A] Thankmar fled into the church dedicated by Pope Leo to the blessed apostle Peter.

The army pursued him even into the church, especially Henry’s retainers, who grieved over the injury to their lord and sought to avenge it. They did not hesitate to cut through the doors with iron, but entered the sacred building armed.

Thankmar stood beside the altar, with his weapons laid upon it together with a golden torque. When he was being pressed from the opposite side by weapons, a certain Thiadbold,

an illegitimate son of Cobbo, wounded him amid insults and immediately received a wound from him in return; in a short time he lost his life in terrible madness.

A certain soldier, named Maincia, pierced Thankmar through the back with a spear from a window adjoining the altar and killed him there beside the altar.

Maincia himself, a supporter of fraternal discord,

[Col. 0166B] later lost his life miserably in the battle of Birten, after wickedly snatching gold from the altar.

The king, unaware of these events and absent, was indignant when he heard of the soldiers’ rashness. But while the civil war was still raging, he could not punish them.

Moved by his brother’s fate and displaying the clemency of his character, he spoke briefly in praise of his courage and industriousness. But he condemned Thiadric and the three sons of that man’s paternal aunt, who had joined hands with Thankmar,

to death under Frankish law and had them perish by strangulation.

From there he turned the army, eager for battle and enriched by the city’s plunder, toward Larun.

The men of that place, fiercely resisting at the command of the city’s prefect, did not cease to hurl stones against stones and weapons against weapons.

Overwhelmed by the battle, they requested a truce against the commander’s orders.

[Col. 0166C] When this was granted,

the commander’s protection was denied them.

Therefore, leaving the city, they surrendered themselves to royal authority.

In that battle Tamma, the cupbearer, formerly famous for having successfully carried out many other undertakings, became renowned.

When Everhard heard of Thankmar’s death and of the defection of his soldiers,

his spirit broken, he prostrated himself before his captive and asked for pardon—and wickedly earned it.

[Note: [Col. 0166D] The church was built in 785, as the Annals of Lorsch record for that year. No one known to me except Widukind reports that Pope Leo consecrated it. A charter granted by the same Leo to the church in 799, in the city of Heresburg itself, survives; see Meibomius, *Sources* III, p. 21.]

[Note: [Col. 0165] After the entry into the sacred building, 1 adds *tunc*, “then.” Printed reading: add. tunc 1.]

[Note: [Col. 0165] For *Thiadboldus*, “Thiadbold”: *thiadbodlus* 2, 3; *Theobaldus* α. Printed reading: thiadbodlus 2. 3. Theobaldus α.]

[Note: [Col. 0165] For *Maincia*, the soldier’s name, 1 has *mancia*. Printed reading: mancia 1.]

[Note: [Col. 0165] In 2, *fautor*, “supporter,” is corrected to *auctor*, “author/instigator.” Printed reading: fautor corr. auctor 2.]

[Note: [Col. 0166D] Compare chapter 17.]

[Note: [Col. 0165] For *indignatus*, “indignant,” 2 and 7 have *dedignatus*, “disdaining.” Printed reading: dedignatus 2. 7.]

[Note: [Col. 0165] For *fervente*, “raging,” 2 has the form *ferventi*. Printed reading: ferventi 2.]

[Note: [Col. 0165] For *contristari*, “to be distressed,” α has active *contristare*, “to distress.” The latter fits the sense “he could not distress/punish them.” Printed reading: contristare α.]

[Note: [Col. 0165] For *Thiadricum*, “Thiadric”: *thiedericum* 2; *thiadericum* 3; *theodericum* α. Printed reading: thiedericum 2. thiadericum 3. theodericum α]

[Note: [Col. 0165] For *junxerant*, “had joined [hands],” 3 has *vinxerant*, “had bound [hands].” Printed reading: vinxerant 3.]

[Note: [Col. 0165] For *strangulo*, “by strangulation,” 3 and a. have the form *strangula*. Printed reading: strangula 3. a.]

[Note: [Col. 0165] For *Laras*, the place-name: *Lares* 3; *Larun* 7. Printed reading: Lares 3. Larun 7.]

[Note: [Col. 0165] For *consulto*, “counsel/consultation,” 2 has *consulta*, “counsels” (or a different inflection). Printed reading: consulta 2.]

[Note: [Col. 0166D] That is, against the will of the duke or prefect.—They intended, that is, to consult Duke Everhard. P.]

[Note: [Col. 0165] For *concessis*, “[these things] having been granted,” 3 has *concessit*, “he granted.” Printed reading: concessit 3.]

[Note: [Col. 0165] At the denial of the duke’s protection, 3 and α add *non*, “not,” reversing the negative statement. Printed reading: add. non 3. α.]

[Note: [Col. 0165] For *negatur*, “is denied,” 1 has *negavit*, “he denied.” Printed reading: negavit 1.]

[Note: [Col. 0165] For *tradiderunt*, “they surrendered,” 3 has equivalent *tradidere*. Printed reading: tradidere 3.]

[Note: [Col. 0165] For *ea*, “that [battle],” 1 has *et*, “and.” Printed reading: et 1.]

[Note: [Col. 0165] For *Tamma*: *tammo* 2, α, 7; *Dammo* 3, variants of the cupbearer’s name. Printed reading: tammo 2. α. 7. Dammo 3.]

[Note: [Col. 0165] For *et*, “and,” α has *et de*, “and of.” Printed reading: et de α.]

### 12

[Col. 0167A] At that time Henry was still exceedingly young,

hot-tempered,

and enticed by an excessive desire to reign. He released Everhard from his guilt on this condition: Everhard was to conspire with him against the king, Henry’s lord and brother, and, if possible, place the royal diadem upon Henry’s head.

Thus a pact was struck between them.

Afterward Henry returned freely to the king and was received by him with purer faith and affection than he himself brought on his arrival.

[Note: [Col. 0167] *Erat*, “was,” is absent from 1. Printed reading: deest 1.]

[Note: [Col. 0167C] Henry, born between 919 and 922, was then in his sixteenth or eighteenth year.]

[Note: [Col. 0167] *Fervens*, “hot/ardent,” is absent from 3. Printed reading: deest 3.]

### 13

At the urging especially of the excellent and most religiously distinguished man Fritheric,

the successor of Archbishop Hildebert,

Everhard approached the king, humbly sought pardon,

and surrendered himself and all his possessions to the king’s judgment.

Therefore, lest so great a crime remain uncorrected, the king sent him, as though into exile, [Col. 0167B] to the city of Hildesheim.

But after not much time he was mercifully received back into favor and restored to his former honor.

[Note: [Col. 0167] For *Frithurici*, “of Fritheric,” 2 and α always have *friederici*. Printed reading: friederici 2. α semper.]

[Note: [Col. 0167C] Hildebert died on May 31, 937.]

[Note: [Col. 0167] *Veniam*, “pardon,” is absent from 3. Printed reading: deest 3.]

[Note: [Col. 0167] For *Hildinensem*, “of Hildesheim”: *Hildenensem* 3; *Hildesheimensem* α. Printed reading: Hildenensem 3. Hildesheimensem α.]

### 14

While these events were taking place, our ancient enemies, the Hungarians, suddenly burst into Saxony

and, setting up their camps along the banks of the river Bode,

spread from there throughout the entire region.

The duke, sent from the camp with part of the army, moved his standards toward evening on that day around the city called Stederburg.

The townspeople, seeing that the enemy had been made sluggish both by the journey and by the heavy rain,

boldly burst through the gates,

first terrifying them with a shout, then suddenly rushing upon their opponents. After killing very many of them and capturing a large number of horses together with several standards,

[Col. 0167C] they forced the rest to flee.

The cities they encountered, observing the enemy’s flight, harried them with weapons everywhere. After striking down most of them, they forced the duke himself into a certain muddy pit and overwhelmed him.

But the other part of the army, turning northward and led by the skill of a certain Slav to a place called Thrimining,

perished because of the difficult terrain and after being surrounded by armed men, and struck excessive fear into the rest.

The commander of that army escaped with a few men, was captured, and led to the king; he was ransomed for a great price.

When this was heard, all the enemy camps were thrown into confusion [Col. 0168A] and sought safety in flight.

They did not appear again in Saxony for thirty years.

[Note: [Col. 0167] For *Saxoniam*, “Saxony,” 3 has *Saxones*, “the Saxons.” Printed reading: Saxones 3.]

[Note: [Col. 0167] For *Badae*, the river-name rendered Bode, α has *Bode*. Printed reading: Bode α.]

[Note: [Col. 0167] For *Stedieraburg*: 2 corrects *stederburg* to *stedieraburg*; 3 has *Stediereburg*; α *Steidiereburg*. Printed reading: stederburg corr. stedieraburg 2. Stediereburg 3. Steidiereburg α.]

[Note: [Col. 0167C] Stederburg near Wolfenbüttel.]

[Note: [Col. 0167] For *segniores*, “more sluggish,” 3 has *seniores*, “older.” Printed reading: seniores 3.]

[Note: [Col. 0167] For ablative *portis*, “through/from the gates,” 3 has accusative *portas*, “the gates.” Printed reading: portas 3.]

[Note: [Col. 0167] For *compulerunt*, “they forced,” 3, and perhaps 1, have equivalent *compulere*. Printed reading: compulere 3. 1?]

[Note: [Col. 0167] For *habuere*, “they had [in their path],” α has equivalent *habuerunt*. Printed reading: habuerunt α.]

[Note: [Col. 0167] For *luti*, “of mud,” α has *loci*, “of a place.” Printed reading: loci α.]

[Note: [Col. 0167] For *altera autem pars*, “but the other part,” 3 has plural *alterae autem partes*, “but the other parts”; α has *alter autem Ung. exercitus*, “but the other Hungarian army.” Printed reading: alterae autem partes 3. alter autem Ung. exercitus α.]

[Note: [Col. 0167] For *in locum*, “into a place,” α has *in loco*, “in a place.” Printed reading: loco α.]

[Note: [Col. 0167] For *Thrimining*: *thriminig* 1; *triminig* 7, the same place-name. Printed reading: thriminig 1. triminig 7.]

[Note: [Col. 0167C] He means the forest now called the Dromling. Meibom. It was a marshy region, the source of the Aller and the Ohre; the Annals of Corvey cited above call the district [Col. 0168C] Belxa. P.]

[Note: [Col. 0167] *Omnia*, “all,” is absent from 1. Printed reading: deest 1.]

[Note: [Col. 0167] For *quaesierunt ... apparuerunt*, “they sought ... appeared,” 3 has the equivalent forms *quaesiere ... apparuere*. Printed reading: quaesiere---apparuere 3.]

[Note: [Col. 0168C] I have noted above that Widukind wrote this as the year 967 was drawing to a close.]

[Note: [Col. 0167] The same note is repeated at *apparuerunt*, “they appeared”: 3 has *quaesiere ... apparuere*, “they sought ... appeared.” Printed reading: quaesiere---apparuere 3.]

### 15. (DCCCCXXXIX)

After this, Henry, burning with the desire to reign, prepared a celebrated feast at a place called Salaveldum [Note: [Col. 0167] Salaveldum in 3; Solaveldun in α.] [Note: [Col. 0168C] Saalfeld.]. Since he was great and powerful, by royal dignity and authority he gave many gifts to very many people, and for that reason associated many with himself in this faction. There were nevertheless many who [Note: [Col. 0167] “Which” in 1.] thought it preferable to conceal the matter, solely so that they might not be found implicated in the fraternal discord [Note: [Col. 0167] “To the king” in 3.]. Yet they gave advice by which the war might more easily be brought to an end: namely, that he should leave Saxony under military protection and throw himself against the Lotharians, a feeble race of men; and so it happened that the king defeated them at the first attack and exhausted them in a single engagement.

Thus, with the advice of his fellow soldiers, Saxony having been left, as we have said, and the cities of Saxony—or those in the land of the Thuringians—having been entrusted to military protection [Note: [Col. 0167] The words “as we have said … cities” are absent in 3.], he himself went with his friends against the Lotharians. The report of this terrified everyone everywhere, because they had no knowledge at all of the reason for the king’s sudden withdrawal and unexpected war [Note: [Col. 0167] “They had no knowledge” is singular in 1.].

When the king heard this report, at first he did not believe it; finally, having established the certainty of the matter of the war, he delayed no longer but followed his brother with the army [Note: [Col. 0167] “Pursued” in 2 and α.]. When he approached the city fortified by his brother’s garrisons, called Thortmanni [Note: [Col. 0167] Thormanni in 1; Throtmanni in 2 and 3.] [Note: [Col. 0168C] Dortmund.], the soldiers who were in it, mindful of Thancmar’s fate, did not dare to await the king there. They left the city [Note: [Col. 0167] “The city” in 2.] and surrendered themselves to the king.

There was a man named Agina [Note: [Col. 0167] α always has Hagina.] who was supposed to administer that city on Henry’s behalf. [Col. 0168C] The king bound him with a solemn oath to the effect that, if he could, he should recall his lord from war to peace and concord, or at least return himself to the king. Thus dismissed, he went to his lord. The army led by the king reached the banks of the Rhine.

### 16

At the time when Evurhardus was at war with the king [Note: [Col. 0168C] “At the time of the earlier war,” in a. 938.], Hadaldus was sent to Isilberhtus for the sake of concord and peace. He was in charge of the king’s bedchamber [Note: [Col. 0167] “Haaldus, a very noble man and related to the king,” is certainly a fabrication of Falkius (p. 584).]. Since the matter had not yet openly inclined toward either side [Note: [Col. 0167] “He might incline” in 3, α, and 7.], he was received indignantly, and the reply was postponed from day to day [Note: [Col. 0167] “A reply” in 1.].

But sensing the duke’s hostility and no longer content with such evasions [Note: [Col. 0167] “Despised” in the variant reading], he said: “By royal command I order you to be presented before the king’s tribunal on the appointed day, with the people as witnesses [Note: [Col. 0169] “I confer royal authority upon you,” he says, “with the people present,” in i. i. r. t. f. α; “with the people as witnesses” in 2, 3, and α. This is a passage which W. himself may appear to have altered.]; otherwise, know that you will be judged an enemy.”

In the same way he dismissed Bishop Bernhard [Note: [Col. 0169] Berthardus in 1.] [Note: [Col. 0169D] Of Halberstadt.], who had been sent by the king, dishonored and without a definite answer. It is also said that he repeatedly tampered with the seals of the royal letters. After this statement [Note: [Col. 0169] Absent in 1.], however, he began to treat the envoy somewhat better [Note: [Col. 0169] “Better” in 3.] and had him escorted away with honor.

### 17

[Note: [Col. 0169] This chapter 17, omitted in the manuscript, has been inserted here.]

Thus Henry and Isilberhtus, preparing their forces for war [Note: [Col. 0169] “Preparing” in α.], resolved to meet the king at the Rhine. Agina too, mindful of his oath, went ahead of the army, crossed the Rhine, and presented himself to the king. After greeting him in the humblest words, he said:

“Your brother, my lord, wishes you to reign for a long time, safe and unharmed, with a great and extensive empire, and commits himself to hasten to your service [Col. 0169B] as quickly as possible [Note: [Col. 0169] “His whole service” in α; the words are absent in 1.].”

When the king asked whether he had been thinking of peace or war, he looked ahead and saw a very large multitude proceeding slowly with raised standards and moving toward the part of his army that had already crossed the Rhine. Turning to Agina, he said: “What does that multitude want, or what is it?”

He replied quite calmly [Note: [Col. 0169] “Knowledgeably” in 3.]: “It is my lord, your brother. If he had deigned to incline his mind to my persuasion, he would have come otherwise [Note: [Col. 0169] “He would come” corrected to “he would have come” in 2.]. I have come exactly as I swore [Note: [Col. 0169] “He came” in 2.].” [The preceding reference to the part of the army has the uncertain reading “qui [quae?]” in the source.]

When the king heard this, he did not conceal his inner grief in the movement of his body, because there were no ships by which he could cross the Rhine. The great river offered no other route [Note: [Col. 0169] “Would offer” in 1.], and the urgency of the sudden battle allowed those stationed on the farther bank to think of nothing else than either that they must fall in the presence of their enemies [Col. 0169C] or defend their lives by arms [Note: [Col. 0169] “Might be obliged to fall” in 3; the phrase is absent in 2.].

Therefore the king stretched out his hands in supplication to God [Note: [Col. 0169] “To the Lord” in a.] and said [Note: [Col. 0169] Absent in α.]: “God [Note: [Col. 0169] “Lord” in α; “the Lord” in 3.], author and ruler of all things, look upon your people, over whom you have willed me to preside, so that, rescued from their enemies, all nations may know that no mortal can oppose your ordinance [Note: [Col. 0169] “Your ordinance” in 1], you who can do all things and live and reign forever.”

Those who were on the farther bank sent their baggage and every impediment across to a place called Xantum [Note: [Col. 0169] Xanctum in 2; Sanctum in 3.] [Note: [Col. 0169D] The Continuation of Regino under the year 939 and Liudprand IV. 23 report that the battle was fought near Biertana (Birthen); therefore Widukind also calls this battle the Biertan battle in ch. 11 and III. 16.]. They themselves, however, prepared to await the enemy [Note: [Col. 0169] “Were awaiting” in the variant reading].

Since there was a pool between our men and the enemy, the Saxons divided their comrades: one group rushed upon the enemy from the front, while the other followed from behind, crushing the enemy in the midst [Note: [Col. 0169] The words from “the other” through “the enemy” are absent in 1.]. Though few, they pressed hard upon the many.

For it is said that there were scarcely more than one hundred armed men among our forces [Col. 0170A], whereas the opposing army was quite large. But since they were pressed from the front and equally from behind, it was not apparent on which side they ought chiefly to take precautions.

There were also some among our men who knew how to speak partly in the Gallic language [Note: [Col. 0169] “Who partly knew the Gallic language” in 1.]. They raised a loud cry in Gallic [Note: [Col. 0169] “Raised it high” in α.] and urged the adversaries to flee. The latter, thinking that their own allies had shouted in this manner, began to flee as soon as the cry was raised.

On that day many of our men were wounded [Note: [Col. 0169] “Many from our side” in 2.], and some were even killed. Among them was Ailbertus [Note: [Col. 0169] Eilbertus in α; Albertus in 3.], surnamed Candidus. Wounded by a weapon of Duke Henry, he died after only a few days had passed.

All the enemy were either killed, captured, or put to flight; all their baggage and all the enemy’s equipment were divided among the victors [Note: [Col. 0169] “Equipment” misread as “supplicant” in 1.]. On the side of the Lotharians, Godofridus [Note: [Col. 0169] “Frid” in 2; Godefridus in α.], surnamed Niger, was said to have fought well in that engagement. Maincia too, whom we mentioned above, fell on that day.

### 18

Dadi [Note: [Col. 0169] Dedi in α.], a Thuringian [Note: [Col. 0169] “Thuringian” in α.], sent word to the governors of the cities that were in the eastern part belonging to Duke Henry [Note: [Col. 0169] “Who” in the main text; “which” in α.] about the king’s victory and the fact that the duke himself had fallen in battle. He acted shrewdly so that they all surrendered themselves to royal authority.

Henry, however, did not leave this act unavenged [Note: [Col. 0169] “This deed” in α.]. Only two cities remained to them out of all the rest: Mersburg [Note: [Col. 0169] Always Mesburg in 1.] and Scithingi [Note: [Col. 0169] Scitingi in 2; Schidingi in α.]. After the victory, the king decided [Note: [Col. 0169] “Was ordered” in 3.] to pursue his brother and his brother-in-law.

### 19

When he heard of the defection of his cities [Note: [Col. 0169] “Henry” is added in α.] and was broken by the king’s recent victory, he set out with only nine armed men [Note: [Col. 0169] “With new men” in 3.] and, approaching Saxony rather slowly [Col. 0170C] [Note: [Col. 0169] “Slow” in 2; “slowly” in 7.], entered the city of Mersburg [Note: [Col. 0169] Mesbug in 2.].

When the king learned of this, he too returned to Saxony and besieged with his army the city in which his brother was. But since he could not withstand a stronger and larger force, after roughly two months Henry surrendered the city and went out to the king [Note: [Col. 0169] “Entered” in α; “engaged” in 7.].

A thirty-day truce was granted him, so that he might withdraw from Saxony with the soldiers attached to him. If any of them wished to approach the king, he would have the opportunity for pardon. After this, Saxony rested from its internal wars for a few days.

### 20

The barbarians, however, encouraged by our weariness, ceased nowhere from burning, slaughter, and devastation, and they planned to kill Gero, whom the king had placed over them [Note: [Col. 0170D] In addition to the district of Suevon, Gero had already ruled Nordthuringowe in 937, and in these years he seems to have been appointed margrave of the Saxon frontier.].

Gero himself, forestalling deceit with deceit, destroyed in a single night nearly thirty barbarian princes who, drunk at a splendid banquet and buried in wine, were helpless [Col. 0171A]. But since he was not sufficient against all the barbarian nations—for at that time the Apodriti too had rebelled [Note: [Col. 0171] Abotriti in α; the form is always used there], and after defeating our army they killed its duke, named Haicam [Note: [Col. 0171] Haincam in 1.]—the army, led out repeatedly by the king himself, harmed them, afflicted them in many ways, and brought them almost to the point of utter calamity.

Nevertheless, they chose war rather than peace, preferring every misery to their dear freedom. This race of men is hard and enduring of labor [Note: [Col. 0171] “This kind of men” in α.], accustomed to the lightest fare; what is usually a heavy burden for our people, the Slavs regard as a kind of pleasure.

Many days indeed passed while the one side fought variously for glory and a great and extensive empire, the other for freedom against the most extreme servitude. In those days the Saxons suffered many enemies: Slavs from the east, Franks from the south, Lotharians from the west [Note: [Col. 0171] The words from “Franks” through “west” are absent in 1 and 7.], and from the north Danes as well as Slavs. For this reason the barbarians prolonged the conflict.

### 21

There was a certain Slav left by King Henry who, by the law of his people and by paternal succession, was lord of those called the Heveldi [Note: [Col. 0171] Hevelli throughout α.], a man named Tugumir. Won over by a large sum of money and persuaded by an even greater promise, he declared that he would betray the region [Note: [Col. 0171] Absent in 1.].

Accordingly, having escaped as though secretly [Note: [Col. 0171] “Because” in α.], he came to the city called Brennaburg [Note: [Col. 0171] Brandenburg in 3.]. Recognized by the people and received as their lord, he soon fulfilled what he had promised. For, inviting his nephew—the only one remaining of all the princes of the people [Col. 0171C] [Note: [Col. 0171] “Of the peoples” in 1.]—to come to him, he captured and killed him by treachery [Note: [Col. 0171] “Captures and kills” in 1.], and handed over the city and the whole region [Note: [Col. 0171] Absent in 3 and 7.] to royal authority.

After this deed, all the barbarian nations as far as the Oder River [Note: [Col. 0171] Odora in 3.] likewise subjected themselves to the royal tributes.

### 22

Henry, therefore, leaving Saxony, again went to the Lotharians and stayed for some time with his brother-in-law, namely Duke Isilberhtus [Note: [Col. 0171] Isberhtus in 1; Isilberthus in 3.], and his soldiers.

The king again led an army against Isilberhtus [Note: [Col. 0171] Histberhtus in 1.], and the entire region of the Lotharians subject to his rule was given over to fire. Besieged in the city [Note: [Col. 0171] “Fortress” in 4.] called Kievermont [Note: [Col. 0171D] Properly Chèvremont, near Liège.], he escaped from there and departed. Since the siege made little progress because of the difficulty of the terrain, the king returned to Saxony after devastating the region on every side.

### 23

Knowing that a certain count of Duke Isilberhtus, named Immo [Note: [Col. 0171] Giselberthum in 3.], was exceedingly crafty and cunning, he thought it better to contend against him by arts than by arms [Col. 0172A]. Immo, being extremely shrewd, submitted himself to the better and stronger man and took up arms against the duke. The duke bore this most bitterly, because he had to endure as his adversary the man to whose counsel and loyalty he had hitherto entrusted himself above all.

The duke’s indignation was also increased by a herd of pigs cleverly captured by Immo [Note: [Col. 0171] “For the duke” in 3; “of the duke himself” in α.]. When the duke’s swineherds were passing by the gates [Note: [Col. 0171] “The pigs” in 3.] of the city, Immo had a piglet driven before the gate and, with the gates opened, received the entire herd of pigs inside the city.

Unable to bear this injury, the duke gathered an army and besieged Immo. He is said to have possessed very many swarms of bees [Note: [Col. 0172D] Some think that this story arose from the German word Imme (plural impi), “bee.”]. Breaking them open, he threw them against the horsemen [Note: [Col. 0171] “Threw” misspelled as “progecit” in 1.]. The bees, stinging the horses with their barbs, drove them into madness, so that the horsemen began to be in danger [Col. 0172B].

Seeing this, Immo looked out from the wall and threatened a sortie with his companions [Note: [Col. 0171] “Threatened” in 3.]. Thus, by such stratagems, the duke was repeatedly deceived by Immo and lifted the siege.

As he departed, he is said to have said: “With Immo thinking along with me, I easily held all the Lotharians captive; now I am unable to capture him alone together with all the Lotharians.”

### 24

Evurhardus, considering that the war had lasted so long, no longer remained quiet. Indeed, despising the king and disregarding the force of his oaths, he joined hands with Isilberhtus [Note: [Col. 0171] Hisberhtus in 1; Iselberthus in 3; the latter form occurs frequently.] and together conspired to kindle wars [Note: [Col. 0171] “They might conspire” in α.].

Not content with the western kingdom alone [Note: [Col. 0171] “Despised” in 1.], they plunged with an army into the territory east of the Rhine to ravage it.

When this was heard in the king’s camp—for at that time the king was fighting against Briseg [Note: [Col. 0171] Brisag in a.] [Note: [Col. 0172D] Compare SS. I. 618; III. 324.] and other cities that belonged to Evurhardus—many men withdrew from the camp [Note: [Col. 0171] Absent in 3.], and there was no longer hope that the Saxons would reign.

The king, however, used such steadfastness and authority in that great disturbance, although he was rarely surrounded by soldiers [Note: [Col. 0171] “In the presence of” in 3.], as though no difficulty had confronted him. For the chief bishops too, abandoning their tents and every other possession, themselves also fell away from their loyalty.

### 25

To disclose the cause of the defection and reveal royal secrets is beyond us; yet we think that the demands of history must be met. Whatever we do wrong in this matter, may it be pardonable [Note: [Col. 0171] “Pardonable” in 2.].

The chief bishop was sent to Evurhardus for concord and peace. Since he was exceedingly desirous of these things [Note: [Col. 0171] “Most desirous” in 3, 1, and perhaps A.], he gave his oath as a mutual pledge and is said to have declared that, for that reason, he could not desist from him [Col. 0172D] [Note: [Col. 0171] The text seems to require this correction; 1 and 2 read “to be foolish,” while 3 reads “to defect.”].

The king, sending through the bishop replies appropriate to his office, wished nothing that the bishop had done without his command to pertain to him [Col. 0173A]. But because the bishop did not wish to submit to the king’s authority as to one preeminent, he withdrew from him [Note: [Col. 0173] “From him” absent in 2.]. The king sent him to the city of Hamburg [Note: [Col. 0173] Hammaburgensem in 1; Hammenburgensem in 2; Hommaburgensem in 3.] as though into exile, while he sent Bishop Rothardus [Note: [Col. 0173] Ruthardus in A; Ruodhardus in 3.] [Note: [Col. 0173D] Bishop of Strasbourg.] to New Corvey.

Within a short time, however, he mercifully forgave both, received them into his favor [Note: [Col. 0173] “Received” in 2 and 3.], and restored them to their former honor.

### 26

To restrain the presumption of the dukes [Note: [Col. 0173] “Of the duke” in 2.], Herimannus was sent with an army [Note: [Col. 0173D] He seems to mean Herimannus, duke of the Alamanni.]. He found them on the bank of the Rhine, with a large part of the army absent because they had already crossed the Rhine with the booty [Note: [Col. 0173] “Had crossed” in 2.].

Thus Duke Evurhardus, surrounded by the weapons of the soldiers, received many wounds and bravely returned them; finally pierced by weapons, he fell. Isilberhtus, however, fleeing, boarded a ship with many others [Note: [Col. 0173] “With several” in 2.]. Overburdened by its load, the ship foundered and sank, and the duke himself, submerged with the others, was never found [Note: [Col. 0173D] Nothing certain is known about the day of his death.].

When the king heard of the victory of his soldiers and the death of the dukes [Note: [Col. 0173] Absent in 2.], he gave thanks to almighty God, whose timely assistance he had often experienced. Appointing Oddo, son of Ricwinis [Note: [Col. 0173] Ricwini in 2; Ricuinis in 3.], over the region of the Lotharians, to rear his nephew, the son of Isilberhtus, a boy of the highest promise named Henry [Note: [Col. 0173] “So that he might administer the kingdom too” is added in 6; I would almost suppose it omitted in the manuscripts.], he returned to Saxony.

The boy’s mother was married to King Hluthowicus [Note: [Col. 0173] Luthuuicus in 1; Ludwicus in A.], and Henry, the king’s brother, leaving the Lotharians, withdrew into the kingdom [Note: [Col. 0173] “Region” in 3.] of Charles.

(DCCCCXL.) The death of the dukes was followed by a very harsh winter, and the winter by a severe famine [Note: [Col. 0173] “A famine followed,” with “severe” omitted, in 2.] [Note: [Col. 0174D] Compare the Cologne Annals under 939 (Mon. I, p. 98) and the Greater Annals of St. Gall under 940 (ibid., p. 78).].

### 27

After this Immo [Note: [Col. 0173] Ymmo in A, always.]—whether truly or falsely, I do not know [Note: [Col. 0173] “Truly” in 3.]—took up arms against the king. In midwinter, surrounded by an army, he surrendered himself together with the city [Note: [Col. 0173] “The world” in A.] and thereafter remained faithful and useful.

### 28

The nephews of Isilberhtus also subjected themselves to royal servitude [Note: [Col. 0173] “Remained subject” in 1.], while nevertheless retaining the cities they held. Kievermont was still held by Ansfridus [Note: [Col. 0173] Anfredus in 3.] and Arnaldus [Note: [Col. 0173] Arnoldus in 2, 3, and A.]. Immo sent them the following message:

“I think of myself no differently than you do; but concerning you it is well known that you are princes of this people. Therefore no one doubts that each man is stronger with two hands than with one. [Col. 0173D] It is certain, then, that three surpass one in strength. [Col. 0174A] And now what necessity compels us to serve the Saxons, except our own discord? When they surrounded you with arms, did they rejoice in victory? It is certainly shameful for victors to serve.

“I abandoned our common lord, the best of all mortals, who nurtured me from childhood, always counted me among his friends, and honored me with great power, and I joined myself to a Saxon at the risk of my life [Note: [Col. 0173] “I joined myself to the Saxons” in 1; “to Saxony” in 3 and 7.]. Now, as you know, having received insult instead of honor according to my deserts, I have been surrounded by arms and have almost been made a slave from a free man [Note: [Col. 0173] Absent in A.].

“So that you may know that I wish in good faith to advise what is beneficial to us all, I shall betroth my only daughter to you, Ansfrid, so that I cannot be marked among you by any suspicion of disloyalty. Therefore grant an opportunity for mutual discussion [Note: [Col. 0173] “For mutual conversation” absent in 1; that phrase appears in A.], and from my own person you will test the loyalty that you cannot yet test through a messenger.”

Although they had hearts of iron and had long suspected him, they nevertheless yielded to such cunning and, softened by persuasive words [Note: [Col. 0173] “Softened by words” in 2.], granted him an opportunity for a face-to-face meeting [Col. 0174B].

But he had armed men hidden in suitable places. By treachery he captured both men and sent them under guard to the king, with a message sent along in these words:

“Arnaldus [Note: [Col. 0174D] The name is supplied by the editor.] is more high-spirited but softer; he does not need chains [Note: [Col. 0173] “Bonds” in A and 3.] or blows [Note: [Col. 0173] “Blows” misspelled in 1.]; threats [Note: [Col. 0173] “Less” in 1.] reveal everything he knows. Ansfrid, however, is harder than iron [Note: [Col. 0173] “Is harder than iron” in 2; “he is hard with iron” in A.]; if the most severe tortures are applied to him, that is a serious matter.”

When the king had received them, he punished them for some time by committing them to custody. Later, joining them to himself through the leniency of his favor, he released them in peace.

Since causes are so linked with causes and things with things [Note: [Col. 0173] “And things with things” is absent in 1; 3 reads “and matters with matters.”] that they ought not to be distinguished at all according to the order of the statements [Note: [Col. 0173] “Are” in 2.], let no one accuse me of confusion in the succession of times because I have placed later events before earlier ones.

### 29

The king, therefore, always merciful toward his brother’s grave hardships [Note: [Col. 0173] A and 3 always read “toward him.”], granted him several of his cities for his own use [Note: [Col. 0173] “Granted for his use.”] and permitted him to live within the region of the Lotharians [Note: [Col. 0173] “In the land” in 2; “in the country” in 3.].

### 30

At that time the war with the barbarians was raging [Note: [Col. 0173] In manuscript 1, chapter 30 begins with the words “And when the soldiers …”]. As the soldiers enrolled under the command of the governor Gero were weakened by frequent expeditions, and could be supported less adequately by gifts or tributary rewards because tribute was being refused everywhere, they were sharpened by seditious hatred against Gero.

The king, however, was always close to Gero for the common interests of the state [Col. 0174D]. Thus it happened that, excessively embittered, they turned their hatred against the king himself as well [Col. 0175A].

### 31

This cause did not escape Henry [Note: [Col. 0175] The words “the cause … escaped him” are in 2.]. As usually happens when something sweet is offered to embittered minds [Note: [Col. 0175] “As usually happens in arms, while their minds are embittered” in A.], he easily persuaded such men to join him, hoping to reign again, since he knew that the army was hostile to the king [Note: [Col. 0175] “They knew” in 2.].

Finally, after many messengers had gone back and forth and small gifts had been sent to one another, he gathered almost all the soldiers of the eastern regions to himself.

(DCCCCXLI.) The matter proceeded to such great wickedness that, after a powerful conspiracy had been formed, at the approaching Easter festival, when Henry himself had come to the palace [Note: [Col. 0175] Absent in 2 and 7.], they planned to kill the king and place the diadem of the kingdom upon Henry [Note: [Col. 0175] “To place it” in 2 and 7.].

Since there was no public betrayer of these plans, yet the supreme divinity always protecting him, the ambushes became known to the king shortly before Easter [Col. 0175B]. Surrounded day and night by the force of his faithful soldiers, and diminishing nothing of the dignity or majesty of kingship before the people during that solemn festival, he brought great fear upon his enemies.

After the solemn day, however, chiefly on the advice of the Franks who were then attending him—namely Herimannus [Note: [Col. 0175] Herimannus in 1.], Udo, and Conrad [Note: [Col. 0175] Chuonradus in 3 and frequently thereafter.] surnamed Rufus [Note: [Col. 0175D] This should be Conrad, or Curcipoldus, nephew of Duke Eberhardus, who was sent with Udo against Eberhardus and Giselbertus in 939 and died in 948; or Conrad, son of Werinherus, who later became the king’s son-in-law and duke of Lotharingia.], he ordered those secretly betrayed to be arrested or killed.

Among them was Erich [Note: [Col. 0175] Erik in 3.], who, apart from this fault, was foremost among all the others in every good virtue and was exceptionally brave and excellent. When he understood that armed men were hastening toward him, conscious of his offense, he mounted a horse and took up arms. Surrounded by bands of enemies, mindful of his former virtue and [Col. 0175C] nobility, he chose to die rather than submit to the domination of his enemies.

Pierced by a lance, he fell—a man beloved and distinguished among his fellow citizens for every virtue and skill. The others, conscious of the plot, were held over until the following week [Note: [Col. 0175] “The following week” in 2.], and, paying the punishments deserved by their crimes according to the laws [Note: [Col. 0175] “The law” in 1.], they were beheaded. Henry, however, fled and renounced the kingdom.

### 32

That year certain portents also appeared [Note: [Col. 0175] “Appearing” in 1.], namely comets. For they were seen from the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November until the Kalends themselves [Col. 0176A] [Note: [Col. 0175] “Novembers” in 3.].

When they were seen [Note: [Col. 0175] “Having been seen” in 1.], many mortals were terrified [Note: [Col. 0175] “Many mortals” in 1.] and feared either an excessive pestilence or certainly a change of kingdom, because before King Henry’s death many prodigies had indeed been displayed. The sun’s brightness outside was almost entirely invisible through the air without any cloud [Note: [Col. 0175] “The air” in 2.], while inside, through the windows of the houses, a redness like blood poured in [Note: [Col. 0175] “May appear” in 1.].

Rumor also reported that the mountain where the Lord of all things himself was buried vomited flames in many places. The left hand of a certain man, moreover, which had been cut off with an iron weapon, was restored to him after almost a full year while he slept. As a sign of the miracle, a bloody line marked the place of its joining [Note: [Col. 0175D] This miracle did not occur at the time of Henry’s death; from Flodoard under the year 944 it appears to have happened during these years.].

(DCCCCXLII.) But the comets were followed by a very great inundation, and the inundation by a pestilence among cattle [Col. 0176B].

### 33. (DCCCCXLIII.)

When Oddo, governor of the Lotharians [Note: [Col. 0175D] Flodoard reports that Oddo died in 944; the Continuation of Regino places his death in 943. In Calmet, *History of Lotharingia*, proofs, p. 340, it is stated that Otto confirmed a charter of Bishop Adalbero; the chronological indications, however, do not sufficiently agree among themselves. Nothing certain is known about Henry’s death.], and the king’s nephew Henry had died, the government of the region was granted to Conrad. The king also betrothed his only daughter to him [Note: [Col. 0176D] Compare I. c. 37. The Continuation of Regino reports that the wedding took place in 947.], because he was an energetic and brave young man, excellent at home and in military affairs [Note: [Col. 0175] “In military service” in 3.], and beloved by his fellow soldiers.

### 34

In those days Bertholdus [Note: [Col. 0175] Bertoldus in 2 and A; Bertholdus in 3.], brother of Arnulfus [Note: [Col. 0175] Absent in 1.], administered Bavaria. Fighting against the Hungarians and proving victorious, he became renowned through a celebrated triumph [Note: [Col. 0176D] Bertholdus, already made duke of Bavaria in 937, defeated the Hungarians with great slaughter near Wels.
