This victory seems to belong under the year 943 in the Greater Annals of St. Gall, although the Continuation of Regino and the Salzburg Annals place it under 944. Aventinus recorded August 11 (IV. 23, 17).].

### 35

The king, advancing from day to day, was by no means content with his paternal kingdom. He went to Burgundy and brought the king, together with his kingdom, under his own authority [Note: [Col. 0176D] From Flodoard under 940 it appears that this had already happened long before.]. By arms he subdued another Hugh [Note: [Col. 0176D] Flodoard reports that in these years Otto dealt with Hugh the Great now as a friend, now as an enemy.], and made him subject to himself [Note: [Col. 0175] “Subdued” in 2.].

(DCCCCXLIV.) We see the golden clasp granted to the king as a gift [Note: [Col. 0175] “Of the kingdom” in 3.], marvelous for the variety of its gems, shining on the altar of the protomartyr Stephen [Col. 0176C] [Note: [Col. 0175] The words “shining on the altar …” are absent in 2.].

## Restored apparatus omitted from the translated chapters

- **Chapter 15 — *videlicet*:** alpha reads *scilicet*, also “namely.”
- **Chapter 15 — *et sese inferret*:** witnesses 3 and possibly 1 read *ut sese inferret*, “so that he might bring himself”; the conjunction changes from “and” to purpose.
- **Chapter 15 — *inferret*:** witness 2 reads *inferior*, “lower/inferior,” a corrupt or syntactically different form.
- **Chapter 15 — *Lothariis*:** witness 3 reads *Lotharius*, “Lotharius,” for “to/among the Lotharians.”
- **Chapter 15 — *consulto*:** witnesses 3 and 7 read *consultu*, “by the counsel,” for *consulto*, “after consultation.”
- **Chapter 15 — *traditis*:** witness 3 reads singular *tradito*, “having been handed over,” for plural *traditis*, “having been handed over.”
- **Chapter 16 — *Isilberhtum*:** witness 1 spells the name *isberthtum*.
- **Chapter 16 — *responsio*:** witness 1 reads ablative *responso*, “by/with the answer,” for nominative *responsio*, “the answer.”
- **Chapter 16 — *de die in diem*:** alpha reads *a die in diem*, “from day to day,” for “from the day to the day.”
- **Chapter 17 — “my lord,” he said:** witness 2 orders the words *dominus, inquit, meus*, “my lord, he said,” rather than *dominus meus, inquit*.
- **Chapter 17 — *adessent*:** witness 2 reads *essent*, “were,” omitting the prefix that gives “were present.”
- **Chapter 17 — *ulteriore ripa*:** witnesses 3, alpha, and 7 read *ulteriori*, an alternative dative/ablative form meaning “on the farther bank.”
- **Chapter 17 — *cadere debere*:** witness 3 reads *deberet*, “he/it ought”; witness 2 omits *debere*, “to have to.”
- **Chapter 17 — *vitam defendere*:** witness 3 reads *defenderet*, “he might defend,” for infinitive *defendere*, “to defend.”
- **Chapter 17 — *pars una*:** witness 1 reads *pars uno*, changing the feminine agreement “one part” to the masculine/neuter form *uno*.
- **Chapter 17 — *Neque enim*:** witness 3 omits “For indeed/not indeed.”
- **Chapter 17 — *nostratium*:** alpha reads *nostratum*, another genitive plural form meaning “of our men.”
- **Chapter 17 — *tuae dispositioni*:** witness 1 reads ablative *tua dispositione*, “by/under your ordering,” for dative *tuae dispositioni*, “to your ordering”; thus no mortal can oppose God’s ordering.
- **Chapter 18 — *hoc factum nequaquam*:** alpha reverses the order to *nequaquam hoc factum*, “by no means this deed.”
- **Chapter 18 — *remanserant*:** alpha reads *remanserunt*, “they remained,” for pluperfect “they had remained.”
- **Chapter 20 — *Ipse dolum*:** alpha adds *vero*, “however”: “He, however, anticipated deceit with deceit.”
- **Chapter 20 — *et Apodriti*:** witness 3 omits *et*, “also/and.”
- **Chapter 20 — *gravi oneri*:** witness 1 reads *gravioris*, “of a heavier [thing],” and witness 2 abbreviates *gravioris oneris*, “of a heavier burden,” for “a heavy burden.”
- **Chapter 21 — *a populoque*:** alpha places *populo*, “by the people,” in the alternative order printed in the note.
- **Chapter 24 — *ut initio*:** alpha reads *in initio*, “at the beginning,” rather than *ut initio*, “as at the beginning.”
- **Chapter 26 — *ad coercendam*:** witness 2 reads masculine/neuter *ad coercendum*, “for restraining,” for feminine *ad coercendam*, agreeing with “presumption.”
- **Chapter 28 — *mandatum hujuscemodi*:** witness 2 reverses the order to *hujuscemodi mandatum*, “a command of this kind.”
- **Chapter 28 — *mandato ... directo*:** witness 2 omits *mandato*, “the message/command,” leaving “these words likewise directed.”
- **Chapter 30 — *barbarorum bellum*:** witness 2 abbreviates and changes the phrase as *b. barbarum*, “a barbarian war”; A and witness 3 read *bellum barbarorum*, “the war of the barbarians.”
- **Chapter 31 — *Quae causa ... latuit*:** witness 2 reads plural *causae ... latuere*, “the causes ... lay hidden,” for singular “the cause ... did not escape Henry.”
- **Chapter 33 — *quia erat adolescens*:** A and witnesses 2 and 3 read *qui*, “who was a vigorous young man,” for *quia*, “because he was.”

36. (945.) Therefore, when all kingdoms were silent before him and all enemies yielded to his power, at the urging and intercession of his holy mother he remembered his brother, wearied by many labors [Note: [Col. 0175] Add “he remembered him again” in 1.], and appointed him over the kingdom of the Bavarians, Berthold already being dead [Note: [Col. 0175] Berthold in 1 and 3; Bertold in 2 and A.] [Note: [Col. 0177A] He died in 945, according to the Continuation of Regino; on November 23, if Aventinus may be trusted (IV. 23, 21).]. He made peace and concord with him, and this faithfully endured with him to the end [Note: [Col. 0177] “remained” in 3 and 6.].

Lord Heinricus himself was married to the daughter of Duke Arnulf [Note: [Col. 0177D] Judith.], a woman of outstanding beauty and remarkable wisdom. The peace and concord of the brothers, pleasing to God and beloved by men, became celebrated throughout the whole world, while they increased the commonwealth in unanimity, defeated their enemies, and ruled their subjects with paternal authority [Note: [Col. 0177] “presided” in 3.].

Having therefore received the duchy of the Bavarians, he did not languish in idleness; instead, he departed, captured Aquileia [Note: [Col. 0177] “Aquilegam” in 2 and A.], defeated the Hungarians twice by arms [Note: [Col. 0177] “defeated them by arms” in 2.], swam across to Ticinum, and, after capturing great booty within the enemy’s territory, brought his army safely back to its homeland [Note: [Col. 0177] “into the homeland” in 3.] [Note: [Col. 0177D] We have no certain information about this expedition of Heinricus. Hansiz thought of the Tiza (Theiss), a river of Hungary; I hesitate to agree with him, since Heinricus may perhaps have defeated Hungarians in Italy who were allied with the patriarch of Aquileia. Cf. Staindel, *Chronicle of Bavaria*, under 948.].

To set forth the character, bearing, and appearance of such men and such greatness, whom supreme clemency destined for the delight and adornment of the world [Col. 0177B], is wholly beyond our virtue [Note: [Col. 0177] “virtues” in 1; absent in 3.]. Yet we cannot entirely conceal the devotion that we have toward them.

Finally, the lord of all things, eldest and best of the brothers, was especially distinguished for piety; in action he was the most steadfast of all mortals. Apart from the awe imposed by royal discipline, he was always cheerful, generous in giving, sparing in sleep, and while sleeping always saying something, so that one might think he was always awake. He denied his friends nothing and was faithful beyond what is human. For we have heard that certain men were accused and convicted of sin, yet he himself became their advocate and intercessor, refusing in any way to believe the charge, and afterward treating them as though they had never sinned against him [Note: [Col. 0177] “having been set after him” in 3; “having been preferred” in 3.].

His intellect was exceedingly remarkable. For after the death of Queen Edidis [Note: [Col. 0177] “Edidis” in 1.], although previously unlearned, he learned letters so thoroughly that he knew how to read and understand books completely [Note: [Col. 0177] “understand” in 1.]. Moreover, he knew how to speak the Roman language [Note: [Col. 0178D] Widukind seems here to mean not Latin—for it is easy to demonstrate that Otto did not even understand Latin (Flodoard, under 948; Liudprand, *History of Otto*, ch. 11; Ekkehard, *On the Disasters of the Monastery* II. 139)—but the vernacular language of Gaul, called Gallic above and elsewhere very often Roman (Nithard III. 5; cf. *Histéraire littéraire de France*, vol. VII, Preface, pp. XI ff.).] and the Slavonic language [Note: [Col. 0177] “Slavonic” in 2; “Sclavonic” in 3.] [Note: [Col. 0177] “knew” in 3.]. But he rarely deigned to use either of them [Note: [Col. 0177] “deigned” in 3.].

He was frequent in hunting and loved board games, sometimes exercising the grace of horsemanship with royal dignity. To these qualities was added a bodily stature displaying all royal majesty. His head was scattered with gray hair [Note: [Col. 0177] Absent in 1.]; his eyes, flashing and emitting a certain brilliance by a swift reflection like lightning [Note: [Col. 0177] “of a flash,” corrected in 2 to “of lightning.”]; his face ruddy; his beard long [Note: [Col. 0177] Add “in addition” in A.], contrary to ancient custom; his chest covered with something like a lion’s mane [Note: [Col. 0177] “of a lion” in 2; “lion-like” in 3.]; his belly well proportioned; his gait once swift, now more ponderous; his dress native, and never that of a foreigner [Note: [Col. 0177] “which was never foreign” in 2.]. Whenever it was necessary for him to wear the crown, fasting is always said to have preceded it [Note: [Col. 0177] “to cut” in 2.].

Heinricus, however, excelled in gravity of character and for that reason was described by strangers as less gracious and cheerful. He possessed an exceptionally steadfast spirit and was himself faithful to his friends, so much so that he honored a soldier of modest means by marrying him to his wife’s sister, making him his companion and friend [Note: [Col. 0178D] Judith’s sister—Adelheid?—married Count Burchard.].

He was of excellent bodily form, and in his youth his distinguished appearance drew everyone toward him. The younger brother, Lord Brun [Note: [Col. 0177] “Lord Bruno” in 3.], was great in intellect, great in learning, and great in every virtue and endeavor. When the king had placed him over the untamed people of Lotharingia [Note: [Col. 0178D] 953.], he cleansed the region of robbers [Note: [Col. 0177] Add “thus” in 3.] and instructed it so thoroughly in lawful discipline that the highest justice and the highest peace held sway in those parts.

37. Therefore, when internal and external wars had ceased, divine and human laws prevailed with authoritative force. In those days a severe persecution arose against monks, certain bishops asserting that it was better for monasteries to contain a few illustrious in life than many negligent men [Note: [Col. 0177] “thinking it better” in 2, 3, and 7; “seeming” in 6.], forgetting, unless I am mistaken, the saying of the householder who forbade his servants to gather the weeds, but required both weeds and wheat to grow until the harvest (Matthew 13:29). As a result, many conscious of their own weakness laid aside the habit, abandoned the monasteries, and avoided the heavy burden of the priests.

Some, however, thought that the supreme pontiff Frithericus [Note: [Col. 0177] “Fridericus” in 2 and A; “Friederichus” in 3.] had done this not sincerely but deceitfully [Note: [Col. 0177] A has “thought that he had done this”], so that he might somehow disgrace the venerable man and the abbot Hadumarus [Note: [Col. 0177] “Hadumarem” in 2.], who was most faithful to the king [Note: [Col. 0177] “however he could” in 2; “could” in A.].

38. He was indeed a man of great prudence and industry [Note: [Col. 0177] Absent in A.]. In his time the famous church of Fulda was consumed by fire [Col. 0179A] [Note: [Col. 0179D] In 937; a new church was dedicated in 948; see Flodoard, under that year.], and he restored it and completed it with much greater splendor [Note: [Col. 0179] “greater adornment” in 2; add “was” in 3.].

He kept the pontiff under guard, since he was culpable in a second conspiracy [Note: [Col. 0179D] Cf. above, ch. 25.], at first honorably, but quite severely after he had criticized letters written by him. The pontiff, once released, sought vengeance. Unable to prevail against so great a man by legal means [Note: [Col. 0179] A has “and only then”], he attempted, by pontifical authority, to advance from the humblest monasteries toward the most distinguished ones on equal terms. But such deceptions were poured out in vain. For the abbot remained in the king’s favor and friendship, and, circumstances intervening, the pontiff did not accomplish what he had planned.

39. The king’s sister [Note: [Col. 0179D] Gerberga.] therefore bore three sons to King Hluthowicus: Karolus, Lotharius, and Karlomanus [Note: [Col. 0179] “Carlomannus” in 1 and 3; “Karolomannus” in 2.].

King Hluthowicus himself [Note: [Col. 0179] “but” in A, 2, and 3.] was surrounded by his dukes and captured by the Northmen [Note: [Col. 0179] “Normans” in 1; “Northmen” in A and 3.]. On the advice of Hugo, he was sent to Lugdunum [Note: [Col. 0179] “Lucdunum” in 1.] [Note: [Col. 0179D] That is, Laudunum, Laon; see Flodoard, 945–946.] and handed over to public custody.

The Northmen took his elder son Karlomanus [Note: [Col. 0179] “Carlomannus” in 1 and Sigbertus; “Karolus” in A, 2, and 3.] with them to Rothun [Note: [Col. 0179] “Rothum” in 3.] [Note: [Col. 0180D] Rothomagus, Rouen.], and he died there. When the king heard this, he grieved greatly over the misfortune of his friend [Note: [Col. 0179] “friends” in 1.] and ordered an expedition against Hugo into Gaul for the following year.

40. At that time (946), while the king was staying in the forested fields hunting [Note: [Col. 0179] Absent in 3.], we saw there the hostages of Bolizlav [Note: [Col. 0179] “Bolizlai” in A.], whom the king ordered to be presented to the people [Note: [Col. 0179] Absent in A and 2.], rejoicing greatly over them.

41. That year was marked by the grievous misfortune of the whole people, namely the death of Queen Edidis, of blessed memory. Her final day was commemorated on the seventh day before the Kalends of February [Note: [Col. 0179] “the sixth day before the Kalends” in A.], amid the groans and tears of all the Saxons.

Born from the race of the English, descended from a stock powerful no less in holy religion than in royal authority, she was illustrious. She shared the kingdom for ten years and died in the eleventh. She inhabited Saxony for nineteen years. She left a son named Liudulfus, who at that age was second to no mortal in any virtue of mind or body [Note: [Col. 0179] “to no one” in 3; “of mortals” in A.], and also a daughter named Liudgarda [Note: [Col. 0179] “named Liutgarda” in 3.], who had married Duke Conradus. She was buried in the city of Magathaburg [Note: [Col. 0179] “Magdeburg” in A.], in the new basilica, on the northern side [Note: [Col. 0179] “toward the north” in A and 3.], facing east.

[Col. 0179] HERE ENDS THE SECOND BOOK [Note: [Col. 0179] Thus A; 1, 2, and 3 omit this.].

# BOOK III

## TO LADY MAHTHILDIS, DAUGHTER OF THE EMPEROR: THE PREFACE OF THE THIRD BOOK BEGINS

[Note: [Col. 0179] Thus 1. “Prologue to the third book,” A. “Witichind’s Letter to Queen Mathildis, daughter of Emperor Otto,” 3. All this is absent from 2.]

[Col. 0179]

[Col. 0179C] Just as the appearance of heaven and earth, the voices, faces, and characters of human beings vary in a thousand ways through concordant discord, yet are compelled under the guidance of one light and one understanding, by the providence of God who governs all things, so imperial dignity, which has poured you forth upon the world as its most serene splendor and brightest jewel, is the single rule of justice [Col. 0180C] and standard of uprightness.

Therefore I humbly beseech you to receive into the embrace of your glorious clemency the work of our labor, which is received differently by people of differing character because it lacks clarity of intellect and expression [Note: [Col. 0179] Add “in” in A.]. Let not our foolishness, but rather our greater devotion, be considered in it [Note: [Col. 0179] “in it” in 1, 2, and 3.].

[Col. 0179] HERE ENDS [Note: [Col. 0179] “Here it ends” in 1.] THE PREFACE.

## THE CHAPTERS BEGIN

[Col. 0179C] 1. How the king made his son Lindulfus king after him.  
2. Concerning the expedition into Gaul, the dispute between the king and Duke Hugo, and King Luthowicus.  
3. How the king went to Lugdunum.  
4. How he went to Rothun and returned from there to Saxony [Col. 0179D] [Col. 0180C].  
5. How Hugo met the king near the river Char.  
6. Concerning Liudulfus, the king’s son, and how he went to Italy.  
7. Concerning Bernharius, king of the Lombards.  
8. How the king led an army against Bolizlavus.  
9. How the king took a queen as his consort, and Liudulfus [Col. 0180D] therefore departed from him in sorrow.  
10. After celebrating his marriage, the king returns to Saxony, and Bernharius follows him in order to make peace with him [Note: [Col. 0181] “to make” perhaps?].  
11. Concerning the assembly of the people near the city of Augsburg [Note: [Col. 0181] “Angustana” in the manuscript.] and the miracle that occurred there.  
12. Concerning the king’s sons.  
13. Concerning the plots that were prepared against the king.  
14. Concerning the Easter preparations.  
15. Concerning the king’s son, son-in-law, and the pontiff Frithuricus.  
16. Concerning the assembly of the people at Fridesleri and the counts Dadanus [Note: [Col. 0181] “Dano,” corrected to “Dadano” in the manuscript.] and Wilhelmus [Note: [Col. 0181] “Uulhelmo” in the manuscript.].  
17. Concerning the battle of the Lotharingians with Duke Conradus.  
18. Concerning the siege of Mainz and the dispute between Heinricus and Liudulfus [Col. 0181B].  
19. Concerning Ecberhtus [Note: [Col. 0181] “Etberhtus” in the manuscript, repeatedly.], the king’s cousin.  
20. How the Bavarians joined Liudulfus.  
21. Concerning Arnulfus and his brothers, and how the army requested and received permission to depart [Note: [Col. 0181] “receives” in the manuscript.].  
22. Concerning the king, and how many fell away from their allegiance.  
23. Concerning the Saxon army that went to Mainz.  
24. Concerning Thiadrichus and Wicmannus.  
25. Concerning Ecberhtus and Wicmannus and Duke Herimannus [Note: [Col. 0181] “Hirimannus” in the manuscript, repeatedly.].  
26. Concerning the king’s arrival in Bavaria.  
27. Concerning the pontiff Frithuricus and the other pontiffs.  
28. How the king returned to Saxony without accomplishing his business.  
29. Concerning the lawsuits of Herimannus and his nephews.  
30. The Avars join the Bavarians, but the king meets them [Col. 0181C] with a powerful force.  
31. The Bavarians, exhausted by war, discuss peace.  
32. Concerning the king’s court at Cinna.  
33. Concerning the pontiff Frithuricus and Duke Conradus.  
34. Concerning Liudulfus, who departed angrily from his father, and how the king pursued him.  
35. The battle at Horsadal.  
36. The siege of the city called Renesburg [Note: [Col. 0181] “which” in the manuscript.].  
37. Liudulfus seeks peace but does not obtain it, and concerning the death of Arnulfus.  
38. Peace is granted to Liudulfus, and the king returns to Saxony.  
39. Heinricus goes to Nova urbs.  
40. How the king mercifully receives his son [Col. 0181D].  
41. Concerning the death of the pontiff Frithuricus.  
42. How the Ucri are captured by Gero [Col. 0182A].  
43. How Raeinesburg surrenders and he restores the territory to his brother.  
44. Concerning the famous triumph that the king obtained over the Hungarians.  
45. Concerning Thiadrichus’s battle against the Slavs.  
46. Concerning the portents that occurred meanwhile.  
47. Concerning the fall of Duke Conradus.  
48. Concerning the three dukes of the Avars.  
49. Concerning the king’s triumph.  
50. Concerning the king and Wicmannus’s stratagems.  
51. Concerning the army that nearly captured Wicmannus in the city of Suitleiscare.  
52. How the city of the Cocarescimi was captured.  
53. How the king avenged that devastation.  
54. Concerning Gero the governor [Col. 0182B].  
55. Concerning Stoineffus, king of the barbarians, and the soldier who killed him.  
56. Concerning the king, who became glorious through repeated victories.  
57. Concerning Liudulfus, who left his homeland on account of his friends.  
58. Concerning the letters announcing his death.  
59. Concerning Wicmannus, who secretly entered Saxony.  
60. How Wicmannus was received on Gero’s pledge.  
61. Concerning the prodigies that appeared on garments.  
62. Concerning the emperor’s illness.  
63. Concerning the king’s second expedition into Italy.  
64. Concerning Wicmannus, and how he rebelled again.  
65. Concerning the Danes, and how they became fully Christian [Col. 0182C].  
66. Gero released Wicmannus because of his oath.  
67. How Gero [Note: [Col. 0181] “therefore” in the manuscript.] conquered the Lusiki.  
68. Concerning the two petty kings and Wicmannus.  
69. Concerning Wicmannus’s death.  
70. Having taken up Wicmannus’s arms, the emperor, now made emperor, wrote a letter to be sent into Saxony.  
71. Concerning the Greek envoys and their deception.  
72. Concerning Gundtharius and Sifridus.  
73. Concerning the people of Constantinople and their emperors.  
74. Concerning Mathildis, the emperor’s mother, and the deaths of Bishops Bernhardus and Wilhelmus.  
75. Concerning the emperor’s return from Italy and his death [Col. 0182D].  
76. How the people chose his son as ruler in place of his father.

[Col. 0181] HERE END [Note: [Col. 0181] “Here ends” in the manuscript.] THE CHAPTERS.

## BOOK III BEGINS

[Note: [Col. 0183] Thus 1. “The prologue ends. The third book begins,” A; this too is absent from 2.]

[Col. 0183]

[Col. 0183A] 1. After the death of Queen Edidis (946), the king transferred all his maternal love to his only son Liudulfus [Note: [Col. 0183] Absent in 3.] and, having made a will, appointed him king after himself. He was still a tender youth, being no more than sixteen years old.

2. As the king was setting out on campaign into Gaul [Note: [Col. 0183] “Gallic” in 2, 3, 6, and 7.], having assembled an army at the city of Camaraca [Note: [Col. 0183] “Cameraca” in A.], he hastened to enter the kingdom of Karolus in order to avenge the injury done to his kinsman Hluthowicus [Note: [Col. 0183] “of the kindred” in 1.].

When Hugo heard this, he sent an embassy and swore by the soul of his father [Col. 0183C] Rotbertus [Note: [Col. 0183C] King Rotbertus; cf. above, book I, ch. 30.], who had long ago perished while resisting God and his own king [Note: [Col. 0183] “the king” in 2.] [Note: [Col. 0183] “resisting” in 1.], that he possessed such a supply of arms [Note: [Col. 0183] “armed men” in 3.] as the king had never before seen. He added contemptuous words, speaking vainly and arrogantly about the Saxons [Col. 0183B], saying that they were unwarlike and that he could easily swallow seven Saxon weapons in a single drink [Note: [Col. 0183] “absorb” in 3.].

To this the king gave a sufficiently famous reply [Note: [Col. 0183] “gave” in 2, 3, and 6.]: that he, for his part, would have such a multitude of straw hats presented to him as neither he nor his father had ever seen.

[Note: [Col. 0183C] Codex A: “Such a multitude of straw hats as would have to be presented to him, as neither he nor his father had ever seen. And indeed, although the army was very large—namely, thirty-two legions—hardly anyone was found who did not use a straw hat.”

Codices 2 and 3: “Such a multitude of straw hats as would have to be presented to him, as neither he nor his father had ever [absent in 2] seen [‘seen’ in 3]. And indeed, although the army was very large—namely, thirty-two legions—no one was found who did not use a straw hat, except the abbot of Corvey, named Bovo [‘named Bovo and this one’ omitted in 6], with his three followers. This was a wise and distinguished man, shown to us by God, not granted” [Col. 0183D] [Note: For he presided over the monastery for only six years, 942–948.].

“The grandfather of this father [that is, Bovo], the father of this Bovo [Col. 0183D] [Note: Bovo, as is clear from the Annals of Corvey, was abbot from 900 to 916; King Conrad visited Corvey in 913; the elder Bovo governed the abbey from 879 to 890.] became famous by reading Greek letters before King Cuonradus; and he in turn had a grandfather of the same name who, as the elder, surpassed him in every virtue and wisdom. But he himself was also the grandson of Warinus, who became a monk from being a soldier and was the first of all to be regularly elected abbot at New Corvey [absent in β]. Since Warinus was of admirable holiness, he brought, to increase his virtues and to Saxony of blessed memory, a precious treasure—namely, the relics of the precious martyr Vitus.”]

Such a multitude of hats woven from stalks [Note: [Col. 0184C] We append here chiefly a passage from Ratherius, bishop of Verona, from which it is clear that hats made of straw were characteristic of the Saxons. I copied it from a tenth-century royal manuscript at Munich, fol. 7:

“ This saint, naked or half-naked, rolled about on the very uneven ground day and night for seven years. We sinners, asking forgiveness, put on over our hair a shaggy hat—hair that in mourning we ought to have torn out—in order not to be chilled; his cap was snow, hail, and rainy wind. A sufficiently harsh winter cold, which would surely wash away the crime he had committed. Instead of the hat which it is customary, even among the generality, for those lamenting countless offenses or offenses of the same kind to stuff with foreign skins, his head was covered in winter with down. That straw chamber of the Saxon custom, which they place upon the crown of the head to avoid the sun’s heat, was Phoebus to him, himself flame-vomiting.” PERTZ.]

Such a multitude of hats, therefore, as neither he nor his father had ever seen. And indeed, although the army was very large—thirty-two legions, to be precise—no one was found who did not use such a covering, except the rarest individuals.

When Hugo became certain of the king’s arrival [Col. 0184A], and was also terrified by fear, he released Hluthowicus [Note: [Col. 0183] “Luthuvicus” in 1, consistently thereafter.]. Thus released, Hluthowicus met the king and joined his army with his companions.

3. The king then went with his army to Lugdunum [Note: [Col. 0183] “Lucdunum” in 1, consistently.], attacked it with arms, and proceeded from there to Paris [Note: [Col. 0183] “Parisium” in A, 2, and 3.]. There he besieged Hugo and also honorably venerated the memory of the martyr Dionysius [Note: [Col. 0183] Add “holy” in 1, by a second hand.].

The army was then led against the city of Rheims, where Hugo’s nephew was bishop [Note: [Col. 0184C] Hugo, son of Heribertus of Vermandois, who had invaded the bishopric of Rheims, was a cousin of Count Hugo. BOUQUET. Nevertheless, see above, col. 153, note 177.], installed against every law of right and justice while the legitimate bishop was still alive [Note: [Col. 0184D] Artoldus.]. Having captured the city by arms, he expelled the unjustly appointed priest and restored the legitimate one to his church and his proper see.

4. From there, gathering from the whole army a force of chosen soldiers [Col. 0184B], he went to the Danish city of Rothum [Note: [Col. 0183] “Rothundanorum” in 2 and A.] [Note: [Col. 0184D] On this siege of the Northmen’s city of Rouen, omitted by Flodoard, see Dudo of Saint-Quentin, dean, book III, in du Chesne, *Scriptores rerum Normannicarum*, p. 130 ff.]. But because of the difficulty of the terrain and the onset of a harsher winter, a great plague struck them. With his army unharmed but his undertaking unfinished, after three months he returned to Saxony, granting King Hluthowicus the cities of Rheims and Lugdunum, together with the other things taken by arms.

5. (947.) Hugo, having experienced the king’s power and the valor of the Saxons, did not allow him to enter his borders hostilely any longer. When the king went on the same expedition the following year [Col. 0185A] [Note: [Col. 0185] “as he went to him” in 2.], Hugo met him near the river called Char [Note: [Col. 0185] “Car” in A, 2, and 3; “Kar” in 6.] [Note: [Col. 0185D] The Chiers.], submitted, and entered into an agreement according to the king’s command; thereafter he remained useful to him.

6. When the king saw that his son Liudulfus had become a man, he gave him a wife distinguished for wealth and nobility, the daughter of Duke Herimannus, named Ida. After he had received her, his father-in-law soon afterward died (949), leaving him all his possessions together with the duchy.

Having received this authority, Liudulfus cast off the tranquil disposition he had maintained as a boy [Note: [Col. 0185] “when a boy” in 1.] and, leading armed soldiers into Italy, captured several cities there and placed them under guard. He himself then returned to Francia (950).

7. At that time a savage and avaricious man had usurped power and ruled in Lombardy, one who sold every form of justice for money: Bernharius [Note: [Col. 0185] “Brenharius” in 2; afterward “Bernharius”; consistently “Berngarius” in 8.] [Note: [Col. 0185D] That is, Berengarius.]. Fearing the power of the queen, a woman of singular prudence, left behind by King Hluthowicus [Note: [Col. 0185D] She was the widow of Lotharius.], he afflicted her in many ways in order to extinguish or at least obscure the glory of so great a splendor [Note: [Col. 0185] A has “the splendor of the duke.”].

8. At that time the king set out on military service against Bolizlavus [Note: [Col. 0185] “Bolizlaum … Bolizlai” in A.] [Note: [Col. 0185D] It is unusual that he calls Boleslaus, king of Bohemia, a king; Frodoardus does the same under 950. MEIB. Cf. Dobner on Hagecius III, pp. 640–642.], king of the Bohemians. When the city called Nova [Note: [Col. 0185D] Nova urbs (Nivunburg in an Ottonian charter, *Monumenta Boica* XXVIII, p. 183) seems to have been a part of the city of Prague. It is Nivunburg, in whose suburb, Beheim, Otto issued a donation for Saint Emmeram on July 16; the city was called Neumberge as early as 1343, and today Niemburg or Nimburg, east of Prague at the confluence of the Elbe and the Mrlina.] was about to be captured, where Bolizlavus’s son was shut up under siege, the king prudently broke off the battle so that the soldiers would not incur danger while plundering the enemy’s spoils [Note: [Col. 0185] “the soldiers … incur” in 2.].

Considering the king’s valor and the immeasurable multitude of his army, Bolizlavus [Note: [Col. 0185] “Bolizlaf” in 2 and 3.] came out of the city and preferred to submit to such majesty rather than suffer utter destruction [Col. 0185C]. Standing beneath the standards, hearing the king [Note: [Col. 0185] “approaching” in 1.], and giving his answers, he at last obtained pardon. Then, made glorious by complete victory, the king returned to Saxony [Note: [Col. 0185] “returned” in 3 and 6.].

9. (951.) Since the king was aware of the aforesaid queen’s valor, he decided, under the pretext of a journey to Rome, to set out. When he had entered Lombardy, he attempted to test the queen’s affection for him by means of golden gifts. Having tested it and found it faithful, he took her as his wife, and with her obtained the city of Pavia, which is the royal seat.

When his son Liudulfus saw this, he departed sorrowfully from the king, went to Saxony, and stayed for some time at Salaveldun, a place fatal to counsels [Note: [Col. 0186D] Cf. II. 15.].

10. After celebrating his marriage in Italy with royal magnificence [Note: [Col. 0186D] The day of the wedding is uncertain; it was certainly celebrated before Christmas.], the king set out from there in the splendor of his new marriage to celebrate the coming Easter in Saxony, bringing great joy and favor to his homeland.

King Bernharius, persuaded by Duke Conradus, to whom Pavia had been left to guard with a military garrison [Note: [Col. 0185] “left” in 2.], followed the king into Germany in order to make peace with him and obey everything he should command.

As he approached that royal city [Note: [Col. 0186D] Magadaburg.], the dukes, prefects, and leading palace officials met him a mile from the city. He was received royally, led into the city, and ordered to remain in the lodging prepared for him [Note: [Col. 0185] “prepared” in 3.]. For he did not deserve to see the king’s face for three days.

Conradus, who had brought him and shared his sentiments, took this badly. Together with the king’s son Liudulfus, they regarded Heinricus, the king’s brother, with suspicion in this matter, as though he were driven by an ancient jealousy, and avoided him. Heinricus, knowing that the young man had been deprived of his mother’s support [Note: [Col. 0185] “destined” in 2.], began to despise him, to such an extent that he did not even spare him insults.

Meanwhile, the king spoke with the king. Received into the favor of the king and queen, Bernharius gave a pledge of submission and designated a day and place near the city of Augsburg [Note: [Col. 0185] “Augusta” in 3 and 6.] for a voluntary treaty [Note: [Col. 0185] “of the treaty” in 3; absent in 1?] [Note: [Col. 0185] “day and place” absent in A and 3.].

11. When the assembly was held there [Note: [Col. 0185] Absent in 2.], Bernharius clasped the hands of his son Adalberhtus [Note: [Col. 0185] “the hands of his son” in 2.] in his own hands. Although long ago, while fleeing from Hugo, he had submitted to the king [Note: [Col. 0186D] Cf. Liudprand V. 12.], he now, with his allegiance renewed before the whole army, subjected himself and his son to the king’s service.

Thus dismissed, he returned to Italy with favor and peace [Note: [Col. 0185] Absent in 2.]. There a hailstone of extraordinary size, hurled from heaven amid thunder [Note: [Col. 0185] “thunder” in 2; “of thunder” in 3.] and a violent storm, provided a great miracle for many who saw it.

12. Sons were born to the king by the most serene queen: the firstborn, Heinricus [Note: [Col. 0186D] It is uncertain in what year he was born and died; nevertheless, there is mention of a son in 953 (Flodoard, under that year). The Merseburg Necrology gives April 7 as the day of his death.]; the second, Brun [Note: [Col. 0185] “Bruno” in 3.] [Note: [Col. 0186D] Brun died on September 8, 957, according to the Fulda Necrology.]; the third, designated by the majesty of his paternal name [Note: [Col. 0185] Add “Otto” in 3.], whom the whole world already hopes will be lord and emperor after his father [Note: [Col. 0187D] Otto was born in 955, if we accept the testimony of the Continuation of Regino.].

They also had a daughter named after his holy mother [Note: [Col. 0187D] That is, Mathildis, whom the Annals of Quedlinburg also report as having been born in 955.]. We do not presume to say anything about her, since her glory surpasses everything that we can say or write [Note: [Col. 0187] “can say” in 3.].

13. (953.) Indeed, while the king was traveling through the regions and cities of the Franks, he heard that an ambush was being prepared for him by his son and son-in-law. Therefore, the supreme pontiff was recalled. He had been leading, as usual, a stricter life with hermits and solitaries before Easter, but he received the king at Mainz and ministered to him there for some time [Note: [Col. 0187] “was ministering” in 2.].

When the wicked plans were exposed and noticed by the son and son-in-law, they sought and obtained, with the pontiff’s counsel, a place in which to clear themselves of the charge [Note: [Col. 0187] “they sought” in 3.]. Although they were plainly accused of the crime, the king nevertheless yielded to their proposals in everything [Note: [Col. 0187] “in everything” absent in 1.], because of the narrowness of the place and time.

14. When the Easter preparations had to be made at Aachen [Note: [Col. 0187] “at” in 1.], he discovered that nothing worthy of him had been prepared there [Note: [Col. 0187] “to be” in A.] [Note: [Col. 0187D] Although it should perhaps not be added here, it seems necessary to supply, with Reineccius: “Therefore, when he had gone to Saxony.” Cf. Continuation of Regino, 953.]. He was properly cared for with maternal joys and services, and magnificently welcomed in his homeland—the king whom she had almost lost in Francia [Note: [Col. 0187] “in childhood” in 2.].

15. [Note: [Col. 0187] In 1, this chapter begins with the words “he was strengthened by the presence of his friends and his own people.”]

For, strengthened by the presence of his friends and his own people, he declared void the agreement that he confessed he had been forced to make [Note: [Col. 0187] “beginning” in 1.]. It was proclaimed to his son and son-in-law that they must hand over the authors of the crime for punishment, or else he would regard them as public enemies [Note: [Col. 0187] “public enemies” in 3; absent in 2 and 7.].

The pontiff intervened on behalf of the previous agreements, as though he intended to promote peace and concord. For this reason he became suspect to the king and wholly despised by the king’s friends and counselors.

We do not presume to judge rashly about him [Note: [Col. 0187] “something necessary” in 3.] in any way. But what we approve about him—that he was great in prayer day and night, great in generosity with alms, and outstanding in the word of preaching—we have judged unworthy of silence. As for the cases brought against him [Note: [Col. 0187] “the acts” in 2.], the Lord is the judge.

16. Since no end was being made there to these matters, a universal assembly of the people was ordered to meet at the estate called Fridesleri [Note: [Col. 0187] “Fridislar” in A.], in order to examine these cases [Note: [Col. 0187] “to be examined” in 3 and 7.].

When Heinricus, the king’s brother, was present there [Col. 0188A], he brought many serious charges against the supreme pontiff. For this reason he incurred the anger of the king and of nearly the entire army, since they judged him wholly culpable on the basis of the pontiff’s statements [Note: [Col. 0187] “their statements” in 3.].

Moreover, because he was still carrying a stern disposition from the recent injury [Note: [Col. 0187] A and 3 have “a harsher disposition”], the king condemned to exile men of the highest rank, once dear to him and faithful to his brother in the Britannic war, after they had been handed over to that brother, while they were giving an account of themselves after being accused and were unable to clear themselves [Note: [Col. 0187] Add “not” in 3 and 7.].

They were Thuringians by origin, men of prefectural authority, named Dadanus [Note: [Col. 0187D] Dadanus is undoubtedly the same man whom he called Dadi above (II. 18). Cf. Wedekind, *Notes* I.] and Willehelmus [Note: [Col. 0187] “Uulelmus” in 1; “Wilhelmus” in A and 3.].

After this, many who were conscious of crimes became sufficiently terrified [Note: [Col. 0187] Absent in 3]. The assembly was dissolved, the multitude dismissed, and the king withdrew into the eastern regions.

## Critical apparatus: English translations


1. **add. iterum recordatus est 1** — Witness 1 adds *iterum recordatus est*: “he remembered again.”
2. **Bertholdo 1, 3; bertoldo 2, A** — The name is “Berthold” in 1 and 3; 2 and A spell it *bertoldo*.
3. **Obiit a. 945 …** — He died in 945, according to the continuator of Regino; on 23 November, if Aventinus (IV.23.21) is to be believed.
4. **et 3** — Witness 3 adds “and.”
5. **permansit 3, 6** — 3 and 6 read *permansit*: “remained/endured,” for the text’s “persevered.”
6. **Judithae** — “Judith.”
7. **deest A** — A omits *fit*, “becomes/is made,” after “throughout the whole world.”
8. **praesumit 3** — 3 reads *praesumit*: “takes precedence/assumes,” rather than “presides.”
9. **aquilegam 2, A** — 2 and A spell Aquileia as *aquilegam*.
10. **superavit armis 2** — 2 reverses the words: “overcame by arms.”
11. **Ungarios a. 950 …** — The Annals of Hersfeld report that the Hungarians were killed by the Bavarians in 950.
12. **in p. 3** — 3 reads *in patriam*: “into the homeland.”
13. **De hac Heinrici expeditione …** — Nothing certain is known of this expedition of Henry. Hansiz thought of the Tiza (Theiss), the river of Hungary; I doubt this, since Henry may instead have defeated Hungarians allied with the patriarch of Aquileia in Italy. Compare Staindel’s Chronicle of Bavaria, under 948.
14. **nostrum 3** — 3 reads *nostrum*: “our,” rather than *nostrae*.
15. **virtutibus 1; deest 3** — 1 reads *virtutibus*: “virtues”; 3 omits *virtutis*, “of virtue.”
16. **deest 3** — 3 omits “and.”
17. **posthabitos 3** — 3 writes *posthabitos* as one word: “having been set aside.”
18. **In sequentibus Widukindum …** — In what follows, any reader can readily see that Widukind had Einhard’s *Life of Charlemagne* before him. P.
19. **edidis 1** — 1 spells Edith’s name *edidis*.
20. **intellegere 1** — 1 reads *intellegere*: “to understand.”
21. **Non de lingua Latina …** — Widukind apparently means not Latin, which Otto can readily be shown not even to have understood, but the vernacular language of Gaul, called above “Gallic” and elsewhere very often “Roman”; compare Flodoard 948, Liudprand, *History of Otto* 11, Ekkehard II.139, and *Histoire littéraire de France* VII, introduction XI ff.
22. **slavicaque 2; Sclavonicaque 3** — 2 has *slavicaque*, “and Slavonic”; 3 has the fuller spelling *Sclavonicaque*.
23. **sciebat 3** — 3 reads *sciebat*: “he knew,” rather than “he knows.”
24. **qua 2; quod 3** — 2 reads *qua*, “by which”; 3 *quod*, “which/that.”
25. **dignaretur 3** — 3 has *dignaretur*: “might deign.”
26. **deest 1** — 1 omits *capite*, “head,” before “grey hair.”
27. **fulgoris corr. fulguris 2** — 2 corrects *fulgoris* (“of brightness”) to *fulguris* (“of lightning”).
28. **f. citharae percussione 2** — 2 perhaps reads *citharae percussione*: “at the striking of a lyre.”
29. **add. ad A** — A adds *ad*, “to.”
30. **leonis 2; leoninum 3** — 2 reads *leonis*, “of a lion”; 3 *leoninum*, “lion-like.”
31. **ut 3** — 3 adds *ut*, “so that/as.”
32. **peregrino sit 2** — 2 reverses the order: “may be foreign.”
33. **caedere 2** — 2 reads *caedere*, “to cut/strike,” for *praecedere*, “to precede.”
34. **melioris 1** — 1 reads *melioris*: “of better [rank/quality].”
35. **deest 1** — 1 omits *socium*, “companion/associate.”
36. **Judithae soror …** — Judith’s sister (perhaps Adelaide) married Count Burchard.
37. **dominus Bruno 3** — 3 reads “Lord Bruno.”
38. **An. 953** — The year was 953.
39. **add. ita 3** — 3 adds *ita*, “thus.”
40. **affirmantibus 1** — 1 retains *affirmantibus*, “asserting.”
41. **arbitrari 2, 3, 7; videri 6** — 2, 3, and 7 read *arbitrari*, “to judge/think”; 6 reads *videri*, “to seem.”
42. **esse 2** — 2 reads *esse*, “to be.”
43. **patrisfamiliae 1, A, 3** — These witnesses read *patrisfamiliae*, “of the householder.”
44. **servo 1** — 1 has singular *servo*, “servant.”
45. **deest 3** — 3 omits “and.”
46. **fridericum 2, A; friederichum 3** — The name appears as *fridericum* in 2 and A and *friederichum* in 3.
47. **arbitrati sunt fecisse A** — A reverses the wording: “they thought that he had done [it].”
48. **hadumarem 2** — 2 spells the name *hadumarem*.
49. **quomodo 2** — 2 reads *quomodo*, “how/in what manner.”
50. **possit A** — A has present *possit*, “may be able,” for imperfect *posset*, “might be able.”

51. **deest A** — A omits *vir*, “man,” in “a man of great prudence.”
52. **A. 937; ecclesia nova dedicata est a. 948; v. Flod. h. a.** — The church burned in 937; the new church was dedicated in 948; see Flodoard under that year.
53. **majori 2** — 2 reads *majori*, “greater,” for *majore*.
54. **add. est 3** — 3 adds *est*, “is/was.”
55. **Cf. supra c. 25** — Compare chapter 25 above.

89. **bertharius cod.** — The manuscript spells Bernhard *bertharius*.
90. **facturus?** — Perhaps *facturus*, “about to make [peace].”
91. **angustanan cod.** — The manuscript spells Augsburg *angustanan*.

100. **explicit c.** — Witness c has *explicit*, “ends.”

151. 2 reads *relicto*, “having been left.”
