### 17

When the Lotharingians perceived that King Otto was offended with Duke Conrad—and since they had long been hostile to him because he governed the duchy over them against their will—they took up arms against him. [Col. 0188B; witness 1 reads *sumit*, “takes up,” singular rather than *sumunt*, “they take up.”] He, however, undaunted, displaying a lion-like spirit—witnesses 2 and 3 read *exercens*, “exercising,” and witness 7 *exhibens*, “displaying,” instead of *exerens*, “bringing forth”—brought his standards against theirs and personally routed an incredible multitude of them, while the blood of his friend whom he had lost in battle—namely, Conrad, son of Eberhard—sharpened him like a most savage beast. [Witness 1 reads *sera*, “fierce,” rather than *fera*, “wild.”]

[Note: Whether Conrad should be regarded as the son of Eberhard, Duke of the Franks, some have denied (Wenck II, p. 655 n. a.), while others have defended the identification (Leutsch, p. 40 n. 75). Concerning this battle, fought against Count Raginer, see Flodoard, under the year 953.]

Thus, with the hand of brave soldiers supporting that most valiant man—witness 3 reads *suppetente*, “supporting,” instead of *subpeditante*—and with fresh troops continually being added to the opposing army, the battle continued from midday until evening. At night the fighting was broken off, and no one rejoiced in victory.

### 18

Around the Kalends of July—witness 3 reads “from the Kalends of July”—the king set his army in motion and attempted to seek out his son and son-in-law with arms. He either captured the cities of the opposing party that lay in his path by force or received their submission, until he reached Mainz, which his son entered with an army and, in a most pitiable sight, awaited his father there in arms. [Witness 1 reads *dicto*, “having been said,” rather than *dictu*; witness 3 omits the word.]

There a war began, more than civil and harsher than every calamity. Many siege engines were brought up against the walls, but the townspeople destroyed or burned them. [The words “against the walls … destroyed” are absent from witness A.] There were frequent battles before the gates, while the enemy’s forces were rarely routed outside. [Witness A reads *stationis*, “of the station,” rather than *stationes*, “stations.”] For by delaying, the whole situation changed repeatedly—witness 1 reads *rex*, “king,” rather than *res*, “matter”—since those within feared the successor, while those outside feared the ruler of the kingdom. [Witness 2 reads *regens*, “ruling,” rather than *dominatorem*, “ruler.”]

When the siege had lasted nearly sixty days—witnesses 1 and 3 read a corrupt form corresponding to “until it exceeded”—discussion of peace arose. Accordingly, a cousin of the king, Ecberhtus, was given as a hostage into the city. [Witness 1 spells the name *Etberhtus*; witnesses 2 and 6, and always witness A, *Ekbertus*; witness 3 always *Ecbertus*.]

[Note: Concerning his relationship, see the Quedlinburg Annals under the year 955. Scheidt has demonstrated in *Orationes Guelficae* IV, p. 568 ff. n., that he and the younger Wichmann were brothers.]

This arrangement left everyone a free path into the camp, so that anyone might clear himself of the charge and negotiate concerning peace and concord. The son and son-in-law entered the camp, prostrated themselves at the king’s feet, and declared themselves ready to endure everything for their offense, provided at least that, having been received into his allegiance as friendly supporters, they would suffer no adversity.

The king, however, finding no way to inflict deserved penalties upon his son, demanded that the abettors of the plot be identified. But they, bound by reciprocal oaths and in a certain manner constrained by the craft of the ancient enemy, denied everything absolutely.

Meanwhile immense joy arose in the camp, and news spread from the camp everywhere that those in the city would not leave it—witnesses 2 and 3 read “would not be going out”—until they had obeyed everything commanded by the king. [Witness 2 reads “until everything commanded by the king should be obeyed.”] These hopes, however, were conceived in vain. For when they did not obey the king’s edicts—witnesses 3 and 7 omit *non*, “not”—Heinricus, moved against the young man, said:

“You boast that you have done nothing against my lord the king, and yet the whole army knows you as a usurper and invader of the kingdom. If I am accused and found guilty of the crime, why do you not lead your legions against me? Move your standards against me.”

Then, picking up a straw from the ground—witness 1 reads *vestucam*—he said:

“You will not be able to snatch this from me or from my authority. What possessed you to trouble your father with such actions? You are acting against the supreme divinity when you resist your lord and father. If you know or can do anything, pour out your fury upon me; I myself do not fear your anger.” [Witness 1 reads *evove*, “call forth,” rather than *evome*, “pour out.”]

The young man made no reply to this. But when he had heard the king, he entered the city with his men.

### 19

[Note: Since chapter 19 is not found as a heading in the manuscript, I have inserted its number here, following the table of contents.]

The king’s cousin Ecberhtus, having been given as a hostage into the city, was corrupted by persuasive words—witness 2 reads *suasilibus*, “persuasive,” with a different spelling—and became hostile to the king, although he had already been angry with him because he had been reproached for an ill-considered engagement—witness 3 reads *incepti*, “undertaken,” rather than *incauti*, “heedless”—in which he had lost an eye.

[Note: Hence later writers frequently call him “the one-eyed.”]

### 20

While these events were taking place, on the following night the Bavarian counts of the king’s brother—witness 2 reads “to the count,” and witness 1 “the king’s brothers”—abandoned him—witness 1 reads “abandoned them”—and joined Liudolf. Proceeding with them, he captured the royal city called Rainesburg—witness 1 spells it *Raeinesburg*, witness 3 *Reinesburg*, and witness A *Regnesburg*—along with the other very strongly fortified places in that region. He divided all the duke’s money among his soldiers—witness 2 reverses the order, “the duke’s money”—and forced the duke’s wife, together with her sons, kinsmen, and friends, to leave not only the city but also the region.

We believe that all this was brought about by God so that the man who had wished to place the most serene king over many peoples and nations might learn that he himself could do little, but that in God he could do everything. [The note in witness 2 indicates that *quem* should perhaps have been written where the text has *qui*.]

### 21

The younger Arnulf was with his brothers; he had devised such a scheme against Heinricus because Heinricus was being installed in his father’s kingdom, while Arnulf himself had been deprived of his paternal honor. Moreover, the army, exhausted by prolonged labor, requested and received leave, while the king, with only a very few men, followed his son into Bavaria. [Witness 1 reads *regem*, “the king,” rather than *rege*, “with the king.”]

### 22. 953

For he was extraordinarily patient under hardships, beyond what can be believed of a man delicately reared from adolescence. In the end, when the multitude fell away from its allegiance, there were very few who supported the king’s cause. Among them was a certain Adalherhtus—witness 1 spells the name *Adalberthus*, witness A *Adelbertus*, and witnesses 2 and 3 *Adelbertus*—and a few others with him.

[Note: He was a powerful Count of Swabia. See the Greater Annals of St. Gall under the year 954 and the *Life of Saint Ulrich* X. 38–39.]

### 23

While the king was waging war against Mainz—witness A spells the name *Maguntia*—Duke Herimannus was administering Saxony.

[Note: The same action attributed above to Sigifridus (II. 2) is here attributed to Herimannus; nevertheless, he had not yet been established as duke at that time (Wedekind, *Notes* II).]

When a new army was supposed to be sent from Saxony to reinforce the old one, Thiadricus and the younger Wichmann were placed in command.

[Note: Thiadricus seems to be the same man who succeeded Gero in governing the northern march. See Leutsch, *Gero*, p. 92, II. 149. Wichmann was the son of Wichmann, mentioned in II. 4 and II. 9; see Wedekind, *Notes* II.]

[Note: The account given by Widukind concerning the expedition of Thiadricus and Wichmann must have occurred earlier. At that time Liudolf had withdrawn to Regensburg and Conrad to Metz, and they could not have joined together to meet these forces. Widukind himself indicates that the army was led not into Bavaria but into Francia; perhaps chapter 25 allows us to infer that these events occurred before Ecberhtus’s defection. They are related here so that the causes of the movement in Saxony may become clear.]

When they reached the frontier of the Franks, they were suddenly surrounded by Duke Liudolf and Duke Conrad and driven into a certain deserted fortress. As they attempted to besiege it, the standard-bearer lost an arm when a wheel was thrown at him before the gate. After this, the battle was calmed and a three-day truce was granted for their return to Saxony.

### 24

[Note: Following the table of contents, I have placed chapter 24 here and numbered the chapters in this way thereafter; in the manuscript the order is frequently confused.]

Thiadricus was tested by Liudolf with great promises. Wichmann, however, thoroughly corrupted—the manuscript first reads *correptus*, “seized,” corrected to *corruptus*, “corrupted,” in witness 2—began to accuse his uncle, Hermannus, and call him the robber of his father’s inheritance and the plunderer of his treasures.

[Note: The name of the uncle is Hermannus.]

It is difficult in every respect to express how the man himself, by no means ignorant of the plan, kept watch with such wisdom and prudence against his relatives and declared enemies. [Witness 1 has the misspelling *difficele*, “difficult.”]

### 25

Ecberhtus joined Wichmann, and together they rose up with the same purpose against the duke, allowing him no respite whatever. [Witness 2 reads *dede*, “gave,” rather than *dant*, “give.”] But he, breaking the young men’s fury with noble patience, took care that no tumult should grow in those regions while the king was absent.

### 26

At the king’s sudden arrival, the Bavarians neither turned toward peace—witness 1 reads “returned”—nor dared to undertake open war. Instead, shut within their walls, they imposed great labor upon the army and brought desolation upon their own region. Since the campaign therefore made little progress, the army spared nothing—not even human lives—but laid everything waste. [Witness 3 reads “from its hands” rather than “from human lives.”]

### 27

Meanwhile the supreme pontiff, as he himself said—witness 1 reads *agebat*, “was conducting,” rather than *aiebat*, “was saying”—because of fear of the king, having lost his pontifical office, was leading the life of a hermit with other solitaries.

The other bishops likewise felt no small hesitation in Bavaria, since they favored the king’s cause by sometimes assisting him and sometimes aiding the opposing party—witness 1 reads “opposing persons,” and witness 3 “other parties.” For they could neither detach themselves from the king without danger—witness 1 reads *qui*, “who,” rather than *quia*, “because”—nor adhere to him without harm to themselves. [Witness 3 omits *sui*, “of themselves.”]

### 28

After spending three full months there—witness 3 places “full months” before “three”—the king departed from Mainz—witness 1 has *Mogontio*, witness 2 *Moguncia*, while witness A generally has *Maguntia*—and, with the campaign unfinished, finally returned to Saxony around the Kalends of January.

[Note: That is, between 14 and 31 December. The king had already celebrated Christmas in Saxony; see the Continuation of Regino under the year 954.]

He had lost two prominent and powerful men, Immede and Mainwercus—witness 2 spells the latter *Meinuuerco*, as does witness A—both of whom died from arrow wounds: one at Mainz, the other while traveling toward Bavaria.

### 29. 954

When cases were pleaded before the king, Hermannus and his nephews, all who adhered firmly to justice praised the duke’s judgment—witness A reads “the judgment of the duke”—deciding that the young men should be punished. [Witness 2 reads “should be judged.”] But the king, loving them—witness 2 reads “sparing them”—spared them and handed Wichmann over to military custody within the palace alone.

### 30

Meanwhile he heard that the Avars, entering Bavaria, had joined the opposing party and were preparing to attack him in open war. Yet, quite undaunted by such a necessity, he never forgot that by God’s favor he was lord and king. He gathered a strong force and advanced to meet his fiercest enemies.

They, however, turned away from him—witness A and witnesses 3 and 7 read “turned aside”—accepted guides from Liudolf, and ravaged the whole of Francia. They inflicted such slaughter first upon the king’s friends that they captured more than a thousand households belonging to a certain Ernustus—witnesses A, 2, and 3 spell the name *Ernestus*—who was of the opposing party and held them under his own authority; then they did the same to all the others, to an extent surpassing belief.

On the Sunday before Easter they were publicly served at Worms—witness 1 spells the city *Wurmacia*—and presented with very large gifts of gold and silver. From there they set out for Gaul—witnesses 2 and 3 add “from there in Gaul”—and returned to their homeland by another route.

[Note: The Continuation of Regino under the year 954 says: “They returned through Italy.”]

### 31

Exhausted by the civil and foreign war—for after the Hungarians had departed, they were being pressed by the royal army—the Bavarians were compelled to negotiate peace. Peace was granted until the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July—witness 3 reads the seventeenth—and a place was appointed at Cinna—witness 2 reads *Ricina*—for an accounting to be given and a response to be delivered.

[Note: Cinna is Langen-Zenn near Nuremberg. See Wedekind, *Notes* I.]

### 32

When an assembly of the whole people was taking place at the appointed location, the king began this speech:

“I could endure it if the indignation of my son and of the others who are plotting against me tormented me alone, and did not disturb the entire Christian people. It would be a small matter that they had invaded my cities like robbers and torn regions from my authority—witness 3 has “regions,” while witness A reads “previously”—if they were not sated with the blood of my relatives and dearest companions.

“Look: I sit deprived, without my sons, while I suffer a most grievous enemy in the person of my son. The man whom I loved most and raised from a modest station to the highest rank and honor has my only son against me.” [Witnesses 2 and A read “has turned my only son against me.”]

[Note: That is, Duke Conrad.]

“This might somehow be tolerable—witness 2 reads *tollerabile*—if the enemies of God and humanity were not introduced into these matters. Now they have left my kingdom desolate, my people captured or killed, my cities destroyed, my temples burned, my priests slain. The streets still run with blood. Laden with my gold and silver—the wealth with which I enriched my son and son-in-law—the enemies of Christ return to their homes.” [Witness A reads *remeant*, “return,” witnesses 2 and 3 correct *remeunt*, “return,” and witness 7 has *redeunt*, “go back”; witness 2 reads *referri*, “to be carried back,” rather than *referti*, “laden.”]

“What crime, then—witnesses 3 and 7 read *ergo*, “therefore”—what treachery remains, I cannot imagine.”

After these words the king fell silent.

Heinricus, praising the king’s judgment, added:

“Since the enemies, twice defeated in open battle—witness 2 has the singular “defeated”—are being hired wickedly and most shamefully, so that a way may again be opened for them to inflict harm, I would rather endure every calamity and every hardship than ever receive the common enemy into allegiance.” [Witness A reads *fide*, “faith,” rather than *fidem*, “allegiance”; witness 2 has the infinitive “to receive.”]

After these words Liudolf stepped forward and said:

“I admit that I secured them against me with money, so that they would not injure me or those subject to me. If I am declared guilty in this matter, let the whole people know that I did this not voluntarily but compelled by the utmost necessity.” [Witness A omits *non*, “not.”]

Finally, the supreme pontiff entered to give an account. He promised that he would declare in whatever judgment the king commanded—witness 2 reads “whoever”—that he had never thought, wished, or acted against the king; that he had withdrawn from the king under compulsion of fear; that he had understood the king to be offended with him—witness 2 reads *qua*, “by which”—and that, though innocent, he had been overwhelmed by the gravest accusations; and that henceforth he would preserve faith by every means of oath. [Witness 3 reads *juramentis*, “by oaths,” rather than *argumentis*, “by means.”]

The king replied:

“I do not demand an oath from you, except that, insofar as you are able, you assist the cause of peace and concord.” [Witness 2 reads *consilio*, “by counsel,” rather than *consilium*, “the cause.”]

When this had been given, he dismissed him in loyalty and peace. [Witness 1 reverses the order, “he dismissed him.”]

### 33

Since the pontiff and Duke Conrad could not induce the young man to submit to his father and endure his father’s judgment, they withdrew from him, joining themselves to God and the king. [Witness 3 reads *se*, “themselves,” rather than *sese*.]

### 34

On the following night Liudolf departed from the king with his men and entered Rainesburg with an army. [Witnesses 1 and 2 spell the city *Reinesburg*, witness 3 *Reinespurg*, and witness A *Regensburg*.] The king, following his son, encountered a city called Horsadal—witness A, 2, and 3 spell the name *Horsedal*—and besieged it.

[Note: Probably Rossthal in the district of Cadolzburg. See Wedekind, *Notes* I.]

### 35

When battle was joined, no mortal had ever seen a harder engagement around a wall. [Witness A reads “had seen.”] Many were killed on both sides, and more were wounded; the darkness of night separated the combatants. [Witness 1 has a misspelling corresponding to *dirimere*, “to separate”; witness A and witness 3 read *diremere*.]

At daybreak the army, wounded by the two-sided battle, was led away from there—witness 3 adds “the army”—since it seemed unwise to remain longer while those men were striving toward more serious dangers. [Witness 1 reads “greater dangers.”]

### 36

They therefore traveled three days to Rainesburg. [Witness 1 spells the name *Raeinesburg*, witness 3 *Reinespurg*, and witness A *Regensburg*.]

[Note: The manuscript’s *itin­er* means *iter*, “journey”; the witnesses vary between *itinere*, *iter*, and *itur*.]

The sites of the camps were occupied and surrounded with fortifications, and the siege of the city was carefully begun. But since the multitude did not allow siege engines to be brought against the walls, the two sides sometimes fought fiercely before the walls. [Witness 2 omits *est*, “was”; witnesses 6 and 7 supply it.]

The prolonged siege compelled those shut inside to undertake some action in the conduct of the war. [Witnesses 2 and 3 read “those shut inside” in the dative.] They judged that if they were forced to it, hunger would torment them worse than dying bravely in battle.

It was therefore ordered that cavalry should burst out through the western gate, as though they intended to attack the camp, while others boarded ships and, as the cavalry battle was being fought, should invade the camp, which would be left undefended, by way of the river adjoining the city. [Witness A and witness 3 read “river” rather than “water”; witness 2 reads “the city adjoining the river.”]

The townspeople gathered at the signal of the bell and carried out the agreed plan, which was already known in the camp. For that reason the besiegers too prepared themselves energetically.

Because the cavalry delayed its breakout—witness 1 has a corrupt form of “in breaking out”—the fleet drifted farther from the city. [Witness 3 reads “the besieged” rather than “the fleet.”] The men leapt from the ships and rushed into the camp—witness 1 has “they rushed.” Finding the soldiers armed—witness 2 has “finding them”—they panicked and sought flight; surrounded on every side, they were cut down.

Some, terrified and straying, were unable to re-enter the ships—witness 3 supplies *non*, “not”—and were swallowed by the river. Others crowded into the ships beyond their capacity and were drowned. The result was that scarcely a few of the many survived.

The cavalry, exhausted and defeated by the opposing cavalry, with many wounded, was driven back into the city. [Witness 1 reads “in the city.”] The victorious royal army returned to the camp, bringing with it only one man struck by a mortal wound before the gates. [Witness 1 reads “they returned.”]

All the city’s livestock was brought to a grassy place between the rivers Rain—witness 1 reads *Raim*, witness 3 *Rein*, and witness 2 “was on the land”—and Donov. [Witness 1 and 3 read “Danube,” witness 7 *Donan*, and witness 2 “the river”; witness 2 has the singular *fluvius*.]

But the king’s brother Heinricus captured the animals and divided them among his companions. The townspeople, worn down by frequent battles, also began to suffer from hunger.

### 37

Accordingly Liudolf left the city—witness 1 adds “he went out”—with the leading men and requested peace, but did not obtain it because he refused obedience to his father.

Then, having entered the city, he attacked Gero, who was besieging the eastern gate with arms—a man renowned for as many victories as battles. Fierce fighting continued from the third hour until the ninth. [Witness A and witness 3 add *est*, “was.”]

Before the city gate, when his horse fell—witnesses 1 and 2 read “from the horse,” a distinction adopted here—the rider Arnulfus was stripped of his armor and immediately pierced by weapons—witness 2 corrects the singular *telo*, “weapon,” to the plural—and died.

After two days, his death was reported by a woman fleeing the city because of hunger, since previously it had been uncertain. At his death the townspeople were greatly disconcerted and were already negotiating peace.

### 38

Thereupon, through the intervention of the leading men, Liudolf again left the city with his companions. After it had been besieged for a full month and a half—witness 1 has the feminine singular “complete”—he obtained peace until the appointed day, when these matters were to be judged. The site of the council was designated at Frideslari. [Witness A reads *Frideslar*. Witness 3 omits “of the council.”]

The king then returned to his homeland. [Witness 3 reads “the king returned from there to his homeland.”]

### 39

Heinricus, however, gained the New City.

[Note: Perhaps the more recent part of the city of Regensburg, on the left bank of the Danube, which our author called by this name.]

Nearly all of Rainesburg was burned down on the following night. [Witness A reads “was burned”; witness 3 “burned”; witness 6 “was consumed by fire”; witness 7 “was set on fire.”]

### 40

While hunting for exercise in a place called Suveldun—witness 2 corrects *Seveldun* to *Suveldun*—the king’s son prostrated himself before his father with bare feet, touched by profound repentance. [Witness A reads “if the son”; witness A also has “before his father.”] With a tearful speech he first drew tears from his father—witnesses 1 and 3 read “from his father”—and then from everyone present.

[Note: Suveldun is perhaps Saufeld in the district of Berka on the Ilm, in the land of Weimar. See *Acta Societatis Historiae Thuringicae Saxonicae* IV.2, p. 172.]

Received into favor through his father’s love, he promised that he would obey and assent to his father’s every will. [Witness 1 has *spondit*, “he promised,” rather than *spondet*, “he promises”; witness 1 also reads “and they assented.”]

### 41

Meanwhile it was announced that the supreme pontiff had fallen ill and was considered beyond hope. The king’s hearing was therefore postponed for a short time. [Witness 3 reads “postponed” with an expanded form.]

Those who were present praised the supreme pontiff’s end as wholly worthy of commendation. After the pontiff’s death, a general assembly of the people was held. [Witness A supplies “was held.”]

[Note: On 17 December, at Arnstedt; see the Augsburg Annals for this year.]

After a year and a half, Mainz—witness A reads *Moguncia*—was handed over to the king together with all Francia. The son and son-in-law were received back into favor, which they faithfully enjoyed until the end.

### 42

That year the Slavs called Uchri—witness A reads *Flavi* here and thereafter—were defeated by Gero with great glory, while Duke Conrad, sent by the king, was assisting him.

A vast amount of booty was carried off, and great joy arose throughout Saxony.

### 43. 955

In the following year the king celebrated Easter with his brother—witness 1 reads “the king at Easter,” witness 3 “Easter, the king.” Afterward he led an army against Rainesburg, again tormenting the city with weapons and siege engines.

When it was deprived of the support of the Saxons and harassed by hunger, the townspeople came out through the gates and surrendered themselves, together with the city, to the king. He condemned the leading men to exile but spared the remaining multitude. Glorious in victory, he returned to his homeland, with the entire Bavarian region restored to his brother.

### 44

Entering Saxony around the Kalends of July, he encountered envoys of the Hungarians, ostensibly visiting him because of their ancient loyalty and goodwill, but in reality, as some thought, observing the outcome of the civil war. [Witness 2 reverses the word order, “the civil war.”]

After keeping them with him for several days—witness 3 reads “several”—giving them some small gifts, and sending them away in peace, he heard from messengers of his brother, the duke of the Bavarians:

“Look, the Hungarians are spreading out and invading your territories, and they are preparing to engage you in battle.” [Witness 1 adds “and.”]

Hearing this, the king, as though he had endured no hardship in the previous war, set out against the enemy. He took with him only a very few Saxons, because the war against the Slavs was already pressing. [Witness 3 reads *Sclavonicum* rather than *Slavanicum*, both meaning “Slavic.”]

After pitching camp on the borders of the city of Augsburg, he was met by an army of Franks and Bavarians. Duke Conrad also came to the camp with a powerful cavalry force. At his arrival the soldiers were encouraged—witness 2 reverses the word order—and now wished that the battle would not be delayed.

He was naturally bold in spirit and—something rare among bold men—good in counsel. [Witness 2 reads “of good counsel,” witness 3 “with good counsel,” and witnesses 6 and 7 “good in counsel.”] Whether he went against the enemy on horseback or on foot, he was an irresistible warrior, and at home and in war he was dear to his companions. [Witness 3 reads “in war also.”]

Accordingly, the raiding columns of both armies reported that one army was not far from the other. A fast was proclaimed in the camp—witness 3 reads “ordered”—and everyone was ordered to be ready for battle on the following day. [Witnesses 3 and 7 read “for the following day.”]

At first light they rose, exchanged peace, and pledged under oath their services first to the duke and then each to the other. [Witness 2 reads *promisso*, “by a promise,” rather than *promissa*, “pledged.”] With their standards raised, they advanced from the camp—witnesses 3 and 6 read “out of the camp”—numbering nearly eight legions.

The army was led through rough and difficult places, so that the enemy would not have an opportunity to disrupt the columns with arrows, which they used with great ferocity, while thickets protected the army.

The Bavarians arranged the first, second, and third legions, under the command of the officers of Duke Heinricus. For he himself was absent from the battle because he was suffering from bodily illness, of which he also died.

[Note: He died on 1 November.]

The Franks organized the fourth legion, whose leader and commander was Duke Conrad. [Witness 2 omits “was.”]

In the fifth legion, which was the largest and was also called the royal legion, was the prince himself, surrounded by chosen men drawn from all the thousands of soldiers—witness 3 reads “from many”—and by vigorous youth. Before him was an angel, in whose keeping was victory; he was enclosed by a dense column.

The Swabians formed the sixth and seventh legions, commanded by Burghardus. [Witness A, and witnesses 3, 6, and 7, spell the name *Suevi*; witness 1 *Burgardus*, witness 2 and A *Burchardus*, and witness 3 *Burcardus*.]

[Note: Burghardus appears to have been the son of Duke Burchard, who was killed in 926. He married Hadwig, daughter of Heinricus, and after Liudolf’s deposition received the duchy of Swabia in 955.]

The eighth contained one thousand chosen Bohemian soldiers, equipped more with weapons than with good fortune. All the baggage and equipment were placed there as though it were the safest position, since it was the rearmost. [Witness A supplies an additional *et*, “and.”]

But events turned out otherwise than expected. [Witness A reads “than was expected.”] The Hungarians, without delaying, crossed the river Lech, surrounded the army, and began harassing the rearmost legion with arrows—witness A and witness 3 read *lacessere*, “to harass,” rather than the corrupt form in the base text. Then, making a charge with immense shouting, they killed or captured some—witnesses 3 and 6 add “others”—seized all the baggage, and forced the remaining armed men of that legion to flee.

They attacked the seventh and sixth legions in the same way, routed many of them, and put them to flight.

When the king understood that the battle was in front—witness A and witness 7 omit “was”—while the rearmost troops were in danger behind him, he sent the duke with the fourth legion. They rescued the captives, recovered the booty, and drove back the enemy raiding columns. [Witness A, witnesses 2 and 3 read “disturbed” rather than “drove back.”]

After the enemy’s raiding formations had been routed everywhere, Duke Conrad returned to the king with the victorious standards. In a remarkable turn of events, while the veteran soldiers—accustomed to the glory of victory—hesitated, he celebrated the triumph with the new troops, who were scarcely experienced in warfare. [Witness 1 has the feminine *ignara*, “inexperienced,” rather than masculine *ignaro*.]

### 45

While these events were taking place in Bavaria, the prefect Thiadrichus fought various engagements against the barbarians.

[Note: See chapter 23. “Prefect” appears to designate the same man whom Widukind seems elsewhere to call the margrave; see II. 30 and III. 54, 67 concerning Gero, and III. 51 concerning Heinricus. In II. 33 Duke Oddo of the Lotharingians is given this title in a charter of 932 (Schannat, *Traditions of Fulda*, p. 234), although that document can scarcely be considered genuine. The name Meginwardus, Count, also occurs.]

When he attempted to capture one of their cities, he pursued the enemy as far as the entrance of the gate—witnesses 2, A, and 7 add “up to”—forcing them inside the wall. He took and burned the town and captured or killed everyone who was outside the wall. [Witness 1 reads *prae*, “in front of,” rather than *foros*, “outside.”]

When he was returning after the fire had already died down, and half of his soldiers had crossed a marsh adjoining the city—witness 3 omits “was adjoining”—the Slavs saw that our men were hemmed in by the difficulty of the terrain—witness 1 has a misspelling of “difficulty”—having neither an opportunity to fight nor much room to flee. [Witness A has “they had no opportunity to fight.”] They therefore pursued those who were returning from behind, with a great shout.

They killed about fifty of them—witness A omits “about”—after a shameful flight had taken place among our men. [Witness 2 adds “and they killed.”]

### 46

[Note: From this chapter onward, the chapter numbers in the manuscript agree with those in the table of contents.]

Meanwhile immense terror seized all Saxony, which trembled for the king and his army because of this reverse. [Witness A reads “the adverse event”; witnesses 1 and 3 vary between “the adverse event” and “the adverse thing.”]

Unusual portents also terrified us. Finally, in many places, temples shaken by a violent storm caused excessive horror to those who saw and heard it. Priests of both sexes perished by a stroke of lightning, and many other things occurred at that time, dreadful to relate and therefore to be passed over by us.

Seeing that the entire weight of the battle was now approaching from the front—witness 2 reads “was”—the king addressed his companions for their encouragement—witness 1 omits “for their encouragement,” and witness 3 supplies “his”—in this manner:

“My soldiers, you yourselves see that we need courage in this great crisis, since you face the enemy not far away but standing before you. Until now I have gloriously used your tireless hands and ever-unconquered weapons, and I have conquered everywhere outside the soil and dominion of my kingdom. Am I now to turn my back in my own land and kingdom?

“I know that we are surpassed in numbers, but not in courage and not in weapons. For we have learned that, for the most part, those men are entirely without weapons. And what is our greatest consolation is the help of God.

“Their only protection is boldness as a wall; ours are hope and divine protection. Let it now shame the lords of almost all Europe to surrender their hands to their enemies. Better that we die gloriously in battle, my soldiers, if that is where the end lies, than preserve a servile life subject to our enemies—or perish by strangulation like savage beasts.

“I would say more, my soldiers, if I knew that words could increase courage or boldness in your hearts. Let us now begin our conversation with swords rather than tongues!”

After these words, he seized his shield and holy lance—witness 3 reads “sword and shield”—and was the first to turn his horse against the enemy, performing the duty of a most valiant soldier and excellent commander.

The bolder of the enemy—witness A reads “the hearers”—first resisted—witness A reads “resisted,” witness 3 “they resisted,” and witness 6 “they resisted”; then, when they saw their companions turn their backs, they were struck with terror and, mingling with our men, were destroyed.

Of the rest, some, with their horses exhausted, entered nearby villages. Surrounded by armed men, they were burned together with the walls. [Witness 2 and witness 6 read *moenibus*, “walls,” rather than *moeniis*, “fortifications”; witness 1 adds *quoque*, “also.”]

Others swam across the adjoining river, but when the far bank could not support them as they climbed it—witness 1 has “higher bank,” witness A “higher”—they were overwhelmed by the river and perished.

That day the camp was invaded and all the captives rescued. On the second and third days, the remaining multitude from the neighboring cities was so thoroughly destroyed that scarcely anyone escaped. [Witness A reads “departed.”]

But the victory over so savage a people was not won without bloodshed. [Witness 1 omits *adeo*, “so.”]

### 47

Duke Conrad—witness 1 reverses the word order—fighting bravely, burned with the fervor of his spirit and the heat of the sun, which was excessive that day. As he loosened the fastenings of his armor and sought air (the printed *aurum* is evidently an OCR error for *auram*), he fell, pierced in the throat by an arrow.

By order of the king his body was honorably collected and transported to Worms—witness 1 spells the city *Wurmatia*, witness 3 *Vormacia*—where he was buried, a man great and renowned in every virtue of mind and body, with the tears and lamentation of all the Franks.

### 48

Three leaders of the Hungarian people were captured and presented to Duke Heinricus. They were punished with the evil death they deserved: they were hanged and died. [The words “an evil death … punished” are absent from witness 1.]

### 49

After a famous triumph, the king became renowned—witness 1 reverses the order—and was called by the army “Father of the Fatherland” and “Emperor.”

Accordingly, honors and worthy praises were decreed to the supreme divinity in each church. The king also sent word through messengers that the same should be done for His holy Mother. [Witness 1 adds *ut*, “that.”]

He returned victorious to Saxony amid rejoicing and the greatest joy and was most gladly received by his people. [Witness 3 omits “by his people.”] For no king before him had rejoiced in such a victory within the preceding two hundred years.

[Note: Widukind seems to have had in mind Charles Martel’s victory over the Saracens in 732.]

[The words “For they themselves were absent from the Hungarian war, being reserved for the Slavic battle” are absent from witness 1. Although they might be attributed to some glossator, since both witness 2 and witness A contain them, I did not wish to omit them.]
