- **N157 · Col. 0195 · after `praedicato , jussum est omnes in crastino`:** source note: crastinum 3. 7. — Witnesses 3 and 7 read *crastinum*, “the next day.”
- **N159 · Col. 0195 · after `sacramento promissa , erectis signis procedunt castris`:** source note: e castris 3. 6. — Witnesses 3 and 6 read *e castris*, “from the camp.”
- **N160 · Col. 0195 · after `0195D] praefuerunt praefecti ducis Heinrici; nam ipse`:** source note: ipso 3. 1? — Witness 3 and perhaps 1 read *ipso*, “himself/by him.”
- **N161 · Col. 0195D · after `valitudine corporis laborasset, qua et mortuus est`:** source note: Obiit die 1 Novembris. — Editorial notice: he died on November 1.
- **N162 · Col. 0195 · after `laborasset, qua et mortuus est . Quartam`:** source note: add. vero 3. — Witness 3 adds *vero*, “however.”
- **N165 · Col. 0195 · after `et dicebatur regia, ipse princeps vallatus lectis`:** source note: electis 2. 7. — Witnesses 2 and 7 read *electis*, “chosen men.”
- **N166 · Col. 0195 · after `regia, ipse princeps vallatus lectis ex omnibus`:** source note: multis 3. — Witness 3 reads *multis*, “many.”
- **N167 · Col. 0195 · after `princeps vallatus lectis ex omnibus militum milibus`:** source note: militibus 2. 7. — Witnesses 2 and 7 read *militibus*, “soldiers.”
- **N172 · Col. 0195 · after `novissima. Sed aliter res acta est ac`:** source note: quam A. 7. — A and witness 7 read *quam*, “than/whom.”
- **N173 · Col. 0195 · after `[Col. 0196B] cunctantes, Lech fluvium transierunt, circumeuntesque`:** source note: circueuntesque 2. 7. — Witnesses 2 and 7 read *circueuntesque*, “and going around.”
- **N175 · Col. 0195 · after `coeperunt, et inpetu cum ingenti vociferatione facto`:** source note: facta 1. — Witness 1 reads *facta*, “having been done/made.”
- **N176 · Col. 0195 · after `ingenti vociferatione facto , aliis caesis vel`:** source note: aliis 3. 6. — Witnesses 3 and 6 read *aliis*, “others.”
- **N179 · Col. 0195 · after `quarta legione, captivos eripuit, praedam excussit, latrocinantiaque`:** source note: latrocinantium 2. — Witness 2 reads *latrocinantium*, “of robbers/brigands.”
- **N180 · Col. 0195 · after `eripuit, praedam excussit, latrocinantiaque hostium agmina proturbavit`:** source note: perturbavit A. 2. 3. — A and witnesses 2 and 3 read *perturbavit*, “disturbed.”
- **N181 · Col. 0195 · after `Conradus ad regem revertitur; mirumque in modum`:** source note: immodum 1. — Witness 1 has defective *immodum* for “excessively/beyond measure.”
- **N184 · Col. 0195 · after `praeside Thiadrico adversus barbaros. Cum capere nisus`:** source note: uisus 3. — Witness 3 reads *uisus*, “having seemed/been seen.”
- **N188 · Col. 0195 · after `videntes nostros in arto sitos ob difficultatem`:** source note: diffucultatem 1. — Witness 1 misspells *difficultatem*, “difficulty,” as *diffucultatem*.
- **N189 · Col. 0195 · after `sitos ob difficultatem loci, nec copiam habere`:** source note: haberet A. — A reads *haberet*, “might have.”
- **N190 · Col. 0197 · after `tergo revertentes clamore magno. Peremerunt [Col. 0197A]`:** source note: et peremerunt 2. — Witness 2 adds *et peremerunt*, “and they killed.”
- **N193 · Col. 0197 · after `quinquaginta viros foeda fuga nostrorum facta. 46`:** source note: inde ab hoc capite codicis numeri cum indice conveniunt. — Editorial notice: from this chapter onward the codex’s chapter numbers agree with the index.
- **N194 · Col. 0197 · after `omnem Saxoniam trepidam pro rege et exercitu`:** source note: exercitui A. — A reads dative *exercitui*, “for/to the army,” for genitive *exercitus*, “of the army.”
- **N195 · Col. 0197 · after `et exercitu ejus pro hac re adversa`:** source note: adverso 1. adversam 3. invasit adversa A. — Witness 1 reads *adverso*, “adverse”; witness 3 *adversam*, and A “the adverse event invaded,” changing agreement and syntax.
- **N197 · Col. 0197 · after `ex adverso jam adesse conspiciens rex, exhortandi`:** source note: hortandi 1. — Witness 1 reads *hortandi*, “of encouraging,” for *exhortandi*, the same meaning with prefix.
- **N198 · Col. 0197 · after `conspiciens rex, exhortandi gratia allocutus est socios`:** source note: deest 1. add. suos 3. — Witness 1 omits *socios*, “companions”; witness 3 adds *suos*, “his.”
- **N199 · Col. 0197 · after `allocutus est socios hoc modo: Opus esse`:** source note: esset 2. — Witness 2 reads subjunctive *esset*, “might be,” for infinitive *esse*, “to be.”
- **N200 · Col. 0197 · after `hoc modo: Opus esse nobis bonorum animorum`:** source note: bonis operibus 3. — Witness 3 reads *bonis operibus*, “good works,” for *bonorum animorum*, “good/courageous spirits.”
- **N201 · Col. 0197 · after `extra solum et imperium meum ubique vici`:** source note: vici ubique 2. — Witness 2 reverses the order to *vici ubique*, “I conquered everywhere.”
- **N202 · Col. 0197 · after `Dei. Illis est sola pro muro audatia`:** source note: audacia pro muro A. — A reverses the order to *audacia pro muro*, “boldness in place of a wall.”
- **N203 · Col. 0197 · after `colloquium incipiamus! Et his dictis, arrepto clipeo`:** source note: gladio et clypeo 3. — Witness 3 reads *gladio et clypeo*, “sword and shield,” for *clipeo ac sacra lancea*, “shield and sacred lance.”
- **N204 · Col. 0197 · after `ac optimi imperatoris officium gerens. Hostium audaciores`:** source note: auditores A. — A reads *auditores*, “hearers,” for *audaciores*, “the bolder men.”
- **N205 · Col. 0197 · after `imperatoris officium gerens. Hostium audaciores primum resistere`:** source note: restitere A. 3. restiterunt 6. — A and witness 3 read *restitere*, and witness 6 *restiterunt*, all “they resisted,” for infinitive *resistere*, “to resist.”
- **N206 · Col. 0197 · after `villas proximas intrant, circumfusique armatis, cum moeniis`:** source note: menibus 2. 6. — Witnesses 2 and 6 spell *moenibus*, “walls,” as *menibus*.
- **N208 · Col. 0197 · after `alii flumen contiguum transnatantes, dum ripa ulterior`:** source note: alterior 1 altior A. — Witness 1 reads *alterior*, “other/farther,” and A *altior*, “higher,” for *ulterior*, “farther.”
- **N209 · Col. 0197 · after `consumpta est, ut nullus aut rarus evaderet`:** source note: discederet A. — A reads *discederet*, “departed/might depart,” for *evaderet*, “escaped/might escape.”
- **N212 · Col. 0197 · after `eo die nimius erat, accensus aestuat, vinclisque`:** source note: vinculisque loricae 6. — Witness 6 reads *vinculisque loricae*, “and the fastenings of the cuirass.”
- **N213 · Col. 0197 · after `juxta regis imperium honorifice collectum transportatur Wormatiam`:** source note: uurmatiam 1. vormaciam 3. — Witness 1 spells Worms *uurmatiam* and witness 3 *vormaciam*.
- **N214 · Col. 0197 · after `praesentati, mala morte, ut digni erant, multati`:** source note: mala---multati desunt 1. — Witness 1 omits the span from *mala*, “evils,” through *multati*, “punished.”
- **N215 · Col. 0197 · after `0198B] 49. Triumpho celebri rex factus gloriosus`:** source note: gloriosus factus 1. — Witness 1 reads *gloriosus factus*, “made glorious.”
- **N218 · Col. 0197D · after `tanta victoria quisquam regum intra ducentos annos`:** source note: Widukindus de Karoli Martelli victoria 732 de Sarracenis reportata cogitasse videtur. — Editorial note: Widukind appears to have had in mind Charles Martel’s victory over the Saracens in 732.
- **N219 · Col. 0197 · after `est. [Nam ipsi bello Ungarico aberant, Slavanico`:** source note: sclavonico 3. — Witness 3 reads *sclavonico*, “Slavonic.”
- **N220 · Col. 0197 · after `ipsi bello Ungarico aberant, Slavanico certamini reservati`:** source note: nam ipsi---reservati desunt 1., quae quamvis glossatori cuidam tribui possent, quum tam 2. (3.) quam A. exhibeant, omittere nolui. — Witness 1 omits the span from *nam ipsi*, “for they themselves,” through *reservati*, “preserved.” Although it might be attributed to a glossator, the editor retained it because witness 2, witness 3, and A contain it.

### 50

[Source cols. 0197–0199A]

Therefore, as we related above, when Wichmann failed in giving an account of himself against his uncle, he was kept under guard within the palace. But when the king wished to depart for Bavaria [Note: “Therefore” in manuscript A3.] [Note: This refers to the expedition undertaken in 954, after the Hungarians had been put to flight (ch. 31).], Wichmann, pretending illness, refused to make the journey. The emperor then admonished him that, having been abandoned by his father and mother, he had taken him in place of his sons, had liberally reared him, and had advanced him to his father’s honor; he begged him not to trouble him, since he was already burdened with many other concerns. Hearing nothing useful in reply, the emperor departed, entrusting him to Count Ibo [Note: “Bono” in manuscript 2.]. After spending several days with him, Wichmann then asked permission to go into the forest for hunting [Note: Another reading: “After this he asked that he might go into the forest for the purpose of hunting”; manuscripts 2 and 3 respectively read *inire* (“to enter”) and *intrare* (“to go in”).]. There, taking with him companions whom he had concealed, he proceeded into his homeland; after occupying several towns [Note: One manuscript adds “there.”], he joined forces with Ecberht and took up arms against the emperor. The diligence of Duke Herimann, however, easily crushed them and drove them across the Elbe [Note: Manuscript A has “transabiamque”; manuscript 3 has “trans Albimque,” both meaning “across the Elbe.”]. When they realized that they could not resist the duke, they allied themselves with two barbarian sub-kings, Naco and his brother, who had long been hostile to the Saxons [Note: Compare the Greater Annals of Saint Gall under the year 955.].

### 51

[Source cols. 0199A]

When the army was led out by the duke, they were found in a town called Suithleiscranne [Note: Manuscript 1 reads *qui* (“which”); manuscript A: “suithelei scrannae”; manuscript 3: “Suuithleiscranne.”] [Note: Hahn and H. G. II, p. 62 n. i., and Wedekind, *Noten* I, considered the town to be Schwedt; Leutsch, *Gero*, p. 97 n. 153, proposed another view.]. They were almost captured together with the town, unless they had been roused by someone’s shout [Note: One manuscript reads “aroused”] and had leapt to arms. Nevertheless, after killing about forty armed men before the town gate and taking possession of the slain men’s spoils [Note: Manuscript 2 omits “up to”; manuscript A has “of the slain”], Duke Herimann withdrew [Note: Manuscripts 2 and 7 read “he withdrew”]. Those who helped him were the governor Heinricus and his brother Sifridus [Note: Manuscripts 2 and 3 consistently have “Sigifridus”], eminent and brave men, outstanding both at home and in war [Note: Another reading has “and in military matters.”]. This occurred at the beginning of the Lenten fast [Note: One manuscript reads “at the beginning of Lent” or “of the fast.”].

### 52

[Source cols. 0199B–0199C]

But after the following Easter the barbarians invaded the region, with Wichmann as their leader—not for command of the realm, but for this enterprise alone. Without delay Duke Herimann himself also arrived with a military force. Seeing that the enemy army was formidable and that his own forces were exceedingly small [Note: Another reading: “were present”], while civil war pressed upon him, he judged it more prudent to postpone the engagement while matters stood in doubt and ordered the multitude, which had gathered in the greatest numbers in a single town because they distrusted the others [Note: One manuscript reads “because they differed”], to seek peace by whatever means they could. The soldiers, however, took this decision very badly, especially Sifridus, who was an exceptionally fierce warrior.

Nevertheless, the citizens of Cocarescemiorum [Note: This word was erased in manuscript 1; manuscript 1 has “convocare,” and manuscript 2 “sceniorum.”] [Note: The location of the town remains disputed; compare the books cited below. The Slavonic name indicates that it lay either near the Elbe or on the opposite bank, not far from Magdeburg, where several places bear some resemblance to the name. P.] did as the duke had ordered and obtained peace on the following terms: the free inhabitants, with their wives and children, were to climb unarmed over the wall, while their slaves and all their property were to be left for the enemy in the middle of the town.

When the barbarians rushed into the town, one of them recognized his own slave in the wife of a certain freedman. When he tried to drag her away from her husband, he received a blow from a fist [Note: Manuscript 1 reads “by a blow”; manuscript A has “a thrown blow.”] [Note: The manuscripts vary between forms meaning “of the fist,” “of the fight,” and “with the fist.”], and he loudly proclaimed that the agreement had been broken by the Saxon side. Consequently, all turned to slaughter: they spared no one, but put to death everyone of mature age, while they led away the mothers and their children as captives [Note: The clause from “the mothers” through “they led away” is absent from manuscript 1.].

### 53

[Source cols. 0199D–0200B]

Eager to avenge this crime, the emperor, having already achieved victory over the Hungarians [Note: One manuscript reads “having obtained” rather than “having carried out” the victory], entered the barbarians’ territories in a hostile manner. Concerning the Saxons who had conspired with the Slavs [Note: One manuscript has “had conspired”; manuscript A, “are conspiring”], it was judged [Note: One manuscript adds “and judged”] that Wichmann and Ecberht ought to be treated as public enemies [Note: Some manuscripts read “ought to be regarded”], but that the others should be spared if they wished to return to their own people.

An embassy of the barbarians was also present. It announced that they wished, as was customary, to pay tribute to their allies, but that they wished to retain dominion over the region; on these terms they desired peace, otherwise they would fight for freedom with arms. The emperor replied that he certainly did not deny them peace, but that he could not grant it in any manner unless they cleansed the injury they had committed by worthy submission and reparation.

He led his army through those regions, devastating and burning everything, until at last, having pitched camp above the river Raxa [Note: The unanimous agreement of all the manuscripts shows that, contrary to the *Annals of Saxony*, “Taxa” is not to be read and that the river cannot be understood as the Dosse. It seems therefore to be the Recknitz, a river of the duchy of Mecklenburg; the people with whom the war was being waged were crossing it.], which was extremely difficult to cross because of its marshes, he was surrounded by the enemy.

Behind them, the road was blocked by the strength of trees [Note: These words are absent from manuscripts 1, 2, 3, and 7.] and fortified by a host of armed men. In front lay the river and the marsh adjoining the river, while a Slav with a great army prevented the soldiers both from working and from proceeding [Note: One manuscript has singular “the Slav”; others read “the Slavs,” and one has “preventing the Slavs from work and travel.”]. The army was also harassed by other hardships, by disease as well as hunger [Note: Some manuscripts read “and” for “as well as”]. While this continued for several days, Count Gero was sent to the barbarian prince called Stoinef, so that he might surrender to the emperor and thereby gain a friend rather than encounter an enemy [Note: One manuscript writes the name as “Stoinefgero.”].

### 54

[Source cols. 0200C–0201B]

For Gero possessed many good qualities: skill in warfare, sound counsel in civil affairs, sufficient eloquence, and great knowledge [Note: The words “great knowledge” are absent from manuscript 1]. He displayed his prudence more by deeds [Note: Some manuscripts add “more”] than by words; in acquiring he was energetic, in giving generous, and—what was best—in divine worship he showed commendable zeal.

Accordingly, the governor greeted the barbarian from across the marsh and the river beside which the marsh lay. The Slav replied in kind. Then the governor said to him:

“It would be enough for you if you were waging war against one of my lord’s servants, and not also against my lord the king. What army have you, what weapons, that you presume to undertake such things? If you possess any courage, any skill, any boldness, give us room to cross over to you, or give yourselves room to come here to us; and when the ground is made equal, let the fighter’s strength appear.”

The Slav, snarling in barbarian fashion and pouring forth many insults, mocked Gero, the emperor, and the whole army, knowing that the emperor was weighed down by many hardships [Note: One manuscript omits “many.”]. Gero, angered by this, as he was a man of exceedingly fiery spirit, said:

“Tomorrow will show whether you and your people are strong in power or not; for tomorrow you will undoubtedly see us engaging with you.”

Although Gero had long been regarded as famous for many distinguished achievements [Note: One manuscript reads “achievements” in a corrupt form] and insignia [Note: Other manuscripts read “distinguished deeds”], he was now celebrated everywhere as a great and renowned man because he had captured, with great glory, the Slavs called Uchri [Note: The words from “because” through “called” are absent from manuscript A] [Note: Compare chapter 42.].

Gero returned to the camp and reported what he had heard. The emperor, rising during the night, ordered the enemy to be challenged to battle with arrows and other engines [Note: One manuscript has “others” for “other engines”] and made it appear that he wished to cross the river and marsh by force. The Slavs, believing that nothing else was intended than what had been threatened the previous day, united for battle and defended the passage with all their strength.

But Gero, descending with his Ruanian companions [Note: Another manuscript has “Rugian”; another “his own companions”] [Note: The Rani, Ruani, and Rugiani are the same people, the difference being only one of pronunciation. Meib.], from a point nearly one mile from the camp [Note: One manuscript reads “departing” rather than “descending”], quickly constructed three bridges without the enemy’s knowledge [Note: Another reading: “while the enemy was unaware.”]. He then sent a messenger to the emperor and recalled the entire army. When the barbarians saw this, they too hastened to meet the legions.

The barbarian infantry had to run a longer distance before entering the battle and, exhausted by the effort [Note: One manuscript reads “scattered in flight”], quickly gave way to the soldiers. There was no delay: while they sought the protection of flight, they were cut down.

### 55

[Source cols. 0201C–0202A]

Stoinef, meanwhile, awaited the outcome on a prominent hill with his cavalry. When he saw his allies begin to flee, he too fled. He was found in a certain grove with two attendants and, exhausted from the fighting and stripped of his armor, was beheaded by a soldier named Hosed [Note: One manuscript reads “by a man”; another has the corrupt reading “by gold.”].

One of his attendants was captured alive and was presented to the emperor by the same soldier, together with the sub-king’s head and spoils. From that time Hosed was held in honor and distinction. As the reward for so famous a deed [Note: Manuscript A reads “act.”], he received an imperial gift consisting of the revenues of twenty manses [Note: The word is corrected in manuscript 2 from “return” to “revenue.”].

On that day the enemy camp was stormed, many men were killed or captured, and the slaughter continued far into the night. At dawn [Note: One manuscript reads “on the following day”], the sub-king’s head was placed in the field. Around it, seven hundred captives were beheaded [Note: One manuscript reads “seventy”]. His counsellor, having had his eyes torn out, was deprived of his tongue [Note: One manuscript reads “his tongue”] and left useless in the midst of the corpses.

Wichmann and Ecberht, conscious of their crimes, departed for Gaul and escaped in flight to Duke Hugo.

### 56

[Source cols. 0202A]

Having been made glorious and renowned through frequent victories, the emperor gained alike the fear and the favor of many kings and peoples. Consequently he received very many envoys, namely from the Romans, Greeks, and Saracens [Note: Manuscripts 1 and 3 have the same spelling, “Saracens”]. Through them came gifts of various kinds [Note: Manuscript 1 omits this]: golden and silver vessels, bronze vessels also, decorated with marvelous variety of workmanship [Note: Manuscript A and manuscript 7 have the feminine form “decorated”; the editor adopts the distinction of words found in manuscripts 2 and A], glass vessels, vessels of ivory as well, and objects fashioned in every kind of form, fabrics [Note: Manuscripts A, 2, and 3 place “fabrics” after “fashioned”], balsam and perfumes of every kind, and animals previously unknown to the Saxons: lions and camels, monkeys and ostriches [Note: Manuscript 1 has a corrupt form; manuscript A another variant; manuscript 3 the standard form]. The affairs and hopes of all the Christians round about rested upon him.

### 57

[Source cols. 0202B]

(DCCCCLVI–LVII.) Liudulfus, the emperor’s son [Note: Manuscript A and manuscripts 2 and 3 read “the emperor’s son” in the reverse order], wishing to keep faith with his friends, left his homeland and went with them to Italy. While he was there for nearly a whole year [Note: Another reading: “for almost a year”], he died [Note: Another reading: “on the final day”], leaving throughout the Frankish empire a grievous wound from his own wound [Note: One manuscript has “to the whole empire.”].

His funeral was conducted by the soldiers with the honor due to him, and his body was transferred from Italy to Mainz [Note: Manuscript 3 has “Mogontia”] and buried in the basilica of Saint Alban the martyr [Note: In manuscript 1, “in the basilica” is written; “of Saint” is added above the line], amid the mourning and lamentation of many peoples. He left behind a son distinguished by his father’s name [Note: This was Otto, born in 954.].

### 58

[Source cols. 0202B–0202C]

News of his death was brought to the emperor while he was on campaign [Note: Manuscript 1 reads “in Italy”], campaigning against the Redarii. Therefore he shed a very great number of tears over the death of his son [Note: One manuscript reads “who” rather than “therefore”]; but thereafter, while he continued to order his empire, he faithfully entrusted it to God, ruler of all.

### 59

[Source cols. 0202C]

At the same time Wichmann, knowing that Saxony was empty of warriors, departed from Gaul and secretly entered Saxony. He visited his home and wife, and from there again threw himself among foreigners. Ecberht, however, was restored to favor through the intervention of the great bishop Bruno [Note: In manuscript 1 “Egmanu” is written above “berhtus.”].

### 60

[Source cols. 0202C–0202D]

(DCCCCLVIII.) An army was led against Wichmann for the third time [Note: First by Herimann in 955 (ch. 51), and second by the king in the same year (ch. 53)]. It scarcely succeeded in arranging that he should be received under the protection of Gero and his son, and that they should obtain from the emperor that he might enjoy, with imperial favor, his homeland and his wife’s inheritance.

Ordered [Note: Manuscripts A, 2, and 3 read “without being ordered”; the editor says he does not know which is preferable] to do so, he gave a terrible oath that he would never do anything wrong by counsel or deed against the emperor or the emperor’s kingdom [Note: One manuscript reads “by action” rather than “by deed”]. Having thus given his pledge, he was dismissed in peace [Note: Another manuscript reverses the word order] and was encouraged by the emperor with good promises.

### 61

[Source cols. 0202D–0203A]

After the slaughter of the barbarians had been completed, prodigious signs appeared that year [Note: Manuscript A and manuscripts 2 and 3 read “appeared” in another form], namely signs of the cross on the garments of many people. At the sight of these, very many were struck with a salutary fear and dreaded adversity; they also corrected many of their vices in part [Note: One manuscript reads “the same people” rather than “they also”]. Some interpreted the marks as leprosy of the garments [Note: Manuscript A omits this], because a subsequent leprosy would afflict many people [Note: One manuscript has “would afflict” in the plural]. But wiser men declared that the sign of the cross had foreshadowed salvation and victory [Note: One manuscript reads “foreshadowing itself”], and we too give their view our faithful assent.

### 62

[Source cols. 0203A]

At that time the emperor himself also began to fall ill. But through the merits of the saints, whom he continually serves with faithful devotion, and especially through the protection of the renowned martyr Vitus, to whom he opened his mouth [Note: In manuscript 1, “holy” is written above the line], he recovered from his illness and was restored to the world, like the brightest sun after darkness, for every beauty and delight.

### 63

[Source cols. 0203B–0203C]

When matters had thus been properly arranged throughout all Francia, Saxony, and the neighboring peoples round about [Note: One manuscript and manuscript A read “neighboring” in the masculine form], and having decided to set out for Rome, he proceeded to Lombardy (DCCCCLXI) [Note: Manuscript A and manuscript 3 read “into Lombardy.”].

To relate how he besieged King Bernharius [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “Bernhardus”; manuscript 3, “Berengarius.”] of the Lombards for two years, captured him with his wife and sons, and sent him into exile; how he defeated the Romans in two battles (DCCCCLXIV), stormed Rome [Note: One manuscript omits capitalization], subjected the dukes of Beneventum, overcame the Greeks in Calabria and Apulia [Note: Manuscript 3 has the variant spelling “Appulia”], opened veins of silver in the land of Saxony [Note: Manuscript 1 corrects “the land of Saxony” to “the land of the Saxons”; manuscript 6 has “Saxon land”; manuscript 3 reads “in Saxony”], and enlarged the empire with his son in a manner so magnificent—this is beyond the capacity of our weakness to tell. As I declared at the beginning of the history [Note: Compare the preface to Book I.], it is enough that he labored with such faithful devotion.

Moreover, with regard to your dignity and serenity, which the greatness of your father and brother left to the homeland for every honor and to us for consolation, may great devotion magnify this humble work [Note: Another reading: “may it magnify it magnificently.”]. Let this, then, be the end of the civil war and the conclusion of the little book.

### 64

[Source cols. 0203D–0204A]

(DCCCCLXIII.) Wichmann, having been restored to his homeland, remained calm while he hoped for the emperor’s arrival. But when the emperor’s return was delayed [Note: One manuscript omits “was delayed”], he went toward the northern regions [Note: Manuscript 3 has a variant spelling], as though intending to contrive a new war together with Harald, king of the Danes [Note: Manuscript A has “Halard”] [Note: The author means Harald, surnamed Bluetooth, son of Gorm. Meib.].

Harald sent him word that, if he had killed a duke or knew of any other prince, he should know that Harald wished to ally himself with him without deceit [Note: Manuscript 3 has “if he wished”]; otherwise he should not doubt that Wichmann had acted deceitfully [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “had dealt deceitfully.”].

Meanwhile, his acts of brigandage were exposed by a passing merchant. Some of his companions were captured and, as men acting against the public interest, were condemned by the duke and lost their lives by strangulation. Wichmann himself barely escaped with his brother [Note: The author appears to mean Ecberht.].

### 65

[Source cols. 0204B–0204C]

The Danes had been Christians in ancient times, but nevertheless served idols according to pagan custom. It happened that a dispute concerning the worship of the gods arose at a certain banquet in the presence of the king [Note: Manuscript 2 has “royal,” omitting “in the presence of the king.”]. The Danes asserted that Christ was indeed a god, but that there were other gods greater than he, since they themselves displayed more powerful signs and wonders to mortals.

Against this, a certain cleric—now leading a religious life and a bishop [Note: Compare Adam of Bremen II, 26; Poppo received the bishopric of Schleswig.]—named Poppa [Note: Manuscript 2 and manuscript A have “Poppo”], testified that there is one true God, the Father with his only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, and the Holy Spirit, but that images are demons and not gods [Note: Manuscript 2 reverses the word order].

King Harald, being one who is said to be quick to hear and slow to speak [Note: Some manuscripts omit this phrase; another has “to have been”], asked whether Poppa was willing to demonstrate this faith by himself. He replied without hesitation that he was.

The king ordered the cleric to be kept under guard until the following day. In the morning he ordered a piece of iron of enormous weight to be heated in the fire and commanded the cleric to carry the glowing iron on account of the Catholic faith [Note: Manuscripts 3 and 4 omit the words concerning the fire and the iron]. The confessor of Christ seized the iron without hesitation and carried it for as long as the king decreed. He showed everyone that his hand was unharmed and made the Catholic faith credible to all [Note: Manuscripts A and 7 have “made” in the perfect tense].

Thereupon the king, converted, decreed that Christ alone was to be worshiped as God. He ordered the subject peoples to reject idols and thereafter rendered due honor to the priests and ministers of God. This too is rightly attributed to the merits of your father, whose diligence caused the churches and the orders of priests in those regions to shine so brilliantly.

### 66

[Source cols. 0204C–0204D]

Count Gero, therefore, mindful of his oath, when he saw Wichmann accused and recognized him as guilty, restored him to the barbarians from whom he had taken him. Happily received by them, Wichmann defeated, in frequent battles, the barbarians who lived farther away.

He twice overcame King Misaca [Note: Manuscript 1 reads *Misicam* and manuscript 3 *Miscam*; the latter spelling recurs subsequently.] [Note: Misaca was king or duke of the Poles; the Licicaviki are the same people as the Lechi.], whose subjects were the Slavs called Licicaviki, killed his brother, and extorted a great quantity of booty from him.

### 67

[Source cols. 0204D]

At that same time (DCCCCLXIII), Governor Gero most powerfully defeated the Slavs called Lusiki [Note: One manuscript reads “who are called”; the Lusatian people are meant.] and forced them into the extremity of servitude [Note: One manuscript reads “into servitude” rather than “to the extremity of servitude”]. He did so, however, not without suffering a serious wound himself, the fall of his excellent nephew [Note: The editor remarks that nearly everyone has wrongly understood this to refer to the son mentioned by Thietmar, Book II (p. 30).], and the loss of very many other noble men [Note: Manuscript A reads “very many”; manuscript 3 “more numerous.”].

### 68

[Source cols. 0205A–0205C]

There were two sub-kings subject to Duke Herimann, to whom their fathers had left hereditary hostility toward one another. One was called Selibur, the other Mistav. Selibur ruled the Waari [Note: The Wagrii, inhabitants of eastern Holstein, appear to have been neighbors of the Abodrites.], Mistav the Abodrites [Note: Manuscript 3 has “Addrites.”].

Since they frequently accused one another [Note: One manuscript has the words in reverse order], Selibur was finally defeated in the case [Note: One manuscript adds “the other, Mistav”] and was condemned by the duke to pay fifteen talents of silver. Taking this condemnation badly, he considered taking up arms against the duke. But since his forces were insufficient for war, he sent an embassy and requested help from Wichmann against the duke [Note: Manuscript A reads “from” rather than “against.”].

Wichmann considered nothing more pleasurable than being able to inflict some trouble upon his uncle [Note: Manuscript 3 omits the clause] and quickly arrived with his companions to aid the Slav. As soon as Wichmann was received into the town, the enemy immediately surrounded it with a siege. The army led by the duke also besieged the town [Note: Manuscript A reads “besieged the town” with a different case].

Meanwhile, whether by chance or by prudent design I do not know, Wichmann left the town with a few men, as though to obtain reinforcements from the Danes. A few days passed, and the warriors were exhausted and fodder for the beasts had run out [Note: Manuscript A reads “had run out” in the plural].

There were also those who said that the Slav had merely put on the appearance of war and had not waged a genuine war; that it was altogether unbelievable that a man accustomed to warfare from childhood should have prepared military matters so badly; but that the duke had devised this plan so that, by whatever means he could, he might defeat his nephew and at least recover his safety in his homeland [Note: Manuscript A omits “at least”; in that manuscript “safety in his homeland” has the reverse order], which he had completely lost among the pagans.

Thus the townspeople, weighed down by hunger and by the stench of the animals, were compelled to leave the town. The duke addressed the Slav harshly and accused him of treachery and his wicked deeds. He received this reply from him:

“Why do you accuse me of treachery? Look: those whom neither you nor your lord the emperor could defeat are standing unarmed because of my treachery [Note: Manuscript 3 reads “stand unarmed in this matter”; manuscript 1 has “appear.”].”

At this the duke fell silent. He deprived him of the region under his rule and entrusted all his authority to his son, whom he had previously received as a hostage [Note: The words from “whom” through “his authority” are absent from manuscript A]. He afflicted Wichmann’s soldiers with various punishments and gave the booty of the town to his own soldiers. He displayed to the people as a great spectacle a bronze statue of Saturn, cast in bronze, which he had found there among the other spoils of the town [Note: The Bohemian glosses published by Hanka call Saturn “Sytivrat.”]. Having won the victory, he returned to his homeland.

### 69

[Source cols. 0206A–0208A]

When Wichmann heard that the town had been captured and his companions crushed [Note: Manuscript β reads *Wichmannus*; Falke (p. 456) asserts that he copied this passage from that manuscript. Other manuscripts read “afflicted” or “surrounded”], he again threw himself among the pagans toward the east [Note: One manuscript has “returned eastward”]. He dealt with the Slavs called Vuloini [Note: Manuscript A has “Wlovii”; manuscript β, “Uulouuini”] [Note: Adam of Bremen II, 10, and Helmold I, 2, mention the Slavs called Wilini; more recent scholars have placed their settlements by Lake Bellin and the town of Fehrbellin.] concerning how they might harass Misaca, the emperor’s friend, in war [Note: The clause from “he dealt” through “in war” is absent from manuscripts 2 and 3]. This did not escape Misaca’s notice.

He sent to Bolislav, king of the Bohemians [Note: Manuscript β has a corrupt form; manuscript 3 reads “Boluzlavum”] [Note: Manuscripts 2 and β have variant spellings]—for he was his son-in-law [Note: Manuscript 1 omits this] [Note: Misaca had taken as his wife a noblewoman from Bohemia, the sister of the elder Bolislav; she was called Bobrawa in the Slavic language, according to Thietmar IV (p. 97.)]—and received from him two divisions of cavalry. (DCCCCLXVII?)

When Wichmann led an army against him, Misaca first sent infantry against him [Note: One manuscript reads “sent them against him.”]. At the duke’s command, the infantry gradually fled before Wichmann, drawing him farther from the camp. Then cavalry were sent around behind him, and a signal urged the fleeing men to turn back against the enemy [Note: One manuscript omits “to turn back”; another reads “moves” rather than “urges.”].

Pressed from in front and behind, Wichmann attempted to flee. His companions accused him of treachery, since he himself had urged them into battle, trusting in his horse and intending, when necessary, to make his escape easily. Thus compelled, he gave up his horse, entered the battle on foot with his companions, and fought bravely that day, defending himself with his weapons.

But weakened by fasting and by the long journey through which he had traveled armed throughout the night [Note: One manuscript omits “through which”; manuscript A has “than”], he entered at dawn, with only a very few companions, the yard of a certain man, already exhausted [Note: One manuscript omits “already”]. The nobles of the enemy, having found him, recognized from his armor that he was an eminent man [Note: One manuscript omits “the nobles”; another omits “when he had been asked who he was”]. When questioned about his identity, he declared that he was Wichmann [Note: Another manuscript has “to be.”].

They urged him to lay down his arms. They then pledged their faith that he would be presented unharmed to their lord and that they would obtain from him that he return Wichmann safely to the emperor [Note: Manuscript β has “to their lord.”].

Although he was in the utmost extremity, mindful of his former nobility and courage [Note: The whole clause is absent from manuscript 1], he disdained to give his hand to such men. Nevertheless, he asked that they announce to Misaca that he wished to lay down his arms and give his hand to him [Note: Manuscript β has “his hand” in the singular].

While they were going to Misaca, an innumerable crowd surrounded Wichmann and attacked him fiercely [Note: One manuscript omits the second “him”; another has the plural “they attack him.”]. Though exhausted, he felled many of them, then finally took up his sword and handed it to the most powerful of the enemy, saying:

“Take this sword and deliver it to your lord [Note: One manuscript reads “his lord”], so that he may keep it as a sign of victory and send it to the emperor, his friend [Note: Another reading: “deliver it or send it to him”; another: “send it to him”], so that he may know either that he is mocking a slain enemy or at least mourning a relative.”

After saying this, he turned toward the east and, as best he could, besought the Lord in his native tongue [Note: Manuscript A has “god” rather than “Lord.”]. He poured out his soul, filled with many miseries and hardships, into the mercy of the Creator of all [Note: His date of death seems to be indicated by the Luneburg Necrology (Wedekind, *Noten* III, p. 70): 22 September—“Count Wichmann and many others were killed, and Hoico was killed.”].

Such was the end of Wichmann, and such the end of nearly all who took up arms against the emperor [your father] [Note: Manuscript A ends with the words “your father.”].

## Continuation

### 70

[Source cols. 0207B–0207D]

(DCCCCLXVIII.) When the emperor had received Wichmann’s weapons and had thus become certain of his death [Note: One manuscript reads “more certain”], he wrote a letter to the dukes and prefects of Saxony as follows:

“Oddo, by divine will august emperor, sends every expression of affection to Herimann and Thiadrico [Note: Manuscripts 2 and 3 have “Thiederico”], dukes [Note: Manuscript 1 omits “dukes”], and to the rest of the prefects of our commonwealth [Note: Other manuscripts reverse the order of “commonwealth” and “prefects”]. By God’s will, health and every prosperity are proceeding plainly.

“Moreover, envoys of the king of Constantinople, men sufficiently distinguished by rank, have approached us, seeking peace, as we have understood, with great eagerness. However the matter may turn out, they will in no way dare to test us in war, God willing. Unless we reach an agreement, they will surrender the provinces of Apulia [Note: “Apulia” is consistently written in this form] and Calabria, which they have held until now. But if they submit to our will, we intend, in the present summer, to send the wife together with our namesake to Francia, and then, with God as our guide, to set out through Fraxinetum [Note: Manuscripts 3 and 7 have the variant spelling] to destroy the Saracens, and thus to come to you [Note: Manuscript 3 reads “we shall arrange” rather than “we intend.”].

“Furthermore, if the Redarii have suffered such slaughter, as we have heard [Note: We have no information about this war.]—for you know how often they have broken faith and what injuries they have inflicted—let them have no peace with you [Note: Manuscripts 2 and 7 read “with us.”]. Therefore, after discussing this with Duke Herimann [Note: Manuscript 1 has the variant spelling], exert all your strength so that you may bring the work to an end in their destruction. If necessary, we ourselves shall go to them.

“Our son received a crown from the blessed apostolic at the Nativity of the Lord, into the dignity of the empire. Written on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February in Campania, near Capua.”

When this letter had been read before the assembly of the people at the place called Werla, in the presence of the princes and a great multitude, it seemed that the peace already granted to the Redarii ought to remain in force, since at that time war was pressing against the Danes and their forces were insufficient to complete two wars at once [Note: One manuscript reads “against” rather than “adversus.”].

### 71

[Source cols. 0208B]

(DCCCCLXIX.) Trusting sufficiently in the envoys of the Greeks, the emperor sent part of his army, together with many men of princely rank, to the appointed place, where, contrary to the envoys’ pledge [Note: One manuscript omits “contrary to”; another reads “to the envoys.”], the girl was to be handed over to them and brought with honor to his son.

But the Greeks, reverting to their ancestral arts [Note: One manuscript reads “first arts”]—for from almost the beginning of the world they had been lords of many peoples, and those whom they could not overcome by courage they overcame by cunning [Note: One manuscript has singular “by cunning”]—suddenly fell upon the unsuspecting men, who suspected no harm, plundered the camp, killed many, and captured many. They presented the captives to their emperor at Constantinople [Note: One manuscript omits “to their emperor.”].

Those who were able to escape returned to the emperor and reported what had happened [Note: Manuscripts 2 and 3 have “reported” in the imperfect tense].

### 72

[Source cols. 0208C–0208D]

Moved by this, the emperor sent to Calabria, in order to wipe away this disgrace, distinguished men who had already become famous many times in domestic and foreign affairs: Guntharius and Sifridus [Note: Manuscripts 2 and 3 have “Sigifridus.”].

But the Greeks, elated by their previous victory and less cautious, fell into their hands. An innumerable multitude of them was killed, and those who survived were captured. After cutting off their noses, the victors allowed them to return to New Rome.

They extorted tribute from the Greeks in Calabria and Apulia. Made illustrious by such a victory and enriched by the spoils of the enemy, they returned to the emperor [Note: Apart from Widukind, only the Annals of Cava mention this victory; see Pratillo, *Historia Longobardorum* IV, p. 416.].

- **N201, Col. 0207, after `omnibus fere, qui contra imperatorem arma sumperunt`.** Printed note: `patrem tuum unus cod. A., qui his verbis finitur.` English: Only manuscript A adds *patrem tuum*, “your father,” and ends with those words.

### Chapter 72

- **N224, Col. 0207, after `jam saepe claros factos, Guntharium et Sifridum`.** Printed note: `sigifridum 2. 3.` English: Manuscripts 2 and 3 spell the name *Sigifridum*.

- **N226, Col. 0207D, after `spoliis hostium ditati, ad imperatorem reversi sunt`.** Printed note: `Hujus victoriae praeter Widukindum soli Annales Cavenses (ap. Pratillum hist. Long. IV, p. [Col. 0208D] 416) mentionem faciunt.` English: Apart from Widukind, only the Annals of Cava mention this victory (in Pratillus, *History of the Lombards* IV, p. 416).

73. When the people of Constantinople heard that their own forces had fought badly [Note: [Col. 0207] “Having heard from their own people,” 3. In 2, the excised folio omits what follows up to the words in chapter 75, “from foreign lands everything backward,” etc.], they rose up against their emperor and, through a stratagem of his wife, killed him by the ambush of a certain soldier; and, appointing the soldier as lord in his place [Note: [Col. 0207] “as emperor,” 3.] [Note: [Col. 0208D] The emperor Nicephorus Phocas was killed through the plotting of his wife Theophanu by John Tzimiskes on 11 December 969; John was made emperor and sent Theophanu, the daughter of Romanus II and niece of his own wife, away.]. Once he had been established as king, he immediately released the captives and sent the girl to the emperor with a large army and splendid gifts. (972.) The emperor himself promptly handed her over to his son; and, after the wedding had been celebrated with great magnificence, he made all Italy and Germany happier on this account. At the time when these things were being done in Italy, the supreme pontiff William [Note: [Col. 0208D] He had succeeded Frederick in 954.], a wise and prudent man, devout and gracious toward all, was governing the empire of the Franks, which had been entrusted to him by his father.

74. Although his mother was a foreigner, she had nevertheless been born of noble stock [Note: [Col. 0207] “was of noble stock,” 3.] [Note: [Col. 0208D] He was born in 928 (Continuation of Regino).]. When he heard that the emperor’s mother, a woman of remarkable holiness named Matilda (968), had begun to fall ill [Note: [Col. 0207] “mathildam,” 1, 3.], and while he awaited her funeral, his own funeral preceded hers [Col. 0209A] [Note: [Col. 0209] “preceded,” 3.]. If we wish to say something about her praise [Note: [Col. 0209] Omitted in 1.], we fail, because the virtue of so great a woman surpasses every resource of our little talent. For who could adequately describe her vigilance in the worship of God [Note: [Col. 0209] Omitted in 1.]? Every night, in every manner and by every means, she filled her cell with the melody of divine hymns. Her cell was close to the church, where she rested briefly; rising from it every night, she entered the church, while singers and female singers [Note: [Col. 0209] “female singers,” 3.] were stationed in three groups inside the cell, before the doors, and along the road, to praise and bless the divine mercy. She herself remained in vigils and prayers inside the church, awaiting the solemn celebration of Mass.

Then she visited the sick wherever she heard of them, if they were nearby, and supplied what they needed. Then she extended her hand to the poor; then she received the guests, who were always present, with complete generosity. She dismissed no one without kind speech and scarcely left anyone without little gifts or necessary assistance [Note: [Col. 0209] “without little gifts,” 3.]. Often, when she saw travelers at a distance from her cell, she sent them what they needed. Although she carried out such works very humbly by day and night, she diminished nothing of her royal dignity; and, as it is written, although she sat like a queen [Note: [Col. 0209] “royal,” 3.] with the people surrounding her, she was always and everywhere a consoler of the grieving (Job 29:25).

She instructed all her household servants, men and women, in various skills and also in letters; for she herself knew letters, which she learned sufficiently well after the king’s death [Note: [Col. 0209D] Cf. *Life of Matilda*, § 13, at the end.]. Therefore, if I wished to recount all her virtues, the hour would fail me; even if I possessed the eloquence of Homer [Note: [Col. 0209] “omer,” 1.] or Virgil, it would not suffice [Note: [Col. 0209] “nothing,” 1.].

Thus, full of days, full of every honor, full of good works and almsgiving, after distributing all the royal riches among the servants and handmaids of God and the poor, she gave her soul back to Christ on the second day before the Ides of March. [Note: [Col. 0209] “gave back,” 1.] At that same time Bernard, who, as was proclaimed by all the people, was in his generation most worthy of the priesthood, completed his final day. [Note: [Col. 0209] “ended,” 3.] Let no one reproach us for reporting this pious story, since we do not submit to danger concerning the truth. For we heard from a certain solitary that he had seen—in the spirit, I do not know whether in an evident vision—the souls of the queen and the bishop being carried into heaven by an infinite multitude [Note: [Col. 0209] “an infinite multitude,” 3.] of angels, with ineffable glory. [Note: [Col. 0209D] “being carried,” 7.]

Therefore, when the emperor heard of the death of his mother, his son, and the other leading men—for Gero too, a great and powerful man, had already died [Col. 0210A] [Note: [Col. 0209] “was,” 3.] [Note: [Col. 0210D] On 19 May (Fulda Obituary), or on 20 May (Thietmar II, p. 30), 965.]—he decided to refrain from the expedition against Fraxinetum [Note: [Col. 0209] “Fraxinetum,” 3.], to settle affairs in Italy, and to return to his homeland. He was also struck by a report that many of the Saxons had wished to rebel; but because we judge this to have been useless and unworthy of mention [Note: [Col. 0209] “reason,” 3.], we pass it over. (972.) Accordingly, he departed from Italy with great glory: he had captured the king of the Lombards, overcome the Greeks, and defeated the Saracens. With the other victors he entered Gaul, intending to cross from there into Germany and to celebrate the coming Easter at the famous place of Quedlinburg [Note: [Col. 0209] “Quidilingeburg,” 3.]. There, a multitude of different peoples gathered and celebrated with great joy his restoration to his homeland with his son [Note: [Col. 0209] “celebrate,” 3.]. (973.)

After remaining there no more than seventeen days [Note: [Col. 0209] “no more than seventeen days,” 3.], he descended from there to celebrate the Ascension of the Lord at Merseburg [Note: [Col. 0209] “mesburg,” 1; “Merseburg,” 3.]. Sadly he traversed those regions because of the death of the excellent duke Hermann, who, through remarkable prudence, justice, and vigilance in civil and foreign affairs, left an everlasting memory among all mortals who had lived before [Note: [Col. 0209] Here manuscript 2 continues.]. After receiving envoys from Africa [Note: [Col. 0209] “Africa,” 2; “Aphrica,” 3.], who visited him with royal honor and gifts, he made them remain with him [Note: [Col. 0209] “with them,” 2; “them,” 7.].

On the Tuesday before Pentecost [Note: [Col. 0209] “Pentecost,” 1.], he came to the place called Miminlevu [Note: [Col. 0209] “Mimileuu,” 3.]. The following night, rising from bed at dawn according to custom, he attended the nocturnal and morning praises. After this he rested briefly. When the offices of Mass had been celebrated, he extended his hand to the poor according to custom, tasted a little food, and again rested in bed.

When the appointed hour came, he went out cheerful and happy and sat down at table. After the meal, [Col. 0210C] he attended the evening praises. When the Gospel canticle had been completed [Note: [Col. 0209] “of the Gospel,” 2.], he began to grow feverish and tired. When the princes standing around him understood this, they placed him on a seat. As he inclined his head, as though he had already weakened, they revived him [Note: [Col. 0209] “revived,” 1.]; and, after he had requested [Note: [Col. 0209] Add “already” in 2.] and received the sacrament of the divine body and blood [Note: [Col. 0209] “and,” 2, 3.], without a groan and with great tranquility he surrendered his final breath, amid the divine offices, to the piety of the Creator of all [Note: [Col. 0209] “divine,” 2.].

He was then carried into a bedchamber; and, when it was already late, his death was announced to the people. The people [Note: [Col. 0209] “to the people,” 1.] spoke at length in his praise and thanksgiving, recalling that he had ruled his subjects with paternal devotion; had freed them from their enemies; had defeated the proud enemies—the Avars, the Saracens [Note: [Col. 0209] “Saracens,” 1.], the Danes, and the Slavs—with arms; had subjugated Italy; had destroyed the shrines of the gods among neighboring peoples; and had established churches and orders of ministers. As they brought forward many other good deeds one after another, they attended to the royal funeral.

76. When morning had come, although he had long ago been anointed king and had been designated emperor by the blessed apostolic, the son of the emperor, the sole hope of the entire Church, they all vied at the outset to place their hands in his, promising loyalty and confirming by military oaths their service against every adversary. Thus, having been unanimously elected prince by the entire people, he transferred his father’s body to the city which he himself had magnificently built, named Magdeburg [Note: [Col. 0211] “Magadaburg,” 2; “Magdaburg,” 3.].

Thus the Roman emperor and king of nations died on the Nones of May, the Wednesday before Pentecost, leaving to the ages many glorious memorials of divine and human affairs [Note: [Col. 0211] “religious,” 3.] [Note: [Col. 0211] In manuscripts 3 and 4, the following words are added, undoubtedly from manuscript 6, though they are not found in the other codices: “In his first year, which was 937 from the Lord’s Incarnation, the Hungarians, devastating France, Alemannia, Gaul as far as the Ocean, and Burgundy, returned through Italy. The monasteries of Saint Gall and Saint Boniface were burned. Rudolph, king of Burgundy, and Arnold, duke of the Noricans, died.”].

**THE THIRD BOOK OF THE SAXON DEEDS ENDS** [Note: [Col. 0211] Thus in manuscripts 1 and 2.]

**IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 983. JOHN, ABBOT OF SAINT ARNULF OF METZ.**

[Col. 0211]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE

*(In Fabricius, *Bibliotheca medii et infimi Latini*.)*

[Col. 0211] John, abbot of Saint Arnulf of Metz, of the Benedictine order, author of the *Life of John, Abbot of Gorze*, from the year 962, in the *Acts of the Saints*, volume III, February 27, pp. 690–715, with Bollandus’s notes; and in Mabillon’s *Benedictine Centuries*, century V, p. 369. The same author, after the year 951, wrote the *Life and Two Translations of Saint Glodesindis the Virgin*, who is said to have flourished in the time of Childeric, around the year 608. It is found in Labbe, volume I of the *Bibliotheca nova manuscriptorum*, pp. 720–740; also in the *Acts of the Saints*, volume VI, July 25, p. 210; in Mabillon’s *Benedictine Acts*, century II, p. 1087, and century IV, p. 435.

Surius published the Life, though interpolated, on July 25, stating that some manuscripts name a certain Bernard, abbot, as its author, and others Albert, a monk. It is useful to point out that this writer did not compose the *Life of Saint Glodesindis* entirely anew, but revised a version supplied by someone else, perhaps Abbot Bernard or the monk Albert, and enlarged it by adding certain material of his own. This is noted by the authors of the *Histoire littéraire de la France*, volume VI, p. 423, who also add that this writer John was still alive in 977, whereas in 984 he was no longer among the living.

[Col. 0211]

# LIFE OF SAINT GLODESINDIS

[Note: [Col. 0211B] The memory of Saint Glodesindis, always celebrated among the people of Metz, is absent from the ancient Martyrologies, excepting the calendars of Metz. The monk Sigebert mentions her in his *Chronicle* under the year 615 in these words: “Glodesindis of Metz shines forth; fleeing her bridegroom, and receiving from God through an angel the veil for her head, she devoted herself and all that was hers to God.” Her monastery, called Saint Glosina by the truncated form of her name—as often happens—still stands within the walls of the city of Metz, having until now been assigned to Benedictine nuns.]

**ABBESS OF METZ**

By John, abbot of Saint Arnulf of Metz.

*(In Mabillon, *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, century V, p. 1087.)*

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0211B] 1. Your many prayers over a long period, dearest sisters in Christ, pressing me somewhat beyond measure, finally achieved this: I could not deny your love. For what you requested was not only honorable but plainly religious, and I felt that to refuse it would be both unworthy and dangerous. Although I judged my strength somewhat unequal to the task, I was again reminded that charity, which does not compel us to care for what is our own but for what belongs to our neighbors, knows how to open the way to easier success precisely when its cause is pressed by greater difficulties.

Nor should we fear that, in God’s cause, the one for whom the matter is undertaken will fail to assist the person working on her behalf—provided only that faith does not grow weak. You therefore urge me to attempt, in whatever style may be possible, to recount what beginnings of conduct, what intermediate deeds, and what final consummation of life the most sacred virgin of Christ, Glodesindis, whose devoted vigils you continually pursue, displayed, insofar as I can discern from the writings preserved to our age in whatever form of letters they were recorded.

Since it seems improper to resist what has been demanded for so long and with such persistence, I rely on the aid of that same outstanding virgin, who cleaves to God with a pure spirit through her virtues, and likewise on the support of your prayers. Although not without some embarrassment, since I recognize the poverty of my own talent, I will not linger long over extended preliminaries but will proceed more quickly to the narrative.

## THE LIFE BEGINS

[Col. 0213]

[Col. 0213B] 2. In the time of Childeric [Note: [Col. 0213D] “Chilperic” should be read, although in the *History of the Translation of Saint Glodesindis* the author admits that the name of King Childeric was inserted only conjecturally, since other chronological indications are lacking.], the most celebrated of the Frankish kings among historians, in Belgic Gaul—which later changed its name after the people to France—the distinguished virgin of the Lord, Glodesindis, was born from a sufficiently noble lineage. Her father was a most illustrious man and a very renowned duke, named Wintro [Note: [Col. 0213D] This is Quintrio, or Vuintrio, duke of Champagne, mentioned in chapter 14 of the *Chronicle of Fredegar the Scholastic*, who is again said in chapter 18 to have been killed at the instigation of Brunhild in the third year of the reign of Theuderic, Childebert’s son—that is, in the Christian year 598.]; her mother, Godila, was no less distinguished in the brightness of her nobility. From the beginning of childhood she shone forth, marked by many virtues and destined to be an example to many on the way of chastity, illustrious in life and character.

When she had passed beyond girlhood in her parents’ household, having been brought up with complete and every kind of care, and when the time had come for her to be betrothed in accordance with her worthy birth, her parents assigned her in marriage, according to custom, to a certain young man named Obolenus. But while Christ everywhere protected her, she was preserved undefiled in body no less than in mind.

And when the period of betrothal had ended and, as is customary, the young man had received the virgin from her parents, he led her home with a large company to prepare the wedding. But because the holy virgin had already consecrated her body and soul to the heavenly Bridegroom, the aforesaid bridegroom was perhaps, by divine providence, summoned by royal command; and the young man immediately hastened to the palace. When he arrived there, many wicked crimes were charged against him, and the severity of the king was fiercely kindled against him. Thus he was thrust into custody, worn down there by fitting squalor for a full year, and, when that time had elapsed, was brought out, condemned by judicial sentence, and beheaded.

Thus holy virginity, while resisting carnal pleasure with all its strength, regarded the entire pomp of temporal glory as nothing. With the Lord Christ, whom she preferred to all the delights of passing things, fighting on her behalf, she clung in heart and body to the one whom she had always desired; joyful and victorious, she triumphed over the loss of all corruption.

3. The schemes of the adverse power did not fail either. When the father heard of the death of the former bridegroom, he again compelled the venerable girl to enter a marriage chamber. She, who had already absorbed Christ the Bridegroom into the very marrow of her heart, resisted with all her strength and would not allow the mind once fixed upon virtue to be bent toward that defilement by any influence.

Meanwhile, on the appointed wedding day, as the parents’ arrangement pressed forward, the blessed virgin, contemplating the one whom she had conceived with the eyes of her mind as incorruptible, unfading, and immortal, and then observing that this other man would shortly become corruption and a son of man, a worm, reverently rejected her father and sought refuge with God and the holy mother Church.

Her father had a sister named Rotlindis, of memorable holiness and highly renowned at Trier for her religious reputation. He attempted to take the girl with him to her, so that at least through her persuasion the girl’s spirit might be softened and she might not refuse to obey her father’s counsels. But what can blind persistence accomplish against the light of eternity?

The holy virgin, resisting her father’s commands with a manly spirit, chose to seek Metz, or Mediomatricum, a city memorable by land and sea for its population, power, and very antiquity. In that city stands the basilica of the most blessed protomartyr Stephen, which divine activity has often made illustrious through many miracles. When the matter had nearly reached the point of violence, the handmaid of Christ entered it and placed herself as a fugitive between the altar and the confession, where the relics of many saints are contained together with the blood of that martyr [Note: [Col. 0214D] Donatus, in the *Life of Saint Trudo* above, under the year 698, affirms in chapter 8 that his precious blood was preserved in the church of Saint Stephen.].

O devotion to chastity, rightly to be extolled throughout all ages! Mortal weakness, dragged downward by nature itself, though that nature has been afflicted as punishment, descends captive wherever it is led; but this girl, holding herself firmly by the strength of the spirit, shuddered as though before the abyss of a monstrous precipice and, since every other means of escape was closed to her, took refuge in flight alone.

The text here is corrupt: “Nor indeed needy in the bosom … nor were there any from the crowd to compel [her].” Her father was a very powerful duke, wealthy enough to terrify even the rich, and a threatening and dreadful troop pressed around him. But she, readier to die than to lose the flower of virginity and the splendor of glorious integrity, shaken neither by threats nor moved by blandishments, remained undaunted as though in the safest harbor.

Let virgins learn from this present example that it is not beautiful for them to submit to marital bonds, to delight in the abundance of possessions, in crowds of male and female servants, in an array of ornaments of various kinds, or in throngs of attendants. They know that all these things must be lost through various accidents and not without great sorrow, and that none of them can either accompany them or follow them when death breaks through everything. Rather, let them be attracted above all these lowly and perishable pleasures by the delight of that one thing which is the greatest beauty of blessed modesty, uniquely dear to God and the angelic hosts, and by a holy and immaculate desire.

4. But to continue what we began: the girl’s parents followed the fugitive immediately. Astonished at what had happened and inflamed with anger—especially since the attendants of the betrothal, complaining that they had been deceived, urged them on with sharper grief—they attempted by whatever means they could to drag the handmaid of Christ from the sacred place of refuge.

They kept constant watch through the night before the door of the holy building and maintained an attentive guard by day and night, so that, if an opportunity should arise, they might quickly abduct her by force. The venerable girl, stronger in spirit and holding herself immovable with a resolute mind, clung to the most sacred altar and could not by any means be torn away from it even for a moment. And, wonderful to say, she remained in the church for six continuous days, not only never leaving but also abstaining entirely from all food and drink.

But he who gives food to all flesh and fills every living creature with blessing, finding his handmaid deprived of human nourishment, refreshed her with divine sustenance. She, intent upon heaven in constant prayer, is said to have been fed solely by angelic refreshment.

Meanwhile, when faith demanded the reward of such steadfast perseverance, divine consolation appeared, wiping away the long-contracted cloud of sorrow. For as the seventh day, which was Sunday, was now approaching, behold, a man with an angelic face arrived in the sight of everyone, followed by two exceedingly beautiful boys. He went straight to the part of the altar where the most sacred virgin was concealing herself to preserve her modesty, and, in the sight of all, covered the head of the blessed virgin with a veil as a sign of holy religion.

Immediately he was taken from the eyes of those looking on, together with those to whom he had appeared. The magnitude of the event, its astonishment and miracle, struck everyone, while fear itself made them so stunned and empty of mind that they could neither speak nor discover where the visitors had come from or who they were.

5. After the departure of so great a vision, when they came to themselves and saw the holy virgin standing there in that habit, they readily understood that an angelic presence had appeared and that everything they had seen had been done by divine power. They had nothing with which to resist the matter further. They merely prostrated themselves on the ground and submitted at the feet of the blessed virgin; all the swelling of their harshness having been turned into a posture of supplication, they begged only forgiveness for the injuries they had inflicted.

For a heart in which the spirit of piety and the king of gentleness presided, the labor of forgiving was not difficult. At once, as though she had been injured by no one, she set aside everything that had happened and returned to complete favor with her parents and the others.

Here let virgins take heed and learn that nothing is dearer to God, or more familiar to angels, than the treasure of chastity. Christ is present with virginity amid every danger; the heavenly spirits serve it as the most devoted attendants of their emperor’s bride. She alone, undefiled, follows the undefiled Lamb everywhere; and the more closely she clings to him, the more quickly she is heard in whatever she asks.

Behold how promptly that immeasurable grace was present to this handmaid. Truly, the Lord is near to all who have a broken heart, and his salvation is near to those who fear him. With what words do you think she then burst forth in praise of her Creator? In what kind of voice did she pour out a hymn with immeasurable joy, when she recognized that the eyes of that invisible light had been turned so gently upon her, that those most secret ears had so promptly inclined to her voice, and that her prayers had so easily been brought to fulfillment, so that she could rejoice that the holy angel had come beneath the very eyes of mortals, in his almighty majesty, to gladden and console her?

With prophetic exultation, now made a heavenly bride, she could say: “The Lord has clothed me with the garment of salvation and surrounded me with the robe of righteousness” (Isaiah 61:10). Likewise, with the voice of the universal Church gathered from both sexes, she could joyfully proclaim to her one head: “As a bridegroom he placed a mitre upon me, and as a bride he adorned me with an ornament” (ibid., according to the Septuagint).

6. Thus the blessed virgin, overflowing with compassion, mercifully admitted to forgiveness all those who had previously been hostile to her, and thereafter, impatient in nothing toward her parents, submitted herself peacefully to them. She voluntarily hastened to her aforementioned aunt Rothilda, renowned for her great virtue, whom, fearing for her modesty, she had earlier refused to approach in the matter of the marriage with a defiant mind. Now, having received grace, she possessed no small confidence.

There, after spending not much time according to the manner of religious life, and having been fully formed in every pursuit of goodness and in the ordering of conduct and actions according to heavenly discipline—whatever was divinely and humanly fitting and honorable—she returned to Metz, which was dear to her through divine patronage.

At once she undertook the entrance into the stricter life, toward which her holy spirit had long aspired with all its desire. Gathering a company of Christ’s handmaids around her, she took it up with all her strength and resources.

There is a place within the walls of that city, then held by her parents under hereditary right, exceedingly suitable for a more religious institution. The holy virgin requested that it be given to her for divine use, and, having obtained it without delay through their ready generosity, she materially constructed a monastery for maidens of God, still distinguished today by its beautiful appearance; yet she governed it nobly by the more beautiful strength of its virtues. In it she gathered a community of as many as one hundred women serving Christ and devoted herself to it with glorious, vigilant diligence.

What her life was thereafter in this holy struggle, what progress in every kind of spiritual growth came to her through daily practice, under what rigor of discipline she restrained herself, how she became a guide to the others on the heavenly journey and set herself before them as an example to follow, and how she lived for them rather than for herself—all this, with sound understanding and judgment, I believe ought to be commended in writing.

For anyone who considers the matter more attentively will see clearly that the blessed virgin, continually holding before the eyes of her heart that visitation so joyfully poured out upon her from above, preserved in the execution of her outward work a fervor equal to that of her interior devotion.

7. After she had governed that monastery for six years—the number of the days during which she had remained in the church in that wondrous fast of holy preparation for her integrity—she did so happily, pleasing to God and to human beings, magnificent in life and signs. Having faithfully completed the course of her purpose in holiness, she was to receive from the Lord the crown of righteousness and, already to be joined in the bridal chamber to the heavenly Bridegroom whom she had long desired; undefiled, she departed from the world [Note: [Col. 0217C] Namely, on the eighth day before the Kalends of August, on which day her memory is celebrated in the additions to the Usuard Martyrology and in the interpolated Martyrology of Ado. But in what year should Saint Glodesindis be said to have died? Certainly she seems not to have lived beyond the year 610. For she died at thirty, after her father had once and again destined her for marriage. When she sent back the messenger concerning the second betrothal, she was about twenty years old, while her father was still alive; we have said that he died in 698. Moreover, Saint Glodesindis died before Saint Arnulf, who died around the year 640, as the author states shortly below.].

The entire span of her mortality is also confirmed to have been completed in the course of thirty years. Nor is there any need to inquire whether her life had reached the fullness of age, since whatever fruits might have accrued to old age, her youth, brought to perfection in a short time, lacked nothing of them.

For, according to Wisdom, “the understanding of a person is gray hair, and an undefiled life is the age of old age” (Wisdom 4). Indeed, by God’s great gift, the righteous are providentially taken from the world into eternal rest, lest, seeing the evils that are done under the sun, they should linger even briefly amid inward delights, or be corrupted by continual contact with the vices of mortality itself, to which they too are seen to be subject. The same Wisdom bears witness to this: “He was taken away, lest wickedness should change his understanding or deceit deceive his soul” (ibid.).

Meanwhile, her funeral was arranged with the proper honor. According to the custom established by her from the beginning in that monastery, her body was carried to the basilica of the holy apostles, not far from the city walls, toward the southern gate, and there was laid in a crypt sunk far below, on the left side.

For while she was alive, she herself had ordered that this be done, because the cemetery of the holy maidens of that place was then located at the aforesaid church of the apostles. At that time the body of the most glorious confessor of Christ, Arnulf, had not yet been received by the same church in the splendid tomb in which it is now seen [Note: [Col. 0218C] This passage is read differently in Labbe; the reading of Surius, however, appears preferable.]. Arnulf, after a considerable time, was clearly to shine forth there with great marks of life and virtue [Col. 0218B].

From this the place later received its name, both because of his frequent miracles and because of the nobility of his family; and among the people no memory of any other saint is recorded there except under the name of that blessed bishop.

The venerable pledge remained buried in peace in the same place for approximately twenty-five years. Her spirit, already having overcome every change of time, clung amid the rewards of eternity to him who alone truly possesses immortality and dwells in inaccessible light; and she enjoyed life with him truly immortally, because immutably. To him, who alone is immortal and invisible God, be honor and glory unto ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0217]

# HISTORY OF THE TRANSLATION OF SAINT GLODESINDIS, ABBESS OF METZ

By John, abbot of Saint Arnulf of Metz.

*(In Mabillon, *Acts of the Saints*, century V, p. 435.)*

## NOTICE

Three translations of the body of Saint Glodesindis are reported in the following little book. The first took place in the eighth century, in an uncertain year; the second in the year 830, by Bishop Drogo, whose epitaph records the memory of this event in the following verses:

> He solemnly raised the bones of Glodesindis,  
> and laid them in a worthy and distinguished place.

It seemed appropriate to refer the other two to this more solemn translation: namely, the one which I said took place in the eighth century, and the third, which was arranged in 951 by Bishop Adalbero. The following little book commemorates them all.

## AUTHOR’S PROLOGUE

[Col. 0219]

[Col. 0219A] 1. Having, as the dryness of my speech allowed, restored the first parts of the deeds of the holy virgin from the form of those ancient writings into a new presentation, through God’s mercy, before I proceed to explain what remains, I wish to ask the reader—if anyone should not disdain to take these pages into his hands after the earlier ones—to grant me a little goodwill, so that he does not mark me as though I had rashly burst into this undertaking with a certain nobility of mind while perhaps empty of every serious purpose, and so that he does not disdain to learn the reasons with a fair disposition.

First, the same excessively importunate and prolonged demand of the holy sisters, which I declared at the beginning and which outweighed all other considerations, compelled me, since refusing them anything seemed almost an offense against God. Then the subject itself, so clear and worthy by its excellence—indeed, I may say freely, deserving to be ranked with the very best—was sufficient in itself to commend the work and turned my whole desire toward it.

Nor does that writing, although it is handed down under a silent author, detract anything from the power of the events. Scattered, as it were, with seed, though only rarely, it has produced a harvest not barren for our use, a harvest that ought to be extended without limit. For it makes no difference through what indication or from what cavern a most beautiful gem is extracted, provided that it satisfies the avarice of mortals through use and beauty.

And since divine goodness has offered so effective a consolation to our weakness amid the many troubles of this life—a pearl of such great value, rightly preferred to many precious things—I judged it wholly unworthy if shameless and ungrateful silences of the tongue should grow numb before so great a grace. Even if the discourse could not be clothed in eloquence as splendid as the subject deserved, at least a plain account should be supplied, lest the salvation that belonged to all should appear to be shut off from mortals.

2. We do not claim that this novelty of writing will bring anything more certain, nor do we begin an untouched work, since we rely only upon another’s footsteps. But because that history of the blessed virgin had been composed in a simple style, as antiquity perhaps suddenly committed it to memory, and was suitable only for ordinary people, we considered that, since—by Christ’s favor—many people distinguished in the study of the disciplines now disdain the reading of an unsophisticated text with no small degree of disgust, it would not be inappropriate to serve their refined tastes with our labor.

Accordingly, in the first part we have transferred the truth of the deeds, as the earlier writing showed them, into a faithful interpretation, as I believe, up to the death of the blessed virgin. In what follows, likewise with equal purity, with Christ our Lord going before us and the merits of his divine bride favoring us, we shall continue to follow the same footsteps in the order of narration.

3. We are also very pleased that this later portion proceeds along a somewhat more certain route, especially because its knowledge of time is marked more clearly, whereas the earlier parts are somewhat obscured.
