Apart from the name of King Childeric at the very beginning [Note: [Col. 0219] “Hilperic” should be read, as I noted in century II; by that name the author seems not to have known the first Childeric, the son of Chlodovech II.], which was inserted conjecturally and is used throughout the rest of the narrative, the text is so silent about what happened under which king or prince that even Childeric himself, who is found passing judgment in the death of the blessed virgin’s bridegroom, does not provide us with a sufficiently certain date.

If this Childeric is indeed the one in question, tradition merely reports that he lived not long after the time of Charles the Elder [Col. 0220B], and that while Charles was still alive, his father Pippin—previously duke and mayor of the palace, as he was then called—had been elevated to royal power over him. Childeric, sunk in excessive sluggishness and inert idleness, was not merely less fit to govern affairs but entirely useless for every purpose.

Whether this is so or not, I shall not regard as a matter of great importance. The annals and historians that I have been able to consult, apart from the single *Life of Charles*, mention a certain Raganfred, from whose hands Charles seized the principate. Only one annalist briefly notes Childeric and follows the tradition mentioned above: that he was deposed from the kingdom and tonsured, and that Pippin was elevated over him.

But if the man of whom tradition speaks is to be believed to have lived at that time, it is not sufficiently clear how what is found in the present little book can be proved—namely, that the cemetery of the nuns at the church of the holy apostles had not yet been distinguished by the body of blessed Arnulf. For it is certain that blessed Arnulf had been taken from the world much earlier than this Childeric is said to have lived; and, as the sacred writings of his deeds make clear, scarcely a year after his death had elapsed when he was brought to Metz from his place of burial.

Whatever the facts may be, and leaving them for each person to judge according to his own discretion, let us not allow this ambiguity to deprive the remaining matters of much weight. With the Lord assisting our effort, let us now pursue them completely and explain, with a devotion no less than our duty requires, the miracles of virtue that followed the two translations of the blessed virgin and the various cures of illnesses displayed in reverence for her most sacred tomb.

## NARRATIVE OF THE FIRST TRANSLATION OF SAINT GLODESINDIS

[Col. 0219]

[Col. 0219D] 4. As the preceding account has shown, after the most sacred and incorrupt body of the virgin had rested for 254 years in the basilica of the holy Apostles [Col. 0220D] outside the city walls, one of the religious women of the aforementioned convent of nuns declared that she had been divinely warned that, beside the larger church situated lower down, another basilica should be built externally in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God. She related the manner of the revelation as follows:

“I seemed,” she said, “while I was sleeping, to see the blessed virgin of the Lord, Glodesindis, standing upon the city wall and throwing a stone from a distance with her hand, as though marking out a place. She also addressed me, saying: ‘Let a church be built there, and where the stone has fallen by chance, there let an altar be erected to the most blessed ever-virgin Mary.’ Then, pointing to another place at the side, she said: ‘Here let a door be made, so that from the larger church—that is, from the monastery—a passage may be opened for the sisters into this new one.’”

When she awoke from this dream and had reported it to the others, they remained for a long time uncertain what to do, because at that time the place was under royal protection, and they did not presume to undertake such a project unless a petition had first been presented to the king. Accordingly, after the matter had very quickly been brought to the ruler’s attention, and he had readily been persuaded to authorize its execution, the work was energetically undertaken and completed according to the vision. A royal grant of generosity was also added for the same nuns, decreeing that the new basilica, once built, should again solemnly serve as the cemetery of the sisters, and that the body of the holy virgin should soon be reverently transferred from its former tomb and buried there.

Thus the long journey—which had been seen as burdensome for carrying the funerals of the servants of God out of the city [Note: [Col. 0221] Cemeteries were formerly located outside cities, and likewise outside convents of nuns, as can be demonstrated by many examples.]—was shortened, and abundant heavenly protection was provided for the multitude of the faithful. From that time onward, as had formerly been customary, no funeral was carried either to the aforesaid basilica of the Apostles, now celebrated under the name of blessed Arnulf, or to any of the other basilicas around the city. Rather, just as daughters cling to their mother while alive through devoted service, so you may see them, once dead, adhering to her in the due repose of their bodies until the time of their glorification.

5. When the new church had therefore been brought to completion, the whole populace hastened from every direction in eager rivalry to the place of the tomb. After the surrounding earth had been dug away and the stone monument removed, they found the saint still wholly intact in body, displaying no sign in her flesh of so long a burial, but conveying the grace of an entire body as though she had been laid there that very day.

What joy was there, what tears bursting forth from the warmth of inward gladness, possessed that blessed multitude at so great a spectacle! It would be easier to fail in words than to describe it inadequately; indeed, whatever speech might perhaps explain, the devout service of the faithful people at that time expressed far more abundantly. At last, having received the incomparable treasure with pious eagerness, while the sacred orders raised praises to God in a solemn heavenly procession and religious harmony, they carried it to the dwelling prepared for it in the new [Col. 0222A] basilica.

There the nuns, burning with immeasurable devotion toward it, washed and adorned the most blessed body according to ecclesiastical custom, as though she had only then departed this life. During the washing, one of the nuns, afflicted by a long illness and barely clinging to life, came confidently to the place of washing, having conceived no vain hope of recovery, and lightly pressed the saint’s face with her finger. Immediately, when she withdrew her finger, blood followed from the virgin’s face in a wondrous miracle. As all who were present stood equally astonished at the miracle, like that of the Lord’s side, the blood became plainly visible. And although, as I have said, the same religious woman could scarcely retain her final breath, she suddenly perceived the strength already exhausted by disease gradually returning to her; she afterward lived six months as a witness to so great a marvel.

When all the ministry of pious love toward the holy virgin had been completed, they placed her once more in a new sarcophagus on the right side of the altar of holy Mary, Mother of God, and carefully arranged it, heaping earth over it.

6. Some time had passed afterward when, one night, a woman of especially austere life was told in a vision by someone that a mouse was corrupting the body of the blessed virgin beneath the tomb. In the same sleep, the monument seemed to her to be opened, and she herself drove away the mouse, which had already gnawed part of the right big toe.

She awoke at dawn and told the matter to the mother superior and the other sisters. It was immediately decided to summon the ministers of the sacred rites to investigate. After they had performed, according to Christian custom, litanies and prayers for a favorable outcome, they reverently opened the tomb. Finding the right big toe bloodied, as a sure sign confirming the vision, they drove away the mouse; then, since the way farther in was obstructed, they closed and secured the tomb as before.

7. The most sacred body rested in that same place until the time of the most devout emperor Louis, son of the famous and mighty emperor Charles. During that period the blessed virgin frequently manifested herself through numerous virtues, and the healing of many sick people bore witness to her holiness and exceptionally great merit before God.

Although these events were less fully committed to writing because of the negligence of antiquity, memory, nevertheless, passed successively from the accounts of those who came before to those who followed, and—repairing through enduring renewal all things that flee with age and old age—does not cease to report that she always flourished through the display of signs. What a later age recorded, after more sluggish indifference had been set aside, readily shows how much confidence may be placed in the earlier accounts, and likewise that she was renowned for equally clear miracles throughout that long interval.

Yet these things seem to be sought in vain for her commendation, since surely this one fact—that a body granted such a presence of divine power was preserved incorrupt for so many years—surpasses every marvel that could have occurred by any other circumstance [Col. 0223A]. At the same time, it is made clear in what great glory the spirit of her blessed immortality triumphs, free from every change, in the place where it truly is, since here, through the power of her immense merit, she overcame with such potent grace even that which had been given as corruptible and had been subject to the laws imposed upon mortal beings.

8. The Lord wished to display this to human eyes as a commendation of the glory of her most pure chastity, so that it might plainly be evident by what reward he customarily compensates those who, for love of him, despise the flesh and cling only to his embrace; and so that it might be shown that virginity, which does more than is commanded, merits more than is promised.

To be sure, that human flesh might endure intact for some time before the general resurrection of bodies solely by divine gift, although many readings from several reliable writers bear witness in defense of this, it is enough for our present purpose to cite Saint Bede the presbyter; [Note: [Col. 0223D] I read it this way, not “the second,” as in Labbe, where one finds the Life of Saint Cuthbert written by Venerable Bede in volume II.] in his History of His People, a work rightly supported by ecclesiastical authorities as belonging to sound faith and orthodox teaching, he relates of the blessed bishop Cuthbert that, after he had been buried for twelve years, he was found with his body intact. He treats the matter more fully in his book on the man’s Life.

He also records a similar case concerning a certain queen, Edeltrude, of wondrous holiness. Jerome likewise writes that the holy Father Hilarion was found and taken up by his disciple, after some time in the grave, not only with his flesh but also with his clothing undefiled.

For the rest, we do not bring these examples forward to obscure that supreme and singular glory of the Lord, nor to diminish the praise of the saints. Christ, having become a participant in our nature but not in sin, was, as one filled with more abundant grace than the sons of men, truly and naturally God, the Son of God. Thus, according to the prophet, his flesh rested briefly in the tomb in hope of the resurrection that was soon to follow; and when his soul, which could in no way be held by hell, quickly returned to the body, that Holy One of holies experienced no corruption even in the flesh [Col. 0224A] he had assumed as mortal.

There is a very great difference between servants and the Lord. He alone possessed the power to lay down his soul when he willed and to take it up again when he willed. Having freely submitted himself to death, he remained within the confines of the tomb for a short time, then, by the power of his own majesty, broke the laws of death and rose victorious by himself. The saints, however, having departed from this mortal body as wholly mortal by nature, while their spirit flew back to him who had sent it, had their flesh returned to the earth according to the law of the first man.

But because, through a wondrous exchange, the two natures—flesh and spirit—are joined together, and while in the present life they devote themselves to divine things they mutually expend their services in action, so that the spirit performs every good through the flesh and the flesh through the spirit, and while they live together they are regarded as the temple of Christ, as it were an ark of the covenant preserving divine knowledge, then, when the spirit is recalled by its creator, the body in which so many sacred things were long preserved is worthily received and guarded by the faithful in place of God’s temple and of an ark filled with those sacraments.

This continues until, at the end of temporal things, both substances are restored into one structure, as before, and are renewed with greater glory for their friends, with no bonds of division between them. Therefore, if the goodness of God’s power, which did not permit his holy flesh born of a virgin to be subjected to any corruption, also willed that the incorrupt bodies of certain saints should be preserved for a time by a gratuitous gift, the praise of these lesser examples in no way diminishes that supremely unique glory of Christ God [Col. 0224C], who is above all; rather, these things, which would be obscure in themselves, are adorned by the light of that immeasurable greatness.

Let us now continue the account of the second removal or translation of the most sacred virgin, and attend to the conclusion of the work begun with the merits of the one whom the King of angels glorified, his bride, through such splendid manifestations of miracles for the consolation of mortals.

## ACCOUNT OF THE SECOND TRANSLATION

[Col. 0223]

[Col. 0223D] 9. The emperor Louis, whom we mentioned above, son of Charles the Great and surnamed the Pious, after his father had most gloriously completed his reign, possessed the imperial power in no lesser eminence. It was the seventeenth year after his father’s death, when the year 830 from the Lord’s incarnation was in progress, and when a certain Gregory occupied the apostolic see at Rome. He had succeeded two men, Eugenius and Valentine, who had followed one another in rapid succession in death; the former survived only three years, the latter scarcely a month. Gregory was then entering the third year of his pontificate.

The holy see of Metz was at that time held for the eighth year by Drogo, brother of that same emperor Louis [Note: [Col. 0223D] Correctly so; for the Annals of Einhard testify that Drogo was appointed to the Church of Metz in the year 823. Adso the abbot, in his book On the Deeds of Saint Waldebert, abbot of Luxeuil, relates the manner of Drogo’s death, stating that he was swallowed by the River Lignon while fishing. The Necrology of Saint Gall records his death on the fifth day before the Ides of December.], who had also received from that Roman see, by privilege, apostolic vicariate throughout all the regions of Gaul, together with the authority and title of the pallium and of supreme archbishop, and exercised it as a man of the highest dignity [Note: [Col. 0224D] Chrodegang, Angilramnus, and Walo, bishops of the same see, were likewise honored with this privilege.].

Until that time the body of the blessed virgin had remained buried in the right-hand part of the altar of the new basilica of holy Mary, Mother of God, as we have said. But the heavenly providence that cares for all that it has created, and especially for its own people, then wished to demonstrate visibly, through that body as well, how highly the merits of the holy virgin had always been esteemed by God.

For at that time the tomb itself began of its own accord to rise from the ground, in such a wondrous manner that neither the places nearest the tomb in the same earth nor the masonry constructed above it appeared disturbed. When news of this novelty reached the aforementioned bishop, he could not tolerate delay; on the following day he sent trustworthy ministers of the sacred rites, together with the senior archdeacon, whom they call a chorepiscopus, to inspect it. They came, verified everything in accordance with the report brought to them, and immediately reported the matter as certain [Col. 0225B]. Upon receiving their report, the bishop diligently inquired about the same most sacred virgin: who she had been, and what manner of conduct and life she had led while alive—matters that had not yet become sufficiently known.

10. When he had learned everything in due order from those who had been able to see her alive in the body, many of whom still remained, he was greatly stirred by joy mingled with astonishment and, moved by I know not what divine prompting, reinforced by the encouragement of many, quickly resolved to have her raised.

Lest it seem incredible that some people of that time could then have survived, a chronicle extending from the time of King Childeric through Pippin and Charles to Louis proves this readily; it is found to cover little more than eighty years [Col. 0225C], and it is not difficult to demonstrate that such a period may last within the lifetime of one person.

Accordingly, the most reverend bishop himself came to the place with a great gathering of clergy and people. After solemnly offering the pious supplications of their vows, he opened the tomb and, with his own arms, raised the sacred virgin’s limbs from the grave. They were still held intact in their entire structure. Burning with a devotion toward her more wonderful than can be believed, he placed her upon a bier. As all the assembled crowds and peoples vied with one another in proclaiming praises to God and glory to Christ, they carried her in an immense triumph to the larger basilica.

This is the larger basilica still visible today, situated a short distance from the city wall. On its eastern façade, outside the city wall, stood the new basilica of holy Mary, Mother of God, which we described above as having been built as a cemetery for the girls.

The larger basilica itself had from ancient times been consecrated in the name and honor of Saint Sulpicius, bishop of Bourges and confessor [Note: [Col. 0225D] It may reasonably be doubted whether that basilica was originally distinguished by the name of Saint Sulpicius, since Saint Sulpicius, bishop of Bourges and the first bearing that name, was a contemporary of Glodesindis, according to the chronology of Glodesindis’s age that I have established. Certainly, the church seems rather to have borne the name of Saint Peter from the beginning; Saint Sulpicius, bishop of Bourges, was later added as its patron, whether the first or the second of that name.].

It was this church that the blessed virgin, while alive, had founded as a monastery after her parents had granted an estate for divine purposes and laid its foundations. Public documents concerning the possessions of that monastery, in all its records and polyptychs issued in the old style of writing and with the pen [Col. 0226A], contain the name of the blessed Sulpicius; and the entire legal account of the hereditary rights of that place and the reckoning of its properties—which they call the abbey—is designated by his name.

It is also said to have been dedicated to holy Mary, Mother of God, with the blessed apostle Peter added, so that the principal altar was dedicated jointly to her and to the same confessor. In this basilica, a new sarcophagus having been reverently prepared behind the sacred altar, they carefully placed the holy and most precious pledge with the greatest honor and devotion they could provide.

11. Immediately, through the power of Christ, miracles so pleasing and beneficial began to shine forth there that the Lord himself deigned to confirm, by more certain proclamations, how great they believed the glory of the virgin’s merit to be with God [Col. 0226B].

Among these he also continually fulfilled bodily what he declares through the man of God speaking in the Book of Kings to Eli: “Whoever honors me, I will honor; but those who despise me shall be without honor” (1 Kings 2:30).

Because this holy girl—holy indeed, and deserving to be named so often—glorified the Lord in her body, according to the Apostle, and reverently bore him through love of virginity, therefore more abundant grace, leaving aside for now the heavenly reward of immeasurable weight, accompanied her both while she remained in the body during this mortal life and now, after her death, follows those same members with immense honor.

But against the despisers of God and those who trample upon holy things, and against those who, in accordance with Wisdom, see the righteous but do not understand and do not take such things to heart, the words that follow in the same book rightly apply: “The righteous man who has died condemns the living ungodly” (Wisdom 4:16). And shortly afterward: “After this they shall fall without honor and be held in contempt among the dead forever.”

12. But let us now discuss the powers of the miracles themselves more fully. After the body had been taken from the former tomb and placed upon the bier, as the preceding account related, and before it was buried in the second tomb, a man who had been blind for a long time and no longer hoped for any help in recovering his sight suddenly approached the bier, encouraged by a better hope. Without delay, through the aid of the most sacred virgin, he perfectly recovered the light whose return had long seemed hopeless.

Likewise, a woman who had been wasting away from blindness for many years was illuminated there at almost the same hour through the grace of Christ.

13. After the sacred limbs had been placed in the tomb, another woman, similarly afflicted by the loss of sight for a long time, heard of the signs that the Lord was working through the merits of the blessed virgin and of the fame that had already rapidly stirred the whole city. She hastened to the holy tomb as quickly as she could. There, lying prostrate on the ground and imploring divine aid through the Lord’s handmaid, while keeping vigil for several nights, she finally obtained the complete sight she had sought.

[Col. 0227A] 14. At about the same time, three women, exhausted in nearly all their limbs by severe fevers and a very long illness, had repeatedly and uselessly resorted to the empty care of physicians. Having lost their meagre resources, they had doubled their burden of poverty without receiving any remedy. When they heard reports of the great miracles, they hastened in unwavering faith to the tomb of the holy virgin.

As soon as they touched the threshold of the holy church, they invoked the virgin’s aid with trusting prayers and immediately recovered perfect health in all their limbs. In the place where avarice, which is always the companion of bodily cures, had entirely failed—with its power spent upon the bodies or possessions of the wretched—faith alone, which is accustomed to bestow everything freely, restored what belonged to it with its customary speed.

[Col. 0227B] 15. Another woman lay confined to a bed of the most serious illness and longest suffering, so that only her breath seemed to remain. Everything that human hands had applied to her had been entirely futile; indeed, she had already completely abandoned hope that health could ever be restored to her.

By what prompting is unknown, unless perhaps—as later became sufficiently clear—it was by the inspiration of God, whose care extends over all his people. He wished to rescue her by his free goodness from such a pit of despair and would not allow the spark of good action, however faintly kindled in her, to be wholly extinguished. She therefore had herself carried in the hands of others to the threshold of the sacred monastery.

When she had entered the enclosure or atrium surrounding the monastery [Col. 0227C], she began, with whatever voice she possessed, to give thanks to almighty God. She thanked him because divine mercy had allowed her to come there, something she had never hoped for and had not believed could ever happen.

When she began to touch the doors of the holy basilica with her first steps, her illness gradually abated and she began to recover. The nearer she came to the sacred body, the farther the disease seemed to withdraw from her, and she continually felt her strength and health increasing.

Then, amazed at herself as though by a miracle, she began to walk about the basilica here and there, almost as if taking exercise, and loudly proclaimed no small thanksgiving. Shortly afterward she prostrated herself on the pavement of the sacred tomb to pray.

There she poured forth an earnest prayer and spent part of the night between the altar and the tomb [Col. 0227D]. A few days later she was restored to complete health, so that she felt no trace of that long and hopeless illness remaining in her.

16. One day, while the nuns were performing the divine service in the church, an unknown woman who had been deprived of sight, led by another woman, came in the presence of the same maidens of God who were singing, as far as the steps by which one ascends to the altar. When she had passed beyond them and was allowed to approach the altar alone, her eyelids—which had long remained closed in a persistent condition—suddenly parted, allowing her to perceive a little light. In amazement she saw the unknown woman who had been leading her, and, uttering a sudden cry, began to search for the woman who customarily gave her her hand.

When that woman had somehow been divinely removed and did not appear anywhere, the one who had been blind was led by the unknown woman, whom she could still scarcely make out in the uncertain light, to the virgin’s tomb, at the side facing the head.

There she prostrated herself in prayer. When she rose, trembling and bewildered, and stood facing the tomb, she thought that a kind of cloud appeared before the tomb itself. She wondered that clouds, which are accustomed to move high in the air, seemed then to be so near and to touch the earth.

Little by little, a clearer and increasingly brighter light began to be poured into her. Finally, when all darkness had been removed from her eyes, she clearly recognized that what lay before her was indeed a tomb.

Then, astonished and anxious, she remained bewildered, not knowing where she was or how she had arrived there, and seeing nothing around her that she recognized. To increase her fear, she could no longer see the unknown woman whom she had just before been astonished to see walking ahead of her and leading her there [Col. 0228B].

While she was wasting away for a long time in this distress, she eventually came to herself and recognized with complete certainty that the blessed Glodesindis had appeared to her, led her there, and restored her sight through her merits. Breaking into thanksgiving, now seeing everything clearly, she praised the Lord and the holy virgin in a public voice. No longer needing a guide, she went freely in every direction, rejoicing.

17. Not many days afterward, another woman who had likewise been blind for a long time was again led to the holy tomb. There, keeping vigil throughout the night with the other crowds of sick people and awaiting divine aid with prayers [Col. 0228C], she saw the blessed virgin draw near and separate the eyelids of her eyes with her own fingers, as though forcibly pulling them apart.

Without delay, her clear sight was restored, and afterward she lived for many years as a witness to the merits of the sacred virgin.

16. Moreover, a certain man suffered from a wondrous and grievous affliction of the nose, breathing so horribly that no one could easily approach him even from a distance. Various people had often tried to treat him, but all their care had proved futile. When he heard the report spreading far and wide of the joyful healings taking place in the city of Metz at the aforementioned monastery through the glorious merit of the virgin Glodesindis, he hastened to go there.

After he arrived and appeared to enter the church [Col. 0228D], everyone offended by the excessive stench coming from his nose began to flee from him in different directions. The present warning of his anxious suffering reminded him of its cause, and since he could not flee from himself while carrying his punishment with him, he overcame human shame by necessity. He placed complete trust in the one who had not rejected contact with lepers and those flowing with blood, and who had descended to heal the diseases and infirmities of the wretched.

Thus he proceeded with the other sick people to the tomb, which was salutary for all. There he held out a lamp as an offering with his hand, earnestly prayed for the restoration of his health, and awaited the arrival of heavenly mercy. He did not abandon the persistence of his faith until, through the aid of the virgin’s immense merit, he was freed from all the foulness of that obscene odor. Thereafter he enjoyed the ordinary company of people and the customary encounters of greetings and conversation without causing anyone distress.

18. Likewise, a woman who had been blind for ten years and retained no hope of recovering her sight was, as is believed, divinely warned and sought the monastery. When she entered the church and heard the commotion of the sick, many of whom were sitting around the tomb, she called loudly for Glodesindis’s aid, repeatedly invoking her name, and begged God to be merciful to her, a sinner.

Immediately, through the generosity of heavenly power, she received the light and departed rejoicing.

19. Lest we seem to have lingered too long over individual persons and thereby incur the fault of a tedious writer—something rightly to be avoided—let it suffice to reduce the crowd of those healed to a kind of numbered account, noting only whatever may have been more remarkable.

We are careful not to reverse the order in which the working of the miracles successively occurred. Rather, just as the earlier written account reported, joining each narrative to the preceding one according to the order of time, so that whatever happened first was written first and whatever followed immediately afterward was recorded directly after it, and thus the sequence of the entire catalogue was woven up to a definite point, so we follow it throughout, even at the risk of being reproached for the fault of a faithful translator.

20. Five women who had formerly been afflicted with long-standing blindness received, through Christ the Lord’s illumination, the grace of the light they had long desired, to the glory and commendation of the most sacred virgin.

After them, a woman who for three years had carried both feet and one hand twisted out of shape heard of so many miracles and asked to be carried there quickly. Once brought there, she prostrated herself on the pavement of the tomb and testified with much weeping and prayer that she had suffered these things because of her sins. At last, in commendation of the virginity that had been piously and rightly lived, she was straightened in the sight of many bystanders and restored to the full function of perfect health. She departed unharmed.

21. After her, three men and four women who had long been condemned to the darkness of blindness were restored to the sight of light, to the praise of the most illustrious virgin, who always shines with the light of eternity.

22. It is not enough that frequent miracles occurred in the presence of her most sacred body. Many people also felt that abundant assistance had come to them through the grace of Christ when they invoked her name from afar; for Christ both remains and works with his saints in every part of the world. This will become clear from the few examples we set down below.

23. A cleric of the monastery, Fulgubert by name, who was carrying out the office of ecclesiastical service in its proper order, urgently wished to cross the river adjoining the city on the eastern side, called the Sallia [the Seille], because some pressing matter required it.

When he hurried to the bank, he saw no boat there. He waited a long time in case one might arrive from some part of the river. At last, tired from waiting, as often happens, he leaned down briefly upon the ground and fell asleep.

When he awoke, he still saw no means of crossing. As he was considering turning back and blaming himself for the delays he had spent so long and fruitlessly enduring, he suddenly began to call upon the holy virgin by name.

After he had held the cry within him for a few moments, he looked up and unexpectedly saw a boat standing at the place on the bank where he was. Since he could not at all imagine by what human means it had been brought there, he firmly believed that it had been provided solely by the work of God, to whom all things are subject, and by the merits of the sacred virgin whom he had invoked.

Astonished at so great a miracle, he gave immense thanks, as was fitting, to almighty God and the holy virgin, and crossed the river as he had desired. He himself, afterward a faithful narrator of so great an event, solemnly swore that he had invented nothing, but had related it faithfully as it had truly happened to him.

24. A poor man living far from the city, who supported himself solely by the craft of fishing, conceived the intention one day of visiting the monastery of the aforementioned virgin. In rustic simplicity—not blameworthy, however—he did not wish to go there empty-handed, since he had nothing else available. He therefore decided to go to the river and bring a fish, if one happened to come within reach.

He boarded a small boat and cast his net. Contrary to hope, he caught a fairly large fish. But as he hurried to reach the bank, the fish violently struggled free of the net and escaped into the river.

The rustic was deeply distressed and cried in a tearful voice: “Holy Glodesindis, give back what I intended to bring you.”

Having said this, he cast the net into the river again. The same fish that had earlier escaped as fleeing prey was caught once more, and the offering was taken to the monastery and presented there as he had resolved.

25. Numerous and repeated testimonies have likewise shown that this holy woman prevailed with no lesser grace, through her powerful merits, in the healing of those afflicted; the following examples alone will suffice to establish this.

26. Almost at the very time when the rustic whom we mentioned earlier was carrying his fish as an offering and departing, an imperial smith from the village of Judicium arrived at the same place [Note: [Col. 0229D] Jacobus Sirmundus noted this place in his notes on the second capitulary of Charles the Bald. He writes that Judicium, commonly called Judiz, was situated not far from the estate of Theodon [Thionville].].

For eleven years he had been grievously tormented by a demon. He had visited many shrines of the holy martyrs, even in the more distant parts of Gaul: Saint Sebastian of Soissons, whose relics were said to have been brought there from Rome not long before and deposited at Saint Medard; Saint Quintinus of Vermandois; and Saint Dionysius at Paris [Note: [Col. 0231D] That is, in the territory of Paris. The ancients sometimes spoke in this way, as the learned Hadrianus Valesius noted in his Disputation on Basilicas, chapters 8 and 9, and in the later part of his Defense, chapters 5 and 6. The same expression is found in the Life of Adalbero, bishop of Metz, who is said to have sent many gifts to Saint Dionysius at Paris—that is, to the monastery of Saint Dionysius, situated five miles from the city of Paris.], [Col. 0231A] as well as the memorials of many other saints, traveling from one to another in hope of recovering his health.

But his healing was being delayed by a certain divine mystery, not because of any lack of power in the saints. It had most certainly been reserved for this holy virgin, with whom the hand of the Lord worked so effectively.

The skill of bodily medicine also tried, if it could help by any means, to apply many remedies to him, but it had brought him absolutely no assistance. At last, the Lord wished to show more openly that he had so often sought help in distant places in vain, when swifter healing could meet him nearby. When he heard of the great number of miracles taking place at the tomb of the most reverend virgin Glodesindis, he reached Metz as quickly as he could.

Entering the basilica of the blessed virgin [Col. 0231B], he took his place beside her tomb. After he had lain there for some time, that impure and most dreadful spirit, unable to endure the presence of such holiness, was violently expelled and departed, no longer possessing anything of the man.

27. After him, a certain man who had been mute from infancy came there and suddenly obtained complete freedom of speech before the most sacred body. In the same way, a woman who had been mute from birth recovered her speech there through the virgin’s power.

Likewise, a woman who had long been savagely held captive by a demon came there; the adversary was driven out, and she returned in possession of herself and with her mind restored.

A certain lame man from the village of Lauriacum received, at the same place through the virgin’s powerful action, the use of his feet, which severe disease had twisted, so that he could walk freely.

A woman who had been blind for many years, from the village of Arcuntiacum, kept vigil for some time at the holy tomb with the other sick people and was granted sight not long afterward.

Similarly, two other women condemned to blindness received through the blessed virgin the grace of the light they had long lost.

28. Besides these, many and almost innumerable miracles were displayed at the most blessed body of her perpetual virginity from the time of the aforementioned Archbishop Drogo, for approximately sixty years, during the episcopate of Adventius, who succeeded him, while Lothair the Elder and afterward Lothair the Younger were ruling, continuing until the time of Walo, who succeeded the aforesaid Adventius. Because of negligence, these miracles were not committed to writing.

What was done under Walo himself, or under his successor Robert [Col. 0231D], will be explained in the following account.

### 29

Before proceeding to what remains, since circumstances require it and an opportunity has arisen, we thought it appropriate to make a few brief observations about the first two bishops mentioned, and about those who successively followed them, as well as about the condition of the times. The principal reason is that during the episcopate of one of them, namely Adventius, many benefits were bestowed upon the monastery of this holy virgin through royal munificence, and the testamentary edicts of King Lothair the Younger still remain in the possession of the servants of God. At the urging of his wife, Queen Teutberga, and through the intervention of that same Bishop Adventius, these edicts most generously granted them both newly donated possessions and restored earlier ones, as well as immunities for the same monastery, by royal authority.

Queen Teutberga herself then held the governance of that place, and she also rests there. We think it will not displease the reader if we explain who this Lothair was and, taking the occasion, repeat a few matters mentioned above, so that greater knowledge of the chronology may lend greater strength to the narrative.

This was Lothair the Younger, son of that Lothair the Elder who was born to Louis the Pious. After the death of his pious father, and after a long disagreement with his brothers Louis, king of the Germans, and Charles, who later became emperor, arising from their desire for imperial power, they at last engaged one another in a most savage and unprecedentedly bloody battle at Fontenay, a place in the county of Auxerre. Their long-deferred internal hatreds had reached a fatal climax, and the slaughter was grievous; King Pepin of Aquitaine joined them as well.

After peace had nevertheless been made among them and the kingdom divided, this part of France, bounded by the Rhine and the Moselle, together with certain cities and royal abbeys added on both sides for the sake of confirming the peace, fell to Lothair. From that time down to the period in question it has been called the kingdom of Lothair. Not long afterward, Lothair himself voluntarily renounced all worldly affairs, professed himself a monk at the monastery of Prüm, and died there, where his celebrated tomb is still found.

His son and namesake, this younger Lothair, succeeded him. A sufficiently lamentable reputation is circulated about him, concerning his hatred of the aforementioned Queen Teutberga and his unlawful taking of Waldrada in marriage. When this wretched affair had stained the face of the world with a mournful example, it stirred almost the entire world to indignation against it.

Even more appalling, the bishops of the leading sees, Theutgaud of Trier and Gunther of Cologne, became supporters of this detestable marriage. Although they appeared to be men of intelligent judgment and learned in both divine and human letters, they proved themselves the worst possible patrons of folly. Summoned to Rome by Pope Nicholas and heard before the most sacred body of blessed Peter at a synod attended by nearly all the bishops of Italy and many from Gaul, they long tried to embellish their guilt under the pretext of marriage. At last, caught by the deceitful trick by which they thought to catch others, they themselves were caught: with everyone assenting, they were condemned by Pope Nicholas and deprived of their ecclesiastical ranks. The king, together with Waldrada and all who participated in her scandal, was likewise anathematized.

To pass over many other matters, it is enough, as a warning to those who may ever become involved in such things, to say that Gunther himself, defending his action and publicly attacking the pope in many words, declared that he had been bound by an unjust judgment. Treating the apostolic censure with contempt, he returned home without either seeking or obtaining pardon, and, having eaten, celebrated Masses and, on the day of the most holy Supper, performed the absolution and the rite of chrism. His companion Theutgaud of Trier, however, died in exile at Rome under excommunication.

King Lothair, although he promised correction and, as it seemed, restored Queen Teutberga to her honor, later came to Rome. There the pope questioned him about his wife’s fidelity; overcome by fear, he denied his guilt. On the condition that he confess the truth, he heard Mass from the lord pope in Saint Anastasius and, wretched man, presumed to receive the Lord’s body from his hand.

Returning from there to his homeland, he was suddenly struck by a most miserable calamity among his followers, which arose almost at the very gates of Rome. There was neither delay nor rest for the dying, until, while he hurried onward, he reached Piacenza with only a few companions, nearly all his men having already been taken by death. There, while he was sitting unharmed about the ninth hour, he was suddenly struck and became speechless. The next morning he died a pitiable death and was buried there in a basilica of the most humble workmanship.

When Bishop Adventius learned of his death, he immediately sent a messenger to Charles, king of western France. He brought Charles to Metz, accompanied by Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, and in the church of Saint Stephen, called the episcopal residence, placed a second crown upon his head, in addition to the one he already possessed, and established him as king over the two kingdoms.

These matters have been inserted briefly so that the period of the bishop previously mentioned might become clearer.

[Col. 0233C] Walo, as we have said, succeeded Adventius. At that time Berthulf was archbishop of Trier, while Charles was still alive and a certain John held the universal title of pope; from him Walo also obtained the pallium.

After Walo had governed the church for scarcely seven years, the Northmen, having ravaged many parts of Gaul, advanced as far as Trier. While Walo was rashly preparing to engage them with an unequal force, he went to meet the Northmen at a place called Remich, on the bank of the Moselle, where they were advancing threateningly. Since there were no forces available to resist them, it was no longer a battle but a slaughter of wretched men. The bishop was cut down there with the others.

After the slaughter, his body was brought back to Metz and buried in the basilica of Saint Savior, which he had earlier built from its foundations as his own tomb.

During his time, when his death was already approaching, and when a death-bearing event seemed to be foretold by the very portent, oil—not imaginary but real, wonderfully enough—was seen to flow from the side of the holy virgin’s tomb facing her feet. This became known not only to the nuns and sacristans who kept watch beside the sacred tomb by night and day, but throughout the entire city.

Let each person interpret this as he wishes. One thing, certainly, was confirmed by the sight and touch of many: the liquid continued to flow for a long time, so that in appearance and use it plainly resembled palpable oil. It moistened the tomb from the side of the feet as far as the region of the head, and—something even more astonishing—when collected in a vessel it was preserved for a considerable time afterward. Many people who touched or anointed themselves with it for various ailments reported genuine cures.

The common belief was that, as several people claimed had been shown to them in revelations, these were the holy virgin’s tears, by which, as the destruction of the city approached, she strove to turn aside the Lord’s anger. This belief should not be condemned altogether. Although it arose from a simple mind, it can nevertheless be seen to contain some understanding, since oil represents mercy and tears express the movement of forgiveness.

For although in that city of supreme joy there is no grief and no tears at all, where God wipes away every tear from the eyes of the saints, the Lord nevertheless wished to display such a manifestation to human eyes, so that anyone prudent might infer with what sweetness and what light, in the presence of God’s glory, that holy soul rejoiced—she whose extinguished ashes here shone with so pleasing and beautiful a mystery to human hearts and eyes.

The outcome of events nevertheless taught what the blessed virgin had obtained in secret for the city: when it was so near danger from the invasion of the barbarians, Christ, moved ineffably—if not by the virgin’s tears, certainly by her ineffable prayers—made it safe from harm.

### 30

Under the bishop who was appointed to succeed him about a year later, Ruotpert, a most distinguished man of the Alemannic people, a similar flow of oil was seen to issue more frequently from the sacred tomb itself, so that it ran farther from the side of the monument in a stream across the pavement.

The servants of God collected it with a sponge and, after wringing it into a glass vessel until the vessel was filled, reverently hung it over the holy tomb. From this oil, as has been said, many people presumed to obtain remedies for themselves.

### 31

And so that this event might not be considered something similar to vain tales, what happened there through that oil was made public to everyone at the time and thereafter passed from the mouths of many who had seen it down to us.

There was a custodian of that holy church named Doda. One of the sisters, who was responsible for a certain oratory of the holy cross within the precincts of the monastery, persistently begged her to give her the glass vessel containing that divine oil, so that she might keep it in her own oratory with, as she thought, greater reverence.

When Doda, with exceedingly rash levity, stretched out her hand over the tomb where she remembered the vessel hanging, intending to give it to the petitioner, she found it nowhere. Astonished and trembling, she searched more carefully, feeling about again and again, but could in no way sense it, even though the vessel was hanging there just as it had been placed. Thus she was exposed to a sufficiently ridiculous deception.

She summoned the other women, and they too wandered about with her for a long time, always having the tomb before their eyes but never seeing the vessel. With a lamp brought in, they searched around the tomb here and there in a fruitless investigation. At last, after they had been wearied enough by this kind of mockery, they were scarcely able to touch the vessel that had been set down.

The same custodian presumptuously took part of the liquid and sent it as a relic to her brother, the religious priest Angelerius, at the church of Saint Savior in the same city. She gave the other sister the vessel with the remaining portion at her request, and it was carried away to the aforementioned oratory.

Immediately the rash custodian was struck with a punishment sufficiently worthy of her outrageous presumption: she became insane. Nor could she obtain a cure before what had been illicitly given was recovered from both recipients of her foolish generosity and restored intact to its former place upon the tomb. As soon as this had been done, scarcely two hours later, she became sound in mind and fully rational.

Afterward, as has been said, many people who touched the same oil to their aching heads, eyes, or other parts of the body very often felt themselves refreshed by the merits of the holy virgin and completely cured.

### 32

Moreover, during the episcopate of that same Bishop Rotbert, Jesus Christ the Lord deigned to perform many miracles—no fewer than those performed in earlier times—at the same most holy tomb. The following narrative will attempt to set down some of them with the greater confidence because we know for certain that many who witnessed these events have survived into our own time, and no one can refute them when summoned as suitable witnesses. Some of the very people who were healed have likewise lived down to our own day.

### 33

A woman named Hildigard had been deprived of the light of her eyes for eight years. Not without hope, she sought the life-giving tomb. Remaining there on watch through the night, before dawn she was granted pure light through divine mercy, with the virgin interceding, despite all the darkness of night.

Likewise, while a blind young man waited for some time within the basilica for heavenly visitation, he perfectly recovered his sight through the merits of the virgin.

A woman named Osa had been lame for five years. She asked to be carried there and lay sick there for six months, awaiting divine help with unfailing devotion. She did not cease her persistent faith until she received the reward of faithful perseverance: the strength of all her limbs. Rejoicing in her own feet, she returned home, although she had been brought there on another person’s hands.

### 34

Similarly, a certain lame man was once carried on a bed toward evening and placed outside the doors of the basilica. He begged to be allowed to rest inside the holy building that night, but was unable to obtain this. There, before the door, he spent the night in faith that was not empty, until daylight.

Then, behold, in the morning, when strength suddenly came to him, he was thrown from his bed by a remarkable and swift leap. Leaving the bed where it lay, he went with firm steps to the holy tomb, loudly and openly proclaiming that Saint Glodesind was, through divine assistance, the author of his recovery. Giving thanks as much as he could, he glorified with a loud voice the mercy of God and of the holy virgin.

### 35

Another sick man, deprived of every bodily strength, had waited for some time at that very holy place for assistance. One day, overcome by sleep, he fell asleep and saw in a dream the blessed virgin standing beside him. With a certain authority she ordered him to rise and join those who happened at that moment to be working on the pavement, helping to complete the work itself.

He awoke immediately and, recognizing none of his former weakness in himself, sprang up joyfully. As he had been ordered, he approached the work while everyone looked on in astonishment and appeared no less energetic than the others in laboring. He knew beyond doubt that the most blessed virgin had granted him the salvation he had desired.

### 36

A woman named Adelburga was said to have suffered for a long time from a copious flow of blood from her mouth and nostrils, and was already in danger of death, with no remedy available to her from any quarter.

The feast day of the most holy virgin happened to be approaching on the following day. Immediately, presuming upon the hope of recovery through divine consolation, she sent a candle by a vow for her own health, so that it might give light before the holy altar during the night vigil of the solemnity. As soon as it had been brought there, she obtained the recovery she desired, Christ accomplishing it through the holy virgin.

In a similar way, a man named Hilleicus from the village of Fadiliacum had a feeble son, useless in all his limbs. He brought a votive candle for the holy altar and, after pouring out a prayer there on the boy’s behalf, returned home and found his son healthy.

What shall we say of the woman who had long been crippled and, after sending a votive candle there, earned complete recovery before that very candle had been brought into the church? She was from the village of Columbaria and had become so weak in all her limbs throughout the entire summer that she could neither set down a step nor be carried except by other people’s hands. Another woman, similarly long weak and lame, lay bedridden; she was brought to the church and completely healed there.

### 37

Let those who do not fear to violate through unlawful presumption what they have once vowed to the Lord hear this further proof of divine judgment. Let them learn, through more evident punishments, how dangerous it is not to fulfill promises which they refused to recognize through the testimonies of Scripture.

A man of some standing among his fellow citizens at Metz, named Adelmann, had dedicated his daughter, while she was still in her earliest years, by a vow to the service of God and of this holy Glodesind, in the habit of sanctity.

When she grew up, she secretly followed a certain man outside the city into marriage, as they say without her father’s knowledge or consent. After some time had passed in such a marriage, it happened that she wished to visit her parents and relatives in the city. While she stayed there for several days, she was suddenly afflicted with such a paralysis of all her limbs that she could neither rise from her bed nor move from place to place except with the assistance of others.

Then her father, remembering the vow, had her carried to the monastery. After she had been left there and had lain wasting away in sickness for a long time, the servants of God advised her to put on the sacred veil and promise that she would serve God.

This was done, and on the third day she was restored healthy and unharmed, without feeling in herself even the slightest trace of her former suffering. Thereafter she remained in the same monastery under the religious habit.

### 38

Likewise, a woman named Alda had already been dragging her weakened feet for twelve years. Brought to the monastery, she remained there in weakness for six years. Since she repeatedly prayed before the altar that divine help might come to her, one day she was unexpectedly healed so completely that she rejoiced to walk everywhere with an unhindered step.

### 39

A certain demoniac from the village of Marlei, named Wolferus, had been so thoroughly possessed by a most savage and deranged spirit that he boasted that he knew every language and the location of every land.

He was brought to the sacred monastery and detained there for eight days. Through the grace of Christ and the merits of the virgin, the enemy was driven away, and he departed fully restored to freedom of mind.

Likewise, a young man from the village of Lauriacum and four women possessed by foul spirits were similarly deemed worthy of healing there through the help of the most sacred virgin.

### 40

These events are appropriately judged worthy of insertion here, since they display an immense proof of the faith to which the Savior testifies that all things are possible: what nature is evidently shown to deny, holy and innocent virginity is proved capable, through its merits, of accomplishing for its own people.

### 41

Among those who, wearing the religious habit, were accustomed to bring offerings to the altar as laywomen, there was one named Raginaidis. Coming to the basilica of the virgin, she had brought a small vessel full of wine, of the kind customarily carried for sacred offerings. After she had offered it and had distributed among the others who had gathered to make offerings whatever remained, she suddenly tested the little vessel, which she thought entirely empty, and found it filled again with wine as before, to her great astonishment.

[Note: A noteworthy passage, from which we learn that the offering of wine by laypeople during Mass was still practiced in the tenth century.]

### 42

One day a custodian of that same holy church could not find the wine needed for the celebration of Mass anywhere at hand. For some reason she went to a chest in which, for nearly three months already, a small vessel shaped like a little flask—called a *butticula*—had been hanging empty and dry.

When the chest was opened, she saw that the vessel was filled to the very top with wine. It was used to serve the sacrifices then being celebrated. Moreover, a woman of that place who had long been seriously ill asked to swallow a little of the same wine; as soon as she tasted it, she recovered completely.

### 43

On a certain Paschal solemnity, a blind girl, the daughter of a citizen of Metz named John, was brought to the holy tomb. After remaining there for three days, on the fourth day, Wednesday of Holy Week, she fully received her sight through heavenly grace.

### 44

As far as we have been able, we have transferred these accounts from the earlier writings that we found. We have not done so because we deemed that same writing of no account—for it is certainly full of faith and provides the greatest support for the order of events—but because, as I said above, learned men, whose times now flourish by God’s mercy, seemed to desire this.

Even in this undertaking I would not claim any special capacity for learning. To speak frankly, I am more frequently flushed with excessive embarrassment by what I say than by what I write. Unless the goads of certain people who perhaps fall into an imprudent affection for me urged me on, I would remain entirely silent. This is especially because, although I know how those who are present and who approve by personal familiarity whatever falls from my mouth will receive such matters, I clearly perceive that those who come after us will either be wholly ungrateful or will care little about these things.

To them, however, one should apply what Jerome fixed with his sharpest tooth against his detractors in the preface to the *Hebrew Questions*:

> “Foreign merchandise is brought by ship only for those who desire it. Country people do not buy balsam, pepper, or dates.”

Thus, if they despise these things, let them not even read them: I warn and beg them not to begrudge me or obstruct the hope I have faithfully placed in God and his holy virgin, whose boundless love has drawn me.

### 45

Since our account has now reached our own age, we may move through it more freely and briefly record what the Lord has allowed us to see.

After Rotbert, who presided for forty years, had died, and after Wigiric had completed ten years in the episcopate, a certain Benno was appointed in his place. He had long been famous for an eremitical way of life and was appointed through the good intention of the king then reigning, Henry, the father of the glorious emperor Otto.

After he had spent scarcely two years in the sacred order, he was blinded and rendered incapable by the unspeakable and deeply lamentable faction of certain servants. Since he could not perform the office, he abdicated it himself. The prince was then asked to make an election, and, with his consent obtained, this holy see received the lord Adelbero, a man destined for great renown in the future.

Among his other achievements, he determined with exceptional zeal to restore the monasteries within the broad sphere of his care, which for many years had declined greatly, both internally and externally, in spiritual and material resources.

The first of his spiritual works was the monastery of Gorze. [Note: These matters are described more fully in the Acts of Saint John, abbot of Gorze.] There, after the lord Einold, a man of great virtue, had been promoted, and after a large company of religious men had soon gathered there and united under the rule of blessed Benedict in the blessedness of the poor in spirit, Adelbero arranged the remaining monasteries—those outside or within the city, whether belonging to men or women, and even those bearing the name of canonical houses—according to its example.

Thus he also compelled this community of the blessed virgin, under its superior, the lady Himmiltrude, related to him by blood and, more importantly, by spirit, to adopt a monastic discipline.

[Note: Thus, already at that time, these nuns had declined from the monastic life to the looser life of canonesses. Adelbero assigned them the estate of Hasteria in the county of Liège, where certain nuns lived for some time under the governance of a deaness, as is read in the *Chronicle of Val-Dieu*, volume VII of the *Spicilegium*, pp. 529 and 531.]

A separate work would properly be desired concerning the worthy deeds of that holy bishop before God [Note: A little work on the life of this Adelbero survives in volume I of Labbe’s library.]; nor would it be right to enclose so great a majesty within the brevity of this section.

What seems relevant for the present we add briefly below.

### 46

In the twenty-third year of his episcopate, when the year 951 of the Lord’s Incarnation was being completed, an excessive desire arose in the mother superior of that place to restore the church, since its age and small size seemed to demand it.

Because this could not be done without first moving the sacred body, she did not presume to act on her own but disclosed her intention to the bishop. He was entirely pleased that the building should be undertaken and kindly promised his assistance. Yet he hesitated for a long time over the removal of the sacred body, and at last ordered them to seek the Lord’s will concerning it.

The matter was then discussed with the venerable fathers Einold, whom we mentioned above, and Ansteo, likewise a religious man from the nearby community of Saint Arnulf. Since they encouraged the holy bishop and the abbess still further, it was jointly decided that the work should be undertaken.

The feast of the Lord’s Ascension was then approaching, on which the whole people had been summoned by order to attend the solemn Mass. After the most reverend bishop had delivered the sermon for the sacred day, he openly explained the matter and exhorted everyone to pray for the Lord’s mercy, asking that he deign to grant a favorable outcome to the efforts of his faithful.

They carried this out the following day, Friday, with great devotion, making a joyful procession around the sacred buildings. On the next Sunday everyone then gathered at the holy place.

There, after the holy bishop himself had celebrated Mass and had animated the people toward God with much exhortation, while everyone acclaimed and the ministers of the sacred rites raised prayers to heaven in their customary supplications, the venerable bishop approached to open the virgin’s chest. With him came the fathers of the monasteries and the other religious members of the clergy, reverently and worthily submissive to God and the holy virgin.

They immediately removed the most sacred limbs from the coffin prepared for the occasion and transferred them to a nearby house, where they were to be kept temporarily.

On that same day, a demoniac was brought there by his parents. When he had been left beside the coffin in the same house after the people had departed, a short time later, through the assistance of the Lord and the merits of the virgin, he was freed from the mad spirit.

### 47

At almost the same hour, while the nuns remained at the place from which they had removed the sacred body, attending to the sick, a porter brought into the church a little boy who had been completely crippled from birth and whose limbs were condemned by a defective natural formation.

One of the nuns then left him alone inside a small house beneath the coffin where the most holy virgin’s body was being kept. After a short time, the boy suddenly let out a tremendous cry. When the others came running at the sound, he was found healthy, his limbs restored to the functions of nature by divine assistance.

Much later we ourselves saw him, enjoying the same good health, walking everywhere with a vigorous step.

Another little boy, likewise blind and afflicted by deformity in some of his other limbs, was carried there by someone else, brought before the coffin, and suddenly endowed with sight and the soundness of his other limbs through the power of Christ and the intercession of the most sacred virgin. Everyone marvelled and cried out their thanks to God.

Afterward, and almost every day down to the present time, further consolations are provided there through the working of Christ the Lord to those who ask in faith—consolations both for bodies and, what is far more excellent, for souls. There the conscience of each suppliant clearly perceives how great is the efficacy of the prayers he brings away from that place.

Unless distrust alone restrains me, I shall confidently affirm in Christ that no sighs, groans, or tears poured forth from a full heart have ever returned from there without fruit, whatever the need or distress may have been.

---

[Col. 0239]

## The Life of John, Abbot of Gorze, by John, Abbot of Saint Arnulf

[In Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, Scriptores, vol. IV, p. 335.]

## Preliminary Notice

Among the historical monuments that illuminate the condition of the state, the Church, literature, and morals during the tenth century, the life of John, abbot of Gorze, holds a distinguished place.

It was written in a somewhat elaborate style by John, abbot of Saint Arnulf of Metz, a man remarkable for his learning and literary culture and thoroughly knowledgeable about the events he narrated.

[Note: He read the Fathers, as well as the classical authors of the Romans.]

He himself witnessed many of the events he related, while for the remainder he testified that he had received his information from John or from his companions.

[Note: Preface, chapters 48 and 77.]

He also consulted books composed by John, the *Miracles of Saint Glodesind* [see above] and those of Saint Gorgonius, and his writings prove him equally capable of and desirous of the truth.

He was designated by order of Deoderic, bishop of Metz, from among the abbots who sorrowfully surrounded the bed of the dying John, and undertook to write the life of his distinguished friend.

He had completed the first part, comprising the deeds performed by John while he lived in secular dress and his entrance into the monastery, in 978.

[Note: Chapters 7–45. Since Poppo succeeded Balderic in 977, and Deoderic accompanied Otto II to Italy in 980, I have preferred the Christmas of 978, when I suspect that the bishops returning from the Gallic expedition stayed at Metz, rather than the years 977 and 979.]

Around Christmas, Deoderic summoned him to his house and, together with Poppo, bishop of Utrecht, urged him again to resume the work and complete it.

[Note: Chapters 46–48.]

But of the second part, in which he had undertaken to write John’s life during his forty years as monk and abbot, only those portions remain that carry the narrative down to the year 956. Everything else—the return from the embassy to Córdoba, the deeds he performed as abbot from 960 to 973, and the third part, in which the author had promised to write about his death—either perished or, as I am more inclined to believe, was never written because death overtook the author.

[Note: If he wrote the first forty-five chapters during the five years 973–978, it is not surprising that, after surviving another two or three years, he stopped at chapter 136.]

The extent of the historical loss is evident to everyone.

[Note: In a charter of Deoderic, in Meurisse, p. 326, he is already mentioned as dead.]

Our John died before the year 984.

The book on the life of John of Gorze, together with the life and translation of Saint Glodesind, was preserved at Metz in the church of Saint Arnulf. There it was copied by the author of the deeds of the abbots of that monastery.

[Note: Martène, *Collectio*, III, 1199 ff.; Calmet I, *Preuves*, p. 546 ff.]

That author, however, apparently relying on no authority, makes John of Gorze first succeed Ansteo in the monastery of Saint Arnulf and then makes another John succeed him. [Note: He predicted that Count Palatine Theutbert’s wife, Ermentrude, would bear a daughter; this seems to concern the younger John.] He also adds other material about the younger John, which I have included below because its reliability is doubtful.

[Note: “John, when the brothers of Saint Arnulf asked him to become their pastor, consented most graciously. Immediately, through his devotion to learning, he so ennobled the reputation of their place, already famous everywhere, that very many people flocked to his teaching not only from the neighboring cities but from every part of Saxony and Bavaria. We know that some of them were afterward chosen, on account of the merit of their lives and the excellence of their wisdom, either for the episcopal office or to govern monasteries.

Among his contemporaries he stood out both for the elegance of his morals and for the capacity of his intelligence. This John, of pious memory, among the many exercises he undertook within the school of wisdom, composed the responses for the blessed virgin and martyr Lucy in authentic musical form, as well as the life of the blessed Glodesind together with the nocturnal office.

He undertook to write the life of his predecessor, the lord abbot John, but, overtaken by premature death, left it unfinished.”]

The codex was later brought to the monastery of Saint-Germain in Paris and published by Labbe in *Nova Bibliotheca manuscriptorum*, I, pp. 741 ff., and by Bollandus in the *Acta Sanctorum*, February III, pp. 686 ff.

Mabillon published a text based on a single manuscript in the *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, fifth century, pp. 363 ff., and illustrated it with notes.

Since these editions presented a text disfigured by lacunae caused by the age-damaged final pages of the parchment, I resolved to attempt to restore a more complete reading through a new examination of the text.

In part, this succeeded as I had hoped. For, after examining the single codex now identified in the Royal Library of Paris among the Saint-Germain manuscripts as no. 1410—a parchment quarto from the tenth century, itself damaged but still preserving some traces of letters and words—I was sometimes able to restore complete words and even entire sentences.

We therefore present a more complete text than has hitherto been read.

In addition, wherever the original scribe had made a few errors, or where they had been corrected by a second hand of the same period, I have incorporated the corrected readings into the text.

The book ends in the middle of a page.

I have retained the division into chapters established by Mabillon.

## Preface to the Following History of the Life of the Lord John, Abbot of the Monastery of Gorze

[Col. 0241]

[Col. 0241B] It had long been my intention, for the benefit of many, to present in writing our father John, rare in our age as an example in all things belonging to a pious, upright, or honorable life, while he was still alive; and, lest so great a man should lie concealed beneath the obscurity of an uncelebrated name through excessive indolence—which would certainly be regarded as a grave wrong and not without guilt—to entrust him to letters of whatever kind. [Note: [Col. 0241] *committeret* in the copy.]

[Col. 0242B] Meanwhile, as we were occupied with various concerns and perhaps, in place of leisure, awaiting a more difficult task, the accidents of human affairs, as is their custom, suddenly cut short hopes that had been stretched too far into the future. For while we delayed, that most holy man, at the beginning of Holy Lent, [Note: [Col. 0241B] Since he had assumed the monastic habit in 933, he must be thought to have died at the beginning of 973 or 974; [Col. 0242B] he is mentioned in a charter issued on 22 August 973—not 974—in Tabouillot, *Histoire de Metz*.] [974, February 23] on that very first day, after the hour of the evening meal—which, as was always his custom, was exceedingly frugal, consisting only of bread and water—was seized by a very severe fever, and death followed on the fifth day thereafter.

Then, as though with belated sighs, we lamented that the time which had until then been so present had been snatched more deeply from our hands: for we would have learned from him, while he lived—and access to him would of course have been easy if anything were needed—whatever ought to be said about him, and would have learned it better from him himself; provided, however, that there was anyone so intimate with him as to trust that he could draw something of the kind from him. For he had always been so much a fugitive from human glory that whatever he had done he entrusted to God alone, the witness of his works and of his heart. [Note: [Col. 0243] *acordis* in the copy.]

Yet, in a marvelous way, just as those who seek glory are all the more abandoned by it, so, conversely, glory pursues those who flee from it more closely. [Col. 0243B] Hence holy men, the more they desire to remain hidden, are, against their will, revealed all the more conspicuously.

Thus, when this event had almost put our minds to sleep and had grievously cast us down from the beginning of the great undertaking we had conceived some time before, the means by which it afterward gradually restored us, lying prostrate and despairing, to strength, and then drove us, now willing, more and more eagerly onward, was almost this.

When the holy man had immediately taken to his bed from the powerful illness just mentioned, he soon sent an urgent messenger to summon, for the following day, all of us who were found to have charge of monasteries in the surrounding districts. By divine providence, none of us happened then to be absent. There were also added religious men from among the leading members of the household of the holy see of blessed Stephen [Note: [Col. 0243D] The cathedral church of Metz.], [Note: [Col. 0243] *viros* in the copy.] and, in addition, a considerable crowd of lesser persons.

He received each of those who approached him from his very bed with a holy kiss and a face full of joy. Then, according to the time and circumstance, he spoke a few words, addressing particular matters, and afterward, with his customary exhortation to all together, insofar as his illness allowed, he said a little about the misery of this life and the happiness of the other. Having dismissed the multitude with a farewell, the most reverend fathers Kadhroe, [Note: [Col. 0243D] They seem to have been abbots of the monasteries situated outside the walls of Metz: Saint Clement, Vincent, Symphorian, [Col. 0244D] Martin, and Arnulf. Certainly Kadhroe and John presided over Saint Clement and Arnulf.] Berhard, Hudo, and Adelmodus, together with me, the least of them, remained there with some of our holy companions, waiting for his departure.

There, during the four days that remained to him, joined also by the brothers of that holy community who constantly attended him in a single service, while we sat beside him in an exceedingly sorrowful duty and hung upon his sacred mouth—from which, even amid the very struggles of life and death, the grace of saving instruction flowed—we began various conversations among ourselves [the reading *cedi* is uncertain] about how that supreme craftsman, disposer of all things, and most orderly governor could permit this man, who had served him faithfully for so long—a fortieth year in the holy vocation was then his—to be so harshly wearied in the approach to death.

Never had we trembled in the face of a more grievous danger. Rather, a pious thought was burning in each of us: perhaps, in order to attest to the excellence of his life, the Lord might deign to declare him for his glory by some more evident sign.

Amid these waves of feeling, when almost no clearer breeze of reason opened before our troubled minds, each person distrusting his own judgment reckoned, in the excess of grief, what was happening to him, since even the heavenly dispensation did not spare that man of such perfection. [Note: [Col. 0243] *superas* in the copy.]

But reason itself soon restrained this rash movement of the mind. [Note: [Col. 0243] *raro* in the first hand; *ratio* in the second.] [Note: [Col. 0243] *reversa* in the first hand, or *revera* in the second.] Indeed, we refuted it with the sure testimony of Scripture: that human life is to be judged not by the display of the body, but by the strength of merits and conduct. [Note: [Col. 0243] *hostentatione* corrected in the copy.] [Note: [Col. 0243] *aestimanda* in the copy; *aestimanda meritorum* is also supplied in the margin by a second hand, with the beginning cut away.]

Nor should attention be paid to the manner in which someone departs from this life, but to the kind of person he is when he departs. For everyone must inevitably die, whatever the occasion. And death, from whatever cause, is a good thing for the pious. It makes no difference whether an innocent person dies by shipwreck or by fever, provided that he is innocent. Whether he dies from this cause or from that, what must be sought is what kind of person the one who dies is and where he will go after death, not by what means he will leave this life. [Note: [Col. 0243] *sive inde* in the first hand; *vel hinc* in the second.]

With these and similar supports we clearly concluded that the testing of the righteous man—which he himself, always steadfast amid everything, endured wisely and with an even spirit—not only took nothing away from his praise, but also contributed to the fruit of a greater merit.
