For what harm is there to the elect who are striving toward eternal life if they sometimes die harshly? [Note: [Col. 0243] *dicit* in the first hand; deleted by the second.]

That novelty of signs or miracles does not usually establish a distinction of holiness is also clearly shown by the fact that such things sometimes occur through the wicked, while the Church honors many people with the highest reverence and carefully constructed memorials, although it is not said whether they ever shone by even a single sign.

And, to say nothing of others, John himself—than whom, according to the Gospel, no one born of woman was greater—performed no sign; and when he was struck down by the sword in prison, whether he differed from any murderer or robber by any final mark whatsoever is buried in the perpetual silence of all the Scriptures. [Note: [Col. 0243] *destiterit* in the first hand.]

Therefore it is useless to desire some bodily splendor of this kind as a recommendation for so great a man. [Note: [Col. 0243] *propterea* in the second hand, in the margin.] His faith was sufficiently firm and unquestioning; [Note: [Col. 0243] *con* in the second hand.] and it was seen in his works, his holy conduct, and his tireless perseverance in good things to the end that these surpassed all signs and miracles and contributed, not without abundant fruit, to the salvation of souls. [Note: [Col. 0243] *commendatione* in the first hand; *sunt* in the first hand, or *sint* in the second.]

When these and many similar matters were being discussed in mutual conversations within that holy assembly, and everyone was arriving at the same opinion, it was repeatedly declared to be extremely useful and altogether necessary that the life of that blessed man, insofar as it could be seen or learned from the report of those who were older, should be committed to writing in a worthy memorial for the benefit of many. [Note: [Col. 0245] *eadem* in the first hand.]

I, already eager from the beginning of so great an undertaking, was inflamed still more by this consultation. Although I was not unaware of the weakness of my talent, and although my mind, anticipating the labor, seemed to sense that the task would be turned over to me by the others, I nevertheless joined my voice to theirs and repeatedly urged that it be done.

When agreement had immediately followed my hesitant thought, and when all had chosen me especially for this task, I was caught between shame and eagerness at a critical moment. [Note: [Col. 0245] Labbe emended the problematic reading to *metus* (“fear”); Mabillon considers that something must be supplied.] Since no ready answer occurred to me while I deliberated, impatience finally prevailed, and I bound myself, far too rashly and shamelessly, to undertake what I was not capable of completing. And I openly confess that, as an unscrupulous writer, I have taken up a subject unequal to my strength.

Yet I am consoled at last by this hope: whatever the burden may be, I do not doubt that, through divine mercy, it will be lightened by the merits of that same man, who, according to the firm faith I hold, now stands in the presence of Christ’s glory. Although he considered me unworthy while he was with us, he did not judge me unworthy of his holy intimacy; [Note: [Col. 0245] *sua* in the first hand, or *sui* in the second.] and now, as I devote myself zealously to his work of love, I confidently presume that, through the grace of his former friendly kindness, he will not abandon me in his favor.

Moreover, since I have afterward taken many holy men as my encouragers, and since, as a most beautiful crowning summit adorning the entire structure with wondrous light, our lord and most excellent bishop Deoderic—renowned in both divine and human glory, and our special patron—not only urged me but, what was still more compelling, commanded me onward, I trust that I shall not lack the support of so many. Thus, what is impossible for me may be supplied through those whose will I desire to obey by heavenly grace, from whose fullness we have all received whatever good we possess.

We shall therefore leave aside what he did in his earliest years, of which very little knowledge has evidently reached us, and shall attempt, insofar as Christ’s mercy will deign to guide our pen, to set forth only those things by which, as he rose toward perfection, he became of the greatest benefit to many who saw him and wished to imitate him.

First, we shall explain how, while he still lived in secular dress, he flourished through the seed of good action, and how, when that excellent fruit bore more abundantly in the soil of his heart, he then passed over into monastic life. Next, we shall relate with what devotion, labor, and unceasing vigilance in every exercise of virtue—first in the company of others under the authority of a superior, and afterward when placed in leadership—he held the position he had once taken in the spiritual battle and never retreated from it under any assault of the enemy, until, with the Lord fighting alongside him and preserving him, he emerged victorious. Finally, we shall tell what end crowned his struggle when it was happily completed, a struggle to which divine mercy permitted us also to be present.

## TEXT OF THE HISTORY ITSELF

[Col. 0245]

### 7. The secular learning called rhetoric

The rules of secular learning called rhetoric [Note: [Col. 0245] *rhetorica* in the first hand.] are said, among other things, to prescribe, when presenting individual persons, that the ancestors of the person who is to be praised should be traced back as far as possible, and that the line should then be led down by stages to him himself, as though by a kind of thread, so that he might appear more illustrious and distinguished through comparison with those from whom he derives his origin. The comparison is made with a tree whose branches, old with age, have already withered, so that, they say, the fertile root compensates for the sterility of the branches, and what one does not find in the fruit one admires in the trunk.

Let this have been the practice of those who cared only for the things of the flesh and who thought that each person became famous or infamous not so much through his own deeds, whether they were illustrious or obscure, as through those of others. Reason, however, stands against this: very many have drawn distinction from obscure origins, while others have inherited the disgrace of a shameful life from the most distinguished families. [Note: [Col. 0245] *probosae* in the first hand; *mutasse* in the first hand; *mutuasse* (“have borrowed/inherited”) in the second.]

Our religion proceeds by a very different path. In it, the nobility that is celebrated is rather the sincerity of mind and conduct, and the true freedom of the spirit, released from the dominion of vices, than the empty and swollen nobility of the flesh, which vanishes like smoke.

[Col. 0246C] In this religion, the needy man is raised from the dust, and the poor man is lifted from the dungheap, so that he may sit gloriously with the princes of the heavenly people. Nor are proofs lacking. David was raised from the pastures of the flocks to the kingdom, and Peter, together with his companions in poverty, was raised from fishing nets to rule the whole world. The things that are lowly and ignoble in the world are chosen so that the powerful and noble may be confounded. [Note: [Col. 0245] *et* in the first hand.]

But when the very founder of this institution says, “If you remain in my word, you will truly be free, and the truth will set you free” (John 8:31–32)—which means nothing other than “it will make you free”—and when the herald of that same founder says, “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Corinthians 3:17), anyone who may rightly glory in so great a gift of freedom has no need to enumerate that ancient lineage or seek out the names and ashes of his ancestors as a title of praise. Unless, perhaps, we prefer the flesh to the spirit, whose perishable nobility is accustomed to impose upon the spirit the lasting disgrace of ignobility.

### 8. Why, then, is all this being drawn out through such lengthy digressions?

Because writers, whenever they undertake to speak about anyone, customarily begin with matters of this kind: in what region of the earth, under what climate of heaven, from what language or people, under what condition, and from what sort of parents the person was born. As though laying the first foundation for the future account, they immediately cast such things before the reader.

In the case of our subject, whose abundant spiritual nobility is his recommendation [Note: [Col. 0247] *comitatur* in the first hand; *commendat* in the second.], I judge it superfluous to labor over this. [Note: [Col. 0247] *judicio* in the first hand, with the *i* deleted.] The glory of his consummate virtue and the succession of so many perfect men of former times either equals him or brings him very near to them, so that whatever is celebrated in worthy praises for their felicitous deeds is shown to have shone forth entirely in him, as in a most spotless mirror.

Nevertheless, lest some overly curious person accuse us of having done too little, or suppose that our discourse has avoided this part because of a lack of material, we shall insert as briefly as possible whatever of such matters may perhaps be necessary; and we shall devote the time instead to better things, things filled with the richest salutary fruit. [Note: [Col. 0247] *plenissim’* in the first hand.]

### 9. John’s origin

This John, then, was born in the territory partly of Metz and partly of Toul, in a once royal village called Vinderia. [Note: [Col. 0247D] Vendière, somewhat below Pont-à-Mousson on the Moselle.] His parents were certainly not very obscure, [Note: [Col. 0247] “Very noteworthy,” in the margin by a second hand.] and possessed a reasonably substantial estate.

His father was of such advanced age that he was thought to be nearly ninety. Among his own people he was regarded as capable in resources, fair and good to all, and blameless, making himself accommodating to everyone, even to the least. While devoted to the countryside and to managing his household—which he maintained as a considerable one according to the standard of a moderate life—he increased his resources through honest labor. As he grew greatly in property, expenditure, and money through the blessings of the Lord, he devoted himself diligently to hospitality, almsgiving, the honorable support of the Church insofar as he could, and the other fruits of good works.

Finally, in his old age he took a wife of freer birth and younger years, and fathered this John and two sons after him.

### 10. John’s education

John himself was brought up in his father’s house with the more tender care because the old man’s spirit, in keeping with the age at which he had been born, was intolerant of every hardship. [Note: [Col. 0247] *eductus* in the first hand; *educatus* in the second.]

Although he had scarcely been handed over to learn the first elements of letters, [Note: [Col. 0247] That is, “a portion”—by a second hand.] he remained for some time not far from his father’s sight. Later, although his father bore it unwillingly, he was educated at Metz in whatever schools existed there at the time.

For some time he also stayed for study in the monastery of Saint Michael on the Meuse River [Note: [Col. 0247D] Saint-Mihiel.], where at that time a certain Hildebold, a teacher of grammar and one of the pupils of Dom Remigius, [Note: [Col. 0248D] See Ademar III, 5, and Flodoard, *History of Reims* IV, 9.] a most learned master of that age, conducted a school.

As John himself often acknowledged afterward, whether through negligence or through a certain arrogance, as it appeared, he happened to carry away from Hildebold’s teaching only a meager harvest of knowledge, although his father frequently rewarded the teacher quite generously. [Note: [Col. 0247] The construction is understood as “from whose teaching”; the ablative is defective, and the second hand supplied the ending of *necessario dixit*.]

### 11. Responsibility for the household

When his father soon afterward became incapacitated, and John himself seemed already to have entered adolescence, his mother, being younger, remarried, and he alone was left as the administrator of his brothers and of the entire household.

How energetic, careful, and almost superior to other men in intelligence he showed himself in practical knowledge and in the administration of all domestic affairs; how, having grown considerably wealthy through the land, livestock [Note: [Col. 0247] *peccore* in the first hand.], household, and the provisioning and rearing of these; and how much ability he displayed in the practice and arrangement of the various arts useful for a diversified household equipment—so that scarcely anything in worldly business escaped him—I think it better to leave all this unmentioned than to write about it inadequately. [Col. 0248B] Especially since sufficient testimony still survives from many who remember these matters, and those whom such an inquiry concerns can easily be instructed by it.

### 12. Companionship with secular and ecclesiastical men

Until he had reached the full age of manhood, John remained in his own home. Throughout that time, whenever it was appropriate, he attached himself in various offices and affairs to the companionship of various secular and ecclesiastical men, provided only that they lived honorably. From their company he acquired an excellent pattern and example of living. [Note: [Col. 0247] *videndi*, corrected to *vivendi* in the copy.]

For several years he spent time in the household of Count Riquin, a distinguished man of that period, prudent and exceptionally shrewd in every kind of business, and he derived great benefit from him. For he also held, by the same count’s gift, the church of the village from which he originated.

He likewise enjoyed the company for a considerable time of Dado, bishop of Verdun, a man of outstanding intelligence and most celebrated holiness. [Note: [Col. 0248D] He held the see from 880 to 925.] Dado wished to make John a permanent member of his household, because he had recognized in him a well-deserving natural disposition and a lively intelligence [Note: [Col. 0247] *juvaxque* in the first hand; another reading *vivax*, deleted, or *vi...* in the second.], but we have learned little about the reasons why he did not obtain this.

### 13. The church of Saint Lawrence

Afterward, at the border of the territory of Toul, he joined himself in the name of the Lord to a certain nobleman named Warner, on account of the church of Saint Lawrence in the village of Fontaneto, adjacent to that city. [Note: [Col. 0248D] Fontenay on the Moselle.] He devoted himself closely to the nobleman’s service.

On that account he frequently returned to Toul at that time, because, besides this church nearby, he also held another church there, inherited from his native soil, and both belonged to the same diocese.

Thus he received as his ecclesiastical superior and teacher Berner, a deacon of that holy see, a man sufficiently renowned in that region both for his reputation for holiness and for his knowledge of letters. Under him John then began to devote himself to study and reading with increased care.

He grieved that so much of his time had passed, so that he had to begin his studies anew from the beginning. As a little boy he had been entrusted, as has been said, to various teachers for study, and although he seemed to have brought back from them some small amount of learning, his ear, as it were, warmed by their instruction, he had lost almost all of it, stifled beneath the weight of subsequent cares.

Yet, with divine grace assisting the facility of his intelligence, he happily repaired those losses by the success of what followed. From Berner he heard only the first elements of grammar and merely the first parts of Donatus. [Note: [Col. 0249] *B.* in the copy.] Content with this introductory sprinkling, he transferred himself entirely to the divine Scriptures.

Within a short time he displayed so much light of understanding in them that, to everyone’s astonishment, he could readily address any question posed by the wise.

### 14. The church of Saint Lawrence and the holy presbyter

He cultivated the church of Saint Lawrence, which we mentioned, with a unique love, and adorned its ecclesiastical ministry with whatever was necessary, insofar as he could do so with religious devotion.

Whenever he was free, he would have a bed prepared there and would not leave for several days; and he continued through many nights in prayer. Although he still seemed to allow himself some relaxation in the world, in secret, before the eyes of the Lord, he thirsted for spiritual things according to place and time.

There he assigned a certain woman from his master’s women’s quarters [Note: [Col. 0249] *quendam* in the first hand.] to divine services under a veil. Just as she was given over to the holy place with her body undefiled, so she remained holy in flesh and spirit until the appointed end of nature, growing old happily on the support of that church, never touched by any disgrace.

There also he received a certain pilgrim presbyter of advanced age [Col. 0249C] and supported him with every care until he departed in a blessed end. Our father John used to tell us many good things about him: namely, that he devoted himself to the divine work night and day and scarcely ever crossed the threshold of the church except to attend to the needs of the body.

He continually recited the psalms with mouth and understanding so distinctly that you might almost think he was counting their syllables. He occupied most of the night with pure prayer. Fighting with his very thoughts by his own voice, and beating them away as though with his hand, he would say: “Go away, you empty and slothful thoughts; do not take even a little psalm from my mouth!”

He would also often cry out to the martyr in a complaining voice: “Laurence, what are you doing here? Why do you not defend me from these madmen?”

They testified that demons appeared before his bodily eyes in various forms, so that they often cast him, in their extreme hostility, into certain bodily torments, and he would remain unable to rise from his bed for several days.

### 15. The presbyter’s deliverance from the Northmen

This same man used to relate about himself that, at the time when the Northmen were making savage incursions and ravaging the regions around the Seine and the Loire, he had been captured by them and thrown into a well of extraordinary depth, such as are seen in great numbers in the country called Beauce [Note: [Col. 0249D] Beauce, near the Loire.]—for he came from there—and had not been injured in the least.

They then pulled him out and threw him into another, deeper well. When he still could not be crushed in this way, and they decided to draw him out and strike him with the sword, one of them finally said that he had not yet reached the kind of soil in which he was destined to die. He was therefore released, as is believed, by divine intervention. [Note: [Col. 0249] Thus in the copy; it is uncertain whether the subject should be plural, *decernerent*.]

After some hours had passed and the Northmen had gone by, he managed, by crawling, somehow to escape from the well. He then set out on the road and was almost overcome by hunger, for he had gone nearly three days without food. Suddenly, in the middle of the road, he found three loaves lying there. From them he was able to reach the church of Saint Lawrence mentioned above.

He firmly maintained without any hesitation that he had been freed from so many dangers through the power of the psalms, which he always had in his mouth and which, he confessed, he had continually sung while remaining in the wells.

John used often to rejoice that this man had repeatedly admonished him concerning many things he had perhaps done lightly, sometimes rebuked him more sharply, and corrected him in many ways.

### 16. Berner the deacon

He also secretly kept company, in solitary companionship, with many others whom he had found to be of approved life and teaching. Gradually, and as though by degrees, he withdrew himself from every worldly pleasure and strove to apply himself to more disciplined conduct.

He was especially pleased with the aforementioned deacon Berner and held him in the highest honor and esteem because not only did Berner’s teaching and life—which likewise served as a form of teaching—benefit him, but also because, if he happened to see anything in John that deserved criticism, he knew no way to spare him even for a moment. He would immediately rebuke him more severely, and, if the matter required it, even publicly.

Among other qualities with which reputation had sprinkled Berner’s name with a good fragrance, he was distinguished from boyhood by his religious devotion [Note: [Col. 0249] From here onward, the words were written by another hand of the same period.] and especially by a most chaste life. [Note: [Col. 0249] *relionis*, corrected to *religionis* in the copy.] He was biting in his attacks on vices, so that he did not yield even to persons of higher rank. [Note: [Col. 0249] *insignia* in the copy.]

He nevertheless possessed great elegance of speech and exceptional facility in exhorting and persuading. His income was not very ample, but neither was it altogether poor. [Note: [Col. 0249] *multu* in the copy.] He was content with simple food and clothing, although, whenever he had any of these things, his dress was somewhat more refined and almost conspicuous.

Thus, being a man of pure mind, he utterly recoiled, by a kind of inborn nature, from contact with outward filth. [Col. 0250D] The virtue of chastity had so completely permeated his mind [Note: [Col. 0249] *pudititiae*, corrected in the copy.] [Note: [Col. 0249] At this point the earlier hand resumes.] that, if he happened to see that a woman had sat in a particular place, he would never occupy that same place himself, however tired he might be, until she had gone away.

### 17. The example of Geisa

Meanwhile, John was summoned at Metz to serve weekly at the sacred altar in the monastery of Saint Peter, where he also had a nearby house, under the pretext of the church he held, which, together with its own village, was subject to that monastery. Some time after he had begun this service there, an opportunity for his salvation was divinely provided in the following manner.

In the community of girls at that place—which now, happily, continues to flourish through the mercy of the Lord—there was a certain girl who was more remote from the others in conduct and way of life and still very young in years, named Geisa. Her aunt, a religious woman named Fredeburg, was raising her in stricter custody within her own household.

As Geisa daily extended herself toward a more rigorous holy way of life, she had added, among the other ornaments of her holy vocation, the use of a hair shirt beneath all her clothing.

John was still scarcely, or perhaps not at all, aware of this practice. [Note: [Col. 0251] Labbe reads *uistitutu*, corrected to *uestituti* in the copy; *adhuc pa* in the copy, which Labbe does not fully explain. [Col. 0251D] That is, “knowledgeable.”] One day, at an uncertain place, while he was inserting some remarks into a conversation with her, as he was accustomed to do with the others, he caught sight, through the girl’s breast of the finer undergarment, of the shadow of the hair shirt hidden next to her skin.

He immediately put out his hand to discover what it was. When the roughness of the touch revealed the truth to him, he recoiled in great astonishment and with trembling throughout his body.

When he asked what this garment signified, the girl, more modest and with her face covered in blushes, remained silent for some time and then said:

“Do you not know that we ought not to live for or serve this age? I judge the things to which I see most people devoted to be altogether vain and the ruin of souls. My mind is far removed from these things; concern for my own danger alone compels me to live as I do.”

After she had repeated many words of holy desire in this vein, John, stirred from the depths of his heart to profound sighs, said:

“Woe to me, miserable and most slothful, who have prolonged my delays for so long, living not only fruitlessly but even ruinously! Surely I, a man, ought to have surpassed this weaker sex in virtue. For it is the greatest disgrace and humiliation that I not only fail to follow one who is already walking, but that, lazy and wholly clinging to the earth, I neither advance nor even make an effort to move.”

### 18. John’s study of sacred learning

Thus stimulated more sharply, and inflamed beyond anything that the example of anyone else had previously awakened in him, he resolved with firm mind to adopt a more perfect life.

He immediately took up the study of divine reading with all his strength, together with those maidservants of God. First he read through in its entirety the history of the Old and New Testaments in the sacred library. Then he studied whatever books were regularly used in the divine offices at their appointed times in the church: the book called the *Comes* [Note: [Col. 0251D] Attributed to Jerome.], prayers, and whatever books of the sacramentary were used for different purposes; the rules for calculating times and dates, which he had previously reread in large part before the aforementioned deacon Berner; and he committed all this vigorously to memory. [Note: [Col. 0252D] That is, “with perseverance.”]

He also retained wonderfully in his heart, down to what one might call the very last word, the precepts of canonical discipline—that is, the decrees of councils, the judgments concerning penitents, and the order of ecclesiastical acts—as well as the secular edicts of the laws.

He acquired such knowledge of homilies, sermons, and various treatises used in readings of the Epistles or Gospels, and also of the memorable deeds of the saints, that whenever afterward he happened to have an opportunity to speak, it was as though a book lay before his eyes: following the traces in order from the first sentence to the last, as if he were looking at them, he would recite everything in ordinary words.

At the same time he did not hesitate or despair of applying himself to ecclesiastical chants. Although some people, quietly laughing at his supposedly unsuitable age, mocked his ability, the persistence of his good desire completely overcame the difficulty through hard and strenuous labor.

### 19. His spiritual exercises among the women

These were, for the time being, his periods of leisure devoted to holy matters with the aforementioned maidservants of God. From the large number of that same community he also turned many women away from low pleasures toward the flames of heavenly desire by the fire of divine eloquence. They remain to this day witnesses to the order of his life and his virtues. [Note: [Col. 0251] *plurasque* in the copy.]

How greatly he girded himself with strength in his other spiritual exercises—in continence, fasting, vigils, frequent prayer, the remaining bodily labor, and the chastisement of the flesh—and how, preparing himself day by day for better things, he always pressed onward to what lay beyond, with the grace of Christ accompanying him, will perhaps be demonstrated more clearly by the testimony of his subsequent deeds.

### 20. His desire to renounce the world

He burned with his whole desire to despise the world and renounce his possessions. But he could not easily see where he should go, since the abundance of examples had withdrawn itself from this entire region. No monastery at all was heard of throughout the regions on this side of the Alps, and scarcely even in Italy itself, in which the diligence of regular life was maintained.

Because he did not know where to turn, he frequently wore down the thresholds of certain men whom widespread reputation [Note: [Col. 0251] *fulgatior* in the copy.] seemed to distinguish from secular society. He watched their actions attentively and was not inferior in working alongside them. He would spend a month or more, now in the company of one, now of another, serving them in whatever way he could. [Note: [Col. 0251] *co::laborando* in the copy.]

At that time two men in Metz were sufficiently celebrated for the renown of their continent life.

[Col. 0252D] One was Rotlandus, who presided over the school of singers in the household of Saint Stephen and continued day and night in prayers, psalms, and the celebration of Masses in the more remote parts of the oratory of Saint Michael, which was located above the same basilica of Saint Stephen.

The other was Warimbertus, near the basilica of Saint Saviour, not far from the cloisters of the clerics, serving Christ in divine matters with no less devotion.

Many witnesses of their life, which was most pleasing to everyone, still survive; anyone who wishes may learn more fully from them.

### 21. Humbert at Verdun

John remained attached to these men for a considerable time and exercised himself through much labor in the divine work. He also began, at the same basilica of Saint Saviour, a cell of confinement in which he would be shut up permanently.

But, I believe, offended by the inconvenience of the place, situated as it was in the middle of the city, and meditating rather on some secluded place in the forests, he decided for the time being to postpone the plan.

Meanwhile, having heard the reputation of the venerable man Humbert, who was confined at Verdun and was esteemed there by everyone as a holy man, renowned both for his knowledge of the sacred letters and for the testimony of his praiseworthy life, John hurried to him.

After brief mutual conversations in which their young minds came together, he spent several days with him. There he laid down a pure confession of all his transgressions and received from that venerable man a rule for penance.

From that time, it is believed, he completely abstained from meat, and he took up fasts, always dear to him, with unwearied rigor.

### 22. Lantbertus in the Argonne

When he learned that another solitary was living near the same city, in the more remote parts of the forest called Argonna [Note: [Col. 0253D] Still called Argonne today.], he also visited him with the same urgent fervor, wondering whether he might there satisfy his long-conceived desire to dwell in the wilderness.

This solitary, named Lantbertus, was altogether rustic both in conduct and in knowledge. Apart from the fact that his great labor—by which he wore himself down sufficiently and more than sufficiently, with a harshness that seemed almost irrational—commended him to some extent in divine matters, he appeared entirely dull and uncultivated. Whenever he happened to see weaker persons, he could scarcely restrain his laughter.

He paid almost no attention to covering his body or his private parts; and his use of food and drink was likewise very different from that of other mortals.

He would usually reduce an entire *modius* of flour to a single loaf, which would last him a month or even two, until, because of its excessive hardness, it could not be broken except with an ax. From it he would daily take a portion according to weight.

Likewise, he cooked a very large cauldron full at once of vegetables and legumes. He stored it and, each day while anything remained, took a measured amount of it after thinning it with raw water.

At any sudden impulse of his mind he would rush out of the wilderness, enter villages [Note: [Col. 0253] *uulas*, corrected to *unilas* in the copy: variant forms for “villages”.] and cities, and then suddenly withdraw again into his cell.

He usually began Masses in the middle of the night. If his mind so directed him, he would celebrate in the evening, or earlier, or at the dawn twilight. After a fast of two or three days, whenever his body was weakened, no time of day or night was reserved for restoring himself.

### 23

John was not at all disturbed by the various preliminary manifestations of his manner of life. Frequently, indeed, he considered with a kind of astonishment how such great strength could exist in a feeble body—for he was worn out by excessive emaciation and squalor—and he remained with him for some time. He even constructed a cell for himself to live in. At that time many people came there from the neighboring city in order to see him, bringing whatever was needed for necessary uses; and they were kindled in no small degree with holy desire.

Among them was the aforementioned Humbert, who usually came and went, and sometimes remained for several days. There was also a certain man, a Briton by nationality, named Andrew, thoroughly educated in liberal studies, outstanding in strength of character, and—greater than all this—exceedingly devoted to divine things. Driven from his native island by the attacks of the Northmen, after all the inhabitants of that island had either been killed or expelled, he was driven out, together with several other learned and equally wise men. He was received at Montfaucon by the reverend and holy Bishop Dado, mentioned above [Note: [Col. 0253D] Chapter 12], along with some Britons who had arrived with him, and was provided for with considerable generosity.

### 24

After consulting with these men whether it would be healthy and fruitful for him to remain in that place, they, being cautious and not unaware of the hermit’s extraordinary stupidity of character, turned their minds entirely away from living with him. Humbert especially advised him first to attempt to go to Rome to pray at the memorials of the blessed apostles. He himself had already completed that journey some time before, by God’s favor; afterward, returning with life as his companion, they would together carry out whatever reason should commonly indicate [Note: [Col. 0253] *et sequerentur* in witness 1; *vel exsequerentur* in witness 2].

Immediately breaking through every delay in the fervor of his spirit, and having made an expenditure by no means insignificant, he hastened the journey with all speed. He was accompanied by a certain cleric named Bernacer, who long before had lived with that Warimbert mentioned above at the church of Saint Savior in Metz. Bernacer’s handwriting was no worse than that of the other men of his time; he was highly accomplished in the discipline of singing, extremely devoted to the art of calculation, and in every other respect possessed considerable ability. His resources were meager, but he was richly endowed with devotion to divine things.

### 25

After coming to Rome and fulfilling the vows of his holy desire at all the sacred places, he was seized by an even greater longing to press on to more distant regions. Leaving behind some of his companions, he himself, with the aforementioned Bernacer and a few others, traveled more lightly and more swiftly as far as the mountain called Saint Angelo, which is known as Garganus.

On that same journey he also climbed Mount Cassino, renowned for blessed Benedict and crowded with a community of monks. After remaining for several days with those servants of God [Note: [Col. 0253] *remotus* in witness 1], he carefully investigated whatever traces of the holy superior still remained there.

He also entered the inner reaches of the sea inlet adjoining the city of Naples, where he admired the dwellings of the servants of God under the name of Saint Savior, and Mount Vesuvius [Note: [Col. 0255D] *Bebium*; Vesuvius], smoking continuously not far away with its perpetual vapor. Commending himself to their prayers, he bestowed upon those servants of God some blessing from the things he had brought with him.

### 26

At last, with Christ as his guide, he returned home by a prosperous journey, everything turning out favorably for him. Without delay he met with his adviser Humbert. Since no place suitable for their desires had appeared anywhere, Humbert advised him to remain at home for the time being and to perform there whatever pious action he could. Although he accepted this with considerable reluctance, he judged it preferable.

He was, after all, a man who continually kept in mind that the form of this world is passing away: possessing as though not possessing, buying as though not owning, and using this world as though not using it. Already wholly aflame with heavenly things, he seemed to arrange transient matters merely outwardly.

In other respects, no one could easily discern how his life differed from the discipline of a monk. He passed the whole night in vigils, joining nights and days together in prayer; he clung to sacred readings with study scarcely ever interrupted; and he restrained himself with every kind of bodily discipline. With tireless effort every day he followed the author of the cross, raising the cross high enough.

### 27

I truly do not know whether any account could adequately explain the character of his fasts. From the very beginning he imposed such extraordinary persistence upon himself that, if any of those who adhered to him happened to be able to observe these things, they would be astonished at the great miracle: how he could even breathe with his last breath amid such austerity.

Rather, to increase their amazement, after he had commonly spent a day or even two without any food or drink, so that he tasted not even a little, he would proceed, with unbelievable strength intact and a brighter face, agile and steadfast toward any task whatever.

We often heard this very thing from his own mouth as he conversed with us: he frequently prolonged his fast into a second day without taking any food or drink. He admitted that, when some of the brothers who avoided certain harsh practices complained that water was bad for them as a drink, no one had previously hated the taking of water as much as he did, because of his continuous habit of drinking wine:

> “So much so,” he said, “that if on any day I had to abstain from wine, I would reject water with a nauseated stomach, and even bread itself, together with all food, throughout the entire day.”

### 28

Furthermore, I do not think that even the strength of great intellects could adequately explain how swiftly—and as though afraid that someone else might rush in before him—he put on the heavenly armor, or with what strength, relying on Christ, he undertook battle against opposing powers.

Although flesh and spirit resisted one another, and although the better part was always striving for the victory, he nevertheless, always fearful of renewed danger, never lowered his arms. In the midst of these struggles, repelling vices on one side and admitting virtues on the other, he raised a most beautiful structure: the edifice of a life composed in the finest order. Yet these things may rightly be reckoned merely as beginnings, indeed as almost insignificant, in comparison with what he afterward accomplished by divine gift in monastic life.

All these things he performed within the hidden recesses of his house, with God alone as witness and scarcely any of his household aware of them. He took the utmost care that the left hand should not know what the right hand was doing. Like a tender shoot, before it had fixed its roots through sufficient watering, he carefully avoided the touch of hands and winds.

Since the dryness of my intellect is entirely insufficient to make my words equal to the deeds, let us pass over these matters and follow the order of events instead.

### 29

At that time the holy Father Einaldus, afterward the one light of the monks in these regions, was leading his life at Toul as the supreme example of every good thing. In knowledge of both secular and divine letters he was second to none among his contemporaries. At that same see he had first been chief notary and afterward also chief archdeacon. Enriched by an abundance of every kind of wealth, he was touched by love of heavenly desire and distributed everything he possessed, down to what is called a husk, retaining only a simple garment, books, and priestly clothing.

He confined himself in a cell adjoining the clerics’ cloister and spent nearly three years in the highest and most demanding continence. He rarely went anywhere except to the church, either to celebrate Mass or on account of nocturnal prayer. He was content with one servant, who was sent out for whatever necessities were required from outside.

For unless the venerable Bishop Gauzlin, a man especially distinguished in works of mercy, or some religious person sent something, he was supported by no one else. One minor attendant from among the clerics was also left to assist him when he celebrated Mass.

As for the quality of his clothing, food, and drink, the constancy of his hair shirt, the frequency of his fasts, and the austerity of the penance by which he condemned himself, I fear that it would be superfluous to speak, since the magnitude of his deeds exceeds any abundance of words.

### 30

One day, while he was sitting alone in his cell, he suddenly heard a voice, though he did not know where it came from or who uttered it, speaking in a perfectly clear tone:

> “I will raise you above the heights of the earth, and I will feed you with the inheritance of Jacob your father; for the mouth of the Lord has spoken these things” (Isaiah 58:14).

For a little while he was astonished, and, as commonly happens, considered many things inwardly. Then he sent a servant around to inquire whether perhaps some boys from the nearby schools had uttered these words while reciting. When the servant reported that no one had been in any adjoining place throughout that entire interval, the man of prudent intellect faithfully understood that this oracle of divine grace had been directed to him so that thereafter he might more confidently hope for the Lord’s gifts.

He carefully kept it hidden within himself under strong guard of spirit; but afterward events confirmed the truth of all these things.

We have inserted this brief account of the beginnings of so great a man because the subject required it. The abundance of his glorious deeds is otherwise so great that it deserves to be taken up as a work of its own by more learned writers, and can provide the greatest benefit to those who hear of it and wish to imitate it.

### 31

Although John and the same lord Eginoldus were separated by very short distances, neither knew the other except by sight and through ordinary conversation. Both of them were so determined to flee popular glory that they enjoyed only God as their witness [Note: [Col. 0257] *ado* in one witness; *et Deo* in witness C; *ac Deo* in witness M].

Meanwhile, by some chance, the aforementioned Humbert, after the cell in which he had long before confined himself at Verdun had been broken open for an unknown reason [Note: [Col. 0257] *efracta* in witness C], unexpectedly met the same venerable Father Einoldus at Toul. Einoldus had long been one of the few who knew Humbert’s way of life.

The holy man was astonished at his unexpected presence, especially since certain report had reached him that Humbert had been forcibly removed from his confinement. After hearing the reasons for his departure—among which the chief was that he had come in order that they might seek the wilderness together, and there serve the Lord much better, free from all human disturbance, than amid the crowds of cities [Note: [Col. 0257] perhaps *expeterent*, “that they might seek”—the grammar is uncertain]—they secretly formed a plan together.

They crossed the river Moselle, which flows past the town, proceeding alone and far from all observers, and, having found a certain cave in a neighboring woodland, withdrew there as though they intended to become perpetual hermits.

Soon, however, when certain religious men from the town began looking for the holy man, and overcame their love of the place’s difficult access, they found the two men there. They broke up this undertaking by sounder counsel, since such an undertaking could never have seemed advantageous to anyone. The place was so hostile that neither could devote himself to any work there, nor could anyone easily bring them any necessities.

He himself, being a man open to counsel, was not difficult to persuade to the better judgment. He immediately returned to his beloved cell, while Humbert returned meanwhile to his own affairs at Verdun.

### 32

When Humbert began visiting him there again more frequently, they one day engaged in the conversations that such familiarity usually produces. As they questioned one another in turn about whether there might be anywhere at that time people who aspired to holy desires, Humbert brought forward the John of whom we are speaking, whom, as stated above, he knew extremely well.

After saying much about John’s praiseworthy way of life, lord Einoldus said:

> “I have known the man for a long time, and from his frequent visits to me I have come to know him through ordinary experience. But whether he possesses the mind or the inclination toward the things for which he is now praised, I have not yet been able to perceive, even slightly.”

The other replied:

> “He is indeed a man who does not reveal himself indiscriminately to anyone except one whom he knows very well, and even then not easily. Hiding himself completely within, he takes the greatest pains and skill to conceal from human eyes, whenever he goes out in public, the life by which he severely restrains himself in more secret places beneath the eyes of the heavenly Judge. Nevertheless, summoned by you, he will come quickly; and your mutual conversation will readily prove to me that I have said nothing about him beyond the truth.”

He then indicated that he wished to see and speak with John, and arranged matters so that it would be left to John’s decision whether Einoldus should meet him at home or John should visit him at Toul; John was to announce which alternative he preferred.

John, never slow to perform any reasonable duty, said:

> “It is more fitting for a disciple to go out to meet his teacher. I shall meet him at Toul, as is proper.”

When he arrived, and Humbert was still waiting for him there, they greeted one another with great familiarity and courtesy. After removing everyone else from sight, they began to discuss the reason for which they had summoned him.

At length, after a considerable conversation about heavenly matters, each had revealed to the other the faithful secrets of his desire. They then carefully sought counsel concerning the manner in which they should lead their lives, since they were wholly resolved to renounce the world.

### 33

John, believing that the opportunity had now arisen, disclosed to Einoldus the whole course of his association with religious men. He spoke especially of those among whom he then had his frequent refuge at Metz—for he had long since abstained from the others in different places—and explained how unanimously those men themselves had joined together in the same purpose.

Einoldus, whose mind was readily inclined toward this, encouraged John to meet those same men with him. Thus Humbert returned to his own place, while John, after several days, went to Metz. He was greatly pleased by the holy discipline of those men and remained with them for some time.

From time to time, however, when he returned to his own place for a while, the memory of the sweetness he had once experienced seemed to endure the delays of a long absence unwillingly and quickly called him back to their presence [Note: [Col. 0257] A second hand has written in the margin: “Here the sense seems to be …” (*Hic videtur sensus esse*)]. [Note: [Col. 0257] A second hand adds *suam*, “his own.”] [Note: [Col. 0257] A second hand adds *presentiam*, “presence.”]

Those religious persons mentioned above (Chapter 17) were the women at Saint Peter’s: Geisa, her aunt, and several others; Salecho, a cleric of Saint Martin’s on the far side of the Moselle; Randincus, priest of the titular church of Saint Simphorian outside the southern gate of the city, at whose place they met more frequently because of its greater privacy; and the deacon Bernacer, John’s companion from the Roman journey.

The two men of superior life whom we mentioned earlier (Chapter 20), Rotlandus and Warimbertus, had already died.

Together with these people, as though in certain schools of heavenly discipline, the two foremost men exercised themselves every day in the practice of all approved virtues, applying themselves either to readings, to prayers, or at least to mutual exhortations toward heavenly things. By their example they continually urged those with whom they lived to greater and greater things.

### 34

The same venerable Einoldus also completely cut himself off from the properties of the city of Toul to which he had sometimes seemed to return. When he decided to remain with the others as in a permanent dwelling, he likewise urged them all to renounce every possession.

Accordingly, when they consulted more earnestly about these matters, they carefully considered places where they could profess and practice a common life together. Since no place in these regions appeared suitable for what they had conceived in their minds—for the stain of the world had darkened nearly all the monasteries—they decided to choose distant and foreign lands.

When this pleased them all with one mind and one judgment, John declared that on his previous journey through Italy, in the regions around Benevento, he had seen certain places in the wilderness that were highly suitable. There, by the labor of their hands, they could live on simple sustenance after the example of the ancient saints. These places were rich in vineyards, in their situation, and in their vast uncultivated expanses, and were entirely suitable for every other human use.

He also brought up Mount Cassino, which he had climbed and examined with his own eyes, as well as that hidden monastery of Saint Savior within the sea inlet, which overlooks Mount Vesuvius. At last they all agreed that they should decide to hasten their departure there as quickly as possible.

### 35

Then, as it is certain, through divine providence, all these matters were brought to the attention of the bishop Adelbero, afterward the great restorer of divine affairs.

Bernacer, one of the group, was serving at the church of Saint Savior after lord Warimbert, supported by the benefaction of the church’s lord, the great and memorable man Lantbert. After secretly summoning his lord, Bernacer disclosed the whole matter in order, explaining fully the merits of the holiness of lord Einoldus, John, and the others who were with them, as well as their fervor for holy desires.

He also explained that, since no place suitable for serving the Lord had appeared for them in these regions, they intended to seek foreign lands. Lantbert meanwhile instructed him to try by every means to retain them, while he himself waited for a suitable opportunity to bring the matter to the bishop’s attention.

By God’s action, the opportunity came sooner than expected. Lantbert fully explained everything he had learned about the men. He added that it would be a supreme disgrace, to be branded upon all of them in later ages, if these servants of Christ should find the immense extent of the bishopric—which by God’s favor had been so greatly enlarged—closed against them, so that, because nowhere would they be received, they were forced to hurry beneath an unknown sky into some distant land. In that case, all its many monasteries would exist in vain if men so few in number were driven away from them.

### 36

The bishop replied that he had never desired anything more than to retain them near himself. He then asked Lantbert where their dwelling place might be.

Lantbert answered that the monastery of Gorze, not far from the city, could be granted to them very suitably. At once the very prudent man reflected inwardly on what his own desire had once been concerning that place, before he reached the height of pontifical honor. Considering that the matter was being managed not by human counsel but by divine care, he did not hesitate at all to confirm the decision.

Meanwhile, he ordered the matter to be kept secret until there was time to summon them.

That place, once outstanding in appearance, had through long neglect now almost taken on the appearance of a wilderness. Apart from a few men living there in monastic dress, who received scarcely anything in divine alms, the rest of the site was occupied by a foul appearance, all its adornment having been removed.

Whatever external possessions there were were held by Count Adelbertus, a man illustrious by birth but fierce and violent in character, and rarely commendable to any good person for the uprightness of his conduct. He held them through a grant from the bishop in whose service he was a soldier—a favor that was certainly unwelcome.

He was a kinsman of the aforementioned Lantbertus, for he had married Lantbertus’s sister; yet the two were divided by certain hostilities.

When Lantbertus perceived that the bishop’s mind had been inclined toward this plan, he quickly reported to Bernacer that he should persuade the men as much as possible to come before the bishop as soon as possible. He should tell them that they would be asked which place they preferred to choose for themselves, and that, setting all other places aside, they should request Gorze.

### 37

While these plans were being discussed secretly among them, with the others still unaware of everything and occupied with arranging to hasten their pilgrimage, another of their number, named Randincus, suggested that it did not seem entirely right for him, without the bishop’s permission—under whom he was maintained by a canonical stipend and served the aforesaid titular church—either to abandon those to whom he had been assigned or to withdraw permanently anywhere else.

Lord Einoldus did not disapprove at all; indeed, he asserted that the canonical rule was so constituted. The others likewise supported the proposal, urging that it be carried out quickly.

Through Bernacer, Randincus was presented to the bishop in the presence of Lantbertus, a man of great distinction and the bishop’s closest adviser in all matters. When, under the pretext of requesting the religious habit, Randincus’s account made clear what the others also desired, everyone who happened to be present was filled with astonishment mingled with joy. They begged, with voices and prayers, that such men and so great a desire should not be dismissed anywhere, but that a worthy dwelling should rather be provided for them.

### 38

Soon all were summoned into the bishop’s presence and received with fitting honor and reverence. After hearing their conversations and responding in turn, the bishop explained how ready his mind was to receive them. He gave them permission to choose any place they wished within his bishopric.

They asked for and received a short interval in which to consult among themselves. Bernacer, instructed beforehand in secret, named Gorze.

The others hesitated uncertainly, because pilgrimage pleased them much more. John, however, who burned with a greater passion for exile than anyone else, said craftily, as though the proposal were entirely impossible:

> “Excellent. No one could ask for anything better!”

He evidently thought that, if this request were denied—because land could in no way be wrested from Adelbertus, who relied greatly, almost without limit, on his own magnitude, power, and ferocity, as well as on that of his brother Bernuinus, the bishop of Verdun, a man equally fierce in spirit—his own desires would in no way be delayed.

The outcome was entirely different, however, because the Lord arranged it otherwise. When they had immediately reentered the council and reported what had been agreed, the bishop, without delaying in the least or hesitating at all, at once transferred the place into their legal possession, just as he had conceived in the fervor of his spirit long before [Note: [Col. 0261C] Calmet gives the charter in *Histoire de Lorraine*, vol. I, proofs, p. 338].

Not long afterward, in the year 933, he also restored to the monks in full the land taken from Adelbertus. Although this action seemed to involve considerable force, he regarded it as a matter of least account in comparison with the greatness of his devotion [Note: [Col. 0261] Labbe corrected the reading thus: *terram eidem Adelberto sublatam*, “the land taken from that same Adelbertus,” whereas the witness has *querens*, “seeking”; Mabillon accepted the correction]. [Note: [Col. 0261C] That is, the taking away of the land.]

### 39

How zealously he loved and favored both the men themselves and the place above all others must be learned more from the testimony of his eyes than from words. For in a short time all the dwellings of that place, once covered with the most dreadful squalor [Note: [Col. 0261] That is, “the most terrifying squalor”], shone with a new light and an agreeable beauty pleasing to the eyes.

There too, just as he had desired from the beginning, he had a tomb prepared for himself long before his death; and there, through the mercy of the Lord, he was honorably buried.

The grace of Christ enabled him to fulfill in deed what, some time before his ordination, had once occurred silently to his mind as a secret vow. In the time of his predecessor Wigiricus, he had joined a crowd of people who had gone from the city to that monastery on foot, barefoot, compelled by the hardship of a drought. He too had reached the tomb of the blessed martyr Gorgonius, who rested there, and had seen the dreadful condition of the place. Indeed, near the very altars he found foul traces of animals.

There he prostrated himself to pray, groaning deeply at the great insult done to the saints in their sacred places, and, as he afterward used to relate, he burst into these words during his prayer:

> “If you, O boundless mercy of Christ, and you, witness of the Lord who are present here, should ever deign to advance me, unworthy as I am, with your gracious help, to be a minister of this holy seat of yours, then, with you as my gracious helper, I will change this wretched appearance of the place, which I now see with my eyes, into a condition different from this.”

### 40  
*(927, March 1)*

The Almighty heard him. After Wigiricus had died not long afterward [Note: [Col. 0261C] Compare *Translation of Saint Glodesind*, chapter 46], a certain Benno of Swabian descent, formerly famous for his life as a hermit in a vast wilderness near Zurich [Note: [Col. 0262C] In the wilderness of Einsiedeln], succeeded him through the pious zeal of the excellent prince Henry, later the illustrious emperor Otto’s father.

It is uncertain by what abyss of the Lord’s profound judgments this happened, but when the honor of his former holiness and of the renown he had sought in the wilderness had cooled, the matter finally proceeded in a tearful manner. He was blinded in secret by the most wicked servants in 928. Later, in the assembly of bishops, he publicly resigned his office in 929.

Adelbero himself was then raised, beyond everyone’s expectation, to the episcopate of the sacred see of Metz, through the favor of the Lord, with the consent of all and by public ecclesiastical and canonical votes.

Although by both his paternal and maternal lines he was of royal blood extending far back beyond human memory [Note: [Col. 0262C] He was the son of Count Wigericus and a kinsman of Countess Eva, the mother of Odalric, archbishop of Rheims; her husband, Count Hugo, was descended from Saint Arnulf. The relationship of Adalbero is as follows: [Col. 0261] Alberic, in his *Chronicle* under the year 1033, writes that Beatrice and Sophia were daughters of Sifridi, brother of Frederick II], he was somewhat less well provided in property because of the straitened circumstances caused by his mother’s second marriage.

### 41

How his deeds thereafter advanced more successfully from day to day under Christ’s guidance, and how he poured out his zeal above all in the restoration of monasteries, no one should attempt to compress into a short account; nor, if I am wise, should I presume to undertake it myself.

The matter itself is so plainly before everyone’s eyes that whatever is said seems too little, and the multitude of his deeds can in no way be matched by the power of words.

The Church, which he had received almost entirely worn down by the disorder of former times and deprived of nearly all fervor for good studies, both divine and human, he suddenly raised, with the Lord working through him, from—so to speak—nothing to the highest condition. He restored to regular discipline all the monasteries subject to his diocese, which had grown weak and almost hopeless through a long and ancient disease in the work of righteousness. He placed in each one men approved in life and teaching, who, having perfectly renounced the world, might advance the others by their example and discipline.

He changed the clerics’ communities into monastic institutions, because he did not sufficiently approve a manner of life divided between themselves and the world. He rescued the dwellings of holy women from every bite of sinister suspicion, because he could scarcely endure that they should be darkened by reputation, even if not in reality. He subjected them to the same institution as the monks and to observances differing in nothing, according to the discipline proper to their sex.

Nor was he content with the older and more distinguished places. He also marked out as monasteries the cells scattered farther afield in a wandering fashion, where scarcely eight rural clerics—or fewer—performed bare verbal offices [Note: [Col. 0263] *reddebat* in witness C], clothing them in monastic dress and subjecting them to monastic observances.

As circumstances and times required, he restored the lands necessary for their support and those belonging to the places themselves; and, with exceptional generosity, he added lands withdrawn for his own use and transferred them to the monasteries with written charters.

### 42

Although his care held him with marvelous zeal toward all the monasteries, Gorze, as I have said, was always his unique love. It had been the beginning of his works, and the holiness of the aforementioned men Einoldus and John especially delighted him. Because of their excellence in virtue, faith, and wisdom, he afterward used their counsel in almost all divine and human matters.

Hardly anything they decided was ever attempted in vain. On the contrary, whenever he went outside their counsel, he repented of it too late.

### 43

They entered that monastery in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 933, when Henry, king of the Germans, held the kingdom of the former Lotharius in part of France. From him arose the most glorious emperor Otto, surpassing all the praises of earlier generations and born for no less glory than benefit to the whole world.

Western France was held by Louis, son of Charles, who, in the famous battle near the city of Soissons, was neither victor nor vanquished, but was thrust into custody until his death.

As the assembly described above had listed them together, so they all entered in succession into the sacred militia. These were the first and new leaders of the army and the outstanding lights of that age: Einoldus and John; then Salecho, from the clerics of Saint Martin on this side of the Moselle; Randincus, priest of the titular church of Saint Simphorian; and Bernacer the deacon, mentioned above.

With them came two young men: Teuthincus, lord Einoldus’s servant, and Teutherus, who still survives in a good manner of life. He was admitted together with the priest Randincus, his uncle.

For some time they continued to wear clerical clothing. Then, when the bishop came there, they asked for and received an election according to monastic custom concerning the father to be placed over them. Together with the establishment of a regular life, they also exchanged their clothing for the habit of monks.

### 44

With one vote and equal judgment, everyone acclaimed lord Einoldus. He was the first of all to profess before the bishop a regular way of life according to the written institution of blessed Benedict, and, being dedicated to the Lord’s cross, he was clothed in the hood.

The others followed, professing in order to the abbot, and all together under him likewise swore the oaths of the heavenly militia and obedience [Note: [Col. 0263] *patri* corrected to *pari*, “equal”].

Lord John, learned and experienced in external affairs, was chosen to manage matters outside the monastery.

The few monks who remained there from the old manner of life, compelled by the example of the newcomers, also agreed to share their way of life.

At first their income and resources were extremely meager, but the treasure of their inner spirit easily made this tolerable. Their complete faith in God, which knows no lack, urged religious people from different places, drawn into the beauty of this grace then being born, to rush eagerly to one another in competition, each striving to provide whatever necessities were required [Note: [Col. 0263] *necessarius* in witness C].

### 45

For this purpose John himself gathered together whatever possessions still remained to him, as a faithful servant dedicated to Christ—indeed, proving in a small matter how faithful he would be in a greater one—and brought everything there. He left nothing from any of his possessions to any relatives, not even to his blood brothers. Rather, to increase his heavenly glory, he soon brought those two brothers of his into divine service with him.

He gathered together all their possessions, both houses and fields, including a very fine abundance of vineyards, and assigned them to the common uses of the monastery. He imposed this condition, however: while he lived, they were to remain held under the monastery’s authority; after his death, they were not to be reclaimed by any heirs, if any closer heirs should then exist, unless they were first redeemed for the monastery by thirty pounds of silver [Col. 0264D–0265A].

After some time, his mother, widowed by her second husband, came back to him with several members of her household. Since she was already advanced in age, he received her outside the monastery on the monastery’s support [Note: [Col. 0265] *monasterii* in witness C].

There that holy old woman afterward lived for many years in a good manner of life, serving the brothers of the congregation. She and some of her attendants, who remained with her on the monastery’s support, diligently and faithfully performed whatever was necessary concerning clothing. There, in that very service of devotion, she ended her last day.

### 46

When I had reached this point, lifted up by an effort already considerably weaker, and had finally become sluggish in the undertaking, as though exhausted by great labor, I had completely lowered my arms. I thought that no path remained for me by which I could proceed—or that it could be discovered only with difficulty—and that I had become a complete example of a blunted intellect, as though all my strength had been poured out.

Then, unexpectedly, the light of all learning—one who must be named in our own age, born wholly for the usefulness and adornment of every subject—the great and renowned bishop, lord Deodericus, appeared.

With him as my encourager and driving force, and relying uniquely upon him above all others, as I stated at the beginning, I ventured into this excessively bold work.

When he happened to visit me at home, he asked what work I had been ordered to undertake and how much I had completed. Since I was ashamed, conscious of my poverty of intellect, and neither dared to deny the work nor freely offer what I had produced—something in any case inept and full of trifles—and was trembling, hesitating between the two alternatives, he ordered me to bring him the sheets and ran through everything in order.

Then, like those who under a malignant light see things differently from what they are, he began to praise everything in a manner wholly unlike its actual character and to proclaim it openly to everyone he encountered. I could not understand enough of what there was to amaze me.

### 47. (978, December 25)

Perhaps at that time the most illustrious bishop of the Church of Trajectum, or Daventer, and one highly renowned among the company of teachers, lord Poppo [Note: [Col. 0265D] Poppo, or Folcmarus, held office in the years 977–990. We have seen in the *Life of Bruno* that the two names belonged to the same man. Thus, in Thietmar IV.1.2 and in the Saxon Annalist, Poppo should be understood and called Trajectensis; and likewise the abbot of Fulda and of Lorsch, who is called by others Bobbo and by Thietmar VIII.5 Wolcmarus. Another example of a name of this kind, used in two forms, occurs in the *Miracles of Adalheidis*: we have seen Liudolf and Liudgard called Dudon and Dudicha. In the same way, among the English even today the names Robert and William are pronounced Bopp and Dick as well.] had arrived there, summoned by our bishop to share in the joys of the Lord’s nativity feast, together with his father—that is, Poppo’s father—a man exceptionally vigorous in the administration of public affairs and a count palatine named Berno.

After he had repeatedly praised the same work in sufficiently ample words, he turned his face toward me together with Berno and did not cease to kindle my courage with ever greater encouragement and to inflame me with the greatest favor—though I was deeply ashamed—so that I might complete what I had begun without hesitation.

### 48.

When my spirit perhaps began to rise toward some degree of confidence, so that it almost promised itself that what it was being urged toward with such applause might be possible, shortly afterward it nevertheless fell back upon itself. Considering my strength again as it actually was, I compelled myself to remain stuck no less than at the beginning in the sluggish torpor of my own laziness.

But, to break off the delays of hesitation quickly: although these encouragements had aroused me to some extent [Note: [Col. 0265] *animationes*; Mab.], then the love of the man whom we have undertaken to describe—love that knows no diminution—compelled me, above all, to expend whatever strength might remain to me, and to strain beyond my very strength.

Accordingly, taking up the account from his adoption of the religious habit, we shall here pursue what his manner of life was, insofar as we heard it either from all the trustworthy witnesses attached to his pious deeds—religious men, certainly—or from him himself as circumstances allowed—which was rare, since he rejected glory—or from what we ourselves perceived, whose testimony has no superior authority, as will belong to the Lord’s mercy.

### 49.

For the rest, lest the sequence appear interrupted or irregular if matters concerning persons whose relevance to what will be said may appear are inserted—some of whom the preceding account has introduced, while the continuing narrative will bring in many others as causes and circumstances require—for reason itself would resist our supplying the consequences concerning the earlier persons, even if we attempted it.

At the same time, although this incomparable man lived his life in such a way that he lived as a solitary person among multitudes—for anyone who confidently believed that he could aspire to such strength of virtues would strive in vain to withdraw—he nevertheless did not arrogate to himself alone what he had accomplished. Rather, he judged that the others were working with him in whatever that work might be, even if it belonged solely to his hidden life.

Nor had he ever anywhere displayed anything superior to the practice of the common life. Therefore, those who lived together with him will not undeservedly have their deeds included in the account of his actions. They will not thereby incur any envy as though they were his superiors; rather, from their companionship with so great a man, a kind of greater splendor will be heaped upon them, and their distinction and glory will increase [Note: [Col. 0265] *furgor*; manuscript reading, apparently for *fulgor*, “splendor.”].

### 50.

Before I proceed farther, then—since no other occasion perhaps seems likely to offer itself more suitably—I think it proper to speak also of those two venerable men whom the preceding text mentioned (chapter 23), Andrew and Humbert. Both of them, likewise, were no less holy than Einold and John, and they served as incentives and, as it were, goads toward virtue.

For when they had learned, through the report spreading everywhere, that the place mentioned above had received these men and that many people from all directions were hastening toward them out of love for divine service, they too, without delay, hastened there. Though not at the same time, they did so with equal spirit and intention; and after professing the monastic discipline, they neither refused nor were ashamed to submit themselves to the teaching and leadership of those who had previously gone before them and been their teachers.

Andrew’s own brother, Maginfred, followed him, and afterward certain others of the same family. With Humbert, a certain boy named Milo was received, serving him; he was himself of good character and would later prove of no small usefulness.

### 51.

Moreover, what was omitted when the narrative first reached the venerable Humbert (chapter 21) ought briefly to be supplied here: how he too, moved by divine impulse, entered the religious habit.

Although his parents were country people, they were not so impoverished in worldly goods that they lacked resources. While he was still a young man living with them, some acquaintances or relatives had happened to come to their house as guests. When, as the hour happened to require, they were kept there overnight and sought their beds, they placed the little spears that they had brought, as was customary, with the iron points turned upward upon a haystack nearby.

By chance the young man himself had climbed onto the stack shortly before [Note: [Col. 0267] The manuscript reads *consenso*.] and fallen asleep there. Awakened nearly in the middle of the night, he wished to go outside, having previously arranged to go somewhere—I do not know where. As he slowly lowered himself down over the stack, he came into extremely close danger among the upright points. His garment, clinging to his body, was caught and pierced by the iron, and he slid down along the shaft all the way to the ground.

After forcing down the shaft and examining the matter carefully by touch, he stood there and considered the divine protection so immediately present around him, even while he had been attempting something improper. He therefore restrained himself from his undertaking, now resolving on better things, and henceforth devoted his whole mind to serving God.

### 52.

Not long afterward, although his father strongly opposed him, he set everything else aside and departed for Rome. After spending a considerable time in that pilgrimage, he returned and established for himself a reclusory cell at Verdun.

There, through prolonged abstinence and his other zeal for good works, he seemed to benefit many people. He also devoted himself continually to reading and in a short time acquired for himself a considerable treasure of knowledge. It was a marvel [Note: [Col. 0267] The manuscript’s *fuerat* has been corrected to *fuerit*.] that although previously almost entirely without such learning, he suddenly appeared, with the Spirit alone as his teacher, not unlike the learned—indeed, superior to many of them.

During the same period, two religious women of the town were instructed by him in separate cells set apart from him; they received the word of teaching and the rest of his instruction only through the window of his cell.

Two other women in the same city were likewise inflamed by his exhortation. One of them afterward became the mother of many handmaids of Christ [Note: [Col. 0267D] In the year 962.] in the territory of Toul [Note: [Col. 0267] Thus in the manuscript.], at a place called Buxerias [Note: [Col. 0267D] Bouxières-aux-Dames, today in the diocese of Nancy.].

There, after the monastery had been newly constructed by the bishop Gozlin of blessed memory [Note: [Col. 0268D] He died in 963.], and after these two women had first been admitted, a multitude of holy fervor from various parts of the world poured into the place, so that even to this day it seems to shine forth among other places with a certain new grace.

Having therefore spent many years in that more secluded cell [Note: [Col. 0267] *ei gens*; manuscript reading, uncertain.], after—as we mentioned above—he came to Toul through the grace of visiting lord Einold and became known to lord John, he returned to his own place. Soon, when he heard the report of their established residence, he hurried to join them, intending to live with them as well.

In that fellowship he conducted himself thereafter with very devout labor, until, for the sake of religious observance, he was transferred from there to the monastery of blessed Aper at Toul. There he rested in a blessed end while caring for the Lord’s flock.

### 53.

Andrew too, after he had spent a very long period in that sacred service, was sent to Rome, already an old man and reflecting in the whiteness of his hair the purity of his mind. Pope Agapitus had urgently requested in letters from lord Einold that some religious men be sent to him with a suitable messenger, so that he might establish them, with the help of King Alberic, in the monastery of blessed Paul, which he was then attempting to transfer to the monastic order (950).

He was brought there with another brother who, several years earlier, had come from the monastery of Luxeuil to Gorze. After the place had been instructed in regular discipline, he was not long afterward received by the Lord and was buried there.

### 54.

Since we have begun, by mentioning these two men, to touch upon the growth of that congregation, we think it appropriate to add, as briefly as the circumstances permit, what other persons worthy of remembrance came afterward [Note: [Col. 0267] Missing in the manuscript.].

In this way the narrative concerning the man whom we have set out to describe will proceed with a kind of open and unobstructed space, after the preceding matters have first been brought to completion, so that the work may remain continuously directed toward its sole subject, interrupted by no intervening matter.

As a sweet and fragrant [Note: [Col. 0267] The manuscript reads *fraglans*.] odor, in the house where Christ had reclined, was scattered both nearby and far away, all the faithful who were drawn toward it began to converge from every direction with remarkable speed.
