Not only those who had long been inflamed by holy desire, or more secretly inspired by the Spirit, or awakened by divine reading, and who had been awaiting someone to show them the way of right conduct, immediately embraced with complete eagerness what they saw being offered; others too, who until then had appeared cold and sluggish, were stirred by their example and, as though warmed by live coals brought near to them, hastened with the greatest ardor to join their fellowship.

### 55.

Nor were these generally people from the common streets, but rather men of some distinction through urban refinement, reputation, and expenditure; through their resources also the place was increased by a considerable store of possessions.

Among them was Frederick, the uncle of the aforesaid venerable lord Adelbero. As a small child he had been assigned to the monastery of Saint Hubert [Note: [Col. 0269] Correct to “Hubert,” not “Humbert.”] [Note: [Col. 0269D] Saint Hubert.], but, while that place, like the others, languished under their malady [Note: [Col. 0269] The manuscript reads *ceteris*.], he, following the example of his elders, lived indiscriminately with the world.

By that time he had advanced considerably in age, and he appeared to be an industrious man of great intelligence in secular matters. He remained attached to a bishop who was then still relatively young, and on whose advice many affairs were at that time conducted in the episcopal residence.

Moreover, as was fitting for an uncle, he was somewhat severe in spirit and often recalled the youthful endeavors of many people from activities that were not necessary.

At last, reflecting within himself, when he saw the great earnestness of those men of God, he was pierced in heart. Setting aside all the advantages by which he had been wrongly enticed, he hastened to join them.

Not long afterward he was appointed provost of the place, after the abbot, and lord John was assigned to him as an assistant [Note: [Col. 0269] *habatem*; manuscript reading, for *abatem*, “abbot.”] [Note: [Col. 0269] *subpunitur*; variant reading.].

Later, at the request of the bishop Richarius of Liège [Note: [Col. 0269D] In office 922–945.], he was restored to his own monastery of Saint Hubert, appointed abbot according to regular discipline, and maintained divine worship there with excellent monastic observance and praiseworthy strictness of conduct until the end.

He lies at Trier in the monastery of Saint Maximin. While the dedication festival invited him there [Note: [Col. 0269D] In the year 942.], he was suddenly seized by illness and entered his final day; the new church building opened its new bosom for the new guest.

### 56.

In a similar way [Note: [Col. 0269D] Kaddroes too lived at Gorze under Agenold, as we learn from chapter 24 of his *Life*: “Accordingly, rumor had carried his name everywhere, and all peoples spoke of the man’s virtues. The noble bishop Adelbero was nobly governing the noble see of the people of Metz. When much report was brought to him from various regions, it also conveyed the name of this man. Since he was a lover of religious men, he summoned the venerable men Agenold and Ansteus to him, questioned them about the man, and asked how he might reach him. The venerable men just mentioned, having learned of the bishop’s desire, often spoke with the man of God about the matter. It was the solemn day on which the festive memory of the blessed martyr Gorgonius was celebrated (the fifth day before the Ides of September), and Kaddroes himself, a man of God, had also arrived with the crowds flowing together from every direction. Finding an opportunity, they explained the bishop’s wish to him and, prostrating their petitions before him, begged him to consent to remain with them. Who would not love on earth the companionship of those who had already merited eternal dignity in the heavenly camp? Overcome, therefore, by the prayers of the suppliants, he agreed and accepted their charge of a place not far from the city of Metz, renowned for the bodies and relics of many saints, but by then reduced to utter ruin.”]

At about the same time, Odilo, the first man of the Church of Verdun to hold responsibility under the bishop, a man distinguished by birth, adequately supplied with means, and exceptionally energetic in managing affairs, entered this holy poverty. If his being a cleric had not hindered him [Note: [Col. 0269] That is, none of those things which the world’s sphere brings.], he would have been inferior to no one in any position that the world’s sphere embraces. Rejecting all those biting cares [Note: [Col. 0269] *mordatibus*; manuscript reading, apparently for *mordacibus*, “biting.”], he became poor in spirit and gave himself to this holy poverty. He judged its small and humble allowance more glorious and more sufficient than all the wealth of the world.

After the strength of his holy way of life had fully matured, he was requested to reform the monastery called Stavelot, and, having been promoted there [Note: [Col. 0270D] He took part in the synod of Verdun in 947.], he corrected, with Christ’s help, whatever he found perhaps crooked, bringing it into the lines of rectitude. There too he completed the course of nature.

### 57.

At nearly the same time, Angilramnus appeared—so to speak, a specimen and flower of what was then being woven into the heavenly garland—an exceedingly agreeable man and most worthy to behold. First primicerius of Toul, and afterward also of the holy Church of Metz, he was distinguished for nobility and wealth, and for everything that in that age could appropriately constitute glory.

Dragging with him great masses of gold and silver and heaps of other possessions, he sought that holy fellowship, intending that these things should be converted to the uses of the poor, like the possessions of that first apostolic people. He also granted the monastery a considerable quantity of estates to be held under perpetual title.

What marks his subsequent way of life possessed, and with what strength the structure of his virtue afterward endured, will perhaps be heard more agreeably if we first briefly touch upon how its beginnings seemed for a little while to have wavered [Note: [Col. 0269] *facillasse*; manuscript reading, uncertain]. For although he was shaken, he was not completely driven from his position; afterward he fixed his foot all the more firmly because he had grieved that, for a time, he had observed the place he had taken with excessive negligence.

### 58.

When, then, he was received with the wealth we have mentioned, he was treated and honored more gently than the others because he was a man of imposing presence, brought up in luxury, and already well known to all of them. Some of his dependents had also joined themselves to the same purpose.

Meanwhile, because he had not yet completely banished from his heart the reputation that he had once wrongly admitted, he by no means endured being treated like the others. He was somewhat too readily elated by what he had contributed to the place.

As naturally followed, he began to resist rebukes, refuse correction, and, since he regarded all the others as inferior to himself, to pronounce judgment as though from a higher position. If any who were perhaps weaker in spirit had approached him according to their character, he would, at his pleasure, support them against the injunctions issued by their superiors.

Father Einold and the others, already mature in Christ, repeatedly reproached, exhorted, and entreated him according to circumstances and times, and, insofar as his age permitted, rebuked him somewhat more severely. Yet he often answered them almost more harshly than the situation warranted and scarcely restrained himself from insults.

### 59.

What more need be said? When these matters, prolonged over a considerable time, had produced exceedingly unwelcome weariness, one day, while he was being rebuked more sharply for some similar insolence, he suddenly became violently agitated in spirit. He tore himself away from the sight of the abbot and the others sitting there with him, and, unless Christ had intervened to stop him, he would have returned disastrously to the world. He left the cloister.

The brothers, grieving and frightened, followed him. When they found him in the outer portico, where he had sat down after leaving, they fell at his knees and attacked him by every means they could.

At one moment they adjured him by the divine name not to do it, begging him not to lose wickedly the good he had begun well; at another they set before him the perpetual disgrace that would follow him in the world. They urged him to remember the labor already completed, which he was abandoning so shamefully in the midst of his efforts; finally, to remember the strict judgment, which perhaps he could see approaching now that he was already an old man.

They also warned him to beware of the devil’s schemes [Note: [Col. 0271] The manuscript reads *astituas*.], since the devil was eager to snatch away from him the fruit of all his labor.

Repeating many arguments of this kind, while he remained inflexible and demanded only that they return to him what belonged to him—saying that henceforth he would take sufficient care of what happened to him—they pressed him more insistently. With all the strength of a charity that knows no measure, they sought to turn the man’s mind in different directions, renewing speech with speech and prayers with prayers.

### 60.

By the Lord’s cooperation, they did not leave the place until that eye of ancient mercy looked upon him, as it had once looked upon Peter, and changed him, so to speak, into another man.

For he too, pouring forth bitter tears, immediately returned. Stripping his body and carrying bundles of rods in his hands, he threw himself at the abbot’s feet, demanding punishment with loud cries and expressing the magnitude of his sorrow not only through groans but through the gestures of his entire body.

Who, do you think, kept back his tears there? Who, seeing that white-haired man prostrate himself at everyone’s feet, was not dissolved in heart? When he cried out in tearful tones, “Believe me guilty! Strike the rebel! Do not, I beg you, spare the proud, the foolish, and the contemptuous!” who did not proclaim his pardon with joy mingled with tears?

### 61.

At last the father, full of compassion, rose, and with the others who were with him [Note: [Col. 0271] The manuscript reads *aliisque*.] lifted him from the ground, placing the hands of charity beneath him. After graciously forgiving him everything, as such a fall deserved, they received him back into their number with complete joy.

That day was so saving for him that whoever looked upon him afterward could scarcely recognize in him anything of the man he had previously been.

With all his strength, insofar as it lay within him, he continually sought abasement of himself and every form of lowliness. He rejected luxuries and soft things of every kind and embraced what was difficult and more austere.

He could not endure honors shown to him without extraordinary shame; they burdened him more than they delighted him.

He adopted such a frugal measure of food and drink, like a careful observer, that from each item placed before him he gradually removed a little at the daily meals until he returned to a very small quantity [Note: [Col. 0271] The manuscript has *nimiam*, “excessive”; Labbé corrected it to *minimam*, “minimal.”] [Note: [Col. 0271] The manuscript reads *quandam*.]. Sometimes he abstained entirely from certain things, as though they were harmful.

At one time he rejected all smaller fish of a kind, judging that the larger ones could be obtained only rarely; at another, when the very fish he seemed to prefer were offered after having been sought from every direction, he grew, after not much time, almost disgusted with them.

With such determination—victorious, so to speak, over himself—he guarded what he had once resolved in his mind that he would finally be content with little flour porridges, although throughout this period he also practiced frequent fasts, which he had bravely endured even while living in the world, taking only bread and water on fast days.

For, as we have learned from the testimony of many, while he was still in the world it seemed almost nothing to him to pass two entire days without any food or drink at all.

### 62.

What astonished those who saw him was that the vigor of his body remained so lively that he omitted none of the work customary among the brothers. He performed the work in the kitchen, the washing of clothes, the common labor of the garden, the washing of shoes, the weekly order of Mass [Note: [Col. 0271] *ebdomedam*; manuscript reading.], and every duty of the cloister and oratory with vigorous strength. His face also continually remained cheerful and joyful.

Only after some interval of time had his belly sunk from its former corpulence.

The intensity of his prayers and vigils was testified by the hut beside the tomb of lord Chrodegang, which he inhabited as a solitary cell until the time of his calling. As soon as the brothers’ assembly had been dismissed, he would withdraw alone, shutting the door, and continue day and night with groans, lamentations, and countless bendings of the knees.

Since he usually anticipated the brothers’ vigils and spent much of the night in prayer, after those vigils had ended he knew no sleep at all [Note: [Col. 0271] The manuscript reads *lullatenus*.], however much of the night remained in winter or summer, except perhaps on the occasion of a bloodletting—which nevertheless happened very rarely. For the entire period afterward, until the second or third hour, he remained in that holy contrition and in knocking at the heavenly door.

### 63.

I do not know what I should say about the continuity of his silence, since he even avoided the permitted times for conversation among the brothers and instead changed them into the singing of psalms.

If he happened to be addressed, he gave a brief reply and immediately returned to his customary and beloved silence.

For every kind of bodily care—baths and the other forms of refreshment permitted by the common use of the rule [Note: [Col. 0271] Mabillon reads “and baths.”]—he preferred sackcloth, coarse clothing, and a rough manner of dress.

What I am about to say may be the most extreme example, but it greatly proves the strength of his spirit.

When the brothers washed their shoes on Saturday before the *mandatum*, or on Wednesday, according to an ancient custom recently handed down to us [Note: [Col. 0271] This custom again became widespread in many monasteries; compare John’s *Life of Odo of Cluny* II.23.]—he would suddenly come up to any one of them while the brother was holding one shoe to be washed, seize the other from him by force, as though against his will, and wash it.

Likewise, when they washed their faces in the morning or their hands before eating, he would sometimes hurry to the vessel from which water was distributed to the brothers through small channels and hold the stopper that closed the channel while a brother washed; at other times he would offer the towel hanging there for drying. In this way he ministered to the desire of his ardent heart.

### 64.

Many other such practices of service were directed by him toward everyone.

And although these and similar actions were evidence of the humility of his heart, he also could not bear the place in his order in the choir, which he held as the higher one, as though he were impeded by illness, and exchanged it for the very lowest position.

Indeed, after such great austerity, exhausted in strength, he was no longer capable either of standing in the choir or of performing the other work.

How great his purity of life was became especially clear at his end. Not long before his death, one night, hearing something divine—I do not know what—and telling no one anything, he wrote the following in the window of the aforementioned hut the next morning:

“I dreamed that I would die on the fifth day before the Ides of September.”

The truth of this was established very soon. For after a few days he was seized by fever, lay sick in bed for more than a month, and was brought by severe illness all the way to the appointed day.

Throughout that entire period he remained completely without food, sustained only by water. He continued in this way until the Nativity of the holy Mother of God, which is followed on the next day by the feast of the blessed martyr Gorgonius, whose body makes that monastery especially renowned. At that time a very great crowd of religious men had gathered there from various regions.

Most of them visited him. Throughout nearly the entire day, one after another entering to see him, he shared with them salutary words. With his mind and speech unimpaired, he died shortly before midnight.

The multitude that had assembled provided his funeral with the fitting honor and dignity due to so great a man.

### 65.

That same night, and, as could be inferred, at the very hour at which he died, a certain member of that congregation named Adelger, who was resting with the brothers in the monastery called Senones [Note: [Col. 0273D] Senones.] in the Vosges region, saw someone appear in a dream saying:

“Rise, and because lord Angilramnus has died, have the bells rung for him.”

He awoke and roused certain others. He indicated the matter only by a sign, so that it was not clearly understood what he meant. When daylight came, he reported the same thing again, but was still not believed. On the third day, when a letter announcing Angilramnus’s death arrived, it was discovered that the night and the hour had been exactly the same.

### 66.

Having recalled these matters concerning him that ought not to be omitted [Note: [Col. 0273] *quomittenda*; manuscript reading.], since the length of the account prevents us from adequately treating all the members of that fellowship, almost every one of whom was worthy of remembrance for the merit of his outstanding conduct, we must not pass over lord Ansteus, who was later given to us as a father in the monastery of Saint Arnulf.

Here too, after having been the companion of lord Einold in secular dress—and related to him by blood—he left all his possessions several years later and, from being an archdeacon [Note: [Col. 0273] A word has been erased.], was truly transformed into a poor man of Christ. Joining that same fellowship, he shone forth in a life no lesser than that of the others.

In speech, as far as outward expression was concerned, he was extremely eloquent; he was also exceptionally devoted to the study of the sacred Scriptures, although he possessed some knowledge of the liberal arts as well. A certain bodily grace marked the virtue of his spirit.

His face and stature were most becoming; his voice itself was full of strength and, with a modulation more pleasing than anything else, filled the ears in sacred chants.

Nevertheless, insofar as he was able, he made all this serve the desire for heavenly things and the edification of his hearers. Overflowing with words of grace, he was capable of exhortation and of moving people’s minds in every direction, with complete ability in every kind of speech, so that one might call him an orator.

In addition, he possessed no mean expertise in architecture, so that whatever he had once designed could not easily be criticized by anyone’s judgment in the symmetry or measurements of places and buildings.

### 67.

For some time, therefore, he was dean in the same monastery and vigorously carried all the burdens of the abbot. By his life, his speech, and every example of holy conduct, he became a model for the Lord’s flock, so that almost everything seemed to be arranged through him after the abbot.

At last, when the distinguished man Heribert at Saint Arnulf’s—who had been appointed the first head of that place by lord Adelbero the bishop [Note: [Col. 0273] *pontificis*; manuscript reading.] after the clerics had been removed from it [Note: [Col. 0274D] In the year 941.]—departed this life [Note: [Col. 0274D] In the year 944.], Ansteus was appointed pastor, destined to benefit the Lord’s people.

His industry soon became evident there. Building dwellings for the monastic order in a most beautiful design, he made the place, which he had received entirely uncultivated and without any institutions for religious life, entirely suitable for every use in the service of God.

While he applied himself without interruption to constructing the interior buildings, he was no less energetic and prudent in restoring the exterior buildings, which had likewise fallen into miserable ruin everywhere.

He cultivated all the land belonging to the monastery—vineyards, meadows, fields, and woods—in such a way that, although he had found the estate utterly poor and scarcely promising a very meager supply even for a very small number of people, after one year had passed—for he was afflicted by a severe illness resembling pestilence [Note: [Col. 0273] Labbé corrected this to *pestilentia*; the manuscript has *stipilentia*.] [Note: [Col. 0273] The manuscript has *actactus*; corrected reading, “afflicted.”]—it overflowed, by God’s blessing, with every abundance of necessary goods.

After completing all the brothers’ interior dwellings within four years, he turned his mind to surrounding everything externally with a wall in the manner of a fortress.

With the same venerable bishop providing assistance from every side, the work had been carried on for four months and had nearly reached completion, had not the disastrous discord within the kingdom prevented it—the conflict that arose between lord and most glorious Otto, then still king and afterward emperor, and his son Liutolf and son-in-law Conrad (953), and that raged until the incursion against us of the people hostile to God, the Hungarians (954).

Nevertheless, with the Lord’s cooperation, the work was completed more quickly in the following summer.

### 68.

Although he was constantly troubled by concern for these external matters, he never neglected anything pertaining either to purity of life and conduct or to the vigilance of pastoral prudence. Every day he completed the customary measure of prayers, psalms, and sacred readings.

On all Sundays and the more solemn feast days of the saints he celebrated Mass publicly. In addition, he did so privately every Wednesday.

The groans and sacrifices of tears with which he consumed himself in these celebrations cannot even be reported. And, if I may speak with confidence, no one was his equal in the depths of compassion, simplicity of heart, gentleness of spirit, condescension toward the weak, refreshment of the afflicted, and every act of mercy whatsoever.

After completing sixteen years of such labors, and finishing the course of his life in holy perseverance, he died on the day before the Nativity of the blessed Mother of God (September 7, 960). He was placed in a tomb that he himself had prepared long before, from the earliest years of his rule, amid a great gathering of devout men, while lord and venerable bishop Adelbero performed the funeral rites. He was buried on the northern side of the basilica, in the year of the Lord 960.

### 69.

Blidulf, archdeacon of the holy Church of Metz, was at length associated with these servants of God, to the great astonishment of many.

He was supported both by noble birth and considerable wealth, and was skilled in many kinds of intellectual ability—whether this should be called prudence or cunning. He also surpassed the others of that place in knowledge of letters, since he was still a surviving product of the schools of Remigius.

At that time he appeared so devoted to secular affairs that scarcely any trace of religious feeling could be seen in him.

When, as the story goes, he was suddenly seized by illness, he quickly summoned the venerable Einold and professed himself a monk. Immediately taking the habit, he was carried sick to the monastery. After a few days, by God’s favor, he was restored to health [Note: [Col. 0275] The second hand begins again here.], and recovered with a better integrity of mind, destined thereafter to become an example to many.

In holy conduct he appeared inferior to no one.

After several years, touched by a greater fervor for virtue, he sought the hermitage in the more remote parts of the Vosges, accompanied by another man named Gundelach. There, in the sweetness of divine contemplation and through exceedingly severe bodily discipline, he truly died to the world, as the testimony of those who knew him confirms. After spending ten years or more in this way, he died blessed.

He was buried in the oratory of the same cell by his companion, a man equally holy, and left him there as heir to his life and to his very modest possessions.

### 70.

His same companion had formerly come from the monastery of Fulda, many years earlier, conspicuous in the bloom of youth, and had moved to Saint Maximin at Trier [Note: [Col. 0275] *maximum*; manuscript reading, twice.], because of the distinction of his religious life.

Afterward, inflamed by the reputation of lord Eginold, he came to Gorze and remained for some time almost inseparably at his side. At Eginold’s command, he was then assigned, together with the venerable Blidulf mentioned above, to the monastery of the holy man Ogo, a great and distinguished man, formerly abbot at Saint Maximin [Note: [Col. 0275D] See Sigehard’s *Miracles of Saint Maximin*, chapter 12.] and afterward an outstanding bishop of the Church of Liège [Note: [Col. 0275D] In office 945–947.].

After the death of lord Ogo, the two of them returned from there to Gorze. Soon afterward, by common agreement, they withdrew to the more remote hermitage of which I have spoken, and, as has been said, he succeeded lord Blidulf. He inhabited that little place until the end of his life and, distinguished there by his learning and purity of life, rested in peace.

[Note: [Col. 0275] The first hand begins again here.]

71. Isaac, too, a religious man of the church of Verdun, who had conducted himself with becoming propriety in the canonical life and was already venerable in his very gray hair, was received almost two years after the arrival of the aforementioned Blidulf, together with another man of good promise, then younger but now, under the Lord’s auspicious advancement, father of that same holy college, the lord Odolbert [Col. 0276C] [Note: [Col. 0275D] Odolbert sat at Gorze from the year 974 onward; [Col. 0276D] in the year 987 we read of Immo as abbot.]. Isaac, being a man of great simplicity and wholly devoted to the inner goods of the soul, lived without reproach and with the most innocent conduct; he was even granted, through a divine response, foreknowledge of his own end. For one night, while the brothers were sleeping, the lord Einoldus, keeping vigil, suddenly heard a voice calling three times in a prolonged sound: “Isaac, Isaac, Isaac!” When he summoned Isaac in the morning, warned him of his end, and told him what he had heard [Note: variant: *quid*], Isaac replied: “I too heard those same voices, and I recognize that my summons is at hand.” Immediately struck by illness, he died shortly afterward.

Of those, then, who flourished in some way as eminent men in that community, let it suffice to have recalled these; not that everything worthy of remembrance about them has been said—for certainly a separate volume could be composed about each one of them. Many other men of great virtue also existed in that same holy college who deserved to be offered in writing and praise as examples [Col. 0276D] [Note: For example, Rambertus, abbot of Senones. Mabillon.].

72. But from the subject from which we have been separated for some time, a certain cry now calls us back [Col. 0277A]. Having therefore dispatched these matters which we judged unworthy of mention, let us proceed, with the Lord mercifully leading the way, to the deeds of the venerable John, for whom this pen properly labors. First, I wish to describe on what may be called a brief tablet the pattern of conduct and the strength of spirit that were firmly established in him from the very beginning and carried continuously to the end, so that he never swerved in either direction from his wondrous vigor. Just as I would not presume that I could fully accomplish this, so I think it could scarcely ever be comprehended by anyone, however eloquent. Yet it must not be wholly left unspoken, lest the small things that will be said, if buried in a sluggish napkin, deprive the Lord’s gains of those whom they might win.

He maintained such submission to his father and obedience that whatever the latter had once uttered from his mouth as a command, John immediately undertook, like a servant fearing the lash. At the very beginning, while Father Einoldus was deeply troubled by the administration of the place entrusted to him, wondering whether he would have to attend to external matters when he was meditating on very different things in divine contemplation, the lord John approached him and said: “Do not be troubled, lord, by the care of these matters; therefore I shall relieve you of this burden. Direct your mind only to the inner things, as you desire; whatever belongs to external affairs, I shall undertake for myself, with the grace of Christ and aided by your merits.”

Although he thus entrusted everything to John and himself took his leisure in God alone, the lord John never undertook anything, small or great, without Einoldus’s knowledge, counsel, and will. The lord Einoldus himself was witness to this whenever the occasion arose [Col. 0277C]: “He was never disobedient to me,” he said, “nor was there ever anyone who could restore peace between him and me.”

73. The prudent and discerning lord Einoldus also did not cease to exercise him through various changes, in either direction. Often deliberately recalling him from external affairs to internal ones, he even reduced him to the lowest offices, in which John was never seen to refuse, not even by a gesture. Ordered to be provost, he obeyed immediately. When he had laid down the provostship, Einoldus said, “Be dean!” John quietly accepted the yoke. When he left that office: “Take charge of the storeroom!” John at once offered his hand. When another succeeded him there: “Look after the brothers’ clothing!” John resisted no more than before. Thus he ministered to guests, and, when circumstances required it, to the sick, and to all other tasks imposed upon him, with the greatest eagerness and without knowing delay [Col. 0277D].

Whatever money or other things he spent, he returned to the abbot after a week or a month with the total written down in a brief account; likewise, he recorded whatever he had received from outside through any accounts. Although the lord Einoldus disliked hearing these reports, since he knew well that John spent nothing unnecessarily and therefore forbade him to report such matters any further [Col. 0278A], John nevertheless continued to keep everything recorded down to the siliqua, as the saying goes.

74. It is incredible to say with what strength he preserved patience, humility—or lowliness—and, surpassing all these, his fervor of charity toward God and toward everyone. If I wished to recount each of the many occasions on which he frequently provided an example, the writing would run on far too long [Note: *ferrentur*; variant: *ferentur*]. Let us therefore note at least the simpler instances.

The venerable man Fridericus, whom we mentioned above (chapter 55), held the provostship of the monastery, and the lord John held it under him. As his superior, Fridericus often assailed John with severe verbal insults, even publicly and in the presence of laymen [Note: variant: *praesentis*]. While Fridericus continued to thunder on for a long time, John merely prostrated himself again and again on the ground to make satisfaction and maintained uninterrupted silence [Col. 0278B].

When Fridericus repeatedly renewed the same shouting, grew weary with anger, and was already running out of words, John remained motionless for a long time like a voiceless statue. At last, touching a pillar or wall and saying that he was directing his words toward them rather than toward himself, he slipped away from sight. Fridericus, inflamed all the more as though he had been despised, sat down wherever he happened to be. A little later, when his agitation had subsided and his mind had returned to itself more calmly, he secretly brought John aside and, falling at his feet, said: “You have killed me!”

John replied: “In what way have I killed you?”

“Your patience,” said Fridericus, “has killed me.”

“Not so,” the other answered; “your anger has killed you.”

No more was said, and the quarrels immediately ended. This revered man was indeed conspicuous in this one respect, though outstanding in all other respects, and was regarded by everyone as distinguished and eminent because of his great age [Col. 0278C]. The prudent man quickly restrained these very movements of his spirit, which his former manner of life still nourished, and afterward condemned himself by exhausting himself with the most abundant grief and lamentation.

75. What follows is similar. John himself looked after the storeroom, while Bernacer, already mentioned above, kept the brothers’ wardrobe or chamber. One day Bernacer entered the storeroom and found a certain vessel, called an *imapum* [Note: Perhaps the same as *hanapum*, a vessel; in German, *Napf*], placed beneath a wine vessel to catch drippings. Seizing it, he attacked John with complaints, repeatedly asking why he had left a vessel belonging to his own office so damaged, while John insisted that it had suffered no harm.

“For the price of a cartload of wine,” Bernacer said, “I would want it not to have been touched in this way.”

John replied [Col. 0278D]: “Ten little vessels of this kind can be acquired for the price of one cartload of wine.”

The lord Einoldus arrived, and, after Bernacer had already departed, heard the final words John was saying to him from a distance, as John was scarcely finishing: “What is this?” Einoldus said. “Are you quarrelling?”

John immediately prostrated himself on the ground.

“You shall receive nothing,” said Einoldus, “except bread, water, and salt, until I give permission.”

John accepted the command. He told neither Einoldus nor anyone else anything about it, and he abstained continuously for three days [Col. 0279A]. It happened that these were among the hottest days of summer and the days themselves were very long; nevertheless he omitted none of his customary work on that account, but ran about more eagerly and quickly in every task. His bodily health was sound and excessive in neither direction, and by heavenly grace it sufficed, with easy movement, for everything that had to be done.

76. He often endured countless insults even from the lowest people. Some publicly called him a hypocrite, others greedy, others grasping, others a fraud. Some, accusing him of not having renounced the world, thrust before his eyes the members of his household, who served the monastery with their mother, saying:

“You slyly brought your own people here so that you could possess them here more freely and provide for them here better than you could at home. Look—you have even made the monks’ cloister a women’s quarter [Note: variant: *egeneceum*]” [Col. 0279B].

As they hurled these and many other words at his face, he remained immovable like a rock. Nor, so far as I myself have been able to learn from anyone, was there ever anyone who reported having heard an insulting word from his mouth. Even when angered, he maintained this silence amid their shouting. There he did nothing except silently ask forgiveness, prostrate on the ground; and we often observed him doing this even to those who were far below him in rank. For he had devoted his mind to this purpose: that nothing should be so utterly lowly that he would not willingly stoop to it. We have also learned, from men whose testimony is beyond doubt, that he frequently cleaned the brothers’ latrines.

77. Whenever, according to the common custom, he had taken his turn for a week in the kitchen, and consequently in performing the cleaning, he scarcely ever requested a substitute unless some serious necessity occupied him. He himself drew water from the well and carried it on his shoulder [Note: variant: *hausis*], brought it into the kitchen, and hung it over the fire. He poured in the legumes or vegetables he had gathered or cut with his own hands; he washed them, cooked them, and served them. He alone washed the refectory vessels, and he did not assign to another the closely related task of washing the brothers’ feet.

This was common to him with the others. But we ourselves learned from his own mouth that he alone mixed, fermented, and kneaded into dough the flour needed for the whole community—two or three *modii*—with only a little boy pouring in the water; then, in great sweat, he pressed it into loaves, while the bakers carried out the remaining work [Col. 0279D]. Many branded this with the mark of excessive parsimony, although he did it secretly from everyone in a private room. Yet he was a faithful servant devoted to Christ, keeping watch with the utmost vigilance lest any property of the monastery be lost; and, what is greater and truer, he did it so that the sweat of his labor might be rewarded with heavenly prizes.

78. From the following it can readily be judged how little he valued his own personal care. More sumptuous foods, finer clothing, polished footwear, the softness of a bed, the comforts of baths, the use of medicines during any illnesses that arose, and everything whatsoever that contributed to bodily pleasure beyond unavoidable necessity [Col. 0280A]—he regarded these as though they were crimes and rejected them utterly, although he forbade no one else to use whatever of these things they happened to need.

His discernment in this matter was remarkable: although he appeared austere and almost undiscerning toward himself, no one was more compassionate toward others. He fasted, yet urged others to eat; he kept vigil, yet allowed others to sleep; he labored, yet granted others rest. He completely abstained from baths and was said never to have used them throughout his monastic life, except perhaps once, after recovering from a serious illness. Nevertheless, whenever baths were suitable for others, he never condemned or forbade them.

Although he had permanently closed off from himself the taking of food or drink before or after the appointed hour, he suspended no one from it when illness required it [Col. 0280B]. Indeed, he himself freely offered meat to the sick and urged it upon them without being asked. So also with clothing, footwear, and bedding: while he always chose for himself what was cheaper, humbler, sparser, and harder, he provided others with whatever abundance was appropriate, and with garments and bedding more elegant and softer, insofar as this did not excessively hinder their profession [Note: The reading is corrected in Labbé; another reading has “less.”].

79. He watched most vigilantly for the deceitfulness of vices, and in such matters he yielded easily to no one, even if that person was his superior. As soon as he perceived anyone seeking something through vice or fraud, he refused it in every way. For although, as has been said, he became almost mute amid outbreaks of anger, when the moment for correction arrived one could see his tongue grow hot and pour forth sharply piercing words with a certain powerful terror [Col. 0280C].

He had no place at all for flattery—the common disease from which, alas, most of us suffer—in anything that might be encouraged. At the same time he dreaded even the smallest stain of falsehood as something capital [Note: variant: *qo*]. Thus, if circumstances of place or time ever compelled him to say something in favor of powerful people, he proceeded so cautiously between the two paths that he both raised them as much as was necessary and did not exceed the bounds of truth.

Beyond the common practice of men today, we perceived him to be distinguished—or nearly alone—in the apostolic saying, insofar as human nature allowed: “If anyone does not stumble in word, that man is perfect” (James 3:2).

80. If I begin to praise his vigils and fasts, the mouths of all who knew him will overwhelm me, since all will cry out with unanimous wonder that scarcely anyone of this age existed who could equal him in these matters [Col. 0280D]. Since it was almost a perpetual rule for him, after vigils conducted through however deep the night, not to know sleep until daylight, one could hear him, during the interval that monastic custom places between the nocturnal and morning offices, creeping about here and there along various paths. Like a bee, he continually went over the psalms in a quiet murmur: now bending his knees around the altars, now sitting briefly and immediately rising, then standing for some time; again going outside to inspect the sky for the hour of night; then attending to the lamps, either trimming or replenishing them; also inspecting the schools of singers; and sometimes spending whatever remained of the night weaving nets.

Very often he anticipated the common vigils themselves and corrected the dormitory lamps, as though this care had been specially assigned to him—often, as it seemed, even unnecessarily, when they were already giving off a clear light. Then he entered the oratory as secretly as possible and, prostrate before the altar, wore himself out with prolonged lamentations and sighs, audible to the custodians, amid a great flood of tears [Col. 0281A].

81. At times he himself struck the signal for the vigils, and no less diligently than the others carried out the common work of psalms, prayers, and readings. At that time, when the beginnings of the monastic life were still fervent, these offices were extended more abundantly in number, length, and duration; later, the faintheartedness of the weak compelled some of them to be shortened [Col. 0281B].

For the nocturnal prayers, three in number, became much longer as soon as the signal for the vigils was given. After them, while everyone sat together in the choir, thirty psalms—from Psalm 119 to the end of the Psalter—were recited individually in silence, divided into three prayers of ten psalms each. The first ten were for the dead, the middle ten for members of the household, and the last ten for all.

On the shorter summer nights and on feast days, only fifteen Canticles of Ascents were recited, likewise divided among three prayers. The readings at the winter vigils were extended so far that, after nearly two weeks had been spent on the prophets appointed from the Kalends of November, either one of the prophetic books was begun again [Note: printed *repeteretur*; perhaps plural *repeterentur*] or certain other readings were added. Thus we learned that on one occasion this same man completed the whole of Daniel in a single reading, while a third reader had risen to take his turn [Col. 0281C].

Likewise, after the days of the Nativity, the Apostle was read at the vigils; from Septuagesima until the days of the Passion, the Eptateuch [Note: The same as the *Eptateuch*, that is, the Pentateuch together with the books of Joshua and Judges]; and during the Passion itself, Jeremiah was read in full. Much of this is now supplied at the tables.

82. Moreover, after the remainder of the nocturnal course or the customary psalms [Note: Mabillon reads *rursus* (“again”); the printed text has *cursus nocturni*], many usually recited the entire Psalter individually until the signal of dawn [Col. 0281D]. When the others sometimes sought some relaxation in these matters, John, resisting sleep with unbroken strength, yielded to scarcely any weariness. Throughout the entire interval, however long it lasted, he stood awake; and after completing the morning office [Note: variant: *efficio*]—or the first hour, which immediately followed—with the seven penitential psalms and the litany, he at once proceeded to reading.

When sleep occasionally overcame him there, conquering nature itself, he immediately shook himself away from the book and walked back and forth, always muttering some psalm. It was a remarkable spectacle to see him on summer mornings of this kind [Col. 0282A]. We learned that he rarely or never returned to his bed unless bloodletting intervened. For whether in the night or during the intervals, in winter or summer, if the vigils happened to be completed long before dawn and excessive fatigue compelled him, he would lean back on his bed for a little while, but rose again immediately and so hastily that one would not even think he had fallen asleep.

We ourselves often heard him say that from the very beginnings of his monastic life he had carried on this continual battle against sleep in the morning hours, a battle he had never been able to win, since at those same hours sleep always returned to him more aggressively:

“From the old custom of the world,” he said, “I nourished this flattering enemy in myself”—for he kept vigil by night and indulged in sleep until far into the day—“and therefore, although I do not see it, sleep itself announces to me every day that dawn is approaching.”

83. To the higher learning he had acquired before his conversion, he added the practice of reading every kind of book of divine Scripture with such zeal that scarcely any of the most eminent doctors escaped his attention, until, with the Holy Spirit going before him, he reached as much knowledge of Scripture as is permitted to mortals [Note: variant: *nocitiam*].

First, he read through the *Moralia* of blessed Gregory in order, as frequently as possible. He committed almost all the contents of its teachings to memory so thoroughly that in ordinary conversations, whether exhortations or informal discussions, all his speech seemed to flow from those books. He was no less devoted to the reading of Augustine, Ambrose, Jerome, and any of the ancients who came into his hands [Col. 0282C].

Since at that time, when studies were languishing, even the books themselves were scarcely to be found, he read Augustine’s works on John, the Psalms, and *The City of God* in their entirety. Finally, he labored with great concentration over the books *On the Trinity*. When he encountered in them certain matters of dialectical reasoning—especially where, to demonstrate the relation of the Father to the Son and of the Spirit to both, Augustine introduces the category called “relation” (*ad aliquid*), and on that occasion briefly mentions something concerning all ten categories—John immediately desired scholastic instruction to open these matters to him and began the labor of reading with the elementary introductions to the *Isagoge*.

While he struggled for a long time with his innate quickness of intellect and with indefatigable labor, as in all the other matters he had ever undertaken [Note: variant: *indefetigato*], the lord Father Einoldus suddenly cut short his efforts [Col. 0282D]. Einoldus himself had long been deeply interested in these matters and had learned by experience how much labor they required. Not wishing John to waste his time on them, he turned him away with a brief prohibition and urged him instead to occupy his mind with sacred reading, where he possessed an adequate and more than adequate supply of both knowledge and, what is more important, edification [Col. 0283A].

John, who had once sworn not to cross the limits of obedience [Note: variant: *in*], immediately abandoned what he had begun and devoted himself wholly to divine things, as he had done from the beginning. Moreover, he wore himself out through constant use of Gregory’s work on Ezekiel, so that he seemed almost to have committed it to memory. In short, beyond all other writings, he embraced uniquely everything that belonged to blessed Gregory.

84. Nor, among these matters, did he neglect the lives of the saints or the sayings of any of them, written about them in particular works. From these he adopted as the rule of his own conduct Anthony, Paul, Hilarion, Macarius, Pachomius, and the other followers of the desert, as well as Martin, that great and most holy bishop, Germanus, and all those who had lived more austerely and whom he had read [Col. 0283B]. If circumstances had allowed, he might perhaps have attempted to imitate them—a conclusion that could certainly be inferred from the discipline he had undertaken.

Although he was not their equal in bodily labors, I would not hesitate to state with certainty that our age scarcely saw another man more closely their rival in the virtues of the soul. He nearly retained in memory the deeds of a certain John, patriarch of Alexandria, whom they call Eleimon; he brought him back into almost every conversation with pleasing and friendly sweetness, and held his listeners through the great delight of attention with which they heard these accounts from him.

85. Since it seems too laborious to pursue each individual matter, and since knowledge or imitation had made him accustomed to no fewer of these things, everyone regarded it as a wonder that, although he devoted so much practice to them, he nevertheless neglected none of the tasks that had to be performed in external affairs. He ran about attending to different matters, established instructions for arranging each one, and vigorously managed the entire business of the monastery amid so many varied crafts and offices [Col. 0283C].

Although the whole care of the monastery’s possessions rested upon him, he rarely went out to them. Rather, he dictated what had to be done outside the monastery, and, after summoning the ministers, he prescribed what they were to report completed within a month or more [Note: variant: *qq*].

Whenever some more important matter drew him out, and necessity compelled him to remain seated to conduct business, he hastened it as quickly as the affairs permitted and returned to the monastery in haste, sometimes without having eaten. If circumstances or time required him to remain outside, he observed, as far as he could, the monastery’s customary measure of food and drink [Col. 0283D].

He never altered the rule of his bedding: he allowed nothing to be placed beneath him except a feather pillow for his head. In this he followed his own master, the lord Einoldus, who from the very beginning had maintained the practice at home and abroad to the end, so that the disciple truly followed his teacher, walking in his footsteps.

86. Even at the meals of laymen he was greatly burdened by their affairs, although none of them perceived this even slightly [Col. 0284A]. They lacked nothing of whatever abundance they wanted, and John presented himself among them as cheerful, friendly, and accommodating in every way.

But afterward, when he spoke with spiritual men, he repeatedly lamented that he could never take part in the company of laymen, even briefly, without losing something of his customary manner of life and, moreover, unwillingly spending more of the brothers’ property. He expressed himself familiarly in this way whenever discussion arose about brothers who were managing affairs outside: it would not be expedient for them to undertake such matters so frequently in person; they should rather entrust them by word to lay ministers and confine themselves within the cloister.

“No one,” he said, “was ever more dog-like than I, or more deserving of the charge of tenacity, or truly more sparing outside [Note: variant: *partior*], provided that everything I saw the monastery needed was brought into it. But I could never take such care that, whenever I ate with them, I did not spend almost as much as would have sufficed for the brothers’ ordinary daily needs.

“For whenever any traveler—private persons or great men—asked whether some monk was present at one or another estate belonging to the monastery, and happened to find me there, they would turn aside under the pretext of greeting me. They could not suitably be sent away from the table to which they had not been properly invited. Thus I could not ensure that whatever belonged to the brothers outside, or whatever was acquired by any means, was brought into the monastery intact, as I desired [Note: variant: *inferentur*].”

87. Even in legal proceedings, although some criticized him, he never exceeded the bounds of uprightness or justice [Col. 0284C]. When pride or defiance had made certain people stiff-necked or unbridled, he broke their raised necks by treating them on an equal footing with the rest. Even when they tried to secure the patronage of powerful men, he could not be swayed.

His entire intention was directed toward this: that whatever justice obtained should be faithfully brought into the monastery. He was especially careful that the monastery’s purse should never be contaminated by any fraud, or by the deception or misfortune of the poor.

Let each person judge as he wishes; I shall freely declare in good faith that he always hated and guarded against iniquity, and that, with the Lord directing his steps according to his word, iniquity did not rule over him insofar as human nature allowed [Col. 0284D]. Those who think that he served usury and amassed profits from every source under the guise of the monastery’s needs measure him by their own character.

88. They did not think this because they had seen or certainly learned anything of the kind in him. He did indeed lend many things and receive them back, taking care not to be deceived by any trick of debtors, and observing, according to the saying of Persius [Note: Rather Juvenal, *Satire* 1.57]:

> Skilled even at snoring beside the cup with an alert nose,

which John had altered by a better art. As a prudent steward of the Lord’s substance, he watched with the utmost diligence lest any property of the monastery be lost. He often recalled this saying of blessed Gregory to a certain deacon who managed church property:

“These things,” Gregory said, “are neither mine nor yours; act so that you will give an account of them to the one whose they are.”

If grain, wine, salt, or anything else belonging to food was lent, and likewise if clothing was lent, the same measure or quantity was demanded back, so that nothing extra would be required. Silver was lent by a proper weight [Note: One manuscript reads “was lent”; in the margin: “or exchanged.”]. Even what the law of coinage rightfully exacts was not demanded in any way; whatever someone received or gave was repaid on an equal scale [Col. 0285A].

89. Through the labors of the fields and vineyards, in which he excelled with the greatest skill and to which he devoted himself with the greatest diligence, the monastery’s supplies had increased, by the cooperation of divine grace, to such abundance that no want compelled him to undertake any of these measures. Rather, the very labors produced such a surplus for the brothers that many things sold provided enough for whatever was needed immediately or would be needed in the future. From this the entire household economy was sustained, and much was supplied for ornamentation [Col. 0285B].

His only gains from temporal goods were diligently carrying out agricultural work and constructing saltworks—which are found in only one part of that region, called Vicus [Note: variant: *Vic*]—so that in that same place he prepared several vessels called pans, some purchased complete with their sites and some repaired from those belonging to the monastery, all destined to be of great future use [Col. 0285C]. He also worked at blocking rivers with mills for the sake of fish, preparing private fishponds, and caring for herds of cattle, sheep, domestic birds, and wild birds, as well as wild animals, so that there would always be an abundant supply for every use of the brothers and the sick, and also for those from outside, whether present or arriving later.

90. Having brought in craftsmen of various trades from every direction, he first surrounded the entire cloister with a wall in the manner of a fortress. Even today it can be seen to be suitable not only for defense but, if necessary, for assault [Col. 0285D]. Then, because the ancient buildings lay in ruins, he tirelessly set about restoring the necessary workshops and internal facilities as new structures arose.

Finally, he devoted himself to beautifying the house of God with various kinds of ornament. He prepared hangings, coverings of different sorts, and varied vestments for sacred use, so that nothing would be lacking for priestly ministries; he also prepared vessels for sacred use from silver, all in solid and elegant workmanship.

Then he undertook the tomb of the martyr, and, together with all the altars in the various oratories, covered both it and them with silver plates suitably adorned with gold. For this purpose he also covered the ambo used for reading the Gospel and bound it together with durable strength [Col. 0286A].

I say nothing of the crowns hanging from the ceilings with such radiant brilliance; of the lamps, so varied in their places and arrangements [Note: the variant reading is *eam*]; of the candelabra of such weight and workmanship; or, together with these, of the vessels almost beyond naming, all fashioned from solid silver. Finally, there are the number and enormous size of the bells that can be seen, along with the other distinguished works in which his highly skilled intellect shone forth, as it did in almost every craft.

91. These matters themselves slip past the memory, and if I attempt to pursue whatever may follow, the narrowness of my most impoverished speech will not suffice to complete the account. They abound in such profusion that, even if someone could perhaps explain them, they would make the reading not edifyingly delightful but, as I know our age and its habits, altogether tedious [Col. 0286B].

I therefore judge that we should pass on to other matters. Yet lest anyone silently accuse us of being carried beyond what the facts warrant in favor of this man, and of attributing to him what in fact belonged entirely to his master, we do not deny this; rather, we openly affirm that it was so. Everything was carried out by the commands and arrangements of that same father and master, the lord Einoldus, and John never rashly undertook anything unless it had first proceeded from Einoldus’s mouth.

But this objection is quickly answered, since the deeds of disciples redound to the praise of their masters. Nor did the lord John ever claim for himself anything he had done; instead he said: “He ordered it this way, and so I carry it out.” Yet for that reason he cannot rightly be said to have had no share in those works, for all the labor was his, while Einoldus merely gave the instructions [Col. 0286C].

Why, moreover, should a pointless dispute be created among anyone over this, when neither of the two ever found anything in which one disagreed with the other? The father considered whatever the son did to belong to him; the son attributed to his father whatever he himself had appropriately done. With Christ as witness, I confess that no pair more closely united has ever agreed so well through the ages. If this is believed, the reward of faith is certain; if not, no one can prevent me from declaring with certainty what I know with certainty.

92. Although many things come to mind, and my impatience already refuses to hold back from touching on certain of his particular and distinctive qualities, I wish first to discuss as briefly as I can the rule of fasting he had imposed upon himself, since I had almost passed over it [Col. 0286D].

From the very beginning of his conversion, he had resolved to devote all the rest of his time to fasting, except on feast days, or when some unavoidable care of the body, illness, or accommodation to guests required otherwise. For some time he maintained this vigorously, while he still possessed the strength of youth and the confidence in his former worldly discipline. As though it burdened him not at all, he carried it out as something light and scarcely felt, supported by the strength of youth and by confidence in the mortification he had formerly practiced in the world, with an agile body and a cheerful heart and face.

On these days he consumed nothing except bread and water. Even then he took both with such great moderation that he scarcely ate more than half of a loaf which, whole, weighed a pound; nor did he add much water beyond half the measure of wine served to the brothers [Col. 0287A]. He did not touch salt, green herbs, or anything similar that is not forbidden to those who abstain.

The lord Einoldus permitted this for a time while John was testing himself. Later, when he clearly perceived that John had become very weak but was not abandoning what he had begun and was striving beyond his strength, he restrained him moderately and advised him to choose what he could better endure.

John had already so exhausted himself that one day, when he had gone out with the brothers to the garden and applied himself vigorously to the work, his heart suddenly failed him. As he hurried to return to the cloister, he collapsed in the middle of the way and was carried away in their hands [Col. 0287B].

### 93

Accordingly, he adopted a more tolerable rule: he would observe only two Lents each year, one before the Nativity of the Lord and the other before Easter. He began the first at the Ides of September, when the brothers resumed their meal at the ninth hour; then, immediately after the octave of Epiphany, on the third and fifth Sundays he shared the common meal with the others, while he abstained for the remaining four days, content under the rule itself with bread and water alone, as we have said.

[Note: [Col. 0287] Thus L. ep . . . . . . c.]

[Note: [Col. 0287] Thus Mabillon; *reli* is now missing; or perhaps *quos*, incorrectly in L.]

But if any feast day occurred or guests arrived, he likewise altered those abstinences by taking food. Even when he underwent bloodletting—which he could scarcely postpone for more than a month—he did not reject care of the body.

He anticipated the seasons so far in advance and did not wait for the solemnities themselves to draw near, [Col. 0287C] so that, if some unforeseen occurrence required him to miss any of the appointed days, he would still have enough time remaining to make up those same days.

[Note: [Col. 0287] *ipsi* in witness c.]

Thus, when it often happened that, because of the circumstances mentioned or some other accident, an entire week, or perhaps two or more, prevented him from fulfilling his vow, as soon as the desired freedom was restored he would make up the number of days omitted by maintaining continuous abstinence for two or more weeks, with only Sunday free; all who saw it were astonished or distressed. He watched with extraordinary care so that he himself should not omit any of the forty vowed days at one time or another.

It was often possible to see him seemingly foresee even these events, when he appeared suddenly to undertake such a continuation of the fast. For it was observed very frequently that, while he was burning with such zeal, knowing nothing of relaxation, he was subsequently compelled by a messenger or some unavoidable necessity to leave the monastery. As long as he was outside, he carefully attended to the “robberies of the human day”—that is, of human labor—

[Note: [Col. 0287] That is, human labor; compare Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians 4:3.]

[Note: [Col. 0287] Thus the codex; perhaps *lenocinia*, “enticements”?]

and took care that secular observers should not witness his secret practice, for which he reserved a reward from God alone. [Col. 0288A]

Although at other times he also rigorously observed the fixed fasts occurring throughout the year in their proper order—those of the four seasons and of the solemnities, scattered throughout the year—

[Note: [Col. 0287] I have supplied by conjecture the words marked with asterisks in an attempt to fill gaps in the codex.]

whenever circumstances allowed him to do so—for, though always avoiding glory, he often relaxed his practice because of travel or a guest, yet he almost never failed to observe these two annual Lents—during the rest of the year he shared the common life, without any addition or variation, for as long as the brothers’ two daily meals lasted.

### 94

Whatever was prepared for the common meals, he made no distinction: he neither sought inferior food for himself nor rejected finer fare. He never permitted anything to be added to or changed in what had been cooked and served to the others for his own use.

His bread was equal and of the same kind; his wine was of the same measure and flavor, never at any time differing from what was provided for the whole community. On feast days, when the brothers’ customary joy could be displayed in honor of the Lord or the saints with especially rich and carefully prepared food, he freely ate whatever was set before him. “I do not use this; bring or prepare that”—such words were never heard from him. Thus he was never conspicuous in any food or drink.

Indeed, since he was exceptionally knowledgeable about such matters, he himself arranged for the finest foods to be prepared on those days, and consumed them without any apparent affectation. His body had almost always been hardened by a natural resistance to digestion, so that food was digested in him only with difficulty. For that reason he willingly drank herbal preparations and, for the most part, spices that were useful or suitable for this purpose; but, admitting only these, he rejected the other remedies compounded by the physicians’ various arts. [Col. 0288C]

[Note: [Col. 0287] The passage beginning “This certainly” through “exceeded” is absent from Labbe.]

This, certainly, was preserved with the greatest effort: he was scarcely ever, or never, brought into drunkenness or gluttony by taking more food or drink than usual, nor was he ever forced by this to omit any of his customary divine service, whether by night or by day. Thus, outside the monastery too, he appeared to dine with the others as one of them, yet even at the meal he did not exceed the measure of nourishment he had prescribed for himself.

In him it was openly evident, more than in anyone else of his time, that he had been formed and perfected by the highest skill and a kind of discipline in the apostle’s saying, “I know both how to be hungry and how to be filled” (Philippians 4:12). For he never appeared more downcast through hunger, nor more elated after eating.

In short, he maintained this rigor of penitence with extraordinary perseverance to the end of his life, a practice so exalted that no account of ours can adequately express it. [Col. 0288D]

[Note: [Col. 0287] Thus L.; a word is now missing.]

Having now imposed these matters, let us turn our pen to what we have been able to learn about his external deeds. In them, partly the prudence of a keen intellect and the strength of a manly spirit, aided by heavenly grace, and partly the operation of divine power alone, where human assistance could not be present, were revealed.

[Col. 0289A]

### 95

When, as the preceding account has shown, the holy men had gathered there at the place called Gorze, through the ready goodwill of the lord Bishop Adelbero,

[Note: [Col. 0289D] Compare *Miracles of Saint Gorgonius*, chapter 10.]

they were for some time supported chiefly by his help, since he did not yet have the means to restore to them anything from the monastery’s properties, which long before had passed away into the hands of secular beneficiaries.

Then, when certain people, divinely inspired by the reputation of its good report, began to flock there and the number of the holy congregation increased, the resources—still scarcely more than meager—promised only a small stipend in comparison with the size of the community, which was not yet so great, much less equal to the number they hoped would afterward increase day by day.

Moreover, the same holy man Adelbero, with the kingdom then disturbed by various upheavals and himself occupied with many cares, was less able than usual to provide for them. [Col. 0289B] Compelled by this, they had almost decided to seek support elsewhere.

At about the same time (934), Ogo, then provost of Saint-Maximin and later an example of blessedness, had withdrawn from secular life and, with the aid of Duke Gislebert, had restored that monastery to regular observance.

[Note: [Col. 0290D] Compare *Miracles of Saint Maximinus*, chapter 12.]

With the provost’s pious undertaking in mind, they had asked permission to transfer themselves there for a while.

[Note: [Col. 0289] A word is missing—“they granted.” Mabillon supplies it.]

### 96

Meanwhile, as the lord Einoldus restrained their wavering affairs by a sounder judgment—

[Note: [Col. 0289] “Mind” in the manuscript; “judgment” is conjectural.]

one day, among other words of exhortation, he addressed them all as follows:

“Scripture,” he said, “declares (Proverbs 16:7) that when a person’s ways please the Lord, he makes even that person’s enemies turn toward peace. From this we can recognize our negligence: if our minds had applied themselves to divine things with the zeal they ought to have shown, it would have been easy for the Lord to bend this man, make him gracious and beneficent toward us, and turn his heart toward what would be advantageous for us.”

After exhorting them at length concerning matters that would contribute to this end, and urging them to remember the fervor they had possessed at the time of their new conversion, to examine carefully whether anything was now being done among them more languidly, coldly, or negligently, and to strive with complete vigilance to restore whatever they found lacking, he suddenly restored such courage to them that, now individually and now all together, they fiercely joined in a new struggle of religious observance (935).

Each added to his customary and regular practices things more demanding and prolonged; they voluntarily deprived themselves of what was permitted; and they allowed the least possible indulgence to food, drink, sleep, speech, or any bodily comfort, so that they seemed then for the first time to be taking up the beginnings of religious life.

### 97

Meanwhile, the persuasion of the aforesaid Ogo, provost of Saint-Maximin, and of Duke Gislebert urged them to migrate; and the bishop had now been absent from the place for nearly three years. It happened that John of Metz was summoned concerning a certain man who held the monastery’s jurisdiction and administered some episcopal possessions.

The bishop first approached him courteously, asking him not to refuse what he requested.

“Your request,” he said, “is a command.”

“I ask you,” he replied, “to surrender that man to me.”

The bishop, somewhat irritated, since his mind was directed far otherwise, said: “You are now using the example from David’s story, where the rich man, sparing the innumerable sheep he possessed, ordered the one poor man’s ewe, seized by force, to be served to the guest who had arrived. So, while you abound in an infinite abundance of everything else, you are robbing us poor people of this one.”

With raised brows, he turned away, barely indicating by any word the signs of his agitation. John slipped out of his presence.

The monk Frederick of Saint-Hubert, mentioned above in chapter 55, entered at almost that very moment and, judging his mood from his downcast expression, said: “Why do I see your brows hanging so heavily?” For when he was more agitated, he had made this his habitual expression.

“Because of that madman John,” he replied. “Never before have I been so despised by anyone that I was unwilling even to intercede with him for a single man.”

Frederick, aware of the plans being hatched outside, said: “Unless provision is made, you will soon lose all of them. For I have learned that they have already joined themselves to the duke and the provost, since they receive little assistance from you; and arrangements are being hurriedly made to transfer them to Saint-Maximin.”

John was quickly recalled. When he was asked why he had gone away without permission, he stood trembling and silent.

The bishop said: “I did not think you so spirited, nor did I suppose you so difficult in a matter of almost no importance. I ask you, therefore, to surrender the man to me, at least for some period.”

When he understood what the matter was—for money was involved in the agreement—he said: “For as long as you command?”

“For forty days,” the bishop replied.

And he answered: “Even for a year, if you wish.”

[Note: [Col. 0289] Thus L.; a word is now missing.]

### 98

Not long afterward, while the bishop was resting, a certain person appeared to him with a terrifying and threatening face and seemed to say sternly:

“You began a good work well, but you abandoned what you had begun far too quickly. Beware lest this abandonment become for you the cause of greater ruin. Restore what you began, lest you fall into worse things.”

[Note: [Col. 0289] I supplied “Beware lest this” conjecturally in an attempt to repair the eroded passage.]

When he awoke, he reflected deeply on the religious work he had begun and considered, with keen distress, that this admonition had been neglected for so long.

[Note: [Col. 0289] The manuscript has *neglecta*; the correct form is *neglectam*.]

He immediately summoned his chamberlain, whose name was Matzilinus.

“Go with all speed to Gorze,” he said, “and order Abbot Einoldus to come here at once.”

[Note: [Col. 0289] The manuscript has *abbatum*; *abbatem* is the correction.]

The abbot had perhaps spent that very night at Metz and was preparing to return at dawn. After the morning office, he departed; when he had reached the city gate and was waiting there for the keys, a messenger sent to summon him hurried toward him. When he saw and greeted him, the messenger said:

“You have relieved me of my labor, for I was being sent here to summon you, and my lord has ordered you to appear before him at once.”

### 99

When he arrived immediately afterward and the bishop was astonished at so sudden an event, he was ordered to enter. After they had exchanged greetings, the bishop said:

“It has been a long time since, because of other obstacles, I came to Gorze; but, God willing, I had it in mind to go there.”

“We shall see you with the greatest joy,” said the abbot.

“Go ahead of me,” replied the bishop, “and announce on what day I may come.”

The Ember-fast days of the second month were to begin on the following day—

[Note: [Col. 0291D] February, namely the Tuesday after the Sunday called *Invocavit*.]

—and he said that the visit should take place after they had been completed.

“There is no need,” said the abbot, “to delay on this account. I myself shall go ahead today, and tomorrow we shall await you at the hour you specify.”

“At the third hour,” said the bishop, “I shall come.”

The following day, when the bishop had set out and was beginning to approach the monastery, he dismounted from his horse at a place called “At the Cross.” He removed his shoes and proceeded on foot all the way to the monastery.

After he had been received and prayer had been offered, he summoned the community, prostrated himself humbly at their feet, and accused himself of having neglected them until that time. He encouraged them with better hopes concerning himself in the future and, humbly, begged their pardon.

[Note: [Col. 0291] The words corresponding to “and he begged pardon” are now missing.]

After it had been readily granted, he immediately bestowed on them a former monastery possession, which his own brother Gozilin still held as a benefice. It was called Waringis village.

[Note: [Col. 0291D] Waringéville.]

He instructed his administrator that, unless he assigned all the revenues to the abbot in full, he would be punished in the presence of Christ with the curse of Dathan and Abiron if he contrived any fraud or deceit there.

### 100

After the fast-day meal had been served, the bishop departed with complete eagerness. On the following day the abbot set out with some of the elders to take possession of the village.

When they reached, on the way, the fortress called Scarponna,

[Note: [Col. 0291D] Charpeigne on the Moselle, below the confluence of the Moselle and the Meurthe.]

at about the third hour, John’s horse began to limp.

“Why is that horse limping so?” asked the abbot.

“It is suffering because it has lost a shoe,” he replied.

“Do not go farther until it is replaced,” said the abbot. “We shall wait here meanwhile.”

When John hurried down toward the marketplace, someone happened to ask where he was going. He hesitated for a moment.

“It will be useful,” he said, “if you do not conceal it from me.”

“Where are you from?” the man asked.

“From the village of Portus,” he replied.

[Note: [Col. 0292D] Today Saint-Nicolas.]

That village too belonged to the aforesaid estate.

“We are going there,” said John, “to take possession of it by order of the bishop.”

“Listen to me for a little,” the man replied. “The entire money census is still being held there. For when the man who collected it recently brought it to the bishop’s administrator, five solidi or so were missing, and the administrator refused to accept it unless the whole amount was delivered at once. Moreover, the grain from the previous year is still stored there, and the administrator himself has set aside a considerable portion for his own use.”

### 101

John returned quickly after having the horse shod and, having whispered to the abbot what he had learned, they met the bishop’s administrator at about the fifth hour. He happened then to be staying at an estate called Laium

[Note: [Col. 0292D] Lay.]

with Countess Eva, at that time a widow,

[Note: [Col. 0292D] A relative of Bishop Adelbero; see Calmet, volume I, *Preuves*, p. 356 and following.]

whose advocate he then was. His name was Albulfus.

[Note: [Col. 0291] *Albul* is missing.]

After receiving the bishop’s order, he said: “Please remain here today, and I shall provide everything necessary until I send ahead and receive you there with the honor you deserve.”

Although some agreed, John urged them to continue without delay. When certain elders said that these were childish plans, that they should rather rest there that day, and that it was useless to labor without accomplishing anything, the abbot replied:

“It is better for us to hurry.”

John went on ahead more quickly—for they were no more than three leagues away—occupied a house in the village suitable for their meal, and prepared everything else for their arrival with the greatest care.

Then, entering the granary, he found everything in order exactly as had been reported to him, for he was a shrewd investigator of all things. Immediately summoning the collector of the census, he sternly threatened him in the bishop’s name not to allow the total amount still in his possession to be diminished in any way before the abbot and the bishop’s administrator arrived.

Meanwhile, he received the abbot and his companions with the greatest elegance, while the administrator was expected on the following day.
