Late that night the administrator sent a secret messenger, who met the collector and asked him to hand over to his master the money he had brought earlier. The collector replied that the bishop’s word forbade him to do so and sent him away empty-handed.

On the following day, at the appointed time, the administrator carried out everything as ordered and assigned the entire possession to them. It extended over one hundred manses, and its inhabitants were bound by oath.

### 102

Albulfus secretly sent word to the abbot that he should order certain things which he had acquired through his own contract there to be returned to him.

[Note: [Col. 0291] The manuscript has *quodam*; *quaedam* is the correction.]

When it became known that he had nothing there at all, but that everything belonged to his lord’s use, it was perhaps decided to give him ten or fifteen solidi for his good service. The messenger refused unless he received two pounds and reported back to his master:

“You acted foolishly by rejecting what was offered, for now perhaps you will not receive even a penny.”

Later, Albulfus, now openly, said that unless his own possessions were returned, he would bring a complaint against the bishop over the injuries done to him.

[Note: [Col. 0291] Words after “his own” are missing and supplied conjecturally.]

John replied: “We do not shrink from that either; perhaps his property will increase rather than suffer loss.”

He, conscious of the wrongs previously committed, said: “My lords, I do not wish in any way to oppose or obstruct the alms of my lord. I retain so much favor that he has bestowed on me in other matters that, for love of him, I could easily do without these things, even if there were more of them; indeed, if anything belonging to me by hereditary right should be due, I would gladly add it as well.”

Thus the whole matter was settled peacefully. They yielded him a share of the produce,

[Note: [Col. 0293] The manuscript has the masculine form; the feminine is the correction.]

and afterward, both to secure his good will and peace toward them and so that they might use him thereafter wherever there was need of his defense, they also gave him some silver.

### 103

In a similar manner, not long afterward, while the brothers were pressing their frequent petitions concerning a nearby possession and the outcome seemed altogether difficult, so that they had already entrusted the desperate matter to divine help alone, the bishop suddenly summoned the abbot and said:

“Take at last what you have sought with such persistence. And do not return any thanks to me, but to blessed Peter, who terrified me greatly during the night and compelled me to do this.”

[Note: [Col. 0293D] From *Miracles of Saint Gorgonius*, chapter 2.]

### 104

The times were fluctuating amid excessive dissensions, as the kingdom was being pulled in different directions.

[Note: [Col. 0294D] From *Miracles of Saint Gorgonius*, chapter 12.]

Otto, later the great Augustus after his father, the energetic King Henry, had then begun his reign. Under him Gislebert held the duchy of the kingdom of Lotharingia, while Everard held Austrasia in France and certain territories beyond the Rhine. Meanwhile the regions beyond the Rhine remained peaceful. Our own lands were troubled in various ways and did not readily submit to the yoke.

Thereupon a certain Boso, son of Richard, formerly prince of the Burgundians, claimed part of the kingdom for himself and, keeping to strongly fortified castles, utterly refused the rule of anyone else. Holding the fortress of Victoriacum in Champagne, he had usurped among the other surrounding possessions certain properties of the monastery of Gorze as though by hereditary right.

[Note: [Col. 0293] A word is now missing.]

John was sent by the abbot and the brothers to reclaim these, if there might perhaps be some place for petitions with such a man, even through fear of God.

### 105

Obedience had made all difficult or impossible things easy and possible for him. He set out through places infested with brigands and frightening even to a multitude, taking with him only one companion from the household.

When he arrived unexpectedly, he was announced to the count and was admitted into his presence, although it was uncertain what he carried. There he delivered the abbot’s embassy and the request of the servants of God concerning the matter for which he had been sent.

The count, inflamed with anger, said: “What sorcerer brought you here? Where were the guards of mine, that you were able to pass through them?”

“However I was brought here,” John replied, “I have arrived, and I bring you the commands and petitions of the servants of God: restore, for love of God and out of fear or reverence for his saints, what you have seized from their possessions.”

When asked what these possessions were and hearing the answer, the count denied everything categorically

[Note: [Col. 0293] Thus M.; the correction in witness c. has *abnegato*, “having denied.”]

and ordered John to remove himself immediately.

“I can remove myself,” John replied. “But there are many others among us, far more numerous and powerful, who will not cease to follow one another in turn, and you will have no relief from their barking as long as you live.”

“What concern have I for their barking?” the count asked.

“They will cry out continually,” John replied.

“To whom, I ask? To some king of yours whom I do not know? To that duke of yours, Gislebert, whom I regard as the lowest of my servants? The same applies to his bishop, Adelbero, whom I had resolved to help as much as my strength allowed and for whose sake I took vengeance even on his stepfather, Richizo. But since he has now defected against me to Gislebert, let him see what advantage has come to him from that.”

Then John said: “We shall cry out to God, who will accept our person no less than yours.”

### 106

The count, now more agitated, said: “You will not take a horse or a beast of burden away from here.”

“That will be within your power,” John replied. “When no other counsel remains, I shall return on foot; but you will not thereby frighten away the others.”

The count, now more enraged, said: “You will be punished even in your limbs.”

[Note: [Col. 0293] The words corresponding to “you will be punished” are missing.]

“You can easily accomplish that,” John replied. “But it will be no less a punishment for me—a punishment which, assuredly, I shall not grieve over greatly. If you deprive me of my eyes, you will relieve me of great cares and labors, since I shall be able, while sitting, to devote myself more fully to psalms and prayers.”

When the count threatened him with mutilation of his manhood, John said: “You will make me secure from the greatest anxiety.”

He had almost ordered John to be seized when his wife, a prudent woman, intervened. Humbly she warned him not to dishonor himself with such disgrace, lest he should come to be called a man who spared neither monks nor servants of God. Since he denied their requests, she urged him at least to permit John to depart unharmed.

Thus released, and after receiving some travel provisions from the countess, who had received him with sufficient courtesy, John set out hastily. The duke gave him a guide who would escort him safely as far as places free of brigands.

[Note: [Col. 0293] One witness reads “freely”; another reads “places beset by brigands.”]

### 107

At about the third hour they entered a certain village where a market happened to be held that day. Suddenly they saw a crowd throughout the entire marketplace, robbing everyone alike—sellers and buyers—and threatening death to anyone who protested.

John looked at the companion he had brought from the monastery, who was carrying a shield, and said: “That shield has been brought here to our detriment, because you will not be able to use it as circumstances require, and it may perhaps provoke an attack against us.”

“Because you alone among mortal men walk so extraordinarily confidently,” the companion replied, “we shall perish by a death both deserved and appropriate.”

Just then, while they hesitated, the guide whom the countess had provided caught sight of someone known to him. He called that man over and explained the situation.

“You have come here at the greatest danger,” the man said, “and I do not know whether I can get you out of this as well.”

John replied: “You can at least lead us as far as the nearby forest that can be seen from here; the Lord will take care of the rest.”

They passed beyond the crowd and proceeded at a calm and measured pace as far as the forest. At the uncertain reading *Fronte captato* [Mabillon conjectures *Freno*, “with the bridle seized”], they spurred themselves on more vigorously. They crossed the thicket at a rapid run and, now in a safe grassy place, dismounted to take food.

### 108

John drew from a leather pouch some bread, cheese, and fish. [Col. 0295]

[Note: [Col. 0295] *panes* corrected to *panis* in witness c.]

[Lacuna; the conjecturally supplied word appears to be *equi*, “of the horse”:] having loosened the horse from behind him, he urged the guide to eat. While they were eating, the guide, adding a sigh,

[Note: [Col. 0295] I supply *adjecto* conjecturally; Labbe reads *producto*, “having brought forth,” but the letter *a* is visible.]

said:

“It has been three or certainly four months since I have used any food or drink honestly acquired, except what I am eating now. All of us—alas, wretched that we are!—feed only on the spoils and calamities of the wretched.”

John then began a salutary instruction. He exhorted the young man at length against such practices, telling him that it was far better to endure poverty, hunger, and thirst—which God would certainly relieve, as he does for birds and worms—than to persist in things by which God would be offended.

At last the conversation progressed to the point that the young man promised that from that day onward he would abstain from such acts. After they had eaten, John dismissed the young man and reached Gorze when the signal was given for the evening office.

### 109

Not many days had passed when a messenger from Count Boso arrived at Gorze and announced with anxious grief that his lord had collapsed into a grave illness, lay almost beyond hope, and urgently requested that the monk who had recently departed from him be sent to him.

At the abbot’s command John immediately set out swiftly.

[Note: [Col. 0295] The manuscript has *procreditur*; *progreditur*, “sets out,” is the correction.]

The count was told that he had arrived. When John appeared before him, the count said:

“When you recently departed from here, I did not think that the end of my life could overtake me so soon. Here, then, take the estates you requested; only make me their patron, and whatever you lose from them I shall repay in refined gold.”

After he had said and done these things, John withdrew from his sight and returned to the lodging where they had been ordered to receive suitable human care.

[Note: [Col. 0295] The manuscript has *humanae*; this is retained.]

The count, who had been weakened by excessive wasting and had been entirely without sleep for several days and nights, was suddenly overcome by sleep so deeply that he did not awaken from the ninth hour until nearly the third hour of the following day.

At last he awoke and repeatedly called for his wife by name, asking her to bring him something to eat. He had likewise had no opportunity to take anything for several days. After eating it with considerable pleasure, he again fell asleep until nearly the ninth hour. On awakening, he summoned John, declared him the restorer of his health, had him escorted with great honor, and offered himself ready to provide whatever he wished.

### 110

A possession of the monastery had long before passed by way of benefice to a certain count of the palace, Hamedeus, who likewise held the monastery’s property under what is called a *precaria* or *prestaria*.

When he died while still in possession of that estate, which was near the monastery, and before the body had been carried away to Metz for burial in the basilica of the blessed Virgin Mary called “at the hospice,” John at Gorze was informed.

[Note: [Col. 0292D] “At the hospice” is the basilica of the blessed Virgin Mary.]

The bishop happened then to have arrived there. John quickly informed the abbot of the matter and instructed him to approach the bishop.

The abbot entered at once and, with that gravity of his, hesitated for a little before saying:

“Have you heard? They say that your Hamedeus has died.”

“I had heard so,” the bishop replied.

The abbot continued: “He held a certain property of the monastery under a *precaria*. We ask that we be allowed to recover it.”

“Recover it with complete freedom,” the bishop replied.

The abbot reported the matter to John.

“What did you request?” John asked.

“The *precaria*,” he replied.

“I did not advise you to ask for that,” John said. “It would return to us freely. I advised you to ask that the benefice be restored.”

The abbot immediately returned to the bishop and said: “Brother John says that I have achieved nothing useful with you.”

“What, then, is being claimed?” the bishop asked.

“He urged me to reclaim certain properties belonging to the brothers’ table, which Hamedeus was holding.”

The bishop’s entire expression changed.

“You never held any of those properties,” he said. “They have always been assigned as a benefice.”

The real difficulty was that he had several brothers by the same mother, and until that time he had been unable to provide sufficiently for them. Many people held the episcopal properties, and neither law nor prudence permitted him to deprive them of those holdings; they had secured them by force from the possessions of earlier bishops. For that reason he was waiting for some opportunity of this kind, or another, to give something to his brothers.

### 111

Yet divine providence wonderfully opposed this intention of a holy man otherwise proved and distinguished in divine matters. For after the abbot’s reply had almost deterred the bishop from any further attempt, the bishop did go to the evening gathering, which he had once greatly enjoyed and at which he had formerly dined with them very pleasantly. But he merely tasted a little bread and immediately returned.

[Note: [Col. 0295] The manuscript is defective here.]

After Compline had been recited, he lay down. Turning many things over in his mind, he was wearied by sleeplessness until nearly midnight. When he could not fall asleep by any means, he rose, as was his custom, and attempted to devote himself to prayer. But his concentration was so much weaker than usual that, weary and listless, he returned to bed.

[Note: [Col. 0295] The manuscript reads *oratione*; *orationi*, “to prayer,” is the correction.]

[Note: [Col. 0297] The same correction is repeated.]

There, desiring sleep for a long time and exhausted by turning from one side to the other, he gained no result from it. He rose, went to the martyr’s chest, and, prostrate before it, confessed his fault. He promised by a vow to restore the properties in question and placed his staff upon the altar:

“Holy martyr,” he said, “I restore this to you as your own.”

Kneeling, he declared that he had never afterward offered a more intent or more fervent prayer. Rising from prayer, he sought his bed, quickly fell asleep, and, naturally compensating for his earlier restless vigil, prolonged his sleep well into the dawn.

[Note: [Col. 0297] The manuscript has *compensan*; *compensans*, “compensating,” is the correction.]

### 112

He awoke when the sun was already red and, troubled by the remembrance of the hymns he was accustomed to render, reflected at length on the matter. At last he rose and completed the praises.

He immediately ordered John to be summoned. When John was present, the bishop said:

“You have worn me out with a bad night. Go, take the staff placed upon the altar, and possess the estates you requested.”

John fell at his feet and said: “No, my lord; that is not appropriate. Rest for a while, since you are exhausted. Meanwhile, after the signal for Prime has been given and the office celebrated, enter the assembly of the brothers and restore what belongs to everyone as a free gift—not to one man, but to all.”

“Let it be done,” he replied.

### 113

Behold, a crowd of the bishop’s people gathered earlier than usual from various places. For he himself, following his custom, had entered the monastery gate with only two or three clerics and an equal number of chamberlains; after dismissing all his other companions, he remained within as a stranger to secular affairs.

[Note: [Col. 0297] The manuscript has *manasterii*; *monasterii* is the correction.]

Among those who gathered was his brother Gozilin. [Col. 0297]

[Note: [Col. 0297] After this point approximately twenty letters are missing; the restoration is conjectural.]

They had been admitted through the monastery gate, which an incautious ecclesiastical custodian had opened for them, and they proceeded straight to the chamber of the resting bishop.

As soon as John learned of their arrival [the text is defective here], he hurried out to meet them. Since it was forbidden to speak inside the monastery, he signaled them to follow him and made them turn back a long way to the gate, whispering in the custodian’s ear that he should immediately close it behind them.

There he detained them for some time with various words that were not especially pleasant, saying that the bishop, because he had been unable to sleep owing to the discomfort of the night, had only then gone to rest, and advising them to take some food in the meantime—for it was summer.

When they refused, saying that they wanted nothing except an audience with the bishop, he replied: “It is better to do that while he, after completing his customary duties, offers himself for an audience.”

Having delayed them in this way and occupied them with a quickly prepared refreshment, he himself returned inside and struck the signal. After Prime had been recited and the solemn psalms sung, the bishop was invited into the chapter house.

After offering the brothers some exhortation suitable to the occasion, the brothers, already partly informed of the matter, made their request for the properties mentioned above. He refused them nothing and, extending his staff, said:

“Let blessed Peter have what is his, and remember me.”

### 114

When these matters had been completed, those who had gathered immediately burst in, and his brother subjected him to vehement pressure concerning the same properties. After the response had been given to the monks, he continued to press him, saying that the monks already had more than enough from every side and that he ought rather to provide for his own family.

When he accomplished nothing and the bishop departed after eating with the brothers, the same argument was repeated from the very threshold of the monastery all the way to the ford of the river.

[Note: [Col. 0297] One witness reads “boundary”; another reads “threshold.”]

As the bishop was about to enter the ford and had already become thoroughly wearied, he said:

“You are striving in vain. Truly, even if I had granted half the episcopate to these monks, I would not take a footstep of land away from them on account of any one of you.”

There are many other instances in which, whenever opportunity arose, with John intervening, properties alienated from the monastery for many years were recovered. But since the minds of readers are hastening toward the end, and since we are sparing time as much as possible, let us proceed to run through the remainder of his life with our pen.

[Note: [Col. 0297] The closing words are conjecturally reconstructed from the defective source.]

Supplementary textual-apparatus register (keyed to the relevant passages):

- 93: witness c reads *ipsi*; witness c reads *recompensaret*, “he might make up”; at *etsi* (“although”), L now lacks a word.
- 94: at *mutari*, the note says that the word is not missing; at *refectione* and at *eundem*, L now lacks a word in each case.
- 96: witness c reads *comen*; witness c reads *majore*.
- 97: at *Exemplo*, L now lacks a word.
- 98: witness c reads *Repera*; witness c reads *eosque*.
- 101: witness c reads *peccunia*.
- 102: witness c reads *situm*.
- 104: after *possessiones* a word is now missing; witness c reads *hereditatorio*; witness c reads *abate*.
- 105: M has *abnegat*; witness c has *abnegato* (“having denied”).
- 106: witness c supplies the reading noted after “you will not thereby frighten away the others”; the words rendered “a punishment which” are conjecturally supplied. Witness 1 has *ab ea* (“from her”), while witness 2 has *a comitissa* (“from the countess”); witness 1 has the corrupt *com…*, while witness 2 has *ita*; witness 1 has *quidam*, witness 2 *quiddam*; and witness 1 has *libere*, whereas witness 2 reads *a latronibus obsessa libere* (“freely, [after passing] places beset by brigands”).
- 107: the printed reading is *Fronte captato*, perhaps *Monte*; Mabillon conjectures *Freno* (“with the bridle seized”).
- 109: witness c has *du*; witness c has *abisse*; witness c has *humanae*.
- 110: Labbe supplies the lacuna after *beneficii nomine*; *eo* is supplied conjecturally.
- 111: part of the text at the evening gathering is absent from the manuscript; the manuscript has *te* where the printed text has *ante*; it has *juribus* for *viribus* and *defetigatus* for *defatigatus*.
- 112: witness c has *tande*.
- 113: the restoration naming Gozilin is conjectural after a loss of about twenty letters; the manuscript reading at the subsequent marked point is recorded simply as *l.* The restorations “admitted by,” “monastery,” “to speak,” and “to return” are conjectural.
- Closing sentence: “But because the minds of readers hasten toward the end” and “sparing time as much as possible, let us proceed to run through the remainder of his life” are conjectural reconstructions of defective manuscript text.

115. An embassy from the king of Spain, Abderahamen (950?), had perhaps arrived with gifts sent in keeping with royal generosity, prompted by the fame of the glory and distinguished deeds among diverse peoples of Lord Otto, then already a great king and afterward august Caesar.

[Note: *fama gloriae insigniumque factorum* = “the fame of glory and distinguished deeds”; *advenerat* = “had arrived”; *postmodum vero Caesaris augusti* = “and afterward august Caesar.” The readings are conjectural. The apparatus also records *amititiam* for *amicitiam* (“friendship”), *blabsema* for *blasphema* (“blasphemous”), and *imperialibus* (“imperial”) as a manuscript reading.]

The envoys, led by a certain bishop, were received with the solemn dignity appropriate to so great a majesty and were detained for a long time. During the delay, the bishop who led the envoys died. While our people were considering whom they might likewise send back there, and after several matters had been debated at length, this finally was agreed: since that same king was sacrilegious and profane, being a Saracen and utterly alien to the true faith, and although he sought the friendship of a Christian ruler had nevertheless spewed forth in the letter he had sent certain blasphemies against Christ, they should reveal their own voice to him together with the imperial writings they were carrying and, if God should grant the opportunity, be able to change his unbelief.

116. (953.) Around those days our Adalbero, of sacred memory, had happened to visit the palace. Bruno, the king’s brother—later destined to be of great and fortunate service and distinction—was so thoroughly educated in wisdom and prudence, both in public affairs and in all the liberal disciplines, that he surpassed all his contemporaries and almost equaled the ancients. He had also acquired extensive training in Greek learning. He was the confidant of all public and private business at that time and its most prudent counselor; to him the administration of the imperial correspondence had been entrusted.

[Note: The manuscripts read *cu* for *cum* (“with”) and *tunc* for *tum* (“then”).]

While the others were consulting, he named our Adalbero, of sacred memory, as bishop. He added that no one more suitably could be entrusted with this task, since Adalbero himself had many perfect men who, as was sufficiently evident, would yield in no way to human threats: they had already died to the world and would speak with free mouth before any opponents on behalf of the faith.

The bishop was summoned immediately, and he was ordered to prepare two of his men for the embassy to Spain. Having received the instructions, he summoned Abbot Eginold and explained the royal command: he was to select two of his men who could carry out the order.

At first Angilramnus and Wido were chosen, and, by order of the royal majesty, provisions and the means for the journey were prepared from the monastery.

[Note: The conjectural reading *monasterio* means “from the monastery”; the printed form is defective.]

In addition, a certain man from Verdun, knowledgeable about the regions of Spain and ordered to escort them, was commanded to come without any further delay.

[Note: The conjectural reading gives “a certain man from Verdun, knowledgeable [about the regions of Spain].” Another conjecture renders the phrase “with all delay set aside, he was ordered to come.”]

But then Wido, one of those selected, was reprimanded one day in the assembly of the brothers for some negligence—I do not know precisely what.

[Note: The source has a long lacuna here: *pro qua nescio neglegentia ... in conventu fratrum*; Labbeus supplied the missing middle portion.]

He burst forth into such an outbreak of insolence against both the abbot and the whole community that, when the swelling of his excessive anger and madness could in no way be restrained and he would not in any respect submit to regular discipline, he was stripped of his cowl and expelled from the monastery.

This was immediately reported to the emperor.

[Note: The marginal note identifies him as King Otto I.]

The order was given that he be shaved and that another be enrolled in his place.

117. While this matter was being debated for a long time, and everyone absolutely refused, so that no one could be found in so large a community who admitted that he could undertake it in any way, John suddenly and without hesitation volunteered.

The abbot was somewhat displeased, because, while the entire business of the monastery rested upon John, he enjoyed a welcome quiet and would never willingly give it up if it could be avoided. Yet the perfection of charity prevailed, for it does not seek what belongs to itself but rather what belongs to others. At the same time, because he saw that the man desired martyrdom, if circumstances should so bring it about, he preferred to send him to Christ rather than retain him for his own needs.

Thus, with the emperor’s approval, John was sent on the bishop’s embassy. The emperor was all the more pleased, observing that John’s age and prudence made him entirely suitable for this business. He entrusted him with the imperial instructions, letters, and gifts, and made the aforementioned man from Verdun—whose name was Ermenhard—his companion because of his knowledge of the places and regions. John requested that the gifts be handed over to Ermenhard; he himself became merely the bearer of the letters.

Returning to Gorze, he hastened his journey and, setting aside his companion’s delays, departed alone with the letters, commended to the prayers and vows of all the saints. All his expenses were supplied by the monastery. Only one monk was added as his attendant, a man named Garamannus, a deacon by rank and of excellent character in every respect.

Five horses were assigned for riding and carrying the baggage.

[Note: The damaged phrase is conjecturally expanded as “horses were assigned for riding and carrying the baggage.”]

His companion remained in a certain village not far from Toul. He followed John as far as Scarpone, and from there they proceeded toward Longohas [Note: Langres], Belna [Note: Beaune, situated on the road to Lyon only after Dijon], Dijon, and Lyon, intending to go toward Spain.

[Note: The source has a defective phrase concerning the companion’s pursuit of John to Scarpone; the reading “he followed John as far as Scarpone” is conjectural. A manuscript reads *Longohas*; the note identifies it as Langres. Another note records Mabillon’s reading *Viennam*, “now toward Vienne,” in place of *Hispaniam*.]

118. (953.) At Lyon, after loading the baggage onto a ship and having it transported along the Rhône as far as a fixed point, they suffered no small loss—for their ships were attacked, and they lost much of their property. After recovering some of it, they continued toward Spain.

[Note: *Lugdunum* is identified as Lyon. The source reads *Rhodano* (“the Rhône”).]

When they reached Barcelona, they stayed for fifteen days, until a messenger was sent from Tortosa. That was the first city of the Saracen king.

[Note: The manuscript variant is *Bartinonam* for *Barcinonam* (“Barcelona”).]

The governor immediately ordered them to hurry on, but, after receiving them, detained them for an entire month and provided for all their needs, until the king of Córdoba was informed more quickly and royal instructions were sent throughout the individual cities and places that they were to be received with fitting royal honor.

At last they were escorted to Córdoba, the royal city. A house nearly two miles from the palace was assigned to them, where, amid royal luxury—with every kind of provision supplied, even things beyond ordinary use—they were compelled to remain for several days.

[Note: The manuscript reads *regificio* for *regifico*, both referring to royal magnificence or luxury.]

119. (954.) When they had grown weary of the delay and asked those who were caring for them why they were being detained so long from the king’s presence, they were told that the envoys previously sent by their own king had been detained for three years, and that they themselves had been sentenced to remain away from the royal presence for three times as long—that is, nine years.

Meanwhile, certain men from the palace came there to see them and inquire about the reason for their arrival. While cleverly investigating everything and obtaining no definite information from them—for the visitors said that they were permitted to disclose their instructions to no one except the king in person—the palace men boasted that they already knew everything and that, because the visitors were bringing letters to the king contrary to their laws, the greatest danger undoubtedly threatened them. They added that the letters had already come to the notice of the leading men.

And in fact, although this had happened through deception, it was so. For from the city of Toul in our province they had taken with them a certain priest, a companion of the deceased bishop’s envoy mentioned above. He shared everything with them throughout the entire journey. When they reached Tortosa, which was the first city of the Saracen kingdom, he feared for his life: if he returned without letters, having been the companion of the deceased envoy, he might be in danger. Therefore, asking to be shown the letters that had been entrusted to him, he quickly took possession of them.

[Note: The passage is conjectural: *fido sibi poscens monstrari litteras eorum* means approximately “asking, as one who trusted them, to be shown their letters.”]

While they remained meanwhile at Augusta and the other cities they had left behind after Tortosa, he went ahead to Córdoba with the letters.

[Note: The reading “while they remained at Augusta and the other cities they had left after Tortosa” is conjectural. The manuscript has *remerantibus* for *remorantibus* (“remaining”).]

How these became publicly known was not sufficiently discovered; nevertheless, the rumor stirred the nobles and the people.

[Note: The wording “how they became known to the populace” is conjectural; the surviving text is defective around *optimates ... populumque*.]

120. Accordingly, the leading men held counsel among themselves. Since they were investigating whether the matter had already come to the king’s knowledge, and had not sufficiently established that it had, they decided to question the king about it personally.

For a law so unappealable bound them that what had once been established for the entire people in ancient times could never be dissolved in any way. King and people alike were bound together by an equal knot, and every transgression was punished by the sword. If anything was committed by those of lower rank, the king dealt with it; if the king himself committed anything, the entire people took action against him.

Among those laws the first and most dreadful was that no one might ever dare to speak against their religion. Whether citizen or foreigner, without any possibility of ransom, he was punished by death. If the king himself heard such words and did not retain the sword until the following day, he too was condemned to death, and no mercy could intervene.

When those leading men therefore went to the palace and had conveyed this matter to the king through messengers—for access to him was extremely rare, and unless something of the greatest importance arose no one approached him; everything was conveyed only in writing by chamberlains and attendants—he sent back word that nothing of the kind had been brought to him. He said that friends had sent him envoys, that his son had received them in his own house, and that he had not yet learned what they were bringing.

Thus their agitation was calmed. For the rumor had in fact already reached him, and, having secretly sent messengers, he had discovered that it was true; but out of fear of his own people he had suppressed the whole matter in this way.

[Note: The manuscript repeats *parique* (“by an equal”) and has *inferioribus* (“by those of lower rank”).]

121. The king, fearful and anxious on every side, considered that danger might threaten him and tried every kind of stratagem to escape it.

First he sent to them a certain Jew named Hasdeu, whom our people testified that they had never seen or heard of anyone more prudent.

[Note: The wording “whom they had never seen or heard to be more prudent” is conjectural.]

He was to investigate everything thoroughly from the men themselves. Since word had been spread by rumor that he was the bearer of a royal mandate, he first lifted John out of the fear that troubled them, so as to win John’s confidence. He declared that none of them would [lacuna] suffer any harm there, but that they would be sent back to their homeland with honor.

[Note: The passages concerning Hasdeu’s royal mandate and his winning John’s confidence are conjectural.]

He gave them much instruction about the customs of the people and how they ought to conduct themselves among them. The younger men, in particular, were to restrain themselves from every frivolous or wanton gesture and utterance; nothing would be so insignificant that it would not immediately be reported to the king’s knowledge. If they were given the opportunity to go outside, they were not even to approach women with any kind of buffoonery or gesture, since no plague could be more destructive to them. They were not to exceed the law imposed upon them, so that they should be watched by no one with greater strictness; if detected, they would be held in no regard.

John replied to these matters as appropriate and received the advice with complete appreciation. He also poured shame upon his own people through the man belonging to the opposing party. After many exchanges, the Jew cautiously entered upon the matter. He carefully asked what the men who had sent him were carrying.

When he saw John hesitate a little—for they were then speaking privately—he pledged his silence and, indeed, his safe assistance in counsel if it should be needed.

John set everything out in order: the gifts sent to the king and, in addition, the letter to be brought to the king’s ears. Without that letter, neither were the gifts to be displayed nor was it lawful for them to approach the king’s presence. He also explained the letter’s position in words.

“It is dangerous,” said the Jew, “to see the king with this. Be cautious about what answer you give to the royal messengers sent to you. I do not doubt that the severity of the law has already become known to you, and you must prudently consider how to avoid it.”

122. When that man had departed, after several months a certain bishop named John was sent to them. After many requests and replies exchanged in mutual conversation, as is customary among the faithful, he introduced the king’s command: they were to come into the king’s presence with the gifts alone.

“What, then,” John said, “of the imperial letters? Was I not sent chiefly on their account? For he himself sent beforehand certain blasphemous statements, which must also be refuted and overturned by destroying the empty inventions of his error.”

[Note: The conjectural reading is *vana erroris sui commenta*, “the empty inventions of his error.”]

The other, now more moderate, replied: “Consider under what conditions we are acting. We have been brought down by our sins to the point that we are subject to the rule of pagans. The apostle forbids us by word to resist authority. Only this one consolation remains to us amid so great a calamity: their laws do not prevent us from using our own laws. They honor and embrace those whom they see to be devoted observers of Christianity, and they take pleasure in their company, while they utterly detest the Jews.

“For the present, therefore, we seem to have adopted this policy: since no injury to religion is being imposed, we should comply with the rest and obey their commands insofar as they do not hinder the faith. Hence it is now much better for you to remain silent about these matters and suppress that letter altogether than to provoke against yourself and your companions, without any necessity pressing, a most destructive scandal.”

123. John, somewhat more agitated, said:

“It would have been more fitting for someone other than you, who appear to be a bishop, to say such things. Since you are an advocate of the faith, and since your higher rank has also appointed you its defender, you ought not, through human fear, to restrain others from proclaiming the truth, still less to withdraw yourself from it. It would have been far better for a Christian man to endure the grave loss of food than to join himself to food that destroys others among the gentiles.

“Moreover, I hear that you have been circumcised according to their rite—something detestable and impious to the whole Catholic Church—although the apostle’s strong declaration protests: ‘If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing’ (Galatians 5:2).

“And concerning the foods that, because of communion with them, you abominate: ‘All things are clean to the clean’ (Titus 1:15); and: ‘There will be teachers of empty words and deceivers, teaching this and that, and, among other things, abstinence from foods that God created to be received with thanksgiving by the faithful’ (Titus 1:10; 1 Timothy 4:3); and: ‘For it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer’ (1 Timothy 4:5).”

The other replied:

“Necessity constrains us; otherwise we would have no opportunity to live among them. Indeed, we hold this practice as something handed down and observed by our ancestors from the most ancient times.”

John said: “I would never approve that divine ordinances be transgressed through fear, love, or mortal favor. You see that, having turned aside from them, they now abuse you under the pretext of authority [lacuna]. … your consent may be [lacuna] … you seem to make [lacuna] love for the kingdom of heaven; for you admit that necessity compels you to assent to them.

“But I, free from these necessities by the grace of Christ, stand with a mind fixed upon the Lord, by his mercy, and will not be turned by any terror, inducement, or favor from what I have undertaken at the emperor’s command.

“For I will meet him neither without the imperial letter, nor with any part of it removed or altered, not even a single letter. And if anyone rails against what we bear as sound and Catholic faith, and comes forward in opposition to these declarations, I will resist openly, nor, for love of life itself, will I flee from bearing witness to the truth.”

[Note: The source is defective after *... vobis res fuerit consensus*. The surviving words include *necessitate constrictos assentire* (“to assent, compelled by necessity”) and *Domino* (“the Lord”); the lacunae are retained rather than supplied.]

124. (954.) These words were secretly reported to the king. For the king had not yet sent public instructions to which a public reply might be given; that bishop had come only for the purpose of investigation.

The king, whose cunning was said to surpass that of all mortals, devised consultations of every kind, trying to assault the man’s mind now from this direction, now from that, and, like a fortified wall battered by engines devised through various arts, striving to shake the firmness of his heart if any means could be found.

(955.) When, after a month or a period of six or seven weeks, royal messengers were sent to him and asked what he had decided for himself, and they reported that nothing had changed from his original position, the king was driven into various courses by wonder at such steadfastness.

At first he believed that he could terrify him more by fear for the Christians, who freely practiced their religious observances and their own affairs within his kingdom. On a certain day, which was a Sunday, he sent him a letter full of threats.

Only on Sundays, or on the greatest festivals of our religion—Christmas, Epiphany, Easter, the Ascension, Pentecost, Saint John’s feast, the feasts of the apostles, or those of named saints—were they permitted to go to the nearest church, which was dedicated to Saint Martin. Twelve guards, whom they call *sagiones*, escorted them on either side.

When he had gone to the church that Sunday, the letter was handed to him on the very road. Its size was frightening—for it was a square sheep’s hide—and he feared that it might draw him away from the communion of the sacred rites toward which he was going. Therefore he postponed opening it until they had completed the rites and returned to their lodging.

[Note: The manuscript reads *deducentebus*, corrected to *deducentibus* (“escorting”); *terrebat* is conjecturally understood as “was frightening.” The repeated apparatus includes the conjectural phrase “lest it draw him away from the communion of the sacred rites.”]

When he unfolded it, he found threats concerning things that could happen to him, and he confessed that he had never on any other occasion been so shaken by threats.

125. For, after many threats made to him if he did not consent to the king’s commands—threats by which he nevertheless testified that he had not been moved in the least—the final addition was this: if the king killed him, he would leave no Christian alive in the whole of Spain, but would slaughter them all with the sword.

He added:

“Consider,” he said, “how many souls of those killed because of you you will be answerable for before God. They will perish through no other guilt than your obstinacy, although they ought especially to have hoped for peace and safety from you, and although you could obtain from us whatever you wished for them, if only you would cease persisting against us with such obstinacy.”

After he had silently read these words on the road by which they were returning from the church to their lodging, and had for some time been tossed about by great agitation of mind, considering either what counsel he might adopt against them or how he might write back to the king—for he did not have sufficient experience in composing written replies—a saying from heaven suddenly, as he often confessed to us, drove all terror and fear from his mind:

“Cast your care upon the Lord” (Psalm 55:23);

and another:

“Who made man’s mouth? Is it not I?” (Exodus 4:11).

126. As soon as he entered the lodging, he said:

“Brother Garamannus, quickly prepare the hide on which you are to write down whatever I dictate.”

When the other immediately brought out a cut square of hide, John ordered him to take it. With the pen ready, he sat down and began. The abundance of his words overcame the speed of the scribe, so that the scribe repeatedly complained that he could not keep up while so much was being added. For Garamannus was extremely accomplished and practiced in that art.

First he replied point by point:

He had been sent as an envoy and was bound to preserve inviolate his fidelity to the imperial commands. It was not lawful for him, when so great a majesty had entrusted him with his letters—letters that were not sealed—to see the face of the person to whom he had been sent without those letters, or for them to be read before the king to whom they had been sent without him.

If the king permitted this, he would fail in no respect toward the royal honor, because [lacuna].

Otherwise, he would endure every kind of torture rather than transgress anything beyond what had been commanded to him or beyond what the cause entrusted to him required. Just as he had not delayed replying to those who had already tried to terrify him, so, even if every individual member of his body were cut apart by daily mutilations, beginning with the smallest joints and continuing up to the vital organs—for no greater torture could ever be inflicted than if one day one joint of a finger were cut off, the next day another, then one by one on successive days, followed by the arm, shoulder, thigh, shin, and foot, and finally the remaining trunk were pierced—he would nevertheless not be terrified into yielding in any way.

[Note: The conjectural reading is “rather than endure anything beyond what had been commanded or what the entrusted cause required.” Labbeus supplied the phrase “from the smallest joints.” The manuscript has *cruce* where the sense requires *crure* or “shin.”]

He also knew well, from the report of those previously sent to him, that the king himself had already realized that John did not greatly fear death. Therefore it was pointless to try to terrify him with what he regarded as trivial.

As for what the king had written—that, if John were killed, he would leave no Christian alive in the whole of Spain and that God would charge John with responsibility for so great a slaughter—this stood quite otherwise. John was not the cause of their killing; the cause was the king’s own malice and cruelty. While the king paid the penalty for those he killed, John, with those who were slain, would, by Christ’s favor, enter upon a better life.

Yet God could easily change even this outcome, just as Mordecai once instructed Esther:

“If you refuse to intervene now, perhaps the Jews will be delivered through some other opportunity, while you and your household will perish” (Esther 4:14).

So now also God could do the same: after everything had been proclaimed by the king himself, the Lord could help those men at their very necks with swords, in a new and unforeseen manner.

Accordingly, John knew that he could not in any way be moved by threats or terrors of this kind. For the one who had rescued Mordecai, steadfast in his constancy, from the arrogance of Haman by a wonderful ordering of events would not abandon John, since he was involved not on account of insolence but for the sake of obedience; rather, in whatever manner seemed pleasing to him, God would stand by him.

Words of this kind, expanded with many additional statements and supported here and there by the force of suitable testimonies, filled the entire surface of the page. They did not cease to flow from his mouth until the scribe confessed that the hide had been completely filled and that nothing remained.

127. When this was brought to the king, it did not inflame his mind to anger as before; rather, it was referred to the royal council.

[Note: The wording “it was brought before the royal council” is conjectural.]

He had already been warned by his own men, among whom the affair of our people had become widely known, that these matters should be concealed from him, lest he attempt to oppose our emperor. They said that our emperor was a most warlike conqueror of many peoples and that he would avenge every injury—especially injuries to envoys—with an anger more savage than any he had previously shown. Having gathered the forces of many kingdoms, he might eventually subject all Spain to himself by the right of conquest after devastating it with various calamities.

After many such statements had been made, someone happened to suggest that, since the man appeared to possess such constancy and could be judged to possess no less prudence—since even so long a delay had shown him so firmly fixed in his law—and since he therefore might not deny faith to mortals, they should consult him personally about what ought to be done.

Thus, when messengers came to him and he had received these final instructions, he said:

“At last you have approached the matter with wiser counsel. If this had been sought at the beginning, so many periods of time would not have prolonged such wearisome and anxious difficulties for you or for us. Now the answer is quick and easy: let your king send an embassy to our lord the emperor, so that he may write to me what I ought to do concerning the matters entrusted to me. When I have seen his letter again, I will obey in everything.”

128. When this was reported to the king, and the advice was accepted as coming from a prudent source, an inquiry was ordered into who would undertake such a journey. Few or almost none openly came forward, although it had been proposed that whoever went there would return with whatever honor he sought and with gifts of every kind.

At last, among the palace officials, there emerged a certain Recemundus, thoroughly Catholic and very well trained in both our language and the Arabic language of the people among whom he lived.

He held such an office at the royal court that, after hearing outside the palace the cases of various people who came there because of their needs—for all complaints and cases there were recorded and answered in writing—he would bring in the matters he had noted and likewise carry back the written responses. Several others had also been assigned to the same office.

Observing the others’ hesitation, and while the rest hesitated to seize the opportunity perhaps offered to him, he said:

“What will be the reward for a man who sells you his soul?”

[Note: The reading *haesitantibus* (“hesitating”) is conjectural; the preceding word is marked as uncertain.]

For this was their customary expression: whenever anyone was sent as a messenger into the greatest danger, they said to him, “Sell me your soul.” If he returned safely, he was rewarded as generously as possible.

When Recemundus asked this, he was told that whatever such a man requested would be granted to him. He asked only that he be given permission to speak with the envoys in private and then announce whether he ought to attempt the journey.

129. After this was granted, Recemundus approached John and carefully inquired about the customs and institutions of our homeland: what sort of clemency the emperor possessed, how moderate he was toward his subjects, whether he was quick to anger, and whether he was irrevocable in a judgment once pronounced. After many questions of this kind, he finally asked whether John trusted him enough to present a royal embassy to him, lest the one who was being sent repay upon himself the long period during which John had been detained there.

John quickly replied that everything would turn out well. He freed him from all hesitation and fear and assured him that he would everywhere be received with joy and public congratulations.

He said that he would send a letter to his own abbot, who would receive Recemundus magnificently, keep and care for him as long as he wished, and, after presenting him to the bishop, would bring him—either with the bishop himself or with the bishop’s embassy—into the emperor’s presence in peace and favor.

Attracted by these promises, Recemundus returned to the palace and devoted himself to the journey, provided that what he requested was granted. There happened to be a church recently left vacant by the death of its bishop. He requested it as the reward for his labor. His request was readily granted, and he suddenly passed from layman to bishop.

130. Equipped with royal funds and letters, he quickly made for Gaul (June) and reached Gorze in approximately ten weeks (August). He was received there by everyone with congratulations. A few days later, he was invited into the city by the holy bishop Adelbero, stayed with him for several days, and was treated most pleasantly.

Afterward, visiting the various places belonging to the bishop with him, and having arrived already in the declining part of August, he spent autumn and winter with him. Once the feast of the Lord’s Nativity had passed, arrangements were made for his dispatch to the emperor.

Meanwhile, his affairs and several of his people remained at Gorze to be attended to.

Then, around the feast of holy Mary, Mother of God (956; February 2), he was led to the emperor by that venerable bishop, accompanied also by Lord Abbot Eginold, and was honorably received at the palace at Frankfurt (March).

[Note: The source has conjectural readings for “Mother of God,” “accompanied by Abbot Eginold,” and “after his embassy had been heard.”]

After his embassy had been heard, and the envoy’s faithfulness and constancy had been praised with the highest commendation, milder letters were ordered to be carried.

John was written to that the earlier letters were to be suppressed; he was to proceed only with gifts, arrange friendship and peace by whatever means he could concerning the attacks of the Saracen brigands, and hasten his return.

A certain man from Verdun named Dudo was sent to carry the new gifts and instructions.

Thus the Spaniard returned to Gorze, and, after most of the sacred Forty Days had passed (March 30), he set out around Palm Sunday with the imperial envoy and reached Córdoba at the beginning of June.

[Note: The source is cut off after “Thus the Spaniard returned to Gorze.”]

When they soon wished to enter the palace with the new messenger, the king said:

“By no means. Let those who have prolonged the dispute for so long proceed first with the earlier gifts and commands. Then let the second group be brought in order. These men will not see my face at all unless they first visit that monk who has persisted for so long and gladden him with news of his homeland, his loved ones, his king, and his commands.”

131. After everything had been completed, John, now released from nearly three years of confinement, was ordered to appear in the king’s presence.

[Note: The reading “three years” is conjectural; see below, chapter 134.]

When the envoys told him to prepare himself for presentation before the king by cutting his hair, washing his body, and putting on finer clothing, he refused. They concluded that he had no change of clothing and reported this to the king.

The king immediately sent him ten pounds of coins, so that he might purchase garments in which he could decently appear before the king’s eyes. For the custom of the people did not allow anyone to be presented before the royal presence in shabby clothing.

John initially hesitated about whether to accept the money. At last, considering that it would be better spent for the use of the poor, he thanked the king for his generosity and for having deigned to show such concern for him.

Then he added an answer worthy of a monk:

“I do not despise royal gifts. But I shall wear no clothing other than that which a monk is permitted to use—no cloaks at all, nor any garments dyed in any color except black alone.”

[Note: The text is defective; the conjectural wording includes “which a monk is permitted to wear” and “unless dyed black.”]

When this was reported to the king, he said:

“By this answer I recognize his steadfast mind. Even if he comes dressed in sackcloth, I shall gladly see him, and he will please me all the more.”

132. After this, on the appointed day when he was to be presented, preparations of every kind were assembled to display royal pomp.

All along the road from their lodging to the city, and from there to the royal palace, various ranks stood packed on either side. Here infantrymen stood with spears planted in the ground; farther on, they brandished and shook various spears and javelins in their hands and pretended to strike one another. After these came men mounted on mules, wearing a light kind of armor. Then horsemen drove their horses forward with spurs, amid neighing and varied leaps.

There were also Moors of unfamiliar appearance, frightening our people. Amid various displays—which our men regarded with astonishment—they were led to the palace along a road excessively covered in dust. The dust was such as the dryness of the season itself would have raised unaided, for it was the summer solstice.

[Note: The source says that the solstice fell on a Saturday, June 21, 956.]

The leading men came out to meet them. At the very outer threshold, the entire pavement was spread with the most precious carpets and cloaks.

133. When they reached the chamber where the king sat alone, like some divine being accessible to no one or to very few, everything was covered on every side with unfamiliar hangings, making the pavement appear continuous with the walls.

The king himself reclined upon a couch furnished with as much luxury as possible.

[Note: Labbeus supplied *magnifico*, “magnificent.”]

For unlike other peoples, they do not use thrones or chairs when conversing or eating, but recline upon beds or couches, with one leg placed over the other.

[Note: The text is defective; Labbeus supplied the missing wording.]

When John therefore came before him, he extended his hand to be kissed. He admitted no kiss from anyone, whether his own people or foreigners. He never offered the open palm of his hand outside to lesser or ordinary persons; only to the highest-ranking men whom he received with greater ceremony did he extend the middle of his palm to be kissed.

134. Then, when a chair had been prepared, he signaled with his hand that he should sit. A long silence followed on both sides. Then the king began:

“I have known for a very long time that your heart was greatly hostile toward me, since at last I suspended you from my presence. But you yourself know perfectly well that it could not have been done otherwise. I have tested your courage ([Tuam, conjectural restoration; Col. 0309]) and wisdom; foreign [circumstances?] delayed [me], so that I should not see you with the letter ([a. ne v. t. c. episto], conjectural restoration; Col. 0309); but I want you to understand that this was not done out of hatred for you. And I not only receive you now willingly ([olam te n. l. ex], conjectural restoration; Col. 0309), but you will obtain whatever you may ask.””

At this, John—as he later reported to us ([lacuna in the manuscript; Col. 0309])—who had been thinking ([cogitabat, conjectural restoration; Col. 0309]) of vomiting out upon the king some of the gall accumulated through such prolonged anguish, suddenly became so calm that nothing could ever have been more composed in his spirit. He then answered each point in turn:

“He could not deny that at first he had been deeply shaken by so many bitter messages. Yet, even amid those events, he had often reflected silently that these things were being done against him more through feigned than genuine threats. Finally, he had also learned from the deeds and words of the entire preceding three years that all the obstacles of delay had been removed, and that nothing remained which he ought reasonably to suspect had been done out of hatred for him. Therefore, if there had been any such matters, he had entirely cast them from his mind; he rejoiced only in the favor which the king had offered with such gracious magnificence, and he had clearly perceived in this matter a remarkably excellent balance between the strength of the royal heart, its steadfastness, and its measured moderation.”

Having thus won the king over to great goodwill, and while the king was preparing to address him at greater length, John first requested that the imperial gifts be received. When this had been done, he immediately begged permission to return. The king, astonished, said:

“How can this separation take place so suddenly? For so long a period we have awaited one another; now, scarcely having seen each other, are we to break off as strangers? In the meantime, having once obtained the sight of each other, a small measure of knowledge has opened each of our minds to the other; after seeing one another a second time, still more will be established; and at the third meeting the entire fullness of acquaintance, or friendship ([amititiae in manuscript C; Col. 0309]), will be confirmed.” Then you shall be sent back to your lord, and you shall be escorted with the honor due to him and to you.”

When John had assented to this, the second envoys were ordered to be admitted, and, in his presence, the gifts they had brought were presented.

[Col. 0310B]

135. Only then, after both parties had been sent back to their lodgings, was John recalled by the king some time later, and he engaged him in much familiar conversation: concerning the power and prudence of our emperor; the strength and abundance of his soldiers and army; his glory and wealth; the skill and successes of his warfare ([the word is cut off in the source; Col. 0309]); and many matters of this kind.

The king, on the other hand, boasted of how greatly the strength of his army surpassed that of all the kings of the age ([e. r. o, conjectural restoration; Col. 0309]). John answered little ([spondit, conjectural restoration; Col. 0309]), so as somehow to calm the king’s spirit, and finally added ([r. a. m. t. a., conjectural restoration; Col. 0309]):

“I truly confess that I know no king in this age [the remainder is cut off in the source; Col. 0309] who could equal our emperor on land in arms or horses.”

136. But the king, his anger calmed ([ira se, conjectural restoration; Col. 0309]) or lulled, said:

“You praise your king without justification.”

“Whether these things are true or false,” he replied, “he may test for himself.”

The king then said:

“I approve of everything else in both of you; but there is one matter in which he has proved insufficiently prudent.”

“What is that?” he asked.

“That he does not retain the power of his authority for himself alone, but allows each of his men to exercise his own power freely, so that he divides the parts of his kingdom among them—as though by doing so he might make them more faithful and more subject to him. This is far from the case. For thereby pride and rebellion against him are nourished and prepared, as has now happened in the case of his son-in-law, who, after treacherously carrying off his son, exercised open tyranny against him, even to the point of bringing the foreign people of the Hungarians through the very middle of his kingdoms to lay waste to them.”

[Col. 0310D] [Note: In the year 964. Here it will be useful to cite what is read about our John in chapter 30 of the Life of Blessed Kaddroë, abbot of Waulsort, then under Theodoric, bishop of Saint Felix or Clement of Metz:

“But, to give an example from this, John, abbot of the monastery of Gorze, a pillar in the temple of God—whose death, as I do not know who says (Virgil, Eclogue V, 28),

‘The lions of Carthage have groaned,

and the mountains, wild beasts, and forests speak’—

was lying in bed, stricken by a grave disorder of the body. And because he was a man of indescribable abstinence, he tormented his weakened limbs, as he used to do when healthy, with dry foods, compelled by the spirit. Father Kaddroë, hearing this, came to Gorze, led by charity. Not realizing that he could restore him to the children of the Church, he ordered meat dishes to be prepared, and when the hour of refreshment arrived, a little table was set before them. When John shrank from touching the food that had been brought, Kaddroë, knowing that charity does not seek its own interests, and who had long ago resolved, out of love of frugality, not even to touch an egg, took the meat and ate it. When the man of God John saw this, no longer able to oppose his command, he restored his weakened limbs with food until he recovered. What then? Did not Kaddroë serve the charity of Christ in this also? Then he returned to the monastery and took up again the shield of abstinence against spiritual wickedness.”]

IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 983. ODO, DEACON OF AUSCII.

[Col. 0311]

LETTER OF ODO TO GARCIA, ARCHBISHOP OF AUSCII, concerning the church of Saint Venantia, which William, count of Astarac, gave to the church of Auch.

(Gallia Christiana, vol. I, Appendix, p. 159.)

[Col. 0311A]

ODO THE LEVITE TO GARCIA, ARCHBISHOP.

Most holy bishop, you compel me to bring forth a recent work. But because I am unable to struggle against the judgment of the authorities, I blush to violate their prerogative by speaking. For it is indeed dreadful to fall into the hands of the living God, who, as the just Judge, will terrifyingly judge us and require an account not only of wicked deeds but also of an idle word and even of an evil thought on the day of judgment.

And since such a union is found to have been prohibited by almighty God and by the holy canons, so that not only those who perform it but also those who consent to it are judged deserving of punishment, I fear to put my hand to the execution of your command, dreading what the dreadful reading of the Gospel freely declares: “Whoever,” it says, “shall break one of these least commandments and so teach men shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5:19).

This work presses upon me in two ways: by the occasion for, and the precaution against, crimes; and by the reproach of censure from those ignorant of blame. What learned man, then, when he takes this little work into his hands and finds me, its notary, involved in such a mixture of kinship, would not immediately break out in speech, loudly proclaiming that I am a sacrilegious defiler, daring to usurp some counsel contrary to God’s permission? Yet, against the envy of my adversary, a double cause consoles me: both that you, who are the supreme bishop, have been required to act as judge, and that the necessity of the whole Church of Aquitaine, over which with God’s help you preside as mother, demanded it.

[Col. 0311C]

Finally, I know perfectly well that, after the prophetic, evangelical, and apostolic Scriptures by which the Church of God was founded through his grace, I ought also to make this clear: although the catholic Church spread throughout the world is like one bridal chamber of Christ, nevertheless the holy Roman Church has been placed before the other Churches not by synodal decrees but by the evangelical voice of our Lord and Savior, who obtained primacy for it:

“You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven. And whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew 16:18–19).

Therefore I do not doubt that, by the grace of God, the marvelous power of the aforesaid Church has been conferred upon you in its place: by divine clemency you are, in lawful succession, its seventh bishop, with power to close and to open the gates of the blessed life.

It seems a very superstitious and detestable matter for a deacon to undertake what has been commanded by his own bishop, lest I perhaps be found disobedient and deserve to be deprived of the rank mentioned above, and lest I be slain because of my devotion to you, who are pre-eminent. For, with God’s help, I shall make known to all the faithful, and especially to the holy Church of God, to our relatives and successors, what my eyes have seen and my ears have heard. My tongue will not cease to bear witness; and if the Lord fulfills that saying, I shall open my mouth.

Recently it happened that William, son of Arnold, count of Astarac, was about to take his kinswoman as wife. When Archbishop Garcia pressed him with threats so that he would not at all wish to perpetrate this crime, and entirely denied him permission to enter into this union by his consent, affirming that such kinship had been prohibited from being touched by the holy Fathers, and when he saw that he was accomplishing nothing and that the aforesaid count was lending him no ear for hearing, he returned to himself and accepted this counsel from his own people.

Knowing, therefore, that it is better to offer some rudder to a shipwrecked spirit than to leave it without the oars of repentance in the whirlpool of despair, he summoned him and granted him periods of fasting and gifts of alms, as is written in the following little document. Moreover, he received from him a noble town that had formerly been taken by wicked men from the church of Blessed Mary, the episcopal church of Auch.

And, with the aforesaid estate over which the church of Saint Venantia presides restored, [he received] the whole and entire property, with all its appurtenances, both parishes and adjoining chapels, without the participation or objection of anyone, so that he might possess it fully, and, while possessing it, do with it whatever he wished or whatever pleased him, and leave it after his death to his successors. May this charter remain firm, because it has truly been secured upon the Firm One, who is Christ, the rock.

If anyone should wish to disturb this charter and become its adversary, may he first fall under the wrath of God and be subject to a curse at all times; may he succumb to the leprosy of Naaman, be dominated by the ulcers of Job, die the death of Ananias and Sapphira, sink with Dathan and Abiram into the lowest Tartarus, burn with the Sodomites and Gomorrhites in everlasting fire, and be tortured without end with Judas Iscariot, the devil, and his angels. And what more? May he deserve to be filled with every kind of curse and leave to all the living an example of the punishment of wickedness. Amen.

These are the names of the princes and leaders who saw and confirmed this donation:

Bernard, his brother.  
Raymund, his brother.  
Garcia, his brother.  
Agganricus, and his kinsman.  
Atto, bishop of Toulouse.  
Ludovicus of Savannes.  
Enardus of Montalto.  
Arnoldus of Ouran.  
Arnoldus of Mojanac.  
Bernardus of Maurac.  
Arnoldus of Lomagne.  
Fortas of Ballicava.  
William of Galbisan.  
Raymundus of Furesacco, and his brothers.

I ask that, if you may search into these matters, you remember your deacon, most holy bishop.

IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 983. POPE BENEDICT VII.

[Col. 0313]

HISTORICAL NOTICE.

(From Eggs, *Pontificium doctum*, p. 281.)

Benedict VII, a Roman from the counts of Tusculum, son of Count Deodatus, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and bishop of Sutri, after Franco or Boniface VII, the invader of the Holy See, had been expelled through the efforts of his relatives, was proclaimed supreme pontiff in a lawful election on the Kalends of June in the year of our salvation 975.

As soon as he had been elected pope, he turned his attention to restoring the state of the Church and the conduct of the clergy, which had been grievously corrupted by the injustice of the times. For this purpose he celebrated a Roman synod, at which he also restored Arnulf, bishop of Reims, who had been expelled from his see through the sedition of certain people.

Then he turned to repairing churches and monasteries, restoring many of them from their foundations, or founding and endowing those newly established. Among these, he completely restored the monastery of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, together with its basilica, which had collapsed through age, bringing monks there.

He received Sergius, bishop of Damascus, who had been driven out by the Saracens, at Rome with the welcoming embrace of his merciful kindness, and entrusted to him the church of Saint Alexius to inhabit. There Sergius gathered exiled monks and restored monastic observance; after he had lived there for four years, he died a holy death. At his tomb in the same church there is still visible a noble inscription carved in verse, which begins:

“Sergius lies buried here, the metropolitan,

who once for a long time had been of Damascus,

brought by divine will to the sacred threshold of Peter.

In the days of pious Benedict, the gracious bishop,” and so forth.

Benedict also received Lambert, bishop of Kraków, as an envoy to Rome from Mieszko, prince of Poland, so that he might inform the Roman pontiff of the prosperous spread of the Christian faith in his principality, and ask him to send him a royal diadem and command that he and his descendants be kings of the Poles. Lambert left Rome without accomplishing his mission, either because news had arrived of Mieszko’s death, or because the Roman pontiff had been divinely warned to postpone the matter to more favorable times.

At the beginning of Benedict VII’s pontificate, Harald, king of the Danes, who had first imposed the Christian faith upon the people subject to him and had filled almost the whole of the North with churches, died after being wounded by his son and by his own men, who had previously rejected Christ. At the same time, Saint Edward, king of England, is said to have been killed through the plots of his wicked stepmother.

In the year of Christ 983, the emperor Otto II, in the tenth year of his reign, died at Rome on the eighth day before the Ides of November, overcome by a grievous illness of spirit. He was buried in the vestibule of Blessed Peter, which they call Paradise, and covered with a porphyry sarcophagus. He was called “the Bloodstained,” because he ordered the most distinguished Romans, whom he had invited to a banquet, to be killed amid the very merriment of the feast shortly before his death.

After his death, when deliberation was held over the creation of a new emperor, some demanded Otto III, the son of Otto II; others Henry, duke of Bavaria and nephew of Otto the Great through his brother; while the Italians pressed for the matter to be entrusted to Crescentius of Nomentum, a most distinguished man. Then the Germans burst into the midst of the assembly, took up arms, and acclaimed Otto III.

At that time Pope Benedict, an excellent man and a lover of peace, urged everyone, by entreating them, to put aside factional passions and consider the Christian commonwealth, which then especially needed an experienced and skillful governor, in choosing the emperor. Finally, to prevent any disturbance from arising, he approved the judgment of the Germans as equitable and in accordance with the laws, and confirmed Otto III as Augustus Caesar.

During the reign of the same Benedict, the emperor of the Greeks, Tzimisces, who had been taken from the living five years before Otto II, also died. He was famous for military glory and many victories, and was the first of all to order coins to be struck with the image of Christ and the inscription: “Jesus Christ, King of kings.” This example pleased later generations, and the kingship of Christ was asserted over kings, by whose nod empires are established and overturned.

Tzimisces perished, however, through a deadly poison supplied by Basil the eunuch, who feared that he might be removed from the administration of certain cities. Basil II and Constantine IX succeeded to the empire; they ruled jointly for forty-nine years and four months.

In the year 984, on the fourth day before the Ides of July, Benedict himself also died, after having governed the helm of the Church for nine years and two months, full of pious works. His body was transferred to the Holy Cross in Jerusalem and honorably buried there, with an epitaph quoted by Victorellus in his additions to Ciaconius.

[Col. 0315]

LETTERS AND PRIVILEGES OF POPE BENEDICT VII.

I. LETTER OF POPE BENEDICT VII TO THE GAULS AND GERMANS. (Year 974.) He decrees that Lauriacum—that is, Passau—be a metropolitan church; establishes its boundaries and those of Salzburg; and delegates apostolic authority to Pilgrim, archbishop of Lauriacum.

[Mansi, *Councils*, vol. XIX, col. 52.]

[Col. 0315A]

To our most beloved sons in Christ, Hrodebert, of the holy Church of Mainz; Dietrich, of the holy Church of Trier; Adalbert, of the holy Church of Magdeburg; likewise Gereon, of the holy Church of Cologne; Frederick, of the holy Church of Juvavum; and also Adaldag, of the holy Church of Bremen, archbishops; and likewise to the lord Otto, most glorious emperor Augustus, and his nephew Henry, most distinguished duke of the Bavarians; and to the other counts of Gaul and Germany: Benedict, endowed by divine grace, pontiff of the apostolic see—[“the aforesaid,” that is, in the preceding letter]—and servant of the servants of God, sends greeting in the Lord.

We ought always to show ourselves ready and humble toward just requests made in supplication, especially when we are urged by the fraternal prayers of religious fellow priests, who everywhere receive from every boundary of the world the order, rule, and vigor of their proper office from this universal holy Roman Church and from its appointed minister, namely, the vicar of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. Although unworthy, we have succeeded by his grace and gift to the power and rank to which the Lord’s voice says: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church.”

Therefore we judged it worthy to grant our assent to the appropriate petitions of the most reverend archbishop, which he communicated to us through trustworthy persons, namely, his two presbyteral representatives, so that we might restore to him the pallium and the metropolitan dignity of his see, the holy Church of Lauriacum, adjoining the Hungarian frontier. The most ancient testimony of privileges, which he brought with him, bears witness that we owe this entirely to that same Church.

For it was contained in them that, in the time of the pontificate of blessed Symmachus, the bishop of this gracious apostolic see, the aforesaid holy Church of Lauriacum was regarded as a metropolitan church. And insofar as we can gather from this, and also from the passions of the blessed martyrs who were there subjected to various tortures for the faith of Christ during the time of persecution, it is believed that, among all the dioceses of the churches of Pannonia, this church was primitive both in antiquity and in the dignity of an archbishopric.
