For many past ages it had been deserted and reduced to solitude by the repeated devastation of neighboring barbarians, and it remembered no inhabitant professing Christianity, until the unconquered Augustus, the father of grace—that is, the father of our pious emperor, whom the world desires still to survive and rule for a long time—blunted their strength by a military triumph.

[Col. 0316B]

Now, therefore, we break forth with exultant prayers into praise of almighty God, because not only does the frequently mentioned holy Church of Lauriacum, with the terror of its enemies removed, enjoy peace and tranquility together with its inhabitants, but the very men who were formerly its enemies, having now been baptized, profess Christ, whom they once persecuted according to pagan custom. They now desire to have priests and, insofar as those who are still unlearned are able to understand, they venerate them; and their descendants appear to be restoring certain churches in their land which their fathers had consigned to the flames.

For this reason, since the petition of the archbishop of the aforementioned holy Church of Lauriacum is commended by ancient apostolic authority, and since, in addition to its justice, it has also seemed useful to us, we have appointed this archbishop over the peoples newly converted to the faith of the Hungarians and Moravians, and over many other provinces of the Slavs neighboring his parish, with bishops ordained there according to the ancient arrangement [perhaps “disposition”].

For the metropolitan Church of Salzburg had wrongfully appropriated control over the holy Church of Lauriacum, whose episcopal dignity had been obscured and diminished by the devastation of the barbarians. We by no means permit it to be deprived of the apostolic privileges it has received, since these privileges are earlier than those of Salzburg and therefore carry greater authority. This condition of testimony also prevails and holds weight in secular matters.

With the Lord’s help, we easily ward off every accusation and occasion for dispute in such constitutions, separating the two parishes from each other by definite boundaries, while nevertheless establishing everywhere the apostolic sanctions which it is our duty always to defend and, according to the evangelical sentence, not to undo any part of them but to fulfill them.

Therefore, by the authority and power of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and following the example of the blessed pontiffs, namely our predecessors, we henceforth and forever release the same holy Church of Lauriacum and its rulers, now archbishops, from every subjection and jurisdiction of the Church of Salzburg and its bishops, and we elevate it with metropolitan honor.

[Col. 0317B]

And just as in recent times Pope Agapetus of holy memory distinguished the boundaries of these parishes from one another, so we too define them: the holy Church of Salzburg shall have as suffragans the bishops of Upper Pannonia, over whom its bishops appeared hitherto to preside, with such a large and extensive diocese as they have until now possessed in Lower Pannonia. But the holy Church of Lauriacum shall have archiepiscopal authority over the regions of Lower Pannonia and Moesia, whose provinces are Bavaria and Moravia, in which the parishes of seven bishops were contained in ancient times, and its own bishops shall henceforth possess such a large and extensive diocese as they have until now possessed in Upper Pannonia.

Moreover, we enjoin upon them in accordance with the decree of blessed Gregory addressed to the archbishops of the English that the one who is earlier in the time of his ordination shall hold precedence in rank and retain that precedence as long as he lives.

For, after the dioceses of both Churches have been completely determined and every opportunity for quarrelling has been excluded, we strictly prohibit under canonical penalty that either archbishop of these Churches presume to invade the parish of the other, or dare to trouble the other by any quarrels or disputes concerning matters we have now defined.

These matters having been settled, we enthroned our venerable brother in office, Pilgrim, archbishop, at the see of the holy Church of Lauriacum, furnishing him with canonical letters, and sent him the pallium according to the ancient custom of that Church.

We also entrust and delegate to him the exercise of our apostolic authority and representation in the provinces of Bavaria, in the regions of Lower Pannonia and Moesia, and among the neighboring nations of the Slavs dwelling all around, so that there, following the custom of his predecessors, the archbishops of the holy Church of Lauriacum, he may have the power to ordain and appoint priests and bishops, and by his holy preaching prepare for the Lord a perfect people from the aforesaid nations.

II. BULL OF POPE BENEDICT VII FOR THE RIGHTS OF THE ARCHBISHOPRIC OF TRIER. (Year 975.) He grants to Theodoric, archbishop of Trier, and his successors the cell of the Four Crowned Martyrs.

[Mansi, cited above, col. 57.]

[Col. 0318A]

Benedict, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends perpetual greeting in Christ to our dearest brothers, all bishops, and to men of every Catholic dignity and order, both present and future.

Although we are unworthy, etc. Therefore we wish the holiness and diligence of all, both present and future, to know about our brother Theodoric, archbishop and primate of the holy Church of Trier: [The text is corrupt here:] by the constitution of ourselves and our predecessors from the beginning of Christianity through blessed Peter, [and] by the devotion of all Gaul and Germany to that same prince of the apostles. By governing the Church of Christ in his see with great glory, restoring many monasteries that had remained deserted until his time, and visiting the threshold of the blessed apostles more frequently than others, without being deterred by the danger or labor of a longer journey, he has pleased us so greatly that we have judged it just to grant something to be possessed perpetually by him and his Church.

Therefore let it be known to all that, with the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and with the freely given consent of the priests, clergy, and the entire Roman people, we have granted to the holy Church of Trier the cell of the Four Crowned Martyrs, to be possessed forever with all its appurtenances: namely, waters and their courses, meadows, pastures, vineyards, woods, cultivated and uncultivated lands, courts, and dwellings.

All these things we grant by the series of this apostolic decree to our brother Theodoric, archbishop of the holy Church of Trier and our most beloved vicar throughout all Gaul and Germany, and through him to all his successors, to possess, hold, and administer forever: whatever the same cell authentically possesses by various donations of the faithful according to Roman law, or ought to possess by right; whatever has been given, and whatever may be given in any manner until the end of the age; whatever has been taken from the cell by the violence of enemies; and whatever has been lost through the negligence of those dwelling in the same cell—we restore in full and without diminution to our brother Theodoric, archbishop of the holy Church of Trier and our most worthy vicar throughout all Gaul and Germany, and to all his successors through him, from the present third indiction, by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and our own.

If anyone should presume to act against this and attempt in any way to violate what has been decreed by us justly and canonically, let him know that he is to be condemned by the authority of almighty God, of the aforesaid most blessed prince of the apostles, of all the saints, and thereafter by our authority, etc.

Written by the hand of Stephen, regional notary of the holy apostolic see, in the month of January, in the third indiction. Farewell.

Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February, by the hand of Wido, bishop and librarian of the holy apostolic see, in the first year, by God’s favor, of the pontificate of our lord Pope Benedict VII, while our most pious lord, the emperor Augustus Otto, crowned by God, the great emperor, was reigning, in the eighth year of his reign, in the third indiction.

III. BULL OF POPE BENEDICT VII FOR THE MONASTERY OF SAINT BENEDICT AT TRIER. (Year 975.) The monks of Saint Benedict are reintroduced into the monastery of Saint Martin at Trier.

[Hontheim, *History of Trier*, I, 316.]

[Col. 0319B]

In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity. Benedict, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends perpetual greeting in Christ to our dearest brothers, all bishops, and to men of every Catholic dignity and order, both present and future.

Although unworthy, yet by the grace of divine favor and providence we have undertaken the most sacred see of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and the pastoral ministry of caring for the Lord’s flock. We recognize that it is necessary and salutary for us to maintain an urgent and most diligent concern for all the Churches, so that, through our careful administration, they may possess peace, quiet, and protection against every plot, secured to the very end by our authority, for the increase of holy religion.

Therefore we wish the holiness and diligence of all, both present and future, to know that, when our dearest brother Theodoric, archbishop of the holy Church of Trier, came to Rome for the sake of prayer at the thresholds of the blessed apostles, we learned from his account that a certain monastery, where Saint Magneric rests in body, had been deprived by the enemies of God, until his time, not only of religious observance but also of certain possessions belonging to his see.

He renewed its former possessions and everything necessary, confirmed the renewal by the excommunication of himself and of the bishops of his province, and, so that the condition of holy religion might become greater and firmer, placed monks there to serve God as before. He appointed over the place Abbot Engelbert, through whose diligence not only might the place be restored to a better condition, but religion might daily increase more happily and perfectly.

Since, therefore, monastic life is proved praiseworthy in that place, and since we do not wish what our venerable brother and fellow bishop Theodoric restored for the sake of holy religion and his own salvation to be destroyed by any of the archbishops who succeed him or by the power of any earthly authority, we have decreed, through this apostolic privilege and the most authoritative constitution of the holy Roman synod, that the same abbot and all his successors, who will serve God there in monastic observance, shall perpetually possess the privilege of the mitre in the place of a bishop. According to the tradition of Saint Magneric—as is read in his Life—this privilege is known to have been established for abbots.

They shall also possess the same place, with everything belonging to it, namely churches, villages, and all its appurtenances, in complete peace, without contradiction or disturbance from anyone.

When the abbot departs this life, we have decreed by our apostolic sanction that an abbot from the same community shall be appointed to the monastery according to the instructions of the Rule of Saint Benedict. But if, God forbid, no person suitable to monastic discipline is found in that community, an abbot shall be advanced to the monastery from the same diocese with the consent of the archbishop.

Therefore, if anyone should presume to act in any way against this apostolic constitution which we have established for the abbot and the monastery, or attempt in any way to violate what has been decreed by us justly and canonically in a full synod, let him know that he is condemned and anathematized by the authority of almighty God, of the aforesaid blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, of all the saints, and thereafter by our authority, and that he is perpetually pierced by the dart of divine wrath and assigned to eternal punishment with all the impious.

But whoever faithfully strives to observe, preserve, and fulfill this privilege of ours shall effectively deserve to obtain from the Lord the grace of blessing and the fullness of mercy in the heavenly camp among the number of the elect.

Written by the hands of Stephen, notary and regional officer and archivist of the holy apostolic see, in the month of January, in the third indiction. Farewell.

Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February, by the hand of Wido, bishop and librarian of the holy apostolic see. In the year, by God’s favor, of the pontificate of our most holy lord Pope Benedict, while the most pious lord, ever Augustus Otto, crowned by God, the great emperor, was reigning, in the seventh year of his reign, in the third indiction.

[Note: The origin of this monastery of Saint Martin at the Shore is very ancient and, in any event, obscure. Later, when the place had repeatedly been devastated by the force and injuries of barbarians invading Gaul, and sacred things lay violated and neglected, Magneric, archbishop of Trier, in the sixth century, piously cultivated the place—which had been half-ruined and disfigured by the disasters of an earlier age—not only with buildings and roofs but also with the laws and rules of religious life for the men to whom he and his successors as archbishops sometimes withdrew. He wished the name of blessed Martin, whose glory in miracles had become famous everywhere after his death, to remain there, where, while still alive, Martin had delivered the servant of Tetradius, a proconsular man, from the possession of an evil demon, as Sulpicius relates in Book I of the Life of Saint Martin. When ecclesiastical discipline later again collapsed through the injuries of time, especially through the violence of the Normans, Theodoric introduced it here together with the Rule of Saint Benedict.]

IV. PRIVILEGE OF POPE BENEDICT VII FOR THE CHURCH OF TRIER. (Year 975.) He confirms to the archbishop and Church of Trier the right of papal legation, the privileges of riding with the *nacchus* and cross, etc.

[Hontheim, cited above, p. 312.]

[Col. 0320D]

Benedict, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends perpetual greeting in Christ to our dearest brothers, all bishops, and to men of every Catholic dignity and order, both present and future.

Although unworthy, yet by the grace of divine condescension, we have assumed the most sacred see of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and universal teaching authority throughout the whole world. Therefore it is necessary that we exercise the most diligent concern for all the churches, and attend earnestly to ensuring that their rights—established and confirmed inviolably by the authority of that same prince of the apostles and of the other venerable Fathers who followed him—are not diminished or destroyed in our time, but rather suitably strengthened, increased, and advanced.

Therefore we wish all of you to know, in your holiness and diligence, that when our most beloved brother Theodore, archbishop of the holy Church of Trier, came to Rome to pray at the thresholds of the holy apostles, we heard from him—as we had previously learned by hearing and indeed by reading—that this same Church, before all the other churches of Gaul, received the beginnings of the Christian religion and the first foundations of the Catholic faith through the evangelical teaching of the most holy men Eucharius, Valerius, Maternus, and the others, whom the aforesaid apostle Peter ordained and instructed in his own time and also sent there to preach.

Accordingly, with the counsel of the entire order of our apostolic see and by free consent, we have judged it fitting to reconfirm, strengthen anew, and in every way restore to the same holy Church of Trier, and to the aforesaid brother of ours Theodore, and through him to all his successors, the rights and privileges that were authentically granted from the beginning, and down to the present, by the holy Roman mother Church to the aforesaid saints and to their other successors—namely Agritius, Maximinus, Paulinus, Severus, those life-giving and apostolic men—and that are acknowledged to have been destroyed in the ruin, fire, or some other disaster affecting that city.

By the force of this our most authoritative apostolic privilege, we decree that whenever a bishop, priest, deacon, subdeacon, or any ordinary legate is sent from our principal and apostolic see into Gaul or Germany for the benefit of the Church or to hold a synod, the bishop of Trier shall hold the first place among the other bishops after that apostolic legate.

[Note: The Germans, however, did not tolerate papal legates presiding over German councils. The legates of Pope Gregory VII experienced this in 1074; Fleury, *Histoire ecclésiastique*, book LXII, no. 11: “The legates requested on the Pope’s behalf the freedom to hold a council in Germany, but all the bishops strongly opposed it, maintaining that this was unprecedented and contrary to their rights; and they declared that they would never grant anyone the prerogative of presiding over them in council except the Pope in person.” But this has no bearing on the archbishop of Trier, whose right to preside over national councils rested not so much on the privilege of papal legation as on a primacy repeatedly confirmed and often solemnly recognized by the German nation.] [Note: “He shall have the primacy.” The primacy of the Church of Trier has already often been discussed, and more will be said hereafter. Meanwhile see the bull of John XIII, from the year 969, and also that of Leo IX, from the year 1049.]

If the legate sent by the Roman Church is absent, he shall likewise, after the emperor or king, have precedence in sitting, delivering judgment, and canonically promulgating synodal decisions, as one rightly constituted in those regions as vicar of our apostolic see.

Nor is it fitting that the bishop of that Church should at any time be regarded as inferior to the others, since his honor in those regions was established as primary under the very prince of the apostles. And because we know that the archbishop of that Church, namely blessed Eucharius, was ordained by blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, just as blessed Apollinaris of the city of Ravenna was also ordained by him, it has pleased us to permit our brother Theodore, archbishop of the holy Church of Trier, and all his successors through him, that, just as the preachers of both cities were equal in the ordination, blessing, and sending forth of the one blessed apostle Peter to preach the Gospel of Christ to the nations, so they may be equal in celebrating the solemn rites of Mass and in riding with the *naccus* through the stations, and may be equal in every honor. The cross shall be carried before him, just as before the archbishop of Ravenna, wherever it may be carried.

[Note: “Riding with the *naccus*.” A *naccus*, *nattus*, *natus*, or *nactus* is an ornament of a ceremonial horse. On a festival or in a procession the entire horse was covered with a cloth; it was counted among the distinguished privileges if a bishop was granted permission to sit upon and proceed on Palm Sunday and on the Monday after Easter on a white horse covered with an *udo* or *naccus*. No one was ordinarily permitted to do this without special authorization. Du Cange, *Glossary*, under “Equus” and “Nactum.” See also below the bull of Calixtus II, from the year 1120.]

The cardinal priests shall also wear dalmatics when our brother Archbishop Theodore is celebrating Mass, and the deacons, together with the priests, shall use *scandalia*.

[Note: “Let them use *scandalia*.” *Scandalia* or *scandilia* are steps on which one stands or sits at a higher and more honorable level.]

We also permit the weekly priests celebrating Mass at Saint Peter’s, out of regard for his affection, to use dalmatics.

In the same manner we decree that all who live in his parishes, or receive from his bishop ordination and promotion to any ecclesiastical rank, must canonically please, obey, and rightly submit to that same mother Church and its bishop. For, as it appears to have been provided in this matter by the decree of blessed Pope Clement:

> “If all the priests, deacons, subdeacons, and clerics, and all the rulers, both of higher and lower rank, and the rest of the peoples, tribes, and languages do not obey you bishops, they shall be excluded from the thresholds of the holy Church of God, since the Lord says: ‘Whoever hears you hears me; and whoever despises you despises me.’”

[Note: “Cardinal priests.” Thus the pontiff calls the canons of the metropolitan Church of Trier, in a style sufficiently common in that age, as Buddeus extensively demonstrates in his historical treatise on the origin of the dignity of the cardinals, § 15, pp. 40 ff.]

Among all these things that appear to belong to the aforesaid Church of Trier, both within and outside the city—that is, churches with all the possessions belonging to them, and monasteries, both of monks and of virgins, which by decrees or written instruments of kings or emperors, or by the authority of their founders, belong and ought to belong to it, and everything whatsoever that that same Church, wherever and for whatever reason, possesses or ought to possess—we grant and reconfirm, generally and specifically, to the aforesaid brother and fellow bishop Theodore and to his successors, for the perpetual lordship and jurisdiction of the holy Church of Trier, by the tenor of this our apostolic command, to remain valid from the present third indiction and until the end of the age.

If anyone should presume in any way to act against this, or should attempt in any respect to violate what has been justly and canonically decreed by us, let him know that, by the authority of almighty God, of the aforesaid most blessed prince of the apostles, of all the saints, and thereafter of ourselves, he is to be condemned and anathematized, and assigned to eternal punishment with all the impious. But whoever faithfully strives to observe, guard, and fulfill this privilege of ours shall deservedly obtain from the Lord God, in the heavenly camps among the number of the elect, the grace of blessing and the fullness of mercy.

Written by the hand of Stephen, notary, regional officer, and archivist of the holy apostolic see, in the month of January, in the aforesaid third indiction. Farewell.

Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February, by the hand of Wido, bishop and librarian of the holy apostolic see. In the first year, by God’s favor, of the pontificate of our lord, the most holy Pope Benedict VII; in the seventh year of the reign of the most pious lord, father of his country, Augustus Otto, crowned by God, the great emperor; in the third indiction.

### V. Letter of Pope Benedict VII to Theodore, Archbishop of Trier  
*(Year 975.)*

He confirms the monastery of Saint Martin of Trier, restored by Archbishop Theodore, “by the most authoritative constitution of this our apostolic privilege and of the holy Roman synod,” and enlarges its privileges.

[Gudenius, *Codex diplomaticus* I, 9.]

[Col. 0323D]

“If shepherds of sheep, etc.” For the remainder, see the cited author.

### VI. Privilege of Pope Benedict VII for the Monastery of Vézelay  
*(Year 975.)*

[In Achery, *Spicilegium* II, 504.]

Benedict, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Eldrado, religious abbot of the monastery of Saint Vézelay, and to the entire congregation of that monastery, forever.

[Col. 0324A]

Whenever things are requested from us that unquestionably accord with reason, our willing spirit ought to grant them, and to provide fitting assistance to the desires of those who ask. Therefore, since you asked us to make a privilege of the apostolic see for the monastery of Vézelay, over which you are recognized as presiding—a monastery known to have been built long ago by Gerard, a most noble and Christian man, and by his wife Berta, in honor of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ and in veneration of the most blessed ever-virgin Mary, mother of that same Lord Jesus Christ, in the kingdom of Burgundy, in the district of Aval— and which was piously granted by the aforesaid founders to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, by a written testament, we have willingly decided, yielding to your prayers, that this should be done.

Therefore we establish, decree by apostolic authority, and confirm through this our apostolic privilege that no king, bishop, abbot, count, or person of whatever high or low rank, seized by greed or deceived by diabolical suggestion, shall dare or presume in any way to rise against your honor, O venerable Abbot Wido, during your lifetime, or to cause you any trouble concerning your dignity, or to inflict any seizure, robbery, or violence upon any of the monastery’s possessions that were granted and confirmed to you and your predecessors by us and by our predecessors through a written privilege—unless he wishes, by the authority of God, Saint Peter, and our apostolic authority, to be separated from the body and blood of the Lord Jesus Christ and from entry into the Church.

We add this provision to the present chapter in order to exclude the opportunity for greed: no king, no bishop or priest, nor any of the faithful, either personally or through a substitute, shall dare to receive anything, under any form of gift, in connection with the ordination of the same abbot or of clerics or priests, the distribution of chrism, the consecration of the basilica, or any matters belonging to the same monastery. Nor shall the same abbot presume to give anything for his ordination, lest on this pretext the offerings made by the faithful to the holy place be consumed.

Nor shall the bishop of that city or diocese celebrate public Masses there unless invited by the abbot of the monastery; nor shall he announce stations in the same monastery, lest the repose of the servants of God in any way be disturbed by a popular gathering; nor shall he presume to demand provisions or lodging dues from it.

As for receiving the faithful and religious men, and the hospitality that the Apostle commands to be offered to all according to the capacity of the place and its resources, we not only do not deny that it be practiced there, but even recommend it. Yet the size of the congregation should be maintained in such a way that neither an excessive number brings poverty nor too few inhabitants bring abandonment upon the place.

Furthermore, we wish it to be known that a petitionary letter from Gerard, bishop of the Church of Autun, reached us concerning the tithes of four churches—namely, those of Saint Peter, Saint Christopher, Saint Germanus, and Saint Leodegarius—which the aforesaid abbot had obtained from that bishop, just as his predecessors are known to have obtained them from bishops successively appointed to that see. We have confirmed them by our privilege, excommunicating anyone who might bring any accusation against the abbot of that place or its monks concerning those churches, or who, whether the bishop himself or anyone sent by him, might diminish the tithes or transfer them to another parish.

If any king, bishop, priest, abbot, judge, count, or secular person attempts to act against this written decree of ours, struck by apostolic anathema, let him know that he will be deprived of the authority or honor that he holds by his rank and will recognize himself guilty before the divine judgment. Unless he effaces what he has wrongly done, let him be separated from the most sacred body of our Lord Jesus Christ and subjected to the strict vengeance of the eternal judgment.

But let peace be with all who observe the provisions made for that place, so that both here they may receive the fruit of good works and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace.

Written by the hand of Boniface, notary, regional officer, and archivist of the holy Roman Church. Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends, in the month of December, by the hand of John, bishop, by God’s favor, while the most pious lord Augustus Otto, crowned by God, the great emperor, was reigning, in the eighth year, in the month of December and the fourth indiction.

### VII. Bull of Pope Benedict VII for the Church of Saints Apollinaris and Ursicinus at Canossa  
*(Year 975.)*

At the request of Count Teudald, his son, he confirms the foundation of the Church of Saint Apollinaris and the establishment there of twelve canons, made by Count Adelbert in the castle of Canossa.

[Muratorius, *Antiquitates Italicae* V, 207.]

[Col. 0325C]

Benedict, bishop, servant of the servants of God.

Let it be known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God how Count Teudald, son of the already-mentioned Count Adelbert, while visiting the thresholds of the apostles with worthy devotion, asked from our apostolic authority on behalf of his father that we graciously confirm and strengthen by the authority of our apostolic privilege the church consecrated in honor of the holy confessors of God—namely Apollinaris, Ursicinus, and Rusticianus, and also the martyrs Maurice, Alexander, and Victor—which Adelbert himself had built from its foundations on his own property, specifically on the rock called Canuxia, and had dedicated in various ways to divine worship; and to which he had granted, by proprietary right, the tithe of all his territory or estate for the use of twelve canons who, for future times, should be appointed there by him or by his sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons.

Therefore, consenting to his devout petition and offering sincere assent to his good and worthy desire, we have decreed that this privilege, supported by apostolic authority, be made for him, and that, according to the petition and institution and donation of the same Count Teudald and his father, the aforesaid church remain in every respect strengthened by us.

[The remainder is missing.]

Written by the hand of Stephen, notary of the sacred archive of the holy Roman Church. [The remainder is missing.] In the fourth indiction.

Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of January, by the hand of Guido, bishop and librarian of the holy apostolic see, in the second year of the pontificate of our lord, the most holy Pope Benedict VII, and in the third year of the empire of Lord Otto.

### VIII. Privilege of Pope Benedict VII for the Monastery of Saint Pantaleon  
*(Year 976.)*

He confirms the possessions and privileges of the monastery of Saint Pantaleon of Cologne. “For love of the emperor and at the request of the empress, and also on account of the pleasantness of Archbishop Guarinus,” he permits Abbot Christian to use a dalmatic and *sandalia*.

[Wurtwein, *Subsidia diplomatica*, Heidelberg, 1781, quarto IV, 29.]

[Col. 0326B]

“It is fitting for apostolic moderation, etc.” For the remainder, see the cited author.

### IX. Privilege of Pope Benedict VII for the Monastery of Monte Cassino  
*(Year 977.)*

[Gattula, *History of Monte Cassino*, p. 840.]

[Col. 0326C]

Benedict, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Atigernus, beloved son in the Lord Jesus Christ, venerable and religious abbot of the most sacred monastery of blessed Benedict, confessor of Christ, situated on Monte Cassino, and through you to that venerable monastery and its entire congregation, forever.

Since things that accord with reasonable desires should always be granted, our clemency ought not to refuse, when privileges are being granted, the devotion humbly acquired in me by the petitioner. It is written that you asked us that the monastery of blessed Benedict, confessor of Jesus Christ, situated on the aforesaid Monte Cassino, and the monastery of blessed Scholastica, and also the monastery of the Lord Savior consecrated beneath the aforesaid mountain, as well as four monasteries of women—one of Saint Mary in the place called Plumbariola, another of the same Saint Mary in the place called Cingla, the monastery of Saint Sophia built within the city of Benevento, and likewise the monastery of Saint Mary consecrated in the city of Cosenza—and also the monastery of Saint Benedict within the city of Capua, and furthermore the monastery of women consecrated in the same city of Capua called Saint John, together with the churches built in the several places and belonging to the aforesaid monasteries, should be adorned with the privileges of the apostolic see, so that, established under the jurisdiction of the holy Church in whose service, by God’s authority, we are engaged, they might not be disturbed or subjected to the authority of any church or bishop.

Therefore, favoring your pious desires and committing to your petition what it requests by our authority, we entirely forbid any bishop of any church to exercise any jurisdiction whatsoever over the aforesaid venerable places. We have regard only to our apostolic see, and from now on we forbid every innovation and act of violence against those monasteries, so that, unless invited by the abbot of the monastery, no one may presume to enter to consecrate a church or a priest of the aforesaid monasteries or of any cells belonging to them; nor may any bishop presume in any way to celebrate the solemnity of Mass there.

For the consecration of churches in the aforesaid monasteries or cells, we grant the abbot authority to invite whichever bishop he wishes, without impediment from anyone, so that, in accordance with what is contained in the apostolic privileges below, the grants may remain unshaken.

Moreover, together with our priestly college, by this our apostolic privilege we establish that all the places which those venerable monasteries have ever possessed, or which have now been or shall later be granted to them by faithful men in various territories, may not be invaded in any way, nor may tribute be exacted or the monks or servants oppressed, by any castald, bishop, or person, great or small, through any device or stratagem. Rather, to the praise of Christ and the eternal memory of their benefactors, these possessions shall remain forever untouched by all and shall serve only the holy mother Roman Church.

No bishop shall henceforth dare to impose any excommunication upon those monks subject to our holy Church. They shall be permitted to perform the divine offices just as blessed Benedict prescribed for them in his Rule. We also establish that no bishop shall presume to separate from the churches belonging to the said monasteries the people who come there to hear the word of God and confess their sins, whether in the cities or outside them. Rather, the devout people shall enter and leave there canonically, and the churches subject to your jurisdiction shall be open to all.

Since pastoral care has been entrusted to us by God so that we may remain vigilant in all things, lest—as God forbid—the Lord’s sheep be torn by the bites of wolves, we command and order, under the solemn appeal to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, all venerable bishops, priests, abbots, deacons, dukes, tribunes, castalds, officials, and all who fear God. He received from the Lord God our power to bind and loose the sins of men in heaven and on earth, and by God’s divine grace we exercise his vicariate.

By this written decree of ours we forbid all bishops of every church, and all persons endowed with authority of whatever rank, under penalty of anathema and the obligation of eternal judgment, to presume in any way to violate this present constitution granted by us to the aforesaid monastery. …

Written by the hand of Stephen, notary, regional officer, and archivist of the holy Roman Church, in the month of May, in the fifth indiction. Farewell.

Given on the third day before the Kalends of June, by the hand of Stephen, *nomenclator* [sic] of the holy apostolic see, in the third year of the pontificate of our lord Benedict, supreme pontiff and Pope VII, while our lord Otto, crowned by God, the great and peaceful emperor, was reigning, in the tenth year, in the month and indiction stated above.

### X. Privilege of Pope Benedict VII for the Monastery of Saint Peter of Perugia  
*(Year 977.)*

He confirms the goods and rights of the monastery of Saint Peter of Perugia and threatens eternal malediction against those who plunder or disturb them.

[Margarini, *Casinensian Bullary* II, 52.]

Benedict, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Peter, venerable abbot of the monastery of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, which is situated in the place called Quumplorano, and to your successors, forever.

It accords with apostolic moderation to come to the aid, with benevolent compassion, of those endowed with pious religion, and to grant the minds of petitioners their requests with cheerful devotion. For we shall especially earn forgiveness from God, the creator of all, if venerable places of the saints, once established, are undoubtedly brought into a better condition.

Therefore, since your religious devotion humbly requested from our apostolate that we grant and confirm to you the aforesaid monastery of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, with all its houses, cells, buildings, gardens, land, and farmsteads; its vineyards, lands, fields, meadows, pastures, and woods; and also the churches of Saint Lucy and Saint Martha, with all their appurtenances, movable and immovable, and everything belonging to the aforesaid monastery, both what now justly and reasonably appears to belong to it and whatever from now on shall perpetually belong to the jurisdiction of the holy Roman Church, in whose service we are engaged by God’s authority, we have yielded to your prayers and, by the tenor of this our apostolic privilege, grant and confirm to you and your successors the said monastery with all its appurtenances, as written above.

By apostolic censure, under the solemn appeal of divine judgment and the prohibition of anathema, we establish that no pontiff among our successors, nor any other person, great or small, of whatever dignity or order, may ever act against or rise up against this our apostolic privilege.

If anyone, which we by no means desire, is found disobedient to and contemptuous of this privilege of ours, in whole or in part, or presumes to violate it on account of any person, unless he repents, may he receive the curse of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and be assigned with the devil and his associates to the most terrible punishments and eternal fire. May he not be found worthy of the future resurrection of the elect, and may he be separated from communion, from the bosom of the holy mother Church, and from the fellowship of the saints.

But whoever is found to be a helper and defender of the aforesaid monastery, following the path of justice, may be found at the right hand as a participant and remain joined to all the saints.

Written by the hand of Liutulf, notary, regional officer, and archivist of the holy Roman Church, in the month of December and in the aforesaid sixth indiction.

### XI. Bull of Pope Benedict VII for the Church of Ausona  
*(Year 978.)*

[In Flórez, *España Sagrada*, vol. XXVIII, p. 254.]

Benedict, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Fruia, venerable man and bishop of the bishopric of Saint Peter the Apostle, and through him to his successors in that bishopric, forever.

Since the summit of the highest apostolic dignity is recognized as shining forth in the splendor of divine providence, and since in performing the praises of God it strives to display the contest of its labor more earnestly, the proper care of that same apostolic pastoral concern compels us to promulgate abundantly whatever is recognized as pertaining to the stability of pious places and to confirm it by the censure of apostolic constitution.

Therefore, since you asked us for a privilege concerning the aforesaid bishopric of Saint Peter the Apostle, situated in the place called Vicus in the territory of Ausona and Manresa, with all its churches and cells, or castles—one called Monteboi and another Tovos—with all their boundaries and limits: from one boundary extending through Aqualata, and from there crossing to the ford of the same Aedera, then returning along that same boundary and proceeding straight to the boundaries called Jorba, and from there to the boundaries called Clariana; and on the other side crossing from Aqualata, proceeding through the boundaries of Clarmonte, and through the boundaries of Auri Pino, extending through the boundaries of Miralia as far as the boundaries of Rocheta or Villis; with its farmsteads, vineyards, lands, woods, houses, wells of the fields, springs, streams, fields, watermills, mountains and plains, markets, tolls, *raficae*, coinage, pastures, and grazing rights; especially the Church of Saint Mary situated in the city of Manresa, with all that belongs or is adjacent to it, and the churches built or capable of being built within those territories; together with the monastery of Saint Benedict, whose boundaries begin in the east as far as the marker enclosed by the boundaries of Artes, belonging to that same church:

From there it goes along the ridge that leads through the Alsinellias and reaches the boundaries of Solienta. From there it proceeds above the red hill and reaches the estate of Scluvanus and his brothers. From there it ascends above the estate of Count Sunyer. From there it goes by a straight route along the summit of the ridge and reaches the Castle of Gold, and from there to the stream of the Bad Vineyard, and reaches the rocky ford. Having crossed the stream, it reaches the lands of Endalesius, who formerly possessed them. From there it returns to the boundary marker and ascends to the summit of Mount Castrilio, and reaches the boundary of Palatiolum, as far as the ridge beyond the Watchtower. Thus it proceeds along the summit of that ridge and reaches the Little Monastery, and ascends to the *Artiga* of Levigildus. From there it descends upon the estate of Valleformosa, which belonged to Alezinus. Then, having crossed the torrent, it ascends by the *Artiga* that Samuel brought there from the wilderness.

From there it ascends to the hill on the road and descends through Gallicanta, reaching the road of Corneto at the pig-keeper’s cave. From there to the Ubardiola, above the court of Auriolus; then it proceeds along the ridge by a straight route, reaches Mata of Frederick, and descends to the ford of Corneto. Thus it goes to the vineyard of Waldemar. From there to the stream Cordosdinarius, just as Count Borrell fixed the boundary. From there it ascends along the Red Stream and reaches the boundary marker, together with the fisc, with Artes, as is recognized to have been described and delimited in the text of the royal privilege, or as George, the former bishop, defined it when it was adjudicated publicly.

Together with everything generally and wholly belonging to the aforesaid bishopric of Saint Peter the Apostle, or recognized as belonging to that bishopric anywhere in other regions, the boundaries of the entire bishopric are these:

On the western side, the boundaries of Quovecintenigio, Cardona, and Bergetano; on the northern side, Eramala, extending as far as Mount Surocha, reaching the meadow of Campo-Rotundo; then along the ridge, wherever the waters flow, as far as Gurni, and from there to the washing stone; then to the Rock of Latione, descending into the river Teceri; reaching the plantation situated between Gerunda and the boundaries of Ausona; ascending along the ridge as far as Gerundilia; proceeding along the road that comes to Bellampolla; reaching the boundary between Joannetus and Elzeta; reaching the boundaries of Arbucias; extending to the summits between the two landmarks; and as far as the Calma called Area-Mala; reaching the hill of Montenigro; then to the Congustum stream; arriving at the castle of Bertinus; extending as far as the Rock of Saint Genesius; reaching Mount Saint Saturninus and Mount Calvus.

From there to Mount Serratus; reaching the mountain below the castle of Odulinus and the castle of Apiaria; proceeding along the summit of the ridge as far as the river called Anolia; going from that river as far as Hispania; and on the other side according to its boundaries, whether they are now or were from the beginning.

All these things belong by right to the holy Roman Church, in whose service we are engaged by God’s authority. We have issued this command for you to hold them. Yielding to your prayers, through the tenor of this privilege we grant that the aforesaid bishopric of blessed Peter the Apostle remain in its present condition, and that you, without doubt, provide for it from the present sixth indiction and forever, so that it may be administered by you and your successors with all that belongs to it intact, and governed in the fear of God, remaining joined to your bishopric.

You ought to offer praises to the Lord our God in that venerable bishopric. We establish that no payment from it or from anything belonging to it is to be made to anyone except God and by our authority. You must also diligently provide for the building and the preparation of the lamps. Therefore let no delay occur in offering the praises of God or in preparing the lamps; hasten to perform these duties with devout sincerity, and do not allow fear of the future judgment to shake you through the fault of careless negligence. Rather, strive to labor so that, through your efforts, divine favor may preserve what has been decreed by us after just deliberation, unshaken for all future and perpetual times.

If anyone, which we do not desire, should presume with criminal audacity to oppose or in any way transgress what has been established by us for the praise of God and the stability of the aforesaid bishopric, let him know that we bind him with the bond of anathema and assign him to be burned in the punishment of eternal fire by the devil and his most terrible pageants, together with Judas, the traitor of our Lord Jesus Christ.

But whoever proves a faithful observer and guardian of this apostolic constitution of ours and of everything pertaining to the worship of God shall receive manifold the grace of blessing from our most merciful Lord God and deserve to become a participant in eternal life.

Written by the hand of John, notary, regional officer, and archivist of the holy Roman Church, in the month of March, in the sixth indiction. Farewell. Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of March, by the hand of Gregory, bishop and librarian of the holy apostolic see, in the fourth year, by God’s favor, of the pontificate of our lord Benedict, supreme pontiff and universal Pope VII, in the most sacred see of blessed Peter the Apostle, in the month and indiction stated above.

### XII. Privilege of Pope Benedict VII for the Church of Ausona  
*(Year 978.)*

[Flórez, cited above, p. 102.]

[Col. 0331D]

We wish it to be known to all, great and small, throughout the entire province of Ausona and Barcelona, and in Gerunda and Urgell, and to all who are recognized as belonging to this province, concerning this bishop named Froya: he came to the thresholds of the apostles and approached our see before our presence; he showed us all his documents, through which he acquired the property of his bishopric and of all those known to be subject to him.

Thus he requested a privilege from us, and we willingly confirmed it for him, as is found in that privilege. Therefore we ask, and by our apostolic authority command, that if any person—other than Count Borrell himself in person, his wife Ledgardis, and his legitimate son Raimund—should presume any invasion or raise his heel against the aforesaid bishop, that person, of whatever rank or sex, cleric or layman, shall be excommunicated.

### XIII. Privilege of Pope Benedict VII for the Monastery of Cluny  
*(Year 978.)*

He grants Maiolus, abbot of Cluny, the island of Lérins together with the monastery of Arluc.

[D. Bouquet, *Collection* IX, 245.]

BENEDICT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ, Maiolus, most beloved abbot of the monastery of Cluny, and to his successors forever.

Because we know that the monastery of Cluny, which by God’s favor you govern according to the rule, has been entrusted to the holy Roman Church for its defense and expansion, we ought therefore to show ourselves benevolent and beneficent toward that same place. Accordingly, let it be known to all [Col. 0332C] that you asked us to grant, by a privilege of our authority, to your aforesaid monastery the island of Lérins together with the monastery of Arluca [Note: [Col. 0331D] This monastery, which belonged to women, was situated on a very pleasant hill almost beside the seashore and on the bank of the river Siagne. There was formerly, as they relate, an altar in a grove sacred to Venus, from which it received the name Arluca—“altar of the grove.” [Col. 0332D]], and everything belonging to those same places. For, as we have learned from the decrees of blessed Pope Gregory, that island belongs by right and under the jurisdiction of the holy apostolic see.

Therefore, favoring and granting assent to your petitions, we give in full to you and to your successors that same island and the same monastery of Arluca, together with everything belonging to it. If anyone unjustly brings a charge against you or your successors concerning these things, let him know that he will be struck by the sword of excommunication. We further wish you to pay from it annually five silver solidi at the tomb of blessed Peter.

In order that this our authority may possess force [Col. 0332D] and permanence forever, we have marked it with our seal and confirmed it with our own hand.

Written by the hand of Stephen, regional notary and archivist of the holy Roman Church, in the month of May, indiction VI. Farewell.

Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of June, by the hand of John, bishop of the Church of Salerno, in the fourth year of the pontificate of our lord Pope Benedict VII, while our lord Otto, crowned by God, great and peaceful emperor, was reigning in the eleventh year of his reign, in the month of May, indiction VI.

## XIV. PRIVILEGE OF POPE BENEDICT VII FOR THE MONASTERY OF SAINT PETER OF RODA. (Year 979)

[D. Bouquet, ibid., p. 246.]

[Col. 0333A]

BENEDICT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Bishop Hildesind and to all the monks dwelling in the monastery of Saint Peter of Roda: greeting, peace, and apostolic blessing.

Since we judge it most pleasing and entirely fitting to render service to those who serve, and to bestow rewards upon those who give, and since we see that the monastery of Saint Peter of Roda, which you received to possess by hereditary right, has now been handed over to you to be held perpetually under the right and dominion of the blessed prince of the apostles, Peter, and of our venerable Roman see [Col. 0333B], therefore, in turn, by apostolic authority, we grant and confirm to you and to your successors forever the monastery of Saint Peter the Apostle of Roda, with all its adjacent lands, possessions, and boundaries, on this condition: that it remain forever under the protection of blessed Peter the Apostle and of us.

Moreover, without any reservation, we grant to that same monastery all estates or allodial lands that, from this day forward, are or shall be given by the faithful men of your region to blessed Peter the Apostle and to our Roman see, so that they may remain perpetually in the right and dominion of the monastery of Roda, extending from the city of Narbonne [Col. 0333C] to the borders of Spain.

Let it therefore now be known to all the people of your region that this place remains under the protection and governance of blessed Peter the Apostle and under our government and defense. For this reason we admonish all the faithful of your region, under the testimony of Christ, to restore for the benefit of the monastery and of those dwelling in it everything that belongs to the aforesaid place, and, in the name of blessed Peter the Apostle at Rome, to venerate and cherish that place with the greatest devotion.

If anyone is unable, for the sake of prayer, to reach our apostolic see, we grant him permission to venerate that place with the utmost devotion. But if anyone has concealed or retained, without the consent of the brothers, any of the estates or allodial lands of that place, or anything belonging to the aforesaid place, or knows that someone is secretly holding such property, we admonish him under the testimony of Christ and by apostolic authority that, from this day forward, he must not unjustly retain or conceal it, but must hasten to return and disclose it to the aforesaid monastery.

Once these things have been returned or disclosed, together with those that we establish and decree through this our apostolic sanction and through other imperial decrees (divalia, sic), we decree that they remain inviolate and undisturbed forever, until the end of the world.

But if anyone—which we do not believe—should become a rash violator or despiser of this grant or donation, let him be bound under eternal condemnations [Col. 0334A], and let him experience the holy apostles of God, Peter and Paul, as his adversaries in the present and future life. Let him be burned in the lower hell with the devil and perish with all the wicked.

Strengthening this page of our apostolic decree with our own hands, we hand it over to Hildesind, bishop and abbot of that place, and to the brothers accompanying him, to possess perpetually and faithfully, with Christ Jesus our Lord consenting. Whoever, therefore, becomes a helper and defender of our grant or donation should know that he will obtain apostolic blessing and the forgiveness of sins from the supreme keeper of the keys.

Written by the hands of Stephen, notary and archivist, at the see of blessed Peter the Apostle in Rome, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation [Col. 0334B] 979, indiction VII, in the month of April.

## XV. PRIVILEGE OF POPE BENEDICT VII FOR THE MONASTERY OF BISULDUN. (Year 979)

The pope receives the monastery under his protection, confirms its possessions, and grants it other privileges.

[Mansi, Councils XIX, 71.]

BENEDICT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Gausbert, abbot of the monastery of Bisuldun, situated below the castle of Bisuldun on the river Fluvià, and to his brothers, both present and future, who profess the regular life: health, peace, and blessing, [Col. 0334C] so that it may endure in the world. Amen.

Since it is evident that our Lord God continually increases the honor of the holy universal Church through those who propagate the blessed faith, it is necessary for those who receive from him the care of the whole government; and therefore I, Pope Benedict, together with the company of bishops and priests and the entire host of clerics dwelling at the Roman see, serving God under the rule of the most blessed Peter, receive into our protection [something is missing] and strengthen by the privilege of this present document that gift which our beloved son [Note: [Col. 0333D] You will find the foundation charter of the monastery of Bisuldun, by Miro, bishop of Gerona, and the count of Bisuldun, together with his brothers, Counts Oliban and Seniofrid, [Col. 0334D] in the appendix to the Marca Hispanica, p. 919. Martène.] Miro, bishop of Gerona, presented to the Roman Church by a deed of donation for the remedy of his soul and those of his parents—namely, the church of Saint Peter of Bisuldun, together with all the churches, estates, villages, [Col. 0334D] and demesnes given by him, or which may in the future be granted by any faithful persons—as much as it may be able to acquire. In this present privilege we confirm it forever and establish it in complete liberty.

We further decree that the order of the monastery, which is known to have been instituted by the same bishop according to God and the rule of blessed Benedict, shall always be observed inviolably under the governance of its own abbot.

Moreover, whatever goods the same monastery may in the future, by God’s gift, acquire through donations, concessions of bishops, offerings of kings or princes, or those of many of the faithful [Col. 0335A], shall from now on remain firm, undefiled, and perpetual under the protection of blessed Peter and of us.

We grant that, if estates or any offering of property belonging to the holy Roman Church are left by people of those regions, the aforesaid monastery may possess them forever by our benefaction; and that the abbot who presides, or shall preside, over that monastery shall pay five solidi annually to Saint Peter at Rome as a census. If they are unable to come each year, they shall pay twenty solidi every fourth year.

We further establish that, when the abbot of that monastery dies, no abbot shall be appointed there by kings, counts, or any other person. Rather, abbots shall be chosen by all the servants of God dwelling there, according to the rule of Father Benedict, and they shall receive their blessing from the Roman pontiff or his representative.

We therefore confirm and establish that no archbishop or bishop shall dare or presume to impose a sentence of excommunication upon that monastery, upon its churches given by the aforesaid bishop, upon the clerics serving in them, or upon the abbot, monks, and lay brothers belonging to it; nor may they be placed under interdict or excommunicated by anyone except the Roman pontiff.

We also grant that, if anyone comes to the aforesaid monastery for the sake of prayer, he may enter and attend the entire office, unless he happens to have been excommunicated for his own offense.

We likewise grant to the abbot of that place the correction of all his clerics, so that no bishop, [Col. 0335C] nor any ecclesiastical or lay person, may exercise dominion there. Rather, everything ecclesiastical shall remain at all times under the hand and governance of the abbot himself.

He shall receive oil or holy chrism for baptisms and the consecrations of altars from any Catholic bishop whom he chooses.

We confirm and strengthen the cemetery of the entire village of Bisuldun and of all the surrounding villages, as it was established by the aforesaid bishop, and so forth.

Given on the eighth day before the Ides of May, while our lord Otto, crowned by God, great and peaceful, was reigning in the twelfth year of his reign and indiction VII, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 979, in the Spanish era 1017.

## XVI. PRIVILEGE OF POPE BENEDICT VII FOR THE ABBEY OF SAINT RUFILLUS OF FORLÌ. (Year 980)

[In Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, II, 599.]

[Col. 0335D]

[Note: [Col. 0335D] Although this bull is written according to the Ravenna style and differs from the form of other papal letters, I would nevertheless not judge it to be spurious. Jaffé.]

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

In the year, by God’s favor, of the pontificate of the divine Benedict, supreme pontiff and universal pope, in the apostolic [Col. 0336A] see of the blessed apostle Peter, the Lord, year 5; while the divine Otto, crowned by God, peaceful, great emperor, was reigning and ruling; in Italy, year 13; on 22 August, indiction VIII; in the city of Ravenna:

Considering the fall of the human race and fearing the punishments of eternal flames, we have resolved to offer eternal gifts to the Lord, and we perpetually fear being punished with torments. Therefore I, Benedict, bishop of the Catholic Church—indeed, with the consent and authority of the cardinals of the holy Roman Church—grant, humbly offer, and give to the holy and undefiled Church of blessed Rufillus, bishop and confessor of Christ, situated outside the walls of Popilia; and I grant and transfer, in perpetuity and personally, the rights of alienation and dominion to the divine Leo, humble abbot, and through him to the monastery of Saint [Col. 0336B] Rufillus forever, together with what is held and possessed and appears to have been retained by my predecessors [lacuna]: the chapel of Saint Athanasius; six complete estates; the estate of Monendumo; the estate of Saint Athanasius; Lama; Monsignano; Laniagna; Bratula; and the estate enclosed by four roads, namely Spinaria, Pizacita, the cottage (casanista) of Casalbroni, and the stone of Ficta Gibanelli, with fields, vineyards, lands, arbusta (tree-supported vineyards), and trees; and I establish, and so forth [lacuna]. I place in the territory of Corniole the parish church of Saint Apollinaris and that of Saint Prosper, so that I establish the aforesaid monastery and all the things handed over by me under the protection and governance of the holy Roman Church.

I ask that from now on you sing for me this psalm, “O God, come to my assistance,” and repeat three times, “Lord, have mercy” (*Kyrie eleison*). The pontiffs themselves shall not impose upon you or your successors anything else, whether donation or tribute, in any manner, except what was designated by us in this document. But if anyone acts contrary to this [lacuna].

With God’s favor, we asked that this document, from the family of the consul Taber of this city of Ravenna, be subscribed; after it had been subscribed with my own hands [lacuna]. So that the one who offered it to us for confirmation, in the presence of our people, might also have it handed over to you, on the day, month, and indiction VIII, in the city of Ravenna.

I, Benedict, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

I, Mark, priest and cardinal of Saint Stephen, have subscribed.

I, John, priest and cardinal of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, have subscribed.

I, Leo, priest and cardinal of Saints John and Paul, have subscribed.

I, Julian, subdeacon and chancellor, have subscribed the deed of donation [Col. 0336D] and transaction.

## XVII. ROMAN COUNCIL HELD BY POPE BENEDICT VII AGAINST THE SIMONIACS IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 981

[Note: [Col. 0335D] That a synod was held at Rome at this time, in which, among other matters, the case of Giseler, bishop of Magdeburg, was discussed, is attested by Thietmar, Book III of the *Chronicle*. [Col. 0336D] His statement that Giseler obtained that see from the emperor by evil arts deserves no credence, since Adam, an ancient and trustworthy chronicler, calls Giseler a holy man and apostle of the Winuli in Book II, chapter 14. See Baronius under the year 983.]

[In Mansi, *Councils* XIX, col. 77.]

BENEDICT, bishop, servant of the servants of God.

We wish it to be known to all Catholic and orthodox archbishops, bishops, abbots, kings [Col. 0337A] and princes, dukes and counts, and to all who serve Christ throughout the world, how a synod was assembled in the church of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, before his most sacred body, together with our lord Otto, most serene emperor and august ruler, our spiritual son, and with our suffragans, archbishops, bishops, priests, deacons, and all the clergy of the holy Catholic and apostolic Roman Church.

There the chapters of the sacred canons were read concerning whether a bishop might accept any payment for sacred—that is, ecclesiastical—orders. With God’s help and with the assent of that most blessed prince of the apostles, Peter, it was first forbidden in that place by our own mouth and afterward by all the venerable [Col. 0337B] archbishops and bishops residing in that most sacred place that, from this hour onward, no payment was to be accepted for anything from the rank of doorkeeper up to the priesthood, just as is contained in the decrees of the holy Fathers. (Council of Chalcedon, canon 2.)

“If a bishop performs an ordination for money and reduces to a price the grace that cannot be sold, and ordains for money a bishop, priest, or deacon, or any of those numbered among the clergy; or promotes for money a steward, defender, or anyone subject to the rule, for the sake of his most shameful profit, he who is proven to have attempted this shall incur the penalty of losing his own rank. The person who was ordained shall gain nothing from that ordination or promotion, which was obtained through bargaining, but shall be deprived of the dignity or office that he acquired with money.

If anyone has acted as an intermediary in such shameful and impious gifts or payments, then, if he is a cleric, he shall be deposed; but if he is a layman or monk, he shall be anathematized.”

Likewise, in the same decrees (Apostolic Canon 30):

“If anyone obtains this dignity through money, let both he and the person who ordained him be deposed, and let him be entirely cut off from communion, just as Simon Magus was by Peter.”

Indeed, because of that most wicked purchase Jerusalem was captured, since those wicked priests themselves, who ought to have been guardians and teachers of the law, had first become its transgressors. Finally, they had devised a little trick by which to persuade the children of Israel who came from afar not to bring victims with them, but gifts. When people offered these to them, they did not sacrifice them as the Lord had commanded; rather, they reserved them for this purpose: to sell them to one person after another and thereby multiply for themselves the price of the offering.

For our same Lord and Savior Jesus Christ himself—not through prophets, apostles, or any teachers, but by his own action—made a whip from cords and drove everyone from the temple, including oxen and sheep; he scattered the money-changers’ coins and overturned their tables. To those who sold doves he said: “Take these things away from here, and do not make my Father’s house a house of commerce” (John II, 15–16). The house [Col. 0338A] had been so founded by Solomon that it was called the house of God and was [the text is elliptical], as was that most wise king himself. But it became a house of commerce when oxen, sheep, and doves were sold in it.

Therefore, dearest brothers and beloved sons, we who have undertaken pastoral care for our sheep must keep careful watch, lest we hand them over to be torn by wolves’ teeth; and lest, finally, we ourselves, who are called shepherds, be found to be ravening wolves before the merciful and kind judge on the day of the dreadful examination.

For their sake, by asking, beseeching, admonishing, and reproving your holy brotherhood, we command that, putting aside every excuse, you strive with diligent zeal and the greatest concern to fulfill the things that we have sent you to do. For [Col. 0338B], if any of the priests or deacons is unable to receive the gift of the Holy Spirit without payment from his archbishop or metropolitan, let him strive to come to the holy mother, the Catholic and apostolic Roman Church, and receive episcopal blessing there without any simoniacal heresy.

(Saint Gregory, Book IV, Letter 44.)

“However, if the person who has been ordained, after receiving the documents and the pallium, wishes to offer something to anyone among the clergy solely as a token of gratitude, provided that it was not agreed upon, demanded, or requested, we in no way prohibit its acceptance, because his offering brings no stain of guilt, since it did not arise from the recipient’s greed.”

Whoever among the holy orders sees this letter of ours and does not observe the words or examples of the holy [Col. 0338C] Fathers should know that he is not counted among the disciples of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, but is condemned among the wicked and among those who said to the Lord God: “Depart from us; we do not desire knowledge of your ways” (Job XXI, 14).

But those who lawfully guard this teaching and observe it with pious regard shall receive a share with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven, together with that same Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, who now and forever lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages.

We therefore order and command that this letter of ours be carried by the hand of our dearest fellow bishop, Miro, to all the other archbishops and bishops, so that he himself may receive a worthy reward for his labor [Col. 0338D] and struggle and may bear fruit in penitence [perhaps “in patience,” Hardouin].

## XVIII. BULL OF POPE BENEDICT VII FOR THE MONASTERY OF SAINT WALERICUS. (Year 981)

[In Mabillon, *Annals of the Benedictine Order*, IV, 685.]

BENEDICT, servant of the servants of God, to our dearest son Restold, religious abbot, and to the entire community in the monastery of Saint Walericus, which Hugh, most glorious count and our spiritual son, has newly gathered under the rule of blessed Benedict, and to your successors forever.

[Col. 0339A]

We are burdened with great concern for all the churches of God and pious places, keeping watch lest they suffer any loss through need, but rather receive the support of their own advantage. Therefore, because through the intervention of Hugh, the glorious count, you reasonably asked us to confirm for you, out of his great love and affection, the aforesaid monastery of Saint Walericus, together with all movable and immovable property that is known to have been granted by the aforesaid most glorious count Hugh, or that appears to have been granted and donated forever by other Christians, together with everything that in general now belongs to that monastery, as it stands:

Let it be adorned with the privileges and insignia of the apostolic see, so that it may remain under the jurisdiction of our holy [Col. 0339B] mother Church and not be subjected to the jurisdiction of any other church.

Therefore, favoring your pious desires, by our authority we put into effect what is requested. Accordingly, we prohibit any priest of any church from exercising any dominion or authority in the aforesaid monastery, except the apostolic see. Thus, unless he has been invited by the abbot of that monastery, no one may presume in any way to celebrate the solemn rites of Mass there.

Nor, as stated, shall any person, great or small, have permission to take away anything from it or from all that belongs to the monastery of Saint Walericus, situated in the county of Witmau. Thus indeed, [the text is corrupt; it appears to require that it remain securely endowed under the apostolic constitution and privilege] [Col. 0339C].

But if anyone—which we do not wish—should presume by wicked audacity to oppose or in any way transgress the things established by us for the praise of God and the stability of the aforesaid monastery, we declare him guilty and bound by the chain of black anathema, and we assign him to be burned by the Lord with the devil and his most terrible pomp, and with Judas, the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the punishment of eternal fire.

But whoever proves to be a guardian and observer of these things with pious regard may deserve to obtain the grace of blessing from our most merciful God and to become a participant in eternal life.

Written by the hand of Bonizzo, regional notary and scribe of the holy Roman Church, in the month of April, indiction IX. Farewell.

[Col. 0339D]

Given on the first day before the Kalends of April, by the hand of Stephen, bishop and librarian of the holy Roman Church, in the seventh year of the pontificate of our most holy lord Benedict VII, pope in the see of blessed Peter the Apostle; while our lord Otto, crowned by God, great emperor, was reigning in the thirteenth year of his reign, in the month and indiction IX. Happily. Amen.

## XIX. LETTER OF POPE BENEDICT VII TO LIUDOLF, ABBOT OF CORVEY. (Year 981)

It confirms the rights of the monastery of Corvey and grants pontifical ornaments to the abbot.

[In Mansi, *Councils*, vol. XIX, col. 55.]

BENEDICT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Liudolf, [Col. 0340A] religious abbot of the holy church of Corvey, our dearest son, and to his successors forever.

Since the summit of apostolic dignity is recognized to shine forth in the splendor of divine progress when it has striven to display the contest of its labor more earnestly in carrying out the praises of God, the due care of that same apostolic pastoral responsibility compels us to publish abundantly whatever is recognized as pertaining to the stability of pious places and to confirm it by the judgment of apostolic institution.

Therefore, because you asked us that the monastery of the holy martyrs, the protomartyr Stephen and the martyr Vitus, in the place called Corvey, should be adorned with the privileges and insignia of the apostolic see, so that it might be placed under the jurisdiction of our holy [Col. 0340B] see, which by God’s authority we serve, and not subjected to the jurisdiction of other churches, we, favoring your pious desires by this authority of ours, put into effect what you request.

We prohibit every priest of any church from exercising any dominion or authority in the aforesaid monastery, except the apostolic see. Thus, unless he has been invited by the abbot of the monastery, no one may presume to celebrate the solemn rites of Mass there.

We establish absolutely, under the testimony of divine judgment and through the strong and most severe prohibitions of anathema, that no one, whatever dignity or power he may possess, nor any person, great or small, shall ever presume to interfere in that monastery or in its affairs, or in any way to take away or alienate its goods and [Col. 0340C] possessions, or anything that appears to belong to that monastery.

Indeed, by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, before God and his terrible future judgment, through this our apostolic privilege and decree we sanction and decree that the places which have been exchanged or granted by any abbot in that monastery, as well as the other possessions of laymen which have been given and offered to that holy place by kings, dukes, and other Christians, or which may be granted to it in the future, shall belong securely to the aforesaid monastery and shall remain so forever.

We also grant and confirm by apostolic authority that no abbot shall be appointed there from another monastery. Rather, those servants of God who live according to the rule of blessed Benedict shall have the power to elect an abbot from their own community.

Moreover, we grant that on the principal feasts—namely, the Nativity of the Lord, the Epiphany, the Purification of Saint Mary, the day of the Resurrection, the Ascension, Pentecost, and the feast of Saint John the Baptist; on the feasts of the apostles; and on the feasts of Saint Mary and of the saints to whose merits the aforesaid monastery has been dedicated—the abbot of that place may wear the dalmatic and sandals during the solemn rites of Mass.

But if anyone—which we do not wish—should presume by wicked audacity to oppose or in any way transgress the things established by us for the praise of God and the stability of the aforesaid monastery [Col. 0341A], let him know that he is bound by the chain of anathema. We assign him to be burned by the Lord with the devil and his most terrible punishments, and with Judas, the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ, in eternal fires and torment.

But whoever proves to be a guardian of this our apostolic decree, which is directed toward the worship of God, with pious regard and in all things, may abundantly obtain the grace of blessing from the most merciful Lord God and may deserve to become a participant in eternal life.

Written by the hand of John, our notary and of the sacred Roman Church, on the Nones of April, indiction IX.

Given by the hand of Stephen, bishop and librarian of the holy apostolic see, in the year—by the Lord’s favor—of the pontificate of our lord Benedict, supreme pontiff and universal pope of the Church, in the sacred see of blessed Peter the Apostle, the seventh; while our lord Otto, crowned, was reigning, in the twelfth year of his empire, on the fourth day before the Nones of April.

## XX. LETTER OF POPE BENEDICT VII TO THE BISHOPS OF GAUL AND GERMANY. (Year 981)

He reports to all the bishops of Gaul and Germany what was done in the synods. He confirms and enlarges the privileges of the Church of Magdeburg. He adds the following:

“We send this present privilege through the legates of our secretary to the bishops of Gaul and Germany for confirmation.”

“Granted to us, and so forth.” For the remainder, see the cited [Col. 0341C] compiler.

## XXI. PRIVILEGE OF POPE BENEDICT VII FOR THE CHURCH OF PARIS. (Years 980–982)

[Gallican Church, vol. VII, documents, p. 20.]

BENEDICT, bishop, apostolic [bishop] of the holy Roman see, to all fellow bishops and to all princes residing in the region of Gaul: perpetual salvation in the Lord.

[Col. 0341D]

It is fitting for apostolic moderation to come to the aid, with kindly compassion, of those distinguished by pious religion, and to grant the minds of petitioners assent with eager devotion; for indeed the most excellent reward of gain is with God, the Creator of all, whenever venerable places, suitably ordered, have without doubt been brought to a better condition.

Let the praiseworthy gentleness of Your Excellency therefore know that Elysiardus, bishop of the see of Paris, having come to Rome to the thresholds of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, earnestly presented royal charters which, for the remedy of their souls, had conveyed by firm written instrument the church, as well as the privileges of our predecessors concerning it, of the blessed Mary, Mother and Virgin of God, and of the holy protomartyr Stephen, of the aforesaid place. Moved by this consideration, he humbly and devoutly entreated us that, by apostolic authority, we should reconfirm for him the aforesaid charters and the bishopric of the aforementioned see, with all its appurtenances and adjoining properties—namely, the abbey of Saint Eligius; the abbey of Saint Germanus Rotundus; the abbey of Saint Marcellus; the abbeys of Saint Clodoaldus and Saint Martin; the abbey of Saint Peter called Respacis; the abbey of Saint Saturninus of Canrosa; the abbey of Saint Peter called Nigella; the abbey of Saint Martin which is in Campelli; and the abbey of Saint Peter called Caziacus on the Marne—[Col. 0342A]

with all their appurtenances, and whatever the aforesaid church possesses now or is to possess in the future.

Likewise, concerning the stipends of the brethren of that place: the estate of Spedona, with its church, and a small estate called Macerias, with everything that justly and lawfully belongs to them there; which the same aforementioned bishop Elysiardus, moved by the love of God, removed from his own dominion and that of his successors [Col. 0342B]

and assigned for the use of the brethren of Saint Mary of the aforesaid see.

Undresiacum, with its church and altar, in its entirety and with its appurtenances. Aureliacum, with its church and altar and their dependencies; Civiliacum; Lajacum, with its church and altar and everything adjoining it there; Castenedum, with its church and altar and their dependencies; Baniolum, with its church and altar and its appurtenances; Sulciacum, with its church and altar and everything pertaining to the use of the brethren; Christoilum, with its church and altar, and whatever there belongs to the stipends of the aforesaid brethren.

[Col. 0342C]
