For the seven altars belonging to the aforesaid see, the aforementioned bishop assigned them perpetually to the stipends of those brethren from his own dominion, without sale by himself or his successors and without anyone’s opposition: Eleriacum, Steovilla, Rozetum, Cellas and Vernon, Machelum and Samesium, Mintriacum, and Mauriacum, with the churches and everything belonging to them; Viriacum, with everything that appears to pertain to the aforesaid brethren’s use; and also half of the ninth and the tithe, which had been taken away from the property of that church and which are customarily received from those who use them.

Fontenetum, with its church; Vilcena, with all its appurtenances there. Nevertheless, for the security of the religious community, the above-mentioned Bishop Elysiardus requested that we also confirm the cloister of that congregation by perpetual right, so that they might live securely, without disturbance by either the bishop of that place or any other persons; and that each canon might be able to give or sell his own house, with all its substance, to whichever canon he wished from that congregation, and to no one else, as had been established from ancient times.

[Col. 0342D]

We, having examined the provisions of the most pious emperors and of our fathers, were pleased to grant the petition of the same bishop, so that under the right and protection of the holy Roman and apostolic mother Church all these things might continually remain firm and inviolate. By apostolic authority we therefore command the aforesaid canons to choose from among themselves, by the common consent of all, provosts and deans who shall oversee their estates and faithfully administer their due stipends.

[Col. 0343A]

In accordance with this order we command that none of the bishops, in the succession of time, presume to withdraw, diminish, or divert to his own uses any of these things, or grant them to anyone as a benefice, nor impose any impediment upon the brethren in respect of the aforesaid possessions; nor shall they exact services from the same land, nor demand any exactions from it in any matter. If they wish to increase these possessions, they may do so; but they shall have no power to alienate or diminish anything established for the love of God.

We establish, under the scrutiny of divine judgment, by the adjuration of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and by the command of our humility, that no one ever among rulers, kings, marquises, dukes, counts, princes, or any person armed with judicial authority, or established in any order or office, shall exercise any judicial power over the aforesaid property of the bishop or canons, nor on the island itself where the city of Paris is seen to be situated; nor on the royal road, on the side of Saint Germanus Rotundus, from Saint Medericus to the place commonly called Tudella, on the street of the same Saint Germanus; nor on the other lesser roads leading to the same monastery.

[Col. 0343B]

Nor shall anyone presume there to impose any census, toll, river toll, road toll, port toll, ban, fines, or any distraints; nor any reparations, road dues, dust dues, or other levies; nor presume to receive any census or payments from the free men, *albanisci* and tenants residing on the aforesaid land; nor attempt to inflict any harm or damaging injury there, whether in time of peace or of war. From now until the end of the age, as has been said, we decree that all these things are to remain with complete stability under the protection and jurisdiction of the holy Roman mother Church.

[Col. 0343C]

But if anyone—which we do not wish—should wickedly presume to transgress these provisions established by us for the honor of the holy Mary, Mother of God, and of the blessed protomartyr Stephen and the other saints venerated there, and for the stability of the bishopric, let him know that he is bound by the bond of anathema and assigned, with the devil and all the impious, to the most terrible punishment of eternal fire.

[Col. 0343D]

But may whoever has proved to be a pious guardian and observer of these commands deserve to obtain from the most merciful Lord our God the grace of every blessing, absolution and pardon for all his sins, and the blessedness of heavenly life with the saints and elect, forever and ever.

Farewell. Amen.

Given on the third day before the Kalends of January, by the hand of Lord Stephen, bishop and librarian of the holy Roman Church.

## XXII. Bull of Pope Benedict VII for the Monastery of Saint Vincent at the Volturnus  
*(Year 982.)*

[Muratori, *Rerum Italicarum Scriptores* I, II, 464.]

[Col. 0344A]

Benedict, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to John, venerable abbot of the monastery of Christ’s martyr Saint Vincent, and through him to the same venerable monastery and to your successors forever.

Since with great solicitude we are charged to watch over all the churches of God and pious places, lest they suffer any loss through necessity, but rather obtain stipends for their own benefit, it is therefore fitting that with the complete integrity of our pastoral mind we should especially provide for the stability and usefulness of those venerable places, etc.

Therefore, since you have asked us that the monastery of the blessed martyr Vincent, situated above the river Volturnus in the territory of Benevento, in the region of Samnium, together with its possessions and monasteries—namely, the monastery of the blessed apostle Peter situated beside the river Sabbatus, etc.—

[Col. 0344B]

And therefore we grant to you and to your successors, by the authority of our apostolic see, authority to have, for whatever Christian needs arise in the aforesaid venerable monastery, whichever bishop you may wish to invite there, etc., as is read in the other bulls.

Written by the hand of John, notary of the holy Roman Church, in the month of October, on the ninth day, in the eleventh indiction. Farewell.

Given on the sixth day before the Nones of October, by the hand of Stephen, bishop and librarian of the apostolic holy see, in the eighth year, by God’s favor, of the pontificate of our lord Benedict, supreme pontiff and universal pope, the seventh, in the most sacred see of the blessed apostle Peter, in the aforesaid eleventh indiction.

## XXIII. Bull of Pope Benedict VII for the Monastery of Saint Hilary of Carcassonne  
*(Year 982.)*

[Mabillon, *Annales Ordinis Benedictini* IV, 687.]

[Col. 0344C]

Benedict, bishop, servant of the servants of God.

Let it be known to all Christians that Count Rodgarius came, together with his wife named Adhalaice, and with them came Abbot Benedict, to the thresholds of the apostles, the blessed Peter and Paul, into our presence. They asked that by our apostolic authority we confirm for them the monastery consecrated in honor of Saint Saturninus, [Col. 0344D]

where the blessed Hilary lies buried and rests; so that from this hour onward it might not be lawful for any count, viscount, bishop, or any person, great or small, male or female, to presume to remove or alienate anything from its possessions—whatever it now possesses or may acquire in the future—but that the things granted or donated to the aforesaid monastery by the aforementioned Rodgarius and his wife should always remain for the stipends of the monks and for alms to the poor.

These are: the estate called Corneliana, with the church of Saint Peter; the churches situated in the village of Limosum and in Gardia, with the church of Saint Peter; Malchindus and Salsingus; and the other places belonging, or which ought to belong, to the aforesaid monastery.

[Col. 0345A]

After the death of Abbot Benedict, no one shall appoint an abbot there except one whom the monks who serve God there, or who will serve there in the future, have chosen by the consent and more general agreement of the brethren.

All these things written above we grant to you, Abbot Benedict, and to your successors forever, for the love of almighty God and of Saint Peter, and for the redemption of our soul; likewise for the love of Count Rodgarius of Carcassonne and his wife, and of Raymond, my beloved son, so that their reward may endure forever.

But whoever shall be the guardian and observer of this apostolic command and confirmation of ours, may he receive in all things Christian blessing from the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and may he deserve to become a participant in eternal life forever and ever. But whoever is unwilling to observe it shall be bound by the bond of anathema and remain excluded from the kingdom of God.

[Col. 0345B]

Written by the hand of Stephen, notary and archivist of the holy Roman Church. Farewell.

## XXIV. Privilege of Pope Benedict VII for the Monastery of Saint Saviour and Saint Peter of Gembloux  
*(Year 983.)*

[In Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum*, fifth century, p. 300.]

Benedict, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the religious abbot of the venerable monastery of Saint Saviour of Our Lord Jesus Christ and of Saint Peter, newly established there, and to his successors forever.

[Col. 0345C]

Since with great solicitude we are charged to watch over all the churches of God and pious places, lest they suffer loss through any necessity, but rather obtain stipends for their own benefit, it is therefore fitting that with the complete integrity of our pastoral mind we should especially provide for the integrity and stability of those venerable places, and diligently confer assistance there for their usefulness, so that what we are certain to have bestowed upon venerable places for the honor of his holy name, and also for the praise and glory of his divine majesty, may be acceptable to our almighty God, and so that for us, from his richest mercy, a reward for such a pious work may be bestowed in the heavenly citadels.

[Col. 0345D]

Therefore, since you have asked us that, for the love of almighty God, of the lord Otto, most excellent emperor and our beloved son, we should grant and confirm to you the aforesaid monastery, built in honor of Saint Saviour and Saint Peter, with all movable and immovable property which appears to lie beside and belong to the same monastery—whether estates, fortifications, villages, or hamlets, both those existing now and those which will exist until the end of time—situated in the place called Gembloux, we grant and confirm by apostolic authority.

[Col. 0346A]

No abbot shall be appointed there from another monastery; rather, the servants of God living according to the rule of Saint Benedict shall have the power to elect an abbot from their own congregation. The abbot shall be adorned with the insignia of the privileges of the apostolic see, so that, established under the jurisdiction of our holy Church, which by God’s authority we serve, he shall not be subjected to the jurisdiction of any other church.

Therefore we prohibit the bishop of any church from exercising any authority of dominion in the aforesaid monastery, except that he may have permission to confer a blessing. By apostolic censure and authority, and by the authority of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, under adjuration before divine judgment and by powerful and dreadful prohibitions of anathema, we decree that no one ever, whether any of our pontifical successors or any other person, great or small, presume to remove or alienate anything from the property or possessions belonging to the same monastery.

[Col. 0346B]

But if anyone—which we do not believe—whether great or small, should attempt by wicked boldness to act against this apostolic privilege of ours, let him know that he is bound by the bond of anathema, excluded from the kingdom of God, and condemned with all the impious to the punishment of eternal fire. But whoever proves to be an observer of this command, may he obtain manifold grace, mercy, and eternal life from the most merciful God.

Written by the hand of Boniface, regional notary and archivist of the holy Roman Church, in the month of March, in the eleventh indiction. Farewell.

Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, by the hand of Stephen, bishop and librarian of the apostolic holy see, in the ninth year of the pontificate of our lord Benedict, most holy pope, the seventh; while our lord Otto, crowned by God, great and peaceful emperor, was reigning, in the sixteenth year of his reign, in the month and indiction stated above.

## XXV. Roman Judgment Held by Pope Benedict VII  
*(Year 983.)*

Abbot Leo of Saints Cosmas and Damian is compelled to restore many things to the monastery of Subiaco.

[In Muratori, *Antichità Italiane*, I, p. 379.]

[Col. 0346C]

Charter of renunciation concerning Arsule, Rubiano, Anticulo, and other estates, which Leo, abbot of Saints Cosmas and Damian, renounced in favor of the monastery of Saint Benedict.

[Col. 0346D]

In the ninth year of the pontificate of our lord Benedict, supreme pontiff and universal pope, the seventh, in the most sacred see of the blessed apostle Peter; and in the fifteenth year of the coronation of our lord Otto II, great emperor; and also in the month of April, in the eleventh indiction.

So that things legally determined before the present delegated judges may not again [lacuna]. And because the human mind, always engaged in thought, can in no way retain a perfect memory of the present everywhere, the most learned therefore decreed that the things determined by them should be woven into a written record, so that they might remove every question concerning the whole dispute.

This judgment record was drawn up with the assistance and testimony of the judges of the most sacred city of Rome, in the presence of the most holy pope and of the venerable bishops and clergy of various ranks of the apostolic see, as well as of many illustrious men whose names are subscribed below with their own hands. Here their names begin:

[Col. 0347A]

The aforesaid pontiff, together with Giribertus, bishop of the holy Church of Tortona; Peter, bishop of the Church of Pavia—for these two had been sent there by agreement of the pontiff and by imperial command, with responsibility for hearing the truth; Gregory, bishop of the holy Church of Albano; Leo, bishop of the holy Church of Ostia; John, venerable man, abbot of the monastery of Saint Mary situated at Farfa; Roizi, most prudent abbot of the blessed apostle Paul; Peter, priest and abbot of the monastery of Saint Basil, confessor and pontiff; John, venerable deacon of the holy Roman Church; Stephen, by God’s providence primicerius of the apostolic holy see; Leo, by God’s mercy *arcarius* of the holy supreme apostolic see; Aczo, by the grace of God chief archivist and *apocrisiarius* of the apostolic holy see; Rigizo and Benedict, delegated judges; John the consul, called primicerius; Sergius, count of the palace; Aczo, also called Abbo; John, primicerius; Berardus, count of the city of Tivoli; and Agino.

[Col. 0347B]

With all these and many others present in the basilica of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, inside the hospice where the aforesaid pope’s bedroom is situated, Benedict, a humble priest and provost of the venerable monastery of the blessed Father Benedict and Saint Scholastica, situated at Subiaco, appeared in their presence together with John, priest and monk, and Peter, likewise a monk. All these acted on behalf of the abbot, who was not present there because of the serious illness with which his body was afflicted.

[Col. 0347C]

Then the three aforementioned monks, who were the senior members and investigators of the aforesaid monastery, made a public complaint before the aforementioned pontiff, saying:

“Lord, most holy pope, and all of you, we beseech your clemency to hear and attend to our petition, which we have now brought for three years in your sacred Lateran palace; and now may your ears be open to hear us.

[Col. 0347D]

“We speak concerning that Leo, abbot of the monastery of Saints Cosmas and Damian, which is situated at Cave, because he has plotted against our monastery and also wishes to dissipate and destroy the possessions which your holy predecessors of this apostolic chair of the apostle Peter granted from your archive to our monastery as privileges and commands. For he has alienated all the resources of his own monastery and wishes to see our monastery, which is the chief one, undergo the same dissipation.”

Then the aforementioned pontiff said to the judges concerning Leo the abbot: “Why have you acted with such perversity against the monastery of Saint Benedict, from whose teaching you ought to obtain heavenly things?”

And blessed Gregory said: “If you do not wish to relinquish what is yours, take care never to desire what belongs to another.”

In response Abbot Leo said: “May the Lord forbid that I have taken away from their places, or from any resource of the monastery of Saint Benedict, anything belonging to them. But I retain the things which they claim, just as they are contained in our privilege.”

The judges said: “Let them produce the documents before us, and let it be established in those documents what the earlier records show.”

[Col. 0348A]

Then Abbot Leo produced his document and placed it in the judge’s hand, saying: “See whether this is just for us; I shall raise no further dispute.”

Then Stephen, the primicerius, began to read. When the deacon John heard that this document had been issued in the time of Alberic, formerly patrician of the Romans, he said: “It is sufficient for us. Now let us also examine the documents of the monastery of Saint Benedict.”

At that moment Benedict, the priest and provost, displayed these commands from his privileges. Then the aforesaid deacon John and the judges took them together and began to read them.

[Col. 0348B]

The first thing found was that, in the monastery of Saint Benedict written above, the places listed below had been confirmed by Zacharias, of holy memory. The second document was that of the most holy Pope Gregory. The third was that of Nicholas, bishop of Rome, of pious memory. The fourth was the confirmation of Pope Benedict. The remaining documents were constitutions of the most holy emperors Louis and Charles.

When the names of the aforesaid pontiffs and their holy deeds had been heard, as well as the power of the supreme emperor—who was said to have granted nothing else to him except on account of their holiness and for the redemption of his soul—it was clear that anyone who wished to break these provisions or diminish anything without the consent of the brethren could not enter the kingdom of God.

Then Pontiff Benedict, together with the bishops and judges, said: “Let all the places be named.”

[Col. 0348C]

They found the estate of Juventiana, or Seminarium; likewise the place called Saint Paulinus, with the church of Saint Peter, beginning at the water and the arch called Ferrata; also the mountain called Ruviano, where there had been a church of Saint Mary; and the mountain called Arsule; as well as Pantana, called Rudimundi; and the place where there is water called Bullica; likewise Serra, called Saint John; similarly another place called Anticolo; and the mountain called Crufo—all adjoining one another.

[Col. 0348D]

When all these named places, with their boundaries, had been found in the aforesaid privileges, they all said to the aforementioned Abbot Leo and to his congregation who were present:

“With your hearing and seeing this, nothing in these places belongs to your monastery, unless this has been done with the consent of the brethren. Therefore, as you have heard read, let the named places, whose property belongs to the monastery of Saint Benedict, be renounced here and now.”

When the aforementioned Abbot Leo had recognized the truth, he renounced, by the staff, all the places read above, together with his congregation, in every respect to the monastery of Saint Benedict.

Then the pontiff likewise invested the other party, saying:

“Let every possession of the holy Church from which it was taken away, as has been said, be restored completely, and let it remain in its dominion under the power of you and your successors, without any ambiguity, together with everything belonging to the aforesaid places.”

Thus it was sanctioned by all the delegated judges and determined inviolably.

[Col. 0349A]

By order of our lord Benedict, supreme pontiff and universal pope, I, Benedict, archivist of the holy Roman Church, with the consent and promulgation of the aforesaid delegated judges, wrote these words of the judgment. The persons named above subscribed with their own hands for greater and firmer stability, on the day, year, month, and indiction stated above, the eleventh.

I, Benedict, bishop of the holy catholic and apostolic Church, the seventh, have subscribed.

I, Geribertus, bishop of the holy Church of Tortona, was present at this judgment charter forever.

Peter, bishop of the Church of Pavia, was present at this judgment record forever, as written above.

I, John, an unworthy deacon of the holy Roman Church, was present at and subscribed this charter of renunciation.

[Col. 0349B]

Gregory, bishop of the holy Church of Albano, was present at and subscribed this charter of renunciation.

Leo, bishop of Ostia, was present at and subscribed this charter of renunciation, as mentioned above.

Stephen, by God’s nod bishop of the Church of Narni, was present at this charter of renunciation.

Stephen, by God’s providence primicerius, was present at this charter of renunciation.

Leo, called *arcarius* by the grace of the Lord, of the holy apostolic see, was present at this charter of renunciation.

Azo, by God’s mercy chief archivist and *apocrisiarius* of the Roman Church, was present and subscribed.

[Col. 0349C]

Rigizo, by God’s nod delegated judge, was present at this charter of renunciation.

Benedict, delegated judge, subscribed his hand to this brief memorandum.

Sergius, count of the palace, was present at this renunciation.

Berardus, illustrious count of Tivoli, was present and subscribed.

John, consul and duke in the name of God, was present at this charter of renunciation.

I, Benedict, by the grace of God archivist of the holy Roman Church and its writer, after the subscription and delivery of all the witnesses, completed and concluded this document.

## XXVI. Privilege of Pope Benedict VII for the Monastery of Saint Mary of Nienburg  
*(Year 983.)*

[Col. 0349D]

To the monastery of Saint Mary of Nienburg, at the request of “his beloved and spiritual son, the most worthy advocate of the apostolic holy see, the emperor Otto, ever Augustus, who visited the threshold of the apostles with worthy devotion and discussed with him many matters concerning the state of the holy religious life,” he grants “that the same place should enjoy such justice and liberty as the other monasteries possess which, in those regions, are under protection and strengthened by their privilege and appear to be subject to the mundiburdium of their lord the emperor.” He adds certain privileges.

[Knaut, *Gründliche Fürstellung*, 13.]

“Of entrusted oversight,” etc. For the remainder, see the cited compiler.

## XXVII. Bull of Pope Benedict VII to the Soldier Peter  
*(Years 974–983.)*

[Col. 0350A]

To the noble Peter, called Bonicollus, a soldier and *comarchus* of the land of Mudana in the suburb of Ghent, he sends through Balduinus, “a monk of the abbey of Saint Bavo in the district near Ghent, called Boerheim,” “with this present bull, three small bones of Saints Marcellinus, Maximinus, and Quirinus, which may be disposed of for the churches, namely Saint Bavo, Saint John, and also the hall of Saint Pharailde in the city of Ghent itself.”

[*Messager des Sciences de la Belgique*, Ghent, 1837, p. 491.]

“We, distinguished, and also,” etc. Consult, if you please, the cited work.

## XXVIII. Privilege of Pope Benedict VII for the Church of Tivoli  
*(Years 974–983.)*

[Marini, *Papiri diplomatici*, I, p. 229.]

[Col. 0350B]

Benedict, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most beloved, reverend, and excellent brother John, by the grace of God bishop of the holy Church of Tivoli, and through you to the same venerable bishopric and to your successors forever.

Since with great solicitude we are charged to watch over all the Churches of God and pious places, lest they suffer any loss through necessity, but rather obtain stipends for their own benefit, it is therefore fitting that with the complete integrity of our pastoral mind we should provide especially for the integrity and stability of these venerable places and diligently confer assistance there for their benefit, so that what we are certain to have bestowed upon venerable places for the honor, praise, and glory of his holy name may be acceptable to our almighty God, and that for us, from his most abundant mercy, the reward of such a pious work may be bestowed in the heavenly citadels [*sic*].

[Col. 0350C]

Therefore, since your Belovedness has asked us that, by this apostolic privilege of ours, we should grant to you and to your successors all the property of your aforesaid bishopric, namely of the Church of Tivoli of Saint Lawrence, holy martyr and deacon of Christ—for many protections were lost through the negligence of your predecessor bishops—we, moved by your prayers, for the love of almighty God and for his honor, confirm to you and to your successors, for the restoration of the aforesaid Church, the entire bishopric and all the parishes, churches, and monasteries under various names, with all their appurtenances and adjoining properties, situated throughout the territory of Tivoli, specifically within the city of Tivoli [*sic*].

[Col. 0350D]

That is, the entire region called Foro, with Vico Patricius, and Oripo, with the church of Saint Alexander, and the watermills with the ancient channel beside the bishopric. Likewise the church of Saint Paul and the region called Formello, with its steps and everything belonging to them, adjoining one another, and bounded by neighboring properties: on one side by the public paved road descending to the Major Gate and continuing as far as the Dark Gate; on the second side by the wall of the city of Tivoli as far as Putrerula, with the church of Saint Pantaleon, its tower, and marble staircase; and then ascending by the public road as far as the ancient wall of Saint Paul. On both sides it is bounded by that wall, which reaches as far as the city wall.

[Col. 0351A]

Likewise the entire region called Plazzula within the same city: on one side by the wall of the city; on the second side by the paved road leading to the little gate of Vesta; and on the third and fourth sides by the monastery of Saint Benedict.

Also another entire region called Castro Vetere, with the churches of Saint Mary and Saint George, which are deaconries: on one side by the ditch from which water flows toward Vesta, while on both sides it is surrounded by the city wall.

[Col. 0351B]

Moreover, two entire estates adjoining one another, called Sipiano—which is now called the bishopric, with the church of Saint Mary of the Dark Gate [*sic as written in the margin, by the same hand*]—and Lambrione. In them are vineyards with a small building beneath them, olive trees, and everything belonging in its entirety to the same estates. They are situated in the territory of Tivoli and bounded on one side by the public paved road ascending to the Secure Gate; on the second side by the vineyard called Votano; on the third side by the public road descending from the aforesaid city and reaching the paved road; and on the fourth side by the property of your bishopric, as you hold it by other commands.

[Col. 0351C]

Likewise the entire estate called Pozzalia, also called Alefanto, with vineyards and lands and everything belonging to it, situated in the aforesaid territory: on one side by the river; on the second side by Greater Pentonia; on the third side by the estate Quintiliolum; and on the fourth side by Camarti.

Likewise the entire estate called Pluzano: on one side by the river; on the second side by Camarti; on the third side by Cervinariola; and on the fourth side by the estate Purpuranum, belonging to the same bishopric. Also the aforementioned estate Purpuranum in its entirety, with everything belonging to you: on one side by Africanum; on the second side by the river; on the third side by Pluzano; and on the fourth side by Lauretum.

Likewise the estates of Pertusulo and Rosario, with the church of Saint Valentine; the estate Julianum; and the estate Orianum, all adjoining one another in their entirety.

They are situated in the territory of Tivoli, about five miles from the aforesaid city, in the Greater Field: on one side by Staphilianum; on the second side by the paved road on which Ponticello lies; on the third side by the embankment; on the fourth side by Pirantis [Piranis]; and on the fifth side by Colummella.

[Col. 0351D]

Likewise the estate Suberetula; the estate Aramagna; and the estate Bissianum, with the church of Saint Angelus; the estate Trulias; the estate Castamiola; the estate Computum; the estate Turinianum; the estate Jamule; the estate Gimelle; the estate Septem Viae; the estate Matre Saccula; the estate Pracli [Precli]; and the estate Planule—all in their entirety and adjoining one another, with the lands, woods, and everything belonging in its entirety to the aforesaid estates, situated in the same territory of Tivoli.

[Col. 0352A]

Moreover, the entire estate called Barela; the entire estate Casapetra; the estate Tufolo; the estate Tortilianum; the estate Oriali; and the vineyard situated beside Saint Pastor.

Likewise the land and vineyard where the church of Saint Agnes is situated. Also the enclosed vineyard with its crypts and ancient watermills, and the measured land situated at Griptule; and also the entire estate called Cornu; the estate Vineole; the estate Caput Leonis [Capito]; the estate Antonianum, with the church of Saint Mary at Pesile; the estate Carinianum; the estate Lame, with the church of Saint Januarius; the estate Rubetum, with the church of Saint Mary; and the estate Balle Petrosa—all adjoining one another, with lands, fields, meadows, pastures, woods, and all their appurtenances, situated in the aforesaid territory of Tivoli.

[Col. 0352B]

The estate Rosarum; the estate Rejanum, with the parish church of Saint Peter and the church of Saint Thomas the apostle; and the houses and parish church of Saint Stephen, which is called Severinus; and the parish church called Saint Vincent, with its crypts, ruined walls, woods, and all their appurtenances.

Also the entire hamlet called Guaddo, from the estate Ceseranum.

Likewise the estate called Paternus; the estate called Crypta Tabulicia; and Cameto, with all their appurtenances: on one side by the public road; on the second side by Paternus; on the third side by the river; and on the fourth side by Carrarca.

[Col. 0352C]

Especially the entire estate Silicata; the estate Panicianum; and the estate Caccabelli, with vineyards and lands and all their appurtenances: on one side by the paved road descending from the Lucanian bridge [to the Lucanian bridge]; on the second side by another paved road leading to the ancient palace; on the third side by the public road; and on the fourth side by the estate Gostanti.

Indeed, the entire enclosed vineyard above, with everything belonging to it, situated in the estate called Zetula, as it came to the aforesaid bishopric by a charter of donation.

The entire estate Paconi; the estate Piranello; the estate Turriele; the estate Cecili; the estate Serianum, with olive trees; the estate Balbinianum, in which is the church of Saint Victorinus; and the estate Mollica, adjoining one another, with all their appurtenances.

Their boundaries are: on one side a grove; on the second side the stream leading to the bridge of Marinus; on the third side Lumbricata; and on the fourth side the stream Puzzulo.

[Col. 0352D] Moreover, I grant and confirm in its entirety the Marsican road, and the estate called Round Field in its entirety; the estate of Pensionis and the house in its entirety, with the church of Saint Mary and of Saint Severinus, belonging to the aforesaid bishopric. Indeed ([sic]: *Quippini*), and the estate called Cornuti, with the parish church of Saint Stephen; the estate of Parianus, with the church of Saint Mary; the estate of Circulus, with the church of Saint Benedict and Saint Anastasius; the estate of Iron Water; the estate of Paternus; the estate of Maranus and Mount Paternus; the estate of Mars’s House; the estate of Vegeta, which is Projecticus’s House; the estate of Batilianus, with the adjoining lands and woods, situated in the territory of Tibur, bounded on one side by the Greater Ditch, on the second side by the old road that leads to [Col. 0353A] Marinus’s bridge, on the third side by the estate of Calicianus belonging to the holy Roman Church, on the fourth side by the estate . . . , and on the fifth side by the estate of Paulinus belonging to the monastery of Cella Nova.

Furthermore, also the estate called Greater Meadows, with vineyards, lands, and meadows; the estate of Baronianus in its entirety, among the adjoining boundaries, beginning at the stream as far as the ancient aqueduct; on the second side Monetula; on the third side the estate of Romanus; and on the fourth side the river Tiber, extending as far as the other arch, where it is at Poticella. Likewise, the enclosed vineyard situated by itself at the Hadrian Gate; the estate of Ciceianus, the estate of Aflorus, the estate of Ciculanus, and the estate of Paccionus, all adjoining one another in their entirety; the estate of Zizimi [that is, the valley of Cotta] ([sic], written in red letters in the margin), with the parish church [Col. 0353B] of Saint Mary and Saint John; the estate of Marcianellus and the farmstead of Saint Cyricus; the estate of Columnella, or whatever other names they may now be called: bounded on one side by the public road; on the second side by the estate of Apollonius; on the third side by Romanus; on the fourth side by the Long Ditch; and on the fifth side by the aqueduct from which the water runs directly into the public road. Likewise, the estate of Carpinianus and the vineyard between the two Ludi, with the church of Blessed Peter the Apostle [see: outside the walls] ([this note is in the margin, in red]); and the vineyard at the crossroads, with the church of Saint Lawrence.

Indeed, also the estate of the Castle in its entirety, with the church of Saint Angelus; the estate of Balarcese, adjoining one another. Likewise, the estate with its own farmstead, the Long Ditch, and the parish church of Saint [here we have omitted this] ([another hand in the margin]), with vineyards, lands, and all its appurtenances [Col. 0353C]. The estate of Fullonius [Fullonis] in its entirety, and four ounces of the estate called Apollonius. Also the estate of Claudianus, the estate of Julianus, the estate of Tripentis, the estate of Cisternula, the estate of Pontecclum, the estate of Silverius, the estate of Marciana’s House, the estate of Parsi, with woods, olive groves, and lands, with the church of Saint Cecilia and all their appurtenances; likewise the estate of Paternus, with the church of Saint Columba; the estate of the olive groves; the estate of Janula, with the church of Saint Paul; the estate of Anterranus in its entirety, adjoining one another ([sic]), approximately twenty-six miles from the city of Rome.

Furthermore, the estate of Balneolum, the estate of Facundius, the estate of Licinius, the estate of Bassanus, the estate of Barbatianus, the estate of Corsanus, the estate of Long Bico; the estate of Antonius; the estate of [Col. 0353D] Clippus; the estate of Nigilio; Resiarius; the estate of Buccunianus, which is in the territory of Sabina; the estate of Gellus; the estate of Cartelli, which is situated before Lucanus’s bridge; the estate of Corco in its entirety; the estate of Maianus in its entirety, situated beside the paved road; the estate of Jemilianus; the estate of Aquilo; the estate of Mutilianus, beside Saint Stephen’s at Cornuti; the estate situated at the Long Ditch, called *Capra molente*; and Castanneola in their entirety. They are bounded on one side by the colony called Minianus; on the second side by the estate of Veranus; on the third side by the estate of Ilianus; and on the fourth side by the mountain called Vulturella, belonging to the holy Roman Church.

Likewise, the estate of the Holm Oak and the city called Noe; the estate of Petroniliolus and Turricula; [Col. 0354A] the estate of Turritula; the estate of Vicus and Arch, and Cicilianus, Vigilianus, and Aspreta, with the church of Saint Peter, and in the village the church of Saint Valerius; the estate of the Greeks; the estate of Virdilianus, where the church of Saint Magnus is located. All these adjoin one another in their entirety, with houses and vineyards, lands and woods, meadows, pastures, cultivated or uncultivated land; the estate of Melizanus; the estate of Paternus; the estate of Sambuculus, situated in the territory of Tibur, eight miles from that city; bounded on one side by the estate of Minianus, on the second side by Vulturella, on the third side by the estate of Maternus, and on the fourth side by the river called Jubenzanus, and by the mountain called Crufo, belonging to the aforesaid bishopric.

In the same way, on the other side of the mountain, the estates of Caparacia, or the estate called Massa, with the mountain on whose summit [Col. 0354B] stands the church of Saint Angelus, called Faianus; also the place called Trellanus [that is, Giranus] ([in the rubric]), with its estates, namely: the estate of Carpus, the estate of Marra, the estate of Plaza, the estate of Rosarium, the estate of Corianus, the estate of Julianus, the estate of Martellus’s House, the estate of Saint Anatolia, and the valley of Fortinianus, extending to the end of Stella; the estate of Crapola, the Mountain of Living Water. All these adjoin one another in their entirety, with houses and vineyards, lands and woods, fields, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, and all their appurtenances; situated in the aforementioned territory of Tibur, approximately ten miles from that city. They are bounded on one side by the estate of the Greeks; on the second side by the estate of Sassa; on the third side by the estate of Grunzanus; and on the [Col. 0354C] fourth side by the estate of Longianus.

Likewise, the estate of Hercules’s House, with houses and vineyards and all that belongs to it; bounded on one side by the estate of Licilianus, on the second side by the estate of Foranus, on the third side by the estate called Pasinianus, and on the fourth side by the estate of Barbaranus, belonging to the Church of Tibur. In addition, four estates in their entirety, namely Lion’s Head [capud; capito], Priscianus, Caesarianus, and Magianus. All adjoining one another.

Indeed, also the estate of the Villa of the Breach, the estate of Saturanus, the estate of Valneolum, and the farmstead with the church of Saint Secundina, extending to the stream called Trabicella; and the church of Saint Stephen with its farmstead; and the estate of Marcianus, all in their entirety, situated beside the estate of Giranus and Finestelle, in the territory of Trellanus. [Col. 0354D] Likewise, the estate of Cantoranus with its church, the estate of Bulzinianus, the estate of Maranus in its entirety; and the church of Saint Felicitas with its farmstead, extending to the river; all adjoining one another in their entirety.

Furthermore, the parish church of Saint Lawrence, called “at Subiaco,” with the aqueduct and the church of Saint Mary situated above the fortress; the estate of Paternellus; the estate of Bullica, with vineyards, lands, and all their appurtenances, situated in the territory of Subiaco as far as the middle river of the Church of Tibur. The estate of Ponza; the estate called Casa; the estate of Casalupulus; the estate of Canistra; the estate of Scapio; the estate of Caesarea; the estate of Cisinianus, adjoining one another, situated in the territory of Affile; bounded on one side by Affile, on the second side [Col. 0355A] by Turrita, on the third side by Gaianellus, and on the fourth side by Paterclanus.

Likewise, the estate of Orarius and Gratinianus; the estate of Puzzorosanus; the estate of Ponzanus; the estate of Cetreianus; the estate of Torinianus in its entirety, situated in the territory of Subiaco; bounded on one side by Cisianus, on another side by Balneolum, on the third side by Glasteranus, on the fourth side by the estate of Nuscanus, and on the fifth side by the estate of Caprola; on the aforesaid side, the estate of Calcuanus. Likewise, five estates in their entirety called Moreni: Oreta, Plumbariola, Aqua Combula, Pagatianus with its lake and its entrance, situated in the territory of Tibur, approximately four miles from that city, in the Greater Field; also Monticelli and the farmsteads with the church.

These are all the estates, farmsteads, parish churches, monasteries, and churches written above, which appear to be entered above [Col. 0355B]. Moreover, also the churches which your predecessor consecrated this present year in the presence of Bishop Boso, namely those of Saint John and Blessed Juvenal. (This is in the bull of John XIX, dated 1029.)

We also confirm that you may delimit them by their adjoining boundaries and landmarks. Beginning among the boundaries at the Seven Holy Brothers, and extending to the boundaries of Saint John, which is called “at Argentella,” and thence to the Sacred Field, where the artificial *Staphili* are located, and straight on to the great paved road of Palestrina; then descending along that paved road, all the land on the right-hand side belongs to the territory of Tibur and to the jurisdiction of that same Church of Tibur. On the left-hand side, everything belongs to the holy Church of Palestrina. Just as our predecessors defined it by their decrees.

Furthermore, we grant [Col. 0355C] [and confirm to you and your venerable bishopric] to you and your bishopric that at all times you may have the license and power, with all your people, to enter and leave with all your property by the bridge called Lucanus, without paying any rent or making any contribution there for any reason whatsoever. Moreover, we grant you full jurisdiction and the right to hold courts over all the monasteries and churches of your bishopric, both within that city and outside it, and over the monks and handmaids of God, the priests and deacons, and the entire clergy who are under your protection or who shall remain in your diocese, so that you and your successors may have the power to summon and judge them.

Finally, by this our apostolic privilege we confirm to you every customary right which your predecessors were accustomed to possess ([sic]), so that you and your successors may retain it forever without any opposition. No count, castald, or any other man who performs public functions there shall ever be permitted to summon or bring to court, or to require security from, the male or female servants of your church, or the free men who reside in the farmsteads of your aforesaid bishopric, or to subject them to any jurisdiction, without the consent of you and your successors.

As for the aforesaid properties and places contained above—namely, Lipianus and Lambrio, with their vineyards and tabular crypt, and Cannoto, and Pensionis, in which are the church of Saint Mary and Saint [Col. 0356A] Severinus, and Trellanus, and the village with the church of Saint Valerius, and Zizinnus, in which is the parish church of Saint Mary and Saint John, together with the other farmsteads—namely, also in matters of pasture dues and acorn dues—you shall suffer no interference. All the other immovable properties, cultivated and uncultivated, with all their appurtenances and adjacent lands, are as written above.

From this present second indiction, we grant and, through you, perpetually establish the aforesaid places, with their parish churches, churches, houses, villages, and fortresses, cultivated and uncultivated lands, urban and rural properties, and also all the rights and customary practices that have hitherto remained in that same church through past times. From now on we order that they shall always remain inviolate.

Likewise, all the safeguards and every written instrument [Col. 0356B] of charters belonging to your bishopric which have been taken away or diminished by pagans or through human negligence, or burned by fire, shall, through this our apostolic privilege, remain fully and legally effective in every respect, with all their property standing firm. All properties which orthodox Christians and most devout persons appear to have offered and granted, or may hereafter offer and grant, for the sake of their souls or for the welfare of your church, whether by written charter or by spontaneous will, we decree for you and your successors to possess in your church with perpetual stability and perpetual right, without any interference or complaint by any person.

Therefore, establishing and promulgating this before God and before his terrible future judgment, by the authority of this our apostolic privilege we decree, and by the authority of Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, we determine, whether for future pontiffs of the Apostolic See, for those who shall administer ecclesiastical affairs, or for any person, great or small, or anyone endowed with power of whatever rank, that no one shall ever have permission in any way to separate the things piously arranged and granted by us—those immovable properties joined together as one and spiritually united by apostolic writing—or to alienate any one of them from another.

If, meanwhile—which we do not believe—anyone, through rash audacity, should act against those things which have been established by this our authority and by that of our Lord Jesus Christ and Peter, prince of the apostles, whose office we exercise though unworthy, let him be bound by the bond of anathema and be appointed to be burned in the punishment of everlasting fire with the devil and his most atrocious pomp, and with Judas, the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ; may he never be released from the aforementioned bonds of anathema.

But may whoever proves to be a conscientious observer, preserving this apostolic constitution insofar as it concerns the worship of God, deserve to obtain the grace of blessing from our most merciful Lord God and, through the merits of Blessed Lawrence, martyr and deacon, deserve to become a participant in eternal life.

Written by the hand of John, notary of the holy Roman Church, in the month of December and the second indiction.

+ Farewell in goodness. +

[Col. 0357A] Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of January, through the hands of John, bishop of the holy Church of Lavirana and librarian of the holy Apostolic See. In the fourth year, by God’s favor, of the pontificate of Lord Benedict, supreme pontiff and universal pope; in the seventh year in the most sacred See of Blessed Peter the Apostle; while the most devout perpetual Augustus, Otto, crowned by God, the great and peaceful emperor, was reigning, in the fifth year of his imperial rule, in the month of December and the aforesaid second indiction.

ANNO DOMINI DCCCCLXXXIV. POPE JOHN XIV.

[Col. 0357]

HISTORICAL NOTICE.

(From Eggs, *Pontificium doctum*, p. 283.)

After Benedict VII had died, Peter, bishop of Pavia, arch-chancellor of the Emperor Otto, a pious man of great learning, was raised to the See of Peter and consecrated as John XIV through Otto’s efforts, by the Roman clergy and people. When the exiled Boniface learned this, he returned without delay from Constantinople to Rome, intending to invade the See once more. Supported by the efforts of his partisans, and having inflicted punishment on several who had opposed his invasion, he violently expelled Pope John from the See three months after his election. He then bound him in chains and cast him into prison, where for five months he afflicted him in various ways. Finally, after John had been killed by hunger or the sword, he ordered him to be dragged from the prison into public and exposed to everyone’s eyes, so that those who were working for his liberation might no longer hope for anything.

A horrifying sight indeed, and a spectacle to be mourned by all Roman citizens: John, his corpse extinguished by the very emaciation of starvation, crying out for vengeance from heaven and from men against the sacrilegious tyrant.

Nor was the deserved vengeance long delayed on either side. For the savage invader of the Apostolic See, struck by sudden death within four months, fell lifeless from the throne. He became so detested even by all his own followers that they dragged his dead body to the Lateran square with a rope tied to its feet, pierced it with spears and swords, attacked it with stones, spit, and mud, and finally threw it away unburied as though unworthy of burial. Oldoinus writes that the corpse of the unhappy man lay unburied for several days in public contempt and was at last secretly given burial through the efforts of certain clerics. Boniface perished, to be counted among brigands rather than among Roman pontiffs (I use Baronius’s phrase), on the twelfth day before the Kalends of August in the year of salvation 985.

[Col. 0357]

LETTER OF POPE JOHN XIV TO ALONUS, ARCHBISHOP OF BENEVENTO.

(From Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, vol. VIII, col. 69.)

[Col. 0357B] John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most beloved Alonus, venerable and deservedly honored archbishop of the holy Church of Benevento and Siponto, and to your successors forever.

If shepherds of sheep are content to endure sun and frost day and night in guarding their flock, and, lest any sheep should perish by wandering or be carried off and torn apart by the bites of wild beasts, they vigilantly guard and watch over the fold, with how much toil and care ought we to remain watchful, who are shepherds of souls, lest the burden of our negligence torment us before the supreme Shepherd, and lest from the very height of the honors we now possess we should be cast down before all others by the strictest judgment. [lacuna]

We have sent to your fraternity, according to custom, the pallium for the celebration of the solemn Masses. We permit you to use it—while the privileges of your Church remain in their established condition—only as you know that your predecessors and those before them used it: namely, on these feasts, at the Nativity of the Lord, the Epiphany, the Presentation of Saint Mary our Lady, likewise at her Annunciation, at the Paschal feasts, the Ascension of the Lord, and Pentecost; also at the feast of Saint John the Baptist, at the birthdays of the Apostles, at the Assumption of Blessed Virgin Mary, and likewise at her Nativity; also at the dedication of the holy church of your archbishopric, on the day of your consecration, and at the gathering and consecration of bishops; [Col. 0359A] likewise at the feast of Blessed Michael the Archangel and the translation of the body of Blessed Bartholomew the Apostle.

We also grant and concede to you and your successors the authority to ordain bishops in the following cities: Saint Agatha, Avellino, Quintodecimo, Ariano, Ascoli, Bibino, Vulturaria, Larino, Telese, Alife, Termoli, Trivento, and Sessula. We confirm to you and your successors the Church of Saint Michael on Mount Gargano, together with the Church of Siponto itself, and with all their appurtenances, estates, dependents of both sexes, churches, and estates which are recognized as belonging to those churches. Of which, however, [lacuna] honor must be preserved by the modest vitality of your actions.

Moreover, we urge that your conduct should correspond and conform to your dignities, so that, with the Lord as author, you, reverend one, may be conspicuous everywhere [Col. 0359B]. Let your life, therefore, be a rule for your sons, since their progress depends upon your example, so that after your death you may safely say: “My heart was lifted up neither by prosperity nor by the things that flatter us temporally, nor was it cast down by adversity; but whatever it may have been, it was overcome by the virtue of patience.”

Let hatred find no place with you, just as indiscriminate affection must not occupy you. Let the good find you kind, and let the wicked recognize you as discerning. Easily [lacuna]. Let evil suggestion not make justice blameworthy in your judgment; let favor or influence not excuse the guilty. Do not show yourself lenient toward offenders, lest, because you have not avenged what was done, you appear by your tolerance to permit it.

Let there be in you the sweetness of a good shepherd and the stern strictness of a judge: the one to cherish those who live rightly, the other to restrain the restless from wickedness [Col. 0359C]. [lacuna] love. But since zeal against sinners, when it wishes to be an undiscerning avenger, very often passes into cruelty, therefore restrain anger by judgment and reserve discipline, so that, like a father, you may punish faults and not withdraw your affection from the sons whom you correct.

Show yourself merciful, insofar as virtue permits [lacuna]. Let your defense assist the oppressed; let restraint and reason oppose the oppressors. Despise no one [lacuna]; reject no one who seeks justice. Let the guardianship of equity excel in you, so that neither the power of the rich may persuade you to dare anything outside the path of reason, nor the humility of the poor cause him to despair of you, so that, with God’s help, you may be such as sacred reading commands when it says: “It is necessary that a bishop be blameless.”

But you will be able to use all these things beneficially if you have charity as your teacher; whoever follows it will never depart from the right path. Behold, dearest brother, the qualities that, among many others, belong to your priesthood [Col. 0360B]. These accompany the pallium; if you diligently preserve them, you will possess inwardly what you have shown that you received outwardly.

As for the faith which you briefly set forth in your letters, although you ought to have explained it more fully, nevertheless we give thanks to our Redeemer that we recognize it as sound even in its brevity. May the Holy Trinity [lacuna] your fraternity by the grace of its protection, and so direct us along the path of its honor that, after the bitterness of this life, we may together deserve to attain eternal sweetness. Amen.

Written by the hand of Leo, regional notary of the Holy Roman Church, in the month of December, in the twelfth indiction.

Given on the eighth day before the Ides of December, through the hands of John, [Col. 0360C] bishop and librarian of the Holy Apostolic See, in the year, by the Lord’s favor, of the pontificate of Lord John, supreme pontiff and universal pope XIV, the first in the most sacred See of Blessed Peter the Apostle.

[Note: From the reading of the diploma just recited, I observe that, in that century—which by universal agreement was rough and barbarous—this diploma was written in periods and sentences so aptly composed. I think this happened because it was dictated by the pontiff himself; for it has more the scent of a pastoral letter [Col. 0360C] than of a pontifical diploma. The latter, as can be seen in those already recited, were copied from some formularies, since nearly all have the same, and likewise stereotyped, opening, which I find preserved down to the time of Leo IX.]

ANNO DOMINI DCCCCLXXXIV. THEODERICUS, BISHOP OF METZ.

[Col. 0359]

HISTORICAL NOTICE CONCERNING THEODERICUS.

(*Gallia Christiana*, vol. XIV.)

[Col. 0359D] After Adalbero’s death, Bruno of Cologne governed the Church of Metz for a time, and arranged for the staff of Saint Peter to be transferred to the Church of Cologne. At the end of the year 964, however, Theodericus, or Diedericus, a canon of Halberstadt and provost of Worms, was proclaimed bishop by the Emperor Otto I, to whom he was bound by ties of blood, as he was also to Bruno, archbishop of Cologne, through his mother’s family, and to Emperor Conrad I and Count Eberhard through his father’s family. A nearly contemporary writer records the following about him: “Deodericus, a man of imperial lineage and singular intellect, ascended to the episcopal chair by the common acclamation of all.”

He devoted himself to letters at the monastery of Saint Gall under the renowned teacher Kerold. He is said to have declared that, when he learned from ancient tradition that the first letters of the names of the bishops of Metz had been written in metals more or less precious according to each man’s merits, he would perform such great deeds that his name, written in silver, would be marked in gold.

In the year 965 he spent the holy day of Pentecost at Aachen in the company of the Emperor Otto and Bruno, archbishop of Cologne. Shortly afterward Bruno fell ill and wished to be carried to Rheims, where he died, leaving his will in the hands of Theoderic of Metz and Wicfrid of Verdun, the bishops who arranged his funeral. In that same year Theoderic was also present at the assembly of bishops held at Cologne, where the foundation of the collegiate church of Saint Martin of Liège was confirmed.

Around that time he restored the village of Vigiacus and certain other properties to the monastery of Saint Arnulf. He dedicated the church of the monastery of Vergaville, recently founded in honor of the Blessed Virgin and the holy Apostles, in the year 966.

Following his cousin the emperor into Italy, he remained there for three years. Taking advantage of this opportunity, he gathered many relics from various places and arranged for them to be transferred in the year 970 to the monastery of Saint Vincent, which he himself had built two years earlier on the island of that city and adorned with splendid buildings. After receiving the body of Saint Lucy in that same monastery of Saint Vincent, he immediately began building an oratory there in her honor; he dedicated it on the seventh day before the Ides of August in the year 972, with the assistance of his provincial bishops, Gerard of Toul and Wicfrid of Verdun.

In the district of Calvomont, finding a certain place between the Moselle and a neighboring mountain called in the vernacular “Spinal,” suitable for divine service, he built a monastery there and transferred the relics of Saint [Col. 0361C] Goericus, bishop of Metz. He also provided evidence of his generosity to the monasteries of Saint Arnulf and Saint Peter of Metz.

He was a supporter and protector of the Parthenon on the Mount of Saint Romaric; in that capacity he subscribed a charter of Gisla, who at that time was abbess. Together with many other bishops and abbots, he received from Otto II the task of restoring regular discipline in the monastery of Saint Gall.

In the year 976 he became, together with Hildebold, bishop of Worms, an arbitrator in a dispute that had arisen between Werinher, abbot of Fulda, and Gozbert, abbot of Hersfeld, concerning navigation on and use of the river Hursilla. Through the intervention of the Empress Theophanu, he received royal rights in the city of Metz from the prince himself in the year 977.

In the year 980 he attended the assembly at Ingelheim, where it was decreed that the monasteries of Stavelot and Malmedy should remain united. While King Otto was fighting against the Greeks and Saracens in Calabria in the year 982, Theoderic and the Empress Theophanu were awaiting the outcome of the battle at Rossano, where they learned that the imperial army had been defeated and that the emperor himself had sought safety by swimming. Theoderic hastened to bring him aid.

In the year 983 an assembly was held at Verona at which Otto II proclaimed his successor, Otto III, in the presence of the magnates of the empire, especially Theoderic, who enjoyed great influence with the prince and was one of his most trusted counselors. In that same year he attended the funeral of that emperor, who died at Rome on 7 December.

Strongly opposed to the promotion of Adalbero, recently elected bishop of Verdun, he became involved in a serious dispute with Charles, duke of Lower Lorraine, who supported Adalbero. He wrote a very sharp letter to Charles; in return, Gerbert wrote atrocious letters in Charles’s name, as is clear from the letters of Gerbert, two of which are addressed to Theoderic, whom he calls Diederic.

In a letter of Ricuin, bishop of Toul, concerning the monastery of Spinal, Theoderic is called “d’Homelant.” Hillinus of Trier, in a confirmation of the possessions of the same place, names him “Theoderic of Hamolo”; he is also surnamed Sixtus.

He departed this life on 7 September 984 and was buried in the monastery of Saint Vincent, which he had founded. When his tomb was opened after three hundred years, his pontifical vestments were found intact, and his bones were placed in a wooden chest, which is displayed in the choir on the anniversary of his death; the same vestments are used for its celebration.

EPITAPH OF THEODERICUS.

Here Deodericus, born of noble blood,

[Col. 0362C] From the lineage of kings, bearing a celebrated name,

Whom the bloodline of Caesar Otto reached,

Whose counsels gave laws to peoples.

For he shone upon the world like a star in full light,

In distinguished deeds and excellent conduct.

Therefore he deserved to ascend the See of Metz,

Which he governed with the worthy office of a bishop.

For the heavenly King he built this palace,

And adorned it with wondrous and countless things.

When the [uncertain: *ebdenis*] Ides of September had come round,

His life’s departure is enclosed beneath this stone.

[Col. 0361]

VERSES IN HONOR OF THEODERICUS.

(From Sigebert, *Life of Theoderic*, in Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, Scriptores, vol. IV.)

[Col. 0361D] Deodericus, in blood and conduct,

Clearly more renowned than all the renowned,

Shone second only to the king,

Scarcely second to anyone beneath him.

This cousin of the illustrious Caesar

Clung to him in war and at home,

Bearing the second place in the kingdom,

And lightening the emperor’s cares.

[Col. 0362D] Through him all the affairs of the kingdom

And ecclesiastical laws stood firm.

Soldier, senate, and royal court

Looked to his utterances.

While King Otto, with the helm of government,

Tried everywhere to calm

The greatly troubled affairs of Italy

By the laws of peace, removing evils,

[Col. 0363A] This man was there—much there, and intimate—

At the mouth, the ears, and even the emperor’s heart.

Through him those who pleased the emperor found favor;

Without him scarcely anyone prevailed.

With such magnificence did he stand above others

That all honored him with generosity,

Made gracious through him,

So that they might obtain their desires.

He did not demand greedily, but piously and eagerly,

What would be useful,

And what was free from notorious fault,

What would prepare hope of pardon for himself.

For the bodies of your saints, O martyrs,

This holy man’s faith sought,

Having them transferred with whatever care was possible,

So that he might possess them reverently.

The city of Metz rejoiced in this bishop,

Trusting doubly in his protection,

Strong through his holiness

And secure through his nobility.

[Col. 0363]

EPITAPH OF COUNT EVRARD, BY THEODERICUS.

(From Sigebert, in the *Life of Theoderic*, in Pertz, as above.)

[Col. 0363B] In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 978, Deodericus, the humble bishop, builder of this place from its very foundations, with pious devotion entrusted to the stone, according to the human condition, Everard, his nephew and his sole beloved, as long as he was granted life: a boy distinguished by orthodox and royal parents, already promising an excellent nature, and raised from his very cradle with tender affection as the great hope of his family and fatherland. Before he had reached ten years, he was cut down by the untimely sickle of death, a dear pledge amid the immeasurable mourning of the people and his parents. He was buried on the fourth day before the Nones of September.

Another epitaph:

The death of the just is not ruinous, but precious,

Always having the day before the face of God.

[Col. 0363C] That day is full, serene with shining sun;

It is a day without night, and rest without end.

[Col. 0364B] Glad in this rest and relying on the relief of light,

May Evrard remain, so that he may behold

The King who reigns, ruling kingdoms that reign,

Christ, whom he worshiped while he was able to live.

This distinguished boy, ten years old in the flower of life,

Adorning all his pursuits with purity,

Passed from the world on the second day of September.

Reader, say at last: “May he rest in peace!” Amen.

Another epitaph of the same Count Everard:

In this tomb lies a dove without bitterness,

The infant Evrard, noble and pious,

Noble by the blood of the magnificent Deodericus,

The bishop, whose brother was his father.

The coming light of September was the last for these limbs.

[Col. 0364C] Christ, grant him your rest and yourself as his day!

[Col. 0363]

DISCOVERY OF THE SAINTS FOUND BY THEODERICUS, BISHOP OF METZ, AND TRANSLATED TO THE CITY OF METZ.

(From Acherius, *Spicilegium*, old edition, vol. IV.)

[Col. 0363D] In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 870, while the great and most glorious Caesar Augustus Otto, together with his namesake, a youth of admirable character and likewise Augustus, his son, and also his wife Adelheid, than whom nothing could ever have been more just, gentle, prudent, or pious, were governing the scepter of Italy peacefully and firmly with pious and just authority as far as the borders of Calabria, the venerable lord Theoderic, bishop of holy Metz, who was related to that magnificent emperor by blood and bound to him by extraordinary affection and intimacy, and at whose counsel, because of his remarkable wisdom, all the affairs of the palace were conducted, was engaged in that same Italian expedition, in which he served for almost three years.

While he was especially devoted to divine worship and eagerly seeking whatever might contribute to the honor, dignity, or protection of his holy See, and while all things were effectively supplied to meet his wishes, with God’s grace assisting him he gathered a great abundance of the bodies of saints from various places in Italy and endeavored to convey them to his holy See at Metz, where they might be venerated with more worthy worship and honor.

Concerning Saint Elpidius.

The first of these was the holy and venerable confessor of Christ, ELPIDIUS, whom he obtained from the province of the Marsi, with the permission of Albricus, bishop of Marsica, from a certain church near the episcopal See. This See is situated beside Lake Fucinus; what it once was is attested by the ruins of the city and by the large number of churches and monasteries around it.

The bishop himself and the other inhabitants told us that Elpidius had belonged to a company of certain servants of God who, in an earlier age, came from the regions of Greece—seventy in number—to that same province of the Marsi. Shining everywhere in the surrounding places and cities with the light of wondrous signs, wherever the end of their lives came upon them in holy conduct they were placed in venerable burial, and, because of the constant delight of their miracles, they are honored with great reverence by their neighbors far and wide [Col. 0365B].

Three of them rested in the same cemetery: Callistratus, Eutychius, and this Elpidius, who was the third. The emperor had removed Eutychius; and, so that no deception could be practiced in receiving him, since the tomb remained untouched and sufficiently secured and showed no sign of violation from the day of his reinterment, before any of the inhabitants had learned of it, our priest Teudo, together with the emperor’s priest Heriwardus, opened the saint’s chest in the presence only of Bishop Albricus and a few of his clergy—for they had been unable to do so except by breaking through the altar above.

They received the sacred bones, all complete in number and size, of wondrous whiteness and no less fragrant odor, and placed them in a reliquary. (We celebrate his feast on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of October.)

Concerning Saints Eutychius, Victorinus, and Maron.

[Col. 0365C]

Coming recently from there into the territory of the city of Amiternum, which likewise displays nothing but ruins, he received from the same Bishop Albricus, from a monastery subject to his jurisdiction at Reate, the most precious martyr EUTYCHIUS. In the previous year he had already acquired the relics of his blessed companion VICTORINUS, and likewise a portion of Saint MARON, who suffered martyrdom with him. We saw both the places of their passion and the very waters of Cotilae [that is, Cutiliae], breathing a foul odor—the waters in which the martyr had been suspended head downward.

Their passion is preserved in writing by the saints Nereus and Achilleus. The venerable lord Theoderic himself, being present there, received this martyr from the marble chest, strongly secured, with great rejoicing and veneration, on the eighth day before the Kalends of October [Col. 0365D]. Adhelard, son of Gerard, carried these two back to his homeland.

## On Saints Felicianus, Bishop and Martyr

At Fulinias, a fortress not far from Spoleto, the sacred body of FELICIANUS was guarded amid a great throng of people arriving from every direction. Benedictus, bishop of that same fortress of Fulinias, gave him with much weeping through Bertraus the deacon and Heriward the priest, on the fourth day before the Nones of October. He was taken up from the innermost cave itself. His passion has been written down.

## On Saint Asclepiodotus, Martyr

In the woodland called Collis, which adjoins the city of Perusia, where the emperor was then engaged in the autumn hunt, there was an extremely ancient monastery beside the river [Col. 0366A] Tiber. There the river flowed through a moderately shallow ford, but from that point onward increased in the depth of its sea-like waters all the way to the city of Rome.

A tomb once constructed, as it appeared, with marble work and ornamentation, but by then collapsed through age, held the venerably buried remains of the outstanding martyr Asclepiodotus. His tomb had been blocked by a very substantial mass of stones and earth. When Theudo, Bertraus, and Rothardus had finally penetrated it with great difficulty and stripped away the marble nearer to the holy body, they found a monument sunk down to a great depth—indeed, to the very bottom.

Through its middle, from the head all the way to the feet, it appeared naturally divided by a certain boundary, as though by the rock itself; yet, when examined more carefully, it proved to be one continuous whole. One half of the blessed body lay on this side and the other half on the other, with the limbs on either side placed one against the other, except for the head alone, which had been carefully positioned lying in one intact portion.

The sacristan and the others said that antiquity had intended to mark this by such a sign; they themselves firmly asserted that the same martyr had been cut in half while still alive by a cruel form of execution, and that, as testimony to this, he had been placed in the monument divided in this manner.

The venerable pontiff likewise took him up with the honor appropriate to him on the seventh day before the Kalends of October. From the inhabitants we learned that his feast day is celebrated on the ninth day before the Kalends of November. For we were entirely unable to extract an account of his deeds from the bishop of Cisa, to whom the place belonged.

## On Saint Serena and Saint Gregory of Spoleto

The most holy virgin SERENA had rested near Spoleto in the monastery [Col. 0366C] of Saint Savinus the martyr, outside the city walls, where she also shone forth through many miracles. Almost daily a great crowd of people came to her, so that even through the nights the throngs kept vigil there with lamps and other offerings.

When the venerable pontiff had obtained her, with her bones intact throughout her entire body, by sending there the deacon Rothardus together with other faithful men, he also obtained there the relics of the blessed martyr GREGORY of Spoleto, whose passion has been written down.

Apart from what we find in the passion of Saint Savinus—namely, that she had buried that blessed martyr—we were unable to discover anything further about Saint Serena’s deeds. Yet she commends herself by such continual signs of power that, when the testimony of her deeds is set before our eyes through the living reading of them, there is no need to ask what she was like in life [Col. 0366D]. Her day is celebrated on the tenth day before the Kalends of December, on the same day as that of Saint Savinus the martyr.

## On the Chain of Saint Peter the Apostle

Meanwhile, the aforesaid deacon Rothardus, having been sent to Rome, obtained from the gift of Lord Pope John, who was the thirteenth of that name, a considerable portion of the chain of blessed Peter in the basilica called *ad Vincula*, the same portion having been cut away.

Together with it, that same lord pope sent the monastery of Saint Vincent a privilege, along with a dalmatic and sandals granted to its abbot by apostolic prerogative. Adelbert the cleric transferred all these things with Count Cono.

## On Saint Vincent, Levite

[Col. 0367A]

The blessed and great martyr and levite VINCENT was venerated in a certain extremely ancient city called Corduno, which had long since been utterly destroyed and lay twelve miles from Arretium. From a nearby monastery, quite beautifully adorned and likewise frequented by a great crowd, he was taken up.

The deacon Bertraus, accompanied by a certain cleric of the bishop of Arretium—his name was Crisulfus—who knew the place, took him up with great difficulty and at no small risk to his life. They firmly asserted that he had been brought from Spain to Italy.

We later learned the fuller account of this translation when the lord bishop came to Beneventum, having been sent to meet the emperor’s daughter-in-law as she came from Greece. Near Capua, [Col. 0367B] we found a nearly ruined monastery called Saint Vincent’s. The few old monks who were then seen there said that it had once been built by three noble brothers through great and marvelous workmanship.

They said that the body of Saint Vincent had later been secretly brought there from Spain by two monks and held in the greatest veneration for many subsequent years, until, after the same monastery had been devastated by pagans, the holy body was taken from there and transferred to the aforesaid city of Corduno.

At that time the bishop of Arretium also gave, though unwillingly and while placed in the gravest danger before the emperor concerning himself and his possessions, a considerable portion of the blood of the most blessed protomartyr STEPHEN in a crystal vessel magnificently fashioned with gold and gems; in another pyx, some of the blood of the Innocents; and, in small packets attached individually, hairs of Saint Peter [Col. 0367C].

And because his ability to ransom himself was pressing him hard, he secured our venerable bishop as his intercessor through these objects and through the body of Saint Vincent; thus, through the bishop’s intervention, he barely regained the emperor’s favor.

Several Italian bishops had already often tried to obtain this same blessed martyr. Among them was Ambrosius of Bergamo, because the see of his episcopate was dedicated to Saint Vincent. A short time earlier he had fixed the day on which he would receive him, together with those whom he had been able to gather; but, by the Lord’s ordering, the night before the day he had appointed, our men anticipated him [Col. 0367D]. Clerics from Monte Romaric (Remiremont) carried him away.

## On Saints Protus and Hyacinthus

In the region of the Sabines, not far from the city of Rome, approximately eleven miles away, the holy martyrs PROTUS and HYACINTHUS were buried, under somewhat negligent guardianship.

A certain abbot from the monastery of Saint Mary called Farfa, when he asked our venerable pontiff to act as his intercessor with the emperor in his own cause, first offered him a portion, since he knew that the pontiff took pleasure in no other gift so much. Later, however, moved by the extraordinary influence of the lord bishop, he added whatever he was able to find there.

Together with his monks, he swore over the holy Gospels that these truly were the bones of Saints Protus and Hyacinthus. This took place after the Nativity of the Lord, as we were returning from Rome, in the vicinity of the city of Horta [Col. 0368A].

## On Saints Digna and Emerita

While we were then staying in Rome, through a gift from Lord Pope John he received the relics of the holy women DIGNA and EMERITA, whose bodies are buried in the portico of the church of the blessed martyr Marcellus, which stands before the Holy Apostles.

At the same time he received relics of various saints, deposited separately and accompanied by their own annotations, among them a sandal of Saint Stephen. All these things were sent through Willardus, a monk of the monastery of Maurus.

## On Saint Vincent, Bishop

He received another Saint Vincent, a bishop, from a certain monastery in the county of Urbino, approximately one mile from Ravenna, near Petra Pertusa. Its abbot was greatly worn down by his necessary expenses, since he had nothing else to give for the relief of the place; he therefore offered a portion first, but when Bertraus was sent there and acted energetically with considerable skill, he received [lacuna].

We have written down this saint’s passion. He was sent by Count Immo.

## On Saints Vincent and Carpophorus

The city of Vincentia lies not far from Venetia. It is said that, when the Lombards invaded Italy, they first came to this city among all the cities.

In it the martyr LEONTIUS was venerated in a celebrated monastery. The bishop of the place promised our most reverend bishop relics of him if he would appeal to the imperial majesty on the bishop’s behalf.

Soon the deacon Rothardus was sent there. When the bishop had made himself excessively difficult in giving, the deacon’s continuous and insistent demands finally overcame him, and, apart from the few relics he retained for himself, he gave the entire remainder of the body beyond what he had promised [Col. 0368C].

The inhabitants asserted that the blessed CARPOPHORUS too had suffered martyrdom at Rome and had been transferred from that same city not long before. There, they said, a once-noble monastery of Saint Felix could be seen, where the martyrs were reportedly first buried. But after it had been burned by the Hungarians—who are almost neighbors to those very places—and their continual raids prevented its restoration, the bodies were deposited beneath an altar at the episcopal seat within the city.

From that altar, after breaking open the tomb, the aforementioned deacon Rothardus took all of Saint Leontius, but a considerable portion of Saint Carpophorus’s relics.
