They said that the account of their passion had perished in the fire [Col. 0368D]. Their feast is celebrated on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August. Teudo carried them away.

## On Saint Lucia, Virgin and Martyr

The virgin and martyr LUCIA of Syracuse, memorable through the great and universal celebration of the Church, came into the eager devotion of our most religious bishop in the following manner.

Wigericus, our priest—at that time serving as cantor, but now holding the office of custodian of Saint Stephen—was able to explain this matter reliably. He took those sacred bones in his hands from the urn in which they had been held under no slight protection.

She was resting at Corfinium, once an ancient city but now entirely destroyed. We were reliably told that she had been transferred to that place from Sicily by a certain Faroaldus, duke of Spoleto [Col. 0369A].

The bishop of the place himself, placing his hand upon the holy Gospel, confirmed that this was the very Lucia of Syracuse, concerning whom responsories and antiphons are sung everywhere, generally together with the Mass.

## On the Gridiron of Saint Lawrence

When, after the royal wedding had been celebrated at Rome with immense splendor, we were preparing to return to our homeland, Lord Pope, as a final favor—and one more abundant than the others—enriched the venerable bishop with four portions of the gridiron of Saint LAURENCE.

Wigericus and the monk John struck these pieces out from the sacred gridiron itself [Col. 0370A]. They were the heads of the rods that had lain crosswise and been fixed into the outer ribs. For all the rods, which had numbered six on it, had long ago been given as gifts by various popes to different kings from ancient times. One of them, which had still remained until a few years ago, was granted by Octavian to the great Emperor Otto.

When the rods were struck out, the heads which had been held firmly below, nearer to the inner ribs, remained. Yet, when iron was applied and they were struck by hand [or: “with the hand applied”], they were dislodged, although only through laborious effort.

[Col. 0369]

# Letter to Charles, Brother of King Lothar

Written by Gerbert under the name of Theoderic.

(See among the letters of Gerbert.)

# In the Year of the Lord 984. Gezo, Abbot of Tortona

[Col. 0369]

# [On the Body and Blood of Christ]

## Muratori’s Notice of the Following Book on the Body and Blood of Christ

(*Anecdota*, vol. III, p. 237)

While the most distinguished man John Mabillon was examining the libraries of Italy, he encountered two codices in which this very work of Gezo had been copied.

One is preserved in the Florentine monastery of Santa Croce of the Friars Minor, but without a title or preface; the other is in the monastery of San Benedetto at Polirone in the Mantuan territory, as is clear from his *Museum Italicum*, pp. 164 and 207.

Mabillon did not think it worthwhile to publish Gezo’s entire book. He was therefore content to publish only its preface and table of chapters, on page 89 of the second part of the *Museum* just mentioned. He informed us that he would proceed to a complete edition of Gezo’s work once he understood that this would please readers.

I, however, am among those who would have eagerly desired such a favor from the distinguished man. The subject treated by Gezo is a question so vigorously debated by the innovators of our own times that even the smallest fragments of antiquity concerning it deserve to be brought into the public light. Indeed, Gezo’s book, even if it could do nothing more than confirm the ecclesiastical tradition of the tenth century concerning the truth of Christ’s body and blood in the august sacrament—a truth denied by the Calvinists—would deserve to be received by Catholics with willing approval.

For this reason I resolved to make that very work available to the public after I encountered a copy of it, unknown to Mabillon, in a manuscript codex of the Ambrosian Library, shelfmark Q 98.

The one alteration I judged necessary was to omit a considerable number of chapters from the work, since they had already been published among the works of the Holy Fathers. These include passages that Gezo extracted from the books of Cyprian, Ambrose, Augustine, Gregory, and others and incorporated into his own book.

I considered it even more necessary to omit the little book of Paschasius Ratbertus to his disciple Placidus, which Gezo copied almost in its entirety, forming twenty-three chapters of his own work from it.

We learn who Gezo was and when he lived from his preface, where the following words occur: “But how strongly the lord Giseprandus, of reverend memory, our bishop at that time, resisted this decision of my will, both by force and by authority, you are not unaware,” and so forth.

Now Giseprandus, or Giselprandus, bishop of Tortona, as Ughelli shows in volume IV, page 855 of the *Italia Sacra*, flourished around the year 950 of Christ, since he took part in the Council of Augsburg in 952 and is named among the witnesses in a diploma of Otto the Great granted to the church of Asti in 962.

According to the same Ughelli, Giseprandus appears to have lived as late as 981, on the authority of the chronicle of Volturno [Col. 0371]. All this allows us to affirm without danger of error that our Gezo too flourished before the year 1000 of Christ.

Giseprandus had built at his own expense a noble monastery at Tortona under the title of Saint Martianus the martyr, where that saint’s sacred body was also buried. Ughelli cites an illustrious diploma granted by the Emperor Otto IV in 1210, in which much is recorded about that monastery and its founder, Giselprandus.

Gezo was the first abbot of that monastery while the aforementioned bishop was still alive, as Gezo himself testifies in his preface. He continued in that office even after Giselprandus had been taken from the living. Since his book is addressed “To the most beloved brothers, for whom, by divine dispensation, I exercise paternal care insofar as my own weakness permits,” Gezo must be understood to have written to the monks of that same monastery.

After the preface are verses by Lord Odo, that is, the abbot of Cluny, who was famous for the holiness of his life no less than for his published works. He died in the year 942 of Christ, as is clear from his Life and eulogies: volume VII, fifth century, page 124 of the *Acta Sanctorum* of the Order of Saint Benedict, and volume XVII of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, where these very verses are printed on page 313.

The verses that follow, however, have the celebrated Paschasius Ratbertus as their author. Only fifteen of them are known to have been published, in volume XIV, page 720 of the same *Bibliotheca Patrum*, namely through the words “He determines the cause,” and so forth. I therefore think that the verses following these in our codex have not yet been brought into public light. In them Paschasius clearly establishes transubstantiation, as he does in his other writings; Gezo undoubtedly approves the same opinion.

# Gezo’s Book on the Body and Blood of Christ

## The Prologue or Letter of the Following Work Begins

[Col. 0371A]

To the most beloved brothers for whom, by divine dispensation, I exercise paternal care insofar as my own weakness permits: GEZO, servant of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Long ago, dearest brothers, I had resolved, conscious of my very grave sins, to leave my homeland and parents and withdraw to some secluded place where, completely separated from the noise of worldly affairs, I might spend my life in the service of almighty God, continually mourning my sins and, through constant satisfaction in penitence, inviting the most merciful Lord and Judge of all to show mercy.

How strongly the lord Giseprandus, of reverend memory, our bishop at that time, resisted this decision of my will, both by force and by authority, you are not unaware [Col. 0371B]. He maintained that it was not canonical for me, after leaving the Church in which I had been nourished and ordained, to move elsewhere according to my own judgment; and he declared that he would never give his consent to such a course.

This was especially so because he had already resolved to build a monastery in his own Church, where the body of the most blessed martyr Martianus lay buried and at rest. If I had firmly decided to change my purpose, he said, I would find solitude there, and everything necessary for serving God according to my desire would be available.

Because of my inexperience at that time, I accepted this promise reluctantly, since in my feverish longing the wait for so long a period appeared exceedingly protracted. His authority nevertheless prevailed, for failing to obey the commands of so great a man and refusing to heed his counsels would have been called not merely rash but almost insane.

He therefore hastened to fulfill his promise as quickly as possible. Setting aside all worldly concerns, by which he was greatly hindered, he devoted himself entirely to the construction of the monastery [Col. 0372A], granting me permission in good faith to profess the monastic life.

He had not long delayed when, with the Lord’s cooperation, he saw the work beginning to prosper in his hands. He then began with every insistence to press me to assume responsibility for the entire place and to show myself diligent and watchful in winning souls for God.

I resisted and persistently refused the burden of governance. He nevertheless continued to press me and remained unyielding until, accepting no excuse from me, he bound me under an invocation of the divine name: unless on that very day I committed myself to his will and undertook the burden he commanded, he would immediately expel the monks then living there—very few in number—and hand the place over to canons whom he had already prepared [Col. 0372B].

Thus I took upon my weak shoulders the heavy burden of governance, and, compelled by extreme necessity, I became the teacher of a profession whose disciple I had not previously been.

From that time onward, occupied by the most grievous cares of the stewardship entrusted to me over you, while devoting myself as fully as possible to your welfare and considering carefully within myself what would be most beneficial for you, it occurred to me to prepare for you, according to the poverty of my understanding, a sweet and flower-filled cup, soberly tempered with sacred promises, concerning the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood—a cup that might be both a delight and a means of salvation for your love.

As I read through the writings of the Holy Fathers and reconsidered them through as attentive meditation as I could manage, whatever I was able to find in them that was especially clear and well explained for understanding the mystery of so great and subtle a matter, I gathered into the compact body of a single little book. If the favor of the Holy Spirit breathes upon you, it will neither displease you through difficulty of understanding [Col. 0372C] nor fail to please you through its smallness [Col. 0373A].

In this little work I have imitated Paschasius Ratbertus, who composed a splendidly expressed little book on this same subject for a certain disciple of his, Placidus. I have followed the same authorities as he did: the most blessed priests of the Lord, Cyprian, Hilary, Ambrose, Augustine, Gregory, John, Isidore, Isitius, Jerome, and Bede.

From the writings of all these men we have gathered certain flowers of their sentences, very necessary to our subject, exhaling the sweetest fragrance of the Lord’s body and blood. Paschasius’s little book itself we transferred almost in its entirety into our own work, just as we found it, following his meaning rather than his words in certain places and avoiding whatever was superfluous.

But so that the grace of so great a mystery might be commended to your minds more clearly and purely through the favor of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0373B], I have amassed a wealth of miracles which the Lord formerly deigned to reveal to his saints and to those who diligently served him, for his praise and glory, so that he might show what he has prepared in heaven for those to whom he has left so great a gift on earth.

I also kept this in mind: if, perhaps because of slowness of understanding or lack of literary education, the sacrament of this redemption should not be clear to some people from the writings of the Fathers, it might be made manifest through the revelation of signs.

With what reverence and holy fear you ought to stand before the sacred altar, awaiting participation in so great a grace, lest—God forbid—what you desire to receive for salvation should become destruction for those who communicate: this too I have diligently appended to the little book as far as I could [Col. 0373C]. Thus, pleasing God in all things, both I through your advancement and you through my labor and concern, may find mercy on the day of the Lord.

Therefore, dearest brothers, accept with the affection with which it is offered whatever little gift comes from my smallness. Let it not become worthless to you because of my humility, for in the substance of its meaning it is glorious and excellent.

It cannot be despised by a reader without danger. For although it may possess somewhat less in eloquence, nothing can be more outstanding in subject matter, through which eternal and incorruptible life is bestowed upon those who believe worthily.

I beg you, do not undervalue the Lord’s grace. From reading this work, understand how great is the power of receiving eternal life on earth and being nourished daily with angelic food.

Although everything is full of God and we too are always present before the eyes of the divine majesty, it is nevertheless especially necessary before the holy altars to observe and revere both the face of God and the presence of the angels [Col. 0373D], where, through the power of the word of God and his mercy, such great and excellent things are bestowed upon us—things no human being can express.

May God himself, our Lord, the Word, Power, and Wisdom of the Father, preserve and protect in us this same grace which he has bestowed, and may he deign to illuminate more fully the eyes which he has already begun to open for you.

Through him and with him, to the eternal Father, together with the Holy Spirit, be all praise and glory, honor and magnificence and power, from the ages, and now, and always, and throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

The prologue ends.

# The Chapters of the Following Work Begin

I. That human weakness ought not readily to investigate divine things, from the book of Saint Hilary, bishop and confessor, *On the Trinity*.

II. On the origin of the Lord’s body.

III. On the birth of the Son of God from the Father.

IV. That we are often instructed by comparable forms toward understanding divine things.

V. On the substance of God the Father.

VI. On the birth of the Son of God from the Father.

VII. On the generation of the Son of God from his mother.

VIII. That our Lord Jesus Christ naturally remains in us through the flesh he assumed, and that we remain in him through receiving his body and blood.

IX. The Catholic faith of the Church [Col. 0374B].

X. That confidence must not be placed in human wisdom.

XI. On the Word of God.

XII. Cyprian’s true assertion concerning God.

XIII. Augustine on the Word of God.

XIV. That it must not be doubted that communion with Christ is truly his body and blood.

XV. That no one ought to be ignorant of this mystery of Christ.

XVI. What the sacraments are, and why they are so called.

XVII. Whether this sacrament of the mystical cup is made under a figure or in reality.

XVIII. What difference there is between the ancient sacrifices and figures of the Law and the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood.

XIX. What it means to receive the body and blood of Christ worthily for life.

XX. In what ways Christ’s body is spoken of.

XXI. That in this communion one receives either judgment or reward [Col. 0374C].

XXII. Why Christ, who was sacrificed once, had to be sacrificed daily, and what good these mysteries bestow upon those who receive them worthily.

XXIII. Why this mystery is celebrated in bread and wine.

XXIV. Why water is mixed in the cup.

XXV. Whether this mystery possesses something more when it is performed by a good minister, or something less than the Truth promises if it is performed by an evil minister.

XXVI. Why these things do not at all change color or taste in the sacrament.

XXVII. That these things have often appeared in visible form.

XXVIII. By what words this mystery is accomplished.

XXIX. Whether this body may rightly be called bread after the consecration.

XXX. Whether the one who receives more obtains more from it than the one who receives less.

XXXI. Why this mystery was delivered to the disciples before the Passion [Col. 0374D].

XXXII. Why a fragment of the body is mingled in the blood of Christ.

XXXIII. Why the mystery of sacred communion is now generally celebrated by those who are fasting, when the Lord delivered it to the apostles after supper.

XXXIV. What the Lord means when he says: “I shall not drink from this fruit of the vine from now on until I drink it new in the kingdom of my Father.”

XXXV. Whether there is any difference in this mystery for the righteous person and for the penitent who has been reconciled.

XXXVI. What the Eucharist provides to those who receive the Lord’s body and blood worthily or unworthily.

XXXVII. What the blessed martyr Cyprian affirms happened in his presence to those who, having been polluted by sacrificial food offered to idols, rashly received the sacraments of the Lord’s body and blood.

XXXVIII. Why those entangled in capital sins are to be excluded from the Lord’s sacraments.

XXXIX. That Jews are to be excluded from every gathering of the faithful, especially where the offering of Christians is celebrated [Col. 0375A].

XL. How one ought to approach the miraculous sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood.

XLI. On the revelations by which the Lord strengthened the hearts of those doubting the truth of his body and blood.

XLII. A miracle concerning a certain Jew.

XLIII. Likewise, concerning a certain elderly hermit whose doubt the Lord strengthened through the same revelation of the truth.

XLIV. Likewise, a miracle that took place at Rome.

XLV. Likewise, another.

XLVI. On the sacrament of the cup revealed to Blessed Cyprian.

XLVII. How, in the Passion of Our Lord Jesus Christ, the mystical Passover was abolished and the truth of the reality was displayed in his sacrifice.

XLVIII. Whether this lawful Passover is to be eaten by the faithful after a year’s interval, after long intervals of days, or daily.

XLIX. How much the sacrifice of the sacred offering benefits the spirits of the dead.

L. Concerning a certain monk who escaped punishment through the saving Host.

LI. Concerning a certain man whose bonds in captivity were loosed when a sacrifice was offered for him.

LII. Concerning a certain sailor who escaped death through the power of the Lord’s sacrament after enduring the dangers of the sea for a long time.

LIII. For which dead persons the sacrifice of the Lord’s body is beneficial.

LIV. With what discipline and modesty one ought to pray while the priest is sacrificing and each person awaits the hour of sacred communion in his own order.

LV. What must be avoided in prayer.

LVI. Cyprian to the clergy on beseeching God.

LVII. That the most holy altar of the Lord ought also to be adorned in outward worship [Col. 0375C].

LVIII. That nothing is to be placed upon the altar except the most holy offering.

LIX. That sacrifice is not to be offered for murderers and robbers.

LX. Concerning those who give alms but do not forgive sins.

LXI. A very astonishing account concerning a certain priest.

LXII. That the excommunication of any priest whatsoever is greatly to be feared; and that one must consider not what his merit is, but by whose authority he does this—even if the excommunication appears unjust, which God forbid.

LXIII. A highly commendable example of the glorious Emperor Theodosius.

LXIV. Likewise, another exceedingly fearful example.

LXV. How great reverence is owed to the episcopal chair, and concerning Lord Peter, patriarch of Alexandria.

LXVI. How grave a sin it is to violate sacred places or pollute them with any defilement [Col. 0375D].

LXVII. Concerning a certain robber buried in the cemetery of Blessed John.

LXVIII. The letter of Saint Augustine to Bishop Auxilius concerning the case of an unjust excommunication begins.

LXIX. Likewise, chapters pertaining to the same matter.

LXX. On the sacrament of baptism: Saint Ambrose.

The chapters end.

# Verses of Lord Odo on the Sacrament of the Lord’s Body and Blood

To teach that the guests at the heavenly banquet should be clean,

the Lord washed the feet of his servants.

With various gifts, and rejecting many things thereafter,

he preferred this one thing above all: grain and wine.

This he makes sacred—this thing so small, yet of such great height—

so slight in cost, so easy and ready,

yet so sublime that it contains the whole Godhead.

This alone suffices to cleanse the world’s sin.

Hence this gift pleases, because it is made from many things into one:

the body is joined to its head, and the head is joined to it.

This kind, this one thing, pleases; this will endure forever.

It is easy, pure, simple, and full of the Godhead.

# The Verses of Paschasius Ratbertus to His Disciple Placidus Begin

(See among the works of Paschasius Ratbertus.)

## Chapter I — That Human Weakness Ought Not Readily to Investigate Divine Things, from the Book of Saint Hilary, Bishop and Confessor, *On the Trinity*

The blessed Apostle forbids his disciple Timothy to deal with genealogical discussions and to touch upon the interminable fable of controversy. Rather, he teaches that the building up of God is in faith, so that it may confine the measure of human modesty within faithful reverence for God’s omnipotence.

Nor should our weakness extend itself toward perceiving things whose nature does not permit them to be perceived. If, when people gaze upon the brightness of the sun, the power of their concentrated vision is stunned—so that, whenever the keen sight of curious contemplation investigates more carefully the cause of the radiating light, the nature of the eyes draws them back to the point at which their power of seeing dies, and striving harder to see results in failing to see—what should we expect in the things of God and in the Sun of righteousness?

Will not folly overtake those who wish to be wiser than they ought? Will it not encroach upon that very domain of sacred understanding? For an inferior nature will not understand the cause of a superior nature, nor is heavenly reason subject to human conception.

Whatever is submitted to the consciousness of the weak will remain within the condition of weakness. The power of God therefore exceeds the human mind. If weakness reaches out toward it, it becomes weaker still, losing even what it possesses, because the superior nature of heavenly things, which it pursues, overwhelms and weakens its every obstinacy through an embrace greater than itself.

Just as the sun ought to be viewed only as far as it can be viewed, and light ought to be received only as much as is admitted, lest, if we wish to inspect more than we can, we obtain even less than we are capable of attaining, so heavenly reason is to be awaited only insofar as it permits itself to be understood and gives itself to be grasped.

Otherwise, if we are not content with the moderation of what has been granted, we shall lose what has been bestowed [Col. 0376D].

There is therefore something in God that can be perceived—indeed there is, if only you wish to perceive what can be perceived. For just as there is something in the sun for you to see, if you wish to see what you are able to see, but you lose what can be seen when you strive after what cannot be seen, so in the things of God you have something that you can understand, if you wish to understand what you can.

But if you hope to go beyond what you can, you will become unable even to do what you were able to do.

I now advise those who investigate heavenly secrets to speak according to their nature of the mystery of Christ, who was born from a Virgin. How, they will say, was he conceived in a Virgin? How was he born of a Virgin? What cause of origins will they discuss in this matter? And what body was formed within the recesses of the maternal womb? From where is he man? From where is he so truly man?

After this, what human understanding will contain the meaning of the Son of Man’s having descended from heaven while remaining in heaven? For to descend and to remain do not have the same meaning according to bodily causes: the one is a change involved in descent, while the other is the undisturbed state of remaining.

The infant cries, yet he is in heaven. The child grows, yet God remains in the fullness of his being.

And when he ascends to where he was before, and the one who remains descends, by what human understanding will this be contained? For the Lord says: “What if you should see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before?”

The Son ascends to where he was before—what understanding can grasp this? The Son of Man descends from heaven, yet is in heaven—what reasoning can account for this? “The Word became flesh”: what words can express this?

The Word becomes flesh, that is, God becomes man; and the one who is man is in heaven, while the one who is God is from heaven. He ascends while descending, yet he descends without descending. He is what he was, and what he is, he was not.

## Chapter II — On the Origin of the Lord’s Body
The Lord assumed the body in such a way that, conceived from the Virgin, he gave it the form of a servant. For the Virgin bore only through the Holy Spirit what she bore. And although she contributed from herself as much to the birth of the flesh as a woman contributes to the formation of bodies when she receives the beginnings of their development, nevertheless Jesus Christ was not formed through the nature of human conception. Rather, the whole cause of his birth, introduced through the Spirit, retained in the birth of a human being what belonged to his mother, while at the same time possessing in the origin of his birth what belonged to God.

Accordingly, the Lord himself revealed that greatest and most beautiful mystery of the humanity he assumed when he said:

> No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven. [Col. 0377C]

That he descended from heaven refers to the cause of his origin, conceived from the Spirit; for Mary did not give origin to the body, although she contributed everything natural to her sex for the body’s growth and birth. That he is the Son of Man refers to the birth of the flesh he assumed from the Virgin. But that he is in heaven refers to the power of a nature that always remains, which, although it was initiated and established through the flesh taken by itself, did not, by the power of its limitation, confine itself within the region of a bounded body. By the power of the Spirit and the power of the Word of God, while remaining in the form of a servant, he was absent from neither the whole of heaven within nor the whole of heaven beyond, nor from the circle of heaven and the world; he was Lord of heaven and the world. Thus he both descended from heaven, is the Son of Man, and is in heaven.

Because the Word became flesh, he had not ceased to remain what the Word is. For while he is the Word, he is also in heaven; while he is flesh, he is also the Son of Man. While the Word became flesh, he is from heaven, the Son of Man, and in heaven. The power of the Word, remaining without bodily modes, was not absent from the place from which he had descended; the flesh had received its origin from nowhere other than the Word; and the Word became flesh, yet, while he was flesh, he was still also the Word.

The blessed Apostle clearly expressed the mystery of this ineffable bodily birth when he said:

> The first man was from the clay of the earth; the second man was from heaven.

By saying “man,” he taught that the birth was from the Virgin, who, fulfilling the function of a mother, carried out the nature of her sex in the conception and birth of a human being. When he said that the second man was from heaven, he testified that his origin came through the entry of the Holy Spirit descending upon the Virgin. Thus, although he is man and is in heaven, this man’s birth is from the Virgin and his conception is from the Spirit.

The Church knows one God, from whom all things are; it also knows one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom all things are: one “from whom,” and one “through whom.” In the one “from whom,” it understands the origin of all things; through the one “through whom,” the creation of everything. In the one “from whom,” it venerates the authority of the unbegotten; in the one “through whom,” a power differing in nothing from that of the author. Since “from whom” and “through whom” establish in created things the authority of participation, it knows God in the Spirit as an impassible and incorruptible Spirit. For it learned from the Lord that a spirit does not have flesh and bones, lest anyone suppose that bodily sufferings and losses could befall him.

It knows one unbegotten God, and it also knows the only-begotten Son of God. It confesses the Father as eternal and free from origin; it also confesses the Son’s origin from eternity—not originating from himself, but born eternally from him who has always been from no one, receiving his birth from the Father’s eternity.

It knows that one must not form judgments about God by human standards. For our nature is not such that it can raise itself by its own powers to heavenly knowledge. What is to be understood about God must be learned from God, because he can be known only through his own agency. Let there be the cultivated training of secular learning; let there be an innocent life: these may contribute to the joy of conscience, but they will not attain the knowledge of God.

When Moses was a shepherd of sheep in the land of Midian, he saw fire in a bush without the bush being consumed, heard God, asked his name, and learned his nature. Nor could these things have been known about God except through God. Therefore, we must speak about God only in the manner in which he himself has spoken about himself for our understanding.

To God, for whom all things live even among the dead, only that perishes which perishes for itself. For he himself will judge all things and, in accordance with the mercy of his majesty, will temper the punishment deserved by ignorance and error; but those who deny him he will no longer judge—he will instead deny them.

The confession of true faith is that God was born from God as light from light: he gives his own nature from himself without detriment to himself, so that he gives what he has and has what he has given. What exists is born, when nothing other than what exists is born. Birth receives what already was and does not take away what it has received; and the two are one, since what is born comes from what exists, and what is born is neither from elsewhere nor something else. For it is light from light.

## CHAPTER III — The Birth of the Son of God from the Father

God is born from God neither according to the custom of human birth nor through the elements of our origin, as a human being is produced from a human being. His birth is whole, perfect, and undefiled; it is an issuing from God rather than a birth in the ordinary sense. He is one from one—not a portion, not a failure, not a diminution, not a derivation, not an extension, not a suffering, but the birth of living nature from living nature. God proceeds from God, not a creature chosen to bear the name of God.

He did not begin to exist from nothing; he proceeded from one who remains. “To proceed” signifies birth, not beginning. For it is not the same thing to receive substance and for God to proceed from God. Although knowledge of this birth is not contained in words, since it is ineffable, the teaching of faith nevertheless possesses the certainty that the Son manifested himself as having proceeded from God.

This birth alone possesses the mystery that it embraces name, nature, power, and confession, because every birth necessarily possesses the nature from which it is born. What proceeds from one does not subsist as something foreign by possessing the substance of an earthly kind. But what is not foreign to itself is one in the kind of its nature; and whatever is one through birth does not possess solitude.

## CHAPTER IV — How we are instructed by forms that can often be compared with divine things

I appeal to our awareness of human birth: does not the origin of what is born remain within the origin of the Father? For although those lifeless and humble elements from which the causes of birth begin flow into another human being, nevertheless, through the power of nature, they remain within one another. The one who gives birth follows the one born through the origin of the same nature bestowed by him; and, through the birth received, the power of which is transmitted is not taken away from the begetter, if the one born remains.

Let this comparison be recalled by us only for understanding human birth, not as a complete example of the birth of God the Only-Begotten. Human nature is composed of dissimilar things; it is neither preserved from lifeless matter into life, nor does the one who is born immediately live within it, nor does he live wholly from life, since many things in it, when they have grown, wither away without possessing the perception of their own nature.

But in God everything that exists lives, for God is life; and this life cannot be anything except living. His birth is not by derivation but by power. Thus, since everything that exists lives, and everything born from him is wholly power, there is birth but no alteration; there is an imparting of growth but no loss of nature. And since the birth he gave follows through the likeness of an undivided nature, birth, which is living from living, does not abandon its nature by being born.

Fire, containing fire in itself and remaining fire within fire, offers an indication of this truth for the sake of faith. Although there are in it the brightness of light, the heat of nature, the power of burning, and the mobility of heat, it is entirely fire, and all these things are one nature. In its weakness, it depends on and lives through matter, and it fails together with that by which it had lived. Yet by comparison with these things we gain some knowledge of what is incorporeal in God, so that we do not consider it incredible that something should be found to some degree in earthly elements.

I ask, then, whether there is division and separation when fire comes from fire. Or is nature cut off so that it does not remain? Or does nature fail to follow, so that it is not present? When light is kindled from light, through a kind of progress resembling birth, there is no failure of nature, and yet there is light from light. Or does this not remain in that which subsists from itself without failure? Or is this not present in that from which there has been no departure, but from which it has gone forth with the unity of natural substance?

And I ask whether they are not one, when light from light is neither separable by division nor different in the kind of nature. As I have said, these comparisons are offered only for understanding the faith, not for the dignity of God—not so that we should derive knowledge of invisible things from comparable things as though any comparison could satisfy the nature of God. It is fitting and just to believe the God who bears witness about himself.

## CHAPTER V — The substance of God the Father

[Col. 0380B] The Father is he from whom everything that exists subsists. In Christ and through Christ, he is himself the origin of all things. His being is in himself: he does not receive what he is from elsewhere, but contains in himself and from himself what he is. He is infinite, because he is not himself in anything, but everything is within him. He is always beyond place, because he is not contained in place. He is always before time, because time is from him, outside whom nothing exists, and for whom there is always the condition of always being.

This is the truth of the mystery of God; this is the inscrutable name of his nature in the Father. He is known only to the Son, because no one knows the Father except the Son and the one to whom the Son wishes to reveal him. Therefore, let us form our understanding of the Father together with the Son who reveals him, for the Son alone is the faithful witness.

## CHAPTER VI — The birth of the Son of God from the Father

[Col. 0380C] [Note: [Col. 0379D] See Saint Hilary, *On the Trinity*, Book II.] The mind is terrified to approach the Son, and every discourse trembles lest it betray him. He is offspring of the Unbegotten, one from one, true from true, living from living, perfect from perfect, power from power, wisdom from wisdom, glory from glory, the image of the invisible God, the form of the unbegotten Father.

If anyone perhaps charges the mystery of divine generation against the limitation of his own understanding—that is, says that he cannot grasp how the Father generated the Son—although both Father and Son must nevertheless be understood without qualification, he shall hear from me, with still greater sorrow, that I do not know it. I do not know; I do not inquire; yet I shall still find consolation. The archangels do not know; the angels have not heard; the ages do not contain it; the prophet did not perceive it; the Apostle did not ask about it; the Son himself did not disclose it.

Let the grief of complaints cease. For you, whoever you are who ask these questions, I do not bring you back to an example, nor do I stretch you toward immensity, nor do I lead you down into the deep. Will you not calmly remain ignorant of the Creator’s birth while you are ignorant of the origin of creation?

At least this I ask: do you perceive that you were born, and do you understand what is born from you? I do not ask whether you understand the source from which you drew life, from which you received understanding, or from which you acquired your qualities. What is that which exists in you as smell, sensation, sight, and hearing? Certainly no one is unaware of what he does.

I ask from where you grant these things to those whom you beget; how you implant senses, kindle eyes, and attach the heart. Explain these things, if you can. You therefore possess what you do not know, and you bestow what you do not understand. Calmly ignorant in matters concerning yourself, you are arrogantly ignorant in matters concerning God.

### Right Faith

Understanding reaches its limit in these words. The Son is from that Father who is. The Only-Begotten is from the Unbegotten, offspring from the parent, living from living. Just as the Father has life in himself, so life has also been given to the Son in himself.

Perfect from perfect, because wholly from the whole. There is no division or severing, because each is in the other, and the fullness of divinity is in the Son. Incomprehensible from the incomprehensible, for no one knows them except each other. Invisible from the invisible, because he is the image of the invisible God, and because whoever has seen the Son has also seen the Father.

One distinct from the other, because the Father and the Son are distinct. The nature of divinity is not one thing and another, because both are one. God from God: from the one unbegotten God, the one-begotten God. Not two gods, but one from one. Not two unbegotten beings, because he was born from the Unborn.

The one differs in nothing from the other, because the life of the living one is in the living one. In these statements we have touched upon the nature of divinity, not comprehending the totality of understanding, but understanding that what we speak is incomprehensible.

## CHAPTER VII — The generation of the Son of God from his mother

For the sake of the human race, the Son of God was born from the Virgin. The Holy Spirit himself served him in this work, and, overshadowing with his divine power, he established for him the beginnings of a body and laid the foundations of flesh, so that, having been made human from the Virgin, he might receive in himself the nature of flesh, and so that, through the fellowship of this union, the body of the whole human race might exist sanctified in him.

Thus, just as all were established in him through his willing to be bodily, so he might in turn be conveyed into all through what is invisible in him. The invisible image of God did not reject the humiliation of a human beginning. Through conception, birth, crying, and a cradle, he passed through all the indignities of our nature.

What worthy return can we make for the affection of such condescension? The one only-begotten God, whose origin from God is ineffable, is inserted into the human form of a tiny body and grows in the womb of the holy Virgin. He who contains all things, and within whom and through whom all things exist, is brought forth under the law of human birth. He at whose voice angels and archangels tremble, and before whom heaven, earth, and all the elements of this world will be dissolved, is heard in the crying of an infant.

He who is invisible and incomprehensible, whom sight, sensation, and touch cannot measure, is wrapped in swaddling clothes. If anyone recalls these things as unworthy of God, he will confess himself indebted to a greater benefit precisely because these things seem less fitting to the majesty of God.

He did not need to become man, through whom humanity was made. We needed God to become flesh and dwell among us—that is, for the inward reality of all flesh to dwell in us through the assumption of one flesh. His humility is our nobility; his humiliation is our honor. What he, God, is while remaining in the flesh, we in turn become through being renewed from flesh into God.

But lest the cradle, the crying, the birth, and the conception hold the mind captive in anxious reflection, the dignity of God must be recalled in each detail, so that the ambition of his power precedes the humility of his will, and dignity does not abandon condescension.

Let us therefore see what mysteries the conception contains. The angel speaks to Zechariah; a birth is granted to a barren woman. The priest comes forth mute from the place of incense. John, still confined in his mother’s womb, bursts forth into a voice. The angel blesses Mary and promises that the Virgin will be the mother of the Son of God.

Conscious of her virginity, she is troubled by the difficulty of the event. The angel explains to her the efficacy of the divine action, saying:

> The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you.

The Holy Spirit, coming from above, sanctified the Virgin’s inward parts. Breathing within them—“the Spirit breathes where he wills”—he joined himself to the flesh of human nature. What was foreign to him, he took up through his power and authority.

And so that nothing might be disrupted through the weakness of the human body, the power of the Most High overshadowed the Virgin, strengthening her weakness as if by an enveloping shadow, so that the overshadowing of divine power might temper the bodily substance to the generative efficacy of the Spirit entering her.

This is the dignity of the conception. Let us see what dignity follows in the birth, crying, and cradle. An angel speaks to Joseph of the Virgin who is to give birth and says that the one who will be born is to be called Emmanuel, that is, “God with us.”

The Spirit proclaims this through the prophet. The angel is witness: the one who is born is God with us. A new light, greater than that of a star, is sent forth from heaven, and a heavenly sign accompanies the Lord of heaven. The angel announces to the shepherds that Christ the Lord, the salvation of all, has been born.

A multitude of the heavenly host gathers in praise of the childbearing, and the heralds of so great a work express the joys of the divine assembly. Then glory to God in heaven and peace on earth to people of good will are announced.

The magi then arrive; they adore him wrapped in cloths, and, after that secret operation of their empty knowledge, they bend the knee before him placed in the cradle. Thus, through the magi, the squalor of the cradle is adored; through the angels’ divine rejoicing, the crying is honored. Thus the Spirit, proclaiming the birth through the prophet, and announcing the same thing to the angels, and the star of the new light, serve him. Thus the Holy Spirit, coming at the beginning of the birth, and the overshadowing power of the Most High, bring the work to completion.

One thing is understood, another is seen; one thing is perceived by the eyes, another by the mind. The Virgin gives birth; the birth is from God. The infant cries; the angels who praise him hear it. He is soiled by swaddling clothes; God is adored. Thus the dignity of power is not lost while the humility of the flesh is adored.

The course of the rest of his life is comparable, for every period he spent as a human being he filled with the works of God. It is not possible to speak of each event individually. Throughout the various kinds of miracles and healings, only this must be observed: in the assumption of flesh, he is human; in the deeds he performs, he is God.

## CHAPTER VIII — That our Lord Jesus Christ naturally remains in us through the flesh he assumed, and that we remain in him through receiving his body and blood

If the Word truly became flesh, and if we truly receive the Word as flesh in the Lord’s food, how can he not be considered to remain naturally in us? He both assumed, by being born human, the nature of our flesh, now inseparable from him, and joined the nature of his flesh to the nature of eternity under the sacrament of the flesh that he communicates to us.

Thus we are all one, because the Father is in Christ and Christ is in us. Therefore, whoever denies that the Father is naturally in Christ must first deny that he himself is naturally in Christ or that Christ is in him, because the Father in Christ and Christ in us make us one in these things.

If, then, Christ truly assumed the flesh of our body, and if that man who was born from Mary is truly Christ, and if we truly receive under the mystery the flesh of his body, and through this become one because the Father is in him and he is in us, how can unity of will alone be asserted, when through the sacrament the property of perfect unity is natural?

One must not speak of divine matters according to human or worldly understanding. Nor should perversity be wrung from heavenly statements by violence or shameless preaching, contrary to sound and reverent understanding. Let us read what is written, and understand what we have read; then we shall fulfill perfectly the duty of faith.

For concerning the natural truth of Christ in us, unless we learn what we say from him, we speak foolishly and impiously. He himself said:

> My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink. Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him.

No room has been left for doubt concerning the reality of the flesh and blood. For now, both by the Lord’s own declaration and by our faith, it is truly flesh and truly blood. Once received and consumed, they bring about this result: we are in Christ, and Christ is in us.

Is this not the truth? Let it certainly be untrue for those who deny that Jesus Christ is true God. He himself is therefore in us through the flesh, and we are in him, since he has carried into God with himself that which we are.

That we are in him through the sacrament of the flesh and blood he communicates is also testified by him when he says:

> The world will no longer see me, but you will see me, because I live and you will live. On that day you will know that I am in my Father, and you are in me, and I am in you.

If he wished only the unity of will to be understood, why did he set out a certain degree and order by which unity is consummated? Was it not so that, just as he is in the Father by the nature of divinity, we should be believed to be in him through his bodily birth, and he in us through the mystery of the sacraments, and thus perfect unity should be taught through the mediator? While we remain in him, he remains in the Father; and while he remains in the Father, he remains in us.

Thus we would advance toward the unity of the Father, since we too would naturally be in him who is in the Father according to his birth, while he himself naturally remains in us.

How natural this unity in us is, he himself testified as follows:

> Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him.

For no one will be in him unless he himself is in that person; and he has assumed only that person’s flesh who has received his flesh.

He had already taught the sacrament of this unity perfectly when he said:

> Just as the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father, so whoever eats my flesh will live because of me.

He lives, therefore, because of the Father; and just as he lives because of the Father, so we shall live because of his flesh. Every comparison is proposed as a pattern for understanding, so that we may grasp the matter under discussion according to the example set before us.

This, then, is the cause of our life: that we possess Christ, who remains in us bodily through the flesh, so that we may live through him under the condition by which he lives through the Father.

If, therefore, we live naturally through him according to the flesh—that is, having received the nature of his flesh—how could he not naturally possess the Father in himself according to the Spirit, since he lives through the Father?

He lives through the Father because his birth did not introduce into him a foreign or different nature; because what he is comes from the Father, yet he is not separated from the Father by any intervening difference of nature; and because, through his birth, he possesses the Father in himself by the power of nature.

We have recalled these things because heretics, pretending that there is only unity of will between the Father and the Son, used our unity with God as an example. They claimed that we were united to the Son and through the Son to the Father only by obedience and religious intention, and that no natural participation in the sacrament of flesh and blood was granted to us.

Yet, both through the honor bestowed upon us by the Son of God and through the Son’s bodily and permanent presence in us, and because we are bodily and inseparably united with him, the mystery of true and natural unity must be proclaimed.

## CHAPTER IX — The Catholic faith of the Church

The faith of the Church, instructed by apostolic teachings, knows the birth of Christ but does not know its beginning; it knows the dispensation but does not know division.

It does not divide Jesus Christ, as though Jesus were not himself Christ; nor does it distinguish the Son of Man from the Son of God, lest the Son of God perhaps not also be understood as the Son of Man.

It does not take up the Son of God into the Son of Man, nor does it split Christ by a threefold faith. His garment, woven from above, is seamless, so that it does not divide Jesus Christ into Word, soul, and body; nor, conversely, does it take God the Word as assuming a soul and body.

For the Word of God is wholly God to it, and Christ is wholly man. In the mystery of its confession it retains this unity: it believes Christ to be nothing other than Jesus, and preaches Jesus as nothing other than Christ.

I am not unaware of how greatly the majesty of the heavenly mystery obstructs the weakness of human understanding. [Col. 0384D] [Note: [Col. 0383D] See Saint Hilary, *On the Trinity*, Book III.] We cannot easily express these things in words, judge them by our senses, or even encompass them in the mind.

The eternity of the Father exceeds place, time, form, and whatever else can be conceived by human understanding. He is outside all things and within all things, containing everything and contained by no one. He is not changed by an approach that will later recede, but is invisible, incomprehensible, full, perfect, and eternal. He receives nothing from elsewhere, but is himself sufficient for that which remains as it is.

This unbegotten one, therefore, before all time, generated the Son from himself—not from some underlying matter, because all things are through the Son; not from nothing, because the Son is from himself; not as a product, because nothing in God is changeable or empty.

He did not generate a part of himself, divided, severed, or extended, because God is both impassible and incorporeal. These are matters of suffering and flesh. As the Apostle says:

> In Christ the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily.

Yet incomprehensibly and ineffably, before all time and the ages, he brought forth the Only-Begotten from what was unbegotten in himself, imparting to his birth all that God is, through love and power.

Thus the Only-Begotten Son is perfect and eternal, from the perfect, unbegotten, and eternal Father.

Those things that belong to him according to the body he assumed are the expression of his goodness and his will for our salvation. Invisible, incorporeal, and incomprehensible, since he was begotten from the Father, he received within himself as much materiality and humility as there was in us capacity to understand, perceive, and contemplate him. He accommodated himself to our weakness rather than failing in those things in which he existed.

Therefore, the perfect Son of the perfect Father, the only-begotten offspring of the unbegotten God, received everything from him who possesses everything: God from God, Spirit from Spirit, light from Light.

He confidently says:

> The Father is in me, and I am in the Father.

For just as the Father is Spirit, so the Son is Spirit; just as the Father is God, so the Son is God; just as the Father is light, so the Son is light.

From what exists in the Father, therefore, the Son possesses what he is: the whole Son was born from the whole Father. Not from elsewhere, because nothing existed before the Son; not from nothing, because the Son is from God; not in part, because the fullness of divinity is in the Son; not in some things, because it is in all things.

But he was born as the one who could do so willed, and as the one who generated him knows. What is in the Father is also in the Son; what is in the Unbegotten is also in the Only-Begotten. One distinct from the other, and both one. Not two constituting one, but one in the other, because there is nothing different in either.

The Father is in the Son because the Son is from him. The Son is in the Father because the Son is not from elsewhere. The Only-Begotten is in the Unbegotten because the Only-Begotten is from the Unbegotten.

Thus they are in one another: just as all things are perfect in the unbegotten Father, so all things are perfect in the Only-Begotten Son.

This unity in the Son and the Father is power, love, faith, hope, truth, way, and life. One must not slander God concerning his own powers, nor disparage the Son through the mystery and power of his birth; one must not compare anything with the unbegotten Father, nor distinguish the Only-Begotten from him either in time or in power; one must confess the Son as God because he is from God.

Therefore, concerned with the human race, the Son of God first became human so that he might be believed, so that, as a witness to divine realities, he might be one of us, and through the weakness of the flesh proclaim God the Father to us who are weak and carnal.

He accomplished the will of God the Father in himself when he said:

> I have not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me.

This does not mean that he himself did not wish to do what the Father willed, but that he displayed his obedience through the fulfillment of the Father’s will, himself willing to carry out the Father’s will. This accomplishment of the will was itself his will.

## CHAPTER X — One must not place confidence in human prudence

Human prudence must not be trusted so far that it thinks itself perfect in whatever it knows and supposes that the whole substance of reason is contained in what, after examining it in the mind, it considers consistently established everywhere by its own judgment of truth.

For imperfect things do not comprehend the perfect. Nor can what subsists from another fully possess either an understanding of its author or an understanding of itself. It perceives itself only in what it is, and does not extend its understanding beyond the limit established for it by its nature.

It does not owe its movement to itself but to its author. Therefore, because what subsists from an author exists in something else, it is imperfect in itself, since it depends on another.

It is necessary, then, that precisely where it thinks itself wise, it should be foolish, because it does not govern the limitations of its nature. Thinking that everything is contained within the boundaries of its weaknesses, it already boasts falsely under the name of wisdom, since it is not permitted to exercise understanding beyond the power of its own senses.

While the substitution of an imperfect nature boasts that it possesses the wisdom of perfect understanding, it is mocked with the reproach of foolish wisdom.

## CHAPTER XI — Cyprian or Hilary on the Word of God

The designation “Word” applied to the Son of God belongs to the mystery of his birth, just as do the names “Wisdom” and “Power.” Although these have come to exist in God the Son together with the substance of a true birth, they are not absent from God as his own possessions, even though they were born from him into God. For birth does not diminish the begetter when it retains the growth of the one born.

These are therefore appropriate names for God the Only-Begotten. Through birth they complete his subsistence, yet they are not absent from the Father; hence, by the power of nature, they are mutable.

God the Only-Begotten is the Word. But the unbegotten Father was never without the Word—not because the utterance of a voice is the nature of the Son, but because God from God subsists through the power of birth. To show that he is proper to the Father and inseparable from him through the sameness of nature, he is signified by the name “Word.”

Likewise, Christ is the Wisdom and Power of God—not, as is usually understood, an effective movement of inward power or understanding, but the one who, through birth, possesses the truth of substantial nature and is signified by these names of inward realities.

For what subsists by being born cannot be understood to be identical with what is eternal to each. But the Only-Begotten Son, born as subsistent God from the eternal God the Father, has been shown by these proper names to be subsistent, so that he might be understood not to be foreign to the nature of the Father’s divinity. Once he had subsisted, he did not lack these names.

## CHAPTER XII — Cyprian’s true assertion concerning God

There is one Ruler of the world, one Lord, who commands all things that exist by his Word, orders them by reason, and brings them to perfection by his power.

He cannot be seen; vision is too limited for him. He cannot be comprehended; touch is too impure for him. He cannot be measured; he is greater than the senses. Therefore, we esteem him worthily when we call him beyond estimation.

How could God possess a temple when the whole world is his temple? And since a human being occupies a wider space, do you think the power of such great majesty can be confined within a single little building? He must be dedicated in our mind and consecrated in our breast. Do not seek the name of God, and so forth.

## CHAPTER XIII — Augustine on the Word of God

> Now you are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you.

Why did he not say, “You are clean because of the baptism with which you were washed,” but instead say, “Because of the word that I have spoken to you,” unless it is because the Word also cleanses in water? Remove the word, and what is water except water? The word comes to the element, and it becomes a sacrament, itself, as it were, a visible word.

He had certainly spoken of this when he washed the disciples’ feet:

> Whoever has been washed does not need to wash, but is wholly clean.

From where does water possess such great power that it touches the body and cleanses the heart, unless this is accomplished by the Word? Not because it is spoken, but because it is believed.

For in the word itself one thing is the passing sound, and another is the abiding power: this is the word of faith that we proclaim. The Apostle says:

> If you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved.

One believes with the heart for righteousness, but confession is made with the [mouth] for salvation. Hence it is also read in the Acts of the Apostles:

> Cleansing their hearts by faith.

And in his Epistle the blessed Peter says:

> In the same way, baptism will save you—not the removal of dirt from the flesh, but the appeal of a good conscience.

That is, it is the word of faith that we proclaim, through which baptism is undoubtedly consecrated so that it may cleanse.

For Christ, the vine with us and the Father the husbandman, loved the Church and gave himself for her. Read the Apostle and see what he adds:

> That he might sanctify her, cleansing her by the washing of water in the word.

Purification, therefore, would never be attributed to the flowing and unstable element unless the word were added. [Note: [Col. 0387D] See Saint Augustine, Treatise 80 on the Gospel of John.]

This word of faith has such power in the Church of God that, through the Church believing, offering, blessing, and immersing, it cleanses even a tiny infant, although the child is not yet able to believe with the heart for righteousness or confess with the mouth for salvation.

All this takes place through the word of which the Lord says:

> Now you are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you.

## CHAPTER XIV — From the booklet of Paschasius Ratbertus to the disciple Placidus: that there must be no doubt that Christ’s communion is the true body and blood

Every Catholic rightly believes in his heart that God created all things from nothing, and so forth.

(The booklet of Paschasius follows, almost complete, having already been published elsewhere.)

## CHAPTER XXXVI — What the Eucharist provides to those who receive the Lord’s body and blood worthily or unworthily
Instructing the Corinthians, the blessed Apostle says concerning the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood, so that they might know how much reverence they owed it, among other things: “For I received from the Lord what I also delivered to you: that the Lord Jesus, on the night when he was betrayed, took bread, and, giving thanks, broke it and said: ‘This is my body, which is broken for you; [Col. 0388A] do this in remembrance of me.’ In the same way also the cup, after supper, saying: ‘This cup is the new covenant in my blood; do this in remembrance of me.’”

He showed them that the mystery of the Eucharist, celebrated during the meal, is not itself a meal. For it is a spiritual medicine which, tasted with reverence, purifies the person devoted to it. Indeed, it is the memorial of our redemption, so that, remembering the Redeemer, we may deserve to receive greater things from him, proclaiming the Lord’s death until he comes. Because we have been freed by the Lord’s death, by eating and drinking the flesh and blood that were offered for us, accustomed to these things we signify the new covenant—that is, the new law, which hands over to the heavenly kingdoms the one who obeys it.

[Col. 0388B] For Moses too, having received the blood of a calf in a basin, sprinkled it over the children of Israel, saying: “This is the covenant that the Lord has established with you.” This was a figure of the covenant that the Lord called new, so that the one Moses handed down might be the old covenant. The covenant, therefore, was established by blood, because it is the witness of the divine blood’s benefit. In its type we receive the mystical cup for the protection of the body, blood, and soul, because the Lord’s blood redeemed our blood—that is, it saved the whole human being. For the Savior’s flesh was poured out for the salvation of the body, but his blood for our soul, just as it had previously been prefigured by Moses: “The flesh,” he says, “is offered for your body, but the blood for your soul”; therefore, blood is not to be eaten.

Thus, whoever [Col. 0388C] eats this bread or drinks the Lord’s cup unworthily will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. He calls that person unworthy before the Lord who celebrates the mystery in a manner different from that which was handed down by him. For no one can be devoted who presumes to act otherwise than it was given by its author. Therefore he warns that, according to the order handed down, the mind of the person approaching the Lord’s Eucharist must be devout, since judgment will come, so that each person may give an account on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ according to the manner in which he approaches. For those who approach without the discipline of tradition and conduct are guilty of the Lord’s body and blood.

But what does it mean to be guilty except to suffer the penalties of the Lord’s death? He was killed for those who treat his benefit as void. “Let a person examine himself, and so eat of the bread and drink from the cup; for whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not discerning the Lord’s body.” He therefore teaches that one must approach communion with a devout mind and with fear, so that the mind may know that it owes reverence to him whose body it approaches to receive. The one who receives it ought to judge this within himself: that he drinks the blood, under the Lord’s mystery, which is the witness of God’s benefit. If we receive him with discipline, we will not be unworthy of the body and blood, giving thanks to the Redeemer.

“Therefore many among you are weak and sick, and many are asleep.” To prove that the examination of those receiving the Lord’s body would truly take place, he already displays here an image of judgment against those who had received the Lord’s body carelessly: they were seized by fevers and illnesses, and many died, so that the rest might learn from them, and so that the example of a few might terrify and correct the others. They should know that the Lord’s body cannot be received negligently without punishment, and that the one whom punishment has delayed here will be dealt with more severely because he despised the example.

“If we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged. But when we are judged, we are disciplined by the Lord, so that we may not be condemned with the world.” He says this because, if we corrected our own errors, we would not be judged by the Lord; and because we are disciplined, this is nevertheless for our benefit, so that we may be corrected by that very fear. In a few there is the correction of all, lest we be condemned with the world—that is, with unbelievers. For there is no difference between an unbeliever and one who approaches the Lord’s table carelessly.

## CHAPTER XXXVII — What the blessed martyr Cyprian declares happened in his presence to those who, polluted by food sacrificed to idols, rashly received the sacraments of the Lord’s body and blood

“In my presence,” he says, “and with me as witness, hear what happened. Parents fleeing outside, while in their panic taking insufficient care, left a little daughter behind in the care of her nurse. The nurse carried the abandoned child to the magistrate. There, at the idol to which the people flocked, because by reason of her age she was not yet able to eat meat, they gave her bread mixed with wine, which itself also remained from the sacrifice of those who were perishing.”

The rest may be read in Saint Cyprian, *On the Lapsed*.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII — Why those entangled in criminal sins are to be excluded from the Lord’s sacraments

[Col. 0389C]

Since the Son of God himself says, “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink,” this must be understood to mean that the same mysteries of our redemption truly are the body and blood of the Lord, so that we ought to believe them to be pledges of that perfect unity which, in hope now and in reality hereafter, we shall possess with our Head. Hence the sacraments are also called such from sanctification or from a hidden power.

Therefore those who, by the foulness of deadly crimes, have turned away from the health of Christ’s members are suspended from the sacraments themselves by ecclesiastical judgment. For whoever worthily eats and drinks the body and blood of the Lord signifies that he is in God and God in him. But whoever either does not possess the medicine or uses it unworthily testifies, by languishing, that he is far from the physician. For he does not lie who says: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves,” and so forth.

It must also be known that the holy Fathers established this above all for the purpose of excluding those who sin mortally from the Lord’s sacraments, lest, receiving them unworthily, they become involved in greater guilt—as Judas is said, after rashly receiving the bread from his Teacher, to have been more fully seized by the devil, so that the crime he had first conceived through wicked premeditation might then be completed by the most wicked deed—or lest, as the Apostle says concerning the Corinthians, those who presume to receive them incur bodily weakness, infirmity, and death itself. They are also suspended from communion by the fear of this exclusion and by a kind of condemnation’s anathema, so that they may more earnestly seek the medicine of repentance and more eagerly long to recover salvation.

## CHAPTER XXXIX — That Jews are to be barred from every gathering of the faithful, especially where the offering of Christians is celebrated

In the celebration of so great a mystery, great care must be taken that heretics or pagans are not present. Jews in particular are to be barred not only from the thresholds of the church but from every gathering of the faithful. For these most wicked and utterly depraved people, together with their prince, the devil, are accustomed to attack the life-giving sacraments and, insofar as they can, impiously strive to profane and pollute the price of human redemption. This was once openly discovered and punished with a fitting penalty in the time of the most blessed confessor Syrus.

Since the manner in which it happened brings great praise to the Lord, as it is read in the *Life* of the aforesaid confessor, we have thought it proper to insert it in this chapter. After the marks of the temple’s or altar’s dedication had been completed, the most blessed Syrus offered daily praises and sacrifices to God there. One day, while the distinguished bishop was celebrating the solemnities of the Mass in that place, and a multitude of his children—whom, according to the Apostle, he had begotten for God by the seed of the word—were devoutly present at the holy mysteries, a Jew, instigated by an evil spirit, boldly entered, intending to receive the Lord’s body and throw it into a dung heap.

When he reached the hands of the man of God amid the crowds of the faithful, he sacrilegiously received the Lord’s body with his unclean mouth. As soon as he opened his mouth to spit it out, he was struck by a fitting punishment and, unable to form words, began to cry out, heard and seen by everyone. He wanted to close his lips but could not; his rigid tongue offered no service of speech. As though carrying a fiery dart in his mouth, he was tormented by immense pains. The whole church resounded with the cries of his senseless voice, and the assembly of Christ’s faithful rejoiced at the power of so extraordinary a miracle. The saying was fulfilled: “He himself mocks the mockers”; and what the Apostle writes to the Galatians: “Do not be deceived: God is not mocked; for whatever a person sows, that he will also reap.”

But the unbelieving Jew had not heard these proclamations—or rather, this deception (the text is corrupt); he had thought to impose a trick upon the Holy Spirit. The man of God ordered him to be brought before him and said to him when he arrived: “You unbelieving man, full of faithlessness, why have you fulfilled the counsel of so wicked an enemy, so as to regard Christ’s body as something utterly vile? Behold, the hidden persuader has enticed you, wretched man, to do this; divine power will show it to all his faithful.”

The Jew, overcome by excessive pain, did not cease emitting sounds without speech, bearing in his throat the torment of his wickedness. For, according to the prophecy of the most holy Simeon, just as the Word of God is destruction and ruin for unbelievers, so for his faithful it is life and exultation. By a marvelous balancing, the Lord’s body could be seen hanging in the Jew’s mouth, so that it rested neither upon the joints beneath the tongue [Col. 0391A] nor adhered above to the unclean palate.

When the faithful pleaded for his misery, the man of the Lord stretched out his hand and drew the mystery of the holy Eucharist from the sacrilegious mouth, saying: “Behold, now you have been freed. From now on beware, do not do anything like this, and do not presume to repeat it again.” The Jew, falling at his feet, cried out that he would believe in Christ the Lord if he were washed with the water of holy baptism and joined to his devout assembly.

“To you,” he said, “Father of almighty God, I give thanks, because you do not disdain to correct Jewish faithlessness, but in your abundant mercy turn them to faith in your Only-begotten.” After he had been baptized, many Jews who believed with him were reborn through Christ’s holy baptism and joined to the faithful and the spiritual assembly.

## CHAPTER XL — How one ought to approach the wondrous sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood

[Col. 0391B]

We prescribe that confessions be made with particular care, especially concerning disturbances of the mind, before going to Mass, lest someone perhaps approach the altar unworthily—that is, without possessing a pure heart. For it is better to wait until the heart has become sound and free from scandal and envy than to approach boldly the judgment seat. The tribunal of Christ is the altar, and there he judges with his body and blood those who approach unworthily.

Therefore, just as one must abstain from carnal and deadly sins before receiving communion, so also one must abstain from inward vices and the illnesses of a sick soul before joining true peace and the bond of eternal salvation. When a suitable time invites us to the fearful table [Col. 0391C], the greatest care must be taken that no Jew be found there, that no wicked person approach, that the tongue utter no deceptive words, and that no plots be devised in the mind, but that the speech declare what the will possesses.

And now Christ is present there—the one who adorned that table; he himself also consecrates this one. For it is not a human being who makes what is set forth the body and blood of Christ, but the one who was crucified for us, Christ. The words are spoken by the priest’s mouth and consecrated by God’s power and grace. “This is my body,” he says. By this word what is set forth is consecrated. And just as the voice that said, “Increase and multiply and fill the earth,” was spoken once, yet produces its effect through all time, with nature at work in generation, so that voice too was spoken once, yet through all the churches’ tables, even to the present day and until his coming, grants firmness to the sacrifice.

Therefore let no hypocrite approach; let no one with a deceitful mind dare to draw near to such great mysteries, lest he be condemned, earn a sentence, and suffer what Judas suffered. For the devil entered him after he had shared the table—not because he had despised the Lord’s body, but because the shamelessness and wickedness of his mind caused the adversary to dwell in him. Thus you may learn that the devil prepares snares for those who are unworthy and who celebrate the secrets of the mysteries hypocritically, and that those who hurry to communicate without an upright mind are assailed more and more.

[Col. 0392A] I say this not to frighten you, but to make you more cautious. Let no one be a Judas at the table. This sacrifice is spiritual food. Just as bodily food, when it finds the stomach occupied by harmful fluids, injures it more, does greater harm, and provides no help, so this spiritual food, if it finds someone polluted by wickedness, destroys him all the more—not by its own nature, but because of the recipient’s fault.

Therefore let the mind be pure in every respect and the thought pure, because the sacrifice too is pure. Let us prepare a holy soul. From this condition a person may be corrected not over a long period, but in a single day. If you are distressed because of your enemy, release your anger and loosen your enmities, so that you may receive a remedy from the table.

Are you hurrying to the holy and fearful sacrifice? Be ashamed before the mysteries of the offering. Christ has been set forth for slaughter [Col. 0392B]; let us see why he was slaughtered: namely, so that he might reconcile the heavenly things, establish peace among all things on earth, and make you a friend of the angels and of God, who possesses power over all. The Lord gave his soul for you, and you remain an enemy to your fellow servant? And with such a mind you approach the table of peace? He did not even refuse to die for your benefit, and you will not forgive your fellow servant even your anger for the sake of your own liberation?

But perhaps you say: “I have been defrauded by my enemy; he has injured me with many losses and burdened me with great damages.” Whatever you say comes down to a matter of money. He did not crucify you as the Jews crucified Christ; yet Christ, in his abundant mercy, granted the blood poured out for the salvation of those who poured it out.

A swollen breast is hostile to God. This sacrifice was rightly established for the sake of reconciliation. If you despise the commands of the sacrifice, you will not be able to experience the sacrifice’s remedy. Fulfill the purpose for which the sacrifice was made, so that you may enjoy the sacrifice. The Son came for this reason: to reconcile human nature to divine favor. For this reason also, when we do this, he caused us to be called by his name. “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God.”
