Do what the Only-begotten of God did: if you wish to become an author of peace both for yourself and for others, that is why he calls you a son of God. In the celebration of the sacrifice, God commanded nothing other than the reconciliation of a brother. Let these things therefore remain fastened in our minds. Let us hold to the holy kiss, which joins souls, unites minds, and shows us to be one body, since all are seen to have received one body.

And therefore let us mingle with one another in one body—not by the mingling of bodies, but bound by the love of souls—and thus we may be satisfied with the fruits of the divine table. For even if we abound in many good works of conscience, once reconciliation has been despised we can earn no consolation.

## CHAPTER XLI — Concerning the revelations by which the Lord strengthened the wavering hearts of those uncertain about the truth of his body and blood

The grace of the Lord’s body and blood is so great that no human being can conceive it. Through it the world is reconciled to God; through it human beings become gods, and, though earthly by nature, become heavenly in their conduct.

Yet some, insofar as they can, diminish this grace, not believing that what is received is truly the Lord’s body or that what is drunk is truly Christ’s blood, but only a figure, although he himself said: “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink.” In the sacred banquet of his supper, when he handed over to the disciples the sacrament of so great a mystery and transformed the bread into his body, he did not say, “This is a figure of my body,” but, “This is my body.” Similarly, in handing over the cup, he said: “This is the cup of my blood.”

Since this alone ought to satisfy everyone—that which Truth itself handed down to the disciples of truth—nevertheless, for certain people whose hearts had been shrouded in the darkness of unbelief and who could not believe otherwise, the Lord once deigned to reveal the very likeness of human form, just as the truth of the matter requires, so that what was manifested to a few might benefit all for faith and salvation.

I do not consider it irrelevant to insert into this little book, for the greatest edification of posterity, the things we have learned by reading about such revelations, and to leave written down by our own labor the splendid miracles of our Lord Jesus Christ, lest they slip from memory.

## CHAPTER XLII — A miracle concerning a certain Jew

I think it appropriate to publish what I have learned up to now from a certain Hebrew who related it. Nor will it for that reason be thought untrue if, perhaps through the hostile mouths of enemies, a sure account acknowledges the truth in genuine conversation. Greater credence is usually given to such things when enemies attest to truthful statements and support them without the deceit of flattery or false speech.

In this manner, through Balaam, who was certainly an enemy of the Jewish people, the marks of blessing were proclaimed. The “chosen vessel” too is not inappropriately chosen, so that the one who had previously been thought intolerable to the faithful might himself place the name of the majesty of the Lord Jesus before rulers and powers.

But what did he relate? “A certain Jew,” he says, “going to a certain bishop, said that he wished to be initiated into the mysteries of the Catholic faith. The bishop therefore ought to hand down to him the rite of worship, so that, instructed more fully, he might attain his desire and, having become a believer, be joined to the Christian body.

“To this the bishop replied: ‘Leave us, I beg you, hateful race of men; cease, as is your custom, to attempt wickedly. But if, as often happens, you are bound by the necessity of some crime, be content to receive a stipend from the Church, provided that you do not turn out to be a mocker of our faith.’

“To this he replied: ‘No, blessed bishop; I am not approaching you so that you may immediately treat me as a cursed enemy. I wish to be initiated into the mysteries of your faith, because I fear the judgment of the Lord Jesus Christ, whose name is terrible, and I desire to have his protection.’

“But because he persisted in his request, and by an oath had bound himself with an excessive pledge that he would not neglect what he was asking with any sense of security, abandon it under any persecution, or betray it under any circumstances, the bishop ordered that the beginning of his catechizing be given to him through the sign of the cross.

“Easter came. When he reached the sacred waters in which sins are cleansed, he began to resist. It seemed that he was not expressing complaints in words but, roaring through certain groans, was cursing the mystery of baptism itself. The very confused bishop therefore ordered him to be removed immediately.

“But when the man had suddenly turned back to himself, he said to those who, as though driven by madness, were holding him at a distance to one side: ‘Take me to the font. I am no longer out of my mind, and you must not think that I have been captured. Indeed, I now desire to be baptized.’

“Thus, when he had been brought back and again reached the bishop, he said: ‘I beg you, renowned priest, let the sacrament of this holy washing be completed in me.’

“And the bishop replied: ‘I will not do so unless you explain fully the whole circumstance of your terror and the secret of your confusion, and confess in truthful words what stupor came upon you earlier, so that you cursed the water of this sacred stream.’

“Then he burst into tears and unfolded the sequence of his ordeal in this order:

“‘As I stood before the entrance of this font, about to be washed, a crowd of very black demons, like Ethiopians, came. Seizing me, they prevented me by force from approaching the font in the hands of the saints. Other candidates were also present, resisting them and saying: “Do not prevent this man from approaching the mysteries of the holy font. Who are you, that you serve these sacraments in order to punish? For you—you are the ones to whom the burning of the noxious fire is owed, not the splendor of baptism.”

“‘“What have you to do with this man?” they replied. “He is ours, and he must not be thought to belong to you by right.”

“‘When, then, by your command and authority, you had had me dragged away in the hands of certain people and removed from your sight, ordering me to withdraw to the other side, amid the quarrels of the parties a kind of agreement was reached: they would weigh me against my sins on an equal scale, and if the weight of my crimes proved greater, I would depart with them as unclean and would not be led away by the others to be cleansed.

“‘But when the mass of my unspeakable burdens had grown and become hateful under its excessive weight, a certain poor man suddenly appeared—the man whose body I had warmed with my garment a few days earlier. He brought forward the garment and offered it to be weighed against my body.

“‘Immediately, as though some material of immense weight had been added to the garment itself, the garment’s weight outweighed that of my body, and those Ethiopians were cast out and driven away. I was brought back here in the hands of the blessed.’

“After he had affirmed with terrible oaths that these things had happened, he was admitted to baptism and received the gift of the most holy washing.

“When they came to the mysteries of the Mass, he again began, as he had earlier at baptism, to shrink from the Holy of Holies. He gave loud groans and roars and seemed to recoil violently from the sacrament of the mystery itself.

“The bishop, astonished again, said: ‘Why is this troubled man acting madly and roaring with such frenzy?’

“While all of us who were present remained utterly astonished and fixed in place, some approached him and said: ‘Why are you again overcome by stupor? If you do not wish to believe, why do you hypocritically attempt the sacrament of so great a mystery?’

“But he replied: ‘I am overcome by the greatest fear and trembling, for I see the body of a fully grown man laid upon this altar, torn apart limb by limb. I see your hands wet with his blood. Do you not notice that the joints of your fingers, stained with blood, have changed color and become red?’

“Then everyone, together with the bishop, burst into tears and began to cry out loudly: ‘Thanks be to God! Praises to God, who does great and inscrutable things without number! Hosanna to the Son of David! Hosanna in the highest!’

“They marveled together and said: ‘Truly, in this man the prophecy of the psalm has been fulfilled: “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven and whose sins have been covered.”’

“It was not without purpose that the secret of so great a mystery was revealed to him. For, as he related—unless I am mistaken—the man in question (the text is corrupt at *ille qui dixerat*) had his bright soul received by gracious light among those in white on the seventh day; once the bonds of the flesh had been loosed, he completed his blessed life with a beautiful end.

“Through this miracle it became clear that the one who consecrated his body upon the altar in the mystery—and also through the image of truth—is the same one who consecrated it for his disciples in his Passion.”

## CHAPTER XLIII — Likewise concerning a certain elderly hermit whose doubt the Lord confirmed by the same revelation of the truth

[Note: [Col. 0395D] See the edition in Rosweid, *Lives of the Holy Fathers* (*Patrologia*, vol. LXXIII).]

The abbot Daniel related, saying: “Our father, Abbot Arsenius, told of a certain old man from Scetis, where he lived, who was great in this active life but simple in faith. And he was in error, and so forth.”

## CHAPTER XLIV — Likewise, a miracle that took place at Rome

[Note: [Col. 0396D] See John the Deacon, *Life of Gregory the Great*, book II, chapter 41.]

There was a certain noble matron in the city of Rome who, out of devotion and religious zeal, used to make offerings, carry them to the church on the Lord’s Day, and present them to the supreme pontiff, both as an expression of ecclesiastical custom and because of her familiarity with him.

One day, when she approached in the customary order to receive communion from the hand of the apostolic bishop, and the pontiff offered her a portion of the Lord’s body, saying, “May the body of our Lord Jesus Christ benefit you unto eternal life and the remission of all sins,” she smiled.

When the man of the Lord saw this, he withdrew the holy communion from her, placed it separately upon the altar, and entrusted it to the deacon to be kept until all the faithful had communicated. When the sacred mysteries had been completed, blessed Gregory questioned her, saying: “Tell me, I beg you, what arose in your heart when you smiled as you were about to receive communion?”

She replied: “I recognized that the little portion had been taken from the same offering that I had made with my own hands and offered to you, and when I understood that you had called it the Lord’s body, I smiled.”

Then the holy pontiff of the Lord addressed the people concerning this and urged them to implore the Lord earnestly, so that, for the strengthening of many people’s faith, he might show with bodily eyes what the unbelief of this woman’s mind ought to have seen and perceived with the eyes of faith.

When the prayer had been offered, he rose from prayer together with the people and the same woman. In the sight of everyone, while they crowded around to behold the heavenly spectacle, he uncovered the corporal cloth on the altar and found a portion of a little finger stained with blood. He said to the woman:

[Col. 0396A] “Learn, I say, and now at least believe the Truth who bears witness: ‘The bread that I will give is my flesh, and my blood is truly drink.’ But our all-knowing Creator, by the power with which he made all things from nothing and fashioned for himself a body from the flesh of the ever-Virgin through the working of the Holy Spirit, transforms bread and wine mixed with water into his flesh and blood through the sanctification of the Spirit at the Catholic prayer, for the sake of our restoration, while their proper outward form remains.”

He then ordered everyone to pray to the divine power that it restore the most holy mystery to its former form, so that it might be possible for the woman to receive it. This was done. Thereafter the aforementioned woman made great progress in holy religion and faith, was consecrated through participation in the Lord’s sacrament, and all who had witnessed it grew more fervent in divine love and orthodox belief.

## CHAPTER XLV — Likewise, another

A certain man, most noble according to his fleshly lineage and most powerful according to the royal magnificence appropriate to his rank, had obtained familiarity with the apostolic see through intermediaries. He had also been sufficiently instructed in the worship of God and the saints by frequent admonitions in letters sent by blessed Gregory. He sent worthy gifts through energetic and devout messengers to the pontifical see, asking that relics of the blessed apostles and martyrs be sent to him.

The holy Apostle received his envoys honorably and gladly and kept them with him for some time. In the ancient custom of this kind of business, he continually went around celebrating memorial Masses for the holy apostles and martyrs and consecrating relics in their memory, always keeping the aforesaid envoys and their companions with him.

When he had completed the celebrations of those whose relics had been requested, he divided into separate portions the consecrated cloths upon which he had celebrated the holy mysteries and placed each portion individually in its own small reliquary. He secured them with the seal of his holy authority and handed them over to the petitioners according to ecclesiastical custom.

They received the blessing they had requested and obtained with due reverence and set out on their journey rejoicing. But as they traveled for several days on their return, a certain curiosity came over the man who was regarded as first among the others. He said to his companions that they had foolishly undertaken such a long journey, since they did not know what valuable thing they were taking back to their lord.

As their exchange of words gradually increased, at the urging of his companions the individual seals of apostolic authority were broken, the reliquaries were opened, and in each one a single little portion of cloth was found.

They immediately returned indignantly to Rome and went to the archdeacon, complaining: “Why,” they said, “does the Apostolic Lord hold our lord in such low regard? He had hoped that he had obtained such favor with him that the pontiff would wish to mock him in this way and subject us to his dishonor and offense.

“We thought that we were bringing back from here the precious bones of apostles or martyrs, as was fitting for so great a man as our lord. Yet from such a distinguished see, situated at the end of such a long and sufficiently difficult journey, we have been given small pieces of cloth, as though this kind of little cloth could not be found among us. Unless concern for the matter had come to our aid, so that we might discover what we were carrying and thus avoid the foolishness of coming to our lord in this condition, there is no doubt that we would have incurred danger to his honor and favor.”

The archdeacon rebuked them with a gentle reprimand for having burst into such presumption as to break the apostolic seals, and urged them to return and deliver to their lord with honor what they had received.

But they would not at all heed his admonitions. They came into the presence of Lord Gregory, and when the matter had been reported, he bore their foolishness with the greatest patience and ordered them to attend the most holy solemnities of the Mass.

When the appropriate point in his sermon had arrived, he urged the people of God to pray for the grace of the saints, so that they might deign in this matter to reveal their power plainly, in order that those who were less believing and ignorant might learn more clearly what faith is capable of.

After the prayer had been offered, he took the knife from the man who had violated the seals and, upon the altar of the body of Saint Peter, pierced one of the pieces of cloth he had received through the middle and cut it. Blood immediately flowed from it and stained the entire piece.

The envoys mentioned above and all the people saw the astonishing and mysterious miracle of the holy faith. They fell prostrate upon the ground, worshiping the Lord and saying: “Wonderful is God in his saints, the God of Israel; he himself will give power and strength to his people. Blessed be God.”

After silence had been restored, blessed Gregory said among other teachings of the faith to those who had previously thought little of the venerable relics: “Know, brothers, that in the consecration of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, when offerings were made upon the most holy altar for the sanctification of relics in honor of his apostles or martyrs, to whom the relics were specially assigned, their blood always entered these cloths—the blood that was poured out for the name of Christ our Lord.”

Having strengthened all who were present in faith, he again secured the reliquaries with his seal and handed over to them the incomparable gifts they had desired. They returned with joy, reported these events in order to their lord, and fulfilled his desire. He reverently received the precious protection of the saints and honorably placed it in a venerable location, where God deigns to work miracles to the praise and glory of his name even to the present day.

## CHAPTER XLVI — What was revealed to the blessed Cyprian concerning the sacrament of the cup

[Note: [Col. 0397D] See among the letters of Saint Cyprian.]

Writing to Caecilius concerning the sacrament of the cup, the blessed Cyprian says among other things: “Since certain people, either through ignorance or simplicity, do not do in sanctifying and administering the Lord’s cup to the people what Jesus Christ our Lord and God, the author and teacher of this sacrifice, did and taught, I considered it both religious and necessary to write to you about this matter,” and so forth.

## CHAPTER XLVII — How the mystical Passover was abolished in the Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ, and how the truth of the matter was shown in his offering

[Note: [Col. 0398D] See volume III of the works of Saint Gregory.]

We have said enough above concerning the sacrament of the cup, according to what the Lord deigned to reveal to the blessed martyr Cyprian. It remains now to discuss the mystery of the Lord’s body and of our Passover—that is, of the immolation of the new Passover—and how and by whom it is to be celebrated.

Let us set forth the sense and words of the most holy Pope Gregory, so that what was hidden under the veil of the letter in the Law may become clear in the Gospel through the truth of the matter:

“Our Passover,” he says, “is Christ, sacrificed for the apostles.”

If Christ is therefore the Passover, we must consider what the Law says about the Passover, so that, searching more subtly, we may recognize whether its statements appear to have been spoken about Christ. For Moses says: “They shall take from the blood of the lamb,” and so forth.

## CHAPTER XLVIII — Whether this legitimate Passover is to be eaten by the faithful after a year has passed, after long intervals of days, or daily
The observance of this Pasch—namely, reception of the Lord’s body and blood—is customarily celebrated by some after a year has elapsed, by others after fixed intervals of days, and by still others daily, according to the diversity of circumstances. Yet this seems [Col. 0398C] more conducive to human salvation if those who approach the sacrament of so great a mystery do so with a pure and devout mind. For Christ is the bread of life, and this bread is not for everyone, but for the faithful who receive it piously. Just as God the Father is properly the Father of those who understand and believe, so Christ, our God and Lord, the Son of God, is the Father of those who receive his body with faith. At his command we daily ask the Father to give us this bread, so that we who are in him and daily receive the eucharist of his body as food for salvation may not, through the intervention of some more serious offense, be separated from his body while being kept away, not communicating, and fasting from the heavenly bread. He himself proclaims and says: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven; whoever eats [Col. 0398D] of my bread will live forever. The bread that I will give is my flesh for the life of the world.” When, therefore, he says that whoever eats of that bread will live forever, it is clear that those live who touch his body and receive the eucharist of true communion.

Thus, on the contrary, we must fear and pray lest, when someone is kept away and separated from Christ’s body, he remain empty of salvation, as he himself declares and says: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you do not have life in yourselves.” Therefore we daily ask that our bread—that is, Christ—be given to us, so that we who remain and live in him may not depart from sanctification through his body.

[Col. 0399A]

The saints have always burned with this desire: to live for God by the nourishment of this bread. For them temporal life was a loss, and to live was Christ. Among them was one venerable Cassius, named Narniensis, a bishop of the Church. As Blessed Gregory relates, when he was offering the daily sacrifice and making himself, amid the very mysteries of the sacrifices, a pleasing victim to God, he received through a vision granted to one of his priests a command from the Lord, who said:

“Do what you are doing; carry out what you are carrying out. Let neither your foot nor your hand cease. On the feast of the apostles you will come to me, and I will repay you your reward.”

After seven years, when he had completed the solemn Mass on that very feast of the apostles and had received the mysteries of holy communion, he departed from the body.

## CHAPTER XLIX  
### How much the offering of the sacred sacrifice benefits the spirits of the dead

[Col. 0399B]

[Note: [Col. 0399D] See St. Gregory, *Dialogues*, Book IV, at the end.]

But what is surprising if this true and singular protection of the human race provides present and everlasting help to the faithful who remain in the body and are dear to God, when even the spirits of the dead themselves ask this of the living and indicate by signs that they appear to be released through it?

The most holy Pope Gregory, so often mentioned, bears witness that in his time there was a priest of holy conduct who was accustomed, whenever necessity required, to come for the purpose of bathing to a place where the vapors of hot water were exceedingly strong, etc.

## CHAPTER L  
### Concerning a monk who escaped punishment through the life-giving Host

[Col. 0399C]

Since, in order to commend the power of the Lord’s body, we have thought it appropriate to insert several chapters from Blessed Gregory’s *Dialogues* into this little work, it is not out of place to connect a few remaining accounts that confirm what has preceded. For this greatly strengthens the hope of the faithful, who are always anxious through fear of the divine judgment, that which the most blessed Pope Gregory asserts happened in his own monastery in his presence.

There was a certain monk named Justus, a physician by profession, etc.

## CHAPTER LI  
### Concerning a man whose bonds were loosed in captivity after the offering of the sacrifice

[Note: [Col. 0399D] See St. Gregory, as above.]

It is reported that, not long before our own times, a certain man was captured by enemies and carried far away, etc.

## CHAPTER LII  
### Concerning a sailor who, after long perils at sea, escaped death through the power of the Lord’s sacrament

[Note: [Col. 0400D] See the same work.]

For Agatho, Bishop of Palermo, as many faithful and religious men have testified to me, etc.

These things have been related by way of example, so that everyone may clearly understand that, unless their sins have been unforgivable, the victim of the sacred offering can also benefit the dead by contributing to their release.

## CHAPTER LIII  
### For whom the offering of the Lord’s body benefits the dead

[Col. 0400A]

It must be understood that the victim benefits those dead who, while living here, obtained that good deeds performed here by others on their behalf would also help them after death. Among these matters, however, we must consider that the safer course is for each person to do for himself while he lives the good that he hopes others will do for him after his death. It is indeed more blessed to depart free than to seek freedom after imprisonment.

We must therefore despise the present age with our whole mind, especially since we already see that it is passing away. We must offer God daily sacrifices of tears and daily immolate the offerings of his flesh and blood. For this victim alone releases souls from eternal destruction: through its mystery it restores to us the death of the Only-Begotten.

[Col. 0400B]

Although, having risen from the dead, he no longer dies, and death will no longer rule over him, yet, living in himself immortally and incorruptibly, he is again sacrificed for us in this mystery of the sacred offering. For there his body is received; his flesh is distributed for the salvation of the people; his blood is poured out no longer into the hands of unbelievers, but into the mouths of the faithful.

Let us therefore consider what this sacrifice is for us, by which, for our release, we continually imitate the passion of the Only-Begotten Son. For what faithful person could doubt that at the very hour of the immolation, at the priest’s voice, the heavens are opened; that in this mystery of Jesus Christ the choirs of angels are present; that the highest things are joined to the lowest; that earthly things are united with heavenly; and that one reality is made from visible and invisible things?

[Col. 0400C]

Yet when we perform these things, it is necessary that we slaughter ourselves before God in contrition of heart, because we who celebrate the mysteries of the Lord’s passion must imitate what we perform. Our offering to God will then be true for us, when it makes us ourselves an offering.

We must strive, even after the times of prayer, to preserve our mind, insofar as God grants us the ability, in the same state, with its proper weight and strength, lest afterward a wandering thought dissolve it, lest empty joy steal into the mind, and lest the soul through negligence lose the profit of compunction through a drifting thought.

[Col. 0400D]

While the time granted permits it, while the Judge is patient, while he who examines our faults awaits our conversion, let us melt the hardness of our mind in tears and form in our neighbors the grace of kindness. And I say confidently: we shall have no need of a life-giving victim after death if, before death, we ourselves have been a victim to God.

## CHAPTER LIV  
### With what discipline and modesty one ought to pray while the priest celebrates the sacrifice and each person in his own order awaits the hour of holy communion

Since in the preceding chapters we have said much about the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood, it follows that we should set down, at the end of this little work, a few passages from many sources concerning the reverence, manner, and discipline with which we ought to take part in the divine mysteries when the priest sacrifices the sacred victim and await the hour of receiving the most holy eucharist, as [Col. 0401A] our elders handed these matters down to us and as we have been taught by the most holy priests of the Lord—namely, Cyprian and Ambrose—who left them written in their books.

One of them, Cyprian, says:

“When we come together with the brethren and celebrate the divine sacrifices with God’s priest, we ought to remember modesty and discipline. We must not scatter our prayers indiscriminately in disorderly voices, nor throw before the Lord, with tumultuous loquacity, a petition that ought to be commended modestly, because God is the hearer not of the voice but of the heart. He does not need to be admonished by shouting, since he sees the thoughts. Let speech and prayer among those who pray be disciplined, containing quietness and modesty. Let us consider that we stand in the sight of God. [Col. 0401B] We must please the divine eyes both by the posture of our body and by the manner of our voice. For just as it is characteristic of the shameless to make a din with shouting, so it is more fitting for the modest to pray with restrained petitions,” etc.

For the remainder, see St. Cyprian, *On the Lord’s Prayer*.

## CHAPTER LV  
### What must be avoided in prayer, and how prayers should be made

The most blessed Bishop Ambrose, a precious instrument of divine eloquence, explaining that passage of the holy Gospel in which the Lord commands us to pray in a chamber, indicates very clearly with what caution and discipline the divine help must be implored:

“Your chamber,” he says, “is the mind’s hidden place and the soul’s secret recess. Enter into this chamber of yours—that is, enter into the depths of your heart,” etc.

For the remainder, see St. Ambrose, Book I of *On Abel [Col. 0401C] and Cain*, chapter 9.

## CHAPTER LVI  
### Cyprian to the clergy concerning prayer to God

[Note: [Col. 0401D] See Letter 8 of St. Cyprian.]

“Cyprian sends greetings to the priests and deacons, his brothers.

“Although I know, dearest brothers, that because of the love which each of us owes to God, etc.”

## CHAPTER LVII  
### That the most holy altar of the Lord should also be adorned in its external worship

[Col. 0401D]

In the beginnings of the Church the mystery of the altar was not celebrated as frequently as it is now; yet the rarer it was, the more religiously it was performed. In the time of the earlier Fathers, those who shone with natural simplicity were appointed to the ministry of sacrifice, as Eusebius relates in his *History*, in accordance with the saying: “His conversation is with the simple.”

Those who were to participate in this mystery approached with bare feet, because of what was commanded to Moses and Joshua: “Remove the shoe from your feet, for the ground on which you stand is holy ground.”

The holy Pachomius also ordered the bakers that, when they baked the offerings, they should meditate on salutary things and speak nothing vain. Once this was violated in the monastery at Tabenna, Pachomius was immediately informed of it by divine revelation. He promptly sent Theodore and ordered this negligence to be corrected as a transgression of the divine command.

Now, however, the mystery is celebrated much more frequently, but—what must be deeply lamented—with far greater negligence. This negligence is plainly displayed by the very appearance of the church, by the altar vessels, and by the linens [Col. 0402A] and all the other things belonging to the service of the Lord. There is no need to list each item individually. It is sufficiently clear what priests cultivate with greater care: their own possessions, or the things of the altar.

But surely, when charity, which is the fullness of the law, has not yet grown wholly cold, how does such continual persistence in sacrificing endure, unless the malicious enemy does not oppose those who sacrifice in this matter because he knows that here they are burdened all the more? For he did not prevent Judas from receiving the eucharist. He knew that, just as the reception of that mystery restrains the fraud of the devout, so among those who receive it unworthily that fraud advances more freely.

[Col. 0402B]

Against those who neglect the external worship of glory, the Lord complains through Malachi, saying:

“O priests, who despise my name, and you say: ‘In what way?’ In this you despise my name: you offer polluted bread upon my altar and say: ‘The table of the Lord is polluted.’”

Priests pollute the bread—that is, the body of Christ—when they approach the altar unworthily. Although they do not say in words that the table is despised, when they themselves fail to adorn its external worship, they make it despicable even to the laity, because people of carnal mind suppose that the holiness of divine power is absent wherever they see the adornment of magnificence lacking.

## CHAPTER LVIII  
### That nothing should be placed upon the altar besides the most holy offering

There is a church of Blessed Walburgis in which miracles used to occur. Once it happened that the relics of that same holy Walburgis remained upon the altar for several days; immediately, however, the miracles [Col. 0402C] ceased.

At last the virgin herself appeared to one of the sick and said:

“For this reason you are not being healed: my relics are upon the altar of the Lord, where only the majesty of the divine mystery ought to be celebrated.”

When he reported this to the custodians, they removed the reliquary, and immediately miracles began to occur.

If, then, out of reverence for that mystery, the saints do not wish even their own relics to be placed nearer to it, what should be thought of impurities?

## CHAPTER LIX  
### That sacrifice should not be offered for murderers and robbers

On the road leading from the monastery of Alvernia to the marketplace [Col. 0402D] there is a church of St. Peter called *ad Salas*. Near it lived a certain robber who, wishing to plunder two travelers whom he had received as guests, attempted to kill them during the night. But they overpowered and killed him.

When he was being carried to the church for burial, the priest began to celebrate Mass for him. As he was about to come to the words of the Lord’s consecration, a terrifying sound resounded through the roof of the church, and the altar was split down to its foundations. The priest and everyone else, struck with immense fear, fled, and he ceased offering the sacrifice for an apostate.

This is directed against those who promise, for the sake of criminals, that they will pray for them.

## CHAPTER LX  
### Concerning those who give alms but do not abandon their sins

[Col. 0403A]

Whoever gives alms in such a way that he does not abandon his guilt does not redeem the soul whose vices he does not restrain.

This is proved by the deed of a certain hermit who, after having served God with many virtues together with one of his companions, received from the devil the following thought: whenever he was titillated by lust, he should emit semen by rubbing his genital organ, casting it out as though it were phlegm from the nostrils.

For this reason, at his death he was handed over to demons, as his companion [Col. 0403B] saw. Since that companion, unaware of his guilt but remembering his exercises of virtue, almost despaired and said, “Who can be saved, when this man has perished?” an angel immediately stood beside him and said:

“Do not be troubled. Although this man did many things, he defiled them all through that vice which the Apostle calls impurity.”

Of this the prophet says: “Your hands are full of blood.”

Something similar happened in our own time, and, lest its novelty cause it to be disregarded, it deserves consideration.

## CHAPTER LXI  
### A most astonishing account concerning a certain priest

A certain priest in the district of Abitincatinus had despaired of continence. He went to Rome nine times, hoping that Blessed Peter would grant him impunity for his crime, as though he deserved it because of his frequent visits to the place. Although he was unwilling to abandon his sin, he was nevertheless extremely afraid; [Col. 0403C] for this is the custom of the wicked: although they take pride in their guilt and boldly do evil things openly, they are nevertheless forced to tremble in their hearts, so that the very fear becomes a fitting witness to their condemnation.

Thus Adam fled after his sin to a hiding place; yet he fled in fear, and he was very afraid because he answered God harshly. This man, therefore, out of fear, offered what appeared to be a religious service.

But in order to show that God accepts satisfaction only for sins that are abandoned, when the man returned for the ninth time and, as though more secure, resumed intercourse, the wretch died by divine judgment in such a way that, as the unfortunate woman reported, when he discharged his semen he breathed out his soul at the same time.

## CHAPTER LXII  
### That the excommunication of any priest must be greatly feared; that one must consider not the merit of the priest but the authority by which he acts, even when—God forbid—the excommunication appears unjust

[Col. 0403D]

Some years ago, when the feast of St. Andrew fell on the first Sunday of the Lord’s Advent, a certain priest ordered his parishioners to hear both Masses. Among them was a physician who departed after hearing the first Mass. When the priest rebuked him, he answered him harshly. The priest then excommunicated him.

The angry physician returned to his house and, in contempt of the excommunication, immediately took a drink. At once he began to be tormented until he breathed out his soul.

## CHAPTER LXIII  
### A most praiseworthy example of the glorious Emperor Theodosius

The famous Emperor Theodosius was once [Col. 0404A] excommunicated by a certain monk—who, I believe, was not entirely sound in mind—because of a complaint of the monk’s that the emperor had not immediately resolved. The monk departed after writing the excommunication on a small tablet and throwing it down where the emperor could find it.

The emperor, however, considering in the matter not that wandering monk but rather the heavenly King, by whose authority excommunication is customarily imposed, did not dare to dine when the hour had arrived. Although many bishops were standing before him, including the bishop in whose diocese the monk in question lived, and although they gave him permission, he could not be persuaded to taste anything—until the monk had been sought for a long time, finally found, and granted the emperor permission.

## CHAPTER LXIV  
### Another example, greatly to be feared

[Col. 0404B]

We read in the *History of the English People* that a certain bishop excommunicated two brothers who were royal courtiers because they had repudiated their wives.

It happened that the king of that people was passing near their house. Enticed by many flattering invitations to stop and dine with them, he finally consented. When the meal was over and he was returning, he met the bishop who had excommunicated those brothers. When the king saw him, he trembled, leapt from his horse in the middle of the road as he was, and prostrated himself before the bishop.

The bishop approached him with the staff he held in his hand, touched him, and said:

“O king, it is not mine to forgive you, because you acted against God when you knowingly joined yourself to those who had been excommunicated. Therefore this sentence has been pronounced upon you: this year you must die [Col. 0404C] in the very house in which you despised the excommunication.”

And it happened as it is written there.

Behold, the king could expiate this offense only by dying. Behold, the bishop could not forgive even a king prostrate in the dust. From this, therefore, it must be concluded that even the bishop whose excommunication is despised cannot forgive such a crime without the gravest penance.

## CHAPTER LXV  
### How much reverence is owed to the episcopal chair: concerning Lord Peter, Patriarch of Alexandria

When the decisive moment of his passion was at hand, Christ appeared to him in a dream, shining with immense splendor. He was clothed in an exceedingly white *colobium*, but it was split [Col. 0404D] all the way to the feet. Nevertheless, he held the garment tightly against his chest with both hands, somehow covering his nakedness.

Peter, recognizing that this was Christ, said, struck with immense horror: “My Lord, my Lord, who has done this?” He replied: “Arius did this to me.”

For this reason Peter, during the whole time of his episcopate, never wished to sit in his chair, but sat upon the stool belonging to the chair. The clergy and people frequently complained to him about this, but he would not yield, because whenever he ascended the *thisiasterium* (altar), a fiery radiance appeared to him issuing from the seat itself. At the sight of it the holy man was so inflamed that at times he did not know whether he was still in the body.

Once, when the clergy and bishops who were present complained about his manner of sitting, [Col. 0405A] he could no longer conceal the matter and said:

“Why do you afflict my heart? Do you not see the fiery power that flashes from the throne itself, and do you not perceive the spirit glittering?”

When they all lowered their heads and fell silent on hearing so great a thing, he added:

“Believe me, my little sons: if you saw what I see, you would then recognize what priestly power is and what grace dwells in them. In the presence of that majesty I am so terrified that I do not dare to sit in that same chair.”

If this example is properly considered, it can greatly terrify those who despise such things; yet it also causes those who sit upon episcopal chairs to tremble considerably.

## CHAPTER LXVI  
### How serious a sin it is to profane sacred places or pollute them with any defilement

[Col. 0405B]

A certain foolish man named Ratherius had taken refuge in a monastery out of fear of his enemies. One night, while sleeping in a cell adjoining the church, he attempted to have intercourse with his wife. He became so attached to her like a dog that he could not in any way be separated from her.

When he realized that he was being held in this way, he cried out. The report spread and grew. Everyone hurried there. Confused both by the event and by shame, they had the monks summoned. They gave as many gifts as they could to the holy place. After the monks had prayed for a long time, the couple was released.

As the event itself makes clear, the embrace of the married couple, since it was lawful, was punished temporarily because of the unlawful presumption committed against the sacred place where it occurred. The guilt of incest, however, when perpetrated in sacred places, is generally not punished in the present life because [Col. 0405C] it is so great that it ought to be struck not by a transitory but by an eternal vengeance.

Conversely, how much reverence for a sacred place benefits a person may at least be perceived from the following example.

## CHAPTER LXVII  
### Concerning a certain robber in the cemetery of St. John the Apostle

A certain king of the Lombards, as is recorded in the history of that people, had himself buried in the cemetery of a church of St. John, although he remained a heretic. A thief broke open his tomb and carried away the ornaments with which the king had been buried.

St. John himself said to the thief in a vision [Col. 0405D]:

“Why did you dare to touch this man’s body? Although he did not believe rightly, [Col. 0406A] he nevertheless commended himself to me. Since you have presumed to do this, you shall never again enter my basilica.”

And so it happened. Whenever he wished to enter the shrine of Blessed John, his throat was immediately struck as though by a very powerful boxer, and he was suddenly thrown backward as if pushed.

If, then, out of reverence for a holy place, St. John was angered against the violator of the tomb of that heretic, how much do you think God and his saints are angered against anyone who in any way defiles sacred places?

## CHAPTER LXVIII  
### Here begins Augustine’s letter to Bishop Auxilius concerning an unjust excommunication

[Note: [Col. 0405D] See among the letters of St. Augustine.]

## CHAPTER LXIX  
### Other chapters pertaining to the same matter by Blessed Augustine

[Note: [Col. 0405D] See the same source.]

[Col. 0406B]

## CHAPTER LXX  
### Concerning the sacrament of baptism: Blessed Ambrose

[Note: [Col. 0406D] See St. Ambrose, Book I of *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 3.]

“Where the sacrament of baptism is not complete, neither its beginning nor any form of baptism is considered to be present,” etc.

### A brief definition of the eucharist

Christ therefore received our flesh, not a phantom flesh but a natural one; consequently our flesh is also natural, since that flesh was taken from it. Yet that natural flesh which would unite both and make them connatural is itself likewise connatural.

But, as a certain Wise Man says, this does not mean that there are several fleshes or bodies, just as there are not many sacrifices, although the one sacrifice is offered by [Col. 0406C] many persons in different places and at different times. For the divinity of the Word of God, which is one and fills all things and is wholly everywhere, makes it so that there are not several sacrifices but one, although it is offered by many; and the body of Christ is one with that which he took from the Virgin’s womb.

For it must truly and without hesitation be believed that at the very hour of the immolation, in response to the priest’s prayer, the heavens are opened; that what is Christ himself is carried by angelic ministry to the exalted altar; and that he who is both priest and victim, and the contact with him, become one.

“O what sort of hands,” as St. Basil says, “ought the hands of the priest to be, ministers of such great things, which have repeatedly been touched by the angelic [Col. 0406D] service that transports the common Lord on high!”

# In the Year of the Lord 988: Saint Dunstan, Archbishop of Canterbury

[Col. 0407]

# Life of Saint Dunstan by Osbern, a Canterbury Monk

*(In Mabillon, Acts of the Saints of the Order of St. Benedict, Fifth Century, p. 654.)*

## Preliminary Observations

[Col. 0407A]

1. Among the eminent pontiffs of the English Church in the tenth century, I do not know whether anyone deserves the first place more than St. Dunstan, whom, Baronius says, “the outstanding holiness of his life, unshaken priestly constancy, the splendor of his miracles, and all the gifts of the Holy Spirit” adorned; to these qualities one should also add the distinction of his birth.

From this point the writers of the island of Britain—his contemporaries, near-contemporaries, successors, and later authors—seem to vie with one another in celebrating his praises.

Among his contemporaries, “some,” according to Osbern, “although sufficiently elegant, were not sufficiently careful; judging that what was adequate for the nocturnal office of the feast was enough, they wrote only in the manner of addresses to the people. Others, while attempting to explain too carefully how each event had taken place, lost elegance and fell into that kind of speech which the foremost of Roman eloquence calls supported. But those who labored in both respects, so that their works would be festive as well as well ordered according to the events narrated—those writings were consumed in the fire which, not many years ago, the holy Church of Canterbury is known to have suffered, with great loss of its possessions.”

Gervasius records three fires in that church. The first occurred “when Blessed Martyr Elfegus was captured by the Danes and crowned with martyrdom”—namely, in the year 1020. The second occurred “when Lanfranc, Abbot of Caen, undertook the governance of the archbishopric of the Church of Canterbury”—that is, in the year 1070. “The third was in the time of Archbishop Richard and Prior Odo,” namely, in the year 974; the Canterbury monk Gervasius depicts this last fire vividly.

Osbern is to be understood as referring to the second fire, since it is established that he flourished under Lanfranc. After the foregoing, Osbern adds:

“But, they say, some of these works have survived translated into the native—that is, English—language. From them we ask to extract at least this much and translate it once again into Latin.”

2. Of all the writings composed about Dunstan immediately after his death, therefore, only the works of the first and second kinds survived when Osbern wrote: those written merely in the manner of addresses for the nocturnal office, or composed inelegantly though accurately. The works that were accurate and elegant at the same time had been consumed in that fire of the Canterbury church.

I found an author of the second kind in a manuscript codex of the monastery of St. Vaast at Arras. His writing is so full of roughness that it seems to me unworthy of the light of day—especially since the codex of St. Vaast is not complete but mutilated and breaks off at Dunstan’s death.

Let the following serve as a specimen of his discourse: the prologue addressed to Albricus, or Alfric, the second archbishop of Canterbury after Dunstan, runs as follows:

“To the most prudent lord Archbishop Albricus, B., the least of all priests and a humble native of the Saxons, [wishes] the high joys of heaven.

“You, most excellent shepherd, because of the enormity of your widely celebrated learning and through the magnificent, gracious dignity of your privilege, I distinguish from all others—however conspicuous they may be in learning—for my unsurpassable protection, as I attempt with the brilliant pen of suitable eloquence to extend the memorial of the merits of the kindly and blessed custodian, Dunstan. Yet, as you see, at the opening of his glorious life I have defiled the whole design of this little work by touching it with the degenerate style of my faults.

“Therefore, before all others, I openly confess this disgrace of mine to your serenity, and, like winged creatures who seem to beat their wings before they utter the word of profession, I unload and afflict myself with the blows of my own words, prostrate at your knees,” etc.

This is the style of the good orator. I conjecture that its author was Bridferth, a monk of Ramsey, both from the initial letter B of his name, which the St. Vaast codex bears, and from Bridferth’s age. Pitseus records that he was a disciple of Abbo and lived around the year 980.

Whoever this B. may be, the author of this scribal thicket, he is understood to have been Dunstan’s contemporary from the following words, which occur near the end of the life:

“Yet I think it fair to unravel at least those things which I myself either saw or heard, prompted by God’s rightful admonition, as far as I am able, for the sake of charity.”

Finally, he wrote under Archbishop Aelfric, who began to preside over the Church of Canterbury in the second year after Dunstan’s death. Hence his authority in explaining particular events is not to be despised; we shall repeatedly borrow from him and record his statements in notes.

I return to Archbishop Aelfric, whom Gervasius places third after Dunstan, namely after Athelgar and Siricius. William of Malmesbury, however, places Ethelgar immediately before him, saying that Ethelgar held the see for one year. It is therefore surprising that Godwin was so mistaken as to say that Alfric had been omitted by William from his catalogue of the archbishops of Canterbury.

William’s words are these:

“After Ethelgar had been removed from this life, Aelfric sat for eleven years. He had previously been bishop of Wilton and had also earlier been abbot of Abingdon. Concerning him, what some say—that he expelled the monks from Canterbury and installed clerics—does not seem probable. For it is established that monks had been in the church of the Holy Savior from the time of Archbishop Laurence, who was the first to succeed the most blessed Augustine, etc.”

“After him came Siricius, etc.”

3. After the primary writer of Blessed Dunstan’s life, I find no one before Osbern, a Canterbury monk. William speaks of him in the book *On the Kings of the English*, chapter 8, where he discusses Dunstan:

“Cantuaria’s cantor Osbern, who composed his life with Roman elegance, recalls me from wishing to say more—and not contemptible things—about the man. In style he is second to no one in our time; in music, certainly, without dispute, he is first of all.”

It is clear that Osbern’s work is not the one published by Surius, although Baronius and others praise it under Osbern’s name, but the work that we now publish for the first time from the Thuanus–Colbertinus manuscript, in which there are two little books by Osbern: one on the life and the other on the miracles of St. Dunstan. The style of these little books corresponds admirably to the praise that William bestows upon their author.

Osbern is understood to have flourished under Archbishop Lanfranc from the book of the miracles, where he is said to have also carried out the ministry of preaching at Lanfranc’s command. William calls this writer of the life “venerable” in Book II of *On the Bishops of the English*, chapter 2, where he quotes his exact words concerning Algarus, as this author has them in section 41 of the following book.

4. Surius produced another narrator of St. Dunstan’s deeds under the name Osbert, a monk of Canterbury. But I fear that, like Trithemius, he inserted the name Osbert in place of Osbern and attributed to him the life he published, because he had perhaps learned from William and others that Osbern was the author of St. Dunstan’s life.

Nevertheless, we shall call this author Osbert, not Osbern, as Macheuvius and most others mistakenly do, thinking that he is the same Osbern whom they had read about in William.

We understand that Osbert—or whoever the author of Surius’s life may be—wrote not in the year 1020, as it is read in Surius, but rather around the year 1120. This is evident from the book of miracles composed by the same author and abridged by Surius after omitting many passages; we have obtained the complete work from a manuscript of Compiègne.

That book mentions several events that took place in the time of St. Anselm, which we shall report in their proper place. For the present, we are content to set forth what is either not explained so fully in Osbern or is entirely absent there.

The fact that this book has the same author is confirmed by the brief prologue prefixed to it, which you will read in what follows.

5. Besides these authors who wrote about St. Dunstan as a work of special purpose, there are also others who treated him at considerable length. Among the principal ancient authors are William of Malmesbury, in his books both *On the Kings* and *On the Bishops of the English*; Gervasius of Canterbury, a monk, in his book *On the Deeds of the Archbishops of Canterbury*; Roger of Howden, in the first part of his *Annals*; Aelred, Abbot of Rievaulx; John Brompton; among the chroniclers, the Saxon writer after Bede; Matthew of Westminster; and Trithemius, in Books III and IV of *On Illustrious Men of the Order of St. Benedict*.

Among more recent writers are Baronius, Harpsfield, Thomas Macheuvius, and nearly all the English historians.

Ditmarus is mistaken, for in Book VII of his *Chronicle* he confused Dunstan with Elfegus, his fourth successor.

6. “Dunstan,” according to William in Book II, chapter 8, of *The Kings of the English, “first abbot of Glastonbury, afterward bishop of Worcester,” then simultaneously bishop of London, “soon afterward archbishop of Canterbury, a man of great power in the world and of great grace with God, there displayed Martha, here Mary.” His transfer contrary to the canonical provisions from one see to another, and his simultaneous occupation of the sees of Worcester and London, must be attributed not to the desire or ambition of an excellent man, but to his outstanding holiness, the kings’ most urgent will, and indeed the necessity of the English Church; and it was done always against Dunstan’s wishes.

“Dunstan himself,” William adds, “was, after King Alfred, the most remarkable promoter of the liberal arts throughout the whole island; himself a generous restorer of royal places; terrible in his thunder against kings and wrongdoers; justly supporting the poor and those of moderate means, and so much a pursuer of peace even in trivial matters that, when fellow countrymen met in taverns and, already drunk, contended over the proper measure of drinking, he ordered silver or golden nails to be fastened to the vessels, so that, when each man recognized his limit, shame itself would prevent him from drinking more or forcing another to drink more.”

This last detail is not found in the *Acts of Dunstan*, but it chiefly illustrates his zeal against wrongdoers. What he contributed to the restoration of royal places—that is, monasteries—and of the arts must now be investigated briefly.

7. When Dunstan first appeared in the light of England, monasticism had declined so completely since the time of the Danes that scarcely any monastic life remained in more than a very few monasteries.

“Not yet in England,” says Osbern, no. 6, “was the common life cultivated, nor was the practice of abandoning one’s own will cherished among men. Scarcely anyone had heard the name ‘abbot’; scarcely anyone had adequately known a community of monks. Rather, whoever happened to desire such a way of life, wishing to pass into a foreign mode of existence, would leave his native land, sometimes alone, sometimes accompanied by a few of like purpose.”

Osbern himself explains this in the *Life of Saint Odo, Archbishop*, saying that “the zeal for religion, through the many vicissitudes of diverse events, had everywhere begun to grow cold,” and that for this reason Odo had asked the monks of Fleury for the habit of holy religion.

Nevertheless, in certain places the name of the monastic order persisted—leaving aside the monastery of Crowland and others—in the cathedral church at Canterbury. This is expressly attested by Gervase, a monk of that place, who, after reporting Osbern’s words, makes an exception for the church of Canterbury. Yet religion had been so disfigured there that the monks lived more like counts than monks, as Osbert testifies in the *Miracles of Saint Dunstan*.

Almost all the remaining places were occupied by clerics of a more relaxed way of life. This calamity must be attributed not only to the Danes but also to Eadwig, a most depraved king, who, out of hatred for Dunstan, drove the monks from the monasteries.

For Malmesbury we have as our authority William, a monk of that place, in Book II, chapter 7, of *The Kings*: “He drove Dunstan himself, the leader of the monks, into Flanders. At that time the appearance of the monks was shameful and pitiable. For he made the monastery of Malmesbury, which had been inhabited by monks for more than two hundred and seventy years, into a stable for clerics.”

Dunstan could not endure this calamity. Once recalled from exile, he restored the fleeing religious life to the cloisters. On this subject Osbern writes:

“Religion increased throughout England to such an extent that forty-eight monasteries for monks or nuns were founded, with blessed Dunstan assisting in this the venerable men, namely Oswald, first bishop of Worcester and afterward bishop of York, and Aethelwold, bishop of Winchester.” Consult their deeds here.

For this reason, in the name of King Edgar, and doubtless through Dunstan’s initiative, indeed even at his dictation, the *Concordia* concerning the observance of a uniform rite in all the English monasteries was issued. The pious king wished to increase their number to fifty, and Dunstan was the principal instigator of this undertaking. This *Concordia* survives complete in Clement Reyner’s *Appendix*, p. 77, and incompletely in Selden.

8. First of all, Dunstan restored to the monks the monastery of Glastonbury, or Glaston, where the holy man had earlier led a solitary life. For previously Glastonbury, “devoted to royal stipends, was entirely ignorant of monastic religion,” according to Osbern, no. 6.

The place lies among the West Saxons, in the diocese of Wells, in Somerset, a district that had three monasteries for men: Glastonbury, Adling, and Miclan. William discusses these in Book II, chapter 5, of *The Bishops of the English*, and speaks of Glastonbury in the following way:

“Glastonbury is a village situated in a certain marshy retreat, yet accessible on level ground, and attractive neither in situation nor in pleasantness. There King Ine first built a monastery at the counsel of the most blessed Aldhelm, granting it many estates that are still known by name today. Through the varying vicissitudes of time, but by an unbroken succession, the place flourished with communities of monks until the coming of the Danes under King Alfred. Then, like other places, it was deserted, and for some years lacked its familiar inhabitants. Whatever the storm of war had crushed, Dunstan splendidly restored; he had previously lived there as a monk in solitude. Later, through the generosity of King Edmund, he acquired all the former dependencies and many more besides, and established an abbey such as there is not, nor has ever been, in England,” and so forth.

I omit what is said about Glastonbury in the *English Monastic*; but B., the author of Dunstan’s *Life*, adds here several details that must by no means be omitted:

“There was a certain royal island on the boundary of the aforesaid man [Heorstan, Dunstan’s father], called Glastonbury by the ancient usage of the neighboring people. It extended over broad tracts of land, abounded in fish-filled waters, was surrounded by rivers, and was suitable for many human needs and—what is most important—was devoted to sacred purposes. On it, the first neophytes of the Catholic law in that place, by God’s direction, discovered an ancient church, constructed by no human art, but rather prepared from heaven for human salvation. Afterward the very maker of the heavens demonstrated, through many miraculous deeds and many manifestations of mysteries, that this church was—that is, is—consecrated to him and to his holy mother Mary. They also added another oratory, which they dedicated to Christ and to his holy apostle . . . .

“It happened, therefore, for reasons of this kind, that the aforesaid man Heorstan, accompanied by the blessed boy Dunstan, passed through Glastonbury. When they spent the night there for the sake of prayer, behold, a period of the sweetest sleep happily covered the boy. In an ecstasy of mind he saw a certain old man clothed in snow-white brightness, leading him through the pleasant courts of the sacred temple and showing him the monastic buildings that were afterward to be constructed under his pastoral care, indicating that they would be established in the order in which they are now seen.”

Compare the following *Life*.

9. Besides these, Dunstan established five other monasteries from the property that had come to him by inheritance, according to Osbern, no. 16. Dunstan was also the one responsible for establishing monks in the New Monastery at Winchester, as was stated above in the acts of Saint Aethelwold; consult them.

To Dunstan also belongs what we read in B. concerning the dedication of a certain church at Winchester:

“Meanwhile the devout citizens of Winchester invited that same bishop of God to the dedication of a certain new church, which they had built in their city of Winchester, where he himself held episcopal authority, out of reverence for the supreme Divinity, on the southern side of the public street. This church is now said to be nearer to all the churches on the western side. Among many others, Dunstan was present at its consecration with the bishop, as one of the principal men. After it had been dedicated, they compelled the venerable man, together with his companions, in accordance with human courtesy, to spend a joyful day at the prepared feast of charity, in honor of so great a man and in celebration of the consecration.

“But after giving thanks, the bishop rose with his companions as night was approaching, and, having given his blessing, returned to his own place. As they proceeded along the road, they came to a church dedicated to the blessed Pope Gregory. There the bishop stopped and said to B. Dunstan: ‘Here, in the oratory of our holy father Gregory, let us complete our hour of Compline.’ After the prayers had been recited, they approached and joined their heads together so that, according to their customary practice, they might disclose their confessions to one another.”

This passage concerning confession at Compline should be noted:

“When this had been completed, while the bishop was granting remission of sins, a very large stone fell from the high air and, by the Lord’s mercy, landed on the ground with a violent descent between the heads of the two men. It touched only the hair of both their heads and injured neither of them. Unless I am mistaken, that evil one, the enemy of every good work, hurled it in a frenzy from the missiles of his wickedness, as though he intended to avenge a double anger upon both men.”

I thought these matters should be reported here because they are absent from Osbern and Osbert.

10. Something similar also happened to Dunstan himself at the funeral of one of his own brothers, to whom the abbot had entrusted the administration of Glastonbury’s household affairs.

“For this same true man of God,” B. relates, “had, through the human generation of his parents, a certain brother of his own, named Wulwinus. He appointed him as a powerful steward externally in the affairs of his estates, so that neither he himself nor anyone belonging to the monastic profession would wander outside in foolish involvement with secular business.

“This man, after completing the span of his time, was overtaken by a fatal condition and underwent temporal death. For this reason it happened that all the monks of the aforesaid church went out to his funeral, and no one remained at home except the abbot himself and a young scholar who afterward became a bishop and disclosed these events to us, so that they might carry the lifeless body with the sacred rites of burial to the monastery where it was to be interred.

“Meanwhile the abbot and the same scholar were walking to see, as I suppose, whether the brothers had already drawn near with the little body of the deceased. While they proceeded, as usual, always singing psalms, a certain stone missile suddenly came from beyond the old church, flying violently and attempting to strike the head of the blessed Father; but, because God defended him, it could not do so. Nevertheless, it threw the cap that covered his head far away, about one rod’s distance from his head.

“Turning, he said to the scholar walking with him: ‘Hurry, then, and seize this rolling stone as quickly as possible, so that you may bring it back for me to examine.’ When the boy, by the Father’s command, struggled to carry it back because it was exceedingly heavy, the venerable Father Dunstan said:

“‘O hostile enemy, for a long time you have been lying in wait and maliciously preparing the blow of this stone against me. For there was no testimony from many people that stones of this kind, whether very large or small, were found in these regions of Somerset, except perhaps in certain stone constructions. Therefore it was plainly evident from whose wicked hand it had been launched.’

“Nevertheless, after this he ordered that the stone, although it had been hurled for his injury, should be brought into custody and preserved as a testimony.”

I thought it worthwhile to report this, both so that Dunstan’s concern for the monks might be apparent—for he took care to keep them free from secular affairs—and so that his brother Wulfwinus might become known, since he is mentioned nowhere else.

We therefore have Dunstan’s royal lineage: his father Heorstan, his mother Kynedrida, his brother Wulfwinus, his paternal uncle Athelmus, archbishop of Canterbury, and his kinsman Cynewius, bishop.

11. To all these monasteries must be added the western monastery of Saint Peter at London. For when Dunstan was archbishop there, “he had made Wlfinus abbot at Westminster,” according to William of Malmesbury in Book II, where he discusses the bishops of Sherborne, “having furnished a small monastery for twelve monks, where Mellitus had once built a church” of Saint Peter.

12. Moreover, Dunstan restored in England not only monastic life but also literary learning. This is attested not only by William but also by Aelfric in Spelman’s first volume of the *Councils*, p. 618, where we read that from the time of King Alfred the study of letters had declined so far “that no English priest knew how either to compose a letter in Latin or to translate one from Latin, until Dunstan, archbishop of Canterbury, and Bishop Aethelwold revived this knowledge in the monasteries.”

Dunstan is also said to have written several works himself, according to Pits: formulas of archiepiscopal blessings; a short treatise on the Rule of Saint Benedict; and one book *On the Rule of Monastic Life*. In addition, *Against Bad Priests*, *On the Eucharist*, *On Tithes*, *On Hidden Philosophy*, *On the Ordination of the Clergy*, and various letters, some of them against Eadwig.

I would not insist that all these works be accepted as genuine, but it must nevertheless be admitted that some are authentic. First, the *Decree for Concord*, or for a uniform manner of life among monks, was composed by Dunstan under the name of King Edgar; it was discussed above, no. 7, and may perhaps be the book *On the Rule of Monastic Life* praised by Pits.

Next, it is certain that no. 34 of the following *Life* records that he devoted himself not only to reading but also to correcting manuscripts, and that in this work he applied himself to the Rule of Saint Benedict.

Of his letters we have found one written to Wlffinus, bishop of Worcester. We give it below from a manuscript *Pontifical* written six hundred years ago, which is now preserved by the most learned Antonius Faurus, doctor and fellow of the Sorbonne. The same *Pontifical* has prefixed to it a letter of Pope John XIII addressed to Dunstan concerning the pallium; its title in the manuscript must be noted. It reads as follows:

“Here begins the letter of privilege which, at the command of Pope John, after receiving a blessing from him, Dunstan the archbishop received from the pope’s hands; but he did not receive the pallium from the pope’s hands, but, at his command, from the altar of the holy apostle Peter.””

Baronius published part of this letter from William of Malmesbury’s book—as he notes in the margin—*On the Bishops*. I do not, however, find it in William. Whatever the case may be, we reproduce it here in full from a parchment manuscript, especially since it is not found complete even in the new edition of the *Councils*. (Seek this privilege among the letters of John XIII, volume 105 of the *Patrologia*.)

13. Finally, in the ecclesiastical laws of King Cnut, issued in the year 1032, the feast of Saint Dunstan is prescribed for the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June, chapter 24. His memory is likewise found in martyrologies published thereafter.

Here the reader should be warned by Harpsfield that, if he should happen upon those fictitious writings—as Harpsfield himself calls them—which state that the relics of Saint Dunstan were transferred from Canterbury to Glastonbury in the year of the Lord 1012, he should not be easily deceived.

For Eadmer, in the *Life of Saint Anselm*, utterly rejects that fiction. He writes that, when he was a boy, the body of Saint Dunstan was found with its tiara, ring, pallium, and other pontifical ornaments, together with a leaden tablet declaring that it was his body; and that it was carried into the new basilica built by Lanfranc.

Finally, in 1508, Archbishop William Warham arranged for the tomb to be opened, and the head, together with all the bones and the aforesaid tablet, was found there.

Anselm composed a pious prayer concerning Saint Dunstan, with a commemoration of his miracles; it appears in the new edition, p. 297.

Now it is time for us to hear Osbern.

# OSBERN’S LETTER OR PREFACE

[Col. 0413]

## The Occasion for Writing after Others

[Col. 0413B]

1. To all the sons of the Catholic mother Church, their fellow brother, through the rebirth that is in Christ, Osbern sends good peace and perpetual salvation.

[Col. 0413C] The venerable authority of many revered Fathers has often pressed me to commit the life of the magnificent Father Dunstan to the monuments of literature and to commend it to the ears of the Church for the praise of God and the benefit of humanity.

When, by way of excuse, I offered them the true fact that many works on this subject had already been written by men of no ordinary learning, everywhere, and that I feared the criticism of those who might perhaps call us mimics or at least rash men, since they would contend not so much that we had nothing sufficient as that nothing could ever be sufficient for us, they replied that they themselves had more reason to say that they had nothing sufficient than that nothing could be sufficient, and declared that they wished to establish this with plausible supports of argument.

“For,” they say, “some of those whose special duty it was to exercise diligence in this matter wrote, although with sufficient elegance, not with sufficient diligence, but only what they judged adequate for the nocturnal office of the feast, in the manner of sermons for the people. Others, however, while attempting too diligently to explain how each event had occurred, lost their elegance and fell into that style of speech which the leading figure of Roman eloquence calls ‘supported,’ a style accustomed to produce weariness more readily in readers than any benefit in hearers.

“Those who labored in both aspects of composition, so that their works might be equally entertaining and well ordered according to the events narrated, had their writings consumed in that fire which, as is known, the holy Church of Canterbury suffered some years ago, with great loss to its possessions.

“But some of these works,” they say, “translated into the native—that is, English—language still survive. From them we ask that you extract at least this much, and, with God’s help, translate it once again into Latin.”

## The Author’s Modesty; The Division of the Work

2. Thus, whether led by these arguments or by those who advanced them, I was drawn to write. I preferred to obey another’s will by speaking well rather than, in serving my own will, to refrain from speaking well.

Yet I approach this undertaking with no little blush of embarrassment, because I imagine everyone’s eyes fixed upon me, as though I were a man, in the manner of Laelius, promising new victories in eloquence and presuming that I would speak more effectively about matters that others have already expressed adequately.

But I neither criticize them for having spoken less effectively nor promise that I will speak more effectively. Rather, whether what I undertake proves worthy or, in view of the magnitude of the subject, the opposite of worthy, I attribute it to the merit or fault of those whose command and insistence have overcome me and compelled me to write this.

Even so, my own devotion toward that same father and lord of ours ought to be so great that, if no one wished to request these things from me, I would nevertheless not hesitate, for my part, to undertake them. His merits have had such power: in others, when I saw them, and in myself, when I experienced them.

Yet it was not my intention to speak in this little book either of what happened to others while I witnessed it or of what I experienced in myself. It was my intention to speak of these matters in another work, which will be written about the signs performed at his tomb.

For now, I shall strive to complete as truthfully as possible the beginnings of his birth, the course of his life with the increase of heavenly grace, and the exchange of mortal existence for the immortality of the eternal age. I shall omit all those things that were so marvelous that they seem incredible to unbelievers.

I know that I am unequal to recounting these matters, but in the name of him in whom Dunstan faithfully believed and to whom he offered the faithful service of his works, I shall attempt to undertake them.

# HERE BEGINS THE LIFE OF SAINT DUNSTAN, ARCHBISHOP AND CONFESSOR OF CANTERBURY

## (Fourteenth day before the Kalends of June)

[Col. 0415]

## Dunstan’s Noble and Devout Parents

[Col. 0415B]

3. When the magnificent king of the English, Athelstan, was reigning, in the first year of his rule—and in the four hundred and ninety-seventh year after the arrival of the English in Britain—while that same king, having subdued his enemies on every side, was governing the kingdom in peace and harmony, God’s boy Dunstan was born in the West Saxon regions of England.

[Note: Athelstan’s first year is combined with the year of Christ 925 in the Saxon chronology, and Dunstan is said to have been born there in that same year. But this year is only the eight hundred and seventy-seventh after the arrival of the English on the island of Britain; Bede places that arrival in the year 449, in Book I, chapter 15. Osbern made the same error at the end of this *Life*, where he discusses Dunstan’s death.]

His parents were indeed great in worldly dignity, but far greater in the religion befitting Christians.

[Note: Bound by the right of kinship to the royal family; see below, no. 6.]

For they cultivated their minds by living according to such a rule of virtue and labored so earnestly in pious works that, having entered upon the common path of mortals, they deserved to be associated with the angelic spirits, as was later made known to their same son through divine revelation.

It is not unreasonable to conjecture that this happened according to the plan of the Godhead, namely, so that such a great child would have such parents—parents who, while living well themselves, could also hand on to the son born from them a model of living well.

God foresaw that he would be great, having gone before him there with the blessings of his sweetness where all the sons of Adam receive the sentence of their native curse, unless they are restored to their original blessedness through the human form assumed by the Son of God.

God, I say, foresaw that he would be great, to whom so great a gift was granted that, before his mother had brought him forth into the light of this world, he was already made known to the world by signs.

And so that the remaining matters may proceed clearly and orderly, I shall establish the beginning of my account here.

## Light Restored by Heaven in the Candles

[Col. 0415D]

4. As the maternal womb swelled with its sacred burden, the festive day of the Purification of the holy and perpetual Virgin Mary dawned.

People from all around were gathering at the church dedicated to that Virgin at Glastonbury, in order to offer the service of their devotion to Christ, the King of kings, on so solemn a feast. It happened that the boy’s father, Heorstan, arrived with his wife Kynedrida, and, after the sacred lamps had been lit, took part in the solemn Mass.

The clergy had already completed a large part of the daytime service, and the passage had begun to be recited describing how the parents brought the boy Jesus into the Temple, when suddenly the majesty of the Lord appeared in the church.
