It extinguished all the lights of everyone and covered the entire building in dark gloom.

A cold terror then pierced all their limbs; their hair stood stiff, and their knees knocked together. They stood bewildered, expressing their amazement by exchanging glances.

But so that it might become clear to everyone what the majesty that had appeared intended by this event, a light sent from heaven immediately shone in the church and lit the candle that the pregnant woman held in her hand.

If the people had previously been astonished at the loss of the light, they were now seized by still greater wonder and rejoicing. They rejoiced that they had seen the grace of God present, but wondered that it had come to them through a woman.

Everyone therefore went to her, and from her the light was supplied to all.

Thus we have a new John from a new Elizabeth; we have a Jeremiah of our own time. God declared one of these sanctified in his mother’s womb, and the other by an archangel.

And, to make you recognize the more excellent grace: on the day when the Son of God was presented by his Virgin Mother in the Temple, the boy of God was likewise carried in his mother’s womb to the Temple.

“Light for revelation to the nations and glory of Israel,” holy Simeon proclaimed with rejoicing; and Christ, who is the true light, likewise declared by a light that a light had arisen in the land of the English.

## Dunstan’s Birth and Baptism

5. When the time for the birth arrived, the woman gave birth to a son who was small in bodily size but immense in the grace of God that had gone before him.

[Note: Dunstan was born near Glastonbury, as is clear both from Osbern and from B., in the eighth preliminary observation.]

Immediately afterward, having obtained the honor of a second birth, he received in his name Dunstan—meaning the firmness of a rock—the future solidity of his faith, divinely prefigured already at that time, and was so called by the record of his parents.

Then, when the succeeding age had closed the tender years of infancy and his tongue had begun to form articulated sounds, he was carried with offerings of sacrifices to the temple once distinguished by the miracle of his birth. Indeed, he himself was offered as a living victim, holy and pleasing to God.

While they spent the night there in prayer, a man with heavenly features appeared and declared that the place would shortly afterward be exalted, that the boy was to be left there for God, and that he would be proclaimed blessed throughout the ages.

Then, extending the surveyor’s measuring cord across the level courtyard, he said: “This place will be built in this way to prepare the hearts of those who, through this boy, will believe in God in this place.”

Overjoyed by this revelation, they offered immense praises to almighty God, entrusting the boy to the temple so that he might be a Levite for the Lord and the Lord might become his portion, just as was said to Moses when he divided the dwelling places of the Jews among their individual tribes:

“There shall be no lot for the tribe of Levi among their brothers, says the Lord, because the Lord God is their portion.”

Thus Peter, showing that he had a portion in God and not in the world, said: “I have neither silver nor gold, but what I have I give you: in the name of Jesus the Nazarene, rise and walk.”

That is: gold is not my portion; silver is not my portion; Christ is my portion. This is a generous name; this name is fruitful for me.

Having therefore attained the fruit of such a portion as a young soldier of Christ in holy fear, he served the Lord through constant ministry, advancing daily both in knowledge of piety and in the virtue of holiness.

6. At that time Glastonbury, devoted to royal stipends, was entirely ignorant of monastic religion.

For the common life was not yet cultivated in England, nor was the practice of abandoning one’s own will cherished among men. Scarcely anyone had heard the name “abbot”; scarcely anyone had adequately seen a community of monks. Rather, whoever happened to desire such a way of life, wishing to pass into a foreign mode of existence, would leave his native land, sometimes alone, sometimes accompanied by a few of like purpose, and would live as a foreigner wherever the opportunity for such a life granted him freedom.

[Note: Gervase, the monk of Canterbury, uses the same words, except that after these words he inserts: “except in the Church of Canterbury.” One might say that there had previously been no monks anywhere in England. But these authors speak in this way with reference to the period when nearly all the monasteries had passed into the possession of clerics. Certain Gallican writers of that time spoke in the same way.]

This custom still especially persists among the Irish, although it affects many others as well. For what goodwill turns into custom among others, custom turns into nature among them. Many distinguished men among them, nobly educated in divine and secular letters, had left Ireland to travel as foreigners into the land of the English and had chosen Glastonbury as the place of their dwelling because it was both removed from the civic multitude and suitable for human needs, and because of what they especially desired: its renown for the religious veneration of the pilgrim Patrick.

[Note: Especially on account of the honor of the blessed junior Patrick, who is said to have happily rested there in the Lord. Therefore this was not the great Patrick, disciple of Saint Germanus, bishop of Auxerre, as William of Malmesbury supposed in Book II, chapter 5, *On the Bishops*. This junior Patrick seems to have been the elder Patrick’s son. Jocelin is said to have written his *Life*; he also praises Benignus—whose bones William says were preserved at Glastonbury—and two other writers of the same *Life*.]

This Patrick, having once reached that place while evangelizing the kingdom of God, is reported to have shone forth in many ways through his life, teaching, signs, and miracles, and afterward to have rested there in the Lord.

When such men had come to Glastonbury for these reasons, yet could not find there in sufficient abundance everything they needed, they undertook the education of the sons of noblemen in the liberal studies, so that whatever the fertility of the place supplied less abundantly for its own use might overflow through the generosity of those whom they taught.

## Overcome by Illness, He Performs Wonders under an Angel’s Guidance

7. Among the others, then, the most noble boy in Christ, Dunstan, was present—or rather, among them he alone was preeminent. While devoting himself to the study of letters with an intensity greater than his tender age could bear, he was afflicted in his delicate body by a severe illness, so that for several days he paid attention neither to what he himself was doing nor to what others were doing.

The company of his fellow students wept; the entire household wept, as did the servants and the teachers, recalling the boy’s modesty, talent, nobility, and upbringing.

When death was already thought to be standing at the threshold and nothing else was being considered except the rites of his funeral, behold, in the dead of night heavenly medicine revisited him. Christ administered it to him through the ministry of an angel.

As soon as the divine medicine had arrived, so that no delay might be attached to his recovery, he immediately rose from his bed of pain and ran at a measured pace to the church to give thanks to God. On the journey he had as guide the one whom he had had as savior in his illness.

Those who were in the house and responsible for the sick boy’s care were astonished at the greatness of the event. They slowly followed the footsteps of the apparently dying boy, investigating the outcome with eager curiosity.

Before he had completed half the journey, an evil spirit—whether envious of his salvation or suspicious of his future religious vocation—met him accompanied by a multitude of barking dogs and attempted to block the road before him.

Terrified, the boy cried out to Christ; but, protected by the aid of his guide, he seized a rod and brandished it against the face of the opposing apparition, compelling it and its entire company to flee.

O holy and terrible name of Christ, hidden from the wise and revealed to little ones! Behold, the dragon whom God created at the beginning of his creation to mock him is mocked not only by God’s angels but also overcome by a tiny boy.

Truly his pride was dragged down to the underworld; his corpse fell into the depths of the pit.

But in whom could our little boy accomplish these things, except in him who, although he is God blessed above all forever, was born to us as a little child from the Virgin, the Son given to us by the Father?

When Dunstan reached the gate of the church and found it secured with bars, he unknowingly—and as though in an ecstatic state—climbed a ladder that those repairing the upper parts of the church usually leaned against.

From there he proceeded to the other side of the roof, where there was no way down; angelic hands lowered him to the ground, and he was led into the interior of the church through locked barriers.

When daylight arose, and inquiries about the boy had been made among the neighboring houses, he was found in the church, wrapped in gentle sleep among those who were keeping the night watch.

When asked to explain how so extraordinary an event had occurred, he replied that it was not within his own awareness, and he led the minds of those who did not understand into even greater uncertainty.

But those whom we said had followed the boy in order to investigate gave clear and trustworthy testimony about everything that had happened up to the highest summit of the church. The remaining details, since they were hidden from them and from the boy, were shown to have been marvelously accomplished by the power of God alone.

All who heard this were therefore shaken by great fear and wondered what had happened to the boy, saying to one another:

“What does this boy signify, to whom so many and such holy proclamations bear witness? He was blessed before he was born; virtue revealed him as glorious before age could show him grown.

“We see that he has been endowed with singular grace: an angel healed him when he was sick, the devil trembled when he was healed, and the Church, marked with the sign, received him.”

Then they prayed again, saying: “May God increase the boy’s merit for his own glory.”

But he, filled with the spirit of Christ who governed him, turned the ears of his body away from their praises, while in the secrecy of his little heart he blessed God.

From that day he was held in such great admiration that a great multitude of both sexes, although he was still delicate, desired to see him.

But the more distinguished the things he heard about himself, the less he thought of himself.

## He Receives the Minor Orders and Devotes Himself to Reading and the Sciences
### 8. He Receives the Minor Orders. He Devotes Himself to Reading and the Sciences.

His youth was already blossoming into the dignity of adolescence when his parents asked him to receive the sacred orders, so that he who had been chosen for the Lord from earliest childhood might, through such grace, remain joined and clinging to Him. Humbly complying with their wishes, he both assumed the minor orders and maintained them through the propriety of his life. At that age—which is no small adornment—he strove to surpass everyone in service, to outstrip everyone in graciousness and affability; to preserve chastity and flee wantonness; to seek what was honorable and abhor what was shameful [Col. 0419D]; to attend the conversations of his elders and avoid the games of the young; to abstain from food, to moderate his sleep, and to be grave in his bearing; neither to move readily from place to place nor to speak abruptly; to possess great confidence in beginning a good work and perseverance in completing it; always to have God as the beginning of his good conduct and to commend its conclusion to Him.

[Note: [Col. 0419D] B.: “Seeing, therefore, the aforesaid parents the great excellence of their son, they imposed on him the tonsure appropriate to the clerical office and associated him with the renowned monastery of Glastonbury Church, so that [Col. 0420D] there he might serve God and Mary, the Mother of God, day and night,” etc.]

To his good character he added devotion to sacred reading. Through this practice he both avoided the importunities of vices and nourished the growth of virtues. And since study has little effectiveness where natural ability does not supply understanding, God had endowed him with both to such a degree that, through the facility of his intellect, he understood any matter with the greatest keenness, and through the application of study he retained most firmly whatever he had understood. Consequently, it soon came about that he was no less learned than his teachers and himself far more learned than the most accomplished of his fellow students.

He diligently cultivated the sciences of the philosophers, which antiquity defines as the knowledge of the truth concerning things that are and cannot be otherwise: such as magnitudes, some of which remain fixed and without motion, while others turn perpetually according to the principle of motion and never rest at any time; and also multitudes, some of which exist in themselves and others in relation to something else. He cultivated these sciences, I say, with diligent reasoning, perceiving in them a great and abiding perfection [Col. 0420B]. Although he excelled magnificently in all these arts, he claimed with a particular affection the knowledge belonging to that branch of number which instructs music—namely, the music produced by instruments. Thus David took up the psaltery, struck the lyre, modulated his instruments, and touched the cymbals; but not as did those whose sluggishness and luxurious idleness our prophetic shepherd rebukes:

> “You who sleep on beds of ivory  
> and live wantonly upon your couches,  
> who eat lambs from the flock  
> and calves from the midst of the herd,  
> who sing to the sound of the psaltery like David,  
> who think they possess vessels of song  
> while drinking wine from bowls.”

We do not mention these things because we think they are necessary for one striving toward perfection, but so that the manifold graces of God in the young man may be commended [Col. 0420C]. For he preferred to all secular studies the knowledge of piety contained in the evangelical and apostolic writings. Always submitting his own understanding to the authority of the holy Fathers, and referring both matters to those same writings, he rejoiced that he had found true faith, discipline of morals, and—that one and only thing which must be sought above all else—eternal life. Thus, like our David the musician, he possessed vessels of song, because he expended their use only in divine praise.

Moreover, he was skilled with his hands in every kind of work: he could make paintings, form letters, engrave with a chisel, and fashion whatever he wished from gold, silver, bronze, and iron.

Athelm entrusts him to King Æthelstan.

### 9.

Then, having heard the reputation of the venerable Athelm, archbishop of Canterbury [Col. 0420D], who was his maternal uncle—the brother of his mother—he set out to him with the permission of his parents, so that he might both acquire knowledge from such a relative and shape his youthful character according to the example of his life.

[Note: [Col. 0420D] He has been discussed in the eulogy of Plegmund, archbishop of Canterbury.]

The bishop therefore rejoiced greatly at his nephew’s arrival, observing in him physical beauty, vigor of spirit, and outstanding excellence in every honorable quality. Recognizing, through the spirit of God with which he was inspired, that the young man would become a vessel of election, he endeavored to honor him with a higher rank and to commend him to King Æthelstan in a familiar exhortation [Col. 0421A]:

“I commend to Your Excellence this young man, who is exceedingly dear to me and is also bound to the royal line by no small right of kinship, so that he may stand continually in your presence and hear a word from the mouth of my lord the king. In him I shall test your grace, which I have often experienced in the greatest affairs and which I trust I shall experience still more hereafter.”

The king received this with ready gladness of heart, welcomed the young man with the greatest favor, loved him uniquely, and afterward appointed him to preside, in the king’s place, over necessary affairs.

Dunstan, therefore, living in the earthly palace, went out and came in at the king’s command, and whatever work he began prospered in his hands. At one time he rose to pray to God; at another he sat to judge human cases [Col. 0421B]. He conducted himself so wisely and cautiously that he pleased God in all things and, through his own fault, offended none of those who lived piously. For the Lord was with him and directed all his works.

Again, when he saw his lord the king wearied by secular cares, he would play upon the tambourine, the lyre, or any other instrument of the musical kind. By this he gladdened both the king’s heart and those of all the nobles.

### The Lyre Gives Sound from Heaven

### 10.

A certain noblewoman [Col. 0421D] repeatedly and devoutly urged him to paint a priestly stole for her with artistic workmanship, so that she might afterward decorate it with goldsmiths’ work in imitation of the divine worship.

[Note: [Col. 0421D] B. calls her Ethelwina, and relates this event immediately before Æthelstan’s death.] Taking up the lyre in his hands, he hung it on the wall and diligently began the work for which he had come. While he prepared his hand for the work, but his heart and lips for God, the glory of the Lord appeared in the house. It refreshed him with delightful sweetness, but filled the others with extraordinary amazement and fear.

For the lyre which, as we have said, had been fastened to the wall, hanging from its peg as it was, without any impulse from a human hand, resounded with the familiar melody of this antiphon, in a modulation at once exceedingly high and perfectly ordered:

[Note: [Col. 0421D] B.: “which in the paternal tongue we call a *hearpam*.”]

> “The souls of the saints rejoice in heaven,  
> who have followed the footsteps of Christ;  
> and because they poured out their blood for his love,  
> therefore they will rejoice with Christ forever.”

The young girls, the lady of the house, and all the household servants then leapt up, shouting that the man was exceedingly wise and knew more than was expedient [Col. 0421D].

But he, contemplating that heavenly music with the purest gaze of a most pure heart, understood that he was being admonished to undertake the harder paths, to follow more closely in Christ’s footsteps, and not to fear the shedding of his blood if he desired to possess God’s kingdom and eternal life.

Long ago we heard that a braying she-ass uttered words, but we have never heard that a lyre sang intelligently without human touch [Col. 0422A]. The one restrained the man riding it lest he die; the other admonished him not to fear death. The one, fearing angelic faces, crouched down; the other invited all who heard it to behold God and his angels. But these are your great works, O Christ, which you wished to perform in your Dunstan and to have proclaimed to human beings through our ministry.

### Dunstan Flees the Envy of the Courtiers

### 11.

The devil, therefore, inflamed with fury when he saw the young man advancing upon such holy foundations, attempted to lead him into the envy of certain people. He did not know that his evil will was serving God in bringing about God’s good will in the man whom God had predestined to rejoice and reign with him.

He therefore inflamed workers of iniquity with the goads of envy [Col. 0422B], so that by fabricating a lie they might damage the young man’s reputation with the king. They claimed that he had been instructed in evil arts and that he performed most of his works not through divine aid but through the illusions of demons.

When Dunstan noticed that the king’s face was not toward him as it had been yesterday and the day before, he prepared to leave the palace, preferring to abandon the king voluntarily [Col. 0421D] rather than be forced to leave him against his will.

[Note: B. says that Dunstan’s rivals, by a certain false accusation, obtained from the king that he should be expelled from their company; and that, once expelled, he was thrown by them into muddy places of the wrestling-ground [Col. 0422D]. The third author says that the occasion for accusing him arose from the miracle of the lyre.] When those who were the most wicked rivals of his goodness learned of this, they blocked the road with ambushes, scattered his companions, threw him from his horse, inflicted punishments upon him, and finally, after entangling him in bonds, drove him into a nearby cistern.

Meanwhile, he was found by certain men while being defended by a terrifying pack of mastiffs. Through their care and piety he was carried to a village to be nursed.

Then, groaning with a sigh from the depths of his heart, he said:

“O savage madness of my relatives, transformed from human affection into canine ferocity! For the irrational nature of dogs displayed human affection toward me by its flattering kindness, while my kin, having forgotten humanity, showed me the severity of the dogs that attacked me.”

He therefore understood that this was the beginning of the struggle of which the divine lyre-player had forewarned him.

### At Bishop Ælfheah’s Urging, and Then through Illness, He Becomes a Monk and a Priest

### 12.

From there he went to his kinsman, Bishop Ælfheah [Col. 0422D], who at that time presided over the Church of Winchester and adorned his life with virtues.

[Note: B. likewise calls him Ælfheah surnamed the Bald, and a kinsman of Dunstan; he adds that Dunstan was at first drawn away from the religious life by a desire for marriage.] The bishop repeatedly urged him to assume the monastic habit, so that he who already possessed the beginnings of an angelic way of life might demonstrate perseverance in that habit.

Dunstan replied that greater grace belonged to one who had grown old in the world and yet had done what was worthy of a monk than to one who had given himself to a monastery and afterward could do nothing except what had been prescribed for him.

“One,” he said, “is a matter of necessity; the other, of freedom.”

To this the bishop replied:

“For everyone alike there is an ultimate necessity: whoever wishes to escape the fire of Gehenna must strive to extinguish the fire of desire. The fire of desire is not extinguished to any great degree if its fuel is not removed from the human senses. For just as wood is to fire, so are the things subject to the senses to desire. But there will be no removal of fuel unless there is renunciation of secular affairs. From all this it follows that, if you wish to escape the fire of Gehenna, you must strive to renounce the world.

“Moreover, what is chiefly sought in the world is human freedom. Once this has been surrendered, the other things cannot be possessed; and if they are possessed, freedom does not cease to possess them. Therefore, as long as you retain it, you have not given to God what you loved most. In order to give what you love most, let it cease to possess you.”

As the bishop pressed these and similar words upon him each day, and Dunstan postponed his response with arguments either true or plausible, he was one day violently assailed by uncertainty in his thoughts and began to deliberate earnestly about what should be desired most in life: virtue or pleasure, a wife or virginity.

While he was held in this uncertainty, a very serious fever attacked him [Col. 0423D] and brought him to the point of despairing of life.

[Note: B.: “The intolerable pain of swollen blisters covered his whole body, so that he thought he was suffering from elephantiasis.”] He lay sick without any hope of recovery, giving those who looked upon him no sign of a living person.

Then, unexpectedly recovering, he said:

“Here I renounce the laws of pleasure; here I declare myself its eternal enemy. I will make no pact of peace with a wife; virtue alone shall have me as its soldier. For it is madness to endure as mistress of my soul one who neither restores the living to health nor leaves the dying without despair. The Son of the Virgin has preserved me a virgin until now; Mary, the Queen of Virgins, shall have me as a virgin.”

He immediately summoned the bishop and asked that the blessing of the religious life, which he had delayed, be given to him. The bishop, filled with immense joy both at the young man’s recovery and at his conversion, promptly advanced him through the monastic and priestly grace [Col. 0423D], assigning him to the church of the blessed Virgin Mary, to whom his parents’ pledge had dedicated him from the beginning.

[Note: B. says: “He consecrated him as a monk corrected for the Lord,” without any mention of the priesthood. A third author says that this occurred “at the proper time, through the canonical succession of the sacred orders.”]

[Note: The phrase “assigning him to a title” shows that monks were ordained with titles. We learn this from canon 6 of the Council of Chalcedon, in title 6 of the collection of Cresconius, chapter 196, where it is forbidden to ordain a presbyter, deacon, or anyone in an ecclesiastical rank absolutely—that is, without a title—unless the church of a city, estate, martyr shrine, or monastery to which the person being ordained belongs is specifically named. Monasteries, therefore, were counted among the titles. The Mendicants introduced the title of poverty. I have read in the archive of the monastery of Mouzon letters of dismissal to the title of a monastery, issued five hundred years ago.]

### Shut Up in a Narrow Cell at Glastonbury, He Receives the Devil Magnificently

### 13.

When the first days of the way of life he had begun were completed, the bishop instructed him by speech and strengthened him by authority against the devil’s snares [Col. 0423D]. He then sent him away to the place where his birth had begun. There he remained in the church of the aforesaid Virgin, carrying out what the rule of pious religion required.

He built, with his own labor, an adjoining cell—whether it should more properly be called a *destina* [Col. 0424D], a cave, or by some other name, for I do not find the most exact term for it.

[Note: A *destina* is a support or prop of a building or church, in Bede, Book III, chapter 17.] It had less the appearance of a human dwelling than of a tomb.

To testify concerning a thing I myself saw, its length, as far as I can judge, was no more than five feet [Col. 0424D], while its width was two and a half feet. Its height was that of a man standing in an excavation in the earth. Otherwise it did not reach even to the chest, so that, as I have said, it appeared more to be the tomb of a dead man than the dwelling of a living one.

It is therefore clear that he neither slept lying down nor ceased to pray to God while standing. The little door was no different from the wall: what was a doorway to someone entering became a wall once he had entered. In so small a structure it was not possible to make a door except across the whole width. In the middle of the little door he opened a small window, through which light shone upon him as he worked.

I confess that I, miserable and sinful, looked upon the holy place where he sat; I saw some of the works of his hands, touched them with sinful hands, brought them to my eyes, watered them with tears, and worshiped on bended knees. For I remembered how often he had heard me crying out in danger, and how mercifully he had been troubled on my behalf. Therefore I could neither restrain my tears nor, if it had been possible, depart from that place.

This was the young man’s house; this his bed; this his view of the whole world. Yet the spacious and extensive walls of cities cannot be compared with these narrow confines, since through these same narrow confines the sick obtain health today, the furies of demons are brought to rest, and many illnesses recover [Col. 0424C].

### 14.

But lest the devil appear to pity his poverty—he who previously had not allowed him to dwell in the palace—he now tried to drive him from his hut.

Thus, concealing himself beneath the appearance of a deceitful human being, he came to the young man’s cell at dusk. He thrust his head against the window, saw him occupied with craft work, and asked him to make some object for him.

Dunstan, neither perceiving his trickery nor able to endure his importunity, applied himself to the work requested. Meanwhile the devil began to speak in a perverse manner, inserting the names of women and recalling acts of lust; then he assailed religion [the text has *ostendere*, “to display,” apparently for *offendere*, “to attack”], and repeated the same things again [Col. 0424D].

Then the athlete of Christ, realizing who he was, began to heat fiercely the tongs with which he held the iron, invoking Christ with closed lips. When he saw that the tongs were glowing red at their very tips [Col. 0425A], moved by holy fury he quickly snatched them from the fire, enclosed the demon’s mask-like face in the tongs, and, resisting with all his strength, dragged the monster inward.

Dunstan was already gathering strength by standing when the one who had been held—held by no wall—escaped from the hands that had seized him, roaring and howling horribly:

“What has this bald man done? What has this bald man done?”

For Dunstan had thin but handsome hair, and on that account the devil shouted such things about him.

When morning came, a considerable crowd from the neighboring people gathered around him, asking what that cry had been which had so violently terrified them while they slept.

“That was the fury of a demon,” he said, “who nowhere allows me to live. He is even trying to drive me from my cell. Guard yourselves carefully against him, because if you could not endure the voice of one who was angry, how will you be able to endure the companionship of one who is condemned?”

After this day Dunstan remained as though in battle array, challenging the devil to combat through his virtues, weakening his body by fasting, and adorning his soul with prayers. He knew that the devil could be overcome in nothing more effectively than in that which the Lord declared was accomplished through fasting and prayer.

Thus, together with bodily chastity, he acquired such purity of heart that scarcely anything contrived by the evil spirit could remain hidden from him. His reputation therefore spread throughout the entire region, inflaming the hearts of everyone to visit the man of God. Every age and both sexes—the famous and the obscure, the poor and the wealthy, private persons and those in positions of power—all spoke of Dunstan, praised his wisdom, and magnified his virtue.

### A Royal Noblewoman, Devoted to the Blessed Virgin Mary, Approaches Dunstan. Through the Mother of God’s Aid She Refreshes the King

### 15.

A certain woman named Elgifu [Col. 0425D], born of royal stock and possessing great wealth, who had always loved, fostered, and nourished all the royal family with a mother’s affection, came to the man of God, leaning upon the hands of her attendants, desiring to enjoy his most holy conversation.

[Note: B. calls her Cewelfleda; Osbert, Elsgiva; others, Aelfleda. B. says that she lived in a little house at the western side of the church, and calls her a niece of King Æthelstan.]

When she heard a word from his mouth, she was so delighted by the sweetness of eternal life that she thereafter chose neither to return home nor to leave the place, but to remain, live, and die with blessed Dunstan. She therefore established a dwelling for herself near the sacred church; she diligently attended the hearing of God’s word, gave alms to the hungry, clothing to the cold, practiced great continence herself, and showed herself completely ready for every work of justice.

She was so fervent in the veneration of the blessed Virgin Mary that she installed many men of the sacred order in her church, supplying from her own generosity whatever they needed. For this reason her merits had such influence with that same Virgin that whenever necessity compelled her to ask for something, she received it from her almost without delay.

To digress briefly from the subject, so that readers may not grow weary—and the digression does not depart far from our present matter—when the aforesaid king once came to Glastonbury because of the sanctity of the place, she wished to preserve the old custom by which she used to serve kings. She asked him to turn aside to her and graciously accept the meal she had prepared for him.

The king agreed, not without embarrassment—for he knew what she spent upon the poor of Christ—and ordered the officials responsible for the royal provision to ascertain whether everything had been prepared suitably and moderately.

After inspecting everything, they reported that there was an ample supply of all things, provided only that they had enough of the drink made with honey and a sprinkling of myrtle [Col. 0425D].

[Note: B. calls this drink by the single word *medonem*, as does Osbert, who adds that the English were especially accustomed to use it.]

She replied:

“My lady, the mother of my Lord Jesus Christ, Mary, will not permit anything to be lacking in all that befits royal magnificence.”

She hurried into the church of the most blessed Virgin and asked, through her overflowing goodness, that what seemed deficient in the royal provision might be increased.

[Note: B. says that this happened after the celebration of the prayers and Masses.]

The king sat surrounded by a large retinue. The servants drew from the small quantity of prepared liquor, yet the vessel remained so undiminished that one might have thought it the widow of Zarephath’s jar of flour or flask of oil. Indeed, they drew from the vessel throughout the entire day and nevertheless found it inexhaustible.

At this event the king, changed in mind, said:

“We have sinned greatly against the servant of God by burdening her with the excess of our multitude.”

Having said this, he turned his face away and departed by the road he had taken.

### While Ill, She Places Her Affairs in Dunstan’s Hands; He Gives Her Movable Goods to the Poor. Revived by the Coming of the Holy Spirit and Strengthened with Anointing and Viaticum, She Dies. Dunstan Converts Her Inheritance into Churches and Monasteries

### 16.

But now, to return to what we undertook: after completing the glorious struggle of her labors, this same woman began to suffer from a serious bodily illness.

When Father Dunstan entered her chamber in grief, after abundant floods of tears from both of them, after the deepest devotion of a pious confession, and after the sweetest consolation concerning blessed hope and the coming of the Lord the Savior, he urged her to strip herself bare of every worldly possession, lest the prince of this world find anything belonging to him in her who was passing away.

She replied:

“I hold no one in the world as dear as you, because I know you to be the principal author of my salvation—apart from the fact that I believe almighty God to hold the primacy of all goodness. I therefore make him heir of my possessions, and I appoint you guardian of the inheritance, so that whatever you know him to wish may be committed to execution at your discretion.”

When blessed Dunstan heard this, although unwilling, he wished to comply with her desire. He immediately distributed all her treasures that could be spared from her movable possessions to the poor; the rest he reserved for the support of churches.

The sun was already inclining toward sunset, and Dunstan, fleeing the darkness of night, returned to his cell. As he passed the church door while singing psalms, he raised his eyes to heaven and saw the coeternal Spirit of almighty God the Father and the Son descending in the form of a dove. Its body was more radiant than any whiteness, while the flight feathers of its wings scattered the brilliance of flashing fire through the air [Col. 0427A].

Then, truly blessed, he contemplated it with the devout eagerness of his mind and saw it enter the inner chamber of the dying noblewoman. He quickly returned to the place from which it had come and saw the house shining with the splendor of divine radiance. He heard the woman inside the enclosure of the drawn veil giving thanks.

He marveled at the conversation and, patiently listening, waited for her to finish speaking. Then he lifted the veil, entered the inner chamber, asked the name of the star-bearing visitor, and questioned the messenger.

Her face suffused with an extraordinary grace, she smiled modestly and said:

“You saw the star-bearer before you came here, and now you ask with whom I have spoken? He is the one who appeared to you as you sang psalms at the church door. He also condescended to console me by his visitation when I was terrified by fear of the approaching death.

“I therefore announce to all my friends that they must not grieve over my death, because the brightness of eternal life will receive me as I die. But to you, my most illustrious and singular friend, I offer abundant thanks, because, instructed always by your admonitions and assisted by your prayers, behold, I am going to God.

“I give you one final command, if I may dare to call it that: at first light, make me a participant in the sacred anointing [Col. 0427D] and in the Lord’s body, so that, fortified by these life-giving mysteries, I may not be put to shame at the gate when I speak there with my enemies.”

[Note: Formerly it was customary for the anointing of the sick to precede viaticum, as was said in the preface to the first century. B. mentions communion alone, but says that before Mass and communion the noblewoman first took a bath for washing her body. Osbert agrees with Osbern and writes that she requested the viaticum of the Lord’s body together with the sacrament of sacred anointing.]

The venerable Father Dunstan obeyed her command and departed. He returned in the morning as agreed and performed everything, so that, when the Mass was almost completed and she had received the body and blood of Christ, she likewise surrendered her soul to Christ.

After she had been honorably buried in the church of the blessed Mary, Dunstan became concerned both about her estate and about his own [Col. 0427D]. For both of his parents had died and had left no heir other than him.

[Note: Osbert reports the same. Hence it is clear that monks in England at that time retained the power to succeed to inheritances, as they did elsewhere.] First, he endowed that same church with the nearest and richest lands in the whole inheritance. He reserved the remainder for founding five monasteries, separated from one another according to the arrangement of the lands.

In the time of the succeeding kings, these monasteries were increased so greatly through his industry [Col. 0428A] that each contained crowds of many monks, all of whom lived according to the rule established by that father.

### He Learns Heavenly Secrets

### 17.

After this the holy man devoted himself to still greater advances in virtue and prayed that the Lord would show him the glory of the just, so that he who already held it as a matter of rightly grounded faith might love it more sweetly through seeing it revealed.

As he was meditating on such things in his heart, a youth of distinguished appearance appeared to him.

[Note: Osbert says that they “served under the guardianship of the regular life at the command of Father Dunstan.” B. explains the matter in these words: “The king kissed him and, leading him to the priestly chair and setting him upon it, said: ‘Be the powerful prince and occupant of this seat, and the most faithful abbot of the present church; and whatever, from my own support, may be lacking to you for the increase of divine worship or the completion of the sacred rule, I shall devoutly supply it with royal generosity.’ Therefore, after this, the servant of God Dunstan accepted the aforesaid dignity for the purpose of governing by the king’s command; and, following in the aforesaid manner the most salutary institution of St. Benedict, he shone forth as the first abbot of the English nation,” etc. [Col. 0427D–0428D]] Dunstan recognized him as the boy whom he himself had once known in the body and had always loved with holy intimacy. The youth recounted the joys of eternal life.

He told him, however, that in this world he would suffer many things: the snares of demons and the malice of human beings; but that after all these things he would attain the highest ranks, win many thousands of people for God, and, together with them, ascend to the realms of heaven.

But since, out of caution, Dunstan did not give credence to what the youth said, the latter took him by the hand and led him into the church courtyard. Showing him a place that was still undisturbed, he said:

“So that no doubt about what you have heard may touch you, within three days a certain priest will be buried here—a priest who is not yet ill.”

Dunstan rose from prayer in the morning, summoned the clergy together, and came to the place. After setting up a marker, he said:

“If what was shown to me during the night is true, within three days a certain priest will be buried here, although he is not yet ill.”

Hardly had they separated from one another when the former court priest of the woman whom we have just praised arrived. After reaching an agreement with the clergy, he obtained the aforesaid place for his burial and said:

“When God commands me to depart from the body, I ask that my remains be buried in this place.”

The priest therefore left in the evening in good health, returned sick during the night, took to his bed, struggled in agony, died, and was buried in the place marked out by the blessed father.

Great astonishment seized everyone, because that same man had foretold such remarkable things concerning the place, the time, and the person, all of which they afterward saw fulfilled and made evident.

Dunstan himself became exceedingly joyful at the glory of eternal life that had been shown and promised to him; but he was made no less sad and anxious by the other matters.

### Summoned by Edmund to the Palace, He Is Again Driven Out; but after the King Is Saved from a Precipice, He Is Honorably Recalled and Granted His Native Soil.

18. When King Æthelstan had died [Note: B has: “It happened at the same time that a certain deacon of the Glastonbury Church, named Wulfred, underwent temporal death; while he lived, he was likewise distinguished and a familiar friend of Blessed Dunstan. Not long after his departure, he appeared to him, revealing many things unknown concerning heavenly matters,” etc.], his brother Edmund [Col. 0429A] assumed the monarchy. Since he knew with what great virtue the venerable Father Dunstan had once shone at court, how richly endowed he had been with just works and upright counsels, and since for this reason he had always loved him with fraternal affection, he sent messengers to him and asked him to come, so that he might appoint him, whom he knew to be acceptable to Almighty God, to the highest position among the royal nobles and courtiers [Note: Namely, in the year 940, according to William of Malmesbury.].

But Dunstan, whether wishing to obey the apostolic commands that every soul must be subject to the higher authority, or desiring to exalt in the land of the English the kingdom of justice, which had for the most part grown obsolete, consented to the king’s requests. He remained at court according to the circumstances of the times, and subjected both the king himself [Col. 0429B] and all the princes of the English to the laws of justice. But since it almost always happens that the industry of some increases the envy of others, and since whoever cannot rise to the virtue of another attempts to attack that virtue in the one who rises, once again, as formerly, many nobles took offense at Dunstan’s prosperous success and falsely suggested to the king that he should be expelled from their company. The king, however, giving greater favor to falsehood than to honor, deprived Dunstan of his possessions and royal favor and ordered him to be driven from the court [Note: B inserts the following: “There were at Ceodrum, where these things had occurred, certain venerable men—namely, envoys of the eastern kingdom—who were then lodging with the king. Since he had been assigned, as it were, to exile and knew of no other course, he approached them and begged that, abandoned by the king, they should not abandon him, but take him with them to their homeland, even if only as a resident. Taking pity on his sorrow, they promised him whatever advantages their kingdom possessed, if he would accompany them.”].

Thus the first day passed, and so did the second. The third dawn had now come, and the king went hunting with his men. The woodland which he had found for hunting was the exceedingly lofty Mount of Cedars [B: Ceodrum]. Broken through its middle, it displayed to those looking from above a vast chasm and dreadful precipice [Col. 0429C]. The king therefore loosened the reins on the mountain’s slopes and pursued the fleeing stag through every trackless place. Both grew weary: the king from pursuing the stag, and the stag from fleeing for its life. At last, deprived of every freedom to flee, the beast made for the precipice, plunged over it, and, torn into the smallest pieces, perished.

The pursuing hounds suffered a similar death. Finally, a horse carried the king forward. When it saw at close range what fortune had prepared before it, it drew back the reins and tried to turn its rider around; but suddenly, when the reins broke and were flung from his hand, the horse carried the king away at a flying pace. What more is there to say? Completely despairing of himself, yet placing some confidence in God’s mercy, he implored heavenly aid and prayed in confession of his sins:

“God, almighty King, although you are exalted above all things, you look upon the lowly and always recognize the lofty from afar, come now to the aid not of a king, but of a man like other mortals, standing in the supreme [Col. 0430A] peril of death. Do not remember the injuries inflicted by me upon your faithful servant Dunstan; for if you rescue me from this present death through his merits, you shall have me, for as long as I live, devoted to your name and a praiser of his.”

He had not yet fully finished speaking—and this is incredible to say, though nothing is impossible for God—when the animal remained fixed at the very edge of the abyss, as though held there by a divine hand. Then, giving lofty thanks to God in both heart and speech, the king ordered Dunstan, the author of his deliverance, to be summoned. Before all the princes he explained what the Divinity had accomplished through him, took the man’s right hand, kissed it, and said:

“Most holy of men, I acknowledge what evil I committed against you—not, by my faith, because I wished to do so, but because I was compelled by wicked men. Thanks, therefore, to God’s clemency, which not only refused to inflict upon me the punishment I deserved, but also chose to bestow an undeserved benefit, rescuing me from the precipice of death and granting me a longer span of life through your merits. Henceforth, therefore, let there be between us the perpetual integrity of perfect familiarity; let there always be free authority for you to arrange matters at court; and let there be throughout the whole kingdom of the English supreme power for you to judge between a man and his neighbor.

“And so that you may know my affection for you, I give you in perpetual possession the place where I found that you were born, brought up, and had lived, so that whatever you wish to determine concerning it may be left to your judgment. If it should be especially pleasing to your heart to gather there men of the order whose habit you wear, whatever they lack in any matter I shall supply through royal generosity, for your sake” [Note: William, in Book II of *The Kings*, chapter 7, reports the entire privilege, granted in the year 944 and “written in golden letters in a Gospel book,” which the king himself gave.].

He makes the monastery at Glastonbury famous. He mocks the demon’s terrors. He entrusts himself to Saint Andrew. He is familiar with the angels and learns Edgar’s destiny. He sees events occurring in his absence.

19. Dunstan therefore, having received authority over the royal residence called Glastonbury, after a few days began to lay the foundations of a narrower church, to construct workshops according to the model once shown to him, and, when everything had been completed, to gather there a great and distinguished company of monks. Having become their first abbot, he led all who lived with him to such perfection of justice that they seemed like the lights of heaven, dispersing all the clouds of error and the darkness of sins [Col. 0430D].

Then from these same monks bishops were chosen for all the neighboring churches; then abbots were appointed; finally, superiors of various offices were instituted. They were outstanding in the merit of their religious life, illustrious in the wisdom of their learning, and pre-eminent in the defense of the Catholic faith [Note: Osbert adapts to this passage the portent of the lighted candle mentioned above, no. 4, as follows: “Just as the entire community of the church recovered its lost light from the candle of Dunstan’s mother, so it is evident that all the churches of England received the light of true religion from this place, through Dunstan’s teaching and institution.”].

But the evil demon, unable to endure such a spirit of religion, worked with every possible stratagem to overthrow the man from his state of uprightness. One night, while Dunstan was praying in his chamber, the demon presented itself to his eyes as a monstrous wolf; shortly afterward it fashioned itself as a flattering fox. Dunstan smiled at the variety of its forms and said:

“O you who are in every respect like yourself! O forms corresponding to your conduct! In the one you prove yourself bloodthirsty, in the other fraudulent. Go now, enemy, for in the name of him who overcame you as a lion and a dragon, I shall overcome you as a wolf and a fox.”

Seeing that he was suffering great hostility from demons and placing insufficient confidence in his own strength or that of his sons, he called upon the apostle Andrew, the patron of his life, so that he might be a faithful interpreter before God, a constant companion on earth, and an unfailing guardian amid all the storms of this world. Enclosed, as it were, within a wall by Andrew’s continual protection, he lived securely within his cell, transcending the whole world in the height of his mind and resting in perpetual meditation upon the love of divinity.

Thus he often deserved to take part in the sweetest harmonies of the heavenly spirits, while God granted him good hope of his future reward; and, as one who lived on earth in the company of angels, he came to know their fellowship in heaven. Finally, when a son named Edgar was born to the aforementioned King Edmund—a child destined to bear peace and justice—the blessed man heard the blessed angels in heaven rejoicing and singing psalms with great exultation [Note: This is found in William, Book II of *The Kings*, chapter 8]:

“Let there be peace; let there be great joy for the Church of the English, for as long as the child who has been born holds the kingdom and our Dunstan completes the limits of mortal life.”

How firmly this saying was supported by the truth of events will be made clear by the appropriate order of the present narrative.

20. At that same time the man of God, bound by the king’s requests, proceeded to visit the Church of Bath, which was to be established for divine worship. While he was praying there alone after taking refreshment, he was suddenly carried up to heavenly things and saw the soul of a certain disciple whom he had nobly educated at Glastonbury being borne toward the palace of heaven, surrounded on every side by an innumerable multitude of angels and suffused with the radiance of immense light. Immediately he commended it into the hands of divine mercy and invited the lords of the place to commend it as well [Col. 0432A].

While everyone stood amazed and scarcely gave credence to his words, the testimony of a swift messenger [Note: B says that Ceolwius, a superior who had come to transact the monastery’s business with Dunstan, confirmed the event.] proved that both the death and the hour of death had occurred exactly as the man had testified.

He foreknows the king’s death, and buries his body at Glastonbury.

21. On his return from that place, as he went to visit the king, who was most eager to speak with him, he found the devil, resembling a jester, dancing before the riders and boasting as though of some future gain. When he pointed out its presence to the people who were with him [Note: B mentions only one man, Ælfstan, Dunstan’s companion on the journey. Since he did not see the demon’s illusions, he was granted the ability to see them when Dunstan prayed. King Edmund’s murder occurred in the year 946, perpetrated by a robber named Leof, according to William, Book II of *The Kings*, chapter 7. At approximately the same time, that is, in the year 948, Dunstan the abbot subscribed to a charter for the Crowland men in Ingulf.], and by command stripped from it the form that was horrible to all eyes, he was afterward asked what that monster’s insolent joy signified. He declared that it foretold the king’s death and the imminent change of the kingdom.

The truth of events soon confirmed his prophecy. The sun had not yet created the day seven times when the king was killed and the kingdom changed. From this it is sufficiently clear how greatly God’s grace governed this man’s heart: he could so easily detect an invisible enemy and expose its illusions with such truth.

The king’s funeral procession was transferred to Glastonbury, where Blessed Dunstan committed him to the earth amid a great gathering of the grieving people.

He becomes dear to King Eadred.

22. Eadred succeeded to the kingdom by right of his brother. He was an excellent man, a cultivator of justice and piety, greatly loving God and himself greatly loved by God. For this reason, like a good son, he was often scourged by Him with a father’s rod. In the presence of this king the venerable Father Dunstan was so precious that Eadred preferred him to the whole human race. He appointed him keeper of his wills [Note: B explains the matter as follows: “The king entrusted to him all his best possessions—many rural charters, the ancient treasures of preceding kings, and also various riches that he himself had acquired—for faithful safekeeping under the protection of his monastery.”]; he entrusted treasures, soul, body, and kingdom to him; and there was no one throughout the kingdom of the English who would move hand or foot without his command.

Thus Dunstan, as though made king and emperor of the king, extended the rod of equity and the rod of God’s kingdom throughout all the borders of England. He endowed with extensive inheritances those churches which he had either founded himself or which, having been founded by others, had been oppressed by poverty. He brought great joy to the peoples through his power, while peace and justice turned toward one another in mutual embrace and offered each other the gift of a kiss.

After Ælfheah’s death, he refuses the see of Winchester.

23. While these things were taking place, Ælfheah [Note: B calls him “Æthel … bishop of the Church of Chrydon.” That he was bishop of Winchester is clear from the preceding no. 12; Osbert also confirms it here, adding that Elfin was ordained in Dunstan’s place.]—the man with whom we previously said Dunstan had once lived—departed for the life of the spiritual age. The king, thinking that he had found a suitable opportunity to make Dunstan the recipient of greater honor, began to ask him to take up as pastor the Church that had been deprived of pastoral care.

But when he saw that he could not persuade Dunstan of what he was urging, he entrusted the matter to the persuasion of his mother, Queen Eadgifu [B: Aelpwolduy]:

“I know, dearest mother and queen of the whole kingdom of the English, that our common friend Dunstan loves you above all among human beings and takes the greatest pleasure in your works. Whatever he has commanded you for the sake of eternal life—whether in supporting the poor or in endowing churches—you have never ceased to fulfill through diligent execution. For this reason my mind is held by a great hope: if you ask anything of him that would be fitting for both me and him, he will not wish to refuse you in any way.

“It is manifest to everyone that it is fitting for both of us that he should attain the highest priesthood. We know that all honors are inferior to his life and wisdom, and we know that the king of the English is more powerful than many kings of other lands. Therefore approach the man, my sweetest mother, with feminine eloquence, and exhort him through that influence which you possess with him to consent to you, so that he may thereby cling more closely to God and be able to absolve us more powerfully from the bonds of sin.”

The mother, the queen, therefore obeyed her son the king. She invited Dunstan to a banquet and charmed him with her conversation. But he, standing firm and immovable like a mountain, in accordance with the etymology of his name, said:

“I do not wish, lady, that you should ask of me something which, if granted, would disturb my spirit, or, if refused, would offend yours. For I know how difficult it is for each person to plead his own case before the tribunal of Christ, let alone to become the examiner or judge of another’s case.

“Even if this greatest of reasons did not exist, another would greatly restrain me from accepting the episcopate: I see that the lord king is threatened by a persistent illness, and I cannot be separated from him for long, since he has appointed me both father to himself and lord of the whole kingdom.”

When she still wished to hold him, as he resisted, by further arguments, he was moved for a little while and said:

“Know with complete certainty that I shall not be elevated to the pontifical dignity during your son’s lifetime.”

Then, carrying a troubled mind, he withdrew to his chamber. As he turned many things over within himself, sleep overtook him. And behold, there appeared the princes of God’s kingdom and the judges of the world, the venerable apostles of Christ Peter and Paul with Saint Andrew, as though they were meeting him as he came out from the city of Rome and joining him on Mount Gaudium.

They greeted him most graciously. He saw each of them holding a gleaming sword, and all of them courteously offered their swords to him. As he passed his gaze along the swords extended before him, he read on the sword of blessed Peter an inscription woven in golden letters:

“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word.”

The swords of the others bore the names of their respective holders: Paul’s had “Paul,” and Andrew’s had “Andrew.” Meanwhile he looked upon Andrew, whose face was bright and who was winking, and heard him chant beforehand in evangelical words:

“Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls.”

Then blessed Peter ordered him to extend his left hand, and he received a slight blow from a crackling rod. Peter said to him:

“Let this be for you both the punishment of rejection and the sign that you shall reject the pontificate no further.”

At the touch of the little rod he awoke from sleep and understood that he had been visited by divine power. He gave thanks to God, by whose gift he saw himself so honored.

When day dawned and he had recounted to the king what he had seen, the king marveled and resolved the vision in this interpretation:

“Through the weapons of apostolic blessing the power of the pontificate is signified. You should know that, because yesterday you despised the Lord’s yoke, you were rebuked and designated by divine election as a future bishop.

“Moreover, because you saw written on the sword of the blessed apostle Peter the words, ‘In the beginning was the Word,’ and since the Word of God is the only-begotten Son of God, God always with God, but made human among human beings for the sake of human beings, know for certain that you are destined to become the chief of that see which, under the name of Christ, is celebrated in the city of the Cantware as more distinguished than the other Churches.”

By this sign of divine foreknowledge Dunstan was glorified, and by this interpretation of the king he was designated as bishop.

O remarkable sign! O grace freely given to a man! O sincere purity of his heart! The supreme pontiff of the English, Odo, was still living his life among human beings, yet in the eyes of the heavenly Inspector Dunstan was already the supreme pontiff.

It is greatly astonishing that he, still an inhabitant of earth, should yet be admitted among the angelic choirs in heaven; and no less astonishing that the citizens of heaven should visit him on earth. What shall I place first: the man joined to the heavenly beings, or the heavenly beings assigned to the man? I do not know, except that in the one respect he was more blessed, and in the other more secure.

Let others marvel at the various gifts of various virtues divinely bestowed upon certain human beings. I value nothing so highly as seeing a man who, standing amid the storms of this world, transcends the entire world in his mind and rests in the love of the Creator; seeing Martha in his ministry, Mary in his longing, faith working, and charity burning.

But we have said nothing unless we say what remains.

He arranges the funeral of the dead Eadred.

24. King Eadred, seized by a fatal illness [Note: B says: “So that at mealtime he rejected food because of the weakness of his stomach.” His death occurred in the year 955. William of Malmesbury writes of him in Book II of *The Kings*, chapter 7: “Meanwhile he, devoted to the feet of the saints, had vowed his life to God and Dunstan. At Dunstan’s instructions he patiently endured frequent bodily torments, continued his prayers, and made his palace altogether a training ground of virtues. He died amid great mourning among the people,” etc.], fell into bed, and the physicians offered no hope of escaping death [Col. 0435A]. He therefore quickly sent messengers to summon Dunstan, the father of his life, so that he might be a witness of his final decision, receive his confessions, and be a faithful intercessor for him before God.

Dunstan was deeply grieved in soul and went with all possible speed to visit the king, his friend. But God, seeing that he was afflicted by grief of heart and suffering bodily exertion, did not allow him to be touched by further distress. He both eased his sorrow and lessened his labor.

For while Dunstan was on the road toward the palace, and his limbs, exhausted by fasting, were being wearied without respite, a voice descended from the highest heaven and sounded:

“Behold, King Eadred has fallen asleep in the Lord.”

At the utterance of this voice, the horse on which he was riding was struck and died. His companions trembled: they heard the crash of thunder but did not understand what was thundering [Col. 0435B]. Dunstan disclosed the matter to them, commended the dead king’s soul into the hands of the eternal King, and immediately heard from messengers what the angel from heaven had just announced to him.

Entering the palace, Dunstan saw the corpse of the beloved man lying there. The crowds of companions who had once been accustomed to stand beside him in gold now kept their distance. Dunstan marveled at the change and pitied the human condition. Then, wishing to show the same faith to the dead that he had shown in loving him while alive, he took the body’s covering upon himself and performed the duty of burial with the honor owed to it.

He withdraws because of King Edwy’s evil conduct.

25. After him arose Edwy, son of King Edmund, young in age and possessing no aptitude for ruling [Col. 0435C]. He was neither wise himself nor willing to follow the counsel of the wise. Rather, like another Rehoboam, he despised his elders and followed the counsels of boys.

Having acquired these most destructive companions and relying not so much on their counsels as on their madness, he stripped the best men of their possessions, proscribed the wealthy, disinherited churches, undermined religion, and imposed manifold exactions in the cities. His cruelty harmed not only those unrelated to him, but also, in the manner of Nero, raged against men descended from his own line and even against the queen, Eadgifu, the mother of kings, in his madness.

Besides this, burning with lust, he was continually inflamed with the desire for intercourse. The venerable Father Dunstan was deeply offended by these things and frequently rebuked him sharply, at suitable times and places [Col. 0435D]. Edwy laughed at his rebukes and at the same time threatened him with many evils. When Dunstan saw that his efforts achieved nothing, he decided altogether to abstain from conversation with him.

He lives piously at Glastonbury.

26. Dunstan therefore left him and withdrew to the monastery. There he lived at such a height of religious devotion that his holy dedication exceeded all measure [Col. 0436A]. At that place a tower had been constructed [Note: Osbert here inserts the death of the monk Ælfi, who, while walking around the monastery’s workshops with Dunstan, was called three times from heaven. Osbert then adds: “In that very place where Dunstan heard the voice, he built an oratory in the form of a tower under the patronage of Blessed John the Baptist.”], but its summit was not yet enclosed by any roofing.

When the people attempted to raise and set against the highest walls the beam that supported the entire structure, the ropes suddenly broke and the beam began to fall downward. A great cry arose from the entire people, repeatedly calling out to Dunstan. The saint rushed up more quickly, held his raised right hand against the structure, and traced a cross opposite it.

Before his holy hand had finished drawing together its sacred fingers, the beam that had begun to lean appeared to be carried back to the place from which it had begun to fall—not bound by ropes, not lifted by machinery, and not supported by any device of human ingenuity.

If the evil spirit had not envied such glory, whom would it have envied? If it had not poured out the venom of its malice then, when would it have done so? Having no further doubt about the man of God, it decided to direct all the snares of its ambush against him at once.

It therefore transformed itself into the appearance of a bear, approached him while he was praying with a similar gaping mouth [Note: B writes that this happened while he was praying before the altar of the martyr of Christ, George], seized in its claws the pastoral staff that he held in his hand, and tried to drag it toward itself.

But divine Dunstan, powerfully strengthened by the spirit of divinity, pulled the staff back toward himself and raised it high. He beat the fleeing beast with extreme violence and did not cease striking the monster until the whip appeared broken into three pieces upon its back [Note: Osbert adds that Dunstan made another thick and strong staff for himself and adorned its top with encircling silver. Formed above in the shape of a hollow sphere, it contained a tooth of the blessed apostle Andrew, both as protection against demons and out of love for the apostle.].

He attacks the king’s amours and is driven into exile. He lives at Ghent.

27. Thus defeated in himself, the devil sought to conquer his victor through others. Opportunities were not lacking by which he could turn what he was wickedly contriving to malicious purposes.

For when the aforesaid king had publicly fallen into shameful intercourse on the very day on which he had been consecrated, and the entire senatorial order had consequently taken offense, although no one dared rebuke his licentiousness, Dunstan was urged by the unanimous and common wish of all [Note: B: “When the supreme pontiff Odo saw the king’s insolence, especially on the day of his consecration, he said to his co-bishops and his princes: ‘Go, I beg you, each of you, to bring out the king …’ Finally they chose two men whom they knew to be most steadfast in spirit: namely, Dunstan the abbot and Cynewius, bishop and kinsman of that same Dunstan.” Osbert calls him Kinswinus.] to approach the king steadfastly, restrain the royal adultery by divine and human reasoning, and terrify the adulterous woman with the threat of a prostitute’s hanging.

Dunstan did this, and did still more. He found the prince together with the adulteress and her daughter, violently dragged him away from the adulterous bed, placed the crown upon his head, and brought him before the supreme pontiff Odo [Col. 0436D].

But the harlot, rolling her bloodshot eyes, said:

“You have condemned me to death by hanging; I shall deprive you of the beauty of your limbs and condemn you to perpetual exile.”

Seized by the force of this speech, the evil spirit awaited vengeance against the man of God, prompted by the nefarious harlot. The devil therefore stirred up the woman’s spirit, and the woman inflamed the king’s anger [Col. 0437A]. Both threatened Dunstan with exile.

First, at the urging of the king’s edict, all the churches of monastic religion were stripped of their possessions, so that what had always been Dunstan’s greatest joys might now become for him the greatest possible sorrow. Then, when they reached Glastonbury and Dunstan himself had been proscribed after everything had been inventoried, amid the tears of the monks whom he had nourished by his own hand, the lamentations of friends who came to him from every place, and the groans of the poor whom he had refreshed each day with their customary allowances, the sound of the devil clapping was heard in the temple courtyard, like the sharp, rapid laughter of a young woman.

The saint looked upon him with a stern expression and said:

“Do not rejoice so much over my exile, for there is more for you to grieve when I return than you will ever be able to rejoice over while I am in exile.”

At these words, the pallid minister of the pallid kingdom withdrew.

Dunstan, however, mindful of what the divine lyre-player had once proclaimed to him, and indeed remembering the Lord’s promise by which Christ declared that those who suffer persecution for justice are blessed (Matthew 5:10), entrusted himself to the sea. He reached the opposite shore in the land of the Flemings, where he found favor with the distinguished ruler of that country and remained in the monastery of Saint Peter situated at Ghent, because it seemed to surpass the other monasteries of that region both in its practice of virtue and in its philosophical learning.

Yet the madness of the frenzied woman did not cease. After investigating all who had sheltered the man of God during his departure, she proscribed and condemned them and even sent wicked ministers to tear out Dunstan’s eyes.

But by the mercy of divine clemency, whose help never failed him, Gaul had received him before the servants of Jezebel reached the sea. Thus the saint lived in exile, lamenting no loss from exile through God’s grace. He so bound all people to himself by his merits that he considered exile his homeland.

Moreover, the consolation of his apostolic friend sustained him; Andrew allowed him to lack none of the things he desired [Note: B adds that certain persecutors tried in vain to drag him away from the monastery, and that this was signified to Dunstan by a vision. Osbert explains the matter, saying that some of the Glastonbury brothers wished to remove him from the leadership of that monastery, but that God prevented it.].

After King Edwy is driven out, Edgar reigns.

28. Christ’s clemency, therefore, seeing the people of the English deprived of so great a patron, stirred the hearts of men from the River Humber to the River Thames, above which the city of London is founded, against the impious King Edwy [Col. 0437D–0438A]. As though transformed into a single man, they sought not only to reject his kingdom but also to drive him from the throne, because he had acted foolishly in the government entrusted to him, destroyed the wise, admitted the ignorant of good to his counsels, and rushed headlong into lust and arrogance.

They gathered into a crowd and did not cease pursuing the king, who was fleeing with the adulteress and hiding himself in inaccessible places, with weapons. They found the woman near the city of Claudius [Note: Osbert says “near the city of Gloucester,” commonly Gloucester], cut the sinews of her legs, and then inflicted upon her the death she deserved.

They drove the king, wandering by obscure paths through various places, beyond the River Thames. Then they summoned his brother, a young man of excellent character named Edgar, whom we previously said had been designated as the future king by a heavenly oracle, when the angels proclaimed peace and the salvation of the kingdom for his own times and those of Dunstan. They established him as king over all the provinces from the great River Humber to the River Thames, which divided the kingdoms of the two brothers from one another.

Thus the kingdom that had been one was divided between two kings and for some time sweated under serious conflicts of war. Then was fulfilled that truthful saying of the Savior, in which he asserts that every kingdom divided against itself will be destroyed and that house will fall upon house (Luke 11:17).

Edgar advanced daily, like David, in piety and courage and, like Solomon, in wisdom, wealth, and glory. The house of Edwy, however, diminished day by day, while Edwy himself did not cease increasing in his crimes.

Dunstan is recalled from exile. He is ordained bishop of Worcester under the title of archbishop of Canterbury.

29. A few days after his election, King Edgar, diarch (*diarcha*) of all his kingdom, ordered a council to be held. At it all the unjust laws decreed by his brother were abolished, and everything that had been taken away through his violent condemnation was restored. He also recalled the venerable abbot Dunstan from exile in great glory [Note: Namely, in the year 957 according to the Saxon Chronicle, not in 959 as in Spelman and others. What follows concerning Dunstan’s ordination is read in nearly the same form above in the *Life of Saint Odo, Archbishop of Canterbury*. It occurred at the assembly at Bradanford, according to B, which says that Dunstan was first ordained bishop so that he might serve as the king’s counselor, and afterward appointed to the Church of Worcester after Cynewald’s death. “Afterward a great assembly of wise men was held at Brandanford, and there Dunstan was chosen and ordained bishop by all, especially because he had continually attended the royal presence on account of his prudent counsels … Then the shepherd of the Church of Worcester, Cynewald, having been removed by the course of mortal death and temporal life, fell, and blessed Bishop Dunstan, appointed by the king, took over that same church,” etc. Thus B, which says that the king’s great-grandmother was recalled from exile with Dunstan. Concerning Kenewald, see above.], and raised him to an honor greater than any earlier king had bestowed.

He also pressed him with intense requests to accept episcopal dignity. He refused to desist from his entreaties until he drew Dunstan away from his refusal into consent and appointed him bishop of the Church of Worcester, which flourished under the honor of the blessed virgin Mary.

When Dunstan came to Canterbury to be consecrated, and the supreme priest of God, Odo, had joyfully assented after the petition of the clergy and people had been read, it was wonderful to relate: he completed the remaining ministry of consecration not as though upon the bishop of the Hwiccii, but as upon the archbishop of the Cantware, with extraordinary joy.

The surrounding clergy reproached him for acting against the decrees of the Fathers, which prohibit one church from having two bishops and forbid an election of succession to be made by hereditary right. He is said to have answered:

“If human things did not yield to divine things, the authority of men could rightly be brought forward against me. But since God is the author of all things, I cannot fail to do what the Spirit of God has deigned to command should be done. For this blessed man will be the archbishop of this see immediately after my death and a most valiant warrior against the prince of the world.”

Defended by this reasoning of the supreme pontiff, Dunstan proceeded to the people, himself also predesignated as the supreme pontiff of Canterbury. He bore the insignia of Aaron, not shadowed by the veil of the law, but adorned through the grace of Christ by the gift of divine propitiation.

Returning from there to the church entrusted to him and elevated to the pontifical chair, he remembered what he had once promised the exultant devil when royal impiety had assigned him to exile. He therefore rose against him with open hands, divided his limbs with the evangelical sword, and recalled to the Lord’s fold the sheep that were wandering everywhere.

He frees Edwy’s soul from punishment.

[Col. 0439C]

### 30.

Meanwhile, after the death of the most impious King Edwy [Note: [Col. 0439] They assign his death to the year 959; he was buried at Winchester in the New Monastery, according to William in Book II, chapter 7, *On the Kings of the English.], and after he had been transferred into the lot of evil spirits, Dunstan was serving in the church over which he presided, occupied with meditations upon David, knowing nothing of what had happened to the king. And behold, the infernal host, exulting beneath his gaze, began as though to lead a chorus and, as if celebrating victories over captured spoils, rejoiced. The holy man therefore investigates the cause of their joy and hears that the king had died and that his soul was immediately to be handed over to the fires of hell [and freed]; but that this first had to be announced to Dunstan by divine command.

Moved by compassion, Dunstan prostrates himself upon the ground, and a copious rain of tears pours from his eyes. He assails God with prayers and does not cease praying to him until he recognizes that the king’s spirit has been freed. After a brief interval, however, the sorrowful infernal legion returns and breaks out with a great cry in these words:
