“Ah, you man among men! Ah, stranger to faith! Ah, always ungrateful for our benefits! We offered you service, but you have repaid us with punishment. We have come from the region of darkness to avenge your injuries, and behold, confounded by your adverse curses, we return.”

When he commanded the demons to declare the truth, he learned that the king’s soul had been taken from them by angelic power and preserved under a seal until the appointed time; that the demons had no claim over it [Col. 0440A], but that it had passed into the lot of repentant souls.

Then, exulting in the Lord, he restrained their fury with this reasoning:

“What injustice has been done to you?” he said. “If this man sinned, he sinned against Christ and against me. But since I forgave my injuries for Christ’s sake, Christ also forgave his, when I pleaded for his mercy. What Christ and I have graciously deigned to forgive—by what presumption do you dare wickedly to condemn?”

At this sentence the dark spirits, as though struck by a Parthian arrow, scatter like flies snatched up by the wind.

### 31. He Receives the See of London

But Edgar, having become monarch of the whole kingdom, was considering placing the blessed man over the entire realm [Col. 0440B], unwilling that the kingdom should grow without the man whom, even before he became king, he had striven to love more familiarly than all others. Therefore, when the bishop of London had been gathered to his fathers, Dunstan was granted succession to him at the request of the king and the nobles, with all the inhabitants of that city also consenting and loudly acclaiming his name.

They had heard how acceptable he had been to God from his earliest age, how solicitous he had been in the Church over which he presided, and, finally, how approved he had been in every good and excellent matter. For this reason they did not wish to have another when they could have the very best.

Nor did the excuse help him by which he appealed to the authority of the canons: just as they forbid one church to have two bishops, so they do not allow two churches to be assigned to one bishop. “When John,” they said, “the Lord’s beloved, presided over seven churches and their bishops, and blessed Paul possessed at once the care and governance of all the churches.”

Overcome by such testimonies of reason, the blessed pontiff was enthroned as bishop of London. He did not abandon the Church he had previously held, but presided over both, governed both, and was the true and proper pontiff of both.

You therefore possess, most holy Father, Paul’s sword, which he himself had once brought to you as destined for you from heaven and had entrusted to you to use in dividing the enemies of the Church. And although your earlier pontifical power was administered with no lack of evangelical discipline, it nevertheless did not need to be prefigured either by a sword or by the person of its presiding bishop [Col. 0440D], because a sword does not suit a virgin, but it suits men; nor, by changing your place, did you change your service, when you passed from the Virgin Mother of the Lord to the Lord’s Apostle, from Wigracester to London.

Gird yourself, therefore, most valiant warrior; gird yourself with the sword of God’s power, made powerful through him who is also most powerful above the thigh (Psalm 44:4), to fight against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places (Ephesians 6:12).

Divide those who, through wicked crime, abuse an unlawful marriage, and let neither royal power [Col. 0441A] nor the singular exaltation of the Roman pontiff deter you from inflicting punishment. Pronounce sentence upon the silver-dealing seducers of the people, and do not proceed to offer at the sacred altar on Pentecost before vengeance has struck them and justice has come to the people of God.

Leave everywhere the signs of your virtues; everywhere raise the trophies of the Lord’s cross. For shortly you will deserve Peter’s sword, by which, like Peter, you will kill innumerable animals of every kind (Acts 10:13–14) and transfer them into the body of the Church by eating them.

You will deserve, I say, Peter’s sword, marked with the name of the almighty Son of God, so that throughout the whole breadth of England the power of binding and loosing may through him be increased for you, and so that no one may enter the sheepfold who, under your guidance, has not ascended through the door.

How fittingly Dorobernia is called the door of the granary: the granary signifies the breadth of the English kingdom, while the door signifies the primacy of the Church of Canterbury.

### 32. After Odo’s Death, and Likewise Elfsin’s; Berthelin Expelled, Dunstan Is Transferred to Canterbury

Thus Odo, chief of the priests, a man distinguished for wisdom and praiseworthy for virtue, passed from human affairs, led by the hands of angels to paradise. If Dunstan had not succeeded him, he would always have been mourned by the whole English people [Note: [Col. 0441D] William’s words concerning Odo belong here: “How slight, however, is the testimony Osbern bears him, when he says that, because of his holiness and ability, he would always have been mourned by the whole English people unless Dunstan had succeeded him.”]

After his death, when the king urged Dunstan to become chief of the priests, and Dunstan in no way consented to the one urging him, certain men appeared whose hands the bishop of Winchester, Elfsin, had filled with gifts; they demanded that the supreme priesthood be confirmed for him. He had also sought the supreme priesthood before Odo, but Christ, guardian of his Church, had obstructed his ambition.

The king, unaware that they had been corrupted by the bishop’s gifts, and therefore hearing them with a simple mind, entrusted the Church deprived of its shepherd to him to govern. But when he had set out for Rome to receive the pallium from the Apostolic See, he was seized by severe cold among the Alps and miserably died, divine vengeance being requited upon him in a manner worthy of his deeds: he who had grown cold in heart toward the love of heavenly things perished in his body through the severity of cold; and he who had presumed to seek another’s honors died in a foreign land and lost both honor and life.

Once again prayers were poured out to Dunstan concerning the archbishopric [Col. 0441D], but they accomplished nothing in his mind by way of persuasion. Therefore Berthelin, bishop of Dorchester, was chosen for the patriarchate of the Church of Canterbury—a man gentler than capable, and one who knew better how to attend to his own life than to another’s.

After a few days of the pontificate he had received, it became known that he was insufficiently suited to so great an office. Ordered by the king and by the whole people, he left Canterbury and returned, not without embarrassment, to his recently abandoned Church [Col. 0442A]. For the Lord was acting on Dunstan’s behalf, so that he might fulfill the word he had promised by the hand of the kingdom’s princes.

King Edgar, observing the rejection of these men and recognizing that the better man should be called, and that Dunstan alone among all men was one to whom no one could be compared—indeed, one who could be preferred to all—wearied him with prayers a third time. At last, overcome both by the importunity of the king himself and by that of all the bishops, he appointed him primate and patriarch of the first metropolis of the English [Note: [Col. 0441D] The Saxon Chronicle shows that Odo died in the year 961 and that Dunstan was appointed in his place; we preferred it to the other authorities in the Acts of Odo. The matter of the pallium was treated above in Observation 12.].

The Roman pontiff immediately deserved to see him when he had gone to the city of Romulus because of the strength of his apostolic faith or authority [Note: [Col. 0442D] B. adds that Dunstan’s provisions failed on the journey because of his excessive distribution of victuals, but that, when his steward complained, a certain abbot came to his assistance.], and, having adorned him with the sacred pontifical vestments, sent him to the English people as though he were an angel of the Lord of hosts, to display knowledge of the divine law, or as a pillar of light to illuminate the face of the earth [Col. 0442B].

Behold how the things once foretold so long beforehand have been fulfilled through the sword inscribed with the word of God and brought forth through the blessed embassy of the chief of the apostles, Peter.

But what does it mean that he received a third sword from the hand of the third apostle, when he never sat as pontiff in the church honorably maintained under that apostle’s name at Rochester? He certainly sat there in power, although not by bodily sitting; he sat, I say, in authority, he sat in command, he sat in defense, he sat in benefits.

### 33. A Dove Appears during the Sacred Rites. He Draws Water from a Rock

But lest Canterbury should be deprived of the grace of his virtues [Col. 0442C], or the increase of the honor he had received seem to have diminished his former virtue, the Holy Spirit deigned, through certain new manifestations of his grace, to glorify the man in the Church of the Savior in such a way that he himself appeared to be extraordinary, beyond human nature.

For when, on the first day of his arrival, he stood at the sacred altars and distributed the life-giving bread to the people of God, suddenly, while the church was covered by a cloud, the dove once seen by John in the Jordan appeared again (Luke 3:22). It remained above him until the sacrifice had been completed.

When the sacrifice had been completed, it rested above the tomb of blessed Odo, which had been constructed in the form of a pyramid on the southern side of the altar. From that day the pontiff so revered the merit of that man of God [Col. 0442D] that he never passed by without bending his knees and calling him good, saying: “Here rests good Odo.”

### 34.

At about the same time, a certain great and powerful man established a small church for the Savior. The venerable pontiff Dunstan was invited to come and consecrate it and to possess it by his own rightful title.

When water was lacking there for the rite of dedication, and the resulting situation caused embarrassment to the one who had invited him, at the man’s word the dry rock poured forth by God’s grace water which it did not possess by nature. Flowing from that same rock down to the present day [Note: [Col. 0443D] William of Malmesbury makes the same claim: “He leads perennial streams down to this day.”], it offers the faithful a life-giving drink and makes Dunstan’s name famous.

### He Reforms the Condition of England. He Corrects the Books

Dunstan, then, invested by the Roman pontiff, as we have said, with the white robe of his apostolate, and appointed patriarch both to the whole English people and to the other regions subject to the English kingdom, hastened to visit the cities of each district, so that if anyone was unfamiliar with the name of the faith, he might preach to him, and so that he might instruct those already of the household of faith in good works according to apostolic tradition.

It was not easy for any of his hearers not to be teachable, because such subtle understanding of matters and such eloquence of speech were in him that nothing could be found wiser, expressed more elegantly, or heard more pleasantly [Col. 0443B].

When he had been granted rest from external affairs, he then remained more closely with God, devoting himself to sacred vigils, reading the divine Scriptures, or correcting copies of them. His greatest concern was never to be idle from divine works.

At one time he distinguished true judgment between one man and another; at another he calmed the troubled minds of men with peaceful speech; he dissolved the foolish marriages of some [Note: [Col. 0443D] See below, in Osbert’s fragments, what he did against a certain earl who was bound to an unlawful marriage.]; he refuted the heretical opinion of others; here he renewed what had been neglected, there he built new things. He neither undertook unnecessary buildings nor neglected necessary ones.

He aided widows, orphans, and strangers from the just revenues of the Church; he possessed money not as an estimation of profit but as an acquisition of piety; he devoted all his effort to his country and was more concerned to avert its destruction than his own dangers.

Therefore the king, trusting his life to Dunstan’s counsel and receiving everything he said as though it had been spoken from the mouth of the Almighty, established whatever had to be established and condemned whatever had to be condemned.

With this counselor’s support, he drove from every part of his kingdom all the ministers of diabolical wickedness: thieves, sacrilegious persons, perjurers, violators of faith, makers of poisons, and seekers after lust; likewise all who had conspired against their country, those who had raised their hands against their parents, and even women who had murdered their husbands by adulterous deceit; finally, all whom he knew to be living under God’s anger. He banished them all to prolonged or perpetual exile [Col. 0443D].

By this man’s counsel also, all ministers of the churches who, having rejected the ministry of their profession, were accustomed to spend their lives either devoted to hunting [Note: [Col. 0443D] Dunstan also forbade the king to hunt on the Lord’s Day, as Osbert relates below], or occupied with profitable business, or disfigured by the shamelessness of sleeping with women, were decreed either to be restrained by strict punishment or swiftly expelled from the churches [Col. 0444A].

As a result, when the ministers of certain most illustrious churches preferred pleasure to honesty while deliberating what course to choose, they were expelled from those churches by royal sanction [Note: [Col. 0443D] The Saxon Chronicle, under the year 964: “Here King Edgar expelled the priests of the city, namely of Winchester, from the Old and New Monastery, and from Chaterica and Middeltuna, and established monks in their places; and he appointed Ethelgar abbot of the New Monastery, Ordbyrht of Chaterica, and Cyneward of Middeltuna.” Read above the Acts of Saint Ethelwold, bishop of Winchester.] and left their places to better men and to men of another Order.

As a result of these institutions of the most holy discipline, the worship of the divine grew so greatly in the English kingdom that even the noblest and most powerful in the world, despising all the splendors of the world, fled to divine service; and those whom the ecclesiastical Order had admitted competed in virtue, knowing that no one could attain honor whom the merits of virtues did not assist.

Because of the excellence of this discipline, such steadfast peace and such abundance of goods came into being that you might think all the elements of the world, and even God, the Creator of the elements themselves, smiled upon the king’s reign [Col. 0444B].

Thus the pontiff’s wisdom dictated the king’s justice; the king’s justice obtained God’s mercy; and God’s mercy provided abundance of all things.

### 35. He Assigns the King Seven Years of Penance for Violating a Virgin

But the Evil One, wishing to disturb these common joys of the whole Church, inflamed the mind of the most Christian king with love for a virgin devoted to God [Note: [Col. 0444D] Read Osbert on this virgin in the Appendix to this Life.], so that, since he had been unable to cast Dunstan from the path of justice, he might attempt to cast down the man whom Dunstan especially loved and upon whom the strength of the whole religion rested.

After the sin committed against the veiled virgin had been made public and brought before the hearing of the people, Dunstan, overwhelmed with the deepest grief both because of the crime and because of the king’s disgrace, immediately approached him as another Nathan approached another David sleeping with Bathsheba—another Nathan, but far more severe—and fearlessly burst in upon him in fury.

The king rose to meet the approaching pontiff and extended his hand to lead him to the royal throne. Dunstan refused to give him his hand, turned his eyes upon him with a certain indignation of spirit, and said:

“You dare touch the hand of a pontiff, though you did not fear to seize a virgin betrothed by God’s gift? You have committed adultery with the bride of your Creator, and do you imagine that the bridegroom’s friend can be appeased by some service of yours? I do not wish to be a friend to one whose enemy is Christ.”

Terrified, therefore, by the thunder of these words, the king fell at the feet of the pontiff who rebuked him. At once he tearfully confessed his crime and humbly begged forgiveness.

When the pontiff saw this, he was overcome with pity; and, as the king was drenched with tears, he too, wet with tears, raised him from the ground. Then, after explaining the magnitude of the sin at length and rendering him prepared for every satisfaction, he imposed upon him seven years of penance:

- throughout that period he was not to wear the crown of the kingdom;
- each week he was to observe a two-day fast;
- he was to distribute lavishly among the poor the treasures of his ancestors;
- in addition, he was to found a monastery for virgins consecrated to God, so that he who had taken one virgin from God through sin might gather more to him through many generations of the world;
- he was also to expel from the churches clerics who acted wickedly and introduce companies of monks;
- he was to establish laws that were just and acceptable to God, write them down, and command the peoples throughout all the borders of his empire to observe them.

Nothing therefore remained that the king fulfilled less fully or less diligently than his spiritual director had commanded.

When, in the seventh year, the period of penance had been completed as the appointed term returned like a jubilee, the holy pontiff summoned all the princes of the English realm, the bishops, abbots, and every rank of ecclesiastical dignity. In the presence of the entire multitude of the English people, he placed the crown upon the king, while all rejoiced and praised God in Dunstan with indescribable cries of jubilation.

### 36. He Silences the Complaints of the Expelled Clerics

Meanwhile, the clerical Order was living in such disorder in certain places that it not only possessed nothing superior to the life of secular people, but lay far beneath it in disgraceful conduct.

For this reason the troubled shepherds of the churches approached Dunstan as their own primate, explained the bad state of affairs, and sought counsels of correction. But he pronounced sentence by the authority entrusted to him against the wicked men:

“Either one must live canonically,” he said, “or leave the churches.”

As a result, the clerics of many churches, refusing to be corrected under the condition proposed, were expelled by the pontiff’s authority.

When they approached the king [Note: [Col. 0445D] Read Osbert concerning what happened in this matter to the canons of Winchester. William describes the affair in Book II, *On the Kings of the English*, chapter 9, where he says that a certain Elfer “overthrew almost all the monasteries that the most reverend monk and bishop of Winchester, Aethelwold, had built in the province of Mercia,” insolently doing so in order to insult Dunstan. Baronius assigns the Council of Winchester to the year 970 and calls it a general council of all England, convened indeed at the command of Pope John XIII; he proves this from the Acts of Saint Oswald, concerning whom more below. About the same time Dunstan subscribed various charters for the monastery of Crowland in Ingulf.], or those whom the king’s favor had made his intimates, they accused Dunstan of injuries, declared themselves lovers of virtue, and asked that a meeting be held in the king’s presence.

Dunstan, unwilling to oppose what they seemed reasonably to request, came to Winchester after a council had been summoned. There he gained victory over his adversaries by the judgment of the entire council.

When they saw that nothing remained to them by right, they resorted, with the help of the king and the princes, to entreaties. They begged the bishop to have the persons who had been introduced expelled from the churches and the expelled persons restored.

While the man of God hesitated and offered no answer to their requests, something marvelous and unheard of in the ages occurred: behold, the form of the Lord’s body, fixed upon the standard of the cross and placed in a higher part of the house, expressing human features, silenced everyone’s voices, saying:

“Let this not happen.”

At this voice the king and nearly all the elders, terrified almost to the point of death, filled the courtyard alike with shouting and the praise of God.

While these adversaries lived, the disputes ceased, until the former discord was renewed through the succession of their sons. These men departed, taking as defender of their iniquity Heornelinus, bishop of the Scots, a man almost invincible in both ingenuity and eloquence. With swelling spirit they went to the man of God at a village called Calne and brought forward their grievance.

Dunstan, however, broken by long old age and by the great labors of the Church, had by then set everything aside except prayer. Nevertheless, lest the unjust party, once defeated by a divine miracle, should now boast of achieving victory, he hurled this missile of response against his enemies:

“Since so much time has passed without your presenting any occasion for accusation, but now, when I am growing old and devoting myself to silence, you strive to revive your ancient complaints, I confess that I do not wish to conquer you. I commit the cause of Christ’s Church to Christ the judge.”

He spoke, and the judgment of the angry God confirmed what he had said. Immediately the house was shaken, the upper room was loosened beneath their feet, and the enemies were thrown to the ground and crushed beneath the weight of the falling beams. But where the saint reclined with his companions, there was no collapse of the ruins.

### 37. Deaths of Kings. A Change of Kingdom Foretold

King Edgar, however, carried off by an untimely death, left his son Edward as heir both to the kingdom and to his character. When certain palace nobles refused to consent to his election [Col. 0446C], Dunstan seized the standard of the cross which, according to custom, was carried before him, stood in the midst, displayed Edward to them, chose him, consecrated him, and showed him the affection of a father and teacher throughout his life.

What they had shortly before considered grievous was turned into joy for all: they had thought that the young king would be inhuman, would disregard the counsels of the wise, and would do everything according to his own desire. But after they learned that the opposite was true, they themselves adopted the opposite view, and it greatly displeased them that they had disliked the king.

After he had been killed three years later by the treachery of his stepmother [Note: [Col. 0446D] William calls her Elfreda. In Book II, *On the Bishops*, chapter 8, he says that Elfrida, the wife of King Edgar, built the monastery of Wareham in honor of the holy cross, “stricken with remorse over the undeserved killing of her stepson Edward, of whose death she herself was both conscious and the author.” John Bromton says that before his death Dunstan absolved Queen Alfrida, “who afterward,” he says, “living in chastity throughout all the days of her life, happily completed her life in the Lord.”], his brother Ethelred obtained the scepter of rule.

Although this event was displeasing to Dunstan, either because Ethelred had come to the kingdom through the shedding of innocent blood or because he possessed little prudence and courage, it was nevertheless not advisable to resist, since he appeared to be the king’s son and then the nearest heir.

Yet on the day of his consecration, after the crown had been placed upon him, Dunstan is said to have foretold this to him:

“Because you aspired to the kingdom through the death of your brother, whom your shameful mother killed, the sword will not depart from your house, raging against you throughout all the days of your life and destroying those born from your line, until your kingdom is transferred into a foreign kingdom [Note: [Col. 0447D] This happened during the time of the Danes, shortly after Dunstan’s death, as related below in his Translation.], whose customs and language the people over whom you rule do not know.

“Nor will your sin, and the sin of your mother, and the sin of the men who took part in her wicked counsel be expiated except by prolonged vengeance.”

### 38. The Deaths of Athelwold and Others Are Foretold

At this time it happened that Athelwold [Note: [Col. 0447D] We related his life above under the year 984, to which the Saxon Chronicle assigns his death.] the bishop of Winchester came to Canterbury with another bishop, from Rochester. Their arrival brought great joy to Dunstan, because through his care they had been raised, by education, learning, and various disciplines of virtue [Col. 0447B], to the highest honors of the Church.

After several days had passed in mutual conversation and rejoicing, the archbishop left the city, wishing to proceed to the place of the Mansionary of Christ Church. They accompanied him and escorted him until the road divided them, directing each man separately to the place where he intended to go.

When evening was already approaching and they were still far from their destination—for they had left the city somewhat later than the hour required—the bishop of Rochester begged the archbishop to turn aside to a nearby estate of his church and spend the night with him; in the morning, if he wished, he could continue his journey.

He graciously agreed to the request and said:

“If our brother Athelwold wishes to come with me, there will be no delay in my coming.”

The bishops therefore agreed to this, and together they entered the lodging prepared for them.

The golden light had already driven away the shadows of night when the blessed men set out and climbed a hill. From there they were to part from one another with reciprocal words of peace.

The high priest of God extended his hand to bless and dismiss the lesser bishops who had been seated with him. At once he burst into tears—so great a flood that he could scarcely force a voice from his holy breast.

The bishops were alarmed at this unusual action and anxiously sought the cause of his tears. After a short while they received this answer to their questions:

“I weep for this reason: I know that you will soon die.”

They replied:

“Do not bring such a dreadful prophecy upon us, most holy Father. We shall not die; rather, we shall see one another safe and sound again and again.”

He confirmed what he had said with this response:

“What I have said must happen. You will die to this world but live to God. You will die, no longer remaining in this life, but you will go to God and live eternally with him.”

The bishops therefore turned away from one another, sorrowful for one another, but each more concerned for himself with pious fear.

The bishop of Rochester, returning to his city, fell gravely ill as soon as he entered it and, after a few days, as the truthful prophet had foretold, departed from this world.

Athelwold, however, before reaching the city of his own see, was seized by his final bodily illness and entered the dwelling of the heavenly see.

The venerable Father was deeply saddened by his death, whether because Athelwold had always been devoted to the most holy religion, or because he had left the living a major occasion for dispute over appointing a successor. He therefore asked the Lord to be a merciful provider for the abandoned Church.

At once, while he prayed, his familiar companion, the apostle Andrew, appeared and told him that God had heard his prayers. He instructed him to bring Elfegus, abbot of Bath, and to appoint him, by divine counsel, bishop of the Church of Winchester.

Thus Dunstan immediately obtained from God, through the apostle as interpreter, whatever he himself had desired. He in turn repaid the apostle with honor, striving to show him devotion in every service, building basilicas in his name and adorning those that had been built with gifts.

### 39. The Siege of Rochester. The King’s Avarice Is Punished

At a certain time, when the aforesaid king was besieging the city of Rochester because of certain disputes, and, finding it difficult to capture it, was invading the patrimony of the blessed apostle by laying it waste, the most blessed pontiff commanded him to cease from his folly, declaring that Andrew was as ready to provide assistance as he was vigorous in avenging wrongdoing, and that the king would experience his power himself if he did not stop harassing his inheritance.

Dunstan, disregarded by the king, sent the same warning again through messengers who hurried back and forth. In addition, he sent one hundred pounds of silver. The king accepted the money and withdrew from the siege.

As soon as this was reported to the pontiff, he was astonished at the man’s greed and arranged to write to him:

“Because you have preferred money to God, silver to the apostle, and your greed to my will, the evils that the Lord has spoken will swiftly come upon you—evils such as have not existed from the beginning of the English people’s rule until that time.

“Nevertheless, these things will not happen while I live, because the Lord has also spoken this.”

All these events happened in this way, as one may read in the annals and see in our own times.

### 40. He Sees His Mother in Heaven and the Blessed Mary

But now, in order to address more confidently in the service of devotion that blessed man of whom we are speaking, and thus proceed with tearful eyes to his happy passing: what contemplation could be greater, O wondrous Father, O incomparable Father? What contemplation could exceed the minds of all mortals—that in this mortal life you should see either the Mother of God or your own mother in eternal life?

You were led into heaven; you were present among the blessed ranks; you delighted in the melodies of the angels joining that same mother of yours to the eternal King as in a bridal chamber, while their instruments resounded with the sweet chant, “Kyrie eleison” [Note: [Col. 0448D] B. writes that this occurred in the little church of the blessed Father Augustine.].

When you were accused of remaining silent, because amid such joys of eternal life you alone ceased from divine praises, although you ought especially to have rejoiced in honor of your parent, and when you replied that you were ignorant of such great sweetness, how briefly and sweetly were you taught by the citizens of that city, so that you burst into these words in song:

“O King, Ruler of the nations, save the Christian race still journeying on earth, so that they too may return from enmity to grace, and that through them the losses caused by the fall of the angels may be restored.”

But with what lips of exultation shall I proclaim that you saw the Mother of the Lord and Savior, Queen of the world and Lady of the angels, with your virginal eyes—not surrounded by a vestal choir, but encircled by a virginal crown?

Happy your eyes, which were able to see her whose most chaste womb deserved to bear the Maker of heaven and earth! Happy your eyes, to which it was granted to see her whom the angels revere as more beautiful than the daughters of Jerusalem, whom human beings desire, whom hell fears, and whom every creature marvels at as its mistress.

Nor were you happy only because you were able to see that unique glory of the whole world. You were also able to hear her honey-sweet voice, by which she encouraged her virgin companions to praise together the King of the ages, temporally begotten from her flesh. She sang the following words of the wise man and senator Sedulius:

“Let us sing to the Lord, companions; let us sing his honor.

“Let the sweet love of Christ resound from a devout mouth.”

When this had been taken up by other virgins, others recited the verses that follow:

“The first fell headlong, proud from the great light:

“So when man grew arrogant, the first fell headlong.

“Because of the merit of one, all the lesser ones perished:

“All are saved because of the merit of one.

“She alone was a woman through whom the gate of death was opened;

“From her alone, a woman, life returns.”

And in this manner the pairs of verses of the entire poem proceeded, with those first verses always being repeated that were spoken by the Mother of the Lord:

“Let us sing to the Lord, companions; let us sing his honor.

“Let the sweet love of Christ resound from a devout mouth.”

### The Author’s Apostrophe

These things, most worthy of pontiffs, you were able to see with the keenest power of bodily eyes transformed into spiritual power; these things you, intimate investigator of heavenly mysteries, were able to hear; you were able to be present at such great and astonishing events.

O holy purity of your soul, and pure holiness, which the supreme dignity of the heavenly city so honors! O glory and reward of virginity, who so rejoices together in the dignity of both virginal and angelic nature!

But behold, it is beyond the strength of the living to linger over the praises of your life while you lived in the body; how much less shall we be able to speak fitting praises of you who have passed away and reign eternally with Christ?

May almighty God, through your most powerful merits [Col. 0450A], grant that we may at least describe the end of your life in however small a measure of praiseworthy speech; so that, although we were not permitted to have you always living bodily among us, we may at least, by contemplating your most precious death, recognize your eternal life, love it after recognizing it, and by loving it obtain from God through you, most compassionate Father, some portion of blessed reward.

Meanwhile, let the devout hearers of so many miracles learn from your example to live soberly, frequently celebrate sacred vigils, and devote themselves to chaste prayers. You deserved to share in such and so many joys because, while others slept, you remained awake in holy desires, prayed, and thought without interruption upon your final hour.

Yet it was not sufficient to do these things in the secrecy of your chamber [Col. 0450B], unless you also visited by night, amid the cold, the church of the blessed Father Augustine [Note: [Col. 0449D] Osbern correctly gives the year of Dunstan’s death as 988. He is mistaken, however, as at the beginning of the Life, in assigning the year of the English arrival in Britain: according to Bede, it occurred not in 428, as he supposed, but in 448. The day of the Ascension noted here agrees with this.], and from there proceeded to the nearby temple of the aforementioned virgin to see this glory of God.

### Signs Are Given Concerning Dunstan’s Death
### 41. The year twelve short of a thousand from the Incarnation of the Word, and the five hundred sixty-third from the arrival of the English in Britain

Thus, in the year twelve short of a thousand from the Incarnation of the Word, and the five hundred sixty-third from the arrival of the English in Britain, the most holy and God-beloved Dunstan, leaving behind the fleeting light of the present life, reached the light endowed with blessed and eternal joy, where he shines like the sun from the radiance of God and eternally possesses the everlasting day—in the thirty-third year of his patriarchate [Note: [Col. 0449D] Rather, the twenty-seventh, as it is read both in William [Col. 0450D] and below in the account of his translation. For Dunstan succeeded Odo in the year 941, according to the Saxon Chronology.], and approximately the seventieth of his birth—when he was already filled with every gift of virtue and wearied by his desire to see God [Col. 0450C].

His venerable passing, foretold both by himself and by others through many revelations, brought joy to him and profound grief to others: joy to him, because he rejoiced that what he had possessed more delightfully through hope during life, he would see in reality and enjoy forever; grief to the rest, because they thought that no one who might thereafter excel equally in divine and human matters would appear on earth.

But, setting aside the varied accounts of his many revelations, we shall demonstrate each of the matters we have proposed by only one testimony for each. The feast of Christ’s Ascension preceded the day of blessed Dunstan’s glorification by three days [Note: [Col. 0450D] William reports this word for word in Book II of *On the Bishops of the English*, chapter 2, where he speaks of the bishops of Helmeham. Among them he lists Algar as the fifth, and from this passage infers his holiness.].

As the dawn of that great day arose, a certain priest named Algar [also Elfgarus], eminent in learning and conduct, whom we later learned shone forth as a noble bishop at Helmeham, was keeping an all-night vigil in the Church of the Savior, performing the sacred honors of the Lord’s Ascension and stretching his mind toward contemplation of heavenly things. Transcending himself and all the affairs of this world, he saw Dunstan presiding on the episcopal throne and dictating canonical ordinances to the clergy.

And behold, through all the doors of the church there entered infinite hosts of invading angels [Col. 0451A], shining in the whitest robes, glittering with golden crowns, proclaiming “Holy” with the Cherubim and Seraphim, and as though bearing a divine message. When, in ordered ranks, they stood beside the seated bishop, they addressed him with this greeting:

“Greetings, our Dunstan,” they said. “If you are ready, come and enjoy our gracious fellowship.”

Dunstan replied: “You know, holy spirits, that today Christ has ascended into heaven, and that it is our duty to refresh God’s people both by word and by sacrament; therefore I cannot come today.”

Then the holy spirits said: “Be ready to cross over with us to Rome on Saturday and sing ‘Holy’ eternally before the supreme pontiff.”

### On the feast of the Ascension the holy man speaks to the people and announces his death to his followers

### 42.

When, therefore, the day of eternal recompense had been announced and Dunstan had been divinely persuaded to consent, the angels who had appeared immediately disappeared. But the priest, who had been such an evident observer of these events, watched in astonished silence to see their outcome.

While, amid the sacred joys of that same day, the Gospel reading was being recited in which we read that our Lord Jesus Christ appeared to his disciples after his resurrection and, reproaching their unbelief and hardness of heart, gave them the command to preach the Gospel of the kingdom throughout the whole world, to announce faith and baptism, to offer salvation to believers, and to threaten condemnation to unbelievers [Col. 0451C]; and while, to confirm these things, he entrusted them with the power to perform signs—casting out demons, speaking new languages, taking up serpents, extinguishing the poison of deadly drink, and laying hands upon every illness for healing (Mark XVI, 14–18)—when this Gospel reading had been proclaimed, and afterward it was added how Christ ascended into heaven before the eyes of those to whom this power had been entrusted (Acts I, 9), the bishop came forth from the sanctuary to discuss these same things more extensively with the people and to impress the remembrance of God’s mercies more deeply upon their hearts.

He spoke, therefore, as he had never spoken before, showing by what reason the Son of God had assumed flesh, why he had accomplished the salvation of the human race only by dying, how, rising from the dead, he had conquered the prince of death, and how, attended by angels, he had entered heaven.

Then he taught that the blood of Christ is incomparably superior to all creatures, and that the world could place such confidence in the shedding of that blood that, even if someone possessed the sins of the entire world, he ought not despair because of either the number or the magnitude of his crimes, provided he had the Mediator of God and humanity as his advocate.

Amid these happy joys of a blessed promise, the bishop was brought back to the altar, transferring, by the Lord’s all-powerful words, the appearance of bread and wine into the true substance of Christ’s body and blood.

The hour of blessing the people had now arrived, and the blessed man again came forth to the people, wishing to announce his departure to them, but he was recalled by his love for the sweetness of his children. Accordingly, he exhorted everyone to direct their whole attention toward that place where Jesus Christ, our head and beginning, had gone before them on that very day. Having given them the blessing of his authority, he prayed that the Holy Spirit might be present with them, as the Son of God had promised when the heavenly cloud received him as he returned to the Father: “I will send you the Spirit of truth, so that he may remain with you forever” (John XIV, 16).

When the most blessed bishop had dwelt at length on these matters, they saw that his face was like the face of an angel of God, so that it was truly and visibly recognizable [Col. 0452B] that the Holy Spirit whom he invoked had deigned to reveal the presence of his majesty.

When he wished to turn back to the altar, the people sighed after him, still desiring to see his desirable face and enjoy his conversation—as though they had been taught by the instruction of that same Holy Spirit that they would not see him again in the flesh.

After confirming them three times in the love of the eternal Trinity, and after offering the kiss of his peace and charity, he could no longer conceal the glory that awaited him. He asked them to remember him, said that the day of his calling was at hand, and declared that he would not remain with them any longer in this world.

Then one would have thought that the whole day of judgment had arrived and that all the ages had gathered into their final hour, so great was the confusion of the grieving people, so mingled with tears were the cries of the clergy, and so pitiable was the distress of widows and orphans [Col. 0452C].

The priest who had witnessed such a marvelous ecstasy in the church, having recognized that he himself had experienced it not in an image but in the reality of things, openly disclosed to everyone, amid great groans, what he had seen.

The most precious Father consoled their grief kindly, as far as he could, returned to the altar, and, having received the meal of eternal life, entrusted both himself and all committed to his care to the eternal Shepherd.

### He is refreshed by food and carried from the earth; he addresses his followers

### 43.

Then he entered the refectory joyfully and nourished all who gathered around him both with bodily food and with the sustenance of spiritual life.

After the meal—or rather, after the final supper—he again entered the church of Christ with the brothers. He marked out the place of his burial, visible to all ascending to Christ’s altar, and went up to the upper chamber to rest, in keeping with the season of summer.

The grieving household of the church surrounded him as he rested and, whether troubled by fear for themselves or by his death, filled the place with dreadful lamentation and tears. While he comforted them with the holy reasoning he always used and instructed them more carefully in the hope of the future age, they saw the man moved from the earth by an invisible power of God and, once moved, lifted to the highest roof of the house.

Those who had stood nearer a moment before, terrified by the extraordinary miracle, all fled from their seats. Yet they stood leaning against the walls and thresholds of the enclosures, gazing upward from a distance [Col. 0453A], wishing to see how the matter would end. They thought that he would either be carried away with his flesh like Elijah or be taken from them in some other unusual manner.

But soon, gently lowered with the same sweetness by which he had been carried upward, he summoned all who had fled and soothed them with this address:

> “You have seen, my children; you have seen, my dearest ones, where God is calling me, where God’s ineffable mercy is inviting me. The path of my journey has been shown before your eyes, so that none of you may distrust the reward of attaining heaven if he has been a diligent follower of my life.
>
> “Neither will the dwelling of Erebus hold my soul, nor will the foul face of the abyss hold my soul; neither will unquenchable fire nor the undying worm hold my soul. What I embrace is above; above is the place to which I climb.
>
> “Therefore, imitate my life if you wish to be followers of my journey. Learn always to know the will of God, and, when you know it, wish to prefer nothing to it. But if you recognize that you have deviated even slightly from doing his will, turn at once to implore his mercy, lest, while you have shown less reverence than you ought, you be judged not only transgressors but also unbelievers.
>
> “Do not seek merely to appear good, but to be good; and do not seek merely not to appear evil, but not to be evil. For this is the greatest evil among human beings: all wish to appear good, but do not wish to be good; no one wishes to appear evil, yet they do not wish not to be evil.
>
> “Always pursue peace, and do not cease pursuing it before you grasp it in heaven. And, so that you may be able to attain it effectively, always hold in your mind that one who is most sweet; continually give thanks to him; humbly obey his commandments—him who willed that the unique sacrifice for all should be offered, in whom he was pleased that all fullness should dwell, and through whom he willed to reconcile all things, making peace through the blood of his cross, whether the things on earth or those in heaven (Col. I, 19–20).
>
> “I also declare to you that the nation of the English will suffer dreadful and prolonged evils from foreign peoples, but at the end of days God’s mercy will drip down upon it. It will be useful for you to remember these words, so that, whether these events occur for the correction of sins or for the perfection of virtue, you may always subject your souls to the divine disposition. Do not, like wicked children, love the one who flatters you; and do not despise the one who instructs you—which may this be far from you.
>
> “Indeed, no human being possesses either punishment so grievous or merit so excellent that it can earn the vision of almighty God, the vision of blessed eternity, the vision of eternal truth, of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Rather, if God does not regard the natural goodness of his mercy, a person suffers nothing that he does not deserve, by the just judgment of God, because of his own fault.”

### He receives the viaticum and is led into heaven by angels

### 44.

In these words the most blessed Father felt the strength of his body gradually failing, although his spirit did not know failure from its integrity. Thus he remained, serene in face, sober in understanding, and constant in instructive speech, throughout that entire day and the following Friday, so that all who came to commend themselves to him and seek the blessing of so great a Father declared that they had been refreshed and strengthened in many ways in the love of the divinity.

The promised Sabbath of blessedness had already dawned, and the time for Dunstan to rest from all his labors was now approaching, when suddenly a great crowd of children came running—children whom he himself had tenderly nurtured within the bosom of Mother Church and had led to a more excellent perfection of spiritual grace. With shouts and excessive wailing they complained that he was leaving them abandoned and that they were not permitted to die with him [Col. 0454B].

But he commended them into the hands of almighty God and strengthened them with a gracious blessing, then ordered the mystery of holy communion to be celebrated before him.

When he had received it with outstretched hands, offered from the heavenly table, he began to entreat God in this prayer:

> “Glory to you, almighty Father, who have given those who fear you the Bread of life from heaven, so that we may remember your wonders, which you have worked in the midst of the earth, sending us your Only-Begotten, true man born from a true Virgin.
>
> “To you, holy Father, we render due thanks: you created us when we did not exist, and when we were sinners you made us participants in this grace through that same Son of yours, our God and Lord, who does everything with you and the Holy Spirit, governs all things, and reigns throughout infinite ages of ages.”

As he spoke these words, his soul poured itself out from all the depths of its being toward the God whom he had always desired. He saw the blessed angels who had invited him to the heavenly banquet standing nearby and preparing heavenly service for him.

His happy soul rejoiced in their venerable company and gladly departed from the dwelling of his most holy body, setting out with them to contemplate the glory of the eternal Creator.

Behold how he was honored whom God judged worthy of honor! Behold how he entered into the joy of his Lord, who had proved a faithful distributor of the teaching entrusted to him! O entrails of God’s mercy, whose sweetness this man of God had always experienced! O heart of a man always ready for the will of God, who could say: “My heart is ready, God, my heart is ready” (Psalm LVI, 8)!

Behold, now he sings psalms in his glory, illumined by the light of the vision of God’s glory.

### He is buried

### 45.

The venerable priests of the Lord received the venerable body of the high priest and carried it into the basilica of the great Lord and Savior, amid the immense murmur of grieving crowds densely surrounding the bier, tearing their faces, beating their palms, and crying out in bitter voices: “Alas, alas, dearest father!”

There, in the place he had designated two days earlier [Note: [Col. 0453] According to Osbert, “which was before the steps by which one ascended to the altar of the Lord Christ.”], he was buried with every care [Col. 0455A]. Afterward, the place was decently covered with a more elevated structure, and he left to all—a sorrowful yet beloved memory of himself, both to those singing psalms in the choir and to those ascending by the steps to the altar.

I call it sorrowful because they had his tomb daily before their eyes, yet could not see his venerable face. I call it beloved because, although they lacked his visible presence, they knew that his invisible and incorporeal spirit rejoiced in heavenly faith and prayed more earnestly to God for mercy on their behalf.

### Events after his death

### 46.

After his death—if it should be called death, since eternal life followed it—all things took on such a contrary movement that everything seemed to mourn Dunstan’s death [Col. 0455B] and unable to endure his absence.

There was a change from supreme peace to intolerable war, from immense joy to overwhelming sadness, from abundance of all things to want of all things. Finally, the air itself was changed; the natural alternations of the seasons fell into discord with one another. Heaven did not heed the earth, nor the earth what was sown in it. A hostile invasion left a foul face everywhere: cities were destroyed, churches plundered, altars dug up, and the priests of the Lord killed.

Among them was the man of virtues, Elfegus, who was the fourth archbishop of Canterbury after the great Dunstan. After he had converted a great multitude of enemies to the Christian religion and daily rebuked those whom he could not convert from the error of unbelief, he was captured by those same people. After they had destroyed his city, slaughtered the innocent population, and both stripped and burned the holy church, he was led away in chains, tormented for seven months by various tortures, and, after all this, stoned to death by their hands; thus he sent his spirit to heaven in triumph.

Thus were fulfilled the things that the angels had foretold to Dunstan concerning prosperity, and that Dunstan had foretold to King Æthelred concerning adversity. Yet amid the severe troubles of the agitated people, the mercy of heavenly compassion was not absent. It displayed such marvels of radiant grace in memory of him that they were a terror to the reprobate and a consolation to the afflicted.

For his heavenly spirit did not act otherwise than if he came daily to earth again in his risen body. But we cannot relate everything about him because of its vastness, nor do we think that we should refrain from everything, lest it appear that there is nothing for us to relate.

Some things we have excerpted from his books of miracles, which now scarcely survive; others, performed upon others in our own age, we have seen, or, performed upon us, we have ourselves experienced. But here this little book ends, so that what we have undertaken may be taken up from another beginning.

> The just man, naked of vice, enters the blessed dwelling;
>
> The dark host grieves that it has been expelled from it.
>
> This man seeks heaven; that steep mass of Stygian fire
>
> He leaves, and the light earth is accustomed to float.
>
> A different dwelling and different rewards—how far
>
> The rising sun is distant from the setting sun.
>
> Over this one the Lamb commands, surrounded by a joyful host;
>
> Over that one Pluto presides with his wicked band.
>
> That dwelling burns with perpetual frost, snow, and hail;
>
> This dwelling always possesses springtime days.
>
> This one, adorned by a noble leader and a gracious citizen,
>
> Is festive in song and peaceful in unending quiet.
>
> You, venerable Dunstan, mingled with pious throngs,
>
> Practice joyful games in this region.
>
> The people of the star-dwellers show how great your merit is,
>
> For, having served you, they carried your soul to the stars.

# HERE BEGINS THE BOOK OF HIS MIRACLES

By the same author, Osbern the monk.

### The author asks faith of his readers

### 1.

In the preceding little book we said from which parents the venerable Father Dunstan was born and distinguished, whose kings’ reigns he ennobled, what progress he made in virtue, and how he gloriously migrated to the heavenly kingdoms.

Now, however, we intend to relate what his blessed spirit deigned to perform in this age after the laying aside of its bodily burden, so that all the English peoples of future times may recognize what honor and reverence they owe to a man of such great name.

But since we know that most, indeed nearly all, of the things to be written occurred in our own times, while a few happened in other periods but were reported to us by the most truthful testimony of the most trustworthy men, we invite all who deign to read these things to believe them for this reason: just as they will wish to be believed if they should perhaps wish to write about events occurring in their own times, so let them believe us when they hear narrated things that we were able to see.

For whatever estimate of truthfulness they wish to be held by those who come after them, they ought rightly to grant to those who came before them. If no events worthy of being written down should happen in their times, let them not immediately accuse us of falsehood, as though what does not occur at one time through the hidden providence of God could not occur at another time for the correction or reproof of human beings, since the grace of miracles always requires an appropriate occasion in circumstances and time.

Is Peter, the prince of the apostles, to be believed less because in our times he did not heal a lame man at the Beautiful Gate of the Temple? Or did the blessed evangelist John therefore not drink poison without harm and raise those who had perished from poison, because some impostor and slanderer has not seen these things?

It would be as though someone, hearing a pilot or charioteer praised because the one knows how to steer a ship skillfully in a storm and the other how to guide horses expertly into a course, should argue that this is beyond human nature merely because he believes that it cannot be done.

This must not be admitted. Rather, it must be believed that each thing depends upon its own time and order. Let those, therefore, who deign to read these things deign also to believe that, just as through the merit of our faith—by which we believed things we had not seen to be true—we were enabled to see some things, so they may one day receive the reward of faith and be able to see what they were able to believe with unquestioning faith when we narrated it.

Now we shall proceed to what we proposed and, as far as we can, relate briefly and clearly the order in which each event occurred.

### A blind man sees

### 2.

There is a village near the city of Canterbury called Leoham by its inhabitants. A certain man lived there who was afflicted by long-standing blindness of the eyes.

He was therefore warned in a dream to go to Dunstan, the father of his country, bewail the evils he had committed, and expect that through him he would recover the light he had lost.

The man told his family what he had seen. They approved and arranged for him to undertake the journey. Thus the blind man entered Christ Church and asked to be allowed to spend the night there.

“I have received such an instruction,” he said.

The following night, at midnight, all kinds of fragrances began to be perceived from the tomb of the man of God, while the blind man was meanwhile tormented by extremely severe stabbing pains in his eyes.

He cried out loudly, was miraculously healed, praised God, and joyfully praised Dunstan.

### Likewise, three blind women

### 3.

Three women also lived together in one house. They had been struck by similar blindness for a long time and were oppressed by the burden of poverty.

When the great Dunstan had lived in the body, he used to feed them, among the other poor dependents of the Church. After hearing news of the miracle, they encouraged one another in turn, saying:

“Why are we sitting here, when we hear that the father of our life has come to life again? Let us go to him, bewail our calamity, and ask for help. He who was accustomed to drive away our poverty will deign to dispel the blindness of our bodies. He will have compassion on us, who are dying of hunger, so that, once our sight has been restored, he may show grace to these poor women, who will henceforth live by the work of their hands.”

They spoke thus and, using a staff as their guide, began to travel along the road leading to the city.

When they reached the church door, they joined hands and entered. Falling before the memorial of the man, they expressed their grief in this supplication:

“Holy father, serene father, look upon these dependents of your mercy, so that either, as is your accustomed practice, you may provide them with food, or restore the light of their eyes by which they may pass through life.”

Again they said: “Most merciful and most powerful one, have pity on these, your poor little women.”

They prayed in this way, and while they were praying they clearly saw, bringing great joy to the people.

### A paralyzed priest is healed; in his ingratitude he relapses and dies

### 4.

A certain priest, Ceowlfus by name, superintendent of the people of Folcan, was a very wealthy man and held great distinction among his people.

For many years he had been so crippled by paralysis of all his limbs that he could neither visit his nearby estates nor touch the threshold of the church unless he were carried there on a litter.

His intimates therefore advised him to allow his wretched body to be carried to the memorial of Lord Dunstan. At first the rich man delayed out of embarrassment, scorning the company of the poor who were gathering there from every place in hope of recovering their health.

But when he had become unbearable even to himself because of the magnitude of his pain, he ordered a bier-like contraption to be fitted between the sides of horses and had himself placed upon it and dragged to the church doors where the aforesaid saint rested.

There, supported on the shoulders of his attendants, he was carried inside, followed by a considerable crowd of relatives calling upon Dunstan’s name in mournful voices.

On the second day, when the sick man had fallen into agony, he felt as though a human hand were moving throughout his body and touching every nerve of his entire body. Then, crying out, he leapt from the ground, stood on his feet, and, restored to complete health, began to exclaim:

“Blessed is the Son of the living God in his good servant Dunstan, and blessed is his good servant Dunstan in him. Truly merciful, truly almighty is Christ, who has servants so powerful and endowed with such great compassion.”

Immediately, after offering hymns and praises most devoutly to the Lord, he who had been carried by the hands of others ran on his own feet, mounted a horse, and departed rejoicing and cheerful with his whole retinue.

But after a few days he held a banquet in his house and summoned all his friends and acquaintances so that they might rejoice with him and congratulate him on the health he had obtained.

While they were feasting in great joy, they began to praise and glorify God, who, although powerful, had not rejected a powerful man, but had granted him, along with his poor, a period for repentance.

At this he replied indignantly:

“Do you count me among the other poor because you assert that I was healed among them? It is not so, for even if Dunstan had not existed, this would have happened to me.”

At these words his whole body trembled, and in a single moment he was struck by the same illness with which he had previously been dismissed, so that not one of all his limbs remained untouched by the attack.

He therefore cried out pitifully and shortly afterward died miserably.

### Health is restored to an invalid

### 5.

From that day great fear and great veneration for the holy man of God increased. Every day, now one, now several sick people, brought from distant regions, were restored to complete health.

Among them, a young man was carried on the shoulders of many people. He had a handsome face but had been unable to speak from birth, so that during fifteen years he had neither raised his head upward nor directed his step downward.

They lifted him high above their heads and offered him to the saint with these prayers mingled with tears:

“O Christ, salvation and creator of all, who willed that human beings should excel the other living creatures in this respect also—that they can speak and walk with upright heads—restore in this son of ours whatever nature left unformed or whatever illness hostile to health corrupted after it had been formed.

“For it belongs to you alone to bring what is not into what is, and to change what is into whatever forms you wish. Hear, therefore, the prayers of those who beseech you, for your own sake and for the sake of your beloved Dunstan.”

Then the sick man was lowered from the shoulders of those carrying him so that he might be brought closer to the saint’s memorial. As soon as he touched the tomb, he stood on his feet, raised his head and shoulders upward [Col. 0459B], and, with his tongue released—the tongue that had never before spoken—began to cry out in a loud voice: “Glory to God in the highest, alleluia.”

He continued thereafter in the full power of speech he had received, so that until the end of his life he spoke everything not only fluently but also eloquently.

### A woman born blind is given sight

### 6.

A poor woman also arrived with the rest of the crowd, carrying in her arms a three-year-old daughter who had been born from her womb without the light of sight.

After devoting herself anxiously for several days to prayer for her daughter’s recovery, and sensing that she had received no answer, she begged the entire clergy to assist her before God’s saint. She trusted that they would obtain what they desired all the sooner because they served him more familiarly than other people.

Moved, therefore, by compassion for the mother’s grief and the girl’s illness, the monks [Note: [Col. 0459] Thus the monks still constituted the clergy of the Church of Canterbury at that time. See nos. 16 and 21.] began to implore the saint with the most urgent prayer, asking him to deign, in his customary goodness, to come to the aid of their affliction.

On the tenth day, while the girl happened to be lying in her mother’s lap, she suddenly opened her eyes and saw everything clearly. Leaping for joy, she said:

“Mother, what are these beautiful things that I see?”

Her mother replied: “Do you see, my dear?”

She answered: “That beautiful man ordered me to see these beautiful things.”

The news was therefore shouted throughout the church that the girl, blind from birth, had been given sight by the great bishop Dunstan. Everyone crowded around the mother and daughter.

But since some of the clergy could not believe that sharp vision was present in eyes that were open, they wished to see a sign by which the truth could be investigated. They threw apples across the church floor, as is customary when playing with children, to test whether the little girl could follow and seize them without error.

She immediately leapt from her mother’s lap, pursued the rolling apples through their various winding paths, seized them, and returned swiftly to her mother.

Then it was discovered that the girl could see with her eyes open, although previously those eyes had appeared open without light.

### Likewise, an old woman who was blind

### 7.

An old woman was likewise brought to the memorial of the holy bishop so that, in extreme old age, she might recover the light of her eyes that she had lost in youth.

After devoting herself to prayer without obtaining any remedy for her health, she left the city, wishing to return to the place from which she had come.

She had already begun to cross the bridge of the river Stour when, suddenly deprived of the assistance of her guide, she cried out:

“Dunstan, Dunstan, I have not obtained from you the light I hoped for, and now I have lost my guide.”

Wonderful to relate, and difficult for the faithless to believe, she immediately saw very clearly some young men carrying timber across the middle of the bridge. She returned to the city with them and told everyone what had happened.

### The punishment and salvation of an excommunicated man

### 8.

What shall I say about Clement the German, whose name is more appropriately “Madman” than “Clement”? Because of the fault of lust and stubbornness, a priest had handed him over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh and had bound him with a sentence of malediction for seven years, so that he was not only continually trembling throughout his body in the same place but was also carried from place to place in an unsteady, rushing motion.

When he was brought into the Basilica of the Savior before the memorial of the great Dunstan, and the responsory “Behold the miracle” happened to be begun at the nocturnal vigils, he leapt high into the air, vomited out a demon together with blood, and thereafter remained quiet both in place and in body for all time, according to every proper quality of a sane person.

### A man who suddenly rises

### 9.

Or how shall I narrate the miracle performed in you, Elward—a man of gigantic stature, if the weight of a most severe illness had not pressed upon you for thirty years while you lay prostrate on the whole earth beneath the mass of your body?

Afterward, when you were offered to dear Father Dunstan and miraculously healed by him, you became not only beloved by everyone because of the miracle of the health you had obtained, but also an object of wonder because of the spectacle of your bodily size.

You learned thereafter, as a musician at banquets, to soothe the minds of the diners with song and to vary the melody on the pipes while singing. But you received this mark of exalted honor: all people, with one accord, called you Dunstan’s man and servant.

### A bow-legged man at last regains a straight gait; the author now relates what he himself saw

### 10.

It is also worthy of no small admiration that we learned the following from the report of a certain venerable old man, approved in every form of religious observance.

He said that the same father and lord of ours appeared in a dream to a certain bow-legged man and ordered him to come to the place of his bodily rest to be healed.

The man came to the place but found no health at all after praying for many days. Broken by weariness or despair, he departed and attempted to return by the road along which he had come.

He had already traveled nearly half the distance when the one who had previously appeared to him while he slept met him, severe in countenance and dignified in clothing. He asked where the man was coming from and where he was heading.

“I was ordered to go to the holy man of God Dunstan for the sake of recovering my health,” he replied, “but, having achieved nothing, I decided that I should return home.”

Then the other said:

“I am Dunstan, a fellow servant of all the servants of God. Occupied with certain necessary affairs, I could not visit the place of my bodily rest during these days or show my presence to the children remaining there. For Elfric, surnamed Bata, attempted to dispossess the Church of God, but, with me as its guardian, he could accomplish nothing.

“Now, however, the matter has been settled, and I am going to the place of my rest. See, therefore, that on that day and at that hour I find you there, so that through you I may show my grace to my fellow citizens.”

The invalid therefore returned to the city, told everyone what he had heard, and patiently awaited the appointed day.

Most astonishingly, on the day and at the hour when the saint had foretold that he would come, the bow-legged man rejoiced in the health he had received and filled the entire city with ineffable joy.

Thus far we have narrated the things conveyed to our knowledge by the testimony of others. Now we shall devote ourselves to narrating what has occurred in our own age.

### A virgin without sight beholds the light
### 11. A virgin deprived of light sees light

A certain virgin devoted to God came to the city for the sake of prayer. She was wretched because, from the time she had been born, she had never seen the light of this world; yet she was blessed because she had always sought the eternal light with ardent desire. As the birthday feast of the holy confessor of Christ, Bishop Audoen, happened to be approaching—a feast on which the memory of him and of all the others whose relics are contained in the church of the Saviour was celebrated with special veneration—she asked the custodians of the church to allow her to keep vigil there that same night.

Having readily obtained this permission because of the religious character of her life, she remained in the church, standing near the resting place of the blessed Father Dunstan, and spent the entire night in vigils and prayers. We had already begun the nocturnal praises; we were already singing the eighth responsory, “Let your loins be girded,” in measured voices, when the virgin of God, suffering an intense itching in her face, began to rub her eyes with the very firm pressure of her fingers. Immediately blood flowed out abundantly and ran down onto the cloth placed beneath her head. Modestly signalling to those around her, she said: “Give me a vessel to receive the blood, lest the holy ground be stained by its discharge.”

After they had done this, they also brought her water with which to wash her eyes. Meanwhile we boys turned our faces in that direction, glanced at her, and then again signalled our joy to one another by mutual looks and gestures. [Editorial note (Col. 0461): Silence is indicated here, both because it was night and because of the sanctity of the place; for it was unlawful to speak in church. See below, no. 13.] For we suspected—as was indeed the case—that our good father had accomplished something good.

The singing about girding the loins and carrying the burning lamps was now ending for the second time; the singers were now giving glory to the holy and undivided Trinity; and behold, she who had always girded her loins with chastity saw, for the glory of God, the lamps burning in the church, with great joy of heart.

She was therefore amazed at everything she saw. Golden plates, crosses, basins, and the keys of the church were shown to her, and she gazed upon all of them in wonder. She also examined the very human figures with immense astonishment. You could see everyone in the church shedding tears and praising God with modulation of the voice and jubilation of the heart. At dawn, we happened to go in to the teachers, to be beaten for the offences we had committed. And behold, the good man Godricus burst in from the side in a fury, shouting:

“You men here are spewing cruelty upon innocence, while our sweetest Father Dunstan is showing us sinners the sweetness of his mercy. Leave! You see the prerogative of the miracle once celebrated by the Saviour in the man born blind being celebrated again, and yet you dare to do something cruel? Leave!”

Thus we escaped the impious hands, and afterward entered the church. Then the signal of our most blessed father was sounded—the signal which he was said once to have made with his own hands. At its sound, the whole city gathered, wishing to see with their own eyes what they had heard when fame disclosed it. We therefore began with loud and tearful voices to praise the Lord our God, who through his blessed servant Dunstan had deigned to bless our times with such great joys. And although many thousands of people were standing in the church, you would not have seen a single person among them who did not weep piously and sweetly for joy.

### The author as witness of the miracle performed on a girl

### 12.

It was the vigil of the blessed apostles of Christ, Peter and Paul. The day was already declining, and the clergy were conducting the evening prayers in the church. By chance I had been serving at Christ’s altar with another boy of my own age, and, having completed the service, I was beginning to descend the steps. And behold, an old woman with a well-grown daughter came to meet us, falling down upon the steps and crying out:

“Have pity on me, boys of God, so that almighty God may have pity on us, granting you the advancement of virtue and happily bringing your childish years to mature age.”

But we, boys of that age and frightened by what the woman had done, stood rooted to the spot, tearfully asking the cause of her misery. Then she said:

“This daughter of mine whom you see was crippled from the tops of her shoulders to the ends of her fingers. Whether through the midwife’s madness or negligence, she was made deformed and maimed. I have heard that great divine power is present in this place, and therefore we have tried to come here on a long journey to implore him. Tell us what we should do.”

Meanwhile we looked at hands that were scarcely hands at all. The joints did not connect with the joints; rather, a discordant deformation produced an ugly massing of the bones. Her thumbs, bent backward, were rigid and without sensation. The remaining fingers had no recognizable form; certain roots protruding from the palm curved inward and, fixed into the hand, pierced it with their nails. This caused the sufferer unbearable anguish.

We therefore turned our eyes away, saying only: “Good woman, do not ask us what should be done. He who is able both to advise you and to procure the health of your daughter is near at hand. According to their faith, he is accustomed to help all who call upon him.”

Then she seized the hem of her daughter’s garment and drew her to the place. Immediately both women prostrated themselves upon the ground and worshipped the saint, assailing his goodness with tears and wailing. And truly they assailed it, for so quickly did the depths of his mercy open to them.

For Phoebus had not yet raised his head from the sea waves when the girl who had been contracted by disease began, with her veins ruptured, to lift her arms and extend all the joints of her hands. Though from childhood she had been unable to move her fingers, she now handled everything with ease.

Thus we ran up, saw, and wept; and at daybreak we praised the Lord our God with the rejoicing of the whole city.

### The cripple made upright

### 13.

A certain young man lived near the city who had been so weakened from childhood that, from the loins downward, his entire lower body was dead. He supported himself on two sticks, dragging half of his whole body behind him. On the day when the Son of God, having assumed flesh, deigned to die, he entered the church, worshipped with the rest of the multitude the banner of the cross on which, by dying, Christ destroyed our death, and, remaining near the body of the venerable Father Dunstan, awaited the joys of the approaching feast.

When the hour arrived at which our Lord Jesus Christ is believed to have risen from the dead after triumphing over the devil, a great tumult arose in the church: people were shouting that the young man was standing upright with his whole body, although for many years he had been accustomed to drag the lower parts of his body behind him. Although the clergy knew what had happened, they nevertheless waited patiently and joyfully for sunrise.

On the morning of the Lord’s Resurrection, an innumerable multitude from the whole city gathered in the church to see what divine power had done in the man whom they had previously known so well in his infirmity. They saw, therefore, and gave glory to God, crying out that Dunstan had served the good Lord during his life—he to whom, after death, it had been granted not only to live more blessedly, but also to bestow upon human beings the grace of his benefactions.

### Other miracles

### 14.

We also saw a boy who was contracted in all his limbs healed through the same holy man of God.

### The punishment of the novices remitted. A pagan’s corpse ordered to be cast out of the church

### 15.

[Editorial note (Col. 0463D): Osbert: “The feast of Christ's Nativity was approaching. It had long been an ancient custom in this monastery, on the fifth day before the feast, to torture with severe and excessive beatings the boys undergoing disciplined instruction in the schools; this suffering was inflicted upon the wretches not for offences committed, but through custom,” etc.]

One day, when the fury of the teachers was raging against the boys more fiercely than usual and no hope of intercession was available anywhere, they believed that this one and only remedy remained: to flee to the memory of the sweetest Father Dunstan and present him not so much as an intercessor as a defender against the ministers of impiety.

At first light, therefore, they went to him, asking for his mercy with many tears.
