The teachers were sitting in different places where the boys would have to pass, carefully watching for their exit from the church. And behold, the pious Father Dunstan appeared to them with a kindly face. Touching one of them with the staff he carried in his hand—this boy saw him with open eyes but was entirely unable to move—he began to speak:

“Let your weeping now cease, boys, for today I permit no one to trouble you. For this reason I have come, summoned by the tears of your grief. Now I shall go and lull the teachers who are watching for your exit into a very deep sleep.

“But you, boy who see and hear me speaking, once you know that you have been freed through my favour, will show me your gratitude in this: order the provost of this church, in my name, to have the newly baptized child who was recently buried beside me—the son of Earl Harold—cast outside. For it is exceedingly improper that the bodies of pagans should be buried where the divine mysteries are celebrated every day. If he, whether through fear or unbelief, neglects my command, let him know that nothing prosperous will proceed in this church until my command has been carried out in deed.”

[Editorial note (Col. 0463D–0464D): This Harold was king of the Danes, whose son Sweyn or Swegen invaded England in the reign of Ethelred or Aethelred; there, “after long living impiously among the pious, he is overcome by a lingering death and buried in that same place,” according to Thietmar, book VII, p. 94. The same writer, p. 95, records that Harald and Cnut, sons of Sweyn, again undertook an expedition into England in 1016; this is the expedition to which Dunstan's prophecy at the end of the Life, above, should be referred. Thietmar goes on to recount the martyrdom of Ælfheah, Dunstan's fourth successor, which, through erroneous report or lapse of memory, he falsely attributes to Dunstan.]

Having said this, he was received into the tomb. The one who had seen these things—then a boy, but now an elder of venerable age—was the man who had carefully urged us to write them without revealing his name. Immediately recovering his senses, he signalled to his companions and said:

“Did you see Father Dunstan? Did you hear whether he said anything?”

He then recounted everything in order, saying: “He said this and this.”

The boys therefore rose to enter the house of martyrdom [Editorial note (Col. 0464D): This is doubtless called the “house of martyrdom” because in it the boys paid penalties for their faults.] and passed before the first teachers: they were asleep. They passed before the second: they were asleep. They passed before the third and fourth: they were asleep.

A little later, they awoke and, deeply grieved that they had been mocked, were enraged. They resolved to take the fiercest vengeance upon the boys at the third hour of the day, since Dunstan’s protection had prevented them from touching them in the morning. For at that time the custom in the Church was that those whom the first hour of the day had preserved from punishment were punished more harshly at the third hour.

But Dunstan, always and everywhere faithful, so divided the aforementioned teachers from the boys at that same hour that they were free to think not so much about injuring the boys as about dealing with their own humiliation. Thus the boys escaped the danger of that day and, on the following day, watched the vigils of the Lord’s Nativity with joyful hearts.

The one who acted as the Father’s messenger faithfully reported what he had heard to the provost, but the latter, with an unbelieving mind, thought little of the report.

### What followed when this matter was neglected: the translation of Saint Dunstan

### 16.

How often, too, did he appear to the brothers in a nocturnal vision as he was leaving the church? When they wished to hold him back as he departed, he said:

“I cannot remain there because of the stench of the pagan boy, although baptized, who is buried in this church.”

Not long afterward, the church of the Saviour was consumed by fire. The walls fell, and nothing among all the monastery’s buildings remained unburned except two houses without which the monks could not remain—namely, the dormitory and the refectory—and as much of the cloister as was necessary to pass from one house to the other without being drenched by the rain.

From this it was sufficiently clear how great was the care that Father Dunstan had for us. Yet this ruin was changed for the better when the venerable man Lanfranc, archbishop—and at once the holiest and wisest of all who lived on earth in our time—arrived.

[Editorial note (Col. 0465D–0466D): In Osbert: “Lanfranc, abbot of the monastery of Caen, a man outstanding in wisdom, undertook the governance of the see of Canterbury. Arriving at Canterbury, as was fitting, on 18 Kalends of September, in the manner of an elected bishop, he was received by clergy and people as the father of so great a see and a man of immense renown. Having received episcopal consecration at Canterbury on 4 Kalends of September, he wished utterly to demolish and make narrower the church of the Saviour, which the aforementioned fire and age alike had rendered useless, etc. The bodies of Christ's precious bishops, Dunstan and Ælfheah, were raised.”]

When he wished to lay the foundations of a new church, and could not do so without translating the bodies resting within the precinct of the same church, he proclaimed a fast for all the people, so that the saints’ will might be made known as to whether their bodies should be transferred to other places.

On the day appointed for this undertaking, while all the people prayed, the clergy approached with candles, perfumes, and every kind of rejoicing. The priests prepared themselves to raise the shrine of the holy Father Dunstan from the earth without touching his body and to carry it with every care to a place prepared for it.

When they had taken it upon their shoulders, they were detained by certain soldiers of the church who had recently violated King William’s peace by killing two knights, namely the nephews of Scolland, who was abbot of the monastery of Saint Augustine situated outside the city walls. They feared that the deaths of the slain would be requited by their own deaths, and therefore, to avoid this evil, they were unwilling either to withdraw from the saint or to release his shrine.

Both the abbot and all those whose concern it was to grant pardon for the vengeance were summoned. They refused and were unwilling to let the death of the slain pass without vengeance. What, then, was to be done? The sacred body was carried away while the matter remained unresolved, and was placed in the oratory of the blessed virgin Mary.

At first light, while we were still resting in our beds, the abbot burst into the church surrounded by crowds of kinsmen. He ordered the brothers to be awakened quickly and said that he wished to speak with them about an urgent matter. When they had come, he approached the body of the saint, bent his knees, and tearfully burst out in these words:

“We have sinned against you, holy man of God, unwilling to show you the honour of our service in the sight of the people. Behold, now we both forgive the injury and ask pardon for the obstinacy of our minds.”

We marvelled at so sudden a change of affairs. We learned that they had been terrified by a vision of the holy man of God and had scarcely survived that night, because a priest of terrifying appearance, who seemed very like Dunstan in the images made of him, had tormented them with severe tortures and, after torturing them for a long time, had forcibly dragged them to be burned upon a blazing pyre.

Thus, compelled to do what they had refused willingly, they forgave the injury.

### Lanfranc perceives Dunstan’s favour in a temporal case

### 17.

At this time Archbishop Lanfranc entered into conflict with the magnates of the kingdom of the English, especially with the Bishop of Bayeux, Odo by name, who was the king’s brother and Earl of Kent, concerning the rights of Christ Church and certain lands unjustly taken from it in ancient times.

But, placing no confidence in his own powers—for just as he was incomparable in wisdom in the eyes of all, so in the sight of God he had always been especially admirable for his humility—he prayed that blessed Dunstan would be his aid in defending the case of his church. Having offered a saving sacrifice to obtain a favourable hearing, he sat quietly in the place, awaiting the advocacy of the lawyers and at the same time considering what he himself might bring against his adversaries or how he might answer each of their objections.

Then, while he was undergoing an ecstasy of mind, the saint of God appeared to him, standing between two men endowed with angelic dignity. He himself had an angelic face and showed Lanfranc a certain narrowing of the forehead and eyes, as though in assent.

Made confident by this vision that he would win the victory, Lanfranc fearlessly approached the council of the wicked and utterly scattered their defences with a torrent of arguments. He defeated all Christ’s and his own adversaries so completely that what belonged by right to his church was restored to Christ Church in its entirety. The same servant of the Lord gloried that this had been accomplished not by human wisdom but by divine power.

### And in a serious illness

### 18.

Some days later Lanfranc was struck by a very severe bodily illness and was wholly despaired of by the physicians. When he thought that the end of his life was already at hand, he sent a message to the brothers of Christ Church, informing them of what was happening around him. He desired the presence of the elders, so that, if he was not permitted to live longer in the body, they might—“to use his own words”—carry his dead body back with them to the city.

For the venerable Father was ill in a certain estate of the church far from the city, called Ealditune [or Ealdintune]. They therefore came to the place and found everything filled with tears. They wept with those who wept, unwilling to see a man brought to an end by death whom they knew they would never find another like.

But he, unable to bear either his own distress or the misery of his sons—for just as a mother loves her only son, so he loved each of us uniquely—turned his face toward the wall in order to implore the divine mercy with as many sighs as he could.

Immediately, being caught up on high, he saw what seemed to be an army of men clothed in white, with faces shining like the sun, mounted upon white horses adorned with golden trappings, and displaying to one another generous merriment with a certain joyful grace.

As he watched them pass with delighted eyes, he asked whose procession it was. He was told that it belonged to the lord Dunstan and that Dunstan himself was not far away.

Lanfranc therefore waited, examining the faces of each person passing by, eager to recognize above all the one from whom, above all others, he hoped to receive the remedies of salvation. And behold, the most blessed Father Dunstan came, surrounded on either side by groups of venerable elders. In every respect he wore the same appearance as the others, except that from the shoulders upward he rose higher than them all.

Lanfranc humbly advanced to meet him and, drawing up beside the rider, embraced his foot together with the stirrup upon which he seemed to lean, attempting to draw it toward himself in order to kiss it. But Dunstan, as though startled by the act—or perhaps wishing to show honour to Lanfranc—seemed to draw his foot back toward himself with both hands, bending his knee.

In this blessed struggle, Lanfranc returned to what he had been, and found himself so completely healed that no trace of illness remained anywhere in his body. He therefore gave thanks to God, by whose gift he had been able both to see Dunstan and, through Dunstan’s gift, to receive the health he desired.

He then summoned those who were reclining nearby and recounted in order what he had seen, declaring at the same time that he had recovered. But when they thought that he was speaking with an alienated mind, he said:

“Prepare an altar for me, for you will see the man who shortly before seemed scarcely able to move his lips offering sacrifice to God.”

Then, calling the elders who had recently arrived, he said:

“This will be for you a day of good news. Know that our Lord and Father Dunstan has been here and has healed me of every bodily affliction. Return, therefore, to the church, bar its doors behind you, approach the saint’s memorial, bend your knees, and give abundant thanks for the health restored to me.

“For I do not wish to come there in person now, lest people think that I am something extraordinary, as though I had been able to see the saints of God.”

They carried out his commands and brought great joy to the brothers, who had feared that the Father was dying.

### And in the illness of his chaplain

### 19.

A certain priest, the archbishop’s chaplain, had been tortured by so severe an attack of fever for eight months that, his flesh having been consumed, his skin scarcely clung to his weak bones.

At the very moment when the archbishop was restored to health, he too obtained the health he had desired from God. In the morning he entered cheerfully to see the archbishop—for he had learned that Lanfranc had recovered—and asked how his health had been restored. He was then asked in turn to say how he himself was.

“I am completely well,” he said, “because the one who in his mercy looked upon you when you were in danger of death has also, on your account, deigned to grant me health this night.

“I was lying in my bed, which was separated from yours only by a wooden wall, and in a vision I saw the blessed Dunstan celebrating the solemn Masses in the church of the Saviour, while I was serving him in the ministry of the subdiaconate. When I had read the epistle, I approached his feet, as is customary, to kiss them; I asked for his blessing, and, departing with his blessing, I recovered.”

Hearing this, the venerable Father Lanfrancus burst into joy and said:

“No trace of illness could remain in a place which the saint of God has deigned to illuminate by the grace of his visitation.”

### A prisoner’s chains broken. An opposing event

### 20.

At that time two events also occurred among us, which we thought should be attributed no more to blessed Dunstan than to the other saints resting there.

By order of the Bishop of Bayeux, a certain man had been thrown into chains because he had shot and killed a stag in the bishop’s forest after the animal had been roused by dogs and was rushing toward him.

Held in chains in the city of Canterbury, he visited the church day and night, shedding tears for his sins and arousing great affection among the people by the sound of the clanking chains around him. After he had done this continually for two years, one day, as he lay prostrate before the altar of the Lord’s cross, the chains broke apart in the sight of everyone standing around. The fetters were shattered into four pieces, and the nails were broken into tiny fragments.

He himself knew nothing at all of what was being done for him by divine power. When he rose from prayer, the bonds fell from his feet. He picked them up in his hands and proceeded through the midst of the brothers, who were praising almighty Christ for the miracle. He placed them upon Christ’s altar, offering to God as a gift what had been imposed upon him as a burden.

A few days later, when Archbishop Lanfranc had told this story to a powerful man, the latter replied:

“I too can relate something of this kind to Your Excellency, which I think you will regard as no less astonishing.

“Today is the third day since sixteen pirate ships, driven by a very strong wind, were cast upon the seashore. The men inside were partly swallowed by the waves and partly captured by the king’s officers. Together with their leader, a man named Baraba, they were bound in fetters. He wished to be called Baraba because he had always been excessively cruel and had killed a great many people with his own hand.

“But he escaped from his fetters and took the road leading to Canterbury, knowing that he would lose neither life nor limb if he could reach Christ Church as an asylum. When he was already near the city, however, as soon as he saw the church’s pinnacle and the golden cherub, he was repelled as though by the power of a heavenly cherub and could proceed no farther.

“He therefore struggled with all his strength against the empty air, yet always felt it as though it were an iron wall. Astonished, he stopped, then gathered his strength again and resumed the struggle as before. But repelled by the same power as earlier, he sprang back a greater distance than before.

“He tried to return by the way from which he had come; he could run as far as he wished. But if he wished to proceed in the direction he had planned, as soon as he saw the church he could not move his foot.

“Despairing, therefore, of his salvation and of God’s mercy, he said: ‘It is clear that I share the lot of the damned, since I am not permitted even to see Christ Church. What good is it to call upon a cruel Christ from whom one cannot obtain mercy? Let fortune take its course. I shall no longer attempt to flee; I shall return to the place from which I came and die there.’

“Saying this, he hurried back and recounted to many thousands of people what had happened to him. Afterward he paid penalties worthy of his deeds.”

When Lanfranc had heard this, he summoned me and ordered me to preach these things to the people. He added that the first man had been terribly repelled from the church because he had approached it with a deceitful heart, whereas the other had been miraculously freed in the church because he had daily sought to reach it with a devout spirit.

### A monk wishing to depart is prevented

### 21.

This event also deserves to be remembered forever [Editorial note (Col. 0469D): Osbert recounts this miracle more fully below.]: the mercy of Dunstan worked in a remarkable manner concerning Edward, archdeacon of the city of London.

Although he had flourished in worldly pleasures, when he saw that all the goods of this world were narrow and constricted, he betook himself to the one unchangeable and all-sufficient common good, God. He assumed the habit of holy religion in the church of Canterbury, under the rule of the aforementioned glorious man, Archbishop Lanfranc. There he lived honourably for several years and gained great favour among all his fellow inhabitants.

After this, however, the malignant spirit, jealous both of his conversion and of his manner of life, implanted in his mind, through certain hidden and persistent suggestions, a weariness of religion. It wished to lead him into such madness of mind that he would return to the world from which he had come, repeating his vomit and returning to his filth.

For the devil cast into his heart the pleasures of the world, the embraces of women, spacious houses, and the companionship of friends. He did not allow him to consider how sweet the Lord is to those who taste him, how great is the house of God and how immense the place of his dwelling, or how blessed is the company of the angels who praise God for ever and ever.

At last, overcome by the tempter’s persistence, he attempted to leave the church. Having prepared everything that seemed suitable for carrying out this sacrilege, he entered the church [Editorial note (Col. 0469D–0470D): That is, while “the brothers rested on their beds at the midday hour,” according to Osbert, who says that this happened “between the feasts of the Assumption and the Nativity of St Mary.”] to ask Saint Dunstan’s permission to depart and return to the world. He knew beyond doubt that nothing would prosper for him if he did not fear leaving after offending Dunstan.

When he rose from prayer in order to leave through the church door, he found Dunstan standing in the doorway with a staff. He was not then as Lanfranc had seen him, but terrifying in face, threatening in his eyes, and growling through biting lips:

“Go back, wretch, go back! Prostrate yourself before the almighty Lord and vomit from your heart the poison conceived by the devil.”

When the man stood there terrified and trembling, Dunstan raised his staff against him and said:

“You shall not leave; you shall die here.”

After he had said this, the speaker disappeared, and the man to whom he had spoken fell gravely ill. He was immediately taken to his bed, lived for two months in great distress, and afterward completed his life.

When the time came for him to give up his soul, he summoned those whom he had first held dear in brotherly love and recounted in deep contrition of heart everything that he had either arranged wrongly or had recognized as being to his own good.

Another brother, a young man of good character named Adrianus, confessed the same things before everyone, saying that he had both known of the plan and consented to the deed.

### Dunstan gracious to one who invokes him

### 22.

Some time ago, when I was on the island of Thanet, I was walking beside the seashore with a soldier who had invited me for his protection. I was observing the wondrous works of God that are found there and drawing material for good conversation from them.

From there our conversation turned to Father Dunstan, since I always regard it as the greatest gain whenever I find an opportunity to speak about him. At the mention of this name, the soldier suddenly grew completely pale and, as though sighing from the depths of his grief, said:

“Woe to me, ungrateful man, who until now have remained mindful of none of such great benefits!”

Then I said: “And what are these sighs of such distress?”

“You know,” he replied, “how hostile the abbot of Saint Augustine was toward me while he lived, when he wanted to seize the property that had come to me by inheritance.”

“I know,” I said. “And do you also know that his excessive conduct not only did me no harm, but even increased the honour that came to me?”

“I do not deny this,” I said, “but I do not know why you recall it now.”

“You shall know,” he replied. “On the night preceding the day appointed for the settlement agreed between us, while I was at home—for my house is nearby—I remembered that you often used to extol Father Dunstan in your arguments. ‘Now,’ I said, ‘I must find out whether he is as praiseworthy as I have heard.’

“I therefore bent down in prayer and said: ‘God of Father Dunstan, favour our side today.’ Then I entrusted my little body to rest. In my sleep I saw the city of Canterbury, the basilica of the Saviour, and the memorial of the Father. As though leaning upon it, I looked upon a man standing beside me, handsome in appearance, splendidly clothed, and holding a lamp of light in his hand.

“Terrified by his form, I said: ‘Who are you, most beautiful of men?’

“He replied: ‘I am the one whose help you prayed for a little while ago.’

“‘Good heavens,’ I said, ‘how quickly you come to pity the wretched! Do you know what the Lord threatens?’

“He said: ‘Do not fear his threats, nor value them highly at all.’

“Thus the soldier prayed. Afterward, turning to me, he said: ‘You know the rest: how you and I came together, argued, and convicted one another.’

“I said: ‘On that day the saint gave a great sign, because although the others were more numerous and had sharpened their wits, they departed defeated by a few who were less sharp.’

“Then I looked toward those who were present and indicated in words what I now reveal in writing.

### The author recounts a vision of himself
### 23

Now I shall pass to matters that concern my own person, as one perhaps less wise, and so shall impose silence upon my mouth and give my hands their rest.

At one time certain men were persecuting me with bitter hatred, and they were unwilling to cease harassing me until, after inflicting great injuries upon me, they threatened to inflict still greater ones. The minds of those appointed as judges to hear our case had been alienated from me, whether by the favor or by the importunity of my adversaries, to such an extent that they could be swayed neither by entreaty nor by any argument. Despairing, therefore, of human assistance, I decided that I must seek the help of God alone and of this blessed man. Thus, at night, when everyone was asleep, I approached his memory with great confidence and assailed the multitude of his mercies with groaning voice and tearful eyes.

At last, weary in mind and anxious with grief, I withdrew and sought solitude, desiring, as sometimes happens, to relieve the pain of my heart by bodily rest. I had not yet arranged my body sufficiently for repose when, my mind passing beyond all ordinary bounds, I seemed to see in the court of a church a house whose size was marvelous and whose beauty was beyond measure. No one could reach it except by passing through a kind of inundation of waters. Yet the rule for those crossing was that, the nearer they approached the entrance of the house, the less they felt those waters.

I crossed with the others, and, as the waters grew shallower, reached the farther banks of the stream. Immediately, entering the house, I saw it all shining with a brightness greater than that of the sun, surrounded by a company apparently of saints rejoicing in an ineffable sweetness. Before the eyes of those looking there appeared a certain delicate beauty, transparent like crystal. I examined it more carefully, wishing to discover from where the radiance of that immense light flashed forth, and it seemed to me that the same splendor issued from nowhere else than the bodies of the saints.

When I asked what these things were, I was told that this was the clergy of the great Dunstan, and that he had been present shortly before, had celebrated the divine sacraments, and had departed before the communion antiphon had yet been sung, having ordered them to await the one who had lain down at his resting-place. I therefore wondered whether I might be that man.

While I was turning this over in my mind, those men rose, seized me, and set me in their midst, encouraging one another with alternating voices:

“Come, brothers, let us finish the Masses, since he is here for whose sake this delay was made.”

They therefore began to sing psalms in the sweetest and most melodious voices and invited me to accompany what they were singing.

I say to you, my friends: do not be terrified by those who persecute you.

At these voices I immediately awoke and ran to the saint’s tomb. I embraced its middle with both arms and cried out, saying with excessive joy of heart:

“You have come, dearest Father, you have come! You have come to one laboring in distress and humbly asking for your favor. Truly you are a saint of God, and whatever you wish, you can obtain from him. Now I shall approach the judges without fear, and today I shall dread no one’s threats.”

When the judges arrived, whose duty it was to bring the case to an end, those who had attempted to disturb me approached, and I too came forward and brought an accusation against my adversaries. Thus, with God’s help and Dunstan’s patronage, I defeated all who opposed me, so that they themselves fell through their own argument, while I not only escaped the injury done to me but also rejoiced greatly both in my defense and in my triumph.

*The author omits many things.*

### 24

I consider these things sufficient, most dear lords and fathers, either for making known the saintly man’s temporal labors or for commending his everlasting glory to the faithful of the Catholic Church—not because there are not more things, and perhaps greater things, that could be related in connection with these, but because I wished to narrate only those which, as I said in the preface, did not seem to exceed belief.

For who would immediately grant me credence if I said either that he had hung a garment upon a pillar of light, or that he had raised the extreme poverty of a kinsman to the greatest wealth by means of half a coin? Whom would horror not seize if he heard that a monk journeying to Jerusalem [Note: Osbert relates this miracle below. William mentions another, omitted by others, concerning a hanged thief whom Dunstan preserved unharmed.], surrounded by the army of the emperor at Constantinople, had been freed from their most troublesome assault merely by invoking that saint?

Who, I ask, would not be struck with astonishment on considering either that a thief, terrified by the saint, had left unharmed in the church court the objects he had carried away from the place of the saint’s rest; or that a citizen of Canterbury, stealing the property of Christ’s Church in defiance of the saint’s authority, had paid the penalty for his rashness a few days later?

You see the things from which I refrain, because I do not wish to go beyond the judgment of my listeners. Yet if I were to mention them, I ought not to be considered incredible, since there is no difficulty wherever the Lord Christ is the author of the deed.

Then we did as singers at banquets do: when a most beautiful song is being performed, they customarily cut short its middle section, both to remove weariness from their listeners and to arouse a greater delight in hearing it again. Finally, we wished to obey the precepts of eloquence even at the end of this discourse, for those precepts bring the duties of speakers to a close when the minds of their hearers have been moved. For, as Tully says, “Nothing dries more quickly than a tear.”

If I have performed my duty as I ought, I beg you to give thanks with me to almighty God, by whose mercy this was accomplished. But if I have spoken less aptly, the one about whom I have spoken should not therefore be valued any less, since nothing is more unworthy than to diminish the virtue of one who has deserved well because of the fault of the writer.

Rather, let us magnify God in him and vie with one another in exalting his name, giving thanks to him who chose Dunstan before the foundation of the world in his eternal wisdom and wished to bless the ages of the English through the manifestation of Dunstan’s bodily presence. Let us also venerate him in God and raise his merits to the highest honors, certain that whatever our devotion forms in his veneration belongs to the glory of God.

Let us love him with all the inmost feelings of our hearts, and through him let us hope to receive whatever we faithfully ask from God, because God’s mercy can deny us nothing if we strive both to love in our hearts and to honor in our service the one whom he loves.

Glory to almighty God the Father, who made him; glory to the only-begotten Son of God, who redeemed him; glory to the Holy Spirit, who enlightened him by his grace. To the one only living and true God be praise and thanksgiving throughout infinite ages of ages. Amen.

The family into which he was born marks him out; virtue strives to raise him higher;

Our company has it as its task to offer him gifts of praise.

Father Dunstan, outstanding, worthy of veneration throughout the world:

After winter, the joyful seasons of spring follow.

[Col. 0473]

## The Letter of Saint Dunstan to Wulfsin, Bishop of Sherborne

(Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum*, Fifth Century, p. 239.)

[Col. 0473C]

D., archbishop by the grace of God, to his faithful friend Wulfsin, bishop: eternal salvation and peace in the Lord God.

Let us give thanks to God, who ordained us, unworthy and last among his servants, to govern his holy Church in such dangerous and laborious times. And now let us together beseech the clemency of almighty God, that he may help us in every good work.

And you, dearest brother, act manfully and bring to completion, with strength, the work of the Lord that you have in hand, for the reward of our souls and the salvation of many souls. Let your tongue not cease from preaching; let your foot not cease from going about the flock entrusted to you; let your hand not cease from laboring, so that alms may be given through you and God’s holy Church may everywhere be exalted.

Be an example of salvation to all. In you let there be an example of the holiest conduct, in you consolation for the wretched, in you encouragement for the doubtful, in you the rigor of discipline, in you confidence in the truth, in you hope of every goodness. Let the pomp of the world not exalt you; let luxury of food not weaken you; let vanity of clothing not soften you; let the tongue of flatterers not deceive you; let the hostility of detractors not disturb you; let sorrows not break you, nor joys lift you up.

Do not be a reed shaken by the wind, nor a flower falling before the storm’s breeze, nor a wall destined to collapse, nor a house built upon sand. Rather, be a temple of the living God, built upon a firm rock, whose inhabitant is the Paraclete Spirit himself.

[Col. 0474C]

Show yourself gentle and humble toward the better, harsh and firm toward the proud, becoming all things to all people so that you may win all. Have honey and wormwood in your hands; let each person eat from them whatever suits him. Let the one who wishes to feed on kindly preaching receive honey; let the one who needs stern rebuke drink from wormwood—yet in such a way that he may hope for the honey of forgiveness if a rosy confession of repentance precedes it.

Let all your proper duties be performed in order. Let a time be appointed for reading, let prayer have its hours, and let the solemn celebrations of Mass take place at their proper time. Let whoever observes a day observe it for the Lord.

Let joy at banquets be restrained; let the nourishment taken during fasts be chaste. Let the face be washed with repentance; let the head be anointed with the oil of mercy, so that all things may become acceptable to the Lord God, who chose you as his priest.

Admonish the duke and all secular princes to preserve piety and mercy in their judgments and always to love purity of heart and body, because “blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.” Let them defend Christ’s Church, so that the Lord of the Church may become their helper and defender.

Let them be merciful to widows and orphans, so that God may have mercy on them; and let them be gentle and kind toward all people, gathering God’s people rather than scattering them, and keeping peace among themselves, because “blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God.”

And you, dearest brother, always keep the fear and love of God before the eyes of your heart. Let the book of the *Pastoral Rule* of blessed Father Gregory, in which the life of rulers and subjects is carefully distinguished, be read frequently before you. Remember my name in your holy prayers, so that the mercy of almighty God may defend, govern, and protect us, as I believe you wish, so that in the love and will of God we may complete the course of our life.

Do not consider it superfluous or arrogant that I have admonished you; receive it with the deepest affection of charity, because a brother helped by a brother is a strong city.

May almighty God preserve you safe forever.

[Col. 0475]

# Saint Dunstan’s Regular Concord for the Monks and Nuns of the English Nation

(According to Reinerus, *Apostolate of the Order of Saint Benedict in England*, p. 77. (G)*

## Preface

[Col. 0475B]

For the glorious Edgar, by the assisting grace of Christ, the distinguished king of the English and of the other peoples dwelling within the bounds of the island of Britain, from the beginning of his youth—although, as is customary at that age, he followed various ways of life—nevertheless, drawn by regard for God, when a certain abbot repeatedly admonished him and pointed out the royal road of the Catholic faith, began greatly to fear, love, and venerate God.

As the spark of faith gradually shone forth, lest it be extinguished and decay through the torpor of idleness, he began anxiously and diligently to inquire by what merits of holy works it could be kindled into the ardent heat of perfection. For when he learned that sacred monasteries established in various places under his rule were wasting away through negligent neglect and were almost deprived of the service of our Lord Jesus Christ, he, pierced by the grace of the Lord, hastened with great eagerness of spirit and adorned them most fittingly wherever they were located.

After expelling the filth of negligent clerics, he established everywhere throughout the vast extent of his kingdom not only monks but also nuns, appointing Fathers and Mothers over them for the service of God, and enriching them with every good thing, he joyfully endowed them.

Thus, carrying out his royal office as a vigilant shepherd of shepherds, he rescued and fortified from the rabid nets of the faithless the sheep whom, by the Lord’s generous grace, he had diligently gathered, as sheep from the gaping jaws of wolves. He carefully instructed his wife Alphrida to guard the flocks of nuns with the fearless vigilance of a guardian, so that male might assist males and female females, without any suspicion.

[Col. 0475D]

After the rule of holy Benedict had been honorably adopted, very many abbots and abbesses, together with the communities of brothers and sisters subject to them, strove eagerly and joyfully to follow the footsteps of the saints with one faith, though not with one customary practice.

The aforesaid king, greatly delighted by such zeal, carefully examining everything hidden, decreed that a synodal council should be held at Winchester. He humbly sent there exhortatory and peaceful words, beautifully written on a document, and, moved by the grace of Christ, admonished all that, united in one customary practice, they should imitate holy and approved Fathers, preserve the precepts of the rule with steadfast minds, and in no way disagree through dissension, lest unequal and varied practice under one rule and in one country should disgracefully bring reproach upon holy conduct.

Spiritually pierced by the prudent admonition of this most excellent king, not only the bishops but also the abbots and abbesses, raising their hands toward heaven, did not delay in returning immense thanks to the High-Throned One, rejoicing that they had deserved to have such a great teacher.

[Col. 0476C]

For immediately obeying his commands eagerly with all the strength of their minds, and recalling the instructions of our holy patron Gregory, by which he strove to admonish blessed Augustine to establish in the young English Church not only the honorable practices of the Roman Churches but also those of the Churches of Gaul, they summoned monks from Fleury, the blessed Benedict’s monastery, and from the distinguished monastery commonly called Ghent (*Gandavum*).

Gathering from the worthy conduct of these monks whatever was honorable—just as bees gather a honeycomb of nectar from various meadow flowers in a single hive—they placed these customs of conduct into this little booklet, tempered with great and subtle rational discretion, for honorable life and the sweetness of regular observance, so that, by Christ’s helping grace, the Savior of the world, they might be lawfully tasted in a most willing draught and fulfilled with eager, loving devotion, without complaint and with the weariness of distaste removed, by those who still humbly walk, free from the fault of boasting, in the [textually uncertain] way of the Lord’s commandments.

[Col. 0476D]

Therefore, lest individuals, seduced by the pride of arrogance and rashly choosing their own invention, should miserably lose the excellent fruit of holy obedience, and should appear to be Sarabaites—or rather wild beasts—rather than monks or human beings, they unanimously vowed a lawful vow to our Lord Jesus Christ and confirmed it by a spiritual pact: that, as long as life lasted, they would devote themselves to the yoke of the rule and openly preserve these recorded customs in their common way of life.

For the rest, each person may use prayers in the secluded places of the oratory, as far as the grace of the Holy Spirit mercifully inspires him, with God as witness, prudently and with vigilance in good works.

The distinguished Dunstan, archbishop of this country, added this wisely and prudently, speaking with prophetic spirit to strengthen the aforesaid synodal assembly: no monk, nor any man of higher or lower rank, should dare to enter the private quarters of the nuns under the pretext of inspecting them. Those who exercise the primacy of spiritual authority over them should do so for the benefit of discipline, not for secular tyranny of power; and, as blessed Isidore urges, they should carefully regulate their access to the women’s private quarters, so that they in no way contradict their regular observance.

[Col. 0477B]

We have judged that this one matter should be specially attended to by all Catholics devoted to the yoke of the rule: lest the prayers of intercession that by the custom of the Fathers we habitually sing for the king and benefactors, through whose gifts we are fed by Christ’s bounty, should by excessive haste in psalmody provoke God thoughtlessly to anger—far be it from us—rather than wisely invite forgiveness of sins.

Thus, at the urging of our Benedictine Father, everything should be modulated by singing distinctly, so that our mind agrees with our voice and the apostolic saying may be fulfilled: “I will sing with the spirit; I will sing also with the mind.”

If, however, for some need anything must be added beyond the common usage of the rule, let it be done only for as long as the matter for which it is done is improved by the helping grace of Christ. And, in order that the most welcome fruit of obedience may be acquired after the pride of arrogance has been rejected, let that regular degree be most carefully observed in which it is commanded that a monk do nothing except what the common rule of the monastery or the examples of his elders encourage.

Such a practice must by no means be rashly maintained any further unless it has been chosen and handed down by synodal council, with the discretion that is the mother of all virtues, and accepted by all Catholics.

[Col. 0477D]

At the aforesaid synodal assembly, all agreed that the election of abbots and abbesses should be conducted with the king’s consent and counsel, according to the teaching of the holy rule.

The election of bishops should likewise be conducted in the same way as that of abbots wherever regular monks live in an episcopal see, if, by the Lord’s generous grace, a monk of such great advancement can be found there; no one should presume to act otherwise while they share the same manner of life.

If, however, because of lack of ability or deserved punishment for sins, no person worthy of the honor of so great a rank could be found in that community, then someone should be chosen from another known monastery of monks, with the unanimous counsel of the king and of the brothers to whom he is to be entrusted.

When ordained bishop, he should diligently and constantly preserve in all things the same regular practice with his monks that the regular abbot observes, and should not, on account of the episcopate, arrogantly or forgetfully neglect the precepts of the rule. Rather, in proportion as he excels in honor, so also should he excel in conduct.

To prevent secular authority from miserably descending into great ruin and loss, as formerly happened, they wisely prohibited the sacred monasteries from receiving it with severe punishment and anathema, requiring only that the authority of the king and queen, for the protection of the holy place and the increase of ecclesiastical property, should always be sought by an auspicious vow.

[Col. 0478A]

For service to the king and queen, the Fathers and Mothers of the monasteries should, whenever necessary, approach them humbly, with fear of God and observance of the rule, for the benefit of the sacred monastery over which they preside.

They may approach the powerful, whether within or outside the monastery, whenever necessary, not for the purpose of feasting but for the benefit and even the defense of the monastery.

When traveling on horseback or on foot, they should not waste time in idle conversations, but should either devote themselves to psalmody or speak about necessary matters at the appropriate time.

With this in mind, they should complete the canonical hours suitably and with divine compunction, not while riding but after dismounting from their horses and kneeling, unless it is a feast day.

Those traveling should take with them not boys but adults, whose admonition may make them better.

Those remaining at home should love not only the brothers but also abbots, adolescents, and boys—not by embracing them in their arms or gently kissing them on the lips, but with a charitable affection of the spirit, reverently and with great caution, without flattering words.

They should not presume to lead any one of them away privately for personal service, or even under the pretext of a spiritual matter. Rather, as the rule commands, the person should remain continually under the vigilance of his guardian. Nor should the guardian himself have permission to depart alone with any single boy without a third person present as witness. Instead, according to the customary practice, he should go with the whole school, if a reasonable matter so requires, wherever necessity demands, in silence or while devoted to psalmody, with a blessing.

[Col. 0478D]

Unless great necessity compels them, and prudent consideration of what is necessary dictates it, they should by no means wander about making rounds of the villages.

They should not, with rash presumption, visit the banquets of secular people—neither superiors nor subjects—unless perhaps the hospitality of a journey unexpectedly arises.

With the Lord our Jesus Christ’s grace consenting, let us preserve with all our strength, in due measure, weight, and number, the clothing, fasting, abstinence, vigils, silence, the good of obedience, and all the other practices which we have voluntarily accepted through the tradition of our patron Benedict.

Relying on the admonition of the aforesaid king and trusting in the commands of the Fathers, let us diligently set down in writing, as we promised, the customary practices of the holy rule, both those handed down by the aforementioned Father Benedict and those openly preserved through constant observance by his holy followers and imitators, with careful examination and discussion, insofar as our strength permits and the grace of the Holy Spirit instructs us, for the preservation of brotherly unity in charity.

Thus may we receive an eternal reward from him while preserving all things harmoniously and joyfully—him who makes people dwell together in unity, that is, with one manner of life, in the house where Christ the Lord, the Son of the Virgin, is king; he who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God forever and ever. Amen.

## The Chapters Begin

1. How the customary rule should suitably be observed by monks throughout the course of the year at the canonical hours, by day or by night.

2. How the order of hymns should be maintained in winter, and how the other things that must regularly be done should be performed.

3. How the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity should be conducted, and how it should be conducted from that solemnity until Septuagesima.

4. What regular order should be observed from Septuagesima throughout all of Lent.

5. How the daily or nightly praise should be performed during the Paschal feast.

6. How it should be performed on the Saturday of the Easter octave and throughout the entire summer season.

7. How the brother called the Circa should fulfill his office.

8. How the daily or nightly office should be performed during the week of Pentecost.

9. How the Ember seasons should be observed.

10. How the Mandatum should be given daily by the brothers to the poor, and in what order the abbot should act toward travelers.

11. In what order the brothers should perform their cleaning on Saturday, and what offices they should carry out for the salvation of souls.

12. How one should act toward a sick brother, and how the dead should suitably be committed to the earth.

# The Regular Concord

## Here begins the order of how the customary rule should suitably be observed by monks at the daily or nightly hours throughout the course of the year

Beginning with the Kalends of October, with the Lord’s grace assisting the religious way of life, all things—spiritual or bodily—that must be undertaken in the regular practice and in imitation of the holy Fathers, with humble and necessary service, should be begun with a blessing.

This custom, necessary above all as the greatest protection, should be legitimately maintained by all who are subject to the yoke of the rule, in small matters as well as great, with continual observance. Even if individuals have begun something, it must not be interrupted.

Without doubt, nothing firm or strong will remain that lacks the blessing of Christ, who creates all things and governs them with just moderation.

Therefore, at every season, during the nightly hours, when a brother rises from his bed for the divine office, he should first make the sign of the cross upon himself by invoking the Holy Trinity. Then he should say the verse:

“Lord, open my lips.”

After that, the psalm:

“O God, come to my assistance,”

entirely, with the *Gloria*.

Then, if that hour requires it, he should attend to the bodily necessity of nature. Thus he should hasten to the oratory and sing the psalm:

“To you, O Lord, I have lifted up my soul,”

entering with the utmost reverence and caution, so as not to disturb those who are praying. Then, kneeling in the proper and customary place, he should pour out his prayers in the sight of the Lord, more with his heart than with his mouth, so that his voice, through great compunction of spirit and remembrance of his sins, may effectively penetrate the ears of the merciful Lord and, by the favor of Christ, obtain forgiveness of all crimes.

At the first prayer, therefore, he should sing the first three penitential psalms, with the Lord’s Prayer, as follows, interceding first for himself. After these, he should say this prayer:

“I give you thanks, almighty Father, who have deigned to guard me during this night. I beseech your clemency, merciful Lord, that you grant me to spend the coming day in your holy service in such a way that our service may please you with humility and discretion. Through the Lord,” etc.

Then he should come to the second prayer, where he should say the following two psalms for the king and queen and their household, with this prayer:

“O God, who through the grace of the Holy Spirit have poured the gifts of charity into the hearts of your faithful, grant your servants, male and female, for whom we beseech your clemency, salvation of mind and body, so that they may love you with all their strength and complete with total love whatever is pleasing to you. Through our Lord,” etc.

Then, coming to the third prayer, he should sing the two remaining psalms for the faithful departed, with this prayer:

“May the souls of your servants, male and female, we beseech you, O Lord, find fellowship in eternal light—those who, placed in this light, have received your sacrament. Through the Lord,” etc.

Until the boys enter the church, one small bell should be rung continuously. Once the boys have entered, they too should use threefold prayer, so that reverence for the Trinity may be properly maintained by all.

When the three prayers have been completed by the boys, the second signal should be sounded. All should sit in their assigned places in order and sing the fifteen Gradual Psalms individually, in three divisions. The first seven should be sung kneeling, after five psalms have been completed and the prior has given the signal.

When the remaining signals have again been rung and those psalms have been completed, they should begin Matins. When Matins is finished, they should say the two psalms:

“O Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger,”

and:

“May the Lord answer you,”

one specifically for the king and the other for the king and queen and their household, with these collects:

“We beseech you, almighty God, that your servant, our king N., who by your mercy has received the governance of the kingdom, may also receive increase in every virtue, so that, suitably adorned with them, he may be able to avoid the monstrous forms of vice and overcome the enemy, and may graciously reach you, because you are the way, the truth, and the life. Through our Lord,” etc.

“Rule, we beseech you, O Lord, over your servant N., and multiply in her the gifts of your grace, so that she may be free from every offense, not be deprived of temporal assistance, and rejoice in eternal ordinances. Through our Lord,” etc.

For the king and queen and benefactors:

“O God, who have poured out the gifts of charity,” etc., as above.

And thus, when all the regular hours have been completed, let the customary practice always be followed.

After these psalms, let there be a very short interval, as the rule commands and as is suitable throughout the summer. The school should go out with its teacher for the necessary purpose; the others, except those who are in need, should remain in the church devoted to prayer.

After this, let the praises of the day follow. After “Have mercy on me, O God,” etc., let them add two psalms for the king, queen, and household:

“Blessed are those whose iniquities,” etc.,

and:

“Incline your ear, O Lord,” etc.

When these have been completed, let them sing an antiphon of the cross, then an antiphon of holy Mary, and of the saint whose veneration is being celebrated in the present church—or, if that is lacking, of the consecration of the place itself. After these, let there be the same morning praises of all the saints, singing an antiphon in honor of the saint to whom the portico toward which they are going is dedicated.

After these, let there be praises for the dead.

If the office has been completed in daylight, as it ought to be, let them begin Prime without the bell’s signal. Otherwise, let them await daylight, and, when the signal has been sounded, assemble for Prime.

Then, when Prime is finished, let them sing the two psalms:

“O Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger,” etc.,

and:

“Have mercy on me, O God,” etc.

The first is for the temptation of the flesh, with the petitions:

“Examine us, O Lord,”

and:

“Let not the foot of pride overtake us,” etc.,

and the collect:

“Kindle [us] with fire.”

The following psalm is for the deceased brothers, with the collect:

“May they find, we beseech you, O Lord,” etc.,

and the prayer:

“The souls of our brothers,” etc.

Thus, in the customary manner, let them devoutly go through the penitential psalms, with the psalm:

“Incline your ear, O Lord,” etc.,

inserted between them.

When these have been completed, let the litany follow. All, without exception, should complete it in the customary manner, humbly prostrate, when the signal has been sounded.

When it is finished, after the Lord’s Prayer, let the psalm be sung between the prayers:

“In you, O Lord, I have hoped,” etc.,

with the accompanying petitions and prayers.

When these have been completed, let them summon the brothers to reading until the second hour, according to the command of the rule.

Then, when the signal has been given, let them go and put on their daytime footwear. No one should presume to do this before the signal has been heard, except the ministers; nor should anyone then omit it without permission, lest through rash presumption they grievously obscure the merit of obedience.

Afterward, devoted to psalmody, let the entire school wash their faces in the customary manner, together with the teacher and the abbot.

The elders, however, according as God has placed a divine impulse in each of their hearts, should silently and with the full attention of their minds perform their duty in these observances, just as in all prayers, adorning them by singing the canonical hours, the seven penitential psalms, or some other spiritual office for overcoming diabolical temptation.

Thus let them all come to the church.

When the children enter the church, let the sacristan first sound the signal. After the children have completed their three prayers, as the elders had previously done, let each take his place. When the bell has been rung, let them begin the third hour.

After it has ended, let them say, for the king, queen, and benefactors, the psalms:

“How long, O Lord,”

and:

“Have mercy on me, have mercy on me,”

with the prescribed collects following.

Then let them celebrate the morning Mass. At this Mass, on the second feria, the right choir should offer; at the principal Mass, the left. On the third feria, the left should offer at the morning Mass and the right at the principal Mass. Thus, alternating, they should proceed through the week.

Let the same morning Mass be celebrated for the king or for whatever urgent need may arise.

When this has been completed, let them assemble at the chapter house at the signal of the prior, with the prior preceding them. Facing east, let them greet the cross and, bowing their faces, humble themselves before all the brothers standing around. The reason for this humiliation is to be observed at every assembly.

Then, when all are seated, let the Martyrology be read.

When it has been read, let all rise and say the verse:

“Precious in the sight of the Lord,” etc.,

with the prayer and verse:

“O God, come to my assistance.”

Let this verse be repeated three times by all, the prior beginning. They should add the *Gloria* and kneel if the time requires it.

When the prior says, “And lead us not into temptation,” let all rise and, with faces raised, say:

“Look upon your servants,”

adding the *Gloria* with bowed heads.

The prayer follows:

“Direct and sanctify,”

and:

“Our help is in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth.”

When they are seated again, let the rule be read; or, if it is a feast day, the Gospel of that day. From this reading the prior should speak according as the Lord grants.

After this, whoever recognizes himself as guilty of any fault should ask humbly for pardon and seek forgiveness.

Every brother who has been rebuked by the abbot, or by any prior, for whatever reason, should ask for pardon before saying a single word. When the prior asks him what the reason is for which he seeks pardon, he should answer and confess his fault, saying:

“It is my fault, Lord.”

Then, when ordered, he should rise. For if he acts otherwise, he will be judged guilty.

Whoever has been rebuked by any prior for some offense, or has exceeded in any duty, and does not immediately ask for pardon as the rule commands, should be subjected to a greater punishment.

For the more a person humbles himself and declares himself guilty, the more mercifully and lightly he ought to be judged by the prior.

It is necessary that in all our negligences—whether of thought, speech, or deed—we be judged in the present life through true confession and humble repentance, lest, after the course of this life has passed, they set us as guilty before the tribunal of Christ.

When this business of spiritual cleansing has been completed, let them sing the five psalms that are noted below for the deceased brothers.

All these things that we have mentioned should be done after Terce at these times. On Sundays throughout the year they should all be done before Terce, yet in such a way that each brother reveals the guilt of his conscience to the spiritual Father—or, if he is absent, to his deputy—through humble confession.

If the number is so great that everyone cannot come to confession on that day, they should fulfill the same duty on the following day, namely the second feria.

The school, however, whether child or not, must by no means omit this. It should carry it out in the customary manner, like the elders, even though it has not yet been attacked by temptations.

But anyone who requires it on other days, having been stirred by some temptation of mind or body, should not delay in coming devoutly and without hesitation to the salutary remedy of confession.

[Col. 0483A] On feast days, for the sake of observing silence and devotion to study, Prime is to be extended in such a way that, after the chapter has been held and the morning Mass celebrated—which on Sunday is to be celebrated for the Trinity, unless another feast day has occurred—if it is Sunday, they are immediately to proceed to the rite of sprinkling; if it is any other solemnity, immediately to Terce. Meanwhile, while that Mass is being celebrated, the ministers of the next Mass are to vest; and when Terce has been completed, they are immediately to summon the faithful people by the movement of the bells and begin Mass.

After the Peace, the brothers, every day—except those who know themselves to be guilty of some crime or bodily weakness—are not to refuse to receive the Eucharist, being wholly intent upon the regular observance. Let them heed what blessed Augustine says in his book *On the Words of the Lord*: namely, that in the Lord’s Prayer we ask not for annual but for daily bread. And, as he himself testifies there, a Christian can as easily go without ever receiving the nourishment of life, namely the body and blood of Christ, as taste it no more frequently than once a year. “Live,” he says, “in such a way that you may deserve to receive every day; whoever does not deserve to receive every day does not deserve to receive after a year.” Yet those invited to the Lord’s Supper must take care not to presume to approach, without confession and penance, while shamefully infected with some crime, and thus turn the nourishment of life into their condemnation, as the blessed Apostle says, because they do not discern the Lord’s body.

When Mass has ended, time is to be allowed for the ministering brothers to receive the mixed drink on account of Holy Communion, while all the others remain seated in the church; after the signal has been given, let them say the prayer and then celebrate Sext. After Sext, let them go to table. It must always be observed that on Friday the Mass is of the Cross, and on Saturday of Saint Mary, unless a feast day has occurred, in which case the principal Mass is to be celebrated.

On every feast day, whether solemn or ordinary, after Mass has ended, let the psalm *May the Lord answer you* be said for the king, and *To you I have lifted up* for the queen, and so forth, with the succeeding prayers and the appropriate collect—that is, so that their commemoration may be made after Mass as it is made at Mass and at all the other hours. Throughout the entire day, strict silence is to be maintained in the cloister.

Rising from the chapter, let them sing five psalms for the dead: *Give ear to my words, O Lord*; *Rebuke me not in your anger*; *I have loved, because*; *I believed*; *Out of the depths*. After these, let the tablet be struck; and if they have nothing to do, let the prior alone say, “Bless,” with the others responding, “The Lord.” But if they have work to do, after the tablet has been struck, let the prior first invoke divine assistance, saying three times, “O God, come to my aid,” with the brothers responding likewise, followed by the *Glory*, the *Our Father*, and “Our help.”

Then, with the chanting of the canonical course and the psalter, let them perform whatever has been assigned to them until they hear the signal to vest. When they have heard it, let each one leave his work, hastening to the work of the Lord; and when they have come before the oratory, let them bless the Lord who has provided them assistance, saying three times: “Blessed are you, O Lord, for you have helped me and consoled me,” followed by the *Glory*, the *Our Father*, “Our help,” and “May the almighty Lord be gracious to us.”

Entering the church, let them say the prayer. Then let the ministers go to vest; when vested, let them enter the choir and, after the bells have been struck, celebrate Sext. When Sext has ended, let them sing the psalm *May God have mercy on us* and *O Lord, hear* for the king, the queen, and their household, with the appointed collects. The litany follows; when it has ended, the cantor, vested for this purpose in the customary manner, is to begin the Mass. When Mass has ended, let the first signal for None be struck, and let the prayer be said.

After the prayer, let the weekly ministers go to receive the mixed drink, while the other brothers remain in the church devoted to psalmody until, after another signal has been given, they celebrate None. When None has been completed, let them say for the king, the queen, and their household the psalms *He who rules Israel* and *Out of the depths*, with the collects already mentioned. Then let them proceed to table. Rising from table, let them devote themselves to reading or to the psalms, according to the precept of the rule; or, if there is something to be done, let the tablet be struck, and, with the blessing, let them begin what must be done.

Let Vespers be celebrated earlier. While its signals are sounding, after the prayer in the choir, let the younger brothers be seriously occupied individually in the study of spiritual reading, while the elders, intent upon divine prayers, sit nowhere wandering, with the grace of the Lord. At Vespers, after *Have mercy on me, O God*, let them add two psalms for the king, the queen, and their household, namely, *You have blessed, O Lord*, and *O Lord, hear*.

At Vespers, let what we stated above concerning the antiphons after Matins likewise be done after Vespers. Let Vespers for all the saints, for the dead, and the vigil continue until the Kalends of November.

When these things have been completed, let the brothers go to remove their daytime shoes and put on their nighttime shoes. If it is Saturday, let each one wash his feet, and let suitable vessels for this work be assigned to each person. After washing their feet, let those for whom it is necessary also wash their shoes. After this, when the prior has struck the little bell, let them approach with thanksgiving to draw their drinks.

When they rise, let the prior say this verse: “Our help”; and let the others respond: “Who made heaven and earth.” Then, after the tablet has been struck, let them go to the mandatum according to the decree of the rule. When it has been completed, after the signal has been given, let the collation begin in the church; and, when the little bell has again given the signal, let them enter the refectory for the sake of charity. Whenever charity is offered to the brothers while the collation is being read, when the reading has ended and all have risen, let the prior say: “Blessed be the name of the Lord,” and, “Let us bless the Lord,” with the others responding according to custom.

On the remaining days, after changing their shoes, let them go to the refectory at the signal. From there, likewise at the signal, let them go to the collation, which is to be read as time permits and as seems best to the prior; and thus let them proceed to Compline.

When the signal for Compline has been struck, let the prayer be said. When it has ended, after the signal has been given, let them mutually offer one another the salutary remedy of confession. When Compline has ended, and finally *Have mercy on me, O God* has been sung in the customary manner, let two psalms be added, *O God, come to my aid* and *I lifted up my eyes*, for the king, the queen, and the benefactors.

When Compline has ended, so that in this last canonical hour, as at its beginning, reverence for the holy Trinity and undivided Unity may lawfully be offered by the Catholic servants, let the boys first perform three prayers, and after the boys let the brothers do so.

In the first prayer, let them sing the psalms *How long, O Lord?*, and so forth, and *Judge me, O God*; *Lord, have mercy*; the *Our Father*; and the petitions: *Turn your face away*; *A clean heart*; *Do not cast me away*; *Restore to me the joy*; followed by:

> “I give you thanks, holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God, who have deigned to guard me on this day through your holy mercy. Grant me to pass through this night with a pure heart and chaste body, so that, rising in the morning, I may be able to offer you an acceptable service. Through our Lord,” etc.

In the second prayer: *May God have mercy on us*; and *Unless the Lord*; *Lord, have mercy*; the *Our Father*; the same petitions as above; and the collect:

> “O God, to whom every heart is open, every will speaks, and from whom no secret is hidden, purify, through the infusion of the Holy Spirit, the thoughts of our hearts, so that we may deserve to love you perfectly and to be worthily praised. Through our Lord,” etc.

In the third prayer: *Out of the depths*; *Lord, have mercy*; the *Our Father*; the same petitions; and the collect:

> “Most gentle almighty God, who brought forth for your thirsting people a spring of living water from the rock, draw forth from the hardness of our hearts tears of compunction, so that we may be able to lament our sins and, through your mercy, deserve to receive forgiveness. Through our Lord,” etc.

> “Most gentle almighty God, look favorably upon our prayers and deliver our heart from the temptation of evil thoughts, so that we may deserve to be found a worthy dwelling place of the Holy Spirit. Through our Lord,” etc.

When these things have been completed, let them be sprinkled with blessed water by the weekly priest, and thus let them proceed to their rest with the utmost tranquility of voice and reverence. If, after this, anyone should wish, perhaps through the fervor of his devotion, to persist longer in these things, let him indeed do so; but when he hears the signal of the sacristan, who summons those remaining to go out, let him not delay. Every night also, after Compline, their resting place is to be sprinkled while they are lying down, on account of demonic illusions.

## How the order of the hymns is to be observed in winter, and how the other things that are regularly to be done are to be performed

From the Kalends of November until the beginning of Lent, one order of hymns is to be maintained: namely, that shorter hymns be sung on the shorter days, and longer hymns on the longer days. Thus, at Sunday Vespers: *O blessed light*; at Compline: *Christ, who are the light*; at the nocturns: *First of days*; and at Matins: *Eternal maker of all things*.

At the nocturn, Matins, and Vespers throughout the entire year, except on Sundays and the feasts of the saints, ferial hymns are to be maintained according to custom. At distinguished and festive solemnities, suitable hymns are to be celebrated according to customary practice. During Advent of the Lord, Lent, and the season of the Passion, hymns belonging properly to those observances are to be sung, but in such a way that on Sundays, whether by day or by night, during Lent, the hymns that run throughout the whole year—not the hymns concerning fasting—are celebrated.

From the same Kalends, the brothers are to be allowed access to the fire whenever necessity compels and excessive cold presses upon them. This is nevertheless to be done in silence; it is not at all to be done in the refectory. During this winter season also, because of the excessive severity of the rains, a suitable place is to be assigned to the brothers, whose [lacuna] refuge may lessen the adversity of winter harshness and bad weather.

But if the weather is calm, let them use the cloister as they please, with Christ’s blessing. If, out of necessity, they leave the cloister and enter the house designated, as we have said, let the same custom be maintained there in all things as is ordinarily maintained in the cloister. No one at any time, however, leaving the cloister, is presumptuously to go to the aforesaid house to remain there, nor is anyone, leaving the house, to enter the cloister without the prior’s permission.

According to the decree of the rule, let them rise earlier for the vigil, so that, after the nocturnal office has been completed, together with the psalms mentioned above, the vigil for the dead with its Lauds, and Matins for all the saints, the interval until daybreak may be carefully observed while the brothers devoted to psalmody or, according to the precept of the rule, to reading, serve those who have need of them. At the dawn’s first light, when the sacristan has struck the signal, let everyone assemble in the church; after the prayer has been made, let them sing the morning Lauds.

When these have ended, let them say the antiphons mentioned above until the coming of the Lord. These are to be followed by Prime, the special psalms, and the litany. After this, let them leave the church and devote themselves to reading, considering the progress of their souls, until the time mentioned above.

From the feast of Saint Martin, after the brothers have been fed and have entered the church, let the signal for None be given. Let the office of None itself follow; no drink follows None until the Purification of Saint Mary. This is to be done on all solemn days. On the other days, let them follow the order stated above: namely, after the signal has been given, let them put on their shoes and fulfill all the remaining requirements as has been said.

During Advent of the Lord, fat is forbidden—namely, bacon—except on feast days. Vespers is to be celebrated every day according to custom, that is, at its proper time after the meal.

## How the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord, and the period from that solemnity until Septuagesima, are to be observed

On the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord, while the account of his birth is being read by the lector in the chapter, let all rise together and kneel, giving thanks for his ineffable mercy, by which he descended in order to redeem the world from the snares of the devil.

Likewise, on Holy Saturday, while the Resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ is being read by a boy—although it is not found in the martyrology—let the same observance be made because of his most glorious victory, by which, after destroying the prison-bars of Erebus, he brought the faithful with him into heaven and granted us, though restored to life, hope of ascending.

In the evening, let suitable antiphons concerning the completion of the time be sung for the psalms. At the vigil of that night, in the fourth responsory, let two sing it together, so that it may be performed with greater honor. After *We praise you, O God*, let the Gospel be read by the abbot in the customary manner. When the prayer has been said, let the ministers leave in silence, so that they may put on their shoes, wash, and vest in haste. When all the signals have been set in motion, let Mass be celebrated.

After this, let the morning Lauds be sung. When these have ended, let them begin Lauds for all the saints according to custom. If the abbot should decide to celebrate it, let them celebrate the morning Mass, which is to be celebrated at the first light of dawn.

Then, at the appropriate time, when the signal has been struck, let them sing Prime. When Prime has ended, let them come to the chapter. After the other conversations concerning spiritual edification, let the brothers humbly ask the abbot, who acts in Christ’s place, for pardon for their many faults, saying, “I confess.” The abbot is to respond, “May he have mercy.”

Then the abbot himself, prostrating alone, is to ask the same thing from the brothers; the same form of confession is to be observed on the first day of the Paschal solemnity.

When the chapter has been held and the psalms have been said, let everyone vest, so that all may be adorned for Terce. At Vespers on that day, let the antiphons *With you is the beginning* and the others be said. On the remaining three days, let antiphons for the saints themselves be said, with the psalms suitable to the solemnity.

When these have been completed, let *With you is the beginning* be repeated until the Lord’s Octave. On these days, between the feast of the Innocents and the Lord’s Octave, because *Glory to God in the highest* is sung at Mass in honor of so great a solemnity, let all the bells be struck at the nocturn and at Vespers, as at Mass, according to the custom maintained by the natives of this land.

For we have resolved in no way to reject the honorable customs of this land that pertain to the Lord and that we have learned through the practice of the ancients, but rather, as we have said, to strengthen them in every respect. At Matins, however, for the reason stated above, although *We praise you, O God* is not sung and the Gospel is not read in festive fashion, a candle is nevertheless lit, all the bells are struck, and the thurible is carried while incense is offered.

From this time until the Epiphany of the Lord, let the psalms proper to the ferial day be said at Vespers with the antiphon. On the vigil of the Epiphany of the Lord, no fast is observed. Let antiphons from that solemnity be said with the psalms of that Vespers.

On the other days after the Lord’s Octave and the first day of the Epiphany, let the morning Mass be celebrated after Prime; after the chapter, let the tablet be struck, and obedience be performed. The bells are not to be struck at the same time, nor is *Glory to God in the highest* to be sung, unless another feast has intervened, until the eighth day, which is to be celebrated solemnly with twelve readings. From that day until the beginning of Lent, let the order written above be maintained.

On the Purification of Saint Mary, let candles be arranged in the church, to which the brothers are to go in order to obtain lights from there. As they go, let them walk silently, devoted to psalmody, and let all be clothed in white if this is possible or the weather permits. Entering the church, let them say the prayer with the antiphon and collect in veneration of the saint to whom the church they are visiting is dedicated.

Then let the abbot, vested in stole and cope, bless the candles, sprinkle them with blessed water, and incense them. Having received a candle from the sacristan, with all singing psalms, let each take one candle and light it after receiving it.

Returning from there, let them sing the antiphons that are provided until they come before the door. There, after the antiphon *Simeon received the answer* has been sung, let the prayer *Hear us, we beseech you, O Lord* be said. Afterward, let them enter the church singing the responsory *When they brought in the child*. When this has been sung, let them say the Lord’s Prayer; then let Terce follow.

When Terce has ended, if they did not perform the procession while vested, let them vest, and, celebrating Mass, hold the lights in their hands until after the offering, when they are to offer them to the priest. Let this regular order be observed from Septuagesima throughout all Lent.

At Septuagesima, fat is to be discontinued until Quinquagesima. From Quinquagesima onward, let them observe the Lenten abstinence according to custom.
