From Septuagesima, after the three readings have ended, let the six psalms of the later nocturn, like those of the earlier nocturn, be sung with the three antiphons drawn from the melody of the psalms themselves, with the greatest diligence, until the Lord’s Supper.

From the beginning of the fast, on Wednesday and Friday, let them observe the procession until the Lord’s Supper, and from the Octave of Pentecost until the Kalends of October. The order of this procession is to be as follows:

On the Wednesday at the beginning of the fast, after None has been sung, let the abbot, vested in a stole, bless the ashes. After they have been blessed, let the abbot himself go and place them on the heads of each person, since it is his responsibility to impose penance upon them. Meanwhile, let them sing the antiphon *Hear us, O Lord*; *Save me, O God*; and the *Glory*; *Lord, have mercy*; the *Our Father*; *May God have mercy on us*; the petitions; and the collects.

Then let them go where they must go, singing the antiphons contained in the Antiphoner. Coming to the church to which they are going, let them again say the prayer. After the antiphon for the saint and the psalm *To you I have lifted up my eyes*, together with the petitions and prayer, let them begin the litany there and return to the mother church. Afterward, let Mass be celebrated according to custom.

This order of procession is always to be maintained whenever a procession is held. At other times, however, let the antiphon *Arise, O Lord* always be said first, with the psalm and the *Glory*.

When these things have been completed, let the ministers of the altar vest after they have entered the church with the procession, the litany having been prolonged as much as necessary for this. Then, when vested in chasubles, let the priest, deacon, and subdeacon perform their ministries.

This custom of the chasuble is to be observed only during Lent and the Ember seasons, according to the practice of the fathers who preceded us. Whenever the subdeacon wears the chasuble, he is to remove it while reading the Epistle; when the Epistle has been read, he is to put it on again. When the deacon approaches to read the Gospel, he is to remove the chasuble, fold it, and place it around his left shoulder, fastening its other end to the cincture of the alb. When the sacrament of Communion has been completed, he is to put it on before the collect ends.

On the aforesaid days of Lent, once the Lenten observance has been completed, let the signal for Vespers be struck and let the prayer be said. Then, during the interval while the bells are being struck, let those who wish go to receive the mixed drink; those who do not wish to do so are to have permission to abstain.

Since we hold that the ornament of the rule requires us on these holy days of Lent to add something to the service of God beyond the customary measure of our service, we have determined that from the beginning of Lent until the Lord’s Supper, except on feast days, every day after the completion of each hour, we should devoutly pray two psalms prostrate on the floor of the oratory. The order is to be as follows:

[Col. 0489B] After Matins have ended, let two psalms immediately be said: *O Lord, rebuke me not in your anger* [Psalm 6], and *To the Lord*; *Lord, have mercy*; the *Our Father*; the petitions for sins; and the prayer.

At Prime: *Blessed are those whose ways are blameless* and *I lifted up my eyes*, with the rest as above.

At Terce: *O Lord, rebuke me not in your anger* [Psalm 37], and *I rejoiced*.

At Sext: *Have mercy on me, O God*, and *To you I lifted up my eyes*.

At None: *O Lord, hear*, and *Unless the Lord*.

At Vespers: *Out of the depths*, and *Those who trust*.

At Compline: *O Lord, hear* [Psalm 142], and *When the Lord restored*.

Thus, at each hour, one penitential psalm and one psalm of ascent are to be said, so that, cleansed from the bonds of sins, we too may ascend through the steps of virtues to the heights.

During these days of Lent, for the first three weeks let them be unshaven; halfway through Lent, let the excess of hair be removed by the service of shaving.

[Col. 0489C] On Palm Sunday, since a greater procession remains to be performed, let the procession customarily held in the cloister while the morning Mass is being sung be performed only by the priest, who is to carry out the sprinkling and blessing.

When that Mass has ended, let the greater procession be held. As we said was to be done in the earlier procession, so let it be done here: namely, let everyone, if possible and if the time permits, go in ordered silence, devoted to psalmody, and dressed in white, to the church where the palms are. When they have arrived, let them say the prayer of the saint, imploring the intercession of the saint to whom the church is dedicated.

When the prayer has ended, let the deacon read the Gospel *A great multitude*, up to *the whole world has gone after him*. This is to be followed by the blessing of the palms. After the blessing, let them be sprinkled with blessed water and incense burned. Then, when the boys have begun the antiphons *The children of the Hebrews*, let the palms themselves be distributed; and, after beginning the greater antiphons, let them go out.

Coming before the church, let them stop until the boys who went ahead sing *Glory and praise*, with all the verses, as is customary, while the others respond, *Praise and glory*. When these have ended, and the cantor begins the responsory *As the Lord entered*, let the doors be opened.

After entering, when the responsory has ended, let them do as was said above, and let them hold the palms in their hands until the Offertory is sung; afterward, let them offer them to the priest.

On that day, at the Passion, *The Lord be with you* is said, but *Glory to you, O Lord* is not answered. The same is done in the other Passions, except for the Passion on Good Friday, where neither is said: neither *The Lord be with you* nor *Glory to you, O Lord*.

On Thursday, which is also called the Lord’s Supper, let the nocturnal office be performed according to what is contained in the Antiphoner.

We have also learned that in the churches of certain religious men something is done that has arisen as a sign of spiritual reality for the compunction of souls: namely, when everything belonging to the singing of that night has been completed, and the antiphon of the Gospel has ended, with no candlelight remaining, two boys are appointed for this purpose on the right side of the choir, who sing in a resonant voice, *Lord, have mercy*; and two likewise on the left side, who respond, *Christ, have mercy*; and also two on the western side, who say, *Lord, have mercy on us*.

When these have been completed, the whole choir is to respond together: “Christ the Lord became obedient unto death.” Then the boys of the right choir are to repeat what was said above, in the same manner as above, until the choir finishes what was said above. The same is to be repeated a third time in the same order.

When it has been finished for the third time, let them offer the petitions silently, kneeling according to custom.

Let this order be maintained uniformly on those three nights. For, as I believe, this ecclesiastical practice of compunction was devised by Catholics so that the terror of darkness—which strikes the threefold world with unusual fear at the Lord’s Passion—and the consolation of apostolic preaching—which had revealed to the whole world that Christ suffered and was obedient unto death for the salvation of the human race—might be represented most clearly.

We have therefore judged that these things should be inserted, so that, if they please some through devotion, they may have here something by which to instruct those who do not know this practice. Those who do not wish to do it, however, are not at all to be compelled.

On the days following those nights, at no hour is *O God, come to my aid* to be said; instead, the chapter verses of the canonical course are to be said directly, followed by the verse and what follows.

On Wednesday, the same chapters are to be said more loudly, so that they may be heard by everyone; this is not to be done at Vespers or Compline on the other days.

On the aforesaid nights, if Matins should end before daylight, the brothers who wish may return to their rest. Those who prefer spiritual exercises are to remain awake in the deepest silence, which benefits their souls. When morning has come, on the Lord’s Supper, let them assemble for Prime. After Prime has been said aloud according to the canonical custom—namely, *O God, in your name*, *Blessed are the undefiled*, up to *Set the law before me*—let them say the verse, kneel, and perform the remaining parts in silence.

After the *Our Father*, let *My soul shall live and shall praise you* be said silently, to the end of the psalm. When the prior reaches the place of confession, after the signal has been given, let them make confession.

At the other hours likewise, let the remaining chapters be said. At Terce, from *Set the law before me* to *My soul has languished* in a loud voice, and the verse and the rest in silence. At Sext, from *My soul has languished* to *Wonderful are your testimonies*. At None, from *Wonderful are your testimonies* to the end.

At Vespers likewise, let each psalm with its antiphon be sung in a loud voice, but the verse, the Gospel, and the rest in silence. Let Compline also be said aloud; after the first psalm, according to the canonical custom, *In you, O Lord, I have hoped*, and the Gospel *Now you dismiss*, followed by the *Our Father* and *In peace itself*.

On these three days, after Prime has been completed, let them sing the entire psalter together in the choir. After this, let them perform the litany prostrate; then let them devote themselves to reading until, when the signal has been given, they go to put on their shoes. Let them complete the rest according to regular custom.

After the chapter has been held, let the brothers remove their shoes; entering the church according to the manner of obedience, let them wash the floors of the church, while the priests, meanwhile, wash the sacred altars with blessed water together with the altar ministers. On that day no celebration of Mass is to take place at any altar until it has been washed.

When these things have been completed, after washing their feet, let them put their shoes on again. When Sext has been completed, let Mass be celebrated. Beforehand, poor people are to be gathered for this purpose according to the number the abbot has determined. Then, after they have been gathered in a suitable place, let the brothers go to perform the mandatum. Singing antiphons suitable to that work, let them wash and wipe the feet of the poor and kiss them. After water has been given to their hands, let food also be given to them, and let money be distributed among them according to the abbot’s decision.

Then, at the appropriate time, let None be celebrated. After it has been sung, as a sign of the hidden mystery, if it should please them, let the brothers vest and proceed to the door of the church, carrying a staff with the image of a serpent. There let fire be struck from flint. After the fire has been blessed by the abbot, let him light the candle fixed in the form of a serpent.

Then, with the sacristan carrying the staff, let all the brothers enter the choir, and let one candle after another be lit from that fire. On Friday, let the same be done in the same order, and let the staff be carried by the dean. Likewise on Saturday, let it be carried by the provost. After this, let Mass be celebrated.

At that Mass, *The Lord be with you* is not to be said, except by the bishop, and only where the chrism is consecrated. By him alone, after *Lamb of God* has been sung three times, is the kiss of peace to be given to the priests when the Eucharist is received; others are not to presume to give it.

At this Mass, as also at the Communion of the following days, Communion is to be offered both to the brothers and to all the faithful. Nevertheless, a portion of the Eucharist sufficient for all to communicate on the following day is to be reserved from that day. When the celebration of Mass has been completed, let everyone go to receive the mixed drink.

After the mixed drink, let the abbot take with him whichever brothers he wishes and perform his mandatum. When it has been completed, let them celebrate Vespers; afterward, let them provide the brothers’ meal.

At the appropriate time, let the mandatum of those same men be performed, but the brothers are first to cleanse their feet carefully. When they come to the mandatum, let the weekly ministers, according to their custom, precede the abbot and perform the mandatum. He follows them, washing the feet of each in his own basin, with those whom he wishes assisting him in this service; he is to wipe and kiss the feet.

When this has been completed, let the abbot sit in his seat. Let the priors come and perform the same service for him. Then, rising, let him give water into each man’s hands, and let the same service again be performed for him.

Meanwhile, as they wash their hands, let the weekly deacon and the other ministers go and vest. When the signal for the collation has been given, let them enter, with the deacon vested in a dalmatic and carrying the Gospel book, candles and thurible preceding him. Let the Gospel according to John, *Before the feast day*, be read until the little bell is struck.

Then, with the procession preceding, let the whole community follow. When all are seated in the refectory, let the same deacon, standing, continue the following passage of the Gospel, the Gospel book having been placed on the ambo.

Meanwhile, let the abbot go around serving the brothers a drink for each, kissing each one’s hands. When this service has been completed, and the abbot has taken his seat, let *But you, O Lord* be said. Then let the prior serve a drink to the abbot and to the other ministers who were assisting.

When the Gospel has ended and the drinks have been taken, let the procession proceed, and let the brothers remove their vestments and be with the others for Compline.

[Col. 0492B] On Good Friday, let the nocturnal praise be performed as was stated above. After this, let everyone come to Prime barefoot and continue until the cross has been adored.

On that same day, at the ninth hour, let the abbot come with the brothers to the church. After the prayer has been completed, when he has vested in the customary manner with the altar ministers, let him come from the sacristy before the altars for the sake of prayer; then, in silence, let him go to his own seat.

The subdeacon is then to ascend to read the reading from the prophet Hosea, *In their tribulation*. The responsory *O Lord, I have heard* follows, with four verses. Afterward, the abbot is to say the prayer kneeling: *O God, from whom Judas also*. Then another reading is read: *The Lord spoke to Moses*. The tract *Deliver me, O Lord* follows. Afterward, let the Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ according to John be read.

At that Passion, the deacon is not to say *The Lord be with you*, but *The Passion of the Lord*, and the rest, without anyone responding, *Glory to you, O Lord*. When it is read in the Gospel, *They divided my garments*, and so forth, two deacons are immediately to strip the altar of the linen cloth that had previously been placed beneath the Gospel, in the manner of thieves.

After this, let the prayers be celebrated. The abbot, coming before the altar, is to begin the solemn prayers that follow. Let him say the first without kneeling, as though reading: “Let us pray, most beloved,” and the rest.

When these have been completed in order, let the cross immediately be prepared before the altar, with space left between the cross and the altar on either side by two deacons. Then let them sing *My people*. Two subdeacons standing before the cross are to respond by singing in Greek:

> “Agios o Theos, Agios ischiros, Agios athanatos, eleison imas.”

That is: “Holy God, holy strong one, holy immortal one, have mercy on us.”

The choir likewise sings the same in Latin: *Holy God*.

Then let the deacons themselves carry it before the altar, with an acolyte following them with a cushion, upon which the holy cross is to be placed. When the antiphon to which the choir responds in Latin has ended, let them sing there as before: *For he led you out through the wilderness*. The subdeacons are likewise to respond in Greek as before: *Agios*, as above; and the choir likewise in Latin as before: *Holy God*.

Again, with the deacons lifting the cross, let them sing as before: *What more could I have done?* The subdeacons likewise as before: *Agios*, as above; and the choir likewise in Latin: *Holy God*, as above.

After this, turning toward the clergy, with the cross uncovered, let them say the antiphon *Behold the wood of the Cross*; the antiphon *We adore your Cross*; the antiphon *While the Maker of the world*; and *Sing, my tongue*.

Immediately, when it has been uncovered, let the abbot come before the holy cross and prostrate himself three times with all the brothers of the right choir, namely the older and the younger. With a great sigh of the heart, let them sing and pray through the seven penitential psalms, with the prayers appropriate to the holy cross.

In the first prayer, let them say the first three psalms with the prayer:

> “Lord Jesus Christ, I adore you ascending upon the cross; I beseech you, may that cross itself deliver me from the devil who strikes. Lord Jesus Christ, I adore you wounded upon it; I beseech you, may those wounds themselves be a remedy for my soul. Lord Jesus Christ, I adore you descending into the underworld to free the captives; I beseech you, do not allow me to enter there. Lord Jesus Christ, I adore you rising from the dead and ascending into heaven; I beseech you, have mercy on me. Lord Jesus Christ, I adore you who will come to judge; I beseech you, at your coming do not enter into judgment with me, a sinner; rather, I beseech you, forgive me before you judge, you who live and reign.”

In the second, let them say the two middle psalms with the following prayer:

> “Most glorious Lord Jesus Christ, creator of the world, who, being the splendor of glory and coeternal with the Father and the Holy Spirit, deigned for this reason to take flesh from an immaculate Virgin and allowed your glorious palms to be fastened to the gibbet of the cross, so that you might shatter the prison-bars of hell and free the human race from death: look upon me and have mercy on me, wretched as I am, weighed down by the burden of many crimes and stained by the pollution of many wickednesses. Do not deign to abandon me, most merciful Father, but forgive what I have impiously done. Hear me, prostrate before your most glorious cross, which is to be adored, so that I may deserve to stand before you pure and to please your sight, you who, with the Father, etc.”

At Terce, the final two are said with the following prayer:

> “Almighty Lord Jesus Christ, who for our sake placed your clean hands upon the cross and redeemed us with your blood, send into me the understanding and intelligence of how I may have true repentance and good perseverance throughout all the days of my life. Amen.”

Then, humbly kissing it, let him rise. Thereafter all the brothers of the left choir shall perform the same action with equally devout intention. For, after the cross has been venerated by the abbot or by all, [Col. 0493D] the abbot himself shall return to his seat and remain there until all the clergy and people have done the same. Since on that day we celebrate the deposition of the body of our Savior, we have decreed that, if anyone wishes or finds it pleasing, this custom of certain religious men may be followed in imitation, so as to strengthen the faith of the unlearned populace and of neophytes.

On one side of the altar, wherever there is room, there shall be a representation of a tomb, with a kind of veil stretched around it. After the holy cross has been adored, it shall be deposited there in the following manner: the deacons who previously carried it shall come, wrap it in a shroud at the place where it was adored, and then carry it back while singing the antiphons “In peace, in the selfsame place” (*In pace in idipsum*); “He shall dwell” (*Habitabit*); likewise, [Col. 0494A] “My flesh also shall rest in hope” (*Caro mea requiescet in spe*). When they have reached the place of the tomb, they shall lay down the cross as though the body of our Lord Jesus Christ had been buried and shall say the antiphon, “When the Lord had been buried, the tomb was sealed, and soldiers were appointed to guard him” (*Sepulto Domino signatum est monumentum, ponentes milites qui custodirent eum*).

The holy cross shall be guarded in that place with all reverence until the night of the Lord’s resurrection on Sunday. During that night, two or three brothers, or more if the size of the congregation requires it, shall be appointed to keep a faithful vigil there, chanting psalms. When this has been completed, the deacon and subdeacon shall come out of the sacristy with the Lord’s body that remained from the previous day, and with a chalice containing unconsecrated wine, and shall place them upon the altar. Then the priest shall come before the altar and say in a clear voice: “Let us pray, instructed by saving precepts,” and the Lord’s Prayer, [Col. 0494B] followed by “Deliver us, we beseech you, Lord,” up to “for ever and ever.” The abbot shall then take a portion of the holy sacrifice and place it in the chalice, saying nothing, and all shall communicate in silence. When this is completed, each person shall sing the vespertine office privately in his own place; after it has been completed, they shall go to the refectory. When they rise from the table, they shall perform the rest as usual.

After the veneration of the cross has been completed, those ministers or boys who have time shall shave and bathe, if the size of the company is such that the following Saturday would not suffice for this. After the collation, each person shall celebrate Compline standing separately and silently in his own place, in the manner of the canons, as we have said above, and shall complete the rest according to customary practice. During these three days, however, everything in the refectory and chapter [Col. 0494C] shall be done with the blessing and in the customary manner.

## How the daily or nightly praise is to be conducted during the Paschal festival

When the ninth hour comes on Holy Saturday, the abbot shall enter the church with the brothers, and the new fire shall be brought, as stated above. After a candle has been placed before the altar, it shall be lit from that fire. The deacon, blessing it in the customary manner, shall recite the following prayer in a voice as though reading:

“Let the angelic host of heaven now rejoice” (*Exsultet iam angelica turba caelorum*).

Then, in a higher voice, he shall say, “Lift up your hearts” (*Sursum corda*), and the remainder. When the blessing has ended, another candle shall be lit. Then two candles shall be illuminated and held by two acolytes, one at the right corner of the altar and the other at the left.

After the blessing, the subdeacon shall ascend the ambo and read the first lesson, “In the beginning he created” (*In principio creavit*). The prior’s prayer follows: “Let us pray: O God, who wondrously…” (*Oremus, Deus qui mirabiliter*).

The second lesson is “It happened at the Vigil” (*Factum est in vigilia*); the tract is “Let us sing to the Lord” (*Cantemus Domino*). The prayer follows: “Let us pray: O God, whose ancient miracles…” (*Oremus, Deus cuius antiqua miracula*).

The third lesson is “This is the inheritance” (*Haec est hereditas*); the collect is “O God, who [have established] your Church” (*Deus qui Ecclesiam tuam*); the tract is “As the deer longs” (*Sicut cervus*). The prayer follows: “Grant, we beseech you, almighty God” (*Concede, quaesumus, omnipotens Deus*).

When the prayer has ended, the sevenfold litany shall begin at the entrance before the altar. Afterward the abbot shall descend with the schola, singing the fivefold litany as they go to bless the fonts. The prayer “Almighty and eternal God” (*Omnipotens sempiterne Deus*) and the preface follow. When these have been completed, they shall return to the altar with the threefold litany. Before “Glory to God in the highest” (*Gloria in excelsis Deo*) is sung, the master of the schola shall say in a loud voice, “Light them” (*Accendite*). Then all the lights of the church shall be illuminated, and when the abbot begins “Glory to God in the highest,” all the bells shall be rung.

The collect “O God, who have made this most holy night” (*Deus qui hanc sacratissimam noctem*) follows. Then the Epistle “If you have risen with Christ” (*Si consurrexistis*) is read, and “Alleluia, give thanks to the Lord” (*Alleluia, confitemini Domino*) is sung, followed by the tract “Praise the Lord” (*Laudate Dominum*).

Before the Gospel, lights are not carried during this night, but incense alone. When the Gospel has ended, the abbot shall say, “The Lord be with you” (*Dominus vobiscum*), and “Let us pray” (*Oremus*). On this day neither the Offertory nor the *Agnus Dei* nor the Communion is sung, and the peace is not to be given except to those who communicate. Meanwhile, while they are communicating, all shall sing “Alleluia” and “Praise the Lord, all nations” (*Laudate Dominum omnes gentes*), followed by the antiphon “But on the evening of the Sabbath” (*Vespere autem Sabbati*) and the *Magnificat*.

Thus the priest shall complete the Mass and the vespertine synaxis with a single prayer. On that same day, at the time of the washing of the feet, water shall be given only for the hands, and the minister shall offer it to the brothers as an act of charity. Compline shall be celebrated audibly in the manner of the canons.

On the holy day of Easter, the monks shall celebrate the seven canonical hours in the church of God according to the manner of the canons, on account of the authority of blessed Gregory, pope of the apostolic see, who himself prescribed them in the Antiphonary.

At that same time of night, before the signal for Matins is given, the sacristans shall take the cross and place it in its appropriate location. At the beginning of the Night Office, when the Praise of God is begun in the church, the abbot or any priest shall say, “O Lord, open my lips” (*Domine, labia mea aperies*), once only. Then, “O God, come to my assistance” (*Deus, in adiutorium meum intende*), with the *Gloria*.

The psalm “O Lord, how they have increased” (*Domine, quid multiplicati sunt*) being omitted, the cantor shall begin the invitatory. Then come three antiphons with three psalms. When these have ended, the appropriate versicle shall be said, followed by the requisite number of lessons with their appropriate responsories.

While the third lesson is being read, four brothers shall dress themselves. One of them, dressed in an alb as though entering to perform some other task, shall secretly approach the place of the tomb and sit there quietly, holding a palm in his hand. While the third responsory is being celebrated, the remaining three shall follow. All shall be dressed in copes and carry censers with incense in their hands. They shall proceed slowly, as though searching for something, toward the place of the tomb.

All this is performed in imitation of the angel sitting in the tomb and of the women coming with spices to anoint Jesus’ body. When the one sitting there sees the three approaching him like bewildered men seeking something, he shall begin to sing in a moderately loud and sweet voice, “Whom do you seek?” (*Quem quaeritis*). When he has sung this through to the end, the three shall answer with one voice, “Jesus of Nazareth” (*Iesum Nazarenum*). He shall reply: “He is not here; he has risen, as he said. Go, announce that he has risen from the dead.”

At these words of dismissal, the three shall turn toward the choir, saying, “Alleluia, the Lord has risen” (*Alleluia, surrexit Dominus*). After this has been said, the one who is sitting shall again speak as though calling them back and shall say the antiphon, “Come and see the place” (*Venite, et videte locum*).

As he says this, he shall rise, lift up the veil, and show them the place stripped of the cross, with only the linens that had wrapped the cross lying there. When they see this, they shall put down the censers they had carried into the same tomb, take up the linen, and stretch it out toward the clergy. As though showing that the Lord has risen and is no longer wrapped in it, they shall sing this antiphon: “The Lord has risen from the tomb” (*Surrexit Dominus de sepulcro*). Then they shall place the linen upon the altar.

When the antiphon has ended, the prior, rejoicing with them in the triumph of our King, who rose after conquering death, shall begin the hymn “We praise you, O God” (*Te Deum laudamus*). When it begins, all the bells shall be rung together. After it ends, the priest shall say the versicle, “At your resurrection, O Christ” (*In resurrectione tua, Christe*), word for word, and shall begin Matins, saying, “O God, come to my assistance” (*Deus, in adiutorium meum intende*).

The cantor shall immediately begin the antiphon with the psalm “The Lord reigns” (*Dominus regnavit*), followed by “May God have mercy on us” (*Deus misereatur nostri*). This is not sung at that point, but together with “O God, my God, to you I keep watch from dawn” (*Deus, Deus meus, ad te de luce*), according to the manner of the canons.

After the five psalms have been properly completed with their appropriate antiphons, a chapter shall also be given by the priest, followed by the versicle “The Lord has risen from the tomb” (*Surrexit Dominus de sepulcro*), as is customary, recited by a boy. Then the antiphon for the Gospel shall be begun. When it has ended, the collect for all the saints shall be said in the customary manner. For these seven days we do not sing.

At Prime: four psalms, “O God, save me by your name” (*Deus in nomine tuo*) and “Give thanks to the Lord” (*Confitemini Domino*); on the first day only, “Blessed are they” (*Beati*) and “Pay back” (*Retribue*), with *Alleluia*, a chapter, and the versicle “This is the day” (*Haec dies*), recited directly by a boy; then “Lord, have mercy” (*Kyrie eleison*), the Lord’s Prayer with the Creed, and the customary prayers, followed by the collect.

At Terce: the psalm “Put a law upon me” (*Legem pone*) and “Remember your kindness” (*Memor esto bonitatem*), with *Alleluia* and the gradual “This is the day” (*Haec dies*), without a chapter or versicle.

Likewise at Sext, None, and Vespers: “The Lord said” (*Dixit Dominus*), “I will give thanks” (*Confitebor*), and “Blessed is the man” (*Beatus vir*), with the antiphon and without a chapter; the gradual “This is the day” (*Haec dies*) without a versicle; *Alleluia* with a versicle, and the sequence. Then the Gospel antiphon shall be begun, followed by the collect.

Afterward they shall go to the fonts, singing the psalm “Praise the Lord, children” (*Laudate pueri*) with its antiphon, followed by the collect. Returning from there, they shall go to the choir or oratory, whichever seems suitable, singing the psalm “When Israel went out” (*In exitu Israel*), followed by its own collect.

Compline shall be performed entirely according to the manner of the canons. When the psalms have ended, the chapter and versicle shall follow. Thereafter “Now you dismiss” (*Nunc dimittis*) shall be sung with its antiphon, followed by the prayers of the hour, the collect, and the blessing. This order shall be maintained on the remaining six days.

## How the Saturday of the Easter Octave and the entire summer season are to be conducted

On the evening of the Easter octave, the regular order shall now begin fully. Throughout the summer, at the Night Office, only one lesson learned by heart and a brief responsory shall be said on feast days, as the rule prescribes.

On the birthdays of the saints, however, when the labor of work is not suspended, three responsories and three lessons pertaining to the veneration of the saint whose memory we are recalling shall be read at length, if the time permits. On the other festivals, when the labor of work is suspended, twelve lessons with an equal number of responsories and the appropriate psalms shall be read most suitably, both in summer and in winter, as on Sundays.

On ordinary nights, when the twelve responsories are not sung, a very brief interval shall be made after the Night Office has ended, as the rule prescribes. Then, when the signal has been given, Matins shall be sung. If Matins has ended in daylight, as it should, the brothers shall leave the church, put on their shoes, and wash. After completing three prayers in the church, they shall sit in the cloister and devote themselves to reading until the signal for Prime is heard.

If it is not yet day and the prior considers it appropriate, then, after the signal has been given, those who wish may rest in their beds until morning. When morning has come, they shall proceed as described above.

Throughout the summer, except on Sundays and feast days, after Prime has been sung, the morning Mass celebrated, and chapter completed, the board shall be struck as stated above. Everything that must be done shall then be done until the first signal for Terce sounds.

After Terce has been completed and the following Mass celebrated, as the rule prescribes, the brothers shall sit in the cloister and devote themselves to reading until the first signal for Sext is heard at the middle of the fifth hour. When this has been completed, Sext shall be sung; then, after washing their hands, they shall go to table.

After eating, they shall rest in their beds until the first signal for None is heard at the middle of the eighth hour. On hearing it, they shall rise and wash; then, entering the church, they shall sing None. After None has been celebrated and cups have been drunk, the versicle “O God, come to my assistance” (*Deus in adiutorium*) shall be said in the customary manner, and they shall then perform whatever work is necessary.

During the remaining hours, however, since it is the time for reading according to the rule’s command, they shall devote themselves solely to reading and carefully maintain silence in the cloister. At all times, from the first ringing of the vespertine synaxis, silence shall be maintained in the cloister until chapter has ended on the following day, except in the place of instruction. That place is especially called the auditorium because there one must hear what the teacher commands; it is not proper there, or anywhere else, to spend time in stories or idle conversation.

Since the authority of the rule says that silence must be cultivated at all times, nevertheless, at an appropriate time, out of regard for the seriousness of silence, we have permitted necessary matters to be discussed in a low rather than a loud voice, as our patron, blessed Benedict, permitted. At other times we exhort everyone to meditate in silence on God and the salvation of his soul, as he himself judged. The time for reading is also a time for silence.

From the octave of Easter until the octave of Pentecost, one antiphon shall be sung at Vespers and Matins for all the saints. A vigil for the dead [Col. 0497D] and psalms for benefactors are not customarily sung. The litanies before Mass shall also be omitted entirely, since the ecclesiastical order warns against kneeling.

## How the brother called the *circa* is to fulfill his office

In accordance with the rule’s command, a brother must now be appointed who, under the dean, will care for the entire cloister. From the duty of making his rounds, he is called the *circa*. His office is to go around the cloister frequently, lest a brother be found overcome by listlessness or devoted to some vanity.

If he finds such a one, he must on no account keep silent about it in the chapter of the following day, unless that brother, humbled by satisfaction for some minor fault, has obtained this favor from him. The *circa* shall also go around the cloister after Compline, and if he finds any books or garments there, he shall carry them to the chapter of the following day. No one may remove them from the place where they were put without his permission.

He shall have a lantern with which, during the nighttime hours when these duties must be performed, he can inspect what is going on by sight. While the lessons are being read at the Night Office, during the third or fourth lesson, as he judges expedient, he shall go around the choir. If he finds a brother overcome by sleep, he shall hold the lantern before him and return. The brother, having immediately shaken off his sleep, shall ask pardon on his knees. Then, taking that same lantern, he shall go around the choir himself; if he finds anyone affected by this sickness of sleep, he shall treat him as he himself was treated, and then return to his place.

## How the daily or nightly office is to be conducted during Pentecost week

The prayers with the lessons and canticles that are said during the Vigil of Pentecost before the descent to the font begin as follows:

The first lesson is “God tested” (*Tentavit Deus*), followed by the prayer “O God, who in Abraham…” (*Deus qui in Abrahae*).

The second lesson is “They shall seize” (*Apprehendent*); the canticle is “Give ear, O heaven” (*Attende caelum*), followed by the prayer “O God, who through the prophets…” (*Deus qui nobis per prophetarum*).

The third lesson is “They shall seize” (*Apprehendent*); the canticle is “A vineyard was planted” (*Vinea facta*), followed by the prayer “O God, who have brought us to celebrate…” (*Deus qui nos ad celebrandum*).

The fourth lesson is “Hear, O Israel” (*Audi Israel*), followed by the prayer “O God, who are unchangeable” (*Deus qui incommutabilis*). The canticle “As the deer longs” (*Sicut cervus*) follows, with the prayer “Grant, we beseech you” (*Concede quaesumus*).

When the prayer has ended, the sevenfold litany shall begin at the entrance before the altar. Afterward the abbot shall descend with the schola, singing the fivefold litany as they go to bless the fonts. The prayer and preface follow. When these have been completed, they shall return to the altar with the threefold litany.

When this has ended, the priest shall say, “Glory to God in the highest” (*Gloria in excelsis Deo*). The prayer “Grant, we beseech you” (*Praesta quaesumus*) follows. Then the Epistle “When Apollos…” (*Cum Apollo*) is read, and “Alleluia, give thanks to the Lord” (*Alleluia, confitemini Domino*) is sung, followed by the tract “Praise” (*Laudate*). Then Mass shall proceed according to the order.

After the meal, at the appropriate time, Vespers and the remaining offices shall be celebrated as usual. On that Sunday night, the Night Office shall consist of three psalms and three lessons, with a responsory, as it is designated in the Antiphonary. At the remaining hours of the day and during the following week, the regular order shall be maintained. The Vespers of Saturday and of the holy day itself shall likewise be sung according to the normal order.

That week of Pentecost shall be celebrated solemnly like Easter week, except that on fast days “Glory to God in the highest” is not sung, and *Alleluia* is sung in place of the gradual. Vespers shall be said for all the saints. Again, during the octave, “The Spirit of the Lord” (*Spiritus Domini*) is not repeated on Sunday, because we celebrate only the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit; instead, that week is devoted to the Holy Trinity.

At Sunday Vespers on Saturday, the hymn “God, creator of all things” (*Deus creator omnium*) shall be sung; at Compline, “Before the ending of light” (*Te lucis ante terminum*); at the Night Office, “Rising by night” (*Nocte surgentes*); and at Matins, “Behold, now the night” (*Ecce iam noctis*).

This order shall be maintained throughout the summer until the Kalends of November. At the Kalends themselves, when the nights are longer, the hymns shall be sung as stated above. After the two psalms that are said after the Night Office have ended, the vigil shall be held. Because of the shortness of the days, it could not be held in the evening except on those feast days when the brothers are going to dine.

On those occasions, after supper they shall hold the vigil while the ministers dine meanwhile, so that afterward, in accordance with the rule’s instruction, all may come together for the collation. This order of the vigil shall be maintained until the beginning of Lent. During Lent, after supper, and thereafter throughout the entire length of summer, the vigil shall be held in the evening after supper, or after the vespertine praise if there has been no supper.

On the four Ember seasons, which are observed ecclesiastically for the celebration of Mass, the deacon shall say, “Let us kneel” (*Flectamus genua*), according to the Lenten custom. The abstinence from food proper to those same seasons shall be observed with great care, except when one of them falls during Pentecost week. In that case, we have judged it appropriate to proceed somewhat more leniently out of reverence for so great a solemnity.

## How the brothers are to perform the washing of the feet for the poor on ordinary days, and how the abbot is to act toward pilgrims

The washing of the feet, which we have received from the example of the Lord and also by the admonition of the holy rule, shall be offered to the poor with the utmost care, excepting what the brothers perform for one another. Christ is to be adored in them, and it is he who is received.

Therefore, in every monastery there shall be specific places established for this purpose, where the poor may be received. Every day, without interruption, three poor people shall be chosen from among those who are continually fed in the monastery, and the service of the washing of the feet shall be performed for them. They shall also be fed with the same food that the brothers use.

The order for going there shall be as follows: on Saturday, the boys of the right choir shall perform it with one custodian; on the following day, Sunday, the remaining boys of the left choir shall do so with another custodian. Then, on each day of the week, for each weekday, enough brothers shall be assigned to perform this duty that, apart from the abbot, no one may be excused from this obligation of service. The abbot, however, shall not perform it on only one weekday; whenever he has time and opportunity permits, he shall devote himself to it more often.

As for poor pilgrims who arrive unexpectedly, the abbot, with the brothers whom he chooses according to the rule’s command, shall perform the service of the washing of the feet. The father himself, if he can in any way do so, or any of the brothers, shall most devotedly provide every service of humanity in the guesthouse, lest anyone, deceived by arrogance or forgetfulness, foolishly neglect anything in their service that the rule commands.

Let this one matter alone, which the holy Fathers established by synodal decree for the salvation of the soul and especially for the preservation of the virtues, be carefully observed: no one living in the monastery, neither the abbot himself nor any of the brothers, is to eat or drink outside the refectory, except on account of illness.

In all other matters, as we have said, let the most devoted person fulfill his duties with great eagerness of spirit. Let him not delay or cease to minister promptly and fervently to the poor, the eternal vicars of Christ, in a suitable guesthouse, while he desires to hasten to minister to fleeting earthly riches. When pilgrims depart, food and other provisions shall be supplied to them according to the resources of the place.

## How the brothers are to perform cleaning on Saturday and discharge the several duties for the salvation of the soul

On Saturday, in accordance with the rule’s command, they shall perform the washing of the feet and the cleaning with diligent care. Those who do not yet know how these things must be done shall earnestly learn, and let the diligent complete them according to customary practice.

Let no one presume to do anything, however small, by his own initiative and as though it were his own work; let no one celebrate the appointed hours in the church, leave the cloister contrary to what the rule prescribes, or dare, inflated with the swelling of pride, to do even the smallest thing without the prior’s permission.

The greasing of footwear, the washing of garments, and the provision of water are not to be despised; rather, if the grace of the Lord grants strength, they shall all be performed customarily at the appropriate time. Let each person, according to the strength available to him, gladly perform the duties of the kitchen, the bakery, and all other offices, as the holy rule prescribes, lest by treating the least of the rule’s commands as insignificant he pass them over, and thus, as the Apostle says, God forbid, become guilty of all the commandments.

## How a sick brother is to be treated, and how the dead are to be returned to the earth

When someone has been summoned to discharge the debt of common human frailty, and he feels himself weighed down by such great weakness that he can no longer be carried, let that brother come before the abbot or the entire congregation, explain the causes of his illness, and, having received the blessing of all, enter the infirmary. There, let servants of God be present, fervent in the fear of God and brotherly love, who will supply him with whatever he needs; or, if necessary, let the service of attendants be provided with a solicitous brother.

If that sick brother feels that his weakness has increased, his custodian shall report this to the community. From then on, every day after the morning Mass, the priest, having removed his chasuble, shall go with the other ministers of that Mass, carrying the Eucharist, preceded by candles and a censer, and accompanied by the entire congregation, to visit the sick man. They shall sing the penitential psalms, followed by the litany and appropriate prayers, and the anointing with oil on the first day only. Finally, he shall receive Communion.

If the illness has been alleviated, this shall also be discontinued; otherwise, the visitation shall continue until his death. When he is in his final agony, the board shall be struck, and all shall assemble to watch over his passing. The commendation of the soul shall begin: “Come to his aid, saints of the Lord” (*Subvenite, sancti Domini*), and the remainder according to the order of the commendation.

When the man has died, his body shall be washed by those appointed to do so. After it has been washed, it shall be clothed in clean garments: an undertunic, cuculla, hose, and shoes, whatever his rank may have been. If he was a priest, a stole shall be placed around him over the cuculla, if reason requires it.

Then he shall be carried to the church while all chant and all the bells are rung. If he died during the night before dawn, or after the darkness had ended at Matins, and the preparations necessary for burial can be made, he shall be buried before the brothers’ meal, after the celebrations of the Masses have been completed.

If not, brothers shall be appointed to devote themselves without interruption to psalmody, sitting around the body throughout the following day and night, until, when morning has come, the body is committed to the earth.

When everything required by the burial office has been completed, they shall begin the seven penitential psalms there and return to the church. Prostrate before the holy altar, they shall finish those same psalms for the deceased brother. Thereafter, for seven consecutive days, a full vigil shall be held, with everyone making an offering at the morning Mass. At the end of all the regular hours, they shall prostrate themselves and sing one of the prescribed psalms, followed by a prayer.

From then until the thirtieth day, a vigil with three lessons shall be held in the customary manner, with one choir making an offering at Mass. On the thirtieth day, it shall again be held in full. During these thirty days, however, every priest shall celebrate Mass for him daily in a private place of prayer. The deacons shall sing the entire Psalter, and the subdeacons shall devoutly sing the fifty psalms. If they are occupied and cannot complete them on one day, they shall perform them on another.

A letter shall also be sent to each neighboring monastery to announce the day of this deposition, in the following form:

> “Lord N., abbot of the monastery of N., to all the faithful of holy Church, both those set over others and those subject to them. Since the unalterable lot of the hour awaits all, we wish you to know about a certain brother of ours, N., whom the Lord has deigned to call from the prison of this age on the day of N. For him we earnestly beseech you to be zealous intercessors before the Lord, so that, through your intercession, he may feel the support of those with whom he was united in the fellowship of the order.”

If a brother from another monastery, one known and familiar to us, is reported to have died, the brothers everywhere shall assemble when the board has been struck and all the bells rung, as we have said. Prostrate in the oratory, they shall sing the seven penitential psalms, followed by this prayer:

> “May the prayer of the blessed Lady of God and ever-virgin Mary, of your holy apostle Peter, of your holy confessor Benedict, and of all your saints, together with the devout supplication of your present household, satisfy you, our Lord God, on behalf of the soul of our brother N.; may it obtain the forgiveness of all sins for which we pray. Do not permit him to be tormented by the flames of Gehenna, whom you redeemed with the glorious blood of that same Son of yours, our Lord Jesus Christ. Who lives and reigns with you and the Holy Spirit for ever and ever.”

For him, the first, third, seventh, and thirtieth days shall be observed in full, and the remaining days more briefly. His name shall be entered among the anniversaries. For an unknown person, only the commendation of the soul and one day shall be observed.

If those who are greatly needed, whether in spiritual or bodily matters, are weighed down by serious illness, then, as soon as this has been reported by the messenger, the board alone shall be struck and everyone shall assemble in the church. They shall earnestly pray for them, reciting the seven penitential psalms with the litanies and appropriate prayers. Other sick persons shall be treated as stated above.

The aforesaid king, in order to conclude the epilogue of this little book in an orthodox manner, just as he had begun its preface with a faithful and reasonable exhortation, examined the matter with prudent judgment and, with the full authority of his royal power, strictly forbade and commanded that no abbot or abbess should hoard for himself or herself a little earthly treasure for this purpose: namely, so that they might possess the customary tribute, which the natives ordinarily call *Heriatua*, usually given to the powerful men of this country after the death of kings, and so that it might be given for them in imitation of secular custom.

Thus, falling under the anathema of Ananias and Sapphira, they would, in contempt of the rule and to the great detriment of their souls, abrogate all the precepts of the holy rule that forbid private property. In the name of Christ, whose vicars they are, and of his mother Mary and all the saints, he forbade this forever, both for himself and for all his successors, whether it were to be given to an abbot or an abbess.

With benevolent intention, however, he urged this: that the fathers and mothers of monasteries should place in the heavenly treasury, through the hands of the poor and with great and continual contrition, whatever remains after necessary uses, so that, while the body remains on earth, the soul may follow after it by dwelling there where it has most justly sent its treasures.

If anything remains when a prior dies, the succeeding abbot, instructed by the grace of the Holy Spirit, shall distribute it not to fleshly relatives or secular tyrants according to the former’s dictate, but shall wisely dispose of it by assisting the needs of the brothers and the poor, making the arrangement with the counsel of the brothers.

# In the Year of the Lord 988. Adalbero, Archbishop of Reims

[Col. 0503]

## Historical Notice

*(From volume IX of Gallia Christiana.)*

[Col. 0503A] Adalbero, distinguished for the integrity of his morals and trained in ecclesiastical disciplines, was appointed to the episcopal see in 969 through the favor and foresight of King Lothar, according to the appendix to Flodoard, p. 178. But what the author of that appendix omitted is that he had been educated at the monastery of Gorze together with Saint Rothad, bishop of Cambrai, according to the *Chronicle of Cambrai*, book I, chapter 101.

He was the son of Godfrey the Elder, count of the Ardennes; his brothers were another Godfrey, from whom the dukes of Lower Lorraine descended, and Henry. As soon as he was installed, he restored the religion of the Church of Reims, which had grown excessively lukewarm, to a better condition. To make what he had in mind more lasting—I use here the words of the *Chronicle of Mouzon*—he strongly urged the canons to live together and to have their dwellings enclosed within the circuit of the cloister.

For this reason, the same Chronicle, discussing Adalbero elsewhere, reports that he ultimately made the canons of Reims rich from poor men, well adorned from peasants, and religious and table-companions from men who had previously lived separately in cottages [Col. 0503B]. It seeks to prove this from the arrangement of the Reims cloister and especially from the common table, which was in force in his own age, although, “because of the greatness and nobility of that age,” it says, “few traces of strict discipline then remained.”

Adalbero repaired the damage that Odalric had inflicted on the borough of Saint Remigius. He also granted the monks of Saint Remigius the abbey of Saint Timothy for the use of their guests; on this matter, see the Bollandists, August, volume IV, p. 576.

Moreover, he repaired or enlarged the basilica of Saint Dionysius of Reims. He also restored the schools of Reims to their former splendor. After returning from the city of Rome, where he was staying in 970, he placed Gerbert, the oracle of his age, in charge of them.

He made use of Gerbert’s services in many matters, especially in drafting letters, many of which are inscribed in Gerbert’s name and addressed to kings and princes [Col. 0503C], and to the principal men of the Gallican clergy [Col. 0504A]. “Nor is this surprising,” says Marlotus. “For since he shone under Lothar with the dignity of chief chancellor, and various difficult affairs arose amid the troubled condition of the kingdom, what more distinguished writer and secretary could he have employed—one who knew how, through his sharper style and skill in speaking, to bend minds wherever he wished?”

In 971 he replaced the canons at the monastery of Mouzon with monks taken from the chief monastery of Saint Remigius, transferring to the same place the body of Saint Arnulf the martyr. This arrangement was confirmed that same year by John XIII, supreme pontiff, and by a synod convened at Mont-Sainte-Marie in the region of Tardenois, which he presided over in May 972.

In the following year, in December, he convened another synod at the same mountain [Note: [Col. 0503C] Mabillon mentions two synods convened at Mont-Sainte-Marie in the diocese of Soissons, between Basilicas and Fines, in *Benedictine Annals*, volume III, p. 622. There he clearly proves that the first was celebrated in May 972, and the second in 973—or, if it was not celebrated, at least convened.

As regards the first, there is no doubt that it confirmed the institution recently made by Archbishop Adalbero of monks in the monastery of Mouzon. But the Igny codex, in Colvenerius’s appendix to Flodoard, p. 180, and Acherius, *Spicilegium*, volume VII, preface, p. XIX, assign it to the year 983; while the Mouzon codex, in Marlotus, volume II, p. 11, assigns it to 976. Both are wrong, although Marlotus believed that the year 977 should be substituted for the year 976 in the Mouzon codex, while others believed that the year 973 should be substituted for the year 983 in the Igny codex.

Moreover, the signatures of this council, which are found in Mabillon and Acherius, cited above, p. 657; in Marlotus, p. 12; and in Labbe, *Collection of Councils*, volume IX, p. 709, cannot agree with the years 972 or 973, nor with 976 or 977, nor finally with 983. For in those years some of the signatories had not yet become bishops or abbots, some had already died, and others had been deposed.

Marlotus believes—and this is sufficiently plausible—that bishops and abbots often gathered at Mont-Sainte-Marie for a synod, and that the names of those who were present there at different times were collected into one and the same catalogue by some copyist. It is also possible that others—whether abbots or bishops—later added their names to the signatures of those who had attended the council of 972, as confirmation of the matters previously enacted.]

In 974 he likewise restored monks to the monastery of Saint Theodoric. In the following year, in the presence of King Lothar, he transferred the saint’s body from the old tomb into a silver shrine. In the same year, 975, he consecrated the basilica of Blandin and held a council at Reims [Col. 0504B], at which Theobald, usurper of the Church of Amiens, was excommunicated. In 976 or the following year he consecrated Rothad bishop of Cambrai. (*Chronicle of Cambrai*, book I, chapter 102.)

It cannot be said how greatly Adalbero exerted himself to advance peace between the kingdoms of France and Germany. Yet, although he vigorously supported the party of Otto III, he was accused of disloyalty; but he cleared himself of that charge before King Lothar. Nevertheless, he incurred the displeasure of Louis V, Lothar’s son, who not only ordered him either to renew his allegiance by oath or to depart from the city and kingdom, but was also considering bringing a public accusation of treason against him before the assembly of the Franks. But when Louis had been removed from this life, the kingdom passed to Hugh Capet, whom Adalbero anointed king at Noyon on 3 July 987; and in that same year, when Hugh confirmed the privileges of the monastery of Corbie, Adalbero likewise imitated him with his own hand.

Meanwhile Charles, Louis V’s uncle and duke of Lorraine, unable to bear his anger because Hugh had been preferred to him in the kingdom, seized Laon. From there he ravaged the neighboring cities, fields, and estates with plunder and fire, like an enemy. Then, sending letters to the archbishop of Reims once and again through envoys, he complained about him as though he had been the instigator of all the evils that had befallen him.

To this Adalbero replied:

“Who was I,” he said, “that I alone should impose a king upon the Franks? These are public affairs, not private ones. Do you think that I hate the royal house? I call my Redeemer to witness that I do not hate it. You ask what above all you ought to do. How difficult this is to say: I neither know sufficiently, nor, if I did know, would I dare to say it. You ask for my friendship. Would that the day might come when I could honorably assist your interests. Although you have invaded the Lord’s sanctuary, seized the queen to whom you swore the things that we know, committed the bishop of Laon to prison, and disregarded the anathema of the bishops (I say nothing of my superior, against whom you have undertaken an enterprise beyond your strength), nevertheless I cannot be unmindful of the favor you showed me, nor of the enemy’s weapons that you diverted,” and so forth.

After this Adalbero did not live long. In 987, in the month of October, he had gone with the other nobles of the kingdom to assist Hugh Capet in besieging the city. But, severely afflicted by the labor of the siege and the force of fever, he arranged to be taken back to Reims, so that there he might for a while restore his spirit through reading Sacred Scripture and Boethius. As his illness grew worse, however, he finally breathed his last in that same year—either on 23 January, according to the Chronicle of Mouzon, or on 5 January, according to his ancient epitaph (a date that falls in the year 988)—after he had governed the diocese of Reims vigorously for nineteen years. Others say that he died at Laon, to which he had been exiled by Duke Charles.

His body was buried in the principal church of Reims beneath the altar of the Lord’s Cross, with an epitaph engraved on bronze that still existed before the restoration of the former church, as follows:

> Nature, the mother, had bestowed upon you  
> what she considered highest,  
> and, for the increase of merit, upon you, Bishop Adalbero,  
> when she took you, outstanding above all mortals, from the world—  
> on the fifth day of the month that pours forth waters,  
> beneath the burden of events.

Now these words are read on a small stone near the steps of the sanctuary, or beside the eagle:

> ADALBERO, ARCHBISHOP.

The author of the appendix to Flodoard adds:

“Every year the day of his death is reverently commemorated, and a plentiful alms of bread and wine is distributed to the poor; this alms is also called Adalbero’s Mandate. It should also be known how the expense of this alms is prepared: namely, from the house called the hospital of the poor, four sextarii of grain; from the grain chamber, four; from the demesne granary, one modius of grain; and sufficient wine.”

[Col. 0505]

# THE LETTERS OF ADALBERO

(At Duchesne, *Scriptores rerum Francicarum*, vol. II, among the letters of Gerbert.)

## LETTER I. TO ECBERT, ARCHBISHOP OF TRIER

[Col. 0505C]

As we shudder at the weakening of your commonwealth through the indolence of certain men, so we blush for it, both because of the privilege of our affection for you and because of our shared kinship with our homeland. Have so few kings been created that you wish to place a new one before your lord’s son? Perhaps, because he is Greek, as you say, you wish to institute a co-ruler in the Greek manner. Where has the most sacred faith gone? Have the benefits conferred upon you by the Ottos slipped from your mind? Recall your great understanding; consider your nobility, lest you wish to become a perpetual disgrace to your family. If you proclaim that your strength is failing you, seek out those who think better; trust that we shall be supporters and fellow-workers in such affairs. In the disturbance and confusion of everything, who will lift another’s burden?

Finally, if you cannot protect the city of Trier without compromising the dignity of your name, let Reims be sufficient for both of us; and we shall be richer than Eucharius and Sixtus once were. If ratified, this will remove the disgrace from you; if rejected, it will make us free.

## LETTER II. TO WILLIGIS, ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ

Father, we must work together with great steadfastness to secure peace and repose. What else is the disturbance of kingdoms than the desolation of the Churches? For our part, piety and the many benefits of the Ottos toward us do not permit us to oppose the emperor’s son. In short, we have advanced our own affairs in support of him. If it pleases you, we shall establish the agreement of one party permanently by common consent. We shall ask nothing of you except with the fidelity owed to our lord.

We say these things with God as our witness, and in complete trust we entrust them to your prudence. He who tried to extinguish two Ottos will wish the third to survive. Remember that saying of Cicero: “It is foolish to demand faith from those by whom you have often been deceived.” At the same time, since Providence has not without purpose granted you the knowledge and ability to understand what it approves in these matters and what you judge contrary to them, and who support them and who dissent from you, indicate these things to us in secure replies.

Let the depth of your counsel take thought for the affairs of blessed Remigius, your neighbor, lest either a rapacious plunderer seize them, or Otto, who ought to be their guardian, become their devastator. In these matters also, may we be permitted to learn your will.

## LETTER III. TO WALON AND HIS OBSTINATE ASSOCIATES

Until now we have patiently endured your folly. But now, because you make light of synodal decrees, despise the summons addressed to you, and prefer human things to divine ones, we summon you once again to be heard at the assembly of our brothers to be held at Gualdo’s court on the Kalends of July. Come there, however, or on that same day await the sentence of condemnation with whatever disposition you please, together with those who support you.

## LETTER IV. TO NOTGER, BISHOP OF LIÈGE

[Col. 0507A]

Please do not think ill of our friendship, Father, because my brother Godfrey did not visit the king by prior agreement and did not come at the appointed time you desired. A sound deliberation indeed detained him, but an accident caused by an injured foot delayed him. It is therefore for your prudence to plead the cause of your friend, to stand up for him, and to make a faithful promise concerning him, as you know and as is just.

For our part, we have carried out the matter concerning your lord’s young servant according to your decision; and if you change it for the better, with Divine Providence favorable we shall repay it with something better. We shall compensate your affairs as if they were our own. The man whom you know to be close to us and most faithful to you was, as was proper, our interpreter before the royal majesty, and what you requested was firmly obtained without regard to our enemies.

And because everything must not be entrusted to letters, we wished you to attend the appointed assembly, and we shall arrange to await your presence until the third day before the Kalends of June. One must meet the proper time, lest, when you withdraw, it become inconvenient.

## LETTER V. TO WIDO, ABBOT OF GHENT

Those who overturn the principal elements of religion claim the citadel of religion for themselves in vain. Does one who lacks charity, who disregards a promised faith, protect religion? If you have offered us fraternal conversations and caused us to rejoice through messengers of whatever sort, yet—conscience is witness—after so long an interval they retain their own things more tightly than they desire what belongs to others. From among your brothers we adopted one, but ours, who ought to have returned, has been detained.

Write back, then, at least, what has settled in your mind concerning these matters, and whether any of our boys can be educated with you; and, if so, when this ought to be done.

## LETTER VI. TO ECBERT, ARCHBISHOP OF TRIER

Dangerous times do not commit everything to letters that will be entrusted to the most faithful envoys. What you communicated to us through our G. was full of joy and delight, concerning the condition of the Churches of God and of the kingdoms, and concerning the man through whom these things might be accomplished. I feared him as a tyrant, but now we admire him as a man full of faith and wisdom.

Carry out what you promised us concerning him. What you request from us concerning him has been secured, both with the greatest silence regarding your secrets and with the greatest fidelity regarding our actions.

## LETTER VII. TO NOTGER, BISHOP OF LIÈGE

My brother is sending you an envoy by prior agreement, but one entirely uninformed about the present matter, lest he be marked either by falsehood or by negligence. On the fifteenth day before the Kalends of January we shall speak with the archbishop of Trier; whatever we learn more fully, we shall take care to communicate as fully as possible to your prudence.

## LETTER VIII. TO KING LOTHAR

A letter bearing the impression of your name, with unknown signs, delivered only through a trusted messenger, brought us grief. For it orders the enclosure of the monastery of Saint Paul to be entirely demolished, as though it were a fortress of hostile defense. A priest must not be ordered to do what might be fearful even to any tyrant—especially when there are many who would rejoice in such things if so great a pleasure in carrying them out were present.

Moreover, the fact that this place is unsuitable for enemies is proved by nature’s having constructed several sites around the city that are more suitable and, if this pleases the enemy, more convenient to fortify. Know, however, that we have always wished, and shall always wish, to look to your safety and fidelity and to obey you, with divine regard placed before all else. But your order that the guard of the cities be prolonged is not tolerated by the soldiers; they repent of their undertaking, since want and scarcity are bringing everything to ruin.

## LETTER IX. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF TRIER

[Col. 0508B]

I do not wish to conceal from your fatherhood, to whom I owe everything, that I sent the preceding letter solely at the command of my lord. And since my nephew was ready to promise and preserve the faith that you had promised to my lord, he obtained from us the permission that the authority of our ancestors had promulgated. But by what means his fidelity has become sullied is hidden from our understanding.

How, then, shall we either call this man Adalbero, or excommunicate him, or ask others to do the same? Therefore, since we cannot do this according to the laws, neither shall we do it ourselves nor encourage others to do it, lest we seem to drag either ourselves or those who have deserved well of us into an abyss.

And since the heavenly King says, “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s,” we shall always offer pure faith and pure service to our laws, we shall deviate in nothing, yet we shall place the Lord’s interests first. But since at this time few have taken care of the things that belong to the Lord, whenever we zealously defend the Lord’s law we are branded either with treachery or with some other fault. Thus, so to speak, being placed between the hammer and the anvil, we have little hope of escape without loss of soul and body.

If, therefore, you have any compassion; if we have always honored you as a brother, or rather as a father, accept the burden of friendship through counsel and help, so that we who trusted greatly in you in prosperity may not despair of you in adversity. We confess these things, which must be concealed, not to a man, but to the fidelity of a great priest. We call upon the Lord as witness, invoking twice over the fearful avenger against those who reveal these things to our injury.

## LETTER X. TO THE SAME

Although your letters release us from a multitude of cares, we are again entangled in others. For behold, we rejoice in the constancy of your affection and in your faith and devotion toward us. But who has twisted your understanding so that you thought we felt whatever our relatives feel?

I do not know why I should hate Lord Henry; I do know why I should love him. But what outward fruit does that love now bear? For Providence imposes necessity through some circumstances, while blind fortune creates disturbance through others. Finally, pressed by such a mass of affairs, we consider this saying wise rather than poetic:

> “Whatever it is wrong to correct becomes lighter through patience;  
> and if what you wish cannot be done, at least wish what you can.”

This is what we desire: may the arms of sinners be broken, and may God confirm it.

There is one matter requiring explanation. Since I was formerly the most faithful interpreter of your mother and queen, why am I deprived of this business, and why do I learn so many things through others rather than through you? And since, as I have confessed and continue to confess, I owe you everything, I fear for you as I fear for myself. For, in a different manner, the same saying is addressed to us all: “Let whoever stands take heed lest he fall.”

We must therefore deliberate together. To make this possible, make me a participant in all matters concerning your assemblies at Duisburg [reading uncertain]. Also, if it is hidden from your understanding—as rumor has it—what the royal power demands from Duke Beatrice and from your leading men, investigate it carefully and inform me what your disposition toward it is.

For the rest, as we began, we think the very best of you; and with the same faith with which we entrust our affairs to you, we accept yours.

## LETTER XI. TO THE SAME

Just as we never tried to retain the monk Gozbert against your will, so, according to our decision, we shall bring him back to Mouzon on the first day of the Rogations. And because we have made use of him for so long, we shall not be forgetful before you of so great a kindness.

If, therefore, you do not wish him to remain with us longer, let him be received there by your people, since our own are not permitted to proceed farther, both because of the number of enemies and because of the zeal of those who cunningly oppose us.

## LETTER XII. OBJECTION AGAINST ADALBERO

I am accused and held guilty of treachery and disloyalty toward the royal majesty because I granted permission to my nephew, namely a cleric of my Church, since he had both visited the palace and accepted a bishopric as a gift from another king, in a kingdom that the elder King Lothar had reclaimed as his own right; and because afterward I conferred ecclesiastical orders upon him without the permission and authority of my superior.

## LETTER XIII. DEFENSE

When my superior, King Lothar, neither possessed the kingdom of Lorraine nor reclaimed it from my brother’s son, I finally obtained this arrangement, upon giving my pledge: that, if circumstances ever required it, I would return him and his possessions to the king and his people without obstinacy.

But when it was being arranged that my superior should act as advocate for the emperor’s son, and hostages had been given for that reason, he repeatedly demanded my brother’s son through envoys. He rebuked me for receiving him sluggishly and for violating my pledge; he said that his affair was being disturbed by many people and that the man was betraying the position he held. He proclaimed the terrible Judge of the Last Judgment as the avenger of despised faith and kinship.

Since, therefore, my superior had said nothing to me about reclaiming the kingdom, but only about the advocacy, and since he had not prohibited me from granting permission to the cleric, but had even willingly consented—as I learned from my envoys—provided that the young man wished to do what his father had promised to his own people, I released him when he departed and demanded his pledge, so that he might most sincerely preserve the purpose for which the hostages had been given. He has offered that pledge until now, and, as we believe, continues to offer it.

I conferred upon him the orders of deacon and priest, lest, emancipated from us, he become subject to another in receiving them, and lest our Church be exposed to envy by having a subdeacon from among its own raised to the episcopal summit. I did so also because these orders confer neither provinces, cities, nor estates belonging to kingdoms, but rather things belonging to the heavenly kingdom: namely, opposition to vices and cultivation of virtues.

In this matter, where I was being charged with treachery and disloyalty, I have shown, as I think, both that I possessed the greatest faith and that I especially preserved fidelity toward my superior.

## LETTER XIV. TO DUCHESS BEATRICE

[Col. 0510B]

Concerning the matters that you seek to have communicated to you with greater certainty, we know nothing more than what we have either said in person or what you have learned through our embassy. For the rest, we both wish and rejoice if you, as free friends, prosper according to your desire, while the royal honor remains safe. Consider our affairs your own. In the presence of Duke Hugh, confidently presume upon the purity of your intention and your steadfast faith.

Finally, whatever we demand from you, we shall in due time render through your service. Above all, we are grateful that through you we have been informed about many matters. We have heard that the monk Meing., long sought at the request of Abbot Rai., has left Corbie and gone to Rouen. If the opportunity is granted, we shall endeavor to carry out your will in everything concerning him.

## LETTER XV. TO THE SAME

[Col. 0510C]

Since matters are proceeding for you according to your desire, we rightly rejoice with you. And because through you we frequently learn what was unknown, and because we experience the sincerity of your affection toward us, we count this among the foremost things.

But what circumstance so changed the proposed conference of the ladies that Duke Henry alone is coming? Whether this is being done through the deceit of the other party, and which princes will come there, if you know, you will disclose fully and faithfully in response to our entreaties.

## LETTER XVI. TO THE SAME

[Col. 0510D]

I seem to see the excellence of your discernment: peace established among the princes, the commonwealth well ordered, and changed for the better through you. There is only one matter that troubles many people: the archbishop of Trier, delaying his ordination with such great effort, either wishes to surrender himself, together with the duke and the kingdom of Lorraine, into the hands of the Franks, while concealing this from you—something that makes it plausible that a conference is to be held at Verdun—or wishes to contrive something still greater.

Your friend A. is ordered to destroy the ordination of the nephew. Is the archbishop either king or primate of the people of Trier? The faction of the archbishop seems to contain this affair in some way, wherever it may come from. Let your prudence therefore keep watch; investigate toward what point the weight of such great matters is inclining, and take care to learn whether Duke Henry will preserve his faith toward you.

## LETTER XVII. TO NOTGER, BISHOP OF LIÈGE

[Col. 0511A]

The gathering of the bishops, concerning which it was reported that it had not taken place, must be attributed to the lateness of the letter’s delivery. These matters will be discussed upon your arrival, and, if it seems appropriate, they will afterward be deliberated more fully, both privately and publicly.

For the rest, since my brother considers himself and his possessions to belong to you and places much hope for his safety in you, you must restrain the soldier Walter from invading the estates of his Wazo. By doing this, you will both avoid an unfavorable rumor and appear not to have failed in your proper duty.

## LETTER XVIII. TO THE SAME

[Col. 0511B]
