With one who has entered into an account with a wise man, one should not labor through a lengthy speech. What was taken from you by force will be restored. Trust the friend who gives his pledge of faith. If that is not sufficient, let a hostage be received from those whose possessions we have asked to be restored to them in turn; there must be no delay, both because of the necessity of the approaching court and because we have the highest opinion of you.

While we were dictating these things, we received hostages from the besieged fortress, to be returned tomorrow, as we inform you. The lords’ conference is to be held at Metz; we greatly wish you to be present. If the matter has been left as arranged, we are endeavoring through you to learn the cause that has brought it about. Private circumstances will teach you what you will need to know privately.

## LETTER XIX. TO ECBERT, ARCHBISHOP OF TRIER

[Col. 0511C]

The more urgent care demanded by the present circumstances prevented us from carrying out what we had ordered from the city of Verdun concerning the return of our brother G. For necessity both imposes what we do not want and takes away what we do want.

Now at last, lest we appear ungrateful toward those who have deserved well of us, we remit the matter to your clemency as far as we can, asking only this from your customary benevolence: that, on our recommendation, he may experience your graciousness; and, if it can be done with your approval, that he may not be deprived of the studies to which he has resolved to devote himself most diligently.

## LETTER XX. TO ECBERT, ARCHBISHOP

Although I know that no benefits corresponding to your merits can be offered in accordance with my desire, my spirit nevertheless burns, and what it cannot accomplish in deed it pursues in affection. We have often experienced the privilege of your love toward us through letters, often through messengers, often through deeds themselves.

And since you have offered holy petitions to the Lord on our behalf, the benevolence shown to us by the lady Augusta on the sixth day before the Nones of March bears witness to how fruitfully you offered them. On that day the most glorious King Lothar, the brightest star of the Franks, was taken from the world. The man whom you thought deprived of royal favor was not excluded from intimacy.

## LETTER XXI. TO THE EMPRESS THEOPHANO

[Col. 0512A]

Although until now I have always honored you as my lady because of the merits of your most excellent and ever-memorable husband, the Augustus, your recent benefits and those of your son both contain your former affection and greatly increase our faith toward you and yours.

Our Church cherishes, among its chief treasures, the pledge of your friendship toward us. Therefore, if it can be done, let blessed Remigius experience the favor of so great a lady in recovering the possessions that have been lost, both because of his own merits and because of whatever services we may be pleased to render.

Let us also experience the grace that has already been well founded: namely, that you deign to inform us through an envoy, and even better in writing, about the peace and the conditions of peace to be established with our king. We are entirely ready, insofar as it is lawful, to offer the most sincere fidelity. Thus we shall be better able to provide jointly for your safety and ours.

## LETTER XXII. TO MAIOLUS, ABBOT OF CLUNY

[Col. 0512B]

Your exhortation against the invader is indeed excellent. But since it is written, “The things that Jesus began to do and to teach,” why do you plead separate jurisdictions and different regions under heaven, so that you may communicate with one whom you have declared guilty while others do not communicate with him?

The holy Fathers resisted heresies, nor did they think that anything belonged outside their concern if they heard that it had been wrongly done somewhere. There is one Catholic Church spread throughout the entire world. These words are yours—or rather, through you, those of the Holy Spirit. No faithful Christian will fail to find this ambitious audacity detestable.

Therefore detest the invader. Let him perceive that you do not favor him and do not communicate with him, and, through you, that not only every religious person of your order but also, if it can be done, the Roman pontiff presses him with curses.

And just as you learned the matter as it was, so you judged what you had learned according to the dignity of your name. We and all our people, like the most faithful companions, shall follow only such a leader, and we shall never communicate with this invader—approved as so honorable, yet so disgracefully wicked—without your command.

## LETTER XXIII. TO ECBERD [EBRARD], ABBOT OF TOURS

[Col. 0512C]

Your letters have made clear how great is the gravity of your character, how blameless your conduct of life, and how pure your speech. Therefore, the zeal of your piety and severity moved us to adopt your judgment, as did that man full of God, in whom we have great confidence.

We shall therefore remove that treacherous man from our fellowship and from the judgment of our brethren, such great Fathers; and we shall regard as an enemy anyone who dares to say what must not be said against the judgment of the reverend Father Maiolus and the venerated Father Ecberd. If, with Divine Providence favorable, we obtain the support of the princes, we shall add still greater useful measures to these.

## LETTER XXIV. TO THE EMPRESS THEOPHANO AND TO HER SON OTTO

[Col. 0512D]

The sudden and unexpected assault of the king bears witness to the extent to which his anger and fury have burst out against us; it was scarcely repelled without great slaughter on both sides. Those who were supposed to be faithful envoys ordered us to demolish the fortifications under your rule and to offer an oath according to their will, or to depart from the city and kingdom. They invoked the ancient benevolence of the divine Augustus O. toward us and our familiar service to him. These and similar considerations have for the present obstructed our own safety.

Therefore bring certain consolation in an uncertain time, and do not mock us with doubtful hope, since we have never doubted in preserving our faith toward you. On the sixth day before the Kalends of April an assembly has been summoned among the Franks, and there we shall be charged with disloyalty because we granted permission to the bishop of Verdun and because we promoted him to the dignity of the priesthood, and that the same man be demanded back from us, thus making the matter impossible.

If these things take place as described, your faithful servants and ours, Gerbert and Renier, will be unable to meet you at Noyon, as you wished. But let your clemency provide them at Cologne, whither they are afterward to come, with a guide suited to so great a journey.

On the second day before the Kalends of March we shall speak with Counts Otto and Heribert, and, having again given the hostages whom we received, we shall attempt to return my brother to your service. We have expressed briefly the distress under which we are pressed because of the faith we have always kept and must continue to keep toward you.

We await your salutary aid from your side with steadfast spirit, and we beg that the enemies remain unaware of this very fact, lest their anger against us blaze more fiercely.

### Couplets on a Chalice

> From this, thirst and hunger flee; hasten, faithful ones.  
> Bishop Adalbero divides these treasures among the peoples.

### On Gifts

> Virgin Mary, your bishop Adalbero offers you this gift.

## LETTER XXV. TO THE BISHOP OF BEAUVAIS

[Col. 0513C]

For the present we have not thought it necessary to reply to your writings, since at the appointed conference we shall be able to satisfy you more carefully, according to our ability, concerning each matter. And because, for love of us, you put your private affairs second and diligently attend to ours, we count this among the foremost things and store it in a grateful memory, intending to repay you with no lesser benefits if faithless fortune should turn against us.

## LETTER XXVI. TO THE LADY THE EMPRESS THEOPHANO

[Col. 0513D]

On the sixteenth day before the Kalends of June, when my brother had been freed from the darkness of hell, a certain light of your honor seemed to rise. But every effort must be made lest Counts Otto and Heribert corrupt that light with the blind fire of desire.

Therefore you will graciously hear my brother’s just and honorable requests, both on account of his merit and on account of your benevolence toward me. But from unjust requests, and from those which the tyrant irrationally extorted for the destruction of the Churches of God and the disgrace of your family, you will wisely turn away.

Will you permanently alienate from the Church, by oath, the estates of the bishop of Verdun that Count Godfrey unwillingly gives, together with his son Bishop Adalbero, for his ransom? Will you permit those men to build fortresses in those same estates according to their desire, when they are now secretly gathering forces of chosen soldiers in order to attack you if you are at Clermont?

For, because Duke Theodoric seized Satanaca vineyard—as though in vengeance for the queen—they pretend that they are going to invade the town of Juveniacum, intending to commit a crime if they perceive that you are accompanied by only a small force.

I have said these things while entirely anxious for your sake, and I shall carry out with complete fidelity whatever you communicated to me through G., your most faithful servant, who asks that this be granted to him: that he may be the most truthful interpreter of your party.

## LETTER XXVII. TO ECBERT, ARCHBISHOP OF TRIER

For the appointed work, we are sending the designated figures: a marvelous form, nourishing both mind and eyes, which a brother will make for a brother and a sister for a sister. Your great and celebrated skill will ennoble our small material, both through the addition of glass and through the composition of an elegant craftsman.

## LETTER XXVIII. TO THE BROTHERS OF BLANDINIUM

[Col. 0514B]

How long will you abuse the patience of those whom you were once thought to have as most faithful friends? You put forward the language of charity, while preparing to practice robbery. Why do you break apart the most sacred fellowship?

You voluntarily offered certain books to us, but you retain them, although they belong by right to us and to our Church, contrary to divine and human laws. Either charity will be restored through the return of the books together with what belongs with them, or a deposit wrongly retained will be condemned to a deserved punishment.

## LETTER XXIX. TO ECBERT, ARCHBISHOP OF TRIER

[Col. 0514C]

Because we are not enjoying your long-desired counsel, we do not endure it with sufficient patience. We persist and strive to overcome the intervening accidents that disturb us. A synod has been summoned in the regions of the Rhine, as rumor has it; but both more serious illnesses among our bishops and royal affairs disturb the synod that we wished to hold as one body.

Yet, so that we do not languish in idleness meanwhile, we intend for the present to seek the intercession of blessed Otto. Through you we plan to secure our return, so that by this reunion we may punish our prolonged separation. And since our route lies through Verdun, send there, if possible, on the Kalends of November the cross that, as we hope, has been fashioned through your knowledge. Let it be a pledge of friendship.

Thus, while the pleasing work is more frequently brought before our eyes, indissoluble love will increase day by day.

## LETTER XXX. TO ECBERT, ARCHBISHOP OF TRIER

[Col. 0514D]

Although we intend to respond to your benefits at the proper time, the holy fellowship presumes that these same benefits should nevertheless be increased. Therefore, at our request, let Hidilo, my brother’s priest, be released from the bond of excommunication until his case is examined at the next assembly and either he is restored as innocent or he frees us from an unjust demand.

Let the man who is to be the bearer of our books also be the bearer of the *Sacramentale*, most beautifully adorned with gold. For we shall very soon write back certain things that will please you, and through the same bearer we shall deposit a volume inferior in no respect.

## LETTER XXXI. TO THE SAME

[Col. 0515A]

Cut off from the journey we had begun by every difficulty of circumstances, we judged that the harbor of salvation must be sought. For continuous torrents intercept the mountain slopes, and the plains are so covered by unceasing waters that, with villages and their inhabitants swept away and cattle destroyed, they inspire the terror of a renewed flood; those skilled in natural phenomena having removed hope of better weather.

We therefore flee to you as to Noah’s ark and strive with all our strength to visit Trier, intending to return the services of blessed Otto, extorted by force, in devotion to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles.

## LETTER XXXII. TO FELLOW PROVINCIALS

We invite you, with the dearest affection, to join the brothers of our diocese, since we have much to discuss concerning the state of the Churches of God and much concerning public and private affairs—not so much for our honor and advantage as for yours.

Place of discussion: Mont Sainte-Marie of Terdon. Time: the third day before the Ides of December. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXIII. TO ROTHARD, ARCHBISHOP OF CAMBRAI

Upon receiving this letter, excommunicate Baldwin, whom we recently excommunicated, because of his wife, whom he wrongly abandoned; and let the obedience that has been delayed too long through negligence correct the matter. His having gone to Rome and deceived the lord pope with lies will profit him nothing, since Paul says: “If anyone announces to you anything other than what you received, let him be anathema, even if he is an angel.”

Be defenders, therefore, with us, of the divine laws, since you rejoice in sharing the priestly dignity.

## LETTER XXXIV. TO . . . .

Overthrown by your distress, we have been relieved by your relief. We have added, and shall continue to add, whatever supplications we can; and if the art of medicine suggests anything to our efforts, we shall send it as soon as possible.

We are somewhat troubled, however, that you communicated to us so late what was happening around you, especially concerning the case of our brother and nephew. As soon as we read your letter and received our envoy from the palace—who firmly asserted that Ar. had received his son as a royal gift—we immediately learned of it.

In this matter we have no other consolation except that we know the soldiers strongly disagree with him. We shall also work on this matter in whatever way we learn your will.

## LETTER XXXV. TO DUKE CHARLES

If our service can contribute anything to your excellence, we rejoice greatly in this. Since we have not now come to you in accordance with your command, the terror caused by your soldiers, who were ranging everywhere, is responsible.

But if you care about our presence, send men whose faith we dare trust until we can have guides for the journey in safety. And so that you may understand that these words are spoken with great sincerity, remember our counsel and our conversation at the palace of Ingelheim, and see whether what I promised you concerning the long-sought peace between the kings has been accomplished.

Meanwhile, I faithfully advise you to treat the queen and the bishop with the utmost gentleness, as befits your rank, and not to allow yourselves to be enclosed within the walls under any circumstances.

## XXXVI. TO THE LADY THEOPHANO

We have always wished to look to your advantage, and we rejoice in doing so, since we have devoted ourselves and all that belongs to us to your service. Therefore, from such affection and such love, we presume to ask from your munificence what we know was once granted to us through your most faithful messengers: namely, that if any church in the borderland of the kingdoms should become vacant of a pastor, no one else should be appointed to it except the person whom, with sound judgment, we have chosen as entirely suited to your interests.

And because all the provincials know that we have with us Abbot Gerbert, expelled from Italy but remaining steadfast in unfeigned faith, we ask by every means at our disposal that he be placed over that church. To us he is a true son; to you he is in every respect a most obedient servant.

Although we are greatly burdened by his absence, we nevertheless put private concerns after our common benefits. We earnestly beseech you to learn your will concerning these matters as soon as possible through sacred replies.

## LETTER XXXVII. TO THE CLERGY AND PEOPLE. . .

[Col. 0516C]

The bitter death of your father and our most beloved brother has brought us great sorrow and great anxiety. Therefore God must now be called upon with all the depths of our being, so that he may restore to you a father and to us a suitable brother.

Meanwhile, let it be your ever-watchful concern that, according to divine and human laws, the possessions of the deceased bishop, both movable and immovable, be reserved for the future bishop, lest—God forbid—if inadequate provision has been made [the transmitted reading is uncertain], both royal censure and an even more severe divine judgment be imposed upon those who are negligent.

## LETTER XXXVIII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF TRIER, V. V. D. K. A.

Do not rashly believe rumors; since you have often experienced this, experience it now. For, with divine grace going before and the urgency of your prayers lending support, we retain all the affairs of the bishopric as before, and nothing else came of so great a report except this: after midday, when the royal soldiers had been overcome by wine and sleep, the townsmen made a sortie with all their strength. Our men resisted and drove them back, while beggars set the camp ablaze; in that fire the entire equipment of the siege was consumed. These losses must be restored many times over on the eighth day before the Kalends of September. We return you immense thanks, moreover, because you take care of us with such exceptional affection. We both wish and pray that this may continue with holy petitions, which we shall extend to the end with the same resolve and desire.

## LETTER XXXIX. TO DUKE CHARLES

How do you seek counsel from me, when you count me among your most faithless enemies? How do you call me “father,” when you wish to take my life from me? In the end, I have not deserved this from you; rather, I have always fled—and continue to flee—the deceitful counsels of ruined men; I am not speaking of you. Recall—for you tell me to remember—what I discussed with you concerning your safety when you first approached us, and what counsel I gave concerning your approaching the leading men of the kingdom. For who was I to set a king over the Franks by myself? These are public affairs, not private ones. Do you think that I hate the royal family? I call my Redeemer to witness that I do not hate it.

You ask what, above all, you ought to do. Since this is difficult to say, I neither know sufficiently nor, if I did know, would dare to say it. Do you seek my friendship? Would that the day might come when I could honorably be permitted to attend your service. For although you have invaded the sanctuary of the Lord, seized the queen, to whom you swore what we know, handed over the bishop of Laon to prison, disregarded the anathema of the bishops—and I say nothing of my senior, against whom you have undertaken an enterprise beyond your strength—still I cannot forget the favor you showed me when you withdrew the weapons of my enemies.

I would say more, including that your supporters are especially deceivers, and that through you they will, as you will discover, accomplish the business of their own interests. But this is not the time. For it is dangerous to have said these same things and not to have replied to your earlier letters. The situation is unchanged, since we are keeping your letter carefully. Nowhere is faith secure. It would be possible to discuss, deliberate, and communicate the reasons for these matters in any way, if R. K. I. G. H. H. T. Z. V., having given hostages, could reach us; to him it is permissible to entrust such matters. Without him we can and must undertake nothing of this kind.

## LETTER XL. TO THIETMAR, ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ

Worn out by the labor of the siege against Charles and gravely afflicted by the violence of fever, I cannot adequately express my sincere affection for you, dearest brother. I indicate only this much: command, and we shall obey; and let our friendship consist in willing and refusing the same things.

Since, amid the severe heats of cares, philosophy alone can be, as it were, a remedy, wherever we possess its parts imperfectly, let your diligence supply what is lacking. For the present, however, write only what is missing for us in the first volume of the second edition of Boethius, in the book *Peri hermenias*: that is, from the place where it is written, “But it does not run and it does not labor. I do not call it a word when it signifies time,” through the place where it says, “Words spoken in themselves are indeed names and signify something,” in the section on propositions, in the missing part of the commentary. We shall not be unmindful of your favor; we shall not abandon the faith conceived in our heart; whatever you wish, we shall carry out to the best of our ability.

## LETTER XLI. TO CONSTANTINE

We congratulate you, dearest brother, because the invader and enemy of monastic religion has been removed from human affairs, to the salvation of many. Press on, therefore; and if you now have a father worthy of your affection and that of your brothers, let us also have him present through your efforts as soon as possible, at the feast of blessed Remigius, so that our affection—since you have caused us to be somewhat alienated from the men of Fleury—may through you be very greatly reconciled.

But if all this cannot easily be done, may we at least be permitted to enjoy your presence, if we have ever done anything that pleased you, and if you deem it worthy to do what might please us.

## INTRODUCTION OF THE MONKS INTO THE MONASTERY OF MOUSOM

*(From the Chronicle of Mousom, in Acher, *Spicilegium*, vol. VII, p. 642.)*

The text that follows describes how the bishop Adalbero himself, through the Roman letters of the Pope and by the decision of his council, established that this place, Mousom, should have monks—men whom the rule would restrain to live holily, and who would worship the divine Majesty in hope of eternal life, both for himself and for his predecessors.

[Col. 0517D] … In the preceding sequence of our account, we gave a concise report of the life and passing of the holy martyr Arnulf: where he was buried, how he was taken from there and transported to Guiledium, and finally how, by God’s merciful providence, he came to this church of Mousom amid the occurrence of miracles. We set this down in a very rustic and unpolished style; but, after investigating the matter with sufficiently probable reasoning, we have pursued it fully, as the reader will find in its proper place.

Now, because the devotion of Bishop Adalbero toward the aforesaid church arose afterward, and because through this holy man Arnulf the Lord warned his mind, as we have related above, by the visible illumination of miracles, we have judged it not unworthy to send the matter down to posterity as something to be remembered. Thus those who receive divine benefits may fear to be ungrateful; and, understanding how many blessings they obtained through this pastor, provident for their salvation, may recognize that they are always bound to repay his soul with good.

In the second year, therefore, of his ordination, the events took place that we discussed in the earlier account: namely, the translation and bringing into the church of Mousom of the blessed bones of the aforesaid martyr, in the year 971 of the Lord’s Incarnation, the fourteenth indiction, in July, on the ninth day before the Kalends of August.

When the venerable bishop had seen and heard miracles of divine power that were both holy and worthy of praise and wonder—miracles displayed within the brief period of his presence through the merits and name of this blessed man—he did not delay any longer what he had long since conceived in his mind. Rather, he promptly arranged for the work to be done, lest the task that was his intention should become another’s work and, if he neglected it, the loss of merit should be charged against him; while another who faithfully accomplished it would carry away the crown and reward.

Accordingly, having gathered within the secret chamber of his mind, as within a mirror, through the most ample contemplation, the things that are, that have been, and that will follow afterward—for the future is very often inferred from the past—he summoned certain of his nobles, distinguished men both of his clergy and of his military household, who were then present with him. He asked them to hear and report whether they approved or rather disapproved what his mind had long been collecting as a resolve, after requesting their counsel and goodwill, saying:

“I know nothing at all by what counsel and judgment of God I have come to this pastoral care and been appointed to this administration. But, just as I must always fear waves rushing upon me, so often as I consider this burden, so often am I terrified by it.

“For when I consider certain of the most ancient places of this bishopric—places founded long ago under religious observance, when mercy and truth met one another, when justice and peace kissed, when truth rose from the earth and justice looked down from heaven (Ps. 84:11–12)—places that then flourished and prospered under a happy fortune, when ‘the Lord gave what is good, and our land gave its produce’ (ibid., 13); but that are now wholly neglected, with some merely displaying the reputation of their name, others so utterly reduced to ruins that not even the fame of their name remains, and still others, when they ought to have been corrected for the better, having reached worse conditions—when I consider all this, I remain suspended in a shipwreck of great uncertainty, wondering which of them I might first attempt to restore by the skill of my undertaking. I carry within me a mind entangled in doubtful winding paths and barely able to extricate itself.

“For whatever movable property those places possessed or could have possessed—gold, silver, or substantial furnishings of any kind of ornament—has vanished, having been devastated, plundered, or worn away by the old age of time. When will the estates, villages, female and male dependants, churches, mills, and possessions of every kind, seized, donated, confiscated, or assigned under benefices by powerful men, tyrants, and the nobles of the kingdom, return to the places of the saints, whether by the ancient obligation of their rightful claim or by virtue of whatever privileges testify to their ownership?

“How great were the disasters of the kingdom, so poorly at peace; how great the discord of kings and nobles; how great the wickedness arising from the sins of the people; how great the impious and utterly unjust savagery that surged forth from the nations invading Gaul and fighting one another with hostile fury!”

This evil was compounded by the blameworthy life of certain of our pontiffs, who, if anything happened to remain, made for themselves men wholly devoted to them, so that they might be secure through their shamelessness and fraud. They handed everything over to the palace dogs. No one may be named, since guilt seems to arise from uncertainty, and this deed demands pardon more than it promises any favor; and it is better to keep silent about the multitude of faction-makers than to offer any hope of correction. Therefore, let us dismiss these matters and return to the subject.

[Col. 0520B] Of the places about which we are speaking, Mousom is one. It was once distinguished by the name and honor of holy Mary, Mother of God. Made most pleasant by the river Mosa flowing through it, it seems to me highly suitable for the habitation of monks. In accordance with the quality of its air, it provides every pleasure and convenience of human life—except that the yield of vineyards there is not especially abundant. This was neither a concern for its inhabitants nor a matter requiring particular attention, since the nature of vineyards is to love a temperate rather than a cold soil. Yet this causes me little concern, because, if God prospers my resolve, I possess from my patrimony and from the lawful inheritance that has come to me from my predecessors the means to drive this poverty away from it. If they know how to manage it, I could make them true lords and wealthy possessors of the best wine, together with the other blessings of their revenues.

Formerly, the place of Mousom, in honor of the Queen of Heaven and Virgin Mother Mary, had been formally assigned, by the true devotion and resolve of the faithful, to a community of holy women. But when the storm of evils raged—evils of which we have scarcely made mention above—it lost both its name and its being. More recently, the late Lord Heriveus, the most faithful pastor and ruler of this see, loving this place with great religious devotion, restored and organized it for a second time under the title of a community of canons, after those who had occupied it had fallen away.

Finding the church deprived of everything, even of inhabitants, he rebuilt it from its foundations. The flames that had consumed it, the rainwater entering through the roof, and the long neglect that had worn down its walls had left it presenting to onlookers nothing but a dreadful solitude. Once restored and returned to its former condition, it was adorned with prebendaries, according to the dignity of the place from its beginning and the generous multitude of its citizens.

Here a second see of Reims had formerly been maintained. It preserves, under the title of a canonical foundation, not indeed the life of canons, but at least in some fashion the ancient appearance of their name. Yet since their life differs in no way from that of laymen in their manner of living together—for they enjoy marriage, devote themselves to profitable commercial dealings in sons and daughters, and make use of worldly practices—it deeply stirs my mind to ensure that, if it can be corrected, the reverence due to so great a name—namely, blessed Mary, ever virgin—should not remain any longer without the honor of a religious order.

Believe me: my love for this undertaking grows from hour to hour,

> As greatly as the green alder rises in the true spring.

And hear by what means I shall first approach it; I shall explain briefly. In the territory of the County of Port, there is a very small and poor settlement of eight monks with an abbot set over them. The noble matron Freduidis, with her illustrious husband, Count Stephen, because hope of offspring had disappointed them, established it under the law and title of divine service, contributing the estates they seemed to possess there, so that in return for present gifts they might receive from their sons and daughters a better name in the inheritance of heaven.

[Col. 0521B] This settlement, therefore, by the counsel of Lord Gerard, an abbot of venerable life who at that time, by the merit of his name and religious conduct, presided over many monasteries of monks in France—including the monastery of Saint Remigius—they entrusted by a faithful vow to Saint Remigius, so that it might be held as subject to him and preserved through his care.

It had been consecrated in honor of Saint Quintinus and situated at the foot of Mount Aldinac; from the stream of a spring that rises there and flows past it, it is called Tignus. But because of the disturbance caused by the surrounding retainers from the nearby castle—which, because it lies amid marshy mud, is called Cantarana—it was frequently harassed and, suffering repeated troubles, was often forced to abandon its devotion to contemplation.

I wish, if God permits, to exchange this place, together with its abbot and brothers, with the monastery of Saint Remigius, using property of our church, and to make it, once lawfully transferred to me, one with the place of Mousom [variant: Mousomagensis]. Thus, after the abbot has been transferred there with the monks, something larger and better may be made from two things, though each is smaller.

These are the matters I wished you to hear for the present. If they are from God, upon whose mercy we rely, do not hesitate to report what you judge more useful.

They, observing the work of piety and considering the path of good action, immediately replied: “O auspicious intention! And if it achieves its purpose, how certain and happy will be the reward of this good will! It should not be our counsel to delay such things, for this work is a heavenly undertaking. If a good work exists in the will, through God’s help it will reach completion.

“Such resolves, although they may falter because of difficulty, do more harm when abandoned through sloth. For the more arduous and lofty the undertaking one begins, the more worthy one is of being raised by the proclamation of praise if one succeeds in bringing it to completion. Therefore, since the authority of your grace has deemed us worthy to hear what you have proposed, and since God looks upon it with a favorable omen, it seems to us excellent to undertake, and it will be counted salutary for you.”

After receiving this report, the bishop—for nothing is hurried enough for a mind eager to act—immediately went to the monastery of Saint Remigius. He summoned the abbot who then presided, an honorable man named Rodulf, and detained him in conversation with arguments many times repeated and sweetly persuasive concerning his intention. He opened the whole matter of his plan in confidence, removed every avenue of difficulty with the file of his most wise reasoning, excluded all grounds for refusal, and promised emphatically that no loss would come to the place of Saint Remigius. Rather, through an exchange of properties, which would be transferred under mutually agreeable agreements, he promised that the arrangement would be advantageous.

He declared that his own possessions were so considerable—outstanding in the number of bishoprics and in the abundance of property as well as in the dignity of their name—that this small settlement, when joined to another small one, required the proximity of common resources and the strenuous vitality of strength. He said that he would act well and wisely if he hastened, with a ready and faithful spirit, to establish and organize whatever might increase the honor of divine service; and that he would thereby make himself more united in purpose with the abbot, who seemed to be seeking these things.

The abbot asked for an opportunity to consult and deliberate with the brothers concerning what he had heard. This having been graciously granted, he returned to the brothers and, once they had gathered and taken their seats, explained in open and concise words the bishop’s request and the whole depth of his plan.

The brothers, holding different opinions and—such is the disposition of changeable minds, especially of the young—not all marveling at the same things, remained for a time uncertain in their judgment, while the elders’ decision wavered and each man relied more heavily on his own opinion. At first they refused and were unwilling to agree. Why, they asked, should they entrust to another what they had received once to care for themselves? They believed that the vow of the faithful woman who had made the alms-offering ought to remain in force; that what another would carry out was being taken away from them; that the means by which another would grow were being diminished for them; and that this would not be praised among the people, but would seem a reproachful accusation of degenerate and dishonorable conduct [variant: an insulting charge].

When they repeated such arguments and disagreed in various ways, the abbot ordered silence. Raising himself to speak with authority and freedom of voice in order to suppress the noise of their murmuring, he began with an exhortation of piety:

“Dearest brothers, most beloved of God, these are the words of the Apostle: ‘Do nothing through contention or empty glory, but in humility regard one another as superior to yourselves, each considering not his own interests but those of others’ (Phil. 2:2–3). These words of the Apostle are like leaven for good dough in our understanding, so that everything we do may be ‘without murmuring and hesitation’; that we may be ‘blameless and simple, like children of God, without reproach in the midst of a crooked and perverse generation,’ among whom, he says, ‘you shine like lights in the world, holding the word of life’ (Phil. 2:15–16).

“And elsewhere: ‘Be careful to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. There is one body and one Spirit, just as you were called in one hope of your calling’ (Eph. 4:3–4).

“Therefore, my brothers, if the bishop admonishes us in matters belonging to God, no one ought to dare resist him, because the Lord says in the Gospel: ‘Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever despises you despises me’ (Luke 10:16).

“Now, when we consider the intention of our archbishop, his proposal seems to proceed from the fear and love of God implanted in him. Therefore, we can neither justly oppose it nor rashly pervert what we recognize as pertaining to the worship of divine service.

“If you lament the loss of what is being diminished, you are not sufficiently attending to what he is now transcribing to us in compensation for the exchange. But if you are claiming popular approval as your justification, beware that you do not wish to be ‘a reed shaken by the wind’ (Matt. 11:7).

“As for your assertion that the woman’s vow ought to remain, I believe that what will be devoted to the use of the poor and needy will stand supported by a greater mercy, as it is written: ‘He distributed, he gave to the poor; his righteousness remains forever and ever’ (Ps. 111:9).

“Since we have abundance and even more than abundance, we must beware lest, under the appearance of piety and as though defending rectitude, we be accused of wickedness, greed, and covetousness. Therefore I ask you, brothers, that your minds incline toward and accept the sounder counsel, so that, according to the Apostle, ‘all your things may be done in charity’ (1 Cor. XIII, 14).”

By these and many other such health-giving addresses, the stubbornness of those who had first been angered was broken and softened, and they returned to the goodwill of agreement. They assented to whatever the bishop and abbot wished.

From there they went to the bishop and reported the brothers’ obedience: although they had initially wished to resist and oppose him, they had been overcome by reason, had changed their intention, and did not reject the execution of his good will.

The bishop received this graciously and gave thanks. After appointing, by common consent, excellent men of suitable standing as witnesses, the bishop and abbot lawfully completed the compensation for the properties that had been agreed upon through the exchange of what was given and received. To ensure that whatever was assigned to each at that time should remain fixed and unshaken, it was formally confirmed under pledge, with guarantors transferring their legal rights.

After the bishop had obtained by agreement everything he had desired, he set out with his entourage for the castle of Maceria, which his brother Count Godefrid then held as constable. He summoned as quickly as possible the abbot of the poor little monastery of Tignus, named Lietald, and, in the presence of witnesses, the provost of Saint Remigius, and other men of good faith, repeated to him everything that had been stipulated.

He privately instructed him concerning what he wished him to do obediently. He ordered him to board with his monks the ship that the bishop himself had prepared for them and supplied with provisions, and not to alter course until they had first reached Mousom.

Once these arrangements had been made, Lord Adalbero mounted his horses and came to the church of his see to complete the undertaking he had begun. He was received with honor. Then he began addressing the senior clergy of the church, pretending to speak of one matter after another as though casually. Conversing about the site and condition of the place and its buildings, he said that he wished to see whether the church possessed anything in gold or silver, or anything especially valuable in its furnishings or vestments, such as priestly garments.

After examining these things, he said: “These are sufficient for their purpose, but they are not numerous. Yet the one to whom everything belongs can enlarge them.”

On the following day, at about the first hour, the bishop already knew that his monks were close at hand—for a boy placed on watch, keeping them easily before his eyes, reported their arrival with complete certainty. He had all the clergy assemble in the secret chamber, and, with a strong guard of his own men present and everyone seated around him, he began in a lofty manner:

“Very great is the wickedness of this age, and truly the nature of human beings has always been inclined to evil from their youth (Gen. 6:5). Like a ship set in the middle of the waves, unless it is diligently driven forward, it continually moves backward. I shall briefly explain why I have raised this matter.

“This place, assigned under the title of holy Mary, Mother of God, does not possess the honor of religion appropriate to the dignity of its name.

“After that misery which the wickedness of the world brings upon almost everyone, scarcely any knowledge and almost no clerical or canonical wisdom adorns you for knowing and understanding God. I shall not delay you by speaking at length. You are given two choices: let each person choose what seems more useful to him—either to become a monk or, by yielding, to vacate the place.

“Let the one who wishes to become a monk promise it now. Whoever refuses and does not wish to do so must change his seat and leave. Behold, I have monks here who will live under the rule of Saint Benedict.”

For the abbot was already being announced as standing before the doors, coming from the ship with his brothers. Everyone was thrown into confusion—for the speech concerning the monk seemed harsh to them—and no one, except a few constrained by concern for their household property, was willing to follow the good course that the bishop, worthy of God, urged them to undertake.

Thus, after the abbot and monks had been brought into the sanctuary with fitting honor, the bishop said:

“Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together as one. Let it be for you like the oil upon the head, running down upon the beard, the beard of Aaron, and running down upon the edge of his garment; and like the dew of Hermon, which drips [variant: descends] upon Mount Zion, so that here the Lord may command blessing and life forever” (Ps. 133:1–3).

When everyone had answered, “Amen,” the bishop addressed the abbot and brothers:

“Let it not be without purpose or cause that we admit you here, and that, having made this change, we place the order of clergy after you. Rather, weigh what is said: ‘Friend, for what purpose have you come?’ (Matt. 26:50.) ‘Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice before him with trembling; embrace discipline, lest the Lord become angry and you perish from the righteous way’ (Ps. 2:11–12).

“It will be your task to pray for us; ours, with God’s help, will be to arrange provisions for you.

“We shall mark out the enclosure of the monastery and the buildings for your work, and as time proceeds we shall provide whatever is suitable. You, walking with God, must be diligent to conduct yourselves worthily before God and his saints, so that it may rightly be said of you: ‘Behold, the dwelling of God is with human beings, and he will dwell with them. They will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God’ (Rev. 21:3).

“Whoever lived in this place through the many years before you—whether in the days of the holy women or during the second change, when clerics followed one another here—followed their own desires and clung wickedly to their depraved wishes. Having become like a horse and a mule, which have no understanding (Ps. 32:9), they rotted like beasts in the dung of their corruptible life.

“And because they did not approve God as something to be known, he handed them over to a reprobate mind, and their foolish heart was darkened, so that they did things that were not fitting (Rom. 1:28). And, as God speaks in the song of Moses: ‘They provoked me with what was not God and angered me with their vanities; and I will provoke them with what is not a people, and with a foolish nation I will anger them’ (Deut. 32:21). Therefore, do not become participants in their deeds.

“Let the rule of blessed Benedict be for you a model and mirror of good imitation. Let everyone follow it as a teacher, and let no one rashly depart from it.

“I ask and beseech you: let the labor of my devotion be fruitful, so that what I have begun to do for you and desire to accomplish may, through the first fruits of this good harvest pleasing to God, reach the full harvest of divine blessing and eternal blessedness.

“Work and live in such a way, dearest brothers, that on the final day of this life the Redeemer’s mercy may not perish in you, but that, through Jesus Christ our Lord, it may crown in grace the price of our redemption.”

[Col. 0525C] “Behold, now, in the presence of God and witnesses, for your service, for the remedy of my soul, and in exchange for the blessed reward of my predecessors and successors, I withdraw from my table one estate named Odun, with all its jurisdiction. I also withdraw another small estate, Secia, as much of it as falls within my right.

“Likewise, at Romeliacum and Alleicourt, whatever little share belongs to me there, I willingly offer in perpetuity for the use of the monks who faithfully serve my lady, holy Mary, Mother of God, in order to earn her continual intercession; and with the authority that I ought to possess or can possess, I lawfully transfer it.

“From my patrimony, however, the portion that falls to me—if, with the assistance of Christ’s grace, I can prevail upon my brother Godefrid by persuasion in this holy undertaking—I shall give you whatever I possess in the bishopric of Metz, namely in the estates of Bretenacum, Rothila, and Madrengias, amounting to twenty-eight manses.

“Likewise, from the land called Sulci of Saint Remigius, in two places, Roseoli and Castellum, amounting to twelve manses, I shall strive to relieve you, lest lack of sufficiently good wine constrain you.

“As for Berveliacum, situated three thousand [units] from here, I shall strive willingly to acquire it for your use, with all its appurtenances, for fattening your pigs in pasture—wherever [variant: so that] I may be able to wrest it from the hands of those who now hold it as a benefice, on lease, by exchange, or through any other contrivance. Only wipe away the stains of my sins with continual prayers.”

[Col. 0526A] At that time Richard, Count of Metz, possessed this estate from ancient times as a benefice of the bishopric, as though by his own right. The good bishop, drawing it to himself with great effort, as he had promised, lawfully transferred it before his death to this church of Mousom, to be possessed thereafter as its own property.

Thus, addressing the abbot and brothers before a great crowd and urging them to remember him continually by living holily and piously, the bishop dismissed them in peace, blessing them.

It was the month of November, and the seventh day before the Ides was being observed, when the brothers were established in this place. Together with that little monastery of Tignus, the monastery of Mousom received its name and its association, so that, by joining a preposition to a word, it might become an adverb of conjunction, preserving the form of the former name because of the inward affections of the union.

It was the year 971 from the Lord’s Incarnation when these things took place: the fifteenth indiction, the twenty-second epact, the sixth concurrent, the fifty-second year of the nineteen-year cycle, and the nineteenth lunar year.

After these words and deeds, Lord Adalbero followed the teaching of the *Pastoral Book*, which says: “Let the ruler not lessen his care of interior matters through occupation with exterior affairs” (St. Gregory, *Pastoral Care*, II.7, beginning), and let him not abandon attention to exterior matters in his concern for interior ones, lest, devoted to outward affairs, he fall away from what is inward, or, occupied only with inward matters, fail to provide for his neighbors what he owes them outwardly.

Confirming by the strength of his counsel what belonged to the palace, guarding what in the kingdom required attention, and excelling through the authority of his magnanimity, he—one and the same man—built up both the highest and the lowest, the rich together with the poor.

Therefore, after celebrating the Nativity of the Lord, he sent his legates to Rome with letters. He honored Lord John, Pope surnamed “White Hen”—who from the earliest years of youth had been made white by the gray hairs of fitting reverence and angelic dignity—with most magnificent gifts worthy of him; through his envoys he explained what was being done with him and in Gaul, and announced that he was to hold a council in May. If the Pope wished anything concerning his undertaking to be determined there, he was to send a man worthy of the task with his apostolic authority.

He then explained in the greatest detail what especially required discussion concerning the condition of the monastery of Mousom, and the causes of the whole undertaking, informing him about everything according to the justice of his good intention. He humbly requested and implored, by God’s grace, the favor of the Pope’s authority and of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, so that he might deserve to preserve it securely by privilege.

The Pope required the considered judgment of his officials and fellow priests concerning all these matters. By God’s grace, so that he might grant the request of such a man—our bishop—the unanimous counsel of all agreed to this good work.

Accordingly, after summoning a notary and, according to the custom of Roman dignity, preparing and writing documents on sheets made from a papyrus volume, he produced a privilege and established a decree. This decree would protect this church of Mousom, with its monastic and monkish order, in perpetuity for as long as divine clemency should determine that it be preserved. He sent it to be read at Adalbero’s council before the bishops and the general synod.

Thus, after the representatives of the Holy Roman Church had returned to him, together with his own envoys, Adalbero, the bishop worthy of God, gathered in May a council at Mont-Saint-Marie in the district of Tardenois, summoning men from every direction to review the canons and to set the affairs of the holy Church in better order.

There, after arranging and justly ordering whatever seemed necessary and capable of being ordered, he did not forget the resolve for which he had sent to Rome. In the presence of the venerable Fathers and the entire holy synod, Lord Adalbero began as follows:

“Lord Fathers and dearest brothers, hear, I ask, and attend to the prayers of my humility. For just as the Holy Spirit has gathered us here, so, while praying for his coming upon us, we have desired and obtained that whatever we perceive through his inspiration should also be administered through his infusion and cooperation.

“One small matter remains. In it, with God almighty as author, I also ask for your favor, counsel, and blessing.

“Mousom is a place in our diocese, consecrated under the title and name of holy Mary, Mother of God. Formerly, from its beginning, it was famous for its community of holy women. But it could not remain in the condition into which the increasing evils of the world had brought it. Later it was restored twice through the gathering of faithful clerics or canons; but, while everyone sought his own interests and not those of Jesus Christ, its property was dissipated and partly taken away, and it was reduced almost to nothing.

“Therefore, as I believe by God’s inspiration, it seemed good to me to reform that place for the better through the order and discipline of monks according to the rule of Saint Benedict. Having undertaken this, I sought the counsel and authority of our lord, the bishop of the Roman see, concerning the matter.

“As you will now hear, through the grace of Christ he sent us a privilege of his authority, confirmed the decree establishing it under the page of Saint Peter, and struck with the dart of anathema those who rashly attempted to violate it, as is written below:

“‘John, bishop, servant of the servants of God,’ etc. The remainder may be found among the letters and privileges of Pope John XIII.

“Since, therefore, you have both seen and heard the decree of the apostolic lord, if it pleases you that it likewise be confirmed by the unanimous testimony of this holy synod and by a written document of our humility, decree that this has been done.”

Accordingly, when everyone had given assent with one accord, and the document had been drawn up, it was read as follows:

> “Adalbero, by the clemency of divine mercy archbishop of the holy Church of Rheims. Let it be known to all the faithful, present and future, that when a certain episcopal estate had formerly been granted to us through royal favor and kindness, we found some holy places in a state of complete honor and great usefulness, while others, their former dignity having declined, were utterly neglected. Among these was the monastic establishment at Mouzon, constructed in rivalry through zeal for antiquity, originally intended for the life of holy women, but later more suitably organized under the canonical order by our predecessor Herveus and worthily consecrated in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God. Yet, neglected and dishonorably misused on both sides, partly through the removal of its possessions and partly through the evils then prevailing, it fell under an adverse fate.

> “When our mind learned of this, and after we had sought the careful counsel of our faithful, clearly weighing that the same place could not usefully remain in the canonical order because of the world’s misfortune, we established there, as seemed appropriate in hope of eternal things, the monastic life under an appointed abbot, Leotald [variant: Ledaldus], so that the religious inhabitants of that place, using both the possessions assigned to them and whatever might subsequently be assigned, and continually offering their vows to God, might be constant in prayer for us, for our successors, and for all the other orders. Therefore we earnestly implore the paternal care of you who are to be substituted for us there [variant: imploring], that, out of regard for divine love, you may favor with a zeal of fitting piety the beneficial undertaking of this accomplished work, and may deign, through the passage of time, to console and support it with unfailing generosity [text uncertain], so that, happily obtaining God’s grace through it, they may deserve to share in this excellent benefit.

> “Moreover, on the authority of the decrees of the holy Fathers, we absolutely forbid this; indeed, calling upon the divine Name, we entirely prohibit anyone of our order from ever violating such an arrangement through any presumption. Rather, it is to be reverently preserved hereafter as stable and unshaken by perpetual right. For if laymen should bring injury against this undertaking, the dart of excommunication, together with anathema, shall unquestionably be hurled against them.”

Accordingly, in the year 973 [variant: 983] from the incarnation of the Lord Jesus Christ, when a provincial synod had been established and generally convened in the month of May at Mont-Saint-Marie in the district of Tardenois, this decree was solemnly read before the venerable bishops, abbots, and other faithful—[variant: and several other faithful]—who supported this institution of ours with pious assent, indeed also praising and confirming it. The first of them was I, the aforementioned archbishop Adalbero, who, by God’s authority, presided over that council with pontifical authority; subscribing with my own hand, I confirmed the same decree. The others likewise judged that this pontifical statute should be made firm by the laying on of their hands: it had been strengthened on every side by the privilege of apostolic authority at the request of our petition and was therefore to be held by all in reverence as a matter of the highest honor.

I, Adalbero, archbishop of the holy Church of Rheims, subscribed and confirmed this.

I, Wido, bishop of the Church of Soissons.

I, Hildricus, bishop of the Church of Beauvais.

I, Theobaldus, bishop of Amiens.

I, Haldanus, bishop of Noyon.

I, Theudo, bishop of Cambrai.

I, Adalbero, bishop of Laon.

I, Gipuinus, bishop of Châlons.

I, Constantius, bishop of Senlis.

I, Liudulfus, bishop of Thérouanne.

Sign of Albert, archdeacon of Rheims.

Sign of Leudo, archdeacon.

Theobald, archdeacon. Erluin, archdeacon.

Hugo, archdeacon.

Gerannus, archdeacon.

Roger, archdeacon.

Emmo, archdeacon.

Sign of Rodulf, abbot of Saint-Remi.

Odelei, abbot of Saint-Médard.

Ratold, abbot of Corbie.

Berland, abbot of Saint-Vincent.

Adzo, abbot of Saint-Basle.

# In the Year of the Lord 1490. Folcuinus, Abbot of Lobbes

[Col. 0529]

## Historical Notice on Folcuinus

*(Fabricius, Bibliotheca medii et infimi Latini.)*

Folcuinus, also called Fulcuinus, Folquinus, Volquinus, or Fulquinus, abbot in Belgium at Lobbes, or Laubium, wrote from 965 to 990 a Chronicle of the deeds of the abbots of the monastery of Lobbes, founded by Saint Landelin, from the year 697 down to his own time. In it Folcuinus speaks of himself from chapter 28 onward. Mabillon gives the Life of Folcuinus, bishop of Thérouanne in Flanders, who died in 854, in *Acta Sanctorum*, Benedictine century IV, p. 622. To these may be added, from Oudinus, vol. II, p. 475, a homily on the weeds in Matthew 13:25 and following, preserved in manuscript at Leuven, at Saint Martin’s.

[Col. 0529]

# Life of Saint Folcuinus, Bishop of Thérouanne in Gaul, by Folcuinus, Abbot of Lobbes

*(Mabillon, Acta Sanctorum, century IV, p. 622.)*

## Preliminary Observations

### 1

Although Folcuinus, abbot of Lobbes, is by no means an obscure author, this Life, published by him, is nevertheless not of great importance, since it frequently digresses into commonplaces. The reason is that the author knew little about Saint Folcuinus, and what he did know he received from tradition a hundred years after the saint’s death. Nevertheless, the particular facts he reports seem certain; they derive their authority, at any rate, from another Folcuinus, about whom I shall speak shortly. Folcuinus, or Folcwinus—others spell the name Folcoinus or Folquinus—was counted among the saints immediately after his death and was venerated by that name in the monastery of Sithiu.

### 2

What Saint Folcuinus was like before becoming a bishop, neither Folcuinus the abbot, nor John Iperius, nor anyone else has left in writing, whether through carelessness or, more likely, through ignorance. For Folcuinus the abbot, who lived only a hundred years after him, expressly testifies that this was unknown to him. Trithemius did not number Saint Folcuinus among the holy or illustrious men of our order. Arnold Wion included him, for the specific reason that he learned that Folcuinus was venerated in the monastery of Sithiu. When consulted on this matter, the monks of Saint-Bertin recently replied that they could see no reason why Saint Folcuinus should be counted among our monks, since no trace of his monastic life appears in the ancient authors, archives, or manuscripts.

### 3

The holy man took part in several councils: the restoration of Ebo, bishop of Rheims, in 840; the Council of Paris in 846; the Council of Quierzy two years later; and the Council of Soissons, where he is named in 853. In that same year he is numbered among the envoys of Charles the Bald in the king’s capitulary.

Hincmar, bishop of Rheims, wrote a letter, according to Frodoard in book III, chapter 20 of his *History*, “to Folcuinus of Thérouanne concerning a certain priest ordained by him, who complained that he was suffering injustice at the hands of Immo, bishop of Noyon; he also requested that relics of the saints resting in the parish of Thérouanne be sent to him, since he was preparing an altar in the church of the Mother of God to be consecrated by Folcuinus himself and honored with relics from that parish.”

He is also found subscribing the letter of Odo, bishop of Beauvais, published by Sirmond at the end of volume III of the *Councils of Gaul*. Yet either that letter was written before the thirty-fifth year of the reign of Charles the Bald, or Folcuinus could not have subscribed it, since it is certain that he died in the fifteenth year of Charles’s reign, in the year 855 of Christ. His successor Huntfrid will be discussed below under the year 869.

### 4

Folcwinus, a monk and levite of Sithiu, discusses the lineage and principal deeds of Saint Folcuinus in a register of his monastery, compiled by him in 961, as I read in a parchment codex that I believe to be his autograph. It is useful to reproduce here certain excerpts:

> “In the time of Louis Augustus, a certain light of the Church arose, named Folcwinus. So that it might not remain hidden under a bushel, the king himself placed it upon the Church’s candlestick; he appointed him to the episcopate of the city of Thérouanne in the year 827 of the Lord’s incarnation and the fourth year of the aforementioned king. There was much that we could say about his life and virtues, and I would wish to touch briefly upon what he accomplished in this world. But, considering my own foolishness, I shrink even from touching what men of the greatest learning might fear to approach. For these things surpass the disputation of philosophical worldly wisdom. [lacuna] I have brought forth only these matters in his memory with foolish chatter; I leave the rest of his deeds to be investigated by a man of greater ability. [lacuna]

> “Since I remember having mentioned blessed Folcwinus, I would still like to insert here one of his deeds, which I recall having learned when Bishop Wicfrid narrated it. ‘Worn out,’ he said, ‘by long old age, that blessed bishop Folcwinus—who had spent nearly forty years in the episcopate—could no longer publicly celebrate the solemnities of Mass. When the king learned this, while Folcwinus was still alive, he sent him a successor as bishop, contrary to the canons.’”

And so forth, in the same words as in numbers 13 and 14 of the following Life.

> “That bishop had asked that, wherever his death might occur, his body should be carried to the monastery of Sithiu and buried in the basilica of Saint Bertin. After he had died, when his clerics were considering how they should carry him to the place mentioned above, during that very night, while a south wind was blowing, the entire immeasurable depth of water surrounding the island of Sithiu froze so completely that in the morning it offered the bearers of the holy body a firm path over the ice. In wintertime, the severe cold of scarcely seven days could hardly accomplish what happened then. Carrying the blessed man’s body to the monastery of Sithiu, they buried him on the right side of Saint Bertin.”

The same account is found in number 15 of the Life below.

The levite Folcuinus continues:

> “It is also said that this man of God possessed a certain horse which, whenever he wished to set out on a journey, would bend its knees in service to the man of God, so that he might mount its back without any exertion. They say that this horse went before the brothers who carried his bier, but afterward refused to carry any human being,”

and so forth, as in number 16, except that, in place of the words just given, it reads: “the horse going before the bier wept.” This indicates that Folcuinus the abbot was different from Folcuinus the levite.

The levite Folcuinus adds the following concerning his own family:

> “In the year 928 of the most blessed incarnation of Jesus Christ our Lord, in the time of Charles the Recluse, in the first indiction, my father, Folcwinus, who am writing this, came here with his brother from the kingdom of Lothair, with whatever equipment they could provide, wishing to raise the body of Saint Folcwinus, which until that time had been covered by the earth. Both were close blood relatives of that blessed man. After permission had also been requested from the aforementioned count and abbot Adaloff, they came to the tomb of the holy man with candles, incense vessels, and a choir of singers. They raised the body on the Ides of November, on Thursday, at daybreak, and prepared refreshments for the brothers as best they could. They had brought wine and everything necessary with them. When this had been completed, they returned home rejoicing.

> “These men were Folcwinus and his brother Regenwala, sons of Odwin, the son of another Odwin, who was the brother of the blessed bishop Folcwinus. The father of that holy bishop was called Jerome, and his mother was named Ermentrudis.”

This is a genealogical tree of Saint Folcuinus, not previously explained with sufficient clarity. Folcuinus the abbot calls his mother Ercensinda, while this author calls her Ermentrudis; from this it appears that she had two names. His father Jerome was the son of Charles Tudites, or Martel; he was the father of Odwin and Fulrad, abbot of Quintin, and the brother of Bernard, father of Saint Adalhard, abbot of Corbie, whose Life was related above.

### 5

Certain arguments suggest that Folcuinus, or Folcwinus, the levite was different from Fulcuinus, abbot of Lobbes. Both originated in the kingdom of Lothair, and both were monks of Sithiu, indeed at the same time. For Folcuinus the levite compiled the collection of his monastery’s charters in 961, while the other was called to govern the abbey of Lobbes in 965, as he himself writes in the *Chronicle of Lobbes*.

The reasons why I think there were two men are these. First, although Folcuinus the abbot in the following Life uses almost the same words, he nevertheless mixes in certain different details. The levite calls Saint Folcuinus’s mother Ermentrudis; the abbot calls her Ercensinda. The former says that he was a blood relative of the bishop; the latter is silent about this. The first writes that the horse went before the holy man’s funeral, while the other adds that it wept. The abbot also rendered the levite’s statement in number 18 incorrectly, unless the error belongs to the author rather than the copyists.

Finally, two Folcuinuses lived together in the monastery of Sithiu, according to Folcuinus the levite, who, at the end of his Collection, when listing the names of the brothers with whom he had lived in that monastery, names Folcwinus. Folcuinus the abbot here relates a miracle that occurred at the tomb of Saint Folcuinus in the person of Folcuinus the monk, whom I believe to have been Folcuinus the levite. The monks of Sithiu call him this by tradition, although I do not know whether he remained in the rank of levite.

### 6

He writes of himself in his Collection as follows:

> “In the year 947 [lacuna] Abbot Wido, because he pursued the pleasures of excessively vain youth, was accused before the count, deprived of the abbacy, and appointed abbot of the monastery of Saint Bavo. Womar, however, governed the monastic community under regular discipline. At that time I, Folcwinus, who am writing this, was brought here from the kingdom called that of Lothair by my father Folcwinus, already mentioned above, and my mother Thiedala, in the year 948 of the most blessed incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ. On the feast of the Elevation of Saint Bertin, which follows the feast of All Saints, I was offered to Saint Bertin and made a monk—alas!—outwardly only.”

The Elevation of the body of Saint Bertin, as far as I know, is mentioned nowhere before the year 1052 in the various documents published about him in Part I of the second century.

### 7

Folcuinus the abbot expressly writes in the following prologue that he came to the monastery of Sithiu not so much willingly as under compulsion, since the concerns of his relatives had ceased because of their many attacks; he confesses that he was brought up there almost from infancy. In chapter 28 of the *Chronicle of Lobbes* he modestly calls his family “not of the lowest rank,” and in chapter 37 he calls his brother Godescalcus. Abbot Fulcoinus died in 990, six years before the death of Walter, abbot of Sithiu, to whom he dedicated this Life in the manner that follows.

# Author’s Prologue

[Col. 0533]

### 1

To the most beloved brothers in Christ of the monastery of Sithiu, holding with us one and the same faith, hoping in the same hope, and embracing the same charity: Folquinus the sinner, whom they call abbot of Lobbes, wishes the perpetuity of the highest and unique joy in him who truly exists, together with his saints.

Always mindful of you in my prayers, I believe that I shall be perpetual in my affection toward you, because after God one’s neighbor is to be loved in charity. I count your well-being as my own fortune, and I desire that your success and prosperity in Christ may endure forever as though they were mine. Your own zeal first kindled me to this, I confess, when, almost from infancy, after the concerns of my relatives had ceased because of their many attacks, they compelled me to test among you—not, let me say, a reciprocal relationship, but a gratuitous brotherhood. I have made such use of it that I now regard violating it as sacrilege and being deprived of it as an execrable crime.

Indeed, I would rightly call it sacrilege to violate charity, since the Apostle could commend nothing greater than that which God is, as he says: “God is charity” (1 John 4:16). Therefore to violate this is to deny Christ; and this seems to me to be more than sacrilege. Although charity, with an enlarged bosom, admits even enemies, it nevertheless knows that the measure of ordered love is to be directed especially toward the members of the household of faith (Galatians 6:10).

### 2

Beyond this love owed to all who share his faith—that is, the faith called catholic, or universal—I have a particular bond with you: namely, that, having been catechized by you, I may share with you in every good thing, according to the Apostle’s saying (Galatians 6:6). I also have this bond because of the patrons of your place and the relics of the saints, in which you abound beyond all your neighbors and in whose patronage you rejoice with a singular privilege.

Their protection, though I have flowed through many vices, has always been present for me when entreated. Thus I embrace them with a devotion second only to God. It seems useful and a great good for me to do so, and through their merits it is lawful to hope for the highest good.

The intention of this love, which grew up with me from my earliest beginnings, was changed—not entirely, as it seemed to me—from a childish one into the thought that I might satisfy their praise, though they need no praise, if something from the ancients should come into your hands that could correspond to each of their feasts in the several assemblies which the Greeks call *synaxes*, and could stir the minds of the hearers to praise God through love of the saints.

There was, moreover, a considerable supply of material that seemed capable of fulfilling this intention. In the first place, the lives and deeds of those whose primacy gives you joy and whose hereditary succession you have received together with their names—I mean Audomar and Bertin—were sufficiently commended by the authority of the ancients. Since they were their contemporaries, they are linked by such a certain proximity that, when you hear of one, you understand the other, and in the work of one you can easily foresee who the other was.

Saint Winnocus also, since he depended upon one of those mentioned above, had been sufficiently described: how, anointed with the oil of faith and equipped with virtue, he was trained in your school of faith, followed the laurels of his father, ran with the same praise as his teacher, and adorned the world, which rebelled against him, through the power of Christ.

But, O our times, O our morals! The negligence of modern people has so entirely neglected the venerable and universally celebrated Saint Folquinus that there seemed to be no memory of him beyond popular rumor.

### 3

I was therefore angry at this negligence—or rather, it should be called carelessness—and silently grumbled inwardly against those responsible. At last, while youthful modesty and the inexperience of a dull heart struggled within me with love for the saint, afflicted by that Pisonean fault of one who, unable to speak, could not remain silent, I resolved to describe his life. Entrusting my pen to him who makes the tongues of infants eloquent, I emerged like a new Arpinas, an author who had suddenly appeared.

But remembering that sophism of Erisippus: “If you lie, you lie even when you say what is true,” I set down nothing—although I passed over many things concerning him—except what I had received through the tradition of people whose dignity was worthy of approval, since their authority could not be refuted.

Moreover, lest I provide our fellow-countrymen with grounds for slander, as is the custom of certain boys, I entrusted what I had dictated for a time to the cloisters of silence and reserved it for this period, when it might emerge somewhat more polished. Since the work needed a supporter whose authority could strengthen it, I dedicated it to you, and especially to you, venerable Father Walter, to whom, beyond what I share with the others, I owe something singular, whether because you stand in Bertin’s place or because of the affection that has grown up with us.

You—I say, you—I have as the judge and defender of this work. As for detractors, they are not worth much. If they should happen to slander me for failing to observe the modes of connection and other matters treated by those of whom it is said under one heading, “she who speaks sophistically is hateful,” let them know that the Church of Christ has voluntarily rejected these rules, although she is not ignorant of them—especially since it was said long before us that the true law of history is simply to commit to writing for the instruction of posterity those things gathered through the report of common fame.

Let them go, then, and proclaim their own Catos in whatever forms of speech they please, whether those Catos are severe or censorious; let them pursue every little rumor and scrap of popular glory, and, according to one of their poets, let them carry their *nicetetia*—their victory celebrations—in a *ceromatic* neck [the allusion and wording are uncertain].

For us, who philosophize in Christ’s school under the instruction of the apostles, the aim is to temper the serpent’s prudence with the dove’s simplicity, so that, while we provide for the needs of our neighbors through teaching and action alike, provision may also be made for ourselves.

For the rest, brothers, I address you in the words of the Apostle: “Rejoice, be perfected, be encouraged, be of the same mind, live in peace, and remember me, your brother, when reminded of me; and may the God of peace and charity be always with you all.” Amen.

# Here Begins the Life of Saint Folcuinus

### 4

The benign, ineffable, and all-powerful deity, sufficient to itself—for it relies on nothing external, since it is the highest good—distributes and dispenses the riches of its goodness in many ways among those whom it foreknew and predestined before the ages. It changed vessels of wrath, fitted for destruction and long endured, into vessels of mercy; and, so that they might know that the excellence of this grace came from God and not from themselves, it gave them this gift of grace: that it made their punishment known to them, and so forth.

### 5

The blessed mother Church, likewise adorned with such jewels, is the tower of David built with its battlements. So many and such shields hang from it, and such is the armor of so many strong men, that she is fortified and adorned for merit and rescued from the terror of the gates of hell.

Among these battlements, God gave us, not as one of the lesser shields, a patron and defender: the blessed Folcuinus, a bishop worthy of proclamation throughout the ages. Since we wish to illuminate his life briefly and concisely, we do not make a great effort to commend him by miracles. We know that we are speaking to the faithful, for the Apostle said that tongues were given as a sign not to the faithful but to unbelievers. We have little experience of him through miracles, though much through his life; and even if he performed miracles, no one concealed them more than he did. But now, as we are about to speak of him, we ask that he assist us by his intercession with the one whom he loved so greatly.

### 6

To speak, then, of the beginnings of the blessed man’s birth: he drew the distinction of his earthly rank from a long and exceedingly high lineage of nobility. He flourished under King Charles, distinguished both by the wealth of his possessions and by the vigor of his wars, but, greater than these, rightly surnamed “the Great” because of his cultivation of religion and peace.

His mother was Ercensinda and his father Jerome. The former derived from the Gothic people a sufficiently illustrious ancestry, both by birth and by wealth. The latter, as I believe, was the aforementioned king’s uncle and, first among the courtiers, administered the management of public and private affairs.

He also had brothers of the highest rank. Among them, Folrad is associated with the monastery of Saint Quentin. And, to go back still farther, all his ancestors’ ancestors were most noble.

We say this not because such things are glorious for those who possess them, but because they are marvelous in those who despise them. The people of the world welcome those who possess these privileges; we praise those who have despised them for the sake of the Savior.

### 7

When the care of his parents perceived that their noble offspring, almost from infancy, was inclined toward sacred studies, they entrusted him to the schools of the Church to be instructed, as was possible for such a tender age, in the sacred writings. There, as I think, the boy, endowed with a good nature, progressed obediently through a keen intelligence; once he had acquired the rudiments of the first discipline, nothing afterward escaped the liveliness of his mind.
