A constant meditation and the zeal of continual practice bore witness to the purity of his heart, since every such inclination had already completely passed into habit. For it is written: “From his studies it is understood whether a boy’s works are upright and pure” (Proverbs 20:2).

Thus the Lord formed him under the instruction of teachers as one whom he would afterward place over his Church. For it is a rule of pastoral office that no one should dare to preside who has not learned to be subject.

Then, when he advanced, as one might say, with giant strides from virtue to virtue, and after he had learned the sacred writings and the divine law, he attained the perfection of the sacred orders in due succession. Grace conferred such grace upon him through heaven’s favor that he was revered by all with greater reverence and loved with more devoted affection.

### 8

Meanwhile, that spiritual stone, polished by manifold proofs and suited to heavenly ornaments, deserved to be set in the King’s diadem. Therefore, lest he remain hidden under the appearance of a private person, and lest one who had until then benefited only himself fail now to benefit many, he was sought for elevation to the dignity of the Church and acclaimed by the voices of all.

On the shores of the British Ocean, toward the west in the borders of Gaul, a certain people dwells, not extensive in territory but powerful. Historians call them the Morini; now, from their once extremely wealthy city of Thérouanne, which is ruined and almost emptied, they are called Tarvennians.

The priest and faithful historian Orosius mentions this people in the work he wrote for us against the pagans, and he shows with complete clarity that they possessed such a large military population that they would not yield to any Roman army that confronted them [variant: “that they might not succumb”]. He also mentions the city of the Menapii, of which nothing remains except ruins and an empty name.

Perhaps the poet calls them the farthest of peoples because Flanders, which is part of this people, occupies that region of the sea, and no people is known to dwell beyond it, the Ocean preventing this—using the whole for the part in its customary manner. For from the region occupied by the city of Boulogne and the Odraus, the Pharos has an easy crossing to Britain.

[Note: [Col. 0535] Others call it the Burning Tower, popularly *la Tour d’Ordre*, in the harbor near Boulogne of the Morini.]

This people was disorderly in its customs, relying more on arms than on counsel and, as was said before us, possessing much eloquence but little wisdom. Its untamed barbarity, always inclined toward evil, could not easily be restrained except by the prudence and discernment of a great ecclesiastical man.

### 9

The church of this people was without a shepherd.

[Note: [Col. 0537D] Namely Erkembald, whose death therefore occurred in the year 817, according to the preceding observation, no. 4.]

But when the matter of appointing a bishop was under consideration, and all had been carefully examined, no one was found more worthy than Folquinus. In his election the divided people followed no contrary course but unanimously requested that this man be given to them as bishop, with the agreement of the nobles and the entire clergy.

What more is there to say? Thanks be to God, it pleased the imperial authority—namely Louis, who had succeeded his father Charles—and with his consent Folquinus was consecrated bishop of the city of Thérouanne, the Lord’s will guiding everything.

Strengthened, therefore, by spiritual blessing, he increased his works of piety and faith, showing himself in all things such as a servant of the Lord ought to be. Since he knew that he would have to fight against spiritual wickedness, he carried before him the arts and exercises of virtue, the weapons of faith. He moderated the rigor of discipline so that no one was more popular than he when exercising judicial severity; yet, while being popular, he did not abandon the order of severity.

He ordered his life so that he inclined excessively toward neither side. The middle ground was paved with charity. He preferred neither to allow the sheep entrusted to him to act wrongly rather than rightly, nor to spare the wicked in such a way that he would destroy the good. In truth, he knew how to use the sword.

Thus he labored so that he might be either a defense or an ornament to holy mother Church: a defense outwardly, an ornament inwardly. Neither in his words nor in ordinary conversation was there frivolity. He conversed with anyone about something useful, or meditated on that same thing in anyone.

From the very beginning of his episcopate he appeared as well suited to the office over which he had newly been enthroned as though he had presided over it for a long time. In matters of religion and the worship of God—which the Greeks call *theosebeia*, “godliness”—he first followed canonical and apostolic authority: namely, that all entrusted to his care should be of one heart and one soul. Whatever he saw in his church that was indecent or effeminate, he cut away most diligently with a true and spiritual circumcision, regarding as his own loss whatever appeared inept in his subjects and counting as his own gain whatever bore fruitful results through the cultivation of Christ.

He cultivated that Church so diligently that it needed no pruning, since he did not permit any kind of vice even to grow from the root. He offered himself to his people as an example and mirror for imitation. He did not labor for himself alone but sought the salvation of all through the commerce of his labor.

If anyone undertook some great work in religion, he recognized that man as a reserve force supporting him in the divine battle. He was also concerned for Christ’s poor. What he scattered by withholding it from his own table increased for them; he did not reserve it for his belly, as some are accustomed to do, since he was not greatly concerned about the following day.

It is difficult to describe fully what kind of servant of the Lord he showed himself to be. To pursue only his virtues: he contained the sum of all virtues, as though the forms of innate goodness had been firmly implanted in him by nature.

### 10

Sithiu is a monastery of men of God, and it contains many memorials of saints. It belongs to the parish of the bishop of Thérouanne, although it possesses privileges of immunity from emperors, or from the universal pope, and from the bishops of that see itself.

At that time Hugo governed it. His brother was Louis, and their father was Charles. That monastery is properly divided into two parts: the monks occupy the lower section, and the canons the upper; the former rejoice in the patronage of Bertin, the latter in that of Audomar.

### 11

The translation of blessed Audomar, how it was carried out by this blessed bishop, and what occurred between him and the aforementioned abbot Hugo are celebrated in popular report.

[Note: [Col. 0537D] These events were written by Folcard in book I, chapter 8, *On the Miracles of Saint Bertin*, a book found in Part I of the second century, where there is more about Saint Folcuinus. In chapter 7 of that work his privilege granted to the [Col. 0538D] monks of Sithiu at the request of Abbot Hugo is reported; it was granted in 839, in the twenty-second year of his episcopate, an era that agrees correctly with the foregoing.]

Among these events the constancy of the holy man is sufficiently remarkable. It was not easy to resist the abbot, whose birth was so distinguished and who also possessed no shortage of military power. But the man of God placed all these things after the fear of the Lord. Finally, he did not rest until he had restored the holy body, fraudulently removed, to its proper place, even at considerable risk to his own life, and had established a solemn feast in the month of June, when the grain stands with its stalk growing.

Taking precautions for the future, lest the holy body be taken away in the same manner or by any other device, he concealed it in the earth, where it remained hidden from human beings for many years; but it was revealed when the Lord willed.

In the same way he also translated and reburied the body of Saint Bertin.

[Note: Read chapters 9 and 11 of the aforementioned book.]

He decreed that this day should be solemn for us; it is the seventeenth day before the Kalends of August.

### 12

After these events, the more the man of God Folquinus recognized that, through the old age of his body, the day of his release was approaching, the more assiduously he devoted himself to the practice of right action, knowing what is written: “Blessed are those servants whom the Lord, when he comes, will find watching” (Luke 12:37).

Thus, increasing daily from virtue to virtue, he burned with the desire to see the God of gods in Zion. The tears of that inward love bore witness to him, revealing the innermost part of his conscience; while chanting the psalms amid those tears, he very often said: “My soul has thirsted for you, O God; when shall I come and appear before the face of my God?” (Psalm 41:5).

Bringing the eye of his mind less often back to the things he had already accomplished with Christ’s help, and following the Apostle’s saying—“forgetting what is behind and stretching toward what lies ahead”—he devoted himself increasingly to fasting and vigils. He strove to kindle his mind, sharpened by this discipline, toward higher things.

With his loins girded, the lamps of good works lit and filled with oil, he awaited the return of his Lord from the wedding feast, so that he might enter with him into the enduring joy of eternal blessedness and reign with him. Caring for the flock entrusted to him, he supplied them with the wheat of the word as a most faithful steward, urging them to convert while it was still “today,” lest the final day find them unprepared.

### 13

Exhausted by long old age—for he had spent nearly forty years in the episcopate—he could no longer publicly celebrate the solemnities of Mass.

[Note: [Col. 0539D] Folcuinus the monk uses the same words above and says that he received this account from Wicfrid, bishop of Thérouanne, who took possession of the see in 948.]

When the king learned this, while Folcuinus was still alive, he sent him a successor as bishop, contrary to the canons. When the holy bishop heard this, he prepared himself, in episcopal fashion, for the celebration of Mass and, while the usurping successor was present, carried out the entire service with the utmost vigor.

But when the time came to give the blessing, as is customary for bishops, he reversed the order and pronounced a curse instead. The frightened men, having mounted their horses, wished to return home. But halfway along the road the usurping bishop fell from his horse, broke his neck, and breathed out his life. All those who had come with him also died within a year through various disasters.

[Note: [Col. 0539D] Folcuinus the levite writes *equitibus*—“the riders”—instead of *equis*—“the horses”; this usage is frequently found in authors of that period.]

14. Therefore, when the time of his calling approached, although weighed down by advanced old age, he resolved to travel through the parishes of his episcopate, knowing that this was salutary both for himself and for his subjects: if any of the children of the Church had wandered astray from their mother’s bosom, he would bring them back to her by correcting them according to the statutes of the canons and exhorting them through preaching. With such zeal and devotion he made a pious visit to the church situated in Mempiscus, called Hicclesbeke. [Note: [Col. 0539D] It is a village near Woromholt, a little beyond the midpoint of the road from Audomaropolis to Bergas, and is now called Hekelsbeke, on the River Yser, which flows into the Pene.]

While he was staying there for only a short time and was already considering his return, he began to be afflicted by a severe illness. Then, summoning his disciples and commending them to the almighty Lord, he urged them at great length not to abandon the path of the right way. Finally, strengthening them with his blessing, he joyfully surrendered his soul to heaven, to be joined to the assembly of the saints. [Note: [Col. 0540D] Saint Humfrid, his successor, will be treated below under the year 859.]

He died in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 855, in the third indiction, as the seventh day was drawing toward evening. That was the fifteenth year of the glorious King Charles, son of Louis, and the fortieth year of this blessed bishop’s episcopate, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of January. While still alive, he had requested that, wherever his death might occur, his body should be carried to the monastery of Sithiu and buried in the basilica of Saint Bertin. [Col. 0539D]

15. After his death, crowds came from every direction to the funeral of the blessed body. When his clerics were distressed by the difficulty of the journey and began to complain, they turned to divine assistance. Then, during that same night, while a south wind was blowing, the entire immeasurable depth of water surrounding the island of Sithiu froze for almost two miles, so that in the morning it offered the bearers of the holy body a firm passage over the ice.

When the body was carried there, it was received with candles and censers by that most reverent and holy community of monks, who came forth to meet the sacred funeral procession together with an immense multitude of people. After they had completed the rites with all the dignity required by a funeral, the body was clothed as he had been accustomed to stand before the sacred altars, and was brought to the place he himself had chosen for burial. He was buried on the right side of Saint Bertin, amid the profound grief of the assembled people. [Col. 0540A]

16. The elders also report that this man of God possessed a horse of remarkable intelligence. Whenever he was about to set out, as necessity required, the animal willingly bent its knees and offered its back to the holy burden. They say that this horse, so intelligent, wept when it was to be given to the brothers and preceded the bier, and that thereafter it refused to carry any human being. [Note: [Col. 0540D] Folquinus the Levite writes only that it preceded the bier, not that it wept.] Nor did it permit anyone to use it for pleasure after the body of so great a bishop had been laid to rest. Not long afterward the horse died, and when its body was offered as food to dogs, none of them touched it with a bite. For it was not fitting that its exposed corpse should feed dogs and crows, stuffing their throats, above which the frequent prayer of Christ had risen from the heartfelt devotion of the one who sat upon it. Indeed, it is not right to believe that the saint delighted in fables. When the townspeople saw this, they buried the animal according to human custom; thus, as I have said, the brutal ferocity of the dogs revered it with a certain, so to speak, admiration. [Col. 0540B–C]

17. Not long afterward it happened that a monk of the aforesaid monastery of Sithiu, the namesake of this blessed man—for he too was called Folquinus—became seriously ill. He had suffered for a long time and could scarcely walk except with the support of two staffs. One day, overcome by the intensity of his pain, he resolved to proceed as best he could to the altar of Saint Bertin, his patron, in order to pray for the health of both soul and body.

For those who do not know the arrangement of the church, I should explain that, for those entering from the southern side, the tomb of the aforesaid holy Father, placed in front, blocks the way; this is the principal altar of Saint Martin. Consequently, on the right side of that tomb, the tomb of the blessed Folquinus is the first one encountered by those wishing to reach the former tomb.

The monk mentioned above had already reached the tomb of the blessed Folquinus when suddenly, shaken by some indescribable shudder, and with his staffs flying apart in opposite directions, he fell headlong upon the holy tomb. Seizing this opportunity, he tearfully implored God, through the intercession of the bishop buried there, if his soul possessed any merit before God, to restore to him the health he had long desired. He did not remain there long in prayer. At once he rose healed, so that everyone marvelled and gave thanks to God, as he walked on his own feet without anyone’s assistance.

From that day onward the tomb of the blessed man was held in greater reverence. The monk who had been healed, being trained in grammar, expressed the event in elegiac verse and wrote the following on his tomb:

> Here lie the venerable remains of Father Folquinus,  
> Once the bishop who ruled the Morini.  
> For five times four tens of years he was a guide in life,  
> Performing God’s commands with pious mind and deed.  
> On the fourteenth day of December he was taken  
> From the world and rejoices to enter the apostolic choir.

18. Thereafter everyone venerated the merits of the blessed man, so that the Savior’s saying might be proved true: “Nothing is concealed that will not be revealed, nor hidden that will not be known” (Matthew 10:26). The Shepherd of shepherds did not wish the bones of his vicar to remain hidden beneath the earth any longer, but desired that the venerable glory of his holiness should be proclaimed to all. [Note: [Col. 0541C] Here Folquinus is called Christ’s vicar. Wibert, abbot of Gembloux, also applies this designation, among others, to Philip, archbishop of Cologne, as was noted above in connection with the book on the miracles of Saint Adalhard, abbot.]

In the year of the most blessed incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 928, in the first indiction, during the reign of King Charles, two men of distinguished character, living far apart, repeatedly received visions during the quiet of night ordering them to go to the famous monastery of Sithiu and, raising the remains of the venerable holy bishop Folquinus, to prepare them for the honor due to them. [Note: [Col. 0541C] Compare what I noted above from Folquinus the Levite in the preliminary observation, no. 4.]

They joyfully fulfilled the command. Equipped as best they could, they came to the aforesaid monastery of Sithiu, explained to the brothers the reason for their arrival, and asked permission to uncover the urn in which the holy citizen was enclosed. After the brothers had long weighed the matter from every side, they reported it to Adoloffus, then the generous count and abbot of that place. After consulting Stephen, at that time the most reverend bishop of the church of Thérouanne [Note: [Col. 0541C] Folquinus the Levite does not say that the bishop was consulted on this matter.], and with the common consent of all, they came to the holy man’s tomb at daybreak on the Ides of November, with candles, a choir of singers, and all the clerical vestments. They raised the saint’s bodily remains and placed them there; an altar was built at the site of the tomb, and they spent that day in festivity with songs and rejoicing. When the service had been completed and they had refreshed themselves, each returned to his own place. [Col. 0541C–542A]

19. Once these things had taken place, the remains of the blessed man began to shine forth through miracles. The townspeople established the custom that those suffering from fever should frequently visit the altar of the holy bishop, each bringing a candle according to his means; and everyone marvelled that, in proportion to the faith of those who asked, they received healing.

We have often seen women suffering the difficulty of childbirth receive health through the merits of the saint from his stole, which still survives. [Note: [Col. 0541C–542C] John Iperius, abbot of Sithiu, writes in chapter 13: “We preserve one of his processional copes, a mitre, gloves, and sandals, as well as three stoles.” He testifies that contact with these is salutary for women in childbirth. Finally, Folcardus writes in the first book of his work on the miracles of Saint Bertin, chapter 9, that the body of Saint Folquinus was famous for great miracles in his own time, that is, in the eleventh century. I recently inspected these precious κειμήλια [relics or treasures] in person and venerated the relics of Saint Folquinus, placed upon the high altar on the southern side in the splendid basilica of Sithiu, or the monastery of Bertin. Most graciously received by the most reverend lord abbot and the religious monks, I easily obtained permission to examine the remarkable monuments of that place, which provide me with much assistance.]

Thus women who had been burdened with the labor of childbirth for three days or more, and who seemed almost at the point of death, were restored to their former health as soon as they entered beneath that stole while giving birth. Through many other signs also the Lord showed that his saint had been glorified in heaven. Our Lord Jesus Christ, who works and remains with his elect until the end of the age, coeternal and consubstantial with the Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns for endless ages of ages. [Col. 0542C] Amen.

[Col. 0541]

# FOLCUINUS, ABBOT OF LOBBES, ON THE DEEDS OF THE ABBOTS OF LOBBES

*(Monumenta Germaniae Historica of Pertz)*

## Editorial Notice

[Col. 0541D] Following the example perhaps of Ansegisus, who wrote the deeds of the abbots of Fontenelle in the ninth century, Folquinus undertook, toward the end of the tenth century, to write the deeds of the abbots of the monastery over which he himself presided, namely Lobb es. [Note: [Col. 0541D] Folcwinus, Folcuinus, Folquinus, Fulcoinus, Fulcuinus, and Volquinus are the same name.]

He was born into an illustrious family. [Note: [Col. 0542D] *Deeds of the Abbots of Lobbes*, chapter 28. According to Folquinus, the author of the charter-book of Saint Bertin: Charles Martel begot Jerome; Jerome begot Saint Folquinus the bishop and Odwinus; Odwinus in turn begot Odwinus; the younger Odwinus begot Folquinus and Regenwala; Folquinus in turn begot Folquinus the deacon and monk of Saint Bertin.] He must be counted among the descendants of Charles Martel through his son Jerome. [Note: [Col. 0543C–D] I regard him as no different from Folquinus, author of the charter-book of Saint Bertin. The matter is by no means settled by the arguments adduced by Mabillon, *Acta*, IV, I, p. 623; for all the reasons he offers for distinguishing the two are either of no weight or more strongly persuade one that they were the same man. Folquinus the abbot, in the Life of Bishop Folquinus which he published, added some details to what the deacon had written in the Sithiu charter-book in 961, concerning the same saint, his great-grandfather, in the same words. In the charter-book he calls the saint’s mother Ermentrude, whereas in the two manuscripts of the Life available to Mabillon she is Ercensenda; in the charter-book we read that the horse preceded the funeral, but in the Life that the horse, preceding the funeral, wept. Finally, in one place the author says that he was Saint Folquinus’s kinsman, while in the other he is silent; and he writes that at the saint’s tomb Folquinus the monk—although two monks of that name then lived at Saint Bertin—was healed and composed three elegiac verses in the saint’s praise. These facts do not prove that the deacon was different from the abbot. On the contrary, both were of noble Lotharingian stock; both were offered as boys to Saint Bertin and were monks there in 961 and 965; both were accustomed to handling ancient charters; both hold a place among writers; and one published a shorter Life of Saint Folquinus in the charter-book, the other a fuller Life in a work published later. They seem to me to have been one and the same man.] From his father Folquinus, who in 928 had raised the body of Saint Folquinus the bishop together with his brother Regenwala, and from his mother Thiedala. In 947, while still a boy, he was brought from Lorraine to the monastery of Sithiu and, in 948, on the feast of Saint Bertin, [Note: [Col. 0543D] *Charter-book of Folquinus*, in Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, fourth century, part I, p. 623.] “when the cares of his relatives had ceased to assail him with manifold harassment almost from the very cradle,” [Note: [Col. 0544C] Preface to the life of Saint Folquinus, ibid., p. 624.] he was offered to Saint Bertin and became a monk.

There he was taught both sacred letters and those of the Romans. In 961 he collected the charters of the monastery, arranged in a twofold order according to time and subject, inserting the deeds of the abbots, [Note: [Col. 0544C] Mabillon, *De re diplomatica*, p. 235. We await the forthcoming publication of the charter-book itself by the most distinguished scholar Guerard.] and dedicated the collection to Abbot Adoloffus.

In 965, while still a young man, he was placed in charge of the monastery of Lobbes by Bishop Everacrus and was ordained at Cologne on Christmas Day in the presence of Otto I. [Note: [Col. 0544C] *Deeds of the Abbots of Lobbes*, chapter 28; *Annals of Lobbes*.] He governed the abbey for twenty-five years. During that time he not only protected its possessions and rights, but also enlarged the monastery, with the support of Bishop Nothgerus, with buildings, ecclesiastical ornament, bells, and books. [Note: [Col. 0544C] Continuation of the *Deeds*.—In a letter of the people of Lobbes preserved in Balderic, *Chronicle of Cambrai*, I, chapter 105, he is accused of negligence.]

He maintained dealings with learned men of his time, for example with Ratherius, whom he received at Lobbes when he was an exile from Verona but later found ungrateful, and with Adalbero, archbishop of Reims, whom he visited at Reims as the patron of Gerbert and other very learned men. [Note: [Col. 0544C] Ibid., chapter 7.]

He was exceptionally well equipped to write the deeds of his predecessors as abbots. He had examined the charters and letters preserved in the church archives, [Note: [Col. 0544C] Ibid., chapters 21, 16, 8, 6, and 3.] other records of the monastery, very ancient martyrologies, [Note: [Col. 0544C] Ibid., chapter 7.] inscriptions, [Note: [Col. 0544C] Ibid.] a catalogue of the abbots, [Note: [Col. 0544C] Ibid., chapter 9.] and even very brief annals brought down to his own time. He had read the lives of the abbots Ursmar and Ermin, [Note: [Col. 0544C] Chapter 9.] writings relating to the history of the neighboring bishoprics, Liège [Note: [Col. 0544C] Chapter 18: the life of Lambert by Stephen, bishop.] and Reims [Note: [Col. 0544C] Chapter 7: the history of Reims by Flodoard.] the annals of the Franks, [Note: [Col. 0544D] See the Prologue and chapter 2.] and the works of Einhard [Note: [Col. 0544D] Passim; see below.] and Ruotger. [Note: [Col. 0544D] Chapter 25.] From these he borrowed sentences and even entire chapters in an attempt to adorn his narrative.

Yet his talent did not rise above his material. His narrative is often thin and sometimes badly arranged [Note: [Col. 0544D] Especially compare chapters 14–17.], and his language is also liable to faults. [Col. 0543C] [Note: [Col. 0544D] For example, he uses a deponent in place of a passive.] Only when he reaches his own lifetime does he win greater approval. The final chapters of the work prove him—as we have also seen in the case of Flodoard—no less devoted to truth than credulous of miracles.

The book was produced at Lobbes around the year 980. [Note: [Col. 0544D] While Adalbero, archbishop of Reims, was still alive; he died in January 990.] It was preserved in the monastery itself, then at Tournai, and, if Foppens may be trusted, at Gembloux. [Note: [Col. 0544D] *Bibliotheca Belgica*, I.] It became known in later centuries through additions to the work, to Sigebert of Gembloux [Note: [Col. 0544D] *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 136, and the *Life of Wibert*, chapter 13.], to the author of the *Life of Saint Ursmar* published by Chesne [Note: [Col. 0544D] *Scriptores Francici*, I, 688.], and to Trithemius. [Note: [Col. 0544D] *On Illustrious Men of the Order of Saint Benedict*, II, 60. Yet in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, 296, he attributes these works, like Andreas of Bamberg, to Bishop Hilduin.]

Only in the seventeenth century did it appear, together with its continuations, in D’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, having been badly copied from the Lobbes manuscripts. [Note: [Col. 0544D] Volume VI, p. 541, and the new edition, volume II, p. 730.]

When the old materials for our edition had been sought in vain, it finally happened that Bethmann discovered in the royal library at Brussels, and I in Paris, manuscript copies made in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. We are grateful that, chiefly through the work of Waitz, these were brought into use:

**1) C.** Formerly belonging to the monastery of Blessed Mary of Nazareth in the diocese of Morini, later to the Society of Jesus at Tournai; some of its readings are recorded in the margin of the royal Brussels manuscript N. 7816. Several passages of greater importance, the preface, and chapters 25, 30, and following, previously omitted in the Brussels manuscript, derive from this now-lost codex. We regret that it was copied carefully enough, but not wherever it mattered; consequently its readings are often doubtful.

**1\*) C.** Royal Paris manuscript among the books of Saint-Germain, marked “Residu fasc. 90 n. 4,” on paper. It contains a copy of the Lobbes manuscript sent to D’Achery for printing. D’Achery recorded: “The monk D. Simon Guillemot of Saint-Ghislain sent me what had been transcribed in 1660 by Dom Gregory Sergeant, subprior of Lobbes.”

But since he suspected that the scribe had often, especially in Folquinus’s continuation, imposed his own manner of writing upon the text rather than following the manuscript, he used it only for the division of chapters, headings, and the final chapters, generally reproducing Baluze’s copy, to which we shall shortly refer. He was compelled, however, to print the continuation from the Lobbes manuscript. [Col. 0544C]

**2) C.** Royal Brussels manuscript N. 7816, on paper, sixteenth century, small folio, generally copied carefully and collated with the manuscript of Blessed Mary (1). It contains Folquinus together with the continuations, followed by a little history of Lobbes. “Many people say many things about the condition of the monastery of Lobbes,” and so forth. It is mutilated at the end. We also examined it. [Col. 0544B–0545A]

**2\*) C.** Royal Paris manuscript preserved among Baluze’s papers, Armarium II, fascicle 1, no. 3. Waitz observed that these sheets were copied from the Brussels manuscript, which was apparently at that time preserved in the monastery of Rouge-Cloître. [Note: [Col. 0545B] The name of the monastery appears in the upper margin of this copy.] D’Achery reproduced them in his edition. The Tournai scribe inserted the supplements into the text, adopting readings sometimes from the Tournai manuscript and sometimes from the Brussels manuscript; from the continuations he extracted only four and a half sheets. Since the Brussels manuscript survives, we have entirely disregarded this copy as worthless.

**3)** From the treatise *On the Miracles of Saint Ursmar*, written by a monk of Lobbes with the help of Folquinus and his continuation, and attributed by Henschenius to Folquinus in *Acta Sanctorum*, April, volume II, pp. 563 and following, we have extracted various readings.

[Col. 0545B] With these materials, especially the Brussels manuscript, employed, we may present a text that, even if not everywhere authentic, nevertheless comes very close to the genuine text, as comparison with the work of Ruotger demonstrates.

[Col. 0546A] We shall in due course insert into our collection the continuation of the book in which Folquinus, with the assistance of Bishop Nothgerus, is said to have obtained from Otto II the renewal in 972 of the immunity of the monastery of Lobbes, confirmed by Pope John XIII, [Note: [Col. 0545B] The Lobbes annals give 973; but John had died in 972.] and to have made provision for the support and clothing of the poor after his death, leaving an inventory of the books and ornaments that he found in the monastery or acquired through his own efforts. [Note: [Col. 0545B] *Annals of Lobbes*.]

Folquinus died in 990. He had also published the *Life of Saint Folquinus, Bishop of Thérouanne*, which he had dedicated to Walter, abbot of Saint Bertin, as a witness to their long-standing relationship. [Note: [Col. 0545B] Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum*, cited above. Rivet, *Literary History of France*, VI, 454, conjectures that it was written around 970, but that Folquinus added the words “whom they call abbot of the people of Lobbes” with his customary humility; see *Deeds of the Abbots of Lobbes*, chapter 28. Walter is said to have died in 996; we read that three other abbots served between him and Adoloffus, who was abbot in 961.] It seems no less doubtful that he dedicated to the same man the lives of Saints Audomar, Bertin, Winnoc, and Silvinus. [Note: [Col. 0546B] The prologue to the *Life of Saint Folquinus* seems to have given rise to this opinion.] It is equally uncertain that he wrote the numerous sermons and homilies attributed to him by Trithemius. [Note: [Col. 0546B] Compare *Literary History of France*, cited above, p. 458. A homily on the tares, concerning Matthew 13:25 and following, is said formerly to have existed in the library of Saint Martin at Leuven.]

He was buried in the church of Saint Ursmar beside Bishop Ratherius, under this inscription: [Note: [Col. 0546B] Martène, *Collection*, IX, p. 964.]

> Here lies buried the unmarried Folquinus,  
> Renowned for nobility, rising in the name of abbot,  
> Striving in divine matters, skilled in human sophistries;  
> May every reader ask pardon for his sins.

# DEEDS OF THE ABBOTS OF LOBBES

[Col. 0545]

## PROLOGUE

[Note: [Col. 0545] “The prologue to the deeds of the abbots of Lobbes follows”: manuscript 1. Manuscript 2 lacks the prologue.]

[Col. 0545C]

After a long period in which ancient authorities had debated the question in every direction as far as they could, the opinion finally settled in the minds of all philosophers and spiritual fathers, and they instructed us to hold it inviolably: the world is not governed by chance events, but everything is ruled by providence according to the will of the One who presides over it, the creating and almighty Deity, in accordance with the ineffable ordering of his disposition, before anything emerged in time.

[Textual apparatus: [Col. 0545] Manuscript 1 has *dixi* (“I said”) corrected to *Diu* (“for a long time”); it omits *ex tempore* (“in time”). For *cuique quod est esse perfectum est*, the note explains: “that is, whatever exists has perfect being, and to be perfect is what it is.” Manuscript 1* reads *temporis* (“of time”) for *temporum* (“of times”), *creavit* (“created”) for *creaverit* (“has created”), and *quippe* for *quidem*. It has *et hiems* (“and winter”), and *veri quoque autumnus, autumpno ver* (“spring likewise [is opposed] to autumn, autumn to spring”); *campis nive* (“the fields with snow”) for *nive campos*; it omits *in vere* (“in spring”); and reads *marescunt* (“wither”) for *marcescunt* (“wither languidly”). Manuscript 1 omits *de interna summi Imperatoris aula* (“from the inner court of the supreme Emperor”) and *diligit* (“loves”); manuscript 1* has *quicquam potest* for *non potest quicquam*. For “as the Psalmist says,” manuscript 1* has *psal.*; manuscript 1 has *praesta* (the codex seems to have read *psta*). Manuscript 1* gives *Nabucodonosor* for *Nabugodonosor*, *Hoc testatur* for *Testatur hoc*, omits *ad* before “the Persians,” reads *Persos* for *Persas*, and *finem faciens regnandi* for *regnandi finem fecit*; it also omits *sibi* (“for himself”) in the phrase concerning Alexander. For the reference to Alexander, see *Deeds of the Kings of the Franks*, chapter 1 and following. Manuscript 1 reads *dicitur* for *quia*, and the manuscripts have *Aenea* in the phrase concerning Aeneas. Manuscript 1* reads *Hlodoveus* for *Clodoveus*, *delituit* for *Nec distulit*, omits *rex regum Christus* (“Christ, King of kings”), *prospexit* for *provexit*, and *Hlodoveos, Hlotharios* for *Clodoveos, Clotharios*; manuscript 1 reads *quem* for *quae* in “the Wisdom of God, which says.” Manuscript 1* has *aut diruta* for *ante id temporis diruta* and *et* for *aut* in “sprang up again or were begun.”]

The most powerful force of the Deity, for whom whatever exists possesses the perfection of being, always held within itself the forms of things, already perfect in certain primary substances. But when he willed, where he willed, and how he willed, he made them visible to us. Nothing was added to him in time so that he might become Creator, since time itself began when he ordered it, and he arranged all things within time, so that he who is rightly believed to be Creator might also be regarded as Dispenser. [Col. 0545D]

For times consist of days and numbers. When we read or hear that on this day or that day God made this or that, we understand time or number. Therefore God is the Creator of times, since he himself is older than the time of which he is the Creator, and since he created all things in time. [Note: [Col. 0545] “Time” instead of “times”: manuscript 1*.]

Indeed, he made time itself, divided by dissimilar equality into intervals that differ from one another, yet mutually harmonizing according to his will, so that things thought to be confused are not confused, but rather, fitting together by turns, they form an ordered and perfect commonwealth. The elements themselves, through which we subsist, though opposed to one another, come together in such a pleasing equality into the constitution of a single body that, though differentiated, they do not conflict. Indeed, if you remove one from the other, you destroy the human being altogether.

The same principle applies to temporal motion. For what is more opposed than night to day, darkness to light? Summer also resists winter, and winter summer. [Note: [Col. 0545] “And winter”: manuscript 1*.] Spring is opposed to autumn, and autumn to spring. [Note: [Col. 0545] “Spring to autumn”: manuscript 1*.] Who has ever experienced the heat of Cancer and the dog days in winter, or seen the fields whiten with snow and the rivers spread with ice in summer? Likewise, no one has ever tasted new wine in spring or made use of grapes, while the various kinds of grass and flowers with which spring is adorned and rejoices wither languidly in autumn. [Note: [Col. 0547] “Become parched”: manuscript 1*.]

These things, coming in their proper order and occupying their proper place, complete the year. If they were not distinguished from one another, the result would seem rather a kind of chaos and an intolerable time than a year.

An immutable reason contains the mutable cause of these things. With that reason, nothing is new which appears recent to us, and nothing changes which seems changeable to us. It orders everything in such a way that even what is thought to be evil is not disordered. Therefore the highest and principal—indeed the sole—cause of things is the will of God. Hence we sing: “Everything that the Lord willed, he did” (Psalm 134:6).

Nothing happens outwardly unless it is commanded or permitted by the inner court of the supreme Emperor, either for the benefit of certain people or for the punishment imposed by his hidden and just judgment. For who loves more than the one who made? And who rules more orderly than the one who made and loves? Therefore nothing can advance beyond or fall short of what it should do except according to the Lord’s will, while the gift of free choice has been granted to human beings by the grace of God. [Col. 0547A–B]

Nor should we be greatly surprised by the successions or changes of kingdoms that we have either heard about or witnessed. The kingdom belongs to him, as the Psalmist says, and he himself will rule the nations (Psalm 21:29). As Nebuchadnezzar learned, he gives it to whomever he wishes. When he willed, he established kingdoms; when he willed, he changed them.

The most ancient kingdom of the Assyrians bears witness to this. It was later transferred to the Medes and Persians, and its reign came to an end. From them it passed to the Macedonians, whom that Alexander acquired for himself with much bloodshed—the Alexander whom Daniel calls bronze in the statue or a leopard in his vision, a great man indeed, that great whirlpool of misery. Finally, after crossing land and sea and with superior forces, the empire passed to the Romans, not without the nod of God.

So much for kingdoms, although the empire of the Franks subsequently increased. Since it had poured into the Roman strongholds through frequent and successful advances and by military force, in which it was especially abundant, and had attained that height of power, it must nevertheless be counted as part of the Roman commonwealth.

For the same people are joined to the Romans by a certain kinship, since both peoples came from Troy: the Romans followed the standards of Aeneas, while the Franks, led by Antenor, advanced through the Illyrian gulfs to the Maeotian marshes. [Note: [Col. 0547D] Famars; compare H. Müller, who discusses the homeland of the Salic Law, pp. 41–46.] Because of their excessive fierceness of spirit, they received the name Franks. Eventually occupying Gaul and feared by the other peoples of those regions, they exchanged idolatry for the service of Christ.

For their king Clovis, having received the grace of Christ through baptism by Saint Remigius, made his people Christian. Nor did Christ, the King of kings, delay in giving a gift to those who served him as soldiers: he advanced them to kingdoms and increased them with favorable successes. From that time the fortunate and hereditary succession continued through the Clovises, Chlothars, and Dagoberts. And why should it not have continued, when the Wisdom of God, which says, “Through me kings reign” (Proverbs 8:15), confirmed it by faith and strengthened it by equity and justice?

The bishoprics and monasteries that before that time had been destroyed or did not exist bear witness to this. From then on, some sprang up again, while others were begun under new auspices. If we were to write about each of them individually, the page would fail us, especially since this is not our purpose. It is enough to speak only of our own institution; and since we must speak of the place, let us describe the site of the place about which we must speak.

## 1

[Note: [Col. 0547] “Topography of the deeds of the abbots of Lobbes”: added in manuscript 1.]

[Textual apparatus: [Col. 0547] The source prints *oportunitas*, corrected to *opportunitas*, here and below. Manuscript 2 reads *liptinas* for *Liphtinas* and omits *lo* (“a woodland shade”). In the clause concerning the parish boundary, manuscript 1 reads *enim* (“indeed”), while manuscript 2 omits it. Manuscript 1 reads *conatu* (“effort”) for *conamine* (“striving”). For the divine foreordination, manuscript 1 reads *noluit* (“did not will”) for *voluit* (“willed”). Manuscript 2 reads *et* (“and”) for *aut* (“or”) in the final alternative.] 

There is a place within the boundaries of the district which the ancients called *Fanum-martinse*, after the place where the superstitious pagans had consecrated a shrine to Mars. Later generations called it *Haynau*, after the river flowing past it. Through the district of the Sambre, the Sambre flows in a gentle and pleasant channel. Here a certain plain, bordered on either side by projecting hills, together with the shade of the woods and the convenience of the site, makes the place extremely agreeable.

At this place a stream flows down into the Sambre. They call it the Laubac, and some think that it gave its name to the place. [Note: [Col. 0547D] Compare the *Life of Saint Landelin*, *Acta Sanctorum*, June, II, p. 1065, although it seems to have been written after Folquinus.] Others, however, think that the name arose from the suitability of the place for capturing wild animals—for it is surrounded on every side by woodland, and the royal estate of Liphtinas was nearby—and that the forest is still called by its ancient name. [Note: [Col. 0547] “Liptinas”: manuscript 2.] [Note: [Col. 0548D] Lestines. Concerning it, the continuation of the miracles of Saint Ursmar says (*Acta Sanctorum*, April, II, 569): “Liphtinas is the name of an estate in the district of Hainaut, once a royal residence, when peace and justice still met one another upon the earth; now, apparently in the tenth century, it has been distributed among many as a benefice and scarcely suffices in annual revenues for one person.”]

They say that when the king went hunting, he ordered a shelter to be made there to temper the heat of the sun—a structure they call a *lobia*—and that the place therefore received its name from this enduring name, while the stream took its name from the place, not the place from the stream. This seems more probable.

The Germans appear to support this explanation. In their language the place is called *Lobach*: they call a shady woodland place *lo*, [Note: [Col. 0547] Omitted in manuscript 2.] while *bach* means a stream. If the two are joined, they produce “the stream of the shelter.”

The place was suitable for laying ambushes and for banditry. For, as has been said, it was enclosed by forests and made difficult by rocky outcrops; consequently, after committing a crime, the enemy could not be found. [Col. 0548D–0549A]

Taking advantage of this suitability, a certain Morosus, a man devoted to this craft and activity, persisted in banditry in such a place during the reign of Lothar, the seventh ruler after Clovis. Since he was not content with minor crimes and continually planned and committed greater ones, the Lord at last took pity on him. Through Saint Autbert, bishop of Cambrai—for this place lies within the boundary of his church’s parish, although the diocese of Liège also extends as far as here—Morosus was converted into Landelinus; from a Saul he became a second Paul. He put an end to his vices and dedicated the place to sacred pursuits, so that the place he had stained with vices might be consecrated by virtues, and so that, where sin had abounded, grace might also abound, as the Apostle says (Romans 5:20).

In that place he established a church for himself for the time being. He mourned the things in which he had formerly delighted, seeking his livelihood by his own hands and labor, subduing the wantonness of the flesh with fasts and vigils, and applying himself with the utmost effort of his mind to the things of God, so that everyone marvelled when they saw the transformation wrought by the right hand of the Most High.

Through such exercises he became a model to many who flocked to pursue the same devotion, and thus he became the first founder of the monastery of Lobbes.

But the divine foreordination of which we spoke earlier—for God does not reveal his judgments to everyone, since the Psalmist says, “Your judgments are a great abyss” (Psalm 35:7)—willed that blessed Landelinus should depart from Lobbes, so that the place might at some time be free for another who would follow. Otherwise he would have built upon another’s foundation and suffered loss, or the great merits of two men might have been confined within the narrowness of a single place. Perhaps foreseeing this, blessed Landelinus departed from Lobbes and sought Crespin. [Note: [Col. 0549D] Crespin, in the diocese of Cambrai.]

### 2

[Note: [Col. 0549] Dacherius took the chapters from a copy of the Lobbes manuscript (1*).]

Nor were there lacking many helpers and fellow-workers in the enlargement of the aforesaid place, although their names have disappeared: this was during the times of Clothar, son of Clovis, who reigned for four years, and also of his brothers—namely, Childeric II [Note: [Col. 0549] “the second,” 2.], king of the Austrasians, and Theoderic, whom Pippin [Note: [Col. 0549] “Pippin,” 1? 2; frequently so.] defeated at Testric and subjected to himself, allowing him to finish his reign under him after Theoderic’s eighteenth year; also of Clovis, son of Theoderic, who reigned for two years; and of his brother Childebert, surnamed the Just, who reigned for seven years; and likewise of Dagobert, Childebert’s son, who reigned for five years. All these reigned under the aforesaid prince, retaining only the name of kingship [Note: [Col. 0549] “remaining,” 2.].

During this period—just as in the Acts of the Apostles the disciples, when they wished to go into Asia, were forbidden by the Spirit of the Lord; for it was being reserved [Note: [Col. 0549] “because it was being reserved,” 2.] for John [Note: [Col. 0549] I have written *Johanni* according to the consistent usage of the Middle Ages, as also *parrochia*. In the writing of *cotidie*, *chartis*, *auctoritas*, *conicere*, *valitudo*, and others, manuscript 2 is by no means consistent. We know nothing certain about manuscript 1.]—the blessed Ursmar, distinguished by every exercise of virtue [Note: [Col. 0549] “exercises,” 1?], to whom the Lord had assigned Lobbes as a place of apostolic labor, was summoned by the aforementioned prince Pippin and, through the intervention of Hyldulf, one of the kingdom’s chief nobles, accepted the governance of the same monastery [Note: [Col. 0549] “undertook,” 2.].

(689) The indications of his merits were that boy [Note: [Col. 0549D] Compare Anso, *Life of Ursmar*, chapter 1.] and the bread shown beforehand to his mother in an *oromate* [Note: [Col. 0549] *oromate*, corrected to *aromate* in manuscript 2.] and that ascent of the blessed ladder from earth all the way to heaven. How fitting all these things are for the blessed man, we learn from his deeds.

Perhaps it was not without some presage [Col. 0550B] that he received such a name. For Ursmar, they say, is derived from two customary linguistic forms of Gaul [Note: [Col. 0549] Omitted in manuscript 2.]: one Latin, which those who employed it corrupted [Note: [Col. 0549] Omitted in manuscripts 1 and 2; manuscript 2 adds in the margin, “something is missing.” Dacherius published the word from the Lobbes codex? and after “Teutonic” added: “It is said to mean ‘bear,’ which makes no sense.”], and the other Teutonic. The name is plainly appropriate to the blessed man. They say that a bear licks an unformed offspring and completes, by the work of its tongue, what is lacking in nature [Note: [Col. 0549] Omitted in manuscript 1.].

So that blessed man, by preaching, restored all carnal people and all who were wise only in the things of the flesh [Note: [Col. 0549] Manuscript 2: “who were wise only in that which is of the flesh.”] to the form of their original principle [Note: [Col. 0549] The reading is corrupt in manuscript 1: *praept . . ii*.], continually giving birth to a people for the Lord from sons of wrath, so that he could say with the Apostle: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Galatians 4:19).

I would be lying if these exercises of his had not continued down to the dregs of our own age [Note: [Col. 0549] “appearance,” manuscript 1.]. To say nothing of those whom he instructed either by his living voice or whom, through the proximity of time, he made in many respects imitators of himself—though it was exceedingly difficult to equal him in everything—we, to whom the ends of the ages have come [Note: [Col. 0549] “have arrived,” 1?; [Col. 0550D] the thousandth year from the Incarnation was feared.], even though no likeness of our patron’s ability shines forth in us, nevertheless acknowledge [Note: [Col. 0549] “we attest,” manuscript 1.] that whatever we are, however little, we are through his patronage. For we too are the seal [Note: [Col. 0549] “sign,” manuscript 2.] of his apostleship [Note: [Col. 0549] Omitted in manuscript 2.] in the Lord.

It is not especially our task to commend him as famous: a great part of Gaul knows this, and so do those whom he daily restores to health after they have been afflicted by various illnesses.

### 3

Why, then, do we say that he was a bishop? This has often been asked of us. The text describing his life teaches that he was a bishop [Note: [Col. 0550D] Compare Anso’s *Life*, prologue and following.]; but it is entirely silent about the place or time of his ordination, or by whom he was ordained. Yet in documents made during his time and in very ancient parchment fragments preserved in the archives of our church [Note: [Col. 0551] So the edition; manuscript 1 reads “in our church,” manuscript 2 “more closely, our church.”], we find him written under the title of bishop and pontiff.

Our elders give various accounts of this matter. Some say that he was ordained bishop for the sake of preaching—as was appropriate at that time, when the faith was still in its beginnings—in order to restrain the excessive rites of the barbarian people; we also read that the same was done in the case of Saint Amand [Note: [Col. 0551D] See *Life of Saint Amand*, chapter 8.]. Others assign this dignity to the place itself and defend their opinion by a certain reasoning: namely, that a royal place, built with royal munificence and, as has been said, adjoining the royal palace [Note: [Col. 0551] “namely, at Liptines, in French Lestines,” added in manuscript 2; this is a gloss.], would not have been entrusted to anyone unless he had first been ordained a bishop [Note: [Col. 0551] “had been ordained,” 2.].

We shall say below that this dignity also lasted through many of his successors [Note: [Col. 0551D] A later life derived from Folcuin adds (Du Chesne I, p. 688): “Of this, too, so much still remains in that place that the abbot may use sandals and a subdeacon’s tunic, possess the power of binding and loosing, and everywhere wear a gold ring and gloves.”]. Which of these accounts is more truthful we leave to the judgment of our readers [Note: [Col. 0551] Manuscript 2 corrects *lectorum* (“of the readers”) to *lectoris* (“of the reader”).]. Nor do we detract from the holy man in either direction, since, whatever the truth of the matter, we do not deny that he was a bishop.

### 4

Thus, at the beginning of his administration (697), he consecrated the church, which until that time had remained unconsecrated, dedicating it to the Lord in honor of Peter, the chief of the apostles, and likewise of Paul, the teacher of the nations, and of all the apostles of Christ. He enriched the temple with gifts and the altar with many patron saints.

This dedication took place in the year 697 of the Lord’s incarnation [Note: [Col. 0551] “in the year six hundred ninety-seven,” 1.], on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of September [Note: [Col. 0551] “the seventeenth,” Dacherius.], while the Lord reigned forever and Pippin ruled among the Franks.

Because he absolutely would not allow that church to be polluted by the bodies of the dead, he built another in honor of Saint Mary on the summit of the mountain beneath which the aforesaid monastery lies. There he established a cemetery [Note: [Col. 0551] Manuscript 2: *cimitterium*.] for the faithful, and there the people were to assemble; for access to the other church by women was unlawful except at a specified time, as is still the case [Note: [Col. 0551] Corrected from “at a certain time” to “at a specified time” in manuscript 2.].

He also built the monastery at Alne [Note: [Col. 0551D] Aulne on the Sambre.] and subjected it to Lobbes. He likewise built the monastery called Waslare [Note: [Col. 0551D] Wasloi, Walers-en-Fagne, in the diocese of Cambrai], toward the forest of Thérouanne [Note: [Col. 0551D] Thiérache, on the borders of Picardy], in the territory of Fagne [Note: [Col. 0551D] A part of Hainaut], and placed Dodo over it—a very holy man, instructed by him. After remaining there for some time, Dodo desired the wilderness, and, having built a cell in the same forest of Fagne, with the permission and leave of his pious father, lived there the contemplative life. Later, renowned for many virtues, he departed to the Lord. His body was transferred to the monastery called Waslare, where it now rests with the veneration due to it.

Saint Ursmar, always intent on gaining souls, went into Flanders for the sake of preaching, toward the territory of the Menapians, who were still held by the vain superstitions of their people’s rites. Converted to the faith of Christ by his teaching, they made him heir to no small portion of their estates and to the church of Christ at Lobbes.

### 5

(713) The blessed Ursmar, therefore, full of every kind of virtue, having faithfully administered the office entrusted to him and brought the place into equality with the ancient monasteries built by royal munificence [Note: [Col. 0551] So the edition; omitted in manuscripts 1 and 2, where a blank space appears.], was released from the prison of the flesh and brought into the heavenly paradise, where, now and forever, may he happily enjoy God, remembering us, as we ask.

He died in the year 713 of the Lord’s incarnation, while the Lord God reigned over us forever and Pippin held the scepter. Before his death, broken by a long illness [Note: [Col. 0551] Manuscript 2: *longua*], he had appointed Saint Ermin as his successor while he was still alive (711), having poured himself out entirely into him through a special intimacy, as into a beloved heir and most welcome successor.

Ermin, therefore, having been appointed [Note: [Col. 0552D] Compare *Life of Saint Ermin*, chapter 5, *Acta Sanctorum*, April III, p. 375.], began to emulate his teacher, so that, if it were permissible to believe the Epicureans’ account [Note: [Col. 0552D] Folcuin seems to have written “of the Pythagoreans” rather than “of the Epicureans.”] of the transmigration of souls into alternate bodies [Note: [Col. 0551] Manuscript 1 reads “the Epicureans’ account of transmigration”;], he might be thought to represent that same man.

It would be tedious to recount everything, if we wished to tell how assiduous he was in enlarging the place and how careful in the pastoral office entrusted to him, especially since the account of his life speaks sufficiently and abundantly about these matters [Note: [Col. 0551] Omitted in manuscript 1.].

He also had fellow-workers or successors, governors and co-abbots of the same place: Saint Abel, a Scot by birth; Saint Vulgis, a bishop; and Lord Amulwin, likewise a bishop. Antiquity has left nothing certain as to whether they succeeded one another or, while Saint Ermin was occupied with spiritual matters, administered the place jointly. Nevertheless, it did not fail to record that they both held and governed the place of Lobbes and improved it according to the needs of the times [Note: [Col. 0551] “made it better,” 2.].

Saint Ermin governed the same monastery under the aforesaid prince Pippin for three years, and under Charles, son of that same Pippin, likewise senior king and duke, for twenty-two years. Thus, after completing twenty-five years in government, he shared in his teacher’s glory and died on the eighth day before the Kalends of May (737).

### 6

After him Theoduin became abbot. With Karlomannus, mayor of the palace, granting it, our church obtained the estate of Eontanas, watered by the Sambre. The charter of this grant is subscribed as follows:

“Done at the public estate of Liptines” [Note: [Col. 0553] Corrected from *Liptanas* in manuscript 2.], “on the sixth day of February, in the second year of the reign of Childeric.”

And in this stipulation:

“The sign,” it says, “of Karlomannus, mayor of the palace, who made and confirmed this donation.”

This was indeed Karlomannus, Pippin’s brother, who, abandoning the burdensome administration of the kingdom, first became a cleric at Rome and built a monastery on Mount Soracte; afterward he became a monk at Saint Benedict’s on Monte Cassino [Note: [Col. 0553D] See Einhard, *Life of Charlemagne*, chapter 2.].

History records that the aforementioned Childeric reigned under Pippin [Note: [Col. 0553D] See the same work, chapter 1, and the Annals for 749 and 750.], and also testifies that afterward, by order of Pope Zachary, he was tonsured and thrust into a monastery [Note: [Col. 0553] “shut away,” 2.]. From there the sole rule of the kingdom passed to Pippin, with Archbishop Boniface consecrating him.

### 7

Of Abel, mentioned above, we have also learned the following. When we were at Rheims and were conversing with Adalbero, archbishop [Note: [Col. 0553] “Abalbero,” 1? 2.], a venerable man and most learned in the affairs of those regions, we asked about the origin of that city [Note: [Col. 0553] “town,” 2.] and the succession of its bishops. He satisfied us, as time allowed, by producing the pontifical records of that city [Note: [Col. 0553D] Flodoard’s work; see book II, chapter 16.].

In those records it was found that a certain Abel had been bishop in that city and had acquired or established many things there. But what his end was, the writer of the records either did not know or deliberately chose to keep entirely silent.

After examining the chronological calculations from every source [Note: [Col. 0553] This seems the correct reading; manuscript 1 has *veritatis*, manuscript 2 *tantis collatis* in the edition], we proved by an easy argument that this same Abel was both our Abel and a Scot and a bishop. But since his historian was uncertain about his end, perhaps the length of the journey and the religious man’s voluntary withdrawal, together with his love for his heavenly homeland, caused this.

The aforementioned bishop also said that a custom inherited from his predecessors and continued down to his own time required that, during the solemn Mass, in the special commemoration of the dead called the *diptychs* and solemnly performed during the consecration of the Lord’s body, the names of all the bishops of that see be recited individually from a written list, while the subdeacon silently whispered them into the priest’s ear [Note: [Col. 0553] Omitted in manuscript 1.]. He said that he greatly wondered why this man was not found in that commemoration.

As we conjecture, this was done because, although he had previously been ordered to occupy the vacant see as bishop, he later voluntarily renounced that catalogue out of love for God [Note: [Col. 0553] “renouncing it,” manuscript 1.]. It is not heretical to believe this of him, since not resisting heretics is almost the same as favoring them [Note: [Col. 0553] “may be a penalty,” 2.], and so many and such great men at that time would not have allowed anything of the sort to spread. Indeed, by issuing public writings either to prevent or to refute the heresy [Note: [Col. 0553] Manuscript 2 reads “to proclaim”], they would have attacked it with free authority, while the Lord solemnly threatening: “Cursed is he who keeps his sword from blood” (Jeremiah 48:10).

Nor could it have happened that he would seek Ursmar and Ermin—whose manner of life was in heaven—except intending to imitate them, since he could not have been received by them unless he himself had first been tested and trained in the Lord’s camp.

But little has come down to us about Saint Vulgis, the bishop. Nevertheless, in our very ancient martyrologies we find that his feast day is recorded as follows [Note: [Col. 0553] “his birthday,” 2; “recorded,” 2.]:

“On the day before the Nones of February, at the monastery of Lobbes, the deposition of Saint Vulgis, bishop.”

His mausoleum too, in which he lies buried [Note: [Col. 0553] “which was buried,” 2.], can readily be seen.

### 8

The holy bishop Theodulf therefore succeeded [Note: [Col. 0553] Manuscript 2: *susccessit*.] Abbot Theoduin in the administration of the aforesaid place, partly under the aforementioned prince Pippin after he had become king, and for nine years under King Charles, later emperor. He governed it energetically and increased it considerably.

During his time many estates were granted to our church. I would describe them if the donations and testamentary charters were not readily available, and if I were not concerned with brevity.

He died in the year 776 of the Lord’s incarnation, on the feast day of Saint John the Baptist.

### 9

Anso succeeded him in the administration: a good and holy man, abbot only and not a bishop, who governed the same monastery under the aforementioned emperor Charles for twenty-four years.

Anso also devoted himself to letters, according to the capacity of his intellect. There survives a little book on the *Life of Saint Ursmar*, which he composed for his predecessor, Bishop Theodulf [Note: [Col. 0554D] Published in *Acta Sanctorum*, April II, p. 560.], and another on Saint Ermin [Note: [Col. 0554D] There, April III, p. 375.]. In these works, the historical truth, insofar as it could be described by a man of simple eloquence, should be welcomed.

It is not our task to judge the confusion of his statements, which is so great that it is uncertain whether, in setting forth what he knew, he was inclined to do so less learnedly than secular writers, or whether, because of the excellence of the deeds, he deliberately treated the rules of the art as insignificant [Note: [Col. 0553] “so that he was not inclined,” manuscripts 1? 2.].

Anso too died under the aforesaid Charles, in the year in which that same man became emperor (800).

After him [Note: [Col. 0553] Manuscript 2: *quem*.] Hildric, a canon, usurped the same abbacy under that emperor. After him came Ramneric in the time of Lord Emperor Louis [Note: [Col. 0553] “Lodovicus,” manuscripts 1? 2.]. Then it passed to Lord Folrad [Note: [Col. 0555] “Fulrad,” 2.], a most pious abbot and uncle of the aforementioned Ramneric, under the same emperor.

Only the names of the earlier abbots, not their deeds, are known. I believe this is because of the small number of years involved [Note: [Col. 0555] Omitted in manuscript 1.] or because remembering them would have been of little usefulness.

Who the third was, the deeds reveal: he was of great nobility and royal kinship. For he was Charles’s nephew on his father’s side, as is made clear [Note: [Col. 0555] “shines forth,” 2.] by the inscription carved on the wall of the tower of the church of Saint Quentin at Augusta Viromanduorum—for he had also governed that monastery—which reads as follows:

> When renowned King Charles, wielding pious scepters, had completed  
> ten lustres less three years,  
> and, released from human affairs, was leaving  
> the heights of the great kingdom to you, King Louis,  
> Abbot Fulrad, famed for nobility, began  
> to build this work of the venerable hall.
>
> For Jerome was father to this man, and Charles father to that one,  
> who raised high the glory of his own race,  
> waging wars and preserving peace;  
> with God’s help he passed the heights of the kingdom  
> to his offspring.

### 10

In those days the Lord, unwilling that his lamp—which he had kindled by justifying it, made bright by blessing it, and proclaimed through miracles—should remain hidden any longer, but wishing to reveal it to all people for greater veneration, touched the heart of the aforesaid abbot and moved him [Note: [Col. 0555] The conjunction *et* is omitted in manuscripts 1 and 2.] to raise the body of Saint Ursmar, holy, venerable, and to be named with all love, from the tomb [Note: [Col. 0555] The verb *propalare* (“make known”) is *probare* (“prove”) in manuscript 2; *corpus* is omitted in manuscript 2.].

This elevation was performed by order and permission of the man who was then bishop of Cambrai [Note: [Col. 0555D] Halitgar.], with clergy of both orders officiating and a great multitude of people present [Note: [Col. 0555] “officiating,” 2.].

When the elevation had been completed, they treated that day as a feast day [Note: [Col. 0555] The words “for us and for posterity” are missing in manuscript 2.] and decreed that it should be celebrated by us and by those who came after us.

This elevation took place in the year of the Lord 823, one hundred and tenth after the saint’s—indeed, I should not say his death, but his birthday, when he began to live with Christ [Note: [Col. 0555] In manuscript 2, *vere* was deleted before *vivere*.].

From that time the blessed man’s famous reputation began to grow, and, as crowds of sick people flocked to him, it shone forth in miracles of various kinds of healing. These things, whether through the negligence or ignorance of our predecessors, lay unrecorded for a time, and the study of letters was neglected [Note: [Col. 0555] Omitted in manuscript 2.]. We shall set down in their proper places what we have seen or heard, noting only the more remarkable events [Note: [Col. 0555] “remarkable,” 2.], and we shall do this while preserving the order, when, by God’s gift, we reach the dregs of our own age.

### 11

The aforesaid abbot died three years after the aforementioned elevation (826), leaving Ecgard [Note: [Col. 0555D] Manuscripts 1 and 2 read *Ergard*; the edition reads *Eggard*; the Lobbes Annals read *Egard*.] as abbot after him. During his time the first ordination took place in our monastery, with Theoderic, bishop of Cambrai, officiating, while Louis the emperor was still alive.

### 12

When that emperor had been removed from human affairs, Harbert of Corbie was appointed abbot (835), a good and highly praised man, and for that reason promoted to this office by the aforementioned emperor. He was devoted to religion and devoted himself to constructing or [Note: [Col. 0555] “and,” 2.] adorning buildings and objects.

A very famous bell, made at his command and donated to our church, bears witness to this. On it are verses that reveal the abbot and its maker, and the purpose for which it was made, as though the bell itself were speaking:

> By Harbert’s command I am fashioned by Paternus’s art;  
> though unlearned in the Muses, behold, I shall utter tuneful songs.  
> Wakeful by night and by day, I shall sing forth hymns to Christ.

The same abbot also attempted to bring an aqueduct from the forest, cutting through the heights of the mountains, so that it might provide a suitable flow for the use of the mills. But he could not complete the ill-considered work, begun too late [Note: [Col. 0555] “begun,” corrected from *inquoatum* in manuscript 2; compare Einhard’s words in *Life of Charlemagne*, chapter 25.].

For that abbey was violently overrun by Hucbert [Note: [Col. 0555] “Hubert,” corrected to *Hucbert* in manuscript 2; brother of Theutberga, wife of Lothar II.], hateful to God and the saints. After he had gained supreme control of affairs (864), he expelled Harbert, who returned to Corbie, and immediately divided the entire abbey for military purposes, assigning estates to the brothers for their sustenance—estates of small income, as suited the assignor [Note: [Col. 0555] Manuscripts 1 and 2: *delegatis* for *delegans*.].

He then became devoted to a wife and fathered children, retaining for his own condemnation nothing clerical except the tonsure [Note: [Col. 0555] “preserving,” 2.]. His perversity was so great, as common report has it, that he did not shrink from defaming even the majesty of evangelical truth, insofar as it concerned him, saying that what is written by the Lord, who says, “Everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled” (Luke 14:11), was not true—because, if he humbled himself as much as he had exalted himself, he would never have been, as he then was, so exceedingly prominent, but rather utterly rejected and vile in everyone’s eyes.

O tongue that ought to be cut into pieces and thrown to dogs or birds! Perhaps the wretched man did not know, or knowingly and miserably acted the fool, that an exaltation such as his—although permitted by God—is an eternal fall and rejection, as David prays, or rather prophesies, in the Psalm:

“My God,” he says, “make them like a wheel and like stubble before the face of the wind” (Psalm 82:14).

We see a wheel rise upward, only to fall headlong; and from the very point at which it begins its ascent, there it suffers its fall [Note: [Col. 0555] Manuscript 2 reads *in altum* (“upward”) for the corrupt *inante*.]. Stubble, moreover, the higher it is carried by the wind, the more heavily it sinks [Note: [Col. 0555] Omitted in manuscript 1.].

He himself also experienced God’s vengeance upon this matter. For on the very day when his tongue was spewing or barking such things, he fought in battle against Conrad, leader of the Rhaetian [Note: [Col. 0555] Manuscripts 1 and 2 read “Virehensian.”] or Jura regions. First he was pierced through by that blasphemous tongue, and finally he was killed [Note: [Col. 0556D] Compare Regino and the Xanten Annals for 866, and Hincmar’s Annals for 864.]. Such, indeed, was the end of death that the blasphemer deserved.

This occurred during the time when four brother kings were contending over the kingdom of the Franks [Note: [Col. 0557] Omitted in manuscript 2.], or during the reign of the emperor Lothar [Note: [Col. 0557] “Clothar,” manuscript 1.], who had imprisoned his father, Lord Louis, and afterward became a monk at the monastery of Prüm.

### 13

Later, under Lothar the king, son of the aforementioned Emperor Lothar, the same place began to be restored [Note: [Col. 0557] “recovered,” 1? 2.] and, through John, bishop of Cambrai, and a certain Hugh, was considerably replenished both in possessions and in inhabitants by order of that king.

This was the Lothar who had been excommunicated at Rome on account of his repudiated queen and his taking of Waldrada. At her request, and with the king’s consent, our church obtained the royal estate called Hum [Note: [Col. 0557D] Perhaps Ham, south of Marchiennes.]. There were many buildings there, on account of which she stayed there for a long time, while the king visited her in an illicit union.

In the fourteenth year of his reign (868) [Note: [Col. 0557] Omitted in manuscript 2.], therefore, he ordered the revenues of our estates to be recorded; this document is called a *polyptych*. The record was made by the aforementioned Bishop John.

### 14

After this, when the brothers who ruled in the four divisions of France, together with their sons, had died, only Lord Charles remained. Good Pope John blessed him as emperor.

Just as he did for many other places, he both granted and restored many benefits to the monastery of Lobbes. He also appointed his son Carloman abbot of the same place (870).

### 15

Carloman was succeeded in the administration by Lord Franco in the time of Louis (885), the son of the aforementioned Emperor Charles [Note: [Col. 0557D] The author omits that, after Carloman was blinded in 873, Hugh was made abbot in 883; see the Lobbes Annals for 873.].

This Franco was of great nobility and trained in the pursuits of the palace; hence he acquired many things for our monastery. Some say that the monastery called Anthonium [Note: [Col. 0557D] Antoing on the Scheldt, in the diocese of Tournai.], then a house for girls and now for canons, became ours during his time. Others, however, attribute this to antiquity, although they say that it had previously been alienated and was recovered under him [Note: [Col. 0557] Omitted in manuscript 1.].

Thus, after Louis died in the fourth year of his reign, and with the Franks turning in different directions during an interregnum lasting eighteen years, while Conrad, Rudolf, Odo, and Robert ruled in the West [Note: [Col. 0557] Omitted in manuscript 1.], when Arnulf, king of the Noricans, was chosen king of southern France, the aforementioned Franco requested the abbey for the church of Liège (15 November 889) and obtained it with the consent of the brothers. An agreement was first made that half of the abbey should serve for the common use of the brothers laboring there under the rule, while the bishop should appropriate the other half to himself and to his retainers.

It was further added that all the demesne tithes [Note: [Col. 0557] Manuscript 1 reads “unbroken”; manuscript 2 “untithed.”] should be for the use of the poor and pilgrims at the monastery gate [Note: [Col. 0557] Omitted in manuscript 1], and that the annual memorial of King Carloman—of whom Arnulf was the son—should be observed each year, with the bishop preparing an appropriate banquet for that purpose [Note: [Col. 0557] *Obsonium*, corrected from *opsonium* in manuscript 2.].

We wish to insert the royal decree:

> In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Arnulf, king, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0557] The charter is missing from the manuscripts; see it in Miraeus, *Opera* I, 650, to be inserted into our collection of diplomas.]

### 16

Meanwhile, as the state of affairs tottered and the line of natural kings—who, as we said earlier, had always been regarded among the Franks as hereditary—failed, because the aforementioned Louis, whom they say did nothing on account of the brevity of his reign, had left his son Charles scarcely two years old [Note: [Col. 0557] So Dacherius; manuscript 2 apparently reads “one year,” while manuscript 1 is uncertain. [Col. 0558D] Compare Richer I.4.], a certain northern people [Note: [Col. 0557] “northern,” manuscript 1? 2.], of whom perhaps it was said, “From the north every evil shall be unfolded,” whom most call Northalbingians (*Northalbingi*) and others, more commonly, Northmen, engaged in piracy and attacked France in a new and previously unheard-of manner.

First occupying the seas, they then entered the mouths of the rivers that water France [Note: [Col. 0557] Omitted in manuscript 2.], sometimes holding their position and sometimes advancing. Wherever they saw no one resisting, they swept onward in whatever direction seemed good to them.

These Northmen entered France by the four most celebrated rivers—the Rhine and Scheldt from the east, the Seine and Loire from the west—and laid everything waste with fires [Note: [Col. 0557] “advancing,” 1? 2.] and plunder. They spared neither sex nor age, carried away captives, and even profaned the altars themselves with pagan hands.

Because of their fear, many bodies of saints and the best possessions were transported to safer places. But it was not necessary to carry our patrons farther away, since the neighboring fortress of Thuin [Note: [Col. 0558D] See Regino for 879.]—which was our own and extremely well fortified—had made it possible for those who flocked there to remain unharmed [Note: [Col. 0557] Omitted in manuscript 2.]. The distant estates, however, suffered great devastation and desolation.

Hysa is now the name of a river that in antiquity was called Hysara [Note: [Col. 0558D] The Oise.]. Lucan mentions it in this way in his *Civil War* [Note: [Col. 0558D] Book I, lines 399–401.]:

> These men left the shallows of the Hysara,  
> which, carried in its own current through so many waters,  
> flowed into a river of greater renown,  
> but did not carry its name into the sea.

For it flows into the Seine. The Northmen who traveled down it, although they ravaged everything in those regions, nevertheless raged most violently in the area occupied by those settled along the Scheldt, because the most welcome station for their ships—whether for wintering or for avoiding any danger of war—had made them remain there continually.
