Singulphi is the name of an estate. It belongs to our church, and there is a church there of Saint Ursmar and Saint Peter, in which at that time there was a community of twelve canons.

I remember having seen, along with many of our people, a man from those times. We did not inquire very carefully whether he was called by another name, but, apparently out of affection for his patron, he was called from childhood “*bruoderchin*” [Note: [Col. 0559D] German *Brüderchen*, “little brother.”], which we can render, though not very elegantly in Latin, as “little brother.” He testified that he himself had seen and known those men, and that their provost was called Sparnarius [Note: [Col. 0559] Manuscript 2 reads *Sponnarius*.].

That place was so destroyed by the Northmen that scarcely anything remained there except the ruins of its walls. Likewise, at this time the other estates of our church, which were more widely dispersed in Brabant, were exhausted and emptied.

### 17

With the peace of the church thus disturbed and the foundation of the kingdom laid in fear [Note: [Col. 0559] Manuscript 1: *firmamenti*.], the aforementioned bishop Franco, compelled to undertake wars that were just, so far as secular affairs were concerned, and truly necessary, summoned to himself a certain Reginerius, whom they call Longneck, a vigorous man experienced in military matters. Fighting frequently in battle, they were very rarely defeated and often emerged victorious.

The struggle did not cease until their king, Godefrid, worn down by the plague, was converted to the faith of Christ and baptized, and not long afterward killed. Then the peace of Christ was restored to the church (885) [Note: [Col. 0559] “the peace of Christ,” manuscript 2.].

After this, Bishop Franco, knowing that it was unlawful for anyone with bloodstained hands to handle holy things, sent Bericon, a cleric of Liège, and Theuter, a monk of Lobbes, to Rome. He asked and earnestly petitioned that they be ordained bishops to take his place [Note: [Col. 0559] “who would take his place,” manuscript 2.].

Once they had been made bishops, he entrusted his parish to their governance. He himself thereafter grew old in peace and leisure [Note: [Col. 0559] Corrected from *ocyio* to *ocio* in manuscript 2.], departing this life after having completed more than fifty years in the episcopate [Note: [Col. 0559] “having spent,” manuscript 2.].

### 18. (901)

Stephanus follows him, a man devoted to learning and, so far as the canons are concerned, zealous for religion. He rendered the Passion of blessed Lambert, arranged in an unpolished style [Note: Col. 0559: witnesses 1? and 2 read *impolitam* (“unpolished”)], more elegantly lucid [Note: Col. 0559D: Compare *Literary History* V, 170–172; Col. 0559: *divi* (“saint”) in witness 2], and composed from it the sweetest harmony of the melody that is widely celebrated [Col. 0559D].

He also produced a little book from many “flowers” culled from the divine books [Note: Col. 0559: *libris* (“books”) in witnesses 1 and 2?], in which he gathered, with useful commentary [Note: Col. 0559: witness 2 reads *utilis coto*; the reading of witness 1 is uncertain], the chapters for the several festivals of the year, together with collects and verses. In the preface to this little book he shows that he had been brought up from childhood at Mediomatricum, now called Metz [Col. 0560A]. For he sent the same little book to Robert, bishop of that see, to be read and approved.

Some people even in our own age have remembered this bishop. In his time, too, our church was dedicated by him, having been summoned for that purpose and joined by Dodilo, bishop of Cambrai. Which of them dedicated which part can readily be seen on the bases of the columns.

If anyone therefore asks about this new dedication, lest it perhaps have been repeated or performed earlier, we shall dispose of the matter briefly. We have already said above, if the prudent reader remembers, that the earlier church was built under Prince Pippin by Saint Ursmar [Note: Col. 0559: lacking in witnesses 1 and 2], and we recorded the day of its dedication as the fifth day before the Kalends of September [August 28] [Col. 0560D: Chapter 4].

As the abundance of resources increased through the generosity of kings and of other faithful people, that church seemed too small and inadequate to the nobility of the place; it was therefore demolished and utterly overthrown, and this present church, more elegant in form and appearance, was built. Constructed from columns gathered from every direction, together with their bases and architraves, and with all the other skills of stonecutters and masons, it is, in proportion to its size, incomparable with anything around it. Since it is proved, as they say, by eyewitness testimony, it is enough to have touched upon it here.

We do not know its author, whether he was that king or an abbot. If anyone reproaches antiquity for having kept silent about these matters, let him be angry with antiquity, not with us.

### 19.

After this man had died and been buried in the church of Saint Lambert (920), the church was again thrown into confusion over the appointment of a bishop [Note: Col. 0560D: Compare Flodoard’s *Annals*, year 920]. One party demanded Hilduinus, a cleric of that same church, as bishop, with Gislebert, duke of Lotharingia, favoring their cause [Note: Col. 0559: witnesses 1? and 2 read *faciente*, “bringing it about,” for *favente*, “favoring”; witness 2 omits *sibi*, “for them”], the duke who, treating royal majesty with contempt, had usurped the supreme power of the kingdom for himself. The other party sought Richarius, abbot of Prüm, requested by the gift and consent of King Charles [Note: Col. 0559: *Riccarium* corrected to *Richarium* in witness 2].

This Charles, after the interregnum of certain kings who had reigned between rulers, had been summoned and consecrated by Archbishop Fulco at Reims and restored to his paternal kingdom. Since various people in their respective regions despised this new arrangement, some, as is human nature, reconciled themselves to the new king in the hope of winning his favor; others, with hardened brow, ruled independently in their own principalities. Gislebert was one of these; at that time he governed the duchy of Lotharingia [Note: Col. 0559: witness 2 reads *gerebat* (“held”)].

At his command—or rather, under his extortion and pressure—Hilduinus was consecrated bishop by Hermann, archbishop of the see of Cologne, in a new and unprecedented manner, without the sanction of the king or of the nobles of the kingdom.

Therefore letters were sent by the clergy of the other party to the Apostolic See, complaining about these events [Note: Col. 0561: witnesses 1 and 2 read *conquirentes* (“complaining”)]. John was then presiding over the Apostolic Chair. By letters he ordered the consecrator, the consecrated man, and a third person designated by the authority of the king [Note: Col. 0561: witness 2 reads *ordinatorem et ordinatum et inscium regis*: “the ordainer, the ordained, and one appointed without the king’s knowledge”] to come to Rome.

Why say more? They came, while the archbishop was detained by illness. Hilduinus, by some maneuver unknown, evaded judgment [Note: Col. 0561: *Hylduinus* corrected to *Hilduinus* in witness 2]. When this became known, Richarius was acclaimed, chosen, brought forward, and ordained and consecrated bishop by the Supreme Pontiff himself [Note: Col. 0561: *pontifex* and *et* are lacking in witness 1]. He was given the sole archiepiscopal pallium of all his predecessors, and a horse was spread before him according to apostolic custom for his procession.

Thus he returned to Gaul with so great and distinguished a privilege (922), settled the dissension of the opposing party [Note: Col. 0561: witnesses 1 and 2 read *dirimit* (“settles”)], and alone took his seat in the episcopal authority of the church of Liège [Note: Col. 0561: witness 1 reads *Leodiensibus* (“the Liège people”); the printed text has *Leodiensi*].

There would be enough to say about him: how lovable he was to everyone, how generous, and how assiduous in adorning or constructing the furnishings and buildings of the church. He had been less cautious only with regard to monastic life [Note: Col. 0561: witness 2 and the later occurrences read *monasticam* (“monastic”)], and this is remarkable in one who, nourished from childhood on monastic milk, instructed by monastic rods, and trained in monastic observances, had been accustomed to them.

For under him everything among us was for sale. Indeed, an annual exchange—not of obedience, which is properly regular, but of offices—and the harsh purchase of those offices had drained away whatever was best among us; the remainder the crowd of parasites had gobbled up [Note: Col. 0561: witness 1 reads *abligaverat* (“had swept away”)]. But this bishop’s other good deeds and his civilized spirit had covered over this disgrace and had made him supreme among all peoples.

After he had spent twenty-two years in the episcopate [Note: Col. 0561: witness 2 reads *peregit* (“completed”)], he was buried and rests in the church of Saint Peter at Liège, which he himself built.

During these times the study of letters flourished among us. Those who devoted themselves to learning them were highly renowned: Scaminus [Note: Col. 0561: witness 1 reads *Squavinus*], Theoduinus, and the exceptionally perceptive Ratherius. Ratherius, favoring the party of Hilduinus, clung inseparably to him.

For Hilduinus, deprived of the bishopric of Liège [Note: Col. 0561: witness 2 reads *episcopatu* (“episcopate”)], had taken refuge with Hugh, king of Italy [Note: Col. 0561: witness 2 reads *quem confugerat* (“with whom he had taken refuge”)], and had earned the bishopric of Verona (928) through his service and stipendary allegiance. The king’s promise remained that, when an opportunity arose to promote him to higher office, Ratherius would be given to the people of Verona as their bishop (932, August).

How this was done, and how many adversities he endured in that episcopate, the reader will be able to learn better from his own writing, in the letter that he wrote to the Supreme Pontiff and universal pope [Note: Col. 0561D: John XII or Agapetus], complaining about such matters: “To the Supreme Pontiff, etc.” [Note: Col. 0561D: See Ratherius, *Works*, ed. Ballerini, p. 537].

### 20.

[Note: Col. 0561: In witness 2 this chapter is placed after the following one; but the sequence of abbots and the connection of the argument show that it ought to precede.]

In that exile in which Ratherius said that he had been placed (935), while the bishopric was vacant [Note: Col. 0561: lacking in witness 1], he published a book called the *Agonisticus* [Note: Col. 0561D: Edited from the Lobbes autograph in Martène, *Collection*, IX, 786–964; Ratherius, *Works*, p. 9; compare Liudprand III, 52]. He prefixed to it the following title [Note: Col. 0561: lacking in witnesses 1 and 2]:

> Meditations of the heart of a certain Ratherius, indeed bishop of Verona but monk of Lobbes, which, arranged in six sheets [Note: Col. 0561: I correct this from Ratherius, although manuscripts and editions read *digestis*], he judged should be called a volume of prefaces, entitled the *Agonisticus*.

He sent this book for reading or approval to the most learned men whom he knew: namely, to the archbishops Sobbo and Wido [Note: Col. 0561: witness 2 reads *Mucdoni*] [Note: Col. 0561D: of Vienne and Lyon], to the bishops Godescalcus [Note: Col. 0562D: perhaps of Ancyra] and Aurelius, and also to the most distinguished and highly learned in philosophical studies Bruno and Rotbert, archbishops of Gaul [Note: Col. 0562D: of Cologne and Trier], and finally to Flodoard of Reims, sending each of them letters preserved in the archives of our church (937) [Note: Col. 0561D: The letter to Wido, Sobbo, Godescalcus, and Aurelius was published by Martène, loc. cit., p. 965, and in Ratherius, *Works*, p. 525; others, to the archbishops Robert and Bruno, in *Works*, pp. 527, 529. The one addressed to Flodoard is missing].

He also found at Cumi a little book on the life of Saint Ursmar while he was an exile there (939). He corrected it, since it was full of solecisms, and sent it to us [Note: Col. 0562D: *Works*, p. 195].

Later, while he was staying in that part of Burgundy called Provence (940), he received, at the request of a certain very wealthy man, that man’s son, named Rocstagnius, in order to teach him letters. For him he composed a book on the art of grammar, which, in the customary manner of vernacular speech, he called *Sparadorsum* [Note: Col. 0562D: German *sparen* means “to preserve” or “to spare”; hence it was a book by which the boy’s back was spared. The work no longer appears to survive; compare Ratherius, *Works*, Preface, p. XIV], because the boy who was trained in it at school could preserve his back from blows [Note: Col. 0561: lacking in witness 2].

For these services a bishopric was given to him there [Note: Col. 0562D: Nothing is certain about this matter; the bishopric seems merely to have been offered to him; see *Life of Ratherius*, p. LVI]. He left it and returned to Lobbes [Note: Col. 0561: witness 1 reads *Jobiis*]. Richarius was still alive at that time (944) [Note: Col. 0561: lacking in witness 1]. He received Ratherius favorably and permitted him to reside at Lobbes. Not long afterward Richarius died [Note: Col. 0561: Dachery adds: “After he had completed twenty-two years in the episcopate, he was buried and rests in the church of Saint Peter, which he had built at Liège.”].

### 21. (945)

After him, Ogo [Note: Col. 0561: witness 2 reads *bugo*], abbot and monk of the monastery of Saint Maximinus at Trier [Note: Col. 0561: witness 2 reads *Maximi*], was appointed bishop. He died after scarcely two years had passed [Note: Col. 0562D: *exctis* is evidently corrupt; “completed” is intended] (947), leaving Farabert, likewise abbot of Prüm, as heir to his episcopate.

Again under him, as earlier under Richarius, everything among us was for sale, to such an extent that the same place was called “Silver Valley” by the parasites. Then that royal golden crown [Note: Col. 0563: witness 1 reads *argentea* (“silver”)], which had hitherto been most bitterly lamented [Note: Col. 0563: witness 1 reads *decorata* (“adorned”)], a work of extraordinary craftsmanship and considerable weight, was broken and squandered at will [Note: Col. 0563: witness 2 reads *libito*]; its gems were wondrously destroyed and removed from sight.

This was regarded as nothing, provided that the purchaser obtained the annual office. A man was called holier in proportion as he was more lavish in giving, and more useful in proportion as he was more ravenous [Note: Col. 0563: the editions read this way—“the more useless, the more truthful”; witness 1 reads “the last, the more truthful”; witness 2 reads “the worse, the more truthful”]. But these matters are no concern of ours; let the one who did it see to it himself [Note: Col. 0563: lacking in witness 2].

### 22.

At that time Otto, the most powerful southern king, also ruled over subjugated Italy. His brother Bruno [Note: Col. 0563D: Compare Ruotger, *Life of Bruno*, chapters 5–6] was destined to become the one unique and singular glory of Christ’s Church. Like a most precious stone, he shone with the many-sided arguments of the philosophers (952). Ratherius was summoned [Note: Col. 0563D: He had again been expelled from the see of Verona in 948] and was regarded as first among the palace philosophers.

Why say more? He did not cease until he had made that royal and wondrous talent exceptionally perceptive and complete in every discipline. Seeing this, the greatest of the kings of that time [Note: Col. 0563: witness 2 reads *suo tempore* (“of his time”)] summoned him from the schools with all the honor that was appropriate and enthroned him, amid universal acclamation and rejoicing, in the chair of the church of Cologne after Wicfrid [Note: Col. 0563: witnesses 1 and 2 read *Wifridum*], who had recently died.

How he lived there, how he taught, what he did, how he devoted himself for the peace of God’s churches; how diligent he was in enlarging or restoring churches [Note: Col. 0563: witness 2 reads *restituendis* (“restoring”)], in arranging private and public buildings, in organizing matters at home and in the field, and how solicitous he was for the affairs of God’s holy Church—these things are admirable in deed and praiseworthy in speech.

### 23. (953)

It happened at that time that the see of Liège became vacant when Farabert died. As a reward for his earlier teaching, Ratherius was installed there through Bruno’s great diligence [Note: Col. 0563D: With a few exceptions, this entire chapter is repeated from Ruotger, *Life of Bruno*, chapter 38].

Because of his abundant learning and rich eloquence, through which he seemed to flourish among the wisest [Note: Col. 0563: witness 2 reads *doctissimos* (“most learned”)], it was thought that his appointment would be highly beneficial not only to that church over which he presided [Note: Col. 0563: witness 1 or 2 reads *soli* (“alone”)], but also to many others in the surrounding regions.

At the same time, because in those parts certain priests of the Lord, through zeal and contention—the source from which instability and every evil work commonly arise—were scandalizing the unlearned people, often relying, which is disgraceful to say, more than was right upon earthly power, the aforementioned lord Bruno, who already had responsibility for administering the whole kingdom, judged that this man, previously expelled and neglected, could be drawn by so great a benefit into an alliance of faith and truth from which no one could seduce him. He believed that he could finally silence the mouths of his enemies if no occasion for scandal could be found in their bishop [Note: Col. 0563: witness 1 reads *iniqua* (“wicked”) instead of *inimica* (“hostile”)].

But the sinister party prevailed to its own ruin; whatever was done for their salvation they considered harmful to themselves. Why say more? Error was committed, violence was used [Note: Col. 0563: witness 1 reads *sed vitum*], and they did not stop until, by expelling him, they had satisfied their cruelty and wickedness.

All hope of his restoration was taken away (954, December 25). While he was celebrating the Nativity of the Lord among us with festivity and abundance, an extremely serious conspiracy was formed against him at Liège [Note: Col. 0563: witness 2 reads *est Leodii*]. It seemed impossible to calm it unless he were completely removed from there and Baldricus, who was descended from the lineage of the great men of that land, were substituted in the same place.

Countless storms from every direction converged upon this sewer [Note: Col. 0563: witnesses 1 and 2 read *sententiam* (“judgment”); the printed reading is *sentina*]. The ship of the Church, with its rower struggling, tossed upon the waves; the helmsman himself could not withstand the assault of the stormy weather. He therefore yielded—he yielded [Note: Col. 0563: the second *cessit* is lacking in witnesses 1 and 2]—so as not to be overcome by evil but to overcome evil with good; he yielded to the will of his opponents so that he might slaughter them with their own sword, to his own advantage.

They voluntarily bound themselves by the oath of their sacramental faith [Note: Col. 0563: witness 2 reads *spontanea* (“voluntary,” feminine)], promising that, if they deserved to receive the bishop they were requesting, they would thereafter defend the authority of the Church and the emperor’s right with unshakable firmness (955).

### 24. (957)

After Ratherius had spent nearly two years in this deprivation [Note: Col. 0563D: The Ballerini proved this to be false, Ratherius, *Works*, pp. CVI ff.; Ratherius did not return to Verona before 961], his military support failing him, he returned to Italy. So that nothing in such a matter might remain unfinished and trouble those inquisitive investigators of other people’s affairs [Note: Col. 0563: witness 1 reads *investigationibus* (“investigations”)], the aforementioned Bruno, together with his brother the emperor [Note: Col. 0563: witness 1 adds *ipso* (“the emperor himself”)], arranged that the ancient see of the church of Verona should be restored to him, who had already twice been deprived of it (961) [Note: Col. 0563: witness 2 reads *restitueretur* (“should be restored”)].

At the same time he wrote a book (955) which he called the *Frenesis* [Note: Col. 0564D: *Works*, p. 217], because, like a madman, he attacked Baldricus with excessive severity [Note: Col. 0563: witness 2 reads *abjiceretur* (“was cast out”); witness 1 reads *Brunonem* (“Bruno”); the printed text has *inveheretur* (“attacked”)]. He also wrote another called the *Perpendiculum* [Note: Col. 0564D: A work otherwise unknown], and yet another called the *Sirma* [Note: Col. 0564D: Or *Deliberative Conclusion*; see *Works*, p. 293], in which he attacks the same Baldricus, calling him his “usurper” [*pervasorem*; witness 2 reads *invasorem*, “invader”].

There is also a little book of his against the Anthropomorphites [Note: Col. 0565: corrected from *anthrophomorphitas* to *anthropomorphitas*] [Note: Col. 0565D: A sermon preached in Lent in 964 survives in *Works*, p. 581], who depict God—that is, the invisible Godhead itself—through the outlines of bodily members [Note: Col. 0565: witness 1 reads *depingit* (“depicts”)].

There are also his synodical letter to the priests of his diocese [Note: Col. 0565D: *Works*, p. 409], a conjectural account of his life [Note: Col. 0565D: ibid., p. 373], his itinerary while traveling to Rome [Note: Col. 0565D: ibid., p. 437], and very many sermons: on Easter, on the Lord’s Supper, on the Lord’s Ascension, on Pentecost, on the feasts of Saint Mary, and many others [Note: Col. 0565: witness 2 reads “on a feast” in the singular] [Note: Col. 0565D: *Works*, pp. 577–645; compare the same work, Preface, pp. VI ff.; *Archiv* VII, 868–870].

### 25.

[Note: Col. 0565: “At that time a certain people …” Witness 2 then continues with “We, in order to return from our digression to the subject,” omitting chapter 25. The same narrative appears in the *Book of the Miracles of Saint Ursmar*, chapter 1; the readings of witness 3 are indicated.]

A certain people inhabited the bank of the Danube (954) [Note: Col. 0565: witness 3 reads, “A certain people inhabiting the farther bank, a province which the ancients called Pannonia”].

The ancient inhabitants called the province in which they lived Pannonia; modern people call it Hungary. From there the Hungarians came to us, known more by the barbarism innate and natural to them than by their origin [Note: Col. 0565: witness 1 sometimes has *Hungari* rather than *Hungri*].

Under King Henry [Note: Col. 0565: witness 1 reads *Henrico*], their insatiable cruelty crossed the boundaries of the Moravians [Note: Col. 0565: witness 1 reads *Marahentium*], which shortly before they had impiously seized for themselves [Note: Col. 0565: Dachery reads *antea*, “earlier”], and devastated far and wide, with sword and fire, many provinces of his kingdom [Note: Col. 0565: the words “with sword and fire” are lacking in witness 1].

Later, under Otto, his son, a storm of dissension arose [Note: Col. 0566D: From Ruotger, *Life of Bruno*, chapter 10]. I think that Jesus was sleeping in the breasts of the watchmen keeping vigil before the doors of the Lord’s house, so that certain companions of Satan attempted to extinguish the king. When, through God’s mercy, this plan—conceived through the serpent’s hiss [Note: Col. 0565: witness 1 reads “through the hiss of the persecutors”]—was frustrated, they spread the poison of their wickedness throughout the inmost parts of his entire kingdom [Note: Col. 0565: lacking in witness 3].

The leader of this conspiracy was the king’s own son Liudolphus, a distinguished and uniquely illustrious young man who, if he had not believed the seducers [Note: Col. 0565: witness 1 repeats “if he had not believed the seducers”], and had preferred to be an heir (954), not a traitor [Note: Col. 0565: witness 3 reads “and had wished to be”]. With him was Cono, formerly a very powerful duke, as it were a kind of goad [Note: Col. 0566D: From Ruotger, chapter 18]. They had everything, so to speak, in their hands; by striving to have more, they brought about by every means that they would have nothing [Note: Col. 0565: witness 1 reads *habuerunt* (“they had”); witness 3 has “they brought about that they had nothing”].

These men summoned the Hungarians—the ancient plague mentioned above—to invade the kingdom divided against itself, judging that in this way the anxiety oppressing them might either be completely removed or at least somewhat diminished [Note: Col. 0565: lacking in witness 3].

On this occasion [Note: Col. 0566D: witness 3 reads “on this occasion, as we began to say”], that savage people of the Hungarians, bringing such barbarism as our land had never before experienced [Note: Col. 0565: witness 1 reads *barbariam*], enticed by perverse citizens [Note: Col. 0565: witness 1 reads *illata* (“inflicted”) rather than *illecta* (“enticed”)], crossed Germany and many provinces of Gaul, where long ago that noble people of the Franks had settled [Note: Col. 0565: witness 3 reads *insederat* (“had settled”)], and poured itself over the whole land to devastate everything with sword and fire.

The aforementioned Cono fought in this campaign with his followers [Note: Col. 0565: witness 3 reads “Cono, whom we mentioned, fought with his followers”]. But when they reached Maastricht, which the Meuse washes, he separated from them for some unknown reason [Note: Col. 0565: witness 1 reads *desivit* (“ceased”); witness 3 reads “by what faction he dissented from them”].

The Hungarians attacked Hasbaye with fire and plunder [Note: Col. 0565: witness 3 reads “with fire and booty”] and made for Carbonaria. When the news reached us, our community sent Brother Hubertus, a man patient of labor, fleeing from rest, and ready to spend himself for love of the place and of holy religion, to negotiate with them.

After an agreement had been made for two hundred solidi, he returned, having received hostages from them. But our people, not sufficiently trusting—for what trust can there be in the faithless?—attempted to fortify Tudinium, which Raginerus [Note: Col. 0565: witness 1 reads *Ragnerus*], suspecting the military forces of Liège, had previously destroyed [Note: Col. 0565: witness 3 reads “which Raginerus had destroyed not long before”]. But when soldiers were sent again [Note: Col. 0565: witness 3 reads “when the same man had again sent soldiers”], they were prevented from strengthening the fortification [Note: Col. 0565: witness 3 reads “from rebuilding it; God, as was later discovered, especially brought this about to show that they ought to place their hope of defense not in man but in Him and in the protection of His saints”].

What were they to do then, with the enemy threatening? Their hope of taking Tudinium had therefore been removed [Note: Col. 0565: witness 1 reads *potiendi* rather than *potiundi*; witness 3 adds “and the report of plundering and burning was growing more frequent”], and no confidence remained in military power. For that famous and celebrated Lotharingian army, praised throughout all ages, had been dulled by God’s just judgment at the arrival of the Hungarians and was shut up here and there within its own fortifications [Note: Col. 0565: witness 3 expands this to say that the military force, enclosed in its fortifications, had become dull and ineffective].

Our remaining band of monks, beloved of God, and the church’s own faithful militia climbed the mountain where the bodies of Saints Ursmar and Erminus are venerated [Note: Col. 0565: witness 3 reads “the mountain where Ursmar and Erminus are venerated, whose bodies are there”]. They had deliberated for a long time [Note: Col. 0565: lacking in witness 3], and, trusting in God’s help, surrounded it as a fortification with obstacles made from wagons, whatever branches they could find, and hedges [Note: Col. 0565: witness 1 reads *cingunt* (“they surround”)]. We believe that God brought this about to show that divine help is never lacking where human assistance ceases [Note: Col. 0565: lacking in witness 3; witness 3 expresses the same thought earlier in an expanded form].

The holy celebration of the Easter days had already arrived. At the completion of its octave, which was then the fourth day before the Nones of April [April 2] (Apr. 2) [Note: Col. 0567: lacking in witness 3], behold, at the beginning of morning, the air suddenly thickened with a fog of horses [Note: Col. 0567: witness 3 reads “suddenly”], and thousands of helmets emerged, as it were, from the hidden depths of the earth [Note: Col. 0567: witness 3 reads “from the concealed boundaries of the earth”; it also has “thousands of cuirasses and helmets”].

Our people were terrified and anticipated their own death [Note: Col. 0567: witness 3 reads “began to be terrified”]. Those who were more agile climbed what was, so to speak, an image of a fortification—or rather, through the intercession of God’s saints, a true fortification that was to come [Note: Col. 0567: witness 3 expands: “they climbed, I do not say a fortification, but something resembling a fortification—indeed, a true fortification”]. Those who were older or less able remained below in the monastery precincts [Note: Col. 0567: witness 3]. Those who had remained there were captured. The others were besieged [Note: Col. 0567: witness 3 says that there was no distance between the captured and the besieged except death; Theodulphus and Theumarus, who seemed the most distinguished among the captives, were beheaded in the sight of those watching, while the others were scourged and captured].

Two of the monks, Teutmarus and Theodulphus, were beheaded before the eyes of those who watched; the rest were reserved for captivity [Note: Col. 0567: witness 1 reads *captivi* (“as captives”)]. There was no distance between the besieged and the captured except that, according to a certain saying [Note: Col. 0567: witness 1 reads *quaedam* (“a certain thing”)], the death that is awaited is more grievous than the death that is inflicted.

Meanwhile the besieged were pressed hard, and no kind of weapon or engine was spared. Our people, on the other hand, because the matter concerned their lives, joined the help of the clergy to their own, and even with the assistance of the monks themselves [Note: Col. 0567: witness 3 reads *agmine* (“in a massed formation”)], strove with all their strength, although it is unlawful for this order to handle weapons [Note: Col. 0567: witness 3 adds “because the matter concerned their souls”].

The enemy were already breaking in. Some clung to one another in mutual embraces; many were preparing themselves for death, and many others were arranging their surrender [Note: Col. 0567: The editions contain an expanded passage absent from witnesses 1 and 2: “When matters had reached the point of utter despair, only this could be heard: ‘Lord, have mercy’ (*Kyrie eleison*) and ‘Saint Ursmar, help us,’ according to the custom of the people. When they feared an assault, when they clung to mutual kisses, and when many were arranging surrender …”].

Behold, through the consideration of merciful God [Note: Col. 0567: witness 3 reads *miserationis* (“mercy”)], two doves flew out from the inner sanctuary of the temple [Note: Col. 0567: witness 1 reads *abditis* (“hidden places”)], and by circling three times they enclosed the battle line of the besiegers.

After this there followed a very heavy rain [Note: Col. 0567: witness 3 reads “Immediately a very heavy rain followed”], which frustrated their native art of archery by slackening the tension of their bowstrings. Fear and terror also fell upon them so greatly [Note: Col. 0567: witness 3 reads “such panic and fear”] that they hastened their flight [Note: Col. 0567: witness 1 reads *fuge* (“of flight”)], and the princes themselves used whips [Note: Col. 0567: witness 3 reads *flagris* (“with scourges”)] against those who wished to remain.

They led away those whom they had captured for death [Note: Col. 0567: witness 3 reads “those whom they had captured below”]. The church of Saint Paul was burned, and the larger church was attacked but saved by God’s mercy [Note: Col. 0567: witness 3 adds that the church of Saint Paul and the cloister were consumed by fire, while the dormitory escaped unharmed and the monastery, though attacked, was saved by God’s mercy].

Another Theodulphus had partly transported the church’s treasure and its finest possessions to a certain fortification and had partly concealed them in the church itself [Note: Col. 0567: witness 3 reads “so that they would not be found, he had buried them in the church”]. It was later said, and is thought to be true, that the treasure was disclosed by a certain captive who had lost courage to endure suffering. For it was dug up and carried away.

Then everyone together vowed that the day would be a festival for themselves and their descendants. This is the celebration [Note: Col. 0567: witness 3 reads “the solemn observance which is still kept in our times”] entered in our martyrologies in these words:

> On the fourth day before the Nones of April [April 2], the commemoration of the merits of Ursmar and Erminus, by which the people of Lobbes were deemed worthy to be rescued from the siege of the Hungarians [Note: Col. 0567: witness 3 reads *Laubienses* (“the people of Lobbes”)].

Nor must it be left unsaid that all those who had been captured returned shortly afterward healthy and joyful (955) [Note: Col. 0567: witness 3 reads “all returned safe and joyful”; another witness reads “they returned”].

God did not allow the Hungarians to do this with impunity. For when the final day and unavoidable time was already near—when almighty God, favorable to the land of His people and avenging the blood of His servants, wished to repay vengeance upon their enemies [Note: Col. 0567: witness 3 reads “when God wished to repay vengeance upon their enemies”]—the exceedingly fierce pride of the Hungarian people again became excessively and utterly intolerable [Note: Col. 0567: lacking in witness 3], led astray, I think, by the success of the preceding year [Note: Col. 0567: witness 3 reads “by the success of the previous year”].

For, as it has been said most truthfully, “Before destruction the heart is exalted” (Proverbs 16:18) [Note: Col. 0567: witness 1 reads *exaltabatur* (“was exalted”)]. There all who practice iniquity fell [Note: Col. 0567: witness 3 adds “and there they fell”].

Peace in the royal assembly held at Arnstadt forestalled this impending distress. It was fully agreed upon and had already been confirmed in large part through the wisdom of our emperor and his brothers [Note: Col. 0568C: The author copies Ruotger word for word; Col. 0567: witness 1 reads *sapientia* (“wisdom”)]. And truly it became known among tribes and tongues that “God is not a God of dissension but of peace” (1 Corinthians 14:33), as though at its beginning He had worked salvation among His people [Note: Col. 0567: witness 3 reads “for this reason”].

The emperor’s spirit was stirred within him, since he had no time to gather an army [Note: Col. 0567: lacking in witness 3]. But he had confidence through Christ in God [Note: Col. 0567: witness 3 reads “in the Lord”], who is able to save with few as well as with many.

Cono was there, no longer a duke but a soldier, wholly, as was thought, converted to peace, which shortly before he had savagely attacked [Note: Col. 0567: witness 1 reads *expugnabat* (“had conquered” rather than “had attacked”)]. He subdued his limbs with sackcloth and, as is reported, entreated God with groans that, if such were His holy will [Note: Col. 0567: witness 3 reads “if His holy will so existed”], and victory were granted to our king (104) and his army, He might permit him to be slain by the impious men with whom he had previously joined himself wrongly, so that he might be freed forever from their company [Note: Col. 0567: witness 1 reads *non permitteret* (“might not permit”) rather than *permitteret*].

The emperor decreed a fast to be proclaimed [Note: Col. 0567: witness 1 reads *indici quippe sanxerat* (“he had indeed decreed that it be proclaimed”)] on the very vigil of Saint Laurence the Martyr. Through the saint’s intercession he asked God Himself to be a refuge for him and for his people.

The scope of the work undertaken does not permit an account of the war (104), begun at the first light of the holy festival and scarcely completed by evening twilight [Note: Col. 0569: The transmitted reading is *et propositum suscepti operis negat expedire*; witness 3 has “he urges that the war be brought to an end”; the printed reading appears to contain an editorial error]. By God’s merciful dispensation, and with Him fighting for His own, it ended sufficiently successfully [Note: Col. 0569: witness 1 reads *actum est* (“it was done”)]: with the pitiable death of Cono after the victory, the emperor’s most glorious triumph, the barbarian king himself and his dukes and princes taken captive, and trophies set up throughout the whole breadth of his kingdom as far as the frontiers of that people [Note: Col. 0569: witness 3 reads *in regni illius latitudinem* (“through the breadth of that kingdom”)].

All these things await the diligence of a work devoted to the praise and glory of almighty God [Note: Col. 0569: witness 3 reads “all these things await the diligence of the proper work, to the praise and glory of almighty God.”]

26. [Source cols. 0569B–0571B] To return from our digression to the subject, Baldric was presiding over the Church of Liège. He held his uncle Raginerus in the highest esteem, because the latter had greatly assisted him in attaining the episcopate. This Raginerus, after that remarkable liberation from the Hungarians, was the very first—and would that from now on he were the only one!—not to shrink from violating the church of Saint Ursmar.

[Note: [Col. 0569] Witness 2 reads *raginerium* for *Raginerum* and omits *ille* (“that man”). It corrects *Raginerius* to *Raginerus*; the same correction applies below.]

He was pursuing a certain Oduinus with hatred. Oduinus had sought refuge in the aforementioned church, wishing to draw some breath from arms, while his soldiers had been left behind in their positions.

[Note: [Col. 0569] Witness 2 reads *praenominatam confugerat* (“had fled to the previously named [church]”) for *praefatam confugium fecerat* (“had made refuge in the aforesaid [church]”).] Seizing the opportunity, Raginerus hastened there to force him out of the church. He dragged him, unarmed, from the very tombs of the saints, which happened at that time to be open, and beheaded him in the very courts before the entrance of the church.

Let it be that the man deserved to suffer this; but the suitability of the time and the holiness of the place ought to have been observed! As for the place, it had already been sufficiently demonstrated how dear it was to God, how generous in granting protection, and how avenging and severe toward violators. As for the suitability of the time, let him consider it who either reads or hears these things: they occurred during the vigils of All Saints, while Vespers was being celebrated.

Meanwhile Raginerus made a certain Erluinus his intimate associate. He was from the monastery of Gembloux, which a certain Wibertus, distinguished by the titles of worldly nobility, had built on his own property and in which he himself had truly converted from worldly military service. He had appointed Wibertus abbot there, to whom he, a poor man of Christ, regularly obeyed.

[Note: [Col. 0569] Witness 2 reads *gemblacensi* (“of Gembloux”) for *a Gemblaus*. In witness 2, *Wibertus* is lacking; the edition adds *Wibertus nomine* (“named Wibertus”) after *insignitus* (“distinguished”).]

This Erluinus, by constant flattery, fawned upon Raginerus, and gradually and increasingly aspired to the dignity of the abbey of Lobbes. Nor did he desist until, after Blitardus, a monk of that monastery, had been removed, he was advanced to the honor of provost—which at that time was regarded as the greater office—even though the brothers were unwilling.

[Note: [Col. 0569] Witness 2 reads *sedula* (“assiduous”) for *assidua* (“constant”), *dignitatem* (“dignity” or “rank”) for *ambitum* (“ambition” or “aspiration”), and *promoveretur* (“might be promoted”) for *proveheretur* (“might be advanced”).]

He was a man who placed little value on a lie and lacked nothing in cunning. If you looked to religious observance, nothing was outwardly more elevated than he; but if you looked to his voluntary and often self-invited involvement in worldly affairs, and to his indefatigable pursuit of them—something unbecoming in a monk—nothing was more contemptible than he. In speech itself he displayed such great variety that, when he began to speak, he seemed to weigh each word; and at the end, as a rhetorician skilled in cunning, he wove into his discourse many different stanzas of sophistry.

[Note: [Col. 0569] The reading after *quasi* is uncertain in the first witness; the second may read *quoque* (“also”). The second witness has *doctum* (“skilled”) for *doctus* (“learned”).]

Since, as has been said, he had been promoted against the will of the brothers, he was hated by their unanimity. One day, when the time of the vintage was approaching, the brothers were sitting together and discussing some sad matter—though I do not know what—and Erluinus came upon them. They punished him with such a beating of clubs that he was thought to be dead.

[Note: [Col. 0569] The second witness reads *fabulantibus* (“talking”) for *confabulantibus* (“conversing”), and *probably dying* for *thought to be dead*.]

When he sensed that they had gone away, he withdrew after a little while, panting, and fled for refuge to Bernardus, then the advocate. With his assistance he later departed for Ercliacum, where he drained and carried away as much of the wine as was found, and stored it in places convenient to himself.

[Note: [Col. 0569] The first witness has *erdiacum* for *Ercliacum*.]

He further asked Raginerus and Bishop Baldricus to celebrate the Nativity of the Lord at Lobbes, and he obtained this. It was then possible to see “the abomination standing where it ought not.” For the count remained with his wife in the church’s sanctuary, and the table on which the most sacred body of the Lord was consumed was turned into a place for the service of shoes and cups or bowls.

[Note: [Col. 0569] The second witness has *in qua* (“on which”) for *qua* (“which”), *sanctissimum* (“most holy”) for *sacratissimum* (“most sacred”), and *sumebatur* (“was being received”) for *absumebatur* (“was being consumed”); the first witness has *absumebat* (“was consuming”).]

When the celebration of the Christmas days had been completed and they had departed, the brothers lamented together that their own provisions had been diminished so that others might gorge themselves, as that most querulous class of men is accustomed to do. Taking courage, therefore, they went to Fontaines, a village watered by the Sambre. There they seized and carried away all the wine that was found—for Erluinus had concealed a portion there.

[Note: [Col. 0569] The first witness has *sibi* (“for themselves”) after *assumpta*; the second has *fontanos* for *Fontanas*. [Col. 0570] *Fontaine*: Fontaines.]

Erluinus had gone to Bermeriacum to sell the grain that was there, in payment of a debt for which he had pledged the aforementioned provisions. The brothers pursued him with a great multitude of people and raged against him so violently that it was astonishing that he escaped death.

[Note: [Col. 0569] The second witness reads *eum mortem evasisse* (“that he escaped death”).]

But after he had been promoted to the abbacy, he expelled everyone from the monastery except a few.

[Note: [Col. 0569] The editions add: “while always suspecting the brothers.”]

Those who were consequently more enraged—so as not to prolong the story—three of them, who surpassed the others through the aid of their youth and relatives, attacked the dormitory by night, at very great risk to their profession and order. They dragged him out and, after hauling him some distance from the cloister, deprived him of his eyes and also cut away part of his tongue, though not so far as to deprive him of speech.

[Note: [Col. 0569] The second witness reads *pertractum* (“dragged along”) for *protractum* (“hauled out”).]

And because, as he used to say, he desired martyrdom, he deceived himself: immediately afterward he was put on a boat, fearing another attack, and transported to Gembloux. What he ought previously to have foreseen while healthy, he avoided while weak and blind.

[Note: [Col. 0571] The second witness has *Gemblacum* for *Gemblaus*.]

And because, as it is written, “The wicked shall act wickedly, and none of the wicked shall understand” (Daniel 12:10), and elsewhere, “Let the one who is filthy be filthy still” (Revelation 22:11), after the aforementioned violation of the church of Saint Ursmar, Raginerus multiplied his tyranny, oppressed the poor, and made the property of the churches his own rather than God’s (958).

For all these things he was summoned before Lord Bruno, truly the peacemaker, at Saint Salvius. He confessed and, having been convicted and found guilty of injury to the royal majesty, was proscribed and condemned and deported into perpetual exile.

[Note: [Col. 0571] Saint-Sauve near Valenciennes. The first witness omits *laesae* (“injured”) and the second omits *regiae* (“royal”). The first witness omits *damnatus ac* (“condemned and”).]

Thus, although against his will, a great deal was done for his benefit. For the longer a wicked man persists, the heavier and more prolonged a punishment he prepares for himself.

[Note: [Col. 0571–0572] Concerning this, the author of the *Life of Gerard, Abbot of Brogne*, writes: “Henry was a brother of Otto, alike in name to his father but very different in character. For, at the prompting of the reprobate, he treacherously rebelled against his brother. And, to say something briefly about his other brother, Duke and Archbishop Bruno, whose memory is surely blessed, who could adequately match his virtues with worthy praise? Under his most astute administration, which cut out from the roots the barren shoots of the wicked—‘the blemishes of vice,’ according to the Wolfenbüttel manuscript, from which this text is edited—Lorraine flourished again like a fruitful tree, abounding in peace and justice, affirming that his protection had restored the golden little seasons of old. Evidence of this is Raginerus, count of the Hainaut people—‘of the inhabitants of Hainaut’ in that manuscript—widely known by the nickname Long-neck, who, because he tyrannically harassed his provincials and refused to repent, after being warned once and twice, remains to this day in exile in unknown regions, through the energetic action of this two-handed archbishop.”]

27. [Source cols. 0571C–0572A] Meanwhile, when Baldricus died (959), Lord Evracrus, dean of Bonn, was made bishop with Bruno’s permission. He was a man learned in the liberal arts. He appointed Lord Aletrannus—learned in every field, thoroughly trained in the law of God, and eloquent—abbot at Lobbes, with everyone’s consent (960). There he lived as befitted a servant of God.

[Note: [Col. 0571] The second witness reads “most thoroughly learned and most eloquent.”]

Before him, the brothers had been allowed impunity only in matters of personal property and dining rooms; thereafter they lived honestly and in common. Aletrannus, having been instructed in this way, corrected everything according to the Rule.

[Note: [Col. 0571] The second witness has *impunitate* (“with impunity”) for *impunitas* (“impunity”).]

To complete his work, Lord Evracrus restored to him estates that had previously been alienated: namely, Gimiacum, which a certain Folquinus had acquired for himself and his sons on a precarious tenure; Strata, which Adelardus held as a benefice; Gosiniacum, which Heribrandus likewise held on a precarious tenure; and several others.

[Note: [Col. 0571] The editions say that “Evracrus greatly helped him in this restoration.”]

Under him everything was noble, except that very large golden reliquary chests were stolen by night. Nothing of them was recovered except what was wooden.

[Note: [Col. 0571] The second witness reads “except whatever part of them was wooden.”]

There was also a small golden cross, which, after being broken under Erluinus, was given to Raginerus by the brothers as ransom for him.

[Note: [Col. 0571] The second witness reads “as his ransom.”]

After at last, though late, our church had obtained this long-desired peace, it was very quickly bereaved. For Lord Bruno, in whom supreme authority rested, died on the sixth day before the Ides of October (965). Lord Abbot Aletrannus, after being weakened by paralysis for two years and after he had presided for five years, died in great hope of future glory on the third day before the Nones of November, in the year nine hundred … of the Incarnation of the Lord.

[Note: [Col. 0571] The second witness reads: “After he had benefited for two years, he was freed from paralysis, and after he had begun to preside for five years.” The year-number is missing in both witnesses. The second witness calls him “Abbot Aletrannus.”]

28. [Source cols. 0572B–0573C] After this, Lord Evracrus appointed Folcuinus, truly a sinner and young in age, abbot of Lobbes. When the same bishop was at Cologne in the imperial presence, amid a great gathering of the people, he had him ordained there, after the brothers’ reading had first been recited and read. Thus he was ordained by Ingrannus, bishop of Cambrai, on the very day of the Nativity of the Lord (December 25).

[Note: [Col. 0571] Witness 2 reads *Eurarcus Fulcuinum* for *Evracrus Folcuinum*.]

Returning from there and taking possession of his office, he did many things according to his own judgment; and in many matters Fortune made the abbey serve her.

[Note: [Col. 0571] The phrase *unde ... fecit* (“whence ... he made”) is absent in the first witness.]

Ratherius was still at Verona. Weary of the insolence of the citizens, and at the same time suspicious of the innate and peculiar treachery of that people, he was considering returning. He proposed the saying that “one often lives well in a foreign homeland, but dies badly.”

[Note: [Col. 0571] The second witness has *insolentiam* (“insolence”) for *insolentia*.]

He therefore sent the abbot a book which he entitled *The Conflict of Two*, because in it he debated whether or not he should return and anxiously vacillated between the alternatives. At the same time he asked that horses and companions be sent to him, so that he might hasten his journey away from them more easily.

[Note: [Col. 0572] This book is found nowhere; compare Rath., *Cp.*, preface, p. XV.]

It was done: horses and companions were sent (968, July). He came, bringing with him not, I shall not say moderate quantities of gold and silver, but, to use his own words, masses and heaps.

[Note: [Col. 0571] The first witness has *modica* (“moderate”).]

With these he purchased from King Lothair the abbey of Saint-Amand. Having scarcely possessed it for one night, he abandoned it—for he was a man of remarkable fickleness—and returned to the estate of Alne, which he had obtained through the munificence of the lord bishop.

[Note: [Col. 0572] Aulne on the Sambre. The second witness reads: “He left it and returned to Alne.”]

From there, in a similar manner, he bought, for a large price, the monastery called Hautmont. There he gathered together whatever he possessed that was choice among ornaments and ecclesiastical vestments, as well as whatever he had previously given to our church but later reclaimed, after making a donation.

[Note: [Col. 0572] Hautmont, in the diocese of Cambrai. The first witness omits *et* (“and”) after *ornamentis*; the second has *quod* (“what”) for *quaeque* (“whatever”).]

Abandoning this place as well, he returned once more to Alne, after scarcely completing … .

[Note: [Col. 0571] The text reads only *peracto vix* (“after scarcely completing”) in both witnesses. The first witness has *ita* (“thus”).]

The abbot had also given him, with the consent of the brothers, the estates of Strata and Gosiniacum, the small abbey of Saint Ursmar, and another monastery called Waslare. But he always cursed our place and plotted against the abbot, with some people inciting him to this.

[Note: [Col. 0573] The second witness has *haec* (“these things”) for *hoc* (“this”).]

Why delay with many details? Matters came to such a pass that the abbot withdrew from the place, knowing that the bishop also wished this. For there is nothing else we need say about him.

Ratherius, to show the causes of his former enmity, invaded the place. Fearing the abbot’s courage and at the same time his kinship—which was not insignificant—he surrounded the cloister in the manner of a castle, with the assistance, as he said, of money left over from certain princes, which he had purchased for this purpose. He also willingly deprived himself, for this reason, of the church of Saint Dionysius, which he had bought from Count Robert at the fixed price of twenty pounds.

Nor did he pay any attention to what, how much, or to whom he should give anything for that purpose.

[Note: [Col. 0573] The second witness omits *ob id* (“for that reason”).]

What more is there to say? That year proceeded in this way until Bishop Evracrus died and Nothgerus succeeded him.

[Note: [Col. 0573] The first witness omits *donec defunctus est Evracrus episcopus* (“until Bishop Evracrus died”).]

If I continue to describe his gifts of mind and the sum of his virtues, since he is still alive, I shall seem to be flattering him.

[Note: [Col. 0573] Nothgerus died in 1008.]

One thing must certainly be said: he was a man into whom the Spirit of God had bestowed a singular gift of truth and faith.

Not wishing his beginnings to be regarded as trivial or hasty, he summoned the abbots—namely Werinfredus of Stavelot and Heribertus of Andage, together with some brothers—and first investigated the beginnings of the conspiracy. He weighed and examined the evidence he found, and only afterward used judgment on what had been examined.

When he saw that everything was frivolous, he reconciled the brothers to the abbot and restored the abbot himself.

[Note: [Col. 0573] The first witness reads *reconciliavit* (“he reconciled”) for *reconciliat*.]

Ratherius returned to Alne, where thereafter he lived reconciled with the abbot. Later, while staying for a time with the count at Namur, he died. His body was brought to us and, after solemn pontifical rites had been celebrated, was honorably buried in the church of Saint Ursmar, on the northern side.

[Note: [Col. 0573] Compare Einhard, *Life of Charlemagne*, chapter 18. Nothgerus died in 1008. The remainder of the chapter is missing in the first witness.]

29. [Source cols. 0573D–0575A] After, through the grace of God and Nothgerus’s agency, the firmest peace had been granted us, the lord bishop returned to Liège. He spent the remaining time renewing or decorating buildings and increasing ecclesiastical property.

For, to speak truthfully, no predecessor of his, so far as common opinion remembers, enriched the church of Liège with possessions or ennobled it with buildings more than he did. At that time, several buildings also grew up in our monastery, constructed at the bishop’s prompting and through the abbot’s work.

The refectory was begun from its foundations and, with God’s permission, completed quite elegantly. At its entrance he built a vestibule in which, through underground channels, he brought in a watercourse. The water, boiling upward, seemed to spring forth there. He prepared hollow chambers for this upper reservoir, which, filtering water through four openings into other chambers beneath, dripped out a sufficient supply for the brothers.

This refectory was consecrated by Lord Bishop Tiedo with candles, censers, and all the equipment with which a house is to be consecrated.

[Note: [Col. 0573] The first witness has *Nedo* for *Tiedo*.]

He reroofed the church of Saint Paul, which the Hungarians had burned, and attached to it a house for the sick. The cloister ambulatory—if it may be called that, since no other name now occurs to me—had previously consisted of nothing except the chapter house and a wooden building that covered the doorway of the former refectory, and which was annually roofed with shingles. But when they dried out, they served as fuel.

[Note: [Col. 0573] The second witness reads *dicendum* (“must be called”) for *nominandum* (“to be named”), and *nesciebat* (“did not cover”) in the first witness appears against the reading *vestiebat* (“covered”). The first witness has *scidulis* (“small split shingles”), the second *scedulis* (“boards”); the second has *vestiebatur* (“was covered”) for *operiebatur* (“was roofed”), and *deserviebant* (“served”) for *observiebant*.]

He enclosed this with stone and, after constructing a ceiling, covered it with boards fastened with iron nails.

[Note: [Col. 0573] The first witness has *assilibus* (“small boards”) for *asseribus* (“boards”).]

Since the church was already sufficiently elegant in itself, he took care to make it more elegant in its furnishings; he made what was beautiful most beautiful. Because there was no altar panel, he made one of silver. He painted the altar structure itself and its ceiling especially well.

[Note: [Col. 0573] The second witness has *optime* (“excellently”) for *apprime* (“especially well”).]

He also made the Gospel pulpit in such a way that there were four projecting half-seats, placed opposite one another on either side in the form of a cross. These were cast in bronze and, according to the artisan’s choice, chiseled in some places and gilded; their posts were silver-plated on every side. On the northern side they had a cast eagle, very beautifully gilded. At times it drew in its wings; at times, with its wings extended, it opened a spacious place for the book of the Gospels. Its neck, artfully twisted toward the sound as though at the artisan’s pleasure, was turned so as to hear. With live coals inserted, it emitted the fragrance of the incense placed above it.

[Note: [Col. 0573] The second witness has *sculpta* (“sculpted”) for *scalprata* (“chiseled”), *deargentatam* (“silver-plated”) for *deauratam* (“gilded”), and *libito* (“wish”) for *libitu* (“pleasure”). The first witness has *invisis* (“invisible”) for *immissis* (“inserted”); Dacherius adds “and turned back again.” [Col. 0574] A bronze eagle of this kind exists in the basilica at Aachen. 55.]

On the western side of the same ambo, facing the people, he made an altar in honor of the holy cross and all the saints. Before it he placed a silver panel, and above it he raised that life-giving image of the Lord, which he had previously commissioned a certain man, at great expense, to make for our lands, and which was still without equal.

[Note: [Col. 0573] The words concerning the image are absent in both witnesses.]

There is no time to speak of the remaining ecclesiastical ornamentation or of the multiplication of books in the library. It is enough to have touched on this much, and that only in excess of what is required.

[Note: [Col. 0573] The second witness reads *hoc tantum* (“only this much”).]

He also made a silver crown on which he wrote verses. He also made two larger bells, one of which, the largest, he gave to Saint Peter, and the other to Saint Ursmar.

[Note: [Col. 0573] Perhaps “dedicated” for *dedit* (“gave”).]

The following verses were inscribed on this one:

> At the command of Folcuinus, the hand of the craftsman  
> Daniel made me, to the praise of the Trinity.

On the other there was only this:

> Folcuinus, to God and to his patron, Saint Ursmar.

[Note: [Col. 0575] The second witness has *sanctissimo* (“most holy”) for *sancto* (“holy”).]

30. [Source cols. 0575B–0576A] The church across the Sambre, on the mountain that we call the Mountain of the Saints and the common people call the Beautiful Mountain, was begun in his time on the following occasion.

[Note: [Col. 0575] Witness 2 reads *Ecclesiam* for *Ecclesia*; witness 1, apparently reading the abbreviation *eccla.*, has a different construction after *Sambram*.]

At a certain time the earth was parched. Since the rains had been withheld and the burning sun scorched from above, the days of Elijah were feared. All the people and the entire province hastened to the aid familiar to them and repeatedly experienced by them, namely to Saint Ursmar, their patron, who was exceedingly accustomed in such anxieties to restore God’s grace.

[Note: [Col. 0575] The first witness has *timebant* (“they feared”) for *timebantur* (“were feared”). The third witness reads: “All the people and the entire province hastened to the aid familiar to them and often experienced, to the patron Saint Ursmar, accustomed in such anxieties to restore the grace of God.”]

They asked the abbot to order that the relics of the saints be brought out and carried around in the manner of litanies. The abbot reported the matter to the brothers. They praised the devotion of the people and told him that he ought to satisfy them.

[Note: [Col. 0575] The third witness has *permitteret* (“allow”) for *praeciperet* (“order”), and *deberi* (“that it ought to be satisfied”) for *debere* (“that he ought to satisfy them”).]

A general fast was therefore proclaimed and a day appointed. So great a multitude of people poured together that scarcely anyone had ever seen so many gathered in one place.

[Note: [Col. 0575] The third witness has *igitur* (“therefore”) for *ergo* (“therefore”); the first witness reads “a multitude so great that no one had ever seen it,” omitting *conglobatam* (“gathered together”).]

The bodies of the saints, arranged in biers, were brought forth, amid great mourning and mingled joy among the people. Since the crowd was so great that the breadth of any field, however wide, could scarcely contain it, and yet all were pressing forward with popular tumult to greet the bodies of the saints, they decided that the bodies should first be carried to those who were beyond the Sambre, to the aforementioned mountain and the place prepared there.

[Note: [Col. 0575] The third witness has *multo* (“much”) for *magno* (“great”). It expands the passage: “The multitude was so great that no field, however broad, could contain it; nevertheless everyone pressed forward with popular uproar to greet the bodies of the saints. Therefore they decided that the bodies should first be carried to those who were on the farther side of the Sambre.”]

There the people’s devotion was so great that it cannot be adequately described in writing. The church was marked out and begun from the expenses contributed by the people; when, or by whom, it is to be completed rests with God’s providence.

The relics were then brought back to this side as well, and here too the crowd was so great that people were pressed against one another. The Lord showed that this devotion of the people was pleasing to him through the merits of Saint Ursmar. For on that very day, although the sky had been perfectly clear, the air became clouded, and the sound of impending rain arose. The rain afterward poured down so abundantly that it was fully sufficient and made the year’s crops exceedingly fruitful.

[Note: [Col. 0575] The first witness has *perfluxit* (“flowed through”) for *profluxit* (“poured down”).]

And because we have given only a slight foretaste of the virtues of Saint Ursmar, and, as we proposed, have reached the dregs of our own time, God granting it, I should like to linger for a little while at the end of this little work over the miracles of the same father. For we too wish to fulfill what we promised, and thus pay the interest.

[Note: [Col. 0575] The third witness instead reads: “And because we have reached the end of our narrative, and now an opportunity has presented itself for us to give this slight foretaste of Ursmar’s virtues, I should like to linger somewhat more fully at the end of our little work over the miracles of his virtues, so that he who was the beginning may also be the book’s conclusion. Thus, mindful of our promise, we pay the interest, while also receiving it ourselves. We shall relate, therefore, not the many things that were either neglected or forgotten by our predecessors, but those which we ourselves saw or heard from those who saw them.” This material scarcely suits a book written on the miracles of Saint Ursmar.]

31. [Source cols. 0576B] There is an estate called Villa Relia, near us, and in it there is a memorial of Saint Ursmar.

[Note: [Col. 0575] *Vellereille*, identified by Henschenius.]

They say that the same man of God, while he was an exile in the world and frequently visited the king residing at the city of Lyptines, because the place lies beside the road, was accustomed to rest there. There, because of an excessive toothache—a sickness from which he suffered greatly—he had lost a tooth and buried it.

[Note: [Col. 0575] The first witness has the feminine *commoratam* for *commorantem* (“residing”).]

The place had been sacred to the church, but through the negligence of the townspeople the church had been destroyed. Only the neglected altar of the place remained.

[Note: [Col. 0575] The third witness reads: “Only the altar, and that neglected.”]

A certain blind man was there. It occurred to him to enclose the altar with branches, so that it would not be accessible to sheep or dogs. One day he went into the forest, led by a boy. As he drew a branch toward himself in order to trim it with a tool, in the very effort his eyes opened so completely that he could see clearly.

[Note: [Col. 0575] The first witness may read *copularet* (“join”) for *capularet* (“trim”). The third witness adds: “Made happier, he began to rebuild it from his modest means in repayment for the benefit, giving thanks to God, who had glorified Saint Ursmar wondrously through many miracles.” The order of what follows differs there.]

32. [Source cols. 0576C] There was an old woman among us who was supported sometimes by the monastery’s provisions and sometimes by the alms of the faithful. Her right hand was so contracted that the fingernails seemed to have pierced the palm of her hand.

[Note: [Col. 0575] The first witness has *perforare* (“to pierce”) for *perforasse* (“to have pierced”).]

One day, which was a Sunday and the third of the Lenten days, she stood in her usual place in the church of Saint Ursmar. During the celebration of Mass she suddenly trembled, and at once—because of the unexpected relief after the ailment’s long duration—the tendons of her fingers began to extend and her hand to return to its function.

[Note: [Col. 0575] The first witness has “because of the duration of the affliction,” with a corrupt form *diutuitatem*.]

When she noticed this, she filled the church with her cries. The church was full, and everyone followed. “Thanks be to God! Praises be to God!” they said together, no one remaining silent.

Someone ran to me, as I happened to be in the larger church, one after another bringing some new report. As though the matter had not already been announced, the rumor-bearer conveyed the joy by gestures.

We immediately went up to the church. We found her standing and trembling in amazement at the miracle, but healthy. We praised God, and so we departed.

[Note: [Col. 0575] The first witness has *obsequuntur* (“follow”) for *subsequuntur* (“follow afterward”).]

33. [Source cols. 0577A–0577C] A certain woman possessed by a demon was brought by her parents to the tomb of the holy man—dragged rather than led. Chains restrained her feet, hands, and neck. Through her throat and tongue alone she uttered horrible and foul things.

[Note: [Col. 0577] The first witness omits “to the tomb of the holy man.” The third witness has *arctabant* (“bound tightly”) for *arcebant* (“restrained”), and *promebat* (“brought forth”) for *proferebat* (“uttered”). Dacherius follows the latter reading.]

At times one could hear a barking dog, the hissing of serpents, and the bellowing of bulls, as though in a single den there were various monstrous beasts.

[Note: [Col. 0577] The third witness reads “the bark of a dog.”]

It was the feast day of the same father, and more people than usual had gathered for the celebration. She lay there uttering such terrifying sounds that on so solemn a day the Mass could scarcely be heard.

[Note: [Col. 0577] The third witness has *festivitatis* (“of the feast”) for *festivus* (“festive”), and *convenerat* or *coierant* (“had come together”) for *convenerant* (“had gathered”). Dacherius reads *coierant*.]

When the feast was finished and the following day had dawned, the brothers, sympathizing with her, went to the church of Saint Ursmar to pray to the Lord for her deliverance. They resolved to perform a prostrate litany, whose recitation was assigned to me.

When, after the invocation of all the saints, we reached the place, I ought to have said, “By your coming, deliver us, O Lord”; but, terrified by her cries, I anticipated this by saying, “By your birth.”

[Note: [Col. 0577] The third witness has *omnium nominum* (“of all the names”) for *omnium sanctorum* (“of all the saints”).]

Then she—or rather he by whom the wretched woman was tormented—said: “You are lying, and you are speaking out of order.” I was frightened, I confess, and almost beside myself. But when I recovered myself, I continued the litany and began silently to reflect that this same apostate spirit, tortured by God’s judgment, had then also spoken truly, compelled and unwilling.

Because of our sins, nothing was accomplished at that time. Her despairing parents therefore tried to take her back. But when they reached the Sambre, one of them, looking toward the church in the middle of the bridge, said: “Ah, Saint Ursmar, does it please you that we should return from you so sadly, frustrated after seeking health from you from so far away?”

[Note: [Col. 0577] The first witness omits *ut* (“that”). The third witness has *abeamus* (“we may go away”) for *redeamus* (“we may return”), and *longinque* (“from afar”) for *de longinquo* (“from far away”).]

He had scarcely finished speaking when she suddenly collapsed at that very spot in the middle of the bridge and lay there for a while, looking very much like a dead woman.

[Note: [Col. 0577] The first witness has *similima* (“very similar”) for *simillima* (“very much like”).]

What more is there to say? Through God’s mercy and the merits of Saint Ursmar, after a short while she sat up. She asked what had happened around her, took food, was healed of every affliction, escaped the disease, and afterward carried her own miracle everywhere.

34. [Source cols. 0577D] Recently another man possessed by a demon was likewise brought to the aforementioned shrine. While we were occupied with other matters, the church clerics themselves attempted to rebuke him; they immersed him in consecrated water and exorcised him according to the custom of exorcists.

[Note: [Col. 0577] The third witness reads “and, having immersed him in consecrated water, exorcised him.”]

But while he was in the hands of the exorcists, he was suddenly snatched upward, so that he could scarcely be held by his feet; with considerable effort he was brought down again.

[Note: [Col. 0577] The third witness has “was lowered” for “was brought down.”]

Nevertheless, as the clerics persisted in prayer and rebuke, he too was healed, to the praise of God, through the merits of Saint Ursmar.

35. [Source cols. 0578A–0578B] There was a certain Adso in the service of my brother Godescalcus, practicing the shoemaker’s trade. We all knew him as crippled from childhood, so that he could go nowhere except with crutches.

[Note: [Col. 0577] Dacherius numbers this chapter XXXVII. The third witness has *Atho* for *Adso*, and *sutoriam* (“the cobbler’s trade”) for *calciamentoriam* (“the shoemaker’s trade”). The first witness omits “my brother Godescalcus” and has *agentis* (“of one practicing”) for *agens* (“practicing”).]

One day he came to the tomb of Saint Ursmar to fulfill his vows, bringing wax offerings with him, namely two candles. He asked the sacristan to allow him to spend the night there. The sacristan consented, and he spent the night.

[Note: [Col. 0577] The first witness has *solviturus* (“about to pay”) for *soluturus* (“about to fulfill”).]

At midnight, while he was praying and awaiting God’s power, his contracted shins began to straighten and his legs to separate from the long adhesion of his buttocks, not without great discomfort to the sufferer, until he stood fully upright on his feet while the custodians looked on in amazement.

[Note: [Col. 0577] The first witness has the corrupt *duiciva* for *diutina* (“long-lasting”).]

But because of the excessive pain and his unfamiliarity with the practice of walking, he could not walk.

[Note: [Col. 0577] The third witness has *indissuetum* (“unaccustomed”) for *inconsuetum* (“unfamiliar”).]

In his excessive rejoicing he seemed, in a certain sense, to have shown himself ungrateful: without anyone knowing, he left the church in the morning, and even failed to offer praises to God. Once he was entirely free from pain, he joined himself as a follower to the rebellion of Raginerus.

[Note: [Col. 0577] The first witness has *regerianae* and the third *ragenerianae* for *Raginerianae*, “Raginerian.”]

36. [Source cols. 0578C] Abbot Aletramnus, as we have said, suffered from paralysis (974). A certain blind woman was supported by the alms of that Fredesindis who had married Stephen, to whom Brebona was in service.

[Note: [Col. 0577] Dacherius numbers this chapter XXXVIII. The third witness has *Tredesendis* and Dacherius *Fredesendis* for *Fredesindis*.]

One day she came to the shrine of Saint Ursmar for the sake of prayer. As she herself climbed the mountain on which the church stands, at the gap marked off by an ancient oak, she perceived, from within the sanctuary of the church, a little light trembling toward her as though through very narrow cracks.

[Note: [Col. 0577] The first witness has a corrupt and expanded reading: “At the gap which the ancient oak separates, as though something were gradually cutting away her blindness, she began ...” The third witness reads: “As she proceeded from the sanctuary of the temple, she perceived some light, as if it were trembling toward her through very narrow cracks.”]

When at last she proceeded to the tomb of our holy father, she was so astonished at the sight that, when the provost Gosbertus announced it, the event gave occasion for the greatest joy and most splendid praise of God.

[Note: [Col. 0577] The first witness omits “of our holy father.” The third witness has *Cozbertus* for *Gosbertus*.]

This happened on the Friday before the Sunday they call Mid-Sunday.

37. [Source cols. 0578C] In the territory of Wilare, which served us, there was also a certain tenant farmer. While the other tenants were willingly carrying stones for the construction of the church across the Sambre mentioned above, he mocked them and swore that he would in no way undertake that service.

[Note: [Col. 0577] Dacherius numbers this chapter XXXIX. The third witness has *Villare* for *Wilare*, and Henschenius identifies it as a parish between Lobbes and Binche. The first witness has *fui* (“I was”) for *fuit* (“there was”); the third has *fuit nuper* (“there was recently”). The third witness has *diceret* (“said”) for *dejeraret* (“swore”).]

Suddenly he was weakened in the function of all his limbs. But when, although late, he recognized his guilt, he multiplied his vows and was immediately restored to health. He labored more than the others, kindling the rest and exerting whatever ardor of devotion he could.

[Note: [Col. 0577] The first witness has *qua* (“with which”) for *quo* (“with whatever”).]

38. [Source cols. 0578D–0579A] It was the Kalends of August, a solemn day among us because of the commemoration of Saint Peter’s chains. The Sambre had perhaps then risen higher than usual, and the people were streaming together and hurrying to the feast.

While the Masses were being celebrated, and the people from across the Sambre were hastening in a crowd to attend them, the bridge they had crossed collapsed under the weight of the multitude. The riverbed carried far downstream those whom it had received and submerged.

[Note: [Col. 0577] Dacherius numbers this chapter XL. The first witness has *multitudinem* (“the multitude”) for *multitudine* (“under the weight of the multitude”) and *accepera* (“had received”) for *acceperat* (“had received”).]

A great cry arose, and the church was thrown into confusion. Almost everyone went out, anxiously seeking only the corpses. But through God’s wondrous power, they encountered all those companies of submerged people safe and joyful.

Let anyone say here what he wishes; we attribute this deliverance to God, whose proper and singular work it is everywhere to magnify his saints and, through their merits, to raise up those who trust in them by the works of his mercy in their dangers.

[Note: [Col. 0579] The first witness has *fidentibus* (“to those trusting”) for *fidentis* (“those who trust”), and the third witness reads “by their aid” for “through their merits.”]

## Complete source apparatus

The entries below follow the supplied source exactly. Each records the nearby Latin lemma, the printed form and witnesses, and its English meaning.
