- **N026, Col. 0571C, after `domno Brunone vere pacifico apud sanctum Salvium`.** Printed note: `S. Sauve apud Valentianas.` English: Saint-Sauve near Valenciennes.
- **N027, Col. 0571, after `apud sanctum Salvium evocatus, confessus, et laesae`.** Printed note: `deest 1.` English: The lemma is absent from witness 1.
- **N028, Col. 0571, after `sanctum Salvium evocatus, confessus, et laesae regiae`.** Printed note: `deest 2.` English: The lemma is absent from witness 2.
- **N029, Col. 0571, after `proscriptus est, ac perpetuo exilio [damnatus ac`.** Printed note: `d. ac desunt 1.` English: The words abbreviated *d. ac* are absent from witness 1.
- **N030, Col. 0571D, after `eo sibi graviorem et longinquiorem comparat poenam`.** Printed note: `De ac re scribit auctor Vitae Gerardi Broniensis abbatis: «Fuit Ottoni frater Heinricus, patri quidem equivocus, sed longe distans moribus. Instinctu enim reproborum fratri rebellavit infidus. Et ut mentio fiat quantulumcumque de altero fratre ejus, duce atque archiepiscopo Brunone, cujus nimirum memoria est in benedictione, quisnam queat condigna relatione virtutes ejus equiperare? Sub cujus procuratione sagacissima, radicitus amputante improborum spuria vitulamina [ [Col. 0571D] Vitii lamina, cod. Guelferbyt, unde haec edimus.] tanquam arbor fructifera refloruit Lotharingia pacis et justiciae habundantia, [Col. 0572D] asseverans ejus tutamina revexisse aurea quondam tempuscula. Cujus rei indicio est Raginerus comes Hainnoensium [ [Col. 0572D] Hauinoensium, id.] haut ignotus, cognomento Longicollus, qui, quia tyrannice suis inportunabatur provincialibus, et noluit resipiscere, semel et secundo commonitus, nunc usque exulat in ignotis regionibus, procurante industria ambidextri archipraesulis hujus.»` English: On this matter the author of the *Life of Gerard, Abbot of Brogne*, writes: “Otto had a brother Henry, bearing his father’s name but very different in character. At the prompting of reprobate men he faithlessly rebelled against his brother. To mention, however briefly, Otto’s other brother, Duke and Archbishop Bruno, whose memory is blessed: who could adequately recount virtues equal to his? Under Bruno’s most sagacious administration, which cut away the bastard shoots of wicked men at the root [the Wolfenbüttel manuscript, from which this is printed, reads ‘plates of vice’], Lorraine flourished again like a fruitful tree in abundant peace and justice, affirming that his protection had restored a former golden age. Evidence is Raginer, count of Hainaut, surnamed Long-neck, well known because he tyrannically oppressed his provincials and refused to repent after first and second warning; through the resourcefulness of this ambidextrous archbishop he remains exiled in unknown regions.”

### 39

[Note: [Col. 0579] XLI. Dach.] Gislabert, one of the four sons of Count Robert, had recently [Note: [Col. 0579] *deest* (“is absent”) in 1.] come to lodge with us, together with the others who had accompanied Countess Matilda [Col. 0579D] [Note: Wife of Reginar IV, count of Hainaut. It is not sufficiently clear whether Robert was the same as Rasbod, count of Namur, and maternal great-grandson of Reginar I. HENSCH.] [Note: [Col. 0579] *stupraverat* (“had violated”) in 1.] [Col. 0579B]. While dining, he began to disparage the monastic order as though it were insufficiently lavish [Note: [Col. 0579] *profusum* or *improvisum* (“unexpected”) in 1.], although, given the circumstances, sufficient provisions were being supplied to them, since he and his companions had arrived unexpectedly.

When morning came, the knight rode up the mountain to pray [Note: [Col. 0579] *scandens in populo* (“ascending among the people”) in 1.]. But at the very crossing of the steps by which one ascends to the upper monastery, the horse slipped beneath him and, though repeatedly beaten with spurs, could not be made to rise. They thought that, as often happens, the horse was being overcome by illness. The attempt was made a second and a third time; without doubt the four-footed animal lay motionless. His friends and companions—especially our advocate Boso [Note: [Col. 0579] *ab ofo* in 1.]—persuaded him that, if, as his conscience testified, he had perhaps committed some transgression [Note: [Col. 0579] *transgressorie* (“of a transgression”) in 3.], he should make a vow and satisfy God and His Church, and do so as soon as he could [Note: [Col. 0579] *possit* (“could”) in 1.]. He promised. When he descended, he found the horse indeed sound, but he could not ride it except down the mountain.

### 40

[Note: [Col. 0579] This chapter is absent in Dach.; in 3 it is read above, joined with chapter 32.]

Brother Robert, in our time the sacristan of the church of Saint Ursmar [Note: [Col. 0579] *editus* (“published”) in 1.], fashioned from silver a crooked staff, which many call a *tambuca* [Note: [Col. 0579] *cambutta* in 3.], while others call it a *petaculum* [Note: [Col. 0579] *petalum* in 3.], as something portable and proper to Saint Ursmar. He asked us to insert into that staff a small portion of the saint’s body, for the greater veneration of the people.

We did what he had requested. After searching for and taking two teeth from the ashes of the most holy body in the tomb [Note: [Col. 0579] *de* (“from”) in 3.], we inserted them into the staff. When it had been carried from the lower monastery to the upper one, an old woman was standing at the entrance. She was sometimes supported by the resources of the church and sometimes by the alms of the faithful. The Masses were then being celebrated in the church—it was the third Sunday of the Lenten season—and she suddenly began to tremble [Note: [Col. 0580D] Compare above, chapter 32.].

### 41

[Note: [Col. 0579] XLII. Dach.] Such extraordinary wonders are performed by God through the intervention of this blessed father not only at the place of his repose, but many others worthy of wonder have very often been displayed [Note: [Col. 0579] *plura* (“more”) in 3 and Dach.] in places dedicated to his memory at a distance.

Tudinium, a castle adjoining us, contained a place sacred to the memory of Saint Ursmar. At a certain time, namely on the night of the Lord’s Supper, as we heard our advocate Boso [Note: [Col. 0579] “our advocate” in 3.] report, when, according to customary practice, the lamps were extinguished during the nocturnal office, and, after the hymn of the Gospel had ended, those standing in the church prostrated themselves on the ground [Note: [Col. 0579] *terra* (“earth”) in 1; *prosternuntur* (“are prostrated”) in 1.], three drops fell from the top of the roof onto the pavement, in the manner of the drops we see dripping and burning from pork fat. They seemed to some to be setting the church on fire, and to others to be illuminating it.

Although everyone saw this, it appeared to a certain Tietberga [Note: [Col. 0579] *Tiberga* in 1.], a most noble matron who was engaged in prayer [Note: [Col. 0579] “prostrate there” in 3 and Dach.], to drip nearer to her and almost upon the back of her head [Note: [Col. 0579] *birre* in 1.]. Why this happened is unknown to us; yet, since we read that nothing occurs on earth without a cause [Note: [Col. 0579] *legitimus* in 1.], there is no doubt that this too had a reason.

The sacred character of the number three is clear to Catholics [Note: [Col. 0579] *siquidem* (“indeed”) in 3 and Dach.]. Every orthodox person understands that God is fire—not fictitiously, as poets call Vulcan fire, but truly, as the Apostle understood: both from his words, “Our God is a consuming fire” (Hebrews 12:23), and from the fact [Note: [Col. 0579] *quoniam vero* (“but because”) in 1.] that the Holy Spirit, true God in the perfect Trinity, descended upon the apostles in tongues of fire [Note: [Col. 0579] *domini* in 1, an abbreviation for *deum*; *dominum* (“the Lord”) in 3.]. Whether, then, the Holy Trinity produced this threefold [Note: [Col. 0579] *trinam* (“threefold”) in 1.] fiery dripping in order to approve the devotion [Note: [Col. 0579] *approbandam devotionem* (“devotion to be approved”) in 1.] of one of those standing there—devotion which the same Trinity had perhaps then kindled [Note: [Col. 0579] *ignoraverat* (“had not known”) in 1.]—so that it might outwardly show what it was doing inwardly [Note: [Col. 0579] *deest* (“is absent”) in 1.], or rather to commend the patronage of the saints, which is more credible, since the people were devoutly frequenting that place, is hidden from us [Note: [Col. 0579] *nos* (“us”) in 3.]. But it is certainly evident to Him who foresees everything that must be done and governs and directs what has been done [Note: [Col. 0579] *praevidit* (“foresaw”) in 1.].

### 42

[Note: [Col. 0579] XLIII. Dach.] Overcome and weakened by the magnitude, or enormity, of the work we have undertaken [Note: [Col. 0579] *evicti* (“conquered”) in 3 and Dach.], we shall omit many things. We shall mention only this final matter, proclaimed by everyone and known to many from their own experience: no one who ever inflicted harm upon that church is said to have rejoiced for a year.

If, as commonly happens, the monks of the greater monastery—which is the lower one—climb the mountain of Saint Ursmar to make a complaint about harm unjustly inflicted by someone [Note: [Col. 0579] *quibuslibet* (“by any persons”) in 1.], it is believed—and the hope is not empty—that the wrong will never go unpunished. Many have experienced this, and, though late, have groaned over it. Surely he protects by his merits the place which he ruled while living in the body, now reigning with Christ and rejoicing in Him.

### 43

[Note: [Col. 0581] These chapters are placed above chapters 35 and 36 in Dach.; in 3, however, they are read before chapter 24.]

There was a priest named Osingerus [Note: [Col. 0581] “and he still survives here” in 3.] who was so disabled by paralysis that his neck sprang back at the joint [Note: [Col. 0581] *resileret* in 1.]. What more can I say? He could not speak, and the functions of all his limbs had failed, while only his breath continued to labor. Having completed a year in this condition, he was supported by the assistance of another and by the alms of the faithful.

He lay in a village called Fleon, near which was that attendant chapel of the birthplace of Saint Ursmar [Note: [Col. 0581] *vicinia* in 1?; the words “of Saint Ursmar” are absent in 1.]. There stood a little wooden church, which they say he had joined together with his own hands and dedicated on his estate [Col. 0581B]. One day, when some people were traveling with wagons to Augusta Viromandorum to trade [Note: [Col. 0581B] Saint-Quentin.], he asked as best he could that he might be placed on a wagon and taken to the little church mentioned above.

This was done. He was placed in the church [Note: [Col. 0581] *ecclesiola* (“little church”) in 3 and Dach.] and spent the night there. When morning came, trusting in God’s mercy and the intercession of Saint Ursmar, he wished to test whether, raised up, he could sit upright on that very bed by himself [Col. 0582A]. He did so and marveled at what had happened. Then, gradually recovering life, and with strength returning to his limbs [Note: [Col. 0581] “with his limbs reviving, he astonishingly raised himself upright” in 3 and Dach.], he stood up and walked, giving thanks to God and to his patron.

Afterward we made use of his frequent celebration of Masses in that same place [Note: [Col. 0581] *fruiti* (“enjoyed”) in 3 and Dach.]. He himself remained healthy thereafter, except that the neck which had sprung back [Note: [Col. 0581] *reselierat* in 1.] appeared slightly twisted—perhaps, I think, to make known to everyone, as far as possible, the memory of so miraculous a benefit, and to show how powerful the merit of God’s saint is in the presence of the Lord.

### 44

The same priest reported to us that [Note: [Col. 0581] *quia dum* (“because, while”) in 3.] one day, in that very church, which he served in recompense for the benefit already mentioned [Note: [Col. 0581] The words “in recompense for the benefit already mentioned” are absent in 1.], while [Note: [Col. 0581] *dum* (“while”) is absent in 3.] he was celebrating Mass, after the Gospel had been read, he poured into the chalice the vessel that customarily hung beside the altar with wine in it. But the wine was so thoroughly frozen that not even a drop flowed.

He handed the vessel to the cleric assisting him, so that he might melt the ice by the fire. Meanwhile he himself continued the service. While the cleric was delayed, he looked toward the chalice, which was found full of wine, so full that it almost overflowed.

## In the Year of Our Lord 991: Erkenbald, Bishop of Strasbourg

[Col. 0581]

### Historical Notice Concerning Erkenbald

*(Gallia Christiana)*

[Col. 0581C] From childhood Erkenbald was exceptionally well educated in the liberal arts and was always devoted to books. Accordingly, having been promoted to the bishopric of Strasbourg in 965, as his merits required, and having, as we said, already been his predecessor’s coadjutor, he was consecrated by William, archbishop of Mainz. Thereafter he himself consecrated seventeen bishops, among whom are counted the two archbishops of Mainz, Hatto and Rupert.

In 966 he consecrated a church at Altorf. Pope John XIII praises him highly in a letter in which he promises him the protection of the Apostolic See in all matters. He was held in no less esteem by the emperor Otto II, from whom, in the seventeenth year of his administration, he obtained a notable privilege, issued in 982, in the tenth indiction, on the eighth day before the Ides of January, in the fifteenth year of Otto’s empire and the twenty-fifth of his reign. R. P. Laguille reproduces it in the *Probationes historiae Alsatiae*, p. 23.

Erkenbald died in 991, on the sixth day before the Ides of October, according to the Saxon chronicle in Ekkehard, p. 363, and, according to the Fulda Necrology, as the recently cited author Nuperus states. He composed, in verse, the lives of many of his predecessors, and collected that work, together with books gathered from everywhere, in the library of his church.

[Col. 0583]

## Erkenbald’s Sigh

Or a Soliloquy and Prayer to God, Which He Used Whenever He Heard People Singing in Churches

*(G)*

[Col. 0583A] Lord, You who are the possession of all who strive to belong to You; whom everyone who knows loves, and whom whoever does not know does not love—and whoever does not love does not know: grant me not to know myself, but to know and love You.

I would like, Lord, to know what is meant by “Let the heavens rejoice, and let the earth exult,” and what follows. What else does “let the heavens rejoice” mean except “let the righteous exult”? It is written: “Rejoice in the Lord and exult, you righteous.” Let the righteous rejoice; let the unrighteous weep.

What about me? Do I rejoice, or do I weep? I do not rejoice, because I am not heaven. If I were heaven, I would rejoice. But when I cast myself down, tear myself apart, and reduce myself to nothing—“for Your arrows are fixed in me”—You raise me up, console me, and say: “Let the earth exult.” I give thanks. I know that I am earth; but You can make heaven.

It is enough for me: You said, “Let the earth exult,” and “Let the heavens rejoice.” You added “and let the earth exult”; You gladdened the heavens and consoled the earth. I said, “I do not rejoice.” As a sinner I said this; I spoke of what was mine. But of what is Yours You say, “Let the earth exult.” Since You have gladdened what is Yours, I shall deny what is mine and exult. Let me exult in You, because of You, and rejoice in You. You Yourself know whether it is mine.

What do You know? When I recognize myself, I groan or weep; when I recognize You, I recover my senses and breathe again. What is mine saddens, disturbs, and agitates me; what is Yours consoles, steadies, and gladdens me. Through myself I fall; through You I know that I shall rise again.

Because I know that I shall fall, I do not rejoice in heaven, which is the firmament, because I hope that I shall rise again. Let the earth exult, which is mud [Note: The reading *lutilatio* is uncertain; the word may refer to “mud” or “clay.”]. Let the prophet say it; let the psalmist say it; let us too say: “Let the heavens rejoice; let the earth exult.”

If the Ruler of heaven wills it, why should the earth not exult? “Let the earth exult”—what does that mean for it? “Shout for joy, mountains, in praise.” I do not shout for joy; I do not praise. Why? Because I am not a mountain; I am a valley, I am a sinner.

God said to me: “Why do you recite my ordinances and take my covenant upon your lips?” But because it is commanded that every spirit praise the Lord, and because the Lord will come and have mercy on His poor, I shout for joy and praise, while not forgetting whose act this is—the act of the merciful God. God made my weeping, my sin, and my laughter.

[Col. 0583]

## Poems of Erkenbald

### Epigram

By us this book was rightly called an eye;

For it sees many things closed to the sluggish and the idle.

### Quatrain

Truthful man, rejoice in the emblem of your virtues;

You will be secure, because you will travel by a certain road.

But you who lie will soon after your deed be caught;

In deceiving, may you be deceitful in your deceptive speech.

[Col. 0583]

## Municipal Laws Which Erkenbald Gave to the City of Strasbourg

*(Grandidier, History of Strasbourg)*

### These Are the Rights and Laws of the City of Strasbourg Concerning the Peace to Be Maintained in the City and the Prevention of Plunder or Theft from Being Brought Into It

[Col. 0583C] **I.** Following the model of other cities, Strasbourg was founded in such a state of honor that every person, whether foreigner or native, should have peace there at all times and from everyone [Note: [Col. 0583C] The twelfth-century code, the German translation, and Schiller’s Latin edition add that the city of Strasbourg was built on the model of other cities in order to be a free city: “Strasbourg was founded in such a state of honor that it should be a free city, since every person …”].

**II.** If anyone has committed an offense outside the city and has fled into it through fear of punishment, let him remain there safely. Let no one lay violent hands upon him; nevertheless, he must be obedient and ready to submit to justice.

**III.** Let no one bring plunder or stolen goods into the city, or dare to keep them there, unless he is prepared to give an account to every complainant.

**IV.** Let no one bring in a captive unless he presents him to the advocate or judge, who shall keep him for the administration of justice.

**V.** All the magistrates of this city belong to the authority of the bishop, so that either he himself appoints them or appoints those who appoint them. The higher officials whom he appoints shall appoint the lower, according as the latter are subject to them.

**VI.** The bishop must not entrust a public office to anyone except one who belongs to the household of his Church [Note: [Col. 0585B] “Unless he belongs to the household of his Church.” It would do violence to these expressions to believe that they mean “from the diocese of Strasbourg.” They mean that a person had to be attached to the Church of Strasbourg by some office, fief, or dignity. The author of the Chronicle of Ebersmünster, when enumerating the various subjects of the bishopric in section 3, divides them into three classes. He designates the first as follows: “The first ministerial household, which is also properly called military, so noble and warlike that it may indeed be compared with the free condition.”].

**VII.** The bishop personally invests four officials in whom the government of the city consists: namely, the *scultetus*, the burgrave, the toll collector, and the master of the mint.

We shall first deal with the *scultetus*, who is also called the advocate or judge.

**VIII. Concerning the Rights of the Scultetus** [Note: [Col. 0585C] The word *scultetus* derives from the old word *Schultais*, or *Schuldasius*, the name given among the Lombards to local judges, and still preserved in this province for the provosts or mayors of villages. See Wachter’s *German Glossary*, printed at Leipzig in 1737, p. 1472 and following. The word *Schultheizo* was common among the Franks for all who exercised some jurisdiction, whether civil or military. Otfrid, an Alsatian monk of Weissenburg who lived in the middle of the ninth century, translates the centurion mentioned in Saint Matthew, chapter 27, verse 54, by *schuldeizo* in book IV, chapter 34, of his paraphrased translation of the Gospel in Germanic verse. The most certain etymology of *Schulteiss* is *Schuld*, meaning “debt,” and *Heischen*, meaning “to ask” or “to demand,” because the principal function of the *Schulteiss* consisted in judging debts and fines. This is the opinion of Eccard in his notes on the Salic Law, p. 193; Reiz, *Belga Graecissante*, p. 169; Wachter, cited work, p. 1474; and Haltaus in the *German Glossary of the Middle Ages*, p. 1657.].

It belongs to the advocate to appoint under himself two deputy officials, whom he commonly calls judges, sufficiently honorable that the citizens may appear before them in court with their dignity intact.

**IX.** It also belongs to the advocate to appoint three persons whom we call *heimburgen* [Note: [Col. 0585D] The *Heimburge* of the city of Strasbourg, whom in the present day only seven city sergeants called *Gerichis Boten* have imperfectly replaced, were then highly respected persons, since they directed the police. The *Heimburge* were chosen from among the leading citizens [Col. 0586B] of the city to watch over public security.]: one in the inner, that is, the old city, and two in the outer city; and also to appoint the keeper of the stocks [Note: [Col. 0586C] *Cippus*. Properly, this was an instrument by which criminals’ feet were held tightly so that they could not escape. The name was subsequently applied generally to the prison, which the old French called *chep à mestre malfaiteurs*. See Du Cange, *Glossary*, vol. II, p. 624.], or prison, in which accused persons are detained. The duties of each are as follows.

**X.** The advocate shall judge cases of theft, *frevel*, and *geltschulda* [Note: [Col. 0586C] *Frevela* or *Fraevel* formerly meant two things: either an actionable insult subject to a fine, or the fine itself imposed as a consequence. Wachter and Haltaus explain the word more fully in their glossaries, pp. 468 and 486. The latter proves that *Frevel* derives from the old word *Farfalium*, or *Forfal*, meaning “a falling away.” An old document of the abbey of Honau, in Schilter’s *Chronicle of Königshoven*, p. 1156, reads: “The punishment of daily and nightly *Frevel* fines; the payment of fines.” *Geltschulda* can best be expressed as monetary debts.] involving all citizens of the city and all who enter it from this bishopric, unless they raise a reasonable exception, excepting the Church’s ministerials, those who belong to the bishop’s household, and those whom he has appointed to office.

**XI.** He has the power to compel and constrain those who have been judged, which is called the *ban* [Note: [Col. 0586C] *Ban*, also called *Blutbann*, principally means high justice, or criminal jurisdiction, and the right to pronounce sovereignly on the life and death of people. Hence the advocate was called *Blutvogt*, and the executioner *Vicarius Advocati*. This right derived solely from the king or emperor. “No one can confer the ban except the king alone,” says the *Saxon Mirror*, book III, article 64, in Goldast, *Imperial Customs*, p. 162. See Haltaus, *Glossary*, pp. 94, 174, and 1110. According to Wachter, *Glossary*, p. 114, the term *banlieue* derives from this. The old provincial law of Germany forbids anyone who does not possess the king’s ban to condemn a person to any afflictive punishment other than flogging, chapter 74, §2: “He who does not have the ban from the king may not judge except to skin and hair.” See Magerus, *De Advocatia Armata*, chapter 5, no. 443, and Boehmer, *Observations on Peter de Marca*, book I, chapter 12, observation 18, §2.], not from the bishop but from the advocate. For the authority that concerns the shedding of blood—hanging, beheading, mutilating, and similar punishments according to the nature of crimes—must neither be held nor granted by an ecclesiastical person. Therefore, after the bishop has appointed the advocate, the emperor grants him the ban, that is, the punishment by the sword for those condemned in such cases, together with every power of coercion.

**XII.** Since, therefore, he possesses this authority only through the grace of the advocacy, it is just that he deny it in no way to the advocate, the toll collector, and the master of the mint—whomever the bishop appoints and from whom he holds the advocacy.

**XIII.** No one therefore has the power to judge in this city except the emperor, the bishop, or those who hold authority from him.

**XIV.** The judges whom the advocate has under him do not possess the power to judge thefts or *frevelas*, but only *geltschuldas*.

**XV.** The place of judgment is in the market beside Saint Martin’s. Therefore, no one against whom a complaint is made is to be summoned to the house of the advocate or judge, but only to the public place mentioned above.

[Col. 0587A] **XVI.** If, nevertheless, the judges or the advocate summon someone to their houses and he does not come, he shall not for that reason be liable to any composition.

**XVII.** The duty of the keeper of the stocks or prison is to guard carefully all those entrusted to his custody.

**XVIII.** If he loses anyone, he shall suffer the penalty for his fault, unless the prisoner was violently taken from him [Note: [Col. 0587C] The law of the Visigoths, book VII, title 4, no. 3, prescribes the same: “If the gaoler or keeper should presume, by any fraud and without the judge’s order, to release those whom he holds in chains, he shall suffer the same punishment or loss that they themselves would have incurred.” We also read in Louis the Pious’s charter of 824 for the abbey of Ebersmünster: “If a captive escapes, they themselves—the keepers of the stocks—shall be liable.”].

**XIX.** It is also his duty to lead those condemned to hanging to the gallows; bind the condemned person’s eyes with a cloth; erect the gallows; place the ladder; and bring the accused up to the ladder. Then the advocate’s deputy shall take him and hang him with a noose fastened around his neck.

**XX.** If the advocate’s deputy is not present, the accused shall be kept in custody until the advocate refers the matter to the bishop.

**XXI.** Likewise, if someone has received the punishment of loss of skin and hair, the keeper of the stocks shall inflict this penalty.

**XXII.** If someone has been condemned to have his hand cut off, the same keeper shall hold the axe [Note: [Col. 0587D] *Barta*: an axe or hatchet.], while the advocate’s deputy shall wield the wooden mallet and cut off the hand.

**XXIII.** The same deputy of the advocate shall tear out the eyes [Note: [Col. 0587D] Eyes were chiefly torn out from criminals convicted of treachery and betrayal. Haltaus, in his *German Glossary*, pp. 69 and following, gives several examples of this punishment inflicted upon traitors. These criminals were made to lie belly-up on a ladder while the operation was performed, as may be seen in the *Layen-Spiegel*, printed in 1511. The practice of putting out princes’ eyes was common among the Greek emperors.], cut off the testicles, behead the condemned, and carry out all the other punishments according to the variety of crimes.

**XXIV.** It is also the keeper’s duty to obey the toll collector and the master of the mint just as he obeys the advocate.

**XXV.** He must also summon to judgment those who have been formally accused before the advocate or the judges.

**XXVI.** The method of summons is as follows. He shall name the person making the complaint and inform his opponent that he has been summoned, either by word of mouth, face to face, wherever he encounters him, or by sending word to his house—first, second, and third times—with one night’s interval.

**XXVII.** If, after the first, second, or third summons, he does not come, and the judge’s messenger proves by a third party that he made all three summonses, or at least the first face to face, the absent man shall pay the judge thirty solidi [Note: [Col. 0587D] The old German version of these laws, made in the thirteenth century, translates *solidi* as *scellini*. Eccard, in his notes on the Salic Law, p. 13, thinks that *solidus* gradually became *scholigus*, *scolingus*, and finally *scellingus*. But this etymology is more ingenious than true. In general, the word *solidus* was used in ancient laws to designate a certain sum intended to pay fines; gradually the word passed from designating the fine to designating the money with which it was paid. Wachter, *Glossary*, p. 1416, derives *schilling* from *scylan*, which among the Anglo-Saxons means “to divide” or “to separate,” because the shilling is a part of the large solidus divided and separated into several small solidi. The Salic Law, title 1, no. 1, reads: “If anyone has been summoned to the assembly according to the king’s laws and has not come, if no seizure has detained him, he shall be judged liable for fifteen solidi.”].

**XXVIII.** A person summoned to judgment must present himself at the appointed time. He shall wait for the complainant as long as the judge sits in judgment, or he may leave with the judge’s permission. The judge must not deny him permission to leave if he requests it. If the judge accuses him of not having come at the appointed time, he shall swear that he was present, or he shall pay the judge a composition.

**XXIX.** The advocate or judge must judge nothing except what has been brought before him. If he is convicted of doing anything without judicial procedure and a just judgment, he shall lawfully lose his office.

**XXX.** No fellow citizen may bring a complaint against a citizen who is prepared to depart on a journey—that is, who is already boarding a ship or mounting a horse or wagon—and thereby prevent him from leaving. But because the latter has so neglected himself that he postponed his case until this moment, it is just that whatever claim the other has against him be deferred until his return.

**XXXI.** If someone brings a complaint against his fellow citizen outside the city before another judge, he must pay a composition both to the city’s judge and to the person whom he summoned, and must restore to the latter whatever loss he suffered because of the complaint [Note: [Col. 0588D] The old municipal law of Worms, cited by Schannat in *History of the Bishopric of Worms*, vol. I, part II, p. 203, prescribes nearly the same: “If any citizen has brought his fellow citizen elsewhere outside the city, rather than before the bishop and his judges and the judges of the city, to answer a case concerning any matter, he shall pay thirty Worms solidi as a penalty and shall compensate the injured party for whatever losses he has suffered through him.”].

**XXXII.** No composition is to be paid except to the person to whom the composition is owed.

**XXXIII.** Every composition imposed for *frevela* amounts to thirty solidi. The composition imposed for *geltschulda* belongs to the complainant, namely the *missetat* of the person summoned; but one third of that *missetat* belongs to the judge.

**XXXIV.** If someone makes a composition to the judge and the complainant but does not pay it within the specified period, and if the case has been properly pursued to its conclusion, he shall be held in public custody until he first pays the complainant his composition and then the judge.

**XXXV.** If someone insults another by word or deed before the people, and both wish to submit to the judgment of the people, the judge shall decide according to the judgment and statement of the people. But if the person summoned clears himself by his simple assertion, or if the other can convict him by single combat, the matter shall be decided accordingly.

[Col. 0589A] **XXXVI.** If anyone rashly attacks his fellow citizen within the enclosure of his house or courtyard, without a judge or the judge’s messenger, he shall pay the judge thirty solidi for *frevela*; and to the person whom he attacked he shall pay three times his *missetat* [Note: [Col. 0589D] *Missetat*. This word means a bad action or a criminal offense. See the glossaries of Schilter and Haltaus, pp. 590 and 1352. *Missetat* derives from *that*, “action,” and *miss*, which adds to the action the mark of wickedness. See Wachter’s *Glossary*, p. 1082.].

**XXXVII.** In all the courtyards of the brothers from the monasteries, or of the ministerials, in which they themselves do not reside bodily, the *scultetus* or judge has the right to summon the resident to judgment and compel him.

**XXXVIII.** Likewise, he has the right to judge the servants of the brothers of any monastery, namely in cases relating to trade, if they wish to be merchants.

**XXXIX.** Whoever enters the city while being the debtor of someone, if he is summoned before the judge, must be presented to the *scultetus* for justice by the canon or ministerial in whose house he has perhaps taken lodging. If he does not do so, he shall be required to answer for the debtor.

**XL.** Of all compositions imposed for theft and *frevela*, two parts belong to the *scultetus* and one third to the advocate. The following distinction must be observed. If the composition has been imposed in favor of the advocate, he shall divide it by taking one third for himself and giving two thirds to the *scultetus*. For he shall receive the composition assigned to him, and whatever amount he himself has established in receiving the composition—whether small or large—the *scultetus* must neither reduce nor increase it, but shall accept it as fixed.

[Col. 0589C] **XLI.** Conversely, if the composition has been imposed in favor of the *scultetus*, it is his right to receive two parts and give one third to the advocate. Likewise, whatever amount of the composition he himself has established, the advocate shall not cancel.

**XLII.** The advocate must judge only in the bishop’s palace. If he summons someone to his own house, the person who does not come shall not for that reason owe him any composition.

**XLIII.** When the advocate dies, or the advocacy becomes vacant for any reason, the bishop must not appoint an advocate without the election and consent of the canons, the ministerials, and the citizens [Note: [Col. 0589D] This word does not generally mean all the citizens of the city, but only the leading citizens, as the elite among the townspeople. This is the explanation given for the word by Haltaus, *Glossary*, p. 197, and Moritz, *Treatise on the Origin of Imperial Cities*, part II, chapter 9, p. 387.].

**XLIV. Concerning the Office of the Burgrave and His Toll**

[Col. 0589D] It belongs to the office of the burgrave to appoint the masters of nearly all the trades in the city, namely the saddlers, furriers, glove-makers, shoemakers, smiths, millers, those who make wine vessels and pitchers, those who polish swords, fruit sellers, and innkeepers [Note: [Col. 0589D] According to the agreement made in 1263 between Bishop Henry of Geroldseck and the city of Strasbourg, in Schilter’s notes on the *Chronicle of Königshoven* (observation 12, p. 729), and in Wencker’s *De Usburgeris* (p. 24), the bishop’s burgrave was to exercise particular oversight over the guilds, whose inspection alone belonged to him. He had the right to appoint in his name, in each master’s guild, a master concerned solely with matters relating to his trade. At that time the trades formed nine tribes: tanners, carpenters, coopers, fruit sellers, sword polishers, millers, farriers, painters, and saddlers. In the fourteenth century these tribes numbered twenty-eight; in 1442 they were reduced to twenty-four, and in 1482 to twenty.]. He also has authority to judge them if they commit an offense in their trades.

**XLV.** The place of their judgment and correction is in the bishop’s palace.

**XLVI.** If any of the persons mentioned above become disobedient to the burgrave, he shall refer the matter to the bishop.

**XLVII.** It also belongs to the burgrave’s rights to collect certain tolls, such as those on swords carried enclosed in scabbards and offered for sale in the market. But the toll on other swords brought in ships from Cologne or elsewhere shall be collected by the toll collector.

**XLVIII.** On oil, nuts, and fruit, wherever they have been brought from and sold for money, the burgrave shall collect the toll. But if they have been sold in exchange for salt, wine, grain, or any other commodity, the burgrave shall divide the toll with the toll collector.

**XLIX.** Apart from the foregoing, all other tolls belong to the office of the toll collector, although they are collected in different ways.

**L.** If anyone transfers his merchandise from one ship to another, he shall pay four denarii for each ship.

**LI.** Any merchant who enters this city with his pack animals, if he sells or buys nothing, shall pay no toll.

**LII.** Any man or woman belonging to the household of this Church who sells in this city things made by his or her own hands, or things grown by him or her, shall pay no toll. If such a person buys something for personal use and does not intend to sell it for profit, he or she shall likewise pay no toll. If anyone charges that the things sold were not grown or made by that person, or that they were bought for profit, the person shall clear himself or herself by a simple oath.

**LIII.** If anyone buys or sells something worth less than five solidi, he shall pay no toll.

**LIV.** On five solidi he shall pay one denarius; on a talent, four; on a horse, four; on a mule, four; and on a donkey, one denarius.

[Col. 0590D] **LV.** The toll-collector does not collect toll on charcoal or hemp, which the bishops have hitherto received, [Col. 0591A] nor the wine-ban and the breads called *bernbrōt*.

[Note: [Col. 0591C] The *ban-vin*, or wine-ban—called *bannwein* in German—is a right belonging to the lord, who is permitted to sell, or have sold, his wine alone for a certain number of days, fixed differently according to local customs or usages, at specified times and places, to the exclusion of all his subjects, who may not then sell wine. See Du Cange, *Glossarium*, vol. I, p. 980; de la Mare, *Traité de la Police*, book V, vol. IV, p. 796; Schilter, *Glossarium Teutonicum*, p. 83; and Haltaus, *Glossarium Germanicum*, p. 98. The wine-ban enjoyed by the bishops of Strasbourg in their episcopal city lasted six weeks, beginning with the first vespers of Easter. It was later changed into a kind of payment called *bannwein-gelt*, by which tavern-keepers gave the bishop one measure per cartload of wine that they sold during the interval of the wine-ban. “In our city of Strasbourg, a wine-ban was imposed, namely every year from the vespers of Easter until six weeks thereafter, one *ama* from each cartload of wine, which was sold there by the tavern-keepers during the intervening period.” Thus writes Henry, bishop of Strasbourg, in letters of 1252, by which he sold the city his right of wine-ban for four hundred marks of silver. The bishops had previously granted it in fief to the lords of Lichtenberg, who had granted it as a subfief to the nobles of Beger. The wine-ban had been much more extensive until the episcopate of Otto, who lived toward the end of the eleventh century. It appears from a diploma of Emperor Henry V, from the year 1119, that all the wine sold in Strasbourg from Easter Day until 8 September was sold for the benefit of the bishop, who received two pots from every measure. “The sale of wine from the day of Holy Easter until the Nativity of Holy Mary throughout the whole city belonged to the episcopal treasury, so that from each cartload of wine offered for sale two tubs—which we call *ama* in German—were paid to the episcopal treasury.”]

[Note: [Col. 0592C] *Berenbrōt*, or *bernbrōt*, was a kind of due which the burghers were obliged to pay the bishop in bread. *Brod* means “bread” in French, and *beren* is an old Teutonic word meaning “to give” or “to pay.” Schilter, *Glossarium Teutonicum*, p. 101. An ancient manuscript cited by Schilter in the same work, p. 102, fixes the price of each *berenbrōt* loaf at one pfennig. The high officers of the Church of Strasbourg received several of these loaves as part of their revenues. The register of the possessions and fiefs of this bishopric, compiled around the year 1345, states that the grand chamberlain received weekly from the episcopal table seventeen *berenbrōt* loaves, the grand cupbearer eight and a half, and the grand baker, or grand master of the household, seven. Several other persons attached by their duties to the episcopal palace likewise received rents in *berenbrōt*.]

**LVI. On the office of the toll-collector.**

It belongs to the office of the toll-collector to brand with a heated iron all small and large measures for salt, wine, oil, and grain, made by the master of the tavern-keepers; and he must grant them to no one, except perhaps to a fellow citizen for an *ama* of wine [Note: [Col. 0592D] *Ama vini*: a wine measure. See Du Cange, *Glossarium*, vol. I, p. 364.], or a quarter-measure of grain, and for such small matters without charge.

**LVII.** Nevertheless, any citizen who wishes to have such measures for his own use may do so, provided that they are marked by the toll-collector’s knowledge and through him. Likewise, every burgher may keep weights for pounds in his own house, provided that they have been made by the mint-master.

[Col. 0591B] **LVIII.** It is likewise the office of the toll-collector to construct all the bridges of the new city, as many as may be necessary, and of the burgrave to construct all those of the old city, so firmly that everyone may safely cross with his carts and animals. If anyone suffers damage because of the age, excessive wear, or any weakness of the bridges, the toll-collector or burgrave must each legally make restitution within his own jurisdiction.

**LIX. On the office of the mint-master.**

What follows concerns the office of the mint-master. By right he has authority to judge cases involving counterfeit money and the counterfeiters themselves, both in the city and throughout the entire bishopric outside it, without any opposition from other judges.

**LX.** Wherever he finds a counterfeiter anywhere in the bishopric, he shall bring him to the city and judge him according to the judgment of the city.

**LXI.** The coin must be of such a weight that twenty shillings make a mark; these denarii are called *pfundig*. This coin must circulate stably and perpetually throughout this bishopric, unless it has been counterfeited. In that case it shall be changed by a council of wise men according to another design, but not according to another weight.

**LXII.** The place for striking the coin is beside the fishermen (a second codex of the laws reads: “near the market, beside the butchers’ stalls”). The denarii must be struck in a single house, so that all may see one another’s handiwork.

**LXIII.** No one may make denarii except someone belonging to the household of this Church.

**LXIV.** In the place where the money-changers sit, no other person may buy silver except the coiners themselves. Elsewhere throughout the city, anyone who wishes may buy and sell silver, unless this has been forbidden on account of the new coinage.

[Col. 0592B] **LXV.** Whenever a new coin is struck and the old one is prohibited, from the day on which the prohibition is announced, three periods of fourteen days—namely, six weeks—shall be granted. During these periods the mint-master may prosecute anyone he wishes for having accepted the prohibited coin. If that person wishes to deny it, he shall swear with seven others that he did not do so; otherwise he shall pay the mint-master sixty shillings.

**LXVI.** Once the six weeks have ended, he shall prosecute no one except someone whom he has seen accepting the prohibited coin.

**LXVII.** If he sees this, he shall take the denarius, bring him to judgment, and there prosecute him. If the man denies it, he shall convict him with three honorable persons that he accepted it; once convicted, he shall pay him sixty shillings. If he does not wish to convict him, he shall clear himself by his own oath.

**LXVIII.** No one may prosecute anyone, nor may anyone be required to pay a composition, except for denarii called *phundig*.

**LXIX.** If someone receives a hand-penalty before the mint-master, he shall be judged as above before the advocate.

**LXX.** If the bishop wishes to melt silver from his treasury and have denarii struck from it, the master of the mint shall receive it and divide it among the minters, so that they may make denarii from it. If the denarii are *phundig*, he shall return twenty shillings per mark, less two denarii.

**LXXI.** If they are struck at any lighter weight, two denarii less shall always be returned per mark.

**LXXII.** Charcoal shall be supplied to them from the bishop’s treasury. Three *sextaria* of charcoal are allotted to each mark.

**LXXIII.** When the bishop orders a new coinage to be struck, at the outset five shillings shall be made in the design and weight in which the coin is to circulate.

**LXXIV.** The burgrave shall preserve these for as long as that coinage lasts, so that, if the coin should happen to be accused of being counterfeit, it may be examined and certified by comparison with those five shillings.

**LXXV.** The mint-master shall likewise swear that he will strike the coin in the weight and design possessed by those five shillings.

**LXXVI.** When the mint-master returns to the bishop the tools with which the denarii are formed, he shall give him two in the form of coins and two in the form of obols. [Col. 0593C] In addition, he shall return all the other tools so completely that he shall swear that he has no more and knows of no one else who has any. The dies shall be erased and broken, and the fragments returned to the mint-master; or, with the bishop’s permission, he may retain them whole and undamaged.

**LXXVII.** Whoever wishes to obtain the right of the minters shall give the bishop half a mark of gold, the master of the mint five gold denarii, and the minters twenty shillings of heavy coin.

**LXXVIII.** When the bishop wishes to change the coinage, he shall grant the mint tools for six weeks.

**LXXIX.** Any mint-master living outside the city who buys silver in the city shall pay the mint’s due.

[Col. 0593D] **LXXX.** Whoever damages the walls or rampart of the city shall pay forty shillings to the burgrave.

**LXXXI.** Whoever builds over the road shall likewise pay the burgrave for its repair. He must grant permission to no one.

**LXXXII.** No one may place dung or refuse in front of his house unless he intends to remove it immediately, except in the places designated for this purpose: beside the butcher’s market; beside Saint Stephen’s; beside the well in the horse market; and at the place called Gewirke.

**LXXXIII.** The city rampart must extend around the outside sixty feet beyond the wall, and on the inside thirty feet.

[Col. 0594A] **LXXXIV.** Whoever wishes to build a mill shall seek permission from the burgrave and the consent of the burghers. Once he has obtained these two things, he shall give a gold coin to the burgrave.

**LXXXV.** No one shall pay toll on mats, chickens, geese, eggs, leeks, cabbages, or any other vegetables, bowls, or beakers, unless he sells goods worth five shillings.

**LXXXVI.** No one may keep pigs in the city unless he entrusts them to the swineherd.

**LXXXVII.** The enclosure where the pigs are pastured lies between the gate called Vellemannes Burgetor and the next gate.

**LXXXVIII. On the bishop’s rights.**

It belongs to the bishop’s right to have twenty-four envoys from this city, and these only from the merchant class. Their office is to carry out the bishop’s embassies only within the bishopric, to his own men. If they suffer any harm meanwhile, either to their persons or to the goods they take on the journey, the bishop must make restitution to them.

**LXXXIX.** Each of them must perform this kind of embassy three times every year, at the bishop’s expense. The bishop must show them the following honor: on his festivals, whenever he invites his own men, they must have honorable seats before him at the meal, so that they may become all the more well known to those same men.

**XC.** When the bishop enters the city, his horses must be stabled in the lord’s stable, which begins at the hospital and proceeds around the wall as far as the bishop’s orchard.

**XCI.** If he has more horses, his advocate, or his judges, together with the marshal, shall take charge of them and stable them in the houses where lodging is customarily provided for travelers. If he has still more horses, he may not lawfully place them in any other houses of the city unless he can obtain this by request.

**XCII.** If an emperor or king enters, his horses shall be lodged everywhere.

**XCIII.** Each burgher must likewise work five days each year in the lord’s service, except all the minters who belong to the Church’s household; twelve among the furriers; all the saddlers; four among the glove-makers; four among the bakers; eight among the shoemakers; all the smiths; all the carpenters; the butchers; and the coopers who make wine vessels.

**XCIV. On the lord’s estate.**

To the lord’s estate, which lies within the city, the advocate shall provide thirteen oxen for the bishop’s plows, taken from the property of members of the Church who die, and one draft animal, which the master of the estate shall ride and use to carry seed to the fields.

**XCV.** He shall also provide twelve sows and two boars, one for the bishop’s use and the other for the burghers’ use.

**XCVI.** The bishop shall appoint an estate-manager on that estate. [Col. 0595A] The estate-manager shall provide a plow and a harrow [Note: [Col. 0595D] *Egedam*: a harrow.].

**XCVII.** The advocate shall provide everything else that is necessary, except the wages and food of the servants.

**XCVIII.** Each of the two judges shall give five shillings at harvest time, and the master of the millers one shilling, and the master of the tavern-keepers one shilling, for buying bread during the harvest.

**XCIX.** When the bishop’s grain is threshed, he shall give each judge one *maldre* [Note: [Col. 0595D] One *maldre*. The *malder* was a German measure for dry goods containing four bushels, according to the glossaries of Schilter and Du Cange (p. 563 and vol. IV, p. 376). Wachter, in his glossary (p. 1032), derives the word *malder* from *malen*, meaning “to grind.”], because the judges and heralds must guard the bishop’s grain during the harvest while it is being reaped.

**C.** The advocate may not apply the oxen belonging to the bishop’s plows to any other use, except for cultivating his own *schuchbuze*; nor may the bishop transfer them to any other use except his plow.

**CI.** If one, two, or more of these oxen become unfit for cultivation through old age or in any other way, apart from contagious disease, the butchers must sell their meat and give the money to the advocate; meanwhile no other meat may be sold.

**CII. On the furriers.**

There are twelve furriers, who, at the bishop’s expense, must make skins and fur garments as much as the bishop requires. The master of the furriers, taking with him as many of these twelve as are necessary, shall purchase their materials with the bishop’s money either at Mainz or at Cologne. If they suffer any harm on the journey, whether to their property or through captivity, the bishop must make restitution to them.

**CIII. On the smiths.**

[Col. 0595C]

The right of the smiths is as follows: when the bishop goes on the emperor’s expedition, each smith shall provide four sets of horseshoes with their nails. Of these, the burgrave shall give the bishop enough for twenty-four horses, and he shall retain the rest.

**CIV.** If the bishop goes to court, each smith shall provide two sets of horseshoes with their nails. Of these, the burgrave shall give the bishop enough for twelve horses, and he shall retain the remainder.

**CV.** In addition, the smiths must make everything the bishop needs in his palace, whether for doors, windows, or the iron fittings of vessels, provided that iron materials are supplied to them and food for their support is furnished in the meantime.

[Col. 0595D] **CVI.** If the bishop besieges a castle, or is himself besieged, they shall provide three hundred arrows. If the bishop needs more, they shall supply them sufficiently at their own cost and expense.

**CVII.** They must make the fastenings and chains for securing the city gates, with the necessary costs and expenses supplied from public funds.

[Col. 0596A] **CVIII. On the shoemakers.**

Among the shoemakers there are eight who, when the bishop goes to court or on the emperor’s expedition, shall provide cases for candlesticks, basins [Note: [Col. 0595D] According to Du Cange, vol. I, p. 905, and Carpentier, vol. I, p. 413, *bacchinus* was properly a vessel for holding water, from which the French word *bassin* is derived. Gregory of Tours writes (*History*, ch. 28): “With two wooden bowls, which are commonly called *bacchinon*.”], and cups. They shall make, at the bishop’s cost and expense, everything else necessary for these objects or for the sieges of castles, whether bags or boxes [Note: [Col. 0596D] “Whether in *bulgae* or in *bustra*.” *Bulga* is a very ancient Celtic word meaning a leather sack. Festus says: “The Gauls call leather sacks *bulgae*.” See the glossaries of Schilter and Wachter (pp. 228 and 104). The German translation renders *bustrum* as *Laden*, which in French designates a box.], or any other suitable equipment for the aforesaid tasks, made of black leather.

**CIX. On the glove-makers.**

Four among the glove-makers shall provide, when the bishop goes to court or on the expedition, as much white leather as is necessary for cases for candlesticks, [Col. 0596B] basins, and cups. They shall make from white leather, at the bishop’s cost and expense, everything else that may be necessary for these objects and for sieges of castles.

**CX. On the saddlers.**

The saddlers shall give the bishop, when he goes to court, two pack saddles, and four for an imperial expedition. If he needs more, they shall make them at the bishop’s cost and expense.

**CXI. On the cleaners of swords.**

When the bishop goes on an expedition or to court, those who polish swords must clean the swords and helmets of the vice-lord, marshal, steward, cupbearer, chamberlain, and all the bishop’s necessary and regular servants. In addition, they shall clean the bishop’s hunting spears if necessary.

**CXII. On the beaker-makers.**

All the beaker-makers shall make whatever beakers the bishop needs, either at his own court or at the emperor’s when he visits him, or when he is setting out for the emperor’s court, at the bishop’s cost and expense. The master of the coopers shall provide the wood. In addition, he shall provide wood daily to the bishop’s beaker-makers.

**CXIII. On the coopers.**

The coopers, once their master has provided the wood and the bishop’s cellarer has supplied the hoops, bands, and bindings, shall make everything the bishop needs while residing at home, or whatever the emperor or empress need when they are present, for their baths, and also for the kitchen and for the use of the cupbearers. Likewise, when the bishop goes to court, they shall provide all these things at his cost and expense. In addition, they shall bind all the bishop’s wine vessels, large and small, at his cost and expense.

**CXIV. On the tavern-keepers.**

[Col. 0597A]

It is the right of the tavern-keepers, every Monday, to clean the bishop’s privy and granary, if he wishes them to do so.

**CXV. On the millers.**

The millers and fishermen must transport the bishop by water wherever he wishes between Upper Rust and Lower Velletor. The toll-collector shall provide them with as many boats as are necessary. They themselves shall enter the boats with their oars and bring them back to the bishop’s orchard, from which they took them, at the bishop’s expense. The fishermen shall provide two men, and the millers a third. If they lose the boats through their own negligence, they shall pay for them. If they are taken from them by force, the bishop shall make restitution.

**CXVI. On the fishermen.**

[Col. 0597B]

The fishermen must fish for the bishop’s use every year for three days and three nights between the Nativity of Saint Mary and the feast of Saint Michael, [Col. 0598A] with all their equipment, whenever the water is most suitable, between Lower Velletor on the Rhine and Upper Rust; in the Ill, as far as Ebersheim; in the Breusch, as far as Molsheim; in the Schutter, as far as Merburg; and in the Kinzig, as far as Kinzdorf, at the bishop’s expense. Within these boundaries no one may dare exclude them from any water, except water enclosed beneath barriers.

**CXVII.** In the Breusch, from the upper rampart of the city down to the lower one, beside Saint Stephen’s, no one may dare fish without the permission of the bishop or his steward.

**CXVIII. On the carpenters.**

The carpenters must go to work for the bishop every Monday at his expense. When they arrive before the palace early in the morning, they may not leave before the sound of the bell that is rung for Mass in the morning. If they have not meanwhile been taken up for the bishop’s work, they may leave freely that day. They are not compelled to go to work for anyone else, but only for the bishop.

**In the year of the Lord 992, Adso, a monk of the monastery of Dervent in the district of Perthois in Champagne.**

[Col. 0597]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE

(From Oudinus, *Supplementum de Scriptoribus ecclesiasticis*, p. 308.)

Adso, a monk of Saint Benedict, later made abbot of Dervent, flourished around the year 980 and was distinguished by notable learning and by administrative ability in temporal affairs. The author of the book *Miracles of Saint Bercharius, Abbot of Dervent*, published by Jean Mabillon in volume II of the *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, p. 844, extensively celebrates his praises. There, no. 11:

“After Lord Alberic’s life had ended, Adso became abbot. Considering the basilica of the saints formerly built by Saint Bercharius to be very small, he laid the foundations of a great church; and he recovered for the monastery two estates, Drejam and the other called Puellare-Monastery, which had been lost through the negligence of his predecessors,” and so forth.

He wrote the *Life of Saint Bercharius*, found in the Second Century of the *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis D. Benedicti*, p. 831; also the *Deeds of Saint Basolus the Confessor*, found there on p. 67; the *Translation and Miracles of the same Saint Basolus*, found in the Fourth Century of the *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Divi Benedicti*, vol. II, p. 137; and likewise the *Life of Saint Frodobert, first abbot of Celle near Troyes*, which is found in the Second Century of the *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Divi Benedicti*, p. 626, together with the *History of the Translation of the Relics of the same Saint Frodoard*, in the Fourth Century of these Saints, vol. II, p. 243. Finally, he wrote the *Life of Mansuetus, first bishop of Toul*. Adso died in the year 992. Jean Mabillon discusses him in his prefaces to these legends.

[Col. 0597]

## ON THE ANTICHRIST

(See among the works of Alcuin, *Patrologia*, vol. CI, col. 1289.)

[Col. 0599]

# LIFE OF SAINT FRODOBERT, FIRST ABBOT OF CELLE NEAR TROYES, BY ADSO, ABBOT OF DERVENT

(From Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum*, volume II, Camuzat’s *Promptuarium*, and Bollandus.)

## PRELIMINARY OBSERVATIONS

**1.** The *Life of Saint Frodobert* [Saint Fraubert], abbot and founder of the monastery of Saint Peter on German Island, near the city of Troyes in Champagne, was written—“although Lupellus committed it to writing more briefly than was proper,” as is said below, no. 21—by that disciple. His lost work was enlarged and embellished by another anonymous monk of Celle, of much later date, though not lacking authority or learning. We infer that he was a monk of Celle from no. 11 of the following *Life*. From no. 23, where he speaks of Frodobert’s stature, we gather that he lived not long after the translation made in the time of Charles the Bald, since he says: “As those also testify who declare that they have seen the bones of his most holy body.”

Unless, perhaps, this was Adso, abbot of Dervent, who is said in book II of the *Deeds of Saint Bercharius the Abbot* to have “written, at the request of Odo, abbot of Celle, the *Life of the confessor of Christ, Frodobert, first founder and abbot of that monastery [Celle, or German Island], in a most truthful account and simple style,” that is, in the tenth century. Whatever the case may be, this is the only work we have been able to obtain. In the manuscript codex of the monastery of Vallis-Lucens, it is preceded by a poem by an author of no mean ability who lived in the eighth century; it is followed by an account of the translation of Saint Frodobert, written in heroic meter, together with two sermons delivered on the feast of Saint Frodobert. We received all these materials from the monastery through the kindness of the Reverend Father Claude Maillet, former prior. We give only the preceding poem, lest we seem to repeat the same material with equal tedium.

**2.** The monastery of German Island, in the suburb of Troyes, on the western side of that city, was built around the year 650 of Christ in a marshy place called German Island. After the eighth century, because of the tomb of Saint Bobinus, bishop of Troyes, formerly its monk, enlarger, and benefactor, it was called Cella Bobini, and often simply Celle; in more recent times, the monastery of Saint Peter of Celle, commonly Monstier-la-Celle. From this monastery came, besides the bishops Aldobert and Saint Bobinus, Saint Robert, later abbot of Molesme, and others; also Peter, called Peter of Celle, abbot of this monastery, then of Saint Remigius at Reims, and finally bishop of Chartres, illustrious for his writings and learning. Celle now flourishes under the Reverend Fathers of the Benedictine congregation of Saint Vannes.

# POEM ON SAINT FRODOBERT, ABBOT OF TROYES

From the Codex of Vallis-Lucens.

[Col. 0599A]

You who wish to weigh great things in a few words,

Behold: in a small book you can perceive great things.

If it pleases you to pass through ancient annals with study,

Let this new work please you in these matters.

The deeds of great men are celebrated for their strength;

Here, Frodobert, we celebrate your riches.

From earliest childhood, devoted to learning,

You had imbued your tender minds with dripping dew;

Then, placed at Luxeuil under an honorable way of life,

You took up the support of religion by loving faith.

Soon returning to the city of Troyes,

Full of heavenly gifts and upright in goodness,

Spreading the shining teachings of the divine rule,

So that you might benefit many men by your usefulness.

Then Celle pleased you, a dwelling enclosed by strict boundaries;

In it, enclosed, a faithful station was yours.

O how many labors this enclosure imposed,

While alone he holds his face beneath the star-bearing sky!

But the constrained mind, destined to possess its triumphs,

Was the freer in proportion to the strictness with which it lived.

Then a very small wall confined his limbs within a cave;

Now the vast expanse of heaven holds his great spirit.

Its work grew under your leadership, holy Bobinus,

O bishop, magnificent in your merits;

Now, through your counsels, blessed Frodobert rejoicing

Holds the lofty heights of his Church.

This noble work that we see, founded everywhere

With stones brought together, raising lofty roofs—

[Note: [Col. 0599A] This shows that this poet, who seems to have been a monk of Cella, lived shortly after Saint Bobinus, indeed before the ninth century, since, as follows from no. 26 of the following Life, the basilica adorned and enlarged by Saint Bobinus [Col. 0600A] collapsed through age around the middle of the ninth century. Saint Bobinus is commemorated in the Benedictine and Gallican martyrologies on 23 April [IX Kalends of May], the day of his translation; the day of his death is unknown. On him see below, no. 13.]

Within it, under eternal praise, a steadfast company stands:

The monastic glory governed by the Most High.

[Col. 0601A]

There also stand the numerous rewards of a thousand palms

That this hall will bestow upon its deserving members.

Here eyes afflicted by sorrow return to light;

Here grievous hosts of diseases have fallen.

The lame man begins to walk, his joints restored to health;

Here he receives easy paths where earth had denied them.

Here the customary fury of the demon, collapsed into the air,

Ceases to return to the mind and limbs.

Those whom the grievous harms of rising evils oppress—

Here the powers of body and soul return.

If the guilt of harmful crimes has weighed anyone down,

If he seeks pardon here, he carries back healing from here.

[Col. 0602A]

This book contains the rewards, virtues, wondrous deeds, and feasts

Of countless good people.

If anyone wished to recount them, thousands would remain—

Things the page has passed over and this book does not sing.

For if anyone wished to comprehend in sacred books

The pious deeds, an inexhaustible day would be too short.

Let these few things briefly establish faith for the unbeliever;

Let him remain doubtful, and he will grasp no better things.

May perpetual praises remain for you through the ages,

O Frodobert, and have mercy on your flock.

The heavenly kingdom holds you in lasting joys;

At last, make us remain with you in heaven.

# HERE BEGINS THE LIFE

[Col. 0601]

## The period in which Frodobert of Troyes flourished

[Col. 0601B]

**1.** Frodobert was a man of highly venerable life and distinguished, precious memory. The land of the town of Troyes brought him forth as a most holy and blessed citizen, divinely endowed with singular faith and integrity. He was born of parents of modest status, but he was most illustrious for the incomparable brightness of his mind. For from the very beginnings of tender childhood he was most clearly marked out as a vessel of election; in the breast of a child he already acted as a spiritual and perfect man, compensating for his few years by the gift of holiness and grace.

When the sequence of time is examined more carefully, this same precious priest and outstanding abbot is found to have flourished under the Frankish king Clovis, son of Dagobert, and likewise under the younger Chlothar, son of that same Clovis, while Ragnegisilus, bishop, was exercising apostolic authority in the aforementioned city of Troyes. Ragnegisilus was an Aquitanian by birth and already the seventeenth bishop of that city. Among other things, he is said to have built the basilica of Blessed Savina the virgin on land belonging to him, making the church over which he presided his heir; he lies honorably buried there.

Blessed Frodobert lived under five bishops of his city [Note: [Col. 0601D] Namely Ragnegisilus, Leuconius, Bertoaldus, Wammiro, and Abbo Felix, who is recorded in Frodoard, book II, chapter 6, as having exchanged certain things with Leudegisilus, bishop of Reims.], continuing until Abbo, who is known to have been the twenty-first bishop of that same city.

## He is given over to study and fulfills in action what he learns

**2.** But, to return to the order of events: as soon as his age permitted, he was, through the care of his parents, committed to the schools of the aforesaid bishop Ragnegisilus. There, nourished by holy studies, it is impossible to describe what faith and goodness he already displayed in himself. At length, burning intensely with love of the heavenly homeland, whatever he was able to grasp intellectually in the divine readings he immediately transferred with the utmost zeal into the practice of holy works.

Thus, by indefatigably frequenting the pure streams of Scripture, he shaped the face of the inner man as though with the aid of a most splendid mirror. He considered it a very great sin if he read even a little that he did not immediately and effectively fulfill, repeatedly and familiarly saying to himself that not those who merely hear the law, but rather those who do it, are justified before God (Romans 2:13).

Then you might see him eagerly setting before himself the examples of the earlier Fathers for emulation, and you would scarcely be able to determine in which kind of virtue he shone more perfectly. And, in order to offer himself wholly to God as a rational victim and sacrifice a spiritual holocaust, he devoted himself to continual prayer. Unable to endure rest, he imposed upon himself with great insistence the apostolic command that teaches us to pray without ceasing (1 Thessalonians 5:17).

He practiced fasting not so much frequently as continually, taught by the Lord’s authority that by this twofold manner of warfare that most wicked kind of demons can be driven out (Matthew 17:20). Even then, in the schools of divine service, the new soldier of Christ had taken up this armor; having recently professed the heavenly military calling, he prepared himself with ever greater vigilance to conquer spiritual wickedness.

## He drives away a demon by the sign of the cross

**3.** Meanwhile, amid these holy and excellent studies, the hostile assaults of the cunning enemy were not lacking. The adversary of human salvation already envied, in the years of childhood, the excellence of the holiness that would one day be found in him. Thus, as he later related himself, whenever he went to school to learn the Psalter, the devil repeatedly thrust himself before his eyes, shaking his naturally timid spirit by a great display of threats and terror.

But the boy, gifted with divine understanding and not ignorant of demonic fraud and deceit, armed his forehead no less than his breast with the shield of the saving sign. Calling upon God as his helper, he bravely trampled underfoot the enemy’s cunning devices.

## He restores his mother’s sight

**4.** The time had now come for the lamp that had until then been hidden beneath the bushel to pour the radiance of star-like brightness upon the people. For, so that it might become widely and clearly known what merit he possessed before God, divine providence deigned to reveal by a miracle the purity of his childlike innocence, which it favored.

It happened that his mother, deprived of the assistance of her eyes, suffered the loss of light. As she prolonged a night of blindness and consumed her life in sorrow, one day, while caressing her son in her arms, she begged him to make the sign of the cross over her eyes with his hand. When he refused, and his mother pressed him more insistently, he was at last moved by his mother’s pleading. Calling upon the Lord, he traced the saving sign over his mother’s eyes.

Immediately, as the darkness yielded, friendly light returned, and through the merit of her little son a great benefit was bestowed upon the mother. This miracle was promptly spread everywhere; it struck everyone with astonishment, and it also stirred some of them more ardently to imitate a holy life.

## As a cleric, he goes to the then-famous monastery of Luxeuil

[Col. 0603B]

**5.** Thereafter the aforementioned bishop, observing the young man’s exceptional purity of spirit and exalted efficacy in virtue, assigned him to the clerical office and entrusted him with divine ministries. Later, moved by concern for charity and zeal for divine gain, he resolved to send him to the monastery of Luxeuil for spiritual formation, so that, attracted by the imitation of religious men, he might himself grow in virtue and later bring back to his own region the most gracious examples of holiness and perfection.

At that time Walbert was abbot of that monastery, a man renowned both for religion and for his reputation for holiness. When Frodobert arrived there at the bishop’s command, the holy Fathers of the place received him with joyful welcome and assigned him to the fellowship of the community.

His purity of spirit and distinguished simplicity soon became known to all. Everyone marveled at the young man’s exceptional humility, incomparable abstinence, and singular patience; and because he was always intent upon heavenly desires, he lived an angelic life among human beings.

At that time the aforesaid monastery of Luxeuil was almost unique in the Gallic regions, both in the height of its religious life and in the perfection of its learning. For this reason, many people in whom there was zeal to advance in either direction flocked from everywhere to the same place in eager competition.

## His simplicity is suspected and tested by Teudolenus
6. At the time, therefore, when Blessed Frodobert was staying there, Bertoaldus, an apostolic man and bishop of the city of Langres [Col. 0603D], took care to send there, for the sake of instruction, a certain abbot from the monastery of Saint Sequanus, named Teudolenus. Blessed Frodobert frequently visited his lodging, as youthful age commonly prompts young people to seek the companionship of their peers with particular eagerness. But when Teudolenus discovered such purity of spirit in the man of God, he was moved by inquisitive frivolity to investigate carefully whether this simplicity flowed from the inner source of genuine purity or whether, as is familiar in some people, a deceitful mind concealed itself beneath a simulated innocence.

For this reason, both Teudolenus himself and certain brothers of the place repeatedly harassed him with foolish mockery. Yet he contradicted no one, harmed no one, and, when harmed, did not retaliate. He had so ordered his life [Col. 0604A] that by patience he overcame the injuries inflicted upon him, frequently repeating that saying of David: “I have become like a beast before you” (Psalm 72:23). Thus he always preferred unfeigned simplicity to worldly cunning, choosing to be made a fool by the world so that he might be wise in God.

### He gives an outstanding example of simple obedience

7. One day, then, when he had gone to the lodging of the aforementioned Teudolenus, the latter, partly in mockery and partly as a test, asked him to go to the cell of a certain brother in the monastery and bring him a compass, asserting that he needed it for writing. He immediately hurried off and quickly reached the designated brother. That brother, who knew his simplicity and was not unaware of the mockery for which Frodobert had been sent, placed the middle section of a millstone around his neck and sternly ordered him to carry it as quickly as possible to Teudolenus’s lodging.

Without hesitating, Frodobert carried the burden he had been given with equanimity, although the weight of the stone pressed upon him so heavily that he could scarcely advance, moving only every other step. Meanwhile he encountered the most reverend Abbot Walbertus, to whom some of the brothers had already reported what had happened. When the venerable abbot saw Christ’s gentlest sheep burdened with an unjust load, he groaned deeply, grieving both over Frodobert’s suffering and over their frivolity. He immediately rebuked them more severely and ordered him to cast the burden from his shoulders; then he carefully asked why he was tiring himself so greatly.

The man of the utmost innocence replied that the compass he was carrying was necessary for writing [Col. 0604C], saying that he was taking it to the cell of a certain brother at Teudolenus’s command. Since he was wholly without guile, he had no idea what a compass was and thought that it was simply the object placed around his neck.

At last, when the abbot perceived the man’s utterly simple spirit, he burst into tears out of compassion. He summoned those who had dared to weary the holy man with such cruelty, rebuked them more harshly than usual, and imposed upon them the penance of due satisfaction for their rash deed. After they had been corrected in this way, the other brothers thereafter refrained from injuring him.

O man who shared in angelic purity and was blessed in imitation of our Savior! Like a sheep led to the slaughter, when he was mistreated he did not open his mouth. I say it confidently: singularly obedient to the Gospel commandments, he would not strike back at one who struck him; and if anyone pressed him into service for one mile, he would go two miles willingly (Matthew 5:41). To say even more: if someone dragged him to punishment and placed upon him a penal cross, he would accept it of his own accord and, carrying it meekly upon his shoulders, follow Christ the Lord. [Col. 0604D]

### He returns to Troyes and is detained by the bishop. The bishop approves his rigorous observance of the Lenten fast

8. Several years later, he returned to the city of Troyes with some brothers, at the request of his bishop and to visit his parents. After staying for several days with the aforementioned bishop of his city [Col. 0605A], he asked permission to return to the place from which he had come. But the bishop, exercising wiser judgment and considering it improper to release from his presence so great and excellent a man, detained him by force of authority.

When the holy season of Lent approached, Frodobert withdrew into a more secluded cell and began, with earnest prayer and vigils, to constrain himself by the harshest fasts. Although he had always excelled through an incomparable virtue of abstinence, during those days he imposed upon himself a more severe mortification of the flesh, the enemy of his body, so that he spent many successive days without any food at all.

Finally, as the years passed and he exhausted himself through two or three Lents of this kind, this practice of his life became known to the bishop. There were also malicious people who, gnawing at his holiness with an envious tooth, said that he was either secretly eating or wished to kill his body by starvation. Accordingly, when the next Lent was approaching, the bishop, curious about such matters, assigned him a cell within the church’s portico, where he could complete the season of abstinence according to his customary devotion.

The bishop often entered the cell unexpectedly, wishing to discover more certainly how fervently Frodobert pursued holiness and how much grace the goodness of heaven supplied him in the virtue of abstinence. At once the deceit of his accusers was exposed, and the sincerity of his holy way of life, tested by the bishop’s scrutiny, shone forth; what had previously been attributed to pretense now became an increase of divine praise.

### He cures illnesses with sacred oil and drives away demons with the sign of the cross

[Col. 0605C]

9. From that time the fame of his blessedness resounded far and wide, so that crowds of sick people came to him even from distant places, seeking the benefits of healing through the merits of his holiness.
