But the man worthy of God, wishing to remain firm in the citadel of humility, allowed himself to presume nothing about himself and never permitted anything to be attributed to his own powers.

He did nothing more than bless oil and humbly invoke the name of Christ over the sick. When they had been anointed with it, they recovered their strength and returned home having obtained what they had prayed for.

Moreover, in driving out demons he excelled with such power that whenever he impressed the sign of the cross upon the forehead or breast of anyone possessed, the evil spirit, compelled by his command, immediately fled. Such authority rightly attended him in expelling demons [Col. 0605D], so that he could confidently command them, because he had wholly subjected himself to obedience to the divine commandments.

### He discloses his virtues to his own disciples

10. It was the custom of the most holy man, whenever he engaged in familiar conversation with his disciples, to tell them of things he had secretly done, for the sake of edification or example. He did not ostentatiously display his good works, but disclosed them wisely and humbly, so that divine praise might increase through him—or rather, in him—and so that the minds of his hearers might be formed toward the pursuit of holy imitation.

How completely he shunned approval and boasting was shown by his devotion to a solitary life.

### With Clodoveus’s assistance he founds a monastery

[Col. 0606A]

11. In the end, burning to avoid the company of human society, he frequently revolved in his anxious mind where he might establish a dwelling suitable for his profession and purpose. Although many nobles of the region clung very closely to his holiness, he nevertheless considered it improper to ask any of them for a portion of land or property. He was concerned not only for himself but also for those who would come after him, lest the religious brotherhood that he wished to gather in the holy habit should suffer any disturbance or inconvenience from a secular person because of the place of its habitation.

Accordingly, with divine providence assisting him, he went to the royal court and, through the generosity of Clodoveus, once the illustrious king of the Franks, obtained a certain marshy place in the suburb of the city of Troyes [Col. 0606B], which in the ancient manner was called German Island.

Later, after Clodoveus’s death, he approached his son Clotharius in the second year of his reign [A.D. 656]. With the consent of the venerable Queen Balthild, Clotharius’s mother, he again deserved to obtain a privilege of royal authority over the aforementioned place.

Since this document is preserved to this day in the archives of our monastery [Note: [Col. 0605D] It is likewise under the name of the monks of Saint Basolus that Abbot Adso, although of Dervus, speaks in the Acts of Saint Basolus above, under the year 620.], we have thought it superfluous to insert it here, since we acknowledge that it is readily available for anyone who wishes to read it. [Note: [Col. 0605D] It is extant in the *Promptuary of the Antiquities of Troyes*, p. 19.]

12. The place itself belonged, indeed, to the royal fisc, but, as has been said, it was flooded with marshes, overflowing with frequent eruptions of pools, and filled with wild shrubs. It was suited more to the company of beasts and serpents than to that of human beings.

Strengthened, therefore, by these royal authorities, and, above all, fortified by heavenly assistance, Frodobert undertook the dreadful desolation of the place. By applying his chief effort, he had the brushwood uprooted, the pools drained, and a suitable space prepared for habitation.

There Frodobert built a cell and an oratory. At first he lived there alone with a few brothers, devoted to divine contemplation and always occupied with angelic works.

### He increases the monastery in property and persons. Several are subsequently raised to the episcopate

13. The renowned Frodobert then began to enlarge the place of habitation granted to himself and his followers. He transferred all his patrimonial estates and possessions there in their entirety for common use, and eagerly acquired, at a considerable price and under deeds that are still preserved, an abundant supply of male and female servants, fields [Col. 0606D], and vineyards.

Soon afterward the parents of the blessed man also donated to him generous portions of their goods and treasures, with instruments duly completed according to law. As time went on, the place grew stronger through the increasing number of religious men who gathered there, and the generosity of the nobles who flocked to it enriched it and extended the boundaries of its goods and possessions. The number of the monastic congregation also increased abundantly from day to day, making the monastery renowned and famous everywhere.

Nor should this be omitted: several men who later became bishops in the city of Troyes came from the monks of this place [Col. 0607A] and followed the life and discipline of Blessed Frodobert. Among them were Aldobertus, a man of the highest intelligence and exceptional holiness, and also Bobinus, an Aquitanian by birth [Note: [Col. 0607D] Read the poem above.]. Both brought immense benefits to the place itself, enlarging it in every possible way, within and outside it; and thus, completing their final day in the fullness of good works, they received honorable burial within the enclosure of the basilica of the same monastery.

Having arranged these matters, let us return to the order of events.

### Through his merits, wine increases in the Parthenon of Saint Quintinus

14. In the holy man, unfailing grace for spiritual progress flourished, commended not only by example and conduct [Col. 0607B], but also by the customary splendor of miracles. How great his generosity and abundance of charity were will become clear from one simple account.

It happened that, at a certain time, he entrusted two vessels of wine, holding nearly thirty *modii* [Note: [Col. 0607] That Parthenon has been converted into a priory subject to the abbey of Molesme.], to a monastery of girls consecrated to the name of Blessed Quintinus the martyr and situated within the city. The place was especially familiar to him and joined to him by a special bond of charity; it had been particularly entrusted to his instruction and governance.

Since everyone honored him with principal reverence on account of his holiness, each person considered it the greatest blessing to deserve even a moderate degree of association with him. It was most welcome and desirable to all that he should act affectionately toward everyone and in every matter, and that he should presume freely upon everyone.

Because he often summoned many people there to drink in the exercise of charity, one day he entered the storeroom as usual and found the floor covered with an abundance of spilled wine. Fearing that the vessel might have leaked and caused a loss of the liquid, he ordered a brother who happened to be with him to inspect the opening at the top.

When this had been done—wondrous to relate—the wine was seen overflowing from above. It became perfectly clear that the more generously charity drew from it, the more abundantly the Creator’s kindness restored what had been drawn.

This deed is, of course, attributed to his piety. For God commands us to be merciful and to give to those in need, so that much may also be given to us; and in the measure in which we give, he promises that the same measure will nevertheless be measured back to us (Matthew 7:2; Mark 4:24). The divine hand is not merely generous but rich and overflowing.

Nor should one fear that generosity may be followed by poverty, since, as the Apostle says: “He who sows with blessings” (2 Corinthians 9:6), and the one “who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will also supply and multiply the fruits of our righteousness” (ibid., 9:10).

### He devoutly honors the saints

15. It was also customary for the man of God, thirsting tirelessly for his heavenly homeland, to visit sacred places with particular devotion [Col. 0608A] and, whenever the festivals of holy martyrs or confessors came around in the cycle of the year, to observe them with due reverence.

He had especially imposed this upon himself: to observe the holidays of sacred days with a distinctive form of devotion, so that one might have thought he was already dying together with the martyrs themselves and was no longer detained by the concerns of earthly existence.

### At the feast of Saint Quintinus he is disturbed in prayer by a demon

16. Once, when the splendid solemnity of the precious martyr Blessed Quintinus was approaching, the abbess of that monastery, named Rocula, and the other nuns invited him, out of religious devotion, so that the most holy man might take part in the services of the divine celebration and illuminate the joys of so great a feast with the lamp of holiness and exalted merits.

Apart from his incomparable devotion toward the saints, another reason compelled him to visit sacred places on feast days: he provided them with spiritual direction. He did not delay in coming, considering that the desires of the nuns devoted to God ought not to be frustrated.

When the service of the sacred vigils had been completed in the evening and the crowd had returned to its familiar lodgings, the holy man remained in the church and, devoting himself to secret prayers, kept spiritual watch.

The aforementioned abbess, however, extremely curious about what the holy man was doing, hid herself in the basilica with certain nuns and, together with the sisters, carefully observed his exceptional persistence in prayer and the abundant outpouring of his contrition.

Soon the enemy arrived, opposed to human salvation and an especially zealous rival of good works [Col. 0608C]. He could not entirely destroy God’s pure holocaust, but he attempted to defile it with the poison of suspected deceit. He overturned a candelabrum on which a candle had been placed and, extinguishing the light, clearly showed that he was a lover of night and darkness.

Yet the man of God continued in his devotion to prayer. He could not be darkened by worldly darkness, because Christ, the author and most immediate source of light, was present to him. Although his outward eye was dimmed by the darkness of night, his innermost mind, always pure for contemplating God, shone with the lamp of true light.

### He is mocked by a possessed man

17. Meanwhile, after a few days had passed [Col. 0608D], the servant of Christ was customarily going to the basilica of Blessed Aventinus the confessor, in accordance with his devotion. As he was entering the church doors, it happened that a certain possessed man was being tormented by a demon.

Captive to a rabid madness, he opened his wretched mouth to words of insanity. Among the many utterances of his frenzied heart, he repeatedly shouted the name of Blessed Frodobert and insulted the holy man with insolent words, saying that while he was keeping sacred vigils, he had taken away the comfort of light.

But the most steadfast soldier of Christ, aware of the devil’s deception, could be shaken by no artifice of the enemy and terrified by no threatening attack. Christ was his protection and an impregnable bulwark against hostile assaults. Indeed [Col. 0609A], the more fiercely he recognized the demons’ battles against him, the more strongly he prepared himself for spiritual combat against invisible powers of evil.

### He hears angelic voices

18. It is also worthwhile to pass on to the ears of the faithful that, with the Lord’s consent, the secrets of the heavenly court were often disclosed to him. Since he always dwelt in heaven in his mind, divine goodness more frequently offered him a draught of heavenly delight, so that he might run toward it with greater ardor the more eagerly he had tasted its sweetness.

One day the venerable Theudecarius, abbot of the same suburb, came to him for the sake both of visiting and of receiving instruction. It was the custom of all the religious people in the surrounding area frequently to seek out this holy man, so that they might be instructed by his exhortation and strengthened by his most holy blessing.

When it was about the third hour, Frodobert, filled with the Holy Spirit, was engaged with the aforementioned most Christian man, Abbot Theudecarius, in fruitful and spiritual conversation. He heard choirs of angels singing heavenly hymns with harmonious sweetness and ineffable melody to the glory of the holy and undivided Trinity.

After he had drunk in the sweetness of this song for some time with astonished ears, he called the aforementioned Theudecarius to witness the miracle. When Theudecarius later related the event, so wondrous a matter became known to many.

O singular merit of the blessed man! Although he still lived in the world, he recognized angelic voices in heaven, the Redeemer [Col. 0609C] granting this to him divinely—the same Redeemer who, at the third hour, sent the Holy Spirit from heaven to his disciples.

### He restores a woman who was deranged in mind

19. A certain woman of the same region, named Bertha by her parents, had lost soundness of mind and fallen into the alienation of a wretched madness. Fleeing the company of human beings, she was always wandering and unstable, carried from place to place without a fixed dwelling.

Her anxious parents brought her into the presence of the blessed man. Moved by the compassion of his heart, he grieved over the unhappy woman’s condition. He immediately cast himself into prayer, hoping through abundant tears to obtain the restoration of another’s health.

The gifts of heavenly mercy were not long delayed. When he rose from prayer and placed the life-giving sign of the cross upon her head, her pitiable madness immediately yielded, and she recovered the fullness of her understanding with complete restoration of health. She lived for a long time afterward and, as a testimony to his holiness, carried with her everywhere the joy of her restored health.

Through these and similar virtues divine excellence advanced its most beloved soldier, whom it had determined to place at the summit of the heavenly kingdom. During the course of this present age it also did not cease to make him distinguished and famous through frequent miracles.

### Seized by illness, he foretells the day of his death

20. The time was already approaching when Christ would withdraw his athlete from the dangerous contest of this world and establish him, victorious and utterly at rest, in the encampment of heaven [Col. 0610A].

Indeed, the time had come when, in return for the sweat of his many struggles, the torments of his singular abstinence, and all his works of piety, Christ would receive the warrior, already weary in body, to himself; place him in his Father’s dwelling places; adorn him with the emblem of glory and honor; clothe him with eternity and immortality; and join him to the angels and associate him with the apostles.

Accordingly, he was seized by a mild bodily illness, yet remained strong in spirit and strove to pursue the prize of eternal reward. For a long time he had preferred to be freed from the prison of bodily existence so that he might be with Christ, although he was recognized as necessary in the flesh for the instruction of the faithful.

As a consolation of the greatest security, divine majesty added this gift also: it revealed to him the day of his sacred passing from the world. When he had received this revelation, he immediately turned his whole self toward God. He neither feared death nor dreaded the dissolution of the body; rather, he frequently reflected that, if the earthly structure of our dwelling is dissolved, a much better one is prepared in heaven.

Moreover, his consciousness of his past life gave him the least terror and the greatest confidence: he had lived not for the present world but for God; he had always preferred the divine will to his own; and, sighing continually for heavenly rewards, he had set God before his eyes as present.

As his illness grew stronger, he summoned his disciples and declared to them the day of his passing, which he had learned through divine revelation. When the gentlest flock grieved both over the departure and the absence of their most watchful shepherd, he delivered an elevated exhortation and restrained them all from weeping. He asserted that they ought to congratulate themselves rather than grieve, since the man who had lived in exile until then was now being restored to his homeland and summoned to the banquet of his King.

Above all, he repeatedly urged them to preserve, with inviolable constancy until the end of their lives, the rule of holy discipline that they had learned both from his teaching and from observing his conduct.

### He asks that the new church be dedicated on the Lord’s birthday. When the bishop refuses, he obtains an extension of life

21. Meanwhile, the most festive day of the Lord’s Nativity, to be honored throughout the whole world, dawned in heaven and on earth [Col. 0610D].

He summoned two disciples by name: Leo, the most holy man who at that time was the gentle abbot of the same suburb, and Lupellus, who, as his own writing makes clear, committed to letters an account of the holy man’s life and conduct, though more briefly than was fitting. He sent them with the utmost speed to Abbo, the most reverend man and then bishop of the same city, earnestly begging him to consecrate on the day of the Lord’s birth the oratory that he himself had built in honor of the prince of the apostles in the marsh described above.

With God’s help, the congregation of monks had grown, and he had built a second church larger than the first. When the bishop received this request and had carefully considered the matter within himself [Col. 0611A], he excused himself with prudent moderation. He asserted that the request could by no means be fulfilled on the day proposed: the obligations of the feast would occupy him and his clergy more fully, and ecclesiastical custom absolutely did not allow such a thing to be done on that day.

The disciples returned quickly and reported the bishop’s answer to the holy Father. After considering it carefully and recognizing its reasonableness, Frodobert raised his hands to heaven, his face wet with tears, and said:

“May the Lord pardon me, and you, my sons, forgive me, because, having considered the matter with insufficient care, I have compelled your brotherhood to undertake a useless journey there and back.” Yet divine mercy provided that his holy mind should not be frustrated in all its desires. Having received a postponement of his sacred death, he prolonged his life until the octave of the Lord’s Nativity, the Lord so advancing his most holy wishes that on one and the same day, through the hands of the aforementioned bishop, the basilica would receive both its consecration and the burial of the earth containing his sacred body.

### A lector reading the Gospel before him is freed from a headache. The saint dies

22. In accordance with Christian observance, as the celebration of the Lord’s circumcision on the Kalends of January approached, the holy soul was being summoned to its blessed passing by an illness that pressed urgently upon it.

Even then, however, his tongue did not cease its holy admonitions. He tirelessly exhorted the disciples attending him to preserve among themselves an unbreakable bond of charity and, persevering in the practice of saving obedience [Col. 0611C], always to recall the fear of God before their eyes.

As the sun was already declining toward the lower parts of the earth, he ordered that the aforementioned Lupellus, who was accustomed to serve him more intimately, be summoned without delay. When Lupellus had been brought before him, Frodobert ordered him to read the holy Gospel in his presence.

Lupellus, however, was being tormented by a severe headache. Although, as he later reported, he applied his mind with difficulty to obeying the holy command, at the very beginning of his reading all the pain immediately disappeared, leaving no trace of suffering or of his former discomfort.

Meanwhile, throughout the course of the entire night, Frodobert remained intent upon God. As the hour succeeded hour amid spiritual conversations, and after the brothers had solemnly completed in the church the appointed quantity of psalmody and prayers, he again ordered all the disciples to be present.

While the text of the Lord’s Passion was being read before him [Col. 0611D], the holy soul, stripped of the covering of the flesh before the eyes of all, passed happily into heaven.

[Note: [Col. 0611D] Namely, on the Kalends of January, as in the Martyrology of Celle, although in nearly all the other more recent martyrologies it is celebrated on the sixth day before the Ides of the same month, which is the day of his translation. Since he did not long outlive Clotharius, the son of the younger Clodoveus, as is clear from section 11 above, we place his death around the year 673. His relics are preserved there. [Col. 0612D]]

### He leaves Gibitrudis and the nuns longing for him. He was tall in stature

23. When he had thus been taken from the fellowship of human beings, his most reverend nephew Waldinus—who later succeeded his uncle as abbot of the same monastery—immediately hurried to the monastery of Saint Quintinus and reached the renowned Abbess Gibitrudis, to whom he announced the holy man’s death. [Col. 0612A]

At once a new and almost unbearable grief invaded everyone’s hearts, and it seemed that a portion of their salvation had been taken away when so great a Father was absent.

When the entire community of nuns burst into weeping and tears, the venerable abbess, moved by the affection of her heart, rushed at full speed to the holy man’s funeral. While arrangements for the burial were being discussed, she asked whether a coffin suitable for burying the body was available. They replied that a stone monument had indeed been purchased from a distinguished man named Walbertus, but that it was in no way suitable for the height of his body.

For the sacred man was not only splendid in spirit but also handsome and distinguished by a beautiful, tall body, as those too testify who admit that they have seen the bones of his most sacred body [Col. 0612B].

Servants were therefore sent in haste to bring it. Soon it became clear through a remarkable miracle that the man for whom the funeral rites were being prepared was of the highest merit.

Walbertus had sent some members of his household to hand over the purchased sarcophagus to those who had come to carry it. But, by the dispensation of heavenly mercy, such confusion of mind deceived them that, instead of the smaller vessel that had been purchased, they pointed out another, larger and more capacious one that Walbertus had prepared for himself.

They placed it upon a vehicle and brought it as quickly as possible to the place where the holy man had determined to be buried. Thus almighty God, who cares for all things, did not permit anything necessary to be lacking even to the ashes of his chosen servant.

### He is buried by the bishop after the dedication of the new church

[Col. 0612C]

24. When everything pertaining to the burial had been prepared with the greatest care, the aforementioned most reverend bishop, surrounded by a host of suburban abbots, clergy, and people, hastened to the funeral of Blessed Frodobert. His sacred body still lay in the cell, arranged according to Christian custom.

First, as reason required, the bishop undertook the dedication of the aforementioned basilica. When he had completed it with solemn ceremony, he reverently lifted the sacred body and carried it into the church. On the day of that same dedication, namely the Kalends of January, with hymns, praises, and the entire apparatus of the ecclesiastical service, he consigned it to an honorable burial in the same basilica that Frodobert himself had built [Col. 0612D].

Thus the man of God, most carefully entrusted to the bosom of the earth, celebrates with Christ in soul the seventh day of the Sabbath. Undaunted—indeed, secure in glory—he awaits the eighth day, promised generally as the resurrection of us all. Though dead in body, he remains eternally glorious through his living merits.

### He shines with miracles

25. He therefore rested in the same basilica for many years, visited by a great multitude of peoples who flocked there from every direction and continually testified to him through the almost uninterrupted succession of miracles [Col. 0613A].

For who approached his holy memorial to pray faithfully without immediately receiving help from the devotion of prayer? There, various remedies were provided both for souls and for bodies: desired health came to the weak, and blessed forgiveness to those weighed down by the enormity of their sins.

If anyone was held by some grievous affliction, he came to the saint’s protection and, consoled by his benefit, soon found swift relief. Thus the benevolent Creator performed many wondrous deeds through this most elect confessor of his name. He had enriched him while alive with abundant rewards of good works, and after death he exalted him with tireless titles of miracles.

For this reason a remarkable fervor toward the saint was kindled in everyone’s hearts [Col. 0613B]. Many neighboring nobles, as well as religious women, enriched the place itself with substantial quantities of estates, both to obtain the burial that everyone desired there and to ensure that those who served the sacred body would not lack adequate sustenance, and also that those whom the saint’s fame continually drew from distant regions would be assisted by generous hospitality.

### The cause of the neglect of the saint’s cult. Prudentius first removes the bodies and dedicates the new church

26. Meanwhile, as the flow of passing time gradually slipped away, when iniquity increased and the charity of many began to grow cold (Matthew 24:12), that universal fervor for the saint’s service became lukewarm. As religious devotion ceased and the former crowds grew sparse [Col. 0613C], the miracles also became dormant for a time.

The harmful negligence of that period of torpor arose in the following way. The structure of the church that Frodobert himself had built, as was established above, in which his sacred body had long been visited and preserved with due honors, gradually collapsed under the age of its construction and fell into ruin, since no one supported it.

When another church was being built in its place, the venerable body of the blessed confessor remained unmoved and untouched in the crypt of the former basilica.

At that time the bishop of the aforementioned see was a man named Prudentius [Note: [Col. 0613D] Saint Prudentius is commemorated on the eighth day before the Ides of April. He was especially dear to Hincmar, bishop of Reims, and was famous for writings against Gottschalk and for other works. He did not live long after the Second Council of Soissons, to which he subscribed in the year 853.], a Spaniard by birth, distinguished by the discipline of episcopal life and by no ordinary learning in divine matters.

Summoned by the brothers to consecrate the aforementioned basilica, he carefully inquired whether the bodies of any persons were buried beneath the walls that were to be consecrated. When he discovered that there were very many, he ordered that all of them first be removed from the church, declaring that he would undertake the rite of consecration only on that condition.

The aforementioned bishop was still unaware of the outstanding greatness of Blessed Frodobert’s merits, which had been obscured by the neglect of the times. He had neither learned of his life, full of faith and miracles, through reading, nor discovered that any account of it had yet been preserved anywhere. [Col. 0613D]

### Prudentius wishes to transfer Saint Frodobert’s body but is forestalled by death

[Col. 0614A]

27. After the dedication of the church had been completed, Prudentius returned to the city and, from the account of his deeds, learned more carefully of the miracles performed through the most holy confessor.

At first he severely reproached himself for his former ignorance and bitterly condemned himself for having handled the matter of so great a Father with insufficient honor. He then sent the archdeacon of his see with the entire clerical retinue, earnestly ordering that the body of the most excellent man be returned to the church with great reverence.

He also fixed a time and day for his own arrival, so that he might place the body there with fitting honor and, publicly celebrating the festival of its sacred translation with due ceremony [Col. 0614B], establish it as an observance to be kept by posterity in perpetual ritual.

But the fulfillment of this holy desire was thwarted by the burden of an illness that came upon him. Overtaken immediately by approaching death, he was unable to complete what he had piously arranged.

### Otulfus carries this out. The saint’s tomb is glorified by various wonders
28. Thus the matter remained unfinished until the year 872 of the Incarnation of the Word, which was the thirty-first [thirty-second] year of the emperor and king of France, Charles [the Bald]. At that time the most devout and venerable Bishop Otulfus, who was the third [Note: [Col. 0614D] For between Prudentius and Otulfus, Fulcricus occupied the intervening episcopate; he attended the Council of Soissons in the year 866, whereas Otulfus attended that of Pontigny in 876.] to flourish after him, was governing the Church of Troyes. The body had been placed only within the precinct of the basilica and was venerated by the brethren of the place with vigilant devotion, without being visited by gatherings of the people or celebrated with any solemn distinction. Yet heavenly goodness did not permit that luminous star to remain hidden longer in gloomy concealment. It allowed both his merits to become manifest to the world and his effective intercession to come to the aid of the people.

At that time, therefore, the greatness of the divine presence began to reveal itself to very many of the brethren in connection with the place, and to press upon the hearts of God’s servants through frequent apparitions. For some, occupied in more private nocturnal vigils in the church, heard over his tomb melodious voices, as though choirs of clerics were singing; others saw around the tomb what appeared to be an arrangement of exceedingly brilliant lights. Thus it was plainly evident that, where human services were lacking, divine and angelic offices were being supplied to him. Moreover, a dove of milk-white brightness was seen to descend from heaven and, after flying around for some time, to penetrate the hidden interior of the tomb. During the repose of sleep, many likewise seemed to see the same most holy Father emerging from his sacred tomb before the altar of the chief of the apostles and devoting himself to prayer.

Through these and similar wondrous signs it became clearer than daylight that the precious confessor of the Lord, bearing indignantly the neglectful veneration shown him, was decreeing that a burial more worthy of him should be prepared and that the reverence of service [Col. 0615A] should be instituted with greater devotion. This matter also received considerable confirmation from the fact that whenever anyone prostrated himself at the sacred tomb, a devotional spirit and an abundance of compunction flowed into him more generously. And, so that what the clearest visions concerning him suggested might be completed through the devotion of the clergy, everyone’s mind burned insatiably: God was evidently inflaming the hearts of each person by a hidden inspiration and pressing them forward with the goads of holy desire toward the accomplishment of so great a work.

### A New Translation Is Announced

29. Encouraged by such conspicuous miracles, they approached Bishop Otulfus, presenting before him the deeds of so great a Father, and earnestly begging that he himself might become both a co-worker with and an agent in hastening the divine will toward the saint [Col. 0615B]. And, that you might see the Godhead everywhere favoring the prayers of its faithful servants, the bishop, immediately inflamed by the fires of inward inspiration, undertook the matter with such ardor that he afterward urged the abbot and brethren who had petitioned him, by frequent admonitions, to hasten the effectiveness of the work they had begun. He exhorted them to persist in unwearied prayers, so that divine mercy might grant those whom it had made aware of its will also to attain the beneficial fulfillment of their vows.

### When the Tomb Is Opened, Grains of Gold Appear in the Bone. The Sacred Body Is Raised from the Earth

30. Accordingly, they chose as the first day for beginning so great a work the first day of Lenten abstinence [Note: [Col. 0615D] The unpublished poet indicates the day in these verses:

> When, midway through February, he ascends the stepped road,  
> Having entered its fourth part, the twelfth light,  
> When the Reader counts for himself before the Kalends of March;  
> Compelled on every side, they consider the earth’s entrails  
> And deliberate how to search them with the mattock.]

On that day the ineffable favor of divine mercy first manifested this miracle to human eyes [Col. 0615C]. When the abbot and brethren approached to turn over the pavement stones, the stone that had been placed over the sacred monument, although no one pushed it, slid so violently to one side that, while the other stones remained immovably in place, one would have thought that it had yielded under the utmost exertion of those pushing it. Everyone understood that it had been driven back by the power of the sacred body, which seemed voluntarily to present itself to those piously seeking it.

Persisting, therefore, more firmly in the work, they at last reached the casket of the revered body. As they examined its interior with the reverent caution required, grains of the purest gold shone in one of the bones of the most holy confessor, increasing the miracle. I believe that they most clearly revealed a supremely rich treasure which, disclosed by the generosity of the divine gift, was being handled by the devout diligence of the faithful [Col. 0615D]. That night the holy relic remained in this condition and was honored with more sincere continuous praises and vigils.

When the following day began, the bishop took care to be present early. After solemn prayer had first been offered, he reverently approached the sacred tomb with the brethren, who devoted themselves attentively to psalmody and litanies [Col. 0616A]. Together with the abbot and priests, he reverently raised the holy bones, wrapped them in precious linens, and properly placed them in a very clean location. He carefully sealed it with his episcopal ring and, after completing the sacred rites according to custom, returned home [Note: [Col. 0615D] After this, the poet records two apparitions of Frodobert made to Abbot Bodo. In the first, on the seventh day [Col. 0616D] after the raising of the sacred body, Bodo is said to have been informed of the discovery of Frodobert’s true relics. In the second, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, Frodobert is said to have appeared to Bodo while he slept in the crypt and to have summoned the monk Arembert, distinguished in virtue and blood.].

### The One Who Struck His Mother Is Horribly Punished

31. From then onward, with tireless diligence, the arrangement and adornment of the sacred tomb were prepared with greater care. During the delay required for this, we believe that we must by no means omit what miracle the dispensation of heaven deigned to reveal through the outstanding confessor.

A certain man named Ratbert, a native of the district of Leudun, was quarreling with his mother in a field over the division of provisions. As he separated larger sheaves for his own portion while leaving the smaller ones to his mother, she, unable to bear the fraud, earnestly warned her son not to provoke God against himself by acting in such a way. Then the wretched man, inflamed in his furious heart, attacked his mother; grasping her hair with his left arm, he shamelessly dashed the unfortunate woman before his feet.

Divine vengeance immediately followed him. On the next night he was afflicted with blindness in his left eye, and his left arm was likewise so disabled that he was constantly agitating it backward and forward with restless movement, bearing witness to the consciousness of his crime through the very distress of the afflicted limb. Moreover, to increase the punishment, he was deprived of his senses and struck with miserable madness. His mother, exhausted by such cruelty, died a pitiful death on the third day.

For this most abominable crime he was brought by the local priest before Ægile, archbishop of the city of Sens [Col. 0616C]. By the archbishop’s order he was committed to prison and endured the squalor of the workhouse for three years. Eventually, as hunger grew stronger, he was released lest he die from wasting away through deprivation.

### After Visiting Many Shrines of the Saints, He Is Healed at Saint Frodobert’s

32. From there he hastened to the church of Saint Michael, at the place that from ancient times is called “At the Two Tombs” [Note: [Col. 0616D] By the same designation, “At the Two Tombs,” Odo of Glanfeuil designates Mount Saint Michael in the letter prefixed to the Life of Saint Maurus.]. Departing from there, he made for Rome, where Adrian [the Second] was then governing the apostolic see. When Adrian saw him going toward the church of Saint John called the Lateran, he was astonished at the wondrous spectacle of the object that the wretched man was carrying about because of his crime, and ordered him to be summoned before him. After investigating his case with great care, he kindly exhorted him to repentance and commanded him to go once more to the church of Blessed Michael and then to return again to him.

After being dismissed by him, Ratbert happened to enter the district of Troyes. One night he was warned in a dream to carry a candle equal to his own height to the basilica of the holy Mother and Virgin of God, Mary, situated in a village called Falcaria. Since he was unable to go there, being exhausted alike by labor and illness, he arranged to send it through an intermediary.

From there he happened to come to the monastery of Saint Peter, where the precious relics of Blessed Frodobert are venerated. On the Sunday following the Lord’s Ascension, while the priest was conducting the public sacred rites according to custom and Ratbert was engaged in prayer at the church door, he saw—as he later related—a certain cleric of youthful and handsome appearance approach him, seize him tightly around the waist, and shake his entire body with great force.

Thrown to the ground by this assault, he lay motionless for a long time, so that he was almost thought to be lifeless. During this interval he recovered the use of his arm, his senses, and the soundness of his head [Col. 0617B]. Then, rising and taking a draught of water, he fell asleep again because of his extreme weariness. He saw the same cleric he had seen before, who familiarly impressed these words upon him:

“This garment with which you are clothed, hang at Frodobert’s threshold.”

He was wearing only a hair shirt, as penitents do.

Troubled by these words, he confessed that he did not know where Frodobert’s house was and pleaded that he had no other garment. Meanwhile, one of the custodians awakened him. Anxious, he related what he had seen and eagerly asked where Frodobert’s house might be. When he discovered the church itself—before whose doors he had fallen and been restored to health—he was filled with indescribable joy. He rushed into the church, praising and giving thanks to the one through whose favor he had recovered his health and rejoiced that he had obtained relief from his most serious crime [Col. 0617C]. After depositing his hair shirt there, he hastened, in accordance with the apostolic command, to the church of the holy archangel Michael.

It was truly a wondrous event and one that should ordinarily be attributed to the proclamation of divine mercy: he was saved through the intervention of one whose name he had not even previously known. As soon as he learned the saint’s name by divine revelation, he recognized that through Frodobert’s merit he had recovered the health of both soul and body.

Moreover, during those same days, while preparations were being made for the deposition of the sacred body, many benefits came through his merit to the sick, especially to those who, afflicted by various fevers, humbly sought the aid of Blessed Frodobert.

### Translation of Saint Frodobert: 8 January

[Col. 0617D]

33. Meanwhile, as the succession of time passed, the Kalends of January came—the day on which, as we have said, he was released from worldly labors and flew up to the heights of the heavenly city. But because that day is especially devoted to the Lord’s Circumcision and does not permit another celebration to be eclipsed by its arrival, the dignity of Blessed Frodobert, if received on those same Kalends, seemed less celebrated and less solemn. The people, occupied with the ceremonies of the Lord’s feast, would not have had the freedom to gather at will for the joys of Blessed Frodobert.

Therefore the venerable and aforementioned bishop of the city of Troyes, after consulting with the abbot and brethren, judged it fitting that the celebration in question should be postponed for eight days [Col. 0618A], so that they might both safeguard the dignity of the feast and provide more wisely for the desire of the people, who even then were burning insatiably with devotion to the glory of Blessed Frodobert.

Accordingly, when the sixth day before the Ides of January arrived, after the nocturnal office had been completed, they raised the sacred body on devoted shoulders and carried it to the nearby church of Blessed Michael. They decided to do this so that a larger crowd of people might attend and so that the effect of the translation might be made more celebrated on the following day. There, after the matutinal hymns had been performed with greater solemnity, the bishop was invited by messengers sent by the abbot and brethren. Inflamed by the fervor already described, he promptly hastened to be present with a gathered company of clergy and people.

### More Favorable Weather Is Obtained

[Col. 0618B] 34. What miracle also occurred at that time will become clear from a concise account. The season was harsh, and, as winter conditions are, made difficult by widespread marshes. When the following night arrived, while the abbot and brethren were preparing what was necessary for the service of the forthcoming translation, he considered the watery condition of the season and anxiously discussed with himself the disturbance that might be caused by the arrival of the people.

“If only,” said the abbot to the brethren, “heavenly mercy, through the merit of this blessed Father, would bind the softness of the marsh with frost and moderate the difficulty of the journey by the arrival of snow.”

At once the Creator’s clemency received their devout desire and tightened the whole night with intense icy rigor. Around cockcrow, the earth was covered with such a mass of snow that it became plainly evident to everyone [Col. 0618C] that, through the protection of Blessed Frodobert, a suitable and practicable route had been prepared for the people to come and meet his translation.

### The Annual Solemnity of the Translation Is Prescribed

35. When all had been properly provided that the service of so great a day required, the bishop raised the precious mass of the body from the basilica of Blessed Michael. With the hymns lifted on high, it was carried into the church of the chief of the apostles amid such a display of joy and such rejoicing among the people that it became clearer than the sun that he possessed outstanding merit before God, since such great and immense glory shone among human beings.

The incomparable treasure of the most holy body was then placed in the prepared location. When all the ornaments of the tomb had been suitably arranged, an altar was consecrated at the head in honor of the Innocent Martyrs [Col. 0618D]. The worship of the sacred place was conducted with solemn offices, and by episcopal authority the privilege of its feast was established, to be observed unchanged in all succeeding ages. The entire day was spent filled with every joy, and those first services determined with what devotion it ought to be frequented by later generations.

36. Thus laden with so many benefits through the merits of Blessed Frodobert, we both offer and possess inexhaustible thanks and benefits to almighty God, who has deigned to prepare for us, his servants, a special patron of our people and our order. He made him both the founder and propagator of this place from its foundations, advanced it through his dwelling there, illumined it with most blessed examples, consecrated it by his most holy death, and, while alive, caused him to shine through the gift of signs. In death—or rather, happily immortal—he both gladdened his place by his presence, protected it by his patronage, and adorned it with unfailing miracles [Col. 0620A]. To him, the author, guide, and co-worker in all these things, immortal God, be perpetual glory, infinite victory, majesty, and everlasting dignity, from that time and now and forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0619]

# Life of Saint Mansuetus, First Bishop of the City of Toul  
### By Adso

## Prologue

*(In Martene, Thesaurus Anecdotorum, vol. III, p. 1013.)*

[Col. 0619B] To the holy and truly most blessed bishop Gerard, Adso, an unworthy servant of the servants of God, last among abbots, first among sinners: the gift of eternal redemption.

It is supported by sacred eloquence that, just as the power of commanding shines forth in holy prelates, so the devout willingness to carry out commands ought to shine forth in good subjects. For just as the former ought to be acquitted in the sight of divine majesty on account of their just commands, so the latter ought to be saved by an eternal reward when the fruit of obedience follows.

I, who am not untouched by this principle, have undertaken this work after being advanced by your command. I believe it will not be entirely displeasing to the reader, but it is entirely fearful to its author, because, just as the knowledge of past events is obscured by the passage of time [Col. 0619C], so certainty concerning present matters is unrestricted. What you commanded I humbly undertook; what you instructed me beforehand, I completed, however ineptly.

Receive, therefore, this little book composed at your command and gathered through my labor. In reference both to the dove descending upon and honouring the Lord and to the merits of the most blessed Mansuetus, whom you honour and love, I have determined that it be called “Dove-like,” so that it may be called dove-like, distinguished by the deeds of so great a Father.

## Meter by Adso in Praise of Saint Mansuetus the Bishop, to Be Sung Anywhere

The illustrious offspring of Mansuetus, born of a renowned lineage,  
Shone in the world through its own distinctions.

[Col. 0619D] The island of Ireland bore peoples who worship Christ;  
From there he drew his origin and from there he was born.

Of excellent character, he soon, honored by his companions,  
Shone forth in the tranquil pursuits of virtue.

When he reached his tender years with mature understanding,  
He spread throughout the world as a mirror of justice.

An ardor was in his spirit, exiled from his native fields,  
[Col. 0620B] Desiring to travel the Ausonian roads.

Peter flourished at Rome in the height of apostolic power,  
And Mansuetus, following him in love, willingly sought him out.

Peter received the ardent disciple of devotion  
And made the man a sharer in the sacred mysteries.

Touching the holy teachings from Peter’s mouth  
With devout words, he drank deeply of enduring aid from the fountain of salvation.

For a long time, diligent under the Ausonian master,  
He clung to Peter in loving obedience.

Peter raised him to the highest summit,  
And joyfully bestowed upon him episcopal dignity.

Then it pleased him to send proud Gauls as heralds,  
To instruct savage minds by word and faith.

Chosen men come forth from the Roman citadels, ready  
To wage battles for piety.

[Col. 0620C] Among them, O bishop, you are eminent under the name Mansuetus;  
Your rank shines forth in the distinction of your utterance.

They make for other cities in the regions of Gaul,  
Which the traversable world has so that it may seek their counsel.

You alone, Father, entered the rustic city of the Leuci,  
Trusting in the work of piety.

Ever watchful, with blessed Peter leading,  
So that the city of the Leuci might be numbered among the eternal sheep.

Through you the way of salvation first became known to us;  
Through you, Father, may our end everywhere be found.

But if the matter of assisting us deserves to be increased,  
May your companion Aper be equal to you in aiding us.

For you are twin pillars beneath the axis of heaven;  
From here you lead us, ready to raise up our flocks.

May confidence, therefore, now benefit our prayers,  
Which our hearts hold firmly within us.

O Mansuetus, we ask you to defend your faithful,  
And grant that we may be given long joys with the saints.

Be present also to our prayers, gentlest shepherd,  
So that your peoples may possess the blessed realms.

## Acrostic Verses on the Same Subject

[Col. 0621A]

Those whom once the angel of the great counsel  
Instructed through you, raising them to the fitting citadel of faith,  
And enriching them with the grace of his exalted name,  
May your mercy be theirs, since you are our apostle.

Grant that a heavenly dwelling may be given to us,  
So that, joined with all the elect throughout the ages,  
We may deserve, rejoicing forever,  
To praise, bless, magnify,  
And behold God with you.

# Life of Saint Mansuetus

*(In Dom Calmet, Histoire de Lorraine, vol. IV, Proofs, p. 84.)*

[Col. 0621]

## Book One

### Chapter One  
#### How Blessed Peter, Illustrious through Miraculous Powers at Jerusalem, First Sat at Antioch and Then at Rome, Pouring the Word of Life into the Roman World

[Col. 0621B]

After the glorious triumph of heavenly victory, by which the Creator of the ages, having conquered the enemy, entered the kingdom of heaven, the apostle Peter—chosen and designated for apostolic dignity by the presence of the Savior himself—deserved to receive the keys of heaven and to hold the governance of the universal Church.

When, as we read in ecclesiastical histories, he had first poured the rays of divine illumination upon Jerusalem and then upon the regions of Antioch, driving away the darkness of diabolical superstition through manifest truth, he resolved to extend and exalt the dignity of the Roman Empire under the title of Christianity and the standard of the holy [Col. 0621C] Cross. He therefore approached Rome, mistress of the world and head of the earth; and, as God ordained, he became the principal shepherd and teacher of the holy Catholic Church through the instruction of heavenly discipline.

Thus, where a multitude of different nations had converged, the sound religion of Christianity might grow more freely and more powerfully toward God. And when, with anxious care, he had flashed the rays of his holy preaching through the various regions of the earth like the brightest rays of the sun, gathering together crowds of believers, he strengthened them in the hope of eternal salvation. The fame of his holy name had been carried not only to neighboring peoples but also to foreign nations.

### Chapter Two  
#### On the Beginning of Blessed Mansuetus and How, Having Gone to Rome, He Sought the Presence of Blessed Peter the Apostle

[Col. 0621D]

At that time, as we learn from the testimony of Scripture, there was a young man of holy character named Mansuetus, born in transmarine regions from the distinguished stock of noble Scots, but marked far more richly by the nobility of an exceptional mind.

While he was still progressing through the years of tender youth, he was being advanced toward the height of holiness in accordance with the omen of his name, always striving to become nobler through an increase of piety, with his conduct corresponding to his name. Among his other pursuits of good works he was a true lover of innocence: setting aside his own advantage, he more willingly undertook the causes of others; he felt others’ misfortunes as his own; he sought union with gentle hearts, but more earnestly separation from harsh ones; admission into the purity of sanctification, and release from the preliminary course of baser frivolity; complete dedication to the weak and those overwhelmed by poverty; and the taking upon himself of the groans of the wretched [Col. 0622B].

There was in him such an infusion of virtue and piety that he became a source of salvation not only to himself but also to his parents. Moreover, with the effectiveness of his natural intelligence preceded by heavenly inspiration, he loved and pursued the discipline of literary learning so zealously that he had no equal among his fellow students in perceptiveness and no superior in these studies.

When the urgency of divine fervor was inspiring the young man’s mind under favorable auspices, he set out for Rome, where the Christian faith shone forth from the Roman heights under the distinguished name of the skill of Blessed Peter the Apostle [Col. 0622C]. He sought the presence of the one whom he desired with all his inmost being and, submitting himself in everything to the instruction of the apostolic teaching, fixed his eyes upon the one whose holiness he ardently desired.

With the proclamation of divine works going before him, he chose the foremost teacher of Catholic instruction, from whose fountain he might draw what he would later, as became clear, confirm through the truest testimonies.

### Chapter Three  
#### How Blessed Peter Chose Him, Together with Other Most Perfect Men, to Be Sent to Gaul

When Blessed Peter saw signs of future accomplishment and good virtues shining in him, and the brightness of heavenly illumination sparkling forth through clear indications [Col. 0622D], he took the blessed man more closely into his service for instruction in heavenly teaching, the power of confession having established him as a companion. For that most blessed shepherd of the universal Church, seeing the whole world—which he had received from the Lord Jesus Christ as entrusted to him—wrapped in the errors of demons and subject to them, appointed the most perfect heralds of the divine word.

These men, to be sent from him into Gaul and proven by the strength of constancy and the testimony of faith, were to free the peoples of Gaul, who were held under the yoke of the devil, and summon them to the sacraments of divine worship.

From this company [Col. 0623A] we have no doubt came Blessed Maternus, bishop of the city of Trier; Saint Sinicius of Rheims; Clement of Metz; Felix and Caelestis; and Memmius of Châlons. Along with these he had appointed this blessed man as a colleague in their shared ministry, since he had been instructed through long practice of apostolic eminence and had been thoroughly approved in all things through experience of heavenly teaching.

### Chapter Four  
#### How He Was First Ordained by Blessed Peter Himself, Entered Gaul, and Approached the City of the Leuci

Judging him worthy of greater dignity and grace, Peter fortified him with the privilege of episcopal authority, so that the sacrament of priestly office might precede the benefit of divine preaching [Col. 0623B].

The distinguished disciple therefore perfectly carried out the command of his teacher [alternative: “carries it out”]. Armed with the decree, equipped with eloquence, obedient in commands, and faithful in promises, he departed from Rome. Although separated from Blessed Peter in bodily sight through the long windings of the journey already mentioned, he remained united to him in mind. Voluntarily submitting himself to a distant pilgrimage for the kingdom of Christ, he entered among the citizens of the city of the Leuci, prepared to endure every kind of suffering.

That city, watered by streams, rich in pastures, pleasing in the circuit of its walls, and everywhere fortified with locks and towers, had nevertheless been thoroughly polluted and confused by the filth of idols. Entering the boundaries of that city with Christ as his guide and Blessed Peter’s authority going before him [Col. 0623C], he feared nothing from the barbarian multitude and began to preach to the peoples the sacrament of true faith and the worship of the Christian religion.

He taught that idols were vain, deaf, and mute; made by the hand and contrivance [alternative: cement] of human beings rather than existing from the beginning through true reason; possessing nothing divine; and having no connection with the blessed happiness that would follow this mortal life. Instead, they should worship the one God who had created the lands and seas, who held the heights of heaven under his dominion, and who after death would graciously grant bodies the capacity to live. The worship of so many false gods was a mockery of terrible vanity, a loss to souls, and nothing other than an incitement to everlasting torments.

### Chapter Five  
#### How He Earnestly Proclaimed the One True God to the King, the Queen, and the Leaders of the City

[Col. 0623D]

At that time the city in question was crowded with throngs of people, exceedingly rich in material resources, and filled with the commerce of varied goods. A pagan and barbarian king, named Leo, lived there with his wife. Ignorant of God, he and all his people were subject to the rites of idolatry.

When the arrival of the holy man and the preaching of the divine word that he was spreading among the people were reported to him, the king despised and rejected them and passed by the herald of the true eternal God with deaf ears. But the man of God resisted with persistent steadfastness. Near the walls of the city he prepared a small dwelling for himself and recalled all who came to him from the superstitions of demons to knowledge of the true God [Col. 0624A]. He chose rather to hand his body over to various tortures and punishments than to withdraw from the ministry of eternal salvation that he had undertaken at the command of his blessed apostolic teacher.

Thus he persevered unceasingly in the work he had begun. As many days passed in the task through his tireless diligence, frequent reports of this remarkable affair reached the queen. Her attendants and household servants added further details, saying that there was present a certain man who was a foreigner in homeland, unknown in lineage, unlike in speech, wholly different from them in face and dress, yet a worshiper of the Christian faith by his condition. He had come from Italy, from the one whom most of the Romans followed as the standard-bearer and pope of the true [Col. 0624B] faith, and he openly and constantly proclaimed that he had truly been sent by Peter, and proclaimed God, the maker of heaven and humankind.

As the pagan queen’s mind was in some measure moved to listen by the wonder of those reporting this strange event, and since she had free opportunity in the absence of her king, she used the privacy of her chamber to order the man of God to be brought in.

“What is this new religion,” she said, “hitherto unheard of by us, which you are eager to introduce over the worship of our two gods? You announce to us other beings to be worshiped, which until now have remained both unknown and neglected by our race.”

The blessed man understood the queen’s purpose in questioning him and hoped that life would be reborn in her. “There is one true God,” he said, [Col. 0624C] “distinguished in three persons: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. He is the unchangeable beginning of all things, the fountain and origin of blessings. From him the whole race of mortals received the beginning of existence. His power neither began to be nor will it ever cease.

“Through him a remedy of eternal redemption came to the world as it was perishing, after God and our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of the almighty Father, was sent from heaven to earth. He took human flesh through the womb of an inviolate Virgin, appeared visibly to mortals, and was manifested through many wondrous signs of power. Finally, in order to exclude the devil’s dominion, he was hung upon the cross through the unbelief of the Jews, by a voluntary dispensation of his plan; and through the price of his poured-out blood he released from the error of demons those whom he had predestined to become heirs of everlasting life.”

What more need be said? The queen believed, and, if the power of the pagan king had not stood in the way, she would not have ceased to be cleansed in the saving font, joined in lawful marriage. Nevertheless, whenever the circumstances and concerns of the queen permitted, while the king was occupied with other matters, she repeatedly summoned the man of God and earnestly directed her attention to the way of salvation that he clearly demonstrated.

### Chapter Six  
#### How the King’s Little Son Was Instructed in the Rite of His People; and Concerning the Estate Near the City to Which Wild Beasts, Driven by Dogs, Often Gathered

At that time they had a little son who was being instructed in the rite of his pagan parents. Although his tender childhood was still passing through the early years of nature [Col. 0625A], he nevertheless—as later events made clear—was for his parents the beginning and outcome of the belief and salvation that had been delayed for so long.

As we have said, the blessed bishop had chosen, within sight of the city, a remote place covered by the shadowy foliage of forests. There, giving himself more attentively to the Lord alone, he devoted himself to the work he had begun with continual prayers. Relying not only upon his own resources but also upon those of his teacher, the chief of the apostles, he shone through signs and virtues.

He was distinguished in appearance, gentle in conduct, mild in speech, strong in constancy, long-suffering in patience, outstanding in chastity, generous in acts of kindness, inclined toward the sufferings of the needy, prudent in counsel, full of mercy, devoted to the grace of hospitality, constant in prayer, devout in reading [Col. 0625B], abundant in tears, broken by compunction of heart, and proven and perfected in all his other good works.

Many experienced his virtue not only in great matters but also in small and humble events. For whenever, in hunting wild beasts, that class of people engaged in such exercises pursued any animals with the violence of dogs and came to the place where the man of God lived, you would see them stand motionless in astonishment and no longer press on toward the death of the quarry singled out for capture.

For this reason the royal power, often enraged, had determined that the holy bishop of the Lord should be slaughtered. Yet divine power preserved him unharmed amid barbarian weapons and the fiercest customs, so that he might instruct the people of the faithful and cleanse the city of the filth of idols [Col. 0625C]. It did not wish to bring his life quickly to completion through a brief martyrdom, but rather allowed him to remain through the long labors of time, bear more abundant fruit, and cross over to the kingdom of heaven while bringing back many kinds of gain for the ship of the Church that he was destined to steer.

### Chapter Seven  
#### Concerning the Boy’s Fall into the River Moselle and How Saint Mansuetus Complained in a Vision against Both Parents

Meanwhile an occasion arose for the king and a large multitude of pagans to celebrate a public gathering at their games and devote themselves to their customary amusements. While they were occupied with these activities, the only little son of the aforesaid king happened to fall from a wall on which he was then apparently standing [Col. 0625D]. At that point, where a hollow had been drawn back slightly—a bend that fortune had given the builders—the circuit of the wall had turned at an angle, and the boy slipped from the high place and fell by accident into the river Moselle.

The river, whose channel occupied the nearby places in its course, was then flowing close to the city walls. The depth of the waters there was so great that the skillful efforts of the men searching for the boy, who had been swallowed by this chasm, abandoned both art and hope.

The entire city rushed toward death. The country people raised a cry. The father and mother were brought back almost lifeless. Women’s laments resounded. The false gods were invoked in vain under their supposed names. The day turned into mourning, the games into misery, and the celebration into grief. Thus, with everyone exhausted by a twofold affliction of grief and toil, night fell and closed the day [Col. 0626A].

When, after so much labor, their exhausted limbs had been laid down on the bed, both parents were overcome by heavy sleep. Then suddenly, while the king’s wife was sleeping and the two were lying there, Blessed Mansuetus appeared to her in a vision and said:

“Rightly, O queen, are you troubled; rightly are you confounded; rightly are you performing the sad funeral of your son. For if you knew your Creator, and if you and your king had once placed faith in my words, you might have been free from this misfortune—or these events might have occurred in a far more salutary manner, while blessed rest received the soul together with the body of the one who was perishing.

“But what will you do now, if you should be permitted even to recover the body of the dead?”

She, for her part, vowed that she would do whatever he commanded. As she sought longer conversation with the holy man, however, his vision broke off in the midst of their words. She immediately awoke from sleep and told her husband in order everything she had seen.

Then he said: “If only I could obtain the presence of the one whom you call a holy man of God! For I promise that I will assent to his words, provided that through him I may obtain this one thing: that an inanimate corpse and limbs destined to be torn apart may not lack a grave in the whirlpool.”

## CHAPTER VIII  
That Blessed Mansuetus, sought for three days, is at last found; and when the place is shown to him and prayer has been offered, the boy is brought back over the waves and restored alive to his father.

Meanwhile, as night passed away, the following day dawned. The king’s officials searched for the holy man, but on that day he could by no means be found. The labor of those searching in vain continued until the third day, and now hope of finding him was almost abandoned. But as the third day dawned, the man of God was at last found at his own pleasure and presented before the king’s eyes. The king, laying aside the harshness of his former ferocity, said to him:

“O holy man of God, whom we rejoice to have come from foreign lands for our salvation, have mercy on a bereaved parent; have mercy on my dead child, who still lies beneath the waters of death. Now I stand prostrate and believing: I destroy the altars, overthrow the temples and images, reject all the fabrications of demons, avoid sacrificial blood, accept the faith that you proclaim, and promise to worship the God of heaven, whom the Roman world has now recognized through Peter’s teaching. I will subject both myself and my people to the divine laws, if through you I may only be deemed worthy to receive again the dead child whom, as is evident, I so trustingly lost.”

The holy man, who already certainly knew what he would do, moved by these words and pierced by these tears, while at the same time sensing that divine power was present with him for so great a harvest of peoples, ordered himself to be led to the place on the wall from whose summit the prince’s son had fallen and plunged into the whirlpool.

At that place he poured forth a prayer and, placing particular confidence in the Lord, devoted himself to earnest supplication. When the name of Christ had been invoked, before the eyes of all who had encircled the shore, the body of the fallen boy appeared and, drawn up from the depths, began to be carried over the waters. Quickly snatched from the waves, it was immediately brought before the feet of the blessed man.

“Behold,” he said to the father, “the lifeless body you requested. If, however, you resolve to fulfill what you promised, divine mercy will also be present, able to grant you far greater things. For I came for this purpose; for this purpose alone I undertook my pilgrimage: that through me the gate of the heavenly kingdom might be opened to you. Sent by the prince of the apostles, I pursue the affairs of your salvation; rejoicing in the gain of souls, I seek it.”

Then the father and all who were present unanimously professed that, having renounced their idols, they would become worshipers of the true God if the one who lay lifeless were shown, with his spirit returning, to be able after death to breathe again among the living.

At this point the holy bishop, always filled with the deepest compassion, understood through the Spirit that what was being requested had to be accomplished. Again bending his knee, he prostrated himself on the ground to beseech the divine Majesty in prayer, and he urged the Christians who happened then to be very few in number to do the same, preparing them by his heavenly exhortations [perhaps: “forewarning them”]. When the prayer had been completed, the dead man was suddenly shaken in his limbs by the breath of life; at the holy man’s command he was raised to his feet, and, to the amazement of all, restored unharmed to his father.

## CHAPTER IX  
That, at the boy’s resurrection, all began to weep for joy, and concerning the places of punishment to which he had been assigned.

Then all who had gathered for this spectacle began, at the manifest power of God, to weep for joy, to confess the name of Christ together, and to declare that he above all must be worshiped—he who gave the breath of life to all mortals, who restrains the spirits of the dead by the command of his will after their deadly funerals, and who, whenever he wishes, orders them to be recalled above into living bodies.

Then the faithful priest of the Lord turned to the resurrected boy and said:

“Come nearer, and tell your parents yourself what you saw and where you were; make it plainly known to everyone at once.”

Then he, as though newly emerging from the underworld and rising from its shadows, opened his mouth at the bishop’s command, drew deep sighs from his tender breast, and freely began to declare what he had experienced and seen while placed in hell: many and innumerable kinds of torment; serpents flourishing amid the fire-belching flames of Tartarus; immense multitudes of the guilty subjected to different punishments; and the spirits of the wretched, constrained between flames and cold, failing amid their shrieks and, because of that very failing, being renewed again for living fires.

There, he said, there was no recovery to life, but only forgetfulness of every good thing and the unspeakable torment of present punishments. To that place the king and queen themselves, and all who were present, would doubtless come unless they believed the words and deeds of the blessed bishop and submitted their necks to the Christian faith. He himself had been led to those same places of punishment and assigned to the darkness of eternal condemnation, unless the blessed confessor of Christ’s swift intercession had come to his aid—an intercession that rescued him from the evil spirits and the bars of hell and recalled him to the regions above.

## CHAPTER X  
That, after the boy was baptized, all cast down their idols, received the sacrament of baptism together, and by unanimous vote established Blessed Mansuetus in the episcopal seat.

[Col. 0628A]

After recounting these and many similar things, the weeping boy prostrated himself at the feet of the holy man and humbly and devoutly declared that he wished to be washed in the fountain of salvation. He urged his father and mother, and the others for whom he had been especially concerned, to do the same, by whatever exhortations and counsels he could offer. He said that their bishop had been appointed by God for the city, had come for the salvation of its citizens, and had been chosen by divine arrangement and apostolic institution as a holy shepherd, ruler, and guardian of souls; through his coming, he and the whole city together would be saved.

Then, amid the boy’s words and the most evident power of his resurrection, all were astonished by the extraordinary miracle of so great a novelty. Seeing the manifest power of God, which none of them could resist or in any way oppose, they rejected the idols, overturned the altars, cast down all the workshops of the devil, and, stretching out their hands, began together to invoke the name of Christ and to resound with praises in heaven.

Then, bursting forth in loud voices, they all humbly requested the sacrament of baptism, which they had previously stubbornly refused. After first being instructed by the blessed bishop, according to Catholic discipline, in the rule of the holy faith, they then received the grace of baptism: the king and queen, their entire household, the whole military order, and the entire multitude of country people. And there was great joy in that city.

Then the whole throng of the baptized, together with the heavenly companies praising Christ, having obtained a new kind of redemption and been stripped of the squalor of the ancient serpent’s covering, marveling at the divine power and magnificently proclaiming the glorious merits of Blessed Mansuetus, with equal vote and equal agreement chose the holy man as supreme ruler and just shepherd of the whole Church. He had come for the salvation of the entire people; by the election of the whole people he was to hold the rights of a shepherd. Thus all acclaiming him as worthy, glorious, and in every respect beneficial to the citizens, they established him in the seat of pontifical honor—not now as a foreigner, but as their own shepherd, endowed with the privilege of apostolic dignity.

## CHAPTER XI  
That the king ordered the word of salvation to be proclaimed throughout every part of his dominion, and that Blessed Mansuetus, manifested by signs and virtues, built two basilicas within the walls of the city.

[Col. 0628D]

Then the king and his princes, now grounded in the Catholic faith, ordered the word of salvation to be brought far and wide to everyone throughout the boundaries of their dominion. Thus, whether willingly or unwillingly, they were to be converted in truth or driven from their homeland, and no one was to remain within it who was either not baptized or not instructed in the faith so as to be baptized.

Thus the man of God, first consecrated bishop at Rome, and afterward—as the preceding words make clear—raised to the summit of the episcopate of the city of the Leuci by the general acclamation of the peoples, through signs and wonders, cannot be adequately described in speech: so many and such great things he deserved to be freed from by divine aid. Mercy and piety were always present on his lips and in his mind. Episcopal authority did not loosen the restraints of his former strictness and abstinence; he often completed his nights and days in uninterrupted prayer. He so restrained the movements of his spirit with gentleness that, although he knew how to show mercy, he did not know how to grow angry. He was kind to all and merciful to all.

He bore the sufferings of those who came to him in such a way that whoever arrived in grief returned much more joyful, having been thoroughly consoled. He freely cured the illnesses of those who were suffering, not only through his own intercession but also by the authority received from the blessed apostle Peter. Thus he was truly recognized among the peoples as a shepherd and a physician of salvation.

As can easily be found by the diligent reader in his deeds, which were written long before our time, after the same city of the Leuci had been cleansed, as we have said above, of all the superstitious filth of idols, he built within the city walls a temple for the Lord, in honor, namely, of Mary, Mother of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the perpetual Virgin, as well as of the holy protomartyr Stephen. He built another temple beside it, on the southern side, which he dedicated with the solemn attendance of the people in honor and veneration of Saint John the Baptist, at the place called “At the Fountains.”

Afterward he built very many churches throughout the entire province of his diocese. Priests and deacons were appointed there, and divine praise was rendered to the divine Majesty; God, admirable in his saints, is glorified there even to the present day.

At the place where, on his first arrival, he had prepared for himself, as we said, a dwelling in the suburb of the city, he diligently supplied the flock entrusted to him with the daily nourishment of the divine word in the city. At night, however, so that he might devote himself more freely to prayer, he returned to that same dwelling, as though to a habitation privy to his secrets. There, through an abundance of tears, he washed away whatever, while occupied with the salvation of others, he had attended to less perfectly during the hours of the day.

## CHAPTER XII  
That the citizens of Toul are the sign of his apostleship in the Lord, and concerning the constancy and teaching of the blessed apostle Peter.

[Col. 0629D]

Thus, as we have said, the divine worker, persisting without interruption in such great labors through the long exercise of time, could not grow weary, for the fervor of the Holy Spirit inflamed him. According to the Apostle’s saying, even if he was not an apostle to others, he was truly an apostle to this people (1 Cor. 9:2). He acquired them for God through so many signs and virtues and through so many sweat-filled labors and exertions. Although we have perceived that much is lacking in our conduct and conversion—things which that blessed man both taught and cultivated—we are nevertheless all the signs of his apostleship in the Lord (ibid.), because what he received from the very beginning of the holy and universal Church, he afterward poured out upon our people with free authority, armed more with faith than with iron.

Moreover, the blessed apostle Peter, who was chosen first among the number of the apostles, became the confessor of the Son of God, was chosen shepherd of the human race, foundation of the Church, keeper of the keys of the kingdom of heaven, approved by his confession of Christ the Lord, and afterward crowned through his passion. He had completely filled Galatia, Pontus, Cappadocia, Bithynia, Asia, and Italy with evangelical teachings.
