When, under the earlier Claudius Caesar, he had first firmly established the church of Antioch in the Catholic faith and had governed it for seven continuous years, he arrived, taught by the Holy Spirit, to pursue Simon Magus. Simon, fleeing everywhere from the truth of apostolic instruction, attempted to stain the rays of sound teaching with his own darkness. Peter entered Rome in pursuit of that same Simon Magus and, made pastor of the Church by the choice of the faithful, held the primacy of that city for twenty-five years while preaching the Gospel.

According to the histories, against his most illustrious preaching Simon, having indeed become a member of Antichrist, rose with savage mouth. Trusting in the audacity of Nero and the prefect Agrippa, he did not cease to attack the apostolic assertion with the perversity of his falsehood. Therefore, having attempted through magical arts to ascend into heaven, while he was being carried through the air he fell madly to the ground through the power and prayer of the blessed apostle Peter, to be dashed to pieces. After these events, by Nero’s command, he was proscribed in the city of Rome in the thirty-sixth year after the Lord’s passion and, as he himself had wished, was crucified head downward. Peter, having earned the apostolic reward, entered the realms of the heavenly heights, crowned with the glorious blood of martyrdom.

## CHAPTER XIII  
Concerning the death of the blessed man.

[Col. 0630C]

Hearing, as a most faithful disciple, of the passion of his master, the blessed Mansuetus—whose passion deservedly is recalled throughout the whole world—founded a more noble church at the place where, as we have said, he had for a time been lodged not far from the city. Establishing it in honor and memory of the blessed apostle Peter, unquestionably his teacher, he consecrated it with the blessing of Peter’s sacred relic, which he is said to have brought with him. There, when the duty of preaching had been performed, he would fittingly come, desiring to devote himself to God alone; spending many subsequent years gathering multitudes of the faithful into the faith of Christ, he sent them ahead to the fellowship of the angels.

When the athlete of God, chosen and now full of days and advanced in age, had been exhausted by the many daily labors of good works and exercises of toil that we have mentioned, and had been greatly distinguished by virtues and miraculous signs, like a faithful and prudent servant who had distributed to the household of the Lord its measure of wheat at the proper time (Luke 12:32), he was summoned by the Lord’s command to receive the reward of eternal recompense. Having laid aside the burden of the flesh, he gave back his spirit to heaven on the third day before the Nones of September, and received the robe of blessed immortality, destined to reign forever with his Lord.

There he now rejoices, mingled with the companies of angels, and has become a much more excellent and powerful intercessor for his sheep who still dwell on earth. It is impossible now to say how great a multitude of the faithful gathered for the solemn procession of his burial—those whom, through the grace of the Holy Spirit, he himself had transformed by the urgency of his labor into adopted children.

You would have seen enormous crowds of people surrounding the sad funeral of their own father and shepherd, no longer of a foreigner and stranger, and the mournful funeral rites shining everywhere in a kind of ordered confusion, encircled by those who wept and grieved. Thus, amid the procession of those going before and following, the lifeless body was carried to the place of burial and most worthily committed to the tomb in the place where, as we said, he had dedicated a church in honor and memory of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles.

Where he had completed the course of so many struggles and labors, there, by the Lord’s arrangement, he wished his body to have its proper burial. From that time until now, by virtue of his merits, divine power has illuminated that place with signs and miracles for the praise and glory of its own name, so that it may be shown how brightly in the sight of eternal glory in heaven shines the one who daily flashes forth before mortal eyes through the wonder of such great virtues.

Let us, his merits being our intercessors, who are his sheep and flock, venerate his glorious merits with humble devotion and due honor, so that through his interceding merits we may deserve to rejoice with him without end. Now also, since we have learned in part the end of his life and conversion while he lived in the flesh, we have judged it worthy to insert briefly into this narrative who his successor was.

## CHAPTER XIV  
Concerning Saint Amon, who succeeded the blessed man in the episcopate.

[Col. 0631C]

After the glorious passage from this world to heaven of the blessed Mansuetus, the first bishop of this city, as is found in the deeds of the earlier bishops of the city of the Leuci, Saint and most blessed Amon, by the merciful providence of God, was ordained bishop in this see by the common vote and agreement of all and became the successor of the blessed man. He followed the character and institutions of his predecessor to the letter, and it cannot be adequately expressed how greatly he was proved by his works to possess goodness and holiness.

For, surpassing others in every moral excellence befitting episcopal dignity, he not only cultivated the people entrusted to him appropriately on every side through words and examples, but also illuminated them by marvelous and magnificent virtues. Thus, when he bestowed splendor on the celebrations and adorned the times, as it is written (Ecclesiasticus 47:12), he departed from this world at the completion of his life in the oratory which, as we said above, had been carefully built by the holy man in honor of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. There he was fittingly buried with that most holy predecessor of his.

From that time, through the merits and intercessions of both men, the same place has visibly shone with magnificent miracles for the praise of the divine name. The eyes of the blind, oppressed by long darkness, received the desired light after the darkness had been driven away; those languishing under various plagues were freed; many whose nerves were contracted crawled along the ground; and very many afflicted with different and innumerable illnesses rejoiced that, through the intervention of these men, they had carried the joys of health back to their homes.

We read that kings and princes frequently flocked to their patronage and devoutly brought many gifts through their men to relieve the need of the servants of God and the poor. At different times, remarkable signs of virtue were also displayed through the merits of both men. But whether because of the incursions of barbarian peoples or certainly because of the scarcity of writers, these accounts have undoubtedly been omitted or lost. We also know that this city, because of the enormity of the crimes of its inhabitants, was devastated together with the Vandals’ possessions by the persecution of cruel men and afterward burned by the savage ambushes of the ancient enemy in conflagrations of fire.

[Col. 0632B]

This, however, must not be suppressed in silence: it was faithfully reported to us by certain people. Saint Martin, bishop of Tours, most famous throughout the whole world, as is well known, had been very intimate with Saint Maximin, bishop of Trier, so that they often enjoyed conversations together and, when traveling together to Rome to visit the blessed Peter, supported one another with mutual conversations along the way.

Thus, when blessed Martin had arranged to undertake this journey at a certain time, he entered the oratory of the blessed Mansuetus, to which he had turned aside in order to implore divine mercy. Devout as he was, he entered; and suddenly the spirit of a certain holy girl, a religious woman whose body had not long before been buried at that place, repeatedly called the holy man’s name from the tomb.

When the blessed man attended to her prayers, she immediately continued:

“Most holy bishop, mighty in heaven and on earth, have mercy on the soul of the buried woman. Her body is indeed covered here by the earth, but her spirit still languishes in punishments. Bring the patronage of the most holy Mansuetus and your own to her aid. You may believe that she has been saved when, on your return, you no longer hear the voice of the supplicant.”

Then he departed and undertook the journey he had begun, especially concerned to help the woman who had made this request. When the entire journey had been completed and, on his return, he did not pass by the burial place of the most blessed Mansuetus, as was his custom, and perceived no further signs of the deceased woman’s petition, he gave thanks to the Savior, for he recognized that she had been saved through the intervention of both men.

For how could she have perished, to whom the immense mercy of God had granted such intercessors? These events having taken place, since we are turning toward other matters, let us also bring these to an end according to our purpose.

It also seemed not inappropriate to insert the following, which, spread abroad by frequent testimony, still circulates on the lips of many. It was customary for many people to come to these regions from the overseas lands of the Scots. Among them, at that time, a certain poor man is said to have arrived with his wife. For the fame of ancient times had stirred many to seek a very holy man of their own people, as was customary for the Scots when they traveled abroad.

This man, conscious—as the rumor went—of affection and favor, had obtained lodging not far from the church of the holy man and wished to remain there. He possessed very little household property. Among his modest domestic resources, he customarily kept a small pig, of no great size, to be used for his future food.

But, as commonly happens amid so great a multitude of people, when he had been absent for some time and saw that his dear little animal was missing, the poor man understood that it had been stolen. Since he could nowhere discover the identity of the thief and could not bear the loss he had suffered, he went to the sacred church. With a spirit inflamed—as is characteristic of the Scots—he threw himself sorrowfully upon the saint’s tomb, full of complaints, and, to speak in rustic words, said:

“O holy man of God, I say, a Scot—your Scot and mine—have mercy on me and on the Scottish people. Perhaps you ought to help me, who have been placed at a distance. Behold, as I live abroad, why do you allow me to suffer such deprivation? Why do you permit me to be left without my possessions? Restore, I beg you, what I have lost; restore what the wicked thief perhaps is already consuming.”

After continuing with many such words, the poor man returned sadly to his lodging.

[Col. 0634A]

Meanwhile the greedy thief had already strangled the wretched animal with a knife and rejoiced in the hope of filling his belly with the spoils he had stolen. But the holy man did not long delay answering the complaints of his poor servant. While the dead animal was being concealed in hiding, through the saint’s power, when its breath returned, it was raised to its feet and forcibly snatched from the thief’s house. Entering the stable of its companion, it was restored alive and unharmed to its own master, to the great amazement of many.

Thus the presumption of the wicked thief was mocked; thus the poor man was refreshed in the midst of the grave misfortune he had suffered; and thus the evident power of Saint Mansuetus was shown to be marvelous not only in the greatest matters but also in humble ones, provided that he is petitioned with faith. If anyone wishes to be incredulous about this event, it will make no difference to us, since, if it should please one to inquire into it, it may still be corroborat— [text breaks off].

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 0633]

## CHAPTER XV  
Here begins the little work of the following book, concerning the things accomplished through him after his death.

[Col. 0633B]

Since, in the completion of the preceding work, we briefly explained a few things out of many, insofar as divine sublimity had granted to our lowliness what was needed to renew them in the memory of the present age—namely, those things which he performed by the power of God while he remained in the body—we now turn the zeal of our undertaking toward those events that took place in our own age, omitting here what either negligence or the apathy of long antiquity has left untold or neglected.

We present these matters with all the greater confidence because we undoubtedly hold that they occurred nearer to our own time; especially since, first indeed … or, as we have said, with the … savagery of barbarian peoples breaking in, or likewise through the celebrated conflicts of peoples against one another, as the ages succeeded one another, that same place had been deprived of its possessions, its fortifications destroyed, and reduced almost to nothing, [Col. 0633D] frequently also subjected to the rule of secular men.

Meanwhile, after a long succession of time had passed, following Drogon, the illustrious bishop of the city of the Leuci, Lord Goslin, born of the most noble Frankish lineage, distinguished by piety and religion and especially well educated in literary studies, was chosen by the providence of God and ordained bishop in this see. He carefully instructed the clergy, gathered prudent men from every quarter, enriched the city in material resources, adorned it with wisdom, and fortified it through prudent administration.

Considering this place, which, as we have said, had fallen into ruin through various misfortunes, he summoned to himself Lord Herchembold, a venerable father from the place of Saint Aper, the distinguished confessor of Christ, whom he himself had previously appointed abbot there, and entrusted this place to him to be restored to the order of religion.

That venerable man, being exceedingly religious, assigned some monks under the authority of the provosts; and because stipends were lacking there at that time, he arranged for them to be supported at the expense of his own monastery.

## CHAPTER XVI  
Concerning a certain blind woman who was given sight before the door of Blessed Mansuetus.

During the time of the aforementioned most blessed bishop of the Lord, Gauzlinus, while this same place was under the guardianship of the provosts, as we have said, it is enough to relate a few of the many things that happened in its vicinity and came to us by sight or hearing.

Many people knew Wido, count of this city. He had a small settlement not far from the city; because he himself had built it, it has retained Wido’s name to the present day. A certain female servant of his lived there who had remained blind for seven years. She possessed both a husband and children more as sources of accusation than of help. Entirely unaware of what she should do, unfortunate and exposed to the contempt of everyone, especially her own family, she was subjected to her present poverty.

Meanwhile the day approached on which the annual joys of the feast of Blessed Mansuetus were expected on the following day. Enduring her hostile blindness, she joined the crowds who were streaming together, relying on a stranger to guide her. Weeping, she entered the house of the blessed bishop, invoked the friend of the divine Majesty, and, pouring out tears, entreated the mercy of the gentle shepherd to assist her.

As she wished to spend the night in the oratory, she was excluded, together with the others, by the provost of the church. She kept vigil before the door, which was blocked by the crowds, placing her trust in him toward whom she had directed her entire mind.

Then, in the middle of the night, she gave thanks to God in a loud voice and declared that, through the intervention of the saint, burning lamps had become visible to her.

“Ah, holy man of God,” she said, “you have given sight to the blind, strengthened the weak, and comforted the sorrowful. From now on count me as serving your worship, since you have displayed your power upon me.”

Thus she who had come relying on another’s guidance returned freely proclaiming to everyone the Author of the light that had been granted to her.

## CHAPTER XVII  
Concerning a woman who was healed after being tormented by demons and losing her reason.

A certain soldier named Stephen, not among the least distinguished of his peers, lived in the countryside not far from the city. He had a daughter by his wife, whom he loved with tender affection. But, as the enemy commonly pursues what is dearer, confounds what is chosen, and breaks into what is unwary, the devil, as the girl’s sins required, entered the vessel of the girl, confused her mind, took away her strength, and utterly emptied her reason.

Bound with restraints and surrounded by guards, she was brought by her parents, who had invoked the patronage of the saints, at last to the oratory of Saint Mansuetus. She was allowed to spend the night inside the basilica, while one person remained awake and the others were weighed down by sleep.

From the part where she lay upon the ground, demons wandering above the roof of the church—marvelous to relate!—filled the air with the cries of howling and various sounds imitating beasts. They complained publicly that they had nothing in common with the saint and that they could in no way bring back the gift of salvation which they had deservedly taken away.

The man who was keeping watch was terrified and woke the others, so that they too might hear the voices that he heard. But after openly mocking them for several hours, the demons departed in fear and fled; they abandoned the girl and immediately vanished through the power of the saint. The girl rose free, and, with her reason restored, marveled within herself at the enemies to whom she had been handed over.

## CHAPTER XVIII  
Concerning a leper who was healed.

At another time, a certain man struck by the disease of elephantiasis, whose skin, like snow, displayed a penitential appearance, trembling throughout his body, judged that he ought to seek the help of Blessed Mansuetus.

When he had arrived there, the provost of the church appeared to be standing before the doors. As the man wished to fall at his feet, he seemed to indicate what he wanted and what he was seeking.

But he said:

“Alas for me, wretched man, somehow alive yet dead in every limb beforehand, whose life is spent in punishments, whose flesh is constricted by deadly anguish! I have come so that, even if I am not worthy, I may at least touch some small remedy through the benefit of the saint and the divinity.”

The elder, adopting the appearance of one making a demand, said to him:

“What do you have to offer as a gift?”

Immediately displaying the upper part of the garment with which he was covered, the man replied:

“Behold, I have a little salt, given as a gift through the mercy that relieves poverty.”

“Go,” said the elder, “take it and bring it in as an offering to the sacred place.”

Thinking that what he had heard spoken in a jesting manner had been seriously commanded to him, the man hurried into the church, poured the gift of salt before the altar, and prostrated himself in prayer. As he lay upon the ground, he suddenly felt as if the footstep of someone passing had been impressed upon his back.

He quickly rose, and, seeing no one anywhere around, returned to the elder. Already healed, with his color restored to its former state, he rejoiced that he had cast off the badly whitened skin.

## CHAPTER XIX  
Concerning a cleric rescued from fevers.

It is … [lacuna] that this blessed man … [lacuna] also very often bestowed a remedy of the health sought. To repeat a familiar example, we saw a person of no mean rank among the clergy according to worldly standing. When the great force of fever inflamed him with extraordinary intensity, so that he spent many days and nights without food, already almost given up for dead, he was carried by the hands of servants to the sacred church. Bedding was arranged beside the blessed man’s altar, and he was carefully laid down to keep vigil.

After remaining in that place for two days, when the burning fever had been driven away, he perceived the help of the healing medicine so clearly that he returned home safely and freely, whereas he had previously been carried there suffering the fiery torments of illness.

Nor was this the only instance in which the power to drive out such illnesses was displayed. Indeed, we very often saw people oppressed by this anguish implore the help of the holy bishop, and it happened that they joyfully carried home the desired gift of health. If such swift healing has not come to someone, let him know that either he is not worthy of it or, rather, that it has been postponed for his advancement.

At almost the same time, … [lacuna] a very well-known soldier … [lacuna] had been born; he too fully experienced the favor of this holy bishop. Although he was energetic and ready in military affairs, he was no less distinguished in faith and goodness.

When the plague of fevers attacked him, he was brought almost to the point of death. Having lost all the strength of his body, he saw that nothing remained for him except approaching death. With his mind confused, he considered what most ought to be done. Hating food that sustains life and unable to endure rest, he thought only of death.

Then, amid the deadly breaths of the fever and the shrill points of the burning fire, the thought came to him to seek refuge in this saint and, with vows going before him, to implore his aid. He was therefore brought, carried with the assistance of servants. Entering the venerable church, he placed a bond around his neck, dedicated himself freely as a servant to the saint, and vowed to pay an annual due on a fixed day.

That night he kept vigil prostrate before the altar. On the following day, during the solemn celebration of the Mass, he was freed from the livid fury of the illness and returned free and sound to the home from which he had been carried there. Afterward he did not forget the benefit of his rescuer, through which he had so manifestly deserved to be released from those torments.

Moreover, we remember having seen innumerable people worn down by afflictions of this kind who, their entire bodily strength consumed by shrieking flames and thinking only of death, returned home healthy and unharmed through the merits and power of this holy man. If we wished to recount all these things fully, our time would run out before all his great deeds could be contained in writing.

Nevertheless, if we desire to be advanced through the merits of this protector of ours and assisted by his benefits, it is not fitting that we should be counted as strangers to his praises and service. This can easily be recognized from a single event, which we have considered appropriate to add.

At a certain time, as is customary among country people, a considerable number of peasants from the region of Bar—forming a group, taking wagons and supplies—had gone to the villages of Salins (Vic-aux-Salines). Having carried out their purchases of goods for sale and wishing to return home, they brought back their salt merchandise. When they had completed most of their journey, crossed the village of Gundulf (Gondreville), and reached the bank of the Moselle with their wagon, the peasants, filthy from their labor, became somewhat entangled by the necessity of crossing the river.

The inhabitants of that place harshly rebuked them for spending that day laboring at wheeled tasks during the annual feast celebrated that day in honor of so great a Father, as though with rustic minds they were unwilling to share in the common joy.

The peasants, in turn, responded with mockery, saying that these sacred observances did not concern them and that they had nothing in common with this celebration, which they knew to be owed only to the people of the Leuci and to be honored by their civic vows.

As they persisted stubbornly in this attitude, divine vengeance followed. I shall relate something marvelous: such sudden madness came upon the miserable animals that they attacked one another with clashing horns and struck great terror into all who saw them.

The unfortunate peasants, almost departing from human reason, wandered about in every direction, while the oxen, driven mad, paid the penalty for the offenses of their masters. But those in whom some strength of mind remained quickly burst into the church of the blessed bishop, publicly confessed their guilt, and bound themselves by vows and prayers, promising that they would be more cautious in the future if, rescued from their present punishments, they could return freely.

The holy man did not delay in hearing the voices of the mourners. He restored the wretched herd to them and granted them the ability to depart.

By the intervention of the aforementioned lord Bishop Gozlin, a certain Grimauldus, a man venerable for his way of life, once taken from the devout community of the monks of Saint Aper, had been appointed rector and provost of that place by the command of his abbot. He had deservedly been dear to everyone, distinguished by the chief honors of obedience, and esteemed for his excellence in monastic discipline. [Col. 0637D] He therefore enjoyed, for necessary household uses, the assistance of a single cow; this animal, in particular, regularly rendered the household useful service in preparing vegetables. But one day, when it was expected at the proper hour and was not there, the servants searched diligently through various places. It is uncertain by whose fraudulent scheme the animal had been led away. Then the provost said to the servant who had just arrived, grieving, to report the loss to the household: “Go, then, tell that saint who makes use of our services that, if he now wishes to share in our service and assistance, he should quickly restore the necessary animal, which has been taken away by an unjust fraud.” His words did not fall in vain. For on the following day, the same animal, recovered from its thief under bonds, is said to have been swiftly restored to its own stall [Col. 0638A] by the power of the blessed bishop.

The aforementioned lord Bishop Gozlin, of glorious and eternally blessed memory, approved by pious and most holy works, full of days and distinguished by good virtues, as he completed the course of his life, was carried away, amid the great grief and mourning of all, in the forty-fourth year of his episcopal office by clergy and people to the monastery at Buxières, which he himself had built from the foundations long before. There he received the most worthy burial, as he had ordered while alive, among the choirs of virgins whom he had gathered there in considerable number under a stricter discipline of life, to be honored through long ages in the praises of God. His day of deposition is observed on the seventh day before the Ides of September, under the patronage of Mary, Mother of God [Col. 0638B] and perpetual virgin, who endures forever.

## CHAPTER XX  
### Concerning the deeds accomplished through the merits of the blessed Mansuetus in the time of Lord Bishop Gerard

So that the truth and order appropriate to our history may now be maintained, by the preceding grace and power of this most holy and undefiled virgin Mary, and also through the blood of the blessed protomartyr Stephen, on whom the whole city rests, the entire people are sanctified and governed by their merits. This same city of the Leuci, as has been said, was deprived of its ruler, but by God’s arrangement was not allowed to be ruined for long. For, with divine grace favoring the prayers of both orders of the faithful, by the decree of the unconquered victor, namely the lord Otto Augustus, [Col. 0638C] and through the agency of his brother, the lord Bishop Bruno, Gerard, born in the city of Cologne, distinguished by birth among the clergy and by religious observance, was designated as the future bishop of the deserted city of the Leuci. Since he was thoroughly educated in ecclesiastical institutions, while the Lord and Savior reigns forever, in the year 963 from his holy Incarnation, with all the faithful acclaiming unanimously, he was enthroned and installed in this same see.

When, therefore, he first approached the city entrusted to him, he entered the oratory of the blessed Mansuetus, which happened to lie in his path. At his first entrance, by divine prompting, as is believed, the thought came into his mind that there he had marked out for himself, according to the Prophet’s prediction, a rest forever and ever and a chosen dwelling, in the course of that same verse (Psalm 131:14). As is plainly evident, this became for him, with regard to that place, both an occasion of greater devotion and an increase of salvation. For, after the administration of suitable affairs had been arranged, and not long afterward, on the advice of Huncbert, abbot of praiseworthy memory, who at that time gloriously governed the monastery of Saint Aper—whose name, as we hope and desire, is fixed in the book of blessed life—and with the consent of his faithful, he appointed as abbot and rector of that place a man named Adam, of good reputation, shining in character, and well disciplined in words and deeds. From the possessions that appeared to belong to him, he suitably enlarged the place and faithfully instructed the number of those serving God [Col. 0639A] according to the discipline of regular life.

When these things had thus been accomplished, since they are clearly established and [lacuna]—as we continue the sequence of the history begun—let us briefly explain all the works accomplished through the power of the blessed Mansuetus during the time of the present lord Bishop Gerard.

With the rains suspended from heaven, a great sterility, hostile to crops and unusual for that time, had settled upon the barren fields. Then, as the earth cracked open and the laborers’ efforts were almost burned up by excessive heat, cultivation of the scorched earth perished—horrible to say!—and, as the Lord’s scourging had long before demonstrated in punishment of an unfaithful people, the sky above threatened the appearance of bronze, while below the cruel earth displayed one of iron. As this judgment of heavenly wrath grew more evident day by day, the bishop ordered a three-day fast for the people, exhausted by the heat. Since it is not easy to resist divine punishment, they requested that the body of the holy man be carried to the boundaries of the parched fields, so that it might mercifully be set against their drying condition.

Why say more? With the lord bishop and the entire people present, it was brought out from the place where it had long lain. They raised their voices on high; praising God, they resounded with heavenly hymns. Then, as lamentations proceeded around the blessed Mansuetus, a great crash suddenly thundered from the heavens, so that it broke through the voices of those singing and filled the hearts of all with astonishment, showing the divinity of him whose body was being carried on earth. Thus, while the multitude—nearly two thousand people, or even more, who had gathered from everywhere that day [Col. 0639C]—stood amazed, they were led to the place of Saint Aper to which they had decided to go. The clear, sultry sky, which seemed to scorch the earth while Sirius burned, immediately began to thicken into dense clouds, and, when abundant rains fell, it fully supplied the grace of the requested moisture.

What happened meanwhile must not be passed over in silence.

Among this great multitude that had gathered to witness so remarkable a spectacle was Sindebauldus, then count of this city. Together with a certain Immo, a soldier of no little distinction belonging to the lord bishop, he asked to be placed beneath the relics of the holy man as they were being carried. His hand, afflicted by pains and deprived of every human function, was greatly weakened. He had already despaired of being cured in any other way than by burning away, as is customary, whatever caused him severe pain. But after the body of the blessed Mansuetus that he had carried had been set down [Col. 0639D] and the solemnities of the Mass had been completed, he raised his hand, freed from the disease, before everyone’s eyes, as though he had never felt any pain before. He himself remains a reliable witness of this event, should anyone ask him.

From there they departed with that heavenly treasure of theirs and entered the city amid a great, echoing celebration of divine song. Then, devoting themselves to the sacred vigils of that night, they dedicated to the body of the holy man the basilica that the bishop himself had previously built from its foundations. It was venerable in honor of the holy Mother of God and of Saint Mansuetus; from that time onward it has been magnificently illumined by the merits of Saint Mansuetus, and everywhere the bonds of oppressive sin are released.

[Col. 0640A] When these things had thus been arranged, as they wished to return the body of the holy man to its proper seat, they encountered a peasant lamenting in magnificent cries. He had brought in his arms his wretched ten-year-old son, whose limbs were so knotted that the traces of the nerves held his feet fixed to his spinal column. As the boy followed the relics of the holy man toward the church with lamentations, a certain Jew, who had happened at that time to mingle with the crowds, spewing a hundred blasphemies in the mockery of a raging man, attacked the prayers of the petitioner, saying:

“Hey, you! Why do you follow a dead man? Why do you confuse the air with your shouting? Why do you approach one who is motionless, expecting to obtain a benefit, when I, being alive myself and much more capable than a dead man, can help you if you bring your prayers to me?”

When he heard this, the bishop, who was present, was greatly indignant and said to the brothers standing nearby: “Alas for me! What do we venerate, what do we worship? Either there is no power in the saint by which the Church may be gladdened and the madness of the Jews confounded, or else another is being worshiped in his place, and the one who is thought to be here is in no way being retained.”

Meanwhile, while the people were attending to other matters, the boy was laid upon the pavement. The connection of his twisted nerves suddenly broke apart and began to dissolve as blood flowed. As he tried to crawl toward the relics of the holy man with his hand, he stood upright; and, to the amazement of the crowds, he recognized a path he had never known, relying on his own steps. Thus the holy man displayed the grace of his power as he wished and changed the mouths of those who wept into rejoicing. The boy, as testimony to the event, is supported to the present day at the Church’s expense.

Among the other benefits of power experienced by this most blessed man for this bishop, we also add the following, of which we do not doubt that we were assured by the bishop’s own report. While he was still present in the same monastery in the saint’s company, the day of Saturday ended and night descended, since the solemnity of Sunday was expected on the following day. When the brothers rose early for the proclamation of divine service, the bishop, exhausted by the labor of the preceding days, lay in bed, overcome by deep sleep.

Meanwhile, while they were praising God according to their custom, as pale dawn was already returning to the sleeping bishop, a man of venerable appearance stood before him. He was covered with a most brilliant white stole, distinguished in bearing, and of such impressive stature that he seemed to be none other than Saint Mansuetus. When the divine visitor entered the chamber of the resting man, by some compelling power the doors of the adjoining windows suddenly opened, and the whole house shone as a ray flashed forth. Then the radiant man approached the bed of the sleeping bishop and, placing his hand upon his body, gently moved him. The others lying around him were bound in such deep sleep that they could scarcely have been roused even by a loud disturbance. He awakened him, saying:

“Why are you sleeping? While others are keeping the sacred vigils, why are you oppressed by such deep sleep?”

And, to repeat his very words, he immediately added: “For the kingdom of God does not come to those who sleep, but to those who keep watch.”

When he heard this, the bishop was roused from sleep, burst trembling into the church, and, shaken by great terror, was overwhelmed with shame that he appeared to be taking part so late in these services, as though excluded from them. He reports this event, not without shame on his own account, and tells what he endured in the secrecy of that chamber through the power of the excellent blessed Mansuetus.

But since “it is the glory of a king to conceal a word, whereas it is the Lord’s to investigate a matter,” I shall also come to what is shown to have occurred at that time through the merits of this blessed man. Not long afterward, divine severity struck the sins of the peoples, which were liable to punishment for their crimes. By God’s judgment, the devastation of a diseased calamity had flared up among the peoples. For, like the groin plague that once afflicted the peoples of Italy, a certain literal pain [read: lateral] spread everywhere in renewed growth and, increasing through deadly stages, wandered widely through the boundaries of the regions. Thus, under an evil omen, with the sequence of illnesses accumulating, common people died, peoples fell, and hosts of the dead were borne away without distinction of either sex or rank. Anyone seized by such pain was scarcely permitted to survive beyond three days.

What happened in other parts of the earth is uncertain. This calamity descended upon and attacked the city so violently that, as the same bishop recalled not without a groan, he saw ten or seven coffins of the dead being carried in for burial at a single place, apart from those belonging to the other churches. The bishop was hemmed in by the danger of many who were dying. Finally, this plan was put into his mind: that the blessed protector Mansuetus should once again be taken from the place where he had been laid and set between the living and the dead.

[Col. 0641C] Accordingly, after a three-day fast had been proclaimed and a consultation held, it seemed suitable to the bishop that, with crowds of people gathered again from every direction, the body of the holy man should be sent to the church located at Scrofulae [Écrouves near Toul], which is often illumined by miracles of blessed Mary, Mother of God, as though it were to perform a mission before the supreme Empress of the heavenly Emperor, the mother of all his sheep. After this was done, that calamity appeared to moderate its fury somewhat.

But even so, the terror of the frightened people was not cut off. For once again placing the relics of the holy man upon their shoulders, they proceeded with the choirs of singers of every order, their hearts raised to the Lord, toward the principal monastery of that same Mother of God at Buxières [Bouxières-aux-Dames]. There, with the lord Bishop Gerard present, after that night had passed, while they eagerly desired to return, it cannot be adequately said with what incredible multitude the crowds of people, drawn together suddenly from villages, fields, and various regions, mingled in confused order.

From one direction came sacred virgins; from another, innumerable flocks of the Christian faith. They hastened as far as the bank of the Murtensis River, where the venerable body of the holy man was received by the inhabitants of that place, who had requested it as a vow. When the immensity of the waters already seemed to them to have grown sufficiently great, they are said to have crossed the riverbed on foot, their garments loose amid the waves and the waters reaching to their waists, to the amazement of many.

From there the whole popular crowd advanced with joyful rejoicing and, surrounded on every side by throngs, carried the relics of the holy man back to their proper seat, not without the offering of their vow. For clouds had been gathered in the air, and such a great rain, previously implored, had poured down from heaven that it could fully have sufficed for the parched earth.

Finally, as they approached the temple door with praises, a beam of such radiant brilliance was seen to precede that venerable body that, illuminating the entire church, it clearly showed how divine was the object that appeared to be carried into the holy temple. Then the harmony of the song that had begun was broken by the tumultuous sound of the mingled crowd. Their prayers turning in another direction, many began to weep for joy, although they did not know why they ought to weep, except that the holiness of the saint had stirred in the minds of his children the emotion produced by heavenly grace. Nor did the bishop present restrain his tears, for he wonderfully felt with the people the shared abundance of that sweetness.

And behold, that calamity, which we said had poured forth [lacuna] upon human beings, with the grace of the Lord Redeemer favoring the merits of this protector of ours, so departed from its former course that the whole people openly recognized that, on behalf of the house of Israel, Saint Mansuetus stood in opposition on the day of the Lord, having become the most excellent helper of all his sheep.

I also wish to insert into this account of ours what is known to have happened, almost within the memory of us all in an earlier time, to the praise of this blessed man. And since the aforementioned bishop is involved in the matter, the clemency extended by the divine majesty to a sinner does not detract from his eminent person.

Therefore, after the peoples had been struck by the severity of the scourge and had been rescued through the merits of the saints, the aforementioned bishop too was subjected to heavenly discipline, so that, touched by the blow, he might quickly recognize that there is one all-powerful Lord who strikes and heals. To pass over many details: he who had supplied the nourishment of prayers to many others was overcome by a serious illness and, feeling extremely wretched, lay sick in bed.

No power or strength remained in him. His entire body wasted away; greatly weakened, he could take neither sleep nor food. He led a hated life amid anguish and thought only of his approaching death. Anxious, he did not know what to do or where to turn. While he absolved the people, he himself had been absolved from the people and sorrowfully awaited only his end.

We describe the distress of his illness in this way in order to show what great grace followed through the blessed Mansuetus. As the affliction grew stronger and he was already almost at the point of death, having spent three consecutive weeks in a lethal state of sleeplessness, the sick man resolved, under the pressure of his illness, to flee to the familiar refuge of Saint Mansuetus.

But the customary service of his soldiers stood in the way, since, as rumor had it, if he happened to convert to the monastic order, they too would be deprived, together with their lord, of their domestic possessions. This circumstance had confused their minds and intentions. But he who had experienced the force of the labor that tormented him broke through the obstacles of those who tried to prevent him. He hastened to seek the assistance of the holy man and entrusted himself wholly to his intercession before God. He devoted himself earnestly to the prayers of the brothers [lacuna], and, carrying his vows to God and to Saint Mansuetus from the depths of his heart, he did not desist until, through the Lord’s mercy and the power of Saint Mansuetus, he perceived the hoped-for benefits of returning health.

To the present day the same bishop has been accustomed to report this with sighs: how severely he was weighed down at that time by illness, and by how powerful an intervention of the saint he was saved through heavenly medicine. And since I have, in a brief pen, as it were, described some of the powers accomplished through this saint during the lifetime of the bishop, in order to fulfill at his command this little companion-book of his, let us now bring these matters also to an end, aided by his prayers and with the grace of the Lord Redeemer favoring us.

[Col. 0643]

# LIFE OF SAINT BASOLUS THE CONFESSOR  
### By the author Adso

*(In Mabillon, Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict, Second Century, p. 66, from the parchment manuscripts of the monastery of Saint Basolus.)*

## AUTHOR’S PROLOGUE

### 1. The author turns to heaven

[Col. 0643B] Since we have before us the task of describing the distinguished deeds of the most holy confessor of Christ, Basolus, we direct our mouth and heart toward heaven, because, as Scripture testifies, we know that “every good gift and every perfect gift is from above” (James 1:17). We extend our hand to this work with complete hesitation, because, our strength broken, we succumb as unequal in merits and talent to so great a subject, though we judge it sufficiently worthy of one of the leaders of ancient times.

Even if, as the inventions of the pagans relate, Homer or Tullius Cicero were to return from the underworld, he could not enclose in words the whole work of divine power as it was accomplished. How much less could I, a mere little man, who possess neither learning, nor any record of merits to commend me, nor the eloquence of learned speech—something very necessary in matters of excellence? What, then? Even if we are unworthy, shall we remain wholly silent? Perhaps we incur blame if we keep silent about the virtues and deeds of one about whom we can always speak worthily.

Although we possess no sufficiency in ourselves, we nevertheless believe—as Gregory, the king of Roman eloquence, writes—that “the strength which inexperience denies is supplied by love.” Perhaps we shall be the more eloquent because we place no confidence in our own ability. For the more humbly someone lowers himself within his own ignorance, the more he is inwardly raised by the illuminating Spirit; and what proceeds outwardly from true humility is usually more beneficial in spirit to those who hear it. But speech that proceeds from the arrogance of pride does not help the hearer; it disgusts him.

Therefore, because we are constrained by the dryness of our mind, we hasten all the more eagerly, thirsting, to the fountain of living waters, to the degree that we burn inwardly with consuming thirst. We sigh toward him and place our inmost hearts in him, of whom we truly hold it written that “in heaven he has a chair who teaches the hearts of human beings” (Augustine, *Tractate 3 on the First Epistle of John*, near the end).

### From what authorities the writer composes this life

[Col. 0644B] 2. We therefore wish to draw from the source from which we know that streams of innumerable pages have flowed, assigning the whole of it entirely to that grace by whose teaching whatever is brought forth proceeds. But if someone should suddenly arise after us and immediately attack this work of ours, pouring forth the torrents of his eloquence more beautifully in its composition and reproving us for having arranged certain things less competently or rashly, let him recall that we were led not by an impulse to do whatever we pleased, but by the command of venerable Fathers, under whose authority we serve.

We have judged that it would be a greater madness and sin to contradict them. Against every weapon of unexpected objection, therefore, we place our confidence in their defense. We accepted the burden of obedience from those authorities, who, after the honorable observance of monastic discipline had long been abolished, are in our age restorers and renewers of regular service. [Note: [Col. 0643D] Frodoardus, in his *Chronicle* under the year 952, says: “Archbishop Artoldus sends monks to the monastery of Saint Basolus, after expelling the clerics who served there, and entrusts it to the abbots Hincmarus and Rotmarus.” Hincmarus, abbot of Saint Remigius at Reims, and Rotmarus, perhaps abbot of Hautvillers, after restoring the monks at Basolus, arranged for Odo to be placed over them as abbot. Adso succeeded him; he was a contemporary of Gerbert, bishop of Reims, and built a basilica such as still survives, as Gerbert testifies in Letter 7. See Guillelmus Marlot, *Metropolis of Reims*, book IV, chapters 25 and 26.]

When we obey them, we honor the order of our life and preserve unharmed the purpose of our service. But when we rashly depart from their obedience, we offend God, injure our souls, and receive the judgment of condemnation as the reward of disobedience. Therefore, in this matter, let no one hurl weapons of malicious prejudice against us, since we ought not to be blamed if we humbly fulfill the office of the service instituted for us.

### The author’s modesty

3. Nor, on the other hand, do we tie the ropes of any praise around ourselves, since we entirely refuse to be praised by anyone, remembering that we have never done anything worthy of praise. In such an undertaking, one should not seek praise for the writer, but imitate the proportion of the virtues and present an assertion of the deeds in accordance with the truth.

If anyone is to be praised, let him be praised of whom we servants speak; let him be praised who works miracles; let him be praised who has already reached the harbor in triumph—not the one who is still uncertainly steering his oar amid the waves. He is one of the foremost princes of the exalted monks. We, professors of monastic life, most unworthy and having attained not even the smallest particle of his merits, ought to praise and remember him with devoted hearts.

It is just that we should display the devotion of our service and the rite of veneration toward the one whom we have before our eyes as the chief leader of our order, under whose guidance we make our way toward our homeland through varied circumstances and so many dangers. Thus, when he comes in judgment, he may recognize us as his own, seeing that we were not strangers to his service.

Whoever reads these things should understand that our insistence does not compel him to read them. Let him know that we did not wish to introduce one thing in place of another, but that, diligently investigating the order of what happened, we have done as much as our effort could reach, so that so great a confessor of the Lord [Col. 0645C] might not remain hidden among the people. He was an outstanding imitator of the monks in these regions of France and will always be a most merciful mediator for his entire people before the Lord.

### The faithfulness of this history; the author does not preserve the order of events

4. Some matters handed down from the memory of the ancients we have related at greater length; others, reported by the mouths of the faithful, we have committed to our own style. We have also wished to add certain matters in which we ourselves took part, and we have briefly treated those that we learned with the testimony of people who were present.

In our account, however, we have refrained from preserving the order, provided only that we acted so as not to judge that what came to our knowledge should pass by in silence. It is often affirmed by many that diligent antiquity left to the memory of posterity a book of considerable size drawn from the deeds of the blessed man, but that book has not yet been found within our sight to the present day.

But whether that is so, or whether, as the poet sings, “You had heard it, but it was only rumor,” it is not at all fitting for us to remain silent about the virtues and deeds of our special shepherd. We keep vigil before his body [Note: [Col. 0645D] Here Adso speaks in the name of the monks of Saint Basolus. He was abbot of the monastery of Der, commonly Montier-en-Der, in the diocese of Châlons, in the region of Perthois, le Parthois.] and rejoice in the singularity of his patronage.

Nor will it be a burden to us, however widely we know his praises to be spread by others. Rather, our joy will increase if, where we fail, it should happen that another completes the task. For just as no mortal could fully recognize his virtues, which he performed with heaven as witness, so the speech of many cannot in every respect express them.

## PREFACE

### How useful the examples of the saints are; the author suppresses his name

[Col. 0645C] 5. Returning happily to our homeland after the long weariness of this pilgrimage, we possess the necessary examples of the holy Fathers, whom we know to have earned a glorious ascent to heaven through their virtues. Here, as they say, sailing between Charybdis and Scylla, we make our way through the middle course not without great danger, and we must greatly fear loosening our sails either to the right or to the left.

For savage beasts stand ready on both sides. If they see us inclining toward them, they may swallow us into an open abyss and plunge us into deep whirlpools. Since we cannot carefully avoid these hiding places of death by our own efforts, let us therefore explore with care, by the light of the saints who went before us, the paths by which we may hold a safe course amid so many dangers.

We do this properly if we consider their virtues and deeds and take from their imitation examples of salvation; if we order our conduct, reform our life, and make whatever in us displeases God pleasing to the Redeemer through devotion to holy conduct. We recall the memory of the saints with good fruit if we are not reluctant to imitate what we hear with our ears. We celebrate the feasts of the saints with good fruit if our unhappy conscience receives from them the seasoning of innocence. For festive joy is composed not by an abundance of food and wine, but by desire from the Holy Spirit that purifies the mind.

6. Therefore we describe the life and deeds of our blessed shepherd and illustrious confessor of Christ, Basolus, so that we may recall by what path he reached glory. For if we consider how great his glory is in heaven, let us nevertheless turn our gaze back to what he endured beforehand. It does me no good to hear about heavenly things if I do not unfold in my hands the things by which one reaches heaven.

Therefore we present the life of this most holy Father to the faithful as an example. By the fact that he bravely overcame the devil’s temptations, he plainly taught his children that he must be followed along the difficult path. And since pagan philosophers, stirred by the illustrious deeds of their own people, though themselves lost, sought to commit the lost to everlasting memory so that those who had departed equally in soul and body might live on the lips of human beings, how much more worthily do we exalt the glorious triumphs of the saints, whom we do not doubt to reign with God in eternity?

They live better after death, there where they live, since even their bodies, though extinguished, shine daily with such great miracles, there also where they do not live temporally. I recount more patiently the deed that tells of my most blessed confessor Basolus, enrolled with the citizens in eternal joy, than the story that falsely asserts that Hercules, once endowed with gigantic enormity, was carried up into heaven. This man, therefore, while the sun encircles the world with its light, will live among human beings in everlasting glory; but that other, as the tale goes, will be tormented forever by the Ixionian wheel among the inhabitants below, in eternal death.

We therefore briefly bring his deeds to the knowledge of human beings, he who is honored by the praises of angels. As we believe, he will provide no small heavenly glory to his reader, whoever reads his account with love. But lest the rusticity of my style inflict the injury of baseness upon the deeds of the holy man, let the page present only the subject matter, while concealing the author’s name.

## THE LIFE BEGINS

### Basolus’s homeland and nobility; his virtues while still a layman

[Col. 0647B] 7. The most blessed Basolus arose from an illustrious stock of parents in the province of Aquitaine, in the territory of the city of Limoges; by birth and lineage he was of the highest nobility. When, with happy auspices, he had passed beyond the boundaries of childhood and the years of adolescence had arrived with the growth of his sacred apprenticeship, he turned his whole self toward the work of divine service.

At first held by the appearance of earthly military service, he spent those early years of his age among popular ranks in the pursuit of piety. Although he lived for some time in the world in the ordinary manner, he did not subject his holy youth to the vices in which that age is usually deeply entangled. Even then he burned with love for heavenly things and always strove for an increase of virtues.

Although he was held under the outward appearance of a worldly occupation, he implanted heavenly disciplines in his soul, setting evangelical perfection before his eyes even in that condition. He loved father and mother less, so that, with God approving, he might become more worthy. In adolescence, his ever-watchful mind contemplated the churches of God and monasteries, something he would later fulfill more fully.

Faith governed a broad realm in his breast; charity and love continually drove within him a fire nourished without end. With the radiance of chastity shining forth in him, he did not set his foot on slippery ground, lest he draw a stain from what was hidden. He made vigils and sacred prayers perpetual for himself and, as far as he understood, performed them without sluggishness. Devoted to the strict demands of abstinence, temperate in food and drink, he had curbed the arrogance of youth with hard restraints.

No one can adequately describe how much he cultivated patience amid adversity while among secular people. He possessed such generosity toward the poor that whatever resources were granted to him, apart from his daily sustenance, he poured out entirely for the support of the needy.

In all this he was most pious in spirit, most truthful in speech, distinguished by justice, patient in hope, pleasing in demeanor, modest in his walk, serious in character, lovable in gentleness, open in speech, approachable to everyone, gracious in conversation, honorable at home, restrained in public, the sweetness of those who wept, the strength of the weak, the blessedness of those who stood firm, and in him the most fitting radiance of every good quality. [Col. 0648B] He had so greatly disciplined himself that, even under that outward condition, he surpassed in the virtues of the soul some who were practiced in ecclesiastical discipline.

### He approaches the tomb of Saint Remigius in devotion

8. When the flourishing youth of the most blessed Basolus had passed through all these aforementioned degrees of goodness, his spirit, anticipated by God’s gift, was kindled so that he should now renounce the world more fully, abandon all that was his, leave his homeland, enter the kingdom of France, make for the city of Reims in particular, and visit bodily the tomb of the blessed Remigius, whose holy deeds he had long before learned to be many, wondrous, and distinguished. There he would keep vigil in sacred prayers and watchfulness.

Each day, as greater grace grew within him, he turned over more deeply in his mind the truth that he could not ascend to the splendor of seeing God unless, freed from every impediment of the world, he made himself a disciple of the Savior, who says to all his true followers: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matthew 11:29).

The most blessed Basolus carefully embraced this voice, fearing that, placed amid the storms of the world, he might easily suffer the loss of his soul. He considered it the most fortunate kind of victory to despise the world’s deceptive riches, neither to possess nor seek gold and silver, and to pursue true poverty, which grants possession of the spacious palaces of heaven.

Turning these thoughts over in his heart, he brought before his eyes the faith and steadfastness of the ancient and noble patriarch Abraham, who, abandoning the land of his birth and the house of his paternal kin, confidently sought what was unknown to him and departed to wherever he was ordered.

### He decides to leave everything

9. From that point the holy man began to groan more deeply because he had not yet experienced this form of command. Although he had already abandoned his native soil in his mind, he reflected that he still remained in it bodily.

Finally, as they say, taking only that military equipment of his with which chaste youth was accustomed to pass through its first years, not in worldly pleasure but in perfunctory exercise, he was stripped of his parents and clothed in God’s protection. He joyfully began his pilgrimage. Thus, he who had previously been supported by the affection of his own people became a guest on a long pilgrimage and chose an excellent form of possessing: at least, wherever he might lay his head, he would have nothing at all with Christ (Luke 9:58).

But lest you think that this praiseworthy pilgrimage of the man was emptied of the glory of heavenly reward, pay attention for a little while, and you will find in it something greatly worthy of wonder.

### He deserves an angel as guide for his journey
### 10. He Deserves an Angel as Guide on His Journey

When the most holy confessor of Christ extended his foot beyond the boundaries of his own country to travel as a pilgrim, so that divine power might show how great in heaven was he who wandered as a pilgrim on earth, just as from the beginning of the world it had fittingly provided a guide for all its saints when they set out into exile, so also for this man it appointed a guide suited to him. Thus, wherever he directed his foot or his mind, he had with him an angelic guardian whom, by his inward purpose, he had deserved to have as his companion. It therefore seems that this was written of him: “Behold, I send my angel, who will go before you and guard you always” (Exod. 23:20).

Indeed, an angel of the Lord appeared to him as his companion on the journey, one who had already been made a participant through the true worship of the divine majesty, as it is written concerning true worshipers of God: when we cleave to God, an angel is not more powerful than our mind. The Lord also testifies elsewhere concerning the innocent—not by their age but by their purity: “Their angels,” he says, “always see the face of my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 18:10).

For he who once opened the paths of the Red Sea for the Israelite people fleeing Pharaoh’s power, and commanded that a pillar of fire precede them by night and a pillar of cloud by day as they journeyed through terrible deserts, and who, accompanying them with great signs from heaven, led them in haste from the place of their birth into the land of promise—he himself now, for comparable miraculous purposes, appointed an angelic guide for the blessed man Basolus throughout that entire exile of his holy pilgrimage.

Relying upon this guide for the journey, he reached the city of Reims, intending to bring his long labor upon the road to an end. Thus, as is believed, the blessed Basolus was divinely summoned from the Armorican region and the territory of Limoges and entered these parts. Having abandoned the great resources of Aquitaine, he chose for himself holy poverty in the Champagne of Reims: noble in the dignity of his earthly origin, but nobler in heavenly dignity; of noble human descent, but more noble through angelic companionship. God exalted him in this way because he himself had always striven to humble himself in the sight of the divine majesty.

### Many illustrious in holiness flourished at Reims. Among them was Aegidius, bishop of Reims. Fortunatus composed his deeds in verse.

### 11. At that time, when the citizenry of Reims was flourishing, Aegidius was its chief pastor

At that same time, when the civic community of Reims was flourishing, the whole city shone with the varied radiance of saints still dwelling in the flesh, like a kind of heavenly circle of stars adorned in ordered ranks of brilliance [Col. 0650A]. Among them was Aegidius, a pastor of astonishing holiness, who, raised to the episcopate of Reims, became distinguished as the fourth bishop in that see after Remigius, a prelate whose life had been worthy and praiseworthy.

[Note: [Col. 0649D] Frodoardus records in book II, chapter 1: “Romanus is said to have succeeded blessed Remigius; Romanus was succeeded by Flavius, and after them came Mapinius.” In chapter 2, Bishop Aegidius is said to have followed Mapinius. In the year 569, an encomium of Aegidius composed by Fortunatus is reported by the same Frodoardus in the chapter cited above. [Col. 0650D] Concerning the deposition of Aegidius, which took place in 590 at the Council of Metz during the reign of King Childebert, Gregory of Tours, book X, chapters 19 and 20, should be read. The author of this Life appears excessive in his praise of Aegidius. Why, after all, did he favor Chilperic so immoderately, neglecting his own king Childebert?]

This venerable bishop added greatly to that episcopal church by his strength and ability. In character and life he fulfilled the dignity of a bishop; in possessions he exalted the bishopric; he enlarged its boundaries; and, as far as possible, enriched the ecclesiastical household with abundance. He devoted himself to many labors and vigils so that his flock might not suffer loss.

How greatly he flourished in the practice of good works was briefly but eloquently encompassed in metrical form by Fortunatus, an outstanding teacher and most fluent poet. Fortunatus, summoned—as is read—from Italy to Gaul by Aegidius himself, described his life, character, preaching, and pastoral care.

The Frankish nobles therefore loved him greatly. King Chilperic also loved him—Chilperic, who at that time possessed the rule of the Franks and who had secured the administration of the kingdom by his own strength after his father’s death—because Aegidius supported his cause and took part in the counsels of royal government. In the dispute that arose between Kings Chilperic and Childebert over control of the kingdom, this same bishop did not fail to assist King Chilperic, either in support or in resources; consequently, he is later said to have endured many adversities.

### Aegidius receives Saint Basolus as a guest through his parents

### 12.

Meanwhile, Aegidius did not fail to take part in the king’s frequent expeditions. Since Chilperic, king of the Franks, often sought the regions of Aquitaine, the bishop was well known and renowned throughout that kingdom, including the cities of that realm and the territory of Limoges, and was venerated by all on account of his goodness.

As he progressed through many practices of goodness, by which he deservedly ought to have been praised in the judgment of the just, he also merited being especially exalted by God at the time when divine grace illuminated the city of Reims through the arrival of the most blessed Basolus.

Although this man, most acceptable to God in all things, had left his native land and entered these regions of our France, the reader can nevertheless learn from what follows that the aforesaid bishop was the reason for the blessed man’s arrival in these parts. For, as is reported, while accompanying the king’s retinue, he had been received at Limoges by Basolus’s most noble parents with courteous generosity and had stayed with them for some time as a familiar guest.

### Saint Basolus is reverently received at Reims by Aegidius

### 13.

Finally, when the most devoted worshiper of Christ, Saint Basolus, had entered the city of Reims by God’s providence, the news of so great a man’s arrival spread, and it is impossible to say with what devotion many of the citizens hastened to meet him.

Among the others, the beloved pastor Aegidius was not absent when he entered the city. As was fitting for so worthy a man, he welcomed the saint of God. It was also his practice to draw into his city from every quarter persons who were religious and acceptable to God. He rejoiced and was glad that God had sent him, from distant regions of the earth, this pillar of perfect virtue.

But who can imagine how great the inner joy of Christ’s faithful and devoted servant was when the Lord directed the path of his pilgrimage in his sight?

After this, the venerable bishop asked why a man of such great nobility had left his native land and why such fervor for pilgrimage had pleased him. As truth required, the beloved servant of God explained his purpose in due order: he wished to serve God in poverty and had willingly exchanged his native country and family for the exile of this kingdom [Col. 0651B]. He did not intend to return to his own land, but, as many saints of an earlier age had done, to end his life in pilgrimage.

When the illustrious bishop learned of the pious desire of this exiled man, he was filled with immense gladness and praised the Lord with great acclamations—him who always grants gracious assistance to those who trust in him and draws the hearts of many to his service.

### He obtains from Aegidius a place apart from the crowds. He joins the community of the monks of Verzy

### 14.

After this, the man of God Basolus asked the aforesaid bishop to grant him a dwelling where he could live in greater seclusion, since he did not wish to be seen in public and had resolved to avoid the crowds of the people. He declared that he had come for this purpose: that he might perhaps more perfectly fulfill among unknown lands the worship of divine religion which he had not been permitted freely to pursue among his own people [Col. 0651C].

The venerable bishop rejoiced all the more and glorified God’s mercy when he heard that so great a man had chosen him above all others and wished to live within the boundaries of his episcopal territory. Yet he would rather have kept him near himself, had not the man of God intended to live farther from the crowds. Accordingly, with willing spirit, he granted him the opportunity and freedom to search out a suitable and appropriate place to live anywhere in the territory of Reims.

At last, by God’s providence, he found a place in a village which that ancient and first native inhabitant, Viriziacus—Verzy—had named. It lay at the foot of the mountain of Reims. The grove there, shaded by the density of its foliage, covers Rigetium—“the woods of the Route”—while it begins there its origin [Col. 0651D].

From the earliest times, this place had possessed a monastery of regular life; here the prudent industry of an earlier age had provided suitable dwellings for monks. The monks who lived there had limited their community to twelve and followed the customs and practices of the soldiers of the blessed Columbanus [Note: [Col. 0651D] If our opinion concerning the date of Saint Columbanus’s arrival in Gaul is correct, Basolus was admitted to the monastery of Verzy before Saint Columbanus had brought his institution into these regions. Indeed, according to the opinion of others, who say that Saint Columbanus arrived here around the year 570, the Rule of Columbanus had not yet become influential before the deposition, in 590, of Aegidius, bishop of Reims, who had received Saint Basolus. In that year Columbanus laid the foundations of the monastery of Luxeuil, from which he propagated the religious observance he had introduced. But the holy rule, as Frodoardus says in book II, chapter 7, was imposed upon the monastery of Saint Basolus in the seventh century by Blessed Nivardus, bishop of Reims. By this name Frodoardus commonly understands the rules of Saints Benedict and Columbanus together, which were received in monasteries during that century. The ancient documents must undoubtedly be referred to that period.] as we find recorded in ancient documents.

At that time they were governed by institutions established according to those practices; all obeyed the authority of a single spiritual father. They carried on the warfare of heaven with zeal and through distinguished exercises in the service of the Lord. No one exceeded the bounds of the common rule except when the abbot’s judgment established it in the cause of obedience or permitted it because of bodily weakness.

When Basolus came there with the favor and authority of their beloved bishop Aegidius, and the brothers learned of his desire, they immediately received him into their brotherhood with complete unanimity and the utmost devotion. Because of the excellence of his religious life, he was reverently loved and honored by them all.

### He is instructed in the sacred Scriptures

[Col. 0652B] ### 15.

Thus received by the brothers within the enclosure of the monastery, Blessed Basolus was attached to the monastic community and entrusted by Diomerus, the venerable abbot of that place, to a monk named Komarchus, so that he might be instructed in the sacred writings.

Having entered upon the studies of holy discipline, and with divine grace illuminating him, he advanced in a short time to the summit of doctrinal perfection by meditating day and night on the law of the Lord. Nor is this surprising, since, taught by the instruction of the Holy Spirit, by his grace he attained that for the love of whom he had deprived himself of paternal kin with so great a freedom.

### Catalogue of his virtues. Above all his other virtues, he especially cultivated compassion toward the afflicted

### 16.

Who could adequately touch in words upon the extent of his humility, patience, gentleness, meekness, and kindness? He was diligent in reading, devoted to reviewing what he had learned, fervent in prayer, moved to tears, attentive to the utterances of the Psalms, truthful in speech, and constant in divine matters.

He disciplined his flesh with the severity of abstinence, reducing and withholding the food allotted to him by the general rule, so that more might remain to be distributed to the poor than indulged in for the body’s use. He desired rather always to seek food for the soul than to fear that his body might perish through lack of food, ever keeping before his eyes the Gospel’s saying by which he knew the Lord had promised: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied” (Matt. 5:6).

In obeying the decrees of his elders, he was always so ready and prepared that he undertook even the most lowly and despised tasks with the greatest joy.

Throughout his entire life, during all that first period of his training, he loved, cherished, and pursued nothing more than the possession of the virtue of compassion. He devoted himself to it and practiced it so greatly that, although he flourished in many other virtues, he nevertheless employed this one in all things as the finest foundation of all his good qualities [Col. 0653A].

Fully adorned by that primary fountain of compassion, he could show outwardly nothing other than the gift of compassion that had been poured into him inwardly. For he was most compassionate everywhere, everywhere overflowing with abundant mercy: compassionate in wealth, compassionate in modest means; compassionate toward the rich and no less compassionate toward the poor.

If, when pressing circumstances arose, he could not rescue those confined and held by extreme necessity by lifting them up with his hand, he persevered in prayer so that heavenly power might bring them relief.

Therefore, even to this day, anyone driven by the misfortunes of his possessions, constrained by the harassment of some evildoer, or afflicted by pressing illness, if he approaches this saint’s tomb with complete faith, because he has sought one who is compassionate, will joyfully carry away, through the generosity of compassion, the remission he hopes for [Col. 0653B].

Often, too, we have seen popular crowds come to his sacred body, the gathered flock imploring help against their adversaries with vows and tears. Moved by compassion at their prayers, the holy confessor of God raised up those who were half dead, came to the aid of the wretched, released the afflicted, cast down enemies, changed sorrow into joy, and caused happiness to arise for those in grief.

From this, then, learn easily that whoever approached him with compassion did not depart empty of the gift of compassion. For what this blessed man had received, he gave freely; what he possessed, he willingly bestowed; what ought to have been granted, he never refused.

### He constantly strives toward perfection

### 17.

Living for a long time among the brothers in the monastery and serving God with the others under the discipline of monastic observance, he submitted himself so fully to spiritual institutions that he surpassed his companions in conduct and shone among the others with the beauty of prudence.

As the faithful soldier of the Lord grew nobly from virtue to virtue, he began to be regarded as more perfect than the most perfect. Fearing that the divine examination on the scales of justice might find something lacking in the grace of his fervor and steadfastness, he always pressed onward to higher things through daily growth, ever more fervent in holiness and exalted above his former self.

For when, through long testing within the brotherhood, he had been well proved in the common struggle and perfectly polished on every side, so that, according to Scripture, “the righteous may still do right and be sanctified still more” (Rev. 22:11), he hastened toward a solitary contest, intending to fight against the devil, wisely armed with the Lord’s strength [Col. 0653D].

### 18.

Wishing in every way to avoid human society and enter a solitary life, he again chose a place for himself on the summit of a wooded mountain. There he built a cell with an oratory, desiring to live alone so that he might attend more perfectly to the heavenly commandments and gather the fruits of contemplation more sweetly and purely.

Living in that place in greater seclusion for forty years, and fighting manfully and invincibly against the ancient serpent (Rev. 12:9) like a strong athlete, he served his commander faithfully.

How many labors he endured there for Christ, how many exertions he underwent, and how many sufferings of spiritual combat he imposed upon himself—this was witnessed by heaven alone, as he contended alone before the heavenly Judge, whose penetrating and invisible judgment sees all things. Since these matters cannot be recounted in our speech, we leave them to the judgment of the faithful, for the glory of the saints is not diminished where the capacity of our tongue fails.

Constantly devoted to vigils and prayers, the holy man was always either reading or praying. No time passed without meditation on God’s law; no moment was free from works of salvation. He brought his limbs, wearied by continual afflictions, into the service of the spirit; he bent the flesh to the spirit and the spirit to the Savior.
