He was wholly absorbed in reading, wholly absorbed in prayer. Christ was always in his mouth, the Holy Spirit always in his heart [Col. 0654B]; admonitions of eternal life always proceeded from his breast.

### He exhorts the people by word and example to adopt a better way of life

### 19.

When his reputation began to spread among the people—for the religious life of so great a man could certainly not remain hidden for long—crowds of people began to gather around him, seeking from him help for salvation and life.

The most blessed servant of God, wisely instructed through the grace of the Holy Spirit, could not avoid the crowds of people who came to him. He therefore illuminated them with the rays of holy preaching, set them aflame with the Lord’s words, and, by the examples he offered, formed those whom he summoned through his teaching to the love of heavenly things.

The whole people rejoiced in his instruction, blessing and praising the Lord together because he had generously sent them, for the salvation of many, so great a patron in their region.

### He obtains a spring from heaven on the summit of the mountain

### 20.

There can be no doubt that Blessed Basolus, who had first planted the roots of such great goodness and had been known only to God and himself through his innermost virtues, also shone outwardly before men through the branches of signs and was made illustrious by miracles.

When he began to rise to the summit of holy conduct in the place mentioned above, the divine mercy chose to reveal how great was his virtue and merit before God, since he had been seen humbling himself so greatly before the people on earth.

As we have said, he had built his more secluded dwelling on the summit of the mountain, and the holy man was suffering greatly from a lack of water. One day, on that mountain, he attempted to draw water from the depths of the earth for his needs.

When he approached to dig the ground and anxiously endured his lack of water, he turned to the Lord in devout prayer and invoked him—him who had once deigned to bring water from a hard rock for his people, exhausted by thirst in the wilderness.

Immediately, more quickly than words can say, a most abundant spring began to flow in that same place. To the present day it descends from the heights to the lower ground. This spring, flowing from the mountain in service of the man of God, has an ancient name: “It binds bones” (*Legit ossa*).

It is believed that it was so called for a reason. Since, through the function of medicine, it drives away illness and binds human bones—that is, strengthens and solidifies them—we do not doubt that it received its name from the healing effect of drinking its water.

This spring, once leaping forth beneath the saint’s tomb, now bursts forth, as if from a vessel, through the foundations of the church [Note: [Col. 0655D] The spring may still be seen today in the crypt dedicated to Blessed Mary beneath the high altar, distinct from the spring which is conveyed from a nearby place through lead pipes into the monastery [Col. 0656D].]. Its water is sweet to drink and healthful for drinking.

From many experiences of healing we know that if a sick person suffering from any illness has a desire to drink from it or to wash his body in it, trusting in the virtue of the holy confessor, he will by no means, through divine mercy, be deprived of the salvation he hopes for.

### Sight is restored to a boy born blind

### 21.

We must not pass over another remarkable miracle of virtue, which was certainly revealed in that same place by divine power to display the merit of Blessed Basolus, the confessor of Christ.

A certain boy, Aunegiselus by name, had emerged from his mother’s womb into the world deprived of the light of his eyes from birth and was condemned to perpetual blindness caused by an innate defect of the eyes. Heaven and earth were unknown to him in their natural appearance, except insofar as he could perceive anything through hearing or touch.

Unable to bear the misfortune of his blindness willingly, he was led by another to the higher part of the mountain and used to keep vigil as a blind man before the cell of that man of God.

The saint of the Lord compassionately felt pity for his affliction and, turning to the heavenly Physician, sought through prayer to obtain a remedy. Nor did divine favor delay in hearing one who struggled for the healing of his neighbor.

For as soon as the prayer was completed, light long denied appeared amid the darkness. With his face opened to the grace of a new brightness, he recognized a new world that he had never before seen. In the twelfth year of his age, under better guidance, he joyfully carried the light back to his home.

When the venerable monks living on the lower part of the mountain, as we have shown above, heard of this, they were struck by the astonishing novelty of so unusual an event. Lighting candles and carrying the triumphant sign of the Lord’s cross in their hands, they came singing with loud voices of praise to that place, unanimously giving thanks to God.

### He arranged for a stone cross to be erected in the wilderness

### 22.

From that time, therefore, the name of the blessed man began to spread throughout the entire surrounding region, because, as it is written, “A city set on a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matt. 5:14).

When the report of his holiness had reached the knowledge of many, it stirred many hearts to the praise of the Creator and to glory.

On the more elevated northern side of the mountain, which faces the city, before he built his cell there, he had made a place for frequent prayer among the dense thickets of the forest. In that place he fulfilled the vows of prayer and sacred reading, the more secretly and therefore the more purely.

A stone cross had also been placed there, because the man of God considered it exceedingly unworthy for anyone to inhabit a place for long unless it contained this sign of salvation [Col. 0656A]. That cross remains there completely intact to the present day [Note: [Col. 0656D] A cross can still be seen at the very place; a small cell was added to it a few years ago.].

The servant of God also used to carry with him a certain small wooden reading desk, beautifully fashioned by a craftsman and raised a palm’s breadth above the ground. Whether sitting or even lying on the ground, he often recited the Psalms or the sacred Scriptures with their volumes placed upon it.

Pieces cut away from this little table and distributed in faith in divine power, when applied to illnesses—and especially to toothaches—are known to have effected many cures, as the reader will be able to learn in its proper place.

### He protects a boar from hunters. A remarkable miracle at the River Vidula

### 23.

Divine power, according to the ineffable riches of its divinity and glory, had now determined to make this blessed man reverenced even by people of earthly rank, and, on account of the merit of the man who lived there, to support the place for the present with temporal goods on this occasion [Col. 0656B].

There was a certain powerful man named Attila. For the sake of hunting—as is characteristic of that class of men—he had entered his forest adjoining the cell of the man of God.

Nor was the expectation of wild prey disappointed. He pursued, with panting horses, a boar of enormous size fleeing along fresh tracks.

But the monstrous beast, since it is natural for all living things to dread the destruction of death, climbed the mountain where the man of God lived. It came directly to his cell and, as though possessing some sense of reason, laid aside its fierceness and rolled itself, bristling, at the saint’s feet, as if about to implore protection for its life.

The saint, moved by pity for the irrational creature, since he was full of compassion and grace, fixed the pursuers in place by such power that they could see the beast close before their eyes, yet, with open mouths, could not touch it at all.

The aforesaid Attila, being a good man, clearly recognized the power of God and sought pardon for his presumption. He therefore gave the holy man everything around the place that belonged to his jurisdiction, including several estates of his own and also the estate commonly called Septemsalices—Sept-Saulx. He was the first to enrich the saint’s place with the resources he had bestowed.

From that time, it is believed, a custom arose and has been observed in his honor to the present day: if any hunt is undertaken in the aforesaid forest of Rigetium, once it has entered the little woodland within the embankment that projects on either side, neither hound nor hunter dares to pursue it any farther [Col. 0656D].

### Divine vengeance upon one who hunted on Saint Basolus’s feast

### 24.

Since an occasion has been provided by this event, we shall also recount another incident that took place long after the holy man’s death in a similar matter, though with a different outcome. Almost the whole event occurred in the surrounding region [f., “with regard to the region”].

One of the Frankish dukes had stationed his household establishment not far from the monastery of the holy man Basolus. In the bearing, appearance, and dress of this proud and wealthy man there was nothing but the arrogance of secular power.

The day was approaching on which the solemn feast of this holy confessor was to be celebrated. He therefore said to his men: “Be ready before dawn, for tomorrow I have decided to go hunting.”

Some among them who were more sound in judgment tried to turn their lord away from this intention. They told him that the sacred vigil was at hand, that such an undertaking ought rather to be avoided, that reverence should be shown to so great a day, and that he ought instead to rest and keep the day as a holiday.

But he, more obstinate, repeated his words and firmly declared that he would carry out what he had said.

The next day arrived. The horses were saddled, and the equipment suitable for such tasks was prepared. They set out, ready to place the reins on their hunting mounts.

Without delay, pursuing the course of a foaming boar, he sped as far as the embankment of the aforesaid woodland. There, when his horse slipped, he was thrown heavily to the ground and badly injured. Thus afflicted, he was no longer carried on horseback but transported home on the shoulders of men, promising that, if his life were restored, he would henceforth honor that day.

### He preserves a man hanging on the gallows unharmed

### 25.

We shall also relate another miracle, not unworthy of attention, in which it is clearly revealed how great was the virtue and merit of the saint. At the mere invocation of his name, death lost its authority, and the prey it had almost drawn into its jaws to swallow entirely was unable to consume him, overcome by the power of Saint Basolus.

Let others say what they think and wish; I, however, profess and testify that whenever an opportunity arose, if he was asked with true faith—as he ought to have been asked—he helped the needs of the wretched and frequently came to the aid of those placed in mortal danger.

There was a man named Ragenulfus. After a factional disturbance arising from some offense, he had been seized by his adversaries. Since they were unwilling to spare his life in any way, he was brought forth publicly, examined, judged, and finally affixed to the gallows.

While he hung suspended between heaven and earth, his soul already at the point of death, and the noose having tightened so that his wretched soul was nearly forced from him—something worse than other forms of death—the memory of this most holy confessor of Christ suddenly came to him.

With whatever voice he could produce, constricted as he was at the throat, he gathered his breath with all his strength and called upon the holy man of God, Basolus, with all his inmost being. He tearfully begged him to come to his aid in his extreme necessity [Col. 0657D].

Nor was he deprived of the help of his deliverer. For immediately the noose broke; he fell from the height; the painful torture was ended. Fear and amazement fell upon everyone. Freed and released from death, he departed alive.

Many others in different places have likewise escaped mortal danger through invoking his sacred name.

### He summons his nephew Balsemius from Aquitaine

### 26.

During all this, Saint Basolus was most perfect in life, most kind in mercy, distinguished in the integrity of his conduct, pleasant in speech, devoted in preaching, praiseworthy in compassion, and lovable in gentleness. He clothed the naked, restored hearing to the deaf, gave sight to the blind, and drove demons from possessed bodies.

Finally, foreseeing through the spirit of prophecy that the day of his departure was near, he sent to Aquitaine and summoned to himself his nephew, the holy Balsemius, from the city of Limoges.

As soon as he received this message from the Father, Balsemius left those regions and gladly presented himself before him. Blessed Basolus told him that it had been revealed to him through the Spirit that Balsemius should live in the same cell after his death. Like a good son, he obediently embraced these salutary instructions.

Thus, for as long as the most holy Basolus continued to live in the body thereafter, these two most noble men lived with the greatest religious devotion in the fear of the Lord [Col. 0658B].

### The day of his death

### 27.

At last, when divine mercy had determined that so many of his labors were worthy of eternal reward—for he could not otherwise be clothed with the glory of immortality unless he had first been stripped of the mortal covering of the flesh—after forty years, having been tested and found perfect before God, he laid down the burden of the body and entered heaven to be joined to the blessed angelic spirits and to live forever without end.

There he now rejoices, now exults, now enjoys the blessed delight of every good thing—he who never had rest in this life and never ceased until he reached the one whom he had sought, whom he had desired, and whom, sighing from his whole heart throughout this valley of tears, he had longed for.

If anyone wishes to know this man more fully and learn how valiantly he conquered the world by faith, let him read the passage where a new name and the name of the new city, Jerusalem, are inscribed for him (Rev. 3:12). When he understands with what adornments that city shines, let him attribute all of this to Basolus, since he is believed to have been established there forever by God the Creator as, in a certain sense, a citizen and possessor of that city.

Now made blessed amid the delights of paradise, he has no stain. Christ’s right hand embraces him, and Christ supports him with the left beneath his head (Song 2:6); he sleeps in the sleep of peace. Therefore, before him, a place has been made forever in peace, and his dwelling is in Zion (Ps. 75:3).

While the ages endure and night alternates with day [Col. 0658D], the fame of his most holy life will be proclaimed, and we shall never be free from praising him.

This patron of ours departed from this light to the Lord on the sixth day before the Kalends of December, in the place that he had prepared for practicing his holy way of life.

His nephew Balsemius, himself also most holy, remained in the same cell until his own death, following in every respect the good footsteps of his Father [Note: [Col. 0657D] The body of Saint Basolus was raised from its tomb by Hincmarus, bishop of Reims, in the middle of the ninth century. Frodoardus omitted the history of this event; it is given below. Meanwhile, we wish to inform the reader that, apart from his staff, the body of Saint Basolus is most honorably preserved by our community in its own monastery in a silver shrine, which Hugo, the second abbot of that name, ordered to be made and in which he placed the sacred relics of Blessed Basolus in the year 1121 from the Incarnation of the Word, during the reign of Louis, king of the Franks, in the thirteenth year of his reign and the fourteenth year of the archiepiscopate of Lord Rodulfus, as is read on the base of the casket [Col. 0658D].]

[Col. 0659]

## A Little Book on the Translation and Miracles of Saint Basolus the Confessor, by Adso, Abbot

*(In Mabillon, Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict, fourth century, part II, p. 137, from a manuscript codex of the monastery of Saint Basolus.)*

## Preliminary Observations

We stated in the second century, where the Life of the same saint was related, that the history of the translation, or elevation, of Saint Basolus was written by Adso, abbot of Dervy, around the year 980.

Here we present Adso’s work together with several miracles, some of which Frodoardus mentions, though, so far as I know, without making any reference to the translation. Whether Frodoardus borrowed certain passages from Adso, or Adso from Frodoardus, I do not know. One was nearly the contemporary of the other, although Frodoardus died almost twenty years before Adso.

It is not sufficiently clear whether canons or monks existed in the monastery of Saint Basolus at the time when the translation was celebrated. Certainly, in the year 882, canons already occupied the place, having replaced the monks, as is attested by the letter of apology sent by the clergy of Reims to Hildeboldus and the other suffragan bishops. In that letter they cleared themselves of blame for having discussed the future successor before the visitor’s arrival after the death of Hincmarus.

Finally, after the canons had been expelled, the monks were restored in the year 952, as we observed from Frodoardus in the Life of Saint Basolus. Under Abbot Adso II, successor of Odoleus, the first abbot after the restoration, Adso, abbot of Dervy, composed this little book.

We infer from Gerbert’s seventh letter that letters and learning flourished to some extent at Saint Basolus in those early beginnings. In it Gerbert asks Airardus to have Pliny and Eugraphius copied for him from the monastery of Saint Basolus or Orbais.

## [The Little Book Begins]

### Chapter I. The Restoration of the Monastery of Saint Basolus and the Translation of the Same Saint

[Col. 0659A]

After the most blessed Father Basolus had passed from this world into the heavenly kingdoms above, the entire tradition of the ancient Fathers’ institutions gradually perished in that monastery of twelve monks which, as we have said, had once been established at the foot of the mountain. This happened partly because of barbarian incursions and partly because of the frequent and continuing dissensions among the rulers of the kingdom.

At that time other monasteries as well were deprived of their honor, churches were stripped of their possessions, and very many were destroyed.

Therefore, after many days, when peace had returned to the churches, another monastery was built on the opposite side of the mountain, at the place where the saint of the Lord had lived in an outstanding manner. Because of the continual miracles that the Lord deigned to perform through him, the monastery was constructed by Blessed Nivardus, archbishop of Reims, with sufficiently suitable and fitting workmanship, its dwellings arranged around it in a manner appropriate to religious observance.

When the entire work of that place had been completed for the praise and glory of the divine name, and after many cycles of years had passed, the venerable Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, resolved to transfer the body of the most holy Basolus from the place where it had been reverently buried. Having therefore summoned all his clergy and a very great multitude of people, as befitted so important an undertaking, he unearthed the treasure of the sacred body from the place where it had previously lain. After suitable and abundant ecclesiastical furnishings had been prepared, he placed it in the church with songs and hymns, in a much more noble position than before. On the same day on which his most honored body was translated, the church itself was also dedicated in honor of blessed Martin, confessor of Christ, and of our most holy Basolus, its special patron throughout the ages.

This translation, together with the dedication of the sacred church, was carried out on the Ides of October by the aforementioned Hincmar, an archbishop of great authority. On that day the solemnity of the saint himself is celebrated with greater distinction, because, as we have said, the gathering of peoples from different and distant regions caused it to be held with greater fame. From that time onward, through the many intercessions of this saint, many signs of miraculous power were displayed, though they were not committed to writing for the memory of posterity. We, however, have openly set out for the benefit of readers as much as we either saw taking place in our own age or learned had formerly occurred through the truthful report of the faithful, as well as those matters that we ourselves observed briefly recorded by more judicious histories.

## Chapter II. Concerning the man who irreverently took the saint’s staff, whose foot withered

Long after the death of the blessed confessor of Christ, a certain man, noble by birth but puffed up with arrogance and bestial savagery of mind, approached the sacred church as though for the sake of prayer. After praying, he shook himself free of the ground, took the saint’s staff, hung it from his chin, and foolishly and madly placed it upon his foot. Then, mocking, he said: “Behold, this staff shows how short Basolus was in stature.”

Immediately divine vengeance overtook this blasphemy. The foot on which the saint’s staff had been placed withered, rotted away at once, and not long afterward was torn from his body amid severe torments. His body was accordingly arranged to be carried to the temple of the man of God; yet it was fixed in the ground as though it were some enormous stone statue. When it had been brought to the place of Saint Remigius and they decided that funeral rites should also be performed, so that the clod might be lifted, permission was not granted by God and Saint Basolus. At last, however, necessity compelled it to be buried in the territory of Châlons.

## Chapter III. Concerning a monstrous man from the village of Curmolois who was healed

Nor must we pass over what we know was granted by divine will through the intercession of this saint. Many people have learned that the village of Curmolois (Courmelois) is situated not far from the monastery. The time was approaching when the solemnity of the holy confessor was to be celebrated with annual rejoicing. The entire populace had gathered there; a mixed multitude of both sexes filled the festival from every direction.

Among this spectacle of such brilliance, a certain man had also come from the village above and mingled with the throngs of the people. His body was contracted into a mass, and his living body carried his gait buried within it; to those who saw him, he presented a pitiable and horrifying appearance. Nevertheless, he did not refrain from attending the spectacle of that day, but rather became a spectacle himself to the entire people, offering with complete faith, along with the others, the very small tribute of his vow.

When the nocturnal celebration of the heavenly [reading uncertain: *hiems*] solemnity was already to be held, divine traces suddenly burst forth around him. The sinews that had adhered to his back forcibly returned to their proper places; he stood upright upon his feet before the witnessing crowd, and by his newly restored walking increased the joy of the festival for the astonished throngs.

## Chapter IV. Concerning the girl who received sight

Many of our people know the river Axona [Aisne], in whose region there had been a girl whom hated blindness had held from the cradle. For nearly forty years she had been confined in such a painful prison. At last, as the festival day approached, her parents placed her in a vehicle and, after completing a long journey, brought her to the monastery amid the other gatherings of the populace. Having brought offerings in fulfillment of their vow, they also presented her for healing through the merits of the saint.

Nor was the mystery of his abundant compassion absent. In an instant it changed the anguish of her long sorrow into joy. She had come blind; she departed with her sight restored, and afterward, living for many years, she herself carried her miracle everywhere.

## Chapter V. Concerning a blind woman who received sight

We also report another work of miraculous power performed in the same manner, though not entirely unlike this one, near the little river Cosla.

> **Note:** The little river Cosla, or Cosle, flows into the Matrona in the district of Châlons, somewhat above the city. It has a village bearing the same name, where Saint Gibrianus was buried, according to Frodoard, Book IV, chapter 9.

A certain man living among his neighbors inhabited his native soil; the place, as can be seen, lay about eighteen miles from the monastery. He had a wife whom a debilitating condition had long confined in blindness. The anxious husband believed that she would be freed through the merit of this saint.

He therefore saddled an animal, placed her upon it, and proceeded with the festive gathering of the holy celebration. He himself, together with his blind wife, became one of the crowd of those standing nearby. When almost all the journey had been completed by that labor, with only two miles remaining, she also felt the power of Saint Basolus on the road. He did not allow devoted faith to remain deprived of the reward of its labor before it had completed its toil.

For at once the woman abandoned the darkness of the evil possession. With her eyes opened, she saw the pinnacle of the temple from afar and, rejoicing, said to her husband: “Thanks be to God and Saint Basolus! I recognize the grace of the sight that has been restored, and I see the roof of the church shining.”

Then she immediately threw herself down from the animal and, with bare feet, quickly completed the remainder of the journey. She reached the temple to give thanks and added still greater joy to the rejoicing people.

## Chapter VI. Concerning a certain steward named Spernus, and how he was punished

Not long before our own time—namely, in the time of Lord Archbishop Ebo, Frodoard adds, that is, during the reign of Louis the Pious—a certain religious man of commendable life, Benedict by name, was appointed abbot and rector of this monastery. He was a man devoted to simplicity and governed the household of the altar justly and moderately. Benedict enlarged the dignity of the church, adorned it with various gifts, and, after spending a considerable part of his life, rested in a good end.

His brother, named Spernus, was appointed as his successor. Unlike his brother in character, he was seized by a dreadful greed and was filled to the mouth with wine. He began at times to say to himself:

“This brother of mine and predecessor, held back by sloth—or so I think—did not know how cleverly to increase his own profits from the revenues of this household.”

He therefore ordered his own steward to bring the inhabitants of the villages before him as though to a public tribunal. By subjecting them to various punishments, he could violently extort their possessions from them. A trembling and wretched crowd of peasants gathered together; they saw that unjust penalties were being threatened against them. Then all of them had recourse to their well-known aid: they stretched out their hands toward the temple and invoked Saint Basolus with mournful cries.

Nor did he long endure the complaints of his people. Spernus, who threatened evil and breathed out menace, was confounded by divine power in the silence of night while lying in his bed. He lost his senses, burst apart at the middle, and died a most wretched death amid an overpowering stench. The household, released from fear, was entirely freed from its immediate dangers.

## Chapter VII. How the army of the Vandals turned back through the prayers and merits of blessed Basolus

Because of the persistent wickedness of our evils, divine vengeance ordained that these regions of Gaul should be struck by a pagan sword. At that time the kingdom of the Franks had as king Charles, son of King Louis.

> **Note:** He means Charles the Simple, in whose time the Hungarians poured into Gaul, namely in the year 919, according to Frodoard’s Chronicle.

Before his time this pagan people had been unknown and unheard of within the borders of France. Yet without doubt it became the common merit of the entire people that we incurred the dreadful danger of vengeance, because now, with charity having ceased, the mother of impiety reigns everywhere: the law of God is confounded, justice is overthrown, and, according to the saying of the prophecy, adultery, murder, and perjury have inundated the land; “blood has touched blood” (Hosea 4:2), that is, sin has increased by being heaped upon sin without any interruption. Everything has become confused and corrupt.

Among secular people and—what is worse—among those who bear the name of religion, greed now runs without distinction, and avarice has multiplied evils on the earth, while many abandon the straight paths of justice. The number of Christians diminishes daily. Some go into captivity; some perish by the sword; some collapse amid punishments and torments; some are drowned; some have their hands and feet cut off; some are cast into flames and burned; some, led away captive, are cruelly thrown along the roads as lifeless corpses; others return from captivity—alas, pitiable ones.

Villages have been destroyed, and few churches remain outside the cities. With the cultivators killed, the lands have been left empty. When fear of this detestable people first spread through these regions on the wings of rumor, each person seized defensive positions and fortifications. At that time, too, a considerable multitude gathered around the holy confessor. All the clergy assembled together and resolved to make their way toward the city with the sacred relic of their patron.

They left their own dwellings with no little sorrow. That entire household crowd, beating their breasts as they went, had already reached the village called Pusiolos (Puisieux), adjacent to the river Vidula (the Vesle), two miles away. Then the cry of the sorrowful people was raised on high; confused voices of lamentation were heard continuously from afar, crying out and saying:

“O holy one of God, why are you accepting such service from us and gathering such a company around you? Where shall we follow you? Why do you allow your place to remain so empty?”

As they thus prostrated themselves on the ground and entreated the mercy of God and Saint Basolus, they asked that, if anything harmful were about to happen to them because of this journey, he should give some clear sign, so that the people would not have to labor any further. Immediately the saint’s bier was fixed to the ground with such weight that permission was granted only to turn aside to the nearby church, where they passed the approaching night in vigils.

On the following day, with the help of their protector, they all returned to their own homes. At that time, the aforementioned pagan people did not pass the church of Saint Maurice, which is situated on the border of Champagne and the forest of Argonne.

## Chapter VIII. Concerning the man who began to tear away the gilded metal at the top of the tower

Since we have once begun speaking of the pagan people, we must also report what we know to have happened at different times. Because human hardness does not cease from sinning, the scourges of divine judgment cannot cease to come upon us. At another time, another incursion of barbarians again took place within Gaul. In their savage manner, they seized, killed, burned, and devastated whatever they encountered.

When their arrival had been discovered in advance, while each person sought means of preserving his life and everyone feared destruction, the clergy took the sacred body and hurried into the city. Thus the multitude of pagans, finding the monastery’s places empty of human beings and not fearing the divine defender, entered freely. Because the site was suitable, the entire pagan encampment settled there with all its company.

After pursuing slaughter and plunder everywhere, they returned from various regions laden with booty. Meanwhile, when they saw the little tower at the top of the church gleaming with a gilded appearance, one of them, driven by desire for gold and destined for a nearby death, crawled across the roofs, climbed onto the summit of the church, and began tearing away the shining metal.

But while he was irreverently intent upon this work, he experienced that divine guardianship had not departed from the place. Suddenly he was rolled headlong across the roofs and cast down. Reaching the ground with his limbs broken, he was seized by the punishment of death that he deserved.

## Chapter IX. Concerning the barbarian, or Vandal, who rashly grasped the altar’s horn in order to tear it away

Again, another man attempted with unworthy obstinacy to climb upon the sacred altar. When he rashly grasped the horn of the altar, his hand suddenly adhered to the marble beneath it, so that, although it could be torn away, it could in no way be detached.

You would have seen a captive beast standing in one place without chains, fastened there by divine power. Meanwhile the barbarian multitude marveled and trembled, fearing that a similar vengeance might bind them; they experienced in the present moment the unseen divine power through their brutish audacity.

But when some of the others could not bear to leave him thus bound, they placed axes on either side of the hand and cut away the stone. At last they freed the pagan, though a piece of marble remained permanently and inseparably attached to his hand. Carrying this weight all the way to his own land, he was seen by many returning from captivity to reach his people with his arm already withered, an unwilling herald of the power of Saint Basolus.

> **Note:** Hugh of Flavigny mentions this miracle in his *Chronicle* under the year 937, in these words: “In the church of Saint Basolus, when one of the Hungarians, attempting to climb upon the altar, had placed his bow against it with his hand, his hand adhered to the stone and could not at all be pulled away, until the others, cutting the stone around that very hand, compelled the pagan, to the amazement of everyone, to carry away part of the stone.”

## Chapter X. Concerning the man who fell among robbers with his wife

A certain ancient inhabitant of the metropolis of Reims, well known to many of his fellow citizens both by blood and by diligence, used once each year to hasten to the monastery of the holy man of God. He desired to go there more devotedly to provide the brothers of that place with offerings from his possessions, for the increase of righteousness.

On one occasion, when he had decided to come there according to his custom and had taken with him certain gifts from his abundance to offer to the servants of the holy confessor, he encountered robbers on the road. His horse was immediately seized, all the money he was carrying was taken as plunder, and all the ornaments of his accompanying wife, such as women possess, were turned into booty.

After taking these things, the robbers set off, while sorrow and anxiety overwhelmed the unhappy couple because of their loss. But the woman, provoked by grief over the damage, began to call upon the holy man of God with plaintive cries. She said that she would no longer perform service for his servants if he allowed them to depart without providing support against such treatment.

After her cries had been broken by lamentation and sighs, the robbers’ horses stiffened, like fixed statues, immovable to right or left and incapable of bending even slightly. You might have seen the wretched men standing in terror with their booty, and you would have considered with amazement how, by some divine power, they remained like rigid stones in one place because of the injury done to the saint.

When they had remained for a long time turning toward one another, they finally conferred among themselves. They recognized that they were being held by divine power because of their rashness against innocent people and that, unless they repented, they would be completely deprived of the ability to depart. After taking counsel, they timidly returned to those whom they had unjustly stripped of their possessions. They restored everything to them and, covered with shame, begged them to seek pardon for their crimes.

Thus, with the protection of Saint Basolus supporting them and their enemies released on the road, the couple, now more devoted, hastened to the monastery they had intended to visit. They gave thanks to God and his holy confessor for the benefits granted to them, joyfully presented what they had brought, honored the place with gifts, and thereafter each year fulfilled what they had begun with more willing hearts.

## Chapter XI. Concerning the rector who refused to keep dogs away from the spring

Finally, I think we must report what happened when that same place had begun to lose the worship of the sacred religion that it had once maintained with sufficient dignity, after the morals of our age had already become corrupted. The monastery, together with its possessions, was handed over to a certain Frankish layman under the right of domination.

Nor is this surprising, since during those times the recklessness of secular powers had also seized the seats of bishops. Where abbots or religious men had previously been accustomed to sit, gatherings of foolish men, places of earthly pride, and empty multitudes now occupied the sites, just as the holy prophet lamented that the stones of the sanctuary had been scattered (Lamentations 4:1), and displayed in his prophecies those who had exalted themselves in sacred stations.

The man to whom such a great property had been granted for possession was indeed distinguished by birth, but in spirit and appearance he was seen to be excessively arrogant. After this position had been granted to him, the secular man compelled his household to move in with them, occupied the monastery’s buildings, transported his possessions there, arranged his equipment, and decided above all to reside there. In one part he set up women’s hairdressing establishments, and in another great packs of dogs.

Meanwhile, while the dogs wandered about more freely with their reins loosened, as creatures naturally greedy, they carelessly reached the spring of Saint Basolus, which we mentioned above. Since no one prevented them from repeatedly lapping the water of the sacred spring with unworthy draughts, the entire pack of dogs was turned rabid and fittingly expiated its offense against the holy confessor with the punishment of madness.

Nor did the anger thus divinely aroused through so many movements come to rest. The unlawful ruler himself was also seized by a similar vengeance. Delivered into the power of the enemy, he was wholly confounded, lost his senses, was bound with iron, and, surrounded by madness, no longer recognized himself as a human being, because he had contemptuously refused to keep the unclean animals away from the sacred temple.

But when his household members devoutly cried out to Saint Basolus and honored the place with gifts, he was finally cured of his madness. He took care to preserve the reverence whose vengeance he remembered had been exercised against him.

## Chapter XII. Concerning the shameless cupbearer

A certain household cupbearer served this powerful man, attending to his needs. He was a very frivolous man, rejecting the restraints of continence and ready for illicit acts. On the western side adjoining the sacred temple there had once been a small dwelling built in an earlier age. Its enclosures and other assigned features still remain, and the indication of an altar that has now collapsed can be seen there.

That man was accustomed to sleep there. When he was oppressed by having drunk too much wine, he took advantage of the suitable hour of night and irreverently forced himself upon one woman from the group of women, as though blessed Basolus were either absent from his place or, in his clemency, unwilling to punish the crime.

But the one who had always been a friend of chastity did not allow such wicked rashness to remain unpunished near him. In the darkness familiar to him, the man was seized by a demon and miserably lacerated throughout his body by severe punishment. Bound more tightly with twisted ropes, like a savage animal, he was tied to an elm tree.

Imitating the voices of various monsters and barking like dogs, he himself wounded his limbs. After long torments, at the invocation of the confessor of Christ, Basolus, he was released from the demon, so that thereafter he might be chastened and not presume to commit anything so indecent there again.

## Chapter XIII. Concerning the man who went to the church after being warned three times and received perfect health

Nor must we pass over what, after no small lapse of time, had reached the ears of very many people, for there is an innumerable multitude of witnesses to the event. A secession had been stirred up among the leading men of the kingdom after their anger had been kindled, and, since neither party yielded to the other, the entire weight of their fury was felt also by the losses suffered by the fortress of Châlons.

For after a great multitude had been raised up everywhere, with a certain Baso leading them, they attacked the walls, and committed everything to devouring flames. When the reins had been loosened and the fire ruled everywhere, nothing could remain of the municipality, which had been reduced to ashes, as though Trojan fires had somehow sprung up again.

A certain man from the province of Belgica is said to have taken part in this great crime. Divine vengeance did not allow him, any more than the others, to depart unpunished. Shaken by an intolerable disease, one side of his body swelled and became distended like a wineskin, while for a long time he was tortured by living pains, rolling his unhappy soul almost within his throat day after day and awaiting only death as his final escape.

His property was stripped from him, he lacked a household, he was abandoned by his own wife, and he was cast aside by everyone like a lifeless corpse. Amid these fires of punishment, he was warned three times in a vision to visit the monastery of the holy confessor. He had no way of being saved except through the power of Saint Basolus, although until then he had heard neither his name nor the name of the place.

At last he was placed, half alive, upon a bier and carried to the site. There, while still despairing of life, he poured out prayers in his mind and tasted a little of the mixed liquid from the saint’s tomb. His revived limbs gradually began to live again, so that after not much time he was restored to health and attained such complete soundness as he had never before experienced.

There are, finally, many more things reported as having been seen or heard concerning the deeds of this blessed confessor. For the benefit of readers who wish to pursue examples of humility, however, it is enough for us to have published these few. When the reader discovers that only the more outstanding events have been recorded, let him receive these with greater pleasure, freed from the weariness of length, and let his mind nowhere waver through harmful scrupulosity.

For just as a person who is always nourished by one kind of food is burdened by disgust, whereas the mind is drawn more pleasantly to varied fare, so, if we spin out words at excessive length, we heap up a weariness of words from words themselves.

In all this we have taken care above all to speak the truth with due restraint and not to burden the fastidious with excessive detail. Here, therefore, we bring our work to an end. Like those who, after traversing the arduous expanse of a gulf, moor their ship at a quiet station, not without the fruit of reward, so we conclude our labor. We humbly give thanks to God, who through his holy confessor Basolus honors us with the insignia of miracles and assists us with unceasing protections, with the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

> **Note:** In the manuscript there followed a short history concerning the return of the body of Saint Basolus to his monastery, carried out in the first year of the priesthood of Archbishop Rodulfus according to the customary practice. It is customary for the body of this blessed man to be carried each year by the abbot of the monastery and the brothers to the Reims Indictus; after the bishop has delivered a sermon to the people, it is brought back again to the place assigned to it. This practice has continued until now on the second Monday of Pentecost. In that year, therefore—that is, in the year of Christ 1108—a certain Lotharingian named Dominicus, a tall man in body, mocked the clients of Saint Basolus because of the saint’s short stature and refused to render service to the saints. He is said immediately to have been seized by a demon; but soon repenting of what he had done, he was freed from this affliction through the merits of Saint Basolus, with the assistance of Girulfus, a monk of approved life.

# Life of Saint Bercharius, Abbot of Hautvillers and of Montier-en-Der, the First, by Adso

*(In Mabillon, Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict, Second Century, p. 831, from the same manuscript of Compiègne and from Camuzat’s *Promptuarium*.)*

## Preliminary Observations

### 1

The deeds of Saint Bercharius [Saint Bercaire], abbot, were first written by an anonymous author in a rough and unpolished style; afterward, Adso, abbot of Montier-en-Der, polished them in the middle of the tenth century. “The deeds of this saint and our most devout protector Bercharius,” says the anonymous monk of Montier-en-Der near the end of the following book of *Miracles*, “he adorned, as far as he could, with the charm of eloquence, and scattered throughout the regions of Gaul what until then had been held in uncultivated writing and hidden away.”

Frodoard, canon of the church of Reims, had also shortly before Adso touched briefly upon certain deeds of Saint Bercharius in Book II, chapter 27, of his *History of Reims*. We present here Adso’s work, already published by Nicholas Camuzat together with the accompanying book of *Miracles* in the *Trecassine Promptuarium*, collated with the manuscript codex of our abbey of Compiègne, since it was not possible to obtain the older history of Saint Bercharius.

In the manuscript codices, the name of Adso as author is not prefixed to this *Life*. Yet the first verses persuade us that the book of *Miracles*, which usually follows it, is genuinely the work of Adso.

### 2

The name of Saint Bercharius is absent from the ancient calendars. In our very old copy of Usuard, written eight hundred years ago, Saint Bercharius is indeed mentioned by a secondary hand, though one that plainly bears an age of four hundred years, under the seventeenth day before the Kalends of November—the day of his translation, as we shall say below—in these words: “At the monastery of Der, Saint Bercharius, martyr and abbot.”

In the charters, however, of Emperor Louis the Pious, Charles the Bald, and others, Saint Bercharius is praised, and his body is said to rest in the monastery of Montier-en-Der. They call him a martyr, following the custom of medieval authors, who called pious men violently killed for whatever reason “martyrs.” Thus they adorn with the name of martyrs Saint Praejectus of Clermont, Theodard of Tongeren, Leodegarius of Autun, and Arnulfus, killed by robbers in the county of Porcien—as is read in Volume II of Acher’s *Spicilegium*, in the Chronicle of Mouzon—along with Adalbaldus, the husband of Saint Rictrudis, Edward, king of the English, killed by his stepmother, and many others.

In the Acts of Saint Leodegarius, written by an anonymous author, these verses are found in chapter 5:

> “For it must not be thought that he, Leodegarius, feared martyrdom. For when, some time earlier, a certain monk named Bercharius had announced to him during the Lord’s Supper that he would suffer death, he went to the bloody palace of the king on the day of the Lord’s Passion,” and so forth.

Whether this can be applied to Saint Bercharius the abbot is left to the judgment of the reader. Certainly, Saint Bercharius is said to have taken Waimerus, who was responsible for the torments of Saint Leodegarius, with him to Jerusalem, as is related in Book of Miracles, number 11.

### 3

Besides various chapels, Saint Bercharius built two monasteries: first Hautvillers, and afterward Montier-en-Der, over both of which he presided. Hautvillers [Altivillarense], in the diocese of Reims, stands on the Matrona River, four miles from the city of Reims. It was founded according to the rule of Saints Benedict and Columbanus, as is stated in the charter of Nivo, or Nivardus, bishop of Reims, published by the Sammarthani and cited by Frodoard.

Montier-en-Der [Dervense] lies in the district of Perthois [le Parthois] in Champagne, subject to the diocese of Châlons and bordering that of Troyes, on the river Viger [the Voire]. It too was built under the rule of Saint Benedict by Saint Bercharius, as is related in the instrument granted by Emperor Louis the Pious in the year 815, which the Sammarthani reported after Chesne.

Both monasteries still flourish under the Benedictine congregation of Saint Vanne. Hautvillers is distinguished by the veneration of the relics of Saint Helena; Montier-en-Der by the head of that same saint, by its town, and by the spiritual jurisdiction that it exercises over the town itself and the five villages subject to the monastery.

## Author’s Prologue

### 1

Since the holy and universal Catholic Church throughout the world solemnly pays the glorious palms and rewards of merit of illustrious men with the functions of fitting devotion, I too think that we shall deserve punishment for the unproductive sloth of silence if the deeds of one remain hidden whose abundance of virtues is especially rich among us and whose growth in holy formation shines forth—especially since the deeds of those who came before, when recalled to the memory of posterity, become material for salvation.

Therefore, wishing to touch briefly upon the deeds and contests of labor of the blessed Bercharius, glorious abbot and martyr, we undertake this material of narration with all the greater difficulty because we feel ourselves unequal to explaining the greatness of this work. Yet it is not difficult for him to loosen a tongue bound in silence into words whom even the mute elements are known solemnly to proclaim with harmonious voices.

We therefore intend to pursue those matters that either became known through the records of his own holy household and companions or, later, by divine favor repaid through his merits, were able to be handed down to our own age.

## The Life Begins

### Bercharius, a noble Aquitanian

### 2

The memorials of an earlier age have handed down that his origin and the beginning of his lineage were in an Aquitanian district. His parents were venerable in life and very religious, adorned in no small degree by an outward abundance of possessions and—something far more excellent—distinguished by a certain privilege of singular innocence and blessed fruitfulness among themselves.

They preserved the rights of conjugal chastity with faithful integrity, surpassing others in temporal goods, yet burning with devoted zeal for divine works. Through the disposition of heavenly mercy they deserved to receive such a great and remarkable offspring that, through his formation and merits, an innumerable host of those serving in the heavenly ranks might bear the white palms of good fruits, while the manifold cunning of the ancient deceiver might perish after the spoils of faithful souls had been taken from him.

This is easy to perceive if anyone, setting aside loftier matters, deigns to observe the few things that follow. It is established that, when he emerged into the light from his mother’s womb already sanctified by the gift of God, his parents, following Aquitanian custom, gave him the name Bererus [or Bereus], as though he were already, from the very beginning of his birth, the heir of a good inheritance.

### He is instructed in letters under Nivardus
### 3.

At that time, while the Frankish empire was most happily governed by King Childeric [Note: [Col. 0669C] It is customary for authors who have committed the deeds of the saints to writing to assert that each saint was born under the same king during whose reign he flourished. Adso did this here as well. Bercharius was born during the rule of Chlothar II and was received at Luxeuil [Col. 0670C] not by Eustasius but by Waldebert, or Walbert, the abbot, around the year 650. He founded the monastery of Hautvillers around 670 and died, as they say, in 684.], a man extremely powerful in military affairs but exceptionally devoted to the worship of God’s churches, the blessed bishop Nivardus—most famous throughout the whole Frankish world for the greatness of his holiness and religion, living an apostolic life on earth by apostolic authority—presided over the holy Church of Reims.

Since he was filled with authority and grace, and was also requested to visit various regions and peoples, both because of the merit of his life and because of the abundance of his eloquence in teaching, it happened that he at some time sought the borders of Aquitaine and is said to have reached the very estate where the parents of the man of God evidently lived in their own dwelling. For, among the other gifts which this holy man had received through the generosity of heavenly providence, it is certain that he had also flourished temporally through no insignificant titles of paternal inheritance from his ancestors. Anyone who wishes to investigate this carefully can readily recognize it, since almost down to our own times those who are known to have succeeded him in governing his monastery appear to have possessed, by undisputed right over long stretches of time, the villages and estates belonging to that jurisdiction, both beyond the Loire, where Diseias is located, and within the borders of Aquitaine. But because of the evils that arose, these properties appear to have been lost, partly through the negligence of those who became sluggish and partly through the cruel assaults of perverse peoples—properties that had once been assigned for the use of the monks.

But, to return to the completion of what we began: when the holy bishop mentioned above had been received with the dutiful generosity owed to him by the parents of the man of God, as was proper, and when he marveled at seeing in the boy a kind of image of his future condition, already a candidate for good works, he foresaw, by divine inspiration, that the boy should be devoted to the sacred mysteries. Thus encouraged by the authority of the most holy bishop, his exceedingly devout parents, when the proper time had come during the tender years of his childhood, decided that he should immediately be entrusted to the salutary disciplines of literary study. As the gift of heavenly illumination went before him, the earnestness of sacred instruction was accompanied by the shining growth of spiritual gifts.

He did not idly allow himself, beneath the toys of tender childhood, to gather more eagerly from the luminous fountain of letters those acquisitions by which, later, when he had risen to manly strength, he might be able to benefit both himself and others according to the measure of the Lord’s dispensation. Even then he composed the movements of childish fickleness—by which that unstable and fleeting age is often dissolved—with the dignity of innate virtue and proper self-control, so that he would allow nothing else to remain in him besides those efforts in letters to which he had been devoted—unless, perhaps, he was engaged in works of piety or, as nature permitted, was applying himself more devoutly to the sacred exercises of prayer.

### He goes to Reims to join Nivardus

### 4.

Thus, while the boy of holy disposition soon surpassed his peers both in knowledge and in strength of character, and gradually resolved to devote himself more fully to the beginnings of a good purpose and to the perfect training of the heavenly militia, he began, through the desire of his soul burning for the life above, to aspire to higher things. Sufficient in his contempt for earthly matters, and striving with all his strength toward those things that concern the growth of virtues through the constant contemplation of eternal glory, he fixed everlasting things before his eyes without tiring, exchanged perishable things for enduring ones, restrained the impulses of carnal affections through various kinds of affliction, and strengthened the steps of his youth by the power of divine love.

Then, rejecting the ties of relatives and homeland, and carefully reflecting that when those who undertake the beginnings of a new way of life are regarded by the world as foreigners and strangers rather than as its own citizens, he burned with desire to seek the aforementioned most holy Nivardus, bishop of Reims. As we have said, supported by the privilege of apostolic instruction, distinguished by the honor of nobility, and adorned with various kinds of virtue, he shone as the foremost among the Frankish nobles at the royal court and as a man most worthy in life and conduct.

At that time the city was surrounded by companies of saints. Although it stood amid military ranks under its ruler Childeric, it nevertheless breathed, in harmony with its head, as a populous city devoted to the love of divine worship. Drawn by the fame of so great a man, the fortunate young Bercharius—most suitable in ecclesiastical sacraments, faith, habit, and conduct—shared the faith and merit of that blessed old man to whom the Lord had long before said:

> “Go out from your land and from your kindred, and come into the land that I shall show you, and I shall make you grow into a great nation” (Genesis 12:1–2).

Leaving his kindred and homeland, he entered the borders of Francia after a long journey, destined to become, with Saint Nivardus the bishop, a most fortunate citizen—of the holy Church of Reims, as will be evident from what follows—in order to advance the divine work that the omnipotence of the Lord and Redeemer had ordained to be accomplished through these two most fortunate fellow-workers in the gaining of faithful souls.

When the blessed bishop had obtained such a companion, as he had always desired, he was himself occupied with external affairs of public administration. He was frequently required to attend the counsels and actions of the royal government, and, willingly or unwillingly, to bear the burden of episcopal responsibility by heavenly appointment. He therefore rejoiced greatly when he found a familiar assistant and a most devout partner in divine works, who could exercise the ministry entrusted to him both publicly and privately by reprimanding, correcting, and entreating, like a diligent and perfect farmer.

### He is entrusted to Remaclus for instruction

### 5.

Therefore, desiring that Bercharius should be more perfectly instructed in every respect, Nivardus decided that he should be attached to holier and more religious men learned in divine knowledge, whom familiarity had brought to him from every quarter, so that Bercharius might learn through the authority of many instructors what he would later minister to many others.

Among these men, at that time in the court of the Frankish king, the venerable reputation of the blessed Remaclus, a procurator in the palace’s sacred treasury, had grown exceptionally strong everywhere through his titles of prudence and holiness [Note: It is not sufficiently certain whether Remaclus held that office in the palace, or whether Bercharius lived with him at court or elsewhere. See the Acts of Saint Remaclus under the year 664.].

That illustrious man, later a glorious confessor of the Lord and approved by many miraculous signs, was gentle toward all, benevolent toward everyone, moderate in prosperity, most patient in adversity, praiseworthy in life, and affable in speech. He displayed such prudence concerning temporal matters that he never turned his eyes away from eternal things.

The blessed Bercharius preferred, at the command of the aforementioned bishop, to join himself for a time to the sacred instruction of such a great and eminent man, so that, while taking counsel for the weakness of his age and character in what he understood to be perfect knowledge of doctrine, he might bring back from him not so much the acquisitions of knowledge as those of holy purity.

### He goes to Luxeuil

### 6.

Meanwhile, after the just young man had for some time enjoyed the teaching of this blessed man and had tasted, as far as he could, the draught of heavenly wisdom, he eagerly desired to seek the monastery of Luxeuil, since a reputation for religious observance, commended by the strict rules of Saint Columbanus, had reached him.

At that time this monastery possessed a singular renown in every region of Gaul, both because of its many material possessions and because of its practices of divine worship. There, it was said, the discipline was stricter and the pursuit of wisdom more complete. The same blessed Father Columbanus had built this remarkable place from its foundations in the vast wilderness of the Vosges, where he found buildings of very ancient workmanship and waters naturally boiling up of their own accord from the veins of the earth. Later, when he had gathered a number of nearly six hundred monks of the faithful, he became their superior and governed that monastery most nobly for a long time, becoming famous in the same place through many signs of miracles.

Until the most wicked queen Brunhild, because she had judged two sons whom she had borne from an adulterous union with the infamous king Theuderic—the son, that is, of King Sigebert—unworthy of her conversation and blessing [Note: The author is grossly mistaken if he thinks that Brunhild had children by Theuderic, who was Brunhild’s grandson and fathered great-grandchildren upon her through a concubine.], drove him from that place at the devil’s instigation.

As he was about to leave, not without the great sorrow and mourning of everyone, he appointed as superior over that numerous company of brothers Eustasius, an equally holy man, illustrious both for the nobility of his birth and for his life, whom he himself had instructed from childhood and who had been born in the district of Langres. From there Columbanus went to Italy and founded the monastery of Bobbio with no less fitting workmanship, where, perfected in virtues, he rested in a blessed end.

The holy Eustasius, taking the Father’s place, fortified a considerable multitude of monks in the service of the Lord through words and examples, and became the heir of his master’s name and merit. When the reputation of so great a name was heard, religious men flocked there from every direction, and many eagerly offered themselves and their children to be instructed. Above all, they considered it a very great thing if, after enduring for a long time the injury of being tested, they might somehow deserve admission into the community.

What place or city would not rejoice to have a bishop or abbot formed in the discipline of this blessed man, since it is evident that, through the power of his teaching, almost the whole Frankish world was first suitably illuminated by regular decrees?

Therefore Bercharius, the servant of Christ, always desiring to rise toward the institutions of the higher life, hastened swiftly and according to his wish to this place by the authority and favor of his bishop. He was approved as worthy of the zeal of the aforementioned Father [Note: Saint Eustasius governed the monastery of Luxeuil from 613 to 614, when Sonnatius presided over the see of Reims. After Sonnatius came Leudegisus, Engilbertus, and Lando; Nivardus succeeded Lando around the year 650. Bercharius therefore was not admitted to Luxeuil by Eustasius, but perhaps by Walbert, his successor, [Col. 0674D] who governed the place from 625 to 665.], joined the holy company of monks, and associated with them not merely in body but in mind and conduct.

### He orders his life piously

### 7.

Having been received into the common life with the others, and again undertaking, like a newly arrived athlete, the training-ground of the heavenly militia, forgetful of his former contests, as though he had accomplished nothing fully before when placed in the arena of virtues, he began once more to discipline his spirit through divine works. You might have thought that he was then receiving for the first time the beginnings of monastic rigor: always stronger than himself, and made more joyful by the grace of heavenly illumination through the quality of his earlier life.

It is beyond the capacity of my pen to recount how great was the humility of the man of God, how great the virtue of his obedience, how great the gravity of his moderation, how great his charity, his kindness, his gentleness, and the strength of his patience. He carried out the task imposed by obedience at the command of the one who gave it in such a way that, directing his mind toward higher things, he neither sought the gains of human praise nor exchanged the reward of his glory for the price of a perishing thing.

He also sought, in consideration of others, to despise himself. Although in his own judgment he was inferior to everyone, he nevertheless strove, at the summit of humility, to be found superior to all. He was deeply saddened whenever someone in that holy community undertook some demanding task that he himself, with God’s favor, had performed less vigorously.

### Made cupbearer, he is commended for obedience by a miracle

### 8.

It is reported that at this same time he was appointed there as a server of cups [Note: Although authors sometimes use *caliculas* for *caligulas*, here they seem to mean cups or drinking vessels, as the following makes clear.] and, at the command of the superior, took turns being responsible for the storeroom. When he received this workshop of distributing provisions, since holy obedience had made him energetic for every task, he prudently carried out whatever had been entrusted to him.

One day, while he was occupied with such duties, he was suddenly summoned by order of the father. At that moment he had perhaps entered the storeroom and was standing before a vessel, holding in his hand a utensil commonly called a *ducidulum*, used to draw out drink, and was pouring the grain-based drink [Note: This is what they call beer, or *zythum*, because it is produced chiefly from grain or barley. This kind of miracle is related in the Life of Saint Columbanus, no. 26; but it cannot be applied to Bercharius, since it is said to have occurred at Columbanus’s command, and Bercharius could not have seen him as a companion.] from an amphora. Wonderful to relate! At the single command, when he heard the abbot’s name, he hurried away from what he had in his hands, forgetting in the heat of obedience both the care of the vessel and the precaution due to the amphora.

When he stood before the abbot in response to the summons, the drink meanwhile continued to flow into the vessel placed beneath it. After it had reached the surface of the vessel, it began to gather above it like a column and to form a crown in a circle. You would have seen that kind of liquid rising freely, although it could scarcely be contained by the vessel’s edges, just as once, when God’s people passed through, the waters of the Jordan were lifted upward without banks. Thus it became plainly evident how great was the power of obedience, whose fruit can in no way be lost upon the earth.

When he returned, greatly astonishing the abbot, he was amazed at what had happened, since he had not presumed that such a thing could have been done by him. Yet the holy man attributed what had occurred not to his own merit but entirely to that of his abbot.

### He returns to Reims and joins Nivardus, who is planning to build a monastery

[Col. 0675B]

### 9.

When he had now been thoroughly instructed in regular disciplines and fortified on both sides with the weapons of the divine militia, so that through what he had learned by long practice he might now be able to promote the salvation of many in the administration of the Lord’s profit, he returned to the province of Reims, to the bishop Saint Nivardus. As we have said, Nivardus kept watch over the protection of his flock in both spiritual and material matters, repelled the enemy’s ambushes, and enlarged ecclesiastical dignity through abundant success.

For many years he had carried within his heart, through divine inspiration, this desire: that in some settlement of his diocese he should build a house for the service of the living God, wherever the suitability of the resources might offer more fitting advantages for divine service. The greatest obstacle to this plan was that he lacked a person who could share the undertaking, supply the bishop’s desire, and prove energetic in accepting such a great collaboration.

But his mind, long suspended in uncertainty, could not be wholly disappointed in the hope of an intention conceived long before. He therefore seized upon Bercharius, attached him to his purpose, and chose him after consultation—a man capable in the affairs of God, endowed with religion, effective in spirit, and no less agile than prudent in experience of external matters.

Although at that time, as we have said, that city flourished both through the talent of many men and through its distinguished administration of public affairs, Nivardus nevertheless selected this man alone and made him his chief associate. With authority and merit corresponding to the task, he entrusted him with the care of the future construction and, by sound deliberation, decided that he should have special charge of the whole structure.

There was a public estate in the district of Reims, eight miles from the city, which in an earlier age had evidently been given the name Sparnacus—Épernay. Long ago, in the time of Clovis, the great ruler of the Franks, the same wondrous father had acquired it for a substantial price. Blessed Remigius, endowed with and distinguished by apostolic authority, magnificent in teaching and virtues, had anointed Clovis and his army, as is read in his deeds, with the sacred chrism of the regenerating water through an angelic ministry. Remigius had made this estate heir to the Church of Reims, over which he presided by God’s authority.

Finally, the most glorious bishop of God, Nivardus, faithfully carrying out the office of pastoral diligence, would often go out both to visit other places in his diocese and to visit this village. He did not act merely for his own advantage, but, showing himself approachable to all, diligently provided for the salvation of his subjects.

Since he spent days and nights wakeful in the continual desire to build a monastery on one of his estates, which also possessed considerable temporal wealth, he took his domestic companion, the blessed Bercharius, as he often did, and found occasion to plan a customary visit to the aforementioned village.

As they proceeded on the road toward that village, which lay beside the banks of the river Marne, there was a particularly pleasant place belonging to him. Set slightly back in a hollow on the lovely slope of a mountain, with green grass, streams of water flowing gently down from the heights, and trees and vineyards crowded together on every side along the decline, it offered delights to the eyes of those who looked upon it.

### While Nivardus falls asleep, he receives through an angel the command to found the monastery of Hautvillers

### 10.

When the holy bishop had begun this journey and had already reached those parts along the slope of the mountain where the pleasantness of the descending site presented itself more closely to the eyes, he was overcome by such a heavy sleep on the horse-drawn vehicle on which he was traveling [Col. 0676C] that he was immediately deprived of all ability to continue. He called out to his companion, the blessed Bercharius, ordered the entire mounted company that happened then to be accompanying him to halt, and explained more openly by what force he was being driven into sleep.

“Look,” he said, “I am being shaken by an overwhelming sleep that is unlike my usual condition, so that I am entirely convinced that I am incapable of moving forward from here. Let us therefore, amid these pleasant green places, turn aside for a little rest for my wearied limbs, so that when my strength returns through sleep, I may regain the ability to continue the journey.”

Among the broad forests with their spreading branches and green leaves, they chose a beech tree, pleasing for the present need:

> Here, among the alders, this one raised its head  
> as high as cypresses usually rise among pliant viburnums.

They quickly placed themselves beneath this tree in order to rest. The blessed Bercharius, his inseparable companion, hurried to receive the bishop’s head in his lap while he lay stretched out on the ground; the bishop himself reclined beneath the broad shelter of the beech.

What miracle was then shown from heaven I have thought it proper to make known by the service of my pen, so that the truth of heavenly illumination might reveal those whom the density of the forest had concealed.

While the bishop was resting, the holy man Bercharius, with his eyes fixed upon heaven, suddenly saw through the clear air [Note: Frodoard relates this story somewhat differently in book II, chapter 7, of his History of Reims. He says that after the vision of the dove recounted here Bercharius shed tears: “When the blessed bishop awoke from sleep, he found his face wet with Bercharius’s tears, and, asking what caused his weeping, learned that he had wept because of the ruin of his work”—that is, of the church at Villare, built twice by Nivardus and twice overthrown by an uncertain accident. “As they recounted their visions to one another, it is said that the bishop also told these things seen to a certain servant of God named Bavon, whose possession it was. He had an oratory there in honor of the holy Cross and resided there. After learning of the bishop’s vision and intention, he offered him that same possession, together with a portion of an estate belonging to a certain brother of his named Baldin.” Frodoard adds that Theoderamnus, Bavon’s other brother, count of Reims and later bishop of Reims, and his son Gedeon received the monastic habit there.] a dove descending from above, radiant with snowy brightness, and gently settling upon the very tree beneath which they had remained. As he directed his gaze toward it, carefully wishing to discover toward what place the snow-white bird intended to turn, it suddenly released the oars of its wings, sprang from the tree on which it had perched, and cleaving the empty air, flew in a circle around the area where the monastery was to be built. It marked out the place with its circuit, sanctified it by its presence, and, when this circuit had been completed, returned again to the familiar tree.

When the messenger of heaven had repeated the same circles three times as a sign confirming the future work, it disappeared into the open sky. Nevertheless, a foreshadowing of the divine will was disclosed to people dwelling on earth, and a trace of new wonder was left behind.

The holy man, whose soul was pure, understood that this was a heavenly sign, by which the minds of those who doubted might be strengthened and the work long delayed might be founded in the service of God. Blessed is the man to whom the dignity of an angelic vision was shown bodily, in the form of a shining dove, to confirm the testimony of innocence and purity.

There is also something no less wonderful in this event: what Bercharius had perceived with his bodily eyes, the holy bishop, while resting, had sensed through a dream of heavenly vision. After a short interval of rest, when he awoke from sleep and raised his head, already instructed by heavenly revelation, he said:

“O most faithful companion of my desires, how pleasing it is to me that I have turned aside here for a little while, at the proper time, for the sake of sleep. Through God’s grace, you have evidently come to know the mystery of so great a revelation from heaven. Behold, I now proceed from here in joy, following the signs of heaven. What I had long carried in my heart, though delayed for so long, I am compelled by the secret of this wondrous vision to undertake more promptly. But lest this unexpected matter lead you too far astray, I shall plainly explain what I saw.

“First, understand that a house of God is present here, divinely shown to me, an unworthy servant of the Lord Christ, as it once was shown to the fortunate ancient patriarch and as the gate of heaven was shown to him. For as soon as I had lowered my limbs and was suddenly seized by sleep, when scarcely the power of nature could move me in either direction while I rested, I seemed to see from above something resembling the whiteness of snow in the form of a dove. After settling on this tree, it flew with swift course around this place, without uncertainty about where it was heading, and, having completed three equal circles, rose toward the summit of heaven.

“I truly believe that this portent from God benefits the hope conceived in our hearts: what had been undertaken as our desire must now be carried out more swiftly, since heaven has given warning.”

When the holy bishop had finished speaking, the blessed Bercharius, who had made his lap a resting place for the holy man’s head, said:

“Know, most holy father, that whatever you testify was divinely brought before you in the vision of your spirit by this heavenly portent, I also saw bodily through the manifest power of God.”

### With Childeric’s help, he arranges for one church to be dedicated to Saint Peter and another to the Blessed Mary

### 11.

As the two men thus exchanged accounts—one of what he had perceived in sleep, the other of what he had seen with bodily eyes—the matter was brought into full view: that place, marked out by angelic surveying, had been chosen by God in a wondrous arrangement as a site for carrying out the service of divine worship.

Thus, once both had been made certain by the grace of such a revelation and heavenly consolation, and once they had been specially instructed by the designation of the site concerning what had been doubtful, they both rose.
