The most blessed bishop then lifted his eyes to heaven and immediately praised with all the intention of his heart the one upon whom the Holy Spirit had descended from the hidden counsel of the eternal Father in bodily form, like a dove, and who, with heaven opened, had blessed the streams of the Jordan through the baptism of his sacred body for the cleansing of our sins.

With so great and fitting an auspice preceding the establishment of an eternal dwelling, the eminent bishop said to the blessed Bercharius:

“To you and to your diligence I intend to entrust this holy work, so that, since I have no doubt that you are perfect in prudence and holiness, I may rightly appoint you leader in the construction of this heavenly building.”

The man of God, ardent as he was, overflowing in every part of his being with love for the Lord, hostile to every kind of sloth but devoted to tireless effectiveness in labor, gladly accepted the charge and embraced it with a desire as great as the magnitude of his merits, which heavenly grace had increased in him.

And because he had already made himself a temple of the Holy Spirit through virtue, he also desired to establish for the Lord a temple visible to the eyes through the beauty of an earthly structure, trusting everywhere in both divine assistance and the aid of the supreme bishop.

It is certain that he had become so pleasing and acceptable to all the Frankish kings of his time, as well as to bishops and nobles of royal rank, that if anything concerning divine worship or even the necessities of earthly resources was dear to him, he readily obtained it from them. A careful reader will also be able to find this plainly in its proper place below, if he wishes to review the benefactions granted to him at different times by the generosity of royal majesty and the Frankish princes.

Supported by their authority and favor, he now applies himself more earnestly to the business of organizing the construction. He prepares supplies for the expenses and, as a diligent worker, assigns everything that seemed necessary for so great a work.

Thus, in the aforesaid estate, situated, as we have said, on the slope of a mountain, where the hollowed-out terrain opens into a beautiful and generously spreading plain, and where the long banks of the river Marne lie below and around it, the place appealed to the eye with a certain soothing delight of vision. It had received from ancient times the name Altumvillare, or Hautvillers.

Bercharius enclosed the area designated by the angel, precisely as it had been shown from heaven, by laying the foundations around it. He measured all the walls of the building according to the form of the dove passing through the air. He did not cease his work as a worshiper of God until, with heavenly providence granting its approval, and with the kindly assistance of Childeric, king of the Franks, and of the holy bishop, he completed with the desired perfection the work he had undertaken for the glory of God.

### He equips the monastery with property and people

[Col. 0679B]

### 12.

That tree which had once stood as a most luxuriant beech, upon which the dove sent from heaven had previously settled and whose flight in a circle had marked out the site of the monastery, was cut down after deliberation. With the common agreement of everyone’s wishes, an altar was established in the place where it had been fixed, in honor of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles [Note: The diploma of Nivardus, reported by the Sammarthani, adds Paul, or also Saint John and the other martyrs and confessors, whose relics are known to be venerated there.].

For the consecration of the basilica, other bishops also assembled with Saint Nivardus, the metropolitan bishop. All the clergy and numerous crowds of both sexes hastened there, and the Frankish nobles likewise gathered with no less enthusiasm. Through the praiseworthy work of the blessed Bercharius, they all rejoiced with equal intensity in the praises of God.

On the southern slope of the same mountain, the holy man built another church, which he decreed should be honored in the name of Mary, the Mother of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the ever-virgin.

He also wisely arranged the monastery’s enclosures and all the appropriate offices of the community for the observance of the regular way of life. He gathered religious men devoted to monastic conduct and carefully completed everything judged useful for this order.

The most holy bishop assigned abundant revenues from estates for the necessary uses of the servants of God, both from those that appeared to belong to his own jurisdiction and from those that, through the intervention of the blessed Bercharius, could be obtained from the leading men of the Franks. Thus the people serving God in that monastery might grow both in merit and in number through the labors of these two men.

These, then, are the holy beginnings of the great works of this blessed Father of ours, Bercharius. But greater struggles of pious labor in the service of the divine majesty still remain, which the subsequent course of events will later reveal in this work.

Although he was perfect in the sublimity of spiritual discipline and constant in meditation upon divine law, he did not seek temporal glory. Rather, with purity of mind he continually desired eternal glory; he did not wish to bend toward passing happiness or to be dissolved by empty praise.

When the entire structure of that sacred temple had been completed, neither speech can contain nor tongue in any way express how immense was the joy of these two holy men, how gracious the fellowship of their united affection, how great their love of divinity, and how great their ardor for the heavenly life.

### After Nivardus’s death, he becomes renowned for virtues, miracles, and authority

### 13.

While they were gloriously devoted to these pursuits of holy works, spreading the grace of sacred exhortation among the peoples and stimulating the minds of the faithful everywhere toward eternal glory, heavenly mercy decided to reward the praiseworthy life of their bishop Nivardus with the exchange of perpetual joy and to repay his brief labor with the palm of enduring glory.

Perfect in his work and complete in virtues, when the day of the Kalends of September arrived, he was released from the bonds of death and migrated to the Lord. He obtained the robe of blessed immortality, became a fellow citizen with the ranks of angels in the dignity of the heavenly court, shared in the company of the apostles, and became a co-heir with the martyrs and confessors. He enjoys without satiety the sight of the one whose love is known never to have departed from his breast.

Although he paid the debt owed by human condition according to the law of the flesh, he nevertheless lives in the glory of perpetual rejoicing. There, without doubt, he is more powerfully prepared to come to the aid of our miseries if he is called upon from the heart, since he is now seen to be more closely joined to that supreme and invisible Spirit and, through the power of the one who knows all things, has himself become knowing of all things and an answerer of prayers.

At his bodily funeral the entire city of Reims rushed together. Clergy and people of both sexes assembled, and many also came from the neighboring cities. They committed the passing of so great a shepherd to pious mourning, accompanied by the solemn offices of hymns.

His body, surrounded by various crowds of people, was carried with fitting honor to the basilica of Saint Remigius by Saint Bercharius and by the holy bishops who had gathered there on that day, while the entire multitude of his flock followed. It received there a most fitting burial in an outstanding mausoleum, with the most holy man Bercharius left surviving in the aforesaid monastery of Hautvillers as a glorious prelate.

Although he had been deprived of the consolation of so great a father, he nevertheless did not abandon the purpose of the work he had begun. Through examples and words he instructed the minds of those subject to him. He illuminated the place he had begun to build with resources and varied adornment, withholding no effort until he raised it to the summit of supreme perfection.

For, drenched with the dew of spiritual gifts and already joined to the angelic life, a citizen of the heavenly homeland,

> By the doctrine of justice he refreshed Christ’s fold,  
> establishing heavenly temples for the faithful people.  
>   
> No less did he shine, aflame in great deeds,  
> such as the Fathers before him, supported by piety, had performed,  
> giving the peoples the finest examples of a blessed life.

With the grace of the Lord going before him, he became renowned in that place through many signs of miracles. When various misfortunes arose, he opposed them and bestowed many benefits of heavenly grace upon the people: healing for bodies and salvation for souls.

He was also so approachable toward the Frankish kings who succeeded one another at different times, and toward the nobles of the palace, that he quickly obtained whatever he sought from their familiar friendship, and their generosity supplied him fully with the expenses and resources needed to construct dwellings for the servants of God.

If anyone perhaps remains hesitant and incredulous about these things, let him marvel at the walls of the aforementioned place, look upon its buildings, and examine its works carefully. It will become clear to anyone who wishes to know how great was the merit of the man through whom the Lord deigned to accomplish such great and remarkable things.

### He builds a nunnery in the forest of Der
### 14. He builds a convent in the Dervese forest.

When the external as well as internal affairs of the aforesaid monastery of Altivilla had been honorably arranged according to the worship of God, the aforementioned Father Bercharius, unable to endure bodily repose, searched out suitable places with the aim of gaining souls. Departing from there, and with God’s gift going before him, he hastened toward the vast solitude of the Dervese forest. When he reached that place, mindful of the purpose for which he had come, he diligently and anxiously investigated where a monastery might suitably be built.

While he was considering these matters, divine grace guiding him, he came to a certain matron named Waltildis. Ennobled by proud lineage, she rejoiced in the abundance of many estates inherited from her forefathers. From her the holy man, for the agreed price, purchased for himself part of the forest—namely, the place commonly called Mangis Villare. There he built a cell and consecrated it in honor of Blessed Mary; and, as far as he was able, he gathered together with the greatest care a company of girls who would serve God and his Mother.

[Note, col. 681D: That is, a small monastery of nuns. According to Camuzat, it was utterly destroyed and razed seven hundred years ago and was called the Monastery of the Girls. The local people call the place *Peulle Monstier* in French. It lies scarcely three miles from the monastery of Dervaux, likewise situated on the river Vigera. See Miracles, no. 1.]

For, going out onto the public road commonly called Cantilla, he purchased from passersby eight captive girls. Instructing them in holy religion, he established them there as dedicated to God. With Christ’s assistance, the number of virgins then increased until it reached sixty; and over them the aforesaid father solemnly appointed as abbess the niece of the aforementioned matron Waltildis.

### Various oratories as well.

### 15. He searches for other places.

After these things had been properly completed, he tirelessly explored the more secluded parts of the forest, eagerly wishing to discover whether he might find more suitable places for building cells. Coming to a certain place called Lutosas, which he judged suitable for constructing a cell, he strove with the utmost diligence to fulfill his desire.

[Note, col. 682D: The village of Lutosae, Louzes, in the diocese of Troyes, must be distinguished from Villa Lutosa, Leuze, in the diocese of Cambrai, concerning which Balderic writes in *Chronicle*, book II, chapter 43.]

Since he considered himself in no way worthy to undertake this by his own resources, he approached the person who held that estate. At that time King Childeric was nobly governing the kingdom of the Franks and was most willing to grant the requests of the holy man. The excellent father therefore approached him and, with the support of men devoted to the love of God—Leodegarius and Mummolenus, bishops, and also Amalricus and Wlfaudus, nobles—obtained from the king permission to build a basilica for himself in that place. King Childeric, consecrating it in honor of Blessed Martin, generously granted him the surrounding forest for one league from the church.

Blessed Bercharius, however, was not content even with this. Near the place called Puteolus, in that part now called the little monastery, he founded a cell in honor of Blessed Maurice, hoping that he had found a suitable place for building a monastery.

[Note, col. 682D: The place has now been reduced to a small oratory called that of Saint Maurice, a mile and a half from Dervaux, toward the source of the Vigera.] But when this too did not seem suitable to him, he dedicated a certain church over the river Vigera—“la rivière de Voyre”—to the honor of Saint Sulpitius. Nor did he think that a monastery could suitably be established there. With a vigilant mind, like a wise architect, he asked the one who proves himself present to those who seek him to grant him places appropriate to his desires.

**He finds a place for founding a monastery, with the king granting it.**

### 16. He discovers the place destined for the monastery.

At a certain time, when divine mercy no longer wished the mind of its servant to be distracted through various places, it gave him, through preceding signs, the assurance that a place suited to his desires would be found.

As he traversed the hidden parts of the forest, he happened by chance upon a place where he found swineherds. He addressed them kindly and, giving them gold coins as a gift, asked them to show him whatever places they had ever seen, while going around the forests, that were more suitable for habitation. He told them that he intended, by clearing the forests in an appropriate place of habitation, to designate dwelling places for coenobites; that he had tried various places, but nowhere at all had he found secure dwellings in which to remain.

After receiving the reward, they answered the holy man’s desires:

“We, indeed, since firm faith holds us, have resolved, having been rewarded by you, to comply with your wishes, and we are ready to show you, according to our knowledge, a suitable place for dwelling. For we have often found herds of swine there, although we had already despaired of finding them; nor is there any hope of seeking pigs elsewhere, since the swine, always lost and without any guide, seek that place.

“There is also there, lord and father, a beech tree associated with a remarkable miracle. Beneath it we have often seen lights burning without any human approach, and we suspect that something divine is present there.”

“Now,” said Blessed Bercharius, “go ahead quickly; point out the place of so great a portent, and, by making me—who have long been suspended in expectation—more tranquil as I follow you, relieve me of this great burden of anxiety.”

After saying this, the aforementioned father hurried to the place, intending to test the truth of their words. He did not accept the testimony of the shepherds in vain: he believed that the miracle had been divinely wrought, and that God had shown him the place, since God would not allow his servant, intent on various endeavors, to be frustrated by his own labor. For the One who had foreseen that a community flourishing in the execution of good works would be gathered there fittingly marked out the beginnings of the holy man’s work by such a portent.

The place was two full miles distant from the aforementioned place called Puteolus. There Blessed Bercharius, after laboriously uprooting the forest, selected the site for building a monastery.

From there he proceeded to the palace, intending to petition the king’s clemency in this matter. With the assistance, by divine grace, of Saint Leodegarius, bishop, and Almaricus, mayor of the palace, as well as Fulcoaldus, Wlfaudus, Nivardus, and Atelanus—bishops—he obtained from the king the forest belonging to his treasury, called Vassiacus, surrounding the aforesaid place, as far as it is recorded to have been cleared by royal authority, so that from it he might acquire the resources and estates necessary for establishing the monastery.

[Note, col. 683D: Another reading, Azelanus, who seems to have been Attila, bishop of Laon, concerning whom Flodoard writes in *History of Rheims*, book II, chapter 7. Camuzat prints the diploma of this gift in the *Promptuary*, folio 80. Adrien de Valois doubts, in *Rerum Francicarum*, book XXI, whether the Amalricus mentioned here was mayor of the palace. Certainly Nivardus is said above, no. 13, to have died before Bercharius thought of the monastery of Dervaux, whose beginnings are assigned to about 665. Childeric, in the third year of his reign in Neustria, or in A.D. 671, is recorded to have granted estates in a charter reported by Camuzat and the Sammarthani, subscribed by the men named here; there Wlfaudus, not Amalricus, is specified as mayor of the palace.]

[Note, col. 683D: Vassiacus, Vassy, a town on the river Blaise, which flows into the Marne; it is distinct from Flodoard’s Wasciacum, book III, chapter 7.]

[Note, cols. 683D–684D: Namely, Dervaux, concerning which the preliminary observations have spoken. Its beginnings must be placed about the year 665.]

Since, by God’s providence, the king was most willing to favor him in many matters, he went so far as to grant him a hall built with suitable adornment, as befitted royal majesty, in the place called Puteolus, where he frequently used to come for hunting. From this, Lord Bercharius built a church to be consecrated in honor of God and of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and he called it Puteolus—“Puysie”—after the aforementioned place.

**He enriches the monastery with monks, relics, and other gifts.**

### 17. He establishes monks and brings relics.

When the holy man purchased the aforementioned girls, he also acquired with them, for a price, eight captive men. Instructing them in holy religion, he made them the first monks in that place.

Many people, admiring his holy way of life and religious devotion, with God’s favor—who wills no one to perish—abandoned everything they seemed to possess in the world and devoted themselves to God under the monastic rule and the teaching of that holy father.

He therefore brought water from far away to that monastery, provided workshops for all necessary purposes, and arranged the girls’ dwellings in an orderly fashion. He went to Jerusalem and obtained very many sacred relics, and brought back with him excellent ivory tablets.

[Note, col. 684D: His companion was Waimar, to whom Saint Leodegarius, to be consumed by starvation, was entrusted, as is stated in the book of the Miracles of Saint Bercharius, no. 11. Bercharius is said to have brought back from that journey the body of Saint Theodosia. A manuscript codex of Dervaux reads: “In the year of the Incarnate Word 1108, epact 17, on the Ides of September, in the same year in which King Philip died and his son was anointed king, the body of Saint Theodosia, virgin, who suffered many torments, including beheading, at Caesarea in Palestine for Christ’s name, was placed in this shrine by Lord Abbot Rotger, in the eleventh year of his ordination. Saint Bercharius, abbot, nevertheless brought her from that same city with relics of many saints, and fittingly placed her in this monastery, which he had built by royal gift.”]

In the same way, going to Rome many times, he brought back the relics of many saints and, together with the bishops, honorably placed them for preservation in the aforesaid places. Through the merits of those saints, whose relics had been brought there, and through Christ’s grace, those places bestowed richer benefits upon the faithful.

**He foretells his death.**

### 18. Bercharius foretells his departure.

After passing through so many struggles of labor in the stadium of this world for the prize of heavenly life, when the Lord was preparing to reward his laborer with a worthy recompense, he first allowed him to recognize that the time of bodily dissolution was approaching.

With the solemnity of Easter already near, on the Thursday on which the Lord’s Supper was celebrated, the father, solicitous for the flock entrusted to him, devoutly visited the monastery of the girls, intending, as was customary among the faithful, to fulfill the Lord’s commandments.

Amid many words of exhortation and consolation, he also foretold to them what had been divinely revealed to him concerning the dissolution of his own body:

“Know, my little daughters, that, with the heavenly calling approaching, I can in no way remain longer in this body. Do not mourn as though your shepherd had been taken away, since you hold yourselves firmly joined, with certain devotion of heart, to the eternal Guardian and King, to whom you have been espoused. Since you will no longer be supported by any bodily assistance from me, I commend you as my own daughters to the heavenly Ruler.”

At these words of consolation they broke into loud cries and tears. The holy father softened their grief with words of exhortation, bade them farewell, blessed them, and departed. After completing all things with psalms and hymns, he set out on the road back to the monastery, intending to do the same for the poor monks and pilgrims.

**He is attacked with a knife by his undisciplined godson.**

### 19. Daguinus attempts to kill him.

While he was arranging many matters, it happened that he decided that his godson—whom he had received from the sacred font and established as a monk—named Daguinus, should, because of his offenses, be struck with the chastising blow of correction, as was customary.

As later became clear, this man was wicked and disgraceful. With a polished brow beneath a sheep’s skin, he concealed the behavior of a ravenous beast. Thus, handed over through the merit of his own wickedness to the devil together with the traitor Judas, he could not endure the father’s instructive reproaches. His manly bile swelling beneath his breast, he madly sought to deliver the holy man to an unjust death.

At length, when the blessed father, greatly wearied by the day’s anxious labor, had reclined on a little bed with the brothers and surrendered his limbs to sleep—for “he who rebukes criminals incurs hatred”—that same son of Satan, armed with the weapons of impiety, after believing him to be tired and asleep, rushed upon him and attempted to inflict a mortal wound.

In his fury he struck him with a small knife, and the shameless son stained his own hands with his father’s blood. Daguinus seized the iron with which he had struck the saint and, conscious of his guilt, threw it as quickly as he could into a pool that at that time lay within the monastery enclosure, as though it might be hidden there.

You would then have seen the water, as though aware of so great a crime, shrink in fear from receiving the iron. For as soon as it touched the water, it miraculously floated upon the surface like the lightest feather. The homicidal man, meanwhile, having become insane, went to the church and began to strike the bell with bloody hands.

**He pardons the assailant.**

### 20. Bercharius forgives Daguinus.

When the brothers heard the bell at an unusual hour, they rose in great astonishment. Hearing that the holy man had been killed, they ran to his bed, but found that his spirit still trembled within him, though he remained in anguish.

The brothers seized the aforementioned Daguinus and brought him before the holy man, wishing to know what the severity of his mercy would judge concerning so great a crime.

The holy father, mindful of the Lord’s words by which he prayed to the Father for his persecutors—“Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing”—mercifully remitted to him the offense that he had committed against him.

“Brother,” he said, “strive penitentially to make God favorable toward you. As far as I am concerned, I release you from every impiety without reservation. Go, therefore, my son, to Rome, so that the one who, having received the power of binding and loosing, comes to the aid of the body’s various kinds of illness, may show you free from this crime.”

Daguinus therefore departed and, at the blessed man’s command, went to Rome; afterward he did not return.

**He dies; he is transferred to the church; oil flows from his tomb.**

### 21. Bercharius dies and is translated.

Blessed Bercharius, sick for a very long time from the anguish of his wound, was at last released from the flesh and, happy in spirit, joyfully sought the delights of heavenly life.

At the death of so great a man, religious men came from every direction. He was buried in a certain place outside the monastery [another reading: church], which there became powerful through many miracles granted by God.

But when the Lord no longer wished to conceal his saint, because of the aforementioned miracle of the knife and the other signs displayed at the holy man’s tomb, the servants of God judged that the body of the blessed father ought to be transferred from there. They therefore transferred it and buried it behind the altar in the basilica of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, which he himself had built while alive. There, through the support of his merits, many gifts are granted to the people.

Long afterward, oil was seen to spring up from his tomb and flow into a vessel prepared for that purpose. It proved exceedingly beneficial to all afflicted by illness.

Since we, weighed down by the burden of sins, cannot presume by our own strength to attain the summit of good works, let us therefore implore the help of the grace of him who said, “Without me you can do nothing,” so that we who are brought low by the merits of our sins may be raised up by the right hand of his power—he who lives and is glorified with the Father and the Holy Spirit, God, forever and ever. Amen.

## APPENDIX

From a manuscript of the Dervese monastery, communicated by the Reverend Father Filibert Boulanger, Benedictine monk of the Congregation of Saint-Vanne.

### Date of his death.

### 22. The death of Bercharius.

Blessed Bercharius, sick from the pain of a most severe wound, although he could scarcely speak while drawing out long sighs, nevertheless, with exhausted breath, humbly arranged the rites of the Lord’s Passion and Resurrection, as well as the obsequies of his own burial and the place of his tomb. He foretold many future things to his disciples, charging them to observe the fear of God and the practice of holy religion.

At last, about to meet the triumphant Lord with the palm of victory, he was released from the flesh on the morning of the Lord’s own holy Resurrection from the dead and, happy in spirit, sought the joys of heavenly life.

[Note, cols. 685D–686D: The same manuscript reads: “This blessed father Bercharius ended the last day of his life in the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 685, indiction 13, epact 11, on the sixth day before the Kalends of April, on the sacred morning of the Lord’s Resurrection.” These chronological indicators do not agree unless one reads “the seventh day before the Kalends of April,” on which Easter fell in the year 624. Saint Bercharius is entered in the Additions to Usuard on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of November, which is the day of the translation, as will be said below at no. 7. The body of Saint Bercharius is preserved in the church of the monastery of Dervaux: the head in a silver shrine, the remaining bones in a reliquary.]

At the death of so great a man, religious men came from every direction, and he was buried, as he had ordered, in a certain place outside the church, which there became powerful through many miracles granted by God.

### Day and manner of the translation.

### 23. The translation of the body.

But when the Lord no longer wished to conceal his saint, because of the aforementioned miracle of the knife and the other signs displayed at the holy man’s tomb, the servants of God judged that the body of the blessed father ought to be transferred from there.

After consultation with a large college of priests who had assembled for this purpose, it was decreed that this should be done on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of March. They did not, however, dare to touch the earth containing the most holy body, nor did they wish to weary themselves with carrying over a long distance the stone that covered the sarcophagus. Instead, they devised the humblest means of transfer they could.

A suitable arched opening was made through the eastern wall of the church, which was closest to his burial place. Through that entrance the body, together with the sarcophagus, was transferred inside, and they buried it a second time behind the altar in the very basilica of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, which he himself had built while alive. There, through the support of his merits, many gifts are granted to the people.

When, by God’s providence, this monastery began to flourish in the time of Lord Adso, and so forth, as below, no. 15.

# ON THE MIRACLES OF SAINT WALDEBERT, THIRD ABBOT OF LUXEUIL

## Book by Adso, abbot

Published in Mabillon, *Acts of the Saints of the Benedictine Order*, Third Century, p. 451, extracted from a manuscript of Luxeuil by the Reverend Father Constantius Gravellius, then prior.

## Preliminary observations

### 1. The testimony concerning Waldebert.

We presented in the Second Century the eulogy of Saint Waldebert, or Walbert, abbot of Luxeuil, insofar as it could be composed from ancient records.

Afterward the Reverend Father Constantius Gravellius, then prior of Luxeuil and a member of the flourishing Congregation of Saint-Vanne, sent me a book concerning his miracles, with this heading:

“Here begins the Life of the most holy and most acceptable-to-God Father Walbert, abbot of the monastery of Luxeuil.”

Yet the author undertook to write not a life but a book of miracles performed long after Waldebert’s death. The author was Adso, also called Hermiricus, who governed Luxeuil after the middle of the tenth century, succeeding Aalonus, whom he calls both abbot and bishop. In his Prologue Adso also mentions a volume concerning the deeds of Saint Waldebert, which, he laments, has perished through the injury of time.

In the very ancient calendar of Corbie, written nine hundred years ago, which is prefixed to a mutilated and imperfect copy of the books of Isidore, bishop of Seville, concerning the supreme good, the memory of Saint Waldebert is recorded in these words:

“Six days before the Nones of May: burial of Saint Waldebert, abbot,” with no mention of an episcopal title, just as there is none in the little book that follows.

### 2. Luxeuil and the chronology of Columbanus.

You will read more about the monastery of Luxeuil in our Second Century, both in the Preface and in the Acts of Saints Columbanus and Eustasius, abbots.

I placed the time when Columbanus began to inhabit the Vosges shortly before the year 590. This calculation seems to be confirmed by a clause found at the end of Saint Augustine’s Exposition of the Epistle of John, divided into nine homilies. At the end of these homilies, an extremely ancient copy preserved in the church of Saint Peter at Beauvais, written in uncial letters by a certain monk of Luxeuil, reads:

“The work is completed, with the Lord’s favor, at the monastery of Luxeuil, in the twelfth year of King Chlothar, in the thirteenth indiction, *anno Xlsimo Pis Ni* [a corrupt or uncertain reading], having happily completed [it].”

That is, as I interpret it, the fortieth year of our father Columbanus. He must therefore be said to have arrived in the Vosges in the year 585, since the twelfth year of King Chlothar, reigning in Burgundy, and the thirteenth indiction coincide in the year of Christ 625.

It is also worthy of notice in this writing that the indiction was at times used in the Gallican computation while the Merovingian dynasty was reigning.

## Author’s Prologue

### To the sacred assembly of the monks of Luxeuil

[Note, cols. 687B–688B: Supply “Adso.” For he is reported to have written an account of the succession of his predecessors and a brief chronicle; he was a contemporary of Adso, abbot of Dervaux, concerning whom see the Second Century.]

To the sacred congregation of the coenobites of Luxeuil, the abbot who was called Hermiricus by name, though not deservedly so, sends perpetual salvation in Christ the Lord.

As I considered and repeatedly revolved in mind and speech what usefulness or advantage I might bring to the place where, handed over by my parents, I remember having passed the youthful beginnings of my early training amid the two-horned uncertainties of Pythagorean learning, this seemed above all appropriate: that, for restoring to the diligence of those who come after us the memory of past events, I should commit to writing what divine grace is known to have accomplished even in our own time through the distinguished confessors of Christ the Lord, Eustasius and Waldebert, founders and rulers of nearly six hundred monks of Luxeuil.

Between what has already passed and what is hoped to come, human understanding cannot possess free access to knowledge, as though a deep darkness were interposed like a cloud, unless it is assisted externally by the transmission of literary work. Through this, what the preceding course of time has swallowed up is brought before our eyes and judged as though present.

Moved by zeal for this task, we set our hand to the work, so that the things accomplished for the honor of the divine majesty, insofar as our knowledge could reach them, might not remain hidden through the sluggishness of our apathy. This was especially fitting since divine providence had appointed these men for us as patrons, as though by a special gift of privilege: their present intercession might protect us, and the power of their miracles might more clearly illuminate us.

Yet when we praise glorious men in their lifetime, we do not in any way omit—indeed, we judge that he must be set before all others—through whom we do not doubt that they deserved and obtained all these things: he who is glorious in his saints and wondrous in all his works.

We therefore do not touch upon what those aforementioned fathers accomplished either during their lives or immediately after their departure. Rather, after a long interval of succeeding time, we relate what divine mercy wished to declare through them before our own eyes. Of the many things that could be entrusted to memory, we do not remain silent about these, in order to display more tenaciously the reverence owed to such great men.

If anyone desires to know their deeds more fully, let him diligently investigate their acts, which are more extensively contained from the beginning of their deeds in their own volumes. There he will very easily find with how many and what kinds of marks of virtue each of them shines.

### 2. Dedication.

Let your holy fatherhood receive this little work of our devotion. Although you see us lacking the elegance of eloquence, recognize nevertheless that we have taken care lest our sluggishness grow torpid in glorifying the magnificence of divine works.

We pursue these matters in such a way that, if anyone more correctly or more elegantly should arise to complete them, and if any fruit of praise or mortal honor might come to us from them, we willingly profess that we are without that privilege. We are content to yield our place if another, more capable or more eloquent, is substituted, provided that we have merely shown the way to the material that must be learned.

Nor, as we hope, will the Lord frustrate the reward of our labor if the ability to speak has been lacking, since the affection of our devotion has shown itself ready.

# HERE BEGINS THE LIFE

### 3. After Columbanus is expelled from Luxeuil, Eustasius succeeds him.

After the most blessed father Columbanus, as the book written about his life and virtues indicates, had entered Burgundy as an exile from his native Ireland under Sigebert, king of the Franks, and had specially chosen for himself a place that had long been called Luxeuil, he obtained from the Lord such grace for accomplishing works that, with signs and wonders going before him in that place, he soon gathered together a multitude of nearly six hundred monks, arranged in small groups throughout the locality, as can still be seen today.

He instructed them excellently in every holiness, wisdom, teaching, and religious discipline, so that throughout cities and monasteries pastors and rulers were chosen from the disciples of the blessed father Columbanus.

But, instigated by the devil, he was expelled by the most wicked Queen Brunhild. Departing from Luxeuil, he went to Italy and magnificently founded the monastery of Bobbio, where at last, renowned for many signs and miracles, he rested in a blessed death.

The blessed father Eustasius succeeded him as the prudent governor of the congregation of the monks of Luxeuil. Born from the nobler lineage of the people of Langres, he followed in every respect the institutions of his predecessor and, equally renowned everywhere for wisdom, holiness, reputation, and virtues, departed to the Lord. His body was buried in the same place.

### 4. Walbert, formerly a soldier.

Saint Walbert succeeded him in the government. This man, most glorious in his life, although later in order, was not inferior in the quality of his merits. They say that the years of his youth first flourished most excellently in arms.

Although he was illustrious through a famous lineage and, in the district commonly called Ponthieu, exceedingly rich in honors and worldly dignity according to his birth, nevertheless, while engaged in the affairs of the secular kingdom, he did not forget the eternal kingdom. He diligently pursued works of mercy, doing the things that belong to God, not those that belong to men.

No speech is sufficient to explain how great and how excellent the virtue of good works shone in him beneath his military dress. Among many other things, he was especially devoted to clothing the freezing, feeding the needy, offering solace to the weak, refreshing the poor, comforting the sorrowful, and restoring the quarrelsome to peace.

Thus, an excellent soldier amid rank and arms, always preferring eternal things to those that perish, he occupied himself with constant reflection on what he later fulfilled through devotion in deed.

They report that the beginning of his signs arose during this exercise of good works.

### 5. The young man becomes renowned in the district of Meaux.

Within the boundaries of France, in the district of Meaux, there is a famous village called by its ancient name Nant. This village belonged to him by hereditary right from his ancestors, and the place remains especially distinguished to the present day by his birth and childhood development.

For the honor of his name, a notable spring also rises there. From it, the surrounding crowd of villagers, having been sprinkled with its water, considers itself happier to carry home the benefits of health in memory of the blessed man.

As we have said, this village contained a broad and fertile estate belonging to him. For this fortunate man was powerful in other matters as well, and in this field too. Wild geese—which, because of their whiteness or the sound of their voices, country people commonly call *gantas*—gathered in great numbers and repeatedly ravaged the field, beginning with the very scattering of the seed and the growth of the sowing.

[Note, col. 691D: Saint Amalberga the virgin is likewise said to have driven from her field certain birds which it is customary to call *gantas* by the common name.]

The steward, indignant because he could not drive them away by any force, reported the familiar loss to his master. But he ordered him:

“Go quickly, and, following behind them on foot in their full number, shut them up at home.”

With the servant going ahead, you would soon have seen the troubled birds, their wildness laid aside, gathering into a remarkable flock and, at the command of the one who ordered them, entering the house by the fixed path along which they were led.

Thus, after those birds had remained three days without food, the blessed man at last released them—except for one removed from the number by a member of the household, who, conscious of his wrongdoing, rashly and greedily consumed it as food.

The birds, however, once released from confinement, filled the air with a great cry and lamentation, flew around the house, and made known to the ears of the holy man the loss suffered by the community.

As soon as he understood the cause, he investigated what had been deposited and declared that the guilty man deserved punishment for the crime, but that he had not ordered his death. The presumptuous man, exposed in shame as guilty of theft, brought forward the feathers he had happened to steal, together with whatever remained.

The holy man then prayed, restored the dead bird to life, restored the number of the flock, and allowed them to depart rejoicing. After this they never again dared to invade that field.

Thus the Lord was already then willing to reveal these things in his servant, whom he later intended to place, with pastoral authority, over that holy flock of the monks of Luxeuil. If he was able to do such things as a layman in matters so small, how much more must he be believed to have been powerful in greater matters under the holy habit!

### 6. He returns to Luxeuil at Eustasius’s urging and lives as a solitary.

From this point, as he was striving toward higher things, he desired to renounce the world entirely. By God’s will and on the advice of the blessed father Eustasius, he devotedly sought the monastery of Luxeuil, which at that time surpassed the others in the strictness of its regular discipline and excelled in resources and in the number of its monks.

He handed over to it the estates that he possessed most abundantly in various places, laid aside his weapons—which are still kept there today as testimony to his sacred military service—and entered to join the number of God’s servants.

He attained the grace of holy conversion with such perfection that, even while he remained under another’s direction, he displayed signs of virtue through the illumination of the Holy Spirit.

A place is still shown two miles from the monastery: a hollow beneath a projecting rock, gently watered by water emerging from the earth. They say that he established a cell there and fought alone for a considerable time against the trials of either the flesh or the ancient enemy.

[Note, col. 691D: To this very day one may see, and there is preserved in the sacred cave, a hard stone fitted for a reclining man, on which sufferers from fever very often recover health.]

### 7. He succeeds Eustasius and governs excellently.

Moreover, Father Eustasius, as we mentioned above, having been confirmed by many signs and virtues, as is sufficiently recorded in the account of his deeds, entered the heavenly Capitol to be crowned when the Lord called him, bearing the palm of good works.

He retained a magnificent burial place behind the sacred altar of the chief church, within the walls, which he had founded together with Father Columbanus, as was fitting.

Divine providence did not permit the sacred flock to remain without a shepherd. Although there were many in that company of saints whom wisdom and life commended, all nevertheless, with equal vote and equal consent, chose Waldebert, an equally holy man, to take the place of the departed father and appointed him ruler of the place. They were confident in his virtue and merits—qualities which, although they could be increased in him, were undoubtedly capable of moving them to a firm decision.

He did nothing more weakly than before; rather, he restrained himself by the carefully chosen disciplines of a stricter life. Whatever remained incomplete in the affairs or other necessities of either life during the time of those two fathers, Columbanus and Eustasius, this most blessed shepherd Waldebert supplied with every diligence, increased, and polished to the utmost perfection.

He also bestowed upon the monastery villas and abundant estates through public grants. Among them was the village that we earlier called Nant, his own hereditary land, with the adjacent holdings. He handed it over under threat of a curse, so that whoever removed it from that place would fall under eternal malediction.

[Note, cols. 691D–692D: From this passage it is understood—as is also clear from the Acts of Saint Bertin, abbot—that this Waldebert is different from Walbert, count of Arques, disciple of Saint Bertin; nor was he Saint Fara’s brother or bishop of the church of Meaux, as has elsewhere been proved.]

In the district of Ternois he also offered the village called Herlerus, with everything belonging to it, as well as whatever he possessed by full right in Ponthieu.

[Note, col. 692D: Medieval writers sometimes use contracted letters in calling the district of Tarvanna “Tarnensis.” The village of Herlerus, now commonly Herly, adjoins it; it lies in the county of Ponthieu on the Roman roads, between the headwaters of the rivers Agnion and Edivinia, according to Malbrancq, *On the Morini*, book IV, chapter 6.] He established the blessed apostle Peter as the perpetual heir of all his possessions.

Among his other gifts he also offered a cup made from a most precious single topaz, wonderfully inlaid, as is the nature of that stone, with drops of gold. He added an anathema that whoever, on any pretext, removed it from there or rashly attempted to retain it after it had been removed would be tortured forever in eternal flames with the devil and his angels. This was done without prejudice to the authority of the Frankish kings and nobles, whose usage was commonly observed at that time.

### Waldebert is intimate with Bishop Nicetius; he dies and is buried by him.

8. He was especially close to Saint Nicetius, a bishop of great virtues, with this agreement between them: whichever of the two should first depart this life when called by the Lord, the survivor would arrange a suitable place of burial for him. And so it happened. For when, over the course of forty years, the glorious confessor of the Lord Waldebert had increased the place assigned to him—admirably ordered in every kind of virtue—in its possessions and in the number of those serving God, and had adorned it with many miraculous works of power, he departed to the Lord on 2 May, having become a companion and sharer of the citizens above and having been happily introduced to the door of everlasting joy. As throngs of the faithful flocked from every direction to attend his funeral, he was buried in the church of Saint Martin, which is built on the north side outside the monastery, where Saint Nicetius the bishop had constructed, behind the altar, a crypt of marvelous workmanship. By the Lord’s arrangement, he received there a most fitting burial.

[Note: [Col. 0693D] This church still stands in the middle of the town of Luxeuil and is the parish church.]

The body of Saint Waldebert, especially a protection against pagans.

9. In that place, after his glorious departure from life, many miracles have been displayed in honor of the divine name: sight is restored to blinded eyes; for the lame, after the severed connections of their nerves have been repaired, walking is restored; health breathes upon the sick; hateful weakness is driven from the limbs of the afflicted; consolations are granted to the sorrowful and benefits to those struck by adversity. Among these are also exchanges of divine power. Earlier generations, it is said, established with certainty that, when the reverence due to the man lying there had been rendered in pious obligation, so long as the burial of the sacred body remained in human custody, neither the wickedness of unbelievers nor any savage invasion of pagans could prevail there. But after, whether because it deserved less renown or because some circumstance compelled it, the bones of the venerable body were taken from there and carried into the shrine of another church, neither the impiety of the wicked nor the slaughter and disasters of cruel nations were absent. Indeed, long afterward, when pagans suddenly broke in there—

[Note: [Col. 0693D] Namely, the Saracens, apparently in the year 731, according to the statements concerning that year.]

—they tried with all their strength to burn the monastery, but, repulsed by the manifest power of God, they were seen to have brought their fires there in vain. At that time also, as will be stated later, some of the monks were found slain by the pagans.

His successors.

10. When, as we have said, the most blessed shepherd Waldebert departed this life, Saint Ingofred, distinguished and perfected in every kind of virtue, was solemnly appointed in his place. Then, as a long succession of many years passed, fathers succeeded one another in that white assembly of the snow-white ranks of monks, as can easily be found in their catalogue; neither did pastoral authority fail, nor did an abundance of temporal support cease to prosper until their last abbot, named Melinus. Having briefly anticipated this material, as it were, since it has not been our purpose to repeat the deeds of past times, let us omit these matters and return, as we promised, to the times of our own age.

Drogo, also abbot of Luxeuil. The manner of his death.

11. After the death of the memorable Charles the Great,

[Note: [Col. 0693D] Rather, after the death of Louis Augustus, his son, whose sons these were. The author also errs here when he makes Pippin survive the battle of Fontenay and counts Drogo among Louis’s sons, although it is established that Drogo was the brother of Louis Augustus and was made bishop of Metz while Louis was still alive.]

and of the glorious emperor, a great dispute is said to have arisen among four kings—namely Charles, Pippin, Lothair, and Louis—who quarreled and contended with great force among themselves over which of them should obtain the rule of the Frankish kingdom in particular. This kingdom their younger brother Charles had already received alone, by the will of their dying father. Since the impiety of this fraternal quarrel could not be restrained by any means, it was carried so far that, after forces from both kingdoms had been summoned and the battle lines arranged, standards were unfurled for fraternal armies. In that battle, when Lothair’s army fled, Charles, aided by Warin, the most powerful duke of Burgundy, carried away the standards of victory; and thus he alone received the kingdom of the Franks, the other kingdoms having been divided among the rest.

They also tonsured Drogo, a fifth claimant equally eager to rule, who, as one of the same family, appeared to be of a most distinguished disposition, and appointed him bishop in the see of the Church of Metz. For the increase of his honor they also decreed that he should preside as shepherd over Luxeuil. He governed that place, which he had received, so energetically after the efforts of his predecessors and with such power that, owing to the increase of its possessions, in his time it seemed to number fifteen thousand manses. Sometimes he remained there longer than usual, enjoying the pleasantness of the place. Once, while he had gone to the neighboring river Lignon for the sake of fishing and was pursuing a huge fish, he slipped into the water and was suddenly suffocated. His body was carried to Metz and buried in the church of Saint Arnulf, confessor of Christ.

After these events, Louis, surnamed the Pious, was made emperor in France, with Pope Stephen crowning him. In those days the regular order had failed in many monasteries, and the administration of temporal affairs was wasting away through daily misfortunes. Nevertheless, through frequent synodal councils, he restored the condition of the Churches to its former state as far as he could.

Abbot Ansegisus.

12. At that time the dignity of Luxeuil too, along with other things, was already almost tottering as its former rigor withered. Caesar Louis, recognizing this, placed Ansegisus in charge as shepherd, a most worthy man, distinguished in conduct and outstanding in the beauty of wisdom.

[Note: [Col. 0694D] In the commonly circulated list of abbots, Ansegisus is placed before Drogo; and Drogo indeed survived Ansegisus.]

He repaired what had collapsed, gathered together what had been scattered, extended the Church’s site farther, spread the surrounding workshops over larger spaces and behind higher walls, and painted the walls of the Church, together with its other ornaments, in beautiful variety. He collected the capitularies of the Frankish kings that had been enacted in various councils and had them contained in a single volume. Since he was esteemed by the Frankish kings among the nobles of the kingdom, he devoted himself to just and pious works, and brought his life to an end. There, where he had extended the Church more spaciously, he received a worthy burial.

Abbot Fulbert. Gibardus. The unhappy condition of Gaul. Relics carried against invaders.

13. Fulbert, also, a distinguished man, was appointed to the same place in the succeeding period. He arranged the oratories of the saints between the two monasteries with sufficiently beautiful workmanship and adorned them with appropriate furnishings.

Afterward, when the pagans invaded from far away, as we have said, and the monks, terrified by the sudden danger, scattered in various directions, Gibardus—a man most distinguished in birth and learning, who at that time had been appointed shepherd and abbot of the monastery—was away in a distant region. He was pierced by the arrows of the pagans and buried in a place called Martin’s Villa.

[Note: [Col. 0695D] That is, the Northmen. I think this occurred in the year of the Lord 888, when the monks of Besançon were killed by the same people, as John, a monk of Besançon, reports in his Chronicle, volume II of the *Spicilegium*.]

Tetelmus too, an honored monk among his own people, was found not far from the monastery, killed together with certain others. From then until our own times, as the shepherds died one after another, and while Richard, the great duke of Burgundy, was alive, hateful tyrants began to emerge everywhere and to strike one another down in mutual slaughter. The Church of God was thrown into confusion, rights were broken—[i.e., violated]—the statutes of the laws were broken, the possessions of the Church were invaded and seized everywhere by the impious. The holy places were not respected; rather, as the wickedness of the impious prevailed, the entire honor of religion collapsed together. The inhabitants of the monastery of Luxeuil experienced this fully, as their sins deserved; for the hands of strangers seized their villages and possessions as their own inheritance.

[Note: [Col. 0695D] Richard, the energetic duke of Burgundy against the Northmen, died in the third year after the siege of Chartres, according to Hugh, a monk of Fleury. That siege occurred in 891.]

Since there was no king or judge who wished, out of regard for true justice, to resist this wickedness of the impious completely, very many clerics were compelled to carry the relics of the saints against the reckless boldness of those who were plundering their property, so that those whom human power could not restrain might be curbed by the power displayed by God. Hence the inhabitants of this place, having no confidence elsewhere against the wickedness of the perverse, customarily bring forward against them the power of their defender, Saint Waldebert, carrying abroad the substantial relics of his body, so that he who once appeared to have kept the oaths of temporal warfare might also stand forth as a merciful champion amid the misfortunes of his faithful. The proof of this matter presents itself readily, if one considers the power of his virtue, which he displayed so frequently.

The body of Saint Waldebert brought forth first.

[Col. 0696A]

14. A village adjoining the seacoast, called above Herlerium, had been taken away by the force of tyrants. The monks, placed in a perilous and uncertain crisis, sought the aid of Saint Waldebert, their protector. Taking with them a portion of his sacred relics, they set out through the borders of France toward that place.

As they departed, the river Mantne [read: Materna] suddenly came before them. When they wished to cross it, after a great crowd of people had gone ahead, the portion of the sacred relic had remained on this side of the bank. The monks, confronted by the immediate difficulty, did not know what to do. I am about to relate something marvelous. At once, by divine impulse and without human assistance, a boat was spontaneously brought by its rower to the place where the portion of the holy body was being held. The companions, transported across the river by such a remarkable power, were amazed, having never before experienced anything like it.

Proceeding from there, they soon reached the estate of Nant, mentioned above.

[Note: [Col. 0696D] From this we conjecture that Nant, Waldebert’s birthplace, was the town of Nantogilum, Nantueil, which those traveling from Burgundy past the Materna encounter; a Cluniac priory still exists there.]

There he had temporally begun his life and, while living, had made the place illustrious by certain signs of miracles. When his bodily presence was discovered there, it cannot be said how great a multitude of both sexes flocked together. Among the various gifts that, out of gratitude for his benefits, they decided to hang among the branches of the trees along with the relic of the holy man, as the crowd pressed forward, someone happened to offer a wooden cup. One of the servants had received it for safekeeping. When a certain frivolous and insolent young man asked that it be given to him, although he seemed unworthy to receive it, the servant drew his sword and tried to attack the man who was devoted to the service of the holy man.

As he aimed his blow at him, the striker’s right hand was suddenly bound in the air. Thus, without a gallows, that madman was suspended in the sky; he lost his senses, was held fixed to the earth, and could not be released until, through the prayers of those whom he had come to harm, he deserved to be freed.

Fear had so seized the hearts of many at this deed. Finally, after being detained by the people for a while, they resumed the journey they had begun and came to Herlerum, where they were heading. Unjust usurpers rose up on every side, wishing to drive them from the territory, since they saw that their arrival meant loss to themselves. But the power of the holy man subdued the minds of the impious with fear and restored to his own people the domestic estates that had been seized through the plots of strangers. Thus, although with difficulty, after matters had been settled, the monks, attending to the sacred relics, returned happier to their own homes.

The invaders punished.

15. There is another town of no little distinction, called Provincherias, situated nearly twenty miles from the monastery. A certain soldier, highly renowned among his people, had seized this town. Since distress was imminent and the aid of an earthly defender was lacking, necessity commanded that a portion of the holy man’s relics be carried there.

When it had been placed in the church there, the soldier grew angry and began to rage, to be furious, to disparage the saint, and to rave madly, asserting that he would freely subject the Church’s property to his own authority. Finally, one day, swollen with pride and arrogance, he was riding at full speed on a foaming horse through the field beneath the church, with the reins slack. The horse broke its leg and fell headlong; the man barely escaped the fall and was killed nearby by a soldier. He left the village, which has remained freely possessed by Saint Peter to the present day.

16. At another time, a certain soldier named Rotbert, powerful in strength and wealth, together with his nephew Berard, held the village of Caciacum in the county of Dijon, a particularly fine wine-producing estate. Hubaldus, meanwhile, held Molisiacum in the county of Beaune—possessions of the Church of Luxeuil—with sufficiently unjust domination. The monks complained repeatedly to the princes of Burgundy, but could not prevail.

Therefore, after taking counsel with Count Letoldus, at the time when King Lothair, having lifted the siege of the Burgundians, had received the fortress of Dijon under his authority, the monks sought their familiar aid again and arranged for the venerable relic of Saint Waldebert to be carried there.

[Note: [Col. 0697D] Lothair reigned for thirty years from the year 954. From this you may learn the author’s date, since his successor is called Aalonco, elsewhere mentioned as Adaloncus.]

When they arrived, they suitably set up a tent in the middle of the village over the sacred reliquary. Suddenly the armed enemies, fierce in weapons and spirit—Berard with his men—arrived, but did not dare touch the holy relic with its defender. They nevertheless seized the village according to their usual practice, oppressed the household cruelly, and demanded an abundant and excessive levy of food. Thus, after greedily gorging themselves on food and wine, while the monks were suffering from hunger, night came on and they relaxed their limbs stretched out in sleep.

Behold, suddenly, in the middle of the night, their leader, Berard, was seized by fever; his limbs were tortured by dysentery, and he was constricted everywhere by a flow of the bowels. He scarcely waited for dawn before approaching the monks. He fell before the presence of the saint and did penance for his guilt. After health was granted, the village of Caciacus was thereafter and remains freed from an alien possessor and enjoys the liberty of its rightful lord.

17. As for the soldier Hubaldus, although greedy for the property of the sanctuary, he was otherwise a good man, modest both in arms and in conduct. We said that in the county of Beaune, at the village of Molisiacum, he had subjected the monks’ revenues in wine and grain. Terrified by the virtues and miracles of this saint, he thereafter, though unwillingly, abandoned his possession to the Church.

Other miracles.

18. At another time afterward, the same monks in the county of the Alsigodenses suffered the loss of certain possessions when the attacks of tyrants broke out. Driven by this urgent necessity, after deliberation they decided to visit those regions, carrying with them safeguards of faith, namely sacred relics from the members of Saint Eustasius and also of the glorious confessor of the Lord, Saint Waldebert.

[Note: [Col. 0697D] A portion of the relics of Saint Eustasius is preserved in the monastery of Luxeuil, enclosed in an ivory and silver reliquary.]

On this journey they were first lodged not far from the monastery, at a village called Saint Mary’s. Then they made for a place called Campaniolas and finally arrived there on the fourth day, where they had been provoked by the wickedness of their enemies. In that county there was a considerable number of monks and attendants, and with them had gone the abbot and bishop named Aalonco.

When they reached the appointed place, since no other suitable site was available, they set the relics upon the cut trunk of an oak tree in a meadow that opposed them. At the report of so great a marvel, when many people had been stirred up, one might have seen an infinite multitude of people of both sexes suddenly flocking there. They came together in a remarkable throng not only from neighboring regions but from distant districts, places, villages, and towns. Filling the field, they all invoked the name of almighty God and of Saint Waldebert with one voice and harmonious devotion, seeking timely aid for their troubles.

But when divine power wished to show that the bodily benefit of its saints was also present, suddenly there arose from heaven such a crash and such terror, and such a violent sound like thunder, that, with the earth seemingly trembling, the people present could scarcely remain on their feet and no one knew where any of them had been standing.

Stunned and greatly terrified by what had occurred, they eventually recovered their strength and returned to themselves. I am about to relate something marvelous: one could see a bird in the form of a dove descending through the clear air from the heights, flying gently around the sacred reliquary in a familiar manner. Then, after completing its course, it withdrew into the secret recesses of heaven, so that it was plainly proved to have come there.

From that moment the power of both saints began to be displayed. Immediately, two men who had long been deprived of the sight of their own eyes, at the very hour when the aforesaid bird was seen to depart, received back the brightness of light without anyone leading them; rejoicing, they hurried home. Then two others, whose limbs were bound throughout their bodies as though chained by the twisted knots of contracted nerves, were carried by the hands of others to the sacred relics. By the divine power displayed, they were suddenly raised to their feet and returned joyfully to their homes without human assistance. They began to walk, glorifying the Lord, with Saint Waldebert going before them, taught by a new path to tread with free steps the ground that previously they had been unable to walk upon.

19. A fortress is likewise seen to adjoin this place, which in earlier times we know was called Montem Biliardae.

[Note: [Col. 0698D] Montbéliard, a very strongly fortified town in the county of Burgundy.]

It is enough to establish that one of the inhabitants of this town, named Uto, born of no ignoble family, was known to many. With his nerves contracted and deprived of the use of his body, he could not crawl along the ground with his hands unless he rode on a horse or an ass.

He was therefore brought with the greatest devotion to the place where he had learned that the venerable relic of this saint had stood. He came, drenched the ground with tears, invoked the saint’s name, and sought his aid. He did not leave the place until, by divine power, the bonds of his nerves were broken and he returned home, restored to his former health.

20. Since the opportunity of time and of the same benefit has presented itself, it is not burdensome to relate again another event in praise of the divine name, in which this holy man acted differently in a similar matter.

In the county called Warascus, after the custom of the country people,

[Note: [Col. 0699C] Abbot Eustasius and Agilus with him are said to have recalled the Warasci from their errors.]

we know that in an earlier age there was a man named Bernericus. He possessed the freedom of his birth, but his entire body and nerves were so constricted that he had no ability to plant his feet firmly on the ground. Placed in a two-wheeled cart, wherever he had to be taken, he seemed satisfied with one ox and one servant.

When he heard of the saint’s power, he had the ox yoked before the cart and the servant sent ahead; placed upon it, he reached the place where he had asked to be carried. He lay prostrate on the ground for a long time before the saint’s presence, mingling prayers with tears, and promptly promised the familiar ox to Saint Waldebert if he should deserve to be released from this bodily affliction.

The holy man did not disdain to receive the groaning of the suppliant, but he delayed granting health at once. For, having failed to obtain what he had long requested, Bernericus departed in the deepest sadness. After he had gone some distance on the return journey, he said: “O holy Waldebert, is it pleasing to you that I came in sorrow and leave in still greater sorrow?” Saying this, he ordered the cart to stop, got down to the ground, and released the ox to pasture. Suddenly he became well, hastily returned, gave thanks, offered the ox that had drawn him, and, with his steps made firm, returned home in the greatest joy.

21. A certain woman, noble by birth, was likewise afflicted by a very severe illness of the same contraction and deprived of the support of bodily strength. When she seemed to have despaired of obtaining health, she asked to be carried to the same place.

[Note: [Col. 0699C] The relics of Saint Waldebert are still venerated in the church of Luxeuil: his head in a silver likeness, the remaining parts of his body in a gilded-silver reliquary, as the already mentioned Reverend Father Constantine Gravellius informed me, to whom we owe very much in these notes. The translation of Saint Waldebert—perhaps his elevation—is celebrated at Luxeuil on 16 May, as are those of Saints Eustasius and Columbanus.]

When she persisted there in lengthy prayers and tears, she was suddenly healed and stood on her feet, to the astonishment of many.

But when, having obtained health, she wished to depart, she had already set out on the journey when she suddenly fell to the ground and realized that she had again been seized by the same contraction. Looking up at heaven, she groaned and had herself carried back to the place. When she had recovered her former health there, she felt somewhat secure and, wishing to inspect the necessities of life, departed from the place and began to go away.

Thus, once she had again set out on the journey, her body was contracted into a single mass, and she was carried back to the place once more. It happened that whenever she wished to leave, she fell into the same illness, until at last, having recovered her health, she fixed her mind to remain and stayed in that same place until the end of her life.

IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 994. SAINT AYMARD, THIRD ABBOT OF CLUNY.

[Col. 0699]

TESTIMONIES OF THE ANCIENTS CONCERNING SAINT AYMARD, ABBOT OF CLUNY,

from the Cluniac Library, edited by D. Marrier.

I. Saint Odilo, abbot of Cluny, in the *Life of Saint Majolus*, his predecessor.

[Col. 0699D]

After him (Odo) succeeded Heymardus, of happy memory, a son of blessed simplicity and innocence. He was exceedingly diligent in increasing estates and acquiring temporal advantages, and sufficiently devoted to observance. He bore both the loss of temporal light and whatever adversity could happen to him with the greatest patience, without any murmuring or indignation. Indeed, because of the merit of his patience and of his simple and innocent life, Christ enriched this man with so great and such a gift that, in his time, he deemed it worthy to summon blessed Majolus, the author of our salvation, to the love of the monastic order.

II. Glaber Rodolphus, *History*, book III, chapter 5.

After Odo’s death, Heimardus, a simple man, succeeded him in his place. Although not especially famous, he was nevertheless no inadequate guardian of regular observance.

III. Cardinal Peter Damian, *Letters*, book II, letter 14.

[Col. 0701A]

It happened that I learned from the venerable brothers of the Cluniac monastery two remarkable examples of holy humility. One can greatly edify prelates of every kind; the other is able to edify subjects.

Marcuardus [Aymardus, or Ademarus], certainly the ruler of that Church, appointed Majolus as his substitute and secured for his already advanced old age the leisure of repose. While he remained as a private monk in the infirmary, one evening he asked for cheese. The cellarer, being occupied with many matters, as often happens, not only gave it, but also wounded his attendant with harsh replies. He complained of the crowd of abbots, saying that he could not endure the annoyance of so many lords.

When the old man heard this, he suffered no small scandal; and because he had completely lost the light of his eyes, the pain remained more tenaciously in his heart. For the more a blind man is deprived of outward sight, the more subtly he turns whatever he hears over in his heart; and because it is not scattered outward through the senses, it burns more fiercely through the inward stimulus of zeal.

When morning came, he ordered his attendant to lead him by the hand to the chapter house. When he had been brought there, he addressed the Abbot in these words:

“Brother Majolus, I did not appoint you over me so that you might persecute me, nor so that, like a purchaser, you might rule over me as over a slave. Rather, I chose you so that, like a son toward a father, you might truly share my sufferings.”

After much of this sort, being almost moved to anger, he added: “Are you, I ask, my monk?”

When Majolus answered, “I am, and I profess that I have been yours no less than I am now,” he replied: “If you are my monk, immediately yield your seat and return to the place you once knew.”

When Majolus heard this, he suddenly rose and went to the humble place, as he had been ordered. Marcuardus [Aymardus], therefore, as though returning by postliminy, took possession of the vacant seat. He accused the cellarer against whom he had been angry; then, after throwing him to the ground, he rebuked him harshly and finally imposed the measure of penance that seemed appropriate to him.

Having completed the office of so long a tribunal, he immediately stood there dethroned. He ordered Majolus to return to his own seat, and Majolus promptly obeyed without delay.

IV. Sigebert the Monk of Gembloux, under the year 937 [944].

“Saint Odo, abbot of Cluny, died; Ademarus succeeded him.” And under the year 943 [954]: “Ademarus, abbot of Cluny, appointed Majolus abbot in his place.”

V. Vincent of Beauvais, *Historical Mirror*, book XXVI, chapter 68.

[Col. 0701D]

After Saint Odo, Ademarus, or Heimardus, a son of simplicity and innocence, succeeded. He was diligent in increasing estates and acquiring temporal advantage, and devoted to regular observance. He bore the loss of temporal light and whatever adversity might happen to him with the greatest patience, without any murmur or indignation.

VI. Manuscript Chronicle of Limoges, under the year 941.

“At this time Saint Odo, abbot of Cluny, fell asleep in Christ. Ademarus succeeded him. After he had governed the Cluniac monastery for six years, he appointed Saint Majolus abbot in his place, a man of exceptional fervor and admirable abstinence, and a distinguished restorer of monastic discipline.”

VII. Werner Rolewinck, *Fasciculus Temporum*, under the year 934.

[Col. 0702A]

“Adamarus, a holy man, successor of Saint Otho [Odo], abbot of Cluny.”

VIII. Johannes Trithemius, *On Illustrious Men of the Order of Saint Benedict*, book III, chapter 218.

After Odo, Adamarus was the second abbot of the monastery of Cluny, a man learned in the sacred Scriptures and most holy in the conduct of his life. Deprived of the light of his eyes, like another Job, he shone among his brothers as an example of patience and humility. He flourished in the year of the Lord 932 (932), having been elected in the year 944. His feast is celebrated among the Cluniacs on the Ides of September.

IX. Benedictine Monastic Martyrology, under 5 October.

[Col. 0702B]

At the Cluniac monastery, the deposition of Saint Aymard, renowned for holiness and the glory of his miracles.

X. Cluniac Chronicle.

Aymardus the First, third abbot of Cluny, was elected in the year 944. While the brothers were holding a council concerning the election of an abbot, the same most holy Aymardus, returning from Caviniis to his obedience, joined their council, leading before him on foot the horse on which he was accustomed to ride, loaded with fish. Everyone admired his humility. Thus, by the force of his humility, he was elected abbot and consecrated by Rothmundus, bishop of Autun, during the reign of Louis.

This Aymardus was the son of the count of Angoulême, as Richard reports in his Chronicle. Because of his honorable conduct and nobility, he presided over many monasteries in Aquitaine.

Under this Aymardus, Saint Majolus, archdeacon of Mâcon, became a monk. He had been nobly raised from childhood by noble parents.

The venerable father Aymardus was therefore a son of simplicity and innocence. He was diligent in increasing estates and acquiring temporal advantage, and devoted to regular observance. He bore the loss of temporal light and whatever adversity could happen to him with the greatest patience, without any murmur or indignation. Finally, deprived of all bodily health and of the light of his eyes, after a council of the brothers in the year 954, he appointed Saint Majolus in his place.

While Majolus was in the chapter house, Aymardus burst into these or similar words:

“From the courage of a great-hearted king we know that the spirit of fortitude passes into the soldiers; just as, conversely, the negligence of a slack commander inspires his fellow soldiers with a spirit of dissolution. An illness of the head overflows throughout the body, just as, when the head remains healthy, the limbs as a whole rejoice in firm health and gladness. For if a fearful and timid king turns his back, if he has escaped into flight, will not every brave and manly soldier immediately be undone by womanly fear? Who, suffering distress in the head and enduring pain in the principal member, would not at once grow weak in all the powers of mind and body? Where this speech leads is clear.

“I, who provide you with leadership in the heavenly warfare and, in the manner of a head, offer general governance to the whole human body of the Church, am worn down by old age and weakness and cannot offer the response of action appropriate to my office. I have advanced through many days; even in advanced age and old age I feel within myself the natural failure of every strength. The easy passage of the years has plundered my powers while I was unaware. My eyes grow dim, the entire sharpness of my sight is blunted, and the diminished truth of my senses feels the injury to its direction.

“Although the mind perseveres and the spirit conquers the years, having suffered the ruin of my whole body I cannot perform the vigils of the order. Let your prudence provide for itself a shepherd who will go before you on the way of God and, like a pillar of light in the night of stumbling, direct your steps. A ship committed to the winds without a helmsman is accustomed not to sail to port but to be dashed against the rocks and buried amid the waves. A multitude of soldiers in a military camp, unless it is instructed by the laws of its commander, strengthened by his presence, and fortified by his aid, falls into the savage hands of enemies roaring around it. A Church deprived of a ruler, when it lacks the eye of providence by which it may be governed, encounters the pit of destruction.”
