While the venerable old man Aymardus was speaking these and similar words in the power of the spirit, and the minds and eyes of those sitting around were drawn to his face and words, he added:

“The election certainly rests with you, and it was yours, through common deliberation, to appoint a shepherd. But since you have also placed the freedom of your choice in the judgment of our discretion, piously trusting in the mercy of the Lord, I exhort and admonish you to appoint Brother Majolus as a vigilant guardian and ruler over the Lord’s flock.”

Having done this, he asked that Majolus be ordained by the bishop of Chalon, named Holdebadus. After his resignation, the glorious Aymardus lived for nine years at Cluny and died there in the year 953, on 5 October. He lies in the aforesaid old church behind the altar of Blessed Mary.

[Col. 0703]

CHARTULARY OF SAINT AYMARD.

At D. Marrier, *Cluniac Library*, from the Cluniac chartulary.

I. Privilege of Lord Pope Agapetus granted to Lord Aymardus.

[Col. 0703B]

See among the letters and privileges of Agapetus II in volume CXXXIII of this *Patrologia*.

II. Writ of Louis, king of the Franks, concerning Saint John of Mâcon. (Year 946.)

In the name of the Lord God and of our Savior Jesus Christ, LOUIS, by the ordering of divine providence king.

For if we grant assent to the prayers of the servants of God for the sake of the holy Church of God and their interests, we unquestionably exercise royal dignity, and we wish this to remain henceforth established by the firmest right. Therefore let the diligence of all the faithful of the holy Church of God and of our own people, present and future, know that our princes—namely Hugh, duke of the Franks, and another Hugh, duke of Burgundy, as well as Count Letaldus—approached our royal serenity, beseeching us to grant by royal charter certain properties to the monastery of Cluny, consecrated in honor of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul: namely, the church dedicated in honor of Saint John, situated in the suburb of Mâcon, with all properties belonging to that church; also its estate, Hosa, Malorem, Exboscum, and the estate of Senosana, with lands, meadows, woods, larger waters, smaller streams, fishponds, pools, ditches, and the port of the aforesaid Hosa, as well as the other ports, with pastures, outgoings and returns, and all adjoining properties and all fisheries, both those already acquired and those yet to be acquired; together with Arnulf, his wife, and their sons and daughters, and all male and female servants or children belonging to the aforesaid properties, as well as their allods, scattered inside and outside, wherever they may be, except the third portion of Hosa, which belongs to Saint Vincent. Let there also be [lacuna] of Davaiaco, with his wife, sons and daughters, with all his allods and possessions, and everything that he holds in the said county. This we have willingly done both out of love for the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and for the welfare of our kingdom, our princes, and the salvation of all Christian believers; and we gladly assented to their pious and devout petition.

Therefore, prescribing and commanding, we decree that henceforth, by this authority of ours and by the firmest right, the aforesaid witnesses of Christ, the blessed Peter and Paul, or their abbot, or the monks serving those same apostles of Christ, shall hold and possess these properties; and whatever they may wish to do or decide concerning them, they shall enjoy complete freedom to do whatever they choose. And so that this authority of ours may be held more firmly and better preserved for future times, we have ordered it to be sealed below with our ring.

**Sign of Louis, king.**

Rorigus, chancellor, recognized this in place of Acardus.

Issued at the estate of Capriniacum, on the Kalends of July, in the eleventh year of the reign of King Louis, when he also recovered France.

### III. Charter of the same king concerning Tusiacum. (Year 946.)

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Louis, by the favor of God’s clemency king.

For if we grant assent to the prayers of the servants of God for the welfare of the holy Church of God and for their interests, we preserve royal dignity in every respect; and we decree that this shall henceforth remain established by the firmest and inviolable right. Therefore let the diligence of the faithful of the holy Church of God and of our own people, present and future, know that the most illustrious princes of our kingdom—namely Hugh, duke of the Franks, another Hugh, duke of Burgundy, and Count Letaldus—approached the excellence of our royal serenity, beseeching us to grant by royal charter to the monastery of Cluny, consecrated in honor of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, a certain small estate belonging to the viscountship of Lyon.

This estate is situated in the same county of Lyon, on the Saône River. We grant it with everything belonging to it: vineyards and fields, lands, meadows, woods, waters and the larger courses of waters, smaller streams, fishponds, pools, ditches, and port, with outgoings and returns, pastures and all adjoining properties, and all fishermen and fisheries, together with all male and female servants or tenants, their children, and all their descendants, both those already acquired and those yet to be acquired. We cede and transfer the whole of it, in its entirety, for the love of God and of his blessed apostles, for the welfare and stability of our kingdom and of our princes, and for the salvation of all Christ’s faithful, both living and dead.

Therefore, prescribing and commanding, we decree that henceforth, by this authority of our highness and by the firmest right, the aforesaid judges of God—the blessed Peter and Paul—or the abbots and rectors of their aforesaid monastery, and those serving the apostles of Christ in that monastery, shall hold and possess these properties; and whatever they may wish to do or decide concerning them, they shall enjoy complete freedom to arrange and do whatever they choose. And so that this authority of our highness may be held more firmly and better preserved for future times, we have ordered it to be sealed below with our ring.

**Sign of Louis, king.**

Rogerius, chancellor, recognized this in place of Acardus.

Issued at the estate of Capriniacum, on the Kalends of July, in the eleventh year of the reign of King Louis, when he also recovered France.

### IV. Charter of the same king concerning Carilocus and Regniacum, and the church belonging to Saint Martin of Tours, situated in the suburb of Mâcon. (Year 946.)

[Col. 0705D] In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Louis, by the favor of God’s clemency, king of the Franks.

For if we grant assent to the prayers of the servants of God for the welfare of the holy Church of God and for their interests, we unquestionably preserve royal dignity; and we decree that this shall henceforth remain established by the firmest and inviolable right. Therefore let the diligence of all the faithful of the universal holy Church of God and of our own people, present and future, know that the illustrious princes of our kingdom—namely Hugh, duke of the Franks, and another Hugh, duke of Burgundy, as well as Count Leucaldus [Letaldus]—approached the excellence of our royal serenity, beseeching us to grant by royal charter to the monastery of Cluny, consecrated in honor of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, a certain monastery consecrated in honor of Saint Stephen, called Carilocus, and its dependent cell, Regniacum, dedicated in veneration of Saint Martin; also the church belonging to Saint Martin of Tours, situated in the suburb of Mâcon.

These places named above, situated in the county of Mâcon, we grant with all properties belonging to them: namely, churches, estates, persons of both sexes, vineyards, fields, meadows, woods, waters and courses of waters, in their entirety. This we have willingly done both out of divine love and love of the blessed apostles and for our own sake, as well as for the welfare of our kingdom, our princes, and all Christ’s faithful; and we gladly assented to their pious and devout petition.

Therefore, prescribing and commanding, we decree that henceforth, by this authority of ours and by the firmest right, the aforesaid witnesses of Christ, Peter and Paul, or their abbot, or the monks serving those same apostles of Christ, shall hold and possess the aforesaid properties; and whatever they may wish to do or decide concerning them, they shall enjoy complete freedom to do whatever they choose. And so that this authority of our highness may be held more firmly and better preserved for future times, we have ordered it to be sealed below with our ring.

**Sign of Louis, king.**

Rorigus, chancellor, recognized this in place of Acardus.

[Col. 0706C] Issued at the estate of Capriniacum, on the Kalends of July, in the eleventh year of the reign of King Louis, when he also recovered France.

### V. Charter of the same king confirming Affredus. (Year 950.)

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Louis, by the mercy of God’s favor, king of the Franks.

If, devoting ourselves to divine worship, we strive to raise the Church of God to the highest state of sacred religion, we rely upon royal custom and the privileges of our forefathers. Therefore let the prudence of all the faithful of the holy Church of God, present and future, know that Stephen, venerable bishop of Auvergne, approaching our presence, reverently requested that we deign, by a charter of our royalty, to confirm to the monastery of Cluny and to its abbot certain properties which the late Count Acfred had transferred from the right of his own property in the county of Auvergne to God and his saints, for the remedy of his soul and those of his parents, in order that the Rule of Saint Benedict might be established there. This we have done.

Accordingly, we ordered this decree of our highness to be drawn up and given to Aymardus, abbot of the aforesaid monastery: namely, that by it the same abbot and his successors may possess the aforesaid properties in their entirety, as they are contained in the charter of the aforementioned Count Acfred, perpetually and without anyone disturbing them. And so that this benefit of our authority may be preserved inviolate through the succession of future ages, we have ordered it to be marked with the impression of our ring, affirming it below with our own hand.

**Sign of the lord Louis, most glorious king.**

[Col. 0708A] Odylo, notary, reread and subscribed this in place of Archbishop Altaldus.

Issued at the estate of Polliacum on the Loire, on the third day before the Nones of February, in the sixth indiction, and in the fifteenth year of the reign of the glorious King Louis.

[Col. 0707]

## The Election of Saint Maiolus as Abbot of Cluny during the Lifetime of Aymardus, likewise abbot. (Year of Christ 954.)

[Col. 0707A] By the order of divine dispensation, just as the movements of peoples were first restrained by sacred laws through patriarchs and prophets, and then by human consuls and kings, after the time of the incarnate Word, when the fiery sword at the entrance of paradise had been extinguished by the fountain of Christ’s side, so that the kingdom of God might be seized with greater violence, the condition of the churches began to be shaped by the virtuous conduct of apostolic men. Finally, through holy men and abbots, the regular order was established in the minds of their subjects, so that, as they advanced along it, the ascent to the heavenly homeland might appear easy.

Thus it comes about that, the more someone advances by examples of piety, raising himself toward the heights through fatherly care and providing his subjects with guidance for following heavenly things, the more he receives from the Lord, the giver of rewards, a manifold repayment of reward and filial favor. And since whatever is done wrongly by subjects is charged to their prelates, the example of an evil life and the negligence of subjects are avenged by the sentence of divine judgment and the unquenchable fire of Gehenna.

Therefore I, Haymardus, unworthy abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter of Cluny, wish it to be known generally to all present and future that, considering these and similar matters in my mind, worn out by age and weakened also in bodily functions, and recognizing that I am less suited to pastoral care, having been forewarned, chapter by chapter [perhaps: *capituli*, “of the chapter”], by blessed Benedict concerning the appointment of an abbot (Rule, chapter 64), together with all my brothers, sons, and fellow servants, we choose our religious brother and son Maiolus, formerly a cleric of the blessed Peter, and decree that he shall be abbot.

We do this lest, through the insolence of our infirmity, the order decline and suffer any setback, with the Lord’s favor always advancing it toward better things; and lest he offer some pretext of excuse—for just as one who rashly aspires unworthily to governance is judged, so one who is worthy yet refuses is rightly held liable. We therefore summoned a council of bishops and abbots.

And just as the monastery of Cluny, founded with the Lord as its author by Duke William, consecrated in the name of the prince of the apostles, distinguished by the privileges of the Roman See, confirmed by royal charters, and demonstrably ordered by the revered abbots Lords Berno and Odo, so we entrust it to the aforesaid brother to govern, together with all the abbeys, places, and cells acquired anywhere in their time or ours. We bind him under the bonds of obedience, with divine favor, both to preserve the order according to blessed Benedict and the institutions of our Fathers and to administer the properties in their entirety; and unanimously we all proclaim him abbot.

We order the course of this election and his ordination to be established in writing by the counsel, as we have said, of the leading men, the count, ourselves also, and the advocate Leotoldus; and, having confirmed the ordination celebrated according to the rule in the name of Christ, we asked that it be confirmed in writing by our Fathers and brothers. Done successfully at the monastery of Cluny. Amen.

I, Haymardus, abbot, have given my assent to this election.

Maguboldus, bishop of the holy Church of Mâcon.

Childebodus, sinner, at his command.

Eilbadus, bishop and monk, at his command.

Rodulfus, humble abbot of Saint Peter of Chalon.

Richardus, humble abbot.

[Col. 0708D] And one hundred and thirty-two other monks subscribe with them.

## In the Year of the Lord 994. Saint Maiolus, fourth abbot of Cluny.

[Col. 0709]

# Historical Eulogy of Saint Maiolus

*(In Mabillon, Acts, Fifth Century, p. 760.)*

## I. The Writers of His Life and His Praisers

[Col. 0709A]

1. Such is the renown of the first abbots of Cluny and the glory of their deeds that, although several authors have written about them, they nevertheless explain them neither with the dignity they deserve nor as fully as we would wish. Therefore, what we have already done for Saint Odo must also be done for Maiolus and the two who followed him, namely Odilo and Hugh, lest we appear to have neglected their memory by illuminating it too sluggishly. Concerning Maiolus, the Bollandist associates have already reported much in the third volume for May, drawn from ancient authors; but much remains to be said about him from the Cluniac archives, access to which we have been able to obtain.

2. The Bollandists present us with three heralds of Maiolus: Nalgodus, whom they consider a disciple of Maiolus and the author of the first Life; the other two, Syrus and Aldebaldus, likewise contemporaries, who composed a second work on Maiolus through joint efforts; and, third, Saint Odilo, Maiolus’s successor in the abbatial dignity. All of these must be discussed here at the outset, before we proceed further.

3. The first encomiast of Maiolus must certainly be considered to be the monk Syrus. From a manuscript of the church of Saint Martial at Limoges, we received from our Peter Trellius a pure copy of his work, together with a letter of Syrus to Saint Odilo, abbot, prefixed to the Life, in which the author explains the circumstances of his undertaking.

He says that he undertook the work at the insistence of Warnerius, a monk of holy memory. Syrus had been sent to Italy before the work was completed, while Warnerius himself was sent to Alsace and brought the unfinished work with him. After Warnerius had died, Odilo found the work, in the condition in which Warnerius had left it, at the monastery of Morbach, where Warnerius perhaps died. Odilo then entrusted Syrus with completing it. Syrus eventually carried this out, though not in such a way that it seemed to others to be finished in every respect. Therefore, immediately after Syrus’s death, Aldebaldus undertook to put the final hand to the work.

What Aldebaldus supplied, however, serves largely as ornament—that is, certain unnecessary additions by which he seemed to himself to illuminate and connect Syrus’s narrative. The monk Reimbaldus explains the matter; he prefixed a brief poem to this joint work of Syrus and Aldebaldus, from which it will not be out of place to quote the following:

> Since we believe that this master architect will rejoice,
>
> whose deeds are contained here in this little book,
>
> a few things, as it were flowers gathered from a father’s pleasant meadows,
>
> for the praise of Christ, which Warnerius,
>
> the monk of the most revered Life,
>
> by many prayers humbly persuaded Lord Syrus
>
> to write for the common benefit of all,
>
> lest the pious deeds of so great a father
>
> be allowed to remain concealed.
>
> At last, overcome by prayers and by love for him,
>
> he began to publish what he had been able to learn from those who told it.
>
> But, releasing the garment of the flesh through the due course of death,
>
> he left this outstanding work half finished.
>
> Soon the diligent Aldebaldus supplied what was lacking,
>
> adding what was fitting and, as you see, joining it together in order.
>
> [Col. 0710B] In this work he certainly earned worthy rewards for himself.

But so that the reader may understand what belongs to whom: Syrus composed the whole narrative of Maiolus in three books. He was eloquent for his time and inserted several poems here and there into the narrative. Aldebaldus fitted a prologue to each book and added poems in many places; but he omitted no deed reported by Syrus, except that at the beginning of the first book he introduced a narrative about the Saracen attack on the monastery of Lérins, which had nothing to do with the deeds of Maiolus.

The Bollandist associates published this joint work of Syrus and Aldebaldus. We have thought it appropriate to present here the pure work of Syrus, inserting in their proper place what Aldebaldus explained about the disaster at Lérins.

4. Concerning Aldebaldus and Warnerius, at whose request Syrus applied his hand to the work, we read nothing except that Warnerius must have been a monk distinguished for his religious devotion, since Syrus calls him “a man of holy memory,” and Reimbaldus calls him “a monk of the most revered Life.”

Concerning Syrus, we learn only the following, which Jotsaldus—in the printed editions, mistakenly “Lotsaldus”—mentions near the end of the Acts of Saint Odilo in Bollandus, in these words:

> But I myself did not see most of what I am about to relate at the beginning; rather, I learned it from two of his monks, namely Peter, provost of the monastery of Saint Maiolus, which is near Pavia, a religious man, and Syrus, abbot of a certain monastery, through the notes of Brother Boson, a monk of remarkable simplicity and innocence, who reported these things as I had requested when I began this work. The aforesaid brothers were worthy men, very close to Father Odilo, aware of many of his secrets, and companions of his journeys and labors for a long time, etc.

For a long time I was uncertain whether, in Book II of Syrus’s Life of Saint Maiolus, chapter 23, where he discusses the reform of the monastery of Pavia and says, “and there he appointed his abbot,” one should read *Syrum*—“Syrus”—instead of *suum*—“his.” But the manuscript copies, together with the printed editions, stand against this.

5. To these authors, Syrus and Aldebaldus, was added their holy abbot Odilo. He composed not so much a new account of Maiolus’s Life as a laudatory speech, referring the reader to other writers who had previously treated him. Thus we read in chapter 2 among the Bollandists:

> How many miracles the Lord deigned to display through him, both before and after his passing, is testified by volumes arranged by very learned men, written with Catholic understanding and rhetorical pen, and varied in certain places with dactylic meter.

Odilo dedicates his little book to Hugh, later his successor, and to Almanus, both monks, with a letter placed before it, which we shall at some point reproduce in his Eulogy.

6. Last of all, Nalgodus, a monk of Cluny, likewise undertook to illuminate the deeds of Saint Maiolus, during the time of the venerable abbot Peter. At that time he also polished and abridged the Life of Saint Odo, as we reported earlier in its proper place.

Of all these works, we have thought it appropriate to bring here one account by Syrus and to include in this Eulogy any distinctive statements made by other authors, while omitting two little books of miracles, in which very few matters worthy of notice are recorded. They can easily be consulted in the Cluniac Library, in whose appendix they are printed, and in the Bollandist volume for May.

Moreover, in the Limoges manuscript from which we received Syrus’s work, these two books of miracles follow continuously after Syrus’s three books on the Life of Maiolus. In the prologue to them the author suggests that he wrote the Life of Saint Maiolus, when he begins as follows:

> We have described, as briefly as we were able to know, the glorious works of virtue which the providence of almighty God deigned to perform through the blessed Maiolus, his beloved one, while the fragile garment of his body was being quickened by the addition of the life-giving spirit, etc. Now, having laid aside the burden of the flesh, he shines in heaven as a luminous and most holy star, pouring forth accumulations of virtues that have been increased. Some portion of these, at the paternal command of Lord Odilo, most reverend abbot, we have undertaken to commit to writing.

From this one might infer that Syrus was the author of these books of miracles, although they do not seem fully to attain his style. Whatever the case may be, if anything in them proves especially worthy of notice, it will be reported at the end of this Eulogy.

7. Besides these authors, many others made honorable mention of Saint Maiolus, and we shall conveniently use their words in what follows. Among them are Peter Damian in his thirty-third work, Rodulfus Glaber in various places, Vincent of Beauvais, Peter of Equilinum, bishop, in Book IV, chapter 153, John Trithemius, and many chroniclers.

A shorter Life of Maiolus also appears in the appendix to the Cluniac Library, abridged from Syrus’s work. Now let us turn to the deeds of Maiolus.

## II. Maiolus’s Homeland, Parents, Studies, and Canonical Life; the Archbishopric of Besançon Declined by Him

8. Although it is clear that he was a native of Provence—that is, born in Provence—it is not established by the consistent and unanimous testimony of ancient and modern writers what his precise birthplace was. The common tradition of the Cluniacs, led by Peter de Rivo, says that he was born at Valensole, a little town of the diocese of Riez, situated midway between Riez and Manosque. This tradition is supported by the inscription of the church of Saint Martial at Avignon, subject to Cluny, and reported by Honoré Bouche in his *Chronographia Provinciae*, p. 232.

It is indeed established that this place came to Maiolus by inheritance; but whether it was his birthplace may reasonably be doubted on the basis of Syrus, who says that Maiolus came from the town of the Avennici, that is, from Avignon. We read exactly the same words in the joint work of Syrus and Aldebaldus. In another, shorter Life preserved in the appendix to the Cluniac Library, he is called a fosterling of the townsmen of Avignon.

Nalgodus assigns Provence to him as his homeland but is silent about his birthplace; Odilo passes over both matters. I would consider it improper to depart from the authority of Syrus and Aldebaldus.

9. It is surprising that, among all those authors who wrote about Maiolus, none gives the names or dignities of his parents. They thought it sufficient to say that they were of the highest distinction, as though their complete memory ought to reach us intact beneath that covering of words.

Syrus says first:

> He was of illustrious birth, born of very distinguished parents in the town of Avignon; a Provençal by origin, illustrious in the nobility of the distinguished Gauls.

Odilo says:

> Born of a splendid lineage and raised with vigilant care by noble parents.

Nalgodus says:

> A native of the region of Provence, he extended the boundaries of his kinship even to the leading men of Gaul, and from the line of Gallic blood acquired for himself a great summit of nobility.

These words are grandiloquent but nearly empty, except insofar as they show Maiolus to have been born of a very noble family. But where are the names and dignities of his parents?

At that time, it had become customary for nobles rarely to bear titles of their dignity, except kings, dukes, and counts. Nearly all the others were identified by their bare names. Nevertheless, the designation “knight” began to be used for a nobleman in the tenth century, as is clear from many examples, including the charter of Trasmarius, bishop of Noyon, for the monastery of Ham, reported above concerning the translation of Saint Hunegundis; many knights subscribe that charter.

Yet the negligence of those who wished to describe the deeds of Maiolus while passing over his parents untouched can scarcely be excused. One of Maiolus’s praisers, Odilo, nevertheless names his father Folcherius at the end of his eulogy, almost incidentally, and calls him a knight:

> At that time, he says, there was a certain knight in those regions named Folcherius, vigorous in arms, exceedingly wealthy by hereditary right and in other goods and riches, and—as we have said concerning his most noble offspring—shining with a twofold nobility from both parents. He was a man of great counsel and prudent, discerning intelligence, namely the father of this most holy Father of ours, Maiolus, of whom we are speaking.

The epitome published in the appendix to the Cluniac Library likewise calls him Fulcherius.

10. But even if we did not have this favor from Odilo, the Cluniac records would have preserved Fulcherius’s full name for us, since it appears there more than once, as do Fulcherius’s very extensive donations, which demonstrate that he came from a wealthy family.

In particular, Fulcherius donated to Cluny:

> his allod in the county of Riez, in the county of Apt, the estates of Ausnana and Serulion; and in the county of Aix, the estate of Reglana, likewise the estate of Pinetum with its church under the title of Saint Siffredus, likewise in the same valley the estate of Palus; and in the county of Sisteron, Alairacum with the church of Saint Peter, likewise the estate of Adducellum; and in the county of Riez, the estate of Abiacum with the church of Saint Mary, the estate of Pauliacum, Valensole with the church of Saint Maximus, the church and estate of Saint Tyrsius, the estate and church of Saint Stephen of Marges, the estate and church of Saint John of Ardas; in the valley of Mézin, the churches of Saint Stephen, Saint Martin, and Saint Peter, likewise the estate of Fabricas, the estate of Narbonne with its churches, Fagentia with its church, Draguignan, the estate of Arcus, and half of the valley of Centumclaves, the estates of Locatum and Surigerias, the church of Blessed Mary, and the estate of Bonolas,

all these together with their appurtenances.

I have reported these details one by one so that the extent of Fulcherius’s resources may be apparent: the places where they were situated, namely in the counties of Riez, Apt, Aix, and Sisteron; the scale of his generosity toward sacred places; and, finally, how familiar it was in that age for laymen to possess parish churches and to transfer them to monasteries. This can be proved by six hundred examples, many of which we have seen above in the eulogies of Berno, Odo, and Aymardus.

The year in which this donation of Fulcherius was made is not stated in the charter. It is certain, however, that it was made before Maiolus renounced the world, since he withdrew to Cluny only after the death of his parents, as we shall explain later.

The donation also mentions the transfer of Valensole, which Bouche reported under the year 990 and believed was first made to Cluny by the counts of Provence. In the sixth charter of Maiolus’s chartulary, issued during the reign of King Conrad, it is stated that William himself donated to the monastery of Cluny and to Maiolus, abbot, from the properties that Abbot Maiolus and the Cluniac brothers had granted him for life, the estate of Valensole.

After Maiolus, Almeradus, bishop of Riez, remitted to Abbot Odilo certain annual dues that Valensole customarily paid to the bishop. Among the Cluniac churches from Provence, the Cluniac Library lists:

> the deanery of Valensole in the diocese of Riez, where there ought to be five monks, counting the dean, and one resident priest, and where two Masses ought to be celebrated daily.

11. From the Cluniac archive we learn not only the name of Maiolus’s father but also those of his grandfather and brother. One of these was likewise called Fulcherius, the other Cyricus.

This is clear from charter 344 of Maiolus, a *precaria* granted by Maiolus to Arnulfus, bishop of Apt, concerning certain properties of the monastery of Cluny situated in the county of Apt. It is useful to reproduce the document here in full:

> In the name of the Lord . . . I, Maiolus, by the favor of Christ’s clemency, abbot of the monastery of Cluny. We wish it to be known to all Christian believers, present and future, that Lord Arnulfus, bishop of Apt, approached our presence with a request that we grant him, by way of a *precaria*, certain properties belonging by right to the holy apostles Peter and Paul and to the aforesaid monastery of Cluny.
>
> Having therefore sought the will of our brothers, and with their reasonable assent, we resolved to comply with the prayers of the aforesaid lord bishop. Accordingly, we grant to the same Lord Arnulfus, bishop, and to his kinsman Teobertus, properties dedicated to the holy apostles Peter and Paul, situated in the county of Apt: in the estate called Lausnana, and in another estate called Soldo, as far as Mount Clavaniacum; and in another place called Trabalium; and in another estate called Bassus; and in another estate called Siciacum; and in another estate called Borcium; and in another called Soricaria; and in another called Leocola; and in another called Vallis; and the very allod that my grandfather Fulcherius purchased from Bernardus; and in another estate called Jocadas; and in another called Cariaras; and in another called Serulias.
>
> All these properties came to me and to my brother Cyricus by succession from our parents. We, namely I, Maiolus, abbot of the aforesaid monastery of Cluny, and my aforesaid brother, for the remedy of our souls, of our parents, and of all Christian believers, have transferred them to God and to his holy apostles Peter and Paul in the monastery of Cluny.
>
> Accordingly, all the properties adjoining the estates already named, as well as everything that my grandfather Fulcherius and my father of the same name held or acquired in the county of Apt, we grant in full to the aforesaid bishop and to his kinsman Teobertus, on the following condition: the lord bishop shall transfer his own properties, situated in the county or county-district of Apt, in the estate of Lausnana, to God and to his holy apostles Peter and Paul in the aforementioned monastery of Cluny, with this provision: that for as long as the bishop himself and his kinsman live, they shall hold and possess them and shall pay at the feast of Saint Martin five solidi as a census to Cluny. After the death of both, all the properties written above, with every improvement, shall pass to the aforesaid monastery of Cluny without anyone’s opposition.
>
> So that this *precaria* may remain unimpaired and inviolable at all times, we have confirmed it with our hand and presented it to our brothers for corroboration. Maiolus, sinner and humble abbot; Adiblamus; Jacob; Fulcardus; Stephanus; Andreas . . . the sign of Durannus, of Teodericus. I, Brother Clemens, wrote this. Done at Saint Saturninus, in the twenty-third year of the reign of King Conrad.

From this *precaria* we understand that, in addition to the earlier donation of Maiolus’s father Fulcherius, another donation was made to the Cluniacs by Maiolus himself and his brother Cyricus, consisting of the properties which these letters transfer by *precaria* to Arnulfus, bishop of Apt.

His kinsman Teutbertus is called a most illustrious man in another charter, and his wife Raimodis and son Ulricus are also mentioned. Another charter also mentions further properties, in which William, most noble count, and his wife Lucia restore to the Cluniacs under Abbot Odilo:

> the inheritance of Saint Maiolus, namely Dilioda and Seven Fountains in the bishopric of Riez.

Done at the monastery of Podium Odolinum in the year 1036 from the Incarnation, in the fifth indiction, while Emperor Conrad reigned in his tenth year.

From this it again becomes clear from how wealthy a lineage Maiolus was born: his parents enriched Cluny with so many estates and possessions without, as one may reasonably believe, seriously diminishing their family property.

As I consider these matters, a doubt occurs to me: was Maiolus’s grandfather Folcherius perhaps that Folcratus, duke of Arles, whom Lothair is recorded in the Fulda Annals, under the year 844, to have accepted into submission when he was attempting to rebel together with other counts, and, having done so, to have organized Provence?

12. After Maiolus had spent his childhood in his homeland with an unblemished and unimpaired character,

> when adolescence was already claiming him for itself, his parents having been overtaken by the human lot and his estates having been reduced to desolation by barbarian invasion, by the ordering of divine providence he was compelled to leave his native soil and seek the regions of Burgundy,

as Syrus writes.

> Coming to the city of Mâcon, he was received there as a guest by one of his relatives, who among the other leading men of that city bore the distinction of nobility. After he had remained for some time in his lodging, supported by that man’s assistance, he began to associate with the bishop of the same city. Seeing that he possessed a capable and liberal intellect, the bishop sought to join him to the college of canons; he also earnestly urged him in private to preserve his virginity.

At that time Berno presided over the Church of Mâcon; various records testify to his generosity toward the Cluniacs.

13. What that disaster was, of which Syrus speaks here, has not been established with complete certainty. Two kinds of enemies were at that time ravaging Provence: the Hungarians and the Saracens. The latter, carried perhaps from Spain to Italy in the manner of pirates, seized the fortress of Fraxinetum in the Cottian Alps in the year 891 and held it for many years, to the greatest detriment of Lombardy and Provence, until Hugh, king of Italy, attacked them by land and sea. After burning their ships with Greek fire, he compelled most of them to abandon Fraxinetum and withdraw to Mount Mauros in 941. Hugh would easily have reduced them, once surrounded by a siege, had he not feared Berengar and therefore abandoned the assault, making an agreement with them whereby some of them would settle in the mountains separating Italy from Swabia and prevent Berengar from leading an army from Swabia through those mountains.

Those who had been stationed there afterward either completely plundered or inhumanely killed everyone traveling through that region to visit the thresholds of the Apostles. In the same century the Hungarians, repeatedly pouring forth from Germany into Gaul and Italy, inflicted disastrous devastation. Under the leadership of Berengar, the king whom the Lombards had expelled, they ravaged Italy in 924; then, according to Frodoard, crossing the precipitous Alpine passes, they invaded Gaul. Rudolf, king of Cisalpine Gaul, together with Hugh of Vienne, shut them in “among the narrow defiles of the Alpine hills.” Escaping unexpectedly through the mountain’s remote paths, they attacked Gothia, where they were defeated by the aforementioned Rudolf and Hugh.

A little later, that is, in 933, while Hugh, king of Italy, was besieging Rome, the Saracens occupied the Alpine passes and plundered all the neighboring places. Two years later the Hungarians spread through Burgundy and ran riot with plunder, fires, and slaughter. Such great and so frequent disasters unquestionably compelled Maiolus to take refuge in the city of Mâcon, while Provence—that is, his homeland—was being ravaged by so many calamities.

14. Meanwhile, after becoming a canon at Mâcon, he went to Lyon to study. There he had as his teacher Antonius, a man learned in philosophy, “under whom he greatly prospered” (these are Syrus’s words), “not only in learning, but also in conduct and life.”

The antiquity of the academy of Lyon is rightly demonstrated by Hericus of Auxerre, a monk, in Book I of *The Miracles of Saint Germanus*, where he discusses the time of Constantius of Lyon, that is, the fifth century:

> “At that time,” he says, “the city of Lyon, first and foremost among the cities of Gaul, had also raised its head above all others in its professed knowledge and discipline of the arts. There the mastery of what are called the liberal disciplines—disciplines whose orderly progression at the present time is merely a fable—had grown so strong that, as regards its public schools, it was called the gymnasium of the world on this side of the sea. To offer some rational proof, we infer this from the fact that anyone who was moved by a desire to profess the arts was not deemed worthy to be enrolled among the professors until, after being examined here with tested diligence, he had departed.”

By the term “professors” he means those grades that we designate by the titles “master” and “doctor.” Among their number in the advancing tenth century was Antonius, whom virtue and religious devotion had placed over the monastery on the island of Barbarensis, according to Syrus. This place lay in the middle of the Saône, above Lyon. It had once been a celebrated abbey of our order, but had recently been given secular status. Antonius must be included among its abbots, since Syrus expressly attests this.

15. After returning from his studies, Maiolus “ascending through all the ecclesiastical grades, when he had attained the office of levite, was promoted by the same aforementioned bishop even to its summit, as doctrine required”—that is, to the office of archdeacon, as Odilo explains Syrus’s words.

In that dignity he shaped his conduct according to the form of his learning and excelled in Christian virtues, especially in charity toward the poor. This won him everyone’s esteem. But, fleeing praise and popular commotion, he repeatedly withdrew “to the little oratory of Saint Michael, which he himself had rebuilt, across the Saône,” where, “ever wakeful in prayer, he devoted himself more attentively to divine service.”

From there, extending himself for the benefit of others, he freely and willingly instructed clerics who came to him from various regions. Then, when his reputation had spread everywhere, “after the archbishop of Besançon had entered upon the way of all flesh, blessed Maiolus was urged, by the agreement both of the prince of that land and of the entire clergy and people, to assume the summit of the episcopate.” He absolutely refused to consent. Indeed, he became all the more ardent in avoiding glory—which habitually pursues those who flee from it—and began diligently to consider fleeing from the world.

To investigate more precisely the time when this occurred, it is useful here to recall some acts of Maiolus while he was archdeacon. Among them is a charter by which “Acbertus, a man of exceptionally noble birth,” obtained from Maymbold, or Mainbodo, bishop of Mâcon—whom some incorrectly call Magubold—for the duration of his life, churches on his own property, called Scociacus (Escuzolles). The principal church there was dedicated to Saint Andrew, with an additional chapel of Saint John and another of Saint Marcellus.

The charter was subscribed in his own hand by Maymbodus the bishop, Ado the abbot—the dignity of the Church of Mâcon—and Mayolus the archdeacon, in the third year of King Louis, A.D. 939.

Likewise, in the sixth year of the same king, Maimbod leased to “the noble man Achard” land belonging to his church, “situated in the county of Forez.” Among others, Maiolus the archdeacon affixed his hand and sign to the instrument of this transaction before Ado the abbot.

Maiolus therefore continued to be archdeacon until that time, namely until the sixth year of King Louis, which was A.D. 942. That was also the first year of Aymard’s abbacy at Cluny after Odo’s death.

16. “Since Maiolus excelled in such conduct, when the archbishop of Besançon had entered upon the way of all flesh, he was urged, by the agreement both of the prince of that land and of the entire clergy and people, to assume the summit of the episcopate.” He himself, however, consistently refused this out of modesty.

This is reported by Syrus and Nalgodus, and it is not surprising that Odilo omitted it, since he also remained silent about Maiolus’s refusal of the highest pontifical dignity. Odilo, after all, embellished Maiolus’s brief eulogy more by digression than by composing a careful life.

Gerfredus was elected to the see of Besançon in Maiolus’s place; I have no adequate knowledge of his predecessor.

## III. Maiolus’s Conversion to the Monastic Life. His Election as Abbot

16*. Under Abbot Aymard, Maiolus frequently went to Cluny, “and often held conversation and spiritual fellowship with the brothers,” as Odilo relates. Their desire was “to acquire him as their brother, whom they would afterward deserve to have as their father.”

In bringing about this conversion, “the sweet conversation and spiritual exhortation of the venerable man Hildebrannus” was highly influential. Hildebrannus had been one of the earlier Cluniac monks and was provost of the same monastery. He had twice been invited to undertake the office of abbot, but had refused, because he always wished “to obey rather than command, and to be subject rather than preside.”

Maiolus’s conversion was due not only to Prior Hildebrannus, but also to Aymard’s “merit of patience and innocent life,” on account of which “Christ enriched him with so great and such a gift that, in his time, the author of our salvation deigned to summon blessed Maiolus to the love of the monastic order.”

17. After becoming a monk, Maiolus “stood out among the others by a singular virtue,” says Syrus. Aymardus “placed him in charge of the library and entrusted him with the office of apocrisiarius.” Thereafter Maiolus abstained from reading Virgil and other pagan authors and deterred the other brothers from reading them as well.

“An apocrisiarius is one who guards the treasure of the church, and in whose hand is whatever is offered by the people at the altars.” So writes Udalricus, Book III of the *Customs of Cluny*, chapter 12.

It also seems to have belonged to this office that, whenever business had to be conducted outside, the apocrisiarius was sent for that purpose, as among the Romans. Maiolus was once sent to Rome by Aymardus on business. On that journey, at Ivrea (Yporedia), an episcopal city under the archbishop of Turin, he healed the sick monk Heldricus by anointing him with holy oil.

Heldricus had once been “honored in Italy among the other palace officials.” He “renounced his wife together with a great abundance of temporal possessions, laid aside his belt, withdrew to Cluny, and submitted himself to the purpose of blessed Benedict,” being moved to do so, as Syrus relates in Book II, by Maiolus’s reputation.

Whether this was the same Heldricus who was abbot of Saint Germanus at Auxerre will be considered below. Nalgodus calls the sacrament of anointing the rite by which Heldricus was healed by Maiolus. What we said in the preface to the first century about such anointings is relevant here.

18. Other business conducted by Maiolus the monk likewise confirms that he held the aforementioned office of apocrisiarius. In the eleventh year of King Louis, “Hildebrandus and Maiolus pleaded” before Count Leotaldus, Viscount Walterius, and other men faithful to them—elsewhere called leading men—concerning certain lands given to Cluny that had been occupied by some persons.

Likewise, in the second year of King Lothair, “Eldebrandus and Maiolus, Cluniac monks,” were sent by Abbot Aymardus to Maimbod, bishop of Mâcon, who was attending a synod, to request from him the tithes of the churches of Saint Andrew at Evranda and Saint Bonitus.

These and other acts clearly demonstrate that the Cluniac provost, such as Hildebrandus was, and the apocrisiarius were responsible for temporal affairs. Moreover, by comparing the first of these acts, conducted by Maiolus already as a monk in the eleventh year of King Louis, with the earlier document to which he subscribed as archdeacon in the sixth year of that same Louis, we can plainly conclude that Maiolus renounced the world in the seventh or eighth year of Louis’s reign, that is, in 943 or the following year.

## IV. His Election as Abbot of Cluny. Acts under His Rule

[Col. 0719B] 19. The time when Aymardus chose him as his successor also indicates this clearly enough. Maiolus is called abbot as early as the thirteenth year of Louis, as we demonstrated from certain documents in Aymardus’s eulogy. Yet Odilo says that “in the sixth year of his conversion from the world,” Aymardus designated him as his vicar and successor.

Therefore, if six years are subtracted from Louis’s thirteenth year, the seventh year remains; it is consequently reasonable to believe that this was made illustrious by Maiolus’s conversion.

What prevents us from placing his election under Louis Transmarinus, however, is the fact that in the second year of King Lothair, the son and successor of Louis—the year in which Maiolus was sent with Hildebrandus to Maimbod’s synod concerning the tithes of Evranda and Saint Bonitus—his name is placed after that of Eldebrandus in the charter, and he is called not abbot but merely monk.

Besides the evidence brought forward in Aymardus’s eulogy to establish the earlier point, another argument appears in a deed of donation by a certain Maytramus, who gave to “the place of Celsinianas and to Lord Maiolus the abbot” the estate of Becedas “in the month of February, while Louis was reigning as king of the Franks.” It follows that, while Louis was reigning, Maiolus was already being called abbot.

Since Aymardus had not transferred the administration to him in such a way that he himself did absolutely nothing during the first years, as we stated in Aymardus’s eulogy, it happened that Maiolus—who was regarded rather as a coadjutor—was sometimes called abbot by secular persons in public documents and sometimes monk, especially in those acts conducted under Aymardus’s supervision.

The *Chronicle of Malleacum* seems to imply this, saying that Maiolus “in the year 961, the sixth year of his ordination, assumed responsibility for the monastery of Cluny”—that is, that he assumed full administration in the sixth year after his election, although from what has been said the year should be called the twelfth.

We included the letter of his election in Aymardus’s eulogy, and Syrus also reports a fragment of it. There we likewise related, from Peter Damian, a remarkable incident in which an excellent example of Maiolus’s modesty appears. For when Aymardus ordered him to return to a private seat, he consented without resistance; and, after Aymardus had rebuked the cellarer for speaking insolently to him, Maiolus resumed the abbatial chair with equal ease.

[Col. 0720A] 20. During this period of joint administration, public instruments were marked with the name of one or the other abbot, as can be observed in Aymardus’s eulogy.

For the present I add a charter of Girberga, granting the church of Saint Maurice in the county of Chalon, in the estate of Breugis and the estate of Canna, as Bishop Ardradus had held it, in the third year of King Lothair.

I also add a charter of a certain Gauzbertus, who gave in perpetuity to Abbot Heymardus and the monks inhabiting Celsinianas his allod, “which rustic Latin, using an ancient name, called Petrafixa, situated in the suburb of Brioude,” “for the salvation of his soul and of his lord Bertrand and his son Stephen.”

This was enacted at Celsinianas “in the month of January, in the fourth year of the reign of King Lothair, A.D. 958 from the Incarnation of the Lord.”

In the same year, in December, “Maiolus the abbot” bought certain lands in the county of Mâcon, in the estate of Materiacus and elsewhere, “for a price of 400 solidi.”

Two years later Adalradus transferred his possessions in the estate “of Persezeel,” in the vicariate of Ycion, to “the sanctuary called Celsinianas,” appointing as heirs the monks serving God there night and day, “over whom the reverent fatherhood of Lord Maiolus, the foremost father, presides.” Given in February, on the eleventh day of that month, in the year 960 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the fourth year of the empire of Lothair, king of the Franks—sixth should be read—in the second Olympiad.

In the preceding year King Lothair, at the request of his mother, Queen Gerberga, subjected to Cluny the monastery of Saint Amand in the county of Trahesin, which people call Nantua. It was situated “without superiors, as though in uninhabitable places,” “so that, insofar as God should supply the counsel, it might be built in habitable places.” Given on the ninth day before the Kalends of December, in the fifth year of King Lothair, indiction 3, in the palace at Dijon.

At this point we must recall the *precaria* previously published, made by Maiolus the abbot in favor of Arnulfus, bishop of Apt, concerning certain hereditary possessions of his situated in Provence. It was made in the twenty-third year of King Conrad, corresponding to the year 960 of Christ.

Then, in 962, Count Alberic, son of Leotaldus, gave many things to Abbot Maiolus and his monks in the county of Mâcon, “in the eighth year of King Lothair.”

Moreover, in the tenth year of the same king, Amblardus, bishop of Lyon, gave to Maiolus and the brothers themselves the church of Saint Mary of Cantumerula “in the county of Auvergne,” and, in the vicariate of Rander, a vineyard with a wood at Vetreria, and, “in the county of Clermont,” the estate of Luxiacus.

Stephanus, bishop of Auvergne, and Rotbertus the abbot subscribed his deed in the eleventh year of Lothair. Maiolus, the humble abbot, and Heymardus the abbot subscribed a *precaria* made to two levites concerning possessions situated in the county of Chalon.

From that year onward there is no further mention of Abbot Aymardus; all documents bear only Maiolus’s name as abbot. It is worth recalling some of them.

21. Several diplomas of the emperors Otto are found in the archive of Cluny. One is a judicial decision issued “in the city of Pavia, in the chamber of the hall of the house of Lietefredus, bishop of Pavia, behind the church of Saint Cyrus the Confessor, where his holy body rests, with Otbertus, margrave and count of the palace, presiding so that he might administer justice among men together with the other judges.”

Before him “Lord Maiolus, abbot of Cluny, appeared and presented two records,” or instruments. One was issued in the name of the emperors Otto, “on July 16, in the sixth year of his reign in Italy,” and stated that Gaidulfus, son of Peter the judge, had purchased certain lands. There was “one chapel in honor of Saint Mary near Pavia, and also one of Saint Michael,” and he had given them, together with the chapel, to Abbot Maiolus, “so that monks living there under the rule of Saint Benedict might dwell and pray there forever for the soul of Liutardus, bishop of Como.” The other was likewise a record of several donations made to the same monastery.

Maiolus requested that these be confirmed against invaders. This was granted during the reign “of the two Ottos, father and son, in the sixth year of the Italian reign of Otto the Younger, indiction 10”—read: of Otto the Elder and the Younger, in the first year of the latter. This cell was later called Saint Maiolus.

The same Otbertus, margrave and count of the palace, gave to the monastery called Cluny whatever he possessed on the Po below the castle of Vicopiculo, and other possessions, in the tenth year of the elder Otto, the fourth of the younger, indiction 14.

Besides these, I find a diploma of Otto I in duplicate, one of which contains the following:

> “We receive Odo the abbot under our protection and guardianship, together with the abbey of Saint Sabinus, in the place called Tuscana.”

Given on the eighth day before the Ides of July, in the year 969 from the Incarnation, the eighth year of Otto, “indiction 12. Enacted at Plista.”

Who this Abbot Odo was, or what his monastery was, I do not understand. Perhaps it was situated in Italy.

The same Otto, at the request of his wife Adelheid, granted to the monastery of Saint Peter at Pavia a vineyard that had belonged to a certain priest of the cathedral church of Pavia and then pertained to his royal jurisdiction.

In addition, “in the sixth year of Otto and Otto his son reigning in Italy,” a certain Ingelbaudus, son of Ansegisus, living according to Salic law, gave certain estates in the county of Vienne “to the monastery of Cluny, by knife, knotted staff, and by the *vuanton* and *vuaso* of earth into the hands of Lord Maiolus the abbot.”

22. In the thirty-sixth year of King Conrad, Maiolus the abbot granted certain possessions in *precaria* to Hugh, son of Count Lambert, in these words:

> “Let it be known to all the abbots of the sacred monastery of Cluny and to all future monks that I, Brother Maiolus, abbot—although unworthy—of the aforesaid monastery, with the consent of the brothers, grant the possessions belonging to us to a certain noble man, Hugh, to his wife Almodis, to their son Stephen, and to his firstborn”—what we would today call “for three lifetimes”—“the estate of Ambariacus,” etc.

The subscribers are “Maiolus, the most humble abbot; Vivianus, the prior; Ermenfredus, the bishop; Balduinus,” followed by twenty-five other monks. This occurred in 973.

At about the same time Pope John XIII commended the monastery of Cluny—“over which, as he says, our dearest son Lord Maiolus the abbot wisely and blessedly presides”—to the bishops of Gaul. He instructed Stephanus, bishop of Auvergne, to compel his faithful Amblardus to restore what was owed to the monastery of Celsinianas. He also entreated Ado, bishop of Mâcon, in these words:

> “The matter also requires that we say something to you, dearest and beloved brother, Lord Ado the bishop, whom, although we have not seen, we know by name to possess every spiritual goodness. We therefore earnestly request the most kindly sweetness of your fatherhood that, the nearer you appear to be to the school of the aforesaid monastery, the more swiftly your protection, according to your ability, may come to the aid of the brothers’ necessities. They love you out of abundant charity and desire to surround and embrace you perfectly with the arms of complete love. Therefore, always be a protector of the monastery of Cluny, just as you are a faithful lover of blessed Peter.”

This bull lacks chronological notes in the *Cluniac Bullary*.

23. In the twentieth year of King Lothair, Alberic, count of Mâcon, and his wife Ermentrudis gave to the Cluniac monks under Maiolus many estates in the estate of Aponiacus (Apogny).

In 978, indiction 6, at Lyon, before a multitude of people, Amblardus, bishop of Lyon, “gave his possessions in the county of Auvergne to the brothers of the monastery of Cluny, so that they might build a cell in the estate of Nisiacus (Nizy), in the land of Thiers, in the vicariate of Dorat”; namely, the estate of Genreta, Montembrioson, and others.

We read an instrument of the same Amblardus concerning this matter, in which he says that he gives these things to God and to the holy Apostles Peter and Paul, “so that the monks of the place of Cluny might build for themselves at Nisiacus a cell dedicated to God, in honor of blessed Peter, prince of the Apostles, serving God under the rule of Saint Benedict, the father of monks.” He orders his guarantors, that is, the executors of his will—whom others call his almoners—to prepare a charter of this donation.

They immediately do so: “Andreas the provost, Ornadus the dean, Gundramnus the abbot, Hugo the abbot”—the dignities of the Church of Lyon—“Augendus the canon, Stephanus the deacon, Pontio the canon, and Hugo the layman.”

Nisiacus has remained a Cluniac priory to the present day.

24. Pope Benedict VII “entrusted the monastery of Lérins to be organized to Maiolus, abbot of Cluny,” as our Stephanotius reads in the *Lérins Cartulary*.

A papal diploma concerning this matter survives in the *Cluniac Bullary*, issued “in the fourth year of the pontificate of Benedict VII, the eleventh year of Otto’s empire, in the month of May, indiction 6.”

That bull also mentions the monastery of Arluc (Saint-Étienne d’Arluc), now destroyed. Saint Honoratus had built it for nuns on an exceedingly beautiful mountain beside the sea and on the bank of the Siagne River, where Angarisma presided under Abbot Saint Aigulf.

More distinguished than these, however, is a charter of Rodulfus, bishop of Chalon, in which he says:

> “Ageus the canon approached the serenity of our munificence, asking that we eternally give to the Cluniac monks and to Lord Maiolus the abbot a house with its grounds beside the city walls on one side, and on the other beside the canons’ cloister, together with the canonry that he had held from his earliest age.”

He says that he did this voluntarily, with the consent of his clergy, “especially since we hear with our own ears the glory of so great a man, Maiolus, derived from the Lord himself, and daily perceive with the sight of our own light, without closing our eyes in affection for him. For he is truly the radiance of Gaul, having risen for a time in our age, admirable and, if possible, imitable by all.”

Nothing more illuminating can be offered about a living man than this eulogy. I find no canonry granted to the Cluniac monks before this time—what they call a prebend—though many were granted later under Abbots Odilo and Hugh.

After Rodulfus, the following subscribed this charter: “Adelais the countess, her son Hugh, Rotbertus the viscount,” together with the canons, in the twenty-sixth year of King Lothair.

25. In the thirty-fourth year of King Lothair, that is, in 980, Count Gaufredus and his wife Adelheid gave to the place of Cluny, where Maiolus was abbot, their possessions situated in the county of Chalon, in the district of Jemulac, in the estate of Fusciacus.

The subscribers were “Gaufredus the count, Adelheid his wife, and their son Hugh”—namely, Adelheid’s son by her earlier husband, Count Lambert.

In the twenty-sixth year of Lothair, Wido, viscount of the city of Auvergne, and his wife Ausenda gave the church of Saint Mary of Bellomonte in the county of Chalon, likewise under Maiolus as abbot.

26. In 981, Milo, bishop of Mâcon, granted to Abbot Maiolus and his monks, in his synod, the church of Saint Germanus in the estate of Rofeius and the church of Saint Mary in the estate of Pedronus, together with the tithes and everything pertaining to them, “saving synodal service, payments, and offerings.”

In the twenty-eighth year of King Lothair, Count Lambert and his wife Adeleis gave to Cluny the church of Saint Martin of Ingheto in the county of Autun.

I pass over many other churches that were granted to the Cluniac monks: some by Burcardus, archbishop of Lyon, with the consent of the provost and Abbot Hugh; some by the layman Roclenus in the diocese of Lyon, while Conrad was reigning, from the thirtieth to the fortieth year of his reign; some by Walterius, bishop of Autun, in the twenty-ninth year of King Lothair; and others by various donors.

Among these, Walterius gave the church of Montmelard, the church of Saint Mary in the estate of Vallis, and the church of Saint Germanus in the estate of Tirinacus, “where,” he says, “the aforesaid monks daily attend in obedience.”

27. In the thirtieth year of King Lothair, that is, in 984, Maiolus of Cluny and Valorgus of Luxeuil exchanged certain properties between themselves in the estates of Salustriacus and Danaicus in the county of Mâcon. Previously, Abbot Aymardus and Guido, likewise abbot of Luxeuil, had exchanged certain properties there.

In the same year Aynus, archdeacon of Mâcon, gave to Cluny vineyards situated in the county of Chalon, in the estate of Fusciacus. The grant was confirmed by “Rotdulfus the bishop, Gaufredus the count, and Adeleis the countess.”

28. In 985 Count Lambert of Valence granted land for the construction of a monastery in honor of Saint Marcellus. The document drawn up concerning this matter has the following preface, with some passages omitted:

> “I, Lambertus, and my wife Falectrudis give some of our own possessions to God, to Saint Marcellus, and to these monks, namely Odoinus and Durannus, and to those who shall come to the place of blessed Marcellus and live there together in community, for the salvation of our souls and for our sons Ademarus and Lambertus, and so that the church of blessed Marcellus may be rebuilt and a monastery established there. Let neither that church nor that place be subject to any place except to Saint Peter, prince of the Apostles. At all times, the monks living together there shall pay at Rome, every fifth year, five solidi as a census.
>
> “Let no one be abbot in the place of Marcellus, which is called Fellinis, unless he observes the rule of Saint Benedict and lives according to it. Let no monks live there who do not properly maintain fraternal and common life. If any man or any person should wish, for gold or silver or any other wealth, to install an abbot in the place of Marcellus, may all the saints oppose him, and blessed Benedict with the flock of his monks . . . .
>
> “These possessions are situated in the county of Valence: namely, the mountain called Alavinea and the mountain called Medialuna . . . . We give them, and wish them to remain given forever, for the sustenance and support of the monks and for the reception of guests, pilgrims, and orphans serving in the aforesaid place under the rule of the aforesaid father Benedict, for the salvation of my soul, and also for the salvation of my father Guntardus and my mother Ermengardis,” etc.

Among others, Richardus, Lambert’s son, subscribed.

King Conrad confirmed this donation in the forty-sixth year of his reign. Count Ademarus and his wife Roteldis restored this priory to Abbot Odilo in 1035. Concerning this priory, see the *Cluniac Library*, column 1727.

29. In 986, the year marked by the death of Lothair, king of the Franks, a vineyard near the estate of Noglas in the county of Mâcon was given “to Maiolus and his monks, in the first year of King Louis,” who was Lothair’s son and successor.

A charter is likewise to be understood as referring to this same King Louis. In it, a certain canon of Le Puy restored his buildings, consumed by fire and situated within the canons’ cloister, and gave them to Maiolus and the Cluniac monks, “in the year in which King Louis ended his life in youth. Given on Thursday, the third day before the Ides of August.”

In a brief chronicle of the kings of France, preserved in manuscript in the library of the Carmelite Fathers of Cantoennus at Clermont, the last kings of the second French dynasty and their regnal years are recorded as follows:

> “Chlothar, 31; Louis, 1; Charles, his brother, 6 months; Hugh, a stranger, 9.”

This Hugh, son of Count Hugh “of Paris by Hawidis, sister of Otto, began to reign in the year of the Lord 987 and usurped the kingdom.”

Another entry reads:

> “Louis Transmarinus begot Lothair; Lothair begot Louis, who, while still a boy, took Blanche as his wife. With him the kings from the family of Charlemagne also came to an end. A Hugh from another family succeeded him in the kingdom, the son of Hugh the Great. His son Robert succeeded him in the kingdom. Robert’s son then succeeded him, Henry, who now, with God’s protection, governs the kingdom of France as best he can.”

We have taken these entries from our Stephanotius.

A charter, numbered 326 in Maiolus’s cartulary, is dated “in the fifth year of King Hugh, with Charles thrust into prison.” Charles was Louis’s uncle and duke of Lorraine.

30. In 988, a certain cleric named Richardus gave Maiolus and the Cluniac monks the church of Saint Andrew “in the district of Vapincum (Gap),” together with the estate of Rosanis, the castle of Riso, the estates of Sorbaria, Gemma, and others; and, in the “county of Vaison, within the boundaries” of the castle of Malaucène, six manses, half the castle of Minson, and other possessions, so that there—namely, in the aforesaid church—“monks might dwell forever.”

31. Thus far I have related the acts conducted under Maiolus alone as abbot. In 991 he arranged for Odilo to be substituted for him; consequently, most subsequent acts are attributed solely to Odilo, as we shall say in the following chapter, chapter 8.

Before leaving this subject, however, two further acts of Abbot Maiolus must be mentioned, both lacking chronological notes. One concerns the grant of the monastery of Saint Marcellus near Chalon. The charter is as follows, from the cartulary of Saint Marcellus and from the *Cluniac Library*, column 314:

> “I, Tetbaldus, count of Chalon, greet in the Lord all the sons of Holy Church in the name of God.
>
> “I have heard from my predecessors and from neighboring men of ancient times that the most noble Count Gaufredus, who after the death of my most excellent and Christian grandfather, Count Lambertus, took his wife, my grandmother, Countess Adelheid, approached Maiolus, the abbot of blessed memory, and entrusted to him the monastery in the suburb of the city of Chalon. It had been magnificently built by Guntramnus, a most noble and religious king, and there the body of blessed Marcellus the martyr rests.
>
> “He entrusted it to him on the condition that Maiolus restore the religious observance of the monastic order, which had almost been abolished there, cultivate the land and possessions belonging to that place, and that he and his successors, the abbots of Cluny, should have and possess the monastery in perpetuity.
>
> “The aforesaid Count Gaufredus made this entrustment or donation to Lord Maiolus with the counsel of his wife Adelheid and of her son Hugh, then a cleric and afterward a bishop, with the assistance and approval of Duke Henry.
>
> “Later, while the most serene King Robert was reigning, my uncle, Lord Hugh, count and bishop, in the presence of the king himself and of the counts and bishops of this region, handed over the monastery’s gift to Lord Odilo the abbot, successor to Abbot Maiolus, so that he might have, hold, and possess the place by the right of his predecessor.
>
> “I, Tetbaldus, count by the grace of God, approve, desire, and confirm what my predecessors and relatives gave to God, Saint Peter, and the place of Cluny; and I cause it to be approved and confirmed by my wife and my faithful men,” etc.

The sign of Tetbaldus the count; the sign of Ermentrudis his wife; and others.

32. Another charter is that of Maiolus the abbot, by which he entrusted certain obediences to Humbert of Beaujeu under this title:

> “Record of the entrustment that Maiolus, of venerable memory, made to Humbert of Beaujeu concerning these obediences: Algoia, Pola, Scotiolas, and Arpajacus. He said:
>
> “‘I entrust to you the aforesaid obediences, to guard and defend them from evil and perverse men, in place of satisfaction and compensation for the countless evils that you have done us, for which we ought to have excommunicated you. Nevertheless, you must return to our poor what you have taken from them.
>
> “‘I make this entrustment to you not so that you may demand any customary payment in these obediences—which I forbid and excommunicate with the utmost diligence and vigilance—but only so that, if you pass near an obedience with six or ten soldiers and a monk voluntarily admonishes you, you may refresh yourself, and after the meal continue on your way; you must not presume to lie down there.
>
> “‘The sign of Count Alberic, who approved this record.’”

Here one sees that in the tenth century the term *obedience* had already come to mean a dependency or cell placed under one or more monks.

Thus far we have related the principal instruments made under Maiolus. All of them are said to have been made not to Maiolus himself, but either to the monastery of Cluny, over which Maiolus presided, to the monks, or at least into the hands of Maiolus the abbot, just as all other donations made to monasteries were made. It is therefore all the more astonishing that some people dare to assert that various donations were made to the abbot rather than to the monks, contrary to the certain and well-established tradition of the ancients.

All the charters drawn up under Maiolus are numbered 859.

## V. Monasteries Reformed by Maiolus
### 33.

After we have related the various donations made to Cluny, we must now discuss his other deeds. In this regard Syrus transmits much about his virtues, which it is not useful to repeat here. It will suffice to report some matters that require explanation.

First of all, mention must be made of his familiarity with Otto the Great, or Otto I, and with his son Otto II, as well as with Adelaide Augusta, the wife of the former. She employed him to restore regular discipline in many monasteries. Syrus recorded the following about Otto the Great in Book II:

> “The great Otto, who at that time governed the state, having learned from the reports of many people about the virtue of so great a man, ardently desired his presence. For although this man possessed the imperial dignity, he nevertheless had great devotion toward monasteries, since he did not at all hope to hold the empire successfully unless he took care not to displease the supreme King. And therefore he often groaned when he saw those who had devoted themselves to God through the religious habit proceeding along precipitous paths while intent on secular business. And below: His wife Adelaide clung to him; she was beloved by God and lovable to all, and was so joined to him on the royal throne that she guarded a chaste mind for the heavenly King with every vigilance.”

Syrus adds that Maiolus came to the notice of both of them especially through the report of Heldric, who was prominent among the men of the palace. Hence it happened that Otto summoned Maiolus.

> “He loved him so greatly for his salutary teaching that he wished to entrust to his direction the things subject to him in Italy and Germany. Among these was the monastery of Saint Apollinaris, which is said to lie twenty-four stadia distant from the city of Ravenna. He established it—that is, restored it—on the path of blessed Benedict, and appointed his own abbot there. Moreover, prevailed upon then by the persistent request of the august empress, a woman not to be disregarded, he began to labor at a building near the city of Ticinum.”

I think this occurred in 966, when Maiolus was at Ticinum, according to what was stated above in no. 21. The Ravennate monastery of Saint Apollinaris was called Classe. Odilo writes as follows about the one at Ticinum in Book I of the Life of the Empress Adelaide:

> “Afterward, in Italy, near the city of Ticinum, she began a monastery from its foundations, and completed it in honor of the Savior of the world by imperial authority and through her own most generous donation; and she entrusted it to the aforesaid Maiolus to be regularly ordered.”

Nalgodus interprets the monastery as being “in the Golden Heaven.” We said that it had been founded long before that time by Liutprand in the third century, where we discussed the translation of Saint Augustine and the Life of Saint Appianus. Sigefrid, bishop of Parma, also made use of Maiolus’s services. Through his honey-sweet admonitions, Sigefrid established many things suited to monastic use in the Parmese monastery of Saint John the Evangelist, as we saw above in the Acts of Saint John, the first abbot of that place.

### 34.

At about the same time Maiolus, “when he was about to come to Rome” (as Peter Damian records the matter in Opusculum 33), “ordered a certain brother to go with him, because, as he had been asked, he had decided to appoint him prior in the monastery of Saint Paul. But the man, resisting, raised various obstacles of difficulty and, putting forward now one thing, now another, finally obstinately refused to obey. Maiolus bore the brother’s disobedience with equanimity and, leaving him behind, continued on the journey he had decided upon.

“When the brother had remained in the monastery through disobedience, and the other brothers had vehemently inveighed against him, he finally came to his senses and hastened after Maiolus. Soon he reached a certain river, whose fords the man of God had already crossed and where he was still standing on the farther bank. Since the monk, however, had fixed himself on the nearer bank of the river, having no means of crossing in the absence of a boat, and saw his master standing at a distance, he did the only thing he could: he immediately fell to the ground and humbly prostrated himself. And because, while begging pardon, he perhaps could not make his cry heard through the organ of his mouth, he made his tongue of his entire body.

“When Maiolus saw this from afar, he immediately understood what it meant. He at once sent a boat and had the monk brought across to him; and the man of God immediately asked him why he had come. The other at once begged pardon for his past conduct and promised that in all other matters he would fulfill whatever Maiolus might order. Then Maiolus said: ‘Without doubt, you desire penance.’ When the man replied, ‘I do,’ Maiolus immediately added: ‘Then give this man a kiss.’ For by chance a leper, whose skin was covered with swellings, was standing there. The monk immediately rushed to kiss him, and at once the leprosy completely vanished from the man’s cleansed body.”

Peter Damian draws the following conclusion from this:

> “Thus holy obedience found the fruit of its humility, since he earned pardon by correcting himself. But it also displayed a sign of such a manifest virtue: the man whom pride had almost been able to bring to apostate ruin was enabled by humility to exhibit apostolic virtue.”

### 35.

I return to the discipline restored by Maiolus in the German monasteries as well. None of these is expressly named by Syrus or by others, except that Syrus says, in the letter prefixed to the Life, that Aldebald, sent to Germany, took with him Maiolus’s Life, which Odilo later found in the monastery of Morbach. This is evidence that he had adopted the customs of the monastery of Cluny.

Concerning Paterniacum, which is situated in the diocese of Lausanne, Saint Odilo writes as follows in the Life of Adelaide Augusta:

> “In the place belonging to her father Ruodolf—namely, the most noble king—and to her lord and brother Chuonrad, that is, at Paterniacum, where she entrusted her mother, Queen Berta by name, devoted to God in all humility, to burial, she founded a monastery in honor of the Mother of God and, through her munificence and by the command of her brother, King Chuonrad, permanently entrusted it to the most holy father Maiolus and his successors to be ordered.”

But this concerned a new foundation, not a reform; we shall return to it in the Acts of Saint Odilo.

### 36.

Nowhere, however, was the discipline of Cluny propagated so widely as in the Gallican monasteries, of which Maiolus, as abbot, restored not a few to better condition. Among these the chief were the Major Monastery, the monastery of Saint Germanus at Auxerre, Saint John’s monastery at Réomay, Saint Benignus at Dijon, Saint Maurus at Fosses, and others, some of which have already been discussed in the preceding chapter.

### 37.

What Maiolus accomplished at the Major Monastery near Tours is explained by a fragment in the Cluniac library from the deeds of the abbots of that place, which have been published elsewhere in full. It says that Count Odo, at the suggestion of his wife Hermengarde, obtained “thirteen monks of good life and reputation from Cluny” and substituted them for the secular clerics who were then living at the Major Monastery. From these thirteen, “during the reign of Pope Stephen and King Robert, they chose one as their abbot.”

But the author is mistaken about Pope Stephen, since no pontiff of that name governed the Roman See during the abbacy of Maiolus. Stephen VIII died in 943, and Stephen IX did not become pope until 1057.

The author adds that the pontiff “blessed Count Odo as a monk” and, by the authority of his privilege, freely granted the power to elect an abbot: a power released from Cluny, approved by the authority of King Robert. Maiolus is said at first to have resisted, but finally to have yielded after hearing mention of the privileges.

Although these things may be true, I fear that they cannot all be assigned to Maiolus’s time. On the contrary, Maiolus initially bore the title of abbot in that place, as the charter of the deacon Herlannus shows, and later arranged for Gislebert to be appointed abbot in his place, as we shall say elsewhere. The chronicler of Malleac likewise asserts this: he calls Guitbert the first abbot of the Major Monastery after Maiolus, under the year 994 (Chesne, vol. II, p. 836).

Gerbert’s letter to the abbot of the Major Monastery belongs to this reform. It contains these words:

> “Nature preserves its cycles, and the good earth, long unfruitful not by its own judgment, produces flowers and fruits. For behold, the cell of blessed Martin revives troops of monks that had long since died; Martin’s virtue is recognized in his disciples. Among them we rejoice that we have received Osulf, a foster-child of blessed conduct, as an example of life and morals.”
