In the published editions this letter bears the title: “To Adalbert, archbishop and abbot of the Major Monastery.” But I think it should read: “Adalbero, archbishop,” so that the letter was written by Gerbert in the person of Adalbero, archbishop of Rheims, as were certain other letters.

### 38.

I come to the monastery of Saint Germanus at Auxerre. We read the following in chapter 47 of the History of the Bishops of Auxerre, under Bishop Heribert:

> “During the pontificate of this bishop, Duke Henry, his brother, being a lover of every form of religious devotion, entrusted the monastery of Saint Germanus to Lord Maiolus, the abbot, so that he might establish there the path of the regular rule, just as he was known to have done in many places both in Italy and in Gaul among the monks. For a long time the place had been governed by provosts without an abbot. Maiolus received it gladly and corrected thoroughly, with regular discipline, everything he found to be deviant. Afterward the holy and venerable man Maiolus appointed there the honorable man Heldric as abbot; he too formed that place according to the path of the regular rule of blessed Benedict. The aforesaid bishop and his brother, Duke Henry, together with their people, loved him with very great affection.”

This is how the passage appears in volume I of Labbe’s Library. There the History of the Deeds of the Abbots of Saint Germanus at Auxerre has also been published; its first chapter gives a fuller account and says that Heldric was appointed there “in the year of the Lord 989.”

Heldric “was dear to many nobles because of his holiness and religious fervor.” For his sake “the venerable and God-worthy Duchess Gersendis,” the wife of the aforementioned Duke Henry, “asked her husband and obtained that the monastery of Saint Leodegarius, called Campelli, should be entrusted to him, hoping that through him it could be restored to the norm of regular life.

“That same monastery had been restored by Queen Theodrada [or Theograda], of blessed memory—that is, the daughter of Charles the Great, for it was customary to call the daughters of kings queens—and had been dedicated to the monastic order. But now, because of the demands of sin, for more than two hundred years it had been completely extinguished from the light of this holy purpose.”

A diploma of King Robert survives on this matter in Book VI of *De Re Diplomatica*, p. 578. The identification of the monastery of Saint Leodegarius at Campelli must be corrected there: it is not the Campelli in the diocese of Paris, but another place of the same name in the diocese of Langres, where a priory subject to the aforesaid Saint Germanus still exists.

I omit the many other things concerning Heldric that are found in the aforementioned History of the Abbots of Saint Germanus. His death is said to have occurred after approximately twenty-one years of governance, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of January.

This appears to be the Heldric praised by Syrus in Book II of the following Life, in connection with Otto the Great:

> “He was eminent in secular power and had once been distinguished among the other men of the palace in Italy; renouncing his wife and his great wealth, he laid aside his belt, withdrew to Cluny, and submitted himself to the purpose of blessed Benedict.”

The aforementioned History of the Abbots of Saint Germanus says that, at the time when King Robert was attacking Auxerre, Heldric withdrew with Odilo, the abbot of Cluny, “to another monastery subject to his authority, which is called Réomay.”

The History of Réomay, by Roverius, shows that this monastery obeyed Abbot Maiolus, though not in such a way that it was subject to Cluny in the manner in which that subjection later existed under Hugh.

### 39.

Maiolus is also said to have carried out a similar work in the monastery of Saint Benignus at Dijon, according to the Benignian Chronicle. Bruno, bishop of Langres, wishing to restore the place to a better condition, approached Maiolus for this purpose:

> “Moved by his prayers, the reverend Abbot Maiolus gave him twelve monks trained in the discipline of holy religion, learned in divine and human wisdom, and distinguished by noble birth. He appointed one of them, named William, as abbot, and, when the sons asked him for a spiritual father, he sought one for them.”

But more will be said about him in the Life of Maiolus in the following volume.

### 40.

For the same purpose Maiolus was summoned by Richard, duke of the Normans, to Fécamp, so that he might restore monks there in place of the canons. The holy man refused to undertake this unless Richard remitted to his subjects the tax “called *pasnagium*” (*Benedictine Saeculum*, II, p. 975). Since this did not please the duke, the matter was postponed until the time of the aforementioned Abbot William.

### 41.

But especially notable was the reform of the monastery of Saint Maurus at Fosses, near Paris. It is described at length in the Acts of Count Burchard, which we shall relate in the next volume.

There we read that the condition of this monastery had deteriorated under Abbot Magenard to such a degree that the abbot himself, noble indeed but looser in his way of life, “having put aside monastic garments, adorned himself with coverings of costly furs, and placed an excellent cap of *calamint* on his humble head.” This custom had also come into use in other Gallican monasteries.

Burchard, pitying the condition of the place and urged on by the monk Adico, appealed to King Hugh so that he might be entrusted with the task of restoring discipline there. With the king’s consent Burchard went to Maiolus, who, after considerable reluctance, finally agreed and “having taken the more perfect brothers of his monastery,” went there.

The looser monks were given the choice of remaining with Maiolus’s disciples if they wished to live according to the rule; otherwise, they might depart wherever they wished. Most chose the paths of their own hearts. Abbot Magenard himself, “of noble ancestry”—indeed “of the bloodline of Ansoald, a wealthy citizen of Paris”—was “transferred to the monastery of Saint Maurus, called Glannafolium,” which at that time was subject to Fosses.

Saint Maiolus, “receiving the aforesaid place with his monks, began to observe strictly the strictness of the regular order.”

At his request King Hugh granted the village of Mansiones for the support of the brothers, by a diploma preserved in Book VI of *De Re Diplomatica*, p. 576:

> “On the twelfth day before the Kalends of July, in the second indiction, in the second year of the reign of King Hugh,”

that is, in the year of Christ 989, not an earlier year, as the monk Odo in the Life of Count Burchard and others wrongly interpreted it.

But Maiolus was compelled to return to Cluny, and he entrusted the place to “a certain religious man named Teutonus, whom he had brought with him from Cluny.”

When King Hugh died and Maiolus delayed returning there, his son Robert, “on the advice and urging of the count, gave that same Teutonus the gift of the abbacy and ordered him to be appointed abbot.” When this reached the ears of the Cluniacs, “they became very sad, because they wished to reduce the place itself to a cell for themselves.”

I think that Teutonus was appointed abbot there through Maiolus’s care. For at that time the custom of reducing abbeys to cells was not yet in force among the Cluniacs. Rather, co-abbots were appointed under the abbot of Cluny, except in the smaller monasteries, which were then called “abbeys, cells, and obediences,” and are now called priories. We have discussed this matter more fully in the preface.

In the larger monasteries, however, when the man whom the abbot of Cluny had appointed in his place had ceased to live, the monks of that monastery again had the power to elect their own abbot.

### 42.

Such was the monastery of Fleury. It had been reformed for regular life by Abbot Odo, but afterward suffered various disturbances in the election of an abbot after the death of Oylbold, as I think.

When a certain proud monk had been intruded into the government of the place through faction, all those devoted to piety opposed him in defense of the house of God, especially Gerbert, whose letters on this matter survive in several copies.

One is his ninety-fifth letter, addressed to the brothers of Fleury in the person of the abbots of Rheims:

> “Not without reason do we profess that we belong to one fellowship: we are raised up by your good fortune and humbled, even in the opinion of the most distinguished men, by your misfortune. The ambition and wantonness of certain people, together with their detestable audacity, defile this most holy society and most chaste friendship, when through faction a man is placed over you as father whom the most truthful Fathers would not hesitate to condemn. And just as there is one Catholic Church and one fellowship of all the faithful, we have resolved not to depart from the judgments of those who shine in the Church of the Lord like the brightest stars for everlasting ages. Is not the reverend Father Maiolus a most radiant star? Is not Father Egbert a most brilliant constellation? The former, in a letter which he recently sent to our venerable father Adalbero, archbishop—his judgment concerning the appointment of your father had been sought—says among other things as follows: ‘The man’s character had long been notorious among you for his infamous conduct,’” and so forth.

It is not clear whose this letter was, Maiolus’s or Egbert’s, since both had been consulted. Gerbert’s Letter 88 was written “in the person of Adalbero, archbishop, to Maiolus, abbot of Cluny.” From it one may infer that the letter whose words are reported in Letter 95 was Maiolus’s.

Adalbero blames Maiolus because in this matter he writes differently from the way he acts:

> “‘Your exhortation against the intruder is indeed excellent; but since it is written, ‘The things that Jesus began both to do and to teach,’ why do you put forward different commands and different climates of heaven, so that the man whom you have declared guilty may communicate with others while they do not communicate with him? Therefore detest the intruder. Let him perceive that you do not favor him and do not communicate with him, and that through you not only the religious of your order, but also, if possible, the Roman pontiff, are pressing him with curses.’”

Another letter of Gerbert to Maiolus, Letter 70, has the same purpose:

> “Although you are occupied with vigilant care over your own flock, it is nevertheless a greater act of charity if you sometimes heal the contagion of another flock. An intruder, they say, has seized the chief place in the monastery of Fleury, out of reverence for Father Benedict, among the monks. If you are silent, who will speak? If this is not corrected, what wicked man will not hope for similar things? We say these things out of zeal for divine love, and so that, by our judgment, if he is upright he may be received; if he is wicked, he may be deprived, for the punishment of his condemnation, of the fellowship of all abbots and of the monastic order. Your agreement to this will be most welcome to us through your letters.”

From this letter we understand what we said above: the monastery of Fleury was a flock foreign to Maiolus and therefore was by no means subject to Cluny, although it had been restored to regular life by Saint Odo, who was also abbot there.

### 43.

Who that abbot Egbert, or Evrard, was, to whom Gerbert writes on this same subject as to another star of the monastic order, has not been adequately explained.

Three letters of Gerbert addressed to him survive: Letters 81 and 89 against the intruder at Fleury, and Letter 44 on literary matters. The latter is entitled: “To Egbert, abbot of Tours.” The others read “To Egbert,” and in the margin another reading is given: “Evrard” or “Ebrard.”

As we shall say shortly, these letters were written around the year 987. At that time Bernerius governed the Major Monastery, while Evrard governed the monastery of Saint Julian. I think this is the same man to whom these letters were addressed.

Almost the whole of Letter 89 is devoted to his praise:

> “Your letters have made clear how great is the gravity of your character, how upright your way of life, and how pure your speech. Therefore your zeal for piety and severity moved us to adopt your judgment, and that man is full of God, in whom we have great confidence. We shall therefore remove that faithless man from our fellowship and from the judgment of such great Fathers. He was regarded by us as an enemy because he dared to say what ought not to be said against the judgment of the reverend Father Maiolus and the honored Father Egbert. If, with God’s favor, we obtain the support of the princes, we shall join greater useful measures to these.”

By “the princes” Hugh and Robert, the kings of the Franks, seem to be meant. These disturbances appear to have arisen in the first year of their reign, after the death of Abbot Oylbold.

At that time, when part of the monks of Fleury conspired in favor of Abbo, others “resisted this election with great obstinacy,” as Aimoinus writes in the Life of Saint Abbo.

Certainly, Gerbert’s letters immediately preceding and following these were written after the death of King Lothair, although the chronological order of the letters is not precise.

The intruder rejected by Maiolus and Egbert did not survive long. Gerbert congratulates Constantine, a monk of Fleury, on this matter in Letter 142:

> “We congratulate you, dearest brother, because the intruder and enemy of monastic religion has been removed from human affairs, to the salvation of many. Therefore persevere; and if you already have a father worthy of the love of you and your brothers, let us too, through your efforts, have him present soon at the feast of blessed Remigius.”

These matters had to be set out at greater length, both because they redound to the glory of Maiolus and Egbert and because they shed light on the Acts of Saint Abbo.

### 44.

But now it is time to conclude this chapter on the reform of monasteries carried out by Maiolus by observing what he did near the end of his life for the monastery of Saint Dionysius.

> “At that same time,” says Syrus, “he was pressed by the excessive insistence of the king of the Franks to arrange the monastery of Saint Dionysius according to the teaching of blessed Father Benedict. Although he knew that the end of his days was already very near, he nevertheless did not refuse to set out for this purpose, so that he might bring the good work to completion before the end of his life.”

But he was intercepted by death at Silviniacum during the journey.

From all these things it is clear that what Syrus wrote about Maiolus in Book II is true: that he “restored to its former state the discipline of regular life, which had almost collapsed through the negligence of earlier generations, and throughout various parts of the world subjected many monasteries that had deviated from the regular path to the monastic order, both through himself and through those whom he appointed as abbots”—that is, restored them.

## VI. Maiolus’s Captivity under the Saracens; His Refusal of the Roman Pontificate; Otto II Reconciled with His Mother; His Journeys to Rome

### 45.

At the beginning of Book III Syrus discusses Maiolus’s captivity among the Saracens, who at that time occupied the Pennine Alps, ever since the period when, spreading out from Spain into Italy, they had given assistance to Hugh, king of Italy, against Berengar.

Rudolf Glaber likewise records this about Maiolus in Book I, chapter 4. There he reports Maiolus’s letter to his Cluniac monks concerning his ransom, as well as a twofold event omitted by Syrus and others. The Saracens, “when they had offered him at mealtime the food on which they themselves lived—namely, meat and very coarse bread—and said, ‘Eat,’ he replied: ‘If I become hungry, it is the Lord’s task to feed me; but I will not eat these things, because they have not been useful to me.’

“One of them, seeing the reverence due to the man of God and moved by compassion, uncovered his arms and washed them, and, in the presence of the venerable Maiolus, made bread very cleanly on a shield. Having cooked it very quickly, he reverently brought it to him. Maiolus received it, and after first saying a prayer according to custom, refreshed himself with it and gave thanks to the Lord.”

Another event of the same kind is related:

> “Another of those Saracens, cutting a small chip from a piece of wood with his knife, immediately placed his foot upon the book of the man of God, namely the Bible—indeed, the biblical codex—which he customarily always carried with him. When the holy man saw this, he groaned. Some of the less savage men among them noticed it and rebuked their companion, saying that great prophets ought not to be treated as worthless, so that he should place their words beneath his foot . . . .
>
> “Moreover, so that the holiness of blessed Maiolus might become evident, the man who had trodden on his volume with his foot, on that same day and on some pretext, was attacked in truth by divine judgment by the others, who rushed upon him furiously and cut off that very foot. Many of them then began to be gentler and more reverent toward Maiolus.”

Saint Odilo gives the following brief account of Maiolus’s capture:

> “Among the other evils committed by that most wicked people, they captured the most blessed Father Maiolus, returning from the threshold of the apostles, through fraud and ambush. They stripped him of all his possessions, bound him, and afflicted him with hunger and thirst. But he was divinely released and, finally ransomed with the money of his monastery, escaped unharmed from their hands under the Lord’s protection. His unjust capture became the occasion of their expulsion and perpetual destruction.
>
> “Just as after the passion of Christ the Jews were driven out from their own land, so after the capture of his servant and most faithful minister Maiolus, the Saracens were expelled from the borders of the Christians. And just as through Titus and Vespasian, the Roman rulers, the Lord exercised vengeance upon the Jews, so through William, a most illustrious man and most Christian prince, by the merits of blessed Maiolus, he removed the Saracen yoke from the shoulders of the Christians and by his powerful strength snatched from their tyrannical rule many stretches of land that they had unjustly possessed.”

These events occurred around the year 973.

### 45*.

> “Not long afterward,” says Syrus, “when the Roman See had been deprived of its own shepherd, that same servant of God, summoned by the combined request of Otto II and his mother, was compelled to return to Italy from the regions of Gaul. Received by mother and son with the highest honor, he began to be urged by repeated entreaties to accept the summit of apostolic dignity. But for one to whom abasement was more desirable than elevation, the ambition of high office could in no way advance itself.”

He therefore consistently refused this dignity. Nalgodus says that this occurred “when the ship of the Church, deprived of the protection of its helmsman, was buffeted by various troubles amid the uncertainty of this fluctuating life.”

Henschenius, who considered Nalgodus a disciple of Maiolus, referred this to the time when Pope Benedict VI was thrown into prison in 974 and strangled there by a certain Franko, a wicked man who tyrannically invaded the See under the name of Boniface VII.

After he had been driven out to Constantinople, Donus, the successor of Benedict VI according to Henschenius—but the predecessor, as others hold—was canonically installed and died around the end of October 975. When the supporters of Boniface were trying to restore the antipope, and Otto was appealed to by the Romans to preserve their freedom of election, Otto may have summoned Maiolus to Germany, intending to consult him about an affair of such importance before sending his legates to Rome to be present at the election.

But Maiolus was summoned not to Germany but to Italy, as Syrus testifies. Otto did not go there until after his father’s death, and not before the year 980. Nor, during the entire three-year period in which the emperor remained in Italy—up to the year 983, which was the last year of his life—was the Roman See vacant, since John did not die until the following year.

I would therefore readily grant that Syrus, having suffered a lapse of memory at this point, wrote “Italy” instead of “Germany.” In reality, Maiolus visited Otto II in Germany when Otto was staying there with his mother. Yet neither mother nor son could ever persuade him to accept the pontificate offered amid those disturbances.

### 46.

Syrus adds that “at the same time” Otto II became angry with his most pious mother Adelaide, “as though she were a squanderer of the commonwealth.” Although all the princes clearly recognized the innocence of Augusta, none dared “to remove the accusation from the holy mother.”

Maiolus was then summoned by them to Pavia for this very purpose, and through his speech he persuaded Otto to be reconciled with his mother.

Odilo writes that Maiolus was invited by Otto himself in his Life of Adelaide, where he says that she, “loving her son and unable to bear the authors of the discord which certain wicked men were spreading between mother and son, in accordance with the Apostle’s command, giving place for a little while to anger, decided to seek her father’s kingdom. There she was received kindly and honorably by her brother Chuonrad and his most noble wife Mathilda,” who ruled in Provence.

“Germany grieved over her absence; all Burgundy rejoiced at her arrival; Lyon, once the mother and nurse of philosophy, exulted, as did Vienna, the noble royal seat.

“Afterward Caesar Otto, moved by repentance, sent an embassy to his uncle the king and, with the greatest haste, to Maiolus, father of holy memory. He earnestly begged that through their intervention he might merit the favor of his mother, which he had lost through his own faults. He repeatedly prayed and entreated them to hasten, together with Augusta his mother, to meet him at Pavia.

“Having made use of the counsel of such men, the mother met her son at the appointed time in Pavia. When they saw one another, they fell to the ground, weeping and shedding tears with their whole bodies, and began humbly to greet one another. In the son there was humble repentance; in the mother there was generous forgiveness. Thereafter the bond of perpetual peace remained between them both.”

The Saxon, or Magdeburg, manuscript annals place Otto’s discord with his mother in the year 978:

> “The Empress Adelaide went to Italy with her daughter Adelaide, the abbess, because of certain disagreements that had arisen between herself and her son.”

But Adelaide withdrew not to Italy but to Provence, according to Odilo, who was familiar with Adelaide. Since the reconciliation took place at Pavia, it must be assigned to the year 980, when Otto went to Italy.

Indeed, Otto celebrated Easter at Rome in the following year in the presence of his mother, according to the manuscript Saxon Annals. The same Odilo says that Otto died shortly after the reconciliation.

### 47.

To make what we have said about Maiolus in this and other chapters clearer, I think it worthwhile to distinguish his various journeys to Rome and Italy.

First, while still a monk, he was sent to Rome by Abbot Aymard for business, around the year 945, according to what was said in no. 17.

Then, already an abbot, he was at Pavia in 966, when a certain chapel near that city was granted to him for the construction of a cell, as stated above in no. 21.

Syrus records two miracles performed by him at Pavia in Book III, chapters 13 and 16. Add to these what Widric, abbot of Toul, records in the Acts of Saint Gerard, bishop, concerning the mutual sight and conversation of Gerard and Maiolus.

Gerard, setting out for Rome, “entered Pavia, where he rejoiced beyond words to find magnificent men: namely, the holy abbot Maiolus and Adalbert, later a martyr. Each hung upon the other’s words. After spending a long time in mutual conversation, the three holy guests sat down together to dine.”

When Gerard asked for water and refused to accept wine made from water by heaven, Maiolus said:

> “Cease, holy bishop, to be angry with others in this matter; but receive with thanksgiving what the Creator of all things has bestowed upon you by his blessing.”

This appears to refer to Maiolus’s second journey to Rome, that is, to the year 966, which was the third year of Gerard’s episcopal ordination.

After this, that is, in 973, when Maiolus was returning from Rome, he foretold the death of Otto the Great, as related in chapter 10. This was at least his third Italian pilgrimage, during which he was captured by the Saracens on his return.

His fourth journey took place around the year 982. While at Verona, he foretold the death of Otto II.

Syrus explains his devotion in visiting the basilicas of the saints at Rome in Book II.

## VII. Odilo’s Substitution for Maiolus as Abbot; Maiolus’s Death, Cult, and Relics
48. When Maiolus, already advanced in age, sensed his approaching death, he arranged for Odilo to be substituted for him in the same manner in which Odo had been substituted for the still-living Berno, Aymard for Odo, and Maiolus himself for Aymard. Syrus, Odilo, Nalgodus, and others pass over this in silence; indeed, according to Nalgodus, Maiolus is said to have left Cluny “without the care of a shepherd, without the diligence of a steward.” Nevertheless, that Odilo’s election took place while Maiolus was still alive is demonstrated not only by the document of the election itself [Col. 0737A], but also by ancient charters that designate Odilo as abbot before Maiolus’ death. The instrument of election was published in volume VI of the *Spicilegium*, p. 425, and was drawn up in the same words as the charter concerning Maiolus’ own election, which we reproduced above in its proper place. It is therefore sufficient to report only the concluding words found in Odilo’s instrument of election, together with the subscriptions:

“We order that the sequence of this election and his ordination be confirmed in writing by the counsel, as we have said, of the leading men, and also of our count and advocate, Duke Henry, as well as of Otto; and we have confirmed in the name of Christ the ordination duly celebrated, and have asked that it be confirmed in writing by our Fathers and brothers. Done happily in the monastery of Cluny. Amen.

“I, Maiolus, abbot, have given my assent to this election and have subscribed; Rodulfus, king, subscribed; Burchardus, archbishop [of Lyon], subscribed; Hugo, bishop of Geneva, subscribed; Aynricus, bishop of Lausanne, subscribed; Hugo, bishop [of Mâcon]; Teuto, abbot [of Fossat], subscribed; Richfredus, abbot; Ermenfredus, bishop; Burchardus, count; Lambertus, count; Adalbertus, count; Leotaldus, archbishop; Walterius, bishop [of Autun]; Hugo, abbot; Wago, abbot; Theobaldus, abbot; Warembertus, abbot; Willelmus, abbot; Maiolus, provost; Walterius, provost; Gundulfus, David, Aynricus, Sendelenus”—and with them 177 monks.

49. Perhaps some will wonder why so many ecclesiastical and secular men attended this election [Col. 0737C], and indeed the elections of Odo, Aymard, and Maiolus himself. Yet that custom prevailed in certain places at the election of abbots, and it arose from chapter 64 of the Rule of Saint Benedict, where, in discussing the appointment of an abbot, the Rule admits neighboring bishops, abbots, and Christians as witnesses against the election of an unworthy abbot. Whether these or those persons were summoned lay within the power of the electors; sometimes the practice was also introduced by right of the founders. Thus Pope Gregory VII, at the request of Countess Adelheid, decreed and established that the election of the abbot of Saint Mary of Pinerolo should be attended by the abbots of Fruttuaria, Bremet, Saint Solutor of Turin, Chiusi, and other religious men of those regions; this is recorded by Guichenon in volume I of *The Princes of Savoy*, p. 17. Likewise, in the election of the abbot of Lezat, noblemen of the region formerly had a place, as is clear from ancient records [Col. 0737D].

50. As for the fact that the abbots of Cluny were initially accustomed to choose their own successor, this undoubtedly arose from the desire by that means to block the way for outsiders to impose an abbot. The abbot-elect, as observed above, acted as a coadjutor, but took care only of those matters entrusted to him by the surviving abbot. For the Council of Chalon had decreed as follows, around the year 650, in chapter 12:

“Two abbots ought not to be in one monastery, lest, under the pretext of authority, rivalry and scandals arise among the monks. Nevertheless, if any abbot should choose a successor for himself, the man who is chosen shall have no authority to administer the resources of that monastery.”

Thus it often happened that public acts were drawn up in the name of the earlier abbot; sometimes, however, they were drawn up in the name of the later one, as we noted in Aymard’s eulogy.

51. The instrument cited above does not state when Odilo’s election was celebrated; but from charters bearing his name we understand that it took place in the year 991. He therefore entered religious life before that year, although Hugo of Flavigny places it in that very year in his *Chronicle*, and postpones his ordination until 994, as does the *Chronicle of Cluny*—that is, after Maiolus’ death.

The first charter to be considered is that of Humbert, bishop of Grenoble, who gave to the monastery of Cluny “where, as he says, Lord Odilo presides as abbot,” half of the castle of Ursilia, together with the entire borough and the church of Saint Mary, as well as other gifts, “in the year of the Incarnation 991, the third year of King Rodulf.” This charter is subscribed by “Fredeburgis, his mother; Wigo, his brother; and Humbert, bishop of Valence, his nephew.”

Elsewhere, in the sixth year of King Hugh, Abbot Maiolus acquired by exchange certain churches in the county of Autun. A charter of Walter, bishop of Autun, issued in that same year, does not state the abbot’s name. In it he grants to “the monastery of Cluny, joined to him by a special love surpassing that shown to others, where religion flourishes,” whatever belonged to him or to the archdeacons in the churches of his diocese assigned to Cluny, except the synodal offerings. The subscriptions are those of Elinardus, abbot, and, after the provosts and the cantor, Erpertus, abbot, and Ugo, abbot—perhaps these were offices [Col. 0738C]—followed by archpriests and canons.

In the following year, that is, the seventh year of King Hugh, there is a charter in which Bernard, a nobleman, emancipates several slaves “at the request of Vivianus, provost of the monastery of Cluny, and the monks.” He is said to have “renounced that complaint against the aforesaid place of Cluny, over which Lord and most reverend Father Odilo presides by the command of the most holy Father Maiolus.” Likewise, “in the seventh year of King Hugh,” the church of Saint Desiderius was granted to Abbot Maiolus; and in that same year a certain cleric named Beraldus gave the Cluniac monks—“where Maiolus is abbot”—half of the forest of Adrolt. These are the last acts bearing Maiolus’ name in the seventh year of King Hugh, which ended in the year of Christ 994, the final year of Maiolus’ life.

52. This is relevant to what Syrus writes about Maiolus: “Two years before he died, he entirely withdrew from public affairs and confined himself either in the monastery or in some small cell, so that there he might either correct the brothers with diligent care and advance them toward better things by paternal admonition, or, more often, when everyone else had been dismissed, cling alone to God alone and devote himself, in frequent alternation, either to reading or to prayer.”

During that period the event occurred that Widricus, abbot of Toul, reports in the *Acts of Saint Gerard, Bishop*. Gerard died in the same year as Maiolus, on April 23:

“At that same time blessed Maiolus was at Cluny; and at the hour when the venerable shepherd was being taken from this world, after the brothers had completed the divine office, the time for refreshment had arrived. Maiolus himself, calling the brothers to eat, sounded the monastic cymbal.”

Then, having learned by divine revelation of Gerard’s death, he announced it to the brothers and commended Gerard’s soul to them, as we related above in the account of Gerard.

53. Although Maiolus had resolved in his mind to withdraw completely from public affairs, he was nevertheless asked by Hugh, king of the Franks, to reform regular discipline in the monastery of Saint-Denis at Paris. “Although he knew that the end of his days was already very near,” he set out through the territory of Auvergne. “There, in one of his small cells—at Silviniacum [Souvigny], now a place of great renown—he began to be afflicted by his final illness, and at last he fell asleep with the Fathers on the fifth day before the Ides of May. He was buried in the basilica of Saint Peter, where, through his most holy merits, many benefits are bestowed.”

Saint Odilo writes of this:

“Blessed Maiolus was so magnified and glorified, by the grace of the Lord going before him, in the presence of kings and princes and before all the people, that we may undoubtedly say of him what the discourse of Ecclesiasticus repeats concerning Moses, the servant of God: ‘He glorified him in the sight of kings and showed him his glory.’ Hugh, king of the Franks, whenever he saw him, received him with humble devotion and treated him with great honor. At the time of his calling, he asked him to come to him with the intention that the monastery of Saint-Denis might, by his counsel and assistance, be put in better order than it then was. . . . To carry out that undertaking, he gladly set out and reached the place of Silviniacum, where, called by God, full of days and holiness, he departed this life on the fifth day before the Ides of May, as Friday was dawning, after the celebration of that most sacred solemnity on which Christ Jesus our Lord, having subdued the prince of death, ascended to the right hand of the Father and showed his faithful Maiolus the path by which he too would ascend after him.”

All this corresponds to the year of Christ 994, when Easter fell on April 1 under the Dominical Letter G, and the Friday after the Lord’s Ascension fell on May 11. Nalgodus explicitly gives this day and year, assigning Maiolus forty-one years of governance from the year of his ordination. Lambert of Schafnaburg is therefore mistaken when he places Maiolus’ death in the year 991.

54. Odilo continues:

“After his passing, the aforesaid King Hugh honored his funeral and tomb by the presence of his arrival and by royal gifts. At that tomb, by the Lord’s favor, many miracles have been performed and are still performed, and very many benefits have been granted and continue to be granted to very many people. The number and greatness of these things exceed the capacity of the memory of all our people to recount in order. But to make the briefest possible conclusion: at the tomb of this most holy man of whom we speak, whose life and merits we strive to commend to the charity of the faithful, many sick people have been healed and are healed by the grace and mercy of Christ, whatever illness has afflicted them. There the paralytic and the lame are raised up; there those suffering from fever are healed, as are the blind; there those possessed by demons are cleansed, and those terribly and miserably burned by some unknown kind of fire are delivered. Whoever comes there devoutly and faithfully seeks help in whatever necessity returns home safe and joyful, having obtained what he desired.”

Rodulfus Glaber writes similarly in book III, chapter 5:

“For the fame of his holiness brought together from throughout the Roman world very many men and women of both orders, who thereafter returned giving thanks for the healing of various illnesses. At that same time a dreadful plague raged among human beings, namely a hidden fire which, wherever it seized any part of the body, severed it from the body by burning it away. The burning of this fire consumed many people even within the space of a single night. But although remedies for this fearful disease were found at many memorials of the saints, the greatest crowd nevertheless gathered at the churches of three holy confessors: Martin of Tours, Odulric of Bavaria, and this venerable Father Maiolus. Remedies for the desired health were found there.”

That this abundance of miracles continued until the time of Peter the Venerable is attested by Peter himself in book II, chapter 31 of *On Miracles*, where he relates the raising from the dead of a boy by Saint Maiolus:

“This saint,” he says, “as is known to nearly all the peoples of Gaul, was great in life and likewise distinguished for miracles, both while he lived as a mortal and especially after death. Through this grace of miracles he has now shone for 162 years—that is, from the time of his death—to such an extent that, after the holy Mother of God, no saint throughout our Europe has an equal to him in works of this kind.”

Nor were blessed Maiolus’ miracles absent in later times; Pope Clement IV, Honorius IV, and Clement VI bear witness to them in their bulls.

55. Hence it came about that Maiolus was regarded and venerated as a saint immediately after his own death. Thus, according to Odilo’s testimony, the Empress Adelheid, “at the very time when her final day was approaching—that is, in the year 1000—visited the most blessed Father Benedict, namely the monastery of Fleury, with gifts that were modest but her own; and likewise [she visited] Father Maiolus of blessed memory, already crowned with heavenly glory, whom, while he remained in this life, she loved above all mortals in that degree.”

That he was called a saint from the time of his death is indeed proved by charter 145 in his cartulary, which reads:

“I, Arleis, give to God and Saint Maiolus, so that through his merits I may be able to attain eternal rewards, and to his monks a portion of Medio-Planto in the county of Mâcon, in the village of Maziacum, at the place called Triblada, in the sixth year of King Rotbert.”

His feast is counted among the principal solemnities of the year by Udalricus in book I of the *Customs of Cluny*, chapter 11. In chapter 54 he says that a church of Saint Maiolus then existed at Cluny and that a procession was accustomed to be made to it on Palm Sunday. The commemoration of Saint Maiolus is found in most calendars written from the year 1000 onward, and likewise in more recent Roman, Gallican, Benedictine, and other martyrologies.

56. The body of Saint Maiolus was not raised from the tomb immediately after he had deserved to be honored as a saint. First, however, an altar was erected over it by Beggo, bishop of Auvergne; this was once the customary rite by which saints were enrolled in the canon, as was observed in the preface. Read at the end of this eulogy what we shall report concerning the consecration of that altar.

Nearly a hundred years later the sacred body was taken from the tomb. I find Urban II to be the source for this event. Archbishop Joellus of Reims records the pope’s letter in the Cluniac library, column 309, where the pontiff addresses the monks of Silviniacum:

“Since, by the manifold condescension of heavenly blessing, it has come about that we ourselves have deserved to transfer your monastery and the body of blessed Maiolus within the church to another place, we have deemed it fitting—both because of the special affection with which you adhere to the monastery of Cluny, as members uniquely attached to the head, and because of the reverence of your religious life—to fortify you and your place more particularly under the protection of the Apostolic See. . . . Given at Monticulum, . . . on the Ides of October, indiction 3, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1097.”

There follows a bull of Clement IV, which says:

“Since, as we have learned from your representation, because of the glorious merits of the holy confessors Maiolus and Odilo, whose bodies rest in your church, God works many wondrous miracles daily among his saints there, and because of these miracles a multitude of the faithful comes to that same church from various regions, you intend to transfer the body of the aforesaid Saint Maiolus, with due veneration, to another place in that church which is more venerable and suitable; we . . . grant to all truly penitent and confessed persons who come to the said church on the day of the translation of that saint, on this occasion, one year and forty days [of remission]; and to those who come reverently and devoutly within the eight immediately following days and on the anniversary of his translation, we remit one hundred days of the penances imposed upon them. Given at Viterbo on the day before the Ides of March, in the third year of our pontificate”—that is, in the year 1266.

Honorius IV and Clement VI granted other indulgences there. The tomb of Saint Maiolus, adjoining that of Saint Odilo, is seen in the nave of the church at Silviniacum.

57. To this day the relics of Saint Maiolus are preserved at Silviniacum: namely, his principal bones in a chest of silver and copper, placed above his altar in the northern gallery; the shrine of Saint Odilo stands on the other side, and the head of each is kept in a separate shrine. Saint Maiolus’ scapular, one cubit long and one-third of a cubit wide, has a similar counterpart at Cluny. Also visible at Silviniacum are the upper part of the saint’s pastoral staff, made of ivory, and a horn cup. Gaufridus Choleti, prior in the fifteenth century, made reliquaries that had been begun before him by Ildricus, subprior and sacristan. Thus far Silviniacum has remained famous for its religious devotion and the cult of Maiolus; we discussed it in the eulogies of Odo and Aymard.

VIII. Maiolus’ principal disciples, devotees, and miracles

58. Although we have mentioned some of Maiolus’ disciples above, his principal disciples should nevertheless be gathered together here in one place, so that the merit of the teacher may be understood from the character of his disciples [Col. 0742A]. Two among them were especially distinguished: Odilo and Willelmus. The former succeeded Maiolus; the latter was abbot of Dijon and restored many monasteries to a better way of life.

Odilo, writing about him in his little book on the deeds of Saint Maiolus, says:

“And, if I may speak with the peace of the spiritual craftsmen laboring in the same heavenly workshop, one man shone forth especially—he who recently departed from human affairs and who labored more than all of us, namely Lord Abbot Willelmus. Concerning his most illustrious deeds, his praiseworthy life, and his admirable manner of life, our smallness is not sufficient to report fully what it perceives.”

We shall discuss both him and Odilo himself in the following century. We must also add Teuto, abbot of Fossat, and Heldricus of Auxerre, whom we have already praised. Many remarkable things are recalled about Teuto in the little book on the life of Count Burchard. Among other things:

“Teuto, a religious abbot, is said to have been constantly devoted to fasts and prayers and to keeping vigils through the night, and always faithfully to have desired to please God. Since, in the place entrusted to him, he could not preserve the arduous life he desired because of the demands of pastoral care, he chose a district of the city of Reims in which to live. There was there a small estate that the glorious King Charles the Bald had given to the church of Fossat and to Abbot Godfrey as a place of refuge because of the persecution of the Normans; it is also said that the body of Saint Maurus was preserved there for many years. The aforesaid abbot therefore spent a long time there, living an arduous life for Christ. When he went there and desired to remain there, he sent the staff of pastoral care to the brothers through a minister of his service named Walter, whom he himself had raised in the fear of the Lord, instructing them to choose for themselves, according to Christ’s will, a pastor worthy of the office.”

After Teuto had led an arduous and solitary life in that place, he decided to revisit the Fossat monastery. But they opposed him, arguing that, since another abbot had been installed, “he ought no longer to be received, because he had entirely abandoned the care of souls.” Disturbed by this reply, he withdrew to Cluny, where “he happily died on the day before the Ides of September; at whose tomb, as we have heard reported,” says the author, “many sick people afterward recovered their health.”

Abbot Heldricus was discussed above in chapter 7. Among Maiolus’ disciples we must also count many other abbots whom he trained to reform various monasteries. One of them seems to me to have been Egbertus, or Evrardus, that abbot of Tours whom we praised above on the authority of Gerbertus.

Nor should Syrus and Aldebaldus be omitted, the writers of the *Life of Saint Maiolus*, nor Vivianus, who was provost of Cluny under Maiolus after Hildebrandus, and for whom Maiolus was the chief influence in bidding farewell to the world.

Finally, among the foremost should be numbered Willelmus, duke of Provence, called “father of his country.” Of him Odilo writes in the *Life of Saint Maiolus*:

“How greatly Willelmus, governor of Provence, honored him is shown by his life and death. Through Maiolus’ merit and faithful service, Willelmus deserved to receive the habit of blessed Benedict.”

I do not know whether this occurred during that final illness which Syrus recalls in book III. The charter of Leodegarius, a Cluniac monk, does not state with sufficient clarity that this Willelmus was buried at Cluny. It says that he built a cell and church in honor of Saint Marcellinus, pope and martyr, and Saint Saturninus, which Regimbaldus, archbishop of Arles, dedicated, in the village of Sarrianis:

“Willelmus, once duke of Provence and father of his country, while still alive, assigned it to the monastery of Cluny, dedicated to the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and to the place where he asked to be buried, and to blessed Maiolus, who was still living in the flesh; and, when dying, he bestowed and granted it.”

This suggests that, at the point of death, he received the monastic habit according to the custom of those times.

59. Near the end of his little book on Maiolus’ deeds, Odilo praises many Catholic and honorable clerics, religious monks, and reverend abbots who venerated him; saints and wise men who “treated him as a most holy brother”; emperors and empresses, kings and princes of the world, by whom “he was called elder and lord”; and pontiffs of the Apostolic See, by whom “he was honored as the leader of monastic religion.”

He then adds:

“That divine Caesar and great Otto loved him with all his heart; and the wife of that same Caesar, the divine Empress Adelheid Augusta, loved him with the purest charity and dearest devotion. Their son, the Emperor Otto, loved him with humble devotion; so did Conradus, the noble and peaceful brother of the aforesaid empress, and his most noble wife Mathildis, with affection and a no less similar devotion. The more frequently they saw his face, the more they grew in love for him.

“What shall I say of the most noble man Henry, duke of Burgundy? What of Lambertus, a most illustrious and noble count? What of Willelmus? What of Richard, the strongest duke of the Aquitanians and Normans? What of the Italian princes and marquises?

“How greatly Willelmus, governor of Provence, honored him is shown by his life and death. Through Maiolus’ merit and faithful service, he deserved to receive the habit of blessed Benedict.

“Archenbaldus too, the most faithful steward of Silviniacum, the most illustrious among his own people, father of the neighboring region, and strongest protector of the poor—how greatly and in what manner he was devoted to blessed Maiolus is proclaimed in many ways by the aforesaid place, which he adorned and ennobled both before and after Maiolus’ passing with buildings, wealth, and various kinds of ornaments, so that it would have been fitting had one of the kings done such a thing. But this man who now survives, heir to his honor and name, treats that place well and causes no harm to its inhabitants.”

60. A few words remain to be said about the two books of miracles that Henschenius presents in the appendix to the Cluniac Library. These books record cures of the possessed, the blind, the crippled, the mute, the maimed, the insane, and those afflicted by the sacred fire.

I report only two events here. The first contains the erection of an altar at the head of Saint Maiolus, which was the first step toward his canonization:

“After, therefore, the body of blessed Maiolus had first been buried with the greatest honor and reverence, and an altar had been constructed at his most holy head, the brothers serving God there found the following common and salutary course of action. They sent to the bishop in whose diocese the place lay, asking him to consecrate that altar. Accordingly, Lord Beggo, bishop of the see of Auvergne, came and consecrated that altar with great reverence.”

This Beggo presided over Auvergne while Hugh was reigning among the Franks. The author then adds the healing of a cripple and two madmen. On the following day, a certain boy from Cavannis [Chevines], a village in the county of Mâcon, suffering from a severe wasting condition [the Latin is corrupt: *magnum habens aridam*], was restored.

61. “We shall add another miracle, for which we call not only the common people as witnesses, but also King Hugh himself, Count Burchardus, and his son, Lord Rainaldus, bishop of Paris. This king, coming to seek the aid of Saint Maiolus, deserved to find some slight relief from the severity of his illness. One day, after completing the customary prayers, he was leaving the church when he heard that a certain blind man had been given sight in that very place. He ordered the man to be brought to him, so that he might learn the truth from him.

“When he had learned with certainty that such a miracle had been performed upon the poor man, he—being a man of great gentleness—shed streams of flowing tears for joy, together with the persons mentioned above. Thus, with a great crowd of people, praising God and venerating Saint Maiolus, the man who had received sight returned home, while the magnificent king, more joyful, set out on the road to France.”

62. This is followed by a miracle concerning another blind man who had been born in the “forest of Enguilinum,” where “there is a church of Saint Arnulf.” This is to be understood as the church of Saint Arnulf in the Aquiline Forest [Forest of Iveline], in the diocese of Paris.

There follows the healing of Vivianus—who was one “of the brothers of the monastery of Cluny,” although I do not know whether he was the provost mentioned above—who suffered from an articular disease, and shortly afterward the healing of Bernard, a cleric of Chartres, who suffered from paralysis.

This is sufficient concerning the miracles. Let us hear Syrus, whose work, in a manuscript of the collegiate church of Saint Martial of Limoges, from which our Peter Trelius extracted it, bears the following inscription:

[Col. 0745]

THE LIFE OF SAINT MAIOLUS, BY SYRUS THE MONK

LETTER OF LORD SYRUS ADDRESSED TO LORD ODILO, ABBOT

[Col. 0745A] To the spiritual Father, Lord Odilo, abbot, Syrus, the least of the monks, [sends] whatever is most blessed in Christ.

Although I had often and at length hesitated to pursue the venerable deeds of blessed Maiolus in writing, because the persistent request of Warnerius, of blessed memory, pressed me insistently toward this work, many considerations presented themselves that deterred me with no little fear from attempting it.

For that man whose life was being requested for publication was such an imitator of those who pursue virtue that he was tireless in practicing every virtue. Hence it is impossible for anyone to arrange his deeds without conjecturing all his virtues. Yet no one can discuss virtues correctly if he has been empty of them, since a mind that lacks understanding cannot learn through knowledge.

For these reasons I hesitated to undertake what I considered myself unworthy of by any virtue [Col. 0745B]. Finally, the greatness of the subject and the difficulty of the labor moved me again: while my mind contemplated the many deeds of miracles and virtues and examined its own knowledge, terrified by the judgment of truth it did not dare begin what, because of the smallness of its talent, it despaired of completing. Moreover, I feared, not without reason, that I might be charged with rashness if I boldly presumed to undertake what I knew ought to be entrusted to men more perceptive or more gifted than I.

But although this preface, which I knew about myself, might often be advanced as an excuse, he . . . [lacuna] At that same time, it pleased him to send me to Italy and him to you in Alsace; and he carried with him the unfinished work that I was leaving behind, scattered across separate sheets. After his lamentable passing, when it had been presented to your presence in the monastery of Murbach, I was instructed, according to your judgment, to strive to add what was lacking and to correct by rereading whatever had been corrupted through the fault of the copyists, restoring it to its former condition.

Beginning this task, I strove to complete it as best I could in obedience to your command; would that I had obeyed your authority as effectively as I did willingly, and as I ought. Therefore . . . [lacuna] presumption against me . . . [lacuna]

HERE BEGINS THE LIFE

[Col. 0745]

BOOK ONE

[Col. 0745C] I. The praiseworthy power and wisdom of our God, which wonderfully orders the successive times of ages and generations according to the dispensation of the centuries, leaves no period empty of his goodness. Therefore, through the water of salvation and regeneration, he numbers the faithful of his holy Church among the number of sons; he continually strengthens them by the good example of both earlier and present fathers, and suggests that they remain vigilant in seeking the joys of the eternal inheritance.

In this final period of the age, divine mercy brought forth for the world the true and most faithful servant of God, blessed Maiolus. Born of illustrious ancestry, he was begotten by splendid parents from the town of Avennicum [Avignon], a Provençal by origin and renowned among the noble Gauls for his nobility. From the earliest beginnings of infancy he was devoted to literary studies; and, through the providence of heavenly clemency, he shone forth in the house of the Lord like a bright and burning lamp, so that of him one may say the Mosaic words: “I know you by name.”

II. Maiolus praised according to his name.—For Maiolus, as we may rejoice with a pleasing interpreter, seems to mean “great eye.” In accordance with an apt foreknowledge of future events, that pillar of truth and justice was given such a name, since across the fourfold expanses of the earth he extended far and wide the lights of his blessedness.

Because of the works of the life divinely foreknown and appointed for him, it was fitting that he should bear such a name—one that would cause the good fragrance of Christ to waft in the hearts of the faithful in memory of him, so that, according to the Apostle’s testimony, those who wished to imitate the traces of his life and conduct might deserve to become “the good fragrance of Christ.”

For this most blessed Father Maiolus remained, and remains, the good fragrance of Christ in those who are perishing and in those who are being saved, through the fruits of his holiness and piety poured forth in abundance. His sanctified incense, according to the *Song of Songs*, drew after him many, countless in number, who, inflamed by zeal for holiness and fervent with the fire of perfection, cast off the wrinkles of their aged bodies and sloth and rushed into the strength of youth. By the work of monastic perfection they beat the drum of what Saint Father Benedict taught by divine instruction, so that, laying aside the burden of superfluous curiosity, they might fly on the wings of faith and freedom to the heavens.

III. As a boy he displays examples of virtue.—Indeed, this most blessed and beloved Maiolus, anticipated by a divine gift, foretold by his name what paths of praise and virtue he would follow. Even in childhood he displayed, as it were, a certain blameless beauty of more mature age. Knowingly ignorant, he devoted the beginnings of his life to heavenly discipleship; wisely unlearned, he acquired for himself the dignity of a master during the newness of his days.

Thus heavenly mercy, fitting him to itself at that stage of life in preparation for the privilege of his future election, wished him to be subjected to scholarly disciplines, through whom the overflowing treasure of divine generosity would afterward be fully opened to the world [Col. 0747B]. With the Redeemer’s goodness assisting, many too would be improved who enjoyed the praiseworthy kindness of his holiness.

Adorned, then, with manifold gifts of virtue, blessed Father Maiolus, praiseworthy in life and works, made the tender immaturity of his childhood perfect through the firmness of a more mature spirit. At the beginning of his paths, his companions foretold that he would not in the future lack a certain mastery of magnificence; and, insofar as they could discern, they raised him up with great favor and praise.

IV. He comes to Mâcon and lives chastely there as a canon.—As time passed and childhood came to an end, when adolescence was already claiming him, his parents having been taken away by human fate and his paternal estates having been reduced to desolation by barbarian invasion, divine providence compelled him to leave his native soil and seek the regions of Burgundy.

Coming to the city of Mâcon, he was received as a guest by one of his relatives, who, among the other nobles of that city, bore the distinction of nobility. After he had remained for some time in his lodging, supported by his assistance, he came to the attention of the bishop of that city. Seeing that he possessed a liberal intellect, the bishop sought to attach him to the college of canons. He also urged him privately, with the greatest insistence, to preserve his virginity and, as a chosen vessel, to become worthy of God in the Church.

But the Son of the Virgin had long since breathed into his breast a love of chastity, so that he could not endure to be separated from its contemplation even for a moment. From tender youth he had drunk in the sweetness of the Lord; therefore the radiance of purity had grown incandescent in him, and generous grace had enriched the child’s heart with twin gifts. What is usually pleasing and sufficient for two, it had bestowed in overflowing measure upon one.

V. At Lyon he devotes himself to learning.—At that time a certain Antonius flourished at Lyon, endowed with good character and sufficiently learned in philosophy; virtue and religion had placed him in charge of the monastery of Île-Barbe. When the man of God learned this through the report of others, and since he burned with an excessive desire to learn, he went to Lyon and entrusted himself to Antonius’ instruction. Under his guidance he advanced greatly, not only in learning but also in character and life.

At that time the aforesaid city surpassed all those near it both in the religion of virtue and in the study of the liberal arts. Wisdom—wisdom that ought to be sought for its own sake—had been offended by the shameful profits of certain people, by the undisciplined life of many, and finally by the dishonorable laziness of all who sought it only half-heartedly. Because of the intervening scarcity of teachers and the collapse of the studies of earlier generations, wisdom, mortally hating this region of ours, established for some time at Lyon its familiar seat.

There, expertise in what are called the liberal disciplines—disciplines that are said to proceed in an ordered course at this time, though this is merely a tale—grew so strong that, insofar as schools were concerned, the city was called a public academy for the world on this side of the sea. And, so that I may appear to offer some rationale, we gather this from the following evidence: whoever was seized by a desire to profess the arts was not permitted to be enrolled among the professors until, after being carefully examined here, he had departed approved.

The satirist also supports this point. To make the matter clear by the circumstances of an example, in the first book of his work, after attacking the immoral for a long time and with severity, he says that they grow pale from conscience at the crimes they have repeatedly committed,
As a rhetorician about to speak at the altar of Lyons [Note: [Col. 0747D] Strabo, in Book IV of his *Geography*, after discussing the temple erected there by the Gauls to Augustus, says that there was also an altar with an inscription naming sixty peoples, as Henschenius notes.].

In that city, then, as we have said, while listening to philosophers and ecclesiastical men, by the inspiration of divine grace he surpassed all his rivals in wisdom. The eloquence of his speech was then joined to the dignity of wisdom. From the substance of this combination he began to be a vessel of election. [Col. 0748C]

### VI. He joins virtue to his studies.

When he had already begun to be clothed in the blossoming flowers of youth, he so equipped his adolescence with good morals that even at that time he was thought to be a monk. With every vigilance he kept himself whole and undefiled by those vices with which people of that age are commonly contaminated. For he feared to be imbued with them lest, infected by them in tender youth, he should later be unable to rid himself of them when he wished, according to what is written: “A young man, even when he has grown old, will not depart from his way” (Prov. XXII, 6). Having obtained the companionship of good men, and especially of the prudent, he detested followers of disgrace.

[Col. 0748D]

### VII. He is made archdeacon.

Now, ascending through all the ecclesiastical grades, as is customary, when he had attained the office of the Levites, he was raised by the same pontiff already mentioned even to its summit, doctrine requiring this as a matter of justice. Having therefore accepted the office of ministry, and having been devoted to the cultivation of God’s vineyard, so that he might show himself its farmer, he sought the common benefit of many more than his own. Kind toward all, just toward everyone, he harmed no one; he strove to benefit those whom he could. Sound doctrine indeed dwelt in him, because he diligently did what suited his condition, in accordance with the Apostle’s words: “Giving no offense to anyone, so that our ministry may not be blamed, but in everything let us show ourselves as ministers of God” (II Cor. VI, 3). [Col. 0749A]

### VIII. He restrains his senses.

He had read that death enters through the windows and penetrates into the interior of the house through those same windows. Therefore he diligently strove to close his ears with the bolt of prudence, lest the arrow of bloody death should strike the inner chamber. For each sense, while exercising its own office, was compelled to become the instrument of another. Thus his sight, withdrawn from desire, was rendered sincere and pure. From a tongue free of falsehood, flattery and slander were kept far away. Yet, whenever circumstances demanded it, stern correction was not lacking; for if the perfect man is he who does not offend in speech, he is certainly no worse who, seeing one of his brothers sinning, brings him back to the way of truth by admonishing, exhorting, and reproving him, according to the Apostle. [Col. 0749B]

And because he did not wish to sin easily either with his tongue or with his eyes, the saying seems rightly applicable to him: he was just in sight and in hearing. Endowed also with learning and modest speech, his hearing was wholly closed to obscene and shameful things, in accordance with what is written: “Fence your ears with thorns, and do not listen to an evil tongue” (Eccli. XXVIII, 28). His feet were already being drawn back from the broad road of the world, and they strove to advance along the steep path of the heavenly homeland. The teaching of justice by which he was nourished prudently impressed upon him that it is more blessed to give than to receive; consequently, his hands were often held back by restraint from taking, but more often and more readily extended in generosity.

### IX. He is generous toward the poor.

Overflowing with the bowels of charity, he was always concerned for the poor. Loving Christ with all his heart, while he could not, like Martha, minister to him bodily, he refreshed him daily in the needy, according to Christ’s own testimony in the Gospel: “You always have the poor with you, but you will not always have me” (John XII, 8). Hence he himself will say to his own at the end: “Whatever you did for one of the least of mine, you did for me” (Matt. XXV, 40).

Thus, in receiving the poor, he rejoiced to have Christ as his guest. Yet although he was impelled to the work of mercy by that blessedness which is proclaimed among the Lord’s other beatitudes in the Gospel: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. V, 7), nevertheless, bound by the bond of ordered charity, he assisted each petitioner not for luxury but for necessity, according to what each one needed. [Col. 0749D]

### X. During a public crisis he withdraws to the oratory of Saint Michael and finds seven solidi for the use of the poor.

At a certain time, when the abundance of provisions did not appear as usual and bitter famine was constricting the entire region through lack of food, a crowd of poor people began coming to the man of God in greater numbers than usual. Their insistent entreaties continued daily and pitifully, asking that the piety of the man of God relieve their poverty. Pierced by the point of charity, he began to burn with intense concern. The ample supply of provisions in the great storeroom had already been exhausted by similar acts of distribution. On one side, the necessity of feeding those entrusted to his household care urged him; on the other, the will to assist all who were in need pressed him. Everything required for the conduct of human life seemed absent from the storeroom, and the steward of his house declared that the small amount remaining was insufficient for himself and his own, much less capable of relieving the want of so many petitioners. [Col. 0750A]

Then the man of God entered the little oratory which he himself had rebuilt across the Saône in honor of Saint Michael, and to which he had withdrawn from the city because of the public tumult, so that, in secluded quiet, keeping vigil in prayer, he might devote himself more attentively to divine service. Moved by pity for the poor, he began to implore the Lord more earnestly.

When he had prostrated himself face down upon the ground with tears, and had continued long in prayer, weeping profusely, he lifted his eyes from the ground and saw before him seven solidi. He did not wish to touch them, fearing that they might be either a phantom illusion or someone else’s loss, and that he might commit guilt under the appearance of an act of piety.

He left the oratory, sent the solidi he had found to all who were accustomed to come there, and ordered them to inquire whether anyone had lost them. When everyone denied having lost the coins and asserted that the ones found were not theirs, he assigned them not to his own use but to the food of the poor. [Col. 0750B]

### XI. He teaches others.

As he was an eager investigator of the divine commandments, so also was he a diligent practitioner of them. He exercised himself in piety and endeavored to draw others whom he could toward the same. He took pains to form his youth in the good teaching he had acquired, so that no one might despise it, and so that he might be an example of good conduct to others in word, knowledge, and way of life (I Tim. III, 13).

Because he had read the Apostle’s promise that those who serve well acquire for themselves a good standing and great confidence in Christ Jesus, he attended so carefully to the ministry entrusted to him that his progress was evident to all and beneficial to everyone who heard him.

To lend out to many, as it were at interest, the teaching he had acquired according to the grace granted to him, and lest he be condemned with the slothful servant for allowing the talent entrusted to him to lie idle, he summoned clerics to himself from various regions. Those whom he saw to be teachable he gladly and freely instructed.

He was eager to do this because of the words of the prophet Daniel: “Those who are learned shall shine like the brightness of the firmament, and those who instruct many in righteousness like stars forever and ever” (Dan. XII, 3). He did this so that he might be found worthy to be joined, not alone but together with his hearers, to the splendors of the stars.

### XII. He refuses the archbishopric of Besançon and becomes a monk at Cluny.

When the man of God flourished in such and similar virtues, and his name was spread abroad by celebrated fame, the archbishop of Besançon entered upon the way of all flesh. With the consent both of the prince of that land and of the entire clergy and people, the blessed Maiolus was urged to assume the summit of the episcopate.

Yet although his spirit was strengthened by the firmness of authority and raised by the height of virtue, he feared, under the appearance of this dignity, that he might be compelled to seek worldly gain and proceed through secular business toward the glory of the world, which he had rejected in his mind. By guarding humility, he fled the heavy burden of a storm-tossed eminence, following the example of the Creator of all, who, although he had reigned in heaven before the ages, avoided receiving a kingdom on earth. For it is written: “When Jesus realized that they were about to come and seize him to make him king, he withdrew again to the mountain by himself to pray” (John VI, 15). [Col. 0751A]

Therefore the blessed Maiolus, taught by the instruction of the eternal King—who fled the offered glory of high office and afterward willingly came to the gallows of the cross so that he might become his member—placed all his hope in him. He strove by deed to fulfill what Christ had commanded in word. For this command is given in the Gospel: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Luke IX, 23).

Thus the man of God, through the discipline of heavenly devotion, despised the fleeting glory of the world. Touched by the sweetness of the life above, he utterly restrained himself from all the things coveted by lovers of the world.

Accordingly, he sought the monastery in the valley of the hill called Cluny, governed by the venerable man Heymardus, because of its moral integrity and devotion to virtue. There, according to the rule of blessed Benedict, he asked that the aforesaid man receive him and grant him the habit of monastic life.

### XIII. Devoted to obedience.

Rejecting, then, all the resources of earthly possession for the hope of the promised future, he assumed the habit of holy religious life. From that point onward he lived under another’s command, so that he deviated in nothing from the purpose of holy religious life.

Having removed dullness and murmuring far from himself, he stood out above the others in the singular virtue of obedience, fulfilling among the brothers what blessed Benedict commands (Rule of St. Benedict, ch. 71): “The good of obedience is to be shown not only to the abbot, but the brothers are also to obey one another.” Concerning the abbot he was instructed by the apostolic example: “Obey your superiors” (Hebr. XIII, 17).

Indeed, as an imitator of blessed Benedict, whose discipleship he had entered, he put on the humility of a little child. Rejecting the foolish doctrine of the philosophers, he took up the wise folly of God, according to what the Apostle commands: “If anyone among you wishes to be wise in this world, let him become a fool, so that he may be wise” (I Cor. III, 18). Thus he who had previously been a teacher of grammarians began afterward to be a disciple of simple men. [Col. 0751D]

### XIV. Librarian and apocrisiarius (envoy). He rejects pagan authors and gives excellent admonitions.

Just as philosophers apply the intensity of their minds to the argumentative reasoning of syllogisms, so he devoted himself to saying what had to be carried out in daily practice in the monastery. Having learned all these things through diligent care and entrusted them to the experience of his memory, he soon began to appear more learned than everyone else.

The aforementioned Father therefore recognized him as so prudent within the monastic order that he appointed him over the library and entrusted him with the office of apocrisiarius (envoy). He fulfilled this ministry with such authority and such diligence that he became both an example and a source of fear to all who lived with him.

That man of God had read the books of the ancient philosophers and the falsehoods of Virgil, which he himself no longer wished either to hear or to have others read. “The divine poets are sufficient for you,” he would say; “you have no need to defile yourselves with the luxurious eloquence of Virgil.”

Content with the regular life, he was so devoted to frugality that he seemed in no way different from the fellowship of the common life. When he observed their faults as needing correction, he first sang the praises, in each person, of what was praiseworthy in contrast to the fault proper to that person; then, as though unaware, he criticized what needed correction.

Yet he often admonished them all to present themselves inwardly to God as human opinion represented them outwardly by their religious habit.

O man to whom the highest honors are always owed! Out of love for eternal life he embraced voluntary poverty and gave entirely to Christ whatever he found upon the altar of his heart, attributing nothing to his own merits!

### XV. He is sent to Rome and restores his companion to health with holy oil.

At a certain time the abbot happened to send the blessed Maiolus to Rome with another brother for the benefit of the monastery. When they had completed their mission and were returning, they came to Yporediem (Yurée) for lodging. The brother who accompanied him, named Heldricus [Note: [Col. 0751D] He had been a leading figure at the court of Otto the Great, as will be read below in Book II, chapter 22; afterward he became a monk and then abbot of Auxerre, mentioned above in elegy 6.], was seized by a fever and began to be exhausted by its fierce heat.

As his illness worsened and he was now suffering throughout his whole body, he despaired of life and was deeply concerned about his approaching death. The man of God, who was no less saddened by his brother’s suffering than the sufferer himself, was then afflicted by a double misfortune: on the one hand, his brother’s illness grieved him; on the other, the paternal mission he had begun remained unfinished.

Not knowing what to do, he began to implore divine mercy more earnestly. After three days had passed, when he had given himself over to sleep after the morning praises, a venerable man, distinguished by gray hair, appeared to him and said:

“Why are you oppressed by sluggish grief? Why has it slipped from your memory what my brother James commanded concerning the sick: ‘Is any one of you sad? Let him pray with a tranquil spirit and sing psalms. Is anyone among you sick? Let him bring in the presbyters of the Church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord; and the prayer of faith will save the sick person, and the Lord will raise him up’” (James V, 41). [Col. 0752D]

Somewhat heartened in spirit by this vision, as soon as he awoke he promptly put into action what had been revealed through the apostolic message. A wondrous and exceedingly astonishing event followed: on that same day, when the sufferer had been anointed with the oil of sanctification, he recovered and was restored to his former health as though he had suffered no bodily affliction.

On the following day, giving thanks for the Lord’s power, they attempted to bring their journey to its intended conclusion. For the sick man testified that he had been healed by the prayer of faith through the words of blessed James. It is therefore clearer than daylight that the blessed man obtained by his prayers what restored this man so quickly to health. When the brothers had learned of this miracle through trustworthy report, they thereafter began to hold the blessed Maiolus in great veneration, recognizing that through signs of virtue he had become so close to God. [Col. 0753A]

### XVI. He becomes more humble as a result.

But the blessed man, rejecting the glory of praise and desiring in this life to be despised rather than venerated, the more attentively he was honored through the devotion of the brothers, the more he deemed himself worthy of every lowliness and abasement.

Although he was loved by all with charity, he did not wish to be praised by anyone, lest the purity of his heart be stained by vainglory. Therefore, while fleeing to be held in esteem by men, he showed himself beloved of God in his own conscience.

Moreover, clothed in Christ’s tunic, whose footsteps he followed, and adorned with remarkable patience, he always strove, according to the Apostle, to pursue the greater spiritual gifts. Thus, by turning away from vices and advancing from virtue to virtue, he climbed through the fourfold road of obedience to the highest summit of humility.

But because no one can rightly command obedience from those subject to him unless he has first learned to offer it to his superiors, God’s dispensation appointed that he remain subordinate for a long time, so that under another’s instruction he might learn how he could later preside over others without error.

But here I shall take a brief respite from the work of elaboration, so that this book may receive its proper conclusion here, although it complains that it has been forced into an unworthy brevity.

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 0753]

[Col. 0753B] ### I. He is designated abbot but refuses to consent.
