Meanwhile, the man of God Heymardus, seeing the blessed Maiolus borne aloft on the wings of his virtues, despising all earthly things, avoiding the glory of the world, raining down words, outshining others through miracles, and striving with all his strength to advance from virtue to virtue, while seeing himself, by contrast, weak, deprived of sight, worn out by old age, and already a veteran of long service, summoned the brothers together and began to address them:

“You judge that I, deprived of sight, cannot usefully preside over you.” Therefore choose from among yourselves someone who may be your protector and guardian in the service of God.”

When they hesitated and gave no answer to this, he set forth in speech what he had conceived through divine inspiration, exhorting them to elect the blessed Maiolus and asserting that he alone was fit for this office. There was complete agreement among all, and their desire was no different. One could see them all rushing to unanimous consent.

For companies of monks and clerics, joined with noblemen, hastened forward; the rural people joined their voice to that of the urban people; the judgment of all was the same, their voice the same, and all burned with a common eagerness to confer upon Maiolus the title of shepherd. He was renowned for his merits, worthy to be chosen for his nobility, outstanding in doctrine, foremost in noble character, known to princes and held in some measure in awe.

But when he could not be bent by any entreaties to give his consent, the abbot, adopting good counsel, resolved to entrust to him who can do all things what Maiolus denied himself to be capable of undertaking. Therefore, after the conclusion of each canonical hour, when the brothers had prostrated themselves upon the ground over this petition, Psalm 86 was sung. While this was being done for three days, God offered the following sign of his mercy. [Col. 0753D]

### II. At last he yields to the admonitions of blessed Benedict.

The man of God, deeply anxious, having spent almost half the following night sleepless, was nevertheless wearied by prolonged thought. When sleep came upon him so strongly that he still imagined himself to be awake, a man appeared to stand before him, dressed in a religious habit and handsome in appearance, and said:

“Be at peace, brother. Do not hesitate to accept the honor of governance, because divine assistance will not be lacking for you in carrying out this office.” [Col. 0754B]

Then, holding out a little book which he happened to carry in his hand, he said: “Keep this as your companion, and conduct whatever must be done according to its testimony.”

The speaker seemed to him to be none other than blessed Benedict. Strengthened somewhat by this vision, he could no longer hesitate: he understood that divine dispensation was compelling him to undertake this work.

Therefore, casting his care upon the Lord and placing all his ability in the Lord’s will, at daybreak he prostrated himself bodily upon the ground in the assembly of the brothers. In the chapter meeting he made satisfaction to both the abbot and all the brothers, accusing himself of fault and addressing them in this speech:

“Fathers, brothers, do not count it as obstinacy that I delayed obeying your command with a stubborn mind. When I consider in my mind the force and magnitude of governing souls, conscious of my own weakness I perceive that I am wholly unfit to undertake it. My delay in obedience therefore arose because I fear suffering a fall beneath the weight of so great a burden. No one knows another as well as he knows himself. Thus, if you knew me as I know myself, you would never compel me to this office.

“But because your command presses upon me, and I dare not resist it, I now place all my hope in him who can soothe what is harsh, lighten what is heavy, and overcome adversity. I am changed from my former unaltered decision.” [Col. 0754C]

When the brothers heard this, they all gave thanks to God, by whose most gracious mercy they had deserved to be heard in their petition.

Then the lord abbot summoned a gathering of nobles, bishops, and abbots and sought their counsel. In their presence he broke into these words:

“Your diligence is by no means unaware that whatever is done wrongly by subjects concerns their superiors. Therefore the unending fire of Gehenna punishes both the example of an evil life and the negligence of subjects.

“Accordingly, I, Heymardus, unworthy abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter of Cluny, wish it to be known to all present and future generations that, considering these and similar matters in my mind, worn out by age and weakened even in the functions of my body, and perceiving myself to be less fit for pastoral care, after being forewarned by the chapter of blessed Benedict concerning the appointment of an abbot, together with all my brothers, sons, and fellow servants, have reelected our brother and son Maiolus, formerly chosen by blessed Peter, and have decreed that he be abbot.

“We do this lest the order be worn away by the burden of our weakness and suffer any setback, though by God’s favor it must always be advanced toward better things. For just as one who rashly aspires to governance is rightly constrained, so one who is worthy but refuses it is rightly compelled.

“And just as the monastery of Cluny, founded by Duke William under God’s authority, consecrated in the name of the prince of the apostles, distinguished by the privileges of the Roman See, confirmed by royal commands, and organized by the venerable abbots Lords Berno and Odo, is established as such, so we entrust to the aforesaid brother the governance of all the abbeys, places, and cells, wherever they may be, acquired either in their time or in ours.

“We bind him, by the favor of divine providence, with the bonds of obedience both to preserve the order according to blessed Benedict and the institutions of our fathers, and to administer these possessions with complete integrity. And we all unanimously proclaim him abbot.” [Col. 0755B]

After these words, the election was written down, confirmed by the consent of the whole community, and, when an antiphon had been intoned, he was led into the church, blessed, and raised to his seat amid the rejoicing of all.

### III. He governs himself and others through the reading of Sacred Scripture.

Just as one ordinarily examines oneself by looking into a mirror, so he examined himself inwardly through divine reading; from this he shaped the adornment of his mind, while whatever disfigurement was detected was corrected by the moderation of justice.

For this reason he took greater delight in the words of the divine commandments than in the richest dishes of banquets, because through them he was instructed both to shape his own conduct and to teach and correct those entrusted to him.

Yet he offered himself to all as an example of good living. Therefore, just as in rank, so also in action he strove to be first, according to the evangelist’s saying: “Jesus began to do and to teach” (Acts I, 1).

He was so devoted always to reading that, even when traveling, he often carried a little book in his hands. Thus, while riding, his spirit was refreshed by reading.

### IV. How he reads pagan authors.

When he read philosophers and books of secular wisdom, he followed with shrewd diligence what the divine voice commands the lawgiver in the second giving of the Law—that is, Deuteronomy—concerning a captive woman who, after shaving her head, cutting her nails, and removing her hair, cleansed of every impurity, passed into the embrace of the man who had captured her.

Using this likeness, whatever useful things were found in the books of philosophers he deemed worthy of retaining in his memory. But whatever was superfluous—namely, love of worldly things and concern for secular matters—he shaved away as poisonous and deadly; upon these he imposed baldness, and he cut them off in the manner of nails with the sharpest iron.

Thus, through constant reading and formation by the authority of Scripture, he was so strong in canonical and monastic institutions that no one seemed his equal in legal decrees and philosophical arguments.

### V. How he conducts himself toward his subjects.

Composed in virtue and wisdom and endowed also with a most honorable abundance of speech, he adapted himself to each individual so that he was lovable to all, fulfilling the Apostle’s words: “I have become all things to all, that I might gain all” (I Cor. IX, 22).

Whatever he said, he shaped with the gravity of wisdom. His speech was seasoned with salt; though brief and infrequent because of the weight of virtue it carried, it was considered precious for its prudent sweetness.

Therefore, whenever he delivered a discourse for moral edification, he was regarded as both most eloquent and most welcome. With provident piety he governed the flock entrusted to him, urging them, in concordant and holy struggle, to contend against the worst enemy of all the saints, so that each might not cease to do whatever good he could, lest he wish to do it when it was no longer permitted.

He often also brought before them the admonitions of blessed Paul, who says in his Epistle: “Pursue peace with all and holiness, without which no one shall see God.” For it is an old proverb that like is easily gathered with like. Therefore, as a perpetual guardian of virginity, he did not allow those subject to him to be stained by the disgrace of any shameful conduct.

He rebuked sinners before everyone with the zeal of devoted love, so that the others might have fear. Yet the words he uttered in reproof seemed hard and harsh, like goads, according to the saying: “The words of the wise are like goads, and like nails driven firmly in” (Eccl. XII, 11).

Moreover, in the manner of a father, those whom he rebuked with harsh denunciation he afterward soothed—remarkable though it is to relate how holy and pious he was toward them—according to what he saw would benefit each one. From the treasure of his heart he brought forth new and old things: some he addressed with kindness, others with admonitions, others with threats. Thus, becoming all things to all according to the Apostle, he preached the word, standing by it in season and out of season, reproving and entreating with all patience and teaching (II Tim. IV, 2). [Col. 0756C]

But because he was filled with the charity of Christ, who desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth, he rejoiced in the progress of all the good as though it were his own, and he groaned over the wickedness of the evil. Toward the misfortunes of the wretched he was affected as though he himself were suffering.

### VI. How cautiously he conducts himself in palaces. He converts many from the world and reforms monasteries.

Whenever he frequently visited the palaces of emperors or kings in various regions, he sought in them not his own interests but those of Jesus Christ. Through familiar conversation with them, he either assisted the oppressed by his intervention or won some people from secular or clerical life for God, so that, in accordance with the Lord’s command, they might leave their possessions and, removed from worldly cares, strive to serve God in tranquility.

Thus, although he often lived in an earthly palace, his spirit was in no way diverted from the purpose of heavenly life. Preferring heavenly things to human things, he could not therefore be separated from the heavenly King, to whom he clung with his whole mind.

Moreover, lest any tale of obscene rumor about him arise, and so that an example of good living might proceed from his continence, he adorned himself in his walk and in every movement of his body with such a manner of conduct that every action and every word of his was a teaching and instruction of the apostles.

His mouth was so filled from the abundance of his heart that almost nothing other than the divine law resounded upon his lips. And because Scripture commands, “Let the one who hears say, ‘Come’” (Rev. XXII, 17), he drew away from the wickedness of the world all whom he could by persuasion.

Just as he himself yearned with all his strength, through heavenly desire, for the kingdom above, so he wished all people to go there with him, if it were possible. Yet he was not defrauded of the desire conceived within him by true love. For he who is charity, and who fulfills the will of those who fear him, brought the fervent desire of the man of God to fulfillment.

At his admonitions many people abandoned what they possessed, submitted themselves to regular discipline, and, following in the footsteps of blessed Benedict, denying themselves, served the true King with all their strength.

From various regions an innumerable multitude therefore flocked to his monastery. Although diverse in nationality, they were so united in mind that what is read in the Acts of the Apostles concerning the beginning of the nascent Church seemed literally fulfilled in them: “They had one heart and one soul” (Acts IV, 32). [Col. 0757B]

The shepherd rejoiced in the increase of his flock and rejoiced still more that all were devoted to the work they had undertaken. But because he watched over the flock entrusted to him with vigilant care, he deserved by divine grace to rejoice in this life over the fruit of his labors.

For he restored to its former state, by correction, the discipline of regular life, which had almost collapsed through the negligence of earlier generations, just as blessed Benedict had organized it. Throughout various regions of the world, he subjected many monasteries that had strayed from the regular path to the monastic order, both through his own efforts and through those whom he had appointed abbots. [Note: [Col. 0757D] That is, he restored it by introducing stricter discipline. The same is said below in chapter 23, where the monastery of Saint Apollinaris is said to have been brought into the way of blessed Benedict. From this passage it is clear that the abbots were not priors previously placed over monasteries attached to Cluny; we have already demonstrated this with various examples. [Col. 0758D]]

In this he rejoiced and gave thanks to God, seeing that many of those whom he had raised under his care were fit to govern the monastic order.

### VII. He exercises discretion in food.

As a most discerning father, he placed discretion before everything he did. He practiced the common life with such discretion that he both devoted himself to abstinence more than the others and did not provide anyone with material for praising him on account of that abstinence.

He used what the rule allowed and permitted in such a way that pleasure was not nourished, but the body’s necessity was sustained at little expense. Obeying the Apostle’s command, he used wine sparingly. Through holy and moderate fasts his body was continually reduced; thus he avoided the tongue of flatterers and banished vainglory from his mind. [Col. 0757D]

### VIII. At the tables of the rich and in conversation.

Whenever he was compelled to attend the tables of nobles, he tasted what was served in such a way that he avoided superstition and preserved his continence, since moderation is praiseworthy everywhere.

In all things, even in good things, whatever exceeds measure is a fault. His dress was so suitable and moderate that it seemed neither excessively elegant or splendid nor excessively shabby. From such extremes people often either boast insolently or abase themselves indiscreetly.

Therefore, using discretion, he walked midway between the two, so that he could not be accused of boasting on account of costly clothing or of feigned sanctity on account of clothing that was excessively shabby and cheap. [Col. 0758A]

Whenever he joined articulate men and something was proposed from Scripture, as commonly happens, he listened willingly, answered prudently and modestly, and received their words readily and appreciatively.

If anything erroneous was proposed, he refuted it not harshly but with frank modesty. He did not defeat his opponent by clever argument, but instructed him kindly through the examples of venerable teachers. Then he brought forward the sayings of the orthodox together with the thunders of the Gospel and the Apostles. In this way he showed himself both highly learned and apparently free from any display of learning.

[Col. 0758B]

### IX. Devoted to solitude and tears.

When traveling and staying at an inn, wherever he might be, each day he sought out for himself a secluded place, a friend to grief, so that, withdrawn from human beings, he might be joined more closely to God. But we cannot say with how many groans and how many tears he was then afflicted.

Often the ground before his eyes appeared so watered with tears that it seemed flooded by a stream. If some slight matters occurred—things that commonly arise in thought because of human frailty—he lamented them with such grief that one would have thought him guilty of the gravest crimes.

Moreover, because the just person is first of all his own accuser, he often accused himself and proclaimed himself guilty, frequently repeating the words of blessed Job: “Does God not know my ways and number all my steps?” (Job XXXI, 4).

While traveling, he often made his way apart from the others. When he was engaged in prayer or occupied with reading, none of his companions dared approach him, because, according to blessed Job, he was terrifying to his subjects, and “the light of his face did not fall to the ground” (Job XXIX, 24).

For this reason he wished all his intention to remain hidden, lest any opportunity for praise be offered, through which pride might creep into his mind. Yet the less he sought glory, the more it followed him, for, as Augustine says: “Better is the virtue that is not content with human testimony, except with that of its own conscience.”

True virtue is that which tends toward the end where the good of a human being is found, beyond which there is no greater good. Therefore, for one who possesses virtues, it is a great virtue to despise glory: its rejection is visible in God’s sight, but is not disclosed to human judgment.

## X. How many and what kind were his virtues. The raising of souls

Different faithful men are praised for different virtues; but blessed Maiolus is to be praised not for one virtue alone, but for all of them. We ought, however, to praise in him those virtues known throughout Italy, not unknown in Germany, and in which all Gaul rejoices: namely, the restoration of monasteries, peace restored to the churches, concord between kings and princes, undefiled observance of the Rule, and the gain of souls. These souls he snatched—as once David did—by his strong hand from the fiercest bears’ claws and rescued from the bloody jaws of lions, restoring them to the Lord in such a way that, with the righteous man, he could say: “I was breaking the jaws of the wicked, and from his teeth I was taking away the prey” (Job 29:17).

For as often as he took prey from the teeth of the wicked—that is, of the devil—so often, by preaching, he tore a soul away from the bite of error. Indeed, he drove demons out of many whom, snatching them from the devil, he subjected to the service of Christ. To very many swollen with the serpent’s poison he brought relief through the antidote of his exhortation. He healed very many sick in good works through the laying on of hands, strengthening their lives by the example of his own conduct.

Many men of wondrous holiness are recorded who obtained through their prayers that those who had formerly been condemned to infernal punishments might return to their bodies. But if that is marvelous—when a soul, through dissolution, is raised again to this corruptible life—this is more marvelous and more glorious: when it is recalled to its Creator, and, having been alienated from him by perverse conduct, afterward clings to him through upright living, so that it is one spirit with him.

For blessed Maiolus raised many who were dead in mind to the joys of eternal life, and drew those submerged in the waves of the great sea to the shore of firm solidity in the nets of his preaching. Blessed Maiolus is therefore judged in no way inferior to those who raised the dead. But if anyone wishes to investigate with discerning mind, who could ever recount how many sitting in darkness and the shadow of death he showed the straight road and taught to go to the city of their dwelling—namely, the heavenly Jerusalem? Those who limped in good works he taught to run along the saving path.

Yet there are some who praise only those whom they hear performed visible signs; they contend that the workers of invisible things, which they cannot discern, are of lesser merit. Therefore, to show that blessed Maiolus was endowed with the power to perform outward deeds as well, we shall recount a few of the many things he accomplished wondrously.

## XI. He visits Saint Mary of Anici

Once, wishing with humble devotion to seek the Mother of Mercy, namely the Mother of God, he undertook to approach the city of Vallavorum. At that time the whole city rejoiced, and people of both sexes and every age delighted in seeing him. All sought his blessing and eagerly desired to hear his holy discourse. The nobles came to meet him, the common people hastened forward, and the sacred clergy of the church poured out in a dense throng.

Some applauded his praises, others leapt up in applause, and all greeted the common glory with equal devotion. Then, accompanied by a great crowd, he directed his journey to the holy church. He prostrated himself and, as was his custom, worshiped Christ; he drenched the ground with tears and called upon Christ with lamentations—the Christ for whom his tears had made a road as he flew above the stars.

## XII. A blind man receives sight

After he had been inebriated with spiritual sweetness in Christ and filled with the most delightful food of virtues, he returned to his lodging. There a beggar’s hand met him, asking for alms, trained and sufficiently prepared to live from another’s morsel.

Among those who met him was a man who had been deprived of sight for many years. While the others sought bodily assistance, he alone asked for light. He declared that it had been revealed to him by the chief of the apostles that, if he washed his eyes with water in which the man of God had washed his hands, he would recover the light of his eyes after the darkness had been driven away.

When he had been driven back by a harsh rebuke from the saint, he nevertheless did not cease asking those who served him. When Maiolus learned of this, he forbade them under threat to undertake such a thing in presumptuous recklessness. But the man who lacked sight could not rest from asking for it.

Finally, after his request had repeatedly been frustrated, and since he could not obtain in the city what he sought, he attempted to harass the man of God on the road as he was leaving the city by his persistent insistence. In his asking he resembled the man of whom the Lord says in the Gospel: “And if he persists in knocking, I tell you, even if he will not rise and give him something because he is his friend, yet because of his persistence he will rise and give him as much as he needs.”

At a place called Mons Gaudii—where the church belonging to the Mother of Christ looks out from this side—the blind man went ahead of the man of God and waited for his arrival. Seizing the bridle of the approaching horse, he held it and said under oath: “I will not release this horse, even if I am beaten, unless I first obtain what I am asking.”

He also carried water with him in a small vessel hanging from his neck, so that no opportunity for making an excuse might afterward be taken away. Then the man of God, placed in great anxiety, was at last moved to mercy and felt compassion for the petitioner. He dismounted, exorcised the water according to ecclesiastical custom, and infused it with the saving sign of the Lord’s cross. He then made the same saving sign with that water upon the blind man’s eyes.

He presumed nothing upon his own power, yet he did not waver in faith. He had called upon the name of the One over the water and had washed the saving wood in it, and he had no doubt that this One could restore light to the blind man. And because he believed this faithfully, he was not deprived of the effect of his faith.

Then, kneeling on the ground with the brothers who were present with him, he began with abundant tears to entreat the Mother of Mercy. A marvelous thing! The man who had been deprived of sight recovered the light, the darkness having been dispelled, before the man of God rose from prayer.

**[Note: [Col. 0759D] S. Maioli festum ejus miraculi causa in Ecclesia Aniciensi celebrari solitum tradit Odo Gisseius in historia Deiparae Podiensis, ubi hoc miraculum [Col. 0760D] ait contigisse anno 950; at serius accidit. Lege donationem a canonico Aniciensi Maiolo factam in elogio num. 29.]** Odo Gisseius relates in his history of the Mother of God of Le Puy that Saint Maiolus’s feast was customarily celebrated in the church of Anici on account of this miracle, and says there that it occurred in the year 950; but it happened later. See the donation made by Maiolus, canon of Anici, in Eulogy no. 29.

He who had been accustomed to plant his steps only when guided by another returned joyfully to his own home, led by no assistance. The man of the Lord restrained his voice from shouting and gave him this command: “Go,” he said, “in peace to your home, and tell how greatly the power of blessed Mary the Virgin has helped you.”

This miracle has not been commended to us from another source; rather, it has been inserted on the trustworthy report of those who were present.

## XIII. Another case

We know that another sign of power, scarcely different from this one, was performed through the same worker, the Lord of all. In the region of Vienne, in a certain village, a peasant was weeping for his son, who had been deprived of sight.

Lord Father Maiolus, being within his own jurisdiction, had come with his companions to stay at the same place. The peasant therefore took courage, believing that his son could obtain light if his eyes were washed with water in which the man of the Lord had washed his hands. Because he was afraid to approach the man of God about this, he tried secretly to ask one of his attendants.

Having therefore obtained the water secretly, as soon as he washed his son’s eyes with it, he was granted the recovery of the light he had lost.

When the man of God learned this, because he avoided the glory of human praise, he thereafter had the water in which he had washed his hands sprinkled out before him. Yet thefts of this water were often committed, and through it many who had long been weakened by illness were restored in joy to the health they desired.

## XIV. A man suffering from fever is healed

Once, while he was traveling, a brother who accompanied him began to be violently shaken by immense fevers. He was so drenched with excessive cold that he seemed utterly deprived of vital warmth. The brothers who were present covered him with their own garments, but he was in no way able to become warm.

Then the man of God removed his own tunic, clothed the sick man in it, and ordered him to be placed there. He himself withdrew to his customary refuge of prayer.

But what does Christ not accomplish in his saints? At once, as the tunic of the holy man covered the body numbed by cold, a gentle sleep immediately spread through the limbs of the sufferer. A flood of sweat covered the whole body, which previously had bristled with excessive cold, and restored the desired warmth.

After a short interval, when he rose from sleep, he enjoyed his former health as though he had never before been oppressed by illness. From this it may be understood what power and merit his soul possessed within, since his garment outwardly restored health to a sick man.

## XV. Maiolus’s devotion on the Roman journey

Who could adequately explain how often, when he directed his journey to the thresholds of the apostles, he completed that journey, and with what devotion?

He visited all the holy places adjoining the sacred route with spiritual zeal. There he poured out rivers of tears and begged them insistently to come to his aid through prayer. He allowed none of the poor whom he encountered on the road to pass without consolation. Through a faithful servant to whom this care had been entrusted, he assisted each of them, and whatever he had contributed to them, he rejoiced that he had contributed to Christ.

When he reached the apostles’ tombs, it cannot be said how many tears, how many groans, and how much grief he poured out there. With all his desire he prayed that the dissolution of his body might occur here, and that there he might be covered by a humble tomb.

While he was in Rome, his heart exulted in joy more than usual. Because of his excessive happiness, as he himself admitted, he often seemed to see the glorious princes as though he were looking upon them face to face. For this reason he regarded the day of his arrival as festive and most glorious; but his departure he considered devoid of joy and filled with sorrow.

## XVI. Bishop Arpertus of Chur is restored from illness after making confession

Once, while making that journey and crossing the Pennine Alps toward Chur (*Coriam*), Arpertus, the bishop of the aforesaid city, a man venerable for his virtue, had been struck by a severe plague and was continually tormented by the sharpest pains.

When he learned through popular report of the man of God’s arrival, he obtained by his prayers that Maiolus should come to visit him. By then, as the illness grew worse, he had despaired of his life. He resolved to confess his sins to Maiolus, confessing that he had offended in many things, especially through pride, and fearing that he had lost by empty glory whatever good he had done.

While he confessed these and other matters with the greatest sorrow, he felt himself somewhat relieved from the immense pain by the blessed man’s visit, and therefore believed that through Maiolus’s merit he would be restored to health.

Since Easter was already approaching, and the day on which the holy chrism is prepared was now near, he was unable to approach the altar or perform the required service. He therefore began more earnestly to ask the mercy of the servant of God that Maiolus’s own prayer might obtain from almighty God as much strength as would suffice for him on that day when he was to prepare the holy chrism according to ecclesiastical custom.

But the man who was wholly possessed by compassion did not know how to refuse what was justly requested. He immediately went to the oratory, gave himself to prayer with tears, and, having quickly completed his prayer, came out.

The illness began to leave the bishop. On the very day for which the request had been made, he rejoiced to have received such strength through the man’s power that he felt no discomfort of illness in himself. At last he began to rejoice that he had recovered from his infirmity through Maiolus’s prayers, but even more because, as he himself confessed, he had been freed to a great extent from the vice mentioned above.

From this it is understood that the holy man prayed to the Lord more willingly not for bodily health than for the salvation of the soul.

## XVII. The steward’s greed punished

Once, while he was staying in Rome, he decided to set out for the threshold of Saint Paul for the sake of prayer. When he came to the church of the distinguished teacher, he prostrated himself on the ground before the tomb and prayed with tears.

Rising from prayer, he visited the monks of that place with fraternal love. While he spoke with them and, as a devoted father, instructed them in their conduct, they began to ask him to help meet their needs.

Then, since he was always overflowing with the entrails of mercy, he ordered his steward to give them a pound of silver. But the steward, knowing that this would be a small amount among the expenses, prudently granted only half a pound.

Soon afterward, when Maiolus had returned to the basilica of Saint Peter, a certain man appeared and offered him ten solidi. He accepted them and said to the steward:

> “Take these, and learn that you have fallen into guilt:
>
> because, plotting fraud against the needy brothers,
>
> you chose to be miserly. For if you had yielded
>
> what I ordered you to give, you would today have received,
>
> with Christ granting it, twenty solidi returned
>
> as a return at the usual rate.””
>
> Fear seized the man: he realized that the secrets
>
> of his guilt had been exposed to Maiolus,
>
> though he certainly had not expected it.
>
> “This is marvelous, good sir: that the closed chambers
>
> of the prophet’s heart should gape open,
>
> since he is filled with the breath of the holy man.
>
> He is now God; now he receives divine honors.”

## XVIII. The naked man clothed

At another time, while he was traveling, he found a poor man on the road barefoot and without a hooded cloak. Moved by compassion for him, the man of God stripped off the garment with which he was covered and clothed the poor man in it.

When he arrived at the lodging toward which he was traveling, the bishop of that same city offered him another garment of the same make and appearance, but better. When the most blessed man had accepted it, he began to address his companions as follows:

> “We ought not to hesitate to give what is ours to one who can so quickly and so abundantly restore what we have given.”

## XIX. Emperor Otto’s opinion of Maiolus and the monks. The eulogies of Otto and Adelaide

As the reputation of this holiness—through the wondrous deeds that almighty God performed by him—became increasingly known among men, and the fame of his name spread far and wide, the great Otto, who at that time was vigorously governing the commonwealth, learned through the reports of many about so great a man and desired his presence with growing eagerness.

Although this man possessed the imperial dignity, he nevertheless had great devotion toward monasteries, because he did not hope to hold the empire successfully unless he strove not to displease the supreme King. Therefore he often groaned when he saw those who had devoted themselves to God through the religious habit going headlong into secular business.

For the purposes of rule he seemed so well suited that he appeared worthy to be compared not merely with anyone second to him, but—as may be said more plainly—with the first and highest. He undertook nothing trivial, because modesty accompanied his dignity; and whatever he began, by God’s authority, was in no way lacking in effectiveness.

His wife Adelaide clung to him. Beloved by God and lovable to human beings, she was joined to him on the royal throne while preserving a chaste mind, with all vigilance, for the heavenly King. She helped the poor and continually cherished the sick and weak. She rejoiced with those who rejoiced and wept with those who wept; she was the hope of the wretched and the consolation of mourners. Noble in royal lineage, she was in every respect still nobler in holiness.

## XX. Their humility amid the summit of virtues

Although they were placed at the summit of virtues and had no lack of material for pride, she protected herself with such a guard of humility that no example of boasting could be detected in her conduct. She kept in mind what the wisdom of Solomon says:

> “Have they appointed you ruler? Do not exalt yourself, but be among them as one of them” (Ecclus. 32:1).

For if, according to the Apostle, an unbelieving man is saved through a believing woman, and an unbelieving woman through a believing man (1 Cor. 7:14), through the mutual benefit of faith, much more surely did these two, joined together in Christ and having practiced righteousness through faith, obtain the promises promised by the God who does not lie, according to his own testimony.

Both were hearers of the Gospel, and because they were hearers, they were therefore doers, since they had learned from the Gospel: “Whoever receives a righteous man in the name of a righteous man will receive a righteous man’s reward” (Matt. 10:41). Therefore, those whom they saw more devoted in the service of God they held dearer to themselves. But they loved above all others those who renounced false joys and followed the footsteps of blessed Benedict with the greatest readiness of devotion.

## XXI. Maiolus dear to both through Heldricus. He is placed in charge of reforming monasteries

Thus—as has already been mentioned—when the fame of blessed Maiolus had become known through the reports of very many, they delighted in acquiring acquaintance with him no less than in enjoying life. He who opens the entrance to the blessed life to those who knock in faith did not delay to fulfill their desire.

Heldricus, whom we mentioned above (Book I, chapter 15), was preeminent in lay power and had once been an honored man among the Palatines in Italy. Renouncing his wife together with his great abundance of temporal possessions, he laid aside his belt and went to Cluny, submitting himself to the purpose of blessed Benedict.

His intimacy with Maiolus is reported to have produced the occasion through which the Roman prince came to know the holy man. Through Heldricus he summoned Maiolus to himself, and he loved him so greatly for his salutary teaching that he wished to entrust to his governance the monasteries subject to him in Italy and in Germany.

The empress, meanwhile, as though she were the least of handmaids, desired to offer him the services of her devotion, since she hoped through the prayers of blessed Maiolus to be visited by a more abundant grace of the divine presence.

All the nobles venerated him, and all the princes loved him. The emperor had him as his confidential adviser and as a faithful intermediary in secret matters. If anyone had business with the emperor, he sought blessed Maiolus as mediator.

## XXII. The monastery of Saint Apollinaris reformed

At that same time he brought the monastery of blessed Apollinaris—which is said to be set apart from the city of Ravenna by a distance of twenty-four *stadia*—into the way of blessed Benedict, and appointed his own abbot there.

Moreover, yielding to the empress’s insistent and highly important request, he began to labor on the construction of the church of the holy Savior near the city of Pavia.

**[Note: [Col. 0763D] Nalgodus: Juxta Ticinum, id est Papiam, in honore S. Salvatoris construxit ecclesiam, et monasterium, quod vulgo Cella Aurea dicitur, et [Col. 0764D] collapsum pene fuerat in ruinam, restauravit ad unguem.]** Nalgodus: Near Ticinum, that is, Pavia, he built a church in honor of the holy Savior, and restored with the utmost care the monastery commonly called the Golden Cell, which had almost collapsed into ruin.

Meanwhile this second book now calls for its proper conclusion, so that the third may bring what remains to completion, with its evident signs.

# BOOK THREE

## I. Maiolus, returning to Cluny, is captured by the Saracens

The man of the Lord, therefore, as we have said above, had satisfied the empress’s wishes. After a long period had passed during which he had been absent from the monastery of Cluny, he desired to go and visit the brothers.

When everything necessary for the journey had been prepared, he undertook the labor of travel. At last, after great difficulty and the toil of the journey, when they had passed beyond the summits of the Alpine heights, they descended as far as a village situated near the course of the River Drance (*Dransae*), once accustomed to be called the Bridge of the Bear.

For the stream that descends from the mountains, winding through repeated bends as it runs among the Alps, spreads out there, through its winding course, as much level ground as the position of the aforesaid village can occupy.

Many people from different regions were then accompanying blessed Maiolus, because they believed that they could be delivered through his holiness. When they had reached this place without mishap and had crossed the same stream, a force of the treacherous Saracen people suddenly attacked them amid the narrow road’s difficult turns, which present themselves to those descending after only a short interval.

Thrown into confusion by the sudden assault, and attempting many things in vain, they abandoned every better hope and resorted to flight—but without success. For the mad throng of the impious, pursuing them swiftly along the path, threw into chains all whom it was able to overtake.

When one of that impious band attacked one of the man of God’s servants with a weapon from a high cliff, the man of God placed his charitable hand in the way of the incoming missile, so that the servant might be rescued. The scar of the wound inflicted there remained visible for as long as he afterward lived.

He feared nothing for his own death, but he burned with concern for the others and groaned more deeply because he could not help those whom the cruelty of the impious had thrown into confusion. Although he had an opportunity to escape, charity held him steadfast in mind. He desired to lay down his life for those whom he loved, and although he could not rescue them from the hands of the impious, he did not wish to abandon them, overcome as he was by great grief.

Meanwhile, following the example of the Apostle, who, when shipwrecked, saved by prayer the lives of all who sailed with him because he could not free them from the impending danger by human assistance, Maiolus obtained this through his prayers before God: no one from that wretched group would die amid the enemy’s weapons.

The fierce barbarians, having completed their crime, were returning to their hiding places with a multitude of captives when they saw blessed Maiolus sitting alone at a distance on a stone. Swift foot soldiers immediately approached him, laid their criminal hands upon the saint, seized him, and led him away with the other captives.

Then they began to honor blessed Maiolus, whom they regarded as superior to the others, while they mocked those whom they considered lesser and began to disparage the Christian faith.

## II. He is bound because he preached Christ

Immediately, therefore, blessed Maiolus, an excellent warrior, took up the shield of faith and pierced the enemies of Christ with the spear of the word of God. He approved the worship of the Christian religion and undertook to demonstrate through certain and most evident arguments that the one whom they worshiped as God could neither free them from punishment nor help them in any way.

When they heard this, the barbarians’ boasting, inflamed by mad fury, grew into rage. They bound the saint’s feet with an iron fetter, cut out a place beneath the rock, and shut him in a dreadful prison.

When the saint of the Lord saw them raging for their own destruction, he said:

> As a martyr to receive the palm earned by struggle,
>
> and to be drenched in the fountain of his own blood,
>
> he longs, and with fearless face pours forth these words:
>
> “Enough, and more than enough, we have lived up to this point.
>
> Now, O Christ, my ardent spirit longs to enter your presence; I am weary of the road, weary of toil.
>
> Where the shorter paths of the straight road lie open,
>
> it is a joy to go, although the way may be very steep
>
> for those who tremble;
>
> soon it will be granted us to reach the starry fields.
>
> If the tracks of shed blood lead us,
>
> we embrace the title of martyrdom with outstretched arms,
>
> and willingly seek beautiful death through wounds.
>
> Only deign to make us witnesses for your name.”
>
> Saying this, he prepared his spirit for death
>
> and his neck for the executioner.
>
> His decision of death was firmly fixed,
>
> fearless man that he was. But, O Christ, within your purest ranks
>
> lilies, white and fresh, bloom together with roses;
>
> nor does constancy in martyrdom alone win your favor,
>
> nor is anyone a martyr merely because blood has been shed.
>
> Often a devout life has also won crowns for many,
>
> and the pure confession of your priests
>
> is pleasing to you—those whom the perfection of justice clothes.”

## III. He understands that he will be freed from heaven through the merits of blessed Mary

As we have already said, the man of the Lord, bound in iron chains in the dreadful cavern of a dark prison for confessing the name of the divine being, experienced the aid of divine mercy.

When night had followed, and he had surrendered to sleep his limbs exhausted by excessive grief, a vision of the following kind was shown to him by divine providence. A Roman bishop, adorned in apostolic vestments, seemed to stand near him, carrying a censer fragrant with incense.

Made more certain by this vision, he understood that he would be freed from the hands of the impious through the intervention of the apostles. To what he had seen in sleep another, still more evident sign was added.

Because of his love for the Mother of Mercy, he was accustomed to carry in his holy hands a little book concerning her Assumption, which blessed Jerome had published.

**[Note: [Col. 0765D] Hunc libellum non Hieronymi, sed tamen pervetusti auctoris esse eruditi norunt. Qua de re controversia fuit saeculo IX inter Hincmarum archiepiscopum [Col. 0766D] et nostros Corbeienses, qui istum libellum Hieronymo adjudicabant, teste Frodoardo in lib. III Historiae cap. 23.]** Learned men know that this little book is not by Jerome, although it is by a very ancient author. On this matter there was controversy in the ninth century between Archbishop Hincmar and our Corbie monks, who assigned this little book to Jerome, as Frodoard testifies in Book III, chapter 23, of his *History*.

While he lost all the other sacred books, together with everything else he had there, he deserved—so he declared—to have this one preserved for him through the Virgin’s protection.

When he perceived that he had it beneath the covering of his garment, he carefully considered how many days remained from that point until the same Assumption of the Mother of Mercy. When counted, they were found to number twenty-four.

Then he prayed that she would obtain this from her Son through her intercession: that he himself might be rescued from this captivity, so that divine mercy would grant him, among Christians, to celebrate with his fellow captives the solemnity of so great a feast.

When he had finished this prayer and lifted his head toward the rock, sleep immediately overcame him because of his grief. But after a short while, when he awoke, he found himself released from the iron fetters.

When morning came, the barbarians were astonished at this miracle. Seeing that he had been freed from his fetter by divine power, they no longer dared to presume to bind him again. Their ferocity somewhat abated, and they thereafter began to venerate the man whom they had previously held up to mockery.

## IV. He writes to the Cluniacensians for his release. He converts some of them. He pays the barbarians

Then, with the barbarians’ permission, the man of God sent to the brothers a letter written in his own hand, through a monk who had been captured with him. The letter contained the following:

> “To the lords and brothers of Cluny: Maiolus, a wretched captive, bound in chains.
>
> The torrents of Belial have surrounded me; the snares of death have overtaken me.
>
> If it pleases you, send the price of redemption for me and for those who are being held captive together with me.”

When this letter had been read aloud in the chapter at Cluny, the entire stock that until then had flourished joyfully in Christ through his teaching and example was immediately consumed by sorrow in its assembly.

No one can express the extent of everyone’s groaning there at that time. Everywhere among them there was mourning; one voice was heard from all who lamented, one cry from all who grieved, saying:

> “Our harp has been turned into mourning, and our joy into sorrow.”

For, in accordance with Jeremiah’s lament, Christ the Lord had been captured in our sins, to whom we had said: “In your light we shall live” (Lam. 4:20). Behold, he whose instruction in God we gloried in had been caught in the snare of a profane people.

Meanwhile, while these men were being afflicted by his chains, God’s favor was magnifying him through miracles. Those whom the man of God had persuaded by his arguments to worship Christ, after they had turned from the barbarian rite to the Christian profession, often heard—so their sworn testimony affirmed—the voices of many singing with him.

This occurred when the savage soldiers were sleeping at night and the man of God was rendering due praise to the King of kings. Since no human being at that time shared his lodging, they declared without doubt that the voices belonged to angels singing psalms with him.

On the appointed day, therefore, an immense sum of money was assembled—whether from things necessary for use, from the treasures that had until then been preserved for the monastery’s adornment, or from the generosity of distinguished men. The more eminent brothers, together with a great quantity of treasure, hurried to the appointed place.

They handed over to the robbers everything they had gathered through careful inquiry, and first drew out of the hands of the impious all those who had been thrust into chains; finally, they rescued from them the man whom they loved.

By the ordering of heavenly grace, it came to pass that through the captivity of one, many were granted freedom. And just as he had asked of the supreme King through his most holy Mother, so, through the Virgin’s intervention, he deserved to celebrate the feast of the Assumption among the household of the faith.

## V. Maiolus’s patience is tested by this. The barbarians are punished

Since nothing occurs on earth without cause, as Scripture bears witness, we reasonably believe that it pleased divine providence for a man distinguished in holiness to be tossed about by so many misfortunes, so that the man of God, worn down by adversity, might thereby advance, and a benefit granted to mortals by divine gift might result.

Although, in the conduct of this present life, he contracted certain things from human weakness, on account of which he would say, “Forgive us our debts”—for “if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves”—he nevertheless strove, as far as he could, to preserve himself unstained from this world.

But however pure he might seem, we are nevertheless compelled, according to the Lord’s judgment, to confess what we do not dare deny: that he still needed the supreme Teacher to wash his feet, so that in him might be fulfilled what is said: “Let the holy person be sanctified still” (Apoc. II, 11).

Therefore this tribulation was for the man of God a test of patience. For, as Augustine says, no human being possesses such great righteousness that the tribulation of temptation is not necessary to him, either to perfect, confirm, or prove his virtue.

But by the just judgment of God, from the same source from which a trial came upon the venerable father, just punishment followed those who had afflicted him. For they had occupied the narrow passes among the Alps and ambushed those traveling to the thresholds of the apostles without warning.

But when the man who was greatly loved by the Almighty was captured by them, divine vengeance came upon them directly, through the merit of his holiness.

## VI. A disaster arises among them to avenge the injury done to the man of God

To avenge the injury done to the man of God, disaster arose among them. Gradually they began to fail in strength, to such an extent that they admitted with their own mouths that they understood themselves to be punished by a divine blow.

Although they had been enriched with the most noble spoils of the man of God, they suffered greater and greater hardships day after day and began to seek their own quarters at Fraxinetum by the familiar paths.

Meanwhile, after the Christians had reconnoitered their route, the barbarians were traveling securely through the Alps in their customary manner. From far away they heard the sound of those rushing upon them with an attack. The whole forest echoed with the cries of the approaching men and the blare of the trumpets; the hills resounded with the noise.

At once a cold tremor ran through the barbarians’ hard bones. Struck by divine dread, they perceived no aid except the protection of flight.

There was then a great battle between the Christians and the fleeing barbarians. Since the power of resistance had been divinely taken from the latter’s minds, they withdrew, striving only to expose their unprotected backs to their pursuers.

While they fled, many were captured and very many were put to death. Those who escaped for a time and thus postponed their death chose the brow of a certain promontory as a place of refuge.

Yet they would have fallen more honorably amid the weapons of their enemies. For that promontory appears to be cut off on every side by precipitous cliffs, so that, except on one side of the slope, it denies every possibility of passage.

When the Christians occupied this side, and no route of escape remained for the barbarians—and when they could not turn our men away from the siege by any gift—they searched out a low place by which they might lower themselves through leaps to the bottom.

It was inevitable that they should seek the depths, upon whom heavenly wrath had fallen.

## VII. Maiolus receives the sacred books

Meanwhile the heavens turned, and night rushed from the Ocean, enveloping the earth and the heavens in great darkness. All fell silent; but there was no rest for the wretched men, who hastened to complete their undertaking.

At last, with Satan hindering them, they did not reach the place they had explored. Instead, from the summit of the lofty rock they cast themselves into the deep below throughout the night.

When day began to dawn, our men, astonished at the magnitude of the heavenly victory, desired to give thanks to the one by whose powerful will they saw the hostile army overthrown.

They encountered and captured some of those who had escaped drowning on a more remote side of the mountain. These men asked to be washed in the saving bath—for, as we said above (chapter 4), the man of God had instructed them in Christ through saving words. Having been joined to the body of Mother Church, they were accustomed to report how greatly the Almighty had glorified his servant among the barbarians.

The finest spoils were then gathered and distributed in equal portions among the worshipers of Christ. But although blessed Maiolus was absent in body, all who were present judged it wholly unworthy that he should be excluded from the distribution, since he had been present in merit when the enemies were put to flight.

They testified that, to avenge the injury done to him, the enemies had been overthrown by heavenly victory. Therefore they sent to the blessed man, as his share, the sacred books that the barbarians had taken from him.

Thus the Almighty, having brought down the impious through the merits of his servant, freed the way for all who were traveling to Rome.

## VIII. He Refuses the Roman Pontificate

Not long afterward, when the Roman see had been deprived of its proper shepherd, that same servant of God was compelled, at the joint request of Otto II and his mother, [Col. 0769C] to return to Italy from the regions of Gaul. Received by mother and son with the highest honor, he began to be pressed by continual entreaties to accept the summit of apostolic dignity. But he could not in any way allow the ambition of exaltation to advance upon him, since he desired abasement more than exaltation. He did not wish to abandon the little flock which Christ had been pleased to entrust to him; and he wished to live in poverty with the one who had descended from the heavenly summit into poverty.

But when he was compelled by both authorities, he sought to devise a delay and asked for time. Then he turned to the aid of prayer, so that divine revelation might grant him knowledge of what he ought to do and what answer he should give to so great a power. When he rose from prayer, a book of apostolic readings happened to lie before his eyes. [Col. 0769D] Opening it, he found at the very beginning of the margin the passage by whose instruction he believed himself divinely guided. He began to read aloud to those accompanying him what he found inserted there:

“See to it that no one deceives you through philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ” (Colossians 2:8).

He acknowledged that he ought to carry out with every effort whatever the divine reading suggested. Again and again, through alternating appeals, the emperor and the holy mother begged him; the noble bishops who were present persisted, and they pleaded that the imperial request be fulfilled.

But he, enlightened by divine grace, took care to excuse himself with prudent skill.

“I recognize,” he said, “that I lack those qualities which befit an apostolic man; nor do I seem fit to bear the burden of so great a dignity, nor is it proper for anyone to assume a load whose collapse he cannot avoid. Finally, I and the Romans, just as we differ in our regions, so we differ greatly in our customs. If I adapt myself to them, I shall be deprived of my monastic profession. Therefore acquire another, for you can know with certainty that in this life I shall not ascend to the apostolic summit, nor shall I ever abandon the flock entrusted to me.”

From this we can clearly gather that this servant of God possessed great humility: when requested by the supreme earthly ruler, he delayed ascending to the apostolic summit. Yet what he delayed when requested, many far inferior men—whom neither literary learning nor an honorable manner of life advanced—would, if they could, thrust themselves forward voluntarily; they would subject themselves to every kind of contempt through multiplied entreaties, and, in order to be raised to so great a height of dignity, would not hesitate willingly to condemn themselves to the great plague of simony by promising a substantial gift.

But the man of God, whom humility—the teacher of the virtues—taught inwardly, and in whose spirit evangelical poverty reigned, although he was distinguished by the renown of an exceptional way of life, therefore refused to be exalted by temporal rank, so that, removed from worldly business, he might devote himself more firmly to the service of the Almighty; and, distant from the world, might always become nearer to God.

Desiring secrecy, the holy man, filled with divine power,

Was no more skilled at avoiding external favors

Than the frequent comforts of his attendants.

[Col. 0770C] By vow he had resolved to cherish enduring concealment,

And to lead a life free from the court for as long as it should last.

Yet the promise of great Jesus remains unshaken:

He does not permit the city set upon the mountains to be hidden from view.

Whatever glory, withdrawing from human sight, is concealed by his beautiful merits,

Grace reveals by illuminating it with extraordinary signs.

And wherever he had easily directed his steps along the roads,

In cities and villages alike, the crowd came rushing to meet him,

Stirred by his illustrious deeds,

And although the long labor was easily and securely borne—

## IX. He Rebukes the Emperor for His Quarrel with His Mother and Reconciles Him to Her

At about the same time, the emperor mentioned above was angry with his mother because a false accusation was being brought against her before him. Through false informers he was so provoked against her—as though she were a squanderer of the commonwealth and the one who had driven him from power—that he threatened in turn to expel her from the kingdom. None of his leading men attempted to approach him or to remove the false charge from the most holy mother. They neglected to defend her against the charge of falsehood, although she had raised them to the highest degrees of dignity. They all offered the same excuse: they did not dare contradict the imperial majesty.

Behold, urgent messages were carried by the entreaties of all who belonged to the pious party: he should go as quickly as possible and come to the aid of his beloved empress; no safety remained for her unless, having lost her possessions, she also withdrew from the kingdom, with her life in peril:

… he kindles his anger with words,

[Col. 0771A] and, impatient of delay, immediately demands arms.

Swiftly he takes up arms and clothes his limbs in familiar armor.

He had vowed, for the sake of fidelity, to expose his breast

To whatever death fortune might bring.

But when he arrived, he immediately confronted the emperor and rebuked him publicly before everyone.

“Look,” he said, “you who have been raised to the height of passing dignity: why do you despise the commands of truth? He is able to reduce you to the lowest condition who raised you to the heights of mortals.”

When the emperor heard this threat, he suddenly trembled and replied in submissive speech, humbly asking in what respect he had despised the commands of truth.

The man of God said to him:

“It is the command of the one who, although he was God, was born from a virgin’s womb and deigned in the Gospel to submit himself to his mother, that parents be honored. For the Evangelist says: ‘He went down with them to Nazareth and was subject to them.’ If he who made all things by the power of his divinity subjected himself to his mother, why has your arrogant presumption persuaded you to become proud against the mother of him who formed you from vile clay?”

At these words, the emperor restrained the flames of his anger, laid aside his monstrous fury, and declared that he would obey Father Maiolus’s commands in everything. At last, in obedience to the most holy father’s order, he went before his mother, threw himself at her feet, and thereafter, obedient to her as a son to his mother, was never found to have offended her in anything.

Thus he who stood preeminent as the highest prince among mortals, whom no one dared approach in order to reconcile him with his mother, was compelled by the sole command of this man to restrain the crime, make satisfaction to his mother, and obey her as was proper. It is therefore plainly clear that this man, endowed with great elevation of mind, clung to the power above, by which he was able through a command to accomplish what no one had dared attempt through supplication. Because he clung to the one for whom nothing is impossible, he deserved to receive from him the power to command one whose dominion subjected the princes of the earth.

## X. He Foretells the Death of Otto I and Then of Otto II

Among the other miracles that the Lord performed to reveal the merits of his servant, he graciously instructed him with the spirit of prophecy, so that he often foretold future events and announced things absent to those present as though they were present.

Once, while returning from Rome, he said with sighs and tears to the brothers with whom he was traveling:

“Last night in my sleep I saw a monstrous lion, shut up in a cage and bound with an iron chain. Therefore know beyond doubt that the emperor Otto will depart from human affairs this year.”

The outcome proved that this was so. For when he had soon afterward returned to Provence and was staying there for a few days in one of his own cells, a messenger arrived from the regions of Alemannia and reported that the emperor mentioned above had departed this life.

But just as the man of God then reported to the brothers the death of the absent man as though it were present—for the death of the great emperor, although he was far away, had been revealed to him—so afterward he foretold at Verona, as we have related above, the death of that emperor’s son, exactly as it occurred.

For he took both the emperor’s hands in his own, clasped his face, and said:

“If you would heed Brother Maiolus’s counsel, you would turn back from where you have come. Know for certain that if you proceed to Rome, where you intend to go, you will never again see the kingdom of your birth; instead, in Rome, to which you are traveling, you will have your tomb.”

The outcome later proved true this prediction also, which the servant of God had made.

## XI. He Heals a Count

At one time, while he was staying in the regions of Alemannia, news of his arrival spread widely, and an urgent delegation from a certain count came to him. For a long time the count had been weighed down by an excessive illness. Increasing daily in its harmful effects, it had infected his whole body so completely that he could neither rise from his bed nor turn from one side to the other. Food and drink had become so repulsive to him that his body seemed at once like an image consumed by extreme fasting.

Therefore, by a delegation sent to him, he humbly begged the blessed man’s compassion that his weakness might be relieved by some of the food prepared by God’s servant for his own sustenance.

The man whose heart overflowed with mercy received the bread on which he fed, together with almonds and fragrant spices. Then the servant of God turned to his companions:

“Trusting in our familiarity, this man makes his request through his prayers, asking that the Almighty Physician assist him through our prayers. Therefore God’s clemency must be entreated, so that he may deserve relief from his bodily affliction. For he who healed the official’s son by an imperial word is able, while we are absent, to restore this man to his former health.”

As soon as the man of God devoted himself to prayer with the brothers, the one who was absent immediately began to improve. When those who had been sent returned, they learned that their lord had begun to improve at the very hour when they had departed from the man of God.

Afterward he nourished himself with the gift of the man of God and recovered such complete health that, after a few days, he himself went to the blessed man, threw himself at his feet, and offered immense thanks for the benefit he had received.

## XII. Other Miracles

In the region of Viviers, a noble matron was afflicted by a long illness. When she learned that the man of God was staying in the cell of Saint Saturninus, she immediately sought him through a messenger, asking him to bless water for her to drink and to send her oil for anointing, sanctified by the sign of his right hand.

When she received from the man of God what she had requested, the bodily affliction immediately began to withdraw, and her weakened limbs began to be restored to their former function. Once the illness had been driven away, her whole body soon became so healthy that it was as though she had never been infected by any disease.

## XIII

Nor should the following be suppressed in silence: the visit of the blessed man to the one whom he restored to health has until now been celebrated in a widely known account.

His proper name was Hildebrannus, and his occupational surname was Monetarius, “the Moneyer.” He carefully guarded the office he held so that it would not be diminished in comparison with those of his colleagues. Since he was distinguished by good morals, he became known to the blessed man.

Struck by bodily illness, he began to suffer severe distress. When he saw that he was not being relieved of his illness, but felt himself increasingly burdened as the bodily affliction grew, he spent lavishly—as wealthy people commonly do when they believe they can redeem themselves through their resources—on physicians and priests, on monasteries, and on the poor.

Although these expenditures relieved him of the burden of his offenses, he was nevertheless oppressed by an excessive illness. He had already begun to be troubled by the prospect of death, since the severity of the disease had brought him to despair of life.

While he was considering that his final hour might overtake him, word reached him in advance that the blessed Maiolus was coming to Pavia. Seeking to anticipate his arrival by means of a messenger, he begged that Maiolus deem him worthy of a visit.

The most blessed man, filled with compassion, did not deny the petitioner the arrival he desired. The sick man was immediately so filled with joy at the presence of the blessed man that it was as though manifest health had entered with him. [Col. 0773B] At once the man of the Lord approached the sick man and did not disdain to touch his body, weakened by illness, with his healing right hand. As the long illness felt that salutary touch, it fled; health hastened to return so quickly that the man who had long lain sick in bed was able, on the third day, to go wherever he wished in good health.

## XIV

It now seems appropriate to insert the following, which is known to have been reported by widespread and celebrated rumor.

A certain man was fleeing the presence of his own lord, whom he had gravely offended. For he had deliberately delivered his companion to death, and therefore no human being could restore him to the favor of his master. The lord sought him everywhere, so that he too might exact a fitting penalty from him on behalf of his companion.

To escape the danger of death, he trusted no place, but wandered through various regions. By chance he came to the place where the man of God happened to be staying. When God’s servant saw that he was fit to serve in the military, he asked why he was wandering about. It became known that this was the man’s own lord, and the reason why he traveled through different places was disclosed.

The man of God took pity on him, offered him the consolation of hospitality, and promised that he would obtain the favor of his lord. His lord was a vigorous man-at-arms, powerful in temporal affairs, and so immovable in the judgment he had formed in his mind that no one could induce him to change it because of difficulty. Therefore he was hard to appease whenever he became angry.

Soon afterward the man of God approached him and began gently to ask him to pardon his servant. At the voice of God’s servant he was so violently terrified, and his voice stuck so firmly in his throat, that he had no answer to give. Immediately he threw himself prostrate upon the ground, fell at the feet of the man of God, and commended himself to his prayers.

His fellow soldiers had previously asked him on behalf of the servant; both greater and lesser men had joined their entreaties to him, yet none had been able to bend him to spare the servant. But, by the merit of Blessed Maiolus, God’s favor cast him down before everyone, so that he granted pardon to the servant no less readily than the command of God’s servant had decreed.

Thus the Lord works this daily in his faithful, as the page of sacred authority bears witness: he rejects the prudence of the prudent and glorifies those who glorify him.

Because the wretched man fled to the help of the blessed man, he obtained from him a double benefit: he was granted the grace of the Lord, and by repentance he wiped away his guilt.

## XV

Once, while traveling through a certain forest, he proceeded alone after sending the others ahead according to his usual custom. In the midst of tears and frequent sighs, sleep gradually overtook him. The road along which he was traveling was obstructed by the fall of a tree, so that, if he rode beneath its trunk, he would easily have suffered injury unless he carefully protected himself by lowering his head.

When the horse he was riding reached the fallen tree, it remained motionless, as though bound fast to a stake. Then, in a dream, he saw a boy of extraordinary appearance holding the horse by the bridle so that it could not proceed.

When he awoke and saw the tree before his eyes, he revered the mercy of the Almighty, rejoicing that through an angel he had escaped the danger of death. But because he was separated from the others and was offering himself to God in tears, he deserved to be protected from injury by the angel to whom his tearful prayer was being carried before God.

## XVI

The following event, which occurred while he was staying at Pavia, seems especially unworthy to be passed over in silence.

To avoid the gaze of the crowd and thereby cleanse the eye of his mind from vainglory, he anticipated the canonical hours in the silence of night. He went to the church of the most blessed confessor Saint Syrus and, with abundant tears, devoted himself to prayer before the door, asking for indulgence.

**Note:** [Col. 0773D] Saint Syrus was the first bishop of Pavia and also the patron of the principal church. Count Otto, son of King Arduino, made a distinguished donation to that church in the year 1009; you may read it in the Sebusian library, page 234. [Col. 0774D]

One night, when he rose for his customary work and intended, as usual, to go to the church, the one who habitually envies good deeds tried to frighten him through a deceitful attack, if he could.

A deluge of rain, as commonly happens in winter, made the journey difficult. Moreover, a cloud had covered the sky and concealed the glittering stars. Then the tempter began to place before his mind both the density of the darkness and the difficulty of the journey.

But the man of God immediately recognized the suggestions of the evil spirit and, without delay, set out upon the journey he had planned. The author of evil nevertheless tried to ambush the man of God in many ways along the way. But since he could not harm him in any respect, he extinguished the light carried before him in a lantern.

Those who were accompanying the man of God were thrown into confusion and did not know by what light they should proceed. But the man of God did not doubt that the hater of good had caused this event. He restrained his companions’ fear by a sign, certain and confident that the one before whose door he stood could relight the extinguished candle.

Yet because he trusted more in the most blessed Syrus than in his own power, he deserved to attain through action what he had believed by faith. For as soon as he rose from prayer with the brothers, they saw the candle burning by divine fire—the candle which the devil had dared to extinguish for their destruction.

This miracle greatly benefited the brothers, for when they understood how powerful the prayer of the just was, they devoted themselves to prayer with greater devotion.

## XVII. The Book of Saint Dionysius Is Unharmed by Fire

At one time, while reading the *Hierarchies* of blessed Dionysius the Areopagite, and, as usual, storing away during the night in the library of his breast what he had read during the day through meditation, he was overtaken by sleep. It happened that the candle which supplied light to him as he read fell upon the page he was reading.

But what will Christ not accomplish in his saints? The devouring flame consumed the candle, but the leaf upon which it was burning suffered no damage from the heat. The flame possessed the power to burn the candle, but lost that power when it came to injuring the page.

**Note:** [Col. 0775D] Saint Odilo writes that this occurred when Maiolus was once in the monastery of the most holy Dionysius. [Col. 0776D] Nalgodus adds that, after distributing the substance of the word of God among the monks, he delivered a sermon to them.

The man of God immediately awoke from sleep and was greatly distressed, thinking that the book—which could scarcely be found anywhere—had been destroyed by the fire. But when he brushed away the ash and saw no mark of injury on the surface, he offered immense thanks to the one by whose power the fire had lost the force of its nature: although it consumed the dry fuel resting above the candle, it could not injure the book in any way.

## XVIII. He Visits William, Duke of Provence, and Rescues Those Shipwrecked

When William, prince of the Provençals, felt himself weighed down by his final destiny, he believed that he could be saved from the death of the soul through the merits of Maiolus. Having summoned Maiolus to the town of Avignon, he ordered him to pitch his tent on the island which divides the Rhône beneath the aforesaid fortress, so that he might avoid the crowd’s gathering.

But when news of his arrival spread throughout the surrounding region, an innumerable multitude began to converge upon him from every direction. Each person strove to get ahead of the others, and everyone tried to cross first by boat to the man of God.

A ship then appeared so old that, with its cracks open, it could easily have been overwhelmed by the bilge water rushing into it. When those skilled in navigation tried to direct this vessel, overloaded with a multitude of both sexes, toward the man of God, the force of the overflowing river submerged it amid the waves.

The sight was extraordinary: those who were seeking Maiolus’s protection through the safeguard of his prayers were now endangered by shipwreck. Men with women, and women with the little children whom they were still nursing at the breast, were already being engulfed by the deep river when news of this disaster reached the ears of the man of God.

But Christ, who hears those who cry out to him, did not delay in glorifying his beloved Maiolus.

On the bank of the Rhône mentioned above stood a church built by the ancients in honor of Saint Martin. The man of the Lord went toward it while the water covered those who had been submerged. When he saw none of them, he raised his pious eyes with tears, then lowered his sorrowful face toward the ground.

Although those standing nearby did not know at the time what he had prayed in silence for a little while, he nevertheless deserved to obtain effectively what he had sought with a devout mind. For after he had made the sign of the cross and prayed for a short time with bowed face, as we have said, people of different sexes and ages soon appeared swimming in the whirlpool. The violent current had twisted them beneath the water.

The children were carried along the surface of the waves; the women spun about in the river, their garments spread out; and the men tried by swimming to reach the bank. Skilled sailors rushed to them with small boats and drew them all from the river’s abyss.

Another thing also seems remarkable: when a count’s servant was carrying six loaves to the man of God, although he too was caught in the same shipwreck as the others, the conveyance of the entrusted gift protected him so well that he not only emerged unharmed but also brought three of the loaves out of the water untouched.

## XIX. Maiolus Grows More Fervent as Death Approaches; At the King’s Request He Undertakes to Reform the Monastery of Saint Dionysius; He Dies at Souvigny

Thus Maiolus, at an age when others ordinarily live more indulgently, strove to subject himself to the service of the Lord through arduous labor. As though he had only just arrived and youthful strength were surging through his entire body, he devoted himself to divine service with incredible fervor of mind.
