He did not allow his body, exhausted by old age, to rest at all from its customary work. Two years before his death, his body began to be deprived of its strength more than usual, and from this he recognized that the time of his summons was approaching.

Therefore he no longer wished to go out publicly. He desired instead to remain either in the monastery or in one of his cells for the benefit of the brothers: there he could correct them with diligent care and advance them toward better things through paternal admonition; or, with everyone else removed, he could more frequently remain alone with God alone and devote himself more attentively, in continual alternation, either to prayer or to reading.

Although this had been a special concern throughout his whole life, he labored at it with particular zeal as death approached. He often grieved when he recalled spiritual men whom he had seen flourishing in divine religion and fighting courageously in defense of the holy Church. Remembering them, he lamented that he would be deprived of all consolation in this world. Therefore divine reading alone provided him solace.

For this reason he desired in every way to be released and to be with Christ.

At that time the king of the Franks was pressing him with excessive insistence to arrange the monastery of Saint Dionysius according to the teaching of blessed Father Benedict. Although he knew that the end of his days was already very near, he did not refuse to set out for this purpose. He considered it a good completion of his virtues if, having joined to himself in justice and holiness the professors of the monastic order, he could leave them united by the bond of charity.

He took the road toward the territory of Auvergne and there, in one of his cells—namely at Souvigny, now a very famous place—he began to suffer his final illness. At once the wisest of men recognized that the final hour of his dissolution had arrived.

Then there was mourning and grief for all, one voice of lamentation. When the brothers asked him to whom he would entrust the flock committed to him, he is said to have addressed them as follows:

“You will have Jesus, the supreme shepherd, as its protector.”

Because he was leaving the exile of pilgrimage and joyfully going toward his true dwelling, he often recited these verses:

“Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house and the place where your glory dwells,” and so forth.

“How lovely are your dwelling places, Lord of hosts! My soul longs and faints for the courts of the Lord,” and so forth.

“I have chosen to be despised in the house of my God rather than to dwell in the tents of sinners.”

Thus, under God’s protection, with all the members of his body sound and unharmed—with exceptionally clear sight, pure hearing, and a sound memory—just as he had remained free from the corruption of the flesh and had known no stain upon his snow-white chastity, he reached his end, about to obtain an immortal reward.

When the brothers asked whether he was suffering anything, he replied that he had no distress, but saw everything quiet and peaceful, and that he saw the good things of the Lord in the land of the living.

Then they prostrated themselves before him on the ground and began to entreat him:

“Father most blessed, absolve us who have been entrusted to you in the manner of a father; protect us by your most holy prayers. Your faith and your works unite you to Christ, and therefore whatever you ask of him you will more readily obtain while present with him.”

When he had absolved them and strengthened them with his most holy prayers, he ceased ordinary conversation. He now despised human things and raised his eyes upward to heaven. He repeated the same verses until the departure of his soul, so that when an ear was brought close, what he was saying could scarcely be heard. He also frequently traced the sign of the holy cross upon himself with his holy right hand.

Nor does Christ permit his beloved servant through the ages

To be long tormented or to remain apart from the kingdom he has received.

For one whose life was martyrdom, the Ruler invites him, weary from the burden of labors,

To the heights above.

His spirit, burning to emerge from its constricting bonds,

Leaps forth and is carried free into the clear air,

While heaven sings hymns and sounds a joyful cry of triumph.

[Col. 0778B] His companions from above surrounded him with wondrous splendor,

And they carried the joyful victor across the fiery stars,

And set him before the throne of the supreme King for all ages.

He slept with his fathers on the fifth day before the Ides of May. He was buried in the basilica of Blessed Peter, where many benefits are granted through his most holy merits. Our Lord Jesus Christ reigns forever; to him, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, be honor, power, and glory throughout the immortal ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0777]

# The Election of Saint Odilo During the Life of Saint Maiolus, Abbot of Cluny

*(Year 988)*

[Col. 0777C] When, first through the sacred laws given by patriarchs and prophets, then also through human magistrates and kings, the movements of peoples were restrained by divine dispensation; and afterward, when the fiery sword at the entrance of paradise had been extinguished by the fountain of Christ’s side, so that the kingdom of God might be seized with greater violence, the condition of the churches began to be shaped by the pious conduct of apostolic men, and finally the regular order began to be established in the minds of subjects by holy men and abbots, so that through it the ascent to the heavenly homeland might appear easy to those who traveled along it.

Thus it happens that the more a person advances by examples of piety, raising himself toward lofty things through paternal care and offering his subjects guidance in following him toward heaven, the more he will receive from the Lord who rewards him a manifold return of reward and filial affection.

And because whatever is done wrong by subjects is attributed to prelates, the example of an evil life and the negligence of subjects are punished, according to the judgment of divine examination, by the unquenchable fire of Gehenna.

Therefore I, Maiolus, unworthy abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter of Cluny, wish it to be known to those present and to those yet to come, generation after generation, that, reflecting upon these and similar matters, exhausted by age and weakened also in bodily functions, while I recognize that I am less fit for pastoral care, having been forewarned by the chapter of blessed Benedict to take concern for appointing an abbot, together with all my brothers, sons, and fellow servants, we have chosen the religious Odilo—formerly a cleric, brother, and son among the monks of blessed Peter—and have decreed that he be abbot, lest the order decline through the insolence of our infirmity or suffer any rejection, but, with God’s favor, always be advanced toward better things.

And lest anyone offer a device of excuse—for just as one who unworthily and rashly aspires to governance is censured, so one who is worthy but refuses it is rightly considered bound—we have sought the counsel of the bishops and abbots.

Just as the monastery of Cluny, founded by Duke William with God as its author, consecrated in the name of the prince of the apostles, distinguished by the privileges of the Roman see, confirmed by royal decrees, and organized by the venerable abbots Lord Berno and Odo, as well as by Haimard, is known to have been established, so, together with all the abbeys, places, and cells acquired wherever they may be in their time or ours, we entrust them to the aforesaid brother for governance.

We bind him under the bonds of obedience, with divine favor, both to preserve the order according to blessed Benedict and the institutions of our fathers, and to administer the possessions with complete integrity; and unanimously we proclaim him abbot.

We order the account of this election and ordination to be confirmed, as we have said, by the written testimony of the primates, Count Henry our advocate, Duke Henry, and Otto. In the name of Christ we have confirmed the ordination, regularly celebrated, and have asked our fathers and brothers to confirm it in writing.

Done happily at the monastery of Cluny. Amen.

I, Maiolus the abbot, have given my consent to this election and have signed it.

King Rodulf. Burchard, archbishop. [Col. 0779B] Hugh, bishop of Geneva. Aguricus, bishop of Lausanne. Hugh, bishop. Teuto, abbot. Richfred, abbot. [Col. 0780A] Ermenfred, bishop. Burchard, count. Lambert, count. Adalbert, count.

In addition, 177 monks subscribed below; they too signed this election.

Leotald, archbishop. Walter, bishop. Hugh, abbot. Wago, abbot. Theobald, abbot. Warembert, abbot. William, abbot. Maiolus, provost. [Col. 0780B] Walter, provost. Gundulf. David. Aguricus. Sendelenus.

[Col. 0779]

# The Chartulary of Saint Maiolus

*(From the Cluniac Library)*

## I. Charter of King Lothair Concerning Saint Amandus, Granted to the Monastery of Cluny in the Time of Abbot Maiolus

*(Year 960)*

[Col. 0779C]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Lothair, by the grace of God king.

We follow the customs of our royal predecessors when we graciously hear our faithful in appropriate petitions. Therefore we wish it to be known to the minds of the whole holy Church of God and of all our faithful, both present and future, that my lady mother, the most glorious Queen Gerberga, with the consent of her faithful and ours, came into the serenity of our presence with maternal commands and requests, asking that we should subject to the monastery of Cluny and its rulers the monastery situated in the county of Trahesin, dedicated in honor of Saint Amandus, since it was without rulers and was like an uninhabitable place, together with all that belonged to it: villages and all estates, male and female dependents, meadows, vineyards, woods, waters, the courses of waters, returns, and exits.

Granting our assent to her request, as was equitable, we received it in this decree … [lacuna] … and granted the aforesaid monastery of Saint Amandus, with complete integrity, as has already been said, to the aforesaid monastery of Cluny, on the condition that, insofar as God should supply them assistance, they build it up and make the place habitable as they are able, so that Almighty God may continually be praised there with the saints, and so that my most glorious lady mother, who established this arrangement, may, by Christ’s generosity, be granted the reward of eternal happiness together with us.

And so that this may be believed more firmly and possessed more securely, we have confirmed it with our own hand and ordered it to be marked with the ring of our authority.

Sign of Lord Lothair, the most glorious king.

Gebo, humble treasurer, acting in place of Artold, archbishop and supreme chancellor, has acknowledged this.

Given on the ninth day before the Kalends of December, in the fifth year of the reign of the most glorious King Lothair, indiction 3. Enacted at Dijon in the palace [reading uncertain: *ter.*]. Amen.

## II. Charter of Theobald, Count of Chalon, by Which He Confirmed the Donation of the Monastery of Saint Marcellus of Chalon Made to Maiolus, Abbot of Cluny

I, Theobald, count of Chalon, in the name of God, send greetings in the Lord to all the sons of the holy Church.

I heard from my predecessors and from elderly men of the neighborhood that the most noble Count Gaufredus, who after the death of our most distinguished and most Christian grandfather, Count Lambert, took his wife, my grandmother Adheidis, the countess, approached Mayolus, the abbot of blessed memory, and entrusted to him the monastery in the suburb of the city of Chalon, magnificently built by Guntrannus, a most noble and religious king, where the body of blessed Marcellus the martyr rests. He did so on the condition that Mayolus should reform the observance of the monastic order, which had almost been abolished, and cultivate the rights and possessions belonging to that place; and that he himself and his successors, the abbots of Cluny, should perpetually have and possess it.

The aforesaid Count Gaufredus made this entrustment or donation to Lord Mayolus with the counsel of his wife and of his son Hugh, then a cleric and later a bishop, with Duke Almeric’s consent and approval. Later, under the most serene King Robert, my uncle, Lord Hugh, count and bishop, in the presence of that king and of the counts and bishops of this region, handed over the gift of the aforesaid monastery to Lord Odilo, abbot and successor of Abbot Mayolus, so that he might have, hold, and possess the place by the same right as his predecessor.

I, then, by God’s grace Count Theobald, approve, desire, and confirm what our predecessors and relatives gave to God, to Saint Peter, and to the Cluniac place; and I cause my wife and my faithful men to approve and confirm it. As long as I live, I shall be its witness and helper. After my death, whoever comes against this restoration shall not doubt that he will incur the anger of almighty God.

The sign of Count Theobald, who approved and confirmed this charter and ordered his faithful men and friends to confirm it.

The sign of Ermentrudis, his wife.

The sign of Hugh of Mont-Paon.

The sign of Ansedeus of Naviliacum.

The sign of Tetardus of Raon.

## Around the year of the Lord 996. Letaldus, a monk of Miciacum near Orléans, of the Order of Saint Benedict

## Historical Notice

Letaldus, a monk of Miciacum, wrote a book *On the Miracles of Saint Maximinus, Abbot of Miciacum*, which Jean Mabillon published in volume 1 of *The Centuries of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, p. 598. We think that this same Letaldus is the one who polished the *Life of Saint Julian, Bishop of Le Mans*, although Possevinus considers this monk to have been from Le Mans. In those *Miracles*, Letaldus inserts a succession of the bishops of Orléans and of the abbots of Miciacum; he testifies in chapters 11 and following that he lived toward the end of the tenth century, in the time of Bishops Ermentheus and Arnulf and of Abbot Ammon. He must be distinguished from another Letaldus, abbot of Miciacum, whom this work discusses in chapter 4.

(*Fabricius, Bibliotheca medii et infimi Latinitatis*)

## Life of Saint Julian, First Bishop of Le Mans  
### By Letaldus, a monk of Miciacum

*(In the Bollandists, January, volume 2.)*

## Dedication Letter to Avesgaudus, Bishop of Le Mans

### 1. Letaldus the brother sends greetings in the Lord to the most reverend father Avesgaudus

Moved by a desire for both spiritual and bodily healing, I had approached the memory of the most excellent bishop Julian, and had been permitted to enjoy the sweet address of your affection. The same force of charity, which inclined the mind of your sublimity toward my insignificance, imposed upon me a burden—if I should prove capable of bearing it—lovable and agreeable; because I was unequal to it, not so much agreeable as deserving of reverence: namely, that I myself should weave into a clearer and more polished order those things which had been written by the ancients about the deeds of that glorious father in language which seemed to you uncultivated, and should clothe them, as it were, with a certain whitening, for the edification of those who hear them.

### 2.

I have called this work deserving of reverence rather than agreeable because what must be said and written before the face of truth ought to be treated with the gravity of great reverence, lest from the very thing by which God is believed to be appeased he be provoked still further to anger; for nothing pleases him except what is true.

There are, however, some who, while wishing to exalt the deeds of the saints, stumble against the light of truth—as though the glory of the saints could be raised up by falsehood; yet if they had been followers of falsehood, they could never have climbed to the summit of holiness. Therefore what truth accomplished must be told with truth. For if some Father is said to have performed a miracle, it is not the human being but God who works it, who is able to work in and through whomever he wishes.

When, therefore, I recount such marvelous and splendid things about the deeds of this most excellent Father, I neither distrust his merits nor doubt Christ’s power. But when I find these same things in others, I do not clearly see whom one ought rather to believe—unless perhaps the weight of the authority of some distinguished teacher should draw me away from error and, like the weight of an anchor, steady my wavering mind. For many things have been written in the Acts of the aforesaid Father which I also find, in the same sense and almost in the same words, in the accounts of the blessed martyrs Clement and Dionysius and of Saint Furcaeus the confessor.

### 3.

As for the time in which that great man flourished, I have inferred it from the book of Gregory of Tours. In book 1 of his histories, under the consulship of Decius and Gratus, he states that very many bishops were ordained by Sixtus, the apostolic bishop of the Roman see, and sent into Gaul to preach the word of God. Their names and the places to which they were assigned I shall partly give below.

[Note: This was the year of Christ 250, when, after the slaughter of Saint Fabianus, the see was either vacant, as some maintain, or certainly Saint Cornelius was already governing the Church. Nevertheless, these men could have been sent into Gaul by Sixtus either by the authority of Pope Cornelius or, before his election, on the advice of the Roman clergy, among whom Sixtus was prominent; shortly afterward he was placed at the helm of the Church, being fourth after him.]

Since blessed Dionysius is said by Saint Gregory to have been one of their number, and since the deeds of the glorious Father Julian relate that he came into Gaul with that same Saint Dionysius to preach, I think it is beyond doubt that he is shown to have lived under Decius, Valerian, and Gratus as consuls and under Sixtus, bishop of the Roman see; that same Sixtus and the archdeacon Laurentius were tested by that same Decius and, remaining steadfast in their confession of Christ, were crowned by victorious power.

[Note: Rather, Saints Sixtus II and Laurentius were killed under Valerian and Gallienus.]

But if Julian is said to have been sent by blessed Clement, neither the chronology nor the agreement of the ancients permits this. Blessed Clement was deported into exile at Chersonesus under Caesar Trajan; and between Trajan and Decius, under whom we conjecture that blessed Julian lived, many emperors intervened. A diligent reader can readily recognize this in the *Chronicles of Eusebius of Caesarea*, translated by Jerome.

### 4.

We have therefore confirmed, as far as we could, what we wrote about Saint Julian by the authority of the fathers who preceded us, and have published some things simply according to ancient tradition; others, however, which seemed less probable to us, we omitted. Yet nowhere do we advise anyone to distrust the merits of so great a Father. While, by God’s generosity, he performs such great and such marvelous works beside his sacred ashes, it is clear to all who rightly believe that he must have performed far greater and more splendid ones while he was still living in this world.

If this inarticulate rusticity of ours should contribute something either to usefulness or to devotion, we intend, with Christ the Lord’s generosity, to append also those things which have been performed in our own age at his sacred tomb, as soon as they come to our knowledge.

Certainly, as you requested, we have arranged the order of the responsories and antiphons. In them, to avoid tedium, we have composed single bodies from each mode; nor do we wish to depart entirely from the likeness of the ancient chant, lest we fabricate a barbarous or inexperienced melody, as it is said. For I do not approve the novelty of certain musicians who use such great dissimilarity that they disdain entirely to follow the ancient authors. Those who devote themselves to marriages prefer to beget children resembling human beings rather than produce the likeness of some hated monster.

## Author’s Prologue

### 5.

When the world was still enveloped in the darkness of errors and utterly ignorant of the brightness of the true light, and when the ancient cunning of the enemy was raging against the human race, which he had subjected to himself through the first parent, and when worship was being offered to the creature rather than to the Creator—for each person fashioned gods for himself to adore, either from dead human beings or from insensible matter—almighty God, taking pity on human errors lest his own creation should perish forever, brought forth his Word, equal and coeternal with himself, into human sight through the womb of an undefiled virgin as a true man for the life of the world.

Without any diminution of his divine nature, yet truly assuming our humanity without the stain of sin, he lived among human beings, granting the benefits of divinity and enduring the hardships of human frailty. Finally, he offered the flesh which he had taken from the Virgin for our redemption, and redeemed the human being whom he had created by no other price than his own life-giving and precious blood.

Having therefore become obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross, he destroyed the dominion of death, rescued his own from the very seats of Hell, and, accompanied by that ineffable, victorious procession of the conquered enemy, ascended to the right hand of God the Father to reign forever.

He therefore enlightened his Church, which he had acquired for himself by saving blood, through the coming of his Spirit, so that, while she was meanwhile to be exercised by the adversities of the world, she might be strengthened by the invisible armor of the Holy Spirit. Founded upon the rock of faith, she spread through every region of the world, so that, abandoning the vanity of idols, humanity might know the true God and pass from the error of ancestral sin and the filth of ancient paganism into the newness of life.

### 6.

But the ancient enemy, grieving that what he was losing was clearly being gained for God, turned every device of malice toward overthrowing the invincible refuge of the Church. With wicked persistence, in defense of falsehood he struck down some martyrs with the sword, fastened others to the gallows, submerged others in the sea, destroyed others by hunger, tortured others with fire, and tore others limb from limb. Raging with an unspeakable kind of slaughter, he attempted to conquer the Church of Christ.

But the more fiercely his savagery boiled over, the more the unconquerable steadfastness of the saints shone forth in glory. The more cruelly envy attacked them, the more splendid was the glory of their virtue.

### 7.

He therefore first had Nero as a minister of impiety against piety. Then, through the rulers who succeeded one another, increasing the growth of his wickedness for three hundred years and more, he shook the Church of Christ, but was utterly unable to overthrow it.

When it pleased him who allowed his faithful ones to be refined in the fire of temptation that, after so many storms, a serene day should dawn upon his household, the light of truth entered the summit of imperial power. The glory of the world having been laid beneath it, it began to have as defenders and protectors those whom, through the envy of the ancient enemy, it had until then held as hostile opponents.

Then, as after the harshness of a stormy winter,

> when the mildness of spring tempers the gentle breezes,  
> fragrant shrubs burst forth into flowers,  
> and rose gardens, long left bare, are adorned with renewed roses,  
> while the brightness of emerging lilies dazzles wondering eyes,

so, when peace had been restored to the Church, various men shone throughout the world. Wonderful in the light of their virtues and distinguished by the radiance of faith, they were set forth as examples for the gentle in heart who followed Christ’s footsteps.

## Here Begins the Life

## Chapter One: The People of Le Mans Converted by Saint Julian

### 8.

To establish in Gaul the foundation of the new faith and to raise up the still-unformed structure of the Church, heavenly piety sent magnificent and energetic men: Photinus to Lyons, Trophimus to Arles, Paul to Narbonne, Saturninus to Toulouse, Austremonius to the Auvernians, Martial to the Lemovices, Gatianus to the Turonians, Dionysius to the Parisians, and Julian to the people of Le Mans.

[Note: These saints are celebrated as follows: Photinus, 2 June; Trophimus, 19 December; Paul, 12 March; Saturninus, 19 November; Austremonius, 1 November; Martial, 30 June; Gatianus, 18 December; Dionysius, 9 October.]

### 9.

This Julian, therefore, most illustrious in Roman nobility, eloquent in speech, distinguished in justice, and highly renowned for the merit of his faith, was appointed by God as the first apostle to the city of Le Mans. Although he is not an apostle to others, he is one to the people of Le Mans. For, as the blessed Apostle also cries out concerning himself, they are his sign of apostleship in the Lord.

### 10.

This man of God, fortified by faith and girded with the sword of the Holy Spirit, approached the aforesaid city fearlessly to destroy errors and trample underfoot the vanities of demons. But while the novelty of his holy preaching became a stumbling block to some unbelievers and a cause of ridicule to others, the power of miracles rendered them astonished—those whom ancient and ingrained error had made contemptuous of hearing the way of truth.

For through the hands of the reverend bishop Christ performed such great miracles that by his word he drove out demons, cleansed lepers, and granted every sick person help through the medicine of the cross. Finally, when very many came to him to obtain bodily health, they returned, enlightened by the word of faith, with the salvation of their souls as well.

### 11.

This same venerable man, sheltered in a small dwelling outside the city, persevered day and night in his holy purpose. He scarcely took any care of his own body, devoting himself entirely to the salvation of those whom he was striving to withdraw from demonic error.

### 12.

When they had already been captivated by the sweetness of his miracles and illumined by the light of God, and were clinging to his holy fellowship, there arose a considerable complaint about the shortage of water. The man of God approached a place which he thought suitable, planted in the ground the point of the staff which he carried in his hand, and said in the hearing of all:

“Lord our God, who gave drink to your thirsty people in the wilderness from the hard rock, be present also to us, your servants. Open the treasury of your mercy, and command a spring of living water to be supplied to us from the hardness of this soil, so that those present may know that you are the true God, who at the end of the ages sent your Son into the world, so that those who believe in you might be brought into the true land of promise.”

When the faithful had answered, “Amen,” a most vigorous spring suddenly burst forth. It displayed the power of divinity and clearly demonstrated to all standing there the merit of the blessed man.

### 13.

Then those who had already believed were strengthened in faith, while those who were still held by the error of paganism fell at the saint’s feet, begging to be initiated into the sacraments of the holy faith.

It pleased them, therefore, to call this spring—or place—Centonomium, because, through the joy of its manifestation, the number of believers began to multiply as the interest of faith increased. Many there, through the sacrament of baptism, put off the old man and clothed themselves with the new, who was created according to God in the righteousness and holiness of truth.

### 14.

Thus not only ordinary people but also many of the most noble, laying aside the belts of military service and formerly proud necks submitting to the yoke of Christ, attached themselves to the holy man and rejoiced to be instructed by his sacred example.

When the radiance of so great a brightness had already traversed the entire province, like Lucifer the morning star announcing the Sun of righteousness, the city’s ruler, named Defensor—a glorious man and, according to the fleeting honors of this world, exceedingly powerful—struck by the novelty of so many miracles, summoned through intermediaries the bishop worthy of God and humbly begged him to come to him.

[Note: Is this Saint Defensor, the first bishop of Angers?]

### 15.

When the most faithful minister of Christ was approaching the ruler, he encountered before the door of the ruler’s palace a blind man who, falling down before him, begged for help. But after invoking Christ’s name and impressing upon him the sign of the cross, he restored him in an instant to his former health.

When the ruler heard this, he hurried forward, threw himself supplicating at the saint’s knees, and begged that he might deserve to become a participant in eternal life. The venerable bishop carefully instructed him in the word of God, catechized him, and, after a solemn fast had been completed, baptized him together with his entire household and a large crowd of nobles.

The ruler grew in such ardor of piety that he handed over his house to the holy man, so that he might build there a church suitable for divine worship and devote himself without any hindrance to winning souls for Christ. It is impossible, I think, to say how much joy and how great an eagerness produced daily gains for Christ and losses for the devil there.

Every age and both sexes flocked with the most ardent love to hear the word of the Lord, and each strove eagerly to outstrip the others in the holy purpose. They therefore handed over to the holy man a collection of their goods, so that the churches might be adorned with divine honors and the poor of Christ comforted with bodily nourishment.

### 16.

The faithful and prudent steward whom the Lord appointed over his household to give it its measure of wheat at the proper time was as diligent in distributing the word of God together with acts of piety as he was assiduous, according to apostolic instruction, in distributing earthly goods. To the children of the Church living under him in common, he faithfully divided them according to each person’s need.

Yet, amid these present cares, the eye of his mind was by no means dimmed toward the contemplation of eternal things. The more he was supported by transitory goods, the more eagerly he longed for the joys of the heavenly homeland. He knew well what was appropriate on the journey and what was owed in the homeland. On the journey he saw the wages of labor as necessary; in the homeland he desired with all his heart the reward of eternal blessedness.

There are some who labor in pastoral government but do not seek eternal rewards for that labor. Swollen with the honor of precedence, although they preach heavenly things in words, they seek earthly things with all their desire. But this bishop, worthy of God, though he shone with the splendor of virtues, was surrounded by the power of miracles, supported by the throngs of obedient peoples, and enriched by an abundance of temporal goods, did not succumb to any impediment of pleasure. Fixing his mind upon the giver of all good things, he placed present goods, as it were, behind his back, and faithfully set before his face the things promised to the saints in heaven.

## Chapter Two: Three Dead Men Raised

### 17.

In the city where the most blessed man was carrying out his pastoral watch there was a certain powerful and noble man named Anastasius, who had not yet submitted to the Christian faith.

His son, seized by a severe illness, brought to the point of death, finally expired. The father, unable to endure the grief of bereavement, ran to the man of God, crying out and saying:

“Servant of God Julian, who confess that Christ is the true God, by him whom you preach I adjure you: give me back my son.”

The man of God said to him:

“Anastasius, if you believe that he whom I preach is the true God, you will receive your son back in the present life, and you will obtain eternal life.”

Anastasius declared and said:

“If I receive my son alive again, I confess Christ to be the true God and renounce idols completely.”

The most blessed bishop went with him to the house where the boy’s lifeless body lay. While all were weeping and wondering what the blessed man would do, he took the dead boy’s hand and, lifting his tear-filled eyes toward heaven, said:

“Lord Jesus Christ, who raised the son of the widow, carried out beyond the gate, in the presence of many, and recalled Lazarus, four days dead and already stinking, from the dead by the word of your power: command that this boy be raised, so that, when he has been restored in the body, many may rise in soul through faith in you, and those present may know that you are Christ, the Son of the living God, who saved the world at the Father’s command. Through you we return worthy thanks to him, forever and ever.”

When the faithful had answered, “Amen,” the boy rose unharmed as if from sleep. As all wept for joy, he gave his parents ineffable gladness and the other bystanders a great incentive to follow the Christian religion. Immediately, therefore, his father Anastasius believed with his whole household, received the grace of baptism, and was added to the number of the faithful.

### 18.

Thereafter, at a later time, Christ was pleased to work through him a similar miracle for the praise and glory of his name. As the same most blessed man was departing from the city in order to make gain for Christ from those who were perishing and was visiting the districts of his diocese, a dead man was being carried out, accompanied by a great crowd of people: a young man, the son of a certain distinguished man named Jovinianus.

The holy bishop arrived and, relying on his customary confidence in the Lord, ordered the dead body to be set down. Having commanded silence with his hand, he said in a loud voice to the young man’s father:

“Jovinianus, Christ whom I preach, made man for the sake of human beings, raised the dead, drove out demons by his word, and, to display the power of his divinity, worked among human beings whatever he wished. If you believe in him with all your heart as God, abandoning the vanity of idols, and allow yourself to be purified in the font of baptism, you will rejoice both in your own salvation and in the resurrection of your son.”

Then Jovinianus and all the people standing there fell at the saint’s feet. While all begged for mercy, Jovinianus said with tears:

“Great servant of God Julian, if you restore to me my only child and the consolation of my present life, not only will I confess that Christ is the true God, but all this people will despise the fabrications of their gods and will receive with devoted mind the faith which you preach.”

But the man filled with God, bending his knees to the ground and raising his eyes and hands toward heaven, said in the hearing of all:

“Lord Jesus Christ, who are present everywhere, who wished to become human for our redemption, and, appearing among human beings, excluded death from the human race through the standard of your cross: command that this young man rise, so that the power of so great a deed may strengthen the faith of those who believe in you, and the hearts of those who do not believe may be subjected to you, the only-begotten Son of the living God, whom, reigning and ruling with the Father and the Holy Spirit, we confess throughout the ages of ages.”

When the faithful who were present had answered, “Amen,” the young man rose from the bier as if from sleep. Struck by the novelty of the miracle, all began to cry out in a loud voice:

“Truly great is the God of the Christians whom his servant Julian preaches.”

He also said to his father:

“Truly, until now we have wandered from the true God, for the gods whom we worship are certainly demons. For I saw them in Hell, and I saw that they had no rest from their torments.”

Then, when the shouting of all had risen to heaven, Christ was glorified by everyone and Christ the true God was proclaimed. His servant Julian, though strongly and repeatedly resisting, was worshiped by all.

Thus, through the preaching of the bishop worthy of God, a great multitude of rational fish was gathered in the net of faith and drawn from the deep darkness of errors to the solid shore of true belief.

### 19.

Then, like the standard-bearer of a divine army, sowing the life-giving seeds of faith—some going before and others following—he turned aside to an estate called Proiliacus (in the Beauvais manuscript, Perilianus).

As the darkness of night came on, he ordered lodging to be sought for him. But at the very moment of his arrival, the young son of the owner of the aforesaid estate died, his illness having grown worse.

When this was reported to the man of God, he refused to turn aside elsewhere. Rather, in accordance with Solomon’s saying, “It is better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting” (Ecclesiasticus 7:3), he approached the house in which the little child lay, intending to bring the joy of salvation to those who mourned, and took up lodging in a secluded part of it.

He ordered the dead body to be brought before him. After the father, mother, and all other witnesses had been removed, with only a few companions of his holiness remaining there, he prostrated himself on the pavement to pray. Keeping an all-night vigil, he struck at heaven’s secret place with such persistence of prayers that both the bishop rose from the dust and the child from death.

When dawn was already driving the fleeing torches from the sky, the father entered with the mother and a great number of neighbors. They found alive the one whom they had brought in dead. Struck by the extraordinary nature of the deed, they shook heaven with their cries and, changing their vows—or, alternatively, their voices—again lamented, this time for joy.

Immediately they submitted their necks to the Christian faith and handed over to the most blessed teacher the child whom they had desired as heir to their earthly goods, so that he might be instructed in heavenly disciplines, together with the entire inheritance of the aforesaid estate.

### 20.

Aroused by the fame of the deed, the neighbors came running. Some followed him; others burst into the little cell in which the man of God had lain. They embraced with frequent kisses the place where the saint’s feet had stood, and, in order to share in his blessing, eagerly gathered up the traces of his passage.

The most blessed man turned to the prayers of those who followed him, raised his hand, and blessed them all. All among them who were suffering from any illness he restored immediately to their former health.

## Chapter Three: Other Miracles; Adversities Endured

### 21.

Proceeding from there, the most blessed man was already approaching a village called Ruiliacus, situated on the river Leda.

[Note: Elsewhere this stream is called Ledus, and by some Lidus.]

There he encountered messengers from the chief man of the village, asking him to come as quickly as possible, because that man had an only daughter whom an unclean spirit had seized and was cruelly tormenting.

When he reached the village, they presented the maddened girl to him and, falling before his sacred footsteps, begged for mercy. The wicked spirit, unable to endure the holy man’s presence, abandoned at his first command the vessel which it had claimed by unjust right and fled, leaving the girl healthy in the midst of those who were astonished and praising Christ’s power.

Thus it happened that, through the bodily healing of one girl, all the inhabitants of that village reached the true healing of their souls. For, renouncing the vain fabrications of idols and being reborn in the font of baptism, they became participants in Christian adoption.

The aforesaid owner humbly gave the same village, together with all that belonged to it—

[Note: Something such as “the appurtenances” or “belongings” is missing.]

—to the holy bishop and most devoutly begged him to build a church there. The kindly bishop most willingly fulfilled this request and, through the ministry of holy preaching, dedicated a great number of people there to the Lord.

### 22.

Yet one must not believe that so great a herald could have accomplished so many and such great things without the struggle of labor and the snares of the ancient enemy, since the Apostle expressly cries out:

> “All who desire to live piously in Christ suffer persecution”  
> (2 Timothy 3:12).

Although the greatness of the virtues which Christ worked through him blunted whatever adversity arose from the world, the one who had presumed to approach the Mediator of God and human beings, the man Jesus Christ, as though expecting to find some of his own things there, did not cease to direct against this man also—who was a member of that supreme Head—the cunning assailant’s devices of various temptations, as against a very strong wall.

For just as a new farmer entering a shadowy forest uses now iron, now fire, to prepare the soil, hitherto sterile, for the sowing of seeds, so Julian, penetrating the soil of Le Mans, strove to overthrow ancient oaks and age-old beeches—that is, the barren and empty fabrications of ancient paganism. He used the iron of correction to strike the sins of sinners and the fire of burning to render the soil, once cleansed, fit to receive the seeds of divine love.

### 23.

But the remnants of the pagans, which had escaped the shipwreck of error like fragments of planks, could not endure the praise of Christ’s name spreading and the abominable destruction of their images. With one accord they rose up against the saint, calling him a magician who, under the name of piety, was overturning the hearts of the people with empty magic tricks; who was deceiving the eyes of those who saw; who asserted falsehoods as truths; who affirmed that a crucified man was God; who, in error, was abolishing the worship of the immortal gods whom the Roman world had worshiped from ancient times; and who ought to be burned alive, so that by his death an impostor and rash man might be terrified and might not continue attempting to blaspheme against the commonwealth and the reverence due to the fearsome gods on whom the world depended and by whom it was in some manner sustained.

### 24.

Julian was not frightened by these things. Rather, girded more eagerly for battle against the devil, he hastened to the place where their ill-advised religion had established the head of their error.

For in a village called Artinas there was a temple, and in it a statue of Jupiter and countless monstrosities of false gods, which paganism, deceived by various errors, had erected in ancient times for the ruin of itself and of the peoples who followed—or frequented—it.

When Julian prepared himself to destroy these things, clothed in the breastplate of faith, protected by the helmet of salvation, and girded with the sword of the Holy Spirit, an opposing rustic and ignoble mob armed itself in the most obstinate resistance for the defense of gods incapable of offering them any aid.

But Julian, undaunted, entered the temple amid the roaring and chattering voices of the frenzied people. Having invoked the name of the true God, Jesus Christ, he dissolved the enormous and even terrifying image into ashes by the sole authority of his holy command.

### 25.

When the insane people had come to know whom they had until then honored with divine worship, a most savage dragon burst forth from the overthrown image. Making a charge against its own worshipers, with sulphurous breath and the dreadful lash of its tail, it began fiercely to drive the ranks of its devotees toward death.

They, however, sought Julian’s help against their own god—although shortly before they had been shouting that he was a magician and had been striving with all their strength to burn him alive.

But Julian, the athlete of God, raised his right hand aloft with the sign of the cross and commanded the dragon to flee swiftly, harming no one further, and to seek places entirely devoid of human habitation.

At his command the most savage dragon fled with greatest speed and lost the power to harm those whom it was no longer permitted to deceive by practicing fraud among them.

Then all joyfully became partners in overthrowing the shrine of falsehood. Finally, reborn through the holy washing, they were blessed in Christian teaching by the hands of the holy bishop.

### 26.

The swift fame of this deed, running through all the peoples of the entire province, so wiped away every mist of their former error that scarcely anyone could be found who did not confess Jesus Christ to be God and Lord.

When the report of this celebrated deed had been brought to Defensor, the glorious man whom we mentioned above, he was filled with great joy, blessed God, and hurried to the blessed man. He humbly begged him to come to his house, so that together they might give thanks to Christ, the giver of all good things, for the victory over the conquered enemy and might share in a chaste and holy banquet.

The blessed man did not reject his request—for true charity had rightly bound him to the other’s piety—and hurried to satisfy his desire.

But as they traveled, in a part of a newly cultivated field they found a boy bound by an enormous serpent, his feet, arms, and entire body wrapped in the serpent’s viper-like coils.

All who were present were terrified. The man of God approached and said:

“Lord Jesus Christ, who restored the human race, cast down from the glory of paradise by the serpent, through the standard of your cross: free this creature of yours from the serpent by which he is held, so that the serpent may perish and the boy, escaping unharmed through you, may make those present know that you are the liberator and protector of all who hope in you.”

When the man filled with God had finished this prayer and those who were present had said, “Amen,” the serpent burst apart in the middle. While everyone praised God, the boy escaped unharmed.

### 27.

Meanwhile, when he had reached the ruler’s house, he was received with the greatest joy. People of every age and sex flocked together to see so great a man, whose name and reputation for virtues shone with such radiance that it could kindle even the most distant people with the desire to see him.

Two possessed men followed the holy bishop immediately, begging him for the remedy of their salvation. But after invoking Christ’s name, he drove out the enemy and, having enlightened them through the word of his preaching, restored them to their Creator.

They adorned that day with joyful happiness. During the very banquet of the sacred table, their whole conversation concerned the glory of Christ, the destruction of Satan, and those things which pertain to the true care of the souls of people who fear God.

Afterward, that glorious man displayed to the holy man all the abundance of his household goods and humbly begged him to accept everything kindly and retain it for whatever uses he might wish.

But the most blessed man accepted none of these things. Having bestowed a blessing upon him and strengthened his entire household in the faith of Christ, he hurried back to his own place.

28. And when he was already entering the gate of the city entrusted to him by God, those who were imprisoned and bound with chains and harsh restraints entreated the holy man with a great outcry to have pity on them. But he, most compassionate, who was always overflowing with the deepest love in the Lord, humbly approached those to whom this duty had been entrusted and earnestly begged them that, by the grace of his arrival, they should set free those whom their own wrongdoing had made guilty. But those senseless men were moved neither by reverence for the bishop present nor by the praiseworthy merit of so great a man to do what the saint had not merely commanded but had also requested in a suppliant voice.

Thus, spurned by the faithless, he entered the church and gave thanks to Christ for the souls acquired for him; then he withdrew to the lodging of his own house. When bread had been set before him, he refused to recline at table but, silent and sighing, began to await the Lord’s mercy. Then, in accordance with the desire of the servant of God, the prison doors were opened by angelic ministry, all the chains were shattered, and those who had been sitting in the darkness of the prison and of their private confinement came forth into the common light of day without human assistance. Through the middle of the city, with no one preventing them and freed from the burden of their bonds, they presented themselves before the holy man. Rejoicing in the Lord, he then happily took food and honored those whom he had rightly set free by admitting them also to the holy banquet. No one came to reclaim the liberated prisoners, since it was perfectly clear that this had been accomplished for the holy bishop by the power of divine virtue, not by human assistance.

## CHAPTER IV  
### The Death and Burial of Saint Julian

29. When the vineyard of divine worship had therefore been planted in the district of Le Mans, and all the thorns of idolatry and error had been torn out of it, the time was approaching when that blessed cultivator, about to receive from his Lord the fruit of his devout labor, would happily ascend from the snares of this present life to the eternal kingdoms. Accordingly, as the day of his calling drew near, he withdrew to the village where the church of Blessed Martial now stands.

While he lived there for several days and diligently offered his hearers the sweetness of heavenly life, he was touched by a slight illness. Cheerful and vigorous, he awaited the hour when he would receive from the just Judge the crown reserved for his labors and struggles. And because the ship of Holy Church could not sail across the sea of this world without a helmsman, he entrusted the episcopal seat given to him by God, with the common counsel of the clergy and people, to Saint Turibius, whom until then he had had as his assistant and companion in the ministry of holy preaching. For this same Turibius, distinguished in the office of the priesthood, had been sent, as we have received from ancient tradition, together with Saint Pavatius the deacon, by the bishop of the city of Rome to reveal Christ’s grace to the people of Le Mans, as the companion and assistant of Saint Julian.

30. The most glorious shepherd, therefore, chosen [variant: raised] by the common consent of all, summoned his brothers and sons. Having designated his successor, he raised his eyes and hands to heaven, gave thanks for a very long time, and praised the Lord. Commending to the supreme Shepherd the sheep whom he had acquired for Christ, he joyfully and cheerfully gave back to heaven his spirit, enriched with blessed merits.

When he sought the heavenly kingdoms, Defensor—the glorious man most dear to him for the merit of his faith and good works—was not present; but he learned the day of his most holy death through the following revelation. As he sat at table, the eyes of his understanding were opened, and behold, he saw the most blessed Julian, adorned with a priestly mitre, coming toward him with his three deacons and three candles. They placed the candles they were carrying on the table before him and departed.

Then the aforementioned Defender said to those seated with him: “Do you see the glory that I see?” They declared that they saw nothing. But he said: “Did you not see our father Julian here, who has shown us so many blessings and gladdened us with so many miracles? For behold, he has now come here before me with his three deacons and three candles; smiling with the most joyful countenance, he blessed us, left the candles, and departed. Therefore I know for certain that he has departed from this world. And to us, whom he has left by his bodily presence, he will never cease, while living in Christ, to bestow the benefits of his compassion. Let us therefore rise and hasten to bury our most devoted master, so that in heaven we may deserve to have as our helper the one whom on earth we had as our teacher of salvation.”

When he had said this, everyone was amazed. Rising together, they hurried eagerly to the saint’s funeral rites. Indeed, as it is written of that mirror of bishops, Martin, it is impossible to say how great a multitude of people gathered. All came from the fields and villages, and some even from neighboring fortified settlements. On one side were ranks of clerics singing psalms; on the other, companies of sacred virgins, pale from their austerity. Here the urban populace was mingled with noble men; there the hands of country people served the holy man’s funeral rites.

31. But let no one be disturbed because I have compared Julian with Martin. If you examine the matter carefully, you can see that nearly similar things were accomplished by both.

While still a catechumen, Martin clothed a freezing pauper with half of his cloak; Julian, strong in faith, stripped countless people of the old man and covered them with the garment of faith. Martin first chose a solitary life, so that he might enjoy the sweetness of Christ in solitude; Julian sought open combat, so that he might win the souls of many. Martin was seized by the people of Tours and taken to the episcopate; Julian was appointed by God as bishop—and indeed as apostle—of the people of Le Mans.

By the power of the divine Trinity, Martin was a glorious raiser of three dead persons; Julian, restoring an equal number of dead to life, was as many times victorious over death. Those who had conquered the world under Martin’s guidance accompanied Martin’s body; those who, under Julian’s leadership, already possessed the heavenly realms served at Julian’s funeral. What more need be said? They served one King, obeyed one Lord, were sanctified by one Spirit, and were founded upon the rock of one faith. It therefore remains that equal honor and glory should belong to those whom the practice of virtue made equal in Christ’s discipline.

32. As the body of this blessed man was being carried to his own city, the procession came to a crossing of the river called the Sarthe.

**[Note: [Col. 0793D] The Sarthe is a very clear stream that washes Alençon and the episcopal city of Le Mans; afterward, as [Col. 0794D] does the Loir, it joins the Mayenne, which flows into the Loire below the city of Angers.]**

To manifest the greatness of the merit of the man whose relics were being carried, the horses bearing the bier of the sacred remains, while the others could scarcely swim, passed through the powerful currents and the whirlpools of deep darkness and reached the opposite bank without the water touching their knees, to the amazement of all.

33. While the whole city was hastening to meet its shepherd, a certain woman had placed her little son in a kettle. Having set a fire beneath it, she was washing the child’s limbs in warm water. But, startled by the voices of those singing psalms, she abandoned the task she had begun and, forgetting the child, ran with the others to meet the saint.

While she lingered at the most venerable funeral rites, the fire beneath the child grew hotter; the iron vessel in which the little boy had been placed became surrounded by the flames and generated immense heat, pouring its boiling vapors back upon him. Who would have thought that he could survive such danger?

When the blessed mother saw that the sacred relics had drawn near her house and recognized her household hearth, she finally remembered her child and ran up in terror, supposing that he had melted amid the fiery vapors and that the tender limbs of the boy had been consumed. But the ardor of faith, which had driven her out to meet the holy body, extinguished the burning flames of the hearth. Struck by sudden terror, she did not approach her son until she had summoned many people with a loud cry.

34. Although the body of the blessed man was buried according to the law of human nature, it truly shows that he lives in Christ through the frequent consolation granted to the living. For there blindness receives sight, weakness receives the power to walk, demons are driven away, and fitting requests are granted to those who ask in faith, through the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, be honor and glory, now and for everlasting ages. Amen.

# THE BOOK OF THE MIRACLES OF SAINT MAXIMINUS, ABBOT OF MICIACUM

By Letald, monk of Miciacum.

*(In Mabillon, Acta I, 598.)*

## AUTHOR’S PROLOGUE

1. I knowingly and deliberately thrust my hand into the flames, having presumed, a tiny man of parched talent, to attempt a work hitherto untouched amid so many rivers of eloquence, although those who would have been fully capable and sufficiently qualified to accomplish it properly and competently did not presume to do so; and although men now flourish whose sharp judgment and prejudicial verdict I fear.

This is the matter: from the time of Maximinius, a father of most blessed memory, until the present age—to which the counsel of the Almighty, who calls into existence things that are not as though they were, has brought us—that place which the man of God himself had built, namely Miciacum, has at one time flourished, at another lain open to utter degradation, and at another tried to rise again. Amid all these changes, the mercy of compassionate God was never absent; and the abundance of miracles displayed through the merits of that same Father repeatedly consoled the wavering and the fearful. Yet no one could be found who would publish these things in writing, so that they might reach posterity in an orderly account.

I consider this a great loss, since God’s benefits have been handed over to sluggish forgetfulness, and since the place, having fallen into disrepute, has become almost entirely unknown—its former size and character concealed by the silence of nearly all memorials. Whatever could reach anyone’s knowledge, if it had not been accomplished before the eyes of the person to whom it became known, was undoubtedly transmitted either in writing or by the living voice. But whatever was transmitted by neither of these means—whether it happened or did not happen—all will be silent about equally with me. Remove memorials from events, and they must perish; the order of life will become confused and totter and fall.

2. For this reason, although with the presumption of a rash undertaking, yet with the hope of useful benefit, I applied my mind to this task, intending to write about what I had either seen myself or learned through the truthful report of reliable persons—namely, matters that seemed necessary to my purpose.

No one should find it strange in the composition of this work if I insert certain things that seem to have little connection with the subject, since I do this rarely and, whenever a sound judgment is present, not without reason. Beginning with Clovis and offering a brief preliminary account of his skill, I wished for this reason to establish the beginning of my own narrative with the founder whose munificence gave the place of which we wish to speak its beginning. Likewise, when I introduce his sons, I do so for the sake of Blessed Avitus, wishing to commend both his antiquity and his zeal for piety.

Again, when I distinguish the periods of the kings by counting the years down to Childebert, son of Sigebert, I do so for two reasons: to prove that Blessed Launomarus was contemporary with Father Maximinus, though in such a way that, while Father Maximinus was of mature age, Launomarus was still a young man; and because before that same Father Maximinus no one of such authority among the fathers is recorded as having been found in our region—one who formed so many holy and illustrious men by the example of his instruction. It may therefore reasonably be inferred that the holy and venerable man Launomarus himself proceeded from this very discipline, since the dates agree and the fellowship between the communities of Miciacum and Corbion remained unshaken almost to our own time. Finally, as we shall say later, when Heriricus withdrew from this place because he was troubled by it, he went to the monastery of Corbion and completed there what remained of his life.

3. Nor have I included in this little book everything I have learned that took place in this place or concerned it. I was restrained by the confusion of the times; and because I could not distinguish these matters, I thought it better to remain silent about them.

I learned that noble and industrious Fathers had flourished in this same place: Haymo, Stenogaudus, and Dructesindus; also Bertoldus, a most learned man, who is said to have published the earlier Life of Father Maximinus; and Peter, whose learning and zeal still shine today. Among the other benefits he bestowed, Peter brought to this place books of various histories, corrected and arranged by his own labor, and placed them on the altar of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr on the day of the Lord’s Supper, as the books themselves attest. Since the chronology of these men is not sufficiently clear, let this much have been said about them.

Now, as we return to the sequence of our narrative, we pray the boundless goodness of Christ that, supported by his powerful right hand, he may lead us to the landing-place we desire. We also ask that, if a speck has lodged in the eye of our attention, it may be removed with affection and that it may produce not resentment but charity.

# THE MIRACLES BEGIN

## CHAPTER I  
### Eulogy of Clovis; Summary of the Life of Saint Euspicius and Likewise of Saint Maximinus; Distinguished Disciples of Maximinus; The Author’s Opinion Concerning the Arrival of Saint Maurus in Gaul

1. As I had long considered what I should take up first as the beginning of my narrative, when I was about to speak of the virtues of the great and outstanding Father Maximinus, I found nothing more illustrious than King Clovis. He may rightly be placed as the foundation—indeed the first foundation—of the whole history we are about to set forth.

Although this king had initially been ensnared in the error of paganism, he was converted to the faith of Christ through the preaching of Blessed Remigius, bishop of Reims, and also through the exhortation of his queen Chrothildis. He lived subject to Christ with as much devotion as he always strove to remain undefeated in arms.

When Catholic piety was flourishing, he expelled from Aquitaine the Goths, who were covered in Arian impiety. After killing their king Alaric, he forced his son Amalric to flee to Spain. By arms he claimed nearly the whole of Gaul, and made the Rhine, the Alps, the southern sea, the Pyrenees, and the Northern Ocean the boundaries of his empire.

Finally, the terror of his name had spread so far through all the neighboring nations that even Anastasius, who presided over the imperial power of the Roman name, sought his friendship and enrolled him as consul and patrician of the Roman state, sending him letters patent and great gifts.

He was in every respect a vigorous man, whose glory never suffered diminution; he enjoyed favorable fortune and was always especially successful in war. Yet he was hostile to his relatives and put nearly all of them to death for different reasons.

2. The people of Verdun, encouraged by the hope of their neighboring Germans, rebelled against the king. He immediately besieged their city and would have overthrown it if the prayer of the distinguished man Euspicius, who held the honored office of priest in that city, had not restrained his assault and persuaded him to grant pardon even to men guilty of the gravest crimes.

Since the episcopal seat was vacant, the king wished to make this man bishop; but when he could not obtain his consent, he asked Euspicius to become his companion as he proceeded toward the territory of Orléans. Blessed Euspicius arrived there with his most beloved nephew Maximinus, and the king honored him so greatly that he granted him by hereditary right his own estate of Miciacum, where he was accustomed to stay for the pleasures of fishing and hunting. He also granted him Cambiacum and Litimiacum, estates that were famous at that time, together with everything belonging to them, and ordered a royal charter to be drawn up for these possessions.

3. On this very estate, Miciacum, after a basilica and the other necessary buildings had been constructed, Blessed Euspicius lived honorably with his fortunate nephew Maximinus for as long as he remained in this human life.

When Euspicius died and was buried beside Blessed Bishop Anianus, the man of God Maximinus governed the place assigned to him with the greatest distinction. His discipline was so praiseworthy that when the most holy men Avitus and Carilefus, having jointly resolved to seek the desert, reached the banks of the Loire and heard the fragrance of his reputation, they abandoned their former plan and hurried to meet him with the greatest eagerness.

He received them most kindly and, granting them permission to live with him, bound them to himself by spiritual love. He especially enjoyed the almost constant conversation of Saint Carilefus. To Saint Avitus he entrusted the administration of the community’s material resources; under his administration, the grace, generosity, and abundance of the almighty Lord bestowed upon Father Maximinus, through the saint’s efforts, freed almost the entire district of Orléans from the danger of famine.

4. In every respect he was a remarkable Father, to whom it had been granted by divine favor to possess such disciples and such ministers. For not only these two, but many other holy men also adhered to his sacred following—men once admired by the world, but now, because of their virtue, worthy of imitation by all.

Raised to the summit of virtue by his discipline, many of them sought the anchoritic life and steadfastly practiced philosophy in it. Thus, supported by Christ’s help, they cultivated and watered not only the ordinary dwellings of human habitation but also deserts, pathless places, and regions without streams, through the blessing of their lives.

The Perche bears witness to this, irradiated by the two great lights, the blessed men Avitus and Carilefus. Sologne bears witness, preserving the good Viator at Viatoria; so does Dulchardus, near Bourges. The forest called Longinqua also bears witness, a forest that Blessed Leonard made both famous and near through his spiritual exercises and bodily dwelling. For no one should doubt that Blessed Launomarus and Saint Lifard also flourished from this very discipline.

5. Indeed, before Father Maximinus and his uncle Euspicius, no one of comparable authority among the fathers is recorded as having lived in this province and formed so many outstanding men in holiness through the examples of his instruction.

The fact that the most blessed Father Benedict sent his dearest disciple Maurus to these regions at the request of Berthecrannus, bishop of Le Mans, occurred at a later time. The period in which the glorious Father Maximinus flourished has, I think, been sufficiently indicated.

Blessed Maurus entered Gaul when Brunhild was ruling the Burgundians with her grandsons Theodebert and Theoderic, the sons of Childebert. This Childebert was the son of Sigebert, who had brought Brunhild from Spain and taken her as his wife. By her he had a son, Childebert, and he held his seat at Metz, which is the city of the Mediomatrici.

Sigebert was the son of Chlothar, who was born to King Clovis and Chrothildis. Thus the great Father Maximinus preceded the arrival of Blessed Maurus in Gaul by as much time as the reign of the elder Clovis preceded the reign of his great-grandsons Theoderic and Theodebert.

For from the last year of Clovis—which was the first year of Chlothar—up to the first year of Childebert, the father of these men, seventy-five years are counted.

**[Note: [Col. 0799D] He is mistaken.]**

This Childebert, reigning in northern Gaul, sent his mother Brunhild, with her grandsons—namely, the sons mentioned above, Theodebert and Theoderic—to reign in the kingdom of his uncle Gunthram, who had ruled the Burgundians. While these men were ruling, Blessed Maurus entered Gaul with four brothers and the envoys Arderadus and Flodecarius. But enough about this.

## CHAPTER II  
### Blessed Avitus and the Passing of Saint Maximinus

6. While his spiritual father, namely the first Saint Maximinus, was still alive, Blessed Avitus sometimes remained apart in the monastery. Later, about four miles from the monastery, at a place called Maceriae (Maizières), he established a small cell for himself, where an oratory consecrated in his name still remains.

While he was subduing his body at that place in opposition to the spirit, Blessed Father Maximinus, after countless victories won against the devil by God’s gift, departed to heaven full of virtues and holiness, having reached the measure appointed for him.

He was buried by the venerable Bishop Eusebius and the brothers on the mountain beyond the Loire, where by the Lord’s power he had extinguished a savage dragon. Over his venerable body a certain powerful man named Agilis built a basilica in gratitude for the health restored to him. Later Agilis himself was converted to the habit of holiness and still shines today through miracles.

After the glorious passing of the most devoted Father Maximinus, Blessed Avitus was drawn away from the quiet of the desert and appointed by the brothers in his place. He too, remarkable in religious observance, followed without deviation the footsteps of his devout Father.

7. At that time Chlothar and Chlodomir, the sons of Clovis, went against Burgundy. After defeating the armies of Gotmar and Sigismund, the sons of Gundobad, they put them to flight.

King Sigismund fled for refuge to the holy martyrs of Agaunum, but there Chlodomir captured him with his wife and sons and brought him to the city of Orléans. When Blessed Avitus heard this, he came from the monastery to the city to plead for King Sigismund. His prayers were frustrated because Queen Chlothildis, Chlodomir’s mother, hated Sigismund, since her father and mother had been killed by Gundobad, Sigismund’s father.

For this reason King and martyr Sigismund was killed and buried in a well with his wife and sons. Chlodomir, however, did not long rejoice. For when he later entered Burgundy with his brothers and a large army, he was carried on a very swift horse into the midst of the densely packed enemy on the day of battle and fell unavenged.

While his sons were being raised by their grandmother in the hope of their father’s kingdom, their uncles, the dead man’s brothers, brought them away from their grandmother through deceit and promptly killed them.

8. After Blessed Avitus had governed the monastery for a short time, he resolved to return to the sweetness of the anchoritic life, which he had already tasted. Blessed Carilefus, burning with the same ardor, sought the deserts of Le Mans. Within a short time, when many people had gathered to him, he built a distinguished monastery at a place called Aninsula (the Anille River).

Blessed Avitus likewise gathered a multitude of monks in the region of the Dunois and, renowned for many virtues and miracles, shone far and wide.

9. There was also at Miciacum a certain brother whom Saint Avitus loved with particular affection. When this brother was approaching the end of his life, he earnestly begged the brothers who visited him not to give his body burial before Saint Avitus arrived and commended him to the Lord by his prayer.

A message was therefore sent immediately to the blessed man. Hastening his journey, he entered the monastery at an untimely hour of the night. The brother had already died, and his body had been placed in the middle of the church and was being guarded amid the sorrowful service of the mourners.

The man of God entered the church, found nearly everyone asleep, and threw himself upon the pavement to pray. Soaking it with a great shower of tears, he remained long in prayer. Then he rose, stood beside the bier, and called that brother in a few words. The brother immediately answered, as though lightly sleeping, and, raising himself, sat up in the bier.

Awakened by the murmur of those speaking, the brothers saw alive the one whom they had been guarding as dead. Greatly terrified, they fell at the feet of the holy man, and, freeing the brother from his funeral bindings, led him out with immense joy. He afterward lived many years as a witness to so great an event.

Blessed Avitus, fleeing human praise, withdrew again to the dwelling-place of the quiet he desired.

## CHAPTER III  
### Saint Theodemirus

10. Since the brothers of Miciacum could not be without a shepherd, the entire community chose the man of God Theodemirus and placed him over them as pastor.

This Theodemirus was a man of good gravity and held in great respect among his own people even before he assumed the form of holy conduct. At first he was a canon of the Holy Cross and, as many assert, also its dean.

He was moved especially to become a monk for this reason: he had a sister whose clouded eyes deprived her of light. She was brought to the holy and venerable Father Maximinus and, by the Lord’s grace, was immediately given sight.

The greatness of this man of God, Theodemirus, in holy religion is shown by his end, in which all praise may safely be sung. When he was at the point of death, Blessed Lifardus, who was living an anchoritic life in the village of Meung, was warned in a dream to come as quickly as possible and commend the passing of Abbot Theodemirus to the Lord.

He immediately rose and set out. But before he reached the monastery, he lifted his eyes to heaven and saw on high choirs of angels carrying the soul of this holy man into heaven and saying: “Blessed is the one whom you have chosen and taken; he shall dwell in your courts.”

The same Theodemirus had by the sister already mentioned a nephew named Maximinus. We suppose that he was called by this name either because the man of God Maximinus had received him from the sacred font, or because his mother, out of love for the father by whom she had been given sight, preferred to give her son that name.

After his blessed uncle had been buried, the man of God Lifardus and the brothers chose this man as abbot and appointed him in the place of the deceased. As long as he lived, he diligently watched over the flock entrusted to his care, having followed the discipline of the Fathers.

11. The place where the body of the most blessed Father Maximinus had been buried was rich in many signs of virtue and was honored greatly in its earliest period. Since many people came seeking benefits and their requests were granted for many, as often happens, the novelty of these exceedingly welcome benefits began to fade through the negligence of later generations.

When Sigobert was appointed to the episcopate of the Church of Orléans—most noble both in birth and in character—he saw that this once flourishing place had declined from its ancient distinction and grieved deeply. Therefore, with the counsel of the clergy and people, the bones of Saint Maximinus were transferred from that place to a church that the same bishop had built on land belonging to him. The church stood outside the city but near its walls, adjoining the church of Blessed Anianus, which he had bestowed upon Miciacum.

The venerable bishop endowed this church from his own resources, so that it might have clerics to serve God and not lack lamps or other suitable ornaments.

**[Note: [Col. 0801D] Sigobert sat as bishop around the year 670. Only a few traces remain of the church he built in honor of Saint Maximinus, on the western side of the church of Saint Anianus.]**

12. After these arrangements had endured for many generations, the devotion of the monastery of Miciacum and its zeal for monastic life began to weaken, partly through the desire for worldly things, which is the mother of all evils, and partly through hostile incursions, which frequently occurred because of attacks from Aquitaine.

At that time a grave and prolonged conflict between the dukes of Pippin and Waifarius, king of Aquitaine, inflicted no small damage upon the Frankish state. At last, when Waifarius was captured at the fortress of Thouars among the Pictones, supreme power passed to Pippin.

Around these times, as we had begun to say, the place mentioned above was so utterly stripped of its former distinction that no monk could remain there. Their dwellings were either lodgings for secular people and women, or stables for horses and feeding places for dogs.

13. In the time of the divinely remembered Emperor Charles, surnamed the Great, while the Lord of all things was arranging to restore this place to its former distinction, Theodulfus—most noble in birth and character and a bishop of the Church of Orléans, possessing a very keen intellect—was appointed.

He labored with great diligence to restore the place to its ancient honor. When he found in the neighboring regions monks insufficient for accomplishing this, he recruited others from the regions of Septimania.

**[Note: [Col. 0802D] That is, from the monastery of Saint Savior at Aniane, over which Blessed Benedict, restorer of the monastic order, was then presiding.]**

He gave them the place and, adding from his own resources the possessions formerly assigned to it, handed everything over to them. He did not regret this action; for under his administration the glory of the place shone so brightly that the honor subsequently achieved overshadowed the disgrace of its former shame, and later gains compensated for previous losses.

Among his other works, Bishop Theodulfus built a basilica of marvelous workmanship, modeled on the one situated at Aachen, in a village called Germigny, near the monastery of Fleury. There he elegantly expressed his memory in these verses:

> Theodulfus consecrated these temples in God’s honor;  
> Whoever enters them, I ask, let him remember me.

This venerable priest was accused before the king of conspiracy, deprived of his bishopric, and confined for many days. Later, by a marvelous reversal of events, he most readily cleared himself of the charge and, having regained the king’s favor, recovered the chair of his former dignity, though he did not live long afterward.

For it is said that he was killed by poison by men who, while he was in exile, had gained their freedom and already conceived the desire to seize his property.

14. Jonas succeeded him. He greatly honored the inhabitants of the place, adorned it, enlarged the church, and covered its eastern vault most elegantly with leaden bricks.

Jonas flourished not only in human affairs but also in divine matters. The fullness of his faith, learning, and scholarship can clearly be gathered from the book he wrote against Claudius, bishop of Turin and a new heresiarch.
