Claudius taught that the mark of the blessed and life-giving cross ought not to be worshiped at all. “If the cross is worshiped,” he said, “then young maidens should also be worshiped, because a virgin bore Christ; mangers should also be worshiped, because once he was born he was laid in a manger; asses should also be worshiped, because, sitting upon an ass, he came to Jerusalem.” By composing many other impious arguments, he undermined the simplicity of the Christian faith.

Against these deranged errors the venerable Jonas, who was bishop of the Holy Cross, at the request of Emperor Louis produced a remarkable book. He painted it like a garland of flowers gathered from the various sayings of the Fathers and opposed the powerful folly of Claudius so effectively that afterward no one was found who revived the same madness.

The little book itself is kept in our possession. It had been carelessly left in a house consumed by fire and was found intact after the fire.

15. While Jonas occupied the episcopate, many noble and worldly-renowned men laid aside the belts of military service and, stripping off the old man together with his deeds, rejoiced to devote themselves to the Lord in that same place.

Their father in the way of life was the venerable Heriricus, once a close friend of kings but at that time a most fervent observer of the monastic order. Although they enjoyed every spiritual joy together with the necessities required for this life, one thing brought no small sadness to their hearts: they were deprived of the body of their patron Maximinus.

While Louis was emperor, Abbot Heriricus went with the brothers to the palace to request the body of Blessed Father Maximinus, while also not neglecting the other needs of the place entrusted to him.

The emperor favored these petitions. He summoned Bishop Jonas and ordered that the body be returned. It was lifted with great joy from the burial place where Bishop Sigobert had deposited it, as we have already said, and carried to the monastery of Miciacum together with the bones of two of his disciples, namely Theodemirus and Maximinus, whom we mentioned above.

16. Concerning the venerable Abbot Heriricus, who governed the monastery of Miciacum at this time, the following marvel is reported. When he was ill at the monastery of Corbion with the illness from which he died, he summoned a brother who was especially close to him and ordered him to seek peaches for him.

The brother was astonished, since it was not the season for finding them—the days of Epiphany were being celebrated. “Go,” Heriricus said, “behind the crypt of the monastery, and bring back what you find.”

The brother, overcome not by hope of finding anything but by the insistence of the one giving the order, approached the tree at the indicated place and found three peaches of remarkable appearance. The tree had never produced anything like them in its season.

The sick man received them when they were quickly brought to him, gave thanks to almighty God, namely the holy Trinity, and tasted the fruit. After commending the brothers and sons to the Lord, he joyfully departed from the body.

Having learned this through the truthful report of the elders, I have by no means allowed it to remain hidden in silence. I firmly believe that, although there are now few who perform miracles, there are nevertheless many in Holy Church who are not unlike the workers of miracles in the merit of their lives.

17. When Louis, the most pious Augustus, as we believe, sought the heavenly kingdoms, the Frankish empire—long sought by arms and multiplied in many ways by his father Charles—whose noble body had been formed from many nations, was divided threefold; and his three sons, appointed triarchs, received portions of it to govern. The eldest, Lothar, possessed Francia together with Italy; Louis, all Saxony and Germany; and Charles the Younger, Burgundy [Col. 0804B] together with Aquitaine.

After Charles had obtained no small part of the kingdom, while fortune alternated with misfortune, the condition of his realm was first burdened and devastated by the disasters of internal wars, and afterward by foreign disturbances. For the dukes who ought to have defended the empire’s borders placed private quarrels before the common interests; therefore, as they pursued one another with killings and plunder, they gave the barbarians an opportunity to dishonor through plunder and fires the empire won for illustrious kings and feared for so many centuries.

Between Lambert and Rainold, who governed the borders of Neustria toward the Ocean, a long conflict—bringing ruin to both sides—exposed the flank of the fatherland, through which the disaster that would overthrow the Frankish kingdom first entered. First, the power of the Britons crossed the frontier and subjected to its barbarous rule the ancient regions of Nantes (Namnetica) and Angers (Andegavensis), as far as the river Mayenne (Meduana).

18. Immediately afterward the Norman people came out from the sheath of their dwelling-place and, not in the manner of pirates but freely invading the lands while no one resisted, miserably devastated the whole maritime region with fires, plunder, and every kind of cruelty.

Finally, on the day of the Nativity of St. John the Baptist, they attacked and burned the city of Nantes, and while Bishop Gunhard (St. Gohard) was occupied with the solemn rites of the Mass, they cut him down upon the altar of the martyr Ferreolus, which stands on the left side of the church of Blessed Peter the Apostle, the mother church of that city. Raging through the people, they thought no age should be spared.

After the city had been burned (in the year 843), together with all its furnishings and a great multitude of captives, they returned to an island adjoining the monastery of St. Florentius. There they established a settlement, bringing to it whatever they plundered elsewhere. At first, indeed, inexperience in riding prevented longer expeditions; but eventually, becoming more practiced in this activity, they ranged through not only everything nearby but also places far away, filling all things with slaughter (in the year 853).

Then again they boarded their ships, invaded Tours, and, traveling along the bed of the Loire, reached the monastery of Father Maximinus. Finding it empty of people, they plundered everything that came before them; finally, after setting fire to it, they tried to burn the church from the southern side. But he who neither sleeps nor slumbers, who guards Israel, preserved it. After laboring in vain for a long time and achieving none of their wicked purpose, they departed covered in shame.

Here, moreover, it is enough to observe how vigilantly Father Maximinus protected this place, which from the day of its foundation he never allowed to be violated by fire, even in barbarous times. For at that time scarcely any monastery in all Neustria, and in a large part of Aquitaine, escaped the hands of the impious, since the monasteries of St. Martin and of Blessed Father Benedict were also burned by them.

But no one should think that I am pursuing this account to disparage any saint. Rather, I relate it to demonstrate the devotion of this pious Father, who, foreseeing future disasters and the times of those who seek what is theirs, did not allow his little church to be burned, since he foresaw that it would scarcely, or not at all, be restored to its former condition.

19. When Bishop Agio died—under him the city of Orléans, once torn apart, was burned a second time—Walter succeeded him, an energetic man prepared in spirit to endure every hardship. He both built the city walls and encouraged the citizens, worn down by so many disasters, to resist the barbarians.

[Note: [Col. 0805] In Book VI of his Annals of Orléans, Charles Saussey holds that Agius began to occupy the see in 843; he places Anselm I between Agius and Walter.]

Trohannus (Trannin) succeeded him. He accomplished nothing effective, but left posterity a memory of himself through a cruel end. For, being a man of fickle character, he was accustomed, often while drunk, to give or promise many things which, once the wine had been digested, he completely forgot.

A certain noble cleric named Fredricus took advantage of this opportunity. He enlisted as accomplices certain men close to the bishop, and, approaching the bishop after dinner, began to win his favor with various compliments and urbane speech. Once wine had been brought in, while they were drinking, conversation turned to the monastery of St. Maximinus.

A certain monk named Wmarus, himself distinguished according to worldly rank, had also sought the same place and, having approached Fredricus, was awaiting the fulfillment of his desire. But, on the advice of his brother Ermenteus, Fredricus abandoned this undertaking, ostensibly on Wlmarus’s account, and began to look after his own interests. Having the bishop’s supporters as his intimates, he approached the bishop at the hour already mentioned and extorted from him a merely nominal grant of the aforesaid place.

So that the bishop, perhaps moved by repentance, might not presume to deny it, they secretly carried away his staff and kept it until the following day as evidence of the donation. [Col. 0805D] On the next day, when the bishop arose, Fredricus most dutifully appeared before him, giving thanks for what had been conferred and finally presenting the staff as witness. The bishop was confused and unaware of what he had done, but, overcome by the unanimity of the conspirators, consented, willingly or unwillingly. And since poverty in his household pressed him hard, he was presented with a lavish banquet and, now that Fredricus possessed firm authority, consented to the latter’s desire.

When Fredricus came to the monastery, Wlmarus and the other brothers shut the monastery entrance and did not allow him to enter. Therefore Fredricus returned indignantly to the bishop, led him as far as the monastery, and compelled him to rage against the sheep in the manner of a wolf. Thus Wlmarus and the more prominent brothers were expelled, with only five brothers of the lowest and most servile status left behind.

In this way Fredricus obtained what he wanted and acquired the title of abbot, while entirely avoiding the office. For those whom he had left there, treating them as the most abject of men, he kept as stipendiaries on a small allowance, after stripping them of all their other goods.

Unable to endure such harshness toward them, they approached the bishop and laid before him a complaint about their misery. He utterly rejected them and ordered them to be driven from his presence with the greatest insult. Thus despised, they returned to the monastery and, with persistent lamentations, repeated their misfortune to Blessed Maximinus; clinging to the sacred ashes, they continued day into night.

[Col. 0806B] 20. One night, while the bishop was sleeping, two terrifying men appeared before him, distinguished in dress and venerable with gray hair. One seemed to be in episcopal attire, the other an abbot. They appeared to be demanding an account from him: why, neglecting the salvation of souls, he had placed unworthy persons over holy places—men who devoted themselves to luxury and pleasure and, by driving them away, handed the Lord’s sheep over to be torn apart by the bites of wolves.

When the bishop remained silent and could make no reply, they attacked him with whips and departed, leaving him in the most shameful condition. His servants, awakened by his cries, asked the cause of his shouting and could scarcely learn anything from him. But amid sobs and words faltering with anxious trembling, he kept calling upon Evurtius and Maximinus and repeatedly invoking the monks.

[Col. 0806C] Understanding this, they mounted horses and hastened toward the monastery at that very hour. But before the monks could arrive, the bishop was released from the flesh and died.

Fredricus himself, too, did not long enjoy his success. For he was seized by a very severe illness and, unable to bear the presence of St. Maximinus standing over him, leapt from the bed on which he was lying. Thus, overtaken by premature death amid these cries, he breathed out his spirit amid the grief of many.

## CHAPTER IV. Abbot Letaldus and His Successors

21. After these men had thus been punished, at that time no one remained who would unlawfully seek the aforesaid monastery. But those who had returned from the dispersion into which they had been scattered recovered the place, drove the profane and reckless usurpers far away, and chose one of their own number, named Letaldus, a noble man and, for that time, skilled in many ways; they appointed him abbot.

At that time, however, scarcely any monks could be found who lived according to the rule’s regulations. In those days Odo flourished, an altogether venerable abbot, through whom the monastic order began to rise again as if restored to life. He was an outstanding man in character and adorned with every kind of wisdom. He produced many books in which he left to the studious and to lovers of goodness a living image of himself, since the holy man could teach in no other way than he had lived.

[Col. 0807A] 22. After Trohannus, Berno succeeded him; when Berno died, he left the episcopate to Anselm.

[Note: [Col. 0807D] According to Saussey, Anselm reached the year 930.]

After Anselm’s death, Theoderic, an industrious man, succeeded him. He was exceptionally handsome in body, vigorous in youth, lively in intelligence, and gentle in character.

When Abbot Letaldus died, the monastery of Father Maximinus came under the authority of Bishop Theoderic. He loved the place with a special affection, and, if—alas, unhappily—he had not been overtaken by premature death, he would have restored it in every respect to its former dignity. For he possessed the episcopate for scarcely four years and then left the episcopal seat to Ermenthaeus.

A certain Rothardus administered the affairs of the monastery of Miciacum. Between him and Benedict, the provost of Bishop Ermenthaeus, a great dispute arose over the same place: one desired to invade it, while the other resisted. This dispute brought the monastery down to the lowest degree of degradation.

For, since the people of the place lived in a worldly manner, they gave Benedict grounds for accusing the monastery. Bishop Ermenthaeus, however, excessive in temperament and at that time an excessively devoted supporter of worldly interests, gladly listened to the accusations brought against the brothers, concealed their quarrels, and cunningly observed their conflict, secure in the knowledge that profit from this controversy would accrue to him.

As a result, Rothardus, unable to endure Benedict’s accusations, withdrew. Gathering whatever precious goods he could, he went to a certain abbot of the region of Berry named Raimundus, inflicting enormous loss upon this monastery by carrying away its possessions. Above all, he took with him the ancient royal charters concerning the property of that place, which were regarded as both generous and extremely valuable.

23. After Rothardus departed, Benedict poured himself into the monastery as though it were a deserted place, stretched the reins of his greed far and wide, and, forcing his entire household into the place with him, began to live there as he pleased.

For in the brothers’ houses he established horse stables; here he set perches for hawks; there he kept kennels for dogs; elsewhere young men played with shield and rod; in another place female weavers resounded with their sharp combs; here there were gatherings of laypeople; and there a mistress advanced through the crowd surrounded by troops of waiting women. Who among the monks could live amid such things? Who could endure this disgraceful dishonor?

Meanwhile Benedict built a house on the bank of the Loiret River (Ligeritis), which he called Casa Miranda, so that even the proceeds from the fisheries there might not freely serve the brothers.

And because the bishop carried out everything according to Benedict’s counsel, this man, hateful to God, gave him advice that the estates and possessions bestowed upon Blessed Father Maximinus by kings and by any faithful people for the remedy of their souls should be divided at will among his soldiers.

This was done. Benedict himself first seized the choicer possessions, claiming Litimiacum—which King Chlodoveus had granted to Father Maximinus—together with everything belonging to it. Then, after the estates had been divided among the rest of his henchmen, nothing remained of the remnants for the monks.

To each of the brothers who remained there, Benedict’s servant gave only a small loaf of bread and a handful of legumes; wine was given rarely, and when it was given, the measure was not generous. No monastic duties were assigned to the monks; Benedict’s officials arranged everything that had to be done.

24. At that time there flourished among them a venerable man named Gaudebertus. He was distinguished by the priestly dignity of his office, noble by birth, but more distinguished still in spiritual matters. He had a brother, still young, named Bernerius, who later also became an outstanding man and who never thought that anything should be placed above the common good.

These men, together with certain others, remained there, groaning under this miserable servitude.

At that time a certain venerable bishop named Benedict arrived from Brittany and purchased from the bishop this place of which we are speaking, paying thirty pounds of silver.

That holy bishop was adorned with every grace: most noble by birth, tall in stature, lean in body, devoted to all spiritual goods, and especially constant in prayer. Every day he performed the Davidic synaxis, or psalm office, and afterward, standing, he recited the Gospel according to John from memory in its proper order.

He had an uncle named Gradilo. We believe it worthwhile to insert into this work a worthy story about him, which has been transmitted to us, briefly suspending the order of our subject.

25. When this man was the most powerful of the Britons, he abandoned the splendors of the world and came, for the sake of religious life, to the monastery called the island of Herio.

[Note: [Col. 0808D] Herio Island, commonly called l’Isle de Nermontier, or St. Philibert’s Island, within the territory of the Pictones.]

When he had been devoutly received and himself conducted his life with the utmost devotion, he was ordered, because of bodily weakness, to live apart.

His friends, who had loved him when they were still in the world, sent him many gifts, which he carefully arranged to be distributed among the brothers in the monastery. The brothers, however, thinking that he possessed much money and that he would soon leave everything to them, treated him with great attentiveness. No necessity was left unsupplied; everything was available according to their wishes.

But when he lived longer than expected and the flow of money began to fail, the brothers’ diligence began to fail with it, and that money-based charity began to grow cold.

When he noticed this, he employed the following stratagem against their cruelty. He summoned a brother who was especially close to him and ordered sand and gravel to be brought to him secretly. When these had been brought, he filled two chests that served as his bedstead and, as though he had stored valuables inside them, carefully secured them with strong locks.

After this, he summoned the abbot and politely asked why he had neglected to visit him for so many days. The brothers entered with the abbot. They tried to arrange the same chests so that they could sit and listen to what would be said, but they could scarcely move them at all.

Returning anxiously to themselves, they began to blame themselves for having neglected such a great man, who must have been reserving for them so many good things stored in his possession.

Renewing their attentiveness, they provided for his nourishment with every care and diligence. Within a short time, gathered to the Lord, he rested in a blessed death.

26. After his death, all those who had trusted in him were expelled. The cell was closed, and the chests were opened without a key. The hidden treasures were discovered: an immense mass of sand, entirely suitable to the avarice of those who, believing that his servant had stolen the treasures, seized him and tortured him in various ways.

When his oath was not believed, he said: “Take me to my master’s tomb and let his testimony be sought.”

When they agreed, they both came to the monument. His servant raised his voice with tears and said: “Come, master, declare what treasures you left behind, and tell them whether the punishments I suffer are deserved.”

The dead man answered him from the tomb: “They afflict you, though you are innocent and without cause; but such almsgivers are entirely worthy of such treasures.”

When they heard this, they were greatly terrified and did not dare to ask anything further of him.

Bishop Benedict, however, having spent only a very short time at the monastery of Miciacum, returned to Brittany, visiting his homeland once again.

27. Some time afterward, a certain transmarine abbot named Jacob, while staying in the region of Berry, was moved by report and came to that same place, namely Miciacum. Seeing how attractive it was, he reached an agreement with Bishop Ermenthaeus for sixty pounds. After paying this sum, he obtained the place, whose walls alone were empty.

When Cunanus, bishop of St. Paul’s in León, died, Count Alanus, knowing that Jacob possessed much money, appointed him in the deceased man’s place. Although he thereby obtained consecration, he never visited the see to which he had been consecrated [supplied: “he never went to it”], but remained at Miciacum until the end of his life.

While he lived there, a dispute arose between his own men, whom he had brought into the place, and those who appeared to have lived there before him. They did not agree with one another and, like pottery and bronze, could not in any way be mixed.

It happened, therefore, that Tartulphus, a monk of Bishop Jacob, was caught on certain pretexts and, at the instigation of Lambert and Adelard, was beaten most severely. The bishop himself was also insulted and, suffering more fear than danger, was compelled to bring forth from his bosom the key beneath which all his most precious possessions were kept.

When Isaac and Egroalis reported this to Bishop Ermenthaeus, he was greatly angered. He sent Valinus the dean, an outstanding man, with many other nobles, to seek out the authors of the crime and drive them far away once they had been found, and to restore the bishop’s possessions to him with every honor.

Not long afterward, however, Bishop Jacob, realizing that the time of his deposition was approaching and remembering too vividly the wrongs inflicted upon him, distributed his treasures and distinguished ornaments among his own men and sent the rest back to Brittany.

After his death, Benedict arrived as a grim and most zealous investigator, but later than he should have. For, foreseeing while still alive what would happen, the bishop, as has been said, had already sent his men away with the possessions, leaving only Isaac behind after his death.

28. After the death of Bishop Jacob, Albertus and Azenerius, having again offered twenty pounds, summoned Anno, the venerable abbot of the monastery of Gemmeticum (Jumièges), their own brother. At the command of Bishop Ermenthaeus, this venerable man received the aforesaid place to govern.

During his time, the monastery, like a sick man restored to life who recovers from a long illness, began to rise again from the degradation of its downfall. Through this venerable Father, the regular order was first introduced into this place in our own days and flourished there with the greatest fervor.

Although poverty was present in material things, the virtue of charity and hospitality concealed it by covering it, and generous decency overshadowed it. How often we saw wine lavishly served to guests while all of us were content with water; yet this was done with such prudence that the guests themselves knew nothing of it and all thought themselves to have been imbibed with wine.

The grace of God was present in various ways to meet necessity and, by the comfort of its assistance, to relieve the poverty of such modest charity; it also demonstrated the presence of his regard through the very frequent abundance of miracles.

Desiring now to touch briefly upon a few of these, we confess that we shall relate nothing that we have not either seen ourselves or received from those who saw it or learned of it sincerely.

Therefore, having loosed the rope of our narrative’s sail, we entrust our vessel to the Holy Spirit, asking that, as we speak of his Maximinus, he may pour upon us the grace of his dew and bring us to the harbor of our desire.

## CHAPTER V. Two Brothers Miraculously Saved from Death

29. When winter descended more fiercely than usual, so much so that the river Loire, hardened by ice, permitted passage across its frozen back not only to men but also to various vehicles, two brothers, born of the same parents, set out from the village of St. Marcellus, which lies beyond the Loire, wishing to reach the city. One carried cabbages; the other was loaded with straw gathered for preparing meat.

As they crossed the hardened surface of the river, when they had already reached almost the middle of the stream, the ice suddenly dissolved and a kind of slab was torn away with them. Sinking beneath them and driven forward by the force of the river, it rose again; one end lightly striking and mounting upon the remaining solid ice, it sped onward with the utmost speed like an arrow. It did not stop until it had passed beyond the entire sheet of ice and was caught by the opposing currents.

In the middle of the river, where the whole force of the water pressed upon it, the current appeared not to be very large. When the slab reached it, it began to carry the trembling, almost lifeless men away, while both banks were full of shouting people but no help was available. No one could go out to them, and while everyone was afraid, no one dared enter the water.

Thus the men being carried away, now despairing of life, sat upon their hostile vehicle and awaited help from God alone.

When they had rushed past the monastery, one of them, looking toward the church, obtained the assistance of Father Maximinus with a supplicating voice. Immediately, without delay, the slab split in the middle and carried the man who had cried out, safe and unharmed, to the bank.

He ran to the monastery, prostrated himself before the altar, and, giving thanks for himself with immense weeping, anxiously prayed for his brother: “Holy Father, I shall not leave this basilica of yours until you restore my brother to me safe and sound.”

The other brother, meanwhile, had reached the church of the blessed Apostle Andrew, which is in the village of Ostellum. Having implored the apostle’s help, he too was immediately carried to the bank. Seeking his brother, he found him mourning for him. When the latter saw his brother, he began to weep even more from joy and, rushing into his embrace, began to ask how he had been freed.

Afterward they lived for many years and every year most devoutly rendered the service owed to their liberators.

## CHAPTER VI. A Robber Possessed by a Demon and Later Freed

30. Certain followers of Fulk had entered a village of this Father called Bezillis and were raging with much madness to the disturbance of the tenants. Suddenly a message was sent to the brothers and they were informed. They sent some of their number with relics of the saints to ask that the men cease from this harassment.

The venerable Simeon, a man tonsured from the laity but adorned with reasonably commendable habits of modesty and gravity, was in charge of this mission.

As he entered the little enclosure where the robbers had gathered to defend themselves, with the venerable relics of the saints hanging from his neck, one of them seized a stone and irreverently attempted to strike the reverend man. But when he let the stone fall, his own arms and legs were drawn backward by divine power; he collapsed to the ground with a great roar and began to utter the most varied cries.

Seeing this, the others were struck with great terror. They all prostrated themselves on the ground, begging pardon for their offense. At the same time they restored everything they had plundered, declared that they would depart immediately, and begged on behalf of their companion that he might deserve to be freed from this demonic affliction.

The brothers, however, returning good for evil, immediately touched him with water that had been exorcised and poured it over his entire head. At once his body was restored to the use of its feet and hands.

He himself rose unharmed and began in a loud voice to bless God and magnify his servant Maximinus. They quickly departed from there and did not dare add any further act of recklessness in that village.

## CHAPTER VII. A Charioteer Safely Saved amid the Waves

31. The river Loire, adjoining this monastery, is very often a source of profit and sometimes also of harm. For frequently, when it nearly covers this island by overflowing its channel and becomes one sea together with the Loiret, it deprives the islanders of passage and brings them no small hardships.

When this difficulty arose, scarcity occurred in the brothers’ house. The duty of addressing it seemed to belong to a certain servant named Alvaldus. The cellarer harshly reproached him for abandoning his assigned task instead of attending to this need.

Overcome by the insistence, Alvaldus took two asses with him and boarded a small boat, while the water covered almost the entire surface of the island and the wind was blowing against him.

Unable to struggle against the wind, he was swept with his asses into the middle of the sea. There the depth of the rushing river and the opposing wind left him no further hope of safety. The waves raised threatening heaps and covered the boat, so that it seemed not so much that the boat was among the waves as that the waves were inside the boat.

When he could accomplish nothing with pole or oar, he sat in the stern and began with a loud voice to implore the help of the great Father Maximinus.

Immediately the wind ceased. Although the boat was filled with waves, he was led by an invisible hand and reached the harbor of Marogilum (Mareau), himself greatly wondering how he had been able to escape.

Then he returned to the monastery with his asses and brought great joy to all the brothers by his deliverance.

## CHAPTER VIII. One Who Lay Long in the River, Yet Did Not Die

32. Vivianus, a canon of St. Martin, had once been especially close to this place. On one occasion, when he came there, he brought with him a canon of his own community named Constantinus. The brothers received them gladly and detained them for two days with every courtesy.

On the day when they appeared ready to return, a young man from their company entered the cloister at midday, while the brothers were resting, with a bow and arrows.

[Note: [Col. 0811D] Compare the Rule of St. Benedict, chapter 43.]

With some companions, he began to behave with much noise and frivolity, now shooting arrows, now disturbing the brothers by running and shouting. Although he was warned to desist from such great foolishness, he did not comply. Out of respect for those who had brought him, the brothers bore this patiently for the time being.

But when they had left the monastery that day, the reckless young man boarded a boat opposite the church of Blessed Hilary, where the deep currents of the Loiret River sometimes leave no ford.

When he reached the middle of the river, he carelessly lowered the pole he was holding into the water and fell in after it. He lay there from the ninth hour almost until nightfall. Although many searched for him, he could not be found.

When people had given up hope of him and darkness was already settling in, a fisherman named Barbas dragged him out with a hook, placed him in the boat, and carried him to the bank.

No breath could be detected in him; everyone said he was dead. Great grief, especially among the clerics who had brought him, and intolerable weeping brought many people of different ages and conditions together there.

He was carried to the church, hung up by the feet, and after much wine or water had been poured into him, he was taken down in the middle of the night when he appeared to be alive. Gradually returning to himself, he began to wonder greatly what was happening to him.

When he was asked where he had been and how he could have remained alive among the waves for so many hours, he said:

“Because of the recklessness I committed against a holy place, I had indeed been condemned to death. But through the intervention of the great Father Maximinus, I was recalled from the very jaws of Hell and restored to life. And he whom I had injured, in merciful fashion, became himself the author of my pardon and salvation.”

At daybreak he went barefoot and with great humility to the monastery. Entrusting himself to our great Father, he began to ask pardon for his recklessness and to render the greatest thanks for his life. He lived afterward for many years as a witness to so great an event.

## CHAPTER IX. A Cleric Who Fell from the Church Roof Yet Remained Unharmed

33. The venerable Abbot Anno, who holds the greatest place among the memories of the devout, had ordered a bell to be prepared for the uses of the church. According to the custom of certain people, it was baptized and raised onto the church roof.

While those who had carried it up were walking across the church roof, a certain cleric, proceeding incautiously—his name is still Flodonicius—failed to notice a ceiling panel attached by nails and only loosely suspended. Thinking it was firm material, as soon as he placed his foot upon it as though it were free, he immediately fell with a great crash.

First he struck the head of the Crucified One beneath whom Maximinus stood, immediately breaking its crown and arm. Then he fell upon the walls of the screen, afterward upon the wooden steps, and finally was thrown down upon the pavement.

Yet, having fallen in such a way, he lives unharmed to this day through the intervention of Father Maximinus, although nearly thirty years and more have passed since the event occurred.

## CHAPTER X. The Man Whose Hands Clung to a Spade

34. In the time of the same pious abbot Anno, when I was still a very young child—for I shall relate not what I heard but what I saw—a miracle occurred which I shall now describe.

There was a certain tenant named Benedictus, a man of no inconsiderable means, who lived in a village adjoining ours called Godgiacus. He hired a newcomer for pay to dig a portion of his field.

The feast day of this Father was approaching; it is commemorated on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of January by his passing from this life.

The man who had undertaken to cultivate the field, being a newcomer and unaware of so great a feast, was fired by the desire to hasten his work. At dawn on the feast day he took a digging tool, which they call a *bessa* [French *bêche*], and went to the field to work.

As he worked, a voice suddenly addressed him, saying: “Teduine”—for that was his name—“why are you doing this?”

When he turned his eyes here and there and saw no one, he persisted in the work he had begun. Nevertheless, the same voice again asked in the same words why he presumed to do this.

He looked around and, seeing absolutely no one, climbed the embankment surrounding the field. After carefully looking about and finding no one, he returned to his work.

But for the third time the same voice restrained him with the same words. Immediately his fingers stiffened, and his hands clung to the spade so firmly that he could not move them by any means.

He hurried back to his master’s house and, with a great wail, showed what had happened to him. His master, thinking that his hands had stiffened from the cold—for a severe winter had then set in—ordered water to be heated and his stiff hands rubbed with it.

He cried out even more loudly that he was being tormented. Then his master, remembering the feast day, understood the reason for the anxiety that held him and immediately sent him to the monastery, carrying before him the evidence of his guilt.

35. The Sunday Mass was being celebrated, and they had reached the point at which the Lamb of God, who was sacrificed for us, is both invoked and received, when the man entered the church with much shouting and threw himself down before the altar.

At first they thought he was being tormented by a demon; afterward they suspected that he had fabricated the matter through some deception.

They approached and tried to pull his hands away, but could not do so by any means. The elders therefore decreed that litanies should be sung for him, so that he who had bound him by power might deign to release him through mercy.

When the time for the meal arrived, men were appointed to bring food to him in the church and place it in his mouth.

After the meal, a certain brother named Wido, formerly a notable man in the world, approached him and asked what his condition was. When the man replied that he was free, Wido said:

“Rise, then, and approach the altar. Voluntarily entrust yourself to our Father, and you will immediately be freed.”

When he consented, Wido gave him his hand so that he might rise. He was led to the altar, since he could not go by means of his hands, and, entrusting himself with a suppliant voice, he said:

“Saint Maximinus, have mercy on me, and know that, once freed from these bonds, wherever I may be, I shall be your servant.”

As he said this, he fell backward as though he had been struck with tremendous force. The spade leapt far away in the opposite direction with a great crash, causing many to marvel.

The brothers also came running, and with immense rejoicing they seized the bells and began to magnify the Lord for all his mighty works, by which he never ceases to glorify his saints. He demonstrates that they truly live with him, since beside their lifeless ashes he so beautifully and elegantly triumphs over the pride of the living.

That spade hung for a long time from the church ceiling, and every year, on the annual feast day, the man paid upon the altar of his liberator the head-tax owed for himself.

## CHAPTER XI. Brothers Terrified and Miraculously Saved

[Col. 0814D]

36. Since the merciful Father sometimes wins over a son by gifts, sometimes restrains him through the correction of severity, and since favorable circumstances sometimes make a person more secure and thereby bring him down more disastrously, while adversity admonishes everyone to act with greater caution, the divine eye perhaps observed that we had grown too relaxed after so great a miracle. Therefore, at a later time, it pleased him to terrify us with a certain misfortune. We were indeed miraculously terrified, but through the intervention of that same most pious Father of ours we were saved even more miraculously.

37. For in the following summer, at an unseasonable hour of the night, a sudden whirlwind darkened the sky; the depth of the gloom removed all sight, frequent flashes of lightning struck terror, and the winds engaged in fierce combat with one another. We sprang from our beds and were driven into the church, stunned with great fear, unable to remember the psalms [f., “we sang,” and] the litanies. The sacred candle was extinguished and, shaken at its middle, as though unwilling to come to our aid, slipped down to the ground. At this sight our fear increased and our dread grew; the signals that had been taken up were relaxed as terror interrupted us, and no comfort of any kind could be found among us in our agitation.

A certain Waldefredus, the sacristan—not indeed a monk, but tonsured as a layman—more steadfast than the others, was standing outside the church. When he saw a fiery projectile approaching from afar out of the north, he announced it to those who were stunned and overcome with great terror. He had scarcely finished speaking when, behold, lightning descended through the middle of the little tower’s column and entered the church; it began to roll over us, scattering stones and the masonry of the walls amid boiling flames.

Ewrardus, one of the priors, was standing there. As soon as a slight spark touched him, it struck him to the ground as though he were dead. Maynardus, who later presided over the monastery of Fossés (Saint-Maur des Fossés, in the diocese of Paris), was returning from the oratory of Saint Mary. The same spark struck him, hurled his shoes far away, and cast him lifeless upon the pavement. The entire front of the church was like a blazing furnace; our eyes saw nothing but fire. No one concerned himself with those lying on the ground: each awaited his own death.

For a long time, then, that globe rolled about above us, until at last it slipped beneath the reading desk. We thought that the sky had collapsed headlong, and that chaos, gaping open, had fallen upon the earth. Nothing wiser occurred to us than the words: “The day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night.” An intolerable stench followed and cruelly wounded the minds of those who trembled. We carried out those whom we had thought dead; they stank even more horribly than pigs newly scorched. When our senses returned, we began already to mourn them, but they had neither voice nor consciousness. We assigned guards to them and began the morning hymns.

When morning came and they had regained a more vigorous consciousness, we examined them after stripping them. In Ewrardus there was a line, black on the outside but fiery within, extending in a perfectly straight course from the crown of his head to the sole of his foot. Maynardus, moreover, was marked with a cross on his right shoulder. It spread in every direction to the measure of a man’s palm, yet it too was black on the outside and burning within. Maynardus recovered in a short time; Ewrardus, after lying ill for some time, subsequently lived on for many years in improved health.

## CHAPTER XII. The death of Abbot Anno

38. When Anno, abbot of blessed memory, had governed the same monastery piously for nearly thirty years, on the first day of Epiphany he was stripped of the burden of the flesh amid the almost unbearable grief of all who survived him. He left us bereft of his devout charity and, at the same time, deeply saddened by a second loss. For nine days earlier, Bernerius, who administered the office of dean, an outstanding man among the foremost, had completed a praiseworthy life with a praiseworthy end.

Thus deprived, as it were, of two lights, the remaining brothers were left in great care and anxiety. When Bishop Ermenthaeus learned of this, he was overcome with grief. Taking with him his clergy and whatever nobles were available, as well as the reverend Richard, abbot of Saint Benedict, he came to the monastery to console the brothers and arrange the rites of the holy man’s funeral. We buried him in the outer court facing north, beside the tomb of Suthardus, a most distinguished man who loved this place sincerely and cherished its inhabitants with extraordinary affection.

39. Twelve years after the burial of the venerable Anno, the court in which he had been interred began to be enlarged and raised more suitably, after its old foundations had been demolished. When the wooden coffin of the blessed abbot, exposed by the removal of earth from the headward side for the laying of the foundations, appeared, we approached and opened it. We saw that his body and garments were so perfectly preserved that he seemed to have been placed there on that very day.

40. But to return to what happened next: after the venerable abbot had been buried, since the place could not remain without a shepherd, Isaac, whom we mentioned above, was again appointed dean. At about the same time Bishop Ermenthaeus was seized by a serious illness and began to be despaired of. Since he did not recover at all, he was carried to the monastery during the first week of the fast and clothed in the monastic habit. Soon recovering, he lived in the monastery; his conduct was wholly pleasing and never burdensome to anyone.

The brothers, however, preferred to have him as their shepherd. At first he agreed, but later, changing his mind, he began to try to place a certain Hermenaldus, a monk of Saint Benedict, over the brothers. Ernulfus, his illustrious nephew and foremost among the most energetic men, had already been substituted in the episcopate. Since he was extremely pleasant and lovable, the brothers went to him and asked that Hermenaldus not be placed over them.

When their request had been granted and Bishop Ermenthaeus had thereby been defeated, he nevertheless could not be overcome on this point: that one of us should be made abbot. At that time there was in the place of Saint Benedict a dean named Amalricus, a simple man of good reputation, and distinguished according to worldly rank. When he had been summoned, the place having been without a shepherd for a year and eight days, they appointed him abbot.

Ermenthaeus, after living in this place for two years and one month, departed, as we believe, for eternal life on the Kalends of April.

[Note: From this passage the catalogue of the bishops of Orléans must be corrected, for it places Manasses after Ermenthaeus. This observation easily resolves the difficulty of Saussay, who finds it strange that Arnulfus should have begun his episcopate in the year 963 and yet that Manasses, whom he considers Arnulfus’s predecessor, should have subscribed the Synod of Sens in 981.]

41. When his glorious successor saw himself alone, he immediately manifested the love that he bore toward the place. Among the other benefits he conferred, he released to us the revenues of all our churches that seemed to belong to him, and decreed in writing and with synodal authority that they should henceforth be received by no bishop.

Later, when he went to Rome, he had the decree issued and drawn up with apostolic authority copied in our script on parchment and in the Roman script on papyrus. On his return, he placed it in our archive. In that decree he added that no one from any monastery should ever be appointed in that monastery without the consent of the brothers; whoever dared to do so was to be punished with anathema.

By this act he so won the affection of the brothers that, among the other obligations of prayer, it was decreed that every week a sacrifice of praise should be offered twice for him and for his predecessors and successors. But enough of this. Since we have touched only briefly upon the virtues of the great Father Maximinus, let us proceed to what happened in these days, under this abbot.

## CHAPTER XIII. Those who were buried beneath the earth but did not die

42. The guesthouse had collapsed, and we had begun to rebuild it. Across the Loire, however, a certain clay is found from which walls can be raised at little expense in place of masonry. Laborers were therefore assigned to dig it. While they were digging on the sloping side of a mountain and carrying out the earth after entering it, the overhanging mountain fell upon them. It completely covered two of them and crushed the third beneath its enormous mass, with only his head appearing outside.

The monk who had hired them, turned bloodless with fear, rushed up, repeatedly invoking the name of Father Maximinus. But who would have thought that they were alive? Nevertheless, the others rose with all their strength and vied with one another in clearing away the earth, though they declared that those buried beneath so great a mass were dead. After expending much labor, they brought out alive those whom they had believed extinguished.

When those who had been rescued were being carried away on stretchers, they saw clouds moving overhead and, stunned with great fear, thought that the mountain was collapsing again. They said, “Woe, woe! We shall die again; behold, we see the mountain falling.” Through the intervention of Father Maximinus, therefore, they were saved from death, so that their work would not be stained by a fatality, and they remain alive and unharmed to this day.

## CHAPTER XIV. The blind man plunged into the water

43. Abbot Almaricus was standing with some of the brothers on the riverbank while materials were being transported for the construction of the aforementioned house; by his presence he was vigorously encouraging the laborers. Behold, a certain poor man without the light of his eyes, using a guide to lead him, was making his way to a mill in order to beg for alms.

There was a long and narrow plank from the bank to the mill, along which people went and returned. When the blind man reached its middle, his foot slipped—for he could not see—and he fell into the water. Sinking to the bottom and rising again, he began to be carried extremely rapidly by the rushing current.

When his guide saw this, he began to shout as loudly as he could. Since the man repeatedly surfaced, many people hurried together, but their efforts were ineffective against the force of the river. When the abbot and the brothers who were with him saw this and realized that human assistance was lacking, they immediately implored the aid of the holy Father Maximinus in supplication. At once, the man who was being dragged away was carried to the bank by the obedient wave, and a man who was hastening with a small boat pulled him out unharmed.

## CHAPTER XV. The poor man living beneath a rock

44. There was there a very lofty rock whose face, turned toward the south, opened inward with the greatest spaciousness, while its back, presented toward the north, excluded the southwest wind and offered abundant warmth to those wishing to enjoy the sunshine beneath it.

A poor man came there with his wife and six little children. Finding no lodging, he took refuge with his family beneath the same rock and spent there the entire winter and the season of Lent. On the holy day of Easter he came with all his family to the basilica consecrated there in honor of Saint Maximinus—the place from which he had driven out the dragon by destroying it, and in which, as was said above, he had rested.

While the poor man and the family he had brought with him were waiting to receive the life-giving mysteries, the rock that had sheltered him for so many days fell and rolled down with a tremendous collapse. When the poor man returned and saw the once-friendly roof lying in ruins, he gave thanks to the almighty Lord and began to magnify in a loud voice his servant Maximinus, whose merciful intercession had freed him and his family from the impending destruction.

## CHAPTER XVI. The custom imposed by the provost Salomon and abolished by the grace of the Lord

45. As we were writing, according to the ability of our small talent, about the virtues of our most excellent Father Maximinus, it happened that certain venerable men were present. When, at their request, we reviewed what had been said, they confessed that we had omitted many things in which they themselves had taken part, and among many others they recalled to our memory the miracle that we are about to relate.

46. In the time of Anno, abbot of blessed memory, there was a certain prefect named Salomon, an official of Duke Hugh—namely, Hugh the Great or Hugh Capet. He was an insolent man and violently hostile to the monasteries of the saints. He persecuted this place especially with a particular hatred, to such an extent that he attempted to divert the course of the Loire through the land under his jurisdiction. Although he spent much wealth on this effort in vain, he did not achieve his desire.

When he had attempted this kind of wickedness without success, he prepared to harm the place in many other ways. The brothers persisted humbly, but their prayers had no effect upon the wicked man, so they turned to the mercy of the Lord.

When his henchmen came—as people commonly say—to exact assistance according to the custom recently wickedly imposed by them, the brothers went out to meet them with the holy relics and asked why so great a crime was being attempted. But those men, in a proud spirit, took up arms against the defenseless and ordered the ox-drivers to take away a wagon that was already loaded with wine.

One day, refusing to come to the monastery with his officials, Salomon attempted to impose his fiscal exactions in the surrounding villages. He carried wine seized from the vats and presses—for it was the season of the vintage—to the public cellar. Immediately one man, named Fulcherius, was seized by a demon. The others, driven by extreme terror, fled; the oxen, bloodied here and there, could not move the wagon from its place. At last, when the brothers approached, the wagon was taken back to the house of a servant named Daniel, and thus what they had wickedly stolen was restored.

On the following day Salomon himself came to the monastery with complete humility. Having obtained forgiveness, he did not dare attempt anything similar again. Fulcherius too, brought there not long afterward, was restored by the grace of the Lord to health. But the lives of those whose hearts pride hardened were ended by the most cruel death and a horrifying fate.

## CHAPTER XVII. The man who excused himself by trickery when asked to prune the vineyard

47. The season for pruning the vineyard had arrived, and, by order of the abbot, a brother named Haldeisus was seeking several laborers for this work. When he had gathered many but thought that he still did not have enough, he went to the house of a certain Durandus to ask him to come to the work.

When Durandus’s wife saw him approaching, she said, “Look, Lord Haldeisus is coming so that you may go with the others to prune the vineyard.” He replied, “I shall not go. But, lest this man perhaps be saddened, I shall pretend that my arm is disabled, and by this means I shall remain free of blame.”

As he said this, he hung his arm from his neck. When the monk came and asked him to come to the work, he replied that he could not. When the monk persisted, he threw back his cloak and showed him the hanging arm: “Look, lord,” he said, “I would gladly go, but, as you see, I cannot come for this reason.”

The monk, believing him in his simplicity, withdrew. Suddenly the arm of the man who had deceived him was seized by sharp pain and so tormented that he could not move it at all to do anything. Understanding the cause, he said, “Look, wife: what we said in jest, the reality now compels us truly to say. My arm is so tortured that it seems to me to be completely crushed.”

He spent the following night without sleep. In the morning he made a vow, saying, “Saint Maximinus, free me from these pains justly inflicted upon me, and every year I promise to devote one day to your service, wherever I am ordered to go.” After saying this, he recovered without delay, and, fulfilling his vow, he remains healthy and unharmed to this day.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Adelardus, keeper of the horses

48. The keepers of Duke Robert’s horses had entered the meadow belonging to the monastery and, driving in a multitude of horses, intended to graze it bare. The brothers’ provost approached and began to ask them not to do this. Those of sounder judgment, out of reverence for Father Maximinus, left the meadow and, after crossing the Loire, spread themselves through the meadows of Marogilus (Mareuil).

One man, however, armed with a proud spirit, named Adelardus, who seemed to be in charge of the others, attacked the monks with insults. Presuming in insolent words to blaspheme the name of so great a Father, he undertook, with many of his companions, to keep the horses in the same meadow.

But divine judgments followed his pride. For, while he was resting in that meadow during the same night, blessed Maximinus appeared to him in a terrifying manner. Rebuking him for his folly, he struck him with the crooked staff that he appeared to carry. Rising, Adelardus began to cry out that he was dying. When his companions came running, he told them amid wailing that blessed Maximinus had struck him with a mortal blow.

He immediately ordered the horses to be driven out and himself to be carried away. But as his suffering grew worse, he breathed out his spirit in the hands of those carrying him. Because of this, such terror seized his companions that to this day no one has been found who has dared to attempt anything similar.

These are the things that the aforementioned elders confessed we had omitted, along with many others that, wishing to avoid tediousness, we have decided to leave unmentioned. Now let us proceed to what happened in our own days.

## CHAPTER XIX. Those afflicted with the burning disease

49. As the sins of the people increased and provoked the justice of God, around the middle of August a great plague began to ravage the people of Orléans. Human limbs burned with a divine fire, against whose heat no human skill could prevail. This force devastated every sex and every age, but especially the limbs of children.

What could those whom such dire necessity pressed upon do? They sought the intercession of the saints and implored divine aid where human help was lacking. Since such sufferers were brought in crowds to nearly all the places of the saints, an immense multitude gathered especially before this merciful Father, to such an extent that the brothers could not reverently sing the divine offices to the Almighty as was fitting.

Who could have endured so many dreadful groans and the intolerable stench of human limbs burning? Whose heart could have been so hard that it would not be softened by such misfortune? Moreover, so great was the multitude of these wretched people that, if they had all been gathered together in the church, they would have filled the choir and the crypts.

The brothers endured this burden somehow during the day. When night approached, they were driven from the church and remained in the northern portico adjoining it, as well as in shelters made for themselves in the courtyard. At dawn they returned to the monastery and begged for God’s help through the intervention of the merciful Father Maximinus, using these words:

“O most excellent friend of God, who by the gift of the same Creator of all things have accustomed yourself to restrain your abundant benefits from no one who asks, bring us swift aid, lest, while this torment persists, the breath of our life be taken from us. Through you, to whom we flee trusting in your merits, may the divine power appear to us, and may we hope through your intercession for the forgiveness of the most merciful God.”

As they said these things with many tears and the inward mourning of their hearts, they did not cease to kiss the pavement of the sacred church.

50. The clemency of the merciful God received the cry mingled with the groaning of these pitiable sufferers, as the devout intercessor Maximinus pleaded, and deigned to extinguish the burning in all their limbs. Afterwards, the bones of many whose flesh the fire had consumed were cut away with a sharp blade. In some, the flesh had been so violently destroyed that the loosened parts fell away of themselves.

It is impossible for the tongue to enumerate individually how many there were, especially since, as we said above, the people had flocked together in such numbers. Indeed, the greater part of them were taken from this life as soon as they had obtained health. At last I judged it worthwhile to write by name about those who lived for a long time afterward, so that readers might more readily believe the account.

51. A certain countryman named Ingelbertus, together with his son Gilbertus and a daughter whose name has escaped us, was afflicted by the divine fire. They were so ravaged that the father lost his right foot; the son lost his left thigh and his right lower leg down to the knee; and the daughter lost her left lower leg down to the knee. Thus mutilated, they were finally delivered by divine judgment through the merits of the glorious Father Maximinus and lived for many years thereafter.

52. At that time a little boy named Constantinus, whose left-foot instep had been attacked by this diseased affliction, was carried in the arms of his aunt, named Hermentrudis. He remained there for eight days, and the suffering of the disease allowed him no sleep by day or night. The aforementioned aunt then received from a certain servant of God the advice that she should ask the sacristans to allow her boy to sleep inside the church for one of the nights. This was done.

Behold, in the silence of the night the woman saw a snow-white dove enter the church, and at its entrance the whole church become radiant. It approached the altar and settled there for a little while. The boy, however, was immediately seized by sleep and thereafter felt no further suffering from the disease; nor did any trace of the burning appear.

53. There was another boy with the same name, suffering from a similar disease, but he was not saved in the same manner. No mortal can comprehend the judgment of the heavenly Judge. His mother was named Erfrida, while his father had already put off the human condition.

By chance, a certain dog attacked this boy and bit his right foot. Because of this circumstance, he was brought, burned by the fire, to the threshold of our most merciful advocate, Father Maximinus. After remaining there for a little while, he obtained complete health, and to this day he remains in the service of the brothers, employed as a shepherd.

54. A certain man named Laurentius, although a countryman, was born of a noble family and was the father of two sons. The elder of the little brothers was called Tedmarus, and the younger Gilardus. The aforementioned illness attacked the boys’ right calves and gradually occupied their shins and feet with increasing violence.

Finally, for the sake of obtaining health, their father—whose mind was bound by affection for his sons and who could find no means of helping them—first brought them to the basilica of the mother church of the Holy Cross. After some time had passed there, they obtained no remedy of health.

As the urgency of the burning grew, while they continually struck the most merciful ears of the Lord with the cry of inward pain, the father received counsel from one of the faithful to take them as quickly as possible to the threshold of Maximinus, the confessor of Christ. The divine power, he was told, is readily present to all mortals suffering from bodily affliction.

He immediately hastened on the journey with the boys. When he arrived at the basilica of the most merciful confessor, he implored the merit of this aforementioned patron, asking that, by coming to their aid, he extinguish the boys’ burning limbs. The divinity, which distributes great deeds by its own command in every place and time, was not pleased to delay long.

After several days had passed, the boys’ limbs, consumed by the fire, were extinguished, and through the intervention of the renowned Father Maximinus they were restored to health.

55. At the same time, as the sacred vigil of the Lord’s Nativity was approaching, a certain man named Bernerius, who is still alive, was taking part with the other faithful in the watches of so great a solemnity. Keeping vigil according to the solemn custom, he was suddenly seized by a disease of untimely madness. This had perhaps happened to him because of the excessive heat of the baths [that is, their warmth], in which he had been washed that same night for the sake of the grace of so great a feast.

[Note: A trace of this rite survives in the Decrees of Lanfranc. “On the vigil of the apostle Thomas,” he says, “if it is not a Sunday, let the brothers be shaved; and let those who wish to bathe do so, so that all may have bathed two days before the Lord’s Nativity. If it is necessary, they may bathe on the very day of the apostolic feast.” The same author prescribes there the discipline that the monks customarily observed in this work. A much earlier mention of the practice appears in the rule of a certain Father, chapter 12, in these words: “Likewise, for washing the heads of the brothers every Saturday, or for the use of baths on festive solemnities, let preparations be made.” See the notes of our Menardus on chapter 55 of the *Concordia Regularum*.]

For, as the elements were at variance with one another in an unequal temperature—it was then the excessive cold of midwinter—he completely lost his senses. As the bodily disorder increased day by day, he became so violent that he could no longer be restrained by any bonds. His face was marked by a most dreadful pallor, his eyes were suffused with blood, his limbs were pitifully contorted, his whole body repeatedly flung itself headlong, he rolled lamentably throughout the sacred church, and he greedily devoured the pavement and the rushes strewn upon it. He was a guest lodging in a Christian hospice.

Therefore, when his guardians had been exhausted by such treatment, he was thrust, with the doors locked, into the little oratory of Saint John the Baptist for nearly fifteen days. But our singular glory, the most holy Father Maximinus, who through the grace of Christ is a constant healer and physician of such illnesses, quickly expelled the hidden enemy’s plague through the antidote of his merits.

He did not permit the man whom the devotion of the faithful had entrusted to him for healing to remain long without aid. After a few days had passed, the enemy was driven out with the congealed blood of his mouth. The sick man was found before the most sacred altar as though dead; scarcely any vital warmth of his breathing spirit could be detected in his breast.

The faithful immediately carried him from the church in their arms and took him into a small room adjoining the church. Within a few days he was restored to perfect health, aided in everything by the vigilant care of the brothers. Blessed be God in all things.

*The following appears to be by another author.*

56. Another man, whose name has been lost, arrived deprived of the light of his eyes from the very moment of his birth. Spending the night before the tomb of so great a patron, who assists those who implore him, he deserved to obtain an illumination that he had never experienced and had always desired.

While, with steadfast faith of mind, he trusted that the mercy of the confessor’s intercession would grant him what nature had not bestowed, and while he did not cease his cries of continual distress, suddenly, at a certain touch of the most merciful Rabbo, a stream of blood burst from the very sockets of his eyes. Thereafter, beneath the hand of so great a craftsman, his pupil, previously unacquainted with light, feared the unfamiliar radiance, and then stored within his heart the images of things in a corresponding likeness.

O power of the heavenly King, immense and incorporeal in its nature, which willed to make itself physically perceptible to a mortal through spiritual touch! It destroyed the inborn glaucoma and filled the clouded mirror of the eyes with a double radiance.

57. A boy of twelve named Erfredus had lost altogether the ability to walk because the tendons behind his knees had withered. For many years he had been carefully raised and regularly nourished by the monks of Micy.

But that inexhaustible fountain of mercy, which commands innocence’s purity to be practiced with a devout heart, without any admixture of leaven, wished one night to admonish him to seek the help of Father Maximinus if he desired to obtain health for his entire body.

Trusting the heavenly admonition, he entered the inner church at daybreak and, prostrating himself before the sacred mausoleum, appealed in the innocent affection of his heart to the holy merits of the most merciful confessor. There was no delay: the divine kindness came to his aid.

Rising as though by example, and receiving complete health throughout his body, on the third Sunday of the resurrection of the Savior, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1041, at the second hour of the day, he increased the joys of that Paschal solemnity by the considerable restoration of his own health.

Appropriately, a prophetic voice then sounded for him: “The earth is full of the mercy of the Lord.” At this, the entire people, amazed by such great depths of mercy, hastened together, roused by the ringing of the bells.

## THE TRANSFER OF THE BODY OF SAINT JUNIANUS TO THE SYNOD OF KARROFENSE

Described around the year 988 by Letaldus, a monk of Micy.

[According to Mabillon, *Acta Saeculi IV*, p. 434.]

1. To the lord Father Constantinus and the other brothers of the monastery of Nobiliac, brother Letaldus sends greetings in the Lord.

The angel Raphael was sent by the Lord to relieve Tobias’s labors. After rescuing him not only from his troubles but also assisting him with the benefits of divine mercy, and as he was about to return to the one by whom he had been sent, from whom, even in going forth, he had not departed, he addressed those whom he had raised up through the gift of heavenly favor, saying: “It is good to conceal the king’s secret, but it is honorable to reveal and confess the works of God” (Tobit 12).

Therefore it is fitting for us to reveal and confess the works of Christ that he has deigned to perform in our time through his most glorious confessor Junianus, for the praise and glory of his name and for the edification of those who hear, so that all may know that the works he performed in the days of our fathers he also performs with us—not on account of our merits, but through the benefit of his mercy and through the intercession of those fathers whom he has given us as intercessors and set before us as examples worthy of imitation, for the correction of the severity of our lives.

2. Let us therefore undertake the task we have promised, distrustful indeed of our own strength but supported by the aid of divine generosity, namely, of him who says: “Open your mouth, and I will fill it” (Psalm 81:11).

But you, reverend fathers and brothers, assist by your prayers the task that you have imposed through the authority of charity. Let our rusticity not displease you too much, provided that the truth of what happened, alone and entire as it was handed down by you, is pleasing.

When sinners had arisen like grass, and when, like brambles and thorns choking the earthly harvest, every kind of wicked person was devastating the Lord’s vineyard, it pleased the bishops, abbots, and all religious men that a council should be held. At it, plundering would be forbidden, things unjustly taken from the saints would be restored, and the other evils that defiled the beautiful face of the holy Church of God would be struck under the sword of anathema.

This council was therefore appointed to be convened at the monastery of Karrofense, and a great gathering of peoples took place there from the regions of Poitou and Limousin and from the neighboring territories. Many bodies of saints were also brought there, so that by their presence both religious devotion might be strengthened and the insolence of the wicked restrained.

That council, convened, as is believed, by the will of God, was made illustrious by frequent miracles through the presence of the saints. Among the other relics worthy of God, the remains of the glorious Father Junianus were also brought with fitting honor.

[Note: In the synod held around the year 988, attended by Hugo, bishop of Angoulême, who died in 990, the second chapter decrees measures against plunderers. There can therefore be no doubt that this transfer should be referred to that synod.]

3. While these proceedings were taking place, after the relics of the holy Father had been carried out from the monastery, those who bore the sacred burden sat down not far from the monastery and set down their holy load.

At that place, after the most holy relics had been carried away, the devotion of the faithful raised the banner of the cross in memory and remembrance that the relics of the holy Father had rested there. From that time until now, whoever suffering from fever has approached that place, after invoking the name of Christ, has obtained his former health through the intervention of the same Father.

From there, when they had come to a village called Ruffiacus, they received lodging and spent that night in vigils of praise and hymns to God. At daybreak they resumed their journey. Nevertheless, at the same place where the relics had rested, the Christian faithful made a kind of enclosure from pliant willow branches, so that the place where the sacred limbs had been laid might remain protected from the approach of people and animals.

After many days a fierce bull approached and playfully shook the same fence with its horns and ribs. But as soon as it withdrew from the fence, it collapsed and died.

At the same place, a pool had formed from a great rainfall. Retaining the collected water for some time, it invited many people to wash themselves out of reverence for the sacred relics. Among them came a woman suffering from elephantiasis. After washing herself in that water, she was restored to her former health and returned home unharmed.

# THE YEAR OF THE LORD 816. POPE JOHN XV

## HISTORICAL NOTICE

[According to Mansi, *Amplissima Collectio Conciliorum*, vol. XIX, p. 82.]

John, a Roman by birth, was born to Leo, later a priest. After the tyrant had been killed, he was lawfully elected by common consent in the year of Christ 985, during the reign of Otto III.

Fearing what his predecessor had suffered, he withdrew into Tuscany, when he was being harassed by a new tyrant, Crescentius of Nomentum, who, under the title of consul, had begun to occupy the fortress of Saint Angelo. Since he frequently sent embassies to Otto, the Romans, remembering what they had suffered under earlier Ottos because of injuries inflicted upon the pontiffs, immediately recalled the same John through an honorable embassy. They assured him complete security and asked him to return to the City.

When he did so, everyone went out to meet him on his arrival, honored him with devout services and attentions, and subjected themselves to him. He granted the pallium to Libentio, bishop of Hamburg. He sent Leo, vice-bishop of Trier, as an envoy to the king of England and the duke of the Northmen, in order to reconcile them in their dispute.

He disapproved the acts of the false synod of Reims, at which Arnulfus had been removed and Gerbertus substituted in his place, and he successfully arranged for the deposed man to be restored to his see.

[Note: This was not accomplished until the pontificate of Gregory V.]

To repel the tyranny of Crescentius, which grew stronger day by day, he asked Otto, king of Germany, to come to Rome. Before Otto arrived, however, the excellent pontiff died on 7 May, after having sat for ten years, [lacuna] months, and twelve days. He was buried in the basilica of Saint Peter, in the oratory of Saint Mary.

# LETTERS AND PRIVILEGES OF POPE JOHN XV

## I. PRIVILEGE FOR THE MONASTERY OF COELI AUREI AT PAVIA

Fragment. — (Year 986)

[Col. 0827A]

He confirms all the possessions of that place at the request of Abbot Peter, and grants him the use of the dalmatic, sandals, stockings, and gloves, as well as permission to carry a bell in a chapel while traveling—indeed, in honor of Saint Peter and also of “the most holy Augustine, whose most sacred body is buried in that church.” Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of February, through the hands of John, bishop of Nepi, in the first year of Pope John XV, in the fourteenth indiction.

[In Mabillon, *Annales Benedictini*, vol. IV, p. 35.]

## II. PRIVILEGE FOR THE MONASTERY OF SAINT MAXIMINUS. (Year 987.)

[In Hontheim, *History of Trier: Diplomatic Documents*, p. 326.]

[Col. 0827B]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends apostolic blessing to the venerable abbot, our beloved son in Christ, Ogo.

It is fitting for apostolic authority to assist those distinguished by pious religion with benevolent compassion and to grant assent to their religious petition. For we hope to receive a reward from the supreme Creator if, through our efforts, we labor to establish in a better condition the churches prepared for his worship.

Therefore, granting our assent to your religious purpose, we decree by the authority of an apostolic command that the community serving God and Saint Maximinus, just as it was granted to your monastery by our dearest son King Otto and by the other kings or emperors of the Franks, shall henceforth have free power to choose from among themselves [Col. 0827C] as abbot whomever they may select according to God; and that no person of any rank [Note: [Col. 0827D] “Nor any person of any rank,” etc. All this, as relating to the privilege granted by the emperors, concerns civil immunity, not ecclesiastical immunity.] within the monastery, unless invited by you or your successor, shall presume to arrange or exercise anything there according to his own will.

We also forbid by apostolic command that it ever be subjected to any church or see [Note: [Col. 0827D] “That it never be subjected to any church or see by exchange or by any device.” That is, by a suppressive union [Col. 0828D] or another union less primary and perpetual. Compare the notes above on the bull of Pope Agapetus II concerning the year 950], whether by exchange or by any other device. Rather, let it enjoy such liberty and immunity, unharmed and perpetually, as the monastery of Prüm and the other royal establishments do. We command by apostolic authority that the monastery itself remain forever under the protection of the kings and emperors, sons of the holy Roman Church. Let it never be open to any person for exploitation as a benefice or for seizure [Col. 0827D], but let it remain free, for the use and tranquility of the monks [Col. 0828A] there, without anyone’s opposition.

For the increase and completion of monastic tranquility, we also add that no person of any rank, nor any of your successors seduced by an evil spirit, shall presume to alienate even the smallest thing, either from what has now been given to your monastery or from what other faithful people will give day by day.

If anyone, however—which God forbid—should in wicked audacity presume to infringe or in any way violate what has been established for the benefit of the aforesaid venerable monastery, let him know that he is irrevocably [Col. 0828B] bound by the chain of anathema through the authority of almighty God, through the intervention of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, whose office we hold, and through the apostolic constitution of our authority and of the suffragan bishops [Note: [Col. 0828D] “And the suffragan bishops.” From this it appears that this bull was obtained primarily against the archbishop.]

Written by the hand of Theophilus Latinus, notary, regional secretary, and archivist of the Holy Roman Church, in the month of January, in the fifteenth indiction. Farewell.
