Given on the sixth day before the Ides of January, through the hand of John, bishop and librarian of the holy apostolic see, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 987, in the year of the pontificate of the lord John, supreme pontiff and universal bishop XV, in the sacristy of the church of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles.

## III. PRIVILEGE OF POPE JOHN XV FOR THE CHURCH OF NOYON. (Year 788.)

[Colliette, *Memoirs of the Vermandois*, vol. I, p. 577.]

[Col. 0828C]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the whole Gallican Church.

Let the diligence of all the faithful know that our most reverend brother Lyndulphus, namely the venerable bishop of Noyon, Tournai, and Flanders, came into our presence. While we were seated in the seat of holy Jerusalem, he informed us of the needs of his bishopric. It seemed fitting to us, in accordance with apostolic authority and benevolent compassion, to assist him and to grant his request with willing devotion.

For profit, and especially reward, is then laid up with the Lord, Creator of all, when venerable places have been appropriately and orderly brought [Col. 0828D] without doubt to a better [Col. 0829A] condition.

Accordingly, the affection of the aforesaid bishop Lyndulphus humbly and reasonably requested that we sanction and confirm by the security of a privilege the property and laws of his bishopric, as they had been established of old by kings and princes and by our predecessors. Granting assent to his worthy petition, by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and by the confirmation of our privilege, we sanction and confirm that no count or outsider shall have power to seize or constrain a thief within the district of Noyon, or in the villages belonging to that place’s bishop, which were assigned to that district in ancient times.

We have also decreed that in the city of Tournai no count or outside judge shall interfere with the jurisdiction, the mint, or the derivation-tax of one part, nor with the toll; but, just as it was established by the princes of pious memory, so let it remain fixed and unshaken.

Likewise we order that no one cause that bishop or his successors trouble concerning Hileimo, with the mother church and with the chapel that is in Mulius. And in Flanders, concerning the church of Saint Saviour of Gechbecca, Aldenburg, Latfinga, Gestella, and Fleskengem.

As for the abbey of Saint Eligius, formerly assigned by ancient right to religious men laboring under the rule of blessed Benedict, but later, at the devil’s instigation, reduced to the order of canons, and then restored by the venerable bishop Rodulphus to its former rule, after his death wrongly seized by the canons, and now restored by Lyndulphus, our brother, to the monastic order as it had been: we command that it remain in this order.

Only on this condition: that the possessions which Bishop Lyndulphus found in that abbey, and those which he subsequently added, remain with it. He found there Ragemberticurt with its church, Carisiola, Magnulficurt, Verlegium with its church, Mahericurt, Bathbodium, lands at Appiliacum, lands at Bagdinicurt, lands at Andan, lands at Diva, a vineyard on the mountain, lands surrounding the church that belong to it, and small parcels of land in many places; the abbey of Saint Stephen, mills, and Sichericurt. He himself added Bucedrium, Colneium with its church, Gafrimum, Wasemium without mills, saltworks, and Novemvilla—yet only to be ceded during Wido’s lifetime, as we have said above. Thus only, that all [Col. 0829D] the possessions, and whatever the Lord may give in the future, shall at all times serve the use of the monks.

At Lyndulphus’s request we also confirm the gift which Hadulphus, his predecessor as bishop, gave to the canons of that church of Saint Mary and Saint Medard within the walls: namely, the church called Arceium, so that they may hold it perpetually without contradiction.

We have also decreed by our apostolic decision that the gift of Lyndulphus, which he granted for the remedy of his soul to those same canons outside the walls, shall remain fixed and stable: namely, Betonscurt with its ink-making establishment, and the abbey of Saint Godeberta the virgin, which is dedicated in honor of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul. On this condition [Col. 0830A] that four canons out of the sixty serve daily at the body of that blessed virgin, wherever in that city it may lie, together with the toll of that city, in full and everywhere, and whatever he may subsequently grant to those canons.

Therefore, in the seat of holy Jerusalem, under invocation of the divine judgment and by the strongest prohibitions of anathema, we establish that no king, no duke, marquis, or count, neither archbishop nor bishop, nor any person established in any rank or office, shall dare to cause trouble to the property of that bishopric, whether concerning the aforesaid monasteries or anything else listed above, or presume in any way to take away or alienate it. Rather, as has been said, we decree [Col. 0830B] and promulgate that all these things shall remain permanently secure and stable.

If any presumptuous or reckless person is found—whether cleric or layman—who attempts to uproot or wishes to destroy all these things, let him know that he is bound by the chain of the anathema of almighty God, of our lord Peter, prince of the apostles, and of all the saints; that he is hated by God; and that he is to be burned with the devil and Judas, the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the punishment of eternal fire. He shall never be absolved from the aforesaid anathema unless he repents and comes to make satisfaction.

So be it; so be it; so be it.

But whoever is a guardian and observer of this constitution of our apostolic privilege may deserve to obtain the grace of blessing and eternal life from the most merciful Lord God throughout the ages of ages.

[Col. 0830C] Written by the hand of Stephen, archivist of the holy palace, in the month of May and in the first indiction.

## IV. PRIVILEGE FOR THE MONASTERY OF SAINT GREGORY. (Year 989.)

Founded by Gebehard II, bishop of Constance, this place is received under apostolic protection and endowed with various gifts.

[Mansi, *Councils*, vol. XIX, col. 85.]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God. In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, namely the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

We wish it to be known to all the faithful of Christ how Gebehard II, beloved bishop of the holy Church of Constance and our dearest brother, [Col. 0830D] came to Rome for the sake of prayer, to the thresholds of the chief apostles Peter and Paul, and came into our presence. He reported to us that, compelled by God’s will, he had built a church of cenobites on the bank of the river called the Rhine, in honor of blessed Gregory, confessor of Christ, and that in that place he had most splendidly established the rule of Saint Benedict, abbot, and of the brother monks.

There, with the greatest devotion, he offered for their support and provision some of his own estates, which had come to him from his parents, as well as a portion of the property of his holy church—namely, for those monks who, having [renounced the world], do not cease day and night to offer praises to Christ in that holy monastery. Concerning these matters he begged the clemency of our humility [Col. 0831A] that the aforesaid place might remain forever under the protection and defense of Saint Peter and of us and our successors in the pontificate.

On this condition, however, that no king, duke, or marquis, nor even the bishop who at any time may be in that bishopric, nor any person, dare alienate anything from all that the aforesaid Bishop Gebehard has granted there, or remove it in any way from that holy monastery. Rather, we grant that it remain safe, secure, and firm into future times.

We also prohibit by apostolic command, at the request of our aforesaid brother, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that anyone be placed over the same monastery except one whom the brothers serving Christ diligently there have elected by common agreement; and we direct that the bishop confirm the elected man with the title of blessing.

We have likewise decided that the same rule shall apply to the election of the advocate.

If, however—which God forbid—it should ever happen that the bishop of that holy Church is a heretic or schismatic, the brothers of the aforesaid monastery shall, by the authority of the apostolic see, have power to seek ecclesiastical orders wherever they know a Catholic bishop to be found, so that that wicked man may not presume to inflict any injury upon them in this matter.

For if any person of whatever rank or power—which we do not believe—should attempt in any way to violate what our aforesaid brother has granted to the said monastery, and should wish to remove it from the right and jurisdiction of that monastery, unless he repents, let him remain excommunicated from the body [Col. 0831C] and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ and anathematized by all the holy Fathers and by us. Let him not receive Communion at the hour of death, and, even after death, let his name in no way be recited during the solemn celebration of Mass.

But whoever, with pious regard, proves to be the guardian and protector of this our command may deserve to receive the grace of blessing and life from the Lord God himself and Savior Jesus Christ throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

Written by the hand of John, notary, regional secretary, and archivist of the sacred Lateran palace, in the month of April and in the second indiction. Given on the seventh day before the Kalends of May, through the hand of Gregory, bishop of the holy Church of Porto and librarian of the apostolic see, in the fourth year of the pontificate of our lord John, most holy pope.

## V. LETTER OF POPE JOHN XV TO ALL THE FAITHFUL. (Year 989.)

Certain new rights are granted to the monks of Corvey, and older ones are affirmed.

[Col. 0831D]

It is fitting for episcopal authority, and especially for that of the supreme prelate, always to consider devoutly and carefully how they may so exercise care for churches that they do not refuse to provide timely assistance to holy places, in which God is continually appeased by the diligence of those who serve him.

Therefore I, John, servant of the servants of God, prelate of the most holy apostolic see, make known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God that the venerable abbot Thetmarus of the monastery called New Corvey, [Col. 0832A] through the intervention of Hildibrand, bishop of Modena, earnestly sought our clemency, asking that we confirm and strengthen by our authority all the charters of the most glorious emperors, kings, and other princes, as well as the documents granted or written by our predecessors, Adrian and Stephen, and that we add a document bearing our subscription to what had been decreed by the apostolic see.

Accordingly, considering his religious petition, and recognizing that it is the pastoral duty of the servants of God continually to look after their usefulness and welfare, we have decreed that the two monasteries—namely, the monks’ monastery of Corvey and the nuns’ monastery of Herford—concerning all the property which is acknowledged to have been confirmed either in the common charter of the princes or by their commands, shall nevertheless receive such firmness from apostolic sanction that those who promise themselves that they will at some time be able to alter or violate these arrangements shall find nothing by which they can protect themselves.

Let the aforesaid monasteries therefore have free power in all things to dispose regularly of their property. And, to pursue more fully what we understand the holy apostles already mentioned, and before them blessed Gregory and Nicholas of venerable memory, to have decreed concerning the condition of monasteries, we humbly confirm by our subscription these great authorities, so that no bishop of Paderborn may either receive or demand any portion from them, nor exercise authority over those who hold the place of governance, over the communities themselves, or over the monasteries themselves [Col. 0832C]; nor may he possess any domination over them, whether over the clergy, the servants, or anything whatsoever that appears to belong to the monasteries themselves, just as all this has until now been observed and granted by the bishops in whose dioceses the property of those monasteries is situated.

For we grant to the abbot of the aforesaid monastery and to his successors permission to sit beside the altar and to preach and teach the people within his monastery or cells according to God. No bishop, therefore, nor his steward, archpriest, archdeacon, or any person acting on his behalf shall have power to enter those monasteries or their cells, unless perhaps he comes when called for a necessity or out of affection, so that the holy places may not be troubled by his intrusiveness or by the disturbance caused by his ministers.

Nor shall he attempt to create any disturbance in the churches subject to the aforesaid monasteries or among the priests ordained in those churches, either by establishing a new arrangement or by violating an old one. Rather, as they have been regularly and canonically ordered and have remained so for a long time, let them remain undisturbed in future times.

Let him not delay in carrying out whatever ordinations are necessary for the monasteries themselves. Let him also willingly grant the blessings or consecrations of altars and basilicas, as necessity requires, whether in the monasteries themselves or on their estates. Let him not delay to provide chrism and consecrated oil every year, and let him demand no gift for any of these things, lest, attempting to sell the grace of the Holy Spirit, he should thereby—which God forbid—incur condemnation.

This decree must be observed without hesitation or contradiction not only by the bishop of Paderborn but also by the bishops of all places wherever the aforesaid monasteries, churches, estates, or households are known to possess property. No one is to abuse the property of those monasteries by right of authority; rather, everything which, as we have said, is known to have been granted to them in estates, households, or tithes shall remain under the authority of their prelates and under regular administration. We have confirmed these things to them through apostolic and imperial commands, partly together and partly separately.

They shall also always have the power to elect an abbot and an abbess in these places [Col. 0833B], choosing a person who professes the manner of life proper to either monastery both in conduct and in dress—not a canon, layman, or monk of another monastery. In this matter, let the royal authority pay particular attention to us, so that it may appoint no person over these monasteries who has not been regularly elected by the communities themselves.

Accordingly, let the clemency of the present and of all future princes know that this has been sanctioned by the apostolic see, strengthened by our subscription, and secured by the commands of earlier kings: they are to appoint no person over the aforesaid monasteries from any order whatsoever unless that person has been chosen by a worthy election.

But since importunate men seek many opportunities for wickedness, and it is always necessary to repel hostile arrows with the shield of protection, we likewise approve what apostolic authority has decreed: those appointed to govern the aforesaid monasteries are not to be removed by any power unless they are found guilty of a crime for which they ought not to continue in office.

If they are accused of the stains of infamy or of any crime, they are not to be deposed except after canonical or regular examination.

If anyone, therefore, despises the decree of the apostolic see, he will undoubtedly receive the sentence of condemnation which we believe has been confirmed by the divine Spirit through the apostolic voice.

Therefore, sealing our subscription with the impression of our ring, [Col. 0833D] we beseech all our fellow bishops into whose hands this document comes to confirm these provisions also by their authority and subscription. Whoever presumes to violate them shall be bound by the sentence of our whole body with such a bond of anathema that he will have no one whose favor he may court or by whose protection he may suppose himself shielded from the sentence of condemnation.

Moreover, from emperors, kings, dukes, or whatever authority may at that time be established, those who violate these provisions shall be compelled to pay one thousand pounds of the finest gold: half to the aforesaid monasteries and half to the treasury of those rulers.

But let there be peace from our Lord Jesus Christ for all who observe these provisions, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action [Col. 0834A] and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal rest.

Written by the hand of Stephen, first archivist of the Holy Roman Church, in the month of June and in the second indiction. Given on the Kalends of July, through the hand of John, bishop of the holy Church of Ephesus [Note: [Col. 0833D] Were titular bishops already being appointed at that time?] and librarian of the holy apostolic see. In the fourth year of the pontificate of our lord John, most holy pope, fifteenth of that name, in the second indiction.

## PRIVILEGE OF POPE JOHN XV FOR THE MONASTERY OF SAINT NAZARIUS AT LORSCH. (Year 989.)

[Mansi, *Councils*, vol. XIX, p. 419.]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in the Lord, N., the religious abbot of the venerable monastery where the body of Saint Nazarius, precious martyr, rests, in the place called N., which is dedicated in honor of the apostles Peter and Paul and likewise consecrated to Saint Nazarius the martyr, and to your successors forever.

It is fitting for apostolic authority to assist those distinguished by pious religion with benevolent charity and to grant the petition of those who ask with prompt and eager devotion. For the greatest reward is then laid up for us with God, the Creator of all, when venerable places, properly ordered, have without doubt been brought to a better condition by our apostolic authority.

And because your excellence’s praiseworthy gentleness requested [Col. 0834C] that, for the love of our beloved son, the lord Emperor Otto III, and of his beloved mother Theophanu, and of our lady, his grandmother, our spiritual daughters, we confirm the aforesaid monastery, we grant and confirm to you and to your successors the aforesaid monastery, with all movable and immovable property belonging to it that can be described or named.

Beginning with the present third indiction, we establish and confirm by this act that all this shall remain with that most sacred monastery: all urban and rural places, that is, estates and farmsteads, houses and villages, vineyards and boundaries, castles, fields, meadows, pastures, woods, forests, trees, fruit-bearing and non-fruit-bearing trees of various kinds, wells, springs and streams, waters, mills, fisheries, cultivated and uncultivated lands, together [Col. 0834D] with their tenants and households, tithes, customary payments, and all property that in any way belongs or ought to belong to that place from now until the end of the age.

Just as our predecessor, the lord N., most holy pope, granted these things to you by written command, so we too, through this privilege and by the authority of the blessed apostle Peter, grant and confirm them in their entirety, with complete security and tranquility, to you and your successors, to be held perpetually.

After the death of the abbot, no one shall appoint an abbot there except one whom the consensus and common will of the brothers from that community have elected.

We also establish, under apostolic censure, invocation of divine judgment, and the prohibition of anathema, that no duke, count, archbishop, bishop, or any other person, great or small, shall presume to inflict harm or trouble upon that venerable monastery, or to take away or alienate anything from its property. Rather, just as we have confirmed above, so let it be permitted to remain to the end of time, without any diminution.

If anyone, however—which we do not wish—should in reckless audacity arise against this apostolic privilege of confirmation, or presume to violate it in any way, and should not allow it to remain as we have confirmed above, let him know that, unless he repents, by the authority of almighty God and of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and of us, who hold Peter’s office, he is to be bound by the chain of anathema, excluded from the kingdom of God, and burned in eternal fire with Judas, the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ, and with all the impious.

But whoever, with pious regard, proves to be the guardian and observer of this privilege of our apostolic confirmation may deserve to obtain the grace of blessing from our Lord God, the just Judge, throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

Written by the hand of Stephen, archivist of the sacred palace, in the month of October and in the third indiction. Given on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of November, through the hand of John, bishop of the Church of Nepi and librarian of the holy apostolic see, in the year of the pontificate of our lord Pope John V, in the month of October and in the indiction written above, while our lord Otto III was reigning as emperor.

## VII. PRIVILEGE OF POPE JOHN XV FOR THE MONASTERY OF ANIANE. (Year 989.)

[In D. Bouquet, *Collection*, IX, 252.]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greeting and apostolic blessing to his beloved son Raynald, abbot of the venerable monastery of Aniane, founded and consecrated in honor of Saint Saviour, our Lord Jesus Christ, of Mary, perpetual mother of God and ever-virgin, of the holy archangel Michael, of the glorious Peter, prince of the apostles, and of the other saints, and to his successors.

[Col. 0835D] It is fitting for apostolic authority to assist those distinguished by pious religion with benevolent charity and to grant the petitions of those who ask with pious assent, because the greatest reward is laid up for us with the Creator of all if venerable places built through the devotion of religious men are strengthened by apostolic authority and brought to a better condition.

Therefore, since your affection humbly seeks our clemency, asking that by apostolic privilege we grant and strengthen for you and your successors the monastery of Aniane according to the tenor and stipulation of the royal privilege which is known to have been graciously granted to that place by Charles, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans, of pious memory, and also by Louis, his son, we gladly favor your fraternity.

Whatever royal munificence bestowed upon the monastery of Aniane in possessions and revenues from lands, woods, pastures, cultivated and uncultivated lands, waters and their courses, seas, ponds, and river fisheries; in grants of churches with their appurtenances; in the increase and settlement of free people, servants, and tenants; and whatever the pious devotion of the faithful has offered or will offer; everything which at present or in the future is recognized as belonging to or being possessed by the aforesaid monastery of Aniane by you and those entrusted to you—we grant and confirm by our authority, so that you may retain, distribute, arrange, or exchange it for the benefit of the place, untouched and without disturbance from any power or condition. [Col. 0836B]

And because unrestrained greed and the Simonian heresy among your people entirely disregard moderation and discretion, so that you may more freely carry out what belongs to contemplation, we grant that an abbot may be appointed by the sound decision of the community according to the rule of blessed Benedict. Let the person appointed be blessed by a bishop distinguished by the merit of a more religious life, and let the brothers entrusted to him be promoted to holy orders.

Thus, if that abbot is seen to follow the path of religion worthily and laudably, we grant him the authority to impose penance upon those who humbly come to him from anywhere, to excommunicate the wicked, and, by apostolic authority, to absolve those who make satisfaction.

If, however, because of the iniquity and wickedness of the people, it should be necessary for the province to be struck with the sword of excommunication or anathema, we grant by paternal compassion and confirm by apostolic authority that the place of Aniane may remain free from every bond of excommunication, so that the brothers living there may willingly offer prayers to almighty God for our salvation and prosperity and for that of the whole holy Roman Church. Let penitents who devoutly come on the appointed day of the consecration of the aforesaid place be released solely by our absolution, so that they may more abundantly fulfill the propitiatory vows of their devotion and [lacuna] of all.

Whoever, moved by the praiseworthy reputation or example of the aforesaid place of Aniane, asks to be buried there and assigns any quantity whatsoever of his property or substance to be given to the aforesaid monastery [Col. 0836D], shall not be prohibited by the bishop of whose diocese that person is, by any means or pretext, except if, because of scant merit, he is publicly subject to the excommunication of his own bishop.

And so that the community of the aforesaid place may not find even a small pretext for doing less than what is holy, just, and fitting for the holy rule, we prohibit under the testimony of the divine name that any worldly power—whether count or countess, archbishop or bishop, or any secular person—presume by action, device, or malicious pretext to use force against or trouble that monastery, or to take away or alienate anything from its property or possessions, or to exact unlawfully any service payment, or anything contrary to the monastic order.

Rather, whoever proves devoted to that place and community, and contributes any assistance by word, deed, or expenditure of his substance, shall receive from the pious rewarder of all, the Lord, the blessing from above and the grace of our humility.

But if anyone attempts in any way to oppose or violate the sanction and confirmation of this privilege of ours, let him be condemned by almighty God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, with perpetual curse; expelled from the bosom of the holy Church; and handed over with the impious and murderers to the devil, to be burned in the everlasting fires of Gehenna.

Farewell.

Written by the hand of Stephen, sacred archivist [Col. 0837B] of the holy Roman Church, in the month of July, in the fifth month [read, apparently: in the first month, in the fifth indiction].

## VIII. PRIVILEGE OF POPE JOHN XV FOR THE CHURCH OF HAMBURG. (Year 989.)

[In Lappenberg, *Hamburg Documents*, I, 58.]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our beloved brother Liavizo, venerable archbishop of the Church of Hamburg, and [read: and to] his successors forever.

It is fitting for apostolic governance to come to the aid, with kindly compassion, of those endowed with devout religion, and to grant the requests of petitioners with willing devotion. For by this means we shall doubtless earn the greatest reward of profit before the Lord, creator of all, when venerable places have without doubt been brought to a better condition.

Therefore, since you asked us to confirm to you the entire archbishopric of the Church of Hamburg, just as it was decreed by our predecessors, namely Nicholas and Agapitus, bishops of this apostolic see, yielding to your prayers, by apostolic authority we grant and confirm it, together with everything generally and specifically belonging to that aforesaid archbishopric of yours: namely, all that your predecessors acquired through their labors, or that the faithful among Christian peoples have already bestowed there, or shall henceforth bestow, for love of the eternal homeland.

Together with these, we include those who in the present time have been converted to the faith of Christ—namely, the bishops among all the peoples of the Swedes or Danes, and also in those regions of the Slavs extending from the River Peene to the River Eider—so that they may remain under the authority of you and your successors, the archbishops of the Church of Hamburg. Whatever, moreover, by the struggle of your labor and with the favor of divine grace you are able to win from the error of unbelief—whether of people or of places—to the Christian religion, we decree that you and your successors shall possess perpetually and hold inviolate.

Furthermore, we have decreed and enacted that no archbishop, whether the archbishop of Cologne or anyone else, shall claim any authority for himself within your diocese. Rather, we exhort them and all practitioners of true religion to provide you with help and support in every respect, so that, in return for the favor of this benefaction, they may deserve to receive a full recompense from the Lord. For we do not doubt that everything which is proven beneficial to the Church and does not oppose divine commands must be carried out and provided by the authority of almighty God and of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

By this decree, according to the sanction of the aforementioned popes Nicholas and Agapitus, of good memory, we decree those dioceses themselves—the Hamburg diocese [lacuna]. By apostolic authority, therefore, we further order and admonish the bishops of the Churches of Halberstadt, Hildesheim, Paderborn, and Minden to assist you in every respect, so that you may more easily fulfill the priestly ministry and win souls for the Lord Jesus Christ; let them provide you with support in everything.

Nevertheless, we decree that those whom you acquire, and those whom through the grace of Christ you have acquired, shall remain subject to your archbishopric and that of your successors, receiving their reward only from Christ, as Christian and true religion teaches: “Go, teach all nations” (Matthew 28:19).

Although bishops have therefore been consecrated to preach to the peoples in the regions mentioned above, and many more are to be consecrated in those parts, it is nevertheless to be feared that, through the savagery of the barbarians, their number may diminish so greatly in that still-new planting of Christianity that the consecration of bishops could in no way be carried out with their assistance. For this reason, if necessary, we decree that the aforesaid provisions are to be observed by apostolic authority.

We decree, therefore, dearest brother Liavizo, that you shall have the power to ordain bishops within your parish and diocese among all the peoples mentioned above. If anyone should attempt to act against this privilege of our authority, or in any way endeavor to violate it in whole or in part, let him be excommunicated from the body and life-giving blood of our Lord Jesus Christ and separated from entry into the holy Church of God.

But let whoever observes this admonition and command of ours have the blessing of almighty God, of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and of us, who exercise their vicariate.

Therefore, in granting you, dearest brother Liavizo, the privilege of our authority, we also grant you the use of the pallium everywhere on both banks of the River Elbe, on the appointed days, as was customary for your predecessors. In addition, in accordance with the wish of your most worthy petition, we add that on the feasts of the blessed martyrs Lawrence, Maurice, and their companions, and on each feast of the church entrusted to you, you may be vested with the pallium.

May the Holy Trinity deign to preserve your fraternity safe and unharmed for a long time, and, after the bitterness of this age, lead you to everlasting blessedness.

Written by the hand of Stephen, notary, regional secretary, and scriniarius of the sacred palace, in the month of November and the third indiction.

Given on the sixth day before the Ides of November, through the hands of Gregory, bishop of the holy Church of Porto, in the year of the pontificate of our lord John, most holy pope, the fifth; in the year from the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 988, in the month of November and the third indiction.

We send you the pallium, and in addition grant you permission to be vested in this or another garment of whatever kind of bright whiteness may please you. Amen.

## IX. PRIVILEGE OF POPE JOHN XV FOR THE MONASTERY OF SAINT PETER OF RODAS (Year 990?)

[In Cocquelines, *Bullarum privilegiorum ac diplomatum Romanorum pontificum amplissima collectio*, I, 286.]

**[Col. 0839B]**

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Hildesindus, religious bishop and abbot of the venerable monastery of the holy apostle Peter, founded in the county of Peralada, on the mountain called Rodas, beneath the fortress of Verdera, and through you to the abbots who shall succeed you in the same venerable monastery, forever.

Since those things which are known to accord with reasonable desires ought to be granted, the authority of our apostleship must by no means refuse to strengthen the devout dedication of the faithful by granting privileges. Therefore, since your praiseworthy gentleness requested that, by apostolic authority, through this privilege we grant and confirm to you and to your successors forever the aforesaid monastery, with all its dependencies and appurtenances, together with its boundaries and limits, we therefore, favoring your pious desires, decree by our apostolic authority that the aforesaid monastery of the holy apostle Peter, with all that belongs to it, shall henceforth and until the end of the age remain perpetually under the patronage and protection of the holy Roman and apostolic mother Church. Thus, established under the guardianship of our holy Church, which by God’s authority we serve, it shall be subject to no other right or jurisdiction than that of you and your successors forever.

We confirm to you and to your successors the aforesaid monastery with these boundaries and dependencies, and with all that is set out below: namely, from the very rock called Meda, which lies below the harbor of Fraxano, and from that ridge as far as the place called the Three Brothers; from the eastern side, that is, as far as the open sea. From there it goes to the place called the mill of Balasco, and from there reaches the Tamariz; then it proceeds as far as the Fictitious Rock, reaches the matella of Gomesindus, and from there ascends through the land to the fitorio of Mount Pininello. It continues upward to the summit of Mount Pininello, then descends and proceeds along the road to the place called Sorborello; descending, it reaches the enclosure and the farmhouse of the Friulani.

From there it ascends by the aforesaid road to the farmhouse of Salvatore and to the pass; it returns from Vinea Vitula and reaches the summit of the mountain situated there, called Casralio. From there it goes through the Serva to the pass of Ermenardus, reaches the spring or pass of Filmera, and from there the pass of Saint Genesius. Thus ascending and descending, it follows the summit of the ridge called Calmi and reaches beneath the fortress called Pinna Nigra, as far as the vineyards belonging to the Palace. It runs beneath the forest lying to the south below the fortress of Verdera, and as far as beneath the rock called Fitorio. It ascends to the valley of Fulcimannia and reaches beneath the springs of Devolas in the valley of Frujone.

**[Col. 0840A]**

From there it goes through the rocks as far as Mount Inserto, then descends on the western side along the public road to Rocha Ventosa and to the place called the pass of the valley of Budica. From there it ascends to the summit of the cross, then descends to the road of the aforesaid cross, through the valley as far as the stream of Budica. It ascends to the pass of Terrario and reaches the summit of the mountain called Rocha Morena.

Then, descending and ascending on the northern side, it reaches the summit of Uvardia Maurescha and proceeds along the crest of the ridge to Parada of Durandus. It follows the ridge as far as Reiderictz of Saint Genesius and ascends along the ridge to the hill situated above Rovescalium. It descends along the ridge to the aforesaid Meda, which lies in the sea.

Within these boundaries we likewise confirm to you and your successors the church of the Holy Cross, with its tithes and first fruits; the church of Saint John, with its tithes, first fruits, offerings, estates, and everything belonging to that church; the church of Saint Baudilius in the valley of Tabellaria; the church of Saint Stephen in the valley of Subiradellos; the church of Saint Fructuosus; the church of Saint Vincent, situated in the village of Lanciano, with its tithes, first fruits, and everything belonging to that church; the church of Saint Genesius; the church of Saint Peter, with the fortress of Miralias; the fortress of Verdera, with its fortified outwork and its Fitorio and Pinna Nigra, together with all the rocks, lands, and forests within these boundaries, except the forest of Saint Romanus, as is recorded in the charter which Count Gauzfredus and his son Suniarius, formerly bishop, made for the aforesaid monastery.

We likewise confirm forever to the same monastery the pond of Castilione, with its sea passage and islands, as is recorded in the charter of King Louis or in the charter which the aforementioned Count Gauzfredus and Suniarius, formerly bishop, made for the aforesaid monastery; and whatever that monastery possesses in the village of Castilione or within its boundaries; in the village of Palacioli, called Fortianum; in the upper village of Fortianum; and in the smaller Furtianellum, or within their boundaries—whatever it possesses there and, with the Lord’s favor, shall acquire.

We also confirm the entire lighthouse, with its boundaries and limits. It borders on the east upon the boundary of the village called Saccaro or the boundary of the village called Furtiano; on the south upon the boundary of the aforesaid village of Furtiano, situated in the valley; on the west upon the boundary of the village called the Villare of Hildesindus, or upon the stream called Manivolo, situated in the estate of Saint Paul below Saint Martin of Sambuca; and on the north upon the middle course of the stream Manivolo, or upon the boundary of the village called Timim, and upon the Villare of Hildesindus, or within its boundaries—whatever it possesses or ought to possess there, and, with the Lord’s favor, shall acquire—with the ponds and fishponds themselves, and in the village of Saccari and the New Village, or within their boundaries.

Likewise, the Villare of Stagnejolum, with its ponds and little dependent villages; whatever it possesses in the village of Peralada, in the village of Oleastrum, in the village of Saint Clement, in the village of Dudulim, in the village of Noves, in the village of Spedolia, in the villare called Solartila, in the Jewish village, in the village of Pavo, in the village of Palatium, and in the valley of Rodas, or within their boundaries.

Likewise, in the county of Empúries, in the village of Militiano, called Saint Peter; in the village of Armentaria, with its share of the church of Saint Martin; in the village of Chaniano, with the church of Saint Martin and its pond; and in the villages of Suvrana and Dalmalia, or within their boundaries, whatever it now possesses there and, with God’s help, shall acquire.

In the county of Besalú, whatever it possesses in the village of Lertio, in the village of Molendinos, or in the Tapiolas called Figarias, within their boundaries; and the estate called Hortos, with the church of Saint Christopher, its tithes and first fruits, estates, and everything belonging to that church.

In the county of Girona, the farmhouse situated within the walls of that city; the estate of Cumpinus of Burellus, situated within the boundaries of the village [lacuna]; the estate of Securunio; and the estate of Burdulis.

In the county of Barcelona, in Valès, on Mount Signio, in the valley of Tordera, in the village of Laurona, in Agell, within the boundary of Olèrdola, and in Penedès, the estate formerly belonging to Guidisclus.

In the county of Osona, whatever it possesses in the village of Berga, with the church of Saint Cecilia; the village of Nidummalum; and the land beside the fortress of Bolciarenno; and the church of Saint Cecilia with its estate.

In the county of Pallars, near the city of Liminiana, the church of Saint Andrew, and everything it possesses in that county.

In the county of Cerdanya, whatever it possesses in the village of Exi and in the other villages.

In the valley of Conflent, the village of Villella with its boundaries.

In the county of Fenouillèdes, the church of Saint Andrew in the valley of Pidiliano, with the estate situated there.

Near the walls of the city of Narbonne, two farmsteads.

In the county of Roussillon, the church of the Holy Savior with the estate situated there; in the villare of Emilianus; in the village of Apianus, or within their boundaries; the church of Saint Columba with its tithes and first fruits; the adjoining village with its mills; the village of Pollestres with the church of Saint Martin, its tithes, first fruits, offerings, and estates; in the village of Torrilias, the church of Saint Peter with the estate situated there; in the village of Bigaranas, the church of Saint Andrew with its tithes, first fruits, and estate; and in the county of Vallespir, the estate of Campelli and of the valley of Orosa, and the village called Rivo of Hugarios, with its boundaries and limits, together with the church of Saint Michael and its tithes and first fruits.

The tithes, first fruits, and offerings from the aforesaid churches, and the places and estates with all their boundaries, limits, landmarks, dependencies, and appurtenances—whatever the aforesaid monastery presently possesses within the counties listed above, and whatever, with God’s help, it shall acquire—we establish by the tenor of this privilege as belonging to the jurisdiction of the holy Roman Church, which by God’s authority we serve. From the present third indiction, we establish the monastery, villages, estates, and churches, with all their appurtenances as described above, for you and your successors to hold in perpetuity, and to govern and administer with fear of God.

Thus no king, no bishop, and no person established in any order or office may ever dare to bring vexatious proceedings against the affairs of this monastery. Rather, let all these things remain forever as we have ordered above.

By apostolic censure, under invocation of the divine judgment and prohibition by anathema, we establish that none of our successors in the pontificate shall ever presume to use force against or invade the possessions of this monastery.

After the death of an abbot, no one shall appoint an abbot there except the person whom the consent and common will of the brothers from the congregation itself shall have chosen according to God and the Rule of Saint Benedict. No one shall attempt to receive any payment or gift for his consecration. If the bishop to whose diocese the place belongs should refuse to ordain him, he may freely be ordained, by our authority, either by the Roman mother Church or by any bishop whom he chooses.

If anyone—which we do not desire—should presume with wicked boldness to transgress what we have established for the stability of the aforesaid monastery, let him know that he is bound by the chain of anathema and assigned, with the devil and all the impious, to the most dreadful punishment of eternal fire.

But whoever, with pious regard, proves to be the guardian and observer of these provisions may deserve to obtain from the most merciful Lord our God every grace of blessing, the absolution of all his sins, and the blessedness of heavenly life with the saints and elect, forever and ever. Amen.

Written by the hand of Stephen, notary, regional secretary, and scriniarius of our apostolic see, in the month of February and the third indiction. Farewell.

## X. LETTER OF POPE JOHN XV TO ALL THE FAITHFUL (Year 991)

On establishing peace between Ethelred, king of England, and Richard, duke of Normandy, whom he calls marquis.

**[Col. 0843A]**

John the Fifteenth, pope of the holy Roman Church, to all the faithful, greetings.

Let all the faithful of the holy mother Church, and those of both our orders spread throughout the regions of the world, know how it was reported to us by many persons that there was hostility between Ethelred, king of the West Saxons, and Richard the marquis. We therefore became exceedingly sad, since they were our spiritual sons. At length, taking the salutary counsel of beginning the matter, I summoned a certain apocrisiarius of ours, Leo, vice-bishop of the holy Church of Trier, and sent him there with our exhortatory letters, so that they might repent of this hostility.

Passing through the intervening stretches of your lands, he eventually crossed the maritime boundaries and, on the day of the Lord’s Nativity, arrived before the presence of the aforesaid king. Having immediately conveyed our greeting on our behalf, he presented the letters that we had sent him. The king summoned all the wiser faithful of both orders of his kingdom and, out of love and fear of almighty God, of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, and in response to our paternal admonition, firmly granted peace, without deceit, with all his sons and daughters, present and future, and with all his faithful.

For this reason he sent Edelsinus, bishop of the holy Church of Sherborne, together with Leofstan, son of Alfwold, and Ederelnoth, son of Wulstan. They crossed the maritime boundaries and came to the aforesaid Richard the marquis. Richard received our admonitions peacefully and, on hearing the decree of the aforesaid king, willingly confirmed the same peace with his present and future sons and daughters and with all his faithful.

The agreement was made on this condition: if any of them, or the parties themselves, should unjustly commit anything against the other, it should be cleansed by an appropriate settlement. Let peace remain perpetual and unshaken, secured by the pledge of oaths on both sides.

On the side of King Ethelred: Edelsinus, bishop of the holy Church of Sherborne; Leofstan, son of Alfwold; and Ederelnoth, son of Wulstan.

On Richard’s side: Roger, bishop; Rodulf, son of Hugh; and Truteno, son of Thurgis.

Done at Rouen on the Kalends of March, in the year from the incarnation of the Lord 991, the fourth indiction. Richard shall accept no one from among the king’s men or his enemies, nor shall the king accept anyone from Richard’s men, without their seal.

## XI. PRIVILEGE GRANTED TO GREGORY, BISHOP OF PORTO (Year 992)

[In Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, vol. I, p. 114.]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the most reverend and most holy Gregory, brother and fellow bishop of the holy Church of Porto, and through you to the persons who are to possess the following in the same venerable bishopric, and to your successors forever.

Since those things which accord with reasonable desires ought always to be granted, our clemency must by no means refuse the devotion humbly acquired within our hearts when privileges are granted. Therefore, by this present page of our privilege, we grant and offer your petition to you, and at the same time confirm in the aforesaid venerable bishopric, for the love of almighty God, for the redemption of our soul, and for the forgiveness of all our sins, the land belonging to our sacred Lateran palace for the construction of a ditch.

It begins lengthwise at the river beside the wall of the city of Porto, before the gate called the Major Gate, and from there proceeds as far as Trajan’s Lake; then, returning from Trajan’s Lake by another ditch, it reaches the aforesaid river.

We likewise grant you, from our apostolic majesty, permission to draw water from that river and, along its bank, convey as much water as you and your successors may wish and as may be necessary, at all times, for the benefit of the aforesaid lake called Trajan’s Lake, in order to collect fish; and from there, with the water flowing onward through the ditch, to return it to the aforesaid river.

Whatever you may wish to construct in that ditch or concerning the water, we grant you the permission and power to construct it. Since the territory of Porto belongs to the jurisdiction of the holy Roman Church, which by God’s authority we serve, and since, yielding to your prayers, we ought by this written grant to concede and confirm it to you and your successors for their possession, by the tenor of this document we grant and confirm forever to you and your successors, for the right and authority of the holy mother Church of Porto, the aforesaid land for the construction of the ditch, together with the water that at all times flows through that ditch from the aforesaid river into Trajan’s Lake and from there runs through the ditch, along with everything pertaining to the ditch or water, as stated above.

This is to be held from the present fifth indiction, on the condition that every year we receive from you and your successors, by way of rent for our Church, six denarii.

By apostolic censure, under invocation of the divine judgment and prohibition by anathema, we decree that none of our successors in the pontificate, nor any intervening authorities, judges, counts, or castalds who at any time exercise lordship in the city of Porto—whatever their rank—or any other person, great or small, may remove or alienate from the right and jurisdiction of the aforesaid bishopric the said ditch or the river water flowing from it. Rather, let the aforesaid things remain for the use and benefit of that bishopric.

If anyone—which we do not believe—should attempt with impious and unjust rashness to act in any way or in any part against this apostolic privilege of ours, and should fail to observe and guard it in every respect, let him know that he is bound by the chain of anathema, alienated from the kingdom of God, and assigned with Judas, the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ, and with all the impious, to eternal fire. In addition, let him pay as a legal penalty ten pounds of pure gold to the bishop who at that time occupies the venerable bishopric.

But whoever in every respect proves to be the guardian and observer of this apostolic privilege of ours may deserve to obtain the grace of blessing and eternal life from our most merciful Lord.

Written by the hands of Stephen, scriniarius of the sacred palace, in the month of June and the aforesaid indiction. Farewell.

Given on the seventh day before the Kalends of July, through the hands of John, bishop of the Church of Nepi and librarian of the holy apostolic see, in the seventh year of the pontificate of our lord John, most holy pope XV, and the aforesaid fifth indiction. Therefore we decree, and so forth. If, therefore, any person, and so forth. But to all, and so forth. Amen.

## XII. ROMAN COUNCIL FOR THE CANONIZATION OF SAINT UDALRIC, BISHOP OF AUGSBURG, HELD IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 993

[In Mansi, *Concilia*, vol. XIX, p. 169.]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all archbishops, bishops, and abbots residing in Gaul and Germany, greetings in the Lord and apostolic blessing.

When an assembly had been convened in the Lateran palace on the day before the Kalends of February, with John, most holy pope, presiding together with the bishops and priests, and with the deacons and the entire clergy standing by, the most reverend Luitolph, bishop of Augsburg, rose and said:

“Most holy lord and prelate, if it pleases you and all the bishops and priests sitting here, let the little book which I hold in my hands be read before you: the Life and miracles of the venerable Udalric, formerly bishop of the holy Church of Augsburg. Then let whatever seems good to you be decreed.

“Since the presence and assembly of priests bear witness to the Holy Spirit, what we read is certain, for our truth cannot lie, and the following is the saying in the Gospel: ‘Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them’ (Matthew 18). Since this is so, and the Holy Spirit is not absent even from so small a number, how much more should we believe that he is present now, when a multitude of holy persons has gathered together? For the assembly is holy, in keeping with the veneration owed to it.”

When the Life of the aforesaid most holy bishop had been read, the account reached the miracles performed either in the body or outside the body: namely, that he gave sight to the blind, drove demons from possessed bodies, cured the paralyzed, and performed very many other signs, which have by no means been set out in pen and ink.

We received all these accounts, sufficiently polished with elegant and urbane refinement, and by common counsel decreed that the memory of that man—namely, Saint Udalric, bishop—should be venerated with the most devoted affection and the most faithful devotion. For we adore and honor the relics of martyrs and confessors in such a way that we adore him whose martyrs and confessors they are. We honor servants so that the honor may redound to the Lord, who said: “Whoever receives you receives me” (Matthew 10).

Accordingly, since we have no confidence in our own righteousness, may we continually be aided by their prayers and merits before the most merciful God. For the divinely salutary commandments, and the effective teachings of the sacred canons and venerable Fathers, urge all churches, with pious consideration—or rather through the earnestness of apostolic governance—to accomplish the usefulness of their benefits and the integrity of their firmness, so that the memory of the aforesaid venerable bishop Udalric may exist dedicated to divine worship and may always be able to advance the most devoted offering of praise to God.

If anyone—which we do not believe—should attempt with rash boldness to oppose what has been established by our authority, piously and firmly, through this privilege; or should resist or in any way transgress what we have established for the praise of God and in reverence for the aforesaid bishop, let him know that by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, whose office we exercise, unworthy though we are, he is bound by the chain of anathema.

But whoever proves to be an observer with pious regard may receive the grace of blessing in manifold ways from our most merciful Lord God and become a sharer in eternal life.

Written by the hand of Stephen, notary, regional secretary, and scriniarius of the holy Roman Church, in the month of February, the sixth indiction, in the year 993.

### Subscriptions

I, John, bishop of the holy Roman Catholic and apostolic Church, have consented to and subscribed this decree promulgated by us.

John, bishop of the holy Church of Anagni, consented.

Dominic, bishop of the holy Church of Ferentino, consented.

John, priest and cardinal of Saint Damasus, consented.

Leo, priest and cardinal of Saint Sixtus, consented.

John, priest and cardinal of the Holy Four Crowned Ones, consented.

John, priest and cardinal of Saint Clement, consented.

Given on the third day before the Kalends [Nones] of February, through the hands of John, bishop of the holy Church of Nepi and librarian of the holy apostolic see, in the eighth year of the pontificate of our lord John, most holy pope XV, and the sixth indiction.

## XIII. PRIVILEGE OF POPE JOHN XV FOR THE MONASTERY OF BREWNOW (Year 993)

[In Bocsek, *Codex diplomaticus Moraviae*, vol. I, p. 104.]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Anastasius, abbot, and the convent of the venerable monastery of the saints of Christ—Benedict, Boniface, and Alexius—situated at Brewnow: charity, faith, and perpetual peace.

The apostolic see is accustomed to approve pious desires with clemency and to grant benevolent favor to the honorable prayers of petitioners. Since, therefore, your monastery is the first and a new foundation in the duchy of Bohemia, as we have learned from the report of our venerable brother Adalbert, bishop of Prague, its founder, and since it is worthy that this monastery—which is said already to be flourishing in part, both temporally and spiritually, through God’s merciful providence—should be honored by the apostolic see, yielding to the prayers of that beloved brother of ours, Adalbert, bishop of Prague, we grant by the authority of this document that you, son abbot, and the others who shall preside over the same monastery in due course, may use a mitre, gloves, sandals, a maniple, and a belt.

And so that your Church may be regarded as more worthy or greater than the other monasteries, we decree that it shall be the head and mistress in the correction and reform of regular discipline over all monasteries of the Order of Saint Benedict that shall henceforth be built in Bohemia. To you, Anastasius the abbot, and to your successors who canonically succeed you, we grant the first place after the bishop of Prague, above all others and in all matters.

Moreover, placing your monastery under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, we confirm by apostolic authority to you and to those who shall succeed you all your churches, villages, fields, forests, houses, male and female servants, and also the tithes of the provinces of Litoměřice, Bílina, and Bechyně, together with those of all the people of the same monastery, which were reasonably granted to your monastery by our aforementioned brother Adalbert, bishop of Prague, for whose love we write these things—both in lands already cultivated and in those newly brought under cultivation in the future.

Furthermore, out of divine love we wish and firmly command that whichever duke may be in power shall so guard, love, and uphold the holy monastery itself, its father abbot, everything belonging to it, and the liberties generously granted to it by the noble Duke Boleslaus, a Catholic man, that he may desire the prosperity of the present life and wish to receive from our most kindly Creator the prize of eternal blessedness in the future.

After the death of the abbot, no one shall appoint an abbot there except one whom the congregation itself has chosen jointly and with unanimous agreement. Then, if he is a Catholic, the bishop of Prague may, by our authority and as an act of charity, consecrate the person elected, with every trace of simony entirely excluded on either side.

Let no person at all be permitted to violate this document of our grant or confirmation, or rashly oppose it. If anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and that, with Judas, who, having hanged himself, burst open in the middle [Note: [Col. 0847] From the original transumpt of Otokar I, king of Bohemia, dated 1224, of the bull written on a waxed or papyrus-like charter, already consumed by excessive age.], he will remain perpetually subject to eternal damnation together with all the reprobate.

But whoever guards and wishes to observe the provisions set out and written in this privilege may deserve to attain eternal life. Farewell.

Written by the hand of Stephen, scriniarius of the holy Roman Church.

Given at Rieti through the hands of Dominic, bishop of Sabina, on the second day before the Kalends of June, the eighth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 993, in the eighth year of our pontificate, by God’s favor, and in the eighth month.

## XIV. LETTER TO GRIMOALD, ARCHBISHOP OF SALERNO (Year 994)

He grants him the pallium and establishes him as metropolitan of the bishoprics of Paestum, Acherontia, Nola, Bisignano, Malvito, and Cosenza.

[In Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, vol. VII, col. 378.]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most beloved brother, and deservedly honorable Grimoald, archbishop of the see of Salerno.

Because we ought to remember the benefit you have conferred upon us, and because we have recognized that your reverence toward us and toward the Holy Roman and Apostolic Church has especially abounded, we have therefore rightly and justly determined to answer the recompense of your charity, so that it may be clear to all Christ’s faithful that the one who diligently honors the vicar of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, is to be honored with immense honor. With the consent and will of our brothers, we grant and confirm you, Grimoald, our fellow brother, in the rank of archbishop, just as formerly it was granted to Amatus, to whom the archbishopric of your see of Salerno was first bestowed by our See and by our pontiffs; so may you, by our authority, possess it peacefully and guard it more vigilantly. 

For we have decreed that this should be done in the order stated, so that you and your successors may have license and power in perpetuity to ordain bishops and consecrate them in the places subject to you, namely, the bishopric of Paestum with its parishes and dependencies, as well as the bishopric of Acherontia, and likewise the bishopric of Nola, the bishopric of Bisignano, the bishopric of Malvito, and the bishopric of Cosenza with all their parishes and dependencies, as is contained in the earlier grant of the pallium to your church; and likewise in the church of Holy Mary, Mother of God, and of blessed Matthew the apostle and evangelist, whose most sacred body you possess and which has been granted to you and to your successors.

After your departure, therefore, your successors shall come to the Apostolic See and shall receive, according to the decree, the use of the pallium and consecration. If our successors should be unwilling to consecrate them, your holy church shall have permission to be consecrated by bishops who are our suffragans; and our successors shall not thereafter, in perpetuity, have power to consecrate any bishop in all the bishoprics subject to you which they have assigned to you, since this has already been granted to you. Whoever, however, should presume to violate this grant of our decree shall be bound perpetually by the bond of anathema, and this grant of ours shall remain stable and firm forever.

Written by the hand of Benedict, notary and scriniary of the Holy Roman Church. In the month of March, indiction VII. Farewell.

Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, by the hand of Gregory, bishop of the Holy Portuensian Church and librarian of the Holy Apostolic See, in the eighth year, by God’s favor, of the pontificate of Lord John XV, in the month of March, indiction VII.

## XV. PRIVILEGE OF POPE JOHN XV FOR THE MONASTERY OF FULDA (Year 995)

[Dronke, *Codex diplomaticus Fuldensis*, p. 339.]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most beloved son in Christ, Hatto, the most devout abbot of the sacred monastery of Fulda, consecrated by us, and through you to all your abbots and successors who remain there forever in the praise and service of God.

A desire which is shown to concern the purpose of holy religion and the stability of holy places must, with God as its author, be accomplished without any contradiction, so that thereby the vigor of holy religion may be strengthened, the safety and security of those same holy places established, and we too may receive the greatest profit from the Creator of all, God, in the heavenly kingdoms.

Therefore, because Abbot Hatto petitioned us—through the intervention of Lord Otto, the most excellent king, our spiritual son and, by God’s grace, future emperor and most devout defender of the Holy Roman Church, and in fulfillment of the pious vow of his most pious grandmother, the empress Augusta Adalheidis—that the aforementioned venerable monastery, formerly built by Archbishop Boniface of holy memory for the honor of God and of our Lord and Savior, in the place called Boconia beside the bank of the river called Fulda, should be adorned with the insignia of a privilege of the Apostolic See; and that, just as it was placed under the authority of our holy Church, which by God’s authority we serve, through the constitution of the most holy Pope Zacharias and the decrees of our other venerable predecessors, so it should remain throughout perpetual ages and never be subjected to the jurisdiction of any other Church—

therefore, favoring his pious desires, by this authority of ours we commit what is requested to a worthy effect. Accordingly, we prohibit every priest of any Church from having any authority or jurisdiction whatsoever in the aforesaid monastery apart from the Apostolic See. Thus, unless he has been invited by the abbot of the monastery just named, no one may presume in any way to celebrate the solemn rites of Mass there.

Accordingly, in conformity with what stands secured by the firmness of the privilege subject to the Apostolic See, the monastery shall remain undisturbed at all times, endowed with perpetual security in all its places and possessions—both those which it ought to claim for itself from its beginnings and those which it presently holds and possesses, as well as those which divine providence may in future wish to add to the legal property of that sacred monastery from the gifts, offerings, and tithes of any of Christ’s faithful—without contradiction from any person.

Furthermore, the abbot of Fulda shall, by our Apostolic authority, have precedence over the other abbots of Gaul or Germany in sitting in every place and assembly. In addition, for love of the aforesaid King Otto, our spiritual son, we grant to the aforementioned Abbot Hatto permission, by our Apostolic authority, to use the dalmatic and sandals during the solemn celebration of Mass.

By the page of this decree we establish that if any prelate of any Church, or any person invested with whatever dignity, should attempt to violate or transgress the tenor of this privilege, which we confirm and strengthen by the authority of the most blessed prince of the apostles, whose office we exercise, let him be anathema; let him incur the wrath of Almighty God and be excluded from the fellowship of all the saints. Nevertheless, the dignity of the aforesaid monastery shall remain inviolate, supported by Apostolic authority.

Written by the hand of George, scriniary and notary of the Holy Roman Church, in the month of October, on the eighth day before the Ides. Farewell.

Given on the second day before the Kalends of November, by the hand of John, bishop of the Holy Albanian Church and librarian of the Holy Apostolic See, in the month of October, on the thirty-first day, indiction VIII.

## XVI. LETTER OF POPE JOHN XV TO COUNT ARNULF AND OTHERS (Years 991–996)

That they should restore what they took from the monastery of Saint Richarius.

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Arnulf, count; Baldwin, count, with his mother; Gosbert, viscount; and Iliarda, our most beloved spiritual sons: complete greetings and Apostolic blessing.

We admonish you to withdraw from evil works and cling to good works, so that you may deserve to obtain the mercy of Almighty God and be able to acquire everlasting life. Therefore, dearest sons, we command you to take care to restore, for the love of Almighty God, the entire inheritance which you took from the monastery of Saint Richarius the confessor. For if you restore it, you shall have the blessing of Saint Peter and of us; but if you do not obey our admonitions, know that, by the authority of Almighty God and of us, you are excommunicated and accursed, and separated from the Church of God and from the communion of all Christians, unless you come to make satisfaction.

## XVII. LETTER OF POPE JOHN XV TO SEVERAL BISHOPS (Years 991–996)

That they should take care to restore what was taken from the monastery of Saint Richarius.

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Guido [of Soissons], venerable bishop; Fulco, venerable bishop of the city of Amiens; Baldwin, bishop of the city of Thérouanne; our most beloved spiritual sons: affectionate greetings and Apostolic blessing.

If we know that an abundance of health and cheerfulness exists among you, we rejoice no less than if it existed in ourselves. Moreover, we command you, for the love of Almighty God, out of reverence for Saint Peter and with our intervention, to assist this man named Ingilard, so that the monastery of Saint Richarius the confessor may be restored through our help and yours.

Do not fail to send your letters of excommunication to each of those soldiers who took the monastery’s inheritance, so that they may take care to restore everything they took from the aforesaid monastery. You will show thereby that you love the Holy Roman Church, when our entreaty has come to you, if you fulfill it.

## In the Year of the Lord 996. Guido II, Bishop of Le Puy

[Col. 0851]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE

(*Gallia Christiana* II, 695.)

Between Bego and Wido, the published catalogues place the bishops Hector and Peter. But Hector ought to have been placed before Gotescalc; as for Peter, we have no information about him. We must therefore now speak of Wido, and first of all of his illustrious lineage.

He was the son of Fulk the Younger, count of Anjou, by Gerberga, and the brother of Geoffrey, or Godefrey, called “Grisagonella” from his garment, who was also count of Anjou, as the *Deeds of the Counts*, or consuls, of Anjou teach us. Fulk had three sons: the first-born, Geoffrey; the second, Guido, bishop of Le Puy; and the third, Drogo.

Guido, educated in letters at his parents’ command, renounced worldly pomp and assumed the monastic habit in the monastery of Cormery in the diocese of Tours. There, after the intruder Arnald had been expelled, he was elected abbot by the common consent of the brothers, with the king’s approval. At that time the abbot of Cormery also governed the abbey of Villeloin. But when Guido noticed that disagreements existed between the monks of the two monasteries, at the exhortation and advice of Arduin, archbishop of Tours, he granted the monks of Villeloin the power to choose an abbot for themselves thereafter; and they chose Huncbert.

He was also abbot of Ferrières and of Saint Albin of Angers, and he retained responsibility for Cormery until the year 976, when, according to Mabillon, he was made bishop of Anicium.

Several years before his episcopate, he repented on account of the many estates alienated from the monasteries and granted as benefices. He wrote letters in which he adjured those who possessed the lands of their monasteries in this fashion to restore them as quickly as possible; and he himself restored what he had taken in this way. Let us now speak of his episcopate.

Wido, promoted to the bishopric of Anicium against his will at the desire of King Lothair, went there to assume it. His sister Adelais, wife of William, count of Provence, and their sons Pontius and Bertrand, who are called the most noble consuls of Aquitaine, came to meet him. The wise bishop made timely use of their assistance both to secure peace and tranquility by establishing the Truce of God and to restrain those who robbed the Church’s goods, whom he compelled to restore what they had taken.

It is pleasant to read in the documents the pious and courageous deeds accomplished by him, described in an ancient charter which Lord du Bouchet communicated to our Sammarthani. The foundation of the church of Saint Peter of the monastery is recorded there in the year 993. He is said to have lived until 996. But a charter, or decree, concerning the truce and peace promulgated by him, which we published among the documents of the Church of Anicium, proves that he died later. Since Fredolo, bishop of Elne, is named among those bishops who enacted the decree with Wido, and no mention of him is found before the eighth year of King Robert’s reign, while it is certain that in the year 1000 Berengar, Fredolo’s predecessor, was bishop of Elne, it is clear that that assembly of bishops cannot have taken place before the year 1000.

On the other hand, it is established that Bishop Wido did not reach the year 1000 in the episcopate, since Stephen, his successor after Drogo, was deposed in the year 998. Hence we conjecture that Wido, when he noticed that Drogo had either refused the bishopric or had been prevented by death from obtaining it, and that Stephen had been deposed by Gregory V, returned to the episcopal church and, by the authority he possessed, remained there for some time.

## STATUTES OF GUIDO

Promulgated to bring about peace among Christians.

(*Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, Appendix.)

In the name of God, the highest and undivided Trinity. Wido, by the grace of God bishop of Anicium, to those awaiting the mercy of heavenly compassion: greeting and peace.

We wish it to be known to all God’s faithful that, seeing the evil deeds which increase daily among the people, we have gathered the bishops: Lord Pe., bishop of Viviers; Wigo, bishop of Valence; Bego, bishop of Auvergne; Raymond, bishop of Toulouse; Deusdedit, bishop of Rodez; Fredelo, bishop of Elne; Lord Fulcrannus, bishop of Lodève; Wido, bishop of Glandèves; and many other bishops, as well as all the princes and nobles, whose number has not been determined.

And because we know that without peace no one shall see God, we admonish you for the Lord’s name, and so that you may be sons of peace, that in these bishoprics governed by these bishops, and in these counties, from this hour and henceforth, no one shall violate a church, except a church situated within the fortification of a castle—knowingly, unless [the defective text concerns] bishops on account of their dues [Note: [Col. 0853C] Something appears to be missing.].

No one shall make a raid in these counties or bishoprics. No one shall take small horses, oxen, cows, male or female asses, or the bundles they carry, nor sheep, goats, or pigs; nor shall anyone kill them, unless, under the safe-conduct of their owner or owners, he obtains provisions while traveling, as if for his own household. Let no one carry anything away or build, fortify, or besiege a castle, except from his own land, his own allod, his own benefice, or his own commendation.

Let clerics carry no secular weapons. Let no one injure monks, nor those who travel with them and carry no weapons, except bishops or archdeacons on account of their dues. Let no one seize a male or female peasant for ransom except by his own forfeiture [*sorsfactum*; *forsfactum*]. Nor shall anyone seize a peasant who has plowed or worked another man’s land, where the matter is disputed, except from his own land or his own benefice.

No one shall dare to appropriate ecclesiastical lands—episcopal, canonical, or monastic—or dishonor them by any evil customary exaction, unless he has acquired them from the hand of the bishop or with the consent of the brothers by a precarious grant, from this hour and henceforth.

No one shall knowingly seize merchants or strip them of their goods. We also prohibit any layman from meddling in the burials or offerings of the church. No priest shall accept payment for baptism, because it is the gift of the Holy Spirit.

If any plunderer or curser violates this institution and refuses to observe it, let him be excommunicated and anathematized and excluded from the thresholds of God’s holy Church, [unless] he comes to make satisfaction. If he does not do so, let the priest neither sing Mass for him nor perform the divine office for him. If he dies, let the priest neither bury him nor allow him to be buried in the church. Let him knowingly give him no communion; and if any priest knowingly violates this, let him be deposed from his order.

We also entreat and admonish you to come at this time—namely, in the middle of the month of October—to this assembly of God with a good disposition and good will, in God’s name, so that you may obtain the remission of your sins, through our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit.

This is confirmed by Archbishop Dagobert of the see of Bourges and Lord Theobald, archbishop of Vienne.

## CHARTER OF GUIDO

Written while he was abbot of the monastery of Saint Paul of Cormery. He restored what had been taken from the monasteries.

(*Apud* Mabillon, *Annals*, book XLVII, p. 624.)

I, Wido, in the name of God abbot of the monastery of Saint Paul of Cormery, or of the monastery of Saint Savior of Villeloin, which lives under its protection, and likewise of the monastery of Saint Peter of Ferrières and of the monastery of Saint Albans of Angers, wish it to be known to all the faithful of God’s holy Church, both present and future, how I desire to care for, with every affection and effort, the places entrusted to my government.

For formerly, when I abounded in every good thing and shone with worldly prosperity, I set everything aside and devoted myself to Christ’s training, and therefore assumed the monastic burden. But, hindered by secular affairs and moreover provoked by the temptations of the enemy, I have not until now observed the monastic order I undertook in the many ways in which I ought to have done so; rather, through many sins slipping in, I have transgressed it.

Finally, although I ought to have advanced the places under my government toward better things by increasing their goods as far as possible, I sought instead to fall to the lowest depths, taking many things away from them. Now, however, led by repentance, I wish to make up for what I did wrong.

At the urging of Wido, bishop and my maternal uncle, and also at the prompting of Lord Abbot Hynmar—in fact, by divine inspiration—I restore to them with a willing heart the land which, alas, I took from these places. I have made this written document so that if anyone unlawfully holds something which I, corrupted by an evil plan, transferred to him, he may no longer dare to retain it.

I also sent this writing to my brother Geoffrey, count of Anjou, who gladly confirmed it with his own hand and decreed that it should be strengthened by the hands of the faithful.

Sign of Lord Wido, abbot, who ordered this instrument to be made; signature of Wido, bishop; signature of Lord Hynmar, abbot; signature of Nefing, bishop; Brother Wido confirmed with his own hand; signature of Geoffrey, count; signature of Marcoard; Rainald; Warin; Wido; Guato; Odo; Odolgar; Grifer; Burchard; Ernegis; and fifteen others.

## CONCERNING THE CHARTER OF GUIDO

By which he confirmed the Truce of God.

(*Gallia Christiana.*)

There was a certain man born of a noble family of the Franks, named Guido. By God’s providential arrangement, his parents devoted him to the study of letters. Abandoning worldly pomp, he became a monk in the monastery called Cormery and served there valiantly under the rule of Saint Benedict.

When the father of that monastery departed this life, Guido was elected abbot there by the concordant consent of the brothers and was blessed according to canonical custom. Once elevated, he shone with such good character that the fame of his goodness even reached the ears of the king of France. Relying upon his counsel, the king determined what was pleasing to God and useful to the people.
