At that time the Church of Anicium, deprived of its bishop, sent envoys from the clergy and people . . . [lacuna] unanimously to the king, asking him to give them the most useful shepherd—namely, the aforesaid abbot, whose full brother was the most noble Count Geoffrey, surnamed Grisagonella.

The king was therefore greatly pleased. Summoning the chosen man, he urged him with many prayers to go to Le Puy and become there the most faithful shepherd of souls and administrator for himself and the people. Hearing this, Guido did not consent at once; but when the king compelled him, willing or unwilling, he bade farewell to the brothers, took companions with him, and set out with the messengers from Anicium.

When his nephews Pontius and Bertrand, the most illustrious consuls of Aquitaine, heard of this, they came to meet him with their mother Adelais, his sister, offering themselves and their possessions to him. Entering Le Puy with them, he was received by a great procession of clerics and a great rejoicing of the laity, because God had given them such a patron.

After he had been elevated to the pontifical chair, he thought constantly about maintaining peace and about the property of the Church which the plunderers of that land had taken by force. He ordered all the soldiers and peasants of his bishopric to assemble, so that he might hear from them what counsel they would give him concerning the governance of peace.

He himself instructed his nephews to gather an army at Brioude. When all the people of his bishopric had been assembled together in the meadows of Saint Germanus near Le Puy, he asked them to establish peace, not to oppress the property of the poor and of the churches, and to restore what they had taken, so that they might conduct themselves as faithful Christians ought.

When they disdainfully refused, he ordered his army to come from Brioude at dawn after traveling throughout the night. He wished to compel them to swear to the peace, to provide hostages for maintaining it, and to surrender the lands and castles of blessed Mary and the ecclesiastical property which they had seized. This was done with God’s help.

After Almighty God, subjecting all things to him, had granted him a tranquil and serene peace, he summoned the leading men of the Church and said that it was his will that the clerics serving God there should have sufficient food and clothing in common. For this purpose, from the altar offering of blessed Mary, divided into two portions, he gave one part to the canons serving God and his Mother, while reserving the other for his own use.

Moreover, together with Truanus, the excellent dean, a man of great intelligence, he had the rock called the Needle (*de l’Aiguille*) cut away. At its summit he built a church dedicated in honor of blessed Michael, which he likewise gave, with substantial appurtenances, to the aforesaid canons [clerics].

When these matters had been arranged, by the inspiration of divine mercy Lord Guido, bishop of the holy Church of Velay by heavenly ordinance, carefully examined in the secret chamber of his mind how he ought, day and night, to devote himself to the pastoral office entrusted to him by God, for the benefit of his churches and monasteries and for the progress of his soul and of the other matters appropriate to episcopal care.

Recalling that in many respects he had offended against that office, he was struck, while still on earth, by the judgment of Christ’s examination. He began to implore the Lord’s mercy, lest he complete the way of all flesh before making satisfaction, as far as possible, for whatever he had done wrong.

Therefore, with God’s grace coming to his aid, as he diligently and silently considered how, with God’s favor, he might lay down the burdens of his crimes, he remembered that, so that the glory of churches might be increased, monasteries had been built in many cities; but the Church of Anicium, over which he presided, was deprived of such a religious foundation.

Accordingly, striving to increase the glory of the Church of Velay, so that the Judge might inwardly remit the weight of his sins, he resolved, with God’s generosity, to establish a monastery in the city of Anicium [in its suburb].

Making his plan known to his sister Adelais, countess, and to her sons, namely his nephews Pontius and Bertrand, as well as to the entire college of canons, and with everyone praising it, he built in the aforesaid city of Anicium [in the aforesaid suburb] a church under the name of Saint Peter, for the redemption of his soul, of all the bishops who had previously governed the pastoral care of that city, and of his successors, as well as of Stephen, his kinsman, of his sister Adelais, of their sons Pontius and Bertrand, and of all the canons of the Church of Anicium, and for the redemption of their souls and the remission of their sins.

Later, on a certain day, when the aforesaid Lord Guido, bishop, was personally present in the chapter at Anicium, and the canons had been specially summoned for this purpose, there were among them these venerable men: Lord Guido, provost of Anicium and bishop of the Church of Valence; Truanus, dean; Peter, abbot of Saint Peter and bishop of the Church of Viviers; Guitardus, archdeacon of the Church of Viviers; and Abbot Robert, who at that time were canons of the holy Church of Anicium, together with the college of the other canons sitting in chapter.

By the staff of his episcopal office, as an instrument of inquiry, he handed over to the aforesaid church or monastery, with the consent of all the canons, a certain village called Isla [Fascia], in the territory of Vincennes [Viviers], with all its rights and appurtenances which appear to belong to the bishop’s portion, except only the chapel built in that village and consecrated in honor of blessed Cyprian, bishop and martyr, for the lifetime of Truanus the dean.

After his death he likewise gave the chapel itself, with its domain [tithe], or with the entire inheritance which appears to belong to it and which is in that village: one *fustellina* [one Fascia] of vineyard; in the village of Thauliac, one manse; again, from his own property in the territory of Viviers, in a village called Gimellis, two manses, which he acquired from Guido, grandson of Desiderius.

In another place, in the village of Eagle’s Nest, one vineyard which he had bought from Ebrard for ten solidi; in the territory of Velay, in the village commonly called Caciacus, everything that Lord Guido, the bishop, now appears to hold as his domain, namely meadows, vineyards, fields, woods, and two appurtenances.

And in the same Velay, in the place called Lanciacus, one manse which Roffredus [Boffredus], a canon, held as a benefice; also, in the village of Saint Germanus, one appurtenance for raising chickens; and in the same Velay, in the district called Fiver [Fines], one church dedicated in honor of Saint Julian, subject to his episcopate of Anicium. He received it from his nephews Pontius and Bertrand as compensation for their having violently captured the aforementioned Provost Guigo and led him away from the Church of Saint Mary of Anicium to Miniate.

In the city over which he appears to preside, one mill, which Peter sold to him for ninety solidi; and one oven, which he received from Hugh Arcadius [Richard], nephew of the abbot, as the price of a canonical benefice, for sixty solidi; and in the same city, from that land which the common people specifically call the land of Saint Mary, which the bishop of that place has always been accustomed to hold for his own use, the whole burial ground; and in the Lord’s Park, for the pasture of beasts of burden, as much meadow as one man might wish to cut with a sickle in a day; and likewise in the territory of Auvergne, one enclosed holding which he bought from Imbert, a priest, for one hundred solidi.

Moreover, striving to labor for the benefit of all, and so that his successors might receive an unfailing [unfailing?] reward from the giver of all goodness in exchange for their temporal service, from everything offered in the Church of the other Velay churches, the mother which rises more illustriously in the pontifical chair above all subject to it, to Christ, the mediator of God and human beings, for the repose of the dead and the salvation of the living, he assigned one tenth to the aforesaid monastery.

Thus the monks serving Christ in that monastery under the rule of blessed Father Benedict should, under future bishops, always receive a tenth from their half. In addition to all this, he gave one complete canonical holding out of forty, so that, with God’s permission, they might attain good in that enduring fellowship [as he himself might prosper in this fellowship].

All these things written above are read in the following form: Lord Guido, the bishop, handed them over to the aforesaid monastery [as it is read, for the remedy of the souls of all those mentioned above, in the following form], so that, [according to the order of the abbot who presides over that place], the monks living there and serving the Lord Christ for the salvation of the living and the repose of the dead may have, hold, and firmly possess them by proprietary right, and may distribute them for the benefit of their own community and of the monastery itself, so that by improving them they may always remain in that church and never withdraw from it except for the benefit of the church and of themselves.

The congregation of canons, so that they might receive from God a share in eternal reward, promised at his request that, after the death of Bishop Guido, they would ask the future bishops of that place for such severity [fellowship] for the stability of this aforesaid monastery; and they praised the arrangement as something to be maintained as custom and law, just as the portion of their altar and their common life required.

For just as the future bishops of that place promised under oath to preserve everything which the canons appear to hold as their portion from the same Church of Anicium, so they shall promise under oath in no way to diminish the aforesaid possessions of this monastery, or those which, with God’s favor, may be given there.

Finally, for more certain security and stability, so that it might be believed more certainly and held more firmly, the aforesaid Lord Guido, bishop, asked that this charter be written by himself and his successors in the presence of the canons. Strengthening it below with his own hand in written letters, he ordered all the canons of the Holy Church of various orders, whose names are written below, to confirm it with their own hands.

For it seems exceedingly dishonorable and improper, and contrary to every good work, that another should wickedly squander what has been arranged for ecclesiastical benefit, and that anyone should perniciously try to destroy what ought to grow through his own diligence. Therefore, etc.

This was done in the city of Anicium on the Ides of April, on the seventeenth day of the moon, in the year of the Incarnation 996, indiction VI, epact XXV, concurrent VI, successfully.

This charter was confirmed by Guido, provost and bishop of the Church of Valence; Truanus, dean; Peter, abbot [of Viviers], bishop, canon; Ademarus, abbot, canon; Guitardus, abbot, canon; Robert, abbot, canon; Theotardus, canon; Bofredus, canon; Arnaldus; Robert, keeper of the church, canon; Adenan [Eddenus]; Wibernus, canon; and others, etc.

## In the Year of the Lord 997. Saint Adalbert, Bishop of Prague and Martyr

## LIFE OF SAINT ADALBERT

Possibly by John Canaparius, abbot at the monastery of Saints Boniface and Alexius in the City, at the beginning of the eleventh century.

(*Apud* Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae historica*, IV, *Scriptores*, p. 574.)

### NOTICE

At Rome, on the side of the Aventine Hill facing the river Tiber, there stands a monastery consecrated to Saints Boniface and Alexius. Drawn there by veneration for them, Greeks and Latins alike formerly practiced the monastic life under both the rule of Saint Basil and that of Saint Benedict.

Here Adalbert, bishop of Prague, having fled from his homeland, assumed the monastic habit under Abbot Leo. After spending several years in the company of holy men, he finally found among their number the author of his Life.

Several Lives of the bishop and martyr exist. The one recognized as the oldest of all and the principal source of the others was written within two or three years after Adalbert’s death and had as its author a monk of Saints Boniface and Alexius. He wished to conceal his name, but I believe that he was John Canaparius, who was soon to become abbot of the monastery.

Certainly he reveals himself as a monk of Saints Boniface and Alexius by calling both Saint Basil and Saint Benedict “our Father.” He reports the judgment of Abbot Leo [Note: [Col. 0859C] The same Leo who was sent to Gaul in 995 to settle the case of Arnulf and Gerbert.] and the brothers concerning Adalbert’s life and character. He himself, together with the other brothers, knew Adalbert “to be exceedingly learned in secular philosophy” [Note: [Col. 0859C] Chapter 5. Compare chapter 12.], and he communicates to us matters known only to a very few of the monastery’s brothers [Note: [Col. 0859C] Chapter 29.].

He was therefore a man of no slight authority concerning all that had happened at Rome or before Adalbert’s final journey: he had either seen these things himself or heard them from Adalbert and his brother Gaudentius [Note: [Col. 0859C] Chapter 12.], who had remained attached to the holy man as his most faithful companion from childhood [Note: [Col. 0859C] Chapter 16.], from Saint Nilus [Note: [Col. 0860C] Chapter 15.], and from Leo. He seems to have learned the history of Adalbert’s final expedition and martyrdom from Gaudentius, his companion on the journey, whom he honors with particular respect.

Since this is so, some have thought that Gaudentius himself, whom Otto III installed as archbishop of the see of Gniezno in the year 1000, wrote the book [Note: [Col. 0860C] Especially the learned Voigt in *History of Prussia* I, pp. 653 ff., followed by the learned Palacký in *Appreciation of the Oldest Bohemian Historians*, p. 296, and Contzen, *Historians of the Saxon Imperial Period*, p. 138.]. I am moved in mind not to agree with them.

For the author speaks of Gaudentius with greater affection than would allow me to believe that he was speaking of himself; and he narrates Adalbert’s killing with a mind less disturbed than would lead me to suppose that a brother wrote it. I therefore incline rather to the view that John Canaparius was the author of the book. His vision concerning Adalbert’s death is narrated below in these words:

“Behold, in the monastery where that man [Adalbert] had been brought up, the Lord showed such things in a vision to a certain convert named John Canaparius. From the highest heaven . . . [lacuna] Only very few people besides the one who saw these things know the name of one of them; the other was, as he himself still remembers today, Lord Adalbert, for whom the angelic minister had already prepared the banquets of the heavenly table.”

Here we understand the author, following the example of John the Evangelist [Note: [Col. 0861C] Gospel XIX, 26, 35.], to be recounting his own experience. With the modesty befitting a monk, that man—“John Canaparius, a man pre-eminent in nobility of flesh and abounding in riches, who renounced the monastic habit and took up the things of the world” [Note: [Col. 0861C] *Miracles of Saint Alexius*]—calls himself merely “a certain convert.”

Our John, as we learn from the author of the *Miracles of Saint Alexius*, while he was still in the world, had bound many friends, relatives, and faithful companions to himself by sincere affection, inviting them to journey with him to the same place and assume the same habit; but only a few remained faithful to their promises. That he was learned not only in Sacred Scripture and the Fathers but also in the Roman classics is shown by the many maxims extracted from them that he judged should be inserted into his work. After Leo’s death he was elected abbot [Note: [Col. 0861C] Bruno calls him abbot below in the *Life of Adalbert*.], and in the year 1002, on 8 March, he ordered by public authority that the ancient donation of Eufemianus, Saint Alexius’s father, be transcribed [Note: [Col. 0861C] Marini, *Papiri*, pp. 126–127.]. He died on 12 October in the year 1004 [Note: [Col. 0861C]

Baronius and Felix Nerini, in *De templo et coenobio SS. Bonifacii et Alexii*, Rome, 1752, quarto, p. 144, report his epitaph as follows:

> Christ God, most beautiful Maker and Author of all things,  
> receive me, unworthy as I am, my salvation and every good.  
> I beg, I implore, I ask as a servant, I entreat, John;  
> I confess my guilt; mercifully grant forgiveness.  
> I deserved every evil and increased the heap of my offenses;  
> slow to every good, eager for every evil.  
> From head to foot, foulness stains all my limbs;  
> but you, holy God, King, have mercy in your goodness.  
>
> [Col. 0861D] Grant me a dwelling in that region where the hosts of men are,  
> where golden-haired Christ reigns over golden ages.  
> I ask all of you who will come here after me to pour out prayers for me; and, for the sake of charity, which must not be violated, let no one cast his own or another’s corpse upon me. If anyone should presume to do this, let him be accursed and bound forever by anathema.
>
> I believe that my Redeemer lives, and in my flesh I shall see God, my Savior.
>
> From the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ there are one thousand four years. He died in the month of October, on the twelfth day, in the third indiction.]

.

He wrote the *Life of Adalbert* while Nilo was still alive [Note: [Col. 0861D] Cf. chap. 19.] (+1005), Otto III was still alive [Note: [Col. 0861D] Cf. chap. 14.] (+1002, 24 January), and Leo was still alive, before the emperor’s journey to Poland undertaken to visit Adalbert’s tomb (in 1000)—a journey of which he certainly makes no mention—and while Pope Gregory V had recently died (in 999, 5 February), since, had Gregory still been alive, he would scarcely have condemned the emperor’s rash spirit [Note: [Col. 0861D] Chap. 21.]. He must therefore be regarded as having completed the book in 999. The author of the little book on the translation of Saints Abundius and Abundantius attributes the commissioning of it to Otto III [Note: [Col. 0861D] Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, century V, p. 873; we transcribe its conclusion:

> “He departed to the Lord through the palm of martyrdom. When the king heard this, unable to endure the ardor of so great a martyr, he went beyond the mountains into Slavonia with the Roman senate, bishops, and clergy, to bring the relics of the blessed martyr Adalbert to Rome. Taking his hands, he adorned them wondrously with gold and gems, built a church in his name between the two bridges, and entrusted it to great dignity; moreover, he composed with remarkable skill an account of his origin, deeds, and passion and had it written in a little book. Then he began to search for the bodies of the holy martyrs and ordered that, wherever they were found, they should be carried to the church of blessed Adalbert. He was informed that in the church of the blessed martyrs Abundius and Abundantius, which stands near Mount Soracte, there were many bodies of holy martyrs. He sent his bishops, clergy, and monks as messengers to carry them to the church of blessed Adalbert with every honor and care and with hymns to God. They immediately departed and began to inquire where their tombs were. They found in one tomb the bodies of the blessed Abundius and Abundantius, and in another the body of blessed Theodora, who had buried them on her own estate. They also found among them holy martyrs who wore gilded and magnificently adorned garments, and above their altar a carved and richly decorated table. Everything was carried, according to the emperor’s order, to the church of the blessed martyr Adalbert.”]

The friendship that joined the emperor to Adalbert [Note: [Col. 0862D] Chapters 22, 23, 25.] and the author’s favorable attitude toward Otto III and Otto II [Note: [Col. 0862D] Chapters 8, 14, 21, 22, 23.] may likewise confirm that the matter occurred in this way.

[Col. 0861C] The author uses a weighty and concise style, though he employs expressions that sometimes approach the usage of a more recent idiom [Note: [Col. 0862D] Thus in chapter 8: *foret* instead of *esset*, “would be”; *postulans erat*, *exposcens erat*, “he was asking,” instead of *postulabat*, *exposcebat*, “he asked”; *vivere suum*, “his living,” instead of *vitam suam*, “his life.”].

[Col. 0862A] As soon as it appeared, the book became famous throughout Italy and Germany. A few years later it was excerpted by Bishop Bruno in the book he published on the *Life of Adalbert*. In the eleventh century it underwent a third circulation at Monte Cassino and in Germany; thereafter it became known to Leo of Ostia, the author of the translation of Saints Abundius and Abundantius, to Cosmas, dean of Prague [Note: [Col. 0862D] Through Cosmas, the Saxon annalist.], and, through them, to other authors [Note: [Col. 0862D] Not a few of them produced an abridgment of the life.].

Our edition is based on the following resources:

1. The ducal Guelferbytanus manuscript, formerly Lamspringensis, among the Helmstedt manuscripts no. 553, on parchment, quarto, of the eleventh century. It generally offers a sound text, but in several places it has been erased and corrupted by a second hand, likewise of the same century. Since the primary reading was restored with the aid of the other manuscripts, I have taken account of the corrector only rarely. The following agrees with it:

2. The royal Stuttgart manuscript, formerly Zwifaltanus, no. 167, vol. III, on parchment, in the largest folio, from the middle of the twelfth century; our book was inserted in fols. 187–191 by a thirteenth-century hand. I was able to make use of it through the kindness of the most distinguished Moser, chief educational councillor and librarian in the kingdom of Württemberg. The following seems to belong to the same group:

2b. The parchment manuscript of Heiligenkreuz in Austria, twelfth century, folio.

2c. The imperial Vienna manuscript, listed among the manuscripts of ecclesiastical history under no. 5, on parchment, in folio, from the end of the thirteenth century.

2d. The Zwettl manuscript in Austria, no. 24, on parchment, thirteenth century, folio.

3a. The manuscript of the monastery of Windberg, transcribed by Canisius in *Lectures of Antiquity* V, part II, pp. 332 ff.; it no longer exists, and therefore I used Canisius’s text in its place. It is generally good and departs from the earlier manuscripts almost only where the editor attempted to remedy a sentence he had not properly understood by adding certain words. Canisius’s text—

3a* Freher repeated it on pp. 73–84 of the *Bohemian Saints*, and Basnage enlarged it with several notes in the second edition of the *Lectures*, vol. III, pp. 45 ff. [Col. 0862C] In addition to Canisius’s reading—

[Col. 0863A] 3b. The Admont manuscript in Styria, on parchment, twelfth century, folio, and

3bb. The Klosterneuburg manuscript no. 707, on parchment, folio, twelfth century, seem to belong with it, since, like it and the Prague manuscript, they write *Bohemia* at the beginning where the others have *Slavonia*.

3c. The manuscript of the metropolitan library of Prague, on parchment, fourteenth century, folio [Note: [Col. 0863B] See Pelzel and Dobrowsky on it in the preface to the *Bohemian Saints*, vol. I, pp. XV ff.]. We read it as transcribed and furnished with notes by Godefrid Henschen in the *Acta Sanctorum*, 23 April, pp. 178 ff., using the editions of Canisius and Bzovius [Note: [Col. 0863B] Mabillon compared the editions of Canisius, Bollandus, and Bzovius with one another and added excerpts from the second life, Ademar’s second manuscript, the Saxon annalist—who reports material drawn only from Cosmas—and the translation of Saints Abundius and Abundantius.]. Here and there it has been corrupted by Bohuslav Balbín, through ignorance of how to read it or deliberately. For, as we know from the late Dobrowsky, the Prague manuscript, like the others, has “with fierce men,” not “with brave men.” We also find that glosses and words employed to explain the sentence have been inserted into the text. Otherwise, the manuscript comes very close to our no. 2 in many places.

4a. The parchment Admont manuscript, written in the largest folio in the twelfth century [Col. 0863B], which we are pleased to have had compared with the printed editions through the diligence of our Chmel, presents a text so altered at the scribe’s discretion that one can sometimes no longer recognize our author. It frequently adds, cuts, reshapes sentences, and exchanges words for words, although in other places it copied the genuine text with sufficient fidelity. That this was done at the command of Sylvester II may perhaps be inferred from the fact that virtually the same work in—

4b. The Cassinese manuscript no. 145, on parchment, in the largest folio, eleventh century, pp. 209 ff., is attributed to Pope Sylvester II [Note: [Col. 0863C] Bzovius and the catalogue of the manuscript library of Cassino, by Frederick and Placid of Genoa.]. [Col. 0864A] The book published by Bzovius in 1629 [Note: [Col. 0864B] *The Life and Passion of Saint Adalbert Ursinus, Count of Rosenberg . . . published by his contemporary and intimate, Sylvester II, Supreme Pontiff*. Rome, quarto.] and illustrated with notes generally agrees with the Admont manuscript, but it also contains readings of its own that differ both from Admont and from the genuine text. In some places it introduces glosses into the text; in others it comes very close to Canisius’s reading. From this derives—

4b* The Cassino manuscript no. 110, on parchment, in the largest folio, twelfth century, where, from fol. 264 onward, the life is arranged in four readings. The following seems to belong to the same group:

4c. The manuscript of the Vallicellian Library [Note: [Col. 0864B] We have no information about the Vallicellian manuscript designated II.25.] G.N. 99, perhaps the same one praised by Baronius [Note: [Col. 0864B] *Annals*, 980, pp. 839 ff.] and Bzovius as belonging to the library of Saint Cecilia.

5. The royal Brussels manuscript no. 9290, on parchment, folio, twelfth century, formerly of Saint Lawrence in Liège, has lightly altered the text—which clearly must be established by the authority of the other manuscripts—by removing words more difficult to understand and adding others. It was compared with the printed editions by our Bethmann.

6. The royal Munich manuscript, listed among the books of Saint Emmeram at Regensburg under B.34, on parchment, fourteenth century, which the most distinguished Föringer prepared for our use, exchanges words and complete sentences for others, abridges the text, and enlarges it by inserting portions from another life; at the end it presents the *Miracles of Saint Adalbert the Martyr*.

In such a diversity of manuscripts [Note: [Col. 0864C] The manuscript listed in the catalogue of the Göttingen manuscript library (*Archiv* VI, 200) is no longer there today.], since it was clear that the genuine text is found only in 1, 2, and 3, I judged that only the principal passages in which the others disagree with them should be noted.

# HERE BEGINS THE PASSION OF SAINT ADALBERT, MARTYR OF CHRIST [Note: [Col. 0863] Thus 1. “Here begins the life and passion of the venerable man Adalbert, bishop of the city of Prague, who was called Woithec at baptism; his martyrdom is celebrated on the ninth day before the Kalends of May.” 5.]

[Col. 0863]

[Col. 0863D] 1. There is a region in the parts of Germany, rich in resources [Note: [Col. 0863] “Rich,” 6; and it frequently changes words in this way.], exceedingly powerful in arms and in fierce [Note: [Col. 0863] “Brave,” 3c? See the preface.] men [Note: [Col. 0863] “And fierce men,” 4a, b, c.], which its inhabitants call Slavonia [Note: [Col. 0863] “Bohemia,” 3a, b; “Bohemia,” 3c.] by name [Note: [Col. 0863] “By name,” 4b, c.]. Most of it [Note: [Col. 0863] “Most of which is still occupied by the darkness of unbelief; they worship wood or stone or another creature as God,” 4a, b.], overcome by the error of unbelief, worships the creature instead of the Creator, wood or stone instead of God; many are Christians in name only [Note: [Col. 0863] “Held,” 1.] and live according to pagan custom, so that what ought to be a means of salvation becomes for them a cause of danger. Some, however, of the same people believe rightly and perform good works in hope of the reward to come.

Thus, in those regions where the religion of Christianity flourished most beautifully, there was a man named Zlaunik [Note: [Col. 0863] “Zlaunik,” 2; “Slawnik,” 3c; “Zlaunicus,” 3a, 5; “Sclavonicus,” 4a, b.], a citizen powerful in honor and wealth and very distinguished for his love of justice and works of mercy [Note: [Col. 0863] “Distinguished”; 4a omits *perrarus* and has *praeclarus*; 4b omits the phrase.]. He was a great man [Col. 0864D] among all the inhabitants of that land [Note: [Col. 0863] Omitted by 3.], exceedingly rich in gold and silver, and amid his delights a faithful guardian of the divine law, carefully walking according to the priests’ commands [Note: [Col. 0863] “Obedient to the ministers of the Church,” 4a, b.]. He was dear to the entire people [Note: [Col. 0863] “To all,” 1, 2, 3; likewise below. “To the whole,” 1 corrected by 3c; “to all,” 4a, b.], but especially a friend to the poor.

He took a wife worthy of his lineage and herself full of honorable conduct. By hearing the words of life she thirsted ever more, and by putting them into practice she did not satisfy her hunger [Note: [Col. 0863] 4b omits “By hearing the words of life she thirsted ever more, and by putting them into practice she did not satisfy her hunger.”]. She took no pleasure in the finery of matrons or in gold and precious stones, considering of little value what fools regard as greatest. She was holy in conduct, holy in speech, strong, as they say, in fasting, and intimate with God in prayer; to the grieving orphan she was a mother, and to the stranger and widow a most gracious sister. [Col. 0865A] For these and similar virtues, which both of them practiced, nobles and wealthy men honored them, and a very great multitude of the poor revered them [Note: [Col. 0865] “Of the poor,” 3, 4a, b.].

2. Therefore, since from so noble a marriage a holy offspring was rightly destined to be born, among the brave young men whom they had begotten there was born to them a boy more beautiful than all the others (in the year 956). Afterward, in the washing of sacred baptism [Note: [Col. 0865] “Washing,” 1.], he was given the name Woytech [Note: [Col. 0865] “Woieteth” in a passage erased by a second hand in 1; “Woythec,” 2; “Uventius,” 4a and the manuscript of Saint Cecilia; “Vicentius,” 4b; “Woithec,” 5; “Woythiech,” which name means “consolation of the army,” 3c.].

Since his future greatness was still unknown, his parents spared his beauty and, because of the excessive beauty he possessed, destined him for the world. Whatever pious error—or rather, culpable negligence [Note: [Col. 0865] “Not only,” 5; “or,” 3a.]—the parents committed in this matter, the heavenly sword of divine anger soon corrected by exposing their fault. For one could see the infant’s little body suddenly growing enormously, and, because of the excessive swelling, his belly becoming larger than his whole body. With each passing hour greater pain was added, and the danger of death began to threaten.

The parents were distraught; the father’s tears flowed abundantly, and the nurse tore her pale cheeks with crooked fingernails; the brothers stood sorrowful [Note: [Col. 0865] “They wept,” 4b.]; pain raged within the mother’s entrails, and neither voice, mind, nor complexion remained in its settled state. At last, on the very brink of death, they fled to the gracious and merciful Lord and invoked the Mother of the Lord, who more than all the saints is accustomed to come to the aid of human need. They then went to the church with great humility and dejection of heart. Placing the boy upon the altar of Saint Mary, they vowed him to the Lord in an acceptable vow. When these things had been done [Note: [Col. 0865] “Done,” 3a; “completed,” 4a, b.], God’s indignation was turned away, and, his belly having been reduced, the boy was restored to his former beauty [Note: [Col. 0865] The damaged reading in 1 is corrected from *p—ne* to *p—ni*.].

[Col. 0865C] 3. The parents, who had been the cause of this evil, were moved to repentance and glorified the Lord, who knows how to appoint the scourges of his anger for the betterment of human beings. The boy, meanwhile [Note: [Col. 0865] “Adalbert” is written above the line in 1.], advancing in age and wisdom, was imbued at the proper time with Christian letters. He did not leave his father’s house until he had learned the Psalter by heart.

Thereafter, in order to learn the liberal arts [Note: [Col. 0865] “Libral arts,” 1.], his father sent him to Archbishop Adalbert (in the year 972), from whose verbal instruction he never departed in conduct and life. This archbishop presided over the sacred city which in Latin is called “the city of virgins” [Note: [Col. 0865D] Magdeburg.], and in Greek *Parthenopolis*. It was once a city known among the peoples and one of the great cities while the first Otto held the royal scepters [Col. 0865D]; now, on account of sins [Note: [Col. 0865D] The sins of Gisilar, bishop of Merseburg, who had invaded the archbishopric [Col. 0866D] of Magdeburg.], it is a half-ruined house [Col. 0866A] and an untrustworthy stopping-place for sailors (Virgil, *Aeneid* II, 23).

At that time there was [Note: [Col. 0865] 4a, b add “there.”] a certain teacher of the schools, Octricus [Note: [Col. 0865] “Ohtricus,” 3a, c; “cleric,” 4a; “Stericus,” 4b.], a philosopher, under whom a crowd of young men and a great abundance of books flourished, with study increasing greatly [Note: [Col. 0865] “Of free men,” 3a.]. That archbishop, therefore, receiving the boy with great affection, gave him the confirmation of the most holy chrism, named him Adalbert after himself, and handed him over to the schools. An inseparable spirit was always present with him as he learned [Note: [Col. 0865] The reading in 1 is damaged: *semper :::vidus*; 4a has *inviduus*.], and his intellect, reason [Note: [Col. 0865] “Speech,” 2, 3c.], and understanding flowed in a rich stream [Note: [Col. 0865] “They run,” 2, 3a, c, 5; “he runs,” 4a; “running,” 4b.].

4. Throughout the entire period of his school studies he had not imitated those who practiced wickedness, nor had he stood in the counsel of those whose deeds and childish pursuits were useless [Note: [Col. 0865] “Was,” 4a; “useless,” plural in 2, 3a, c, 4b.]. But as soon as the teacher gave him an opportunity by assigning him a somewhat more distant place [Note: [Col. 0865] “Something,” 3a, 4a, b, 5; “a little farther,” 3c.], he fled by hidden paths to the dwelling places of the holy martyrs [Col. 0866B]. There, fulfilling the vows of prayer according to the measure of time [Note: [Col. 0865] “Vow,” corrected to “vows,” 1.], he returned and sat down again in his place before the teacher’s arrival [Note: [Col. 0865] “Where,” 1, corrected by 3a, c; “and there,” 4b.].

At night also, so that his good work might be concealed from human praise, he went around among the poor, the infirm, and the blind, offering them friendly consolation according to the measure of their sufferings. Yet, so that he might not cease from the pursuit of good works, his father and his excellent mother supplied him with everything sufficient [Note: [Col. 0865] “They supplied him with everything,” 2.]. They even offered his teacher gold, silver, and whatever else was most esteemed in human eyes [Note: [Col. 0865] Omitted by 2, 4a.], and purchased instruction at a high price for their dear son [Note: [Col. 0865] “Of their dear son,” 2, 3a, c, 4a, b, 5.].

He, meanwhile, always stretching himself by tireless effort toward every exercise of virtue, advanced most beautifully among his fellow students. When the teacher had departed [Col. 0866C] and the others lightened for themselves the labor of reading with empty games and jokes, he, tasting the honey of Davidic nectar [Note: [Col. 0865] 2 and 5 omit “but he.”], consoled himself with spiritual laughter. When they, dining in the corners of the school, secretly stole sweet dishes from the teacher, he, sending secret prayers to his Lady [Note: [Col. 0865] Thus 1, later corrected to “his Lord”; 4b has “the mother of his Lord.”] [Note: [Col. 0866D] The Virgin Mary, to whom he had been consecrated.], purchased angelic food for himself.

5. Let us now consider, among the other virtues he possessed [Note: [Col. 0865] “What effects of holy simplicity, and what a prerogative of chastity, while still in childhood, he displayed,” 5.], how rich he was in holy simplicity. One day, as he was going from school, a companion who was traveling with him knocked a girl passing by to the ground and, as a joke, threw him on top of her. The students gathered and awaited with immense laughter what he would do. But because he had touched a clothed virgin [Col. 0866D], O good folly [Note: [Col. 0865] “O good folly” is absent in 4a; 4b has “O, through the impact of folly.”]! he truly believed that he had already married her [Col. 0867A] [Note: [Col. 0867] Omitted by 2.].

Then, rising from the hated virgin [Note: [Col. 0867] Omitted by 1.], the thoroughly simple boy gave himself over to the bitterest lamentation, and immediately wet his eyes with a shower of tears: “Alas for me! I have married,” he said [Note: [Col. 0867] “Wretched me,” 3c.], pointing with his finger to the instigator of the crime: “This man made me marry!”

Already then, by performing these and similar deeds, the little boy filled with God fixed the eyes of many upon himself [Note: [Col. 0867] 4a omits “By performing these and similar deeds, the little boy filled with God fixed the eyes of many upon himself.”], and they marveled at his conduct and said:

“God has indeed blessed this boy, who, while still within the threshold of childhood, rises so loftily toward every excellent thing. Thrice and four times blessed will he be if he completes these pursuits of humanity with complete devotion and brings the course of the work he has undertaken to a fitting conclusion!”

Those who knew his father and his extraordinary mother said:

“It is no wonder that one so great has sprung from such parents. His father’s justice flourishes in him, and the image of his mother’s piety blooms in his purple breast.”

How many years he studied is uncertain; but we all know that he was exceedingly learned in secular philosophy [Note: [Col. 0867] 2 omits “philosophy … human.”]. I believe that the Lord wished him to study human philosophy [Note: [Col. 0867] 2 omits “philosophy … human.”] for this purpose: so that afterward he might climb the mountains of divine wisdom with an easier step—or rather, that as a child he should drink the bitterness of the world, so that later, as a man, he might imbibe the sweetness of God with a more eager spirit.

6. After this, the teacher of the schools [Note: [Col. 0867] 4b: “Astericus, in the service of the emperor Otto II.”] entered the emperor’s service and went to the royal court (in the year 981). But Archbishop Adalbert [Note: [Col. 0867] “Adalbert of Magdeburg,” 4b.], the *archimandrite* [Note: [Col. 0867] Properly, *archimandrite* means “chief of cooks”; here it signifies an archbishop.], having paid the debt of nature, had flown from this sea to the shores of everlasting blessedness.

That pupil, returning to his homeland and dear relatives, took up the weapons of Christian warfare under the bishop of the sacred city of Prague [Note: [Col. 0867] “The first, named Tethar,” 3c.]. Not long afterward the same bishop was seized by a most grievous illness, and, bringing his life to its close with a detestable end, his final day came (in the year 982). For, during his last breath, while a large part of his soul still remained, he recounted in a feeble voice to those standing around him, one of whom was the young Adalbert [Note: [Col. 0867] “Lord Adalbert,” 4b.], this little speech [Note: [Col. 0867] “Expression,” 4a; “this discourse,” 4b.]:

“Alas for me! What sort of man I was, and how different [Note: [Col. 0867] Thus 2, 3c, 4b; 1 omits it; 3a has “changed”; 5, “unlike.”] from that man” (Virgil, *Aeneid* II, 274), “what sort of man I would now wish to be! Alas, wretched me! I have lost my days; there is nowhere any fruit of repentance [Note: [Col. 0867] 2 has “there is no fruit.”]! I am lost [Note: [Col. 0867] “He will perish,” 1.]! Where now is my honor and my empty wealth? O rotten flesh and food for worms, where now is the glory and beauty of your vanity? You deceived me, you deceived me, deceitful world, promising me a long life; and behold, with the sword of an unexpected death, how wickedly you have slain my soul!

“Yet my crime would in some way be pardonable before the gracious Lord [Note: [Col. 0867] Omitted by 2 and 5.], except that the crimes of the people entrusted to me add to the heap of my miseries [Note: [Col. 0867] “May add,” 2; “would add,” 3c; “would have added,” 5.]. For pleasures and desires were their law. I neither restrained the frenzied people nor was able to restrain them from willingly perishing [Note: [Col. 0867] Omitted by 1.], the people who even to this day know or do nothing except what the finger of Satan has written in their hearts [Note: [Col. 0867] “What has been dictated,” 4a.]. Woe to me, because I kept silent! This is what grieves me and will grieve me forever.

“For behold, a victim of dreadful death, I shall depart by the straight road to hell, where my worms shall not die, and my fire shall burn forever and beyond.”

Thus he spoke and, sooner than words can tell (Virgil, *Aeneid* I, 142) [Note: [Col. 0867] Omitted by 1, 3a.], fell asleep. Great mourning arose over him. They were afraid with great fear [Note: [Col. 0867] “All,” 3c, 4a, b.], but above all the young Adalbert [Note: [Col. 0867] “Lord Adalbert,” 4b.], who in those days was a delicate soldier.

That same night [Note: [Col. 0867] 4b repeatedly has “the aforementioned Lord Adalbert.”], clothed in a sackcloth tunic and sprinkling his gray head with ashes, he went around to the individual churches. He also distributed generously to the poor whatever he possessed and commended himself and his cause to the Lord in prayer. Even then some secretly promised him the honor of the episcopate, while others promised it openly.

7. After the bishop’s death, an assembly of the abandoned people together with the prince of that land was held not far from the city of Prague. A careful inquiry was made as to whom they should appoint in his place. They all answered with one voice:

“Who else could it be but our native Adalbert, whose conduct, nobility, wealth, and life are in harmony with honor? He knows very well where he himself should walk; he also prudently guides the souls entrusted to him.”

On the same Sunday when this election took place, a certain man is said to have been seized in the church [Note: [Col. 0867] “Into the church,” 3a, c, 4b, 5.] where the episcopal seat is located by a most powerful demon. He began publicly to confess the evils [Note: [Col. 0867] “Sins,” 2.] of which he was conscious. Then the ministers of the Lord’s table gathered, praying for him and driving away the enemy with sacred words.

The most impure demon cried out through his mouth:

“What have I to do with you, and what have you to do with me? You have come to drive me from this dwelling of mine! What good is there in your uttering empty words? I greatly fear the man who is going to sit in this seat; wherever I see or hear him, I do not dare to remain.”

Immediately, foaming, the demon repeated mutterings and horrible words; gnashing his dreadful teeth for a long time, he finally departed, leaving the man healthy.

The next day, before sunrise, a messenger came saying that the previous day Lord Adalbert had been elected bishop by public consent [Note: [Col. 0867] “Assembly,” corrected to “consent,” 1.]. The people and clergy rushed together, glorifying and thanking the Lord, because the evil spirit, willingly or unwillingly, had confessed Adalbert’s election.

8. (In the year 983.) Meanwhile, returning from the Saracen war [Note: [Col. 0867] “Saracen,” 2c, 3a, c; “Saracenic,” 4a, b.], the imperial majesty, namely Otto II, approached Verona [Col. 0868D]. His hand had been strong in battle and his virtue immense in a small body; an Augustus better than his good father and, as fame records, in every respect a most Christian Caesar. Though then both victor and defeated, he had come here to gather the army [Note: [Col. 0867] “To gather,” 1.] and wished to avenge the losses of victory, not knowing that death was already knocking close at hand.

To him, therefore, a Slavic delegation went [Note: [Col. 0869] “A Bohemian delegation,” 3c; “the hand of the Bohemians—the clergy and people,” 4b.], bearing an embassy from the duke [Note: [Col. 0869] “From Duke Boleslaus,” 4b.]. They presented the elected bishop and asked that the popular election be confirmed by his authority. The emperor readily assented to their worthy petition and gave Adalbert the pastoral staff; then he sent him to the archbishop of Mainz, whose suffragan he was, to be consecrated.

After his consecration, on the feast of the friends of our Lord Jesus Christ, Peter and Paul (29 June), he rode with a large retinue toward his beloved homeland. The horse on whose back he sat proceeded neither in the manner of snorting horses nor at a swift pace [Note: [Col. 0869] “Prosperous,” 4a; “very swift,” 4b.]; nor did it carry a bridle glittering with gold and silver. Instead, its mouth was restrained in rustic fashion by twisted hemp [Note: [Col. 0869] “Hemp,” 3a, 4b; “hemp,” 3c; “hemp,” manuscript of Saint Cecilia (4c?).], and it walked according to the will of its rider.

They came to the holy city of Prague, where the illustrious Wenceslaus [Note: [Col. 0869] “Wuecezlaus,” 1; “Wenezlaus,” 3a; “Wuentisclavo,” 4a; “Wenzeslaus,” 4b.] had once held the kingship and had brought his life to an excellent conclusion in the service of God. Later, completing a noble martyrdom beneath the sword of his wicked brother [Note: [Col. 0869] “Consuming,” corrected to “completing,” 1; “completing,” 2, 4a, b.], he proves his merits by clear signs and great miracles even to this day.

There the new pontiff loosened the bonds from his feet and entered the city barefoot. Then, fulfilling the obligations of prayer with humble and contrite heart, he took possession of the episcopal chair amid the great joy of the citizens.

9. Throughout all the days of his episcopate he served the Lord piously and faithfully, but for a long time and with unproductive labor [Note: [Col. 0869] 2, 3a, c, and 4a, b omit “for a long time”; 4b has “and.”; 1 has *et* erased; 4b has “productive.”] he exercised the Christian rule among the people.

He divided the ecclesiastical revenues into four equal parts: the first he assigned to the necessities and furnishings of the church; the second to the needs [Note: [Col. 0869] “Uses,” 4a, b.] of the canons [Note: [Col. 0869] “Clergy,” 4a, b.]; the third he spent with overflowing compassion among the ranks of the poor; and the small remainder of the fourth he kept for his own needs.

Moreover, every feast day he summoned very many poor people who depended on alms [Note: [Col. 0869] Omitted by 2, 3a, c.] to works of mercy, supplying them abundantly with whatever they needed. On ordinary days also, he was accustomed to have three sets of four—that is, twelve [Note: [Col. 0869C] That is, twelve.]—whom, in honor of the apostolic name, he satisfied with food and drink [Note: [Col. 0869] “He used to satisfy,” 4a, b, 5.].

Rarely, except on some feast day [Note: [Col. 0869] “Something,” 2; “someone,” 4a.], did the midday sun see him eating, and never did midnight find him indulging in sleep. His bed stood rigid with straw [Note: [Col. 0869] “Tall straw,” 2, 3a, c, 4a, b; omitted by 5.] [Col. 0870A], feathers, and purple cloth [Note: [Col. 0869] “Rigid,” 2: *rigulus*.], feeding the eyes of men by day. At night, however, either his brother Gaudentius or a man born blind [Note: [Col. 0869] 3c: “or one other, apart from whom.”] occupied it; apart from these, joined to him in his bedchamber by the closest familiarity, no one else in the house lay down with him as a third. He himself, however, slept on the bare ground, or on a soft haircloth [Note: [Col. 0869] “Light,” 3c, 4b.], with a stone for a pillow.

He never went to bed with a full stomach [Note: [Col. 0869] “He went,” or “he goes,” 3c.], and before his sleep was complete he rose to the accustomed banquets of prayer. He had worn down his body and the incentives of the body with the sharpest fasts, nor did he ever wish to give his mind to any pleasure [Note: [Col. 0869] 4a omits: “nor did he ever wish to give his mind to any pleasure.”]. Little rest was granted to his eyes, and no indulgence to his exhausted feet.

10. For he had visited the prison [Note: [Col. 0869] “Prisons,” 2, 4a.] and those confined in prison [Note: [Col. 0869] “In the prison,” 2, 4a, b.], whose long line and endless multitude were immense. No one’s own house was better known to anyone than his own, for he knew which sick person, by name and in which part, was lying down, or how many heads renewed by the hope of recovery life would restore, and how many the fatal hour would send forth rejoicing.

After all these pious services [Note: [Col. 0869] 3a has: “He was a servant of the sacred seed; when it was time, he ran to the hearth.”], if it was the season for sowing, he would hurry to the field; and, when the sowing was completed, he rejoiced that he had worked with his own hands to provide his livelihood [Note: [Col. 0869] 1, 2, and 3c distinguish the clauses in this way; the others place the division after “completed.”].

From there he would come as an undaunted traveler to the sacred buildings; more often, as an importunate petitioner before the Lord, he would knock at the heavenly doors. At one moment he prolonged his prayer with long kneelings [Note: [Col. 0869] “With bendings of the knees,” 2, 3a, c; “with kneelings,” 4a, b.]; at another he watered the prayer with a great stream of the heart’s anguished sighs [Note: [Col. 0869] 4a: “He spent the long day in these pursuits and the whole night in such occupations; these were his habits, this his devotion, this the goal of his life.” 4b: “In these leisurely activities … he used to spend …”; see below.].

From compline until prime no word came from his mouth [Note: [Col. 0869] “No speech,” 2, 3c.], and he observed the silence of the night as though bound by monastic profession. After prime he devoted his efforts to pastoral matters [Note: [Col. 0869] 4a omits “he devoted his efforts”; 4b has “he lingered over the matters to be conducted.”], carefully listening to what the robbed poor man, the stranger, and the widow were lamenting [Col. 0870C] [Note: [Col. 0869] “They were lamenting,” corrected by a second hand in 1.].

When he was free from external cares, he employed himself in Davidic conversations until the celebration of Mass. He did not speak a word to any human being for as long as he stood vested before the Lord’s table [Note: [Col. 0869] “On Sundays,” corrected to “on Sunday,” in 1; 1 omits “table” and adds “ministry” in a sixteenth-century hand.] and sacrificed the angelic bread above the Holy of Holies.

Afterward he either worked at manual labor or, with his beloved chaplains, tasted the nourishment of sacred reading [Note: [Col. 0869] “Tasting,” 1.]. In these leisure activities he spent the long day and in such occupations the whole night [Note: [Col. 0869] 2, 3c insert “he used to”; 4a omits the sentence; 4b has: “He spent the long day in these leisure activities and the whole night in such occupations.”]. These were his habits, this his devotion, this was the goal of his life.

### 11

After Compline, while he was intent upon his customary prayers, a certain poor man—whom an impious robber had left with nothing except life and limbs—knocked at the temple doors with pitiful howls. When he heard this, and none of the wealth he had distributed remained, he began to consider more carefully what he could give him. Since nothing else occurred to him, he entered his bedchamber and took from it the only thing he possessed, a silk cushion. Removing the silk, he scattered the feathers throughout the house; then, returning to the cry of the beggar lying outside, he folded the empty purple cloth into folds and, sending it through the openings of the joined doors, filled the poor man’s hand with this fruitful gift.

The author of this theft remained concealed. When Myzl, the chamberlain of his household, wished to investigate the matter rather harshly among the servants, he forbade him, saying: “By no means did an enemy do this; rather, someone who was in need perhaps took it to satisfy his necessity.”

*[Apparatus: “after” is supplied in 4b; manuscripts read “none” and “nothing remained” in varying forms. For *pulvinar*, manuscripts variously read “feathering,” “feather,” or “plumage.” For “folded,” readings include “filled,” “pressed together,” “folded,” “collected,” and “gathers.” For the doors, one witness reads “open” instead of “joined.” For the deed, one reads “act” instead of “theft.” The name Myzl is absent from 3c; other witnesses read *uuillico* or *uillico*. For *camerarius*, witnesses have *camararius* or “provost.” For *requirere*, some read “inquire.” The word “this” is absent from one witness.]*

### 12

Amid these holy works he did not cease pouring forth words of preaching. He wished to be good not for himself alone, nor to share in heavenly joys except with many; he was close to each person through compassion and, above all, lifted up in contemplation. Thus he sought what was lofty without despising the weaknesses of his neighbors; thus he accommodated himself to the weaknesses of his neighbors without ceasing to seek what was lofty. He knew how to preserve the art of discernment, so that in him there were both mercy that gave just counsel and discipline that raged piously.

But they, falling through a contrary inclination into carnal understanding, refused to follow the good shepherd. In a new manner, although they had been fed with heavenly goods, they were filled with the dregs of sins. He strove to fortify his folds with spiritual aids; they hastened to destroy what he had done by diabolical assaults. He prepared to free the people from captivity to demons and vices; they did not cease binding themselves ever more tightly in every sin.

Therefore the bishop saw that they were hastening by every means to oppose the divine laws. He saw that, with hardened hearts, they were plotting to commit every kind of great and novel crime against God. He saw that the arms of his excellent governance were being frustrated and that he was doing himself more harm than good to the people. Accordingly, he mourned their sin and pursued the ruin of the lost nation with the bitterest grief. At last he considered it better to leave than to waste his efforts among a blind people perishing of its own accord.

Those who learned the sequence of these events from his own account say that this was chiefly brought about for three reasons. The first, and as it were the principal, was the possession of several wives by one man; the second, the detestable marriages of clerics; the third, Christian captives and slaves whom a Jewish merchant had bought with wretched gold and whom the bishop could not redeem in such numbers.

The Lord also appeared to him in a dream, rousing him and ordering him to rise from his sluggish sleep. He said: “Who are you, with such commanding authority, or for what reason do you order me to break my rest?” The Lord replied: “I am Jesus Christ, who was sold; and behold, I am again being sold to the Jews, while you still sleep?” Awakened, he silently pondered within his heart what this vision might mean.

He brought in as a companion to solve the little question a distinguished man, Willico. He held precedence over the others by virtue of the office of provost, and the most holy man made him a participant in all his counsels. When he explained his vision to him, that most gentle hero replied in his own words and thoughts: “When Christians are sold to Jews, Christ himself suffers this sale, since we are his body and members, moved by him and existing through him.”

*[Apparatus: In 2 and 3c, after *desisteret* are written the abbreviated words *s. c. p. et p. c. i. c. s.*, followed by: “Accordingly, disputing about the kingdom of God and urging his righteousness, he ran forth in fervent zeal against many of their wickednesses. But they themselves …”; 4a–b have “But they themselves.” One witness reads “neither without many,” and another “but with many,” for “nor except with many.” *Relapsi* (“having fallen back”) occurs for *lapsi*. The reading *caules* (“cabbages”) in 1 is corrected to *caulas* (“folds”); 3a reads *claues* (“keys”). “Piously serving” occurs for “raging piously.” The words from “He” through “do not cease” are absent from 4a–b. For “they were hastening,” 3c has “they hasten,” 4a and 5 “they would hasten.” From “The bishop mourns” through “nation” is absent from 4a. *Primicialis* occurs for *principalis*. A marginal reading in 4a expands the third cause to “captives, slaves, and souls of Christians.” 3a reads “seeing” for “whom”; 1 omits “a companion”; and 3a supplies explicitly “we are his body and members.”]*

### 13

The holy bishop weighed these matters with an even balance and drew long sighs from the depths of his heart. He feared to remain any longer and, having accepted counsel born of grief, came to Rome in the year 989. With groaning complaints he asked the pontiff of the Apostolic See—John XVI, who occupied the see from 985 to 996; compare below, chapter 21—what he should do amid such danger to himself and his people:

“Entrusted to me, the flock does not wish to hear me, nor does my speech find entrance among those whose breasts are ruled by the commands of demonic servitude; and this is a region where bodily strength rules in place of justice and pleasure in place of law” (John 8:37).

The apostolic bishop replied: “My son, since they do not wish to follow you, flee what harms you. For if you cannot labor fruitfully with others, it is worthwhile at least not to destroy yourself. Therefore, on my advice, seize the leisure of contemplation and sit among those who lead a tranquil life in sweet and wholesome studies.”

Thus encouraged, as though by a divine response, and breathing with ardent desire toward the future joys of the saints, he resolved to abandon his native land and the peoples who knew him best. He wished to depart abroad for the Lord and, as though beneath another sun, to lead a needy old age. Everything hard and rough seemed sweet to him for the sake of his beloved Jesus; to endure narrow poverty for Christ, who is rich, was not so much labor as immense love.

After this deliberation of his mind—“reflection” or “consideration” is supplied in the margin of manuscript 1—he distributed silver generously to the poor and emptied the episcopal chamber.

*[Apparatus: One witness reads “to remain in this” for “to remain”; another has “questions” rather than “complaints.” One reads “in the breasts of the unjust” for “in whose breasts.” One has “will” rather than “pleasure.”]*

### 14

In those days the august empress Theophanu—the manuscripts give *Sthephania*, *Theophania*, *Teophania*, and *Teuphanu*—was in Rome, the mother of the one who then reigned, Otto III, the greatest with God’s help (989–990). She possessed a pious concern for the poor together with the leading men and a most sincere love for those who rightly sought Christ.

When she learned that the exile wished to travel as far as Jerusalem for the sake of prayer, she secretly had him brought to her and arranged for him to receive silver for his journey—so much that the young Gaudentius could scarcely lift it. A marginal addition in one witness instead says that she ordered a great abundance of her own treasure to be given to him for distribution among the poor in the *gazophylacium*, and that, for the love of Christ, she bestowed on him such a weight of gold that Gaudentius, the holy man’s brother, could scarcely carry it in his bosom.

On the following night he faithfully distributed the money to the poor, spending everything down to a single denarius and keeping nothing for himself. Then, sending the boys back to their homeland, he changed his clothing. He purchased a donkey to carry the burdens and took three brothers as companions for the journey.

*[Apparatus: The empress’s name appears as *Sthephania* (2), *Theophania* (3a, 4b), *Teophania* (3c), *Teuphanu* (4a), and *Theophanu* (5). “Who now reigns” is absent from 2; 3c reads “who then reigned.” “Secretly” stands in an erased place in 1. The long erased passage in 1 is supplied in the margin by another hand: “and ordered a great abundance of wealth from her own treasury to be given him for distribution to the poor”; 5 instead reads that she bestowed such a weight of gold, for Christ’s love, that Gaudentius, the holy man’s own brother, could scarcely lift it in his bosom. *Que* stands in an erased place in 1; 4b reads *onagrum* (“ass”). For Cassino, 3c has lowercase *casinum*; 1 reads “sat” for “stands”; 2 “grace” for “glory”; 4a omits from “there also” through “although”; and 1–2 read “art” for “citadel.”]*

Intending to see the Lord’s sepulchre at Jerusalem, he came to Monte Cassino, on whose summit stands the monastery that the most blessed father Benedict, flower and glory of monks, first began to build. There also, as Gregory’s honey-flowing mouth relates (*Life of Saint Benedict*, chapter 8 and following), he spent the final part of his life and wrote with his finger an example of true religion for all who wish to live piously in Christ.

Although he was not recognized there, Providence nevertheless arranged that he be honorably received as a guest. After a few days, when he wished to resume the journey he had begun, the abbot of the place, Manso, approached him, together with men of great distinction, bringing these counsels as though from a divine citadel:

“The road that you began for the sake of acquiring blessedness is far from the straight road and from the one that leads to life. It is indeed a sign of great spirit to be free from the perplexities of the fleeting world; but to change places every day is less praiseworthy. Just as the instability of the winter sea is a danger to sailors, so wandering from place to place threatens danger to its followers. But remaining in one place and enjoying heavenly pursuits more freely—this is commended to you not by us, but by the precepts and examples of great and strong men.”

The prudent hero, accepting this counsel as no less than divinely given, considered putting an end there to his labor and wandering travel.

*[Editorial note: At Cassino there survives a homily of the venerable Adalbert, bishop and martyr, on the nativity of Saint Alexius the Confessor, together with that saint’s miracles. See this volume, columns 895–876. The manuscript note is evidently corrupt in its column sequence.]*

### 15

While he was considering this, God thwarted him, wishing to delay somewhat the desires of his beloved servant, so that what was now bitter and gained through labor might later become sweeter.

For when he wished to live there according to the monastic rule, and everyone from the least to the greatest most willingly desired this, a terrible word suddenly pierced his astonished ears: “It is good that you remain with us.” One cautious old man is recorded as saying, “It is good, he said, that you remain with us”; another witness gives: “One venerable elder one day deposited these words of charity with him: ‘It is good,’ he said.”

“Here you shall put on the monastic habit; here you shall lead a life pleasing to God. Since you are a bishop, you will also be able most fittingly to consecrate our newly built churches and to promote our clerics to ecclesiastical orders.”

On hearing this, the hero—already long disturbed within himself—replied as anger dictated:

“Do you think me a man or a donkey, that when I had ceased being a bishop after removing the care of sons, I should now, under the name of bishop, consecrate your houses?”

Without delay he went down across the slopes of the mountain and, after what was apparently a journey of two days, proceeded to the great man Nilus, whose noble merit in the monastic order shines like a new morning star in the heavenly vault. Under his leadership, and under him as master of divine discipline, a great multitude of disciples served God. All of them, earning their food by their own hands, followed the heavenly footsteps of our holy father Basil according to his rule.

Drawn by this reputation, he approached the holy old man and, falling on his knees, poured out tears for a long time, seeking from him answers and friendly consolation. Abbot Nilus looked at him and recognized at once, in their first conversation, the merit with which he lived before the Lord. “Even to this day,” he said, “I do not remember seeing a young man so fervent in the love of Christ.”

“I would have received you, dear son, if this reception would not harm me and my people while bringing you no benefit. For, as this habit and the hairs of your unshorn beard testify, I am not a native but a Greek. Whatever little land there is that I and my people inhabit belongs to those holy elders and brothers whom you rightly flee. If, as I would greatly wish God to permit, you were to live together with us, they would take what is theirs, I would be expelled in my entirety with my beloved sons, and you would be even more uncertain amid an uncertain matter.

“Instead, accept your father’s counsel and return to the city of Rome, from which you departed. When, with a good angel guiding you, you arrive there, greet in the name of us all our very dear Abbot Leo, and carry him our letter, which says: either let him retain you with him—which I prefer—or, if that seems difficult to him, let him commend you on my behalf to the abbot of Saint Sabas.”

*[Apparatus: A gloss explains *frustratur* as “that is, God did not consent.” For “labor,” witnesses read “prepared” or “made ready.” The witnesses vary between “him” and “and him.” Some supply “it is good, he said”; another gives the longer elder’s speech quoted above. For “consecrate,” one witness reads “dedicate.” The source cites Leo of Ostia for the possibility of consecrating churches and promoting clerics. For Nilus, one witness reads “he went for a journey” rather than “he proceeded.” A marginal note has *thaine*; its precise force is uncertain and the original term is retained. Other readings include “they were serving,” “he serves,” and “he had served.” The phrase “according to the rule of our holy father Basil” is absent from one witness. One reads “from him” or “from that man” instead of “from him.” For “dear son,” one witness reads “dear guide.” One manuscript adds “by hand” after “not.” Another has a corrected reading meaning “you have come from far away.” A long note identifies the inhabitants as the Cassinian saints, elders, and brothers to whom the monastery of Saint Michael was subject. For “they would take,” one reads “others would take”; for “I would be expelled,” one has “I may be expelled.”]*

### 16

Strengthened by this hope, he returned to Rome, the sacred citadel, mistress of cities and head of the world. Inquiring carefully which monastery Abbot Leo governed, he was led by the people to the shrines of Saints Boniface and Alexius—today Saint Alexius, on the Aventine near the Tiber.

After he had entered and was granted the opportunity to speak with the abbot (Virgil, *Aeneid* 1.520), he offered the greeting and the letter sent by Abbot Nilus. After reading it, Leo, trained by long experience to test the spirit, carefully examined everything by subtle means before receiving him.

First he pretended indignation and, with averted face, investigated what sort of mind he possessed. He foretold harsh and difficult things for him and probed all the secrets of his mind with shrewd intelligence. But the man, just and firm in his purpose (Horace, *Odes* 3.3), could be broken neither by a man’s dreadful reply nor by the trials that were to come; nor could they recall him from the resolve he had once embraced.

When Abbot Leo saw that he could not merely turn him from his purpose but, by foretelling terrible things, could even inflame him more, he promised that he would accept him. He decided first to have the apostolic lord meet with the humbled bishop, so that whatever needed to be done might be deliberated according to the judgment of so great a father and the advice of his cardinals.

After everything had properly been completed, on the day when the Lord washed the feet of his disciples and wiped them with a towel, the holy bishop received the monastic habit. On Holy Saturday, when baptized catechumens are released from criminal bonds, the cowl hanging from his head was also released. Thereafter, enrolled among the brothers according to the custom of the rule, he began to desire Christ more ardently, seeking him by the narrow path.

Two of the brothers who had accompanied him, having long seen that he wished to make himself a monk, took flight, shamefully abandoning their shield (Horace, *Odes* 3.7.10). The manuscript’s marginal gloss explains *clipeum* as *clippeti*, “shield,” with the phrase “running secretly” or “walking stealthily” added.

Gaudentius alone remained, following the example of the steadfast man, and with the blessed man attained monastic profession and a praiseworthy way of life. He also remained at his side as his brother, doubled in flesh and spirit, and as his most faithful companion from infancy.

*[Apparatus: One witness supplies “the monastery” after “which.” For the trial, variants include “the coming temptations,” “the rains of coming temptations,” and “the showers of coming temptations.” A note explains that Leo’s purpose was not merely to turn him away. For the day of the foot-washing, one witness adds that the Lord broke and blessed the eucharistic bread for the disciples. “Infants” appears for “catechumens”; “neck” for “head.” One reads “path” rather than “narrow way.” A manuscript has “having abandoned the right shield” or “having thrown away the shield.”]*

### 17

Walking among the brothers in complete obedience and humility, he girded himself as an intrepid novice against the battles of the vices that assailed him. Always taking refuge in humble confession in his thoughts, he did not cease to disclose the secrets of his shaken mind to spiritual men. When the rain of temptations ceased, he blossomed into a new harvest of virtues and shone more brightly than usual after his victory over the vices. He advanced like shining light and grew until the perfect day (Proverbs 4:18).

The obedience imposed on him by his abbot was of this kind: he carried on his shoulder the water used in the brothers’ kitchen and performed a similar service by washing their hands. Thus he rejoiced to serve all the brothers.

Meanwhile the hostile adversary did not delay in attacking the man of God, now by open warfare, now through hidden ambushes. Whenever he carried earthen vessels—sometimes full of water, sometimes of wine—the aforesaid enemy cunningly caused him to slip, so that the vessels were shattered and scattered in pieces, covering the holy man’s face with immense embarrassment. A marginal word reads *thaine*; the Gothic or vernacular form is uncertain and is retained as printed.

When this had happened many times and he had each time prostrated himself to ask pardon, at last God, the avenger of his humiliation, looked upon these affairs. One day, when he was carrying unmixed wine to the brothers’ table, he stumbled and fell upon the vessel himself, and the vessel “fell with a mighty crash upon the marble” (Virgil, *Aeneid* 1.106). From afar the father of the monastery and all the brothers in succession heard how the hero fell, unaware that this fall would be accompanied by the most prosperous adversity. For the vessel was found sound, and the portion of wine undiminished, as though no collapse had occurred.

Likewise, a certain noble woman—called Constantia in the poem on Saint Adalbert—entered this monastery for the sake of prayer. When she had been ordered to perform an act of charity there, she declared that she had not tasted bread for seven years.

Recognizing that this custom of abstinence had attached itself to her through illness, he impressed the sign of the saving cross upon a loaf of bread. Then, placing it before the matron as she ate, he said: “In the name of my Lord Jesus Christ, daughter, eat this bread. You may not violate holy charity; for love of it you have been ordered to accept this small meal.”

At these words the believing woman tasted the gift of the bread and returned to her house with thanksgiving. From then on she used ordinary food and told her fellow citizens of the strange thing that had happened to her; and the voice of all glorified the Lord God.

Nor must it be passed over how the daughter of a certain John, who is now known to hold the office of prefect of the City—John Glosa held the prefecture even after Abbot Leo’s death in 1002, on 8 March; see Marini, *Papiri*, p. 127—began to be afflicted by the most atrocious pain of fever. When the man of God touched her with his most sacred hand, all the illness of her body departed at his command.

*[Apparatus: The witnesses vary between “obedience given by his abbot” and “his father abbot.” Some omit “water”; 1 has *ministrarios* for *ministratorios*. A marginal reading in 1 is *thaine*. A correction in 1 changes “he poured with strength” to “he covered with shame.” One witness omits “God looked upon these affairs.” One witness omits “a certain” before “noble woman.” For the woman’s reception, 4a reads: “when she was doing charity there, and had been asked with much entreaty by the brothers, [she said that] for three full years [she had not tasted] bread”; 4b reads: “when she had been asked, [she said that] for three full years [she had not tasted] bread.” The printed text reads *jussa* (“ordered”). The name Constantia is supplied from the poem on Saint Adalbert.]*

### 18

In the year 994, the archbishop of Mainz, seeing the flock of the blessed prelate proceeding without a shepherd, sent envoys with letters through whom he petitioned the apostolic lord concerning the return of the holy man.

A synod was held at Rome for this purpose—compare the *Life of Saint Adalbert* by Bruno—and a great dispute arose on both sides: on one side were those who feared to lose the monk, and on the other those who demanded their shepherd with authority. Since the two parties long contended against each other with opposing judgments, the envoys’ leader at last scarcely obtained a doubtful victory.

This leader himself was the brother of the duke whose land the bishop being demanded had governed. The apostolic bishop then, moved not so much by inclination as by the law of God, replied:

“We return what they justly demand, although the sons have already degenerated from their good father; and we shall give him on this condition: if they listen to him, let them keep him with God’s blessing and produce under him a hundredfold fruit. But if they do not wish to depart from their customary wickedness, let our man avoid the company of the evil without risking his life.”

When he had spoken these words, the synod ended, and when the assembly was dissolved, each returned to his own home. The envoys departed, leaving the monks sad and the others joyful and greatly exultant.

When they came to Prague after completing the journey, people of every age and sex went out to meet him and received him with immense joy. They gave their hands and promised everything—one witness adds “to amend”—as though they were genuinely rejoicing at his return and wished completely to correct their former life according to his commands.

*[Editorial note: The leader was Christian, son of Boleslaus I and brother of Boleslaus II; his companion was Radla, also called Anastasius and Astericus, Adalbert’s teacher.]*

### 19

But shortly afterward slothful softness seized them, and, neglecting his preaching, they proceeded into every kind of wickedness. Overcome by memories of their former vices, they relapsed into the carnal way, and the pastoral labor and diligent care of the good father perished.

Amid these events a grievous and pitiable crime arose (Virgil, *Aeneid* 4.226). The wife of a certain nobleman was publicly accused of having committed adultery with a cleric. When the dishonored relatives of her husband wished to behead her according to barbarian custom, she fled through the swift air until, by voice and by running, she reached the bishop she desired.

Wishing to free the woman from their hands, he shut her in a monastery of holy women, consecrated under the name and veneration of Saint George and surrounded by the strongest walls. He entrusted the church key faithfully to its custodian, believing that, as a woman among women, she would have consolation in her grief and security for her life under the protection of the altar.

He also wished to take the crime upon himself, so that, by making himself the author of the offense, something great might be accomplished: namely, that through the fruits of penitence either she might be preserved for life or both of them might be ordered to die together. Since he was seeking the crown of martyrdom with this intention, he would certainly have fulfilled what he wished, had Lord Willico not prudently restrained him.

Meanwhile an impious hand, preparing sword and death for the hidden woman, burst with armed soldiers into the episcopal court. They sought the bishop with threats and insolent words, demanding to know who would defend the harlot against divine law and the statutes of the law.

When he, occupied in the leisure of divine contemplation, heard this, and it was as though the hour of divided night had arrived, he broke the silence by reciting a verse and came out of the temple in which he was enclosed. Then, offering kisses of peace to the brothers who were with him, he said: “Farewell, and bear pious prayers to Christ for me, a wretched man!”

Burning wholly with the ardor of martyrdom, he went willingly against the enemy with a desire and speed no slower than that of one fleeing an enemy. Advancing fearlessly through the middle of the troop, he said: “If you are looking for me, here I am.”

But one of them, whose will was always inclined to evil rather than good, replied in the name of them all:

“An empty hope of martyrdom and the noble glory of death hold you. This holiness is certainly mistaken, since it wants our sin to become its own.
