Your wish will not be fulfilled; rather, something will happen that causes greater pain. Unless this harlot is returned to us immediately, we have your brothers, and through their wives, their children and estates, we shall avenge this evil.”

While the enraged Slav was railing against the bishop, behold, a traitor corrupted by gold appeared. Selecting them secretly from the troop, he called them aside and, offering himself as their guide, revealed the house in which the woman was confined and the house’s custodian.

The custodian, seized by them and tested for a long time by threats and then by friendly speeches so that he might hand her over to them, was finally terrified by fear of death. He did not thereby betray the woman entrusted to him to her bloody enemies.

The unfortunate woman was dragged away, though she clung in vain to the altars, and was ordered to undergo the death sentence at the hand of her husband. When he, like a just man, refused to do this, she was beheaded under the sword of a lowly servant and paid the penalty for the misuse of her body with her head.

*[Apparatus: One witness reads “the clerical order” rather than “a cleric.” For “quickly,” one reads “with excessive speed.” One manuscript reads “covered” rather than “surrounded.” For the penitential fruit, variants include “through the fruits” and “for the fruits.” One witness reads “Wiollitona” for Willico. “With excessive threats” is absent from one witness; another has “insolent” with an altered initial consonant. One witness omits “divine.” For the hour, the text has “as though it were an hour of divided night.” For the hostile man’s reply, one witness reads “good things” rather than “good.” The final sentence has several corrections and variant forms, but the woman is killed by the sword of a lowly servant after her husband refuses to execute her.]*

### 20

Since the popular wickedness of this kind and of even greater kinds could not be opposed by the bishop’s teaching, the good shepherd wept when he saw that no signs of salvation were present in the diseased flock.

Wishing to close his eyes to the evils that would follow, he revisited Rome’s sweet walls in the year 995 and exchanged the pastoral reins for the ship of the monastery. The sacred communities of the monastic people rejoiced with him on his return and enjoyed his holiness both through love and through its benefit. Everyone loved him, but above all his abbot, who had placed him in charge of all the companies of brothers after himself—perhaps in 995, when Leo departed as legate for Gaul.

Content with every kind of lowliness and the lowest place, the greater he was, the lower he presented himself to everyone. The richer he was in spiritual wealth, the more he desired to be small, poor, and despised in the eyes of men (Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 7).

His abbot and brothers said of him that he was perfect to the last detail in every virtue and, apart from martyrdom, truly holy. Thus, growing from day to day ever renewed and stronger than himself, he flew to the heights of divine contemplation like a most chaste turtle-dove.

Wishing to show his servant what merit he possessed in his sight, the Lord displayed to him in a vision two orders in heaven, one clothed in purple and the other in snow-white garments. Under different appearances each possessed its singular merit and proper reward; yet for both, food and drink were the perpetual praise of the Creator.

A voice came to him saying: “Between the two you have a place, fellowship at the table, and the honor most suited to you.”

When he explained the vision to his abbot, he narrated the mysteries of his revelation concerning another person, as the most holy Paul did (1 Corinthians 12):

“I know of such a man to whom the Lord has shown these things in a vision and promises that he will bestow these very gifts.”

*[Apparatus: One witness reads “sweet guide” rather than “sweet walls”; the variants are “ship,” “leisure,” and “love” in place of the text’s “ship.” For “after himself,” a note suggests the date 995, when Leo went as legate to Gaul. One manuscript reads “covered” for “content,” another “greater” for “large.” One reads “dove” in the masculine. A fuller marginal version of the vision says: “I know of such a man to whom the Lord showed heavenly ranks, one of which blossomed with a rose-colored appearance, while the other gleamed with the whiteness of lilies; and a voice came to him saying: ‘You have a place among these orders.’” See also the discussion in the preface concerning the author of this book.]*

### 21

In the year 996, Otto III, king of the Franks, the most beautiful offspring of the beautiful emperor, traveled to Rome. Having passed beyond the years of childhood, when his beard was already flourishing with its first down, time and strength, greater than his years, demanded imperial dignity for him.

Since Rome is and is called the head of the world and mistress of cities, she alone makes kings rule; and since she shelters within her bosom the body of the prince of the apostles, she deservedly ought herself to establish the ruler of the world.

In those days her pontiff was seized by a very severe fever and left his body to the earth and his soul to heaven, each to its own beginning.

King Otto, crossing the snows of the Alps with a large force, established his royal camp near the sacred city of Ravenna. There letters arrived to meet him, sent by the Roman nobles and the senatorial order, in May 996. First, they declared that they desired his arrival with all their hearts and promised to await it with the loyalty owed to him, as though they had not seen him throughout the whole period since his father’s death. Then they announced that the death of the apostolic lord had brought no small share of troubles upon both them and him, and they asked for the king’s decision about whom they should appoint in his place.

There was also in the king’s chapel a cleric named Bruno, excellently educated in secular letters and himself descended from royal blood. He was plainly a man of great promise, though, less favorably, possessed of much of the fervor of youth. Because the king favored him, the archbishop of Mainz, Willigis, and his colleague, Bishop Hildebold of Worms, brought him to Rome after he had been chosen by the leading men. He was honorably received by the Romans, and the bishops ordained for this purpose proclaimed him bishop of the city with apostolic honor.

The king also arrived and was received magnificently according to Roman custom. Then, amid the great joy of all, he reached the summit of imperial power on 21 May. The lesser citizens rejoiced with the leading men; the troops of widows exulted with the afflicted poor, because the new emperor gives laws to the peoples, and the new pope gives laws.

*[Apparatus: “A very severe fever” is the reading of the text; variants include “the supreme pontiff,” “whose pontiff,” and “he divided” rather than “left.” For Bruno, the source identifies him as the son of Duke Otto, son of Duke Conrad and Liudgard, daughter of Otto I; it notes that Peter Damian misunderstood this passage and interpreted it as referring to Bruno, archbishop and martyr. One witness omits “of great promise.” Another editorial note suggests that the passage was written after the death of Gregory V, 5 February 999. Willigis appears as *Wilgisus* in one witness; Hildebold appears as *Hildebaldus*, *Ildebaldus*, *Udelbaldus*, *Udebaldus*, and *Adelbaldus*. The source identifies him as bishop of Worms. A variant says that Bruno was ordained bishop with the consent of the whole clergy and people, with the king’s support. One witness omits “the lesser citizens … and the widows.” Another gives the fuller reading: “With the new emperor, the new pope gives laws to the peoples.”]*
22. In those times, that most Christian emperor, who always showed the greatest zeal and diligent care for the servants of God, frequently spoke with Saint Adalbert and kept him as a close associate, willingly listening to whatever he said. Archbishop Willigisus, however, reviving his old complaint, appealed to the apostolic lord concerning the holy man’s return; he joined petition to petition and pressed by every means for him to be brought back. At the apostolic synod, moreover, reviewing the testimonies of the canons, he declared before everyone that he was asking what was just: it was a sin that, while all the churches had their husbands, Prague alone should be widowed of its shepherd. He freely requested that a favorable ear be lent to those making a just request and that her husband be restored to the widowed church. Again, from the journey on which he had set out toward his homeland, he did not cease to repeat the same request in continuous letters; nor did he desist until the apostolic lord promised that he would do what he wished.

The man of God was saddened because he was compelled to leave the monastery. For he had foreseen that no one could turn the people to whom he owed pastoral care from their evil way. Yet this greatly consoled his sad spirit: if he could not produce worthy fruit among the souls entrusted to him, he had been sent as a preacher to outsiders and to the unbaptized. Therefore, leaving the beloved monastery amid many tears of the brothers, he set out beyond the Alps with Bishop Notherius, a man of the greatest discernment [of Liège].

[Note: Col. 0879: “Who” is omitted in witness 2. “Always” is omitted in witness 1. “The greatest zeal” is omitted in witness 2. “And diligent care” is omitted in witness 1. “Willigisus” appears as *vulgi: sus* in witness 1. “Reviving” appears as “seeking” in witness 2 and “lacking” in witness 4a. The words concerning the apostolic lord and the holy man’s return are omitted in witnesses 1, 3a, 4a, and 4b. “Joins together” appears as “calls by name” in witness 2. “The canons” through “should act” are omitted in witness 4a. “Just” appears as *justa* in witness 4b; witness 3c has *justa* in a different context. “Those making a just request” appears as “those asking” in witness 2. “To lend a favorable ear” is supplied in the margin of witness 5. “Restore” appears as *praebe* (“provide”) in witness 3c. “And to the unbaptized” appears as “and to outsiders” in witness 1. “Many tears of the brothers” is omitted in witness 3a.]

23. When they had been making a journey of nearly two months, they came to Mainz (September), where the emperor, returning from the regions of Italy, had taken up residence.

[Note: Col. 0881: Witness 4a reads: “where, abandoning Italy because of the pestilential heat that was unfavorable to himself and his people, the emperor remained in the Alps.” Witness 4b has: “where, abandoning Italy because of the pestilential heat that was unfavorable to him and his people, he remained.”]

The man of God stayed with him for a considerable time, because he was extremely close to him, and by night and by day remained beside him in the imperial chamber like a most beloved chamberlain. This was not because he had been captivated by any love of the world, but because he loved him and wished to kindle him, through gentle words, to love of the heavenly homeland. For by day or by night, whenever the crowd gave him an opportunity, he approached him with holy exhortations, teaching him not to think it a great thing that he was emperor; to consider that he was a mortal man, destined to become ashes from the most beautiful body, corruption, and food for worms; to show himself a husband to widows and a father to the poor and orphans; to fear God as a just and strict judge, and to love him as the pious giver of forgiveness and fountain of mercy; to weigh carefully how narrow is the way that leads to life, and how very few are those who enter by it; to be, through humility, a companion to those who do good, but through zeal for justice to rise up against the vices of wrongdoers.

Adding many other things in this manner, he urged his dear son to despise the goods of the present life, to desire the choice of eternity, to seek what endures, and not to place confidence in temporal and passing things. Serving all who were in the royal household as though he were the servant of everyone, he handled with his hands even the most menial things belonging to them and performed all their services with complete humility. At night, when they had taken their sleep, he took care to arrange their footwear; from the doorkeeper to the prince of the royal household, he washed everyone’s boots with water and, once cleansed of their dirt, returned them to their proper place. In this way he performed many services in the chamber; the more menial each task was, the more willingly he undertook it out of humility. But the author of this service long remained unknown, until a certain Wolpharius, an imperial minister and a chamberlain dear to him, exposed the holy thief.

[Note: Col. 0881: “A considerable time” is omitted in witnesses 1, 3a, and 4b; witness 4a has “much.” “Extremely close to him” is omitted in witness 1. “And by night and by day like a most beloved chamberlain” has “most holy” in witnesses 3a and 4a, “most friendly” in witness 3c, and the words “of the chamber” are omitted in witness 4b. Witness 1 has “in the chamber” rather than “in the imperial chamber.” “Imperial” is corrected from *imperali* to *imperialis* in witness 1. Witness 1 has *camare*, corrected to *camere*; witness 3c reads “of the court or of the chamber.” The following passage through “not to possess” is omitted in witness 4a. “Love of the world” appears as “custom” in witness 1. “Not to think” is omitted in witness 1; another hand adds “if” after “think.” Witness 3c has “he would show himself” instead of the present forms “show himself … would demonstrate … would fear,” and so forth. “Raised up” appears as “elected” in witness 1. “Many” appears as “very many” in witness 2. “Service” appears in the ablative in witnesses 2, 3c, and 4a; it is omitted in 4b, and “serving all” is omitted in 3a. “Care” appears as “dear” in witness 1. The passage concerning the servant’s author has variants: witness 1 reads “Wolpharius”; witness 4a, “Woltharius the royal,” and also “the expression of a certain Wolpharius, a noble fosterling of good character”; witness 4b reads “the report of a certain Wolpharius of good character.”]

24. There too, one night, he saw a dream of the following kind. He imagined that he was approaching his brother’s estate, and that in the middle of the estate stood a house whose construction was pleasing to behold, with walls and roofs of snowy whiteness. Inside were two beds, one assigned to him and the other to his brother; each, as was fitting, bore great honor. But his own little bed far surpassed the other in splendor: it was entirely covered with purple brilliance and silken ornaments, while at its head it was most beautifully crowned with a linen cloth of golden thread.

Above, at the head, the following was written in letters of gold:

> This excellent gift is given to you by the daughter, the bride.

[Note: Col. 0881: “This gift” appears in witness 1, with the same hand glossing *auctentum* (“authentic”) as “authorial, excellent.” “Bride” appears as “being betrothed” in witness 3a. Witness 3c has “gives.” Witness 2 reads: “The bride, the king’s daughter, gives you royal gifts”; witness 4b: “The king’s daughter gives you.” The remainder of the inscription through “you have deigned” is omitted in witness 4a.]

When he explained the sequence of the vision while recounting it to certain people, they said: “See, for with Christ the Lord’s support you will be a martyr. The king’s daughter who gives you royal gifts is the Lady of Heaven, the most holy Virgin Mary.”

Hearing this, he became exceedingly joyful; and entering the chamber of his heart, he gave thanks to the Holy of Holies, the Lord of the angels, and to almighty Christ. Then he worshiped the mother of graces, who sits nearest the king’s throne, with bowed neck and the rejoicing exultation of his spirit:

“Glory to you,” he said, “Virgin, star of the sea, who, as a gracious lady, have deigned to look upon me, your most humble servant.”

[Note: Col. 0881: “Who sits” appears as “and sits” in witness 1. “Virgin” is expanded to “Virgin Mary” in witness 5. “Almighty” appears in the feminine form in witness 1.]

25. At this same time he visited Tours, seeking the assistance of the holy old man Martin. Nor did he pass by Fleury, which had merited to place in its bosom the most blessed body of our confessor and father Benedict. There, too, the sight of the blind, the steps of the lame, the hearing of the deaf, and many thousands of heavenly miracles testify who he is before the Lord.

[Note: Col. 0881: “Tours” appears as “of the novices” in witness 2. “Which” has the form “who” in witnesses 2, 3a, 3c, and 4b. “Our confessor” and “father” are omitted in witness 3c. “Bosom” appears as “flock” in witnesses 3a and 4b. The identification of who Benedict is before the Lord is uncertain: witness 1 has “the Lord” in a scraped-out place; the phrase is omitted in witnesses 3a and 4b; witness 3c has “with the Lord’s permission.” An editorial note explains: “That is, before the Lord, whose authority Benedict possesses before the Lord.” “The sacred conversations of the two beloved fathers” appears as “their sacred and familiar conversations” in witness 2.]

Fed by the sacred conversations of these two most beloved fathers, he returned with a joyful spirit to the imperial residence. There, bringing to light what was on his mind and what he wished to do with God’s will, he began to have a final private conversation with the beloved Caesar. When the conversation was ended, they exchanged kisses of peace and, not without sorrow, separated in an embrace, never again to be joined together.

The holy man, therefore, commending his dear life most earnestly to his beloved Jesus, began, in accordance with the wish of his archbishop, to proceed to the apostate people. He himself understood that they would not obey his counsel, but, lest he be disobedient, he preferred to fulfill the command given to him. This also gave his spirit great hope, because, if not among his own children, he could gather the profits of souls among outsiders and barbarians. For there were many nations round about through which he could either obtain martyrdom for himself or confer upon them the grace of baptism.

But this most criminal people, to whom he was compelled to return, committed a great outrage in hatred of his name. They struck down their own parents, noble and illustrious men, with a wretched wound; they condemned brothers and the sons of brothers—males together with innocent women—to the most savage death; and, laying waste their cities with fire and sword, they reduced all their goods to captivity.

One of his brothers, named Sobiebor, was away on the emperor’s expedition with Bolizlavo, duke of the Palanians, while these evils were being committed at home. But that duke, out of love for the holy brother, comforted him with great promises and friendly resources.

[Note: Col. 0883: “The apostate people” has a marginal gloss, “the treacherous people,” in witness 1. “To proceed” is omitted in witness 1; witnesses 4a and 4b have a greatly shortened version ending “and into Sclavonia.” “If not among his own children” is omitted in witness 1. “Could confer the grace of baptism” appears as “the grace could be conferred” in witnesses 3a and 5 and “baptism could be conferred” in witness 4b. “His parents” and the following words have variants in the witnesses. The name of the brother is given as “Sobiebor” in a note at Col. 0884D. “Bolizlavo” appears as *bolezawo* in witness 2, *bolezlao* in 3a, *boleslavo* in 3c, *bolisclavum* in 4a, and *boleslao* in 4b. “Of the Palanians” appears as *palaniorum* in witnesses 1 and 4a; witness 5 corrects it to *pulaniorum*; the other witnesses have *poloniorum*, *bolaniorum*, or *polaniorum*. “Outside” is omitted in witness 3a. “Their goods” appears as “their names” in witness 3a. Col. 0883D notes “Lubic”; compare the *Prague Annals*. Cosmas, in a poem in Dobner II, p. 40, calls it Kurim, today Kaurzim.]

26. Therefore, thinking that access to them had been closed to him because of these crimes, that most holy hero did not wish his journey to have been in vain. Instead, he turned to the aforementioned duke (997), since the duke was his very good friend, and through his messengers he was able to find out whether they would receive him.

When this had been done, they sent back to him, in great indignation, words full of anger and fury, saying:

“We are sinners, a people of iniquity, a stiff-necked nation; you are holy, a friend of God, a true Israelite, and all is well with you before the Lord. Such a great and worthy man cannot endure the dwellings and companionship of the wicked. Yet whence does this new kind of holiness arise, that an episcopus should seek those so often rejected and so often cast off—not merely by one mind but by minds of many kinds? We recognize,” they repeated, “what false sound is ringing beneath the appearance of piety in this holiness. We do not want him; for if he comes, he will not come for our salvation, but to punish the evils and injuries that we have inflicted upon his brothers and in which we delight. There is no one who will receive him—not one.”

[Note: Col. 0883: “Access” appears as “the journey” in witness 3a. “The most holy hero” is omitted in witness 5. Witness 4b reads, “if the Bohemians would receive him”; witness 3a omits “if they would receive him,” while witness 5 has “the people of Prague.” “They sent back to him” appears as “they sent back words full of anger” in witness 2. *Iras* is read as “to go out” in witness 2. “Stiff-necked” appears as “harsh-necked” in witnesses 1 and 4a. “A new kind of holiness arises” is omitted in witness 3a; witnesses 4a and 4b have “a new holiness arises.” “Minds” is corrected to “nations” in witness 1; witness 3c has “nations.” “We recognize” was written twice in witnesses 3a, 3c, and 4a; witness 4b has the abbreviation *cogn.*, expanded as *agn.* “What is falsely ringing” is printed in the source as “what is corruptly sounding.” Witness 4b adds after “There is no one who will receive him” a long supplement: “For if he comes to us, he does not come for our salvation but in order to punish us for the evils and injuries we have inflicted on his brothers; and because we have done this, we rejoice. There is no one who will receive him, not one.”]

Hearing this and similar words, the blessed bishop overflowed with such laughter of joy that he almost exceeded the bounds of his customary severity.

“You have broken my bonds,” he said. “To you I offer glory and a sacrifice of praise, because their rejection has freed me from the cords and bonds of pastoral care that were around my neck. Today, O good Jesus, I confess that I am wholly yours; to you, ruler of eternal power, be praise, honor, and glory. You have not willed those who do not will you and who, in their desire, turn away from the way of truth.”

[Note: Col. 0883: “The rejected” is omitted in witness 2. “Desire” appears as “desires” in witness 3a; witnesses 3c and 4b have “in their own things.” Witness 4b expands “I said” as “I said, Lord.” “I will sacrifice” appears instead of “I offer” in witnesses 4a and 5.]

27. From there he began sharpening and preparing the sword of preaching against the savage barbarism and profane idolaters. He began to deliberate in his mind with whom he ought first to fight and with whom afterward: whether he should go to the Liuticians, who feed upon the spoils of Christians and the losses of wretched people, or to the borders of the Prussians, whose god is their belly (Philippians 3:19), and whose avarice is joined with death.

At last, the better judgment prevailed over his wavering mind: since this region was nearer and known to the aforementioned duke, he would go to subdue the gods and idols of Prussia. When the duke learned his intention, he gave him a ship and armed it for the security of the journey with thirty soldiers.

[Note: Col. 0883: Witness 2 adds “and afterward” after “with whom”; the words “with whom afterward” are omitted in witness 3c. The readings of “Prussians” are stable in witnesses 3c, 4a, and 4b. “Whose avarice is joined with death” appears as “whose avarice is death” in witness 3a. The duke-related note states that “duke of Prussia” is probably an insertion by the Polish historian Bzovius, who connects it here and above with the duke of Prussia.]

He first went to the city of Gyddanyze [Danzig], whose very broad territories, dividing the duke’s realms, touch the boundaries of the sea. There, with divine mercy prospering his arrival, many throngs of people were baptized. There, celebrating the solemn rites of Mass, he offered Christ to the Father, to whom, after not many days, he was himself to be offered as a victim. Whatever of it remained, which he and the newly baptized had received in communion, he ordered to be collected and, wrapped in the purest cloth, kept it with him to be carried as provisions for the journey.

[Note: Col. 0883: The city’s name appears as *danyzc* in a gloss in witness 1, *gidanie* in 3a, *gidanic* in 3c, *gnesdon* in 4a, *gedanum* in 4b, and *gyddanyze* in 5. An editorial note identifies it as Danzig. “Dividing” appears as “pressing down” in witness 3c. “Of it” appears as “of God” in witness 3a. “Known” appears as “familiar” in witness 1. “They kept it” appears as “they kept” in witness 4b, “they preserved” in witnesses 2, 3a, and 3c, and “to be preserved” in witness 5. “The days” is omitted in witnesses 2 and 4b. “For the victim” appears as “instead of the victim” in witness 1; “to him” and the following words are omitted in witness 2.]

28. On the following day, after bidding farewell to everyone, he was placed in the vessel and went out onto the sea, disappearing from their eyes, never afterward to be seen by them. From there, after making the voyage with the swiftest speed, he left the seashore after a few days, and the ship returned with its armed guard.

[Note: Col. 0885: Witness 1 has “he entered” instead of “they entered.”]

But he, giving thanks to the sailors and to the Lord of the sailors for the benefits they had bestowed, remained there with two brothers. One was the priest Benedictus; the other was his beloved companion from childhood, Brother Gaudentius. Then, preaching Christ with great confidence, they entered a small island which, encircled by a winding river, appeared in the form of a circle to those approaching it.

[Note: Col. 0885D: The river seems to be the Pregel; compare Cl. Voigt, *Geschichte Preussens* I, p. 266 ff.]

The inhabitants of the place came and drove them away with blows. One of them seized an oar from the boat, approached the bishop, and, because he had perhaps been chanting psalms from a book, struck him a great blow between the shoulders. The codex flew from his hands in different directions, and he himself, with head and limbs outstretched, lay prostrate on the ground. But what the pious mind was doing within the body afflicted outwardly, the laughter of his heart soon revealed through the organ of his voice.

“Thanks be to you, Lord,” he said, “because, even if there will be no more, at least I have deserved to receive one blow for my Crucified One.”

[Note: Col. 0885: “The pious mind” appears as “his mind” in witness 2. “Laughter” is omitted in witness 2. “Pious” is corrected from “divine” in witness 1; witness 5 has “divine.” “The Lord” is abbreviated in the source.]

Crossing to the other side of the river [into Samland, today Samland], he stayed there on Saturday (April 17). When evening came, the lord of the village led the divine hero Adalbert across into the village. The sluggish crowd gathered from every side, and they waited with furious voices and dog-like snarling to see what they would do with him.

Then Saint Adalbert was questioned about who he was, where he came from, and for what reason he had come there. He answered them in a gentle voice:

“By birth I am a Slav, by name Adalbert; by profession a monk; formerly a bishop in rank; now your apostle in office. The purpose of our journey is your salvation: that, abandoning deaf and dumb images, you may recognize your Creator, who alone exists and besides whom there is no other god; and that, believing in his name, you may have life and may deserve to receive the rewards of heavenly joy in the unfading courts.”

Thus spoke Saint Adalbert. But they had long been angry, and, shouting blasphemous words against him, they threatened him with death. Immediately they struck the ground with their staffs, placed clubs against his head, and gnashed their teeth fiercely at him:

“Count it a great thing that you have come this far without punishment. Just as a speedy return gives hope of life, so a short delay will bring you the loss of your life. For us and for this entire kingdom, whose jaws we are, one common law and one way of life rule. But you, who belong to another and unknown law, if you do not leave tonight, will be beheaded tomorrow.”

[Note: Col. 0885: “Saint” appears as “the Bohemian” in witness 3c. “Apostle” is abbreviated in witness 1, with another hand adding *apostolicus*. “What they would do” appears as “what he would do” in witness 2. The words concerning what he would do are omitted in witnesses 3a and 4a. “The crowd” is omitted in witnesses 1, 2, and 5. “Blasphemous” appears in witnesses 2, 3a, 3c, 4a, 4b, and 5; witness 1 has “blasphemy.” “This entire kingdom” appears as “this whole kingdom” in witness 3a. An eleventh-century gloss renders “you will be beheaded” in Old High German as *gihafdade werthath*.]

That very night they were put into a little boat and, taken back, remained for five days in a certain village [opposite the city of Pillau].

29. While these things were happening in that region, behold, in the monastery where he had been raised, the Lord showed the following to a certain convert, John Canaparius, in a vision. From the highest heaven, as though flying, two linen sheets came downward to the earth, white as snow and clean, without any filth or stain. Each lifted from the earth its own burden, namely one man; both crossed the clouds and golden stars at the most fortunate speed.

[Note: Col. 0885: The name appears as *sadulerie* in a gloss in witness 1, *campanario* in witness 3c, and *Canaparius* in witness 5. “Two” is omitted in witnesses 1 and 4b. “Their burdens” appears as “so” in witness 4a; the initial letter of “burdens” is erased in witness 1, while the remaining witnesses read “burdens.” “At the most fortunate speed” appears in witnesses 1, 3a, 3c, 4a, 4b, and 5; witness 2 has “at the swiftest speed.” “Crossed the stars” appears as “passed through” in witness 2 and “crossed” in witnesses 3a, 3c, and 4b. The name of one of them is extremely obscure in the manuscript; witness 4a has *onicrotem*, a very modest reading if one supposes that John himself wrote it. The passage concerning the other through “prepared” is omitted in witnesses 1 and 5.]

The name of one of them is known to scarcely anyone except the man who saw these things. The other was, as he himself still remembers today, the lord Adalbert, for whom the angelic minister had prepared banquets at the heavenly table.

But it is unknown what Father Nilus saw concerning him. In a sweet letter he addressed the same man as follows:

“Know, dearest son, that our friend Adalbert walks with the Holy Spirit and will end his present life with a most blessed death.”

Likewise, the night’s rest told Brother Gaudentius, through a woven maze of images, what was going to happen in reality. When he awoke, he asked his beloved father whether he wished to hear his dream.

He answered: “Tell me, if you have something to tell.”

“I saw,” he said, “in the middle of the altar a golden chalice, half-filled with wine, and no one was guarding it. Since I wished to drink the unmixed wine, the minister of the altar opposed me and, as though with some commanding authority, contradicted my bold attempt, because he did not wish to grant this permission either to me or to any human being, since it had been reserved for you as mystical nourishment for tomorrow.”

As he was speaking, sleep fled from his eyes, and a great stupor seized his trembling limbs.

“May God,” he said, “prosper this vision, son! No one ought to put faith in a deceptive dream.”

[Note: Col. 0885: “Dream” appears as “sleep” in witnesses 2 and 3a. “Brother” appears as “father” in witness 5. “What was going to happen in reality” appears as “what was going to happen” in witnesses 2 and 5.]

30. When the purple day was already rising, they set out on their journey (April 23), shortening the road for themselves with a Davidic hymn and continually calling upon Christ, the joy of sweet life. Then, leaving behind the groves and savage thickets, they came, as the sun rose toward midday, to open country [the sacred grove of the Prussians].

[Note: Col. 0885: “Leaving behind the groves” appears in the corrupt reading of witness 1 as “no delay.” Col. 0886D identifies the place as the sacred grove of the Prussians; see Voigt, p. 660.]

There, while Brother Gaudentius celebrated Mass, that holy monk received communion. After the sacred communion he took a little food to ease the labor of the journey. After reciting the verse and the following psalm, he rose from the grassy turf and advanced the distance of a stone’s throw or an arrow’s flight; then he sat down in that place.

[Note: Col. 0887B: The place was between Pillau and Fischhausen; see Voigt, p. 270, who conjectures that the saint was killed because he entered the sacred forest.]

There sleep seized him; and because he was exhausted by the long journey, savage rest poured him fully into slumber. At last, while all were resting, pagan fury arrived: they rushed upon them with great force and put them all in bonds.

Saint Adalbert, standing opposite Gaudentius and the other bound brother, said:

“Brothers, do not grieve! You know that we suffer these things for the name of the Lord, whose power is beyond all powers, whose beauty is above all beauties, whose strength is indescribable, and whose compassion is unique. What is stronger, what is more beautiful than to pour out life for the sweetest Jesus?”

[Note: Col. 0887: “There sleep seized him” appears in witnesses 3a, 3c, 4a, and 4b. “Exhausted by the long journey” appears as “exhausted by the labor” in witness 3c and “exhausted by the journey” in witness 5. “Poured him fully into slumber” appears as “bathed him in sleep” in witnesses 3a, 3c, 4a, and 4b. “Sicco” has a gloss in witness 1 identifying it as a proper name; witnesses 3a and 3c read “Siggo,” witness 2 has *ignens* (“fiery”), and witness 4b has “a certain old man.” Witness 4a instead reads: “What ignoble color has suddenly changed your cheeks? You know …”]

From the raging band sprang the fiery man Sicco, and, hurling a huge spear with all his strength, pierced the depths of his heart. He himself, a priest of idols and leader of the sworn band, inflicted the first wounds as though by right. Then all rushed together, multiplying the wounds, and satisfied their anger. A red stream flowed from its rich source, and, when the spear was withdrawn, seven great wounds lay open. He stood praying to heaven with eyes and hands raised.

He stretched out his hands in the form of a cross and poured forth humble prayers to the Lord for his own salvation and that of his persecutors, crying:

“Lord God almighty, graciously hear my prayer, and do not regard the crimes that these men have committed against me, unworthy as I am, for your holy name; for they do not know what they are doing. Instead, open the door of their hearts, so that they may recognize and understand you as the maker of all things and return to you. Let my passion not be fruitless, either for these men or for others who have remembered me. Grant, I beg you, rest and peace to all in the present age, and deign to bestow eternal life in the age to come, Savior of the world, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit governs all things forever and ever. Amen.”

When he had completed the prayer, his head was cut off, and thus his noble body occupied the earth in a blessed fall. So the holy soul departed to Christ.

The disciples seized their master’s blood-spattered hair shirt and mourned bitterly, saying:

“Alas, our consolation and the hope of our joy! Why do you not console us as we weep?”

But when the corpse of the most holy martyr and pontiff Adalbert fell, savage barbarism, armed on every side, rushed together; and, while its fury was not yet spent, they removed the head of the most holy martyr from his body and tore apart his bloodless limbs. Leaving the body in that place, they fixed the head upon a stake; then, praising their crimes with joyful shouts, each returned to his own dwelling.

[Note: Witness 4b preserves the following expanded version: “His heart was pierced. When Saint Adalbert saw the old man rushing upon him, he said in a gentle voice: ‘What do you want, father? Why do you stain your hands with innocent blood and willingly hand them over, bloodstained, to the devil?’ He then raised his eyes and hands to heaven and said: ‘Lord, help me.’ When his bonds were loosened, he stretched out his hands in the form of a cross and, pouring forth humble prayers for his own salvation and that of his persecutors, said: ‘Lord God almighty, graciously hear my prayer, and do not regard the crimes they have committed against me, unworthy as I am, for your holy name; for they do not know what they are doing. Open the door of their hearts, so that they may recognize and understand you as the creator of all and return to you. Let my passion not be fruitless, either for these men or for others who have remembered me. Grant all people rest and peace in the present age and deign to forgive them eternal life in the future, Savior of the world, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit governs all things forever and ever. Amen.’ When he had completed the prayer, his head was cut off; thus his noble body occupied the earth in a blessed fall. So the holy soul migrated to Christ. The disciples, however, seizing their master’s blood-spattered hair shirt, mourned bitterly, saying: ‘Alas, our consolation and the hope of our joy! Why do you not console us as we weep?’ But when the corpse of the most holy martyr and pontiff Adalbert fell, savage barbarism, armed on every side, rushed together; and, while its fury was not yet spent, they fixed the head of the most holy martyr upon a stake, while they left the body to be torn by beasts. Then, praising their crimes with joyful shouts, each returned to his own dwelling. But to show what merit so great a martyr possessed, almighty God had his body guarded for thirty days by an eagle commanded by the Lord, so that no beast and no bird could approach it. The disciples saw that eagle guarding it by divine judgment. Later, when the unbelieving crowd was still unsated with human blood, they took up his most wretchedly mangled body and cast it into the sea. Then, by the sign of a radiant column stretching from above his body up to heaven, his body was revealed to the disciples. They came with many Christians, removed his body, joined the head to the body, and buried him honorably; they also built a worthy church in his name, where his merits and virtues abound to this day. The most blessed martyr and pontiff of Christ, Adalbert, suffered on the eighth day before the Kalends of May, namely so that on the day on which the Lord Jesus Christ suffered for humanity, he too might suffer for his name, with the help of him to whom be honor with the eternal Father and the Holy Spirit, now and through endless ages of ages. Amen.” The manuscript of Utrecht likewise stated that the body was guarded by an eagle for three days, according to Henschenius, *Acta Sanctorum*, p. 187.]

The red stream burst from its rich vein, and, when the spear was pulled out, seven huge wounds lay open. With his bonds loosed, he stretched out his hands in the form of a cross and, humbly pouring out prayers to the Lord for his own salvation and that of his persecutors, cried aloud. Thus that holy soul flew from its prison; thus the noble body, extended in the shape of a cross, took possession of the earth; thus, pouring out its life with much blood, he at last enjoyed Christ, ever most dear, in the blessed dwellings. O holy and most blessed man, in whose face was angelic brightness and in whose heart Christ always dwelt! O loving man, worthy of every honor, who embraced then with hands and whole body the cross which he had always carried willingly in mind and spirit!

Armed savage barbarism rushed together from every side; its fury not yet satisfied, they removed the noble head from the body and separated the bloodless limbs. They left the body there, set the head on a stake, and, acclaiming their crimes with joyful shouting, each returned to his own home.

Saint and most glorious martyr of Christ Adalbert suffered on the ninth day before the Kalends of May [April 23], while Otto III, the pious and renowned Caesar, was emperor and lord of the realm, on a Friday. He suffered on the same day on which the Lord Jesus Christ suffered for humanity, so that this man might suffer for his God. To him belong mercy forever, honor, praise, and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

[Note: Col. 0887: Witness 1 has “April” instead of “May.” A note at Col. 0888B observes that in the year 997 April 23 fell on a Friday. “Lord of the realm” appears as “lord of kings” in witness 5. “And renowned” is omitted in witness 1. “To whom” appears as “whose” in witnesses 2, 3a, and 5. “Praise” is omitted in witness 1. Witness 5 adds: “Amen. Here ends the Passion and Life of Saint Adalbert, bishop of the city of Prague.” Col. 0888B also notes the chapel constructed at the site of the martyrdom in 1422–1424 and destroyed in 1669; see Voigt, pp. 663 ff.]

# MIRACLES OF SAINT ADALBERT THE MARTYR

[Col. 0889]

1. After his death, divine wonders did not cease, even among foreign peoples. For when his finger fell into the water and was swallowed by a fish that seized it, it shone from the fish’s belly amid the waves like a burning candle, visible to everyone. Astonished by this miracle, the fishermen, eager to catch it with every effort, followed the fish wherever it turned. Before long they caught the fish, cut it open, and drew from its belly the sacred finger of the holy pontiff, flaming like a burning candle.

[Note: Col. 0889: Compare the books of the Life of Saint Adalbert in Dobner, *Monumenta Bohemiae*, II, pp. 56, 59, and the fourteenth-century *Chronicle of Bohemia* in Mencken, *Scriptores rerum Saxonicarum*, III, p. 1647. “Astonished” appears as “struck” in witness 3c.]

2. At about the same time, a certain noble Prussian from among the Pomeranians came to the land of Sambia on some business, that is, to a particular region of Prussia, in which the blessed martyr Adalbert had completed his martyrdom among the inhabitants. When he learned from those who told him that an unknown man, whose speech they did not understand, had been killed among them, he deliberately came to the place to identify the dead man—without doubt moved by the Spirit of God.

When he found the sacred head, he heard it speak to him and say:

“Take me and carry me to Poland, to the city called Gnesen. If, preserving yourself in purity, you carry me all the way there, you and your descendants will be exalted forever above all who dwell in these lands, with honor and riches. But if you defile your way, your last generation will neither prosper for the better nor decline for the worse, but will remain in a middling condition comparable to your equals.”

Stunned by these words, the gentile took the head, placed it in a vessel, and set out toward Poland. But when he had reached his own land near his house, thoughts of seeing his children and his wives—of whom he had two—began to trouble his mind. Overcome by this affection, he hid the venerable head with its vessel in a hollow oak and went home to his family, intending to return as quickly as possible.

When at last he returned, having become a transgressor of the condition of purity, he sought the sacred head but did not find it in the place where he had deposited it. The family of the man mentioned above, as those descended from it themselves also acknowledge, has remained to this day in the same condition through the success of temporal things, just as had long before been declared by that divine oracle.

In the place where the gentile had deposited the martyr’s head, there was once a church consecrated in honor of that martyr; the church and the place itself were held in reverence, and beautiful miracles are reported to have occurred there.

[Note: Col. 0889: “Particular” appears as “special” in witness 3c. “There” appears as “it” in witness 3c. “The last generation” is omitted in witnesses 1 and 5. The city is called *Gnesen* in the source.]

3. It is also read that blessed Adalbert preached Christ in Hungary: first through his messengers, and then in person, converting an innumerable people to the faith by the word of preaching and by many miracles.

It happened that he reached the place where the principal seat of the entire region is located. There was a certain famous idol, more renowned than the others, from which demons frequently used to give manifest responses. For this reason, at appointed times, crowds from the neighboring cities gathered to behold this spectacle and worship it.

When a very great multitude of people surrounded the idol, the holy pontiff, strong in faith and ready to surrender his life to death for Christ, approached boldly. In the sight of everyone, with a torch kindled before the idol’s priests, while all were struck down and astonished by the power of God, he burned the idol completely; no one contradicted him, so great was the authority of his action.

## Supplementary complete apparatus for chapters 22–30

The following register retains readings that cannot be represented by English wording alone; italic source forms are given with their meaning or function.

**22–23.** In 22, witness 2 omits “to whom,” and witness 1 omits “always”; witness 2 omits “the greatest zeal,” and 1 “and diligent care.” Witness 1 has *vulgi: sus* for *Willigisus*; 2 has *quaerens* (“seeking”) and 4a *carens* (“lacking”) for *canens* (“rehearsing/reviving”). Witnesses 1, 3a, 4a and 4b omit the words “the apostolic lord concerning the holy man’s return.” Witness 2 has *cognominat* (“names/calls”) for *congeminat* (“doubles, joins together”). Witness 4a omits the passage from “the testimonies of the canons” through “should act.” Witness 3c reads *justa inquiebat ...* and 4b *justa* for *juste* (“justly”); 2 has *justa petentibus* (“those asking just things”). Witness 5 supplies *accommodare* (“to lend”) in the margin; 3c has *praebe* (“provide”) for *praebere* (“to restore/provide”). Witness 2 omits *cui* (“to whom”); 1 has *et extraneis et* (“and to outsiders and”) for “to outsiders and the unbaptized”; 3a omits “with many tears of the brothers.” In 23, 4a reads: “where, leaving Italy because of the pestilential heat adverse to him and his people, the emperor stayed in the Alps”; 4b has the same sense with “he stayed.” Witnesses 1, 3a and 4b omit “for a considerable time,” while 4a has *multum* (“much”). Witness 1 omits “very close to him” and the words “and by night and day ... chamberlain”; 3a and 4a have *sanctissimus* (“most holy”), 3c *amicissimus* (“most friendly”), and 4b omits “by day”; 1 reads *cubiculo* (“in the chamber”). Its *imperali* is corrected to *imperialis*; *camare* to *camere*; 3c reads *curti vel camerae* (“of the court or chamber”). Witness 4a omits the following passage through “not to have.” Witness 1 has *more* (“custom”) for *amore* (“love”), omits *ne* (“not”), and adds *si* (“if”) in another hand; 3c makes the exhortatory verbs conditional (*exhiberet, monstraret, timeret*, “he should show, demonstrate, fear”). Witness 1 has *electus* (“chosen”) for *erectus* (“roused”); 2 *plurima* (“very many”) for *plura*. Witnesses 2, 3c, 4a have ablative *servitute* for *servitutem*; 4b omits it and 3a omits “serving all.” Witness 1 has *carum* (“dear”) for *cura* (“care”), and omits “cleansed of dirt.” Witness 2 has *humilitate servat et ministrat* (“he keeps and serves with humility”). For Wolpharius: 1 has *Volpharius*; 4a *Woltharius regius* (“royal Woltharius”) and “the statement of a certain Wolpharius, a noble fosterling of good character”; 4b “the report of a certain man of good character”; 2 omits “and a chamberlain dear to him.”

**24–25.** Witness 2 reads *currem* for *curtem* (“estate/court”). Witnesses 4a and 4b read “and a pillow covered with a golden cloth” for the gold-thread linen at the bed’s head, and 4a omits the rest of the inscription through “you have deigned.” Witness 1 preserves *auctentum* and glosses it “authorial, excellent”; 3a has *sponsatur* (“is betrothed”), 3c *donat* (“gives”), 2 “The king’s daughter, the bride, gives you this excellent gift,” and 4b “The king’s daughter gives you this excellent gift.” Witness 2 has *fec.* for “with Christ’s help”; 3a, 4b and 5 read feminine *haec* (“this [woman]”), while 3c omits it. Witness 1 has feminine *omnipotente*; it reads *sed et* (“but also sits”) for “who sits”; 5 expands “Virgin” to “Virgin Mary.” In 25, 2 has *tyronum* for Tours and *hec* for “nor”; 2, 3a, 3c, 4b read feminine *quae* for *qui*; 3c omits “our” and “father”; 3a and 4b have *grege* (“flock”) for *gremio* (“bosom”). Witness 1 has *dominus* (“Lord”) in an erased place; 3a and 4b omit “before the Lord,” and 3c reads *Domino concedente* (“with the Lord granting”). The editorial explanation is: “that is, before the Lord, of whose authority Benedict possesses standing before the Lord.” Witness 3a omits “hearing of the deaf”; 2 has *sacris et familiaribus confabulationibus* (“sacred and familiar conversations”). Witness 2 omits “began,” 3a has *familiarem et extremum* (“familiar and final”), 3c omits “kisses of peace,” and 2 has *saciandos* for “to be joined.” Witness 1 glosses *placitum* as “decree” and *apostatricem* as “treacherous”; it omits “people.” Witnesses 4a/4b abbreviate the account to “he proceeded ... into Sclavonia.” Witness 1 omits “if not among children”; 3a/5 read “the grace may be conferred,” and 4b “baptism may be conferred.” The geographical note reads: “Lubic; see the Prague Annals. Cosmas, in a poem in Dobner II, p. 40, calls it Kurim, today Kaurzim.” The brother is *Sobiebor* (Col. 0884D). Variants are *bolezawo* 2, *bolezlao* 3a, *boleslavo* 3c, *bolisclavum* 4a, *boleslao* 4b; for Palanians: *palaniorum* 1/4a, corrected in 5 to *pulaniorum*, *poloniorum* 2, *bolaniorum* 3a, *polaniorum* 3c, *polonorum* 4b. Witness 3a omits “outside”; it has *nomina* (“names”) for *bona* (“goods”), and 3c *de amissis* (“about losses”) for *amicis* (“friendly”).

**26–28.** In 26, 3a has *iter* (“journey”) for “access,” and 5 omits “most holy.” Witness 4b reads “if the Bohemians would receive him”; 3a omits *se*, and 5 has “the people of Prague.” Witness 2 has *exire* (“to go out”) for *irae* (“of anger”); 1/4a *dire cervicis* (“harsh-necked”); 3a omits “a new kind,” while 4a/4b read “a new holiness arises.” Witness 1 corrects *mentium* (“minds”) to *gentium* (“nations”), as does 3c. Witnesses 3a, 3c, 4a write *agnoscimus* twice, and 4b abbreviates it *cogn.* for *agn.*; 4b/5 read *veniet* (“will come”) for *venit* (“comes”). Witness 2/3a omit “which,” and witness 1 glosses *juvat* as “it delights.” Witnesses 3a/3c read *illusus* (“mocked”) for “blessed”; 2 *bene* for *pene*; 4b expands “I said, Lord”; 4a/5 have *sacrificabo* (“I shall sacrifice”) for *immolo* (“I offer”). Witness 2 omits “cords,” 3a *desideria*, and 3c/4b *in propria* (“in their own things”) for “in desire.” In 27, 3a/4b have *idololatras*, 3c *idololatrias*; 2 adds “and afterwards,” 3c omits it. Prussian forms: *prusorum* 3c, *prussorum* 4a/4b; the printed note says these are stable. 3a reads “whose avarice is death.” *Pruziae* occurs in 1/3a. The note on “duke of Prussia” says the Polish historian Bzovius is to be considered the inserter who attached the phrase here and above to the duke. City forms are *danyzc* (gloss 1), *gidanie* 3a, *gidanic* 3c, *gnesdon* 4a, *gedanum* 4b, *gyddanyze* 5; Col. 0884D identifies Danzig. Witness 3c has *deprimentem* (“pressing down”) for *dirimentem* (“dividing”); 2/4b omit “those days”; 1 corrects *per* to *pro*, 2 omits “as a victim,” 3a *Deo* (“God”) for *eo* (“it”), 1 *noti* (“known”) for *novi* (“newly”), and the verb has *servavit* 2/3a/3c, *servat* 4b, *servari* 5. In 28, 1 has singular *intravit*; the island is encircled by the Pregel, apparently, “cf. C. Voigt, *History of Prussia* I, p. 266 ff.” Witness 2 omits the expulsion, 1 spells *arepto*, 1 corrects *pia* from an earlier form, 5 has *diva* (“divine”), 2 adds “his mind,” and 2 omits “at once.” The place beyond the river is Sambia, today Samland. 2 has *domnum* for *dominus*, omits *heroa*; 4a/4b have *quid primas de* for “what he would do”; 2 future *acturum*; 1 corrects *furibunda* to *furibundo*, and 1/2/5 omit “voice.” The saint’s voice is corrected from *mitti* to *miti*; 3c calls him Bohemian; 1’s *aplus* is supplied in another hand as *apostolicus*. The crowd’s *blasphema* replaces *blasphemiae* in 2, 3a, 3c, 4a, 4b, 5; 2/3a/3c omit “and”; 3a has *toti* for *toto*. Witness 1 preserves the eleventh-century German gloss *gihafdade werthath* for “you will be beheaded.” Witness 1 omits “into”; 2/3a have *navicule*; Col. 0886D says: “opposite the city of Pillau.”

**29–30.** In 29, 1 glosses Canaparius as *sadulerie*, while 3c/5 have *campanario*. Witnesses 1/4b omit “two,” 4a has *honera* (with *h* erased in 1; the others *onera*) for “burdens”; 2 has *velocissimo* (“swiftest”) for *felicissimo* (“most fortunate”), *transeunt* for “cross,” and 3a/3c/4b *transnant*; 4a’s obscure *onicrotem* is noted as a very modest reading if John himself wrote it. Witnesses 1/5 omit “the other ... prepared,” 3a/4b omit “he,” 3a has *angelus*, and 4b “John” for “the man.” Witness 2/5 have *opera*, 1 *quies*, 2/3a *somnum*, and 5 *fratrem*. Witness 2 omits “to me”; 3a *qui* for *quia*. In 30, 1/4b have *exurgente*, 1 *adbreviant*; the corrupt 1 reading is *ne mora* (“no delay”) for “groves.” Col. 0886D: “the sacred wood of the Prussians; see Voigt, p. 660.” Witness 1 corrects *aleu.* to *alleu.*; 2 has *lapis*; Col. 0887B: “between Pillau and Fischhausen; see Voigt p. 270, who conjectures that the saint was killed for entering the sacred forest; p. 660 ff.” Witnesses 3a/3c/4a/4b add *tum* (“then”); 3c/5 read “wearied by labor,” and 3a/3c/4a/4b *perfudit* (“bathed”) for *profudit* (“poured”). Witness 4a adds: “What ignoble color suddenly changed your cheeks? You know ...”; 3a reads *dulce est* (“it is sweet”). Witness 1 has *foribundo*, glosses *igneus* “angry,” and calls Sicco a proper name; 3a/3c *Siggo*, 2 *ignens*, 4b “a certain old man.” Witnesses 1/3c/4b spell *exaturant*. The full long 4b continuation and the Utrecht manuscript’s “three days” are translated above; the final local note is: “on the chapel built at the place of martyrdom in 1422–1424 and destroyed in 1669, see Voigt, p. 663 ff.”

**Explicit glosses for the remaining forms.** In the Eucharist sentence, *servavit* means “kept,” *servat* “keeps,” and *servari* “to be kept.” In the village episode *domnum* is the accusative “the lord,” where *dominus* is nominative “the lord”; omission of *heroa* omits “hero”; *quid primas de* is a corrupt alternative for “what he would do”; and *acturum* means “about to do/would do.” *Furibunda voce* is “with a furious voice,” while corrected *furibundo* is “with a furious [voice]”; *mitti* is an erroneous form corrected to *miti*, “gentle”; *aplus* is corrected by another hand to *apostolicus*, “apostolic envoy.” *Blasphemiae* means “of blasphemy,” while *blasphema* is “blasphemous”; *toto regno* is “the whole kingdom,” *toti* “to/for the whole [kingdom].” *Campanario* means “bell-ringer,” while the gloss *sadulerie* identifies Canaparius as “saddler.” *Transnant* means “they swim/cross over”; *angelus* is “angel,” not “angelic”; *opera* means “by works/deeds,” *quies* “rest,” *somnum* “sleep,” *fratrem* “brother,” and *qui* “who” replaces causal *quia*, “because.” *Exurgente* means “as [the purple day] rose,” *adbreviant* “they shorten,” and *lapis* “a stone” replaces genitive *lapidis*, “of a stone.” The witness-4a sentence is exactly the printed incomplete quotation: “What ignoble colour suddenly changed your cheeks? You know ...”; its ellipsis is retained because the source ends it there. The full witness-4b continuation, including every surviving word through the Utrecht three-day eagle reading, is translated above.

### 4.

Afterward, when the neighboring pagans of Poland refused to accept his preaching, he wished to go to the metropolis of the Poles, which is called Gniezno. He came to a certain village, where he asked for directions to the aforesaid city. But when the inhabitants of the place heard that his language differed greatly from their own, and observed his clothing—namely, his monastic habit, which was altogether hateful to them—they broke into laughter. Although he spoke to them and asked about the road, they did not deign to answer him.

Then the saint of God, filled with the Spirit, who through him performed signs and wonders, said to them: “Because you are unwilling to speak for the honor of God, in his name I command you to be silent, to his glory.” Having said this, he departed from there and, with Christ guiding him, found the right road.

Those impious men immediately became mute. Terrified and bewildered by what had happened to them, they remained in sorrow and groaning. He came farther on to another village and, asking for directions, was likewise treated with contempt. He punished them, as he had the first, with the same penalty, so that those whom the guilt of a similar offense bound might be fittingly constrained by punishment. In both cases he awaited not the vengeance of his injury, but, in a spirit of gentleness, the occasion of their salvation and the glory of Christ, which he sought.

Then, proceeding under God’s guidance to a third village, he asked about the road. The villagers answered him kindly and humbly showed him the way. Giving them thanks, he completed the long journey in a short time, accompanied by a good angel, and reached the city of Gniezno, full of people, very powerful and famous.

He immediately went to the marketplace and confidently preached Christ to the multitude gathered there, announcing the rewards of eternal life [Note: *annunciat*—“announces,” according to c.]. With God cooperating and confirming his sermon by many and varied signs that followed, countless people believed in Christ the Lord.

Thus it happened that his fame, now spreading throughout the whole region, reached those whom the holy bishop had earlier deprived of speech in Christ’s name—not of hearing [Note: c: *i. quos p. q.*; abbreviated reading, with uncertain expansion]. They had remained in that condition, wholly unable to find any means of relief. Accordingly, they all set out together to the man of God, hoping to find grace from him, and found him preaching to a great multitude.

When they recognized him, they fell at his feet before the assembled crowd and, with sighs, tears, and various groanings, asked pardon for their offense. Seeing this [Note: *Hoc*—possibly “here,” according to c.], blessed Adalbert temporarily set aside the work of preaching, to which he devoted all his effort. Turning toward them, and being exceedingly gentle of spirit, he addressed them calmly, saying:

“I know, brothers, I know who you are. I see that the hand of the Lord has touched you and has granted you understanding, so that, recognizing your sin, you might draw near to God, who heals the contrite of heart. Therefore I declare to you that the merciful God, whose servant I am, has granted forgiveness to your error” [Note: *denuntcio*—“I declare,” according to c.]. “For this reason, as his servant, in the name of that God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Creator, I restore to every tongue the service of speech” [Note: *lingua*—“tongue,” according to c.].

When he had said these things and made the sign of the cross over them, the bond of their tongues was immediately loosened. To the astonishment of all, they began to speak and loudly proclaim that Christ was the true God.

Desiring therefore to receive the grace of baptism, he first instructed them in the word of faith at their own request, and caused them to be regenerated from water and the Spirit [Note: *regenerati*—“regenerated,” according to c.]. At last, confirmed in the faith, they all together eagerly begged the most holy bishop, saying:

“We unanimously beseech your holiness, servant of almighty God, to impose upon us, as satisfaction and for the memory of posterity, some great penance for the iniquity which, with a blind and furious mind, we committed against you” [Note: *quam quidem*—“which indeed,” according to c.].

The blessed bishop answered them: “I praise you, sons, because with pious devotion you humble yourselves beneath the hand of God. Nevertheless, know this with absolute certainty: there, together with all your other sins, everything has been forgiven you in baptism. Only maintain vigilance of mind, lest, returning to your former evils or to others, you lose the grace you have received.”

When they persisted more and more [Note: *instaret*—singular, “he persisted,” according to c.], he prescribed that, beginning with Septuagesima and before Lent, before the other Christians began their fast, they should abstain from eating meat until Ash Wednesday. They received this command devoutly, faithfully observed it throughout their lives, and handed it down to their descendants for observance, as though by hereditary right.

While the Spirit of God’s grace preached and performed many miracles through blessed Adalbert, all Poland accepted the Christian faith. It was founded, as if by one of the apostles, upon the firm rock of apostolic faith. The people gratefully and collectively accepted the aforesaid time and manner of abstinence before Easter, to be observed in honor of Saint Adalbert, and observed it inviolably for approximately 230 years, until a certain legate of the Apostolic See, a man of great authority, unwilling that the Polish people should remain longer unlike the other faithful in the observance of the annual fast, dispensed them from the aforesaid statute by apostolic authority around the year of the Lord 1247 [Note: c reads *volens*, “willing,” for *nolens*, “unwilling”; *annos*—“years,” according to c.].

### 5.

It is also read that, when blessed Adalbert wished to cross over to other lands of the pagans, he appointed in Gniezno as archbishop in his place a holy man named Gaudentius, his companion in labor and travel. He was then brought into Pomerania and honorably received by the duke of the land.

Indeed, Saint Adalbert had baptized this same prince earlier in Poland, when he had come there on behalf of the daughter of the duke of Poland, asking that she be given to him in marriage. The duke refused to give her to him before she had received the bath of baptism there from Adalbert, her fellow bishop [Note: *illud*—“that,” according to c.].

Therefore the duke of Pomerania summoned his people so that they might hear the word of God from the holy bishop. When the Pomeranians heard him preaching that the gods whom they worshiped were not gods but demons, and could provide nothing good, they became exceedingly indignant against him and blasphemed him. Those who were considered wiser among them assembled together and attempted to rebuke him for his words [Note: *atemptantes*—“attempting,” according to c.].

But as Saint Adalbert continued to expound the words of life more fully, they confessed that they had been defeated in their deception; nevertheless, they declared that they did not wish to withdraw from their customary worship and ancient traditions.

They were therefore greatly amazed at his wisdom and answers. Attracted by reverence for his venerable person [Note: *illegitti*—probably “attracted,” according to c.], and judging that he was somehow above the common condition of human beings, they asked that he allow himself to be worshiped by them together with their other gods.

When the man of God heard this, he was deeply saddened and, grieving over the magnitude of their error, groaned heavily, pouring forth abundant tears [Note: c reads *profundentes*, “pouring forth”]. Thus he answered them:

“Alas, wretched men! How blind you are, how lost, and how greatly deserving of tears—you who wish to ascribe deity not only to the worst demons but even to a mortal man, although deity can exist in no one except God alone, who created all things.”

### 6.

From there, crossing the sea into Prussia, he joined himself to a certain Prussian who knew the Polish language and whom he quickly converted to the faith. This man received the blessed bishop as a guest and followed him reverently; at his command, he concealed from the others for a time that he was a Christian.

### 7.

It is also read [Note: c reads *et quod et*] that, when his passion was approaching and blessed Adalbert was celebrating Mass, the unworthy pagans saw this and raised an outcry among themselves, saying:

“Behold, this man has come to us and is practicing his incantations and sorceries in order to curse us and make us ill. Let us go and kill him for our protection and for the safety of our country.”

When, like madmen, they rushed against the saint as he performed the sacred mysteries [Note: *concurrentem*—“rushing together,” according to c.], one of them, looking behind him, saw an immense flame of fire that seemed to be consuming the entire village. He loudly called out and reported it to his companions. Because of this, they all returned as quickly as possible.

Recognizing that no harm had happened to them, but seeing that they had been deceived, they spoke to one another in a rage even greater than before:

“It was an illusion that we saw, produced for us by the force of his enchantment.”

A second time, therefore, they rushed savagely against the saint of God. Frightened by a similar vision as before, they hurried back to the village at a rapid pace and found their houses completely unharmed, together with everything they contained, although they had thought them entirely destroyed by fire.

O marvelous power of God! O inscrutable depth of his wisdom and knowledge! He who gently orders all things deceived them with so slight a jest, although they regarded that divine and heavenly sacrament as a mockery, so that through this the wicked deceivers might be corrected and the sacred sacrifices, with the most holy bishop assisting, might be preserved unharmed.

### 8.

It is also read that they cut off his head and suspended it at the top of the tree beneath which he had celebrated Mass. So that it might be seen from afar by everyone on every side, amid the exultation of the wicked, they stripped the entire part of the trunk nearest the top by cutting away its branches [Col. 0893C].

When they had torn the sacred body limb from limb and scattered it here and there, his host was divinely warned by an angel of God [Note: c: *amonitus*, “warned”] to gather the members carefully, so that none of them might be lost, and to preserve them reverently, keeping them hidden in his mind.

Obeying the heavenly vision, he diligently and in holy fear carried out what had been commanded him. Yet, when [Note: c omits *cum*, “when”] he carefully fitted each fragment to the limbs that joined together, he discovered that one finger was missing from one of the hands. A certain one of the faithless had cut it off because of its ring, removed the ring, and thrown the finger into the river [Note: *projicerat*—“had thrown,” according to c.].

The host therefore searched for it anxiously for many days, examining every place here and there, but could not find it. One day his wife, astonished at this, asked him what it was that caused him to go about so anxiously seeking something. At first he refused in every way to reveal it [Note: *voluit*—“he wished,” according to c.], but at last, overcome by weariness at his wife’s persistence [Note: possibly *importunitate*, “importunity,” rather than *inprobitate*], he disclosed the secret to her.

As soon as she heard it, being faithless, she betrayed to the neighbors how the sacred remains had been collected and hidden in her husband’s possession [Note: *eximie*—“excellent,” according to c.; the context requires “sacred remains,” possibly reflecting an OCR or textual error].

Because he had been the author of this betrayal, his mouth was immediately twisted so monstrously that he could scarcely take food or drink and was entirely unable to speak.

The pagans, however, acting upon their judgment against the man, attacked him, inflicted many blows upon him, and threw him into chains. They subjected him to various torments so that he would show them the holy relics.

At last, abandoning God’s commandment, he was abandoned by God. Delivered unjustly into the power of the wicked, he satisfied their will. Nevertheless, the holy members were handed over to profane hands for removal. By heavenly providence, those barbarians reverently guarded them, either because they feared being struck by divine punishment if they failed to do so, or because they intended to sell them to Christians.

Those who had found the holy bishop’s finger in the belly of a fish hastened, as is read [Note: *properantur*—possibly “they hasten,” according to c.], to those whom they knew to possess the venerable members. All saw the finger of the holy body shining with heavenly light. The entire village gathered to behold the miracle and, astonished, thereafter honored the blessed body with still greater reverence [Note: *prodigiti*—probably “miracle,” according to c.].

The Prussians, moreover, knowing that the relics of the glorious martyr were precious to the most Christian prince, the great duke of Poland, Boleslaus, sent messengers to him, saying:

“Know that the god of yours whom we killed is with us. If you are willing to give us a large sum of money, we are ready to send him to you.”

When the most noble prince heard this, he rejoiced with great joy. He sent the demanded price and received the sacred body with due reverence.

A marvelous event is said to have occurred through the power of God. Since the body, which had been the temple and instrument of the Holy Spirit, was to be weighed against the money according to the pagans’ agreement, it was placed on a scale and became so light that it seemed to weigh virtually nothing when placed on an even balance [Note: *quia*—“because,” according to c.].

When it was being carried to the monastery called Gniezno [Note: c reads *deferetur*, “it will be carried”], it arrived there, and with the consent of the aforesaid duke it was first placed there with appropriate reverence.

As the proclamations of the glorious bishop’s miracles increased and resounded far and wide [Note: c: *circumdon*; reading uncertain], the man who had been his host in Prussia, whose guilt had twisted his mouth, came devoutly to the aforesaid monastery. With prayers poured forth and tears, in a contrite heart, he was immediately and completely healed by Saint Adalbert, who restored his ordinary use of speech. Confirmed in goodness, he remained there until the end of his life, serving God and his holy guest and martyr in holy conduct [Col. 0894D].

After some time, when war arose between the neighboring pagans and the Poles, the aforementioned prince feared that he might lose so great a treasure through some unfortunate outcome of the wars. With great glory, he transferred the sacred relics to Gniezno on the eighth day before the Ides of November, where many wonders are performed through the merits of that glorious martyr [Note: *fuerit*—“may have been,” according to c.].

### 9.

Finally, the emperor Otto, who during blessed Adalbert’s lifetime had held him as his teacher, a familiar friend in the commandments of God, and a most beloved companion, fell into a grave illness while staying in Rome. He had already been entirely deprived of hope of recovery by the physicians [Note: *bis scriptum*—“written twice,” according to c.].

Placed at the point of death, he earnestly invoked the apostles and the other holy patrons of the City for the preservation of his life. But when he felt that no help was coming to him in any way [Note: *ullo*—“any,” according to c.], he turned to seek the protection of his holy father Adalbert [Note: c reads *piis*, “pious,” for *pii*, “of his pious”], whose many distinguished miracles he had known. He made a vow that, if Adalbert delivered him, he would personally visit his shrine.

It was a marvelous event, for God is marvelous in his saints. He had scarcely finished speaking when, behold, he suddenly became completely well, to the astonishment of all. Rising immediately, he went to the pope and disclosed to him in order both the miracle and his vow.

The pope rejoiced and blessed the Lord, who so glorifies his saints, in blessed Adalbert, his glorious martyr.

[Note: For what follows, compare the *Chronicle* of Martin Gallus (Gdańsk, 1749, folio), pp. 60–61, where these matters are said to be read in the book on Adalbert’s passion.]

When the aforesaid emperor Otto III came to Poland to fulfill his vow, he was received with great magnificence and glory by the aforementioned duke of Poland, Boleslaus. The duke spread a public road before him, with canopies, rich cloths, and various precious silk ornaments, for two great miles all the way to Gniezno, to the church and the tomb of Saint Adalbert.

When the most Christian Augustus saw around that same duke such abundance and profusion of riches, and such excellence of royal equipment in servants, foods, and drinks, golden and silver vessels, and other acts of generosity—and saw that he himself had been received and entertained by him with such extraordinary royal dignity—he said to the princes who were with him:

“It is more fitting for such a prince to be a partner of the empire than a subject.”

Taking the diadem from his own head [Note: compare the Life of Saint Stanislaus and Voigt, *History of Prussia* I, 277], he placed it upon Boleslaus’s head and, with the consent of the princes present, crowned him king of Poland.

Thus, on the occasion of the veneration of blessed Adalbert, Poland first obtained the glory of a kingdom, and from that time its princes ceased to be subject to the kings of the Romans.

This king of the Poles, Boleslaus, called Victorious and Pious, enlarged the boundaries of the kingdom and the exceedingly famous reputation of his people. His dominion extended from the Danube—the great river of the kingdom of Hungary—to the Sala, a river of Saxony near Halle, and from Kiev, which is the metropolis of Russia, to the mountains of Carinthia [Note: compare the *Chronicle of Martin Gallus* in Sommersberg, *Scriptores rerum Silesiacarum* II, p. 25].

His son Mesco succeeded him in the kingdom [Note: For what follows, compare Martin Gallus, *Chronicle*, p. 68, and Boguphalus, p. 25]. After him, his son Casimir, born of the sister of the aforesaid emperor Otto [Note: from Richeza, daughter of Mathilda, sister of Otto III], surnamed Charles III, reigned. After him, fourth in succession, his son Boleslaus, called the Warlike but most wicked, held the kingdom [Note: c reads *quam* for *quem*, “after whom”].

This Boleslaus killed Saint Stanislaus, a venerable man and bishop of Kraków [Note: *Cracoviensem*—“of Kraków”; c. reads *draconiensem*], because Stanislaus rebuked him for his wickedness. With him the kingdom failed, and from then until the present no king has arisen in Poland.

Therefore, at the aforesaid coronation, Emperor Otto gave King Boleslaus, among the royal insignia, the lance of Saint Maurice and one of the nails of the Lord. To his son Mesco he gave his sister in marriage.

King Boleslaus, among many outstanding gifts [Note: c: *excelencia*, “outstanding things”; compare Martin Gallus, *Chronicle*, p. 61, and Boguphalus, p. 25], offered the arm of Saint Adalbert to the most illustrious emperor. Otto accepted it with the greatest gratitude above all gifts and, rejoicing, returned to his own lands, giving thanks to the Lord, whose kingdom is eternal and whose empire extends over all, forever and ever. Amen.

## Homily of Saint Adalbert, Bishop of Prague, on the Feast of Saint Alexius the Confessor

*(In Bollandus, July, vol. IV, p. 257.)*

### Notice

We possess a copy from a volume described as manuscript 109 of the library of Cassino, written, as it is said, in Lombard letters, with this title: “On the feast of Saint Alexius the Confessor. Reading from the Holy Gospel according to Matthew. At that time Simon Peter said to Jesus: ‘Lord, behold, we have left everything and followed you; what therefore will there be for us?’ etc. Homily of the venerable Bishop Adelbert.”

This homily is now printed more because of its antiquity than because of its merit, since it teaches us nothing new about the saint. The passages that the author writes at the beginning concerning the reward of those who follow Christ in voluntary poverty have been removed, since they belong more properly to ascetical than to historical matters.

Baronius mentions this homily under the year 1001, no. 19, and adds that it was delivered in the church of Saints Boniface and Alexius in Rome; he repeats this under the year 1004, no. 8. Indeed, that it was delivered in this place may be inferred from the words with which the author addresses his hearers at the end.

## Homily of Saint Adalbert, Bishop of Prague and Martyr

> [lacuna] We too, dearest brothers, have often taken an example of this matter, whenever, departing somewhere because circumstances required it, we learned that all the dwellings of the monasteries lay open to us as though they were our own. We saw all people inclined toward our service with the sincerest devotion, and especially in our father Alexius, of blessed memory, whose venerable day of assumption we commemorate today with due solemnity. We see the entire substance of this reading perfectly fulfilled in him.
>
> For, having abandoned everything, he followed Christ when, rejecting all things—his father and mother, his bride with her carnal love, his male and female servants, and all his possessions—and having crossed the waves of the sea with immense labor, he finally reached the city of Edessa in Syria. There he learned the perfect rule of life through long practice. Despising the world, and with his body mortified by injuries and insults, hunger and thirst, cold and nakedness, he followed Christ with all his desires.

For he knew that Christ himself had said in the Gospel: “Unless someone renounces everything that he possesses and follows me, he cannot be my disciple.”

When he had carried out the Lord’s commands there for a long time, he was made known to people by a divine voice. To avoid incurring the guilt of vainglory, he decided to depart from there. Thus, while he was setting out for Tarsus in order to remain concealed, by God’s will he was driven back by force to his homeland.
