When his father received him as a poor man, as you have heard, he remained in his own house as a stranger. O what constancy and what patience were his! Who could tell how many temptations and what storms he endured in the hidden recesses of his most sacred heart, while he saw his father afflicted with such grief because of him and knew that his mother continued night and day in weeping and groaning?

Moreover, he saw his own servants abounding in luxuries and walking about clothed in expensive garments, while he was held in contempt by everyone. He endured, in addition, their insults and mockery, and, as though already dead to the world, lived only in spirit for Christ.

For how could he, still enclosed in a fragile body, have endured so many hardships unless his heart had been kindled and burning within by divine love? Yet all these things were carried out by divine wisdom so that his glory might increase and so that, by the example of his patience, he might instruct us to pursue the same things.

Your fraternity should know how great a glory he earned before God through patience, so that by a divine voice he was called a man of God and his prayer was said to have been accepted for the sin of the entire Roman people.

For it is a mark of great merit, my brothers, that a man should be called a man of God by a divine voice. Since the same Lord called the prophets “sons of men,” and not “men of God,” this man was named “man of God” as if by a certain privilege. Just as he fought in a struggle unlike that of others, so he deserved to be called by the Lord with a special name.

When, inflamed by divine love, he rejected carnal marriage, he deserved to be joined to the Lord’s bridal chamber and to be numbered among that company of the innocent who follow the Lamb and sing a new song before the throne of God and of the Lamb. “These are they who have not defiled themselves with women, for they are virgins, and they follow the Lamb wherever he goes.”

Rightly, therefore, he became a man of God—that is, a temple of God, a guest of Christ, and a dwelling place of the Holy Spirit. He was rightly said to have been heard while praying for Rome, since he devoted himself to leading a singular life in Rome. The Lord’s saying also fittingly applies to him: “Whoever has left wife or children for my name’s sake will receive a hundredfold and will possess eternal life.”

For what he abandoned for Christ, he received a hundredfold. His merit in chastity among the continent, because of the fruit of the spirit, was certainly a hundred times greater than it would once have been among the licentious, because of the desire of the flesh. And the children whom he then refused to have carnally, he deserved now to receive a hundredfold spiritually.

The number one hundred, as has often been said, figuratively signifies perfection. Although we are not worthy even to be called his servants, we are nevertheless his sons, because the pious intercessor before God has gathered us into this house of his under the monastic profession [Note: From this it seems possible to infer that this homily was delivered by Saint Adalbert in Rome, in the monastery or church of Saints Boniface and Alexius].

We are his sons, whom he never ceases spiritually to unite into one family of holy profession, although we were born carnally to different parents. We are his sons if we hold to the path of his virtues by imitation, and if we do not turn aside through sluggishness from the patience he displayed in himself.

Therefore, dearest brothers, it is necessary that, as good sons worthy of so great a father, we take care to follow the examples of his most holy life. Let no enticement of soul or body turn us back from following the footsteps of so great a father, so that we too—who have abandoned carnal desires and earthly possessions, and who, for love of an angelic way of life, have despised marrying and begetting children carnally—may deserve from the heavenly King, through the merit of spiritual virtues, to receive a hundredfold in the present age through the fellowship of the saints, and in the age to come to possess eternal life.

To obtain this, let us implore with the whole devotion of our minds the patronage of him whose feast we celebrate [Note: From these words and from the earlier statement, “whose venerable day of assumption we commemorate today with due solemnity,” it is clear that this homily was delivered on Saint Alexius’s feast, on the same day, as I suspect, on which he is still celebrated among the Latins, 17 July]. He gives us confidence to make this petition, for he promised that he would hear him praying for Rome. May he himself, who urged us to seek the saint’s prayer, deign through his merits to hear us—the one who, three in persons and one in substance, lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## Profession of the Rule of Saint Benedict by Blessed Adalbert

Made in Rome, in the monastery of Saints Boniface and Alexius the Confessors, on 2 April 991.

*(In Bocsek, *Codex diplomaticus Moraviae*, p. 104.)*

> + I, Adalbert, promise my stability, the conversion of my conduct, and obedience according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, before God and all his saints, with Abbot Augustine present.

## In the Year of the Lord 899. Pope Gregory V

### Historical Notice

*(In Eggs, *Pontificium doctum*, p. 287.)*

Gregory V, a German by nation, previously called Bruno, of the Order of Saint Benedict, son of Otto, Duke of Saxony and Swabia, and of Judith, a woman of illustrious lineage, was elected Roman pontiff after the death of John XVI. Because of the integrity of his life and conduct and his extensive knowledge of literature, and at the urging of the emperor Otto, who was then present in Rome, he was elected by the clergy and people of Rome on the sixth day before the Kalends of September in the year 996.

Because of the most generous alms that he distributed daily to the poor, widows, and orphans, and because of the countless other gifts he bestowed upon oratories, churches, and monasteries, he was called Gregory the Minor, to distinguish him from Gregory the Great.

In the first year of his pontificate, he confirmed to John, archbishop of Ravenna, all the possessions that previous pontiffs had granted in earlier years to the Church of Ravenna. He decreed that no toll should be exacted from any Ravennate cleric throughout Aemilia and the Pentapolis.

He forbade Robert, king of the Gauls and son of Hugh Capet, to continue his incestuous marriage with Bertha. Robert therefore left Bertha and, with Gregory’s approval, married Constance, daughter of William, count of Toulouse.

At the request of Miecislaus, who sought this by letters and messengers, he raised Gaudentius, brother of Saint Adalbert, bishop of Prague, to the see of Gniezno in Poland.

He granted the right to wear the pallium to Heribert, archbishop of Cologne, and afterward admitted him among the seven electors to whom the right of creating the Roman emperor was granted.

He invested Otto III, together with his imperial wife Maria, with the crown and title of Augustus in the Vatican basilica.

In the year of Christ 997, when Augustus Otto had departed for Germany, Crescentius, stirred by his old desire to rule, began to harass Pope Gregory with dreadful revolts. Since Gregory, deprived of every military defense, could no longer endure his power, he followed the example of his predecessor John, left the City, and withdrew into Etruria.

At that time a certain John, called Philagathus, held the bishopric of Piacenza. He was a Calabrian by nation, a native of Rossano, and by profession a Cassinese monk. Inflated by his knowledge of letters, in which he excelled, and by the abundance of his money, by which he surpassed others, he had fallen so far into arrogance that he voluntarily called himself archbishop.

The Romans therefore, finding him wealthy and suited to stirring up riots, proclaimed him, with Crescentius as author and instigator, a false pontiff against the absent Gregory.

When Gregory learned this, he went to Germany, both to complain of the injury and to seek the emperor’s assistance. Crescentius, informed of these events, did not lessen his defiance. Rather, as though he regarded Otto’s war as certain, he began to strengthen the walls of the City, construct embankments, dig ditches, and, above all, fortify the Mausoleum of Hadrian—later called the Mausoleum of Crescentius after his name—with various defenses, provisions, and soldiers.

Otto, moved by Gregory’s pleas, returned to Italy in the same year with the strongest forces of every kind, intent on avenging the injury done to his kinsman the pope.

Having brought his army to Rome and moved it up to the City, while the citizens refused to submit, he attacked Rome vigorously. For some time the Romans resisted fiercely, encouraged by Crescentius and the antipope with great hopes of rewards.

But as the Germans grew stronger on every side, and the besieged, suffering from lack of supplies, could no longer withstand such an assault, they voluntarily opened the gates to the emperor and surrendered the City, while Crescentius and the antipope withdrew into the Mausoleum of Hadrian.

Otto entered the City with his men and, after the tenth month had elapsed since Gregory had been expelled, restored him to his see. Having settled affairs in the City, he besieged Crescentius and John the antipope in the fortress.

When the siege dragged on, the emperor, by offering rewards, incited the Germans to press the attack more fiercely. They attacked from every direction and finally captured the fortress, as Ditmarus writes. They raged against everyone. Crescentius was wounded, captured, and thrown from the wall. His corpse was tied behind an ox, dragged through the marshes, thoroughly mocked, and finally suspended from a high beam in the sight of the Romans. A similar punishment was inflicted upon those of his accomplices who remained.

John the antipope, by the emperor’s command, was deprived of his eyes, and his nose and ears were cut off. Placed upon an animal and led through the entire City, he held the tail of his mount in his hands, presenting a bitter spectacle to all.

Then he was sent into exile in Germany. Shortly afterward, worn out by the pain of his wounds and the sorrow of his spirit, he died, having sat for approximately ten months in the Roman see that he had usurped.

While he was seated against Gregory, he sent Peter, a cardinal, as legate to Gaul, so that he might consecrate in his name a church that Count Fulk of Anjou had built in the diocese of Tours. But on the very day appointed for the consecration, the church suddenly collapsed, as though God rejected temples dedicated in his honor by a schismatic or an invader of the Holy See.

Meanwhile, Gregory, with his rivals removed and restored to his rightful see and freedom, consulted with Otto and turned his mind both toward reforming and stabilizing the condition of the Roman Church and toward ensuring that emperors might henceforth be elected peacefully and without tumult. For this reason he convened a council of bishops at Rome.

Although the acts of this council have perished, what had been lost is nevertheless brought back to light from fragments subsequently discovered.

The council held at Rome under Gregory V is mentioned especially in the acts of Saint Adalbert, written by an author of that period. They indicate that the case of Saint Adalbert, bishop of Prague, was discussed at this synod. He had been summoned for judgment by the archbishop of Mainz concerning the establishment of residence in the church that he had left.

More importantly, the constitution attributed by many to the same Pope Gregory concerning the electors of the emperor seems also to belong to this council: namely, the archbishops of Mainz, Trier, and Cologne; the Margrave of Brandenburg; the Count Palatine; the Duke of Saxony; and the King of Bohemia. Matters of such importance were customarily undertaken only after consultation with the Fathers and with the bishops assembled in synod.

Platina should be read here in his account of Gregory V, as well as Baronius, volume X, under the year 996, Bellarmine, and others—especially John Palatius of Venice, volume II of *The Western Monarchy*, book II, chapter 3, where he treats this very question at length and with sound argument.

While Gregory was at the helm of the Church, the Hungarians embraced the Christian faith. At that time there also lived men of exceptional holiness: Romuald the abbot; Boniface, apostle of the Russians, a kinsman of Otto and a disciple of Romuald; Adalbert, martyr in Prussia; Stephen, king of Hungary; Maielus, abbot of Cluny; and Roswitha, a Saxon religious woman, learned in Greek and Latin beyond a man.

Gregory died after administering the pontificate most successfully—which he held for two years, more than five months, and twenty-four days—on the twelfth day before the Kalends of March in the year of our salvation 999. He was buried at Saint Peter’s in the Vatican, beside the ashes of Blessed Gregory the Great, whose imitator he had been in life. The following epitaph still survives:

> Here lies one whom the earth covers, comely in eyes and face,  
> Pope Gregory the Fifth by name.  
> Formerly Bruno, offspring of the royal Franks,  
> Son of Otto by his mother Judith.  
> A German by tongue, learned in the city of Vuangia,  
> He sat upon the apostolic throne while still a young man.  
> For two years, and about eight [five] months,  
> While February counted three times six days.  
> Rich toward the poor, every Saturday he distributed garments,  
> Careful to observe the apostolic number.  
> Using the Frankish, German, and Latin tongues,  
> He instructed peoples with a threefold eloquence.  
> Otto III entrusted to him Peter’s flock,  
> Anointed to the empire by the hands of his kinsman.  
> After he had cast off the bonds of earthly flesh,  
> He was placed at the right side of his namesake [i.e., Gregory the Great].  
>
> He died on the twelfth day before the Kalends of March, 999.

## Letters and Privileges of Pope Gregory V
# I. Letter of Pope Gregory V to Winizo, Abbot (996)

[In Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, vol. III, col. 618.]

[Col. 0901D]

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ the Lord, Winizo, venerable abbot of Saint Saviour’s, situated in the county of Chiusi, in the territory of Monte Amiata: to you and your successors, perpetual salvation in the Lord.

Since whatever the faithful request reasonably and suitably ought always to be granted, out of devotion to our pious founder it is fitting that, in granting privileges, we in no way withhold our generosity. Therefore, because your affection humbly petitioned the apostolate of our exalted office that the aforesaid monastery of Saint Saviour, established in the above-mentioned county and territory, should be adorned with the privileges of the Apostolic See, so that, instituted under the jurisdiction of our holy Church—which, by the Lord’s authority, we govern—it might not be subjected to the jurisdiction or authority of any other church, for this reason we willingly grant through this authority of ours what you have requested. And therefore we prohibit any priest of any church from exercising jurisdiction, power, or authority in the aforesaid monastery, except the pontiff of the Apostolic See, so that, unless invited by the abbot of that monastery, no one may presume to celebrate the solemn rites of Mass there in any way.

Finally, by apostolic authority we establish that no person, great or small, may presume to inflict any disturbance upon that monastery, whether against its servants and dependants below, or against its male or female slaves, or against its free people, or against any possessions belonging to it—in houses, estates, or property of any kind. Likewise we grant and confirm to the same holy monastery the first fruits and tithes from its people or from its precept-holders (*praeceptales*), and that holy baptism may be celebrated in the church of Saint Benedict and in the church of Saint Mary at Lamule, just as has been granted by the royal authorities through the written charter of privilege.

Whatever appears to be contained there, and whatever has been granted to that monastery by our holy predecessors, the pontiffs Stephen, Hadrian, John, Formosus, or by any other of our predecessors, we grant and confirm in its entirety, by apostolic authority, to you and your successors. They may also freely receive chrism and holy oil from whatever church they wish or are able to approach.

By apostolic censure we establish and command that no duke, margrave, count, viscount, *castaldus*, or any person, great or small, may dare to exercise jurisdiction in any of the castles belonging to the monastery, or to judge there, or to hold any court, unless invited by the abbot of that monastery.

We further establish by apostolic authority that neither a bishop nor anyone else from the clerical order may in any way presume to take away or alienate the churches, parishes, cells, estates, or any places or possessions of the aforesaid monastery, nor dare to inflict any dispute, injury, or loss upon its property, possessions, implements, or ornaments.

All these things mentioned above—namely, the tithes, first fruits, and offerings belonging to the aforesaid monastery, as well as baptism, chrism, and oil—we confirm and grant perpetually, by apostolic authority, to you, beloved son Winizo, abbot, and to your successors, through this document of our privilege, from the present ninth indiction, according to the manner stated above. This is done especially so that in the same monastery uninterrupted devout prayer may be offered for the stability of the kingdom of our most glorious emperor Otto III, and for our soul and those of our predecessor and successor pontiffs.

Finally, we establish that, when the abbot departs from this world, neither king, duke, margrave, bishop, count, nor any other person may presume to appoint an abbot there. Rather, after all the brothers of that monastery have assembled together, they are to appoint as abbot from their own community, by common consent and through God’s providence, the man who appears worthy of this honour.

If anyone—which we do not wish—should attempt with rash audacity to oppose what has been piously and firmly established by this authority of ours through this privilege, or should presume in any way to resist or transgress what we have established for the praise of God and the stability of the aforesaid monastery, let him know that, by the authority of God, blessed Peter the apostle, and the three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers, he has been bound by the bond of anathema. He is to be burned with the devil and his most dreadful pomp in the punishment of eternal fire, unless he duly corrects the evil he has committed.

But may he who, with pious regard, proves himself the guardian and observer of this apostolic privilege deserve to obtain from our most merciful Judge, the Lord, this grace of confirmation and blessing, and eternal life with all God’s elect, for ever and ever. Amen.

Written by the hand of Peter, regional notary and archivist of the holy Roman Church, in the month of May, in the aforesaid ninth indiction. Farewell in the Lord.

Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of June, through the hand of John, bishop of the holy Alban Church and librarian of the holy Apostolic See, in the ninth indiction, in the first year of the pontificate of the lord Gregory, supreme pontiff and universal pope, in the first year of the reign of the lord Otto, crowned by God, the great emperor, in the month of May; and in the aforesaid indiction he subscribed.

Theobald, bishop of the holy Bellitrensis Church.

Peter, bishop of the holy Praenestine Church.

Azzo, bishop of the holy Ostian Church.

Abbo, archdeacon of the holy Roman Church.

Crescentius, *ablationarius* of the holy Roman Church.

Amico, venerable man, priest and cardinal of the holy Roman Church.

# II. Privilege of Pope Gregory V for the Church of Cambrai

[Note: In the year of Christ 996, Herluin, bishop of Cambrai, was ordained at Rome by Gregory V, supreme pontiff. When he had complained at the Roman synod about those who had invaded the property of his Church, Gregory fortified that Church with privileges and excommunicated the invaders. Baldric, bishop of Noyon, mentions this matter and Gregory’s letters in his *Chronicle*, book I, chapter 3: “Afterwards, when a synod had been held there with the emperor, the pope presiding with the bishops, abbots, and priests, and when sufficient discussion had taken place concerning the necessary affairs of the Church, Herluin the bishop rose and, with a grave complaint, denounced the ravagers of his parish. He also brought forward a public accusation that, as we have related above, he had recently found the wealth of his predecessor devastated by Walther and others. Therefore, when the pope confirmed it—indeed, when the bishops, abbots, and all who were present there agreed,” and so forth.]

(Year 996.)

[In Mansi, *Councils*, XIX, 218.]

[Col. 0904D]

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Herluin, bishop of the holy Church of Cambrai, and to his successors for ever.

The pastoral office and the dignity of the highest see, which we, although unworthy, exercise, compel us, with Christ’s approval, to guard and govern with vigilant concern not only the mysteries of the holy Church of God that remain with us, but also those situated far away.

Since, as is almost universally known, the affair that arose between Arnulf, archbishop of the Church of Reims, and Gerbert, its invader, intervened, the aforesaid prelate Herluin was unable to be consecrated at Reims according to canonical custom because of their hostility; and, not unjustly, his consecration came before us at the Apostolic See. When we consecrated him, we heard from him a tearful complaint: namely, that in the time of his predecessors that bishopric had been plundered in many ways by wicked men. Therefore he most humbly implored us to provide him, by our apostolic authority, with some aid against the enemies of the holy Church.

Yielding to his prayers, through this privilege of our apostolic authority we decree that no duke, margrave, count, viscount, or any person, great or small, may henceforth presume to invade or plunder the places of the aforesaid Church. If anyone should presume to do so, let him know that, by our authority, with Christ and blessed Peter the apostle as guarantors, he is bound by anathema until he has satisfied the bishop of the aforesaid see or, by coming to Rome, has there purified himself.

It has likewise been reported to us that, when the bishop or other priests of the aforesaid holy Church of Cambrai die, certain persons filled with a devilish spirit customarily seize and devastate the ecclesiastical property left by either the bishop or the priests. By apostolic censure we likewise forbid them to presume to do this any longer. If they do so, whatever their order or dignity, let them know that they have been struck by the bond of anathema until they have corrected this by worthy satisfaction.

We also greatly desire that the brothers residing in the monastery of that Church, and all the communities belonging to it, should firmly hold and possess without any diminution whatever they ought justly and legally to possess, so that, sufficiently aided by temporal resources, they may more confidently seek eternal things without complaint.

Moreover, through this document of our command, we grant and confirm perpetually to Bishop Herluin and his successors that no duke, margrave, count, or any other person, great or small, may dare to hold any jurisdiction, court, or legal assembly in any place belonging to the aforesaid bishopric, unless he has received permission from the bishop of that see or has been invited by him. Rather, he may appoint from among his own people anyone he wishes to perform that office.

If anyone—which we do not wish—should prove a violator of this apostolic privilege, let him know that he is to be burned with Judas the traitor and the apostate angels in eternal fire.

But may he who proves its guardian and observer deserve to obtain from Christ our Saviour blessing, grace, forgiveness of his sins, and eternal life. Amen.

Written by the hand of Petrisgio, notary and scribe of the holy Roman Church, in the month of May and the ninth indiction. Farewell in Christ. In the first year of the pontificate of the lord Gregory, supreme pontiff and pope of the universal Church, and in the eleventh year of the empire of the lord Otto III, emperor.

# III. Charter Granted by Pope Gregory V to Werinfrid, Abbot

[Note: Suspect. Jaffé.]

(Year 996.)

It confirms all the possessions of the monastery and the right to elect an abbot, first from the monastery of Stavelot and then from that of Malmedy.

[In Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 52.]

[Col. 0906B]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and apostolic blessing to Werinfrid, religious abbot.

The summit of the highest apostolic dignity is recognized to shine forth with greater brilliance when, strengthened by the radiance of the divine, it strives to display more zeal in the contest of acquiring praise for God. For this reason, the duty of the apostolic pastoral solicitude entrusted to us compels us to proclaim generously whatever is recognized as belonging to the establishment of pious places and to confirm it by the censure of apostolic institution.

Therefore, because you, brother, asked us to fortify with the privilege of our authority the monasteries built by the venerable Father Remaclus in honour of Saint Peter—namely Stavelot and Malmedy, situated in the Ardennes forest—and because your petition appeared just to us, we grant you our assent through this enactment of our privilege, strengthen it by apostolic authority, and decree, according to the ancient edict of the kings Sigibert, Clovis, and Dagobert, who were also the founders of these monasteries, and likewise according to that of the emperors Charles, Louis, and Otto Augustus, that the defined places, villages, or possessions which those emperors gave to that saint and which he divided between the two churches are to serve the use of the monks. No advocate may infringe them in court proceedings or in military matters; whoever does so we strike with eternal anathema.

Furthermore, as those emperors determined, we decree that when monks from the two monasteries come together into one of them, they shall have complete freedom to elect an abbot according to the rule of Saint Benedict, without pretence, without exclusion of persons, and without regard to money. This condition nevertheless obtains, with the consent of the monks of Malmedy: since blessed Remaclus, founder of both monasteries and formerly bishop and shepherd of the people of Tongeren, preferred to choose for himself a place of burial in one of them, namely Stavelot, they are to have the first opportunity of election if a man of superior merit and greater probity is found among them.

But if the person to be placed over both sites is found not there but at Malmedy, he is to be admitted from that monastery rather than chosen from outside.

If anyone—which we do not wish—should presume with wicked audacity to oppose what we have established for the praise of God and the stability of the aforesaid monasteries, or to transgress it in any way, let him know that he is bound by anathema and is to be burned with the devil and his most dreadful pomp, and with Judas the traitor of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the fires of Tartarus.

But if anyone proves himself, with pious regard, a guardian and keeper of this apostolic enactment directed toward the worship of God, may he receive abundant mercy from our merciful God and deserve to become a possessor of blessed life.

Written by the hand of John, regional ink-notary of the holy Roman Church, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 996, in the ninth indiction, in the month of June, on the second day. Farewell in the Lord.

# IV. Bull of Pope Gregory V for the Monastery of Saint Martin at Tours

(Year 996.)

[In Mabillon, *De re diplomatica*, p. 659.]

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the brothers living in the monastery of Saint Martin, namely to Otto, dean of the distinguished flock of blessed Martin, our patron.

It has certainly and suitably become known to our ears how that same flock has lived up to the present and has possessed both royal privileges and those of our predecessors, the lords Adeodatus and Nicholas, so that, with the episcopal power of the city of Tours set aside, whatever was to be arranged, governed, or corrected within the aforesaid flock was held under the authority of the abbot of that monastery together with his provost, the dean, and the other most reputable men.

For this reason, a very great concern compels us to arrange whatever is recognized as belonging to the stability of noble places. Therefore, according to the ancient custom, it asks that we confirm for this venerable place, by the censure of apostolic institution, the privileges known to have been confirmed by our predecessors of holy memory, namely the lords Adeodatus and Nicholas, so that at the present time they might finally be confirmed for the same place by our apostolic authority.

Accordingly, yielding to your wishes, we sanction by apostolic authority the decrees of the institutions of the previous Fathers and strengthen them, following the apostolic norm. Therefore, supported by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, we decree and establish for your aforesaid monastery all the arrangements that have existed up to now, and that it may have a bishop there, as it has from ancient times. Through the preaching of that bishop, the people who come daily from various regions with devout minds to the threshold of the monastery of that holy confessor of Christ may receive remedies from the Creator of souls.

When the bishop of that holy place departs from this world, and another religious man has been elected by the abbot and the same community, he is to be ordained without any dispute by the neighbouring bishops, as has been customary, so that the length of the journey may not cause difficulty.

If, however—which may it not happen—those bishops, infected by ill will and envy, delay the ordination, then, by virtue of this licence and privilege, he is to be ordained without delay according to the custom, through this apostolic institution, with the testimony of his abbot and his own clergy, who are to bear in their own hands the written decree subscribed below. Thus the light that has shone there for so long through the bishop’s preaching must not in those times be diminished at all or—what would be impious—extinguished.

Nor may the metropolitan of the bishops dare to exercise authority over the venerable monastery aforesaid in the cells of that church, its titles, or its oratories established under its jurisdiction; nor may he perform ordinations there, come to prepare chrism, conduct inquiries, exercise coercion, or summon its priests to himself. Nor may any bishop sell the altars of their churches without their counsel.

Rather, by this authority of our privilege, the bishop from that venerable monastery is to exercise canonical pastoral care and the solicitude of his ministry over the leading and neighbouring venerable places named or subject to it. Whatever must be amended or corrected, he is to carry out in canonical fashion and according to due order, with the consent of his abbot.

If any disagreement—which we do not wish—arises between the neighbouring bishops or between them and the aforesaid bishop, no one may dare, without the abbot’s consent, to coerce or judge the bishop of the oft-mentioned monastery in any matter. If the abbot of that monastery is in no way able to settle the dispute among them, they are to bring it before our apostolic presence so that harmony may be restored.

Therefore, yielding both to the decree of royal generosity and to the wishes and prayers of so many faithful, we establish and confirm by decree of this holy Apostolic See that, as the text of this command contains, the dean, priests, and clergy of that monastery shall possess perpetually and in full all the property granted to them by royal gift, together with all its appurtenances. No person in authority may presume to take anything from their lordship or possession, in which the royal dignity has decided to bestow the benefit of its mercy upon the brothers dwelling in the monastery of blessed Martin.

Under apostolic censure, invoking the divine judgment and imposing anathema, we establish that none of our future pontifical successors, no person endowed with any dignity or power, and no other person, great or small, may ever presume to act against this apostolic privilege and command of ours. Rather, we decree that it remain most firm and stable throughout his time.

If anyone at any time—which we in no way believe—should attempt to violate this decree of privilege, confirmed by apostolic authority, either in whole or in part, and fail to correct his presumption by worthy amendment, let him know that, by the authority of my lord blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, he is bound by the bond of anathema, alienated from the kingdom of God, assigned to the punishment of eternal fire with the devil and his most dreadful pomp, and subjected to perpetual condemnation.

But may he who proves himself an observer and guardian of this apostolic privilege of ours deserve to obtain from our most merciful Lord God the grace of blessing and eternal life.

Written by the hand of Peter, notary and archivist of the holy Roman Church, in the month of September and the tenth indiction.

Given on the third day before the Kalends of October, through the hand of John, bishop and librarian of the holy Apostolic See, in the first year of the pontificate of the lord Gregory V, pope, and in the first year of the reign of the lord Otto III, crowned by God, great emperor.

# V. Consecration of the Church of Saint Prosper

Performed by Gregory V in 997. The following verses were placed on the church wall as a memorial of his generosity.

[In Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, vol. II, p. 270.]

[Col. 0909B]

Bishop Teuzo founded this present church  
And established it for the honour of Saint Prosper.  
To it he transferred the venerable bones  
Of that saint, together with Pope Gregory,  
Fifth in name, who at that time was perhaps  
Travelling to the city of Ticinum  
To conduct there the business of a sacred council.  
The pontiff …, followed by a great crowd,  
Teuzo received them with a father's hospitality beneath his roof;  
The younger prelate John himself had come,  
Destined to depart there from the see of Ravenna.

[Col. 0909C]

Asked by the aforementioned Teuzo,  
With these men he himself made this temple sacred.  
The house, consecrated to so many and such great patrons,  
Here holds, O gentle Prosper, your body.  
With it, the bones of blessed Venerius were also raised  
And laid within the side of this church.

These things were done, by God’s gift, while Otto III rules,  
And on the ninth day of the Kalends of February.  
[The printed reading is *nova*; it is corrected here to *nono*, “ninth.”]

# VI. Privilege of Pope Gregory V for the Church of Ravenna

(Year 997.)

[Coquelines, *Bullarum privilegiorum amplissima collectio*, I, 292.]

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend and holy fellow-bishop John, archbishop of the holy Church of Ravenna, and through that same holy Church of Ravenna to its successors, the archbishops, for ever.

Since the condition of all the ecclesiastical churches of God is advanced by the teachings of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and whatever has fallen is restored through his support, it is fitting that the holy Church of Ravenna, which has suffered a diminution of its diocese and been deprived of the abundance of its dignities, should be restored so promptly that it may not even lose the name of metropolitan church.

Therefore, recognizing that it has been overturned in every respect, we ought to extend our helping hand toward its restoration, so that, refreshed from the fountain of blessed Peter the apostle, it may, with Christ’s help, be restored to its honours.

Therefore let all worshippers of the holy churches of God and all the faithful know that John, archbishop of that holy Church of Ravenna, represented to our apostolic fatherhood that we should confirm to him the commands issued for the holy Church of Ravenna and granted and conceded to it by our predecessors, the pontiffs, who were his predecessors.

Moved by his prayers, inflamed by divine love and by that of blessed Apollinaris, pontiff and martyr of Christ, we have graciously inclined toward him and confirm and establish these things for ever, without any diminution, according to the ancient custom of the aforesaid holy Church of Ravenna.

Therefore we confirm to you, John, archbishop of Ravenna, and through you to the aforesaid Church of Ravenna, and to your successors in that church for ever, the following:

We confirm and strengthen the monastery built in honour of blessed Hilary in the territory called Galicata, with its defined boundaries, namely all its property, all its rights, and all judicial authority to be exercised over the inhabitants of the aforesaid territory. On one side of the territory of Galicata lies Massa Balneo, which belongs to Saint Peter, and the county of Bobbio; on the second side are the Alpine ridges, the boundary of Tuscany; on the third side is the county of Populonia; and on the fourth side is Fagentella, with the river Rap… running along it.

Thus you, John, archbishop, and your successors for ever, shall have the power … over the same monastery of Saint Hilary … together with the authority and public obligations of the aforesaid territory, in whatever way it may seem better to you according to …, to order and dispose of them, without contradiction from us or any of our successors.

Furthermore, we grant, confirm, and strengthen to you, and through you to the aforesaid Church of Ravenna and your successors for ever, the estate called Fiscalia, with all judicial authority and public obligations and with its defined boundaries: on one side, Ariell …, the transverse boundary called …; on the second side, the boundary of Deonorum running into the Po; on the third side, the Po running as far as half the estate called Latus; and on the fourth side … running as far as the estate called Ustuladum.

We also confirm to you, and through you to the same holy Church of Ravenna and your successors for ever, all judicial authority in the place and parish called “Deer’s Horn,” with its defined boundaries.

Furthermore, we confirm and strengthen to you, John, archbishop, two monasteries situated within the city of Rimini: one founded in honour of Saint Thomas the apostle, the other in honour of Saint Euphemia the martyr, with all their property, both within that city and outside it … which same monasteries your church appears to hold by a deed of donation … of Martin, deacon of that church, and Countess Henglerada … and especially by the emperors’ grants. Both these monasteries and the other places belonging by right to the aforesaid deacon are confirmed perpetually to your holy church.

Likewise, all residents and tenants of the aforesaid Church of Ravenna, whether living in the county of Adria, Ferrara, or Comacchio, are to remain exempt from public tax and compulsory service. Rather, they are to render every tax and compulsory service perpetually to you and your successors, the archbishops, and carry out whatever is imposed upon them by the officials of the holy Church of Ravenna.

We also grant and confirm to you … the people living in the fortress … so that they may perform no public service except for you and your successors, under this stipulated condition: no duke, count, viscount, *castaldus* … or any other person, great or small, may impose upon or exact from the aforesaid tenants and residents any public service or compulsory labour … But let them remain secure and undisturbed in all things under your protection and authority, as stated above.

We further establish that the holy Church of Ravenna, with its subject churches, like the most blessed Roman Church, which by God’s authority we serve, may in no way be excluded from its property except after the course of one hundred years.

Moreover, from the river Punctari, with the Argenta marsh and everything belonging to it—fisheries, lands, bird-catching, hunting, both banks with all the buildings situated on the aforesaid river—as far as the sea-port, and also the port of Volana, as far as the place called Cervia, with all its shores, woods, and whatever instruments are stored there, we confirm these things for ever to you and your successors.

We also grant to your Church of Ravenna all stones and rocks, both above and below ground, placed outside works in public buildings, for you and your successors to use and work as they judge beneficial to that church.

Finally, we grant and confirm that no priest residing at Ravenna, nor anyone from the household of the same holy Church of Ravenna, shall be charged or presumed to be charged with any toll, transport duty, or *siliquaticum* throughout Emilia and the Pentapolis.

Establishing and promulgating this before God and his terrible future judgment …, through this document of our apostolic privilege we decree, and by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, we determine and solemnly charge both the future pontiffs of the Apostolic See and those who administer ecclesiastical services, as well as persons great and small and everyone endowed with whatever dignity, concerning all the chapters stated above that have been granted or confirmed by us: they shall in no way have permission to separate the places mentioned above, joined into one and specifically linked by this written page of apostolic authority, or to alienate one from another.

If anyone—which we do not believe—should attempt with rash audacity to oppose what has been piously and firmly established by this authority of ours through this privilege, or to transgress it in any way, let him know that by the authority of blessed Peter the apostle he is bound by the bond of anathema and assigned, with Judas the traitor, to the punishment of eternal fire.

Moreover, let him know that he must pay thirty pounds of refined gold to the holy Church of Ravenna.

But may he who proves himself, with pious regard, an observer in all things, guarding the provisions of this privilege and directing them toward the worship of God, deserve to become abundantly a participant in the grace of blessing and eternal life from our most merciful Lord God, and remain joined with all the saints.

Written by the hand of Peter, regional notary and archivist of the holy Roman Church, in the month of January and the tenth indiction.

[Note: From the statute concerning the day of Pope Gregory’s election, it is clear that the reading must be *indict. X*, as it stands, and not XI. Everything agrees properly.]

Farewell in the Lord.

Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of February, through the hand of John, bishop of the holy Alban Church and librarian of the holy Apostolic See, in the first year of the pontificate of the lord Gregory, pope, and in the first year of the empire of the lord Otto III, Augustus emperor, in the month of January.

# VII. Privilege Granted by Pope Gregory V to Hatto, Abbot of Fulda

(Year 997.)

[Dronke, *Codex diplomaticus Fuldensis*, p. 340.]

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God.

Let it be known to all the faithful, present and future, how, on account of the merit of his dignity, our devotion did not deny to the venerable Hatto, abbot of the Church of Fulda, what the piety of our predecessor had granted.

Therefore, because he petitioned us, we judged it worthy to renew and confirm for that venerable place and the aforesaid church the grant of our predecessor.

For our venerable predecessor consecrated the aforesaid abbot at Rome and, when he undertook the yoke of due submission, granted him permission to celebrate Mass with the dalmatic and sandals.

Considering this, and because he serves our Roman Church more specially than others like him, we have decided that he should be endowed with a more distinguished privilege. Therefore, without any contradiction, by our apostolic authority we grant that he may celebrate Mass with the dalmatic and sandals and may be marked by such a pledge of submission to our Roman Church.

Written by the hand of Peter, regional notary and archivist of the holy Roman Church, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 997, in the month of February, in the tenth indiction. Farewell in the Lord.

Given on the seventh day before the Ides of February, through the hand of John, bishop of the holy Alban Church and librarian of the holy Apostolic See.

# VIII. Letter of Pope Gregory V to the Emperor Otto

(Year 997.)

[In Miraeus, *Opera diplomatica*, III, 563.]

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Otto, Augustus, emperor of the Romans …

Therefore we judged it right and worthy that the honour and power of imperial government should be strengthened paternally by apostolic authority, and to give worthy thanks to God for all the good will and all the benefits granted by imperial authority to this holy place.

And therefore, because you ask us to confirm and strengthen by our generosity and authority the place and Church at the palace of Aachen, begun with good foundations through your devotion, we do so.

And so that these beginnings, which have been well made, may reach an even better conclusion, we grant to the aforesaid Church a distinguished congregation of Catholic clerics … and commend that they live according to a rule.

Furthermore, through the document of our command we establish and decree irrevocably that seven cardinal deacons and seven cardinal priests serve this Church in their ministry. This is under the following condition: no person of any dignity may celebrate Mass upon the sacred altar of the Mother of God established there, except the aforesaid seven cardinal priests, the archbishop of that place, and the bishop of Liège who presides over that diocese.

We firmly confirm this also by anathema, and so forth.

Given in the year 997, in the month of February, in the tenth indiction, on the sixth day before the Ides of February, through the hand of John, bishop of the Church of Saint Alban and librarian of the holy Apostolic See, in the first year of the pontificate of Pope Gregory V and the third year of the reign of the emperor Otto.

[Note: A similar privilege existed in the metropolitan church of Cologne, in which “no one except the seven cardinal priests may perform the divine mysteries.” Thus Pope Leo IX, supreme pontiff, established it in the year 1052.]

# IX. Letter of Pope Gregory V to Willegis, Archbishop of Mainz

(Year 997.)

[In Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae*, III, 694.]

[Col. 0913C]

Gregory, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and apostolic blessing to his beloved fellow-bishop Willegis, archbishop and our vicar.

Please call to mind the decrees of the synod of Pavia, which I, although unworthy, subscribed, together with the archbishop of Ravenna, the archbishop of Milan, and our other fellow-bishops; and devote your assistance so that these decrees may produce beneficial results.

1. It pleased the holy synod that all the western bishops who were present at the deposition of Archbishop Arnulf [Col. 0913D], and who, although summoned under fixed postponements, spurned the synod of Pavia and sent improper cases through a lay person to confound the synod, be suspended from episcopal office. Adelbero, bishop of Laon, who also seized and handed over his own metropolitan, shall be suspended from episcopal office. This was decreed by the authority of Pope Julius, who likewise judged the eastern bishops who refused to come to the synod guilty of deposition, but held those who had been deposed without apostolic authority to remain innocent.

2. It was also decreed that King Robert, who, contrary to the apostolic prohibition, took his kinswoman [Col. 0914A] in marriage, be summoned to make satisfaction, together with the bishops who consented to this incestuous marriage. If they should refuse, let them be deprived of communion.

3. Likewise, the holy synod decreed that the Neapolitan usurper, who caused the archbishop of that place to be seized and had himself installed in the same see through the heresy of simony, be anathematized unless he makes satisfaction.

4. It also decreed that if any bishop, presbyter, deacon, or cleric, while the pope is safe and without consulting him, should attempt either to lend his signature for the Roman pontificate, or to promise a payment, or to give an oath, or to promise any definite support, he shall be deprived of the dignity of his office and of the communion of all the faithful [Col. 0914B], and shall be anathematized.

The synod of Pope Symmachus: The holy synod decreed that no one presume to sell the gift of the Holy Spirit, or to accept money for the consecration of any bishop, presbyter, deacon, or person of any other order; and let the one who gives, the one who receives, and the intermediary be anathema.

5. It also pleased everyone that Bishop Gisilharius [Note: [Col. 0914D] of Merseburg and Magdeburg], who, contrary to the canons, abandoned his own see and invaded another, be summoned to Rome for Christmas and come to make satisfaction; but if he should refuse, let him be suspended from priestly office.

6. We also inform you that, by the common consent of the brethren, we have separated Crescentius, the usurper and plunderer of the Holy Roman Church, from the bosom of the holy Church and from the communion of all the faithful [Col. 0914C]; and we earnestly ask that each of you in his own episcopate give charitable assent to this action.

I, Gregory, bishop of the holy Catholic and apostolic Roman Church, have subscribed.

I, John, archbishop of the holy Church of Ravenna, have subscribed.

Landulf, archbishop of the holy Church of Milan, has subscribed.

Wido, bishop of the Church of Pavia, has subscribed.

John, bishop of the Church of Albano, has subscribed.

Blinwarmund, bishop of the holy Church of Hippo [Col. 0914D], has subscribed.

Sigifred, bishop of the holy Church of Parma, has subscribed.

John, bishop of the Church of Modena. Adam, bishop of the Church of Turin, has subscribed.

Andrew, bishop of the Church of Lodi. John, bishop of the Church of Genoa.

Constantine, bishop of the holy Church of Alba.

Albert, bishop of the holy Church of Brescia.

Liutifred, bishop of the Church of Tortona, has subscribed.

## X. Pope Gregory V’s Bull for the Monastery of Subiaco (997)

[In Muratori, *Antiquitates Italicae*, vol. I, p. 943.]

[Col. 0915A]

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the most reverend and most prudent Peter, presbyter and monk, and most accomplished abbot of the venerable monastery of the holy confessor and father Benedict and of his holy virgin sister Scholastica, situated at Subiaco, and to you and your successors serving there or entering there, forever.

If things that accord with pious desires must always be granted, then surely those recognized as pertaining to the prerogative of divine worship must not be refused at all, because they are not merely to be requested from their benefactors [Col. 0915B], but are without doubt to be demanded in the name of charity. You therefore asked us to grant or confirm to your religious community the aforesaid monastery of Saint Benedict and Saint Scholastica, situated at Subiaco, together with its cells and monasteries, along with its tower and all their furnishings, together with the cave where the most blessed Benedict led an eremitical life, with everything within and around it, including the crypts and all the human-built structures that now exist there; and also the lake with its fisheries and mills, together with the water called Palaneto flowing out from it, with its fisheries and mills, and carrying that water to the place called Mandra. Likewise, its mills and fisheries, extending as far as the place called Ferrata, all joined together in their entirety.

By our authority, all these things are to be confirmed to your monastery, so that no person, great or small, should ever dare, in the water called Timida, or in the water called Augusta, or in the water called Bullica, or in the Flumicello, or in the water of Roccanellum, or in the water called Cona, or in any water throughout the entire territory of Subiaco, or in any of those places, to establish such a mill by any device without the consent of the abbot of the same monastery. Whoever does this shall cause that very mill to accrue to the aforesaid monastery and shall be liable to pay two pounds of refined gold in our palace.

We also confirm to you, to be held in its entirety, the castle called Subiaco, with all its appurtenances and adjoining properties, with all its jurisdiction and donations, together with its acorn tax and pasture tax, and all its public obligations, just as they are customarily paid annually in our palace. We also confirm to you in its entirety the mountain for the construction of a castle called Augusta, and the mountain called Cervaria, with all their appurtenances in their entirety.

Furthermore, the castle called Arsule, and likewise the castle called Anticulum: each castle with its churches, cells, houses within and outside it, vineyards, lands, fields, meadows, pastures, woods, willow groves, trees, fruit-bearing trees, whether of various kinds fruitful or unfruitful, wells, springs, streams, and rivers, with mills, chestnut groves, and marshes, with mountains and hills, shores and appurtenances, cultivated and uncultivated, empty and occupied, together with everything generally and in its entirety belonging to the aforesaid monastery or castles in the territory of Tibur and Subiaco, as marked out and indicated by boundaries [Col. 0916A].

Beginning at the Emperor’s Gate, from which the river overflows, then proceeding to the mountain called Romani and straight to Campolongum, continuing by a direct route to Pereto, where the church of Saint Peter is; from there coming to Staffile, which stands at Camposacro; from there proceeding and arriving at the Arch of Saint George, and thus reaching the mountain of Flaontino; descending from that mountain and arriving at the water also called Ferrata; following that water until it reaches the Arch of Aquaferrata, and along that water until its course ends in the river Tiber [Col. 0916B]; crossing that river and ascending the mountain called Crofeo, which properly belongs to your monastery. From there, over the summits of the mountains, through the hollows of the valleys and the caves of the rocks, it proceeds to the mountains called Gemini; and thus descends to Fenestrelle, and from there reaches the stream called Trave, and descending along that same stream to another stream of Cona, at the place called Crucis; ascending along Cona itself to the place called Oraru; from there again ascending the mountain also called Aquaviva, straight to the Terranean Bridge, and descending along that river as far as the Emperor’s Rock, and from there to Mount Romano.

The city also called Carsoli, with its churches and houses within it in their entirety, and outside it under various names—villages, vineyards, estates, and farmsteads—with streams and mills, with all its appurtenances and adjoining properties, just as your ancient privileges contain them, shall likewise be confirmed to you in all respects, situated within the Reatine, Cicolano, and Marsican territories [Col. 0916C]. Finally, we also confirm to you in its entirety the castle now called Trillano, together with the hill of Ferrari, Monasterellum, and Sassa, or whatever they are called by other names, with their villages, estates and farmsteads, vineyards, lands, fields, meadows, and pastures, and with all their appurtenances, extending as far as Pisciscano.

And the entire estate called Ursano and Sambuci, with the church of Saint Thomas situated in the desert, and the mountain called Gurdiano in its entirety [Col. 0916D], with its estates and farmsteads, together with half of the place called Ylice; and the place called Castaniola, with its vineyards, lands, and every appurtenance; and in that boundary there is the mountain called Buberano, in its entirety, together with the other names and appurtenances.

Again, we also confirm to you in its entirety the castle called Ampolloni, with its churches and houses within it in every respect, and outside it with its vineyards, lands, estates, farmsteads, and everything belonging to that castle. In addition, the place called Pentoma, with everything belonging to it in its entirety; and also half of the widely known castle of Saint Pamphimus, together with half of all its appurtenances. Moreover, the castle of Collemalo [Col. 0917A] in its entirety.

Likewise, the place also called Romani in its entirety; and half of the village called Papi, together with its estates and farmsteads, vineyards and lands, fields, meadows, pastures, woods, willow groves, springs, and streams, with mills, and with everything generally and in its entirety belonging to each of the places and names. All the places already mentioned are situated in the territory of Tibur.

Moreover, we also confirm to you and your successors the cell of Saint Barbara, which is inside the city of Tibur, in its entirety, with the houses and cells within it, with its mills inside that same city and outside it, with estates and farmsteads, vineyards and lands, fields, meadows, pastures, and woods, with all its appurtenances and adjoining properties.

Likewise, within this nourishing city of Rome [Col. 0917B], we confirm to you the cell of Saint Erasmus, situated on the Caelian Hill, with its houses, wine cellar, and hayloft, with the gardens and vineyards around it, with olive trees and various kinds of fruit trees, and with the remaining vineyards and farmsteads; namely, the meadow situated outside the Salarian Bridge, and the farmstead situated at Aquario, and another farmstead called Quinto; and in the territory of Albano, the vineyards situated from the crypt called . . . . . . . at Silice Albanense, and in the place called Zinzinni, or in various places and under various names, wherever they may be found or discovered through any series of documents as belonging to that pious and venerable place, shall always remain under your jurisdiction, from the present tenth indiction and forever, for you and your successors, the abbots, to govern with fear and administer according to the rule.

It was fitting that you implore our reverence to fortify the aforesaid monastery of Saint Benedict and Saint Scholastica by an instrument of apostolic authority, and to confirm by perpetual right all its possessions and appurtenances so that they might remain inviolable. Therefore, yielding to your prayers, by this document of our command we establish and decree that all the urban or rural places—that is, estates, farmsteads, or castles—various cultivated or uncultivated properties situated in the places and under the names set out or mentioned above, just as they were granted to the same venerable place by pontiffs, kings, or God-fearing persons, or justly came into its possession by other means, and just as the aforesaid monastery held them [Col. 0917D] in the times of our predecessors, the popes Gregory, Zachary, and Nicholas of holy memory, shall now also be able to possess them in great security and tranquility [Col. 0918A]. You, likewise, for your venerable monastery, and your successors, the abbots, shall possess and hold them, enjoy perpetual jurisdiction over them and defend them, and may they perpetually contribute to the benefit of that pious place.

Therefore, under the solemn appeal to divine judgment, we promulgate and decree that no person of any public rank, whether man or woman, or any other person of whatever dignity, great or small, should ever presume in any way to exercise jurisdiction over the aforesaid monastery or over its castles, estates, farmsteads, cultivated or uncultivated properties, waters, mills, and fisheries, or over any possession or other property that you appear to hold anywhere; nor should anyone presume to remove or seize any of these things from that place, or by any device or contrivance inflict any injury or malicious opposition upon the monastery of the blessed Benedict or upon all the things annexed to it and belonging to it as set out above [Col. 0918B].

Rather, in accordance with perpetual right, as has been set forth above, let everything prosper in the same venerable monastery, and let the power and authority to administer and possess remain perpetually with you and all your successors, the abbots.

But if anyone—which we do not wish—should attempt with reckless audacity to act or litigate against the text of this apostolic command of ours, piously promulgated by us, let him know that he is bound by the chain of the anathema of our Lord and of the prince of the apostles, Peter, and that he is to be burned in eternal fire with the devil and his most savage punishments, and with Judas, the betrayer of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ [Col. 0918C], and at the same time plunged into the abyss and Tartarean chaos and punished with the impious.

But whoever, with pious regard, proves to be a guardian, obedient, and observer of this salutary command of ours, may he deserve to obtain from the just Judge, our Lord, the grace of blessing and the eternal joys of heavenly recompense, and become a participant in eternal life.

Written by the hand of Benedict, notary of the Holy Roman Church, in the month of September, in the tenth indiction.

Farewell.

Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of July, through the hands of John, bishop of the holy Church of Albano and librarian of the supreme and apostolic see, in the first year, by God’s favor, of the pontificate of the lord Gregory V, supreme pontiff and universal [Col. 0918D] pope, in the sacred see of the blessed apostle Peter, in the first year, in the tenth indiction.

[Note: [Col. 0917D] Ughelli, having this very bull before his eyes, inserted John into the catalogue of the bishops of Albano under the year 828, in volume I of *Italia Sacra*. But he is mistaken. These letters belong not to Gregory IV but indeed to Gregory V—if, that is, you consider them free from every suspicion of forgery. For the indiction does not agree with the first year of Pope Gregory IV. Nevertheless, an error could easily have crept into the copy, so that the scribe may have read X for V; these letters can readily be confused with one another and are nearly alike in form. But since it is clear from Mabillon’s *Annals* and from the Subiaco Chronicle that Peter, abbot of Subiaco, flourished in the year 997; and since, again, Ciampini in the *Catalogue of the Libraries of the Holy Roman Church* and Ughelli himself in his account of the bishops of Albano assure us that in the same year John flourished as bishop of Albano and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, the evidence suggests that this bull should be referred to Gregory V, who ascended the chair of Peter at that time; and that Gregory V should be written in place of Gregory IV. He, however, was elected pope in May of the year 996, in the ninth indiction. Therefore another error must occur in this bull, and either “in the second year” or “in the ninth indiction” should be written. Meanwhile, note the words: “shall be liable to pay two pounds of refined gold in our palace.”]

## XI. Gregory’s Letter to John, Archbishop of Ravenna (997)

It restores the Church of Piacenza and subordinates Montefeltro.

[In Mansi, *Councils*, vol. XIX, col. 200.]

[Col. 0919A]

To our beloved son John, venerable archbishop of the holy Church of Ravenna, and to your successors, the archbishops, forever.

Hoping that the rewards of divine recompense and the labors of our good action may, by the eternal hand, produce fruit, we have deemed it fitting to devote ourselves with joyful mind to every service of divine worship, especially in restoring churches which we have seen dedicated by our predecessors to the use of divine service [Col. 0919B]. Therefore, also considering all the heresies that have miserably arisen in the holy Catholic Church, we, with paternal love, come to the aid of the holy Church of Ravenna, of you, John, its venerable archbishop, and of your successors forever, judging these matters worthy of being cut away.

We permanently restore to you and your successors the Church of Piacenza, unjustly taken from you by my predecessor and assigned, contrary to the canons, under the title of an archbishopric.

Moreover, you also requested from our apostolate that, for the love of almighty God, for the benefit of our soul, and for the welfare of the kingdom of our lord Otto III, the invincible emperor Augustus, we should grant the bishopric of Montefeltro in its entirety, as a gift from us, under the jurisdiction of the holy Church of Ravenna, and permanently fortify you and your successors with the privilege of our apostolic authority, so that from now on you may consecrate as bishop whomever you wish.

Therefore, yielding to your prayers, for the honor of the holy Church of Ravenna and the stability of that venerable place, we decree that the aforementioned venerable bishopric of Montefeltro, with all its integrity—that is, its churches, chapels, houses, farmsteads, courts, estates, colonies, abbeys, cells, lands, vineyards, meadows, pastures, servants of both sexes, and everything legally belonging to the jurisdiction of that bishopric—shall remain safe and entirely undisturbed under the protection of the jurisdiction of the holy see of Ravenna, without any contradiction from anyone [Col. 0919C].

Accordingly, we confirm and decree that the bishop who is appointed to that bishopric at any given time by you or your successors shall render submission without any contradiction; and that the other suffragans shall obey in all things for the advancement of your church. Moreover, under the solemn appeal to divine judgment, we threaten, command, and prescribe that no emperor or king, duke or margrave, should presume in any way to harm you or your successors because of the aforesaid consecration. Rather, from the present tenth indiction onward and forever, you and your successors shall, by our concession and according to ecclesiastical custom, consecrate as bishop in the aforesaid bishopric whomever you may wish to choose [Col. 0920A], with all human opposition removed.

Establishing this by apostolic censure under the solemn appeal to divine judgment and under threat of anathema, we decree that if anyone, of whatever power, should presume with reckless audacity to act against this privilege of apostolic confirmation, or attempt to seize from the jurisdiction of the holy Church of Ravenna the aforesaid bishopric, gift, or right of consecration, unless he repents and accepts these admonitions of ours, then by the authority of God and of us he shall not only be bound by the chains of anathema but shall remain alienated from the kingdom of God. But whoever proves to be a true guardian and observer may deserve to obtain from the Lord the grace of blessing.

Written by the hand of Peter, notary and regional officer [Col. 0920B] of the Holy Roman Church, in the month of July, in the aforementioned tenth indiction. Given on the seventh day before the Ides of July, through the hands of John, bishop of the holy Church of Albano and librarian of the holy apostolic see.

## XI. Pope Gregory V’s Letter to Abbo, Abbot of Fleury (997)

[In Mabillon, *Benedictine Annals*, IV, 107.]

To the especially venerable lord Abbo, abbot, Gregory, servant of the servants of God, greetings in Christ.

Because the bearer of your letter was hurrying to return as quickly as possible, I was scarcely able to prevail upon him to delay for the duration of the evening office. Therefore, using brevity, I offer thanks for your ever-new benevolence toward me [Col. 0920C], asking, as you instructed, that you send us at present Brother R., who may report to us on your well-being, on the king’s promise [Note: [Col. 0919D] This promise of King Robert perhaps concerned his divorce from Queen Bertha, his relative, whom he had married contrary to ecclesiastical regulations. The archbishop of Canterbury, whose safety troubled the pontiff, is Ælfric, who may at that time have been ill.], and on the safety of the archbishop of Canterbury.

I ask one thing: that you send from your missal books an excellent one, so that whenever I see it amid the solemnities of Mass, I may remember my special friend and never prove ungrateful for your benefaction. Farewell.

## XIII. Pope Gregory V’s Privilege for the Abbey of Saint Ambrose (997)

[In Mansi, *Councils*, vol. XIX, 203.]

[Col. 0920D]

After our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, for our redemption, deigned to appear from the Virgin’s womb—being true God before the ages and true man at the end of the ages—he granted to the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, the power of binding and loosing in heaven and on earth, and also granted the opening of the gates of the heavenly kingdom; he deigned to establish the Church upon the solidity of faith, according to his truthful word: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it; and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and whatever you bind [Col. 0921A] on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew 16).

After those who most sincerely serve God as his vicars, free from the thickness of clouds, had worthily received such great power and had assumed the care of universal governance, among them the mercy of almighty God also deigned to number our smallness, we wished to make known to all believers that, by this privilege of our authority, we most fully confirm the abbey established in honor of the renowned confessor of Christ, Ambrose, and of the venerable martyrs Protasius and Gervasius, where their sacred bodies are buried, together with all its churches, oratories, courts, estates, and districts belonging to it [Col. 0921B], namely Basiliano, Monte Feliciano, Leveniano, Ceresola, Lemonta, Capiate, Oleoducto, Campilioni, Anticiaco, Colonia, Verederio, Cavenaco, Villa Alba, and Cugniano, and together with everything belonging to the aforesaid abbey.

The order is that the monks of that monastery, together with the abbot who now is or who shall be in the future, may have, hold, and possess the aforesaid churches, oratories, courts, estates, male and female slaves, male and female Aldiones, without contradiction from any person, great or small, and may distribute them for their use and expense as they judge best, by our apostolic authority granting this.

But if anyone—which we do not believe—should in the future, at the devil’s prompting, attempt to act against the firmness of this apostolic concession of ours, and should disturb the monks of the aforesaid monastery in any of the things we have granted to them, let him be a dreadful anathema from the three hundred and eighteen Fathers, let him be consigned to flames through the fraudulent collusion of Judas and Ananias, and let him be accursed now and in the future by the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and by the blessed apostle Peter; let him remain perpetually bound by the guilt of the offense, and be expelled from the Catholic Church until he has endeavored to appease, with worthy satisfaction, the monks of the aforesaid abbey and their Father.

Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of May, through the hands of John, bishop of the holy Church of Albano and librarian of the holy apostolic see; in the second year, by God’s favor, of the pontificate of the lord Gregory, supreme pontiff and universal Pope V, in the most sacred see of the blessed apostle Peter [Col. 0921D]; while the lord Otto III, crowned by God, the great and peaceful emperor, was reigning, in his second year, in the month and indiction written above, the eleventh.

Written by the hands of Peter, notary and scriniary of the Holy Roman Church, in the month of April and in the eleventh indiction. P. Farewell.

## XIV. Pope Gregory V’s Letter to Gerbert, Archbishop of Ravenna (997)

He sends the pallium, adorns the Church of Ravenna with many privileges, and enlarges it with many gifts.

[In Mansi, *Councils*, vol. XIX, 201.]

[Col. 0922A]

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Gerbert, archbishop of the holy Church of Ravenna, our spiritual son, and through you to that same church and to all your successors, the archbishops, forever.

Because, moved by the benevolence of the apostolic see and by zeal for ancient custom, we have placed your fraternity over the Church of Ravenna, we have judged it fitting to confer upon you the insignia of the prelates of that church, together with the use of the pallium, which you are to use at specific times and in specific ways, just as you know that your predecessors used it.

We nevertheless admonish you that, just as you rejoice to have received from us the use of this distinction and the honor of the priestly office, so also you should strive to adorn the priesthood received in Christ by the integrity of your character and actions. For you will be conspicuous in a corresponding honor if the goodness of the mind agrees with the attire of the body, so that, outwardly well ordered and inwardly upright, you may truly say to God with the prophet: “I set God [more correctly: ‘God’ (*Deum*), HARD.] always before me, for he is at my right hand, so that I shall never be shaken” (Psalm 15).

But so that you may recognize the sweetness of the charity founded in us, from our free generosity, after the death of the empress Augusta Adelaide, we give to you and your church the district of the city of Ravenna, the entire riverbank, the mint, the toll, the market, the walls, and all the gates of the city.

If, however, other privileges granted to anyone should appear to be binding upon the holy Church and contrary to this privilege of ours, we have judged by the authority of God and Saint Peter that they are to be reduced to nothing; and what we are doing we establish and command to remain untouched [Col. 0922C].

We also give to you and to your holy church the county of Comacchio after the death of the empress Augusta Adelaide, so that you, your holy church, and your successors may freely hold and administer it forever, together with everything belonging to it.

And so that what has been well done may be well preserved and strengthened for the better, we confirm to you, your holy Church of Ravenna, and your successors the privilege granted by our benevolence to your predecessor John, together with the churches of Montefeltro and Cervia and everything that we granted to him, and we decree that it remain perpetually intact: namely, the monastery of the apostle Saint Thomas and of the martyr Euphemia, with all their property in its entirety, and with all their cultivated and uncultivated goods and possessions [Col. 0922D], situated both in the city of Rimini and outside it, specifically in the counties of Pesaro, Rimini, and Montefeltro.

All these things your church and your predecessors have held for a hundred years already, and, by God’s grace, you hold them peacefully: namely, the castle called Ligabizzi, with all its appurtenances, and the court of Saint Hermetes, with the aforesaid church and its farmsteads and appurtenances; namely, the castle called Galliola, with all its appurtenances; and also the fortress called Granariolo, with all its goods and possessions.

And the castle called Montecorlino, with all its integrity; and also the entire castle called Crucis, with all its goods and possessions [Col. 0923A].

And so that the fatherhood of our goodness may, with the greatest affection and abundance in Christ, nourish the filial devotion of your piety, by the authority of almighty God and of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, we confirm, establish, and command to remain unshaken, by this privilege of ours, the charter concerning the bishopric of Reggio, with all its adjoining properties, granted by the venerable Otto Augustus to you, your church, and your successors, so that you and your successors may freely hold, defend, govern, and administer it to the honor of God.

We also confirm to you and to your church, and give it forever, Cesena with everything belonging to it; and by apostolic authority we command that from below the highway as far as the sea no one dare exercise any district jurisdiction or hunting rights unless you or your successors have ordered it. Rather, without disturbance from anyone, you may exercise authority over everything there and issue commands for your honor and benefit [Col. 0923B].

All privileges formerly conferred upon your church by our predecessors, and all commands granted by kings or emperors out of regard for God, we confirm and strengthen by this privilege of ours, in accordance with God’s will and the authority of Saint Peter, and we desire and command that they remain valid forever.

Therefore, if anyone should attempt with reckless audacity to act against the provisions piously and firmly established by this privilege of ours, let him know that by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, whose office we unworthily exercise, he is bound by the chain of anathema and is to be burned in the fire of eternal punishment with the devil and Judas the betrayer [Col. 0923C]; and thus let him be irremediably ensnared, so that he may never be released from the bonds of anathema.

But whoever proves to be an observer of all these things, preserving the authority of this apostolic constitution of ours, which looks toward the worship of our God, may receive in abundance the grace of blessing from our most merciful God and become a participant in eternal life.

Written by the hands of Peter, notary and scriniary of the Holy Roman Church, in the month of April, indiction XI. Farewell.

Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of May, through the hand of John, bishop of the holy Church of Albano and librarian of the holy apostolic see, in the second year of the pontificate of the lord Gregory [Col. 0923D], supreme pontiff and universal pope, in the most sacred see of the blessed apostle Peter, in his second year, while the lord Otto III, crowned by God, the great and peaceful emperor, was reigning, in his second year, in the month and indiction written above.

## XV. Pope Gregory V’s Letter to Alphano, Archbishop of Benevento (998)

[In Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, II, 353.]

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Alphano, most beloved and most reverend archbishop of the holy Church of Benevento, greetings in the Lord.
