Since the summit of the highest apostolic dignity is recognized to shine forth in the splendor of divine advancement [Col. 0924A], and strives to offer the contest of its labor in celebrating the praises of God, the proper concern of that same apostolic pastoral care has compelled us to promulgate whatever pertains to the stability of pious places and to confirm it by the censure of apostolic institution.

Therefore, because you asked us, venerable archbishop, to grant to you and your successors forever the entire archbishopric of the holy Church of Benevento, over which by God’s favor you preside, and to confirm everything granted by our predecessor, the lord John, most holy pope, at the request of the lord Otto, the invincible emperor, by privilege to your predecessor Landulf, archbishop of that see, we, favoring your pious desires [Col. 0924B], by this authority of ours commit to fulfillment what is requested of us through the intervention of the lord Emperor Otto, granting to you and your successors the right to retain the use of the pallium, as it is written.

Moreover, we grant to your fraternity and to your successors the right, in the aforesaid diocese, in the places where bishops formerly existed, to consecrate bishops forever, who shall be subject to your authority; namely, at Termoli, Bovino, Quintodecimo, Ariano, Trivento, Larino, Lucera, Sant’Agata, Avellino, Ascoli, Volturara, Telese, Alife, and Sessula.

We also confirm to you and your successors the church of Saint Michael on Mount Gargano, together with the Church of Siponto and all [Col. 0924C] their appurtenances, and all their properties, with churches, families of both sexes, estates, and everything that appears to belong to those churches.

We grant to Alphano, your cleric and nephew, the entire archbishopric after your death, to be held with all its appurtenances, such as the cities and whatever castles were formerly possessed by your predecessors, the bishops.

Moreover, decreeing by apostolic censure under the solemn appeal to divine judgment . . .

[The remainder cannot be read as far as the end. As for the basis on which Vipera reported the entire document, he must see to that himself. At the end of the document one reads:]

“by the hand of Antonius, notary and scriniary of the Holy Roman and Apostolic Church, in the month of April and in the eleventh indiction . . . . . .”

## XVI. Pope Gregory V’s Privilege for the Monastery of Saint Genesius in the Diocese of Bisuldunum (998)

[In Coquelines, *Enlarged Collection of Pontifical Diplomas*, I, 296.]

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God.

Source/review notes: The final proposed edit is invalid because the source specifies multiple emperors named Otto; it requires correction.

Driven by the care imposed upon us by the charge entrusted to our consideration, and moved by the ardor of Christian religion and zeal for divine worship, we are impelled to reflect upon the stability of venerable places and the security of those who serve God, so that, through this pious labor, the souls dedicated to Christ—those who have devoted themselves to him throughout the days of their lives—may persevere undisturbed, and so that what Christians have established for the praise of God may likewise remain [Col. 0925A] firm to the end. Therefore we wish it to be known to all bishops, dukes, margraves, counts, and faithful members of the holy Church of God, present and future, that our beloved spiritual son Bernard, the glorious count of Bisuldunum, represented to our apostolic office that we should fortify, according to canonical custom and by a privilege of our confirmation and authority, the venerable monastery established in honor and under the name of Saint Genesius and Saint Michael the Archangel.

Moved by his salutary prayers, and desiring the condition of all God’s Churches to be preserved, while unwilling that the right of any sacred place should in any way be violated, we decree by this privilege of apostolic authority, and enact from the present eleventh indiction, for the honor of the blessed Genesius and Saint Michael the Archangel and for the stability of that venerable place, that the aforesaid venerable monastery—which our aforesaid spiritual son in Christ, Bernard, built in the present time and thereafter, according to canonical custom, from his own property and from his county, for the love of almighty God and for the redemption of his soul, and placed under the jurisdiction of Saint Peter, without submitting it to the right or authority of any other church—shall remain secure.

He has donated, or granted in perpetuity to the aforesaid monastery, from his own possessions and from his county of Bisuldunum, the following: first, the church of Saint Vincent, with its tithes, first fruits, and cemeteries, situated near the castle of Bisuldunum; the church of Saint Mary and Saint John, with all their alods and properties, situated near the walls of Bisuldunum [Col. 0925B]; together with the property which the aforesaid monastery of Saint Genesius and Saint Michael is seen to possess in the borough of Bisuldunum, at Casellas, Berrechar, Geffanum, Porciolas, Furvellos, and in all places; the church of Saint Martin of Jucunianum, with its tithes, first fruits, and offerings; the church of Saint Mary situated at Faxis, with its tithes, first fruits, and offerings; and the church of Saint Fructuosus situated at Ursinianum, with its tithes, first fruits, and offerings [Col. 0925C]. Likewise, the church of Saint Sylvester situated at Maurus, with its tithes, first fruits, and offerings; also the alod of Saint Raphael, as it is marked out by its boundaries and limits; likewise the alod of Saint Raphael situated at Adanum, and that situated at Evora, as they are marked out by their boundaries and limits [Col. 0925D]; the alod of the aforesaid Saint Raphael situated at Carravia, as it is marked out by its boundaries and limits; also the alod of the estate of Marialdus, with its boundaries and limits, as it belongs by right to Saint Raphael; and the church of Saint Quentin, with its woods and all that belongs or is adjacent to it; the church of Saint Cornelius situated at Garno, with all that belongs or is adjacent to it; and the alod of the aforesaid Count Bernard, which he is seen to possess at Ribellas, with its houses, vineyards, lands and woods, meadows, pastures, fisheries, and all other alods belonging to the monastery or to those churches.

All the churches mentioned above, with their alods and properties, situated within the county of Bisuldunum, as the aforesaid Count Bernard has already donated them to the aforesaid monastery, together with the other things that would take too long to enumerate, which he has donated everywhere or may hereafter donate—whether houses, farmsteads, estates, manses, churches, cells, lands or fields, vineyards, meadows, pastures or grazing lands—and with everything belonging by right to the aforesaid monastery, we grant and confirm as canonically protected under the guardianship of our apostolic see, so that they may remain safe and undisturbed in every respect.

Accordingly, we decree and confirm that no emperor, king, or any other person, great or small, shall presume to exercise any authority in the aforesaid monastery, whether for a hearing, an enforcement action, or a homicide case [Col. 0926A]. Rather, let them judge and decide matters through judicial proceedings according to canonical law; authority and power over these matters shall always remain in their hands. Let them be permitted to live in quiet and peace and to serve the Lord God alone according to the canonical rule. At all times they shall be exempt and free from every public levy and disgraceful service, so that no one may dare to harass or disturb them, except that they shall pay two solidi each year to the altar of Saint Peter as a census.

Proclaiming this by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, before God and his terrifying future judgment, through this privilege and decree of our apostolic office we enact and decree that no one, whatever dignity or power he may possess, nor any person, great or small, shall ever presume to interfere in that monastery or in its affairs, or in any way take away or alienate its possessions, properties, or anything that appears to belong to it [Col. 0926B]. Rather, the places granted or to be granted in that monastery by the aforesaid Bernard, Count of Bisuldunum, and also the other possessions of places that other Christians may later grant to it in that holy place, shall remain firmly in the right of that monastery and shall remain there forever.

Nor shall anyone have the license, as has been said, to take away from them anything belonging to that monastery, or from all the things belonging to it, whether from a great or a small person, so that this venerable place, which rests upon the provisions and privilege of the apostolic decree, may remain securely endowed [Col. 0926C]. But if anyone—which we do not desire—should presume with wicked audacity to oppose or in any way transgress what we have established for the praise of God and the stability of the aforesaid monastery, let him know that he is bound by the chain of anathema and appointed to be burned with the devil and his most dreadful pomps, and with Judas, the betrayer of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, in the punishment of eternal fire: the worm that does not die and the fire that is never extinguished shall neither wish nor be able to spare him [Col. 0926D].

But whoever, with pious regard, observes and in every respect safeguards this apostolic decree of ours, directed toward the worship of God, shall receive manifoldly from our most merciful Lord God the grace of blessing and shall deserve to become a participant in eternal life forever and ever. Amen.

Written by the hand of Peter, notary and scriniary of the holy Roman Church, in the month of April, in the eleventh indiction. Farewell.

## XVII. Privilege of Pope Gregory V for the Church of Montis Majoris (998)

[In Baluze, *Miscellanea*, Luc. edition, vol. III, p. 6.]

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God.

It is fitting for apostolic governance to come to the aid of those endowed with pious religion through kindly compassion, and to grant the requests of petitioners with eager devotion. For by this we especially earn a reward from God, the creator of all, when venerable places established for the better are undoubtedly brought into a more favorable condition [Col. 0927B].

Therefore let it be known to the whole community of believers that, by this privilege of our authority, we strengthen and confirm forever, in its entirety, the abbey established at Montis Majoris in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God and ever-virgin, our Lady, and of Saint Peter, together with all the churches, oratories, estates, and farming properties belonging to it that have been granted to that holy monastery by faithful Christians, or that appear by any documents to belong to that pious place.

The monks of that monastery, together with the abbot who shall be in office at the time, shall possess, hold, and administer the aforesaid churches, oratories, estates, farming properties, male and female slaves, male and female dependants, without contradiction from any person, great or small, and shall distribute them for their use and expenses as they judge best, with our apostolic authority granting this [Col. 0927C].

Moreover, by our gift and apostolic authority, we grant and confirm forever for the use and support of the aforesaid venerable monastery the entire castle called Biduino, with the territory belonging to it there and with all its adjacent and appurtenant properties, which Ismido donated by a deed of gift to the Lord God and Saint Peter under the jurisdiction of our holy Roman Church.

The arrangement is that after his death, and after the deaths of his three sons—namely Bermundus, Faraldus, and Lotgerius—the whole of that castle of ours shall pass into the power of the monks of the aforesaid monastery [Col. 0927D]. As long as those three sons live, they shall hold and possess half of the aforesaid castle. When one dies, his portion shall revert to the monastery; and so, as the others die, their portions likewise shall revert to the holy monastery.

As a census for the right of Saint Peter, according to what Ismido established, the monks shall pay three pounds of frankincense to the altar of Saint Peter within five years.

All the places mentioned above, with all their appurtenances, we grant by the authority of this privilege to the monks of that monastery to hold and possess forever, so that no duke, bishop, prince, margrave, or any person, great or small, may dare to molest or disturb them concerning any of the aforesaid things that appear to belong there [Col. 0928A].

Moreover, under the proclamation and confirmation of divine judgment and the prohibition of anathema, we decree and strengthen this provision: no bishop or any priest shall presume to come to that venerable monastery to perform any ordination or consecration of priests or deacons, or to celebrate Mass, unless he has been invited by the abbot of that place. Rather, the monks of that place shall be permitted to receive whatever grade of ordination they wish, wherever they wish.

The abbots who are to be consecrated shall be chosen jointly from that congregation with the counsel of the brothers, and they shall summon whichever bishop they wish to consecrate them [Col. 0928B].

But if anyone, with rash audacity—which we do not believe will happen—should attempt to act or proceed contrary to the terms of this apostolic confirmation of ours, let him know that he is to be bound by the anathema of our Lord’s apostle and prince, Peter, and burned in eternal fire with the devil and his dreadful [companions] and pomps, and with Judas, the betrayer of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ; and that he shall likewise be cast into the abyss and Tartarus and perish with the impious.

But whoever proves to be the guardian and observer of this privilege of ours shall receive from the Lord the grace of blessing and eternal life.

Written by the hand of Peter, notary and scriniary of the holy Roman Church, in the month of April and in the eleventh indiction [Col. 0928C].

## XVIII. Bull of Pope Gregory V concerning the election of Arnulf as Bishop of Ausona (998)

[In Mansi, *Councils*, vol. XIX, col. 227.]

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God.

The most salutary divine precepts and the venerable statutes of the holy canons admonish us, with thoughtful consideration and indeed through the effort of apostolic governance, to advance the usefulness and convenience of those things entrusted to us and the integrity of their stability, so that the means of providing for useful works, insofar as they are dedicated to divine worship, may remain secure and may be able to prosper for a very long time in the praise owed to God [Col. 0928D]. The solicitude entrusted to us undoubtedly urges us to remedy this with pious consideration, so that through it, once divine clemency has been appeased, a reward may be assigned to us in the heavenly courts.

Therefore we wish it to be known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God, present and future, how a synod was held on the seventh day before the Ides of May in the basilica of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, before his shrine or altar, with all the bishops of the Roman Church and those from beyond the Alps, as well as the deacons of both orders of our holy apostolic see and of the Roman see [Col. 0929A]. Among them was the most glorious and serene lord Otto III, Augustus, emperor, with the dukes, counts, and a very large body of troops from beyond the Alps and among the Lombards.

There, seated at the feet of the aforesaid Augustus, Ermengaud, count and son of Borrell, the most noble margrave of the Aquitanians or Goths, with his nobles and clerics, and Arnulf, the bishop, and Guadaldus, the bishop’s advocate, disputed with one another in that assembly or synod concerning the bishopric of Ausona.

Guadaldus complained before the apostolic and imperial presence that the aforesaid Arnulf was violently and unjustly taking the aforesaid bishopric of Ausona from him, together with Raymond, the margrave of that province. Bishop Arnulf replied that he had taken the bishopric from him neither by force nor unjustly, but that he held it justly and legally [Col. 0929B], that he had been consecrated by his own metropolitan, the metropolitan of Narbonne, to whose diocese it ought to belong, and that Guadaldus, while Fruianus was still the bishop of Ausona, had been fraudulently and unlawfully ordained by another metropolitan, Odo, archbishop of the province of Gaul, and had been condemned and anathematized by Pope John, our predecessor, and by the assembly of the bishops of the Roman Church and many others.

The aforesaid Bishop Fruianus, he added, had complained that Guadaldus had caused him to be killed, together with his brother and kinsman and several others.

While they were making these statements, we began, with attentive mind and the greatest diligence, amid litanies, psalms, and prayers, and while reciting the Catholic faith, to consider how we might bring a trustworthy account to the regular course and examine the matter according to canonical and apostolic authority [Col. 0929C].

Then, according to canonical and apostolic authority, we bound the aforesaid Count Ermengaud, together with his clerics and nobles, by the rod of excommunication and our ban, ordering them to strive to report to us, for the love of God and of the prince of the apostles Peter, whatever they truly believed about the matter.

They then declared with one mind and one voice that everything we had heard from Bishop Arnulf was true and correct: that Guadaldus had usurped the bishopric for himself while Bishop Fruianus was alive, had been unlawfully intruded by another metropolitan, and had afterward caused the aforesaid Fruianus to be innocently killed by the aforesaid Guadaldus.

Thereafter we and the assembly of bishops carefully examined the aforesaid Guadaldus through questioning, to determine whether the things they had alleged against him were true [Col. 0929D]. Since he could not deny them, he confessed with his own mouth that he had secretly seized the aforesaid bishopric for himself while Bishop Fruianus was alive, that he had been ordained by another metropolitan and not by the diocesan of Narbonne, and that he had stirred up the uprising by which the aforesaid Bishop Fruianus had been killed by his own men.

When we had heard these things, and trusted his words more than the testimony of the others, we began to search the holy canons. In reading them we found chapters established by the holy Council of Nicaea: no one may usurp a bishop’s episcopate while that bishop is alive, nor be ordained by any metropolitan other than his diocesan, even if the clergy and people should elect him; rather, according to his own confession and according to canonical and apostolic authority, the perpetrator of such an act must be deposed [Col. 0930A].

Finally, obedient to the commands of the canons, with the Roman, Lombard, and transalpine bishops judging, and with the agreement and judgment of the lord Otto, Augustus, emperor, we ordered our archdeacon Benedict and Robert, the offering-bearer, to depose Guadaldus.

They immediately obeyed our orders, and, as is the Roman custom, pulled the ring from his right hand, broke the pastoral staff over his head, tore his chasuble and dalmatic, degraded him from the episcopal order, and made him sit upon the ground [Col. 0930B].

After all this had been carried out, at the command of the lord emperor, with the Roman, Lombard, and transalpine bishops judging, and with the agreement and acclamation of Count Ermengaud, together with the clerics and nobles from that region who were present there, and with the Roman senate and the Roman, Lombard, and transalpine troops, we established and elevated the aforesaid Bishop Arnulf in the episcopal order of the Church of Ausona, confirming and strengthening him by the privilege of our authority.

We gave him the ring and pastoral staff, and granted him, in the place of the apostles and of ourselves, the power of binding and loosing. We established for him the aforesaid bishopric, together with the decree of the lord Augustus and all its appurtenances belonging to that see, or that ought to belong to that see [Col. 0930C].

No person or judicial authority shall presume, with rash audacity, to break into, invade, seize, dishonor, or tear apart anything in the aforesaid bishopric or see against this Bishop Arnulf or his successors, or against the church—or property—of Saint Peter or Saint Mary situated in the town of Ausona; nor shall anyone presume by force to take away, claim, or extort anything. This includes parishes, treasuries, estates, castles, the mint, tolls, grazing lands, or anything else that can be said or named, as well as the abbatial properties belonging to the right of the Church.

But if anyone comes to violate the strength of this privilege of ours, or the right of the churches mentioned above, or the decrees of the bishopric, or the canons serving God there, or if he causes them any trouble or injury, let him know—unless he repents—that by the authority of blessed Peter and the other apostles, and on our behalf, he is excommunicated and bound with fiery chains together with Judas, the betrayer.

Written by the hand of Peter, notary and scriniary of the holy Roman Church, in the month of May, in the eleventh indiction.

Benedict, archdeacon of the holy Roman Church, who deposed Guadaldus.

[Col. 0931A] John, deacon of the holy Roman Church, who is called Homo.

I, Notker, bishop of the holy Church of Liège, have subscribed.

Benedict, deacon; John, deacon of the holy Roman Church.

Peter, abbot, who sat in the synod that records this privilege and subscribed.

I, Otto, by the grace of God emperor of the Romans, Augustus, have subscribed.

In the third year of the pontificate of the lord Gregory, supreme pontiff and universal fifth pope, in the most sacred see of the apostle Peter; in the second year of the reign of the lord Otto III, crowned by God as great and peaceful emperor; in the month of May; and in the eleventh indiction [Col. 0931B].

John, prefect and count of the palace, and appointed judge.

## XIX. Letter of Pope Gregory V to Constance, Queen of the Gauls  
*[Note: [Col. 0931D] Wife of Robert, king of the Franks.]*  
(998)

That those who had plundered and burned the estates of Bishop Julian may be restrained by ecclesiastical and royal authority.

Since I know that Your Devotion thinks diligently about heavenly life and the remedy of her soul, I consider myself gravely at fault if I remain silent about what ought to be suggested for fear of almighty God, and if I do not carefully remind Your Holiness concerning ecclesiastical peace.

The recent complaint of my brother and fellow bishop Julian has deeply distressed me, especially since his estates—that is, the estates of his church—have been plundered by the most wicked brigands and burned in nocturnal fires like the property of thieves [Col. 0931C]. Moreover, these same wicked men have refused to make amends for it according to the decrees of our predecessor Boniface, on the grounds of immunity; and the laws of the world have likewise wished this matter to be treated in the following way, as the common law bears witness, where it is written:

> “If anyone comes with an armed band of up to four men into another person’s village to commit wrongdoing, the leader shall pay 900 solidi for the unlawful presumption. His followers, however, shall each pay 80 solidi. But if they set fire to anything there, they shall pay ninefold compensation and shall restore the plunder fourfold.””

If the laws of the world have wished such justice to be observed, why should divine law be inferior? For in the presence of Truth itself, Zacchaeus was praised when, if he had defrauded anyone, he promised to restore fourfold.

Since it is the highest good in kings to cultivate justice, preserve each person’s rights, and not permit what belongs to power to be done against their subjects, but to ensure what is equitable—and we trust that you both love and earnestly strive for this [Col. 0932A]—therefore, in the month of November of the present year, the eleventh—corrected to the twelfth—indiction [Note: The correction to the twelfth indiction, which I have supplied, is certain. The letter was written in November of the year 998, when Constance was married by King Robert. It could not have been written either in the preceding year, when Constance was not yet queen, or in the following year, when Pope Gregory had already died, from February onward. In November 998 the twelfth indiction was in progress, having begun on the Kalends of September, which was the beginning of the pontifical indiction; indeed, it continued for some time afterward, as appears from the letters of Gregory VII, especially book I, letter 19. Gregory does not indicate of which city Julian was bishop. Perhaps Angers, since a copy of this letter was transcribed from an Angevin manuscript. If so, Julian should be added to the catalogue of the bishops of Angers. There will be room for him, since around this period there is a considerable gap in *Gallia Christiana*. Gabriel Cossart.]

—we send Peter, our brother and fellow bishop, from the bosom of the holy Roman Church, so that, once the brothers of that province have been assembled, the immunity, unlawful presumption, and sacrilege may receive such an end, through canonical authority and your royal dignity, that afterward the members of the devil and wicked sons may not presume to do such things in the holy Church, even while you reign there.

## XX. Privilege of Pope Gregory V for the Monastery of Cluny (999)

[*Cluny Charter Collection*, 10.]

[Col. 0932B] Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Odilo, abbot of the monastery called Cluny, consecrated in honor of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and situated in the county of Mâcon, and through you to all your successors, the abbots, forever.

The desire that is shown to concern the stability of religious superiors and holy places must, with God as author, be fulfilled without any delay. Whenever they seek our agreement for their useful interests and the customary protection of apostolic authority, it is fitting for us voluntarily to assist them with benevolent regard and to secure their rightful purposes for complete safety, so that through this a supreme reward may also be inscribed for us by God, the creator of all, in the heavenly courts [Col. 0932C].

Therefore, because you have asked us to fortify the aforesaid monastery by a formal act of apostolic authority, to confirm that all its appurtenances shall remain there inviolate by perpetual right, and to strengthen it by the page of our privilege, free from the yoke or authority of every person, we have bent to your prayers, at the intervention of the invincible and pious lord Otto, Augustus, emperor, and for the remedy of his soul.

By this privilege of our authority we establish and decree that all places and monasteries belonging to the aforesaid monastery of Cluny—which have been granted to that place by Christians, kings, bishops, dukes, or princes, or acquired by your predecessors in the abbacy, namely Berno, Odo, Aymard, and your predecessor, the blessed Saint Majolus, or whatever else appears to belong to that same place—you shall possess peacefully and with complete security, without anyone’s opposition; and through you all your successors shall possess them forever [Col. 0932D].

This includes the monastery of Cluny itself, founded by the most powerful former duke William in the district of Mâcon, together with all the properties surrounding that place and situated in other regions belonging to it:

In the county of Mâcon, a cell dedicated in honor of Saint Martin; also the nearby church dedicated in honor of Saint John; the estates called Cavinias, with a church; the estate of Solustriacum, with a church; Escutiolas, with a church; Galliniacum, with a church; Rufiacum, with a church; Masilias, with a church; Clairmannum; Petroniacum; the estate of Bargeserena; Arpayacum; Darboniacum; Besorniacum; the church of Saint Columba; Vitreria; the estate of Burgulium; the castle of Lurdonum; the estate of Blanuscum, called Cotta; and the monastery called Carus Locus, with everything belonging to it [Col. 0933A].

Also the cell called Regniacum, with everything belonging to it; the church of Saint Victor, with everything that appears to belong there; likewise a cell dedicated in honor of Saint Victor, with all its appurtenances; the churches and lands situated beside it, for which we gave the church of Saint Jangulfus; the estate of Eguiranda, with the church of the apostle Saint Andrew and with its other churches and all its appurtenances; and all the churches, lands, and everything else that the aforesaid place appears to possess in that county [Col. 0933B].

In the county of Chalon, the cell of Bellomonte, constructed in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God, with everything that appears to belong to it; also the church of Campilocus, with everything that appears to belong to it; and the estate called Juliacum, with the churches and lands formerly granted to that place by Bishop Manasse; together with all the churches and lands that the aforesaid place appears to possess in that county [Col. 0933C].

In the bishopric of Autun, the cell of Oradellis, constructed in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God, with all its appurtenances; also the churches and lands that the cleric Theotardus recently transferred to the aforesaid monastery of Cluny.

We also confirm and strengthen by our apostolic authority the grant made by Lord Walter, bishop of Autun, concerning the monastery called Magabrense, belonging to his Church, with everything belonging to it. Also all the churches, lands, and whatever the aforesaid place of Cluny appears to possess in that bishopric [Col. 0933D].

In the county of Auvergne, the monastery of Silviniacum, where your predecessor Saint Majolus rests, with everything belonging to that place; the cell called Firmitas, with everything belonging to it; the cell called Scuriolas; the church dedicated in honor of Saint Sulpicius in the estate called Langiacum; and the cell called “at the Wood,” constructed in honor of Saint Peter.

Also the monastery called Rivis, consecrated in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God, with the estate of Lipsacum and all its appurtenances; the church called Manrengum, with the other lands recently transferred to that monastery by Eustorgius, a most noble man [Col. 0934A]; and the small cell situated nearby in that county, consecrated in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God, which is called “at the Mountains.”

Also the monastery of Celsinianum, with its cells, churches, estates, and lands, namely Carniacum, Burnunculum, Abalniacum, Ginniacum, and Cardonetum, together with all the churches and lands belonging to that monastery of Celsinianum; the cell situated in that county where Saint Florus rests, which the cleric Eustorgius transferred to the aforesaid place, with everything belonging to it; a cell in the town of Brioude belonging to the aforesaid place; the cell of Riliacum, with its estate and everything belonging to it; and the nearby chapel constructed in honor of Saint Savior in the estate called Saraciacum [Col. 0934B].

Also all the churches and lands, and everything else that the aforesaid Cluny appears to possess in that county; dwellings with a chapel situated in the city of Avici, which the cleric Lord Grimald transferred to the aforesaid place.

In the bishopric of Viviers, the cell of Mizoscum, with everything pertaining to it; the cell of Mount Rumpon; the cell “at the Springs”; and the cell of Riorus, with everything that the aforesaid place of Cluny appears to possess in that bishopric.

In the bishopric of Uzès, the monastery dedicated in honor of Saint Peter and Saint Saturninus, situated on the bank of the Rhône, with the castle of Coloncella and the estate of Tulleta, and with everything belonging to it on both sides of the river.

In the bishopric of Troyes, a cell constructed in honor of Saint Amandus [Col. 0934C].

In the bishopric of Orange, a cell at Podium Odolenum; and a small monastery constructed in honor of Saint Pantaleon, with everything belonging to it.

In the bishopric of Gap, a cell constructed in honor of Saint Andrew, granted to the aforesaid monastery of Cluny by the cleric Ricaud, with all its appurtenances; also the small monastery of Ganagobium and the estate of Valentiola; and everything that the aforesaid place of Cluny appears to hold or to have, namely whatever property it has by gift and written record, as well as the estate and castle of Sarrianum; and everything it possesses in the land called Provence.

In the bishopric of Valence, whatever the place of Cluny appears to possess in the estate called Ales and on Mount Sion, and everything that the same place appears to possess in that bishopric [Col. 0934D].

In the bishopric of Vienne, the monastery called Taderniacum, with the cell called Causella, the estate called Braeost, and the estate called Insula, together with all the churches, estates, and lands that the aforesaid place appears to possess in that bishopric.

In the bishopric of Lyon, the cell of blessed Mary called Taluzatis; the cell of Poliacum; the small cell of Artedunum; and the cell of Amberta, with the churches, estates, and lands belonging to it; the cell of Saviniacum; the estate of Ambariacum; the church of Saint Andeolus; the church called the Oratory; the estate of Romanis; the cell of Cavariacum; the small cell of Luiniacum; and the estate of Tusciacum [Col. 0935A].

Also all the churches, estates, and lands that Wichardus, when dying, transferred to that place of Cluny, together with everything that the aforesaid place appears to possess in the aforementioned bishopric.

Also the monastery of Paterniacum, constructed by the empress Augusta Adelaide and granted to the monastery of Cluny by royal decrees of King Conrad and his son, King Rudolf, with everything it appears to possess in Burgundy, and with everything that the Augusti emperors Otto granted to that monastery in Alsace.

Also the monastery called Romanum, with everything belonging to it, we grant to the aforesaid monastery of Cluny, and to you and your successors, to possess forever.

All the places and monasteries written above, with their cells, churches, estates, villages, male and female slaves, woods, vineyards, fields, meadows, waters and watercourses, and all cultivated and uncultivated lands belonging to the aforesaid possessions or jurisdictions, we grant by the authority of this privilege of ours to that place of Cluny, and to you and your successors, to hold and possess forever [Col. 0935B].

No duke, bishop, prince, or any person, great or small, shall dare to molest or disturb you concerning any of the aforesaid properties and tithes that appear to belong there.

Moreover, under the proclamation and confirmation of divine judgment and the prohibition of anathema, we decree and strengthen this provision: no bishop or any priest shall presume to come to that venerable monastery to perform any ordination or consecration of a church, priests, or deacons, or to celebrate Mass, unless he has been invited by the abbot of that place [Col. 0935C]. Rather, the monks of that place shall be permitted to receive whatever grade of order they wish, wherever it pleases you and your successors.

The abbots who are to be consecrated shall be chosen jointly from that congregation with the counsel of the brothers, and they shall summon whichever bishop they wish to consecrate them.

Whatever lands you now hold, and whatever you and your successors may acquire, we grant to you to possess forever.

But if anyone, with rash audacity—which we do not believe will happen—should attempt to proceed or act contrary to the terms of this apostolic confirmation of ours, let him know that he is to be bound by the anathema of our Lord’s apostle and prince, Peter, and burned in eternal fire with the devil and his most dreadful pomps, and with Judas, the betrayer of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ; and that he shall likewise be cast into the abyss and the chaos of Tartarus and perish with the impious [Col. 0935D].

But whoever proves to be the guardian and observer of this privilege of ours shall receive from the Lord the grace of blessing and eternal life. Amen.

## XXI. Bull of Pope Gregory V confirming the rights of the monastery of Pettershausen on the bank of the Rhine in the diocese of Constance (999)

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Gregory, also called Bruno, by the grace of God bishop of the holy Catholic and Apostolic Roman Church and servant of the servants of God.

The desire which is shown to pertain to religious purpose and the stability of holy places ought, with God as its author, to be fulfilled without any delay. Whenever our assent or the customary protection of apostolic authority is sought for some benefit or advantage of the holy Church, it is fitting for us willingly to come to the aid of the request in view of our benevolence, and to strengthen the approved purpose with sound reasoning for its complete security, so that from this the veneration, safety, and protection of holy places may be advanced, and so that for us also the supreme reward of gain may be appointed by the Creator of all things.

Therefore, at the will and request of the Emperor Augustus Otto III and Lampert, bishop of the holy Church of Constance, we fortify with apostolic protection a certain monastery on the bank of the Rhine, near Constance, in the village called Petrishusa, constructed by Gebehard, bishop of blessed memory, in honor of Saint Gregory. We adorn it with the precepts of the Roman Church in such a manner that the monastery itself, now governed by Abbot Pericherus, together with everything belonging to it—various estates, cultivated and uncultivated lands, colonists and households, and whatever the same Bishop Gebehard, by hereditary right or by any acquisition, granted to that monastery, or whatever he exchanged from the episcopal property, or permitted without an exchange—may remain established and undisturbed under the apostolic protection and guardianship of blessed Peter.

The same applies to whatever the aforesaid Bishop Lampert granted to that monastery in any transaction, together with the estates of Siggerus called Tuscenanch and Wengiu, situated in the district of Thurgau under the countship of Count Berthold. One of these was acquired from episcopal property through Bishop Gebehard; the other was acquired from the property of the same monastery through the aforesaid Abbot Pericherus. Whatever, moreover, is granted or has already come to be granted to that pious place by any person who fears the Lord shall likewise remain established and unshaken, under the testimony of Christ. [Col. 0936C]

This also we now entirely forbid by apostolic command, with the consent of the Emperor Augustus Otto III and the aforesaid Bishop Lampert, who requested that these things be done: no one is to be appointed over the same monastery except one whom the common agreement of the brothers serving God there shall elect. It shall belong to the bishop only to confirm the person so elected. We decree the same concerning the election of an advocate. Once an abbot or advocate has been elected, it shall be his concern to care for the monastery’s property and to resist those who dissipate it.

If anyone meanwhile—which we do not believe—should presumptuously attempt to oppose, contradict, or in any way violate what has been piously and firmly established by this authority of ours through this privilege, or what has been decreed by us for the praise of God and the stability of the aforesaid monastery, let him know that, by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, whose office we exercise, although unworthy, he is bound by the bond of anathema and is to be burned with the devil and Judas, the betrayer of Christ, in eternal fires. [Col. 0937A]

But whoever, with pious regard, proves to be an observer of our life-giving decree shall receive manifoldly the grace of blessing from the Lord, the just retributor, and may deserve to become a participant in eternal life for ever and ever. Amen.

## XXII. Letter of Pope Gregory V to Martin, Abbot (A.D. 999)

*[History of Languedoc*, vol. I, documents, p. 155.]

Gregory, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved son Martin, most reverend abbot of the venerable monastery of the holy apostle Andrew, Saint Michael the archangel, and blessed Martin the confessor, founded on the summit of the mountain called Andaon, above the river Rhône, and to his successors, the abbots, forever. [Col. 0937B]

Since the highest summit of apostolic dignity is recognized to shine forth in the splendor of this divine contest, so that it may strive with particular diligence to display the labor of its service in the exercise of God’s praises, for this reason we are compelled by the duty of the same apostolic pastoral concern to promulgate abundantly whatever is recognized as pertaining to the stability of pious places and to confirm it by the judgment of apostolic institution.

Therefore, because you have asked us to grant or confirm to your religious community the aforesaid monastery of the holy apostle Andrew, Saint Michael, and Saint Martin, so that these three churches may always remain one monastery, we decree by apostolic authority that the monastery, together with the entire mountain on which the churches are situated, with everything beneath and around them [lacuna], with houses and estates there and everywhere, with all movable and immovable goods and substances and with things that move themselves, whatever has been granted or bestowed there from the day of its foundation until now, and whatever has now come or shall in the future come there by any means, shall remain firmly and permanently under the protection of the abbot for all time, without anyone’s challenge or hindrance.

Finally, we also confirm that, wherever bodies of the dead, whether male or female, are devoted to burial there, no bishop, canon, cleric of the canons, or deputy [lacuna] authority shall exercise any hostile opposition or malice against you or against the servants of the monastery. For places which have not been constituted among the number of other pious places, you may possess them by paying an annual rent; and we grant all these things to you to hold under the jurisdiction and authority of our most holy Roman Church, which, by God’s will, we serve. [Col. 0938A]

Know, dearest brothers, the traditions of the paternal rules before the eyes of your mind and body, so that every superior may know how he ought to command his subjects. Let us not impose harsh things, unsuitable for every brother, lest the subject’s contempt arise from the indiscretion of the one who commands. Let there be measured vitality in the duties of care and outstanding vigor among the brothers, so that, while complete tranquility is bestowed in accordance with the rule, those who serve well through the line of obedience may attain the everlasting joys of the heavenly homeland.

From the present twelfth indiction and forever, we grant and confirm to you the aforesaid monastery and mountain, as they came to you by the charter of exchange from Aldebert and his brother Adalelmus, together with their wives, namely Leucinda and Beliilde, and with Poncione and his brother Combertus, together with their wives, namely Adalinde and Unia; also with the priest Berengarius, together with his two brothers, namely Perone and Nectale; and with Dabbatus, together with his three sons, whose names are Garibertus, Silvester, and Poncione, so that by the privilege of this present confirmation he may securely possess all things which [lacuna] unshaken.

Therefore, by the authority of God, the holy apostle Peter, and our own authority, we establish that, whenever the abbot dies, no one may enter there as abbot unless he is such a person as pleases God and all the brothers; and that the person whom the community approves may be consecrated without offense.

If any bishop, margrave, count, viscount, gastald, or any other person of high rank—which we do not believe—should oppose or in any way violate what we have established for the love of almighty God [lacuna], let him know that, under the solemn warning of divine judgment, he is bound by the bond of anathema, alienated from the kingdom of God, and to be tormented without end with the devil.

But whoever proves to be a pious helper and observer of this decree of ours shall receive the grace of blessing from Christ the Lord and may deserve to become a participant in eternal life.

Written by the hand of Benedict, notary of the holy Roman Church, in the month of January and in the aforesaid twelfth indiction. [Col. 0938D]

## Around the Year of the Lord 999: Hrotswitha, Virgin and Nun of Gandersheim in Germany, of the Order of Saint Benedict

## Preliminary Materials to the Works of Hrotswitha

*(From the edition of Heinrich Leonhard Schurzfleisch, published at Wittenberg in Saxony in 1707.)*

## Historical Notice on Hrotswitha

*(From Meibom the Elder.)*

Laurentius Humfredus, an Englishman who spent some time in exile in Germany for religious reasons, strives to claim Roswitha, the poetess, for his own country. He maintains that she was the daughter of Hederic, king of the Northumbrians, by his wife Bregsinda, and was otherwise called Hilda, a woman of great distinction and learning who spent thirty-three years in the monasteries of Britain and Gaul.

But he is mistaken about the period, and other witnesses are Georg Fabricius, *Origins of the Saxons*, book II, and Heinrich Bodo, *Manuscript Chronicle of Gandersheim*, who state that Roswitha was a girl of Saxon origin. Some confuse her with Roswitha, the fourth abbess of Gandersheim—Bruschius calls her Rodeswinda—who succeeded Christina III, the daughter of the founder Ludolf, in the government of the monastery. But these too are mistaken about the chronology. [Col. 0939B]

The *Chronicle of the Monastery of Saint Michael at Hildesheim* speaks of the abbess Roswitha in this way:

“Walbertus, the seventh bishop of Hildesheim, after Christina, abbess of Gandersheim, had died, brought Roswitha into the administration there. She surpassed the others in logic and rhetoric, as her books and writings testify; for she composed a highly distinguished book on logic.”

Nicholas Selneccerus, a theologian, writes the following about the same woman in part I of his *Pedagogy*, under the heading “On Usury”:

“Of Roswitha the abbess, daughter, as is said, of the king of Greece, it is related that she extorted from the devil a document by which a certain boy had bound himself to him, having written it in his own blood.”

Our poetess Roswitha was educated from adolescence in the monastery of Gandersheim. She herself testifies to this in the preface to her history of the blessed Virgin Mary, in the following words:

“Thus, secretly from everyone and almost furtively, sometimes laboring alone at composing, sometimes destroying what I had poorly composed, I strove, as far as I was able—although it was scarcely necessary—to put together some sort of text from sentences of Scripture which I had collected within the enclosure of the Gandersheim monastery. At first I was instructed by the most wise and kindly teacher Rikardis, and by the teaching of the others in her place; afterward, with the willing favor of the gracious Gerberga, of royal disposition, under whose authority I now live in the abbey, who, though younger in age, was more advanced in learning, as befitted an imperial niece, and who taught me several authors that she herself had previously learned from the wisest teachers.”

From these words it can be inferred that Richarda and then Gerberga were Roswitha’s teachers, and that Roswitha soon succeeded them in the same office. That there were also lectures and theological exercises there is clear from Roswitha’s writings. For she presents much from Scripture elegantly, and in the preface just mentioned she admits that, at this immature age, she had taken certain things from the apocrypha out of ignorance; although they are doubtful, she nevertheless considers them worthy of being judged favorably.

The most noble Martin Friedrich Seidel, Brandenburg councillor, after publishing portraits and eulogies of several distinguished men who had greatly aided and adorned the March through their studies and counsels, inserted among them a portrait of our nun Hroswitha of Gandersheim. He calls her “Helena of Rossow,” a noble family of which several members still survive today.

*[H. Meibom the Younger.]*

Trithemius lists Roswitha’s works in his *Book on Illustrious Men of Germany* in the following order:

“Rosvida, a virgin and nun of the Gandersheim monastery in Saxony, noble, of the order of the holy Father Benedict, devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, and well trained in the disciplines of secular literature, outstanding in talent and distinguished in eloquence, no less remarkable in conduct than in learning, wrote many excellent little works both in verse and prose. Surpassing her sex in talent, she transmitted her name to posterity with great glory. Of these I have read the following:

“One book addressed to Abbess Gerberga, in heroic verse, on the life and conduct of the undefiled Mother of God and Virgin Mary.

“One book, in the same verse, on the Ascension of the Lord.

“One book on Saint Gangulf.

“One book on the passion of Saint Pelagius the martyr, who suffered at Córdoba in these times.

“One book on the fall of Theophilus, the vicar of the Lord, and his repentance.

“One book on the fall of a certain young man, converted by Saint Basil.

“One book on the passion of Saint Dionysius, bishop and martyr.

“One book on the passion of Saint Agnes the virgin.”

She composed all the works mentioned above in elegant heroic verse. [Col. 0941A]

She also wrote six comedies, imitating Terence, of which the first is entitled:

“The Conversion of the Prince Gallicanus, including the passion of the martyrs John and Paul.”

The second concerns the passion of Agape, Chionia, and Irene, virgins.

The third concerns the resurrection of Callimachus and Drusiana through Saint John.

The fourth concerns the fall and conversion of Mary, the niece of the hermit Abraham.

The fifth is entitled “The Conversion of Thais, the Harlot.”

The sixth recounts the passion of the holy virgins Faith, Hope, and Charity.

She also wrote in verse:

“One book on the deeds of the Emperor Otto.

“One book of various epigrams.

“And some letters that are not inelegant.”

The rest of what she composed has not come to our knowledge. She flourished in the time of Otto I and Otto II, most illustrious emperors.”

Thus far Trithemius, whose words are repeated by Gesner’s *Bibliotheca*, which adds that Roswitha possessed knowledge of the Greek language.

Heinrich Bodo, a monk of Clus, in the manuscript *Chronicle of Gandersheim*, mentions a poem by Roswitha on the foundation of the Gandersheim monastery, preceded by Lives of the bishops Anastasius and Innocent, its patrons. But this work has not yet seen the light of day.

The works mentioned by Trithemius were first published by Conrad Celtes, Protucius the Frank, in 1501. He retained the spelling customary among medieval writers, for whom names such as Rudolfus, Rutbertus, Ramwardus, and similar forms commonly began with an aspiration. Aventinus also mentions this in book I of his *Annals*, in the list of names prefixed to the work.

She composed a panegyric on the praises of Otto the Great at the urging of Abbess Gerberga, as she testifies in the preface. In the second preliminary poem she hints that the Emperor Otto II wished to see the poem itself. Her diction is tolerable and bears the character of the age in which she lived; she made many errors in prosody, which ought to be forgiven on account of her sex.

## Dedication

To the most reverend and serene princess and lady, Lady Henrica Christina, Duchess of Brunswick and Lüneburg, principal abbess of the Gandersheim monastery of the Holy Roman Empire, elevated to that dignity, and so forth.

I humbly and obediently offer and deliver to your Serenity works which by every right are owed to you: the works of Hrotswitha, a virgin born of illustrious rank and once a most religious priestess in the ancient monastery of the Holy Roman Empire at the river Ganda, over which your Serenity presides with the highest authority of an abbess.

She left behind many writings in oration, prose, and verse. She also illuminated with the highest praise of piety and learning the monastery founded by Ludolf, great duke of Saxony, and consecrated to the religious observances of your ancestors—especially in that age of the emperors Otto—and she filled nearly all the finest regions of Europe, particularly Germany and Saxony, where she was born and educated, with the extraordinary fame of the talent that shone forth in her.

She was a most holy virgin, to be preferred to men who, according to the standards of that age, were highly learned in Greek and Latin; and she deserves the greater praise because learning was rarer in those times. She demonstrated through both words and ideas the ornament of writing. Although she did not always reproduce the finest style of expression, nevertheless, since she was eloquent, she held the first place among all those who, in a less polished age, devoted themselves to the elegance of literature.

Accordingly, the religious priestess Hrotswitha read ancient and corrected writers distinguished both in prose and in verse, and proposed them to herself for imitation. She brought a great abundance of words to the resources of the Latin language and examined the disciplines of the ancients, so that through variety in writing she might commend the skill of her mind.

Thus she devoted labor and effort to divine and human wisdom, which is the mother of all good arts, and with firm and resolute mind entered upon this path and method. She did not consider the liberal arts a disgrace to herself; rather, she acquired many of their ornaments, not being unaware that no one can advance to the praise of learning without the pursuit of wisdom. It is entirely true what Cicero wrote: no one can worthily perform his proper duties without philosophy, which supplies arguments for discovering and establishing things.

She therefore traversed all disciplines and arts. Among geometers she drew lines, and she accurately learned the varieties and intervals of sounds. Moreover, she adapted the stories of poets to the use of life; for this reason she studied the extremely learned comedies of Terence and, after making a selection, brought them into conformity with the rules of piety.

She also devoted herself to the study of antiquity and diligently investigated and examined the customs of the ancients and both sacred and secular history. Thus, in the tenth century after Christ, she alone seemed especially worthy to commit to writing the life and deeds of the great and most august Emperor Otto I, so that by this very work she might provide learned assistance to men to whom such tasks are appropriate and rescue his name from the injuries of time and the oblivion of posterity.

These great and unusual accomplishments of Hrotswitha, cultivated through care and vigilance in the monastery which your Serenity so wisely governs in our own time, rightly belong to your Serenity, who even now fosters divine and human arts. Just as the great abbess Gerberga II, in the midst of the barbarism of her age, rescued the study of literature and the good arts from destruction and ruin, so your most reverend Serenity, together with your most reverend and serene associates in princely care—Duchess and dean Maria Elisabeth, Duchess of Mecklenburg and canoness; Eleonora, Duchess of Brunswick and Lüneburg, and others—continues kindly and generously to protect them to this day, to adorn them with benefits, and to preserve them munificently. You transmit their glory to posterity, who, so long as human beings exist, will willingly and steadfastly proclaim the divine and lofty virtues of your Serenity.

For my part, I rest in the prayers which are to be offered to God for your royal Serenity, and I continually venerate your praises, greater than I can either express or imagine. I pray God, the founder of the most exalted families, to keep your most reverend Serenity safe in the greatest tranquility of mind, to increase you with perpetual happiness in all things, and to avert every harm from you as far as possible.

May he daily raise up the most serene line and the whole Guelphic nation, founded and strengthened thus far by the blood of so many and such great heroes and joined by royal and imperial relationships and affinities; may he preserve it, for the comfort of the common fatherland and the protection of the Roman Empire, always safe and flourishing in every condition, so that, with your most serene father safe, your most serene brothers and sisters safe, and all the kinsmen of your most serene house safe, the affairs of the Empire may be established most happily through the counsel and courage of the Guelphs, and their glory and happiness may be made equal to the eternity of the world itself.

Wittenberg in Saxony, the twelfth day before the Kalends of June, in the year of restored salvation 1707.

Your most reverend Serenity’s most devoted servant,

Heinrich Leonhard Schurzfleisch, Doctor of Both Laws, Professor of History.

## Schurzfleisch’s Preface to the Reader

When, in the previous year, I was devoting labor and effort to the Christian poets of antiquity whom I was preparing to publish, and was once again bringing Commodianus and Orientius before your eyes, I was advised by the timely counsel of certain persons to turn my attention to the poets of the Saxon people. In particular, I was urged to reprint those who are scarcely seen any longer in our regions, who are very rare and not easily encountered, and who display the rougher character of their age, so that they might be cleansed of the inelegant manner of writers and made easier to read without disgust.

Therefore, in order to satisfy their entirely reasonable request, I first wished to turn to the poetesses whom Saxony, after it accepted the Christian faith, later fostered in its bosom, so that they might illuminate their homeland, in ages lacking more cultivated learning, through their writings and might hand down to posterity events worthy of remembrance.

Among these was Hroswitha, whom more recent writers call Roswitha without the aspiration: formerly a priestess and virgin of Gandersheim, German by nation, descended from the Saxon people, the glory of Saxon virgins, and without doubt distinguished by the nobility of her birth, since the ancient monastery at Gandersheim scarcely admitted virgins except those born of noble and eminent rank.

The name of this religious virgin is pronounced by several writers with the middle syllable shortened. I do not approve this, however, since I judge that it should rather be pronounced with length. The authority of Roswitha herself leads me to do this, for she pronounces the middle syllable long when, in the preface to her history of the undefiled Mother of God, she says:

“Hroswithae votis carminulisque novis.”

“By the vows and little new poems of Hroswitha.”

Other passages of Roswitha may be compared with this, such as those at columns 1082 and 1083 and elsewhere, where the middle syllable of the name is likewise found long.

Nor do I agree with Martin Friedrich Seidel, who presents a portrait of Roswitha with the inscription “Helena of Rossow, commonly Roswitha, nun at Gandersheim” in his book entitled *Portraits and Eulogies of Several Distinguished Men*, and so forth. He proves this neither by any testimony of a writer nor by any documentary charter. To rely solely on the indication of the portrait and its inscription—perhaps drawn in the memory of our fathers or our own age—and to place such confidence in it is nothing other than telling fables and making elaborate nonsense. I think it ought rather to be regarded as a painter’s conceit, or the work of lovers of that art, than judged to be a true portrait of Roswitha. [Col. 0944A]

The same image also appears in the work of Meibom, but he offered no judgment concerning the image—and, what is the principal point, concerning its inscription—which I find surprising.

She separated herself from the unlearned multitude and had Richarda and Gerberga as teachers both of life and of learning. She learned not only Latin literature but also Greek, and, according to the circumstances of her age and the capacity of the tenth century in which she lived, cultivated and polished her mind in both forms of discourse, prose and verse.

She did not regard the teachings of philosophers as foreign to her studies. Rather, she embraced in memory and mind the best arts useful for discussion and capable of bringing adornment to speech. She also retained splendidly all the examples of antiquity that instruct the wise and drew a large part of her wisdom from the memorials of the annals. Nor did she neglect the mathematical sciences, in which, as is clear from her comedies, she showed herself outstanding and learned. Through her virtue she stirred men who had neglected these studies in a dark age, and virgins to virtue. In piety and holiness alike she left to grateful posterity an example of virtue and, as it were, ascended by steps into heaven.

The Emperor Otto II was by no means unaware of this. He delighted in the virgin’s studies and earnestly urged her to compose an account of the life and deeds of his father, the Augustus Otto the Great, who had died in the year of Christ 973 at Memleben, formerly a monastery of the Benedictine order in Thuringia on the river Unstrut, and had been buried in royal fashion at Magdeburg, in the cathedral church he himself had built.

Nor did she refuse this to Otto the son; rather, yielding to the requests of the Emperor Augustus, while Gerberga II, abbess of the holy virgins, likewise commanded and urged her, she adorned the rough and unpolished age with the power of her poetry. She composed the history of Otto the Great and pursued his deeds in verse that was not inept, though less polished, nevertheless true and expressive in accordance with the trustworthiness of history, specifically in heroic meter.

Certainly this poem confirms Roswitha’s prudence. In it she reviewed the wars of Otto the Great, explained the causes of the enlargement of the Empire through him, showed thorough knowledge of the customs, institutions, and laws of the state, and proved that she was not ignorant of the antiquity of her homeland.

For the religious virgin truly judged that Otto the Great had rightly rejected Pope John XII, formerly called Octavianus before his pontificate, through a proper zeal, although Baronius and Bellarmine disagree: the former in his entries for the years 964 and 966, the latter in book II, chapter 29 of *On the Roman Pontiff*, response to argument 4. They say that Otto the Great’s zeal in deposing John XII, though good, was not right and was not according to knowledge.

Alphonsus Ciaconius and Augustinus Oldoinus undertook especially to defend this opinion in their *Lives and Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs and Cardinals*, under the year 956, p. 715. Roswitha’s words in the *Life of Otto the Great* are these:

“Thus, pierced by the sharpness of a righteous zeal,

He caused the supreme pontiff, perpetrating certain perverse acts

And not deigning to yield to his repeated admonitions,

To be deprived of the honor of the apostolic See,

Appointing another worthy to bear the name of ruler.”

On the deposition of John XII, Theodoric of Niem deserves to be read, and Meibom from him in his notes on Roswitha; also Johann Heinrich Boecler in his commentary *On the Affairs of the Ninth and Tenth Centuries from the Birth of Christ*, especially the section on Otto; Johann Conrad Dieterich in his *History of Otto the Great*; and Hermann Conring in *On the Boundaries of the Empire*.

What Jean Launoy brings by that title against Baronius may be read in his letters, part IV, letter 1, written to Louis de Maraes, a theologian of Paris.

The religious priestess also conveys several things worth knowing about Ludolf, the son of Otto the Great. This deserves all the more attention because her account departs so far from the testimony of other writers. For what is related in the supplement to Regino concerning the civil dissension instigated by Ludolf does not agree at all with Roswitha’s narrative. Boecler nevertheless thinks that this account by Roswitha in the *Life of Otto the Great* is not entirely sincere and is mixed with a certain pretense.

Now, in order also to establish this through the testimony of authors—that the virgin and priestess Roswitha was illustrious by birth, German by nation, and descended from the Saxon people—I thought it useful to cite the evidence.

First, this is indicated by the most ancient manuscript of Roswitha’s works, written by a woman, since its title calls her “our native virgin and German nun, of Saxon stock.”

Moreover, I have at hand Heinrich Bodo, formerly a learned and diligent monk at the monastery of Clus, which is close to the church of Gandersheim. In his *Chronicle of Gandersheim*, entitled *A Treatise on the Construction of the Gandersheim Monastery and also on Its Completion and Decline*, which appears in volume II of Meibom’s *German Affairs*, he calls this illustrious virgin Roswitha a Saxon.

His words, found in Meibom, vol. II, p. 490, are these:

“Under that second most illustrious lady Gerberga, the illustrious virgin and nun Hrosvita lived and flourished, born in Saxony, distinguished by extraordinary talent and learning, and admirable in both forms of writing.”

Johann Trithemius calls her a noble virgin in volume I of the *Annals of Hirsau*, where he says:

“In these times also flourished Roswitha, a nun of our order in the Gandersheim monastery in Saxony, a noble virgin, most devoted to the divine Scriptures and likewise to secular literature, learned to write both in verse and in prose, and deserving of veneration no less for her learning than for the merit of her life, and so forth.”

He testifies to the same in the *Catalogue of Illustrious Men*, p. 129 of the Frankfurt edition published by Marquard Freher.

Johann Cuspinian, in his account of Otto the Great, relates the following:

“Roswitha, a nun, encompassed the deeds of Otto in verse. Although, as the circumstances of the age required, the verses are neither elegant nor sufficiently polished, it is nevertheless astonishing that a woman’s talent, raised and born in Saxony and in the very midst of barbarism, could accomplish such things.”

Lilius Gregorius Gyraldus, a truly learned man, though deserving of better fortune, as Barthius reports of him in his *Remarks* on book V, poem II of Statius’s *Silvae*, says in dialogue V of his *On Historical Poets*:

“Among the Saxons, something which seems almost miraculous to me, flourished Roswitha the nun.”

Georg Fabricius says the following about Roswitha in book II of his *Saxon Origins*:

“The Saxons have the better right to boast of Roswitha the poetess.”

He also mentions her in his book *On the Poets of Germany*.

Caspar Bruschius, in his *History of Monasteries*, calls Roswitha our countrywoman, a Saxon girl.

Antonius Possevinus also confirms this with clear testimony, writing in his *Apparatus to the Sacred Library*:

“Rosvidis, whom some call Rosvitim and others Roswidam, Saxon by origin and family, of very noble status.”

All the others—such as Gabriel Bucelinus in part I of his *Sacred and Profane Topographical, Chronological, and Genealogical Description of Germany*; Gerardus Joannes Vossius in book II, chapter 41 of *On Latin Historians*; Johann Heinrich Boecler in his commentary *On the Affairs of the Ninth and Tenth Centuries from the Birth of Christ*; Casimir Oudin in his *Supplement on Ecclesiastical Writers Omitted by Bellarmine*, p. 311; Cave in his *Literary History of Ecclesiastical Writers*, p. 412; and most recently Élie du Pin in volume VIII of the *New Library of Ecclesiastical Authors*—agree unanimously and in the same judgment that our Roswitha was an illustrious virgin.

Nor does Heinrich Meibom depart from them in his *Life of Roswitha*, where he demonstrates that this illustrious virgin was German by nation and descended from the Saxon people.

The epigrams of the Literary Fellowship also bear upon this matter. They were composed for Roswitha’s works when Conrad Celtes first published them and were again appended to this edition after Celtes’s preface. Specifically, the epigrams of Johann of Dalberg, Johann Trithemius, Heinrich of Bünau, Ololiki of Stein, Willibald Pirckheimer, Johann Tholophus, Heinrich Groninger, Johann Werner, Martin Mellerstadt, Conrad Celtes, Johann Lateran, Johann Stabius, Urbanus Praepusinus, and Sebastian Sprenz confirm unanimously that Roswitha was our countrywoman, illustrious in the nobility of her birth, and descended from the Saxon people.

It was therefore not English by nationality, as Laurentius Humfredus, an Englishman, mistakenly thought; for he strove to claim her for the English nation and boldly, rather than truthfully, maintained that this Roswitha was none other than the virgin Hilda, who had notably distinguished the province of Northumbria, in which she was born, and all Britain. But Humfredus is greatly mistaken, since both geographical and chronological considerations refute him.

For it is clear from Bede that Hilda, a most holy virgin and once the glory and ornament of English virgins, after completing her thirty-third year, renounced the claims of the world and devoted herself to the sacred order. She departed from Northumbria, her native land, for East Anglia, to whose king she was related, intending from there, after crossing the sea, to go to Gaul and dedicate herself and her life to God in some monastery there. Nevertheless, she persisted for a full year in her intention of travelling while in East Anglia, until, contrary to expectation, she was recalled to her native land by Bishop Aidan.

When this had happened, she received, as Bede says, a place belonging to one household “on the northern side of the River Wear,” and there likewise spent one year in the religious life with very few companions; or, as Matthew of Westminster says, she became abbess of Hertesey. Later she presided with the utmost care and devotion over the monastery she had built at Streanshalch, situated in the county of York, and continued in that way of life until her death.

A clear testimony is found in Bede, *Ecclesiastical History*, book III, chapter 33. The wording is as follows:

> In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 680, Hilda, the most devout handmaid of Christ and abbess of the monastery of Streaneshalch, after the many heavenly works which she performed on earth, passed from this world on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of December, to receive the rewards of heavenly life, when she was sixty-six years old. Dividing these years into equal portions, she had spent the first thirty-three in the secular habit, conducting herself with the greatest distinction, and consecrated the following thirty-three, with still greater distinction, to the Lord in the monastic life, etc.  
>   
> When she had decided, after abandoning the secular habit, to serve Him alone, she withdrew to the province of the East Angles—for she was related to that king—desiring, if she could somehow manage it, to leave her native land and all that she possessed, reach Gaul, and lead a pilgrim’s life for the Lord in the monastery of Calae, etc. For in that same monastery her sister Hereswid, mother of Ædulf, king of the East Angles, was at that time, subject to regular discipline, awaiting the eternal crown. Emulating her example, Hilda too, with the intention of travelling abroad, was kept for a whole year in the aforesaid province; then, recalled to her homeland by Bishop Aidan, she received a place belonging to one household on the northern side of the River Wear, where likewise for one year she led the monastic life with very few companions, etc. It happened that she was entrusted with founding or organizing the monastery at the place called Streanshalch, and she fulfilled the task imposed upon her without slackness.

The evidence found in the *Anglo-Saxon Chronicle* also supports this purpose. The work was published at Oxford in 1692 through the efforts and diligence of the distinguished Edmund Gibson, chaplain and librarian to the most reverend Archbishop of Canterbury. Its words, in Latin translation, are:

> And in the same year Hilda, abbess at Streonesheale, died.

William of Malmesbury, in book I of *The Deeds of the Kings of the English*, calls this monastery Streanshale and at the same time notes that it is now called Whitby. His words are:

> Their principal monastery, at that time for women but now for men, lies thirty miles north of York. In the ancient language it was called Streaneshall, and now it is called Whitby. It was begun by Hilda, a woman of distinguished religion, and Edelfleda, the daughter of the same king, who succeeded her in its government, greatly enlarged it with vast royal resources.

William Camden, author of the substantial work entitled *Britannia Magna*, gave this monastery its more recent name, Whitby, when he wrote:

> Such was the abbey of Whitby, founded by Lady Hilda, granddaughter through her son of King Edwin.

This makes it surprising that Gerardus Joannes Vossius, in book II, chapter 41, *On Latin Historians*, should have called the monastery in which Hilda was abbess Herethow. That name plainly does not fit and departs considerably from the description given by English writers.

In this monastery of Streoneshalch—which Bede interprets as “Bay of the Lighthouse,” an interpretation with which Philip Brietius also agrees in his *Parallels of Ancient and Modern Geography*—a synod was held in the seventh century, in the year of Christ 664. It is now called Pharentis, or, as others write, Farensis. The dispute between the English and the Scots concerning the date of Easter was dealt with there.

William of Malmesbury, in book III of *The Deeds of the Bishops of England*, frames the question as follows:

> They sought to determine what was most correct: whether Easter should be celebrated, according to the custom of the Britons, Scots, and the whole northern region, from the fourteenth moon, when Sunday arrived, through the twenty-second; or whether it would be better, according to the practice of the Apostolic See, for Easter to be celebrated from the fifteenth moon through the twenty-first on Sunday.

But the Scots, whose cause Hilda supported, lost the dispute.

The English writers rightly adorn the great priest Hilda, a virgin of most holy conduct, outstanding virtue, and profound learning, with no ordinary praises, in proportion to her deserts. Thus Godwin, in *The Bishops of York*, calls her “a most holy woman”; Foxe, in his *Acts*, “a learned and devout woman”; Spedus, book VII, chapter 20, “pious and learned”; Leland, in Bale, century 10, chapter 16, “an incomparable woman”; and Illyricus, on the authority of Leland and Bale in his *Catalogue*, “a mother of mercy, distinguished by the gift of miracles.” Bale himself, century 1, chapter 80, calls her “a pious, prudent, and learned woman,” and in chapter 94 “a most holy woman”; William of Malmesbury, in book I of *The Deeds of the English Kings*, calls her “a woman of distinguished religion.” Simeon, a monk of Durham, also mentions this Hilda in Selden, p. 75 of the London edition; as the preface attests, that work owes a great deal to him.

On the authority of these writers it is now sufficiently and abundantly established that Hilda was English by nationality, that she presided over the sacred virgins in the monastery of Streanesheale which she herself had built, that she continued to discharge that office of abbess there until her death, and that she was buried in the same monastery, although her bones were later transferred to Glastonbury because of the Danish incursions.

From these facts we can prove, on geographical grounds alone, that Hilda was entirely different from our Roswitha. Hilda was English and a great priest in Streoneshalch—or, as others call it, Streonesheale—a monastery situated in the county of York. Roswitha, however, was German by nationality, Saxon by race, a priestly virgin, commonly called a nun, in the monastery of Gandersheim, where from adolescence she studied the liberal arts under Richardis and the virgin abbess Gerburga. Roswitha was their pupil, as she herself testifies in the preface to her *History of the Blessed Virgin Mary*.

Moreover, it is nowhere recorded that Roswitha was the same person as Hilda. Georgius Fabricius therefore rightly states in book II of *Saxon Origins*:

> The Saxons have better grounds for boasting of the poetess Roswitha than the English; for we neither heed nor tolerate Laurentius Humfredus when he claims her for his own country.

Gerardus Joannes Vossius agrees with him in book II, chapter 41, *On Latin Historians*, where he says:

> For Humfredus is refuted both by places and by dates, since Hilda was English in the monastery of Herethow and died in the year of Christ 680, while Egfrid was reigning in Northumbria, as is clear from Bede, book IV of the *Histories*, chapter 23.

Furthermore, it is nowhere recorded that Hilda came to Germany and there learned the liberal arts, which at that time had almost died out among us and were cultivated more in England than among us during that obscure age.

It should also be added that in the period when Hilda lived, the monastery of Gandersheim had not yet been founded. We read, on the testimony of Caspar Brusch and Gabriel Bucelinus, that it was founded by Ludolph, duke of the Saxons, at the persuasion of his wife Oda, in the year of Christ 842, in honor of Saint John the Baptist, the Forerunner, and Saint Stephen, the first martyr; and that in the year of Christ 852 it was consecrated and endowed by Saint Altfrid, the fourth bishop of Hildesheim.

But when I examine the words of the founder Ludolph’s charter, they seem to signify something else. On its authority it is clear that the first site of this monastery was established at Brunteshusen, now Brunshusen; that afterward, because the place was too confined, it was moved by the same Ludolph, with the consent of his wife Oda; and that it was transferred to a more celebrated building on the River Ganda, not far from Brunshusen, constructed in honor of the bishops Anastasius and Innocentius. There the ancient monastery beside the Ganda, which still exists today, may be seen.

As for the year of its foundation, I admit that it is not expressed in the charter; nevertheless, if we may rely on reasonable conjectures, it can be determined without difficulty.
