For if Ludolph went to Rome in the year 853, and undertook that journey after beginning the monastery, I am led to believe that the year of its foundation ought to be assigned to the year of Christ 852.

This charter is preserved in Bodo, whose little work is contained in volume II of Meibom’s *German Affairs*. More recently Leuckfeld reproduced it from the Gandersheim archive, correcting and publishing it anew in his *Antiquities of Walckenried*. His words are:

> Since it is written, “The wealth of a man is the price of his soul,” therefore I, Lutholph, duke of Saxony, wish it to be known to all the faithful of Christ, present and future, that after beginning the monastery of maidens which, moved by divine inspiration and likewise persuaded by the counsel of my beloved wife Oda, I began to build at Brunnistashusen in honor of the Forerunner and Stephen the first martyr, and after receiving letters from our lord Luodovicus, the most invincible king of the Romans, to the most holy Pope Sergius, I, together with my aforesaid wife, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 853, in the first indiction, at Rome and in the presence of that supreme pontiff, fully transferred into the right and ownership of the prince of the apostles, for the remedy of my soul and of the souls of those to whom I was indebted, the aforesaid monastery and all the inheritance of my property which I possessed—namely, the Gandersem district, the Aluunge district, the Ruderinge district, the Dengdiamarcu district, the Lachtiandorp district, and many other places with households of both sexes, etc.
>
> When, by the cooperation of divine grace, we had returned home safely and had been gratefully received by the holy community, we saw that the same place was too confined for the sacred community of maidens. Therefore, in a certain forest belonging to our inheritance, beside the River Ganda, which is otherwise called the Echtterna, in the year from the Lord’s incarnation 856, in the fourth indiction, we built a church in honor of the aforesaid confessors, not far from the earlier site, but in a more celebrated building.

My conjecture is splendidly confirmed by the *Catalogue of the Bishops of Hildesheim*, taken from the *Chronicles of Eggehard, abbot of W rages, addressed to Egbert of Corvey*, when it records that the monastery at Brunethusen was founded in 852 and that the monastery at Gandersheim was begun four years afterward, namely in the year of Christ 856. It says:

> In the year of the Lord 852, Altfrid began, with Ludolph, the first duke, a monastery at Brunetshusen; and four years after this, he began a nunnery at Gandesheim.

This catalogue is found in Leibniz, in his book *On the Writers of Brunswick Antiquities*.

Engelhus also teaches the same thing, though he omits the years. He says that the first monastery of nuns was begun at Brunteshusen and that four years afterward it was built at Gandersen. Engelhus’s testimonies can be read in his book entitled *Lives of Those Born from the Most Noble and Serene House of the Dukes of Brunswick*, which is inserted in Mader’s *Brunswick Antiquities*, p. 24, and also in his *Chronicle*, which Mader likewise first published from manuscript codices, p. 170.

In my opinion, therefore, Johannes Justus Winckelmann should be corrected in his *Description of Ancient Saxony and Westphalia*, where he states:

> Bruno, duke of Saxony, built a monastery at Brunshusen.

Engelhus is also mistaken in thinking that the monastery at Brunteshusen was built in honor of the bishops Anastasius and Innocentius, whereas it was dedicated to John and Stephen.

At a later time, some canons were also introduced into this monastery of Gandersheim with the consent of emperors and pontiffs. They still possess this right, although they are no longer so numerous. For on the testimony of Doctor Jacobus Andreae, in an address delivered at Tübingen in 1571 on the duty of princes to protect monastic colleges and foster literary studies, we read that the monastery of Gandersheim contained twenty-four virgins, twelve canons, and eight vicars, all nevertheless subject to the jurisdiction and obedience of the abbess and deaness.

It is also appropriate to observe concerning Gandersheim that the most serene Julius, duke of Brunswick, greatly valued this place because of the literary studies which had always flourished there and had been preserved even amid barbarism. Such was his affection for it that, when religious affairs were being reformed, he adorned it with a school.

But when it was later observed that this distinguished school was not situated in a sufficiently convenient place, being close to the Hercynian Forest and exposed to many floods and the dangers arising from them, it seemed best to the same most serene Duke Julius to transfer it to Helmstedt. There it was later increased by privileges and honored with the dignity of a university.

Johannes Caselius speaks of this in a certain work which he composed for the wedding of the hero Henry Julius of the Guelphs and the heroine Elizabeth of Cimbria:

> Thus, beside the stream called Ganna, he laid the first lines of the university, etc. He transplanted the tender shoots from the gardens of Gandesheim into the valleys of Helmstedt, so that, in suitable soil, they might rise to the proper height of trees and themselves bear the many fruits hoped for by the commonwealth. In that place he established a colonnade for disputants, summoned many teachers of letters, assigned generous salaries to the doctors, added prizes, etc.; in short, he founded a new university in every respect.

Meibomius expresses the same view in his *Riddagshausen Chronicle*, p. 391:

> The same prince opened a distinguished school, he says, in the most ancient—and, if our annals deserve any credence, the very first—city of Gandesia, situated on the River Ganda not far from the Hercynian Mountains, etc. When the school soon afterward moved from Gandesia to the Elm, Windruvius went there with his fellow students.

When I was young, the following explanation of this transfer was commonly given. Gandesium, situated, as I have said, at the foot of the Hercynian Forest, was repeatedly troubled at the beginning of spring, when the snow melted and abundant water flowed down from the high mountains in floods. Thus the books and literary equipment of both teachers and students were endangered, etc. Moreover, Gandesium was farther removed from the center of Saxony and seemed to lie almost in a corner or secluded place, so that it was thought to be less frequented.

Helmstedt, however, besides lying almost midway between the large and populous cities of Magdeburg and Brunswick, in an open and healthy location, had neighboring regions converging upon it: the duchies of Brunswick and Lüneburg, the archbishopric of Magdeburg, and the diocese of Halberstadt.

Furthermore, Humfredus’s claim is contradicted by chronological considerations, and the passage of Bede mentioned above provides evidence enough. It indicates that Hilda died in the year of Christ 680 and therefore ceased to live in the seventh century. The previously mentioned *Anglo-Saxon Chronicle* teaches the same thing, whose translator rendered the words as follows:

> In this year, 680, Archbishop Theodore summoned an episcopal synod at Haethfeld, in order to correct the errors concerning the faith of Christ. And in the same year Hilda, abbess at Streoneshale, died.

By contrast, Roswitha, the Saxon poetess and nun of Gandersheim, began to flourish three hundred years later. She flourished under Otto II, as is clear from her preface to Otto II; that is, as Du Pin says in his *Chronological Table of Ecclesiastical Authors* for the tenth century, in the year of Christ 973. Onuphrius, Gerardus Joannes Vossius, Gottfried Olearius, and Oudin, however, assign the period in which she flourished most greatly to the year of Christ 980, while Antonius Possevinus places it in 990. In this connection one should consult Coccius, *On the Signs of the Church*, century X; Canisius, *Ecclesiastical Chronicle*; and Jacobus Gualterius, *Chronographical Table of the State of the Catholic Church*.

In that preface, it is worth noting in passing, she compared Otto I with David and Otto II, his son, with Solomon—an unfailing indication of future prosperity, had he not been snatched away by premature death, so that he might afterward increase the glory received from his father without limit. For Otto II died in the flower of his age, in the very thirtieth year of his life, while engaged in restoring the war he had waged unsuccessfully in Italy. He was buried at Rome in the portico of Saint Peter in the year of Christ 983. His body was later transferred to the new basilica.

In this connection one should read the *Cassinese Chronicle*, book II, chapter 9, and Aringhus, *Roman Subterranean Antiquities*, book II, chapter 9, p. 173. Many doubt whether he was taken off by grief or by poison. Certainly Italy brought imperial glory to his father, but destruction to his son and grandson; nor did matters proceed better or more honestly with their successors.

Yet Johannes Trithemius departs from these considerations in his book entitled *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, published in 1601 by Marquard Freher together with others. He assigns the nun Roswitha of Gandersheim to the time of Pope Leo IV, or shortly afterward, around the year of Christ 860, p. 178. For he says there:

> She was a contemporary of John the Englishman, or, as others write, a contemporary of Joanna the Briton.

In this connection one should read Lilius Gregorius Gyraldus, volume II of his *Works*, dialogue 5, *On the History of the Poets*, in the latest edition presented by Johannes Jensius.

Paulus Colomesius, in his notes in the same place, rightly teaches that Trithemius is mistaken in this reckoning and likewise remarks that he had written more, and not ordinary material, about this Joanna the Briton in his short works and historical miscellanies.

On the other hand, if we consider the sequence which Trithemius arranges there, he included Roswitha among those writers who flourished after the year 1000 and thereby led several writers who followed his opinion into error. Charles du Fresne could not avoid this error in his *Index or Nomenclator of Writers of Middle and Low Latin*, which he prefixed to his *Glossary*, when he says there, p. 146:

> Roswitha, a nun in Saxony, lived around the year 1120.

Dufresne adds that her works were published separately; perhaps he meant that they were published together. For Roswitha’s *Panegyric*, which alone was published separately, as is indicated at the end of this preface, does not include her other works.

Trithemius again departs from these chronological considerations, apparently having entirely forgotten himself, and makes calculations contrary to his earlier ones in the *Chronicle of Hirsau*, volume I of the *Annals*. There he places Roswitha in the year of Christ 971 and correctly assigns her to the tenth century. Although the old, incomplete edition of this *Chronicle*, published by Marquard Freher at Frankfurt in 1601, gives a difference of one year and assigns the year of Christ 970, it likewise lists that same year 970 in the *Catalogue of Illustrious Men* and repeats it on p. 129.

It is therefore astonishing that Trithemius was so inconsistent with himself, that he utterly confused the chronological calculations, heaped error upon error, and assigned Roswitha now to the ninth century, now to the tenth, and now to the beginning of the twelfth.

Nevertheless, some have tried to defend Trithemius from this error. Among them Antonius Possevinus must be named above all, in his *Sacred Library Apparatus*. He was indeed a learned man, but open to serious criticism, as David Biondellus censured him in his *Pseudo-Isidore*, calling him a copyist of Baronius, although Valerius Andreas Desselius, in his preface to the *Belgian Library*, and Daniel Georg Morhof, in the *Polyhistor*, chapter 16, treated him more mildly.

Possevinus thinks that Trithemius could not have been ignorant of the fact that our Roswitha flourished in the tenth century and that it is scarcely credible that he should have made such absurd chronological calculations. Rather, he believes that they must have been inserted in these places by some ignorant or deceitful outsider, with several words added here and there.

Possevinus says in his *Sacred Apparatus*:

> I think it belongs to someone other than Trithemius. For the impostors of our age have inserted many such things into the writings of Catholic scholars, etc.

He means that this was done in the second edition of Trithemius’s *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, where they inserted material that Trithemius had never contemplated.

Gerardus Joannes Vossius, in book II, chapter 41 of *On Latin Historians*, noticed the same error of Trithemius but likewise freed Trithemius himself from suspicion of error, believing that the material had been added by someone who understood chronology poorly. Vossius’s words are:

> Nor was this unknown to Trithemius, etc.

What troubles Vossius here is why Trithemius should place Roswitha among the writers who flourished after the year 1100. But the answer is readily given: in the *Catalogue of Illustrious Men*, Trithemius does not observe the chronological order precisely, nor does he always calculate the ages of writers according to their years.

Humfredus would therefore have made a more plausible, though not more truthful, claim if he had confused Hereswitha, an Englishwoman and wife of Anna, king of the East Angles, with our Roswitha. Perhaps, because of some similarity of names, he would have found more applauders and might have persuaded them of this and led the credulous into error.

For while her husband was alive—and with his consent—Hereswitha, the Englishwoman, departed for Gaul and entered some monastery there, whose name the writers do not mention.

What is read in Mabillon, in volume II of the Benedictine *Century*, in the eulogy of Saint Theoledcheda, concerning this matter rests on an uncertain foundation and is not weighty enough to persuade me to adopt his opinion.

Against Mabillon, it is more correct to maintain that Hereswitha the Englishwoman did not become a nun of the monastery of Calae in Gaul, founded, according to the testimony of the Sammarthan brothers in *Gallia Christiana*, by the holy Bathilde, wife of King Clovis II; nor of the monastery of Jotrum, likewise situated in Gaul and founded by Saint Ado, brother of Blessed Odo; nor was she buried at Jotrum, as Antonius Pagi splendidly demonstrates in his *Baronian Criticism* against Mabillon, volume II, under the year of Christ 680. On that occasion Pagi corrects Bede’s error, since Bede took one monastery in Gaul for the monastery of Calae.

Matthew of Westminster was also deceived by Bede when, under the year of Christ 680, he writes that the aforesaid Hereswitha was a nun of the monastery of Calae. This plainly does not agree with the chronology. For the chronology shows that Hereswitha the Englishwoman had become a priestly virgin before the year 647, at which time the monastery of Calae had not yet been built.

To return to Hilda: she did indeed contemplate a journey to Gaul, but she never reached it, or rather she always remained in England. Henry Meibomius the elder contradicts this view in his *Life of Roswitha*, believing that Hilda spent thirty-three years in the monasteries of Britain and Gaul.

But when I examine Bede’s words more closely, they teach the opposite and confirm, against Meibomius, that Hilda never entered Gaul. The whole difficulty lies in these words: “she was kept in the aforesaid province.” I think they should be understood as referring to East Anglia. I therefore affirm that Bede’s meaning—obscure at this point—is that Hilda migrated from her native Northumbria to East Anglia, remained there for a year while considering a journey to Gaul to visit her sister Hereswitha, and was then recalled by Aidan, bishop of Lindisfarne, to her native Northumbria.

The holy virgin’s plan to travel outside Britain, however, came to nothing, since Bede’s words admit another interpretation. He does not assert that she was detained there, but merely records that she was kept in the aforesaid—that is, the same—province. That province was clearly East Anglia, of which the Anglo-Saxon priest had been speaking, and certainly not Gaul, which that writer had not previously called a province.

Matthew of Westminster, under the year 680, supports my opinion, using these words:

> In the year of grace 680, Hilda, abbess, after having spent thirty-three years in the habit of holy religion at Streneshalh, departed from the world to the Lord. This most blessed virgin, being of noble descent from the line of King Edwin and converted to the faith through the preaching of Saint Paulinus, later, after abandoning the secular habit, resolved to transfer herself to the monastery of Calae, where her sister Hereswita, mother of Aeldulf, king of the East Angles, was happily serving God. But she was detained by Bishop Aidan and made abbess at Hertesey, and afterward at the monastery called Strenefhalh, which she herself had founded, etc.

Antonius Pagi likewise supports our opinion in his *Baronian Criticism*, volume III, under the year of Christ 680, confirming Matthew of Westminster’s view with weighty arguments. Among other things Pagi says:

> For anyone who carefully reads the entire passage of Bede quoted above will understand that Bede indicates nothing other than that Hilda went from Northumbria, her native land, into East Anglia; and that, while there considering a journey to Gaul, she remained for a year until she was recalled by Aidan to her homeland, that is, to Northumbria. Hilda therefore did not carry out her plan of travelling outside Britain, since Bede does not affirm this; indeed, he writes that she was kept in the same province, and therefore in the province of the East Angles, of which he had been speaking, not in Gaul, which Bede had not previously called a province.

As for the teachers of the conduct and learning of our Roswitha, she had several, but names two in particular, to whom she attributes all that she received and whom she adorns with the highest praises. So that the lasting memory of these women might reach all posterity, she expressed their merits solemnly in the preface to her work, composed in verse. Her words are:

> First, under the instruction of the most wise and kind-hearted teacher Richardis, and under the teaching authority of others in their turn; then, through the gracious favor of Gerberga, of royal disposition, whose authority I now obey in the abbey, who, though younger in age, was more advanced in knowledge, as befitted an imperial niece, and who herself had first learned several authors from the wisest teachers, she instructed me with great devotion.

It is therefore clear that the later teacher, Garburgis, called Gerbirga by others, was the superior, commonly called the abbess, in this monastery. The same cannot be said of the earlier teacher, nor can it be inferred from the words of the preface just mentioned.

Nevertheless, some maintain that Roswitha’s first teacher, Richardis, was likewise abbess of this monastery, relying on no other foundation than the fact that she is named earlier in the preface. I do not agree with them. Rather, I join the party of those who deny it and maintain that Richardis—or, as others call her, Rikkardis—was a nun of this monastery but was never raised to the dignity of abbess.

From the words of the preface mentioned above, one may conclude only that Richardis was a wise and learned virgin, that she lived in the monastery, and that she taught Roswitha. Richardis cannot therefore immediately be called abbess, since that title could also apply to a priestly virgin; and, most importantly, she is nowhere so described.

The succession of the abbesses of Gandersheim, which I compiled from Bodo’s collection, is as follows:

I. Hathumoda, called Habundis by others.  
II. Garburgis I, called Gerbirga by others.  
III. Christina.  
IV. Hroswita.  
V. Luthgardis I.  
VI. Windelgardis.  
VII. Garburgis II. Under this Garburgis our Roswitha lived and flourished as a nun, and to her she dedicated her poem.  
VIII. Sophia.  
IX. Adelheidis I.  
X. Beatrix.  
XI. Adelheidis II.  
XII. Frederuntha.  
XIII. Agnes I.  
XIV. Adelheidis III.  
XV. Berta I.  
XVI. Luthgardis II.  
XVII. Adelheidis IV.  
XVIII. Adelheidis V.  
XIX. Mathildis.  
XX. Berta II.

But no abbess named Richardis appears here who was a contemporary of the period in which Roswitha lived and flourished as a nun of Gandersheim.

Nor is the name Richardis found in the succession of these abbesses preserved by Gabriel Bucelinus, which differs from the earlier list in many places in part II of the *Sacred Topographical-Chronological Genealogical Description of Germany*. Bucelinus’s list of abbesses is as follows:

I. Habundis II.  
II. Gerbirga I.  
III. Christina.  
IV. Rodeswinda.  
V. Wendelgarda.  
VI. Gerberga II. Under her, says Bucelinus, flourished the most learned nun of that same monastery, whose distinguished monuments of historical and poetic genius survive.  
VII. Sophia.  
VIII. Athelheides I.  
IX. Bertha.  
X. Loicardis.  
XI. Atelheides II, etc.

I am therefore certain that Richardis, or Richarda, should be counted not among the abbesses of Gandersheim but among its nuns.

I must nevertheless admit that the succession of the earliest abbesses of that monastery found in Bucelinus is mutilated and must likewise be supplemented and corrected from Bodo’s *Chronicle*.

Gaspar Bruschius follows the same order as Bucelinus in the first century of his *Principal Monasteries of Germany*, p. 66. But he freely admits that it is incomplete.

This is the same Bruschius whom Lazius accused of plagiarism and whom Franciscus Guillimannus repeatedly and again censured in his *Chronology of the Bishops of Strasbourg*, and indeed on the basis of genuine tables and the earliest monuments. Christian Matthiae reports his death in the *Historical Theatre*, p. 1030: he died miserably, pierced by a shot in East Francia.

[Col. 0957A] Henry Meibom rightly praises this monk Bodo in his notes on the same man, and correctly affirms that the Chronicle was continued by him down to the year 1550, although, as I remarked earlier, some portion of that work perished through the injury of time. Indeed, what still survives is said not to have been carried beyond the time of Abbess Bertha II, who attained this dignity in the year of Christ 1223. Yet Meibom does not approve everything, especially what Bodo reports concerning the princes of Saxony. Nor does he agree with Bodo in the frequently cited Chronicle on the point that Bodo makes Windelgard, abbess of Gandersheim, responsible for having a church outside the town built and dedicated by her in memory of the Blessed Virgin, and thus deserving the title of foundress; and that Gerburg later converted it into a Benedictine convent and made it suitable for thirty women. For Bodo says as follows in Meibom, vol. II, p. 491:

> “Windelgard built a church outside the town in honor of the Virgin Mother of God; she also blessed it and dedicated it to God.”

Again, in Meibom, p. 494:

> “That church outside the town, which Lady Windelgard caused to be built, the most illustrious Lady Gerburg, the second of that name, converted into a convent of virgins of the order of Saint Benedict.”

But Meibom contradicts this in his notes on Roswitha’s panegyric. Rather, he determines that the foundress of this church was Gerburg II, abbess of Gandersheim, daughter of Henry the Quarrelsome, duke of Bavaria, and sister of Henry Hezelon, likewise duke of Bavaria, [Col. 0957C] and he rightly proves this from the charter of confirmation of the emperor Otto II, which explicitly asserts it. The words of the charter are these:

> “Let the diligence of all our faithful, both present and future, know how our niece named Gerburg, abbess of the convent of Gandersheim, intending to build there from the foundations a certain monastery situated in the upper part of the city, entirely anew, in honor of Saint Mary, in hope of heavenly joy, established it with the consent of her religious women who were already dwelling there, and gathered thirty religious women there into a fellowship for divine service.”

But the Chronicle of Hildesheim by Jacob Reutelius, in Christian Francis Paulini, departs once again from Meibom’s opinion and defends the view favored by Bodo. [Col. 0957D] Its words in § 9 are these:

> “Sighard, called Gebhard by others, consecrated Windelgard, abbess of Gandersheim, who built a church outside the town in memory of the Blessed Virgin and dedicated it herself.”

Nevertheless, Johann Georg Leuckfeld praises this monk Bodo and commends his exceptional diligence, especially because he inspected and thoroughly examined the Gandersheim archives and wished to report in his Chronicle the letters of foundation and donation, as well as the charters of immunity and privileges necessary to know. Even so, he could not escape criticism, because he is greatly deficient in the diligence of transcription: he recorded the earliest and authentic instruments of grants only perfunctorily, and in many places departed from the authority of the ancient archival documents.

[Col. 0958A] Moreover, this too must not be omitted here: our Roswitha, a religious woman, must in no way be confused with the abbess Hroswitha, who is fourth in order in the preceding list of abbesses. For our Roswitha, whom we are discussing here, remained a religious woman and was never raised to the dignity of abbess. Therefore the distinguished Johann Heinrich Boecler must be corrected in his *Commentary on the Affairs of the Ninth and Tenth Centuries from the Birth of Christ*, under Otto II, p. 362, where he says:

> “Roswid, or Hroswitha, a noble virgin, also belonged to this period: first a religious woman, afterward abbess of Gandersheim.”

There he confuses an abbess with a religious woman, just as the scholar Christian Kortholt was led into the same error, [Col. 0958B] in chapter 3, *Tenth Century*, p. 392, of the book entitled *Ecclesiastical History of the New Testament*, believing that Roswitha the abbess and Roswitha the religious woman were one and the same. For he writes as follows:

> “To these may be added Roswitha, or Hrosvita, a noble virgin, first a religious woman and afterward abbess of Gandersheim.”

Having related these matters, I think it will not be out of place to proceed next to enumerate the monuments of Roswitha’s intellect, which she left to grateful posterity. For this religious virgin wrote works of various kinds: at one time *Lives of Martyrs and Saints*; at another, comedies, written in emulation of Terence and encouraging undefiled virginity; and at another, a history of Otto the Great. She wrote more, but those works were either lost through the injury of time or stolen. A witness to this fact, beyond all exception, [Col. 0958C] is Henry Bodo, a monk of Clus, in his *Syntagma*, p. 452, in Meibom, where he mentions a certain poem on the building of the Gandersheim monastery, written by our Roswitha.

But this poem, as Meibom correctly reports, was never published and is not found today in the convent of Gandersheim, as the Reverend Johann Georg Leuckfeld reports in his *Antiquities of Walckenred*, recently published in the German language, p. 243. Before him, Henry Eckstorm published in Latin the *Walckenred Chronicle*, or *Catalogue of Abbots*, which appeared at Helmstedt in 1617. Furthermore, the aforementioned Leuckfeld reports that, as far as conjecture can determine, the monks of the neighboring monastery of Clus, belonging to the Benedictine order, stole it and transported it elsewhere, especially at the time when Julius, duke of Brunswick, sent Dr. Jacob Andreae to those regions in the year of Christ 1568 for the purpose of reforming religion, despite the opposition of Magdalena de Columna, abbess of the Gandersheim convent. For when the monks of Clus were warned of Duke Julius’s intentions and terrified by fear of a new change, they gathered their finest possessions and the documents of their monastery and arranged for them to be transported elsewhere. Thus it happened that the aforesaid poem of Roswitha, which shortly before Bodo, a monk of Clus, had obtained and had been granted permission to use outside the Gandersheim convent, suffered the same fate.

[Col. 0958D] But scarcely anyone knows where it was taken, and learned men rightly lament its loss [Note: [Col. 0959] See the preface of D. Pertz to the poem mentioned, which we print below. EDIT. PATROL.]. In this connection it is worth reading the agreements concluded in the year of Christ 1571 between the most serene Duke Julius and the abbess of Gandersheim concerning religious matters. In these the abbess pledged her word that, in return for what she possessed by right, she would order the abbot of Clus and the members of his monastery to apply themselves with every effort and care to restoring in good faith the ancient documents of the monastery and the charters of grants, and to bringing them back into the monastery. But the outcome did not answer the promise.

It will also be useful to consult the excellent Wilhelm Ernst Tentzel, a man highly experienced in this branch of scholarship, in the *Monthly Acts*.

Nor should this be left unmentioned: quite recently a certain distinguished man from East Francia informed me through a friend that some unpublished booklet of Roswitha was preserved in the monastery of Riddagshausen; he voluntarily notified me so that I might borrow it for my purposes and add it to the work now under my hand. I, who seek nothing else than to appear to deserve well, at least in some measure, of the commonwealth of letters, applied myself with every effort and care to obtaining permission to inspect and copy it, but I was disappointed in my hope. For in reply to the letters I wrote for this purpose, I received the following answer: that, even after the archival papers had been inspected and thoroughly examined, nothing of that kind could be found in the monastery of Riddagshausen.

Moreover, Casimir Oudin, in his *Supplements concerning Writers Omitted by Bellarmine*, p. 331, and L. Elias [Col. 0959C] Dupin, in the new *Bibliotheca of Ecclesiastical Authors*, written in the French language, vol. VIII, attribute to our Roswitha the *Itinerary of Saint Willibald I, Bishop of Eichstätt*, as Surius presents it in the *Lives of the Saints* for the month of July, specifically under the year 750, after transcribing it from volume IV of Canisius’s *Ancient Readings*, and as it is found in Jean Mabillon’s *Third Century of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, vol. II.

The heading of this *Itinerary* is as follows:

> “The Itinerary of Saint Willibald, bishop of Eichstätt, written by a religious woman of Heidenheim, a blood relative of that saint.”

But another *Life* of this Willibald, which is found in Mabillon, *Third Century*, part II, recognizes not this religious woman of Heidenheim but another anonymous person as its author. Furthermore, the aforesaid writers, Oudin and Dupin, assign to the religious virgin Roswitha the *Life of Saint Wunibald*, first abbot of Heidenheim, as its author, as it is read in Henry Canisius’s fourth volume of *Ancient Readings*. There Canisius testifies that he transcribed the *Life of Saint Wunibald*, although uncultivated and obscure and teeming with faults, exactly as it was read in the monastery of Rebdorf, near Eichstätt.

Laurentius Surius transcribed it from Canisius’s volumes and inserted it in his book entitled *On the Approved Lives of the Saints*, under the month of December and the year 740. Yet he could not deny that in certain places he had, as he himself says, altered the style because of its faults, as can be seen in the margin there. [Col. 0960A] The heading of this *Life* reads:

> “The Life of Saint Wunibald, abbot, written by a religious woman of Hildenheim, etc.”

But Oudin and Dupin are seriously mistaken. For in the places just mentioned Roswitha is never named, nor is her name mentioned there at all. Nor do Canisius and Surius, having learned otherwise, assert this. Rather, it can be proved from the *Itinerary of Saint Willibald* and the *Life of Saint Wunibald* that these works were composed by one and the same religious virgin of Heidenheim, a contemporary of those times, whom some call Hildenheimensis. This is also clear from the following consideration: in the *Life of Saint Wunibald* these words are found:

> “After this, then, when that sagacious man desired to fulfill his vowed wishes, and, God so disposing, had immediately begun the journey he desired and longed for, and as we have related more fully in another account concerning his brother, and now recall by repetition, etc.”

Some experts in this field understand this religious woman to have been Saint Walburga herself. Relying especially on the authority of Adelbert, abbot of Heidenheim, they maintain that Saint Walburga wrote accounts of the deeds of her brothers Willibald and Wunibald. Adelbert’s words in his preface to Eberhard, bishop of Bamberg, in Jacob Gretser, p. 320, are these:

> “Whoever, therefore, wishes to know the family and life of Saints Willibald and Wunibald will be able to learn them fully from the writings of Saint Walburga, their virgin sister.”

Medibardus also supports this opinion, commemorating the matter in his verses on Saint Walburga as follows:

> “Surviving both brothers, she briefly but truthfully wrote the most distinguished Life of each.”

Yet Philipp, the thirty-ninth bishop of Eichstätt, in his *Commentary on the Patron Saints of the Church of Eichstätt*, which Jacob Gretser first brought to light, criticizes Medibardus and says that he fell into error because he relates that Saint Walburga survived both brothers.

Gretser then expresses doubt in his observations on Bishop Philipp’s *Commentary*:

> “Whether, as his words seem to say, Adelbert means the *Hodoeporicon* and the history of Willibald found in Canisius’s fourth volume, and believed that these were written by Saint Walburga, or whether he saw other accounts composed by that same virgin, I am unable to affirm.”

Certainly, most of what Adelbert reports, if not everything, is found in the *History of Willibald* and in the *Hodoeporicon*. An anonymous writer rendered the *Hodoeporicon* in a somewhat more polished style, cutting out several passages, as can be seen in volume IV of the *Ancient Readings*.

Yet Canisius departs from Adelbert and Medibardus in volume IV of his *Ancient Readings*. He believes that the author of these works was not Saint Walburga, the sister of Willibald and the first abbess of the monastery of Heidenheim, but another religious virgin of Heidenheim, a contemporary of those times, yet a blood relative of Willibald and by nationality an Englishwoman or Anglo-Saxon. [Col. 0961A] This opinion is also the one that pleases me above the others.

Willibald, the first bishop of Eichstätt, was not of Suevian nationality, nor was he a Scot, although later D. Olear insisted on this in his table; rather, he must be counted among the English or Anglo-Saxons. This was correctly judged after Gretser, in the observations on Philipp’s *Commentary*, chapter 3, by Oudin in his *Supplement to Bellarmine*, p. 199, and by Dupin in volume IV of the *New Bibliotheca of Ecclesiastical Authors*. Cave also agrees with them in his *Literary History of Ecclesiastical Writers*.

Nor should this Willibald, bishop of Eichstätt, be confused with the Willibald who wrote the *Life of Saint Boniface*, which was later augmented by Othlo, an eleventh-century monk, with letters, acts of councils, and several other materials. These men were different and must be distinguished from one another, although Serrarius, book III of *Mainz Affairs*, note 1; Mabillon, in his preliminary observations on that *Life*; and Cointius, in his *Ecclesiastical Annals* under the year of Christ 712, no. 12, led by error, treated these different men as the same.

Yet I cannot deny this: no King Richard of England, who was the father of Saint Willibald, bishop of Eichstätt, and likewise of Abbot Wunibald and Saint Walburga, abbess of Heidenheim, is found in the succession of the kings of England. Nor is a king of that name found anywhere in the English records, much less in Bede, who carefully reviewed the genealogies of the kings. I pass over the more recent writers William of Malmesbury, Matthew of Westminster, [Col. 0961C] Henry of Huntingdon, Florence of Worcester, Ethelwerd, and others, among whom there is no mention of King Richard, who is assigned to this period.

Nevertheless, I do not wish to detract in any way from the credibility of this history, even though Münster in his *Cosmography*, Pantaleon in *Illustrious Men*, Martin Crusius in his *Suevian*, or rather *Volusian*, *Annals*, Nauclerus, the Anonymous Chronicle published at Nuremberg in the year of Christ 1494, and likewise Philipp in his *Commentary on the Patron Saints of the Church of Eichstätt*, as well as finally the *Eichstätt Breviary*, all agree in holding that Richard was a duke of Suevia. Nevertheless, I agree with Bale and Gretser when they report that there was a Richard distinguished by the nobility of his birth and closely related to kings.

Peter Stevartius, in the third note on the aforementioned book, believes that there is no obstacle in the fact that writers pass him over, since he may have been a king not by administration but by lineage, not by office but by title. Furthermore, Charles Cointius confirms this opinion in his *Ecclesiastical Annals* under the year of Christ 738, no. 5, though somewhat differently. Cointius holds that Richard was a subking, and proves from Bede, book IV, chapter 12, that those who governed western Saxony for a time after the death of King Cenwalh, until Ceadwalla recovered the kingdom, were subkings.

Bede’s passage is this:

> “When Cenwalh had died, the subkings took the kingdom of the people and held it divided among themselves for about ten years.”

And shortly afterward:

> “After the subkings had been defeated and removed, Ceadwalla assumed the rule.”

From this Cointius judges that our Richard belonged to the number of those subkings.

Bollandus likewise calls Richard a king. In his work, the *Life* of Richard, composed chiefly from the *Acts of Saints Willibald and Wunibald*, is read under the seventh day before the Ides of February; that day in the ecclesiastical calendars is dedicated to the memory of Saint Richard.

But Pagius departs from both opinions in volume III of his *Critical Notes on Baronius*, under the year of Christ 750. He reports that Saint Richard was not king of England but a noble and very wealthy Englishman, and on this account criticizes Bollandus and Cointius for allowing themselves to be led into error by Baronius, although Baronius has nothing with which to prove it except the supposed epitaph of Saint Richard, written long after his death and more properly assigned to fable than to history.

Baronius himself seems afterward to have recognized this error in the appendix to that year, where he called Saint Richard not king of England but a man distinguished by birth and accomplishments.

As for the *Life of Saint Walburga*, also called Saint Walpurgis, it was written by Wolffhard, a monk of the monastery of Hasenried seven hundred years ago. Canisius later brought it to light, though not in its entirety, and inserted it in volume IV of his *Ancient Readings*, where only two of the four books are presented. We owe all four books, complete, though accompanied by the Canisian materials, to Peter Stevartius, through whose care they appeared at Ingolstadt in the year of Christ 1616. [Col. 0962C]

Philipp, the thirty-ninth bishop of Eichstätt, also embraced the *Life of Saint Walburga* in an extensive commentary, which is found in Canisius, volume IV of the *Ancient Readings*. This commentary by Philipp was later abridged by an anonymous writer and first published by the often-mentioned Peter Stevartius, who joined it to the *Life and Miracles of Saint Walburga* composed by Wolffhard.

Medibardus, or Medingaudus, also included the *Life of Saint Walburga* in verse. Moreover, the Magdeburg Centuriators, in century VIII, and Josias Simler, the epitomator of Gesner, as well as Bale, in century II of the *Writers of Britain*, report that Saint Willibald committed to memory the Life and deeds of Saint Walburga, his sister. But if this work ever existed, it either perished through the injury of time [Col. 0962D] or lies hidden in some obscure place, buried beneath neglect and decay.

It is therefore surprising that Oudin and Dupin fell into the error of believing that these *Lives of Saint Wunibald and Saint Willibald* recognized our Roswitha as their author, when the considerations of time and place utterly contradict them. Indeed, Trithemius alone could have taught them this, since, when reviewing Roswitha’s works, he did not mention these *Lives* even once. Yet it is known that he collected nearly six thousand manuscripts of ancient books with the greatest care and effort and afterward composed from them his work entitled *On Illustrious Men of the Benedictine Order*. We read this in Bilibald Pirckheimer’s dedication of Fulgentius, dated 1519, to the Reverend Mother Pirckheimer, in the Hagenau edition; and the same is confirmed by his testimony in the *Treveltian Memoirs* for April 1705, p. 312.

For what expert in German affairs could be persuaded to believe that one could cut Hildesheim out of Heidenheim? These monasteries are entirely different and lie far apart. One is situated in East Francia; the other lies within the borders of Old Saxony. The religious woman who wrote the deeds of Saints Wunibald and Willibald must be assigned to the former and in no way to the latter.

Therefore the monastery of Heidenheim, which Cointius also calls Hildenheimium at the end of volume V, in the later index of bishoprics [Col. 0963A] and monasteries, must not be sought in Saxony or investigated in Thuringia, as Antonius Pagi mistakenly thought in volume III of his *Critical Notes on Baronius* under the year of Christ 725. Its location must instead be placed in Franconia.

Heidenheim was a monastery of both monks and religious women, though the monastery of the religious women was in a place separated from the monastery of the men. Marcus Welser likewise notes this in book V of his works, p. 147. For he says there:

> “Willibald’s brother Wunibald founded the monastery of men at Heidenheim; their sister Walburga founded that of women. It has now been reduced to secular status.”

It follows, benevolent reader, that I should explain the reason for my undertaking: why I have again taken up the labor of publishing Roswitha’s works. Its principal motive was that I had been publicly invited to do so by a certain man of noble distinction, whose authority carries great weight with me. He judged that the labor would be worthwhile if I arranged for the little works of Roswitha, a Saxon virgin, which more than two hundred years ago—specifically in the year of Christ 1501, not 1505, as the illustrious man supposed in his introduction to the recently published book entitled *Collection of Writers on Brunswick Affairs*—were published at Nuremberg by Conrad Celtis, and which are now scarcely known in our regions, to be printed again and cleansed of their inelegant manner of writing.

The pleasantness of the work especially induced me to undertake this project, since I understood that for me, born in ancient Saxony, it would be not only honorable but also glorious for the ancient Saxon people if I pursued the plan I had begun and demonstrated to the learned world what sort of virgin Saxony had produced and nurtured in her bosom, especially during those obscure centuries when the liberal arts and letters were absent from men and had almost died out in Germany.

Certainly, her marvelous intellect was so greatly admired by all that it proved itself to surpass not only the capacity of her age but even that ordinarily attributed to a woman—an example of a most learned woman greatly honorable to Saxony and destined to be transmitted to all posterity.

I also judged these little works altogether useful to read: both because of the pious and chaste spirit of the virgin and the religious conduct that shines forth in the six comedies she wrote in emulation of Terence, through which she encouraged consecrated virgins to cultivate chastity by means of a new literary form; and because of the *Lives of the Blessed Virgin Mary, the Martyrs, and the Saints* that she left in writing and that Baronius repeatedly praised in his *Martyrology*; and because of her history of Otto the Great, which gives the reader no small light for understanding what took place in Germany at that time.

Moved by these considerations, I applied myself to preparing a new edition and bringing Roswitha’s complete works, exceedingly rare among us, to light again. At the same time, I wished to point out that many before me had wanted to perform this task but had never actually done so, either because they were prevented by other serious occupations or because they were satisfied to publish again only Roswitha’s *Panegyric in Praise of and on the Deeds of Otto the Great*.

Thus the aforesaid *Panegyric of Roswitha* was published separately and attached to Justus Reuber’s *Collection of Writers on Germany*, at Hanover in 1619; it was then printed again at Frankfurt am Main by the Aubrian press in 1621 and joined to the *History of Widukind*, under the care of Henry Meibom the Elder, who added certain notes. More recently it was inserted by the younger Henry Meibom—an especially close friend of my brother, but one who died in recent years, to the great loss of Germany—in the first volume of his *German Affairs*.

Finally, regarding Conrad Celtis, it is worth observing that he concealed the monastery from which the manuscript of Roswitha had been lent to him. This is shown by the following words found in Celtis’s preface to Roswitha:

> “When I had recently traveled abroad for her sake,” he says, “and by chance entered a monastery of the order of Saint Benedict, I discovered a very ancient codex, written almost in Gothic letters and by a woman’s hand, under the title and inscription of a virgin and religious woman of Germany, of Saxon nationality. It contained the works listed at the beginning and in the table of contents of this volume.”

For this reason Johann Aventinus, in his preface to the *Life of Henry IV, August Emperor*, could scarcely restrain himself from criticizing Conrad Celtis, whom he calls his teacher in the *Bavarian Annals*, p. 1, because he concealed the name of the monastery of Saint Emmeram at Regensburg. Theodo I, not Theodo II, founded it, although writers on Bavarian affairs treat both Theodos as one person. The monastery still shines with the great renown of both city and order, and Celtis had taken all his materials from its library; moreover, he had arranged for his edition to be printed from an old copy of Roswitha preserved there.

Aventinus’s words are these:

> “There also exists”—in the library of Saint Emmeram at Regensburg—“a copy of venerable antiquity of Roswitha, a consecrated woman, which Conrad Celtis, having received on loan, arranged to have printed through his own efforts. But why he concealed this, I cannot sufficiently wonder.”

Concerning the same Celtis, it should also be noted that he was the first poet in Germany to be crowned laureate by imperial hands. On the advice and at the urging of Frederick III, elector of Saxony, he obtained the poetic crown from Emperor Frederick III, father of Maximilian I, at the castle of Nuremberg in the year 1491. He was the first among the Germans to bear the title and insignia of that dignity. Writers report that this laurel crown is still preserved today at Vienna.

Conrad Celtis attained this dignity in the thirty-second year of his life. Therefore Eschenbach’s chronological error must be corrected when he says that Conrad Celtis was crowned by the emperor in the year of Christ 1487; he ought to have written 1491. This is clear from the following consideration: if Conrad Celtis was born in the year of Christ 1459 and obtained the poetic laurel in the thirty-second year of his age, as Eschenbach himself admits, it follows that he was crowned by the emperor not in 1487 but in 1491.

Before Eschenbach, the same error had already been made by Johann Peter Lotichius in part III of the *Poetic Library*, p. 9, and by Paul Freher in the *Theatre of Men Distinguished for Learning*, p. 213.

Here one may consult the preface of Conrad Celtis itself, prefixed to his four books of *Amores*, as well as his book of *Odes*, published at Strasbourg in 1513, to which his *Life*, composed at that time by the Rhenish Literary Society, was prefixed. At the end of this book his epitaph is also displayed; it teaches that Celtis died in the year of Christ 1508, on the day before the Nones of February; that he lived forty-nine years and three days; and that he was buried at Vienna beside the church of Saint Stephen.

On the authority of the tombstone and the poems composed for his funeral, Conrad Gesner in his *Bibliotheca*, and his epitomator Josias Simler, can therefore be conveniently refuted when they say:

> “Conrad Celtis flourished in the year of the Lord 1370.”

He had certainly not yet been born at that time. He saw the light in 1459 and flourished especially around the end of the fifteenth century and the beginning of the sixteenth.

His homeland on the Main, not far from the Franconian city of Würzburg, is mentioned in his *Life*, which Melchior Adam transcribed in his book entitled *On the Lives of German Philosophers*. But the place is not designated there. Although Gerardus Johannes Vossius, in book III, chapter 10, *On Latin Historians*, and after him Andreas Christian Eschenbach, in his *Dissertation on Sacred Christian Poets*, no. 53, as well as Matthew Merian in the *Topography of Franconia*, define his homeland and report that it was Schweinfurt in East Francia on the Main, which the common people call Suinfurt, they are refuted by Celtis’s own testimony.

Conrad Celtis confirms this in his booklet *On the Origin, Location, Customs, and Institutions of Nuremberg*, in the following words:

> “As the forest proceeds along that region with the river, it soon receives its name from the hills where it rises toward the left, and in the Frankish language is called Steigerwald, that is, ‘steep forest.’ Then, where the Main has drawn nearer to the Rhine, it waters the very ancient city of Ἐρέβιπολ [Erebipolis, ‘city of Erebus’], the metropolis of the Franks, from which our origin also comes.”

> “I am persuaded that beauty of form befits a body,
>
> And that I was no sluggish slave of love.
>
> Add a lineage illustrious in the long pedigree of forefathers,
>
> Where the Main bends its horns amid chilly waters.
>
> Here, where the city of the Franks rises in an illustrious valley,
>
> And is called a *polis* from the Greek name of Erebus.”

These statements concerning the places therefore testify, on the authority of Conrad Celtis himself, that he was born not far from Würzburg.

The same is indicated by his *Life*, composed by the Rhenish Literary Society, whose words are these:

> “Conrad Celtis, Protucius, of the honorable Celtic family, honored among the leading men of Francia, on the river Main, not far from Herebipolis, the metropolis of the Franks in Germany.”

The name Protucius is fictitious and was assumed by him, perhaps because he concealed the name of his homeland.

It is therefore surprising that Paul Freher, Gerardus Johannes Vossius, and after them Eschenbach assigned Celtis’s birthplace to Schweinfurt, which should instead be sought elsewhere and placed not far from Würzburg. Certainly, if he had first seen the light at Schweinfurt, he would not have written that he was born not far from Würzburg. For the town of Schweinfurt lies far from Würzburg, at a distance of five miles.

Trithemius, however, again departs from these writers. If I examine his words, found in volume II of the *Annals of Hirsau*, p. 636, they claim an entirely different homeland for Celtis and confirm that he came from the village of Wupfeld, which is nearer to Schweinfurt. He speaks as follows:

> “Conrad Celtis, German by nationality, East Frankish by homeland, born at Wulfeld, near Schweinfurt.”

But this does not in any way agree with Celtis or with the words of his *Life*. For if he had been born at Wupfeld, he would more accurately have written that he had been born near Schweinfurt, since the village of Wupfeld is situated near Schweinfurt.

Concerning laureate poets, one may consult Scaliger in his *Readings on Ausonius*, and likewise book I, section 41, of his *Christian Poetics*, where, citing Martial, he reports that heroic poets at Rome were accustomed to be presented with an oak crown. One may also consult Thomas Reinesius, *Various Readings*, book I, chapter 19, where he cleansed Scaliger’s opinion of printers’ errors that excessively obscured the sense and defended Scaliger against Caspar Hoffmann, a Nuremberg medical professor. Charles Paschal likewise wrote on the subject in his learned work *On Crowns*, as did Johann Friedrich Heckel in *On the Crowns of Poets*.

This was indeed a most ancient custom, worthy of all praise, for honoring poets. It had been interrupted for several centuries, but in the year of Christ 1341 the senate of the city of Rome first restored it and conferred the dignity of poet laureate upon Francesco Petrarch, as his *Life* testifies. It is therefore surprising that the author of the *Menippean Satire* mocks so ancient and praiseworthy a custom, one that emperors had often sought, as Suetonius testifies.

These, benevolent reader, are the matters concerning which I thought I should give you advance notice. Farewell, and favor my efforts.

Wittenberg in Saxony, the twelfth day before the Kalends of June, in the year of restored salvation 1707.

[Col. 0967]

## CONRAD CELTIS’S PREFACE TO FREDERICK III, ELECTOR OF SAXONY

*(Edited from the 1501 edition of Hrotsuitha’s works.)*
[Col. 0967A] Through a difficult and lengthy journey, not without loss to my purse and good health, most illustrious prince, I traversed the borders and inner regions of our Germany—lands which you and your brother, the archbishop of Magdeburg and primate of Germany, possess far and wide. I willingly and cheerfully undertook that labor and the dangers of travel, so that I might seek out ancient and as yet unprinted books and, if I found any in the Hercynian Forest, the Alps, the Obnobian Mountains, and the vast wildernesses and even marshes of Germany, in monasteries and religious houses of the Druids, founded with the greatest wealth by our emperors and dukes, bring them to light through the art of printing, invented by our own people, for the good fortune of our age.

Many noble and worthy motives had indeed impelled me to this undertaking. [Col. 0967B] Nor could the empty talk of certain slanderers and detractors deter me from what I had begun. When such men see in another something beyond their own powers—or something which, through their own idleness and the dullness and slowness naturally implanted in their minds, they themselves cannot attain—they immediately rail against and obstruct a virtue to which nothing is impassable or inaccessible, and accuse as sacrilegious those who cannot read the ancient books, or whatever literary works were brought into Germany under Constantine, Charlemagne, Arnulf, Frederick, Conrad, and Otto, those most illustrious and religious emperors, or were born among us; nor can they read those Greek and Roman works written in ancient script.

To them I give this most gracious answer: it is a most beautiful thing for a German man, and a credit to the whole German nation, if someone, out of love for literature and his homeland, undertakes journeys and gathers whatever ancient Greek or Latin copies he can obtain by gift, exchange, loan, or payment, and commits them to print. While they are being printed or transcribed, they may return, with interest and, so to speak, after an interval of leave granted and received, to their proper places and monasteries. [Col. 0967C]

Therefore, when I saw many distinguished and remarkable copies carried by Italians from Germany into Italy and printed there, like outstanding and rich spoils taken from us, I reflected that it ought, by right of succession and inheritance, to fall to me—a man born in central Germany and the Hercynian region, and the first among the Germans to receive, under your direction and instruction, most illustrious Prince Frederick, the ornaments and insignia of literature and the imperial laurel from Caesar—to draw out hidden books from obscurity like an excellent hunter and offer them to my fellow Germans as a rich provision. Through them they might see and understand the diligence and unceasing labors of our ancient fathers and ancestors in literature and in our Christian religion. [Col. 0967D]

Moved by a kind of compassion, and feeling extraordinary sympathy for the labors of the ancient Germans, I wished to preserve the things they had written with great expense and vigilance when, seven hundred years ago—for previously we had used Greek—we received Roman letters together with the Christian religion. I wished to preserve them because, through the negligence and carelessness of our own age, and while we pursue attractive vices, they were not sufficiently protected from the violence of the sky, dust, mildew and decay instead of the study of letters, and—let me say it with a groan—even from beetles (*blaptis*).

[Col. 0968A] A remarkable desire for the histories of Germany and of the neighboring nations also came upon me: if I found books concerning our kings and emperors, or accounts of their deeds and sayings clearly committed to writing by foreign or native authors, I would publish them, or insert them into the illustrated history of our Germany which I have undertaken, or take from them material for writing.

When, therefore, I had recently gone abroad for this purpose and happened to enter a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, I found a most ancient book, written in an almost Gothic script and in a woman’s hand, under the title and heading of a German virgin and nun of Saxon origin. It contained the works listed on the front and in the index of this volume.

It is incredible to say how greatly I was seized by astonishment and joy when I read a German woman speaking in Latin prose and verse after six hundred years—for that many years have passed from the time of the first Otto to our own age. I was especially astonished at three things in her, which are granted to very few, as John Dalburg, bishop of Worms, the glory of all of us and an extraordinary ornament of both literature and the episcopate, recalls in his distich: that she had written such things in girlhood and as a woman, born amid barbarism and in a harsh homeland. [Col. 0968B]

I was also astonished by her ancient inflections and constructions of words and names—for example, *sois* for *sibi* (“for himself/herself”), *tis* for *tibi* (“for you”), and *mis* for *mihi* (“for me”)—as well as by the forms and usages of her words, such as *debrius* for *ebrius* (“drunk”), and many things of the same kind.

I say nothing of the liberal arts and mathematical disciplines in which she shows herself learned and remarkable: for example, her discussion of tones and music in *Paphnutius*, and of the force, power, and natures of numbers in *The Faith*. But if the composition of her language in verse and prose has caused some readers to wrinkle their noses, let them, I ask, show indulgence—not to her, but to those times of hers, [Col. 0968C] when, because of the flood of barbarians, Italy, the mother of letters, employed no other eloquence.

All the Decretals and Clementines are witnesses, as are all the letters and rescripts of that period and age. The book itself is a witness, as are the books of Gregory the Great’s *Moralia* and of other writers of that century, in which the arrangement of expression is very different from that found in the *Digest*, in Saint Jerome, and in Augustine. There everything is directed toward rhythm and the harmonious sonority of the middle and ending, which Cicero likewise calls a color “falling and concluding” in the same manner.

Accordingly, it was not so much the writings of this German virgin that delighted me as those of our own Cimbrian woman, or of that Velleda or Aurinia whom the Roman writers mention, recalling their exceptional courage in war and the prophetic power divinely inspired in them.

It would be a long undertaking, most illustrious prince, if I wished to list the virtues of German women, both those who have been taken from human life and those who are still living. Nor do I value Sappho, Clelia, or Jerome’s Eustochium and Paulina, or among the Hebrews Ruth, Judith, and Esther, as highly as I do Anna the German, most learned in every musical instrument; or Agnula of Frisia, remarkable in Sapphic poetry, civil and divine law, and philosophy; or our own beloved Charitas, the sister of our host Willibald Pirckheimer, who is fluent and spontaneous in the Roman language and in writing letters.

No sex or age, anywhere on earth, is too weak or incapable for virtue and learning, provided that intelligence, industry, education, and instruction are present.

When, therefore, most illustrious prince, I had long considered to whom I ought to dedicate a work by so remarkable a woman, you immediately came to mind during those decisive and electoral days at Nuremberg. When I presented the book of this poetess of ours to you, [Col. 0969C] you immediately ordered and arranged that it be printed. A privilege was also granted by the imperial senate, under a fixed and proper penalty, forbidding anyone to print this or any other copy for ten years after me and my associates in the free and imperial cities.

Accept, therefore, most illustrious prince, the literary gifts of that woman, born of your nation. Because they are more enduring, you value them more highly than if we had offered you something transient and perishable. For your love of eternal and, so to speak, immortal literature and of the Christian religion is so great that you easily surpass and excel all the other princes of Germany, and many bishops as well, to whom the care and patronage of letters ought properly to belong.

You rightly follow and cling to the footsteps of that first Otto, whose entire patrimony and extensive empire you and your brother Ernest, archbishop of Magdeburg, possess by a kind of hereditary right, by title, and almost by blood and kinship. You received this formation from your ancestors and from the most illustrious prince Ernest, who surpassed and excelled all the princes of his age in religion, piety, justice, and singular clemency and generosity. He was most fortunate in the fruitful offspring of his most illustrious wife, born of the ancient and noble Bavarian family, with which, even before they had adopted religion, the Saxons had marriages and alliances.

From that most noble and religious woman your father had a numerous and illustrious offspring. Of them, two most distinguished young men, ordained to sacred office, were sought as bishops by the richest and most powerful Churches in all Germany, Mainz and Magdeburg, while you and your brother John were left for the native lands and the commonwealth of the most powerful duchy. In that realm you shine and stand out through singular prudence, counsel, wisdom, and modesty, and through your love of peace and concord—a feeling rare among the princes of Germany. You are the fiercest enemy and opponent of brigandage and perjury. [Col. 0970A]

It would not be easy for me to say how much you have spent for the concord of our princes and for strengthening the peace and union of Italy, France, and your Germany, or how many years for that purpose you have spent far from your homeland with the emperor Frederick, with whom the Roman empire now breathes, and with Maximilian, the unconquered king.

You have no concern for your native land or your extensive duchy, and no anxiety about taking a wife. Whatever wealth, strength of spirit, and counsel are in you, all of it you spend, give, and offer to the Christian commonwealth and the Roman empire, and for the preservation of its majesty.

Those are divine gifts of your most noble spirit and excellent body, bestowed by birth and by the sealed stars, as astrologers say. From the beauty of your face, the modesty of your eyes, and a certain singular grace, you draw and carry away the favor of men toward yourself. Among these virtues, your endurance and patience in labor and vigil are admirable.

Whenever you are free from public affairs, or devote yourself to the hunt for the relaxation of your spirit, your extraordinary devotion to literature becomes evident. At one time you listen to and read poets, at another orators and historians, then physicians and theologians, and then jurists, [Col. 0970B] and you take pleasure in them. At other times you delight in mathematical disciplines, numbers and measurements, and the observation, nature, and movements of the stars. You honor and enrich with your gifts and benefactions music and painting, and those arts which the Greeks and Romans held in admiration and the highest esteem, as well as their excellent masters.

You act as the emperor Sigismund once did. He honored and placed above the nobles in his court those who surpassed other mortals in excellence of intellect and exceptional arts. When asked why he did this, and why he despised those born of noble and illustrious families, he is said to have replied:

“I rightly honor and prefer to all other mortals those whom nature, our mother, and God have endowed with exceptional intelligence. Nature and God alone can create such men; but it lies in my power to make men noble by title and estates at any hour.”

Therefore, most illustrious prince, on account of those outstanding gifts of your mind and body, all who excel in intelligence or in any exceptional art honor and respect you, and rise in deference and service to you and your most illustrious family. Among their number I too offer, dedicate, and commend myself wholly to you and to your most illustrious brothers, the archbishop and John.

Farewell, most illustrious prince, and when you are free from public affairs, read and turn over the pages of our German poetess, dedicated to your name. Farewell once more. From imperial Nuremberg, our literary lodging, the house of Willibald Pirckheimer, most devoted student of both languages and of philosophy.

[Col. 0971]

## Epigrams of the Literary Fellowship

Composed at the assembly of princes and during the decisive days of the Empire at Nuremberg, for the works of Hrotswitha, the most illustrious German virgin and nun.

John Dalburg, bishop of Worms, prince of the Literary Fellowship throughout Germany.

[Col. 0971A]

What an age granted to few in her native land and sex,

Hrotswitha supplied through her maidenly intelligence.

### Another by the same author

Praise belongs to Affro in the theater, to Flaccus on the lyre, to Maro in war:

Learned Hrotswitha bears a many-sided laurel.

John Trithemius, abbot at Sponheim.

Why should we not praise the writings of a German girl?

If she were Greek, she would already certainly be a goddess.

Add that she sang these verses at so ancient a time:

Thus Phoebus returns from a world six hundred years away.

Heinrich of Bunau.

How greatly the pious powers of heaven favor the Germans,

you can now know from this learned virgin.

She reverently recounts the holy prophets of old,

[Col. 0971B] and sings chaste songs, more than Sappho.

Ololikos of Stein (also called Gitelvolff).

What do you think of this German woman, Greek, what do you think, Italian?

She sings Latin words no less than your women do.

Willibald Birkhammer, Nuremberg.

> If Sappho is the tenth of the singing Muses,
>
> Roswitha is recorded as the eleventh Muse.

### Translation by the same author

If Sappho is the tenth of the Muses, sweetly singing,

Hrotswitha must be written as the eleventh of the Aonian choir.

John Tholophus, provost.

As the lyre bestowed songs upon the Thracian poet,

the radiant star that gleams in the northern sky,

so the same power poured words and the lyre into Hrotswitha,

a chaste poetess born in Saxon lands.

Henry Groninger.

[Col. 0971C] Envious man, you never cease attacking divine poets

as though they were lying and empty-talking men.

Do you not see how much this nun can accomplish in verse,

this eloquent virgin singing sacred histories?

John Verner.

[Col. 0972A]

Hrotswitha is now the greatest glory of the German lands,

skilled at joining Latin measures in song.

Nor does she less carefully depict unbound speech,

following the comic works of free-speaking Terence.

Martin Mellerstat, physician.

As great as the glory once was of the great Ottos in arms,

so great is your glory, Hrotswitha, in history.

Conrad Celtis.

If, having fashioned a worthy cento, she constrained lofty-speaking Maro,

and the other learned men whom Latium had produced,

if they read this woman born of Saxon blood,

they would have praised in verse the work of our poet.

John Lateranus.

Once born in the northern land,

a noble virgin of the Saxon race,

whose ancient name is remembered as

[Col. 0972B] Hrotswitha,

she sang divine fervors,

modulating the holy Lives of the Martyrs,

and with great skill, learnedly recounts

the deeds of the Druids.

Phoebus enrolled her among the sacred number of ten sisters,

pitying her labors,

and heaped upon himself honors worthy of her

with everlasting praise.

John Stabius, mathematician of Ingolstadt.

Although our homeland may be called barbarous,

deprived both of Greek doctrine and of Latin,

nevertheless with this pen a German heroine,

Hrotswitha, could accomplish what Latin men could scarcely do.

Urbanus Prebusinus.

As learned Sappho was among the Greeks in the arts of the Muses,

so Hrotswitha was among the Latins in poetry.

Sebastian Sprentz.

[Col. 0972C] As Greece once flourished through her seven wise men,

and renowned Rome brought forth her prophets,

so the honor and splendor of the homeland is celebrated in every land.

Hrotswitha is a girl worthy to be read by Germans.

# Works of Hrotswitha

(From the editions of Schurzfleisch and D. Pertz.)

## Comedies

[Col. 0971]

## Hrotswitha’s Preface to Her Six Comedies

[Col. 0971D] 1 There are many Catholics—a fault of which we cannot wholly clear ourselves—who, for the sake of a more polished style, prefer the vanity of pagan books to the usefulness of Holy Scripture. There are also others who cling to the sacred pages and, although they reject the other pagan works, read the fabrications of Terence with great frequency; while they take pleasure in the sweetness of his language, they are stained by acquaintance with wicked things.

Therefore I, the strong voice of Gandersheim, did not refuse to imitate the man whom others honor by reading, by writing in such a way that, through the same kind of composition by which the shameful incestuous acts of wanton women were recited, the praiseworthy chastity of holy virgins might, to the extent of my little ability, be celebrated. [Col. 0972D]

Yet this very thing often makes me blush and suffuse myself with deep shame: compelled by this kind of literary form, I have considered in thought and represented through the office of the pen the detestable madness of illicit lovers and their wickedly sweet conversations—things which are not even permitted to our ears. 2 But if, in my embarrassment, I were to neglect these matters, I would neither fulfill my purpose nor set forth the praise of the innocent as fully as I could. For the readier the flatteries of lovers are to entice, the higher is the glory of the heavenly Helper and the more glorious the victory of those who triumph, especially when feminine weakness conquers and masculine strength is subjected to shame.

I do not doubt that some will object to me that the worth of this composition is much lower, much more restricted, and altogether unlike that of the author whom I proposed to imitate. I concede this in their judgment; nevertheless, I declare that I cannot rightly be reproached on the grounds that I wished to assimilate myself abusively to those who far surpassed my sluggishness in a higher science. Nor am I so presumptuous as to compare myself even with the least of the pupils of those authors. I strive only, although wholly unable to do so adequately, to return to the giver, with humble devotion of mind, the talent that I received.

For that reason I am not so much in love with myself that, in order to avoid criticism, I should cease proclaiming the power of Christ, who works in the saints, to the extent that he himself grants ability. If my devotion pleases anyone, I shall rejoice; but if it pleases no one, whether because of my own lowliness or the rusticity of defective speech, I am nevertheless glad for what I have done. While in my other little works, through a heroic wreath, I bind the lowliness of my own labor to the work of my ignorance, in this dramatic composition I cultivate it in an ordered sequence, and by abstaining from the destructive pleasures of the pagans I avoid them.

[Col. 0973]

## Letter of the Same Author

To certain wise supporters and correctors of this book, before she published her works.

[Col. 0973C] 3 Hrotswitha, an ignorant woman and wholly unworthy of any virtue, sends greetings and lasting joy to you, who are fully learned and well mannered, not envious of another’s progress but, as truly wise men ought, rejoicing in it.

I cannot sufficiently admire the greatness of your praiseworthy humility, nor adequately repay with fitting thanks the fullness of your magnificent kindness and affection toward my usefulness. For although you have been nourished especially by philosophical studies and perfected in knowledge far superior to mine, you judged the work of a worthless little woman worthy of your admiration. You praised, with fraternal affection and rejoicing, the giver of the grace working in me, thinking that I possessed at least a little knowledge of the arts, whose subtlety far surpasses my feminine intelligence.

In fact, until now I had scarcely dared to show the rusticity of my little compositions to anyone except a few intimate friends. Hence the work of composing anything further of this kind almost ceased: just as there were few who, when I presented my work, would examine it, so there were not many who would either point out what needed correction or encourage me to attempt something similar.

But now, because the testimony of three persons is established as true, strengthened by your judgments, I venture more confidently to devote myself to composition, if God should at some time grant me the ability, and to submit myself to the examination of any wise men.

In all this I am pulled in opposite directions by different emotions, namely joy and fear. I rejoice in my heart that God, by whose grace alone I am what I am, is praised in me; but I fear that I may be thought greater than I am. For I do not doubt that both things are wicked: to deny God’s gratuitous gift and to pretend to have received what I have not received.

Therefore I do not deny that, through the Creator’s sustaining grace, I know the arts *by dynamis*—that is, in capacity—for I am an animal capable of learning; but *by energeia*, in actual exercise, I openly confess that I know nothing. I also acknowledge that a discerning intelligence was divinely bestowed upon me, but, because of the neglect of teachers’ diligence, it lies uncultivated and torpid through the negligence of my own slothful inertia. 4

Therefore, lest God’s gift in me be nullified through my negligence, if I have been able to pluck some threads or even scraps from little pieces torn from the garment of philosophy, I have taken care to insert them into the work, so that the worthlessness of my ignorance might be ennobled by the admixture of more distinguished material, and the giver of intelligence might rightly be praised in me all the more because a woman’s understanding is thought to be slower.

This is my purpose in composing; this alone is the reason for my labor. I do not boast by pretending to know what I do not know; as far as I am concerned, I know only that I do not know.

Because, bent like a reed by your favor and request, I handed over to you for examination the little book which I arranged with this purpose, but which until now I preferred to conceal because of its worthlessness rather than bring into public view, it is fitting that you should investigate and correct it with no less diligent care than you would the sequence of your own labor. Then return it to me, finally reformed according to the rule of correctness, so that, with your instruction showing me where I had chiefly gone wrong, I may be able to recognize my faults.

[Col. 0975]

# Six Comedies of Hrotswitha

## I. Gallicanus

### Argument of *Gallicanus*

The conversion of Gallicanus, a military commander who, when he was about to go to war against the Scythians, became betrothed to Constantia, the most holy virgin and daughter of the emperor Constantine. But in the battle, after being placed under extreme pressure, he was converted through John and Paul, Constantia’s chief officers, hastened to baptism, and chose a celibate life. Later, when ordered into exile by Julian the Apostate, he was crowned with martyrdom. John and Paul too were secretly killed at Julian’s command and secretly buried in a house. Before long, the executioner’s son was seized by a demon; after confessing his father’s deed and the merit of the martyrs, he was saved beside their tombs and was baptized together with his father.

## The Comedy Begins

### Act One

**Characters:** Constantine, Gallicanus, Constantia, Artemia, Attica, John, Paul, and the Princes.

### Scene I

[Col. 0975A]

**CONSTANTINE**

I am weary of delays, Gallicanus, because you postpone attacking in war the people whom you know to be the only ones among the Scythians to resist the Roman peace and recklessly oppose our commands, although you know that, in view of your valor, this duty of defending the homeland has been reserved especially for you.

**GALLICANUS**

For I have always striven, with hands and feet earnestly devoted to your service, O Augustus Constantine, to answer the wishes of your Augustal excellence with the accomplishment of my deeds, and I have never withdrawn from anything that had to be done.

**CONSTANTINE**

Is instruction necessary? For I keep it fixed in my memory. [Col. 0975B] Hence I admonished you, more by exhortation than by reproach, to comply with my wishes.

**GALLICANUS**

I shall now strive to do that very thing.

**CONSTANTINE**

I am glad.

**GALLICANUS**

Nor will love of life be able to draw me away from carrying out what you command.

**CONSTANTINE**

I approve, and I praise your goodwill toward me.

[Col. 0976A]

**GALLICANUS**
