But the highest devotion to fulfilling servitude demands the highest recompense of reward.

**CONSTANTINE**

And not unjustly.

**GALLICANUS**

For the difficulty of any labor is borne more tolerably if it is relieved by the unshaken hope of receiving a reward.

**CONSTANTINE**

That is clear.

**GALLICANUS**

Therefore, I ask you to set before me now the reward for undertaking this danger, so that I may not be broken by the sweat of combat as I fight tirelessly, encouraged by the hope of recompense.

[Col. 0976B]

**CONSTANTINE**

The reward which seemed most worthy and most gratifying to the entire senate I have never denied you and shall never deny you: namely, admission to our intimacy and the highest dignity among the palace officials.

**GALLICANUS**

I confess it, but that is not what I am seeking now.

**CONSTANTINE**

If you desire something else, you must state it.

[Col. 0977A]

**GALLICANUS**

Indeed, something else.

**CONSTANTINE**

What?

**GALLICANUS**

If I dare to say it . . . .

**CONSTANTINE**

You may—and rightly so.

**GALLICANUS**

You will be angry.

**CONSTANTINE**

Not at all.

**GALLICANUS**

Certainly.

**CONSTANTINE**

[Col. 0977B] No.

**GALLICANUS**

You will be moved to indignation.

**CONSTANTINE**

Do not fear that.

**GALLICANUS**

I shall say it, since you have ordered me to: I love Constantia, your daughter.

**CONSTANTINE**

And rightly so. It is fitting for you to love your lord’s daughter honorably and to honor her lovingly.

**GALLICANUS**

You interrupt what I was going to say.

**CONSTANTINE**

I do not interrupt you.

[Col. 0977C]

**GALLICANUS**

And, if your piety should approve, I eagerly desire to become betrothed to her.

**CONSTANTINE**

He seeks no minor reward, but the highest one, and one previously unheard of among you, princes.

**GALLICANUS**

Alas! Alas! He rejects me; I knew it. Join me, I ask you, in prayers.

**PRINCES**

It befits your dignity, excellent emperor, not to refuse him this out of respect for his worth.

**CONSTANTINE**

As far as I am concerned, I do not refuse; but I think it must first be carefully investigated whether my daughter gives her consent.

**PRINCES**

That follows.

**CONSTANTINE**

I shall go and address her on this matter, if you wish, Gallicanus.

**GALLICANUS**

Gladly.

### Scene II

**CONSTANTIA**

The emperor approaches us more sorrowful than usual. I am greatly astonished at what he may want.

**CONSTANTINE**

Come here, my daughter Constantia; I wish to speak with you briefly.

[Col. 0978A]

**CONSTANTIA**

I am here, my lord; command me. What do you wish?

**CONSTANTINE**

I am exhausted by anxiety of heart and afflicted by grave sadness.

**CONSTANTIA**

As soon as I saw you coming, I detected sadness, and although I did not know the reason, I was disturbed and frightened.

**CONSTANTINE**

I am saddened on your account.

**CONSTANTIA**

On mine?

**CONSTANTINE**

On yours.

**CONSTANTIA**

I am terrified. What is it, my lord?

[Col. 0978B]

**CONSTANTINE**

I am reluctant to tell you, lest you become sad.

**CONSTANTIA**

I shall be much more saddened if you do not tell me.

**CONSTANTINE**

The commander Gallicanus, whose frequent success in triumphs has won him the first rank of distinction among princes, and whose aid we need so often for the defense of the homeland . . . .

**CONSTANTIA**

What of him?

**CONSTANTINE**

He desires to take you as his betrothed.

**CONSTANTIA**

Me?

[Col. 0978C]

**CONSTANTINE**

You.

**CONSTANTIA**

I would rather die.

**CONSTANTINE**

I knew it beforehand.

**CONSTANTIA**

Nor is it surprising, since with your consent and permission I vowed to God that I would preserve my virginity.

**CONSTANTINE**

I remember.

**CONSTANTIA**

For no punishments will ever be able to compel me not to keep inviolate the sacred promise of my resolve.

**CONSTANTINE**

That is fitting. But I am greatly constrained by this situation, because if, as a father ought to do, I consent to your remaining steadfast in your resolve, I shall suffer no slight damage in public affairs. But if, God forbid, I resist you, I shall be subjected to eternal punishments.

[Col. 0978D]

**CONSTANTIA**

If I despaired of divine aid being present, I above all, I especially, would have cause for grief.

**CONSTANTINE**

True.

**CONSTANTIA**

But now there is no room for sadness, since I rely upon the Lord’s compassion.

[Col. 0979A]

**CONSTANTINE**

How well you speak, my Constantia!

**CONSTANTIA**

If you deign to seek my advice, I shall show you how you can escape both dangers.

**CONSTANTINE**

Would that you could!

**CONSTANTIA**

Pretend that, once the expedition has been successfully completed, you will satisfy his wishes. And, so that he may believe you willing to bring about my agreement, persuade him to have his daughters Attica and Artemia remain with me, as a pledge to secure your love, and to take my chief officers John and Paul with him on the journey.

[Col. 0979B]

**CONSTANTINE**

And what shall I have to do if he returns victorious?

**CONSTANTIA**

I think the Father of All must first be invoked, so that he may turn Gallicanus’s mind away from such an intention.

**CONSTANTINE**

O daughter, daughter, how greatly you have sweetened the bitterness of your sorrowful father through the sweetness of your speech, so that after this I am moved by no anxiety concerning the matter.

**CONSTANTIA**

There is no need.

**CONSTANTINE**

I shall also entrap Gallicanus with a cheerful promise.

[Col. 0979C]

**CONSTANTIA**

Go in peace, my lord.

### Scene III

**GALLICANUS**

I am consumed by curiosity, princes, until I discover what my senior Augustus has been doing for so long with his lordly daughter.

**PRINCES**

He is persuading her to be willing to grant what you desire.

**GALLICANUS**

Would that the persuasion might prevail!

**PAULUS [read: PRINCES]**

Perhaps it will prevail.

**GALLICANUS**

Be silent, be quiet: the Augustus is returning, not with the gloomy face with which he departed, but with a very serene expression.

**PRINCES**

Good fortune.

**GALLICANUS**

For if, as they say, the face is the mirror of the mind, the serenity of his face perhaps indicates the gentleness of his spirit.

**PRINCES**

So it is.

### Scene IV

**CONSTANTINE**

Gallicanus!

**GALLICANUS**

What did he say?

[Col. 0980A]

**PRINCES**

Go forward, go forward; he is calling you.

**GALLICANUS**

Propitious gods, favor me!

**CONSTANTINE**

Go safely to war, Gallicanus. When you return, you shall receive the reward you desire.

**GALLICANUS**

Are you mocking me?

**CONSTANTINE**

Am I mocking you?

**GALLICANUS**

How fortunate I should be, if only I knew one thing.

**CONSTANTINE**

What one thing?

[Col. 0980B]

**GALLICANUS**

Her answer.

**CONSTANTINE**

My daughter’s?

**GALLICANUS**

Hers.

**CONSTANTINE**

It is quite unreasonable in this matter to seek the answer of a modest virgin. The outcome of events, however, will show her consent.

**GALLICANUS**

If I knew that, I would care nothing for the answer.

**CONSTANTINE**

You may test it.

**GALLICANUS**

I eagerly desire to do so.

**CONSTANTINE**

She has decided that her chief officers John and Paul shall remain with you until the day of the wedding.

[Col. 0980C]

**GALLICANUS**

For what reason?

**CONSTANTINE**

So that through their conversation you may learn beforehand her life, morals, and habits.

**GALLICANUS**

Good advice, and one that pleases me greatly.

**CONSTANTINE**

In turn, she wishes your daughters to remain with her for the time being, so that through their companionship she may become compliant toward you.

[Col. 0980D]

**GALLICANUS**

Hurrah! Hurrah! Everything answers my wishes.

**CONSTANTINE**

Have them brought here quickly.

**GALLICANUS**

Are you standing there, soldiers? Run, go, and bring the daughters to wait upon their lady.

### Scene V

**SOLDIERS**

Here are the illustrious daughters of Gallicanus, well suited to your companionship, lady Constantia, because of the clarity of their beauty, wisdom, and goodness.

[Col. 0981A]

**CONSTANTIA**

Good. *(Let them be introduced honorably.)* Christ, lover of virginity and inspirer of chastity, who, through the prayers of your martyr Agnes, rescuing me alike from bodily leprosy and from the error of paganism, invited me to the virginal chamber of your mother—for in that chamber you were revealed as the true God, begotten before all ages by God the Father, and likewise as the true man, born in time from a mother—I humbly beseech you, true and co-eternal Wisdom of the Father, through whom all things were made and by whose ordering all things exist and are governed: draw Gallicanus after you and recall him from his unjust intention, since he is trying to extinguish your love in me by stealing me away; and deign to assign his daughters to yourself as brides. Pour into their thoughts the sweetness of your love, so that, abhorring carnal union, they may deserve to enter the fellowship of holy virgins.

**ARTEMIA**

Hail, Constantia, imperial lady.

**CONSTANTIA**

Greetings, sisters Attica and Artemia. Stand, stand; do not fall down, but offer me a kiss of love.

**ARTEMIA**

We have come with eager minds to serve you, lady, and have submitted ourselves with complete devotion to your authority, provided only that your favor toward us may abound.

**CONSTANTIA**

We have one Lord in heaven, to whom the devotion of our service is owed. In faith and love of him, it is fitting that we persevere with the integrity of our bodies preserved, so that we may deserve to enter the palace of our heavenly homeland bearing the palm of virginity.

[Col. 0981C]

**ARTEMIA**

We resist nothing, but strive to obey in all your commands, especially in recognizing the truth and preserving our resolve of virginity.

**CONSTANTIA**

Your answer is entirely appropriate and worthy of your nobility, and I do not doubt that through the inspiration of divine grace you have come—or, according to another reading, are destined to come—to belief.

**ARTEMIA**

How could it happen that, while serving idols, we should have sound understanding without the illumination of heavenly compassion?

**CONSTANTIA**

The steadfastness of your faith awakens in me hope for Gallicanus’s conversion.

**ARTEMIA**

Let him only be admonished; there is no doubt that he will believe.

**CONSTANTIA**

Let John and Paul be summoned.

### Scene VI

**JOHN**

We are here, lady, whom you called.

**CONSTANTIA**

Go quickly to Gallicanus, remain at his side, and gradually persuade him of the mystery of our faith, if perhaps God should deign to win him through us.

[Col. 0982A]

**PAUL**

May God grant success! We shall apply a steady succession of exhortations.

### Scene VII

**GALLICANUS**

You arrive opportunely, John and Paul. I have long awaited your arrival with anxious minds.

**JOHN**

As soon as we heard the voice of our lady who commanded us, we hastened to obey you.

**GALLICANUS**

I take much more pleasure in your service than in that of others.

**PAUL**

Not undeservedly, for it is commonly said: “He who serves those he loves is himself beloved.”

[Col. 0982B]

**GALLICANUS**

True.

**JOHN**

The love of the lady who sent us reconciles us to your companionship.

**GALLICANUS**

I do not deny it. Assemble, gather together, tribunes and centurions, and all the soldiers under my authority. John and Paul are here; their absence had held me back from proceeding.

**TRIBUNES**

Lead on. *(They accompany him as a group.)*

**GALLICANUS**

First we must enter the Capitol and the temples, and appease the divinities of the gods by the rites of sacrifice, so that the outcome of the battle may prosper.

[Col. 0982C]

**TRIBUNES**

It is necessary.

**JOHN**

Let us withdraw for the time being.

**PAUL**

That is fitting.

### Scene VIII

**JOHN**

Look, the commander is coming out; let us mount our horses and go to meet him.

**PAUL**

And quickly.

**GALLICANUS**

Where have you come from? Where have you been?

**JOHN**

We packed up our little baggage and sent it ahead, so that we might accompany your journey unencumbered.

**GALLICANUS**

Good.

### Scene IX
GALLICANUS.

O tribunes, by Jupiter! I see legions of an innumerable army, terrifying with various weapons.

TRIBUNES.

By Hercules, the enemy!

[Col. 0983A] GALLICANUS.

Let us resist bravely and engage manfully.

TRIBUNES.

Is it advantageous for us to engage with so many?

GALLICANUS.

And what would you rather do?

TRIBUNES.

Submit our necks. 10

GALLICANUS.

May Apollo not permit this!

TRIBUNES.

By Pollux, it must be done. See, we are surrounded on every side, wounded, and killed.

GALLICANUS.

Ah, alas! What will happen, when the tribunes reject me and surrender themselves? [Col. 0983B]

JOANNES.

Make a vow to the God of heaven that you will become a Christian, and you will conquer.

GALLICANUS.

I vow it, and I will fulfill it in deed.

THE ENEMY.

Hail! King Bradan, the hope of victory’s fortune mocks us. See, our right hands grow weak, our strength fails; and the wavering of our hearts also compels us to withdraw from the weapons.

BRADAN.

I do not know what to say; the very suffering that you endure weighs upon me. It remains for us to surrender ourselves to the general.

[Col. 0983C] THE ENEMY.

Otherwise we shall not escape.

BRADAN.

General Gallicanus, do not rage to our destruction, but spare us and use our servitude as you wish.

GALLICANUS.

Do not tremble, do not fear; but, after giving hostages, make yourselves tributaries of the emperor and live happily under Roman peace.

BRADAN.

It depends upon your judgment how many hostages, and of what sort, you wish to accept, and how great a burden of tribute you wish to impose upon us.

GALLICANUS.

Lay down your arms, my soldiers; let no one be harmed, [Col. 0983D] let no one be killed. Let us embrace as allies those whom we were pursuing as public enemies.

JOANNES.

How much more powerful is earnest prayer than human presumption!

GALLICANUS.

Indeed.

PAULUS.

How effective will heavenly mercy be for those whom humble devotion commends to God!

GALLICANUS.

Clearly so.

JOANNES.

But what is vowed in turmoil must be paid in tranquility.

[Col. 0984A] GALLICANUS.

I agree; therefore I eagerly desire to be baptized as soon as possible and to devote the rest of my life to God’s service.

PAULUS.

It is right.

SCENE X.

GALLICANUS.

See, as we enter, the Roman inhabitants of the city rush out bearing the customary insignia of praise.

JOANNES.

That is to be expected.

GALLICANUS.

Yet the title of triumph is owed neither to our strength nor to that of the gods.

PAULUS.

[Col. 0984B] In no way—but to the true God.

GALLICANUS.

Therefore, I think the temples should be passed by.

JOANNES.

You think rightly.

GALLICANUS.

And that the thresholds of the apostles should be entered with humble confession.

PAULUS.

O happy are you in holding such an opinion! Now you show yourself to be a true worshiper of Christ.

SCENE XI.

CONSTANTINUS.

I am astonished, soldiers, that Gallicanus has kept himself from our sight for so long. [Col. 0984C]

SOLDIERS.

As soon as he entered the city, he hastened toward the house of Saint Peter; then, prostrating himself on the ground, he offered grateful thanks to the Most High for the victory he had received. 11

CONSTANTINUS.

Gallicanus?

SOLDIERS.

The very man.

CONSTANTINUS.

Incredible.

SOLDIERS.

See, he is approaching; you can question him yourself.

SCENE XII.

CONSTANTINUS.

I have waited for you a long time, Gallicanus, in order to learn the manner and outcome of the battle.

GALLICANUS.

I will tell it in order.

CONSTANTINUS.

For the moment I care little about that, so that you may explain what I desire more greatly.

GALLICANUS.

What is that?

CONSTANTINUS.

Why, as you were going to the temples of the gods and returning, you entered the shrines of the apostles.

GALLICANUS.

You ask?

[Col. 0985A] CONSTANTINUS.

Out of curiosity.

GALLICANUS.

I shall explain.

CONSTANTINUS.

I am eager to hear it.

GALLICANUS.

I confess, most sacred emperor, that, as you said, when I was setting out I entered the shrines and humbly entrusted myself to the demons and gods.

CONSTANTINUS.

This was the ancient custom among the Romans.

GALLICANUS.

A bad custom.

CONSTANTINUS.

The worst.

[Col. 0985B] GALLICANUS.

When the tribunes arrived with their legions, they surrounded me on every side as I went forth.

CONSTANTINUS.

You were setting out with a very pompous display.

GALLICANUS.

We advanced, encountered the enemy, engaged, and were defeated.

CONSTANTINUS.

The Romans defeated!

GALLICANUS.

Completely.

CONSTANTINUS.

O terrible event, unheard of in every age!

GALLICANUS.

[Col. 0985C] I repeated the unholy sacrifices, and the gods who might help were not present; but as the engagement grew fiercer, very many of our men perished.

CONSTANTINUS.

I am confounded to hear it.

GALLICANUS.

At last the tribunes rejected me and surrendered themselves.

CONSTANTINUS.

To the enemy?

GALLICANUS.

To the enemy themselves.

CONSTANTINUS.

Ah! What did you do?

GALLICANUS.

[Col. 0985D] What could I do except seek flight?

CONSTANTINUS.

No.

GALLICANUS.

Yes, indeed.

CONSTANTINUS.

With what great anxieties was the steadfastness of your heart then pressed!

GALLICANUS.

With the greatest.

CONSTANTINUS.

And how did you escape?

GALLICANUS.

My close companions, Joannes and Paulus, advised me to make a vow to the Creator.

[Col. 0986A] CONSTANTINUS.

A saving counsel.

GALLICANUS.

I put it to the test. As soon as I opened my mouth to make the vow, I felt heavenly assistance.

CONSTANTINUS.

In what way?

GALLICANUS.

A young man of extraordinary stature appeared to me, carrying a cross upon his shoulders, and ordered me to follow him with drawn sword.

CONSTANTINUS.

Whoever he was, he had been sent from heaven.

GALLICANUS.

[Col. 0986B] I proved it. Without delay, armed soldiers stood beside me on the right and left, whose faces I did not recognize at all, promising me their assistance.

CONSTANTINUS.

A heavenly army.

GALLICANUS.

I have no doubt. But when, following the one who went before, I entered safely [leg. *securus*] into the midst of the enemy’s ranks, I reached their king, named Bradan. He was immediately seized by incredible fear, fell at my feet, and surrendered himself and his people, declaring that tribute was to be paid to the ruler of the Roman world to the very end.

CONSTANTINUS.

Thanks to the author of prosperity, who does not permit those who hope in him [Col. 0986C] to be put to shame.

GALLICANUS.

I learned this by experience.

CONSTANTINUS.

I should like to learn what the fugitive tribunes did afterward.

GALLICANUS.

They hastened to be reconciled.

CONSTANTINUS.

Did you receive them back for nothing?

GALLICANUS.

Should I receive for nothing those who abandoned me to danger and themselves to the enemy? Not so.

CONSTANTINUS.

Then how?

[Col. 0986D] GALLICANUS.

I proposed a price for earning favor.

CONSTANTINUS.

What price?

GALLICANUS.

Namely, the religion of the worshipers of Christ: whoever chose it would receive favor and higher honor than before; whoever rejected it would at the same time be deprived of favor and of military service.

CONSTANTINUS.

A sound proposal, worthy of your authority.

GALLICANUS.

As for me, baptized and instructed in the faith, I subjected my whole self to God, even to the point of renouncing your daughter, whom I loved above all, so that by abstaining from marriage I might please the offspring of the Virgin.

[Col. 0987A] CONSTANTINUS.

Come closer, so that I may rush into your embrace. Now—now I am compelled to reveal to you what I had been trying for a time to conceal.

GALLICANUS.

What?

CONSTANTINUS.

This, namely: my daughter, and your daughter as well, are devoted to the same religion that you have chosen.

GALLICANUS.

I rejoice.

CONSTANTINUS.

And they burn with such love for preserving virginity that [Col. 0987B] neither threats nor blandishments can call them back from their purpose.

GALLICANUS.

May they persevere; that is my desire.

CONSTANTINUS.

Let us enter the palace, where they themselves reside.

GALLICANUS.

Go ahead; I will follow.

CONSTANTINUS.

See, they come forward with the glorious Augusta Helena, my revered mother, and everyone’s tears flow for joy.

SCENE XIII.

[Col. 0987C] GALLICANUS.

Live happily, O holy virgins, persevering in the fear of God; preserve the honor of virginity inviolate, so that you may be found worthy of the embrace of the eternal King.

CONSTANTIA.

We shall preserve it all the more freely because we perceive that you do not struggle against us.

GALLICANUS.

I do not struggle against you, I do not resist, I do not forbid; rather, I willingly yield to your vows in this matter, so completely that I will not compel you, my Constantia, whom I acquired at no small price—the price of my life—to desire anything other than what you have begun to desire.

CONSTANTIA.

This is a change wrought by the right hand of the Most High.

GALLICANUS.

[Col. 0987D] If I had not been changed for the better, I would not have assented to your promise. 13

CONSTANTIA.

May the friend and protector of virginal chastity and of every good intention, who turned you back from your unjust purpose and marked my virginity as his own, deem it worthy that, in place of our bodily separation, we may one day go together into eternal joy.

[Col. 0988A] GALLICANUS.

May it be so, may it be so!

CONSTANTINUS.

Since the bond of Christ’s love unites us in the fellowship of one religion, it is fitting that, as a son-in-law of the Augusti, you should live honorably with us within the palace.

GALLICANUS.

No temptation is more necessary to avoid than the lust of the eyes.

CONSTANTINUS.

I cannot disagree.

GALLICANUS.

Therefore it is not expedient for me to look frequently upon the virgin [Col. 0988B] whom you know I love more than parents, more than life, more than my soul.

CONSTANTINUS.

As you wish.

GALLICANUS.

See, with Christ’s favor and through my efforts, you have an army four times as large. Permit me now to serve the emperor whose aid enabled me to conquer and to whom I owe everything I have lived through happily.

CONSTANTINUS.

Praise and rejoicing are especially due to him; every creature ought to serve him.

GALLICANUS.

But above all, the one who grants more generous help in time of need.

[Col. 0988C] CONSTANTINUS.

As you say.

GALLICANUS.

I set aside the portion of the property that belongs to my daughters, and reserve a portion for receiving pilgrims. With the remainder, I wish to enrich my own slaves after granting them freedom, and to provide support for the needs of the poor.

CONSTANTINUS.

You are prudently arranging your possessions, and you do not weep without hope of eternal reward.

GALLICANUS.

I also ardently desire to be joined as an inseparable companion to the holy man Hilarianus in the city of Ostia [Note: The latest editor of Hrotsvit’s Comedies, Q. Magnin, advises that *Ostiensi* should be read here instead of *ostendi*. EDITOR], so that there I may spend the rest of my life in God’s praise and in receiving the poor. [Col. 0988D]

CONSTANTINUS.

May Simple Being, for whom “to be” is always “to be able,” permit your being to flourish through prosperous success according to his will, and may he who reigns and is glorified in the unity of the Trinity lead you to the joys of eternity.

GALLICANUS.

Amen.

ACT TWO. CHARACTERS: THE EMPEROR JULIAN, CONSULS, SOLDIERS, TERENTIANUS, JOANNES, WORSHIPERS OF CHRIST.

[Col. 0989]

SCENE I.

[Col. 0989A]

JULIANUS.

14 It is judged to be a considerable disadvantage to our empire that Christians exercise freedom of choice and boast that they ought to follow the laws which they received in the time of Constantine.

CONSULS.

It would be shameful if you tolerated it.

JULIANUS.

I will not tolerate it.

CONSULS.

It is fitting.

JULIANUS.

O soldiers, gird yourselves and strip the worshipers of Christ of their own possessions, by bringing forward the sentence of Christ [Col. 0989B] who says: “Whoever does not renounce everything that he possesses, N. P. T. M. V. E. S. P. T.”

SOLDIERS.

There will be no delay on our part.

SCENE II.

CONSULS.

See, the soldiers are returning.

JULIANUS.

Is this your second return?

SOLDIERS.

The second.

JULIANUS.

And why so swift?

SOLDIERS.

We shall tell you: we decided to enter the fortresses that Gallicanus retained for himself [Col. 0989C] and to seize them for your service; but, if any one of our men set foot inside, he became either a leper or a demoniac.

JULIANUS.

Return and compel him either to leave his homeland or to sacrifice to the idols.

SCENE III.

GALLICANUS.

Do not weary yourselves, soldiers, by offering useless persuasion, because, in my estimation of eternal life, I regard as worthless everything that exists beneath the sun. Therefore I leave my homeland and, as an exile for Christ, seek Alexandria, desiring there to be crowned with martyrdom.

SCENE IV.

[Col. 0989D] SOLDIERS.

Gallicanus, expelled from his homeland as you ordered, went to Alexandria, where Count Raucianus arrested him and killed him with the sword.

JULIANUS.

O, well done!

[Col. 0990A] SOLDIERS.

But Joannes and Paulus despise you.

JULIANUS.

What are they doing?

SOLDIERS.

They roam about freely and distribute Constantia’s treasures.

JULIANUS.

Let them be summoned.

SOLDIERS.

They are here.

SCENE V.

JULIANUS.

I know, Joannes and Paulus, that from your cradles you were bound to the service of the Augusti.

JOANNES.

[Col. 0990B] We were.

JULIANUS.

Therefore it is fitting that, remaining at my side, you should serve in the palace where you were raised from childhood.

PAULUS.

We will not serve.

JULIANUS.

Will you not serve me?

JOANNES.

We have said so.

JULIANUS.

Do we not appear to be an Augustus?

PAULUS.

But unlike the earlier ones.

JULIANUS.

[Col. 0990C] In what respect?

JOANNES.

In religion and merit.

JULIANUS.

I should like to hear more fully.

PAULUS.

We mean to say this: the most glorious and renowned emperors Constantine, Constans, and Constantius, under whose rule we served, were most Christian men and gloried in being servants of Christ.

JULIANUS.

I remember, but I do not wish to follow them in this.

PAULUS.

You imitate worse things. They used to attend the churches [Col. 0990D] and, casting off their diadems, prostrated themselves and worshiped Jesus Christ.

JULIANUS.

You will not compel me to do this.

JOANNES.

That is why you are unlike them.

[Col. 0991A] PAULUS.

For because they devoted themselves to the Creator, they adorned the pinnacle of imperial dignity and made it blessed through the insignia of their goodness and holiness, and they prospered with success according to their prayers.

JULIANUS.

Certainly I do.

JOANNES.

Not in the same way, because divine grace accompanied them.

JULIANUS.

Trifles. I too once practiced such things in my foolishness and held clerical office in the Church.

JOANNES.

What do you think of that, Paulus—a cleric?

PAULUS.

A chaplain of the devil.

JULIANUS.

But when I discovered that there was no usefulness in it, I turned to the worship of the gods, whose favor raised me to the summit of kingship.

JOANNES.

You cut short our speech so that you would not hear the praise of the righteous.

JULIANUS.

What is that to me?

PAULUS.

Nothing; but what concerns you must be added. For after the world was not worthy to possess them, [Col. 0991C] they were received among the angels, while the unhappy state was left to you to govern.

JULIANUS.

Why call it unhappy for that period?

JOANNES.

Because of the character of its ruler.

PAULUS.

You abandoned all religion and imitated the superstition of idolatry. For this iniquity we have withdrawn both from your presence and from the company of your people.

JULIANUS.

Although I have been sufficiently dishonored by you before many, I nevertheless wish, sparing your audacity, to raise you among the foremost [Col. 0991D] in the palace.

JOANNES.

Do not weary yourself, because neither threats nor blandishments can compel us to yield.

JULIANUS.

I will grant you a reprieve of ten days, so that, finally coming to your senses, you may hasten of your own accord to be reconciled to the favor of our dignity. Otherwise I shall do what must be done; I will not be made a laughingstock by you any longer.

PAULUS.

Carry out today what you intend to do, because you will not be able to call us back either to greet you, or to the palace, or to the worship of the gods.

JULIANUS.

Go away, depart, and carry out what I have ordered.

[Col. 0992A] JOANNES.

Let us not treat the reprieve we have received as worthless, but entrust the matter to heaven and meanwhile commend ourselves to God through fasts and supplications.

PAULUS.

That is fitting.

SCENE VI.

JULIANUS.

Go, Terentianus. Take soldiers with you and compel Joannes and Paulus to sacrifice to the god Jupiter. But if they resist with stubborn hearts, let them be killed—not openly, but in the greatest secrecy, because they served in the palace. 16

SCENE VII.

TERENTIANUS.

The emperor Julian, whom I serve, has sent you, Joannes and Paulus, through his clemency, a golden image of Jupiter, to which you must freely offer incense. If you refuse, you will suffer the death sentence.

JOANNES.

If Julian is your lord, keep peace with him and enjoy his favor. We have no other lord but our Lord Jesus Christ, for whose love we desire to die, so that we may deserve to enjoy eternal joys.

TERENTIANUS.

What are you waiting for, soldiers? Draw your swords and kill the rebels against the emperor and the gods; bury the dead secretly in the house and leave no trace of blood.

[Col. 0992C] SOLDIERS.

And what shall we say if questioned?

TERENTIANUS.

Pretend that they had been assigned to exile.

JOANNES, PAULUS.

You, Christ, reigning with the Father and the Holy Spirit as one God, we invoke under this danger; by dying we praise you. Receive the souls expelled from their dwelling of clay for your sake.

SCENE VIII.

TERENTIANUS.

Ah, alas, O worshipers of Christ! What is wrong with my only son?

WORSHIPERS OF CHRIST.

He gnashes his teeth, spits, and twists his crazed eyes; for he is full of demons.

TERENTIANUS.

Woe to the father! He is being tormented.

WORSHIPERS OF CHRIST.

Before the tombs of the martyrs Joannes and Paulus he rolls upon the ground and confesses that he is being tormented by their prayers.

TERENTIANUS.

My fault, my crime. For at my urging and by my command that unhappy man laid impious hands upon the holy martyrs.

WORSHIPERS OF CHRIST.

If he sinned at your urging, he is paying the penalty while you share his suffering.

[Col. 0993A] TERENTIANUS.

I obeyed the orders of the most impious emperor Julian.

WORSHIPERS OF CHRIST.

That is why he himself has been struck by divine vengeance.

TERENTIANUS.

I know it, and I am all the more terrified because I remember that no enemy of God’s servants has escaped unpunished.

WORSHIPERS OF CHRIST.

Rightly so.

TERENTIANUS.

What if I run and, repenting of my crime, throw myself before the sacred tombs? [Col. 0993B]

WORSHIPERS OF CHRIST.

You will deserve pardon, provided that you are cleansed through baptism.

SCENE IX.

[Col. 0994A]

TERENTIANUS.

Glorious witnesses of Christ, Joannes and Paulus, imitate the example of the Master who commands the same, and pray for the offenses of your persecutors. Have compassion on the anguish of a bereaved father and pity the misery of the frenzied wretch who is my son, so that, both of us washed in the font of baptism, we may persevere in the faith of the Holy Trinity.

WORSHIPERS OF CHRIST.

Spare your tears, Terentianus, and spare your heart’s distress. See, your son is coming to his senses and, through the intercession of the martyrs, has recovered his health.

TERENTIANUS.

Thanks to the King of eternity, who granted his soldiers such great honor that not only do their souls rejoice in [Col. 0994B] heaven, but their dead bones in the tombs also shine with various signs of miracles, as testimony to their holiness—through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns.

II. DULCITIUS.

[Col. 0993]

ARGUMENT OF DULCITIUS.

The martyrdom of the holy virgins Agape, Chionia, and Irene, whom the governor Dulcitius secretly visited under cover of night, desiring to be sated with their embraces. But as soon as he entered, deprived of his senses, he embraced and kissed pots and frying pans in place of the virgins, until his face and clothing were stained with a horrible blackness. Then he handed the virgins over to Count Sisinnius, by order of the emperor [leg. “by order of the emperor, to be punished”], who, after also being mocked in wondrous ways, finally ordered Agape and Chionia to be burned and Irene to be pierced.

CHARACTERS: DIOCLETIAN, AGAPE, CHIONIA, IRENE, DULCITIUS, SOLDIERS.

SCENE I.

[Col. 0993C]

DIOCLETIAN.

The distinction of your lineage, your free birth, and the serenity of your beauty require you to be joined in marriage in the imperial palace, a union which our command would approve if you were willing to deny Christ and offer sacrifices to our gods.

AGAPE.

Set your worries at rest, and do not let our preparation for marriage trouble you, because we cannot be compelled by anything either to deny the name we confess or to violate our chastity.

DIOCLETIAN.

What does this madness that agitates you mean?

AGAPE.

[Col. 0993D] What sign of madness do you detect in us?

[Col. 0994C] 18 DIOCLETIAN.

An obvious and considerable one.

AGAPE.

In what respect?

DIOCLETIAN.

Especially in this: abandoning observance of the ancient religion, you follow the useless novelty of Christian superstition.

AGAPE.

You recklessly slander the state of almighty God. Beware.

DIOCLETIAN.

Of what?

AGAPE.

Of yourself and of the state which you govern.

[Col. 0994D] DIOCLETIAN.

This woman is raving. Remove her.

[Col. 0995A] CHIONIA.

My sister is not raving, but she rightly rebukes your foolishness.

DIOCLETIAN.

This one rages even more violently; therefore let her likewise be removed from our sight, and let the third be examined.

IRENE.

You will find the third rebellious and utterly resistant to you.

DIOCLETIAN.

Irene, although you are younger in age, become greater in rank.

IRENE.

Show me, please, how.

DIOCLETIAN.

Bend your neck to the gods, and be an example of correction to your sisters and the cause of their release.

IRENE.

Let those who wish to incur the wrath of the Thunderer bow down to idols. As for me, I will not dishonor my head, anointed with royal ointment, by submitting it to the feet of images.

DIOCLETIAN.

The worship of the gods brings not dishonor but the highest honor.

IRENE.

And what dishonor is more shameful, what disgrace greater, than to venerate servants as masters?

DIOCLETIAN.

I do not advise you to venerate servants, but the gods of lords and princes.

[Col. 0995C] IRENE.

Is not anyone a servant who is bought from a craftsman for a price, as a purchased slave?

DIOCLETIAN.

This presumptuous loquacity must be removed by punishment.

IRENE.

That is what we desire, that is what we embrace: to be torn apart by punishments for the love of Christ.

DIOCLETIAN.

Let these obstinate women, struggling against our decrees, be caught in chains and kept in prison filth for examination by the governor Dulcitius [leg. *praesidis*, “governor”].

SCENE II.

[Col. 0995D] DULCITIUS.

Bring out, soldiers, bring out the women whom you hold in prison.

SOLDIERS.

Here are those whom you summoned.

DULCITIUS.

Good heavens! How beautiful, how lovely, how exquisite these young girls are!

SOLDIERS.

Certainly, they are handsome.

DULCITIUS.

I am captivated by their appearance.

SOLDIERS.

That is believable.

[Col. 0996A] DULCITIUS.

I am consumed with desire to draw them to my love.

SOLDIERS.

We doubt that you will prevail.

DULCITIUS.

Why?

SOLDIERS.

Because they are steadfast in faith.

DULCITIUS.

What if I persuade them with blandishments?

SOLDIERS.

They despise them.

DULCITIUS.

What if I terrify them with punishments?

SOLDIERS.

[Col. 0996B] They consider them worthless.

DULCITIUS.

And what will happen?

SOLDIERS.

Think ahead.

DULCITIUS.

Place them under guard in the inner building of the workshop, in whose forecourt the servants’ vessels are kept.

SOLDIERS.

Why in that place?

DULCITIUS.

So that I may be able to see them rather frequently.

SOLDIERS.

As you command.

SCENE III.

[Col. 0996C] DULCITIUS.

What are the captives doing at this hour of night?

SOLDIERS.

They are occupied with hymns.

DULCITIUS.

Let us approach more closely.

SOLDIERS.

From a distance we shall hear the ringing sound of their voices.

DULCITIUS.

Keep watch before the doors with lamps; I shall enter and sate myself, at least, with the embraces I desire.

SOLDIERS.

Enter; we shall wait.

SCENE IV.

[Col. 0996D] AGAPE.

What is making that noise before the doors?

IRENE.

The wretched Dulcitius is entering.

CHIONIA.

May God protect us!

AGAPE.

Amen.

CHIONIA.

What is the meaning of the clatter of pots, cauldrons, and frying pans?

IRENE.

I shall investigate. Come closer, please, and look through the cracks.

[Col. 0997A] AGAPE.

What is it?

IRENE.

See, that madman, out of his mind, imagines that he is enjoying our embraces.

AGAPE.

What is he doing?

IRENE.

Now he fondles pots with his gentle lap; now he embraces frying pans and cauldrons, lightly offering kisses.

CHIONIA.

Ridiculous!

IRENE.

For his face, hands, and clothing are so dirty, so befouled, that the blackness clinging to him presents the appearance [Col. 0997B] of an Ethiopian.

AGAPE.

It is fitting that his body should look as he is possessed by the devil in his mind.

IRENE.

See, he is preparing to leave. Let us observe what the soldiers waiting outside the doors do when he goes out.

SCENE V.

SOLDIERS.

Who is this demoniac—or rather, the devil himself—coming out? Let us flee.

DULCITIUS.

Soldiers, why are you fleeing? Stop, wait, and lead me with the lamps to my bedchamber.

SOLDIERS.

The voice of our superior, but the image of the devil. Let us not stop, but hasten our flight; the phantom intends to destroy us.

DULCITIUS.

I shall go to the palace and tell the authorities what humiliation I am suffering.

SCENE VI.

DULCITIUS.

Gatekeepers, admit me to the palace, because I have a private matter for the emperor.

GATEKEEPERS.

What is this vile and detestable monster, covered in torn and blackened rags? Let us beat him with our fists, throw him down the steps, and never again allow free access here.

[Col. 0997D] DULCITIUS.

Woe, woe! What has happened? Do I not seem to be dressed in the most splendid clothing and gleaming over my whole body, while everyone who looks at me despises me as though I were a horrible monster? I shall return to my wife, so that I may learn from her what has happened to me. 20 See, she is coming out with her hair unbound, and the whole household follows her with tears.

SCENE VII.

WIFE.

Alas, alas! My lord Dulcitius, what are you suffering? Are you not in your right mind? You have become a laughingstock to the worshipers of Christ.

DULCITIUS.

At last I realize that I have been mocked by their sorcery.

[Col. 0998A] WIFE.

This has greatly confused me; this above all has saddened me: that you did not know what you were suffering.

DULCITIUS.

I order the wanton girls to be brought before me and publicly stripped naked after their clothing has been torn away, so that in turn they may experience what our mockery can do.

SCENE VIII.

SOLDIERS.

We sweat in vain, we labor uselessly. See, the clothing clings to the virgins’ bodies like hides. Moreover, the governor himself, who was pressing us to strip them, has remained sitting and cannot in any way be awakened from sleep. Let us go to the emperor and disclose to him what is happening.

SCENE IX.

[Col. 0998B]

DIOCLETIAN.

It pains me greatly to hear that the governor Dulcitius has been so mocked, so humiliated, and so disgraced. But, lest worthless little women boast that they can mock our gods and the worshipers of the gods with impunity, I shall send Count Sisinnius to exact vengeance.

SCENE X.

SISINNIUS.

O soldiers, where are the wanton girls who must be tortured?

SOLDIERS.

They are being tormented in prison.

SISINNIUS.

Keep Irene back and bring out the others.

SOLDIERS.

Why do you make an exception of one?

SISINNIUS.

Out of consideration for her childhood. Perhaps she will be converted more easily if the presence of her sisters does not frighten her.

SOLDIERS.

Very well.

SCENE XI.

SOLDIERS.

Those whom you ordered are here.

SISINNIUS.

Give your assent, Agape and Chionia, to my counsels.

AGAPE.

Whether we will give it?

SISINNIUS.

Offer libations to the gods.

CHIONIA.

To the true and eternal Father, to his coeternal Son, and to the holy Paraclete of them both, we pour out without ceasing a sacrifice of praise.

SISINNIUS.

I do not advise this to you; I forbid it by threats of punishment.

AGAPE.

You will not forbid it, nor shall we ever sacrifice to demons.

SISINNIUS.

Lay aside the hardness of your hearts and sacrifice. Otherwise, [Col. 0999A] in accordance with the command of the emperor Diocletian, I shall have you killed.

CHIONIA.

It is fitting that you obey the commands of your emperor for our death, whose decrees you know us to despise. But if, by sparing us, you delay, it is just that you should be killed.

SISINNIUS.

Do not delay, soldiers; do not delay to seize these blasphemers 21 and throw them alive into the fire.

SOLDIERS.

Let us set about building the pyres and hand them over to the ravening flames, so that we may put an end to their insults.

AGAPE.

Not to you, Lord, not to you belongs this extraordinary power: that fire should forget the force of its nature in obeying you. But we are weary of delay. Therefore we ask that the bonds of our souls be loosed, so that, when our bodies have been extinguished, our spirits may applaud you with us in the heavens.

SOLDIERS.

O new, O astonishing miracle! See, their souls have departed from their bodies, and no traces of injury are found; nor have the fire burned either their hair or their clothing, let alone their bodies.

SISINNIUS.

Bring out Irene.

SOLDIERS.

At once.

SCENE XII.

[Col. 0999C] SISINNIUS.

Fear the death of your sisters, Irene, and beware of perishing by following their example.

IRENE.

I desire to follow their example by dying, so that I may deserve to rejoice with them eternally.

SISINNIUS.

Yield, yield to my persuasion.

IRENE.

I will not yield to one who advises such a crime.

SISINNIUS.

If you do not yield, I will not grant you a quick death, but will delay it and multiply new punishments day by day.

IRENE.

The more harshly I am tortured, the more gloriously I shall be exalted.

[Col. 0999D] SISINNIUS.

You do not fear punishments; I shall bring forward something that you will dread.

IRENE.

Whatever adversity you inflict, I shall escape through Christ’s assistance.

SISINNIUS.

I shall have you taken to a brothel and your body shamefully polluted.

IRENE.

It is better for the body to be stained by any injuries whatsoever than for the soul to be polluted by idols.

SISINNIUS.

If you become the companion of prostitutes, once polluted you will no longer be counted among virgins.

[Col. 1000A] IRENE.

Pleasure produces punishment, but necessity produces a crown; and guilt is not called guilt unless the mind consents.

SISINNIUS.

In vain I spared, in vain I pitied this child.

SOLDIERS.

We knew it beforehand: she cannot in any way be bent toward the worship of the gods, nor can she ever be broken by terror.

SISINNIUS.

I will spare her no longer.

SOLDIERS.

Rightly so.

SISINNIUS.

Seize her without pity, and drag her away cruelly to the brothel, dishonored.

IRENE.

They will not take me there.

SISINNIUS.

Who can prevent it?

IRENE.

He who governs the world by his providence.

SISINNIUS.

I shall test that.

IRENE.

And the sooner the better.

SISINNIUS.

Do not be terrified, soldiers, by the deceptive predictions of this blasphemer.

SOLDIERS.

[Col. 1000C] We are not terrified, but strive to obey your commands.

SCENE XIII.

SISINNIUS.

Who are these 22 who are attacking us? How like the soldiers to whom we entrusted Irene they are! They are the same men. Why are you returning so quickly? Where are you rushing, so breathless?

SOLDIERS.

We are looking for you yourself.

SISINNIUS.

Where is the woman whom you dragged away?

SOLDIERS.

On the brow of the mountain.

SISINNIUS.

Which mountain?

[Col. 1000D] SOLDIERS.

The nearest one.

SISINNIUS.

O senseless and stupid men, incapable of all reason!

SOLDIERS.

Why do you complain? Why do you threaten us with voice and expression?

SISINNIUS.

May the gods destroy you!

SOLDIERS.

What have we done against you? What injury have we inflicted on you? Which of your orders have we transgressed?

SISINNIUS.

Did I not order you to drag the rebel against the gods to the place of shame?

[Col. 1001A] SOLDIERS.

You did order it, and we applied ourselves to fulfilling your commands; but two unknown young men appeared, claiming that you had sent them for this purpose, to lead Irene to the summit of the mountain.

SISINNIUS.

I did not know that.

SOLDIERS.

We recognize that.

SISINNIUS.

What were they like?

SOLDIERS.

Splendid in dress and exceedingly reverend in appearance.

SISINNIUS.

[Col. 1001B] Did you follow them?

SOLDIERS.

We followed them.

SISINNIUS.

What did they do?

SOLDIERS.

They stationed themselves to Irene’s right and left and directed us here, so that you would not be unaware of the outcome of the affair.

SISINNIUS.

It remains for me to mount my horse and go there, and investigate who they were who mocked us so freely.

SOLDIERS.

Let us hurry there together.

SCENE XIV.

[Col. 1002A]

SISINNIUS.

Ah! I do not know what to do. I have been destroyed by the sorcery of the worshipers of Christ. See, I am circling the mountain, repeatedly finding the path, yet I can neither grasp the ascent nor retrace my way back.

SOLDIERS.

We are all being mocked in wondrous ways and are exhausted by excessive weariness; and if you allow that madman to live any longer, you will destroy both yourself and us.

SISINNIUS.

Whoever among my men you are, stretch your bow vigorously, shoot an arrow, and pierce this sorceress.

SOLDIERS.

It is right.

[Col. 1002B] IRENE.

Wretch, be ashamed and lament that you have been shamefully defeated, because without an array of weapons you were unable to overcome the tender youth of a little girl.

SISINNIUS.

Whatever disgrace has befallen me I endure more lightly because I have no doubt that you will die.

IRENE.

This is the greatest cause for joy to me and for grief to you, because for the severity of your wickedness you will be condemned to Tartarus. But I, about to receive the palm of martyrdom and the crown of virginity, shall enter the heavenly bridal chamber of the eternal King, to whom belong honor and glory forever.

III. CALLIMACHUS.

[Col. 1001]

ARGUMENT OF CALLIMACHUS.

The resurrection of Drusiana and Callimachus. He loved Drusiana not only while she was alive, but also, through grief and the blindness of illicit love, loved her dead in the Lord more than was right; consequently he perished miserably from the bite of a serpent. But, raised again together with Drusiana through the prayers of the holy apostle John, he was reborn in Christ.

CHARACTERS: CALLIMACHUS, FRIENDS, DRUSIANA, ANDRONICUS, SAINT JOHN, FORTUNATUS.

SCENE I.

[Col. 1001C]

CALLIMACHUS.

Friends, I wish to speak with you privately for a little while.

FRIENDS.

Use our conversation for as long as you wish.

CALLIMACHUS.

If you do not take it amiss, I would rather for the moment separate you from the company of others.

[Col. 1002C] FRIENDS.

Whatever seems useful to you is what we should follow.

CALLIMACHUS.

Let us go to a more secluded place, lest someone arriving interrupt what must be said.

FRIENDS.

As you wish.

SCENE II.

[Col. 1003A]

CALLIMACHUS.

For a long time I have anxiously endured a grievous pain, which I hope can be relieved by your counsel.

FRIENDS.

It is right that, by sharing compassion with one another, we should endure whatever fortune inflicts upon each of us through the outcome of both our situations.

CALLIMACHUS.

If only you had wished to share my suffering by sympathizing with me!

FRIENDS.

Explain what you suffer, and, if the matter requires it, we shall sympathize; otherwise, we shall try to turn your mind away from its wicked intention. [Col. 1003B]

CALLIMACHUS.

I love.

FRIENDS.

What?

CALLIMACHUS.

Something beautiful, something lovely.

FRIENDS.

You have named neither one individual woman nor all women. Therefore the particular woman you love cannot be known from this.

CALLIMACHUS.

A woman.

FRIENDS.

When you say “a woman,” you include them all.

CALLIMACHUS.

[Col. 1003C] Not all equally, but one in particular. 24

FRIENDS.

What is said of a subject is known only through some particular subject. Therefore, if you want us to identify the individual, first name the substance.

CALLIMACHUS.

Drusiana.

FRIENDS.

The wife of this prince Andronicus?

CALLIMACHUS.

Her.

FRIENDS.

You are mistaken, my friend: she has been washed in baptism.

CALLIMACHUS.

[Col. 1003D] That does not concern me, if I can draw her to my love.

FRIENDS.

You cannot.

CALLIMACHUS.

Why do you despair?

FRIENDS.

Because you are seeking a difficult thing.

CALLIMACHUS.

Am I the first to seek such a thing, and have I not been urged to attempt it by the example of many?

FRIENDS.

Pay attention, brother: the very woman for whom you burn, following the teaching of the holy apostle John, devoted herself entirely to God, so completely that she could not even be recalled to the bed of Andronicus, a most Christian man, much less consent to your vanity.

CALLIMACHUS.

I asked you for consolation, but you are bringing me despair.

FRIENDS.

The one who pretends deceives, and the one who offers flattery sells the truth.

CALLIMACHUS.

Because you withdraw your assistance from me, I shall approach her and persuade her heart of my love by blandishments.

**AMICI.**

You will not persuade her.

**CALLIMACHUS.**

[Col. 1004B] Indeed, I am forbidden by fate.

**AMICI.**

We shall see.

## SCENE III

**CALLIMACHUS.**

Drusiana, my heartfelt love speaks to you.

**DRUSIANA.**

I am greatly astonished, Callimachus, at what you intend to do with me by this conversation.

**CALLIMACHUS.**

Are you astonished?

**DRUSIANA.**

Very much.

**CALLIMACHUS.**

First, about love.

[Col. 1004C] **DRUSIANA.**

What about love?

**CALLIMACHUS.**

Simply this: that I love you above all others.

**DRUSIANA.**

What force of kinship, or what lawful condition of upbringing, compels you to love me?

**CALLIMACHUS.**

Your beauty.

**DRUSIANA.**

My beauty?

**CALLIMACHUS.**

Indeed.

**DRUSIANA.**

What is that to you?

[Col. 1004D] **CALLIMACHUS.**

Alas! So far, little; but I hope that later it will concern me.

**DRUSIANA.**

Begone, begone, wicked procurer! I am ashamed to exchange words with you any longer, for I perceive that you are full of diabolical deception.

**CALLIMACHUS.**

My Drusiana, do not repel one who loves you and clings to your love with all his heart; repay love with love.

**DRUSIANA.**

I despise your procurer’s blandishments and loathe your wantonness, but I utterly scorn you yourself.

[Col. 1005A] **CALLIMACHUS.**

So far I have found no occasion to become angry, because perhaps you are ashamed to confess what my love for you accomplishes within you.

**DRUSIANA.**

Nothing except indignation.

**CALLIMACHUS.**

I believe that you will change this opinion. 25

**DRUSIANA.**

I certainly shall not change it.

**CALLIMACHUS.**

Perhaps.

**DRUSIANA.**

O senseless madman! Why are you deceived? Why do you mock yourself with empty hope? By what reasoning, with what madness, do you suppose that I will yield to your folly, when for so long I have abstained from the bed [Col. 1005B] of my lawful husband?

**CALLIMACHUS.**

By the faith of God and humanity! If you do not consent, I shall not rest or desist until I have ensnared you by cunning plots.

## SCENE IV

**DRUSIANA.**

Alas! Lord Jesus Christ, what benefit was there in undertaking a profession of chastity, when this madman has been deceived by my appearance? Regard, Lord, the fear I feel; regard the anguish I suffer. I do not know what I should do. If I expose him, civil discord will arise through me; if I conceal it, I cannot resist these diabolical snares without you. Command me, O Christ, to die quickly in you, lest I become the ruin of this pampered [Col. 1005C] young man.

**ANDRONICUS.**

Woe to me, unfortunate man! Drusiana has suddenly died. I shall run and summon holy John.

## SCENE V

**JOANNES.**

Why are you so deeply sorrowful, Andronicus? Why are the tears flowing?

**ANDRONICUS.**

Alas, alas, lord, I am weary of my own life.

**JOANNES.**

What are you suffering?

**ANDRONICUS.**

Drusiana, your follower . . . .

[Col. 1005D] **JOANNES.**

Has she been stripped of her humanity?

**ANDRONICUS.**

Ah! Yes.

**JOANNES.**

It is hardly fitting that tears should be shed for those whose souls we believe to rejoice in rest.

**ANDRONICUS.**

I may not doubt that, as you say, her soul will rejoice eternally and that her body will one day be raised incorruptible; nevertheless, this greatly burns me: in my presence she invited death to come by desiring it.

**JOANNES.**

Do you know the reason?

[Col. 1006A] **ANDRONICUS.**

I know it, and I shall explain it to you when I recover from this grief.

**JOANNES.**

Let us approach and celebrate the funeral rites carefully.

**ANDRONICUS.**

There is a marble tomb nearby in which the body may be placed; let the care of guarding the tomb be entrusted to our steward Fortunatus.

**JOANNES.**

It is fitting that she be buried honorably. May God make her soul rejoice in rest.

## SCENE VI

**CALLIMACHUS.**

What shall I do, Fortunatus, since not even Drusiana’s death [Col. 1006B] can recall me from my love?

**FORTUNATUS.**

It is pitiable.

**CALLIMACHUS.**

I am lost unless your ingenuity helps me.

**FORTUNATUS.**

How can I help you?

**CALLIMACHUS.**

By enabling me at least to see her dead.

**FORTUNATUS.**

Her body is still intact, I think, since she was not wasted away by illness but was released by a mild fever, as you experienced.

**CALLIMACHUS.**

O, how happy I would be if I could ever experience that!

[Col. 1006C] **FORTUNATUS.**

If you appease me with gifts, I shall surrender it for your purposes.

**CALLIMACHUS.**

Take for now what I presently have at hand, and do not doubt that you will receive much greater rewards.

**FORTUNATUS.**

Let us go quickly.

**CALLIMACHUS.**

There will be no delay on my part.

## SCENE VII

**FORTUNATUS.**

Here is the body: neither is the face corpse-like, nor are the limbs decayed. Use it as you please.

**CALLIMACHUS.**

O Drusiana, Drusiana, with what affection of heart I cherished you, [Col. 1006D] with what sincere love I embraced you to the very depths of my being! Yet you always rejected me and opposed my desires. Now it lies within my power to assail you with whatever insults I wish.

**FORTUNATUS.**

Look, look! A horrible serpent is attacking us.

**CALLIMACHUS.**

Woe is me! Fortunatus, why did you deceive me? Why did you persuade me to commit this detestable crime? Look, you will die from the serpent’s wound, and I am dying from fear.

## SCENE VIII

**JOANNES.**

Let us approach, Andronicus, the tomb of Drusiana, that we may commend her soul to Christ in prayer.

[Col. 1007A] **ANDRONICUS.**

This is fitting for your holiness, that you should not forget one who trusts in you.

**JOANNES.**

Look: the invisible God appears to us visibly in the likeness of a most beautiful young man.

**ANDRONICUS.**

I am terrified.

**JOANNES.**

Lord Jesus, why have you deigned to reveal yourself to your servants at this place?

**GOD.**

I have appeared because of the resurrection of Drusiana and of the one who lies beside her tomb, so that my name may be glorified in them.

[Col. 1007B] **ANDRONICUS.**

How suddenly he was received into heaven!

**JOANNES.**

For that reason I do not fully understand the matter.

**ANDRONICUS.**

Let us hasten our steps; perhaps, when we arrive, you will discover what you say you understand less well.

## SCENE IX

**JOANNES.**

In Christ’s name, what is this miracle that we see? Look: with the tomb opened, Drusiana’s body has been cast outside, and beside it lie two corpses entwined in the embrace of a serpent.

[Col. 1007C] **ANDRONICUS.**

I surmise what it signifies. This Callimachus himself loved Drusiana illicitly while she lived; she, bearing this with difficulty, fell into a fever from grief and invited death to come.

**JOANNES.**

The love of chastity compelled her to do this.

**ANDRONICUS.**

After her death, this madman, gathering together the sickness of his unhappy love and his distress at being rejected, was wasting away in spirit and burning all the more intensely with desire.

**JOANNES.**

It is pitiable!

27 **ANDRONICUS.**

I have no doubt that he hired this wicked servant to provide him with an opportunity to commit the crime.

**JOANNES.**

[Col. 1007D] O incomparable wickedness!

**ANDRONICUS.**

Therefore, as I see, both were consumed by death, lest they carry out the crime.

**JOANNES.**

And not unjustly.

**ANDRONICUS.**

Nevertheless, this is especially worthy of wonder: why was the resurrection of the man who wished to do wrong foretold by the divine voice rather than that of the man who consented—unless perhaps the former sinned through ignorance, deceived by carnal pleasure, while the latter acted out of sheer malice?

**JOANNES.**

How strictly the heavenly Judge examines all deeds, and with what just balance he weighs the merits of each person, cannot easily be grasped or explained by anyone, because the subtlety of divine judgment far surpasses the shrewdness of human understanding.

[Col. 1008A] **ANDRONICUS.**

Therefore we have been exhausted by wondering, because we cannot skillfully distinguish the causes of the events that take place.

**JOANNES.**

The outcome often teaches the differences between things after the deeds have been done.

**ANDRONICUS.**

But now, blessed John, do what you are about to do. Have Callimachus raised, so that the knot of this uncertainty may be undone.

**JOANNES.**

I think that first, after invoking Christ’s name, the serpent must be driven away, and afterward Callimachus must be raised.

[Col. 1008B] **ANDRONICUS.**

You judge rightly, lest he be injured further by the serpent’s bite.

**JOANNES.**

Withdraw from this place, cruel beast, for he is about to serve Christ.

**ANDRONICUS.**

Although it is an irrational animal, it has obeyed what you commanded with an ear that was not deaf.

**JOANNES.**

It obeyed not by my power but by Christ’s.

**ANDRONICUS.**

For that reason it vanished more quickly than the word was spoken.

**JOANNES.**

[Col. 1008C] Unbounded and incomprehensible God, simple and beyond estimation, who alone are what you are; who, joining two different things, fashion a human being from this and that, and, separating the same things, dissolve what had been one—command that, with breath restored and the structure rejoined, the parts once more brought together, Callimachus may rise again as a complete human being, so that all may magnify you, who alone perform wondrous deeds.

**ANDRONICUS.**

Amen. Look, he is drawing in the vital air, but in astonishment he still lies motionless.

**JOANNES.**

Callimachus, rise in Christ’s name, and, whatever the truth of the matter may be, confess it. Make known whatever faults enslave you, lest the truth remain hidden from us even briefly. 28

[Col. 1008D] **CALLIMACHUS.**

I cannot deny that I approached for the purpose of committing the crime, because I was wasting away from unhappy illness and could not restrain the heat of illicit love.

**JOANNES.**

What madness, what insanity deceived you, that you presumed to inflict an insult of dishonor upon the chaste remains of another?

**CALLIMACHUS.**

My own folly and the fraudulent deception of this Fortunatus.

**JOANNES.**

Have you been made so wretched by a threefold misfortune that you were able to carry out the wickedness you desired?

[Col. 1009A] **CALLIMACHUS.**

Not at all. Although I did not lack the possibility of wishing, I entirely lacked the ability to act.

**JOANNES.**

How were you prevented?

**CALLIMACHUS.**

As soon as I drew aside the covering and attempted to assail the lifeless body with insults, this Fortunatus—who had been the fuel and kindler of the evil—perished, drenched in the serpent’s poison.

**ANDRONICUS.**

A good deed!

**CALLIMACHUS.**

A young man of terrifying appearance appeared to me. He honorably covered the exposed body, and from his fiery face bright sparks leapt into the tomb. One of them sprang back and was carried toward my face, while at the same time a voice said: “Callimachus, die so that you may live!” After these words, I expired.

[Col. 1009B] **JOANNES.**

This is the work of heavenly grace, which does not rejoice in the destruction of the wicked.

**CALLIMACHUS.**

You have heard the misery of my destruction; do not delay the healing of your mercy.

**JOANNES.**

I shall not delay it.

**CALLIMACHUS.**

For I am utterly ashamed, deeply grieved, [Col. 1009C] anxious, groaning, and sorrowful over the gravity of my wickedness.

**JOANNES.**

And not without reason, since a grave offense demands no slight remedy of repentance.

**CALLIMACHUS.**

Would that the hidden recesses of my inward parts were opened, so that you might perceive the bitterness of the grief I suffer and grieve with me in my sorrow!

**JOANNES.**

I rejoice with you in such grief, because I perceive that you are being healthfully saddened.

**CALLIMACHUS.**

I am weary of my former life; I am weary of wicked pleasure.

**JOANNES.**

And not without reason.

[Col. 1009D] **CALLIMACHUS.**

And I repent of my offense.

**JOANNES.**

And rightly so.

**CALLIMACHUS.**

I am displeased with everything I have done, to such an extent that I have no love or pleasure in living unless, reborn in Christ, I may deserve to be transformed for the better.

**JOANNES.**

I do not doubt that heavenly grace is appearing in you.

**CALLIMACHUS.**

Therefore do not delay, do not hesitate to raise one who is weary and lift one who mourns with consolations, 29 so that by your admonition and teaching I may be transformed from a pagan into a Christian, from a frivolous into a chaste man, and, taking the path of truth under your guidance, may live according to the proclamation of the divine promise.

[Col. 1010A] **JOANNES.**

Blessed be the only Offspring of the Godhead, who is also a sharer in our frailty: he killed you, Callimachus, my son, by sparing you, and by killing you gave you life, so that he might free his creature from the destruction of the soul under the appearance of death.

**ANDRONICUS.**

An extraordinary event, worthy of all admiration!

**JOANNES.**

O Christ, redemption of the world and propitiation for sinners, I do not know with what praises I should celebrate you as you deserve. I am struck with awe at your kindly clemency and your merciful patience: sometimes, by tolerating sinners in a father’s manner, you gently allure them; sometimes, by chastising them with just severity, you compel them to repentance.

[Col. 1010B] **ANDRONICUS.**

Praise be to his divine compassion.

**JOANNES.**

Who would dare to believe, who would presume to hope, that your mercy would raise to life and restore to pardon this man whom death found intent upon criminal vices and carried away once it had found him? May your holy name be blessed forever, for you alone perform astonishing wonders.

**ANDRONICUS.**

Come, holy John, and do not delay in consoling me. For conjugal love for Drusiana does not allow my mind to be at rest unless I too see her quickly rise again.

[Col. 1010C] **JOANNES.**

Drusiana, may the Lord Jesus Christ raise you.

**DRUSIANA.**

Praise and honor to you, Christ, who have made me live again.

**CALLIMACHUS.**

Thanks to the author of salvation, who has granted you, my Drusiana, to rise in joy, though you met your final day amid profound sorrow.

**DRUSIANA.**

It befits your holiness, venerable Father John, that, having raised Callimachus, who loved me illicitly, you also raise this man who proved the betrayer of my death.

**CALLIMACHUS.**

[Col. 1010D] Do not deem this betrayer, this evildoer, worthy, apostle of Christ, to be freed from the bonds of death—he who deceived me, led me astray, and provoked me to undertake a horrible crime.

**JOANNES.**

You must not begrudge him the grace of divine mercy.

**CALLIMACHUS.**

He is not worthy of resurrection, since he caused another’s destruction.

**JOANNES.**

The law of our religion teaches that a person should forgive another if he himself desires to be forgiven by God.

**ANDRONICUS.**

Just.

[Col. 1011A] **JOANNES.**

For when God’s only-begotten Son, also the Virgin’s firstborn—the only innocent, the only undefiled, the only one who came into the world without the stain of ancient sin—found everyone oppressed beneath the heavy burden of sin,

**ANDRONICUS.**

True.

**JOANNES.**

That is to say, he would have found no one righteous and no one worthy of mercy; nevertheless, he rejected no one and deprived no one of the grace of his compassion. Rather, he gave himself for all and offered his beloved soul for everyone.

**ANDRONICUS.**

[Col. 1011B] If the innocent one had not been killed, no one would justly be freed.

**JOANNES.**

Therefore he does not delight in the destruction of human beings, whom he remembers to have purchased with his precious blood.

**ANDRONICUS.**

Thanks be to him.

**JOANNES.**

Therefore we must not begrudge others the grace of God, which we rejoice to possess abundantly in ourselves despite having no preceding merits.

**CALLIMACHUS.**

Your admonition has terrified me.

**JOANNES.**

But lest I seem to resist your desires, he shall not be raised through me, but through Drusiana, because she has received grace from God for this purpose.

[Col. 1011C] **DRUSIANA.**

Divine substance, who truly and uniquely exist without material form, who fashioned humanity in your image and breathed the breath of life into what you had fashioned, command that the material body of Fortunatus, its warmth restored, be fashioned once more into a living soul, so that our threefold resurrection may be turned to your praise, venerable Trinity.

**JOANNES.**

Amen.

**DRUSIANA.**

Awaken, Fortunatus, and at Christ’s command break apart the restraints of death.

[Col. 1011D] **FORTUNATUS.**

Who raised me by taking my hand? Who gave the command that I should rise?

**JOANNES.**

Drusiana.

**FORTUNATUS.**

Did Drusiana raise me?

**JOANNES.**

She did.

**FORTUNATUS.**

Had she not been carried off by sudden death several days ago?

**JOANNES.**

Yet she lives in Christ.

[Col. 1012A] **FORTUNATUS.**

And why does Callimachus remain modest, with a grave expression, and no longer rage in his customary love for Drusiana?

**JOANNES.**

Because, transformed from his wicked purpose, he is truly a disciple of Christ.

**FORTUNATUS.**

No.

**JOANNES.**

Yes.

**FORTUNATUS.**

If, as you say, Drusiana raised me and Callimachus has believed in Christ, I reject life and freely choose death, because I would rather not exist than perceive such an abundance of the grace of virtues in these people.

[Col. 1012B] **JOANNES.**

O wondrous envy of the devil! O malice of the ancient serpent, who gave death to the first-created pair 31 and always groans over the glory of the righteous! This most unhappy Fortunatus, filled to overflowing with the gall of diabolical bitterness, is compared to a bad tree that produces bitter fruit. Therefore, cut off from the company of the righteous and cast away from the fellowship of those who fear God, let him be sent into the fire of eternal punishment, to be tormented without any interruption of relief.

**ANDRONICUS.**

Look, swollen by the serpent’s bites, he is again sinking toward death and will die more quickly than the word can be spoken.

**JOANNES.**

Let him die and be an inhabitant of hell, since out of envy of another’s advancement he refused to live.

[Col. 1012C] **ANDRONICUS.**

Terrible.

**JOANNES.**

Nothing is more terrible than the envious, nothing more wicked than the proud.

**ANDRONICUS.**

Both are pitiable.

**JOANNES.**

One and the same person is always afflicted by both vices, because neither exists without the other.

**ANDRONICUS.**

Explain this more clearly.

**JOANNES.**

For whoever is proud is envious, and whoever is envious is proud. The envious mind, unable to bear hearing another’s praise and seeking to make those more perfect than itself seem inferior in comparison with itself, disdains submission to those more worthy and proudly strives to be preferred to its equals.

[Col. 1012D] **ANDRONICUS.**

It is clear.

**JOANNES.**

Thus this most wretched man was wounded in mind, because he could not endure being judged inferior to those in whom he could not fail to recognize the greater grace of God.

**ANDRONICUS.**

At last I understand why he was not counted among those who rose: he was soon to die.

**JOANNES.**

For he is worthy of both deaths, since he dishonored the appointed funeral and pursued the risen with unjust hatred.

[Col. 1013A] **ANDRONICUS.**

He has died in misery.

**JOANNES.**

Let us depart and leave the devil’s son to him. Let us celebrate this day with [Col. 1014A] joy, both for the wondrous transformation of Callimachus and for the resurrection of both of them, giving thanks to God, the just judge and most discerning examiner of hidden things, who alone examines all things subtly and arranges all things rightly, and will assign each person rewards or punishments according to what he foreknows that person deserves. To him alone belong honor, power, strength, and victory, praise and jubilation, throughout endless ages of ages. Amen.

# IV. ABRAHAM 32

## ARGUMENT OF ABRAHAM

[Col. 1013]

The fall and conversion of Maria, the niece of Abraham the hermit: after living a solitary life for twenty years, she lost her virginity, returned to the world, and did not fear to join herself to the company of prostitutes. But after two years, restored by the admonitions of the aforementioned Abraham, who sought her under the guise of a lover, she cleansed the stains of her crimes through a lavish outpouring of tears and continuous practice of fasting, vigils, and prayers for twenty years.

**SPEAKERS:** Abraham, Ephrem, Maria.

## SCENE I

[Col. 1013B]

**ABRAHAM.**

Brother and fellow hermit Ephrem, are you willing to devote this convenient time to conversation with me, or do you wish me to wait until you have completed your divine praises?

**EPHREM.**

Our conversation ought to be praise of the one who promised to be present among those gathered in his name.

**ABRAHAM.**

I have approached to speak of nothing else except what I know accords with the divine will.

**EPHREM.**

Therefore I do not withdraw from you even for a moment, but give myself entirely to your purpose.

[Col. 1013C] **ABRAHAM.**

Something I must do is seething in my mind, and I hope that your will may answer my desires.

**EPHREM.**

If we are commanded to be of one heart and one soul, we are compelled to will and refuse the same things.

**ABRAHAM.**

I have a tender niece deprived of the comfort of both parents. Out of compassion for her orphanhood I am drawn to her with great affection, and on her account I am wearied by continual anxiety.

**EPHREM.**

And what have you to do with worldly cares, conqueror of the world?

[Col. 1013D] **ABRAHAM.**

I am concerned only that the immense radiance of her beauty [Col. 1014B] not be darkened by the filth of any defilement.

**EPHREM.**

Is such concern not blameworthy?

**ABRAHAM.**

I hope not.

**EPHREM.**

How old is she?

33 **ABRAHAM.**

If one monthly cycle were added, she would have lived on vital breath for two Olympiads. [The wording is uncertain.]

**EPHREM.**

An immature girl.

**ABRAHAM.**

[Col. 1014C] Therefore I am not without concern.

**EPHREM.**

Where does she live?

**ABRAHAM.**

In my little dwellings. For at the request of her relatives I undertook to raise her; but I have decided to distribute her wealth to the poor.

**EPHREM.**

Contempt for temporal things will allow a mind directed toward heaven.

**ABRAHAM.**

My mind seethes with eager desire to betroth her to Christ and place her under his instruction.

[Col. 1014D] **EPHREM.**

Commendable.

[Col. 1015A] **ABRAHAM.**

I am constrained by her name.

**EPHREM.**

What is she called?

**ABRAHAM.**

Maria.

**EPHREM.**

So it is. The excellence of so great a name deserves the emblem of virginity.

**ABRAHAM.**

I do not doubt that, if she is gently urged by our exhortations, she will prove willing to yield.

**EPHREM.**

Let us approach her and instill in her thoughts the security of a celibate life.

## SCENE II

[Col. 1015B]

**ABRAHAM.**

O adopted daughter, O part of my soul, Maria, yield to my paternal admonitions and to the most salutary teachings of my companion Ephrem. Strive to imitate in chastity the author of virginity, whom you equal in name through that shared name.

**EPHREM.**

It is greatly unfitting, daughter, that you, who through the mystery of your name rank with Mary the Mother of God above the stars in the heavens, never to fall, should roll about on earth below, inferior in merits.

**MARIA.**

I do not know the mystery of my name, and therefore I do not understand what you mean through this circuitous speech.

[Col. 1015C] **EPHREM.**

Maria is interpreted as “star of the sea,” around which, so to speak, the world and the people who are called are carried.

**MARIA.**

Why is she called the star of the sea?

**EPHREM.**

Because she never sets, but directs sailors along the straight path of their journey.

**MARIA.**

And how could I, so very little and fashioned from earthly clay, attain by my merits to the place where the mystery of the name shines?

**EPHREM.**

Through the unimpaired integrity of your body and the purity of your mind.

[Col. 1015D] **MARIA.**

It is a great honor for a human being to be made equal to the rays of the stars.

**EPHREM.**

For if you remain incorrupt and a virgin, you will become equal to God’s angels. Then, accompanied by them, casting off the heavy burden of the body, you will pass through the air and rise above the ether; you will traverse the circle of the zodiac and will not halt or moderate your steps until you embrace the Son of the Virgin in the luminous bridal chamber of his Mother.

34 **MARIA.**

He who thinks little of these things lives like an ass. Therefore I despise present things and deny myself, so that I may deserve to be enrolled among the joys of such great happiness.

[Col. 1016A] **EPHREM.**

Look, we find the maturity of an old mind in a youthful breast.

**ABRAHAM.**

That is what the grace of God is.

**EPHREM.**

It cannot be denied.

**ABRAHAM.**

But although she has been enlightened by God’s grace, it is nevertheless not beneficial for an immature girl to use her own judgment.

**EPHREM.**

True.

**ABRAHAM.**

Therefore I shall make her a small cell near the entrance, adjoining my dwelling. Through its window, by visiting her frequently, I shall instruct her with the Psalter [Col. 1016B] and the other pages of divine law.

**EPHREM.**

That is fitting.

**MARIA.**

Father Ephrem, I entrust myself to your intercession.

**EPHREM.**

May the heavenly Bridegroom, to whom you have clung in affection from your tender age, protect you, daughter, from every deception of the devil.

## SCENE III

**ABRAHAM.**

Brother Ephrem, whenever anything is brought upon me by the changing fortunes of life, I approach you first and consult you alone. Therefore do not be hostile to the complaint I am pursuing, but offer help for the grief I suffer.

[Col. 1016C] **EPHREM.**

Abraham, Abraham, what are you suffering? Why are you grieving beyond what is permitted? It was never right for a hermit to be disturbed in the manner of worldly people.

**ABRAHAM.**

An incomparable grief has come upon me; an intolerable sorrow afflicts me.

**EPHREM.**

Do not weary me with a long circumlocution of words; explain what you are suffering.

**ABRAHAM.**

Maria, my adopted daughter, whom I raised for four times five years with the greatest care and instructed with the greatest skill . . .

**EPHREM.**

[Col. 1016D] What of her?

**ABRAHAM.**

Alas for me! She is lost.

**EPHREM.**

How?

**ABRAHAM.**

Miserably; then she secretly escaped.

**EPHREM.**

By what snares did the deceit of the ancient serpent ensnare her?

**ABRAHAM.**

Through the illicit affection of a certain pretender who came in monastic dress and frequently visited her under the pretense of visitation, until he bent the untrained youthful mind toward love of himself, to such an extent that she leapt through the window to commit the crime.

[Col. 1017A] **EPHREM.**

I tremble at hearing this.

**ABRAHAM.**

But when the unhappy girl realized that she had been corrupted, she beat her breast, tore her face with her hands, ripped her clothing, pulled out her hair, and uttered loud cries of lamentation.

**EPHREM.**

And not unjustly, for a fall of this kind must be mourned with a whole fountain of tears.

**ABRAHAM.**

She lamented that she was no longer what she had been.

**EPHREM.**

Woe to that unhappy woman!

[Col. 1017B] **ABRAHAM.**

35 She grieved that she had acted contrary to our admonitions.

**EPHREM.**

And greatly so.

**ABRAHAM.**

She bewailed that she had rendered the exertions of her vigils, prayers, and fasting fruitless.

**EPHREM.**

If she had persevered in such contrition, she would have been saved.

**ABRAHAM.**

She did not persevere, but added worse things to those that came before.

**EPHREM.**

I am shaken to my very entrails and dissolved in every limb.

[Col. 1017C] **ABRAHAM.**

After punishing herself with these lamentations, overcome by the excess of her grief, she was rushing headlong into the pit of despair.

**EPHREM.**

Alas! What a grievous destruction!

**ABRAHAM.**

And because she despaired of being able to obtain forgiveness, she chose to return to the world and devote herself to vanity.

**EPHREM.**

Ah! Such a victory for spiritual wickedness had previously been unknown among hermits.

**ABRAHAM.**

[Col. 1017D] But now we are the demons’ prey.

**EPHREM.**

It is astonishing that she could have escaped without your knowledge.

**ABRAHAM.**

Meanwhile, I had been mentally terrified by the fear inspired by a vision that had been shown to me. If my mind had not been dull, it would have prefigured her fall for me.

**EPHREM.**

I should like to hear the form of the vision.

**ABRAHAM.**

I thought I was standing before the door of the little room. Then a dragon of extraordinary size and terrible stench arrived in a swift rush, found a little white dove beside me, seized and devoured it, and immediately disappeared.

[Col. 1018A] **EPHREM.**

The vision is clear.

**ABRAHAM.**

But when I awoke and considered in my mind what I had seen, I feared that some persecution of the Church was impending, one that would draw certain faithful people into error.

**EPHREM.**

It was right to fear that.

**ABRAHAM.**
