Therefore I prostrated myself in prayer and begged the one who knows the future to reveal to me the interpretation of the dream.

**EPHREM.**

[Col. 1018B] You acted rightly.

**ABRAHAM.**

On the third night, when I had given my weary limbs over to sleep, I thought that the same dragon had writhed about, torn apart at my feet, and that the dove had emerged unharmed.

**EPHREM.**

I rejoice to hear this, and I do not doubt that your Maria will someday return to you.

**ABRAHAM.**

When I awoke and moderated my earlier grief with the consolation of this vision, I recovered my presence of mind enough to remember my foster daughter. I also remember—without grief—that during an interval of two days I did not find her engaged, as usual, in the praise of God.

[Col. 1018C] **EPHREM.**

You remembered too late.

**ABRAHAM.**

I confess it. I approached, struck the window with my hand, and called her repeatedly by name.

**EPHREM.**

Ah! You called in vain.

**ABRAHAM.**

At that time I did not yet understand this. I asked why she was neglecting the divine offices, but I received not even the faintest sound of a reply.

**EPHREM.**

And what did you do then?

**ABRAHAM.**

[Col. 1018D] When I discovered that the one I was seeking was absent, fear tore through my inward parts and terror made my limbs tremble.

**EPHREM.**

Nor is that surprising. Certainly I too am suffering the same thing now as I listen to you.

**ABRAHAM.**

Then I polluted the air with mournful sounds, asking what wolf had snatched away my lamb and what robber had taken my daughter captive.

**EPHREM.**

You had good reason to lament the destruction of the one you had raised.

**ABRAHAM.**

At last people who knew the truth came and told me that the matter was as I have now explained to you, and that she was devoted to vanity.

[Col. 1019A] **EPHREM.**

Where does she live?

**ABRAHAM.**

It is unknown.

**EPHREM.**

What will happen?

**ABRAHAM.**

I have a faithful friend who, traveling through cities and villages, will not rest until he discovers what land has received her.

**EPHREM.**

What if he finds her?

**ABRAHAM.**

[Col. 1019B] I shall change my clothing and approach her under the guise of a lover, in the hope that, at my admonition, she may return after her grave shipwreck to the harbor of her former peace.

**EPHREM.**

What, then, if the eating of meat and the drinking of wine are placed before you?

**ABRAHAM.**

I shall not refuse them, lest I be recognized.

**EPHREM.**

You are exercising entirely sound and commendable discretion if you loosen the reins of stricter observance for a time, so that you may win the erring woman for Christ.

**ABRAHAM.**

I am all the more encouraged to undertake this because I find that you agree with me in this matter.

[Col. 1019C] **EPHREM.**

He who knows the secrets of hearts understands with what intention each thing is done. In his most discerning judgment, a person is not held guilty of transgression if, by temporarily descending from the rigor of a stricter way of life, he does not refuse to become like the weaker, so that he may more effectively recall the soul that has gone astray.

**ABRAHAM.**

Meanwhile, it is your task to help me with prayers, lest I be hindered by diabolical deception.

**EPHREM.**

May the supreme Good himself, without whom no good is done, bring your will to perfection in goodness.

## SCENE IV

[Col. 1019D] **ABRAHAM.**

Is that my friend whom I sent two years ago to search for Maria? It is he.

**AMICUS.**

Greetings, venerable Father.

**ABRAHAM.**

Greetings, affable friend. I waited for you for a long time, but now I had given up hope that you would come.

**AMICUS.**

That is why I delayed: I did not dare to disturb you with an uncertain report. But once I had investigated the truth, I hastened my return.

**ABRAHAM.**

Did you see Maria?

[Col. 1020A] **AMICUS.**

I saw her.

**ABRAHAM.**

Where?

**AMICUS.**

How miserable it is to say!

**ABRAHAM.**

Tell me, I beg you.

**AMICUS.**

She has chosen to live in the house of a certain procurer, who cherishes her with tender affection—and not without reason, for every day no small amount of money is brought to him by her lovers.

**ABRAHAM.**

By Maria’s lovers?

[Col. 1020B] **AMICUS.**

By them.

**ABRAHAM.**

Who are her lovers?

**AMICUS.**

Very many.

**ABRAHAM.**

Woe is me, O good Jesus! What monstrosity is this? I hear that this woman, whom I raised for you as a bride, follows other lovers.

**AMICUS.**

Has it not long been customary among prostitutes to delight in the love of others?

**ABRAHAM.**

Bring me a swift, well-bred horse and military clothing, [Col. 1020C] so that, having laid aside the garb of religion, I may approach her under the guise of a lover.

**AMICUS.**

Here is everything.

**ABRAHAM.**

I beg you, bring me a hat as well, with which I may cover the crown of my head.

**AMICUS.**

That is especially necessary, lest you be recognized.

**ABRAHAM.**

What if I bring with me the one solidus I have, to pay the stable keeper as his fee?

**AMICUS.**

You cannot reach Maria for a meeting in any other way.

## SCENE V

[Col. 1020D] **ABRAHAM.**

Greetings, good stable keeper.

**STABLE KEEPER.**

Who is speaking? Greetings, traveler.

**ABRAHAM.**

Do you have a place suitable for a traveler to spend the night?

**STABLE KEEPER.**

Certainly; our little lodgings must be denied to no one.

**ABRAHAM.**

Commendable.

**STABLE KEEPER.**

Come in, so that supper may be prepared for you.

[Col. 1021A] **ABRAHAM.**

I owe you much for your cheerful welcome, but I expect even more from you.

**STABLE KEEPER.**

Ask whatever you wish, and I shall strive to grant it.

**ABRAHAM.**

Accept this small gift that I bring, and arrange for the very beautiful girl whom I have seen moving about here with you to join our meal.

**STABLE KEEPER.**

Why do you wish to see her?

**ABRAHAM.**

Because I take great pleasure in knowing her, since I have often heard her beauty praised by many people.

[Col. 1021B] **STABLE KEEPER.**

Whoever praised her appearance said nothing false. For she surpasses other women in beauty of face.

**ABRAHAM.**

Therefore I burn with love for her.

**STABLE KEEPER.**

I am astonished that, in decrepit old age, you breathe love for a young woman.

**ABRAHAM.**

I came for no other reason whatsoever than to see her.

## SCENE VI

**STABLE KEEPER.**

Come forth, Maria, and show our [Col. 1021C] new guest your beauty.

38 **MARIA.**

Here I come.

**ABRAHAM.**

What confidence, what firmness of mind can remain to me after this, when I see the woman I raised in the hiding places of the wilderness adorned with a prostitute’s appearance? But this is not the time for what is held in the heart to be revealed on the face. I manfully restrain my welling tears and conceal the inner bitterness of my sorrow beneath a feigned expression of cheerfulness.

**STABLE KEEPER.**

Fortunate Maria, rejoice, because not only do your contemporaries, as before, come to you, but even men already worn out by old age flock to you in love.

[Col. 1021D] **MARIA.**

All who love me receive an equal return of love from me.

**ABRAHAM.**

Come, Maria, and give me a kiss.

**MARIA.**

I shall not merely sip sweet kisses, but shall also caress your aged neck with frequent embraces.

**ABRAHAM.**

That is what I want.

**MARIA.**

What do I feel? What astonishing novelty am I drinking in as I taste this? Look: the fragrance of this scent brings to mind the fragrance of the abstinence to which I was once accustomed.

[Col. 1022A] **ABRAHAM.**

Now, now I must pretend; now I must persist in the jokes of a wanton boy, lest I be recognized because of my solemnity and she retreat into hiding out of shame.

**MARIA.**

Woe to me, unhappy woman! From what height have I fallen, and into what pit of destruction have I collapsed?

**ABRAHAM.**

This is not a suitable place for lamentation, where a gathering of banqueters is assembling.

**STABLE KEEPER.**

Lady Maria, why are you sighing? Why are you wet with tears? Have you not lived here for two years, and has no groan ever burst from you, no sadder word ever escaped?

[Col. 1022B] **MARIA.**

Would that I had been taken by death three years ago, before I came to such enormities.

**ABRAHAM.**

I did not come to mourn your sins, but to join myself to your love.

**MARIA.**

I was moved by a slight contrition, and therefore I said such things. But let us eat and be merry, because, as you have warned me, this is not the time to mourn our sins.

**ABRAHAM.**

We have been abundantly refreshed and abundantly drunk through your generosity, good stable keeper. Give me leave to rise from supper, so that I may place my weary body on a bed [Col. 1022C] and restore it with sweet rest.

**STABLE KEEPER.**

As you wish.

**MARIA.**

Rise, my lord, rise; I shall go with you to the bedchamber.

**ABRAHAM.**

I am pleased. I could in no way be compelled to leave without you accompanying me.

## SCENE VII

**MARIA.**

Here is a dining room suitable for us to inhabit; here is a bed made up with bedding that is by no means cheap. Sit down, so that I may remove your shoes and spare you the fatigue of taking them off yourself.

[Col. 1022D] **ABRAHAM.**

First secure the door with bolts, lest anyone find an opportunity to enter.

**MARIA.**

Do not worry about that; I shall ensure that no one is given easy access to us.

It is time, once the covering has been removed from my head, to reveal who I am. O adopted daughter, O part of my soul, Mary, do you recognize this old man who nourished you with a father’s love, who betrothed you to the Only-Begotten of the heavenly King?

**MARY.**

Alas for me! It is my father and teacher Abraham who is speaking.

**[Col. 1023A] ABRAHAM.**

What has happened to you, daughter?

**MARY.**

A grievous misery.

**ABRAHAM.**

Who deceived you? Who led you astray?

**MARY.**

He who cast down the first-formed pair.

**ABRAHAM.**

Where is that angelic way of life which you practiced on earth?

**MARY.**

Utterly lost.

**ABRAHAM.**

[Col. 1023B] Where is your virginal modesty? Where is your admirable self-restraint?

**MARY.**

Emptied out.

**ABRAHAM.**

Unless you repent, what reward can you still hope for in return for the sweat of your fasts, prayers, and vigils, when, as though fallen from the height of heaven, you have been plunged into the depths of hell?

**MARY.**

Ah, woe!

**ABRAHAM.**

Why did you despise me? Why did you abandon me? Why did you not disclose to me the outcome of your ruin, so that I, together with my beloved Ephrem, might perform fitting penance for you?

**[Col. 1023C] MARY.**

After I had fallen and collapsed into sins, I did not dare, polluted as I was, to approach your holiness.

**ABRAHAM.**

Who has ever been free from sin, except the Virgin’s Son alone?

**MARY.**

No one.

**ABRAHAM.**

To sin is human; to persist in sins is diabolical. The one who falls suddenly is not rightly reproved, but the one who neglects to rise again quickly.

**MARY.**

Alas for me, wretched woman!

**ABRAHAM.**

**[Col. 1023D]** Why do you fall down? Why do you lie motionless on the ground? Rise and listen to what I shall say.

**MARY.**

I fell, shaken by fear, because I could not bear the force of a father’s admonition.

**ABRAHAM.**

Consider my love for you and lay aside your fear.

**MARY.**

I cannot.

**ABRAHAM.**

Was it not for your sake that I abandoned the desirable dwelling of the desert and almost entirely abandoned every observance of the regular way of life, so much so that I, a true hermit, became the companion of revelers, and though I had long cultivated silence, I uttered playful words so that I would not be recognized? Why do you look at the ground with lowered face? Why do you disdain to mingle words with me in reply?

**[Col. 1024A] MARY.**

I am confounded by consciousness of my own guilt. Therefore I do not dare either to raise my eyes to heaven or to begin a conversation with you.

**ABRAHAM.**

Do not lose confidence, daughter; do not despair. Emerge from the abyss of despair and fix the hope of your mind upon God.

**MARY.**

The enormity of my sins has cast me into the depths of despair.

**ABRAHAM.**

Your sins are indeed grave, but heavenly [Col. 1024B] mercy is greater than every creature. Therefore break through your sorrows, and do not neglect through sloth the little time granted for repentance, so that divine grace may abound where the abomination of crimes has abounded.

**MARY.**

If there were any hope of earning his forgiveness, I would certainly not lack the will to repent.

**ABRAHAM.**

Have pity on the weariness which I have undergone for you, and lay aside your deadly despair, which we know to be more grievous than all sins committed. For whoever despairs that God wishes to have mercy on sinners sins irremediably: just as a spark from flint cannot set the sea ablaze, so the bitterness of our sins cannot alter the sweetness of divine kindness.

**[Col. 1024C] MARY.**

I do not deny the magnificence of heavenly mercy; but, considering the enormity of my own crime, I fear that I am not sufficient for the satisfaction required by worthy repentance.

**ABRAHAM.**

Let your guilt be upon me; only return to the place from which you came forth, and begin again the way of life which you abandoned.

**MARY.**

I have never resisted any of your wishes; whatever you command, I obediently embrace.

**ABRAHAM.**

Now I confess that you are truly the daughter whom I nourished; now I judge that you are to be loved above all.

**[Col. 1024D] MARY.**

I possess a little gold and clothing; I await your authoritative decision concerning them.

**ABRAHAM.**

What you acquired by sinning must be cast away together with the sins themselves.

**MARY.**

I thought they should be distributed to the poor or offered upon sacred altars.

**ABRAHAM.**

A gift acquired through crimes is shown not to be sufficiently acceptable to God.

**MARY.**

I shall trouble myself no longer about these matters.

**[Col. 1025A] ABRAHAM.**

Morning is shining; it is becoming light. Let us go.

**MARY.**

It is your part, beloved Father, to go ahead like a good shepherd before the sheep that has been found, while I follow behind, walking in the same footsteps as the one who leads.

**ABRAHAM.**

Not so; I shall go on foot, but I shall place you upon a horse, lest the roughness of the journey wound your tender feet.

**MARY.**

O, what shall I call you, and what recompense of thanks shall I offer you, since you compel me, unworthy as I am of compassion, not through terror but through gentle condescension to repent?

**[Col. 1025B] ABRAHAM.**

I ask nothing else of you except that, by clinging to God’s service, you persist in it for the remainder of your life.

**MARY.**

I shall cling to it with a willing mind and persist in it as far as my strength permits; and, even if the ability to act should be lacking, the will shall never be lacking.

**ABRAHAM.**

It is fitting that with the zeal with which you served vanity, you should now serve the divine will.

**MARY.**

May it come to pass, I pray, through your merits, that the will of the Divinity be accomplished in me.

**ABRAHAM.**

**[Col. 1025C]** Let us hasten our return.

**MARY.**

Let us hasten; for I am weary of delays.

## SCENE VIII

**ABRAHAM.**

With what speed we have traversed the difficulty of the rough journey!

**MARY.**

What is done devoutly is accomplished easily.

**ABRAHAM.**

Behold your deserted cell.

**MARY.**

Alas for me! It is conscious of my crime; therefore I fear to enter.

**ABRAHAM.**

**[Col. 1025D]** And rightly so; for the place in which triumph follows the enemy must be fled.

**MARY.**

And where do you decree that I should devote myself to repentance?

**ABRAHAM.**

Enter the inner cell, lest the ancient serpent find another opportunity to deceive you.

**MARY.**

I do not resist; I embrace whatever you command.

**ABRAHAM.**

I shall approach my familiar companion Ephrem, so that he who alone with me grieved over your ruin may rejoice with me in your recovery.

**[Col. 1026A] MARY.**

That is fitting.

## SCENE IX

**EPHREM.**

Do you bring me any joy?

**ABRAHAM.**

And great joy.

**EPHREM.**

Good; and I do not doubt that you have recovered Mary.

**ABRAHAM.**

I did indeed recover her, and I have brought her back to the sheepfold.

**EPHREM.**

I believe it happened through the grace of a divine visitation.

**ABRAHAM.**

Without a doubt.

**[Col. 1026B] EPHREM.**

I would like to know how, in accordance with that occasion, she has ordered her life and conduct.

**ABRAHAM.**

According to my will.

**EPHREM.**

That is especially beneficial for her.

**ABRAHAM.**

Whatever I proposed that she should do, however difficult, however burdensome, she did not refuse to undertake.

**EPHREM.**

Praise­worthy.

**ABRAHAM.**

For, clothed in sackcloth and continually disciplined by vigils and fasting, she compels her tender body, through the strictest observance of the law, to endure the command of the soul.

**[Col. 1026C] EPHREM.**

It is just that the foul stains of wicked pleasure be removed by the harshness of punishment.

**ABRAHAM.**

Whoever understands her lamentations is wounded in mind; whoever feels compunction is himself pierced with compunction.

**EPHREM.**

That is what usually happens.

**ABRAHAM.**

She labors with all her strength so that she who was the cause of their ruin may become an example of conversion.

**EPHREM.**

It follows.

**ABRAHAM.**

[Col. 1026D] She strives so that, the more disgraceful she was, the more radiant she may appear.

**EPHREM.**

It is more delightful to hear this, I pray, and I rejoice with heartfelt joy [Note: [Col. 1025] D. Magnin restores this passage as: “It is more delightful to hear this, and I rejoice with heartfelt joy.”].

**ABRAHAM.**

And rightly so, for the angelic ranks, rejoicing, praise the Lord over the conversion of a sinner.

**EPHREM.**

Nor is it surprising; for He takes greater delight in the repentance of a wicked person than in the perseverance of any righteous person.

**[Col. 1027A] ABRAHAM.**

Hence she is praised all the more justly because it was thought impossible that she could repent.

**EPHREM.**

Let us rejoice with her and praise; praising, let us glorify the Only-Begotten and venerable, beloved and merciful Son of God, who does not wish those whom he redeemed with his sacred blood to perish.

**[Col. 1028A] ABRAHAM.**

To him be honor, glory, and jubilation through infinite ages. Amen.

# V. PAPHNUTIUS

**[Col. 1027]**

## ARGUMENT OF PAPHNUTIUS

The conversion of Thais the prostitute, whom the hermit Paphnutius, just as Abraham had done, approached under the guise of a lover and converted, and, after imposing penance, confined for five years in a narrow cell, until, reconciled to God through worthy satisfaction, she fell asleep in Christ on the fifteenth day after completing her penance.

**CHARACTERS:** PAPHNUTIUS, DISCIPLES, THAIS, YOUNG LOVERS, ANTONIUS, PAULUS.

## SCENE I

**[Col. 1027B]**

**43 DISCIPLES.**

Why, Father Paphnutius, do you wear a gloomy face, not your usual serene one?

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

The face of one whose heart is grieved also grows gloomy.

**DISCIPLES.**

Why are you grieved?

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

Because of an injury done to the Creator.

**DISCIPLES.**

What injury is this?

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

The very injury which he suffers from the creature formed in his own image.

**[Col. 1027C] DISCIPLES.**

You have frightened us by what you said.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

Although that impassible majesty cannot be affected by injuries, nevertheless—to transfer metaphorically to God the feelings of our frailty—what greater injury can be named than that the one whose rule the greater world obediently obeys should have the lesser world alone struggling against it?

**DISCIPLES.**

What is the lesser world?

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

The human being.

**DISCIPLES.**

The human being?

**[Col. 1027D] PAPHNUTIUS.**

Indeed.

**DISCIPLES.**

What human being?

**[Col. 1028B] PAPHNUTIUS.**

Every human being.

**DISCIPLES.**

How can that be?

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

As it pleased the Creator.

**DISCIPLES.**

We do not understand.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

It is not apparent to very many.

**DISCIPLES.**

Explain it.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

Pay attention.

**DISCIPLES.**

And with ready minds.

**[Col. 1028C] PAPHNUTIUS.**

For just as the greater world is formed from four contrary elements, which nevertheless, according to the Creator’s will, harmonize through an ordered proportion, so too the human being is composed not only from those same elements but also from parts still more contrary.

**DISCIPLES.**

And what is more contrary than the elements?

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

Body and soul, because although those elements are contrary, they are nevertheless bodily; the soul is neither mortal, as the body is, nor a bodily thing, as the soul is spiritual.

**DISCIPLES.**

So it is.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

Yet if we follow the dialecticians, we do not admit that they are contrary.

**DISCIPLES.**

And who could deny it?

**[Col. 1028D] PAPHNUTIUS.**

**[Col. 1029A] PAPHNUTIUS.**

One who knows how to argue dialectically, because nothing is contrary to substance—*ousia*—but substance is the receiver of contraries.

**DISCIPLES.**

What did you mean when you said “through an ordered proportion”?

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

This, namely: just as high and low sounds, harmonically joined, produce something musical, so discordant elements, suitably brought into concord, produce one world.

**DISCIPLES.**

It is strange how discordant things can be harmonized, or harmonious things be called discordant.

**[Col. 1029B] PAPHNUTIUS.**

Because nothing seems to be composed of similar things, nor of things joined by no rational proportion and differing from one another in every substance and nature.

**44 DISCIPLES.**

What is music?

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

One of the disciplines of the philosophical quadrivium.

**DISCIPLES.**

What is this “quadrivium” of which you speak?

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

Arithmetic, geometry, music, and astronomy.

**DISCIPLES.**

Why “quadrivium”?

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

**[Col. 1029C]** Because just as paths proceed from a crossroads, so from one principle of philosophy the straight developments of these disciplines proceed.

**DISCIPLES.**

We are reluctant to ask questions while investigating the three, because we can scarcely penetrate with our minds the tangle of the discussion that has begun.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

It is difficult to grasp.

**DISCIPLES.**

Tell us something superficial about the one we have just mentioned.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

I know very little to say, because it is unknown to hermits.

**[Col. 1029D] DISCIPLES.**

What does it do?

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

Music?

**DISCIPLES.**

Yes, it.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

It discusses sounds.

**DISCIPLES.**

Is it one or are there several kinds?

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

They are said to be three; but each is joined to the other by a relationship of proportion in such a way that what occurs in one is not absent from the other.

**[Col. 1030A] DISCIPLES.**

And what is the difference among the three?

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

The first is called cosmic or celestial, the second human, and the third is practiced with instruments.

**DISCIPLES.**

In what does the celestial consist?

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

In the seven planets and in the celestial sphere.

**DISCIPLES.**

How?

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

In the same way as that which is found in instruments: as many intervals and corresponding progressions, the same harmonies, are found in these as in strings.

**[Col. 1030B] DISCIPLES.**

What are intervals?

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

Dimensions measured between the planets or between strings.

**DISCIPLES.**

And what are progressions?

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

The same as tones.

**DISCIPLES.**

Knowledge of these matters does not concern us.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

A tone is formed from two sounds and possesses the ratio of the *epogdoos*, or the sesquioctave number.

**[Col. 1030C] DISCIPLES.**

The more quickly we strive to pass through what we first proposed to investigate, the more difficult things you continue to put before us.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

That is what this kind of discussion requires.

**DISCIPLES.**

Explain briefly something about the harmonies, so that at least we may know the meaning of the term.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

A harmony is called a balanced combination of melody.

**DISCIPLES.**

Why?

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

Because it is formed now from four, now from five, now from eight sounds.

**[Col. 1030D] DISCIPLES.**

Since we know that there are three, we wish to distinguish the names of each.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

The first is called *diatessaron*, as though “from four,” and possesses the epitrite or sesquitertian proportion; the second is *diapente*, which consists of five and is in the hemiolic or sesquialter ratio; the third is *diapason*. This is in the double ratio and is completed by eight sounds.

**45 DISCIPLES.**

Do the sphere and the planets produce a sound, so that they may deserve comparison with strings?

**[Col. 1031A] PAPHNUTIUS.**

And a very great one.

**DISCIPLES.**

Why is it not heard?

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

They explain this in many ways. Some maintain that it cannot be heard because of its constant continuation; others, because of the density of the air. Some say that the enormous magnitude of the sound cannot enter the narrow passages of the ears. There are also those who say that the sphere emits so delightful and sweet a sound that, if it were heard, all human beings together, neglecting themselves and setting aside every other pursuit, would follow the sound leading from east to west.

**DISCIPLES.**

**[Col. 1031B]** It is better that it not be heard.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

The Creator foresaw this.

**DISCIPLES.**

Let that suffice concerning the celestial kind; continue with the human.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

What about it?

**DISCIPLES.**

Where is it perceived?

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

Not only, as I said, in the joining of body and soul, and in the emission of a voice now deep, now clear, but also in the pulses of the veins and in the measurement of certain limbs, such as the joints of the fingers. In these, by measuring, we find the same proportions that we mentioned above in the harmonies, because music is called a concord not only of voices but also of other dissimilar things.

**[Col. 1031C] DISCIPLES.**

If we had known that this knot of a question was so difficult for the unlearned to solve, we would have preferred not to know the lesser world rather than undergo so much difficulty.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

It does no harm that you have labored, since you have experienced what you previously did not know.

**DISCIPLES.**

True; but we are weary of philosophical discussion, because we do not know how to measure with our understanding the difficulty of your reasoning.

**[Col. 1031D] PAPHNUTIUS.**

Why do you mock me, when I am plainly ignorant, not a philosopher?

**DISCIPLES.**

Then from where did you get these things which you have set forth while tiring us?

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

A tiny drop of knowledge, flowing from the full wells of the learned, I did not sit down to collect; rather, passing by by chance, I found it and lapped it up, and have tried to share it with you.

**46 DISCIPLES.**

We rejoice in your kindness, but we are frightened by the Apostle’s statement: “For God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the sophists.”

**[Col. 1032A] PAPHNUTIUS.**

Whether fools or sophists practice perversely, they deserve confusion from God.

**DISCIPLES.**

So it is.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

Nor does knowledge of what can be known offend God, but rather the injustice of the one who knows.

**DISCIPLES.**

True.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

And to whose praise, more worthily and justly, should knowledge of the arts be turned than to that of the one who made what can be known and gave knowledge?

**DISCIPLES.**

**[Col. 1032B]** To no one’s.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

For the more wondrous the law by which one recognizes that God has established all things in number, measure, and weight, the more ardently one burns with love for him.

**DISCIPLES.**

Not unjustly.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

But why do I linger over matters that bring us so little pleasure?

**DISCIPLES.**

Lay bare the cause of your grief, lest we be broken for too long under the weight of curiosity.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

If you ever experience it, you will not be pleased to hear it.

**[Col. 1032C] DISCIPLES.**

The one who pursues curiosity is often saddened; yet we cannot overcome it, because it is familiar to our frailty.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

A certain shameless woman lives in this country.

**DISCIPLES.**

A dangerous matter for the citizens.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

She shines with wondrous beauty and is befouled by horrifying depravity.

**DISCIPLES.**

How pitiable! What is she called?

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

**[Col. 1032D]** Thais.

**DISCIPLES.**

That prostitute?

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

The very one.

**DISCIPLES.**

Her infamy is unknown to no one.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

Nor is that surprising, because she does not deign to proceed to destruction with only a few; rather, she is ready to entice everyone through the allurements of her beauty and drag them with her to destruction.

**DISCIPLES.**

Mournful.

**[Col. 1033A] PAPHNUTIUS.**

Not only do frivolous men squander the worth of their own possessions by honoring her, but powerful men also ruin the costly variety of their furnishings, enriching her not without harm to themselves.

**DISCIPLES.**

We shudder to hear it.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

Crowds of lovers flock to her.

**DISCIPLES.**

They destroy themselves.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

Those madmen, while each strives to approach her with blinded heart, heap insults upon one another.

**DISCIPLES.**

**[Col. 1033B]** One vice prepares another.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

Then, once the contest has begun, they either break one another’s faces and noses with their fists or drive one another away with weapons, and they wet the threshold of the brothel with the filth of flowing blood.

**47 DISCIPLES.**

O detestable outrage!

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

This injury to the Creator, which I lamented, is the cause of my grief.

**DISCIPLES.**

You are right to grieve over this, and we do not doubt that the citizens of the heavenly homeland grieve with you.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

**[Col. 1033C]** What if I approach her under the guise of a lover, in case she can perhaps be recalled from her purpose of frivolity?

**DISCIPLES.**

May he who instilled in your thought the desire to do this also grant you the power to accomplish it.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

Meanwhile, support me with continual prayers, lest I be overcome by the snares of the vicious serpent.

**DISCIPLES.**

May he who cast down the king of the dwellers in darkness grant you triumph over the enemy.

## SCENE II

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

Behold, young men in the marketplace. I shall approach them first and ask where I may find the woman whom I seek.

**[Col. 1033D] YOUNG MEN.**

Look, some stranger is approaching us; let us find out what he wants.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

Ho, young men, who are you?

**YOUNG MEN.**

Residents of this city.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

Greetings.

**YOUNG MEN.**

And greetings to you, whether you are a native of this country or a newcomer.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

I have now arrived as a newcomer.

**[Col. 1034A] YOUNG MEN.**

Why have you come? What are you seeking?

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

It must not be said.

**YOUNG MEN.**

Why?

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

Because it is a secret for me.

**YOUNG MEN.**

It would be better for you to disclose it, because if you are not one of us, you will find it difficult to conduct any business among us without the advice of the inhabitants.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

What if I speak and, by speaking, bring some obstacle upon myself?

**[Col. 1034B] YOUNG MEN.**

Not from us.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

I yield to your cheerful promises and, trusting in your good faith, reveal my secret.

**YOUNG MEN.**

There will be no treachery on our part and no opposition of any kind will confront you.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

From the report of certain people I have learned that a woman lives near you, lovable to everyone and gracious to everyone.

**YOUNG MEN.**

Do you know her name?

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

I know it.

**[Col. 1034C] YOUNG MEN.**

What is she called?

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

Thais.

**YOUNG MEN.**

She is the fire of our people.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

They say that this woman is exceedingly beautiful and the most exquisite of all.

**YOUNG MEN.**

Those who reported this told no falsehood.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

For her sake I shortened the tedious length of my journey; I have come to see her.

**YOUNG MEN.**

**[Col. 1034D]** No obstacle prevents you from seeing her.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

Where does she live?

**YOUNG MEN.**

There—the dwelling is nearby.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

This is the one you indicate?

**YOUNG MEN.**

The very one.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

I shall go there.

**YOUNG MEN.**

If you wish, we shall go with you.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

I prefer to go alone.

**[Col. 1035A] YOUNG MEN.**

As you wish.

## SCENE III

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

Are you Thais, the one whom I seek, inside here?

**THAIS.**

Who is this unknown man who is speaking?

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

Your lover.

**THAIS.**

Whoever honors me with love receives an equal return of love from me.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

O Thais, Thais, what great stretches of a most arduous journey I have traversed so that the opportunity might be granted me to speak with you and gaze upon your face.

**[Col. 1035B] THAIS.**

I do not withdraw my appearance, nor do I deny you conversation.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

The secrecy of our conversation requires the solitude of a more private place.

**THAIS.**

Behold a well-prepared and pleasant bedchamber for living in.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

Is there another place farther within, where we can converse more secretly?

**THAIS.**

There is indeed another hidden place, so secret that its innermost recess is known to no one except me—and God.

**[Col. 1035C] PAPHNUTIUS.**

Which God?

**THAIS.**

The true one.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

Do you believe that he knows anything?

**THAIS.**

I know that nothing is hidden from him.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

Do you think that he overlooks the deeds of the wicked, or that he maintains his justice?

**THAIS.**

I believe that each person’s merits are weighed on the scales of his justice, and that punishment or reward is reserved for each according to what he has done.

**[Col. 1035D] PAPHNUTIUS.**

O Christ, how wondrous is the patience of your kindness toward us: you see those who know you sinning, yet you delay destroying them!

**THAIS.**

Why do you tremble, your color changed? Why do tears flow?

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

I shudder at your presumption; I weep over your destruction, because you know these things and yet have destroyed so many souls.

**THAIS.**

Woe, woe is me, unhappy woman!

**[Col. 1036A] PAPHNUTIUS.**

You will be condemned all the more justly because, with greater presumption, you knowingly offended the majesty of the Divinity.

**THAIS.**

Alas, alas, what are you doing? Why do you threaten an unhappy woman?

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

The punishment of Gehenna awaits you if you remain in your crime.

**THAIS.**

The severity of your correction has shaken the innermost recesses of my fearful heart.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

O, if only you had been shaken through and through by fear, so that you would no longer presume to consent to dangerous pleasure.

**[Col. 1036B] THAIS.**

And what place can dangerous pleasure henceforth retain in my heart, where only the bitterness of inward grief, together with the new dread of conscious guilt, now rules?

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

This is what I desire, so that, once the thorns of vices have been cut away, the tear of compunction may emerge.

**THAIS.**

O, if you believed—O, if you hoped—that I, a filthy little woman covered a thousand times over with countless stains, could in any way be cleansed or by any form of compunction earn forgiveness! [lacuna]

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

[Col. 1036C] There is no grave sin, no crime so monstrous that it cannot be cleansed by the tears of repentance, if the deed is carried out.

**THAIS.**

Show me, I beg you, Father, by what action I may earn the gift of reconciliation.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

Despise the world; flee the company of lewd lovers.

**THAIS.**

And what shall I have to do then?

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

You must withdraw to a secluded place, where, examining yourself, you can lament the enormity of your crime.

**THAIS.**

**[Col. 1036D]** If you hope that this will be effective, I shall not add even a moment’s delay.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

I do not doubt that it will help.

**THAIS.**

Give me a little time, a brief interval, so that I may bring out the money which I wrongfully accumulated and have long kept.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

Do not trouble yourself about it. There are those who will make use of what has been found.

**THAIS.**

I am not troubled because I wished either to keep it for myself or give it to my friends; nor do I intend to distribute it to the needy, because I do not think the price of atonement is suitable for a work of charity.

**[Col. 1037A] PAPHNUTIUS.**

You judge rightly. And what do you intend to do with what has been amassed?

**THAIS.**

To consign it to the fire and reduce it to ashes.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

Why?

**THAIS.**

So that what I acquired wrongly, not without injury to the Creator of the world, may not remain in the world.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

O how changed you are from what you once were, when you burned with illicit love and seethed with the heat of greed!

**[Col. 1037B] THAIS.**

Perhaps I shall be changed for the better, if God consents.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

It is not difficult for him, whose substance is unchangeable, to change things as he wills.

**THAIS.**

I shall go and complete by action what I have resolved.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

Go in peace, and return to me quickly.

## SCENE IV

**THAIS.**

Come together; hurry, my wicked lovers.

**LOVERS.**

[Col. 1037C] It is the voice of Thais calling us. Let us hasten our arrival, lest we offend her by delaying.

**THAIS.**

Hurry, come near, so that I may converse with you.

**LOVERS.**

O Thais, Thais, what does the pyre you are building mean? Why are you piling beside the pyre such a variety of precious riches?

**THAIS.**

You ask?

**LOVERS.**

We are sufficiently astonished.

**THAIS.**

I shall explain at once.

**[Col. 1037D] LOVERS.**

That is what we wish.

**THAIS.**

Look.

**LOVERS.**

Stop, stop, Thais! What are you doing? Are you mad?

**THAIS.**

I am not mad; I am thinking soundly.

**LOVERS.**

Why this destruction of four hundred pounds of gold, together with a variety of other treasures?

**THAIS.**

Everything that I extorted from you unjustly, I wish to burn in the fire, so that no fuel for hoping that I shall yield again to your love may be left to any of you.

**[Col. 1038A] LOVERS.**

Wait a little, wait, and reveal the cause of your disturbance.

**THAIS.**

I will not wait, nor will I converse with you.

**LOVERS.**

Why do you disdainfully despise us? Are you accusing us of some disloyalty? Have we not always satisfied your wishes? And you pursue us gratuitously with unjust hatred.

**THAIS.**

Let go; do not tear my clothing by pulling it. It is enough that until now I consented to you by sinning. The end of sinning is at hand, and so is the time of our separation.

**[Col. 1038B] LOVERS.**

Where are you going?

**THAIS.**

Where none of you will see me hereafter.

**LOVERS.**

Good heavens! What marvel is this? Our delight, Thais, who always strove to abound in riches, who never withdrew her mind from wantonness and gave herself wholly to pleasure, has suddenly destroyed without hesitation such splendid treasures of gold and gems, has scornfully rejected us, her lovers, and suddenly disappeared!

## SCENE V

**THAIS.**

Here I am, Father Paphnutius; I come most ready to obey you.

**[Col. 1038C] PAPHNUTIUS.**

Because you delayed in coming, I was greatly constrained by fear that you had again become entangled in worldly affairs.

**THAIS.**

Do not fear that, because something quite different occupies my mind. I have arranged my household affairs according to my will, and I have publicly renounced my lovers.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

Since you have renounced them, you can now be joined to the heavenly Lover.

**THAIS.**

It is your part to prescribe for me, as with a ray of light, what I ought to do.

**[Col. 1038D] PAPHNUTIUS.**

Follow me.

**THAIS.**

I shall follow you in walking; would that I might also follow you in action!

## SCENE VI

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

Behold the convent in which a noble community of sacred virgins resides. I desire that you remain there and spend the period appointed for repentance.

**THAIS.**

I do not resist.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

I shall enter and win over the abbess, the guide of the virgins, to receive you.

**[Col. 1039A] THAIS.**

What do you command me to do meanwhile?

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

To go with me.

**THAIS.**

As you command.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

Behold, the abbess is coming to meet us. I am amazed who could have told her so quickly that we were here.

**THAIS.**

Rumor, which is hindered by no delay.

## SCENE VII

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

You arrive opportunely, illustrious abbess; I am seeking you yourself.

**[Col. 1039B] ABBESS.**

You arrive welcome, venerable Father Paphnutius; blessed is your arrival, beloved of God.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

May the grace of the All-Father pour upon you the blessedness of eternal blessing.

**ABBESS.**

What have I done to deserve that your holiness should deign to visit the smallness of my dwelling?

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

Your assistance is needed in a matter requiring some concern.

**ABBESS.**

Only indicate with a brief word what you wish me to do, and I shall fulfill your commands and strive with all my strength to satisfy your wishes.

**[Col. 1039C] PAPHNUTIUS.**

I have brought a half-dead little goat, recently snatched from the teeth of wolves. I desire that, through your compassion, it be nourished and, through your care, restored, until, casting aside the harshness of a kid’s skin, it is clothed in the softness of a sheep’s fleece.

**ABBESS.**

Explain more clearly.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

This woman whom you see established her life in the manner of a prostitute.

**ABBESS.**

How pitiable.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

And gave herself entirely to wantonness.

**[Col. 1039D] ABBESS.**

She destroyed herself.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

But now, at my urging and with Christ cooperating, she flees in obedience from the frivolities she pursued and has acquired a chaste mind.

**ABBESS.**

Thanks be to the author of her transformation.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

Since the sicknesses of souls, just like those of bodies, must be treated with remedies, it follows that she, separated from the customary disturbance of worldly affairs, should be shut alone in a narrow cell, so that she may examine her crimes more freely.

**[Col. 1040A] ABBESS.**

This is of the greatest benefit.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

Order that a cell be built as quickly as possible.

**ABBESS.**

It will be completed in a short time.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

Let no entrance and no access be left, but only a small window through which she may receive a little food, which you must provide sparingly to her on fixed days and at fixed hours.

**ABBESS.**

I fear that the delicacy of her tender mind will find the difficulty of so great a labor hard to endure.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

**[Col. 1040B]** Do not fear this: a grave offense may perhaps desire that a remedy be hoped for.

**ABBESS.**

True.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

I am increasingly weary of delay, because I fear that human visitation may corrupt her.

**ABBESS.**

Why do you endure this delay? Why do you not shut her in? Behold, the cell you desired is complete.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

Good. Enter, Thais, a dwelling sufficiently appropriate for lamenting your crimes.

**THAIS.**

[Col. 1040C] How small, how dark, and how inconvenient for a tender woman to inhabit!

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

Why do you curse the dwelling? Why do you dread entering? It is fitting that you, who until now have been uncontrollably wandering, should at last be restrained in a solitary place.

**THAIS.**

A mind accustomed to wantonness is often impatient with its former life.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

Therefore it must be tightened by the reins of discipline until it ceases to struggle against them.

**THAIS.**

My wretchedness does not refuse to do at once what your fatherhood commands; but there is a certain inconvenience in this dwelling, difficult for my frailty to endure.

**[Col. 1040D] PAPHNUTIUS.**

What inconvenience is this?

**THAIS.**

I am ashamed to say.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

Do not be ashamed; disclose it fully.

**THAIS.**

What could be more inconvenient, or more uncomfortable, than that in one and the same place I must attend to the body’s different necessities? There is no doubt that the dwelling will quickly become uninhabitable because of the excessive stench.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

Fear the enduring cruelty of Gehenna, and cease to fear what passes away.

**[Col. 1041A] THAIS.**

My frailty compels me to be afraid.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

It is fitting that you pay for the sweet pleasure of evil blandishments with the discomfort of excessive stench.

**THAIS.**

I do not refuse; I do not deny that, not without cause, I am filthy and should inhabit a foul, dirty hut. But this pains me more severely: no place has been left in which I can fittingly and chastely invoke the name of the awesome Majesty.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

And from where do you have such confidence that you presume, with polluted lips, to utter the name of the immaculate Divinity?

**THAIS.**

**[Col. 1041B]** From whom should I hope for forgiveness, and by whose mercy can I be saved, if I am forbidden to invoke the one against whom alone I have sinned, and to whom alone the devotion of prayers ought to be offered?

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

You must indeed pray not with words but with tears, not with the ringing sound of a voice but with the groaning of a contrite heart.

**THAIS.**

And if I am forbidden to pray to God with words, how can I hope for forgiveness?

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

You will deserve it all the more quickly the more perfectly you humble yourself. Say only: “You who formed me, have mercy on me.”

**THAIS.**

**[Col. 1041C]** His mercy is necessary, lest I be broken in the doubtful struggle.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

Fight manfully, so that you may happily obtain triumph.

**THAIS.**

It is your part to pray for me, so that I may deserve the palm of victory.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

No prompting is necessary.

**THAIS.**

I hope so.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

[Col. 1041D] It is time for me to return to the desired hiding places of solitude and visit my beloved disciples. Therefore, venerable abbess, I entrust this captive woman to your care and compassion, so that you may both moderately nourish her delicate body with necessities and sufficiently refresh her soul with health-giving admonitions.

**ABBESS.**

Do not be concerned for her, because I shall cherish her with a mother’s affection.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

I shall go.

**ABBESS.**

Go in peace.

## SCENE VIII

**DISCIPLES.**

Who is knocking at the door?

**[Col. 1042A] PAPHNUTIUS.**

I am.

**DISCIPLES.**

The voice of our Father Paphnutius.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

Remove the bolt.

**DISCIPLES.**

O Father, greetings!

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

Greetings.

**DISCIPLES.**

We were exceedingly constrained by your prolonged absence.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

It is a joy that I was absent.

**DISCIPLES.**

**[Col. 1042B]** What has happened to Thais?

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

According to my will.

**DISCIPLES.**

Where does she live?

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

In a small cell, lamenting what she has committed.

**DISCIPLES.**

Praise be to the most high Trinity.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

And blessed be his awesome name now and forever.

**DISCIPLES.**

Amen.

## SCENE IX

**[Col. 1042C] PAPHNUTIUS.**

Behold, three months of Thais’s penance have passed, and I do not know whether her compunction is acceptable to God. I shall rise and go to my brother Antonius, so that it may be revealed to me through his intercession.

## SCENE X

**ANTONIUS.**

What unexpected joy has occurred? What new happiness has come to me? Is this my brother and fellow hermit Paphnutius? It is he.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

It is indeed I.

**ANTONIUS.**

You have come well, brother; by coming, you have made me happy indeed.

**[Col. 1042D] PAPHNUTIUS.**

I rejoice at seeing you no less than you rejoice at my arrival.

**ANTONIUS.**
What is this reason, so acceptable and so welcome to us, that has brought you here from your hiding place?

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

Here I am, in good health.

**ANTONIUS.**

That is what I desire.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

Three years ago a certain prostitute named Thais lived near us. She not only gave herself over to perdition, but was also accustomed to drag many others with her to destruction.

**ANTONIUS.**

Alas, a lamentable habit!

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

I approached her disguised as a lover. I soothed her wanton spirit, sometimes flattering and calming it with gentle encouragements, sometimes frightening it with sharper warnings and threats.

**ANTONIUS.**

Such moderation was necessary for her wantonness. [The text has *ejus*, “of her,” though the syntax is somewhat compressed.]

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

At last she yielded, rejected her blameworthy way of life, chose chastity, and consented to be shut up in a very small cell.

**ANTONIUS.**

I am so delighted to hear this that every vein within my breast seems to leap for joy.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

It befits your holiness. Although I rejoice beyond measure at her conversion, I am nevertheless troubled by no slight anxiety, because I fear that her tender nature may find prolonged hardship difficult to endure.

**ANTONIUS.**

Where true love is present, compassionate devotion is not absent.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

Therefore I earnestly implore your love: may you and your disciples persist with me in united prayer until it is shown from heaven whether the divine kindness, softened toward mercy, has been moved by the penitent’s tears to grant pardon.

**ANTONIUS.**

We willingly consent to your request.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

Nor do I doubt that God will mercifully hear you.

## SCENE XI

**ANTONIUS.**

Behold, the Gospel promise has been fulfilled in us.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

What promise is that?

**ANTONIUS.**

The one that promised that those who agree in prayer can obtain everything.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

What has happened?

**ANTONIUS.**

A certain vision was shown to my disciple Paul.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

Call him.

**ANTONIUS.**

Paul, come here and explain to Paphnutius what you saw.

**PAUL.**

In a vision I saw a little bed magnificently spread in heaven with bright white coverings. Four radiant maidens stood before it, as though keeping watch over it. But when I looked upon the joy of its wondrous splendor, I said within myself: “This glory belongs to no one more fittingly than to my father and lord, Antonius.”

**ANTONIUS.**

I do not consider myself worthy of such blessedness.

**PAUL.**

When I had said this, a divine voice thundered, saying: “This glory is not to be kept, as you suppose, for Antonius, but for Thais the prostitute.”

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

Praise to your sweetness, O Christ, only-begotten Son of God, because you have deigned so mercifully to console my sorrow.

**ANTONIUS.**

He is worthy of praise.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

I shall go and visit my captive.

**ANTONIUS.**

It is time for you to promise her both hope of pardon and the consolation of eternal blessedness.

## SCENE XII

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

Thais, my adopted daughter, open the window so that I may see you.

**THAIS.**

Who is speaking?

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

Paphnutius, your father.

**THAIS.**

From where comes such joy to me, such great happiness, that you deign to visit me, a sinner?

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

Although for these three years I have been absent in body, I have nevertheless been greatly concerned for your salvation.

**THAIS.**

I do not doubt it.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

Explain to me the history of your way of life and the manner of your repentance.

**THAIS.**

I can explain this much: I know that I have done nothing worthy of God.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

If God were to observe iniquities, no one would endure.

**THAIS.**

Yet if you wish to know what I have done, I gathered the multitude of my crimes within my conscience as though into a bundle and continually examined them by reflecting upon them, so that, just as the nostrils are never free from the annoyance of a foul odor, the fear of Gehenna would never be absent from the eyes of my heart.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

Because you punished yourself with repentance, you have therefore merited pardon.

**THAIS.**

Would that it were so!

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

Give me your hand, so that I may lead you out.

**THAIS.**

Do not, venerable Father, do not drag me, filthy as I am, away from these impurities; but leave me to remain here, in the place suited to my merits.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

It is time for you, with fear lightened, to begin hoping for life, because your repentance is acceptable to God.

**THAIS.**

May all the angels offer praise to his mercy, because he did not despise the humility of a contrite heart.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

Be steadfast in the fear of God and remain in his love. For after fifteen days you will put off your human condition, and, when your blessed course has been completed, you will, with heavenly grace favoring you, depart to the stars.

**THAIS.**

Would that I might deserve to escape punishment, or at least to be burned more mercifully in a gentler fire! For I am not worthy to be given unending blessedness.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

The free gift of God does not weigh human merit, because if it were granted according to merits, it would not be called grace.

**THAIS.**

Therefore let the choir of heaven praise him, and every shoot of the earth, and every species of living creature, and the confused whirlpools of the waters—him who not only tolerates sinners but also freely bestows rewards upon the penitent.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

It has been his custom from ancient times to prefer showing mercy to striking.

## SCENE XIII

**THAIS.**

Do not leave, venerable Father; remain with me as a consolation at the hour of my dissolution.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

I am not leaving, I am not departing, until I commit your body to burial while your soul applauds above the ether.

**THAIS.**

Behold, I am beginning to die.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

Now is the time for prayer.

**THAIS.**

You who formed me, have mercy on me, and grant that the soul which you breathed into me may return to you by a blessed return.

**PAPHNUTIUS.**

You who, made by no one, truly are form without matter [manuscript reading: *materiae*, “of matter”], and who caused the simple being of a human being—who is not what he is—to consist of this and that: grant that the diverse parts of this human being, soon to be dissolved, may happily return to the beginning of their origin. May the soul, infused from heaven, be mingled with heavenly joys, and may the body rest peacefully in the gentle lap of the earth, its own material substance, until, when the ashy dust has come together and the life-giving breath has entered the renewed limbs again, this same Thais may rise again perfected, as she was, a human being, to be placed among the bright-white sheep and led into the joy of eternity. You alone are what you are; you reign and are glorified in the unity of the Trinity through infinite ages of ages. Amen.

# VI. WISDOM

## ARGUMENT OF THE WISDOM

The passion of the holy virgins Faith, Hope, and Charity, whom the emperor Hadrian killed by various tortures in the presence of their revered mother Wisdom, who encouraged them by maternal admonitions to endure their sufferings. After their bodies had been perfected through martyrdom, their holy mother Wisdom gathered them, embalmed them with spices, and honorably buried them five miles from the city of Rome. On the fortieth day, after completing her sacred prayer beside their tombs, she too sent her spirit ahead to heaven.

**PERSONS:** Antiochus, Hadrian, Wisdom, Faith, Hope, Charity, Matrons.

## SCENE I

**ANTIOCHUS.**

Since I desire that you, Emperor Hadrian, should prosper in favorable success according to your wishes, and that the condition of your empire should flourish happily and without disturbance, whatever I think could confuse the state or wound the tranquility of your mind, I wish to tear away as quickly as possible and utterly undermine.

**HADRIAN.**

And rightly so. For our prosperity is your happiness, since we do not cease daily to increase your highest degrees of dignity.

**ANTIOCHUS.**

I rejoice in your generosity. Therefore, if I perceive anything arising that seems to struggle against your power, I do not conceal it, but, impatient of delay, bring it forward.

**HADRIAN.**

And deservedly so, lest you be accused of treason if you conceal what ought not to be concealed.

**ANTIOCHUS.**

I have never been liable to guilt of that kind.

**HADRIAN.**

I remember. But report anything new that you know.

**ANTIOCHUS.**

A foreign woman recently entered this city, accompanied by three little daughters of her own.

**HADRIAN.**

What is the sex of the little ones?

**ANTIOCHUS.**

All female.

**HADRIAN.**

Can the arrival of such tiny women possibly bring any harm to the state?

**ANTIOCHUS.**

Very great harm.

**HADRIAN.**

What harm?

**ANTIOCHUS.**

The loss of peace.

**HADRIAN.**

How so?

**ANTIOCHUS.**

What can break civic harmony more than disagreement in religious observance?

**HADRIAN.**

Nothing more serious, nothing worse—as the Roman world testifies, infected everywhere with the stain of Christian slaughter.

**ANTIOCHUS.**

This woman of whom I speak urges our people to abandon the rites of their ancestors and devote themselves to the Christian religion.

**HADRIAN.**

Is her exhortation prevailing?

**ANTIOCHUS.**

Excessively. For our wives despise us in disgust to such a degree that they refuse to eat with us, much less to sleep with us.

**HADRIAN.**

I admit it: there is danger.

**ANTIOCHUS.**

It befits your position to take precautions.

**HADRIAN.**

Naturally. Let her be summoned, and let it be determined in our presence whether she is willing to yield.

**ANTIOCHUS.**

Shall I summon her?

**HADRIAN.**

I certainly wish it.

## SCENE II

**ANTIOCHUS.**

What is your name, foreign woman?

**WISDOM.**

Wisdom.

**ANTIOCHUS.**

Emperor Hadrian has ordered you to be brought into the palace and presented to his sight.

**WISDOM.**

I do not tremble at entering the palace with my noble company of daughters, nor do I fear to look directly upon the emperor’s threatening face.

**ANTIOCHUS.**

The detested race of Christians is always ready to resist rulers.

**WISDOM.**

The ruler of the universe, who does not know defeat, does not permit his own people to be overcome by an enemy.

**ANTIOCHUS.**

Curb the outpouring of your words and proceed to the palace.

**WISDOM.**

Show us the way by going before us; we shall follow, hastening along.

## SCENE III

**ANTIOCHUS.**

This is the emperor himself, whom you see seated on the throne. Consider beforehand what you will say.

**WISDOM.**

Christ’s teaching forbids that; it promises us instead gifts of unconquerable wisdom.

**HADRIAN.**

Come here, Antiochus.

**ANTIOCHUS.**

I am present, lord.

**HADRIAN.**

Are these the little women whom you reported as belonging to the Christian religion?

**ANTIOCHUS.**

They certainly are.

**HADRIAN.**

I am astonished at the beauty of each one, nor can I sufficiently admire the dignity of their appearance.

**ANTIOCHUS.**

Stop admiring them, my lord, and force them to worship the gods.

**HADRIAN.**

What if I first approach them with gentle speech, in case they should perhaps be willing to yield?

**ANTIOCHUS.**

That is better. For the weakness of the female sex can more easily be softened by flattery.

**HADRIAN.**

Illustrious matron, I gently and quietly invite you to worship the gods, so that you may enjoy our friendship.

**WISDOM.**

I neither wish to satisfy your wishes by worshiping the gods nor desire to enter into friendship with you.

**HADRIAN.**

Although my fury has so far been restrained, I am moved by no indignation toward you; rather, I am concerned with a father’s love for your welfare and that of your daughters.

**WISDOM.**

Do not, my daughters, set your hearts upon this Satan’s serpent-like seductions; reject them with disgust.

**FAITH.**

We reject and despise such trifles in our hearts.

**HADRIAN.**

What are you saying in that muttering tone?

**WISDOM.**

I was speaking a few words to my daughters.

**HADRIAN.**

You appear to have been born of the highest lineage, but I nevertheless wish to learn from you more fully your homeland, family, and name.

**WISDOM.**

Although the pride of blood should be considered of little importance by us, I do not deny that I derive my origin from a distinguished stock.

**HADRIAN.**

That is credible.

**WISDOM.**

For my parents were among the most eminent rulers of Greece, and I am called Wisdom.

**HADRIAN.**

The brilliance of noble birth shines in your face, and the name Wisdom gleams upon your lips.

**WISDOM.**

You flatter in vain; we are not moved by your persuasive words.

**HADRIAN.**

Tell me why you came, or why you approached our people.

**WISDOM.**

For no other reason than to recognize the truth, so that I might learn more fully the faith you are attacking and consecrate my daughters to Christ.

**HADRIAN.**

Explain the names of each one.

**WISDOM.**

One is called Faith, another Hope, and the third Charity.

**HADRIAN.**

How many years have they lived?

**WISDOM.**

Daughters, do you wish me to weary this fool with a discussion of arithmetic?

**FAITH.**

Yes, mother; we are happy to listen.

**WISDOM.**

O emperor, if you ask the ages of the little girls: Charity has completed a diminished, evenly even number of years; Hope a diminished, evenly odd number; but Faith an excessive, oddly even number.

**HADRIAN.**

By such an answer you have made me understand nothing of what I asked.

**WISDOM.**

Nor is that surprising, because under this definition not one number alone falls, but several.

**HADRIAN.**

Explain it more clearly, otherwise my mind cannot grasp it.

**WISDOM.**

Charity has now completed two Olympiads, Hope two lustra, and Faith three Olympiads.

**HADRIAN.**

Why, then, is the number eight, which consists of two Olympiads, and ten, which is completed by two lustra, called diminished? Or why is twelve, which is completed by three Olympiads, said to be excessive?

**WISDOM.**

A number is called diminished when the sum of its parts, joined together, produces a quantity smaller than the number of which they are parts—for example, eight. Half of eight is four, its fourth part is two, and its eighth part is one; reduced to one sum, these produce seven. Similarly, ten has a half, five; a fifth, two; and a tenth, one; joined together, these add up to eight.

Conversely, a number is called excessive when its parts, added together, grow larger, as with twelve. Half of twelve is six, its third part four, its fourth part three, its sixth part two, and its twelfth part one; this accumulation amounts to sixteen.

To pass over the principal type, which has received the balanced moderation of a middle limit between unequal excesses: a number is called perfect when it is equal to its parts and is neither increased nor diminished, such as six, whose parts—three, two, and one—restore the same number, six. In the same way, twenty-eight, four hundred ninety-six, and eight thousand one hundred twenty-eight are called perfect.

**HADRIAN.**

And what are the remaining numbers?

**WISDOM.**

All are excessive or diminished.

**HADRIAN.**

What is “evenly even”?

**WISDOM.**

A number that can be divided into two equal parts, and whose part can again be divided into two equal parts, and the part of that part likewise into two equal parts, and so on in order, until it reaches an indivisible unit—such as eight and sixteen, and all numbers that are produced from these by doubling.

**HADRIAN.**

And what is “evenly odd”?

**WISDOM.**

A number that admits division into equal parts, but whose parts immediately remain indivisible, such as ten and all numbers produced by doubling odd numbers. This number is contrary to the preceding one: in the former, only the lesser term is released through division; in the latter, only the greater term is suited to division. In the former, all its parts are equally even in name and quantity; in the latter, if the denomination is even, the quantity is odd, and if the quantity is even, the denomination is odd.

**HADRIAN.**

I understand neither the term you used nor “denomination” or “quantity.”

**WISDOM.**

When numbers of any kind are arranged in order, the first is called the lesser term and the last the greater. When, by making a division, we say what fraction of the number a part is, we give its denomination. When we count how many units there are in each part, we state its quantity.

**HADRIAN.**

And what is “oddly even”?

**WISDOM.**

A number that admits not only one division, like an evenly even number, but also a second, and sometimes a third or more, although it never reaches an indivisible unit.

**HADRIAN.**

What a painstaking and intricate [the text reads *plexibilis*; corrected here contextually from the suggested *plectilis*] question has arisen from the ages of these infant girls!

**WISDOM.**

In this the surpassing wisdom of the Maker and the wondrous knowledge of the world’s Craftsman must be praised: he not only created the world from nothing at the beginning and set all things in number, measure, and weight, but also, through the succession of times and the ages of human beings, granted that an astonishing knowledge of the arts could be discovered.

**HADRIAN.**

I have tolerated your reasoning for a long time so that I might make you obedient to me.

**WISDOM.**

In what matter?

**HADRIAN.**

In the worship of the gods.

**WISDOM.**

In this matter, certainly, I do not consent.

**HADRIAN.**

If you resist, you will be subjected to torture.

**WISDOM.**

You may attack the body with punishments, but you will not prevail in forcing the mind to yield.

**ANTIOCHUS.**

The day has passed and night is approaching; it is not time for arguing, because the hour of dining is near.

**HADRIAN.**

Let them be placed under guard beside the palace, and let a three-day respite be granted them for deliberation.

**ANTIOCHUS.**

Guard these women, soldiers, with every care, and leave them no opportunity to escape.

## SCENE IV

**WISDOM.**

O sweet little daughters and dear little ones, do not grieve over the narrow confinement of prison custody; do not be frightened by the threats of the punishments that hang over you.

**FAITH.**

Although our little bodies tremble at the tortures, our minds burn with desire for the rewards.

**WISDOM.**

Overcome the tenderness of childish age with the strength of mature understanding.

**HOPE.**

It is your task to help us with prayers, so that we may be able to conquer.

**WISDOM.**

This I constantly pray for, this I earnestly implore: that you persevere in the faith which, from the time you were still in your rattles, I never ceased to pour into your minds.

**CHARITY.**

What we learned while suckling at the breast in our cradles we shall in no way be able to forget.

**WISDOM.**

For this purpose I nourished you abundantly with maternal milk; for this purpose I delicately raised you, so that I might give you not to an earthly bridegroom but to a heavenly one, and thus deserve to be called the mother-in-law of the eternal King because of you.

**FAITH.**

For love of that bridegroom we are ready to die.

**WISDOM.**

I take greater delight in your reasoning, daughters, than in tasting the sweetness of nectar.

**HOPE.**

Send us before the judge’s tribunal, and you will discover how much boldness his love has given us.

**WISDOM.**

This is what I desire: to be crowned by your virginity and glorified by your martyrdom.

**CHARITY.**

Let us go with our little palms joined, and let us put the tyrant’s face to shame.

**WISDOM.**

Wait until the hour of our summons arrives.

**FAITH.**

We are weary of delays, yet we must wait.

## SCENE V

**HADRIAN.**

Antiochus, order those Greek women to be brought before us as prisoners.

**ANTIOCHUS.**

Come forward, Wisdom, and present yourself with your daughters before the emperor.

**WISDOM.**

Come with me, daughters, steadfastly, and persevere together in faith, so that you may happily receive the palm.

**HOPE.**

We are coming, and let him accompany us—the one for whose love we are being led to death.

**HADRIAN.**

Our serenity granted you a three-day respite. Therefore, if you have deliberated about anything useful, yield to our commands.

**WISDOM.**

We deliberated about the greatest possible good: namely, that we should not yield.

**ANTIOCHUS.**

Why do you deign to exchange words with this obstinate woman, who wearies you with insolent presumption?

**HADRIAN.**

Should I release her unpunished?

**ANTIOCHUS.**

By no means.

**HADRIAN.**

What, then?

**ANTIOCHUS.**

Urge the little girls, and if they resist, do not spare their infancy. Have them killed, so that the rebellious mother may be tormented more sharply by the funerals of her daughters.

**HADRIAN.**

I shall do what you advise.

**ANTIOCHUS.**

Only then will you prevail.

**HADRIAN.**

Faith, look upon the revered image of great Diana and offer libations to the sacred goddess, so that you may enjoy her favor.

**FAITH.**

O foolish command of the emperor, worthy of every contempt!

**HADRIAN.**

What are you muttering mockingly? Whom are you ridiculing with that wrinkled brow?

**FAITH.**

I ridicule your foolishness; I mock your stupidity.

**HADRIAN.**

Mine?

**FAITH.**

Yours.

**ANTIOCHUS.**

The emperor’s?

**FAITH.**

His.

**ANTIOCHUS.**

O abomination!

**FAITH.**

For what can appear more foolish, what more stupid, than for one who urges us, after despising the Creator of the universe, to offer veneration to pieces of metal?

**ANTIOCHUS.**

Is this not the height of madness and great insanity: to have called the prince of all things stupid?

**FAITH.**

I said it, I say it, and I shall say it as long as I live.

**ANTIOCHUS.**

You have only a short time to live, and soon you must be consumed by death.

**FAITH.**

This is what I desire: to die in Christ.

**HADRIAN.**

Let twelve centurions, taking turns, tear her limbs with whips.

**ANTIOCHUS.**

And rightly so.

**HADRIAN.**

O bravest centurions, come forward and avenge the insult done to me.

**ANTIOCHUS.**

Just so.

**HADRIAN.**

Find out, Antiochus, whether she is willing to yield.

**ANTIOCHUS.**

Faith, do you still wish to dishonor the emperor with your customary exchange of insults?

**FAITH.**

Why should I do so less than usual?

**ANTIOCHUS.**

Because you are being restrained by blows.

**FAITH.**

Blows do not compel me to be silent, because I feel no pain at all.

**ANTIOCHUS.**

O unhappy obstinacy, O defiant boldness!

**HADRIAN.**

The body is wasting away under the tortures, while the mind swells with pride.

**FAITH.**

You are mistaken, Hadrian, if you think I am being wearied by punishments. It is not I who am failing; rather, the feeble torturers are exhausted and stream with sweat from their weariness.

**HADRIAN.**

Have the twin portions of her breast cut away, so that at least shame may restrain her.

**ANTIOCHUS.**

Would that she could be restrained in any way!

**HADRIAN.**

Perhaps she will be restrained.

**FAITH.**

You have wounded my untouched breast, but you have not harmed me. Behold: instead of a fountain of blood, a fountain of milk bursts forth.

**HADRIAN.**

Let her be placed on a grating laid over burning fires, so that the force of the heat may kill her.

**ANTIOCHUS.**

She deserves to perish miserably, since she is not afraid to struggle against your command.

**FAITH.**

Everything you prepare for my pain is turned into rest. Thus I lie comfortably upon the grating, as upon a peaceful little boat.

**HADRIAN.**

Let a pan full of pitch and wax be placed over blazing fires, and let this rebel be thrown into the boiling liquid.

**FAITH.**

I leap in willingly.

**HADRIAN.**

I approve.

**FAITH.**

Where are your threats? Behold, unharmed, I swim and play amid the boiling liquid; instead of the force of the heat, I feel the coolness of morning dew.

**HADRIAN.**

Antiochus, what must be done about this?

**ANTIOCHUS.**

We must take care that she does not escape.

**HADRIAN.**

Let her be beheaded.

**ANTIOCHUS.**

Otherwise she will not be overcome.

**FAITH.**

Now is the time for joy; now is the time to exult in the Lord.

**WISDOM.**

Christ, unconquerable triumphant conqueror of the devil, grant endurance to my daughter Faith.

**FAITH.**

O venerable mother, say the final farewell to your daughter; give the kiss to your firstborn, and do not let any grief afflict your heart, because I am going toward the prize of eternity.

**WISDOM.**

O daughter, daughter, I am neither ashamed nor saddened, but I bid you farewell in exultation. I kiss your mouth and your eyes, weeping for joy, and pray that beneath the blow of the executioner you may preserve inviolate the mystery of your name.

**FAITH.**

O sisters born from the same womb, give me the kiss of peace and prepare yourselves to endure the coming struggle.

**HOPE.**

Help us with constant prayer, so that we may deserve to follow in your footsteps.

**FAITH.**

Obey the admonitions of our holy mother, who urged us to despise present things so that we might deserve to receive eternal things.

**CHARITY.**

We willingly obey our mother’s admonitions, so that we may deserve to enjoy eternal goods.

**FAITH.**

Executioner, come forward and fulfill the duty imposed upon you by killing me.

**WISDOM.**

Embracing the severed head of my dying daughter and repeatedly kissing it with my lips, I congratulate you, Christ, who have granted victory to this tiny girl.

**HADRIAN.**

Hope, yield to my exhortations as I counsel you with fatherly affection.

**HOPE.**

What are you exhorting me to do? What counsel are you giving?

**HADRIAN.**

Take care not to imitate your sister’s obstinacy, lest you perish under similar punishments.

**HOPE.**

Would that I had deserved to imitate her by suffering, so that I might resemble her in reward!

**HADRIAN.**

Lay aside the callus of your heart, kneel and offer incense to great Diana, and I shall honor and exalt you with every affection as though you were my own child.

**HOPE.**

I reject your fatherhood and have no desire for your benefits. Therefore you are deceived by empty hope if you think I shall yield to you.

**HADRIAN.**

Speak more sparingly, lest I become angry.

**HOPE.**

Become angry; I am not concerned.

**ANTIOCHUS.**

I am astonished, Augustus, that you tolerate being insulted for so long by this worthless little girl. I am bursting with fury because I hear her barking so recklessly at you.

**HADRIAN.**

Until now I spared her childishness; I shall spare it no longer, but shall inflict the punishment she deserves.

**ANTIOCHUS.**

Would that you would!

**HADRIAN.**

O lictors, come forward and beat this rebel with raw sinews until she is destroyed.

**ANTIOCHUS.**

It is fitting that she feel the severity of your fury, since she regards the gentleness of your mercy as worthless.

**HOPE.**

This mercy is what I desire; this gentleness is what I long for.

**ANTIOCHUS.**

Wisdom, what are you saying as you stand beside the corpse of your dead child, lifting your eyes upward?

**WISDOM.**

I call upon the All-Father, that he may grant Hope the same perseverance in endurance that he granted Faith.

**HOPE.**

O mother, mother! How effective, how readily heard, I find your prayers to be! Behold, while you pray, the panting torturers raise their right hands and poise the blow, yet I feel no touch of pain.

**HADRIAN.**

If you regard the whips as worthless, you will be confined by harsher punishments.

**HOPE.**

Bring on, bring on whatever is cruel, whatever deadly thing you can devise. The more fiercely you rage, the more completely defeated you will be put to shame.

**HADRIAN.**

Let her be suspended in the air and torn with hooks until, her entrails ripped out and her bones exposed, she fails and bursts apart limb by limb.

**ANTIOCHUS.**

An imperial command, and a wholly fitting punishment!

**HOPE.**

You speak with fox-like deceit and flatter with changeable cunning, Antiochus.

**ANTIOCHUS.**

Be quiet, wretched girl; your loquacity must now end.

**HOPE.**

It will not happen as you hope; even now confusion will come upon you and your ruler.

**HADRIAN.**

What is this new sweetness I feel? What astonishing fragrance do I smell?

**HOPE.**

The pieces falling from my lacerated body give off the fragrance of paradise, and against your will you are forced to admit that punishments cannot harm me.

**HADRIAN.**

Antiochus, what must I do?

**ANTIOCHUS.**

We must resort to new tortures.

**HADRIAN.**

Let a bronze vessel full of oil and fat, wax and pitch, be placed over fires, and let her be thrown into it bound.

**ANTIOCHUS.**

If she is handed over to Vulcan’s authority, perhaps she will not find a way to escape.

**HOPE.**

It is not unfamiliar to Christ’s power to make fire gentle by changing its nature.

**HADRIAN.**

What? Antiochus, I hear something like the sound of surging water.

**ANTIOCHUS.**

Alas, alas, my lord!

**HADRIAN.**

What has happened to us?

**ANTIOCHUS.**

The boiling heat, after the vessel broke, burned the attendants, and that sorceress appeared unharmed.

**HADRIAN.**

I confess: we have been defeated.

**ANTIOCHUS.**

Completely.

**HADRIAN.**

Let her head be cut off.

**ANTIOCHUS.**

Otherwise she will not be destroyed.

**HOPE.**

O beloved Charity, O only sister! Do not fear the tyrant’s threats; do not tremble at punishments. Strive with steadfast faith to imitate your sisters, who are going ahead to the palace of heaven.

**CHARITY.**

I am weary of this present life, weary of earthly habitation, because I am separated from you even for a little while.

**HOPE.**

Lay aside your weariness and strive toward the reward. For we shall not be separated for long, but will soon be joined together in heaven.

**CHARITY.**

Let it be so, let it be so!

**HOPE.**

Courage, illustrious mother; rejoice, and do not let the sorrow of maternal affection touch you because of my suffering. Set hope before grief when you see me dying for Christ.

**WISDOM.**

Now I rejoice, but then I shall rejoice in perfect exultation, when I have sent your little sister, killed under the same conditions, ahead to heaven, and I follow last.

**HOPE.**

The eternal Trinity will restore to you forever the full number of your daughters, without any diminution.

**WISDOM.**

Take courage, daughter; the executioner is attacking us with his sword drawn.

**HOPE.**

I willingly receive the sword. You, Christ, receive the spirit cast out from its bodily dwelling in confession of your name.

**WISDOM.**

O Charity, illustrious child, my only hope from my womb [the printed text repeats the element in *uterimei*], do not grieve your good mother, who awaits the completion of your struggle. Despise the present good, so that you may reach unending joy, where your sisters shine with crowns of unstained virginity.

**CHARITY.**

Support me, mother, with holy prayers, so that I may deserve to share in their joys.

**WISDOM.**

I pray that you will be made firm in faith to the end, and I do not doubt that everlasting rejoicing will be granted to you.

**HADRIAN.**
