Charity, I am sated with the insults of your sisters and exceedingly angered by their lengthy speech. Therefore I shall not contend with you for long: either, if you obey my wishes, I shall enrich you with every good, or, if you resist, I shall afflict you with every evil.

**CHARITY.**

I embrace what is good with all my heart and utterly detest what is evil.

**HADRIAN.**

This is especially healthful for you and pleasing to me; therefore, out of my mercy, I propose something easy for you.

**CHARITY.**

What?

**HADRIAN.**

Say only, “Great Diana!” and I will no longer compel you to sacrifice.

**CHARITY.**

I certainly will not say it.

**HADRIAN.**

Why?

**CHARITY.**

Because I do not wish to lie. My sisters and I were begotten by the same parents, instructed in the same sacraments, and strengthened by one and the same steadfastness of faith. Therefore know that our will, our agreement, and our understanding are one and the same, and that I shall never differ from them in anything.

**HADRIAN.**

What an insult—that I am despised even by such a tiny little girl!

**CHARITY.**

Although I am tender in age, I know how to confound you with argument.

**HADRIAN.**

Take her away, Antiochus, and have her suspended on the rack and savagely beaten.

**ANTIOCHUS.**

I fear that blows will not prevail.

**HADRIAN.**

If they do not prevail, order the furnace to be heated for three continuous days and nights and throw her amid the raging flames.

**CHARITY.**

O powerless judge, who doubts that he can overcome an eight-year-old child without the weapons of fire!

**HADRIAN.**

Go, Antiochus, and complete the duty imposed upon you.

**CHARITY.**

I shall comply by satisfying your savagery, but it will not harm me at all, because neither blows will be able to lacerate my little body nor flames to blacken my hair or clothing.

**HADRIAN.**

She will find out.

**CHARITY.**

Let her find out.

## SCENE VI

**HADRIAN.**

Antiochus, what has happened to you? Why are you returning more sorrowful than usual?

**ANTIOCHUS.**

When you experience the cause of sorrow, you will be no less saddened.

**HADRIAN.**

Tell me; do not conceal it.

**ANTIOCHUS.**

That wanton little girl whom you handed over to me for torture was flogged in my presence, but not even the surface of her delicate skin was torn. Then I threw her into the furnace, which was glowing red from its excessive heat.

**HADRIAN.**

Why do you speak evasively? Explain the outcome.

**ANTIOCHUS.**

The flame burst out and burned five thousand people.

**HADRIAN.**

And what happened to her?

**ANTIOCHUS.**

To Charity?

**HADRIAN.**

To her.

**ANTIOCHUS.**

She wandered playfully among the flame-belching vapors, singing praises to her God. Those who watched carefully also reported that three bright-white men had walked about with her.

**HADRIAN.**

I am ashamed to see her any longer, since I cannot harm her.

**ANTIOCHUS.**

It remains for her to be killed by the sword.

**HADRIAN.**

Let this be done without delay.

## SCENE VII

**ANTIOCHUS.**

Uncover your hard neck, Charity, and endure the executioner’s sword.

**CHARITY.**

In this I do not resist your wishes but willingly obey your commands.

**WISDOM.**

Now, now, daughter, it is time for rejoicing; now it is time to rejoice in Christ. There is no anxiety to gnaw at me, because I am confident of your victory.

**CHARITY.**

Mother, press a kiss upon me and commend my spirit, which is going to Christ.

**WISDOM.**

May he who gave you life in my womb receive the soul which he breathed into you from heaven.

**CHARITY.**

Glory to you, Christ, who have called me to yourself with the palm of martyrdom.

**WISDOM.**

Go, sweetest child [the printed *Vate, protes* is evidently corrupt; translated contextually], and when you are joined with Christ in heaven, remember your mother, now an exhausted matron, who gave birth to you.

## SCENE VIII

**WISDOM.**

Come together, illustrious matrons, and bury my daughters’ corpses with me.

**MATRONS.**

We embalm the little bodies with spices and honorably celebrate the funeral rites.

**WISDOM.**

Great is the kindness and wondrous the devotion that you show me and my dead.

**MATRONS.**

We carry out whatever is useful to you with devoted minds.

**WISDOM.**

I do not doubt it.

**MATRONS.**

Where do you wish to choose the place of burial?

**WISDOM.**

At the third mile from the City, if the distance does not displease you.

**MATRONS.**

It does not displease us; rather, we are glad to follow the raised funeral procession.

## SCENE IX

**WISDOM.**

Here is the place.

**MATRONS.**

This place is indeed suitable for preserving the relics.

**WISDOM.**

To you, earth, I entrust the little flowers of my womb for safekeeping. Keep them warm in your material embrace until, at the greater resurrection, they grow green again in glory. And you, Christ, meanwhile fill their souls with splendors, granting peaceful rest to their bones.

**MATRONS.**

Amen.

**WISDOM.**

I give thanks for your kindness and for the consolation you have brought to my bereavement.

**MATRONS.**

Do you wish us to remain here with you?

**WISDOM.**

No.

**MATRONS.**

Why not?

**WISDOM.**

So that no inconvenience may be imposed upon you because of my comfort. It is enough that you remained with me for three nights. Go in peace; return safely.

**MATRONS.**

Do you wish to leave with us?

**WISDOM.**

Not at all.

**MATRONS.**

And what do you intend to do?

**WISDOM.**

To remain here, if perhaps my request may come to pass and what I desire may be fulfilled.

**MATRONS.**

What do you ask? What do you desire?

**WISDOM.**

Only this: that, after completing my prayer, I may die in Christ.

**MATRONS.**

It remains for us to wait until we can also commit you to burial.

**WISDOM.**
As you wish. Adonai Emmanuel, whom the Godhead of the All-Father brought forth before time, and whom the virginity of his mother bore in time; you, who wonderfully subsist as one Christ from two natures, neither dividing the unity of the person by the diversity of the natures, [Col. 1062A] nor confusing the diversity of the natures by the unity of the person: for you let the joyful serenity of the angels and the sweet harmony of the stars rejoice; let the knowledge of everything knowable praise you as well, and everything formed from the substance of the elements, because you alone, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, are form without matter. Yet, by the Father’s will and the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, you did not refuse to become a passible human being in your humanity, while your divinity remained impassible. And so that none of those who believe in you might perish, but that every believer might live eternally, you did not disdain to taste our death and to destroy it by your resurrection.

I also recall you, perfect God and true man, having promised that all who, out of reverence for your name, would either abandon the use of earthly possessions [Col. 1062B] or place after it their affection for their fleshly relatives would receive a hundredfold recompense and be granted the prize of eternal life. Animated by hope in this promise, [69] I did what you commanded, willingly leaving behind the offspring whom I bore. Therefore, merciful one, do not delay to fulfill your promises; but make me, as soon as possible, released from bodily bonds, rejoice at the reception of my daughters, whom I did not hesitate to offer for slaughter on your behalf. Thus, while they follow you, the Lamb of the Virgin, and sing the new song, may I rejoice more sweetly in hearing them and be gladdened by their glory. And although I cannot sing the song of virginity, may I nevertheless deserve to praise you eternally with them—you who are not yourself the Father, but are the same as the Father, with whom and with the Holy Spirit, one Lord of the universe and one king, you reign and rule through the endless ages of immortal time over the highest, middle, [Col. 1062C] and lowest order of reason.

MATRONS.

Receive it, Lord. Amen.

[WORKS WRITTEN IN VERSE.]

[Col. 1061]

PREFACE OF HROTSVITHA TO HER WORKS WRITTEN IN VERSE.

[Col. 1061D] I offer this little book, adorned with little outward ornament but fashioned with no little diligence, to the benevolence of all the learned for correction—of those, that is, who do not take pleasure in disparaging one who errs, but rather in correcting errors. For I confess that I have erred to no small degree, not only in discerning the natures of syllables but also in composing phrases, and that many things deserving reproach lie hidden in this arrangement. [70] Yet easy pardon is due to one who confesses her errors, and pious correction to her faults.

But if it is objected that certain parts of this work, in the judgment of some, were taken from apocryphal writings, this is not the crime of wicked presumption but an error of ignorance. For when I began to spin the thread of this composition, I did not know that the things on which I had decided to labor were doubtful. But once I recognized this, I refused to destroy the work, because what perhaps seems false may prove to be true.

Since matters stand thus, I greatly need the assistance of many people for the defense of this little work’s completion—just as, at its very beginning, I was supported by scarcely any sufficiency of my own strength. For I was neither yet vigorous in mature age nor advanced in knowledge; nor did I dare, by consulting anyone learned, [Col. 1063A] to clarify the purpose of my intention, lest I be forbidden on account of my rusticity. Therefore, secretly from everyone and almost as though by stealth, sometimes laboring alone to compose, sometimes destroying what I had badly composed, I endeavored, as far as I could—although it was hardly necessary—to prepare some sort of text from sentences of Scripture that I had collected within the precinct of our Gandersheim monastery.

First, under the instruction of the most wise and gracious Rikkardis, my teacher, and of others teaching in their turn; then, through the ready favor of the gracious Gerberga, of royal lineage, whose authority I now serve—the abbess who, though younger in age, was, as befitted an imperial niece, more advanced in knowledge—who herself had earlier learned several authors from the most learned and taught them to me with great kindness. Although metrical [Col. 1063B] composition seems difficult and arduous for female weakness, yet, trusting always in the help of the ever-merciful heavenly grace [Col. 1064A] and not in my own powers, I undertook to accompany the verses of this little work with dactylic rhythms. I did so lest the talent entrusted to me, my little gift of intelligence, should be destroyed by negligence while lying torpid beneath the obscure rust of my breast; rather, struck by the hammer of devoted diligence, may it return at least a slight ringing of divine praise. Thus, if no opportunity were given to gain anything else by trade, it might nevertheless be transformed into some instrument of ultimate usefulness.

Therefore, whoever you are, reader, if you are wise in the right way according to God, do not disdain to offer the help of your uprightness to this needy page, which is fortified by the authority of no teacher. If anything should perhaps be judged rightly composed, attribute it to God; and attribute the generality of its faults to my negligence—not, however, by reproaching me, but by showing indulgence, because the right of rebuke is broken [Col. 1064B] where humility of confession intervenes.

[HISTORY OF THE UNVIOLATED MOTHER OF GOD.]

[Col. 1063]

ARGUMENT OF THE HISTORY OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN.

Joachim and Anna, of the lineage of David, after having lived sterile for a long time and after having been rejected by the priests in the Temple because of their barrenness, at last, through long prayers and vows, received a divine child named Mary. They devoted her in the Temple to chastity and the eternal service of God. Tender, joyful, and steadfast, she climbed the Temple steps to everyone’s amazement and surpassed the other virgins in holiness of life.

When the priests wished to betroth her and sought a husband for her by casting lots among the rods, the lot fell upon Joseph’s rod, he being of David’s lineage. For immediately a dove, settling upon his rod, flew toward heaven, while all praised the divine choice. Joseph, himself a virgin, was betrothed to her; shortly afterward an angel, having greeted him with a divine salutation, announced that God, the creator of all, would take flesh through the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit.

Trusting the angel’s word, she migrated with Joseph to Bethlehem by decree of Caesar Augustus and bore her firstborn, Jesus Christ, the Savior of the world. Both the shepherds and the Magi who came from the East bore witness to his divinity. When this report reached Herod, he ordered all the infants born in that year to be killed, so that he might remove the heir of the kingdom. Warned by an angel, Joseph withdrew into Egypt with the mother and child in order to escape the king’s cruelty. Immediately the images of the Egyptians fell forward to the ground, nodding, and proclaimed to their priests that the true God had been born.

The story also recounts miracles of the child concerning serpents and dragons while they spent the night in a cave, as well as concerning lions and leopards, which presented themselves gently and tamely to the child; it also recalls the palm tree bending down with its fruit into his mother’s lap and the spring that burst forth at the child’s words when they were suffering from thirst on their journey.

[Col. 1063]

TO GERBERGA, ABBESS IN GANDERSHEIM, NIECE OF EMPEROR OTTO THE FIRST.

[Col. 1063C]

Hail, most illustrious royal offspring,

Gerberga, renowned in character and learning.

Receive, gracious and serene mistress,

These little poems that I offer you for cleansing.

Kindly correct their uncultivated verses,

Which your excellent learning can build up.

[Col. 1064C]

And since you are certainly wearied by varied labor,

Deign, in play, to read these rhythms now.

Try also to cleanse this rather soiled Camena,

And support it with the flower of your teaching,

So that devotion may sustain the praise of its lady pupil,

And the poems of a faithful teacher’s disciple.

[Col. 1063]

PREFACE TO THE HISTORY OF THE UNVIOLATED MOTHER OF GOD.

[Col. 1063D]

Unique hope of the world, illustrious mistress of heaven,

Holy mother of the King, bright star of the sea,

You, pious virgin, by bearing restored to the world

The life that the aged virgin had lost;

Deign graciously to be present to your servant,

Hrosvitha, with her little prayers and new poems.

Now, serving you through the labor of a woman’s Camena,

I, suppliant, sound out dactylic rhythms for you,

[Col. 1064D]

Desiring at least briefly to touch upon

The smallest portion of your praise, Virgin,

The clear beginnings of your blessed birth,

And also to set forth your royal offspring.

Yet I acknowledge that fragile strength exceeds itself

When I attempt to sing you with deserved praises—

You whose merits the whole world cannot worthily sing,

And who shine beyond the praises of the angels.

[Col. 1065A] 73

Since, therefore, in your virginal womb you carried

Him who rules all things by his authority,

He who once commanded the foolish she-ass to speak

In praise of his holy name,

And who, through an angelic word, made you, young virgin,

Conceive worthily from the Holy Spirit,

And made you, without any stain upon your modesty,

The mother of his offspring, unlike all others in merit—

[Col. 1066A]

If he is willing, he can release my tongue

And touch my heart with the dew of his gracious gift,

So that, by his granting the gift of his gentle mercy,

I may compose what pleases him and sing you, Virgin,

Lest I rightly be condemned as a companion of ungrateful little sluggards,

Who are reluctant to sing psalms according to their ability to the Most High;

But rather may I deserve, added to the ranks of virgins,

To praise the purple Lamb eternally.

[Col. 1065]

HISTORY OF THE BIRTH AND PRAISEWORTHY LIFE OF THE UNVIOLATED MOTHER OF GOD, WHICH I FOUND WRITTEN UNDER THE NAME OF SAINT JAMES, THE BROTHER OF THE LORD.

[Col. 1065B]

When a thousand lustrums of the passing world had been completed,

And the happy sixth age had begun,

In which God commanded whatever the truthful prophets

Had already foretold to be fulfilled in faithful mercy,

Those who had soon foretold that Jesus would come into the world,

Born from the stock of Judah—

There had arisen in the land of Israel, under the ancient law,

An elder, descended from the royal stock of great David.

For they say that he bore the name Joachim.

From his mother’s breast he had been brought up in the commandments of the law,

And he was righteous and earnestly devoted.

This also was continually his greatest concern:

[74] To pasture well the flocks of his great flock,

Showing himself to be regarded as a true shepherd,

Since he was worthy to be the earthly parent

Of the one who did not refuse to carry the lambs upon his shoulders,

Leading them to the joyful rewards of life,

About to suffer death for love of us,

And to purchase the guilty at the price of his precious soul.

This hero, Joachim, of whom I shall tell,

Was a fortunate patriarch with such a grandson.

Adorning himself with every peaceful effort of good deeds,

He divided into three parts everything he possessed,

Giving one part to widows, strangers, and young girls.

More often he gave a part in the Temple to those serving there,

And he kept one small portion for his entire household.

By doing this frequently in benevolent piety,

He finally received a worthy reward:

His modest substance was multiplied so greatly

That it surpassed all the wealth of the great men of his people,

And the earth bore no other powerful man like him,

Whom such abundance of all things could support.

[Col. 1065D]

When he had now happily lived through four cycles of five years

In the fullness of prosperity,

He betrothed to himself a very beautiful beloved,

Anna, radiant in beauty and praiseworthy in character,

Born from a noble family, descended from David,

Whom he joined to his own love in a lawful covenant.

[Col. 1066B]

But they say that she remained sterile for a considerable time

And offered the faithful man no hope of offspring.

At last, when twenty years had passed,

It happened that Joachim, during a festival,

Stood among the ministers of the altar in the Temple,

Who were seen to be worthy to place the incense.

When Ruben, the scribe of the sacred Temple, saw him,

He addressed the man who had become hateful to him with bitter words:

“You may not touch the holy incense,” he said,

“Nor may you offer gifts for sacrifice to the Lord,

Because he has despised you, denying you the gift of offspring.”

The noble man gave no reply,

But departed grieving and sought the forests in sorrow,

Where he had once often been accustomed to pasture his flock.

As he proceeded through trackless country to a distant land,

[Col. 1066C]

Taking his own shepherds with him,

He hid there in secret places while tending the flock,

And afterward he did not wish to return to the abandoned homeland,

For he had endured deep shame in his heart

Because of Ruben’s bitter words, for which he blamed himself.

After five glorious months had passed,

His wife, despairing that he was still alive and safe,

Wept through the days and knew no consolation.

She poured out these prayers to the Lord in sorrow:

“Ruler of Israel, sole lover of the people,

You who always revive the sorrowful with gentle mercy,

Why did you wish to take away from me my beloved companion,

Adding grief to one who is always sad and mourning,

Because I have always remained sterile, with no offspring in my womb?

But now I sigh from an even greater wound of sorrow,

[Col. 1066D]

Because I do not at all know what it may bring about, [lacuna]

for the devoted friend of the law, devoted to the lawful Lord.

O how happy I would be if only I could know

Whether bitter death suddenly swallowed him,

Or whether he still enjoys the warm breath of life.

Certainly, if I knew, I would have no right to grieve.

Only when he succumbed to the dark shadows of death

Would I honor his funeral with the greatest and most noble ceremony,

[Col. 1067A]

Entrusting his illustrious body to a fitting tomb.”

When these things were finished, she raised her eyes

And saw, on the branches of a laurel tree,

Birds surrounding their feathered young

With a sweet murmuring.

As she watched this, she sang in a sorrowful voice:

“King of heaven, beneath whom the starry axis is subject,

[76] You who are surely able to arrange all things rightly,

May praise for all mercies always be yours,

Because, in your clemency, you have granted all living creatures,

Fish, cattle, serpents, and birds,

To rejoice diligently with their young.

But you have finally decreed that I alone,

A wretched woman, should remain sterile,

As a matter of just judgment.

Therefore I invoke you, the All-Father, as witness

With steadfast heart to the vow I made at the beginning of my marriage:

If in your mercy you would grant me the fruit of my womb,

I would immediately present it to you properly in the consecrated Temple,

And dedicate it to your service according to the lawful custom.”

While she was forming such words with pure lips,

An angel suddenly descended from the starry height,

Bearing great consolation for such great sorrow.

Standing before her, he spoke these friendly words:

“Cast sorrow from your heart; put away grief.

By the counsel of the supreme God, trust in the offspring

That will proceed from your womb at the appointed time.

This child will truly become a wonder to all peoples.”

He spoke, and, flying back on his golden-winged feathers,

Cut through the air.

But Anna, greatly terrified by the angel’s words,

Went sorrowfully home, lay down upon her bed,

And, trembling, prayed through the day according to the rule of the psalms,

[Col. 1067C]

Spending the following night in pouring out prayers.

Afterward she ordered her maidservant to come before her,

And questioned her while she stood beneath her eyes:

“Why did she despise me, or why did she come so late,

When I feel that something extraordinary may be happening to me?”

The frivolous servant girl, on the contrary,

Replied with a word touched by insulting, servile muttering:

“If God has despised you and made you sterile,” she said,

“Tell me, I beg you, what does that have to do with me?”

But Anna patiently endured this insult,

Pouring out only bitter tears in deep sorrow.

[77] At that very hour, certainly, the angel previously mentioned appeared to Joachim among the mountains, shining,

Where the afflicted man had then been hiding while pasturing his flock,

And ordered him to return more quickly to his abandoned companion.

Moved in his heart by these instructions, he said:

“She has now remained with me for twice ten years,

And the Lord has given me no offspring by her.

Moreover, I left the Temple full of bitter insults,

Confounded because of that very cause,

And you urge me to return, to submit myself once more to shame,

To me who am despised and filled with so many evils.”

To him the heavenly messenger, with gentle words,

Said: “Believe that I am a heavenly voice,

Made the guardian of you by the mercy of the heavenly King,

Who, through me, has granted that Anna, who is righteous,

Should be consoled while she poured forth blessed little prayers in tears.

But now I have come from the hinge of heaven on your account,

Bringing the immense joy of a great gift,

And I tell you this: the very noble Anna

Will soon conceive a daughter worthy of veneration for all ages.

She will be holy among all the daughters of humankind;

The Holy Spirit will deservedly rest in her,

And through her the highest blessing will come to the world.

She is said to have had neither a first like her

Nor a successor like her.

Now try to return to your blessed companion,

Who will joyfully bring forth such glory for the whole world.

And always render sweet thanks to the Creator,

Who is pleased to grant you such an offspring,

Such as the prophets certainly never possessed,

And such as all the elect after this will not possess.”

To him Joachim, rejoicing in these promises, said:

“If your grace toward me, your servant, remains certain,

Deign for a time to rest beneath my roof,

[Col. 1068B]

And do not disdain to taste the food prepared for you.”

But the angel replied in a lovely voice:

[78] “Cease, I beg you, from now on to call yourself my servant.

Believe instead that you are a companion of the angelic host.

For I have no need to eat earthly food;

The presence of the supreme Lord always nourishes me.

Therefore I instruct you to bring to the Lord, as a sacred offering,

What you are trying to place upon my table.”

Then he quickly took a year-old lamb from the flock.

Hoping that the ancient reproach of Ruben had ceased,

He sacrificed it to the Lord with a joyful heart,

Placing it upon the fire as the precept of the law requires.

When these offerings had duly been completed as the angel commanded,

he was lifted up in the altar’s smoke and proceeded to the stars.

Then the grace of the merciful Father gradually

Began to shine upon the world with bright rays,

And the earlier discord began to reach a stable end,

When the heavenly citizens first promised

That earthly beings would have their fellowship—

Those whom previously they had despised because of the merits of their ancestor Adam.

At that time the mercy of the All-Father was not hidden from the angelic host:

In pity he soon ordained to send his own Son

Into a virgin womb,

So that he who was born without beginning from the supreme Father

Might take flesh within a virgin’s womb in the fullness of time,

And might save all people by his sacred blood.

Thus the cunning enemy of the human race would not afterward

Rejoice in holding the world fast in evil snares;

rather, the divinity of the Father, the Son, and the gracious Spirit,

powerful in equal form under a threefold name,

[Col. 1068D]

would rule the world lawfully and steadfastly to its end.

After the angel had crossed the star-bearing Olympus,

Joachim could scarcely bear the proclamation of such a great matter.

Struck at last by the dart of great fear,

He lay stretched upon the ground through the power of the heavenly gift,

Terrified, he lay unconscious

[79] for perhaps a sixth part of that day, if I am not mistaken,

until the sun ended its course at evening.

Meanwhile the boys came back, weary, with the flock.

When they saw their master lying prostrate nearby,

They began, in sorrow and confusion of mind,

To ask the reason for his recent terror.

Yet they could scarcely lift him.

[Col. 1069A]

When he had told them what the heavenly messenger had said,

They urged him to obey the commands from above

And return swiftly to his abandoned homeland.

He left the forests after gathering the flocks

And joyfully led the boys with him.

When thirty days had passed,

The angel appeared to holy Anna as she prayed,

And spoke these words in peaceful language:

“Rise up in spirit and proceed with a serene face

At once to the gate commonly called the Golden Gate.

There, perhaps, you will find that your lawful husband,

Returned in complete peace, is still alive.”

She quickly fulfilled the beloved command.

Impatient of delay, she went to the gate

And waited for her husband with joyful heart.

[Col. 1069B]

When she saw him with astonished eyes,

She ran to meet him across the flower-bearing field,

Threw herself lovingly upon his neck,

And finally gave thanks to the Most High in these words:

“Praise to you, supreme Giver of all good things,

Who grant me such joys, though I do not deserve them.

Behold, I feel my own husband present and safe—

I who for so long have remained widowed,

And who, though sterile, have conceived the joys of offspring.”

When these words were heard, all the Hebrew people rejoiced together

And sang praises to God with joyful heart.

After this, when nine months had certainly passed,

The great day arrived on which the most noble Anna

[80]

Bore a daughter worthy of veneration through all ages.

Eight days later the chief priests came,

As custom required, to assign a name to such a girl

And to sanctify her as well.

In their presence Joachim poured forth this prayer:

“King of heaven, who alone gives names to the stars,

Deign to show from heaven, through shining signs,

The name of this tender girl.”

He had spoken, and suddenly a strong voice sounded from above,

Commanding that the remarkable girl be called Mary.

Since this name in the Latin language corresponds to “star of the sea,”

The holy girl deservedly received it,

Because she is the splendid star that shines forever

In the bright diadem of Christ, the eternal King.

After the turning of the two-year limit,

Her fortunate mother took Mary from the breast,

Weaning her in the customary manner,

[Col. 1069D]

And promptly presented her in the Temple with a worthy offering—

Her who was ultimately to become the Temple of the Lord.

There, joined to the holy virgins, the little girl remained always

In divine songs,

Which the heavenly citizens deservedly honor with praise.

After this, standing at the threshold of the sacred Temple,

She suddenly ran boldly up the fifteen steep steps,

Forgetting her age and already filled with God,

Without turning her face backward to seek her parents,

As infants commonly do.

At this, all the assembled people and the ministers of the Temple

Were greatly amazed.

The chief priests themselves praised the deed first,

Saying that by so great an act the little girl

Was quickly foreshadowing something great in herself—

Truly great and deservedly astonishing to all.

What could be believed greater, or what could be greater,

Than that a girl should carry in her virginal womb

[Col. 1070A]

The great creator of the world and her own parent?

Nor is it strange that she began thus to set her steps upward,

Although she was an infant, small in her milk-fed limbs,

Since, holy Father, you enriched her with your sacred Spirit

When she had been enclosed in her holy mother’s womb,

Knowing beforehand that she alone was worthy

To bear your own Son, born through the ages;

He who afterward, clothed in the covering of bodily form,

Made the ascent of the steps plain to all for eternity,

By which they strive to return to their abandoned homeland—

He whose name is Christ, to whom be heavenly praise. Amen.

[Col. 1070B]

The mother, fortunate in such a deed,

Sang this praise to the eternal King:

“Almighty ruler, sole lover of mercy,

In your clemency you have done wondrous things for your own people,

Looking with compassion upon my humble mind as well,

And granting the joys of a daughter to one who had already despaired.

After this I dare to bring offerings to you,

Nor do I fear that my enemy will henceforth prevent me,

joined to the sacred ministers, from visiting the Temple.

For this the heavenly citizens diligently praise you,

Singing a fitting song eternally. Amen.”

When these words of prayer were finished,

The blessed parents returned,

While little Mary remained in the Temple.

No human tongue can comprehend,

[Col. 1070C]

Nor can the enduring world, though it gives voice,

fully declare the splendid fame of this child,

Nor the life and character of the marvelous girl.

Who could praise in worthy songs through the ages

This girl, who, taken from the cradle immediately,

Shone upon the whole world with mature virtues

And displayed nothing childish in her tender limbs?

She was most righteous in the precepts of the law,

And always devoted to David’s songs.

[82] Wise, humble, fervent in the sweetness of her mind,

Pleasing to all and radiant with every virtue.

No ear had ever heard her utter a curse

Or any offense against a human being;

Indeed, no one had ever known such a thing about her.

She was always gentle and most pleasing to all.

Whatever speech flowed from her mouth

Was seasoned with the honey of heavenly grace.

Whenever anyone blessed her with friendly words,

She immediately took care to give thanks to the supreme Lord,

Nor did she thereby restrain her tongue from divine songs.

As a noble example to all her companions,

She placed herself before them in universal goodness.

They say that her face, shining with snowy whiteness,

Surpassed the rays of the blazing sun

And completely overcame the human gaze.

What shall I say of her fingers, proven by sufficient skill in their work?

For the little girl completed her tasks with a practiced hand.

Indeed, setting a severe standard for herself,

She lived more strictly than everyone else in the Temple.

Therefore, among the other virgins who were joined together there,

[Col. 1071A]

She devoted herself so greatly to continuing in sacred prayers

And always steadfastly in divine songs.

After the darkness of night had been dispelled

And dawn spread light over the eastern region,

As Phoebus climbed higher through the serene sky,

The third hour of the day had suddenly arrived.

Then she relaxed her white fingers from their work,

After skillfully laboring over purple threads.

But as soon as Phoebus descended at the ninth hour,

The famous girl devoted herself again to prayers as usual

And persisted in them with earnestness of mind,

Until the holy virgin received sacred food from an angelic minister.

For every day the powerful priests gave her,

According to custom, food supplied from heaven.

She promptly gave it to the needy through her devotion.

[Col. 1071B]

[83] Finally, heavenly citizens, descending from the stars,

Often consoled her with friendly words,

So that she might learn to despise earthly love

And preserve a chaste mind for the eternal King.

Whoever, weak in his languishing limbs, merely touched her

Quickly returned healed.

When her fame flew throughout the world,

The priest Abiathar often urged the other priests

Of the Temple, without sparing a costly gift,

To wish to betroth the illustrious Mary

To the son of an excellent man in a lawful union.

But the chaste girl prevented this from happening,

Rejecting the illustrious alliances of royal lineage,

And declared that she would never submit

Her noble body to anyone’s marriage.

[Col. 1071C]

Then the powerful priests said to her:

“Is not God worshiped, and is he not worthily revered,

Within the lawful posterity of the people of Judah?

Nor is it fitting for such a girl to remain unmarried.”

The virgin, steadfast in mind, replied:

“God rejoices to dwell in a pure Temple

And in sober minds;

He does not delight in those whom wanton desire

Stains with great sin.

We know that Abel deservedly received a double crown:

He was the first righteous man born to the world’s first parent;

one crown for the martyrdom accomplished through his brother’s murder,

And a second, brighter one for virginity.

We believe that Elijah sought the hidden heaven,

Because he remained truly powerful in virginity

And never defiled his body with bitter stains.

[Col. 1071D]

I have certainly learned this through the teaching of the law,

And, learning it, I have diligently fixed it in my heart.

I know how to preserve my maidenly modesty.”

When she had completed fourteen full years,

The Pharisees said that it was not customary

[84]

for a virgin of so great an age to wish to remain unmarried.

After this, under the sacred honor of the Lord,

They decided that the whole people should gather,

So that together they might attempt to resolve so great a matter.

When everyone was assembled beneath the Temple roof,

Abiathar, whom I have already mentioned, the priest under the law,

Climbed the lofty steps.

The high priest then spoke these words to the assembled people:

“Ever since this most noble Temple was built

[Col. 1072A]

Through the zeal of the great king Solomon,

As you know, there have always remained within it

Girls of conspicuous appearance and tender age,

Daughters of noble families, of famous royal stock,

And likewise of priests and prophets,

Who have rightly remained renowned among all the people.

But, once they reached full maturity,

They were joined to husbands worthy of such women,

And from that time onward they pleased God even more.

Yet the virgin Mary hopes, by an unusual custom,

To be able to please him by rejecting men for the Lord’s name.

Now, since it is not certain that she can fulfill so great a vow,

It remains for us to entreat the Most High in worthy prayers,

So that he may perhaps make known to us his command,

Since it is lawful for her to be joined in a legal covenant.”

[Col. 1072B]

When the people had approved this plan,

All the priests first cast lots.

Among the twelve tribes of Israel,

The lot immediately marked which one of Judah’s descendants

Would be worthy of the distinguished girl.

When one man had thus been selected above all the others,

They ordered all the men of the same lineage,

Whom chance had kept unmarried,

To assemble on the following day at the second hour

And bring fresh rods in their right hands.

When all the pious men had been carefully selected,

The worthy elder Joseph arrived with them,

[85]

Carrying a bent rod beneath his finger.

But the supreme priest, joyfully raising the rods,

Offering a holocaust to the Lord of all,

Asked with poured-out prayers what should be done.

[Col. 1072C]

Immediately he received these divine instructions,

Which he was to carry out at the appointed time.

He was warned to place the rods that had been brought

In the famous inner sanctuary of the Temple,

And to command that, collectively, on the following day,

The royal descendants should come again

And each take up his own rod once more.

For he had been told as a clear sign

That the noble virgin should be entrusted to the man

from whose rod a dove would duly fly forth,

immediately seeking the lofty sky.

When at last the men held three thousand rods,

Gathered at the appointed time,

And none of them displayed the sign foretold to the people,

The high priest again offered venerable incense

[Col. 1072D]

And devoted himself to prayer with a pious heart.

As he prayed, a heavenly voice immediately said:

“The short rod of the just elder Joseph,

Which lies in the Temple and should not be disturbed by anyone,

Will alone deservedly fulfill the memorable sign.”

When these things were finished, a priestly voice sounded,

Ordering Joseph to come into the middle of the crowd.

He was lowly and without beauty of appearance,

And did not wish to stand among such distinguished companions.

Rather, he preferred to remain in the last place.

But as soon as he heard the voice calling him,

He proceeded fearfully, ordered to take hold of the rod.

At once a shining dove came forth from it

And soon was carried into the hidden heaven.

[Col. 1073A]

When this had happened, the entire people raised praises,

Giving thanks to the Most High with joyful heart.

[86] He had been pleased to show the righteous man by a new sign.

But Joseph, mindful of his advanced age,

Protesting that he had begotten sons,

Is said to have asked the priests with great embarrassment

Whether they would not give Mary, beautiful as she was,

Not to him personally, but as a bride to his son.

When they perhaps refused, he also declared that he had received a sign,

And that the holy girl ought not to be entrusted to anyone

Except to the man whom the Lord alone had made worthy.

He began to ask that other girls be sent with Mary

For the sake of consolation—

Girls who, like foster-sisters, companions, and peers in age,

Would know how to console her with the sweet comfort of conversation,

So that the virgin, without delay, would not become subject to shame

By being placed under an old husband.

The priests, acting as parents, immediately ordered this to be done.

But the elder had labored in vain by asking,

For the virgin had been dedicated not to him but to Christ.

When the priests yielded to the petitioner’s prayers,

Joseph took the girl into his keeping,

Together with, if I am not mistaken, five girls,

Whose names are believed to have been these:

Sephiphona, Zabel, Susanna, Rebecca, and Abigea.

They were assigned the work of the sacred Temple,

To be carefully completed:

purple with fine linen, linen with wool, and silk;

but the shining purple to be worked for holy Mary

Is believed to have been intended for the precious veil of the Lord’s Temple.

[Col. 1073C]

The girls present, inflamed with anger,

Spoke in this way as an insult:

“Is it established that you will henceforth be our queen,

Since the purple is believed to be woven for you alone,

Although you are not a little younger than we are?”

But she, as always, bore this patiently

And did not answer them with any word.

[87] Then her ever-faithful guardian,

The angel, descending from the star-bearing court,

Said: “Virgin, I beg you, do not let such words disturb you.

For these girls have certainly spoken like prophets:

With voices foretelling the future,

They have already declared what is to come.

For you alone will be a powerful eternal queen,

And illustrious mistress of the star-bearing heaven.”

After this she sat quietly in a private room,

Working the purple threads with blessed fingers.

The supreme angel Gabriel also stood before her,

Having descended from the starry court of heaven.

He addressed the virgin’s honor with friendly words,

Relating what had been foretold by all the prophets.

He declared that from her chaste womb

The Most High’s offspring, far older than the world,

Would deign to be born,

And he recounted the wondrous manner of the virgin birth.

Therefore it is not possible for our speech to set forth

The noble conversation, completed in a long discourse,

Of the virgin, the blessed eternal mother of Christ,

And the paranymph who told of the sacred birth of so great a child.

Nor is it necessary for us to sing in dactylic strains

The great sorrow and harsh grief of Joseph,

[Col. 1074A]

By which he had already been tormented in his heart in vain,

When he suddenly perceived that the girl was pregnant,

Nor how, saddened, he was consoled at night

And ordered to care for the inviolate virgin

And the child born from the stars for us.

All these things are shown by the Gospel books,

and finally exceed our fragile powers.

Passing over these matters, since they are known to all,

we shall speak only of those things from them

that are believed to have been said more dearly in the Temple.

When an edict was flying throughout the stable world,

Ordering that all subjects selected from everywhere

Be enrolled and declare themselves for the census of Caesar Augustus,

[88]

Joseph had proceeded to the city of Bethlehem,

With Mary, who was betrothed to him and pregnant.

[Col. 1074B]

When they were near the city’s famous walls,

the gracious young virgin saw, not with bodily eyes but with the eyes of her mind,

two little groups standing nearby:

one laughing, and the other weeping.

When she told this to the aged Joseph,

she heard him say:

“Keep yourself properly upon the beast beneath you alone,

and, I beg you, do not speak superfluous words.”

He had spoken, and she saw before her a youthful lord,

who explained to her the mystery of the peoples.

Speaking such hallowed words on behalf of the Virgin:

“Why do you say that Mary did not speak true words?”  
He was indignant that she alone should perceive the secret, for he rightly saw the Jewish people weeping, who would soon depart from the Lord with an evil heart, while joy was stirring among the Gentiles,

[Col. 1074C] because they would attain the great sacrament of faith.”

Having said this, he gently turned toward gracious Mary and told her that the time had come for her to give birth to Christ. She descended from the beast of burden, as she had been instructed, and entered a properly prepared cave beneath the earth, which had been wholly deprived of the light of the present world and which perpetual darkness had always possessed.

But as soon as the mother, about to give birth to everlasting light, entered it, the cave began to shine with flashing rays. From that time onward the heavenly light never failed there throughout the whole period during which the blessed mother remained inside.

Certainly, in the tranquil balance of the night, that same maiden gave birth there to her child, rejoicing in the divine one, venerable throughout all ages, whose name is Jesus, to whom be praise, glory, and power. He came to fulfill the ancient prophecies of the seers, who had foreknowledge that he would come to save the world; and, making peace, he reconciled the inhabitants of the earth with the citizens of heaven.

89. When he had been born from the sacred womb of the chaste virgin, an angelic host immediately surrounded him, praising the Maker of the world with bowed voices and praying to the child sent to us from heaven. But his mother, the ever-venerable Mary, suddenly laid his tender limbs in the august manger, wrapping Christ, the everlasting King, in swaddling clothes.

Meanwhile the devout Joseph, departing from her, soon brought two midwives with him, who were called by the names Zelomi and Salome. Zelomi alone entered, while Salome hesitated to touch the cave, which was filled with splendor.

Then, reverently examining the virgin birth, Zelomi, exclaiming and fully believing in so great a sign, said:

“What can this extraordinary birth of one who has not been married mean? Behold, a child has just been born of royal stock; plainly he shows that the mother is without a husband. And the virgin parent alone tenderly nurses her child at breasts rightly filled from heaven. There is no pain for the mother, nor any defilement for the child; rather, I believe that such things have occurred by divine ordinance.”

Salome, scorning these words spoken without falsehood, said that she would not believe what she had heard unless she herself proved it by touching the sacred Mary with her hand.

Therefore, entering, she began to extend her right hand, boldly attempting to touch chaste Mary with her palm. But such audacity brought a fitting punishment: the right hand that had attempted the deed was immediately paralyzed, and she was tormented by grievous pain.

Then Salome, crying out, deeply saddened in her bitter heart, lamented the sudden loss of the use of her right hand, reciting, in Jewish fashion, the merit she believed she had earned. Yet, trusting sufficiently in her feigned righteousness, she is said to have addressed these sorrowful words to the High-Throned One:

“Witness and consoler of all sufferings,

90 you know that I was diligent in observing your commandments, and that, for your sake, I was always abundantly generous to all the poor gathered from the ends of the earth. Whoever came mourning from me also departed more joyful; and now, in return for such merits, I suffer this grievous loss.”

Then a radiant young man appeared and said:

[Col. 1075C] “Touch only the swaddling clothes of the little child. Go quickly to those royal cradles, and he himself will restore you to better health.”

When she followed the instruction of the one who offered her consolation, touching merely the smallest thread of the cloth, she immediately felt herself healed throughout her entire body. In a melodious voice she gave thanks to the Lord, who had deigned to grant her such healing.

After everything had thus been set in order, the shepherds’ vision was fulfilled: the sign given to them concerning the little child to be found in the manger, the circumcision of Christ himself, and the fitting bestowal of his glorious name.

The Magi, royal astrologers, chosen from the rising of the sun and skilled in the law of the stars, came. Seeking the famous city of Salem, they also approached Herod, the king of steadfast heart, and questioned him about the recent birth of a king. They said that they had very recently seen a new star, which indicated that the King of the Jews had been born.

The impious king was troubled in his secret heart. He summoned the scribes quickly and learned from them that Christ was certainly to be born in the region of Bethlehem, in accordance with all the songs of the prophets. Then, deceitfully sending the Magi away, he ordered them to search for the newborn child and to report him to the king, whom he desired to have killed while pretending that he wished to worship him.

Following the star as it showed them the straight path, they quickly proceeded and entered the royal dwelling of the little child,

[Col. 1076A] 91 painted with no variety of color but suitably adorned in honor of so great a star. Bowing down, they planted kisses upon the child’s feet and prayed with humble supplications poured forth in a low voice. With three gifts they worshiped the heavenly King, signifying that he was both man and God and that he would die.

Soon afterward, warned in a dream during the night, they returned joyfully to their homeland by another route.

When these things had thus been accomplished, Herod, the worst of enemies, was brought to Rome by order of Augustus—either so that, as Roman law required, he might be cleared of the grave charge laid against him, or so that he might justly suffer the bitter penalty of death. For he was said to be guilty of treason against the imperial majesty; and rightly he was suspected of desiring, with plots prepared in a fox’s heart, to destroy the divine offspring of the heavenly King.

For I believe that it happened by divine providence that he was then ordered to go to Rome, so that, once he had been removed, all the prescriptions of the law might soon be fulfilled more completely in the child Christ.

For when forty days had been completed in due succession from the virgin birth, the Maker of heaven, now in the tender limbs of a human child, was presented in his own temple with the appointed small offering. He was received into the trembling arms of the righteous Simeon, and the Lord of the world was blessed with fitting praises by that aged and righteous Simeon, as well as by the famous Anna, whose words foretold the future.

[Col. 1076C] When these matters had also been completed in accordance with the requirements of the law, they immediately returned to their native city of Bethlehem.

For, after almost two months had passed, the perverse enemy, returning from his bitter exile, pondered sorrowfully what the Magi had said: that they had seen the beautiful star of the newborn King.

92 Recalling this, he questioned the leaders of the kingdom, asking whether the Magi had returned in good faith, or what information they had given him about the newborn Christ.

They immediately answered together in firm words that they did not know whether the Magi had perhaps returned, nor had they learned anything from them about the newborn King.

Enraged by these answers, the furious King Herod sent orders that all the infants then in the region of Bethlehem should immediately be killed,

[Col. 1076D] hoping that he could thereby destroy Christ while he was still alive.

But Joseph, the venerable man, warned in a dream, went to Egypt, leading with him through the trackless ways of the vast wilderness Jesus, together with his tender mother, while Christ ruled over the newly encountered earthly fear.

But heavenly piety performed these things according to its customary manner, so that the ancient darkness of Egypt might soon be illuminated and utterly driven away by its own light.

It happened, then, one day that holy Mary wished to rest with her child beside a cave. She had been laid down upon the ground, sufficiently weary, and was gently warming Jesus in her lap. Many dreadful dragons came forth from the cave, before which she herself had been resting.

[Col. 1077A] When Joseph saw them, he was astonished and began to cry out in great fear. But the child Jesus lovingly rose from his mother’s lap and stood there gently upon his sacred feet, facing the dragons, who were roaring with troubled minds.

They immediately fell forward, tamed, praying to the Maker of the world with silent gestures. Then Jesus himself, leaving by the paths of the vast wilderness, went before them and ordered them to follow him.

At this sight Joseph and the consecrated Mother of Christ became as lifeless, according to the custom of frail flesh; they were greatly terrified and feared that the child might be harmed.

93 But he, the observer of the mind and witness of the heart, turned toward the frightened ones and answered:

“Why do you handle only my infant limbs and do not in your minds acknowledge the everlasting power within me?

Although I am a little human being in human limbs, I am nevertheless an almighty man, endowed with the supreme divine power. It is fitting that all the beasts of the forest should be tamed before me, once their former rage has rightly been laid aside.”

After this, magnanimous lions together with leopards, and also creatures of every kind gathered from everywhere, came when they realized that the offspring of the Maker was present. They prayed in submissive voices to the tender child and rejoiced around the illustrious Mary.

When she, at last frightened by this extraordinary sign, looked upon it, Christ is said to have spoken to her more cheerfully:

“Do not let the novelty of this gracious sign move you carnally, O virgin, my powerful and beloved mother. These creatures have come solely for the sake of service, not because they wished—or could even wish—to harm you.”

At these words the anguish of her heart departed. The beasts, however, went ahead joyfully, showing the straight road through the wilderness.

Nor did any of them depart during the night. Joined faithfully to Joseph’s beasts, they forgot their rage and their natural fury, and peacefully grazed upon a little hay.

There was such harmony among them that, as once timid lambs joined their sides to wolves, so gentle lions lay peacefully with oxen. And not without reason: the true peace of heaven, which governs the boundless heavens, had established them in a covenant and changed their minds into a faithful disposition.

Afterward, exhausted by the rays of the summer heat, Mary rested beneath the shade of a beloved palm tree. Then, turning her bright eyes upward, she saw that the palm was laden with ripe fruit.

[Col. 1077D] 94 When she saw this, her tongue formed these words:

“I greatly desire this palm tree, so heavily laden, if it is possible for me to eat some of its fruit.”

The aged elder Joseph, righteous under the rule of the law, answered her words without gentleness:

“I am exceedingly amazed that you wish to say this when you see the branches, rising from a great trunk, touch the stars and strike the depth of heaven.

But I am thinking with the utmost concern only of whether I may at least obtain pure water, since there is not a drop of spring water in our wineskins.”

Thus the venerable hero spoke, as though he despaired that the present Christ could do everything, because he was concealed in bodily limbs.

But the child, lovingly reclining in the lap of his beloved mother, turned joyfully toward the palm and, exercising his fatherly authority, immediately said to it with serene countenance:

“Tree, bend your branches from the highest point of your crown, so that my mother may gather from you as much as she wishes.”

He spoke, and the mighty tree bent its nourishing branches before the feet of gracious Mary in obedience to his command. When it had been entirely stripped of its fruit, it remained bent down and did not rise to seek its former height; it awaited the command of Christ, which had been rightly proved.

Then he himself said: “Now rise suddenly, palm tree, so that afterward you may be a companion among my trees, which stand planted in the groves of paradise. Draw immediately from your root the hidden waters of a little spring, flowing in a sweet stream.”

Everything was quickly fulfilled according to his word.

The companions of the Child, examining the fresh spring, offered sweet thanks with rejoicing hearts and quenched their sad thirst with the newly flowing water.

95 When they were about to depart through the regions of the vast wilderness, Jesus spoke thus to the palm tree itself:

“Palm tree, by my command I order you: let an angel descend from heaven from on high, take a branch from the summit of your crown, and immediately plant this very branch in paradise. In return I now grant you such great glory that afterward you shall be called the palm of the supreme triumph; and whoever wins a famous battle shall be told of the victor: ‘You have come to the palm of the great triumph.’”

When he had spoken these words, an angel came down from the stars, took a branch, and carried it upward. At the sight of this, all who were present were astonished and, trembling, fell prostrate upon the ground.

Jesus immediately consoled them, saying:

“Certainly you need have no fear. I ordered this branch to be carried through the stars, so that it might soon be planted as a delight in the great garden. And just as here in the wilderness it fulfilled my commands by satisfying us with great abundance, so there may it provide the holy with everlasting sweetness.”

[Col. 1078D] After such great signs had now been repeatedly seen, Joseph, reflecting upon the everlasting power of the Child, spoke these words in a low murmur:

“Behold, the excessive heat is cruelly scorching our limbs. Now, if it pleases you, whose everlasting kingdom endures, command us to travel by the paths across the vast sea, with cities placed nearby, so that, once a sure resting place has been granted to us, it may enable us to cover such a great distance more quickly.”

Jesus, glorious in divine power, answered him:

“For I shall suddenly shorten the long road through my own power, and what could scarcely be traversed in thirty days I shall cause to be covered within the space of one day.”

At these words they soon saw Sonites, the great Egyptian city, lofty with its famous walls.

[Col. 1079A] Entering it, they approached the threshold of a temple in which the pagan people were accustomed, in their perverse custom, to place and worship their foolish false gods.

But as soon as holy Mary entered with the Child, all the images of the false gods fell suddenly and together face downward to the ground, now recognizing that the everlasting King had come and that the true God, adorned with great power, was present.

Now what had once been spoken in verse by a prophetic singer was fulfilled:

“Behold, the Lord will soon come upon a light cloud, before whose holy face all the images of Egypt must surely be shaken.”

After these things had been recited to Affrodosius, the very powerful ruler of the city, he hurried there with many companions.

When the impious priests of the temple perceived this, they hoped soon to destroy with various punishments those who had inflicted such losses upon their foolish gods.

But when he saw the beautiful images scattered everywhere upon the ground, his heart was suddenly kindled by heavenly love and by sacred faith. His mind was changed, and he stopped and joyfully said to his friends:

“Behold, plainly the Lord who is powerful above all is present. Perhaps our gods themselves, with silent murmuring, rightly testify that he alone is the true God.

It remains for us, prostrate in the manner of their own fallen gods, to worship the everlasting King with devoted minds, remembering what he did to King Pharaoh, who rejected his sacred commandments more than was right, lest he thrust us into the dark pit of death.”

He spoke, and, prostrating his entire body upon the ground, he rolled himself before the feet of holy Mary, praying continually in a faithful voice for the Child’s favor, whom the rejoicing mother carried lovingly in her lap.

97 O Christ, praiseworthy glory of your power! O wondrous and ever-renewed transformation wrought by your sacred right hand! You are able, by a silent nod, to dispose all things.

Who, then, could worthily marvel at the great gifts of your mercy, or proclaim them with fitting praise, only-begotten Son of God, like your supreme Father?

For our sake you performed such astonishing deeds. You, born without beginning from the heavenly Father, by the Father’s command filled the womb of your mother, taking from her a bodily form in due time.

You who can guide the world by your own hand did not refuse to be bound in humble swaddling clothes. You who sit upon a starry throne above the heavens bent low, confined in a little manger.

You who give names to the many stars, and who alone can rightly number the drops of rain and the sands of the sea in a certain reckoning, patiently kept silent like a frail child

[Col. 1080B] at the time when you tenderly suckled virgin breasts.

Moreover, you fled from Herod, a king without any fear, solely out of mercy, so that you might compassionately demonstrate the true form of your flesh.

Then, without delay, you caused the stony hearts of the unconquered pagans to soften and to perceive your solid kingdom enduring throughout the ages, so that, warned by divine signs, they might know you to be the one whom you made the ages by your word alone and whom the songs of all the prophets proclaimed.

Let glory remain for all ages to your Father, and eternal praise to him from all created things, for he did not spare you, his beloved Son. And to you, Christ, be perpetual honor, victory, and power, you who redeem the perishing world by the shedding of your blood,

[Col. 1080C] 98 together with the Holy Spirit, throughout all the ages of the world, through whom every heavenly grace is granted.

What gifts can I now repay to the Maker for all that he himself has worthily rendered to me, who, in his customary mercy, treated me, an unworthy servant, with kindness? Although I am weak, he made me able to offer thanks.

Above all, I ask that the angelic hosts of heaven never cease diligently praising the true God with me.

[Col. 1079]

[THE HISTORY OF THE ASCENSION OF THE LORD]

ARGUMENT OF THE HISTORY OF THE ASCENSION OF THE LORD

After the Savior of the world, Christ Jesus, had fulfilled by all his miracles, his Passion, and his most bitter death everything that the holy prophets had foretold about him—as is found in the Evangelists and in Luke’s Acts of the Apostles—he rose from the dead and was seen for many days among the disciples, teaching them. Finally, summoned to the Father, he called the disciples together and, amid the greatest joy, ascended into the heavens by the Father’s command, accompanied by the whole company of the holy Fathers and the choir of angels. Among them David struck his harp before the Savior, as he entered heaven in triumph.

HISTORY OF THE ASCENSION OF THE LORD. John the bishop translated this narrative from Greek into Latin.

[Col. 1079]

[Col. 1079C] After Christ, clothed in a bodily veil, had completed the sacred and venerable span of time,

[Col. 1080C] which he graciously spent with earthly little human beings, he alone who could live without any stain,

in order to demonstrate through himself the joys of everlasting life, once disastrously lost, and, after his triumphant, holy, and gracious death, which he patiently endured for our sake,

while, as victor, he shattered by a great struggle the fiercest weapons of the enemy of the human race,

99 and freely paid in full the price of his own blood, laying down his beloved life upon the cross,

and after the glorious accomplishment of his rising again, with forty days of time having passed,

during which he repeatedly appeared to his beloved disciples, he showed that the one who had been slain by death was truly he himself, and that he could not be held by the tight bonds of death, he who alone had been without the stains of Adam’s sin,

[Col. 1081B] finally, appearing again to those same beloved friends on the lofty summit of the Mount of Olives, he stood there, soon to ascend to the starry court, and addressed his ministers with these words:

“As the Father promised me, his beloved one, to the world, so I send you, my beloved friends.

But go quickly into all the nations and teach them the commandments of everlasting life. Let them believe and cleanse themselves swiftly in the sacred water, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and likewise of the gracious Spirit, so that they may lay aside the sins of their former impurity.

By my power drive away various diseases. By your authority also compel fierce robbers to leave the cavern of the heart they possess, while preserving the sweetest love of the mind for those whom they always try to harm with bitter hatred.

From this all nations can clearly know that you are truly my beloved disciples, if you love your enemies with pure hearts.

Remain mindful to the very end of all that I suffered for your sake, though without cause.

Can the cherubim not see my face in the Father’s kingdom, such as it now shines?

But the Jews spurned it with their filthy spittle and maliciously struck my jaws with slaps. They fixed my hands with bloody nails to the wood,

100 hands with which I beautifully fashioned the first man from clay and with which I finally stretched out the lofty heavens.

For if I look upon the earth, it trembles in fear, nor is it able to convey the terror of the Mighty One.

And while they savagely went before me and shook their heads, the wicked Jews mocked me.

Although I patiently endured these things at the hands of the condemned, I did not wish to destroy them with a just vengeance. Rather, while freely suffering death upon the wood of the cross, I prayed more mercifully to the almighty Father to forgive them immediately for such great crimes. By this example I taught what must be done, so that my heavenly doctrine might become true and trustworthy, and so that no one might dare to say with deceitful words:

‘Behold, he himself refused to suffer this, yet he persuaded us to endure it; and what he did not do, he told us that we must do.’

I willingly endured the dangers of death first, sorrowfully, like a true shepherd faithful in the goodness of his heart, laying down my beloved life for my own sheep.

I also fulfilled, with abundant faithful mercy, everything that the earlier prophets said about me.

And now I ascend, surrounded by the Father’s power, victorious to the supreme Father, enthroned above the heavens.

But I ask that the hearts of you faithful ones not be troubled, for I shall not leave you as abandoned orphans in the world. Rather, I shall soon send you the gracious gift of the Holy Spirit, who will teach you the truth inwardly.

Moreover, I myself remain with you all to the very end, throughout all the ages of the world.”

When he had said these things, he finally turned and spoke in a gentle voice to his own mother, Mary:

“Do not grieve, I ask you, chaste maiden, when you see me ascending into the lofty heavens. For I do not leave you, the illustrious lamp of the world,

101 nor, as I depart, do I abandon my holy temple. Nor do I leave behind the incorruptible crown of life.

I have found you alone among all women to be chaste and worthy to give birth to my sacred body.

Certainly, when I order you to depart from the world, I shall send to you not only the hosts of heaven’s inhabitants; I myself shall come and take up your blessed soul, far more radiant than the shining sun, and, gently escorted by angelic hymns, I shall soon place it reverently in the starry court.

But for now I command John to remain faithfully with you, he who shines richly with the jewels of virginity, so that your illustrious life may shine forth more brightly, continually surrounded by the chaste services of virginity.”

Immediately, as he spoke these words, an angelic host surrounded him, praising him with sweet-sounding hymns, and soon he was suddenly covered by a serene cloud.

There the ranks of the ancient prophets also gathered. Among them David stood in the midst, a king skilled in singing, and, playing his harp, he proclaimed in these words that the Son had sought the throne of his heavenly Father:

“Exalt the mighty God above the high heavens, and let your glory be over the whole earth.”

Addressing the angelic hosts, he urged them:

“Exalt our God with melodious song, praying repeatedly upon his holy mountain. This God, the Lord, is our God, for he is holy.”

And Christ Jesus, returning with a smiling face, said again to his beloved disciples:

“Peace be with you, brothers, ever truly faithful to me, you who have done my will and will continue to do it. Behold, I finally give you my abiding peace, and I leave that peace with you forever.”

He said this, and, lifted up immediately by his own power, ascended above the heavens, victorious over cruel death,

102 surrounded by the service of a radiant cloud.

When the teaching people of faith looked up at him with fixed eyes, as the gates of heaven were opened and he went upward, while all the stars served him, two men, having descended from the starry realm, stood beside them clothed in white garments. They spoke to them in thoroughly angelic words:

[Col. 1083A] “Men of Galilee, I ask you, why do you stand gazing with astonished faces and uplifted eyes?

This same Jesus, taken up while you marvel, who has ascended beyond the high heavens, will come as Judge in the form in which he goes into heaven.”

When David saw Christ lifted above the heavens, he struck his harp, filled with divine praise, and sang this fitting song of great joy:

“God has ascended in great rejoicing above the stars; the Lord has mounted amid the blast of the sacred trumpet.”

After this, the voice of the Father thundered from his lofty throne, saying to the Son in divine speech:

“You are truly my beloved and only Son, in whom I have always rightly been greatly pleased.

You are without beginning, the true Word of the Father, and alone my true Wisdom from heaven.

But now, victorious, rest at my right hand, rejoicing; I shall rightly place all your enemies beneath your holy feet as a footstool throughout the ages.”

After Christ had brought human nature, now restored from the grave, into the lofty throne of the Father, all the angelic hosts praised him with submissive voices: him who would reign forever, who conquered death by dying and redeemed the world, so that he might make his servants reign throughout the ages.

Whoever reads these things, let him say with a merciful heart:

“Pious King, spare and have mercy upon wretched Hrosvitha, and cause her to persevere in the heavenly praises, she who has sung your wondrous deeds in praise.”

[Col. 1083]

[THE PASSION OF SAINT GANGULF]

103 ARGUMENT OF THE GANGULF

Gangulf, born of the noble family and blood of the Burgundian kings and initiated into the Christian religion, purchased from a certain poor rustic a little garden with a most delightful spring, whose charm Hrosvitha describes most beautifully. Whenever he was free from military service and public affairs, he was accustomed to withdraw to this garden for the sake of prayer and the relaxation of his spirit; his household greatly disliked this practice.

It happened, therefore, that the spring dried up. But when he fixed his staff in the earth, he restored it with a very abundant flow, so that its water drove away every kind of disease from those who drank or bathed in it.

At length he married a woman who was incontinent and unchaste, and who had given herself over to the unrestrained lust of her attendants. When this became known to the holy man Gangulf, he rebuked her for her incontinence. She then plotted against Gangulf through her attendants; he was killed by them and buried in a place called Nil terra, where he became famous for miracles.

When this was reported to his wife, Ganea, she denied the truth of his miracles and regarded them as no different from the rumbling of her own belly. Therefore, as punishment for her faithlessness, her belly rumbled continuously for as long as she lived.

PREFACE TO GANGULF

[Col. 1083B] O gracious Maker of light, Fashioner of the world and of all things,

you who paint the heavens with varied stars,

you alone rule and reign in the starry court, holding all things in your light and governing them by your command.

You who through your own Son made the ages and the threefold structure of things from nothing,

and who, after rightly creating the first man from earth, poured the life-giving breath of your divine mouth into him, so that the work of your own finger might be established,

deign to flood the heart of your servant, Hrosvitha, with the dew of your gracious gift,

104 so that in polished verse I may be able to compose the pious deeds of the holy Gangulf, the outstanding martyr,

and always praise your blessed name. After the battles, you grant your servants fitting rewards for the slight wound of their mortal life, commanding them to live in the light-filled kingdom.

THE PASSION OF SAINT GANGULF THE MARTYR

[Col. 1083]

[Col. 1083C] In the time when Pippin ruled the eastern kingdom

and held the royal scepter of the Franks for the people,

and rightly governed the kingdoms of Burgundy with magnificent authority, subduing his subjects properly beneath his reins,

a famous young man was raised in those regions, mighty in arms and remarkable in body,

named Gangulf, handsome in the excellence of his character, beloved and agreeable to all.

They say that he was born from royal stock and was royal in his outstanding conduct.

Hope for him depended upon his mother’s womb: upon him who created all things from nothing by his word.

Yet he did not consider himself worthy of so great a lineage, but surpassed the distinction of his family by his merits.

For his illustrious mother, blessed by such offspring, brought this child forth into the light of the world. Soon he was washed in baptism from the ancient sins that our first parents had acquired.

Anointed with chrism and marked with the sign upon his forehead, he was admitted among the shining children of the Church. Then, while he still cried in his milk-fed body in the cradle, he was nourished on the doctrine of the full and threefold faith.

As often as he suckled milk, so often did he receive the sacred teaching of faith, suspended at his mother’s two breasts.

[Col. 1084C] While he lived on such nourishment, scarcely carried along by the flood of milk, he began to burn with a weighty intellect. While still in his tender limbs he meditated upon the gray hairs of old age, and he was often occupied with sacred studies.

105 Soon, while still beardless but flourishing in complete virtue, the favor of Pippin, the gracious prince, ordered him, not undeservedly, to be presented at the royal court, honoring such a young man ardently in his heart.

Although the king’s piety, entirely just though it was, enriched him with so glorious a gift, so that from his earliest years he was a royal governor, he was nevertheless not raised up by swelling pride.

Rather, with humble heart he despised such honors, sighing for the gifts of the heavenly court.

For the wealth inherited from his father had come to him in great abundance, and he distributed it to the poor with such devotion as though he perceived Christ himself smiling with a gracious face among the wretched needy.

Often, following the example of Job and of the blessed man, he himself became a hand to the maimed, a foot to the gout-afflicted, and a careful eye to the blind, giving all peoples a noble example.

Nor did he labor less in human affairs, making himself equal to the highest lords.

For if the ancient tale, whether falsely reported or not, had not deceived us with invented and doubtful matters, this saint whom my hand has now begun to portray was accustomed to follow the path of four-footed animals.

He diligently wearied his handsome limbs in hunting, submitting to the command of his beloved lord. His weapon never knew how to yield defeated before the enemy, when the armed bands had been arranged.

He always carried away his triumph from the enemy, safe through heavenly divine assistance.

Certainly, my Muses are not able, by composing dactylic verses, to weave into measured song how many signs the King of kings varied in this beloved man, according to his supreme goodness.

Nevertheless, although my speech is uncultivated, I shall bark out one deed among the many famous and varied ones.

106 As the event itself proves, he led the troops, marching ahead to capture a people sufficiently swollen with the pride of war. He soon emerged victorious from his customary battle, without his purple blood being shed.

After the hostile peoples had been brought under his own law and authority, he recorded the tribute and returned once peace had been granted.

It happened that, while leading the way, he traveled near the enclosed property of a certain poor man. There, hidden from view, was a little garden painted with fresh flowers and covered with the foliage and branches of many plants.

A little spring also flowed there, clear with glasslike brightness, watering the fields with a murmuring stream.

When the illustrious lord directed his eyes there, surveying the clear bubbling of the little spring, captivated for a while by the beauty of the cold water, he stopped and delayed his journey for a pleasant brief interval.

He sent a servant and asked that the owner of the flower-bearing place come to him.

The man immediately fulfilled the commander’s order and quickly emerged from the place where he had been instructed to go.

When the commander himself saw him approaching, he immediately addressed him in gentle conversation. Humbly, with all the sweetness of his mind, he formed these words with his tongue:

“Dear friend, I ask you to be generous to my request and sell me this pure little spring, which, clear in its glasslike and sweetly murmuring waters, runs before these fields and waters them—and yours as well.

In return I shall immediately pour out for you a substantial weight of tested silver.”

But when the joyful promise, giving forth its ringing sound, passed into the ears of the insignificant person, his face rejoiced and all the veins began to quiver, veins that had lain hidden in the secret place of his heart.

[Col. 1086B] Then the wretched man burst into these words, knowing that his doubtful hope exceeded what he could have believed:

107 “O glory of our land, second to none in compassion, whom the eastern people honor in mind and faith, what worthy thing can my little tongue say to you?

Is not our welfare placed in your hands? And whatever you decree by word that I must do, although it may be sufficiently difficult and burdensome, nevertheless it is right for me to obey you, blessed lord, as I have long obeyed the supreme lord.

If it pleases you to make me, an old farmer, depart from here, I do not resist but follow your commands.”

He said this and restrained his words between pressed lips; after his many words, his tongue said nothing further.

The royal man, in his goodness, received these words from the speaker and quickly fulfilled his promise to the poor man, assigning him one hundred solidi.

When he had completed this, he departed swiftly on his return, intent upon making his way toward his neglected homeland.
