Then those who did not know the venerable sign, which the Most High had formerly destined to perform, began in silent whispers to slander the commander and to despise his work of piety as though it were a crime.

But believe me: the rustic’s pious deception had not remained hidden; soon the secret words spoken to him were to be revealed.

The man who gave voice with his eloquent tongue then addressed his companions in these words:

“Why, dear companions, do you wish to rebuke me with words that are excessively insulting?

You say that I have acted foolishly by giving money to an unknown and foreign man, that I am deprived of such a valuable little garden and grieve over it, even though I have properly sold the little spring.

As though wealth were not my own right hand, which is graciously generous if I give gold for small gifts.

It is not fitting that the reason for the price assigned to the property be disclosed to you in these words.

108 Rather, it is better to settle your agitated minds, and I ask you to desist from such speech. Instead, trust me, a man who understands the matter, and let the empty winds and wandering airs have their say.

Then let us quickly return to the little garden that has now been left behind and see whether the spring’s channel is clear as usual, murmuring among the many-colored flowers with its rippling stream over the slippery ground.

Then it will be evident that the rustic has withdrawn himself from those profits, leaving me completely deprived of both.”

After he had said this, one of them hurried back, covering such a great distance. Exhausted, he reached the previously mentioned field, where the water had been sold to the pious master.

Yet, although curious, he did not immediately touch with his feet the threshold of the flower-bearing little garden. Instead, he positioned himself beside tangled paliurus-thorns, shaggy brambles, and thistles, by which the whole surface of the uncultivated ground was covered. He did not shrink from approaching the thorny growth.

Eagerly joining his eyes to the prescribed enclosure, he began to inspect the little stream of glass-clear water.

But, although he brought his eyes close, he peered in vain.

Because the fountain had completely ceased and was absent from that place.

Then, turning over in his mind the narrow junctions, he clearly saw that he could not discern the little enclosure; and, proceeding slowly, stiffly, with neck held proudly, he turned his steps into the small court, hoping that beneath the pleasant leaves some little stream might perhaps be hidden, covered by the many-colored crowns of the flowers.

When he sought the pool and rejected the bottom because of thirst—the bottom that had once luxuriated in abundant waters—he lay stretched upon the ground, mocked by empty hope, and began to lick the sandy places, trying to see whether he could lap up a small drop; but he could not even moisten his parched tongue.

[Col. 1087C] 109 At last he perceived the pious miracles of Gangolf’s shrine, and grieved that he had been unwilling to believe in the saint’s holy merits.

After this, when he had returned and rejoined his companions, he saw a cloud conspicuous in the air, flying near the beloved servant of Christ’s head, finally resembling a small white cloak. Fixing his eyes upon it, he began to explain in words the sudden failure of the fountain that he had learned of, and urged his companions to lay aside their doubt and now become convinced of the saint’s merits.

While they were speaking such words among their friends, they arrived at the walls that had been built around their lord’s own little shrine, with various trees spread around it. Here Christ’s beloved friend directed his steps, gladly entering the splendid little court; carrying the staff in his outstretched hand, he fixed it in the ground and immediately went into the house.

There countless servants were properly competing with one another, energetically attending to various duties. They themselves placed tables laden with food, finally asking to be allowed to relieve their late hunger. But first he ordered the weakened crowd to come forward, the crowd that his table was accustomed often to feed; and, when that crowd itself had been fully satisfied by his own hands, he finally applied himself to the table that had been set.

The Franks, scattered throughout the house, reclined together, tasting the gifts of Bacchic joy. Meanwhile the eastern star was urging sleep, and approaching night threatened black darkness. Friendly rest suddenly followed the meal, creeping through their limbs because of the drunkenness.

The pious leader began to pass the sleepless night, praying to his Lord in an attentive voice. After night, conquered and dispersed when the darkness was torn apart, had withdrawn, and the rising light had encircled the heavenly region, 110 the servants came, chosen from among the recruits, carrying their dear lord’s little shoes. They knocked at the hall, which had been closed because of the night’s lateness, asking that the entrance now be opened.

But the leader remained silent for a little while and pretended to be asleep. Then, as though awakening from heavy sleep, he ordered the inner bars to be released by the guard and the dining hall to be opened to the soldiers.

[Col. 1088B] After these men had been admitted, he reached out his white hands for water, but by the Lord’s command, the heavenly-throned one, water was lacking.

Then the man, secure and blessed by Christ’s favor, quickly sent one of the outstanding servants to bring him the staff that he had mentioned, which he had fixed late in the small court. The servant, running swiftly and leaping across the grassy fields, cast his slippery, wandering eyes about, searching for the staff buried in the earth at that time. When he found it, he seized it with his outstretched fingers and pulled it from the ground, leaving a small hollow behind, so that afterward it might become a visible sign.

As soon as this had been done, the little cloud that had previously flown empty through the air fell down. Split open at that very spot, it poured out the swelling waves of the fountain mentioned above, and fixed in place the watery veins of the spring, where the tiny staff had been planted.

But the boy was astonished and sent his voice through the air, urging the soldiers to run more quickly. He told them of the joy of the new sign, which the king of the angelic host had granted. At once all of them, shaken by so great a sign, raised their astonished faces toward heaven, and, with all their palms spread toward the stars, they sang little songs of praise to God.

Behold, one of the palace servants took a basin in his hands and quickly filled it with the conspicuous water. 111 With joyful face he went to the holy Gangolf, to tell him of the extraordinary sign.

[Col. 1088D] Standing before so great a man with serene countenance, he addressed him with these words from his excellent mouth:

“Joyfully, and as you deserve, receive these very rare gifts, which the small earth did not bestow upon you, but the King of heaven himself, from the highest summit of heaven, sent through the wondrous service of a cloud.

“Thus it is clear that we now share great joy, because you have been granted so glorious a distinction.”

At once, in contrast, the pious leader spoke with serene face and returned this answer:

“It is not fitting for us to attribute these merits sufficiently to ourselves, since I have never earned anything so very small. It remains for us instead to sing manifold thanks to Christ, who is always present to his own servants.”

He spoke, and, washed, bathed himself in the renewed fountain as usual, and sang this hymn to the heavenly Lord:

“O ever-present piety, the one hope of our life,

O greatest power of divine grace!

Who could equal, in worthy songs, the work of the omnipotent Maker, God,

who makes new things correspond to former signs,

who rules the ages through his own Son?

“These are the miracles of your own power, Christ, who once ordered sweet milk to flow for the Jewish people from a rock, and made the bitter salt-water sufficiently sweet.

“Therefore, merciful Thunderer, mindful of your power, by which you justly rule the threefold structure of the universe, you have now wished to entrust this judgment to our lands—a noble testimony of great glory—so that those who dwell throughout the smooth-rolling world may often learn that you alone are, and have always been, God.

“Grant this also now, Lord Jesus, in answer to prayer: let this liquid wash away various illnesses, 112 so that everyone who feels himself saved and strong may praise you with sweet-sounding voices.”

He said this, and healing followed the voice that spoke; the water became health-giving. Praise be to you, Lord.

Afterward, as the machinery of the world rapidly flew onward, Fame, the herald of the sign and of so pleasing a marvel, went forth. It urged not only the farmers of the surrounding region, who had been granted the gift of the golden-flowing water, but also the feeble pilgrims gathered from far away and from every direction, to hasten and receive the gifts of the medicine without payment, merely by tasting a little of the fountain.

You might often see an uncultivated crowd lying prostrate, rolling their weakened limbs along the bank, so that you could believe those afflicted with various diseases to be feeble members of the Jewish people who once, scattered in the porticoes of Solomon beside the pool of Bethesda, competed for the water when the heavenly physician stirred the pool, so that the first person might wash away his various illnesses. They had obtained this remarkable privilege under such a law that, as soon as the one who descended afterward entered it, he would cast off his disgrace—while many, hanging on in the hope of life, eagerly begged that the physician, suddenly falling from the heavenly vault, might quickly disturb the little pool even with his foot.

In no other way did these people, greedy for health, desire to touch even the smallest drop of the fountain. At the first taste, their former health restored, they struck the stars with sweet-sounding songs, returning thanks to Christ for so great a gift, because through the merits of the saint he had given the afflicted a welcome benefit.

They likewise raised the worthy man in praise above the heavens, since they held him to be the cause of such blessings. If there were time to extend praises equal to his merits, and to recount the excellent character of so great a little leader—

113 Before the day reaches its appointed end, night is veiled by the Olympian garment, before our reasoning can attain its goal.

But leaving these matters to be treated by learned poets, let us paint what we have begun with a fragile reed.

Certainly, while the people of the Franks rejoiced in the East at the illustrious merits and goodness of their leader, the venerable elders, through the great petitions of the nobles, sought to flatter this beloved friend of Christ and the entire glory of the nation. They wished him to join to himself, by the lawful bond of customary marriage, a maiden worthy of him, so that the renowned royal offspring of the race might not come to an end through the extinction of descendants.

At last, moved by these admonitions and by the gentle counsel of the fathers, Gangolf, the venerable leader, joined to himself a companion conspicuous for her own rank, royal by birth and radiant in appearance. He ordered her always to lead a pure life, governed by chaste conduct and pursuits.

[Col. 1090B] Alas, however, the greedy, crafty, bitter serpent—the wife’s undisciplined mind! For, unhappy woman, Gangolf’s bold cleric was burning with an excessive desire for his own mistress. Overcome by the serpent’s bitter deceit, she quickly grew inflamed toward crime, clinging to the servant in the secret heat of her heart and rejecting her lawful lord for the sake of the servant.

Then the hostile deceiver scratched out the crimes that had been devised by his own deceit and exposed them. Unable to endure delay, he cast them into the empty air, finally spreading his delight abroad.

When this grievous matter had been made known to the common people, to all the native inhabitants of the Frankish nation, the report, fashioned by the striking of tongues, reached the subtle ears of Saint Gangolf, the beneficent leader, entering through narrow passages as a message of no little sorrow.

114 The most worthy hero groaned at so sad a crime and was struck by a great arrow of grief. Within the narrow chamber of his heart he revolved two opposing considerations, grieving bitterly over them: first, vengeance to be prepared under the law of punishment for the terrible crime of so great an offense; but afterward, pardon to be bestowed according to his customary mercy. Thus he grieved for a time, deeply uncertain.

At last, however, he piously imposed a deserved punishment. He did not wish to publicize the crime any further, but was concerned only to prevent the wretched woman from committing the crime again and from thereafter living recklessly in wrongdoing.

While he was easing his pious mind amid these cares, it happened that he ran into his own little court, opposite the entrance of the fountain previously sent to him through the wondrous service of a cloud from heaven. There, while Gangolf himself stood blessed, his wanton wife suddenly appeared.

He immediately addressed her in peaceful words, dictating the following with a sufficiently solemn mouth:

“I have often learned of the bad reputation attached to you: that you have been shamefully corrupted in your own marriage bed. But I delay treating you publicly with pity until I perhaps learn that you were not guilty.

“I do not order a great crowd to assemble at once, summoned from every side by weeping counsel, so that a knowledgeable court may weigh by subtle judgment the cause and the punishment deserved for so terrible a crime.

“Instead, I shall advise you merely to dip your right hand into the cold water of the present fountain. If no harm immediately comes to you, then no further judgment is necessary.”

Then she, trusting more than was right in her proud heart, while the demon strengthened her hardness, finally placed her bared palm into the water, hoping that no harm could happen to her.

115 But amid the icy waves she learned what the exalted right hand of our God could do. Certainly, though bold, she had been burning in the damp sands; she was fiercely burned by watery flames, and she who had disdainfully refused to yield to peaceful words was compelled to yield to eternal justice.

“O Christ, whose change is ever easily brought about in us!

“O equal power of God, the just judge!”

For the skin of her arm, dipped in the water, was burned away—she who had boastfully pretended sorrow. Immediately, when she withdrew her palm, she bore the raw evidence of the crime she had denied.

When these matters had thus been laid bare, the conscience aware of its deceit trembled, and there was no longer hope of pardon in this life. She was certain only that she must die and be cleansed of her corruption by the swift imposition of death’s punishment.

But the lord Gangolf, an excellent ruler and judge, softened the deserved anger of his mind. He ordered the guilty cleric to be expelled immediately from his homeland and sent away, so that the criminal might mourn his evils there to the very end.

He was expelled from his homeland and given into exile. Gangolf granted the miserable woman pardon out of compassion, but thereafter did not place her in his own marriage bed.

After this, as the fame of blessed Gangolf grew—the fame that praised his beneficent life—the cunning deceiver and captor of men guilty of wrongdoing, stirring up the old bile of envy, tried by every fraud of ancient craft to empty his good reputation, lest the people, persuaded by so great an example, bow their proud necks before the Lord.

For a long time he labored with malicious deceit, but he could not harm the famous little leader, because the power of love for that great man grew much stronger in the hearts of the people as the days passed.

116 At last the deceiver surrounded with the weapons of deceit the wretched man whom Gangolf had driven from his homeland because of his crime; he bade him burn with thirst for noble blood and spare his own lord no longer.

Thus suddenly drenched in gall, the miserable man burned for the death of the just and pious man. Returning to Ganea with equal malicious ferocity, he revealed to her everything that he had devised.

She, alas, subject to his wicked wishes, desired the crime to be committed at once. Secretly she laid impious ambushes for the just man, utterly forgetful of the former pardon by which she had duly been released from the punishment prepared for her; nor did she permit her guilty life to escape death.

Still more ungratefully she consented to her wicked companion, and burned with a slavish flame. When night, conscious of the deceit, covered heaven with darkness, the condemned she-wolf perceived that the time had come when they could wickedly destroy holy Gangolf, and announced this to the perverse arms-bearer.

With drawn sword he cut through the consecrated thigh of Saint Gangolf, the outstanding martyr. He abandoned his homeland, fleeing with his wife, carried away by unrestrained love for his mistress.

But just as unlawful love had known no restraint, so vengeance knew no delay: suddenly, by heaven’s act, he poured out the entrails that had long been swollen with the joy of his deed.

Thus the wretch, struck down by the exalted avenging right hand, lost Ganea, bought at the cost of his life.

For the holy martyr, wounded by a secret blow, while he drank the swift taste of death and breathed his last in his final hours, had an angelic assembly standing close by. With their voice they summoned the steadfast witness to lay down his frail earthen body, woven from weak veins,

117 and, sweetly gladdened by angelic hymns, immediately to take the starry paths of heaven.

Quickly breathing out his soul, the martyr, well washed in the radiant purple blood of the Lamb, was lifted from the air and carried through the serene stars. He was brought to the gate of heaven and set before the Lord.

There, it is said, he soon received from Christ a rare laurel crown, and in his hands the palm branch of everlasting reward. He was joined to a shining robe, among the white ranks held in the joyful hall of heaven because of his wound.

Meanwhile the splendid funeral procession was prepared, and the rites adorned the lifeless body. Everyone lamented the death of so great a patron, especially his wretched servants.

A rich place was chosen for the venerable tomb, which the elders of former times are said to have called Nil. There they buried the limbs of blessed Gangolf, scattering the sacred ashes with tears.

Afterward they often visited the holy bones, seeking a sure protection. The bodies of nobles were also laid prostrate before the sacred tomb for various needs of unstable life.

Even the one who bears the scepter, prostrate upon the marble, kissed it and drank kisses from the marble tomb, reflecting upon the gift, hope, and words by which, through the merits of the blessed martyr, Christ might be propitious to him.

What can I say of the crowd thrown down before the threshold of the church, or how can I speak of its countless vows? No mind can comprehend these things, nor can any letters express them.

But, on the other hand, the most prosperous witness himself grants such gifts of sweetness that everyone immediately feels all things to be favorable, for the sake of which they earnestly implore the outstanding witness.

Here, when sight has happily been restored to the blind, a man soon drinks in the bright flashes with his eyes; 118 ears long closed are opened to voices, and movement is returned to powerless feet. Here, too, illness is driven from various sufferers, as their weakened limbs are finally cleansed.

I cannot adequately tell of the splendid gifts that this excellent people harvest. Not only are those who have the good fortune to be fellow citizens of so great a man refreshed by love for their beloved patron; those who happen to dwell in distant lands likewise experience the martyr’s ready aid.

Hence the land of Nil boasts itself fortunate throughout the world, since it cherishes the sacred bones in its gentle embrace.

Finally, since I began briefly to touch upon the excellent deeds of the holy martyr Gangolf, it remains for me also to recount in a slight narrative the wretched woman, Ganea, unworthy of his marriage, who gave the sign that rightly condemned her to the abyss, in keeping with her own deserts.

Certainly, when the very joyful fame of the victorious witness was already striking the stars of the lofty heavens and, steadfast, was traversing the whole circumference of the world, spreading the joys of so great a glory, a certain joyful and devoted little man was running from the tomb, adorned with various signs.

He encountered the woman mentioned above and stopped, looking at her with astonished eyes. He addressed her, according to her merits, with bitter words, shaping his speech as follows:

“Unhappy adulteress, destined for all the flames, do you now regret the deceit, or repent of the crime that you devised with an unjust mind against the Lord’s holy servant, following only the lustful counsel of your companion?

“Taking pity on you, I reveal the best medicines of sound counsel, which you must immediately undertake: seek the sacred tomb as a penitent and wipe away your stains with poured-out tears.

119 There, because the body of the holy witness has been buried, fragments shine forth with no small signs.

“Although you are unworthy, I hope that you, poor woman, can obtain pardon if you mourn your guilt.”

But her mind, badly devoted to all destructive vices, refused to go along the straight path of life. Embracing only the slippery pleasures of the present life, she did not care about the perpetual joys of her homeland.

When this unhappy woman, the author of the crime she had committed, disdained to yield to peaceful words because she believed herself to be wholly destined to perish and did not desire to retain hope in enduring blessings, she twisted her bloodshot eyes deceitfully toward the one who spoke no false words.

She impatiently shook her ungoverned head at him and barked these words with her poisonous mouth:

“Why do you speak, uselessly pretending that such great miracles are diligently performed because of Gangolf’s merits? These things that are reported are certainly not proved true, since there are no signs at his tomb—unless the final part of my own back produces miracles as wondrous as his.”

She spoke, and a marvelous sign followed the word, corresponding to that particular part of her body. Thus she produced a sound made by an obscene modulation, such as makes one ashamed to utter the word with one’s tongue.

And afterward, whenever she formed any word, she returned that uncultivated sound each time, so that she who had refused to preserve the modesty proper to a lawful marriage became an immoderate cause of laughter for everyone, and carried throughout the years of her life the sign of her own disgrace.

[Col. 1093]

THE PASSION OF SAINT PELAGIUS, MOST PRECIOUS MARTYR, WHO IN OUR TIMES WAS CROWNED WITH MARTYRDOM AT CORDOBA

120 ARGUMENT.

Abdrahemen, tyrant of Mauretania, following the sect of the Saracens, crossed into Spain and afflicted all the Christians with punishments or compelled them to join his sect. When he had captured Cordoba, the distinguished city of Spain, he killed the city’s leading men or accepted money in their place.

When he imposed upon a noble citizen a sum of money so great that the man could not pay it to the tyrant and was to be led to prison, the son, moved by affection for his father, submitted to the chains in his place.

When the young man’s beauty was reported to the tyrant, he was led from prison and brought before the tyrant so that he might submit to his lust. When the tyrant pressed him with many entreaties to commit the shameful act, the young man struck the tyrant, who was seeking his kisses, with his fist.

The tyrant, because the youth rejected his embraces, cast him with a sling and a catapult over the wall into the river that flows around Cordoba. His body, battered against the rocky banks, was recovered by fishermen and mutilated by the tyrant’s guards; finally, the citizens buried it with the greatest reverence.

PREFACE OF HROSVITHA ON PELAGIUS

[Col. 1093]

[Col. 1093D] Illustrious Pelagius, strongest martyr of Christ,

and good soldier of the King who reigns through the ages,

[Col. 1094D] Look upon Hrosvitha, poor woman, with gentle compassion,

me, your little servant, subject to you with devoted mind,

[Col. 1095A] who worship you in my mind and bring forth a poem from my heart.

Grant that the dark cave of my obscure breast

may be watered more gently from the heavenly dew,

so that I may be able worthily to marvel at your praises

[Col. 1096A] and mark with my pen your famous triumph,

you who nobly conquered the world, stained with death,

and purchased a shining palm with your blood.

THE STORY FOLLOWS

[Col. 1095]

[Col. 1095A] In the western regions there shone the bright glory of the world,

the Augustan New City, proud in the fierceness of Mars,

which the Spanish colonists held richly cultivated:

121 Cordoba, famous and wealthy, so called from its name,

illustrious in delights and splendid in all its possessions,

[Col. 1095B] especially filled with the seven streams of wisdom,

and always renowned for unbroken triumphs.

Formerly it had been well subjected to Christ the just,

and had poured forth to the Lord children made white in baptism.

But suddenly its military power, which had established good laws, changed them. By spreading the error of an impious doctrine, it harmed the faithful people.

For the treacherous race of the unconquered Saracens attacked the harsh inhabitants of this city in war. It seized for itself the royal power and the city’s strength, extinguished the good king washed in baptism, who had previously held the royal scepters deservedly and had governed the citizens with just restraints for as many years as he lived.

After he had been overcome by hostile iron and the remaining people had been defeated in so great a slaughter, the leader of the barbarian race, also the architect of the battle—a thoroughly perverse man, profane in life and conduct—claimed the rule of so great an empire for himself.

He placed his wicked companions in the ravaged countryside, filled the mourning city with no small number of enemies, and polluted the ancient mother of pure faith with barbarian custom—an atrocious thing to say—mixing pagans among the just inhabitants, so that they might persuade the people to dissolve their ancestral customs and to become defiled along with them in the profaned shrine.

But the tender flock, which was to be guided by Christ the shepherd, immediately rejected the sad command of the perverse tyrant. They said that they preferred to die and to defend the law by death rather than live foolishly as servants of newly introduced sacred rites.

When the king learned this, he perceived that it would not be without harm to himself if he brought bitter destruction upon all the wealthy citizens of the city, which he had repeatedly taken through the struggle of mighty battle.

For this reason, changing his earlier decree, 122 he immediately sanctioned a law and publicly proclaimed this doctrine: whoever wished to serve the eternal King and to preserve faithfully the customs of his fathers might do so lawfully, without any subsequent punishment, provided only that no citizen of the aforesaid city dared thereafter blaspheme the gods made of gold, whom whichever prince held the scepter might worship; otherwise, he would have to submit his head to the sword without delay and suffer the final sentence of death.

When these arrangements had been made, he rested in a pretended peace, while the faithful city, buried under a thousand evils, repeatedly suffered.

But if the love of Christ and martyrdom inflamed any people sufficiently to persuade them by their words to overthrow the marble images that the prince, adorned with a diadem, worshiped prostrate in body with Sabaean incense, [Col. 1096B] he immediately condemned them to the punishment of decapitation. But their souls, washed in blood, sought the heavenly realms.

For many days Cordoba endured such misfortunes, subjected for a long age to pagan kings, until, in our own times, a certain descendant of the royal line happened to assume the kingdom of his ancestors.

Worse than his fathers and stained by the luxury of the flesh, he was called Abdrahemen. Proud in the splendor of his kingdom, he treated the worshipers of Christ, as his father had done, by weighing out the judgment of faith previously mentioned. Nor did he mercifully abolish the thoroughly unjust decree which the author of the crime, the treacherous ravager of the city, had enacted when he overcame the faithful king in battle.

Instead, turning it over in his mind and preserving it deep in his heart, he repeatedly soaked the fields with innocent blood, consuming the holy bodies of righteous men who burned to sing sweet praises to Christ and to rebuke with their words the foolish gods of the tyrant.

Moreover, this sacrilegious man boasted in his court with such arrogance, piling up deserved punishments for himself, 123 that he believed himself to be the King of kings, and that all peoples should bow their necks to his rule. He did not consider any people so filled with ferocity that they would dare to test his armies in battle.

While he grew still more swollen with pride and boasted of this license, he heard that a people lived in distant places, situated in the region of Galicia and proud in war, worshipers of Christ and rebels against idols. They were continually trying to despise his laws and denied that they wished ever to be subject to wicked masters.

When the king learned this, the demon’s anger boiled within him. He carried the serpent’s ancient bile in his heart and long revolved, in flaming cunning, the insult he had suffered, considering what he should do against such enemies.

At last, when the deceit had perhaps become known to everyone, he addressed the lordly nobles of the wealthy city, barking these words with a poisonous mouth:

“It is no secret that kings submit to our rule and live under the governance of our laws—all the peoples whom the deep Ocean surrounds.

“But I do not know what confidence holds the Galicians captive, that they reject the treaties of our grace and finally prove ungrateful for our ancient kindness.

“It remains, therefore, that we attack the Galicians with armed force, driving on these rebellious enemies, until, struck down by our weapons for all ages, they unwillingly submit their necks to our chains.”

After he had made this boast and recalled the cause of his deceit, he ordered the people to assemble in collected ranks, equipped with various military standards, so that he might go with them to destroy the faithful race. He displayed his face beneath a jeweled helmet, placed iron coverings upon his luxuriant limbs, and with such pomp sought the place he had mentioned, intending first to test the people in war, as though he were immediately to win so great a triumph.

124 After capturing the prince and twice six of his companions, he ensnared them and bound them tightly in chains.

When these losses had been inflicted upon the nobles with great ferocity, the most faithful people yielded, defeated, to their enemies and was subjected to the yoke of the perverse and unjust king.

Then, when the first treaty had again been restored, the twelve companions proceeded bound with thongs, together with the defeated ruler of the captive people.

The companions were quickly released when their chains were undone, being redeemed for a considerable price from their own treasure. But the king ordered that the leader’s price be doubled, beyond what he could pay from his own wealth.

When, on his own account, he brought before the greedy king whatever precious things he was accustomed to possess at home, he fell only slightly short of the agreed amount of gold.

When the king perceived this and turned over deceit in his mind, he said that he was unwilling to release the dear leader with the people unless he first paid the entire tax demanded of him—not merely the amount of gold that was lacking, but as much as the king desired in order to put the people’s ruler to death.

The man was born from an illustrious family, alone among them, endowed with every bodily beauty and adorned with a splendid form. His name was Pelagius; he was beautiful in the radiance of his appearance, wise in counsel, and shining in complete goodness.

Having scarcely passed beyond his boyhood years, he had already reached the first flowers of youthful age.

When he knew that the king would be sufficiently harsh toward his father, he consoled his grieving parent with these words:

“O my dear father, willingly receive my words, and perceive readily what I advise.

“For I know that your life is declining through old age, that your limbs are entirely drained of their own strength, and that you cannot bear even a light labor.

“But I, strong in my limbs, shall be subject for a time to harsh masters. Therefore I advise and entreat you with gentle prayers 125 to offer me, your dear son, to the king, until you are able to pay the entire price, so that your gray hair may not perish in tight chains.”

The old man replied in a stern voice:

“Stop speaking such things, dearest son, stop, lest you bring my gray hairs into hell through grief.

“Does not my whole life depend upon your safety, and can I live any length of time piously without you?

“You are all my honor, you are the great glory of your parents, and you are also the sole hope of the people subject to us.

“Therefore it is better for me to leave my dear homeland and also to enter proud Spain in chains than to entrust you, my hope, to the chains of old age.”

Pelagius could not endure his father’s continuing in this way. He soothed the mind of his dear parent with words and persuaded him by gentle speech to do what he had advised.

At last the venerable father consented to his entreaties and handed over his son, poor man, to redeem himself.

Then the king ordered Pelagius to be taken away with him and returned joyfully as a victor to revisit his homeland.

No one should believe that this deed of the king, whereby he at last prevailed over so splendid a company, was done because of Pelagius’s merits; rather, it happened by the secret judgment of the just Judge, so that the people, properly seized by so great a scourge, might mourn the sins of their entire nation—or because Pelagius, destined to die for Christ’s law, might perhaps reach the place where he could give himself to death and pour out a stream of blood for Christ, offering his life to the Lord, well cleansed by death.

When the savage king reached the wealthy city, carrying the splendid triumph of the defeated people, he immediately ordered the excellent friend of Christ to be bound and plunged into the black darkness of a prison and to be fed with little food, nourished by scanty fare.

For Cordoba preserves beneath a vault a dreadful place, shut away from light and marked by darkness, 126 which is said to be the greatest source of pain for the wretched.

There Pelagius, a pre-eminent child of peace, was confined, compelled by the impious command of the king.

There the city’s leading men came diligently, attempting to soothe the young man’s mind out of compassion. When they had seen the beauty of the captive’s face and tasted the very sweet words of his mouth, coated with the honey of rhetorical speech, they wished to release such beauty from its chains.

They also made this suggestion to the king, who then held the scepter. They knew that he was certainly the supreme head of the fortunate city, corrupted by Sodomite vices: he ardently loved handsome young men in appearance and wished to join them to his own friendship.

Remembering this, and taking pity on Pelagius, they made the following suggestion to the king:

“It is not fitting, strongest prince, for your scepter to order that a handsome boy be harshly punished, or to bind the tender limbs of an innocent captive, if you wish to see his radiant form and at least taste his softened speech.

“You should wish to join such a young man to yourself, to take him into the first rank of military service, and to have his fair body serve you in the court.

The king, softened by these words and compelled by them, ordered Pelagius to be pulled from his harsh bonds, his entire body cleansed in a pure bath, his limbs clothed in joyful purple, and his neck adorned with jeweled metal, so that he might properly become a soldier in the court.

When these things were urgently demanded by the proud command of the ruler, the martyr was immediately brought forth from the black caves and presented in the court, dressed in royal clothing.

When he was placed among the palace attendants, he surpassed his clothed companions in the brightness of his appearance.

[Col. 1099A] Everyone turned his eyes toward him in astonishment. 127 The king, at first sight, was captivated both by the young man’s face and by the sweet words he spoke, and he burned to love the beauty of one born from royal stock.

At last he ordered Pelagius, whom he desired excessively, to be placed with him upon the royal throne, so that he might become the object of the king’s passion, closely joined to him. With lowered brow he kissed the dear youth and embraced his neck in affection.

But the soldier of Christ could not tolerate such love from a pagan king stained by the luxury of the flesh. Instead, mocking him, he brought his ear to the royal mouth, turned away with great ridicule from the kisses that had been refused, and spoke the following from his excellent mouth:

“It is not fitting for a man washed in Christ’s baptism 128 to submit his sober neck to a barbarian embrace, nor for a Christian washed in sacred chrism to seek the unclean kiss of a demonic servant.

“Therefore embrace the foolish men in licit affection, those who appease your foolish gods upon the ground with you, and let your companions be those who are also slaves of an image.”

But the king, stirred by no anger, gently addressed the beloved youth:

“O wanton boy, you boast that you may freely despise the mercy of our law, which is so gentle, and audaciously mock our gods so often.

“Does your present youthful age not warn you of the danger, or of the fact that you may perhaps deprive your grieving parents of you? Our worship demands that blasphemers be tortured, that you be subjected to death and your throats pierced, unless they yield and reject their blasphemous reasoning.

“Therefore I advise you with paternal encouragement to spare such harsh words, and to bring with me a steadfast love of mind. Do not try thereafter to offend our command. With great zeal observe my words and follow them, since I cherish you in my heart and wish also to honor you,

129 so that, surpassing all the attendants of the court, you may shine as the other in my proud kingdom, through my favor.”

He spoke and clasped the martyr’s face with his right hand, embracing his consecrated neck with his left, so that he might plant at least one kiss upon him.

But the clever witness confounded the king’s playfulness. Suddenly he struck the royal mouth with a blow of his fist and delivered such a forceful stroke with his face turned downward that blood immediately dripped from the wound, staining the beard and wetting the garments.

Then the king, turning in no small anger, ordered Pelagius, the nursling of the heavenly King, to be thrown over the walls by a war engine that repeatedly pierces fighting enemies with stones, so that the noble witness, dashed against the river’s banks—the river that flows near the famous city in a broad stream—might quickly be broken apart and perish limb from limb.

The attendants obeyed the king’s command and soon prepared an unheard-of punishment. They cast Pelagius, destined for martyrdom, far beyond the great walls of the famous city by means of a sling.

Although huge rocks hemmed in the sweet body of the witness as it fell from every side, the friend of Christ nevertheless remained unharmed.

Certainly the report quickly reached the royal ears that the martyr’s battered body could not be cut apart; he therefore ordered it to be impaled upon the sharp rocks of the bank.

More deeply offended because he had been utterly defeated, the king immediately ordered that Pelagius’s head be cut off with a drawn sword and thus carried out the final sentence.

At last the executioners, trembling before the royal commands, cut down the faithful witness of Christ with a sword and entrusted the dead body to the waters to be preserved.

For the soldier, with the king’s deathly power overthrown, eternal victor, flies through the starry heavens, gently led by angelic hymns from heaven.

129 The true Judge, enthroned above the stars of heaven,

[Col. 1100B] From his right hand duly received the shining palm,

In place of death, for martyrdom brought to its praiseworthy end.

Nor is he defrauded of the prize of fervent love,

For which he finally gave himself in bonds for his father’s life,

Leaving behind his native land and the people subjected to him.

At last no tongue among the devout is able to express

The little golden crown, flashing with heavenly light,

Which, well preserved through virginity, shines forth,

Joined to the heavenly ranks and received into the heavenly seat,

While he eternally modulates a song to the Lamb: Amen.

After the executioners, following the king’s decrees,

Committed the sufficiently noble remains of the dead man

To the bosom of the waters and fixed them among the rocks,

So that the sacred ashes might be in a tomb without due honor,

Christ, who does not allow his own saints to be lost,

[Col. 1100C] Nor even a small portion of their head or perhaps a single hair to be plundered,

Did not permit the faithful witness to remain in the water,

But duly provided him with a worthy resting place

That would preserve the sacred limbs in a holy tomb.

For fishermen, cutting through the waters with their oars

And catching the wandering shoals with various nets,

Saw the body at the furthest edge of the shore,

Tossed amid the martyr’s resounding waves.

Seeing this from afar with careful eyes,

They quickly set their sails and raised the body.

But they no longer recognized the appearance of the venerable person,

Because his limbs had been smeared with purple blood,

And the noble head lay far away, torn from the stream.

Yet they understood this and believed it with ready hearts:

[Col. 1100D] Whoever this man was, he had died for Christ’s law,

Since only those are condemned there to capital punishment

Who, washed in the sacred waters of baptism,

Do not fear repeatedly reproving the king’s religious practices.

When they found the head and set it upon the neck,

They recognized the radiant face of Pelagius,

130 And, with compassionate hearts, broke into such words:

“Alas! He lies lifeless, the sole hope of his own people.

And the glory of his country lies dishonored, without a tomb.

Do we not know that for many ages

The bodies of holy men have always suffered,

Whom the beheading had shown to be faithful?

And who would doubt that a body may be a praiseworthy witness,

When the trunk of the headless man lies miserably without honor?”

[Col. 1101A] When they had spoken these words, they placed the sacred limbs in the boat,

And, turning their sails, rowed swiftly at last

Toward the gate of the city famous among all peoples.

Here too, having drawn up the keel, they proceeded,

And secretly sought the monastery consecrated to Christ,

Within the city’s not inconsiderable venerable walls,

Carrying the sacred funeral remains of the dead witness,

Which they intended finally to sell for a great price on land.

The faithful crowd received it with joy and hymns,

Celebrating the sacred funeral rites according to custom,

And generously paid the sailors an increased price,

Burning with love to purchase the saint’s body.

When it had been purchased—not for a small payment—

A land rich enough to preserve the limbs was chosen,

And, after the supreme pomp had been restored to the tomb,

[Col. 1101B] The sacred fragments were buried beneath a mound of earth.

Then the greatest Ruler of the star-bearing court

Commanded that it shine with flashing signs in the tomb,

So that, while the soul reigned blessedly in heaven,

The dead limbs might reign with equal glory.

Finally, the assembled populace, seeing people from the city

Afflicted for a considerable time by various diseases,

Saw them cleansed there, their foul limbs freed from decay,

And saved freely, without payment, by the gift of healing.

For people still hesitated to regard the holy man as of such great merit,

though such great miracles occurred through his agency.

At last the head of the monastery and leader of the people,

Considering the best remedies of sound counsel,

131 Perceived that Celsithron must be invoked with devoted mind,

So that he might now graciously and openly,

In his customary compassion,

Reveal the secrets of the doubtful matter and remove uncertainty.

This persons of both sexes desired at once,

And, voluntarily joining together for three days,

They applied themselves to sweet hymns

And to sacred prayers.

[Col. 1102A] When these vows had certainly been fulfilled with devoted hearts,

They perceived that the gentle King of the heavens had been softened

By their prayers, poured forth with earnest murmuring,

And that he was inclined, by his judgment, to resolve the doubtful case.

They quickly compelled the threatening furnace to burn,

Having piled up the fires with all their strength.

When the fire raged in the furnace’s spacious cavity,

The servants then took Christ’s severed head,

And, touching it with such words in flattering speech, said:

“Pious King, noble ruler of the starry court,

You who know how to discern all things with just judgment,

Let the merit of this saint be tested by fire.

And, if he is supported by the honor of such goodness

That these gifts of salvation have arisen from his merits,

Command the flame not to touch the skin of his forehead,

[Col. 1102B] And return all the hairs of his crown unharmed.

But if his merit should perhaps prove to be lesser,

At least give a sign by ordering the surface of the skin

To be damaged, according to the nature of fragile, perishing flesh.”

Saying this, they entrusted the bright head to the fire for testing,

At least to the rising waves that poured forth flames.

At last, after the space of a full hour,

They lifted the same head from the swift flames,

Examining it with their eyes to see whether the heat had caused damage.

But it now shone more brilliantly than pure gold,

Entirely free of odor and untouched by so great a heat.

Then, raising their faces upward, the faithful crowd praised Christ,

The Most High, with a song sung in measured verse.

He had so often caused the fragments of the steadfast witness,

Who had died for him, to shine with such great signs.

[Col. 1102C] 132 Having duly enclosed these remains in a venerable mausoleum,

He is worshiped there with truly worthy reverence,

Known to the credulous people by his merit to the very end,

And always rejoiced in as a patron granted from heaven.

[Col. 1101]

THE FALL AND CONVERSION OF THE VICEDOMINUS THEOPHILUS.

ARGUMENT.

Theophilus, a young man of exceptional character and ability, is entrusted in Sicily [read: Cilicia] to his grandfather, a bishop, who appoints him archdeacon (the bishop’s “eye” according to the canons; here he is called the vicedominus). After his grandfather’s death, the people offer him the bishopric. He declines it before the metropolitan. Another man is elected, who removes him from the office of archdeacon. Seeing himself despised and rejected, he consults a Hebrew in order to regain his former office. The Hebrew summons the devil, and Theophilus devotes himself to him; he is restored to his office. At last, moved by repentance, he implores the help of the glorious virgin Mary. Through her intercessions he finally recovers the document he had given to the devil and devotes himself entirely to a life of holiness.

THE STORY BEGINS.

[Col. 1101]

[Col. 1101D] After the light of faith, growing through the regions of the world,

Had freed Sicily from the dark shadows of error,

A man of great distinction was raised in those parts,

Powerful in nobility and radiant in the splendor of his merit.

His name was Theophilus,

Consecrated by the pure waters of baptism.

[Col. 1102D] The devoted care of his parents therefore marked him out

For divine service from his earliest years,

And, dutifully attending to his beloved nephew,

His grandfather entrusted him to a certain bishop,

A man of great wisdom,

So that he might educate him through flourishing study,

And water the field of his intellect and mind

[Col. 1103A] 133 With streams of wisdom flowing from a sevenfold source.

When the pious boy had sufficiently drunk from these,

He was immediately advanced, step by step,

To an office well suited to him,

Which, as we know, is called in the language of the people the vicedominus.

Having attained this splendid dignity,

He showed himself subject to the bishop and modest toward the clergy,

Pious toward the people, and kind toward everyone,

And vigilantly presided over the flock entrusted to him.

Above all, he gave clothing and food with a generous hand

To Christ’s least and most wretched children,

To chaste widows, and also to all travelers,

And never closed his lodging to wandering beggars.

Thus the whole devotion of the people

Depended upon him with tender affection of heart;

[Col. 1103B] They venerated him lovingly as a dear parent.

Meanwhile, a man of the highest merits,

Having received his heavenly summons,

Was guided into the heavens.

When he had died and been placed in the earth,

All the people cried out in agreement,

Answering the wishes of the clergy, who desired the same thing:

That this vicedominus, distinguished by his outstanding merits,

Should aspire to the summit of the episcopal see

And assume the care of the flock of the supreme bishop.

They quickly hastened to persuade their metropolitan bishop of this,

Sending letters,

For by his judgment a pastor wise and worthy of such an honor

Was to be established for the church.

When he had learned of the man’s kindness and goodness,

He promised that he would fulfill the petitioners’ wishes,

[Col. 1103C] And ordered the man himself to come as soon as possible,

For he had perceived how greatly the people loved him.

But Theophilus steadfastly rejected such an honor

And refused to obey the bishop’s command by coming,

Until he was dragged there against his will,

With the crowds gathering around him.

When he was presented before the bishop’s eyes,

134 He cast himself down upon the ground and raised his voice,

Declaring that he was stained by many vices

And unfit to rule Christ’s holy people.

After he had poured forth these complaints again and again,

The supreme bishop finally yielded under compulsion,

And allowed this man, who had rejected such an honor,

To depart free from the charge that had been imposed upon him.

He appointed another, worthy of the title of ruler,

Who, after only a few days,

Secretly seduced by the flattering counsels of certain people,

Quickly placed another vicedominus over his subjects,

And removed Theophilus, worthy of the highest honors,

From the office which he had held for many years.

[Col. 1103D] But Theophilus, patiently enduring the loss of his fragile honor,

Drove all sadness from his heart,

And rejoiced that he could now devote himself

With so much greater freedom to the service of Christ,

Since he was free from various cares.

Then the most savage enemy of the whole human race

Attacked his patient mind,

Using the same deceit by which he had deceived our first parents,

And struck the inner chambers of this just man,

Frequently bringing to his fragile mind

[Col. 1104A] The enticing pleasures of his former power

And the heavy lot of the contempt he had recently suffered.

Nor did he withdraw the snares of these ambushes

Until he had led Christ’s servant away as his captive.

Without delay, this strong man, renowned for his life and merits,

Foolishly cast aside all strength of mind.

He made no effort to withstand the wicked temptations,

But, overcome, yielded and wasted away in anguish of mind.

The man who had formerly refused to rule the people

Now longed for the pomp of an inferior office.

At last, deceived and blinded in his heart,

The wretched man hurried to a certain wicked Hebrew,

Who had deceived many faithful people by magical fraud,

135 And, licking his feet with his prostrate body,

Begged his evil help with tears.

[Col. 1104B] The malicious man, rejoicing over the sinner’s fall,

Ordered him to return on the following night without doubt,

Promising that the despised office would readily be restored

If he would merely obey his counsels

And thereafter remain under the authority of his masters.

The unfortunate man, badly ensnared by these flattering instructions,

Longed to bind himself in obedience to the fierce demon,

So that he might thus earn the shadowy gift of honor,

Not marked with the holy sign of the salutary cross,

But trusting rather in demonic counsels.

The accursed magician quickly led him with him

Across the city, secretly through the darkness of night,

And brought him into a place full of many phantoms,

Where infernal inhabitants stood dressed in white,

Holding many candles in their hands.

[Col. 1104C] Among them sat the wicked prince in the middle,

Who is the king of death and offspring of perdition,

Counseling his doomed servants with crafty deceit,

Urging them diligently to display every kind of accustomed cunning

And to seize all the snares prepared for capture.

He brought the wandering man, who desired his own ruin,

Swiftly before the wicked council.

The man immediately prostrated himself at his master’s feet

And explained in words the reason for which he had come.

Then the savage demon spoke against him as follows:

“Tell me,” he said, “what assistance can I offer to a faithful man

Washed by the water of Christ’s baptism?

If he wishes to be mine and will deny Christ in writing,

And likewise deny his youthful Mother,

Through whose childbirth I suffer such grievous loss,

I shall immediately free him by my power,

And openly grant him such an honor

That the bishop himself will not dare to oppose his commands,

Seeing everyone serving him,

[Col. 1104D] 136 Those who now despise him and refuse to honor him.”

The wretched man did not contradict any of these words

Spoken with the flattering cunning of the serpent,

But eagerly desired that what the perverse dragon had suggested should be done;

He betrayed himself and gave himself entirely to perdition.

Of his own accord he wrote and handed over a document of his ruin,

In which he declared that he wished to be

Among the black spirits as their companion throughout the ages,

To suffer eternal punishments.

When he had completed this,

The phantom disappeared in every direction,

And he himself returned joyfully with his wicked companion.

[Col. 1105A] On the appointed day, the bishop ordered the leading clergy

And likewise the principal members of the people to appear,

Together with Theophilus, who was brought before them all.

He addressed him with exceedingly flattering and friendly words,

Cheerfully submitting himself to Theophilus’s authority,

And lamented with pious complaints that he had sinned,

Because he had presumed to reject the holy man.

But Theophilus, rejoicing at the sudden gift of such great honor,

Raised himself in a proud mind beyond measure,

And arrogantly compelled the ranks of the subject peoples

To bow beneath his harsh commands.

Having entirely rejected the honor of the heavenly homeland,

He busied himself solely with love of earthly pomp.

And, while he longed for empty riches,

And, as the magician instructed him,

Never ceased wickedly to offer manifold thanks to Satan,

He believed that such prosperity had come to him

Solely from Satan’s generous gifts.

At last the boundless heavenly compassion of the Father,

Who never desires the destruction and death of the guilty,

But rather wishes to grant joyful life to those who turn back,

Pitied the fact that the merit of the kind man

By which he had once shone most famously before the world

Had perished.

This same venerable compassion,

Which gently seeks out all who are in need,

And acts in the divine manner,

Struck the erring man’s mind with worthy fear.

137 Without delay, the wretched man, pierced by the greatest sorrow,

Began constantly to set before the eyes of his heart,

Trembling,

What torments he had deserved forever by denying God,

And with what punishments he would have to be joined in Avernus.

As he considered these things with the deepest grief,

He is said to have uttered the following continual lament:

“Alas for me, wretched and stained by every disgrace!

Woe to me, doomed man, because of the crime of my own vow,

Who denied in writing the Son of the supreme Father,

And likewise the sweet Mother of the divine Son!

Alas, through what savage punishments shall I be handed over for ages,

And in what unending darkness shall I be confined,

Who, wretched, chose to submit to Satan’s authority

And to be joined to the darkness of the abyss,

Deceived by the vain love of worldly pomp?

What shall I, a great sinner, say at that

Time of the holy judgment of the dreadful Spirit,

When each person receives the reward of his deeds,

Measured on a perfectly just scale,

[Col. 1105D] According to the varying quality of his merits?

Or who then will perhaps take pity on me,

When scarcely even the just are saved according to their merits?

For the Mother of Christ, mighty Lady of heaven,

The spotless, radiant temple of the Holy Spirit,

The same virgin, chaste after the joys of childbirth,

Who has always been most gentle toward those who turn back,

And never delays her tender compassion,

Alone is able to bring me the remedy of pardon,

If she deigns to ask her Son on my behalf.

But if I begin to entreat her with polluted lips,

Whom, in my frenzied heart, I recently denied,

I fear that I shall be consumed by flames sent from heaven,

Because the world cannot endure my grievous crime.”

[Col. 1106A] Nevertheless, compelled by the cause of his pressing sorrow,

I humbly sought her swift compassion,

So that, in her mercy, she might save my perishing soul by her prayers.”

138 He said these things to himself amid bitter and deeply mournful complaints.

Then he quickly drove the cares of the world from his heart

And hastened without delay to a temple dedicated

To the honor of the undefiled virgin

And the venerable Mother of God.

For forty days he remained there,

Weeping over his sins with a contrite heart,

Denying himself all the pleasures of food

That delight those who eat,

And likewise very often denying himself the sweet rest of sleep.

Keeping vigil in sacred prayers with the greatest effort,

And breaking his body through such labor,

He cleansed the stains of his corrupted soul with tears.

[Col. 1106B] When he had performed these things well,

And, exceedingly weary during the night hours,

Had laid his limbs down to gentle rest,

The most chaste Mother of the eternal King,

The same Lady of the world,

Appeared to him in sleep—

She who is ready help, hope, and consolation,

The support of those who pray with devoted hearts—

And frightened his fearful heart with these words:

“O man, why do you keep vigil at the threshold of our temple?

Or why do you presume to hope for my swift compassion,

You who, with perverse heart, denied my Son at last,

And denied me, his mother?

Tell me, I ask, with what eyes could I gaze upon the face

Of my divine Son, radiant with heavenly light,

Or in what way could I presume to stand before his dreadful throne,

Asking pardon for you?

[Col. 1106C] Yet I freely forgive you at once,

With the devotion of my mind,

All the sins perhaps committed against me,

Because I love every kind of Christ-worshiper exceedingly.

But I especially love with tender affection of mind,

Console, and embrace in my own arms

Those whom I see praying to me,

Devoting themselves frequently to hymns,

And keeping vigil in my temple.

But the powerful force of maternal love compels me,

And therefore makes me burn with excessive zeal for you.

139 You presumed to be handed over to perdition

By blaspheming and despising my holy Son,

Who is the eternal God, begotten from God the Father,

Before the ancient beginnings of a serene origin;

Who deigned to take from me, in time,

A body subject to human death,

For love of the human race.

[Col. 1106D] When the man, grieving in spirit, heard the chaste Mother of Christ say this,

He replied bitterly:

“O my lady, I know—and I waste away from knowing it—

That I have sinned more than was right.

Captured by empty hope,

I committed a crime greater than any punishment

By despising God, who was poured forth from you without stain.

For this reason I am not worthy to seek the gift of pardon.

Yet you give us an example of the salvation we may hope for:

Those who have fallen into many different crimes

Have obtained pardon for their sins after their fall.

Did not the Ninevites find the gentle compassion of Christ

After an interval of three days,

When they tormented themselves with worthy lamentation?

Did not David, the prophet of God and also ruler of the Jewish kingdom,

Who ruled the Lord’s people,

Suddenly overcome by unlawful love for another man’s wife,

Fearlessly, through deceitful ambushes,

Deprive an innocent man of life without cause,

So that he might lawfully possess the embraces of his beloved?

But, after he learned, terrified by the warning of the prophet who came to him,

that he must lament his twin sins,

He quickly erased the stains of his heart in silence with tears

And received again the gift of prophecy.

What should I say of Peter, blessed according to Christ’s testimony?

Although he had received the power equally to loose and to bind,

And the keys of the star-bearing court,

On account of the clearly expressed truth of the faith,

He refused to acknowledge that he knew Christ as God,

Fearing the voice of a wicked servant girl,

[Col. 1107B] Not once or twice, but finally three times,

And denied his beloved master as though he had never seen him.

140 But because he duly lamented his sin with his mouth after his fall,

He merited the healing of abundant pardon.

He was also ordered to preside over the faithful flock

And became, by right, the shepherd and prince of the holy Church.

Instructed by such and so many examples, and by many others,

I hoped that through you I might quickly seek similar compassion from Christ.”

The holy Mary spoke to him with a gracious face,

Reviving his sadness with the honeyed sweetness of her tongue:

“If the wicked deed you committed troubles you,

It is fitting that with the consent of your heart you confess

What, in your mad speech, you denied:

That the one whom I bore is the Son of the supreme Father,

Who will come as judge to renew the world through fire.

After this I shall presume to pray for you.”

Then the vicedominus, weeping again, replied:

“O most holy beloved Mother of God and of Christ,

You who revive all the faithful with gentle compassion,

By what means, by what right, could I ever presume

With polluted lips to pronounce the holy, venerable, great name

Of the Most High?

I am wretched: I blasphemed in wickedly written documents

Christ, baptism, the cross of Christ, and you, his chaste mother,

And all the pious sacraments of heavenly salvation.”

Hearing these pitiful complaints, the discoverer of virginity

Spoke again more mercifully in gentle words:

[Col. 1107D] “Although you are greatly stained by grave sins,

Nevertheless, as I instructed you, do not refuse to confess the Lord,

Since he became human solely for our sake,

So that he might provide those who turn back with hope of pardon.

Now, obeying these commands and following the instruction,

He poured forth such words with tears toward heaven:

‘I humbly worship, praise, embrace, and adore him,

Christ, born timelessly from the heavenly Father,

Sent in our times from the seat of his Parent.

141 From you, O chaste one, and also from the Holy Spirit,

He put on the garments of our fragile flesh.

I do not doubt that he is true God and also fully human,

Who therefore endured these things for our sake:

To be touched by reproaches,

Struck by blows and slaps,

And beaten repeatedly with sacred scourges upon his back,

While the appearance of his radiant face was stained with spittle.

And when crowned with thorns and given gall to drink,

He fulfilled in every respect what sacred Scripture had foretold.

Finally, with his sacred hands stretched out upon the cross,

Like a true shepherd adorned with the honor of goodness,

He died and laid down his precious life for us,

And deigned to receive burial.

Then, descending to the underworld,

Breaking open the prison of the abyss,

He destroyed death and bound the father of death.

He drew his righteous ones from the prison of Tartarus,

And thus, a victor accompanied by no small company,

Returned to the heights and resumed his own body,

[Col. 1108B] Which had been enclosed in the tomb beneath the great stone.

The third day saw him alive throughout all ages,

And his blessed disciples often saw him,

Now dining with them, now speaking to them

In sweet words about the kingdom that was to come.

After this, while their astonished eyes looked on,

He lifted the very flesh he had assumed above the stars,

In which he will come to conduct the future judgment,

And will render good or evil to all according to their merits.

Believing these things in this way,

Holding them firmly in the faith of my heart,

And asking for your customary compassion,

I commend myself, O most holy Virgin, to your Son,

And obtain pardon from him for your sinful servant.’”

When he had wept out these words in continual lament,

The holy Mother of God, the same mighty Lady

[Col. 1108C] Of the heavens, answered him in friendly words:

“Because of the gracious mystery of holy baptism,

And because of my love for my beloved Son’s leader [dux; reading uncertain],

Whose sacred blood, I know, was poured out for the perishing world

And by whose price you were entirely purchased,

I proceed and diligently prostrate myself

At the sacred feet of him whom I bore,

The just Judge of all.

Nor will I spare prayers poured forth with striving zeal

Until I compel his gentle compassion

To pardon you such great sins.”

When she had said this, the consecrated virgin suddenly departed,

Leaving the wretched man the consolation of the salvation

That he had received as a believing member of the people.

Certainly, after three days, she came to him again in a vision,

Revealing the gift of restored pardon,

[Col. 1108D] And spoke these words with a joyful face:

“Behold, man of God, the sorrowful contrition of your heart

Has been accepted by God the Father and the eternal Son,

And your tears have earned pardon for your sins.

Nor shall you ever be seized by infernal punishments

If after this you wish to remain faithfully without deceit.”

Immediately he replied with humble prayer:

“Certainly I shall preserve the teachings of the sacred faith,

And after this I shall no longer transgress wickedly

By neglecting any of your commands,

My most pious lady,

For after the Lord I hope that you alone can bring healing,

So that you choose me as fuel for punishments rather than for Tartarus [reading uncertain].

But it is not surprising that through you I should now be saved.

Through you the whole world, by God’s gift, is plainly freed

From the deadly crime of the ancient mother.

And whoever seeks you, appealing with unwavering hope,

Does not depart abandoned or return confounded.

For this reason I, sufficiently corrupted by the greatest crimes,

Humbly and with devoted mind implore the perpetual fountain

Of your compassion, gracious Mother of God,

That you immediately take from his hands the writing of the wicked document

By which I subjected myself to the destroyer’s authority,

and receive me back, wretched as I am.

For I fear that my wretched soul may perhaps be harmed

At the time of judgment by great peril

[Col. 1109A] If it is not now withdrawn from the savage robber.”

After saying these things, he again awoke with open eyes.

He prostrated himself in prayer and wept repeatedly,

And then spent three successive days fasting.

[Col. 1109B] After this he rose from sleep early in the morning

And found the document placed upon his breast.

When he saw it, his limbs immediately trembled and went weak,

And he gave thanks to Christ from the depths of his heart,

And likewise to the youthful Mother of Christ.

After this, when the sacred day had happily dawned,

The day that takes its venerable name from the supreme Lord,

He entered the church, filled with people according to custom.

There, during the solemnities of the sacred Mass,

The bishop was teaching those standing by with evangelical words.

The vicedominus prostrated himself before the sacred altar

And also kissed the feet of the same bishop.

Then, in a clear voice before everyone,

He related in order all that had happened:

Both what he had done when overcome by deadly counsels,

[Col. 1109C] And what he had merited through the maiden’s intercession.

When he had fully recounted these things in an orderly manner,

The bishop, touched by terror at the wondrous deed,

Thundered forth these words in an astonished voice:

“Come here now, all you faithful who rejoice,

And, praising the pious deeds of God with faithful hearts,

Believe now that the Lord, kind in his own compassion,

Never delights in the death of the sinful,

But rather wishes to give future life to those who turn back.

Come, beloved brothers, all of you pay attention

To how mercifully the good Lord tolerates all those who pray,

When he knows that they have turned back after grievous sins.

Who would not marvel?

Who would not humbly venerate

The much-praised compassion of sweet Christ,

By which he always raises up those who seek him?

[Col. 1109D] He has now, in his compassion, pardoned the sins of this man,

Through the prayers of that illustrious one

and of the holy Mother,

[Col. 1110A] Through whom the curse of our nature has perished,

And through whom blessing has come to the whole world.

Therefore remember us, most holy Mother of God,

Who praise you in mind, faith, vow, and voice,

So that he himself, the gracious shepherd,

May deign to preserve his faithful flock,

The ancient deceit of the dragon having been driven away.

But we, poor and powerless in every virtue,

Continually proclaim you, untouched and eternal Mother of the King,

And the King and Lord of the heavens born from you,

Singing together in frequent hymns,

For our brother, dying in sin, perished,

But after he perished, through you, holy Virgin, he lived again.”

After these words he burned the accursed document

And immediately celebrated the mystery of the Mass with devotion.

When he had completed this,

His face shone with wondrous brilliance,

Like the rising sun,

So that the radiance of his mind

And the purity of his soul

Were revealed through his shining face.

From that point the people standing by,

Struck by overwhelming fear,

Began to resound thunderous thanks to the Most High,

Who had chosen to reveal the merit of the venerable man.

Then he immediately returned to the sacred resting place

Where he had received the gift of heavenly compassion,

To be broken by the opposing force of fragile bodily sickness.

As the illness increased over the course of three days,

His spirit was freed from the prison of corruptible flesh

And ascended, rejoicing, to the heavenly court,

Strengthened by the help of the holy Lady Mary.

The extinguished body was then buried by the efforts of the people

With the highest honor in the proper place,

[Col. 1110C] Where he had obtained the pardon he had sought with tears.

Such was the end of the desperate and sinful man,

Who learned to lament his own guilt

And diligently punished himself with worthy complaints.

Therefore praise and power be to Christ throughout all ages,

Who had struck down the ancient enemy of the human race,

Snatching the work of his hand from the serpent’s mouth.

And may blessed light be with his gracious and sweet Mother,

Who mercifully brought consolation to the wretched man. Amen.

The only-begotten Son of the Most High,

Existing before the ages of the world,

Who, pitying humanity, descended from the Father’s citadel,

And assumed true flesh from a virgin,

So that he might calm the deserved bitterness of the first woman,

May consecrate the pious food of the table set before us,

[Col. 1110D] Making these dishes health-giving to those who taste them.

May the right hand of the Maker, who governs all things,

Bless what we are, what we taste, and whatever we do!

[Col. 1109]

THE STORY OF THE CONVERSION OF THE DESPERATE YOUNG SERVANT OF PROTERIUS THROUGH SAINT BASIL. Hrotsuitha offers the book to Gerberga, her abbess.

Behold, my lady Gerberga, I bring you new little verses,

Joining poems to the verses written above.

[Col. 1111] How the sinful man also earned beloved pardon,

I sing with dactylic measures, rejoicing in the melodies.

Do not despise them because they are exceedingly flawed,

But praise the works of God with a gentle heart.

PREFACE TO PROTERIUS.

[Col. 1111]

[Col. 1111A] Whoever wishes to grasp a sure example of pardon,

And also the great gifts of God’s abundant compassion,

Let him read through these little verses with a humble heart,

And let him not despise the fragile sex of a woman,

Who sang these measures with a fragile pen.

[Col. 1112A] Rather, let him praise the heavenly compassion of Christ,

Who does not wish to destroy sinners with a punishment they deserve,

But prefers to restore those who turn back to everlasting life.

Whoever examines the present account

Will rejoice and rejoice again,

For it proves that truth stands.

ARGUMENT.

[Col. 1111]

146 There was a certain noble man named Proterius,

From the city of Caesarea in Asia Minor, most eminent.

He had a beautiful and only daughter,

Whom he devoted to chastity.

He had a delicate servant,

Who, seized by love for the girl,

Approached a magician and sought his advice concerning marriage with her.

The magician replied that he wished to fulfill the girl’s desire

And make her insane with love,

If the servant would devote both himself and his soul to the devil.

The servant agreed.

After giving the demon a written document,

He obtained possession of the girl,

And the wedding was celebrated.

Afterward, however, when the girl discovered that he had been devoted to the gods [i.e. demons],

She sought a divorce from the marriage,

Led him into the church,

And through Saint Basil the document was recovered from the demon.

The man was restored to the Christian faith and to the Church.

THE STORY FOLLOWS.

[Col. 1111]

[Col. 1111B] At the time when Basil,

A man rich in virtues,

Ruled the holy Church with just moderation,

Having obtained the office of ruler of the Caesarean see,

A very distinguished man lived in those parts,

Named Proterius,

A count, revered by the people,

Powerful in nobility and wealthy in possessions.

He had one child, a daughter,

And no other heir remained to his great property.

He loved her with tender affection,

With dutiful feeling and paternal devotion,

Wishing that the never-dying soul of his daughter

Might be adorned with the jewels of perfect virginity

Rather than that her mortal body be adorned

With the fleeting pomp of the world.

He arranged for her to associate with holy maidens,

Who, clothed in a sacred garment and dedicated to Christ,

[Col. 1111C] Were likewise kept within the enclosed confines of a monastery.

But the teacher of crimes, who deceived the first-formed man,

Detesting the righteous man’s praiseworthy vow,

Made his own servant burn madly

With love for the girl mentioned above.

The very wretched man,

Pierced by the arrows of love,

Burned all the more intensely in his heart

The more his passion increased.

He remembered that he was unworthy of such a marriage

And did not dare to reveal the new torture of his heart.

147 At last, while seeking a magician,

He found one and revealed to him

The bitter secret of his sorrow,

Promising him a considerable reward

If he could join the mind of his master’s tender daughter

To love for her servant.

Then his perverse companion replied:

[Col. 1111D] “For I confess that I am not powerful enough

To join a servant in marriage with his own lady.

[Col. 1112B] But if you properly strive to obey my master,

Who is acknowledged to be the prince of eternal darkness,

He himself can certainly fulfill your desire at once,

Provided that after this you do not wish to venerate Christ’s divinity.”

The wretched man, badly blinded in his frenzied heart,

Promised that he would consent to these instructions.

Then the magician ordered his servant to write:

“Great prince of hell, mighty ruler of the abyss,

Grant your servants always permission to tempt

Those who have been washed in the fountain of baptism,

So that they may perhaps assign some of them to you,

Snatched away from Christ’s flock,

And so that the portion that follows you may always increase.

For this reason, rejoicing greatly,

I have sent you this man,

With the purpose that, once his plan has been completed,

You may duly make him your disciple.”

Having written this document,

He also gave it to the wretched man

To stand above the tomb of a pagan during the night

And, standing there, humbly to give it to the lord of the abyss.

Therefore, if you desire to enjoy the embraces of your master’s daughter,

First deny Christ with your mouth, as prescribed.

The wretched man, immediately embracing this wicked command

And delightedly following the path by which the magician ordered him to go,

Humbly prayed for the help of the ancient dragon,

Who tries to bring death to his own friends.

Without delay, the infernal servants came swiftly,

And the malicious spirits led the wanderer,

Rejoicing greatly, to a council of the dwellers in darkness.

148 There, the inventor of crime and every deceit,

The prince of doomed legions, himself doomed,

[Col. 1112D] Sat in the midst, surrounded by a raven-black army,

[Col. 1113A] Secretly stretching cunning snares before the unwary,

And unfolding the ambushes he had previously devised.

He asked what each of his servants had done in their crimes.

When he examined the letter sent to him,
