He used these words,

Growling like a lion in anger,

And terrifying the wretched man with savage speech:

“You Christ-worshipers have never remained faithful to me.

But as soon as I fulfilled your pleasant desire,

You immediately fled back again to your Christ,

Utterly rejecting me after receiving such great gifts.

You believe that Christ possesses such compassion

That he would not delay returning pardon

To anyone who asks for it,

And that, once converted, he would not reject him after any crime,

But would grant him the sacred baptism of Christ’s worshipers.

Therefore confess that you wish to remain with me forever

And suffer torments in hell.

Then hand me the document written with your own hands.”

I shall show more quickly how much my power can accomplish.

Soon afterward the wretched servant, ensnared by these evil counsels, wrote his own ruin with a laughing heart and gave the cause of his destruction to the hideous enemy.

The latter, rejoicing exceedingly in his condemnation, immediately sent the infernal ministers from his glad heart, so that they might make the mind of the unhappy virgin burn with incestuous love for her own servant. The fragile mind was struck by the blandishments of love.

She, born of a noble lineage, suddenly cried out, desiring that the servant’s companionship be granted her, and poured forth these words to her father:

[Col. 1113C] “Now pity your daughter, dearest father, and quickly give me to the young man whom I love, lest I die sorrowful, wasting away through the weariness of my heart.”

When her father heard this, he spoke with bitter tears:

149 “Alas, alas! What are you suffering, as though you were your father’s only hope? Tell me, I beg you: who has deceived you with treacherously flattering words? Or who has surrounded you with feigned blandishments? Did I not, desiring that your heavenly homeland be restored to you, finally dedicate you to Christ, your heavenly Bridegroom, so that you alone would worship him in your chaste mind forever, and, after the bonds of death, would resound his praises with the heavenly hosts, added to the virgin choirs?

“And now you burn with lustful love for a servant!

[Col. 1113D] “But now, my child, I shall entreat you in a subdued voice: cease from such great folly, lest you wickedly disgrace your entire noble family. Yet if you attempt to persist in this evil undertaking, you will disgracefully bear a child without delay, dearest daughter.”

But she, utterly scorning her father’s counsel, said to her parent with a biting expression:

“If at last you delay fulfilling my desire, you will learn that your illustrious offspring will soon die.”

Then the old man, against his will, overcome by bitter threats, gave his daughter to the servant in marriage, and at the same time bestowed upon them a small but valuable portion of property. Afterward, with a bitter heart, he said to his daughter:

“Unhappy child of an unhappy parent, you who are the honor and the grief of your mother who bore you, [Col. 1114A] and the shameful disgrace of our entire family: you now rejoice wretchedly in the servant dear to you, and afterward you will be seized, grieving, by eternal punishments, because of such a marriage, contracted through Satan’s deception.”

Christ, the beloved Savior of the world, felt compassion for them—he who, through the flood of his poured-out blood, mercifully saved those captured and held in the enemy’s hidden bonds, and who is pleased to offer gracious help to the fallen.

Soon the erring woman was told that her wretched husband was not a Catholic, nor did he wish to set foot across the threshold of the holy temple, because he was surrendering himself to the power of the greedy serpent, denying the sacred faith of the sect and even the name of Christ.

150 When she recognized that she had been miserably deceived, and heard the speaker’s words with attentive ears, she fell to the ground, her limbs trembling and weakened. She tore out the hair from the crown of her head and repeatedly struck her breast, scattering these words toward heaven amid her tears:

“Whoever refuses to listen to loving parents is never saved; this is proved by what has happened here.

“Alas, alas! Why was I born to behold the light of day? Or why was I not immediately consigned to the grave, unhappy that I might not fall into the dark pit of death?”

While she continued to speak in sorrow, her wicked husband suddenly arrived and falsely swore that the things said about him were untrue.

But she answered him with a firm denial:

“If you are not now guilty of a grave offense, come with me joyfully to the holy church tomorrow, and there celebrate the solemn rites of the sacred Mass.”

Overcome by this sound reasoning, the unhappy man confessed the cause of the crime he had committed. Then she laid aside her womanly softness, assumed manly strength with a prudent heart, and immediately ran to the blessed Basil. She also fell prostrate before his sacred footsteps and, with a troubled heart, spoke these words:

“Holy man of God, mercifully help us wretched beings, and drag us from the dark jaws of the savage enemy, who boasts that he can destroy our frail minds.”

When she had disclosed to him the nature of so great a crime, the Lord’s bishop turned to the wicked servant. He addressed him with kindly words, asking whether, after his crime, he wished to turn his mind back to Christ.

But the man, despairing of salvation, said to him:

“If it could be done, I would willingly desire it in my mind. But the deed remains fixed in my mind, since I wickedly handed myself over to the enemy in a letter I wrote, and with a blinded heart denied the name of Christ.”

The man of God replied:

“Do not pretend that you must despair of forgiveness, as though every hope of seeking pardon had been taken from you. The only-begotten Son of the Father, the most merciful Judge of the world, never rejects anyone who turns to him. If you lament your guilt, he rejoices to provide healing.

“Therefore now abandon the deadly depths of sin, and flee to the sure harbor of mercy, [Col. 1115A] which receives safely all who turn toward it.”

With these admonitions he corrected the wretched little man. He also voluntarily shut him in a dark cave, so that there he might lawfully lament his enormous sins.

After three days he came to him again, asking whether he could endure such a struggle.

The man, utterly exhausted, answered him:

“I scarcely endure the punishments of the black spirits. They continually strike me with whips, and very often assail me with hard stone missiles. Moreover, they always confront me with bitter reproaches, saying that I did not previously approach them unwillingly, but freely, giving myself over to their power without compulsion.”

Then the physician of the languishing soul, well instructed, ordered that the exhausted man be refreshed and immediately withdrew.

After a short time he came again, asking what the man was then suffering in the dark cave.

He replied:

“Certainly I am better, holy father, because I hear the terrible voices only from farther away.”

Then the bishop, rejoicing secretly in his heart, went out, following his previous custom.

At last, after forty days had passed, during which the fallen man lamented his bitter sin, he found joyful the one whom he had believed would be sorrowful.

When he marveled at the joy dear to him, the sinner, now thoroughly cleansed by abundant tears and confident of forgiveness, said to the holy man:

152 “I certainly hope, holy father, that through you I shall be saved, because in a dream I saw you engage in combat for me with the savage and wicked serpent, [Col. 1115C] whom you suddenly conquered by heavenly power.”

When the bishop heard the speaker’s words attentively, he sang Christ’s praise for his mercy. He drew the captive’s limbs out of the black place and, under cover of night, brought him to a cell of his own, which was joined to the side of the consecrated church.

There he ordered the faithful people to assemble, so that they might spend the night together in devoted prayers, and so that the good Shepherd, through his accustomed mercy, might join the straying sheep to the flock of his own fold.

When the sun had risen and driven away the black shadows of night, the bishop took the aforesaid little man by the right hand and entered the church, bringing him with him.

As soon as he touched the venerable threshold with his sacred feet, the demon, secretly hiding there with evil designs, appeared. He suddenly dragged the man upward with great force, seizing his left hand by a hidden trick.

Then Basil, acting with a firm command, said to him:

“Wicked thief, return the workmanship of the eternal King, and quickly abandon the prey you have seized by theft.”

The common enemy of all replied to him, filling the air with perverse barking:

[Col. 1116B] “Why do you strive by force to take from me my own servant, who of his own accord submitted his neck to my chains? The letter which he himself certainly handed to me I shall show Christ at the future time of judgment.”

The holy man again gave him this answer:

“By the command of Christ himself, the just Judge, I hope that you will immediately return that very little letter.”

After these words, the faithful crowd prayed to the Most High, pouring forth prayers from a devout heart, so that he might strengthen his faithful shepherd against the enemy.

At once the deceitful document fell from above [Col. 1116C] before the feet of the holy and beloved shepherd.

Then the people, rejoicing with their worthy bishop in a devout heart, sent their voices with songs of praise all the way to heaven, praising Christ, benign in his accustomed mercy, who had drawn the captive back from the mouth of the ancient lion.

Let us also, applauding, send our voices toward heaven, praising the Lord Christ with a joyful heart, so that in his mercy he may grant us such hope of forgiveness.

To him alone let glory, victory, and power remain forever as a song of praise. Amen.

[Col. 1115]

# THE STORY OF THE PASSION OF THE HOLY DIONYSIUS, ILLUSTRIOUS MARTYR

## Argument

Dionysius, an Athenian philosopher, visited the Egyptian prophets because of the study of astronomy. After being instructed by them, he observed an eclipse of the sun without the moon’s interposition at the hour of the Lord’s Passion. Returning to Athens, he erected an altar to the unknown God, as Lucan says:

> “And an altar dedicated to the sacred rites  
> Of the unknown God of Judea, among the images…”

When the apostle Paul saw it and inquired about the founder of the dedicated altar, he discovered that it was Dionysius the philosopher. He converted him to the faith and ordained him bishop of Athens.

When Dionysius had been encouraged through a vision, while staying with the presbyter Polycarp, to undergo martyrdom, he came to Rome to Clement, the first pope after Peter. Clement entrusted him with a mission to preach the Gospel in Gaul and Paris. There, under Domitian and during the rule of Sisinnius, governor of Gaul, he was crowned with martyrdom together with his companions, and left an effective proof of his holiness: after he had been beheaded, his headless body carried its severed head for two leagues to the place appointed for burial.

## The Story Begins

[Col. 1117]

[Col. 1117A] When the Maker of the highest, middle, and lowest order was suffering the bitter punishment of death upon the cross, nocturnal darkness spread around the world, and the sun, laying aside the brightness of its serene rays, celebrated the Lord’s funeral rites in the service of Christ.

When the blessed astrologer Dionysius saw this—at that time he was studying the art in the lands of Memphis, the art that teaches the movements of the stars and the course of the sun—he was astonished. He began to investigate in the books he read whether an eclipse of the sun could then be taking place.

But when he perceived that the darkness was greater than usual, he considered it worthy to record the day and year, suspecting that something astonishing was perhaps being signified, something that the mystery of the darkness would later disclose.

He conjectured that the benevolent God, attested by these signs, [Col. 1117B] hitherto unknown, would soon be acknowledged by the world.

When he had drunk his fill from the streams of that aforementioned art, he sought Athens and returned to his native city. Among the profane images of foolish gods, he ordered an altar to be constructed and set up, assigning it suitable painted inscriptions, and decreeing that it should be consecrated in honor of the unknown God.

When the teacher Paul saw it, he kindly asked in generous words who this unknown being was. Dionysius himself, the city’s first man, explained the reason for which he had built the altar. Thus, as their alternating speeches contended, the man who had been unbelieving yielded, thoroughly overcome, to faith.

After this, Paul went out and gave sight to a blind man, whom he ordered to hurry into the city. When the aforementioned ruler saw him restored to sight and believed in the sign wrought by divine power, he quickly hastened, eager to go with his beloved wife to the place where he knew Paul to be blessed. A great company of his household accompanied him; they too had been baptized together, and were completely cleansed from the old filth of sin.

And the man who had been leader of the people who worshiped images was therefore appointed bishop over a Catholic community.

155 Once made bishop, he was adorned with remarkable goodness and diligently fulfilled the office entrusted to him. By letters to those absent and by words to those present, he led them to follow the worship of the true faith.

For once, as he traveled, scattering the seed of the Word as well, he is said, when evening was already approaching, to have sought hospitality with a holy Cretan presbyter named Carp.

The latter was deeply troubled by bitter sorrow, and anger burned in him beyond what was lawful, because some pagan, through perverse persuasions, had caused a Christian to abandon the sacred faith.

The bishop perceived that the presbyter was sorrowful and kindly asked him the cause of his sadness. Gently soothing him with benevolent admonitions, he urged him to lay aside his excessive anger and pray for the condemned sinners, so that, quickly converted and reconciled to Christ, [Col. 1118A] they might receive the gift of his mild mercy.

He repeatedly admonished him that hope of forgiveness should be denied to no one who was willing to lament his guilt.

But the man, devoted to sorrow and scorning mercy, instead, gnashing his teeth and wasting away in the fury of his heart, proceeded to curse the wretched people with harsh words, declaring that those who had dared to live without the true God were worthy of neither form of life.

After he had finally carried out this grievous course of action, he arranged his limbs for sleep with a sufficiently troubled mind.

Immediately a vision was shown to him, with the cells of heaven opened, and it calmed the turbulence of his spirit.

He had seen the Most High, flashing with wondrous brightness, seated and surrounded by angelic ministers. From heaven a great fire descended swiftly, as though it had been sent forth as an avenger of certain crimes.

When he turned his eyes downward again and surveyed the earth, he saw a dreadful abyss gaping below, filled with various serpents and furnished with punishments.

156 Above it, the wretched people were slipping about on their feet and clinging to the upper shore, weeping. Serpents that had emerged tormented them and forced them to enter the deep abyss with them.

When Carp saw this, filled with still greater fury, he lamented that the wretched had not been hurled down, and, repeating his curses again in a confused voice, immediately prayed that divine vengeance might destroy the guilty.

He had spoken, and Jesus, benevolent in his accustomed mercy, ready to show pity from the throne of heaven, began to address Carp, reproving his harshness:

[Col. 1118C] “Strike me, if you can, rebellious Carp, you who thirst so eagerly for the destruction of the guilty.

“Behold, I am the ruler of heaven and the destroyer of death, ready in mercy to suffer again for the human race, if sinners cannot otherwise be saved—those who, after committing sin, learn to lament their guilt.

“I do not consider it a small matter if the work of my right hand should perish: that which I made beautiful, that which I restored after it had been corrupted.

“Choose now either to follow sweet mercy and reign with me forever in heaven, or, through the harsh savagery of your cruel mind, to be handed over without end to the punishment of the deep abyss.”

The man, exceedingly justly chastened by these admonitions, became gentle and was made an example of mercy for all to imitate.

[Col. 1118D] After this, the bishop, renowned for the fame of his highest merits, resolved to seek proud Rome, desiring to offer himself to death for Christ together with Peter, Paul, and the teacher.

But those men received the martyr’s palm before he himself, on his arrival, had entered the gates of Rome. Clement, Peter’s disciple and venerable throughout the world, was then properly governing the summit of the apostolic See.

He received the bishop who was arriving with loving devotion and honored him worthily with the greatest affection. Finally, after a long period of time had passed,

157 during which the venerable servants of the Lord remained there, [Col. 1119A] when the most gentle heavenly mercy of the King had wished to tear apart with the rich beam of eternal light the black darkness of ancient errors, by which the western regions were then grievously surrounded, the holy pope, first warned by the divine Spirit, addressed the bishop in fitting and friendly words, urging him to scatter the seeds of the divine Word among the nations.

“Behold,” he said, “O soldier of Christ, brother Dionysius: a great harvest of the Lord is growing throughout the regions of the world, producing countless ears of ripe grain, but very few workers stand ready for the harvest.

“Therefore you, who steadfastly drink from the sacred fountain of books and are most learned in divine worship, go forth safely, following the example of Paul your teacher, and bring many peoples under Christ’s command.

“I believe that you have the same authority of jurisdiction which we know Christ gave to his teacher Peter, and which I, as his successor, have lawfully received: to release those who have been converted in mercy and to bind the guilty.

“Now receive the Gauls to be taught, as I entrust them to you, and let Gaul be marked by your strong teaching, so that she may rightly be celebrated as the worthy disciple of an apostolic man.

“Do not fear to enter rebellious nations, which still snarl savagely against the truth. Only trust that you will be preserved in the starry hall of the Most High Father with an eternal reward proportionate to the suffering you endure for Christ.”

Encouraged by these kindly exhortations of the pope, the bishop hastened to the borders of the western region and soon set foot within the walls of the city of Paris.

[Col. 1119C] There, because of the fertility of the beautiful place, all the nobles of Gaul frequently gathered.

When he began to scatter the sacred seeds of the divine Word, Christ mercifully deigned to perform many miracles through him, so that the softening of the rebellious people’s hearts might lead them to forgiveness whenever they repeatedly saw the signs.

But when the number of the believing people had greatly increased, as the day of Christ’s inspiration had spread and grown among all, the savage deceit of the ancient dragon raged at this.

It scorned the loss of so many souls, which it had previously held in the bitter snares of error. Therefore the father of deceit and teacher of wickedness soon incited the unjust king Domitian to issue savage decrees of death against Christians.

[Col. 1119D] He sent his evil orders throughout his entire kingdom, commanding that all worshipers of Christ be condemned to death.

Accordingly, Sisinnius, governor, immediately giving wicked assent to this abominable command, ordered that the bishop be brought before him in chains—the man whom he had rightly learned to be the teacher of the Gauls. After first having him beaten with harsh whips and repeatedly subjected to bloody punishments, he ordered him shut away in the black darkness of a prison, together with his two disciples, whom no fate would ever force to be separated from their beloved teacher.

But the illustrious bishop did not cease, even in the prison’s caves, to render worthy service to the Lord. He taught the people who gathered diligently and celebrated the solemn rites of the sacred Mass as usual.

When he was about to break the heavenly bread, a new light suddenly shone in the sorrowful cave. In it the splendid Ruler of the starry court appeared, accompanied by an angelic host, and consoled his beloved disciple. Giving him the holy body, he comforted him with these words:

[Col. 1120A] “Receive, my beloved, the venerable body which I shall soon reveal to you in its mystery.

“For your reward remains with me, excellent and everlasting, and the highest salvation is granted in the Father’s court to those who devoutly strive to obey your commands.

“Stand firm, preserve the faith patiently, so that the renown of your praise may grow. Whatever you ask of me in sacred prayers, you will be able to obtain through the gift of my mercy.”

Rejoicing in such strong consolation, the witness no longer feared to suffer any torment for Christ’s name.

After this, the three witnesses were led out of prison together, compelled by the order of the proud prefect, and were asked whether they wished to yield to harsh punishments.

In complete harmony, they confessed in a clear voice that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are the true God, alone and eternally one. They testified that they preferred to die for Christ’s name and to be torn limb from limb by renewed punishments rather than ever submit their necks to false gods.

The profane prefect was even more offended by this. Like a lion roaring in no small anger, he ordered that the necks of Christ’s athletes be cut off and that all who had been washed in baptism be killed by the sword.

After countless executions had been carried out as he commanded, the bishop was dragged together with his venerable companions to the place of martyrdom, where the sentence of decapitation was to be completed.

They went joyfully, singing praises to the Lord and ready to give themselves over to death.

Then the bishop, raising his eyes and hands toward heaven, poured forth these fitting thanks to the Most High:

[Col. 1120C] “My God, my Maker, my most merciful Ruler, who mercifully grant me to live upon the vital breath, you have given me the light of profound understanding, so that I might search out the secret of your mysteries.

“You alone I praise; with all my heart I bless you, and with all my limbs I offer you devoted thanks for all the gifts of mercy bestowed upon me.

“And I beg you, great and everlasting King of majesty, to deem me worthy to grant me an everlasting crown, and to grant it also to my companions, who are now dying for you.

“And preserve your people with fatherly mercy, the people whom I have fed and nourished for you with the word of faith.”

When he had duly completed these prayers, the two disciples together with the holy bishop knelt down, bending their necks, and received the executioner’s blow.

Their celebrated confession remained such that, even after their bodies had fallen silent when their necks were cut off, their tongues, still moving, sang praises to the Lord.

The severed body of the dying bishop suddenly rose, shining with a clear radiance. Carrying his own head firmly in his arms, [Col. 1121A] he descended with steady steps from the deep mountain where he had completed his precious martyrdom. He crossed two thousand paces of the difficult road and came to the place worthy to preserve his body.

As he descended and moved swiftly along, angelic hosts accompanied him in serene light, resounding Alleluia to God with ringing voices.

After these signs had occurred, the faithful people gathered. They honored the martyr’s venerable body at the very place he had marked for himself when he came to rest after his journey, placing it in a tomb with the highest honor and celebrating the funeral rites of so great a patron with mourning.

There Jesus Christ made his power shine forth through glorious signs on account of the martyr’s venerable merits.

[Col. 1121B] Sight is granted to the blind, speech to the mute, hearing to the deaf, and firm steps to the gout-ridden, when the holy witness prays. The sick, weakened by various illnesses, come there frequently and return joyful, their limbs renewed.

Here too, not rarely, gracious comfort is given to the sorrowful, and the gift of forgiveness is brought from the citadel to sinners—those who pour out the sacred vows of their prayers at the martyr’s tomb while lamenting their own guilt.

May his holy intercession continually commend us to Christ, and, by praying for forgiveness of our sins, obtain that he mercifully pardon our faults and grant us a share in everlasting life, so that we may deserve to praise him joyfully forever.

He who, after the hard struggles of his saints, will always grant his martyrs the double reward of honor: while their holy souls rejoice together above the heavens, their dead limbs too rejoice in the tomb, [Col. 1122B] repeatedly glorified and resplendent with the titles of miracles.

To him belong perfect salvation, everlasting victory, power, praise, honor, dominion, and every glory forever and ever.

[Col. 1121]

# THE STORY OF THE PASSION OF SAINT AGNES, VIRGIN AND MARTYR

## Argument

Agnes was a Roman girl of exceptional beauty and a Christian. The son of Sempronius, count and prefect of the city, fell desperately in love with her. At first he tested her with words and gifts, hoping that she would return his love.

She steadfastly declared that Christ was her Bridegroom, to whom she had dedicated herself in perpetual chastity. Finally, the prefect dragged her to the temple of Vesta, where the Vestal virgins served the goddess Vesta—that is, the eternal fire—and ordered her to sacrifice to her.

When she refused, the prefect, driven mad with anger, had her taken to a brothel, intending to expose her to the lust and mockery of all. When frenzied young men wished to assault her, an extraordinary light immediately covered the brothel and repelled those who sought to violate the virgin.

At last the prefect’s own son came, more insolent than the others, and attacked the virgin. He immediately fell headlong to the ground and breathed out his life.

His father, grieving over his son’s sudden death, accused the virgin of magical arts. But the virgin, in order to show that the deed had been accomplished by Christ’s power and not by magic, resurrected the dead man to the praise of God.

When the father saw this, he was uncertain what to do with the virgin and accepted the faith of Christ. When the matter was reported to the priests, they, fearing for themselves and their idols, stirred up a tumult and wished the virgin to be put to death.

The prefect, now a believer, withdrew so that he would not be forced to condemn a believer, and another was substituted in his place. This man cast her into the fire. The flame, fleeing from the virgin’s body, consumed and burned many of those standing nearby.

Finally, when the virgin consented to die, she was pierced through by the executioner’s sword. Her parents received her body for burial, while her spirit was joined to the choirs of virgins with Christ.

## The Story Begins

[Col. 1121]

[Col. 1121C] The virgin who, wishing to despise the empty splendors of the world destined to fall and the fragile luxury of the flesh, deserved to be called the eternal Bride of the King—she who, for the honor of her angelic virginity, wishes to shine in the starry court of her heavenly Bridegroom, joined to the heavenly beings with a radiant crown, and, following the Lamb, to sing a melodious song—may she preserve with pure and sincere love the sign of praiseworthy virginity that she bears.

She who marks her head for Christ with a sacred veil may cling steadfastly to him with tender devotion and place him above all other friends: he who, shining exceedingly with beautiful radiance, rightly surpasses all the sons of women.

[Col. 1122C] Many sacred maidens, once properly inflamed with love for him and steadfast in heart, chose to die and be killed by savage punishments rather than corrupt the honor of their distinguished virginity.

Among them was Agnes, a virgin renowned throughout the world, adorned with worthy praise by the right of her Bridegroom. By proclaiming Christ’s beauty, unlike that of all others, she commends to the sacred virgins the pledge of his love—he who alone was born of a virgin, and who is the Bridegroom and glory of chaste souls.

Thus Agnes, a virgin most illustrious in merits, whom our unadorned Muse sets forth in song, was a most noble inhabitant of the famous city of Rome. She came from a renowned lineage of blessed parents, [Col. 1123A] whom illustrious nobility and noble authority exalted.

Her origin corresponded to her nobility. She was beautiful in face, adorned with the splendor of faith, exceedingly distinguished in merits, and celebrated throughout the world.

Already washed in the pure water of sacred baptism and cleansed from the stains of ancient sin, she devoted herself wholly to Christ with a benevolent mind. Striving to preserve her blessed virginity, she courageously scorned every carnal affection and undertook the hard struggle of the celibate life, so that, victorious over the enemy who urged corruption, she might deserve to be joined to the holy heavenly beings in the sky.

But when two periods of five years had passed in swift succession, and she had also completed three further years of age, the son of Count Sempronius, prefect of the city, [Col. 1123B] a distinguished youth in the flower of his lineage, saw the beauty of her lovely appearance.

Suspended by an excessive affection of heart for her, he chose her alone above all others to love. He considered himself fortunate and worthy of honor if he deserved to enjoy the sweet companionship of so exceedingly beautiful a girl throughout his life.

Therefore he approached her, accompanied by many friends, wishing to marry the venerable Bride of Christ. Carrying many gifts from his ancestral treasures, he foolishly hoped that he could corrupt the virgin’s steadfast mind with gifts and join her to his shameful love.

But Christ’s virgin scorned the gifts as dung, immediately disdaining the weight of the gold offered and the bright splendor of various gems. She is said to have reproached the mad young man with these words:

[Col. 1123C] “O son deservedly condemned to eternal death, O hunger for crimes, scorner of the Almighty, depart from me quickly; flee and go away.

“Do not think that you can corrupt my pure heart, which has been anticipated by the noble love of a more excellent Lover. I bear the sweet love of him whose beautiful sign of faith I carry on my forehead and throughout my entire body. He marked me and bound me tightly to himself, so that my mind would no longer presume to seek another friend, but would learn to embrace only him.

“He, powerful in virtue and radiant with every beauty, surpasses all heavenly and earthly beings.

[Col. 1123D] “The Father Almighty, without a mother, generated him before the ancient ages of the world, equal in divinity and not lesser in majesty; through him he made the ages for himself.

“And, without a father, his mother bore that same one, nursing her own Maker, born in time. At last the sun’s splendor and the moon’s gleaming brightness marvel at his exceedingly beautiful form, while the circles of the world praise the Lord with their shining rays. All the stars, serving at his command, complete their course throughout the ages according to the orders given them.

“To him all the angelic hosts continually offer service, crying out his worthy praises.

“Wondrous is your goodness and exalted your power; sublime your glory, everlasting the harmony of your peace, praiseworthy your mercy, and exceedingly benevolent your will.

[Col. 1124A] “Such is my Lover, whom I love, and whom, I confess, alone above all others must be worshiped.

“He has betrothed me to himself with such a pledge of love, endowing me as a bride with a radiant crown. He has encircled my neck with precious gems and hung shining earrings from my ears, providing me with splendid garments of varied adornment.

“His sweetness certainly flowed from his mouth; it nourished me and fed me with sweet food, like honey’s nectar or an abundance of pleasant milk.

“Moreover, he built for me an everlasting bridal chamber, shining with various gems and golden metals. In it instruments resound with melodious harmonies, singing a sweet song to me throughout the ages, while also modulating the praises of my beloved Bridegroom.

“They continually urge me toward chaste devotion to him, whom I shall love secretly in the affection of my heart, and I suffer no loss of maidenly modesty.

“But when I may perhaps deserve to use his embraces and, like a bride, be led into his radiant bridal chamber, I shall remain a virgin, undefiled and chaste.

“To him alone I shall owe the keeping of perpetual faith; to him I entrust myself with all the effort of my heart.”

When the wretched man heard this, pierced by the darts of love, he groaned, repeatedly drawing long sighs because he had not obtained what he had sought with his blind heart.

Grieving over this and wasting away in excessive sorrow, that most foolish of men fell into bed. He falsely pretended to be ill and concealed the love that had been the great cause of his pain.

[Col. 1124C] Before long, evil rumor made it known that the prefect’s son was bound by excessive sickness.

Physicians immediately gathered as though in an army formation and applied medicines suited to various illnesses. But none of these helped the mad young man.

At last they understood, and soon reported to his father, that this was not a symptom of illness but of a powerful love from which his son was suffering.

When the father heard this and discovered the cause of the illness, he turned swiftly into anger, growling like a lion. In raging fury he began to ask who possessed such imperial power that the proud virgin, relying on vain hope, believed she could disregard the son of one who, deservedly renowned among all the people, had been advanced to the highest honor.

When he had said this and barked in excessive fury, he learned that this very Agnes, washed in sacred baptism and a Christian from her earliest years, [Col. 1124D] declared Christ to be her Bridegroom because of her love for preserving her virginity.

When he learned this, he rejoiced with a wicked heart, hoping that he could rightly drive the tender girl through savage punishments to worship the gods and thus finally satisfy his rage, which had been inflamed by the contempt shown to his sick son.

Therefore he ordered her to be brought quickly before him. When she stood there, trembling from no fear, he first coaxed her excessively with friendly persuasions.

[Col. 1125A] Then he harshly compelled her with bitter reproaches to join herself willingly to the love of his son, to worship the images of the gods, and to deny Christ.

But Christ’s virgin could be overcome neither by punishments nor by any blandishments. She kept without deceit the pledge she had made to her first Lover, secured by the sign of faith.

The prefect, renewing his wicked persuasion, said:

“If you truly wish to remain an untouched virgin, quickly submit yourself to the great goddess Vesta and associate yourself with her priestly maidens, so that you may become worthy to serve her forever.”

The prefect said this, but Agnes answered:

“If I was right to scorn your son, who possesses reason and uses all his bodily senses, but is governed by a soul that will never die—even though he rightly ought to be shut in the depths of the abyss for the many errors he has committed, unless, coming to sound understanding and repenting, he has himself washed in the pure water of baptism—by what threats, or by what persuasions, do you think you can finally compel me to worship images?

“What help in life can I hope for from these lifeless and profane monsters, the work of craftsmen, which, formed from metal, bear only the false appearance of limbs, perform no function of a moving body, and show nothing of a living creature? They cannot benefit themselves, nor can they help me.

[Col. 1125C] “When she had spoken these words, the prefect Sempronius said:

“‘I recognize that you are flourishing in your earliest years, small in understanding and tender in age. Therefore, sparing your childish simplicity, I prudently bear with you, wanton girl, so that by this forbearance I may soon bend your neck beneath the sacred feet of venerable Vesta and make you placate, as is right, the power of our gods.

“‘But if, scorning my mild mercy, you resist and do not follow my commands, I shall no longer spare you. I shall exercise just force and order you to be shut away in the recesses of an obscene house, [Col. 1125D] where women rejoice in shameful crimes. I shall make you the companion of polluted prostitutes, so that you, born from a noble lineage and endowed with distinction, may become every disgrace and shameful confusion to your family.’

“But the sacred virgin, greatly trembling at these threats, courageously gave the prefect this answer:

“If you knew the true God whom I worship, and his power, which endures without end and by which he always mercifully strengthens his own ministers and shatters all the deceptions of the ancient enemy, you would not pour such words from your mouth, nor repeatedly heap so many dreadful threats upon me.

“Therefore I, who, by following the better faith of Christ, know him and am known by him, hope never to be defiled by the stains of sin, since his heavenly right hand defends me, and to overcome all the impurities of fragile flesh.”

[Col. 1126A] At these words the governor, stirred to even fiercer anger, ordered the venerable bride of the heavenly King to be dragged naked from her clothing, and naked in every part of her body, through the whole gathered crowd,

168 and commanded her to be shut up in the chambers of a brothel, where lustful young men, deprived of reason, delight in conversation with sinful women.

But Christ, granting consolation to his own bride, did not permit her to be touched by any insults.

Yet when she was stripped completely of her covering, at once her hair grew abundantly and densely. Falling in long locks from the crown of her head, it descended until it touched the tender soles of her feet, and her whole body was covered by her hair as though by a garment.

And when, sadly, she crossed the threshold of the brothel,

[Col. 1126B] she immediately sensed a sweet fragrance of perfume, and saw the shameful place shining with wondrous brightness, though previously it had been filthy with dark shadows.

And when, compelled, she entered the filthy chamber, an angel of the Most High stood graciously before her—he had been the unquestionable guardian of her body—and offered her a garment gleaming with snowy brightness, fashioned very suitably to her measure.

Having put it on, she raised her voice toward heaven, continually resounding sweet thanks to Christ, whose aid she had experienced under so great a burden of danger, and by whose fatherly assistance she had been protected, lest the ancient enemy be able to corrupt her by his deceits.

Meanwhile the young men, raging with blinded hearts, came running from every direction in gathered bands,

[Col. 1126C] vying with the wicked zeal of perverse minds to see who might enter first, or who might discover whether the virgin, supported by the protection of her Christ—she who had always despised carnal loves—could now persevere in the vow she had begun.

Nor was there any delay: they perceived, and could not deny, that no one who believes in the Lord and hangs upon him in firm hope will ever be put to shame throughout eternity.

For whoever, driven on by his proud spirit,

169 rashly enters the foul recesses of the house, as soon as he saw rays of light shining wondrously, and the angelic guardian of the dazzling garment, seized by immense terror at the astonishing sign, immediately fell prostrate at the sacred feet of the girl and begged that the bonds of his errors be loosened.

He declared that the true God ought rightly to be worshiped, and that he consoles all who worship him.

Thus the place of crimes became a house of prayer.

At last the governor’s son, wickedly insane, came—the blessed virgin had endured violence on his account. As soon as the wretched man entered with a laughing heart, he neither praised the Lord nor rendered honor to the one whose grace shone in the gloomy chamber. Rather, rejoicing, he confidently approached the building, hoping to enjoy the virgin’s sweet embrace, since he was already languishing with a lawful love for her.

But Christ’s compassion and exalted power, firmly resisting his perverse desire, protected his own servant from corruption and handed the wretched man over to reprobate death.

[Col. 1127A] For as soon as he had hastened there at a swift pace, where Agnes had sung praises to the Lord in supplication, the unhappy man suddenly collapsed, his limbs giving way, slain by Christ’s power.

When his father heard this, the wretched man came in tears, accompanied by a great crowd of people. Calling himself miserable, he raised his voice on high and addressed the holy girl with these words:

“O wicked and cruel woman, in whose tender body there is no womanly heart, but only savage ferocity and an excessively bloody will, gnashing your teeth in beastlike fashion, tell me what cause compels you to destroy my son, who was all the honor of his family and the hope of his father, once born from the stock of such a fortunate offspring,

[Col. 1127B] but now, to my misery, the son for whose funeral I am bereaved?

170 “From this it is evident, therefore, that your excessively corrupt mind drinks deeply from the streams of magical deceit, since you have been able to kill the youth flourishing in his first years by taking away his sweet life.”

But the holy virgin was not broken by these insults. Indeed, she did not return a bitter answer; rather, pouring sweet words from her resonant mouth, she spoke eloquently in well-ordered reasoning:

“I was not the cause of death for the young man who perished; rather, he himself was the kindler of his own death, because in his folly he had despised the God whose glory shines forth in this chamber.

“But now, so that his majesty and exalted power may become fully clear throughout the world,

[Col. 1127C] I humbly ask his gracious compassion to command that the rigid body grow warm again and restore a new man to his limbs, revived once more.”

She spoke, and ordered all who stood nearby to withdraw. Then she prostrated herself on the ground and, pouring forth prayers in tears, asked the Lord that forgiveness be granted to the sinful man.

As she prayed and pleaded for the wretched man’s life, an angel stood beside her, raised up the one who lay prostrate, and offered him the comfort of friendly conversation. By the powerful word of God he commanded the dead man suddenly to live again, drawing breath once more.

The man rose from the ground as soon as he was commanded, his entire body fully restored to strength. Scattering sweet praises toward heaven, he immediately offered thanks with a joyful mind

[Col. 1127D] to Christ the victor, giver of death and life.

Then, wholly restored to his original form, he came forth alive, he who had been bound by death. Presenting himself to his sorrowing father, he became a cause of rejoicing to the man for whom he had been a cause of grief.

Then, repeatedly striking the depths of heaven with his cry, he used these words to persuade them earnestly:

171 “Believe, Roman citizens, I beg you; all of you believe that Christ is the true and eternally one God, with the Father seated on high and with the Holy Spirit, always reigning, holding the scepter of heaven.

“Under his authority, he embraces all things and governs everything with the reins of immeasurable goodness. He alone is to be prayed to, worshiped, and loved.

“He first, by sudden death coming more quickly than I, deigned to put an end to my great folly, when I was wandering and desiring perverse things; and afterward, as usual, ready to show mercy to one who had gone astray, he was moved by the exceedingly earnest prayers of the virgin Agnes and restored me renewed to life.”

[Col. 1128A] But when the father saw his son emerge alive again, perfect in appearance and full of beauty, the son whose death he had mourned with bitter tears, he was immediately awestruck with wonder at the extraordinary novelty of the sign, yet rejoiced with a glad heart.

Then, embracing his neck with fatherly affection, he gave tender kisses to his beloved child. Calling out that Christ was the true God, he declared that he recognized his swift compassion, and that bitter death had yielded to his command, returning alive the one whom it had been swallowing as he died.

Indeed, all who stood there, filled with wonder, joyfully raised praises to heaven, praising the holy and blessed name of the Lord.

The bishops, however, unable to bear this with their cruel hearts, stirred up a considerable revolt, calling Agnes sacrilegious and criminal.

They said that she ought to be killed immediately by bloody punishments, because on her account their images and all the laws of their sacred rites were being held in contempt.

Then the governor, saddened and troubled in heart,

[Col. 1128C] grieved for the holy girl with sorrowful mind. Yet, completely uncertain about her, he did not know what course he ought to follow or what action remained to be taken.

172 He did not wish to destroy her, but neither could he defend her.

At last he withdrew in grief and left another to exercise the office of judge with lupine ferocity. This man was called Aspasius and followed a profane ritual. He quickly ordered Agnes to be thrown into the fire, wickedly agreeing with the bishops’ evil wishes.

But the chaste body, which needed no cleansing from any defilement and which carnal love had not inflamed, was not harmed by the fire then present, nor could the flames touch it.

Finally, by divine power, the flames were divided and gave spacious room to the virgin’s prayers. Bursting forth, raging with excessive heat and fury, they first destroyed all the executioners by burning them; then, licking the surrounding unbelieving crowd on every side, they quickly struck down many bands of people.

[Col. 1128D] But the devout virgin alone stood unharmed by the heat, playing amid the crackling locks of flame. With her palms turned toward the stars, she prayed to God, using this prayer on her lips in a melody of praise:

“Father of the Word, all-parent, creator of the world, who, reigning with your beloved Son before all ages, and with the Holy Spirit, coeternal with both, are rightly praised, worshiped, venerated, and loved:

“I praise you alone; in praising you I bless you; and to you I devotedly render perpetual thanks, because, supported by the protection of your Son, I have never succumbed to the deceit of the ancient serpent.

“Rather, with chaste body, pure heart, and secret inner being, I have thoroughly passed beyond all the impurities of the flesh,

[Col. 1129A] while likewise overcoming the punishments of the sacrilegious tyrant.

“Therefore, rejoicing greatly in you over this act of devotion, I now hasten to come to you with joyful mind, desiring to undergo the laws of death and quickly be released, so that I may truly deserve to behold without end

“you whom I have sought and whom alone I have always loved.

173 “In your mercy, receive graciously within the chambers of your kingdom the soul driven from the body for your sake. There, exercising your rightful power under the threefold name, you, one King of the universe, rule through the ages of the threefold realm, and govern all these things with the scepter of supreme divinity.”

When the prayers of the one praying had thus been duly completed, the fires were extinguished: the entire pyre suddenly died out, and the ash itself, growing cold in its embers, became so completely devoid of heat

[Col. 1129B] that it retained not even a single spark.

As this astonishing sign was now becoming clear, the more Christ’s power revealed itself to the world, the more the unjust judge was tormented in his bitter spirit, breathing out the fury of a greater rage.

He could not tolerate the holy girl’s remaining alive after so many miracles had repeatedly been performed through her. Therefore, driving in his sword and piercing her tender throat, he cruelly pierced the neck of the outstanding martyr.

By doing the opposite of what he hoped, he benefited the one whom he had freely wished to harm: he sent to heaven the woman whom he had wickedly tried to remove from the world.

But when, wounded by the deadly blow for Christ’s sake, she returned her final breath to the Lord as she died, and, her faith preserved, joyfully fell asleep in him,

[Col. 1129C] bands of angels, descending swiftly from heaven, stood beside her soul, shining with snowy brightness and suffused with the light of heavenly radiance. They gently received it and joyfully lifted it through the air.

With fitting hymns resounding in divine praise, they carried her swiftly beyond the fires of heaven and led her into the star-bearing palace of her heavenly Bridegroom. From him she immediately received a radiant crown, as the honor due to her pure virginity.

[Col. 1130A] Nor, therefore, was she deprived of the sign of her triumph: she took up the palm of martyrdom, to be borne without end. Thus, a blessed martyr and victor in a twofold contest—

174 of body and of mind, always resisting the flesh—she enjoyed the doubled prize of the eternal kingdom and shone brightly among the virgin hosts,

like lilies mixed with beautiful rosy redness amid the delights of flowers glowing in varied colors.

Meanwhile the sacred care of her noble parents, having prepared the venerable funeral with great ceremony, covered her completely with every honor in the earth’s embrace.

Nor did the solicitude of parental love neglect even the tomb of the consecrated virgin itself, which had been made venerable for preserving her remains, but kept watch over it during the nighttime hours.

[Col. 1130B] While the ever-watchful parents, according to their custom, celebrated vigils for their child with faithful devotion, a vision of this kind was shown to them from heaven.

They suddenly saw companies of virgins descend, falling swiftly from the hinge of heaven, beautifully adorned and dressed in perfect splendor. Among them they saw their Agnes, shining with similar brightness, martyred for Christ.

At her right stood a lamb whiter than snow.

She knew that they were worthy of honor because of their faith. She addressed them gently in friendly conversation, saying:

“Now rejoice with me, and rejoice forever, for I am in the light-filled palace of the heavenly King, eternally joined to these holy virgins.

“And now in heaven I am united to him in the sweet embrace of love whom I always worshiped on earth with faithful mind, desiring to behold him without end.”

[Col. 1130C] After these words she suddenly departed from them.

They, made exceedingly joyful by such great consolation, dried the tears poured out over her death and sang praises to the Lord with melodious voice—he who, after difficult struggles, mercifully grants the rewards of eternal life to his holy witnesses.

---

# Hrotsuitha’s Poems on the Beginnings of the Gandersheim Monastery and on the Deeds of Emperor Otto I

(Apud D. Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae historica*, *Scriptores*, vol. IV.)

[Col. 1129]

## Preface to the Poems

[Col. 1129D] About seventy years after the Saxon poet expressed in verse the deeds of Charlemagne and the conversion of the Saxon people to the Christian faith, Hrotsuitha, a nun, undertook to celebrate in Latin verse the beginnings of the Gandersheim monastery in which she lived and the deeds of the emperor Otto the Great.

[Note: [Col. 1129] In the preface to the *History of Mary*, at the end of the *History of the Resurrection of the Lord*, in the preface to *Gangolf*, and in the preface to *Pelagius*, the name is consistently written HROTSUITHA; only once, in the preface to the comedies, do we read HROTSVIT.]

She was, as may rightly be believed, born in Saxony during the reign of King Otto I.

[Note: [Col. 1131C] “Since I was not yet vigorous in mature age, nor making progress in learning,” she herself writes modestly of herself to the abbess Gerberga in a preface composed around the years 960–965; and in the poem on the construction of Gandersheim, verse 526, she says that she was born long after the death of Duke Otto, who died in the year 912. Therefore she must scarcely have been the niece of the abbess Hrotsuitha, who died in 927.]

She was entrusted to the monastery founded by Count Liudolf, the great-grandfather of Otto I, which received its abbesses from his descendants, and there she devoted herself to learning letters. While she was neither strong in mature age nor, as she modestly says of herself, advancing in knowledge, “she strove to compose some kind of text from the sentences of Scripture that she had gathered within the ark of the monastery.”

In writing books she first benefited from the instruction of Rikkardis, a most wise and kind teacher, and of other women who taught in her place; later she studied under the guidance of the abbess Gerberga.

[Note: [Col. 1131C] Preface to the *History of the Blessed Virgin*.]

Gerberga was the daughter of Henry, duke of Bavaria, and Judith, the daughter of Duke Arnulf. From approximately the year 959 she governed the Gandersheim monastery for more than forty years.

[Col. 1131B] [Note: [Col. 1131D] She died in the year 1001, on the Ides of November.]

At the beginning of her rule, although younger in age, she was more advanced in learning, as befitted an imperial niece. She piously instructed Hrotsuitha in several authors whom she herself had previously learned from the wisest teachers.

[Note: [Col. 1131D] Preface to the book on the history of the Blessed Virgin Mary and the poem to Gerberga, verses 6–12.]

Hrotsuitha, who delighted in the study of sacred and classical books, first tried her hand at writing in the *History of the Blessed Virgin Mary*, in metrical form, and in poems on the Ascension of the Lord, Saint Gangolf, the passion of Saint Pelagius of Córdoba, and the steward Theophilus. Later she added poems on Proterius, the passion of Saint Dionysius, and Saint Agnes.

[Note: [Col. 1131D] See the preface to Gerberga in the poem on Proterius.]

In all these works she followed her books, although she had heard the passion of Pelagius from an inhabitant of the city in which he suffered.

Then, when she had noticed that “many Catholics read the inventions of Terence very frequently and, delighted by the sweetness of his language, were stained by knowledge of wicked matters,” she imitated that poet by writing six Christian comedies, “so that, in the same kind of composition in which the shameful acts of wanton women were recited, the praiseworthy chastity of holy virgins might be celebrated.”

[Col. 1132A] [Note: [Col. 1131D] Preface to the comedies.]

She composed all these works not for the sake of boastfulness or empty glory, but “so that, with the devotion of a suppliant mind, she might consecrate to God’s service the talent received from him.”

[Note: [Col. 1131D] Ibid.: “So that I may return the talent I received to its giver.”]

Nevertheless, she did not lack fame. Adorned with the praises of philosophers,

[Note: [Col. 1131D] Letter to certain learned men.]

she soon became so widely known that the modest virgin could call herself, in her own words, “the loud voice of Gandersheim.”

[Note: [Col. 1131D] Preface to the comedies.]

In the summer of the year 965, Otto II, then ten years old, obtained from the virgin a promise that she would undertake to celebrate in verse the deeds of his father, the emperor Otto.

[Note: [Col. 1131D] Preface to Otto II, verses 6–7. Since the book seems to have been begun before the death of Bruno, archbishop of Cologne, who died on 11 October 965, and completed after news of Otto II’s Roman coronation in 967, on 25 December, had reached Saxony, but while Archbishop William and Queen Mathilda were still alive—they died on 2 March and 14 March 968—I infer that the poem was requested by King Otto during the summer of 965, when he was staying longer than usual in Saxony.]

She began the work, intending to carry it through the Roman coronation of the year 962, without the aid of any book, but following the reports of those who brought her the events to be recorded.

Since she openly says this,

[Col. 1132C] [Note: [Col. 1132C] Preface to Otto I, verses 14–23.]

the book offered to the Ottos and, so to speak, dictated by their relatives William, Gerberga, and their other attendants, presenting only what seemed agreeable to them, can by no means be marketed as history in the strict sense.

Yet even so the book should not be despised. Its simple and clear narrative, generally following the order of events, and several matters that one would otherwise seek in vain commend it.

[Note: [Col. 1132C] For example, the time when Duke Henry married Judith, and the seemingly authentic narrative of Adelaide’s rescue.]

The virgin must sometimes be said to have harmed the truth more by what she omitted than by what she reported.

[Note: [Col. 1132C] For example, in describing the rebellions of Duke Henry, whom one must remember was Gerberga’s father.]

Thus, to the great detriment of history, nearly half the work has been lost—namely, almost the entire narrative of the events occurring in the years 953–962.

The book, completed at the end of January or in February of the year 968,

[Note: [Col. 1132C] See note 11; thus it was completed at the same time in which Widukind completed the first part of his work.]

was offered to the abbess Gerberga. From her it was handed over to Archbishop William, who sent it to the Ottos after judging it.

The death of William, which occurred on 2 March,

[Col. 1132C] should not be thought to have harmed the book, since soon afterward Hrotsuitha began another poem, namely, on the foundation of the Gandersheim monastery and on the ancestors of the Ottos.

[Note: [Col. 1132D] Certainly after the earlier poem had already been completed; for the mention of the Roman coronation of Otto II in verse 79 proves that the Gandersheim foundation was not begun before the year 968, while verses 81–82 mention the book on the praise of the Ottos.]

[Note: [Col. 1132D] Trithemius did not see this poem. He lists the remaining works of Hrotsuitha, as they already existed and still exist in the codex of Saint Emmeram, now in Munich, in his *Chronicon Hirsaugiense*. But the works he lists at the end—“also a book of various poems and epigrams, and certain letters not without elegance”—must be understood not as lost little works, but as poems, epigrams, and letters dispersed throughout the codex. This is shown by the fact that the unique codex has a blank membrane at the end, and that Celtes published the codex as it is today as early as 1501, whereas Trithemius began the *Chronicon Hirsaugiense* indeed in 1495 but did not complete it until 1511. He therefore must be thought not to have seen the fuller codex. In *De SS. ecclesia*, chapter 391, he omitted these items.]

In this book she relates the history of the monastery under its first abbesses, the daughters of Liudolf and Oda, down to the death of Christina in the year 919. She drew it from writings preserved in the monastery: the *Life of Hathumod*,

[Note: [Col. 1133D] Verses 104 and following.]

the documents of Liudolf the founder,

[Note: [Col. 1133D] Verses 118 and following.]

those of Louis the Younger and Arnulf,

[Note: [Col. 1133D] Verses 444 and following.]

and the accounts of the elders,

[Note: [Col. 1133D] Verse 522.]

since she herself was much later than the events she narrates and admits that she did not know any of the men and women whom she celebrates.

[Note: [Col. 1133D] Verse 526.]

Both poems, a testimony to pious character and to learning—rare above all among women of that age—prove that their author read the classical poets of Rome assiduously.

In another place she herself confessed that she had erred in distinguishing the nature of syllables and in composing expressions.

[Note: [Col. 1133D] In the preface to Book I.]

Here too she sometimes made mistakes both in meter

[Note: [Col. 1133D] For example, *Gandersheim*, verse 270, and *Otto*, verse 230. She also admits hiatus.]

and in the forms of words.

[Note: [Col. 1133D] For example, she uses a deponent with passive force in *Gandersheim*, verse 239, and *Otto*, verse 459, *veneratur*; in the prologue to *Otto II*, verse 38, *tueantur*; she uses a passive with deponent force in *Otto*, verse 593, *recitati sunt*, and verse 141, *moderat*. Following Terence’s comedians, she writes in this way.]

On the other hand, the ancient forms *mis* and *tis*, used instead of *mei* and *tui*, show her study of Plautus and Terence.

She takes pleasure in using diminutives frequently.

[Note: [Col. 1133D] Words such as *gratiola*, *perpaucula verbula*, *locellus*, and others of this kind occur.]

The poem *On the Beginnings of the Gandersheim Monastery*, preceded by the hexameter Lives of the most blessed bishops Anastasius and Innocent,

[Note: [Col. 1133D] Bodo, in Meibom, *Scriptores*, II, 494.]

was preserved throughout the Middle Ages at the place itself. It passed into the Gandersheim chronicles, such as we read them after Eberhard translated them into the German language at the beginning of the thirteenth century.

[Note: [Col. 1134C] Leibniz, *Scriptores*, III, 149 and following. From it derives the rhymed chronicle of the Brunswick dukes in Leibniz III, 1 and following.]

In the middle of the sixteenth century, with some leaves omitted and several sentences worn away by age, it was entrusted to Bodo of Clus, a canon.

[Note: [Col. 1134D] He says that he used it in his *Syntagma Gandersheimense*, in Meibom, *Scriptores*, II, 479, 494.]

It is said that he never restored it, but secretly carried it away together with the other codices and documents of the monastery of Clus.

[Note: [Col. 1134D] Leuckfeld, *Antiquitates Gandersheimenses*, p. 276.]

The poem itself therefore remained hidden until the beginning of the eighteenth century, when Johann G. Leuckfeld discovered a fifteenth-century copy.

[Note: [Col. 1134D] According to Harenberg, whose testimony is uncertain, p. 1074. Leibniz, in the *Acta Eruditorum* for 1708, p. 488, calls the book “not very recent.”]

Leuckfeld obtained it by purchase from the abbess of Gandersheim. At approximately the same time it appeared in Leuckfeld’s *Antiquitates Gandersheimenses*, p. 410 and following, and in Leibniz’s *Scriptores rerum Brunsvicensium*, vol. II, p. 319 and following.

[Note: [Col. 1134D] Already in 1708, in the *Acta Eruditorum*, p. 487, it had been announced that the poem had been incorporated into Leibniz’s second volume, which, however, was not published complete until 1710; Leuckfeld therefore anticipated it in 1709.]

Leuckfeld published only the text as it was read, in sufficiently corrupt form, in the codex. Leibniz, however, corrected many passages by conjectures that testify to ingenuity and learning, and for this purpose also made use several times of Bodo’s book.

Using both editions, and perhaps also the Gandersheim codex itself or its copy,

[Note: [Col. 1134D] These may have been the “two manuscripts” whose owners, he asserts on p. 1074, did not wish to reveal their names.]

Harenberg, in his *History of Gandersheim*, p. 469 and following,

[Col. 1134A] corrected Leibniz’s text on the authority of those editions, though often also according to his own judgment and “the most evident prosodic principles”; yet he did not correct it everywhere.

In preparing the materials for our edition, when I visited Gandersheim in the spring of 1835, I learned that not only had Hrotsuitha’s codex, which had been acquired in the previous century, been removed, but I also found that all the other codices of the library had either been carried away or ruined by damp and rain.

Having abandoned every hope of obtaining the codex, and learning that it had been deposited neither in the Göttingen or Wolfenbüttel libraries nor in the archives of the Duchy of Brunswick, I used in its place:

1. A copy of the codex transmitted to Leibniz and corrected in his own hand, which I preserve in the Royal Library at Hanover; and

[Col. 1134B] 1b. The Leuckfeld edition;

2. Bodo’s *Gandersheim Syntagma*, which borrowed much from Hrotsuitha’s work;

3. Leibniz’s conjectures, many of them noted by him in the margin; and

4. Harenberg’s edition.

With these aids I attempted to restore the text as far as possible.

I was much more fortunate with the poem on the deeds of Otto, which I restored with greater success by means of the unique codex:

1. Formerly belonging to Saint Emmeram at Regensburg and now preserved in the Royal Library at Munich, which I examined there in 1833.

The codex, written in a hand from the end of the tenth or beginning of the eleventh century, in quarto,

[Note: [Col. 1134D] Compare *Archiv*, VII, 409–411.]

contains three works by Hrotsuitha: namely, legends of the saints, comedies, and our poem. Each page contains twenty-four verses. There is almost no punctuation, except for a point at the end of most verses. The scribe did not understand the text very well and sometimes corrected his own errors.

The first letter of each verse is written alternately in red and black. A larger letter indicates that the author is beginning a new subject.

To the great loss of literary scholarship, one quire and, elsewhere, six leaves have fallen out. This must have happened before the end of the fifteenth century, when Conrad Celtes arranged for the codex to be printed, adding in his own hand the headings of chapters as he thought appropriate and quite a few corrections.

[Col. 1135A] 2. The Celtes edition appeared in *The Works of Hrotsuitha*, published at Nuremberg in folio in 1501.

In many places the text departs from the unique codex, partly through the editor’s error and partly because Celtes judged that passages which seemed corrupt ought to be emended.

In this respect he undoubtedly sometimes served Hrotsuitha well, and certainly surpassed all the other editors by a great deal. At other times, however, without sufficient reason, he altered by his own judgment a text that was genuinely good or at least tolerable, or allowed it to be reproduced carelessly.

Moreover, by failing to weigh the chapter headings carefully and inserting them into the work, he caused learned men to doubt Hrotsuitha’s reliability, since they believed that she had written against the truth of history. This blemish will finally be erased in our edition.

The Celtes edition, corrected in a few places by Justus Reuber according to the well-known rules of grammar, was reprinted in 1584 in the *Scriptores Germanici*. In 1621 it was published by Heinrich Meibom together with Widukind in folio, enlarged by the *Life of the Nun* and historical notes, which our readers may dispense with without any loss, but with the text altered incorrectly in several places.

For the fourth time it was inserted in 1688 by Heinrich Meibom the Younger into the *German Writers*, vol. II, p. 709 and following,

[Col. 1136A] with the text even more corrupt.

Heinrich Leonhard Schurzfleisch repeated the Meibomian text in his edition of *The Works of Hrotsuitha*, p. 175 and following, in 1707, preceded by a dissertation on the life and works of our poetess and accompanied by an index of Latinity. Yet, using the first edition, he corrected Meibom’s reading in several places and, departing from the earlier editors in five passages,

[Note: [Col. 1135B] In the preface to Otto I, verse 27; in the preface to Otto II, verse 12; and in verses 321, 434, and 752.]

has the true reading of the codex, perhaps transmitted to him at his request by the monks of Saint Emmeram.

Finally, in 1726 Georg Christian Joannis compiled a sixth edition in the second edition of Reuber’s *Scriptores Germanici*, combining the Meibomian and Schurzfleischian editions. Once he also arrived by conjecture at a true reading neglected by the editors.

[Col. 1136B] Since matters stand thus, I restored the text according to the authority of the unique codex and undertook to emend only passages that were plainly corrupt, using either Celtes’ conjecture or my own.

[Note: [Col. 1136B] The diphthongs *ae* and *oe*, which in the codex are very rarely represented by a simple *e*, have been consistently restored.]

I therefore adopted the division into chapters as the codex presents it, replaced the headings inserted by Celtes into the text and full of errors with the numbers of the years, and now offer a better edition of the work.

[Col. 1135]

# Poem on the Beginnings of the Gandersheim Monastery

Textual apparatus for the following verses: [Col. 1135] In verse 1, manuscript 1 supplies *supplex* (“suppliant”). In verse 5, I have consistently emended the name to *Liudulfus*; the printed editions read *Liudulfus*. In verse 11 manuscript 1 has *pdixi* for *praedixi* (“I mentioned before”); in verse 12 it has *pnobilium* for *praenobilium* (“very noble”); and in verse 18 it has *Hludovici* for *Hludowici* (“of Louis”). In verse 19 source 3 conjectures *primis* (“earliest”), whereas manuscript 1 has *primus* (“first”). In verse 25 source 4 has *majori* for *majoris* (“of greater”); in verse 26, *fit par* (“he becomes equal”) is absent from manuscript 1 and was supplied by source 3; verse 27 has *Quinque* (“five”) in source 4 instead of *Quique* (“and who”); verse 31 has *conjunx* for *conjux* (“wife”); and source 2 wrongly read *Prodae* for *Aedae* (“of Aeda”). In verse 37 manuscript 1 reads *Promissura* (“would promise”) for *Possessura* (“would possess”), while source 3 conjectured *Promeritura* (“would deserve”). [Col. 1137] Manuscript 1 has *pulcrae* for *pulchrae* (“beautiful”); the editor states that he consistently corrected this spelling. It reads *nec non* (“and also / not only”) for *nec* (“not”), *effatu* for *affatu* (“with speech”), *trepidas* (“you tremble”) for *trepides* (“do not tremble”), and *Nunctio* for *Nuntio* (“I announce”). Source 3 conjectures *clarescet* (“will shine”) and source 4 also reads it, whereas manuscript 1 has *clarescat* (“may shine”). Source 3 reads *domnae* (“of the lady”), manuscript 1 *domni* (“of the lord”), and copy 1b *domini* (“of the lord”); *claram* (“illustrious”) is absent from source 4. The editor corrects *inclytus, sylva, sydera* in manuscript 1 to *inclitus, silva, sidera* (“renowned, wood, stars”), and notes that he made the same orthographic correction elsewhere. Source 3 conjectures *pater* (“father”), while manuscript 1 and copy 1b have *patris* (“of [his] father”); source 3 conjectures *fecit* (“he caused”), while manuscript 1 has *facit* (“he causes”).

[Col. 1135C] Behold, my humble devotion, suppliant with lowly mind,

is eager to unfold the beginnings of fortunate Gandersheim,

the monastery which the powerful dukes of the Saxons, rightful in authority,

Liudolf the great, and his illustrious son Otto,

who completed the work begun, constructed.

The proper order of these matters now demands

that the illustrious construction of Gandersheim

be sung in fitting verse by our monastery’s poet,

since it is known that the same duke whom I mentioned,

Liudolf, reverently built it.

He, born from a very noble line of parents,

and answering in his origin to his own nobility,

grew honorably among all the Saxons

in excellent character and in the practice of goodness.

For he was vigorous, exceedingly handsome in appearance,

wise in speech, and cautious in all his actions,

and alone the hope and entire glory of his family.

[Col. 1135D] Thus, enrolled in the military service of the great Frankish king Louis

almost from his earliest years,

and honorably raised to the highest dignity,

he soon received the countship of the Saxon people.

[Vers. 17] And quickly endowed with the greater authority of office,

[Col. 1136C] he became the equal of princes and inferior to no duke.

He surpassed all his ancestors in piety

and was no less distinguished by the splendor of his honor.

His wife, therefore, was the very noble Oda,

born from the illustrious line of powerful Franks,

the daughter of Billung, a kindly prince,

and of the noble Aeda, a woman of good reputation.

[Note: [Col. 1135] The second edition wrongly read *Prodae*.]

This Aeda had been accustomed frequently to entrust herself and her whole life to the Lord in prayer.

By persevering diligently in pious works,

she deserved, having been well instructed by heavenly promises,

to learn, through the blessed Baptist of Christ, that her descendants

would one day possess the glory of imperial authority.

Therefore, once, when dawn was cleaving the nocturnal darkness

[Col. 1136D] with the radiance of its shining light,

she lay prostrate beside the sacred altar, as was her custom,

consecrated under the honor of John the Baptist,

striking the innermost chambers of heaven with continual prayer.

And while she was relaxing her mind in those devotions,

she saw before her the feet of a man standing nearby.

Somewhat disturbed, she pondered deeply in her heart

[Vers. 40] who he might be, who had presumed to disturb her solitude

at that hour so suitable for prayer.

Turning her face slightly from the ground and lifting it,

she saw a young man gleaming with wondrous brightness,

clothed in a garment of long-haired yellow material,

as though it had been woven from the hairs of a curved camel.

On his beautiful face, of extraordinary whiteness,

a small beard, matching the dark color of his hair,

formed a kind of shining emblem of radiance.

When the matron saw him and believed that he was not mortal,

she was struck with astonishment and, in the manner natural to a woman’s mind,

suddenly fell prostrate, compelled by great fear.

But he, reviving her trembling spirit with gentle speech,

said: “Do not tremble, nor be afraid in confusion;

but, once the heavy terror of fear has been driven away, recognize

who I am. I have come bearing great consolations for you.

[Col. 1137B] “For I am John, who deserved to baptize Christ in the clear waters.

Because you have frequently honored us, I announce this:

your illustrious offspring will establish a cloister for holy virgins,

a peace and triumph of the kingdom,

while their religion remains steadfast through the devotion of kings.

“Thus your descendants will one day shine throughout future ages

at the summit of so great an honor,

so that at that time no earthly king

will by right be able to equal their power.”

He spoke, and suddenly returned and entered the heavens,

leaving the kindly matron a sweet consolation.

This great promise of magnificent distinction

marked out particularly the illustrious offspring of the lady Oda,

from whom was born the renowned duke Otto.

He fathered King Henry, well suited to the scepter,

[Col. 1137C] who was the father of the venerable Otto Augustus,

the one who, supported by the king’s perpetual power,

after he ruled the Saxon kingdom in place of his father,

blessed by divine will a second time,

deservedly received that same seat of Roman empire

and the scepter of imperial authority.

His blessed namesake and likewise blessed son,

by the pious and enduring king’s kindness,

he caused to ascend the same imperial seat

and to enjoy an equal share of dominion in equal splendor.

This brief page of the book demonstrates these matters

more fully in the work that I wrote about the causes of these events.

[Col. 1137D] Namely, the poem on the deeds of Otto.

Now our devoted pen must be turned

to completing the work already begun.

But when the venerable Oda had been joined

[Vers. 86.] [Col. 1137D] to Liudolf, her elder, in a lawful union,

[Col. 1138A] she advanced in renown among all our countrymen

through her character and deeds, walking along the path of piety.

Living according to the example of her venerable mother, she commended herself wholly to the Lord in sacred prayer, holding in her heart her mother’s counsel to establish a monastery. Hence she frequently urged her husband, with exceedingly gentle persuasion, to build at his own expense, from his own treasures, a monastery suitable for divine praises, in which maidens consecrated to the Lord under the sacred veil might dwell in chastity to the end and devote themselves to the service of their holy Bridegroom.

Therefore, faithful in yielding to these counsels, the man readily consented to the prayers of his chosen wife; and thus, alike in their common effort and intention, they both immediately began to serve God.

They possessed a small church situated on the heights beyond the banks of the Gande; hence they called the celebrated place Gandersheim. There, while a more suitable site was being sought for the worthy celebration of the Lord’s service, they joined many maidens together in a common way of life and resolved that their daughter Hathumod should become like them in habit and their perpetual companion.

And so that she might become the ruler of the maidenly flock, they first entrusted her, for respectful instruction, to a certain venerable abbess who, succeeding in the place of those who had formerly presided, had at that time obtained the see of Herford.

With such purpose Liudulf, the distinguished husband, and his wife meditated divine service. Thereafter, having received letters from their own lord, namely the beneficent and pious King Hludowic, they went to Rome with a considerable retinue by his permission, and visited the seat of the holy father with fitting gifts and gracious prayers, asking through his assistance that they might be able, according to God’s will, to accomplish their vows.

At that same time the blessed Pope Sergius held the primacy for governing the Church. When he had read the king’s letters sent to him, he perceived that a duke worthy of the highest honor had arrived; and, inquiring into the reason for which he had come there, he showed himself gracious toward him in gentle speech.

The duke Liudulf, prostrate with his wife and entreating him as a supreme pontiff rightly worthy of veneration, used these words, filled with every sweetness:

“Renowned pope, do not be harsh toward your pilgrims, who have come from distant shores of the earth to venerate you with the gifts of our service.
