With all the effort of our ardent minds we strive to establish a monastery to be consecrated under the honor of the Lord. Therefore it has seemed especially right to us to seek from you the certain consolation of counsel and duly to disclose our purpose to you in prayer—you who rule as head of the Church throughout the whole world—so that, if our devotion should perhaps please you, with the assistance of your fatherly goodness we may accomplish in deeds what we bear in our vows.

“And you—we most justly ask your counsel—accept our gifts with a merciful heart and, moved also by love for the everlasting King, grant us sacred relics of saints, in whose honor the whole monastery may fittingly be dedicated and by whose sacred merits it may be protected.

“And so that it may remain free from the yoke of earthly kings throughout the ages and suffer no violence from worldly lords, we entrust it solely to the authority of the apostolic ruler, both for defense and for governance.”

Thus spoke the duke. And the supreme bishop Sergius began in this way:

“I embrace you with a gentle heart, my son, and I likewise embrace your beloved wife. Rejoicing in your pious undertaking, I rejoice with you, nor do I believe that it is lawful for me to refuse you what you request.

“There were once two powerful rulers of this Church: the most holy bishop Anastasius of this see, and his sacred fellow apostle Innocentius. After the shepherd Peter and the teacher Paul, they shone forth with the highest distinction in the merits of the Church. Their bodies have been preserved with such great care up to the present by all the rulers of this city that no one has ever removed even a fragment, and the full number of their sacred limbs remains intact.

“But since I ought by right to grant the pious petitions, I shall freely give you relics of both, openly cut from their sacred bodies, if you confirm to me by an oath that you will cause these relics to be venerated in the temple of the monastery already mentioned, built under your protection, to the end of time, with sacred hymns resounding there night and day and with a splendid light always burning.

“Just as you requested, we also assign this monastery to the authority of the apostolic see, so that it may be secure from earthly lords.”

The duke, rejoicing in his heart at these promises, said that he would soon respond to the sacred commands of the supreme pontiff with dutiful deeds, and that he would promptly undertake the building of a church worthy of it.

As the true judgment of many learned men relates, there was at that time, close to the monastery, a little wood surrounded by shady hills, by which we too are encircled. In the wood there was also a small village in which Liudulf’s swineherds were accustomed to lodge. Within the enclosures of a certain man, they laid their weary bodies down to rest at night, while they were supposed to pasture the pigs entrusted to them.

Once, when the venerable feast of all the saints was to be celebrated after only two days, the swineherds themselves saw many bright lamps burning in the wood amid the darkness of night. At this sight they all stood amazed, wondering what the new vision of shining light meant for them, as it cleaved the night’s darkness with wondrous radiance. Trembling, they told this to the master of the house, pointing out the place that the light had flooded.

Desiring to test clearly by sight what he had heard, he stayed outside the dwelling in their company and kept watch through the following sleepless night, not closing his eyes, though weighed down by sleep, until once again they saw lamps burning—surpassing the former ones in their increased number—at the very same place, but apparently earlier than on the previous night [the printed wording about the hour is corrupt; see textual note 31].

As soon as Phoebus scattered his first rays from heaven, this bright sign of a happy omen became known to all through the joyful report. Nor could the worthy duke Liudulf remain unaware of it: the report quickly reached his ears.

He himself, keeping careful watch on the sacred night of the approaching feast to see whether the heavenly vision would afterward display any such sign, observed that same wood throughout the night with many others. No sooner had the black night covered the earth and the forested valley all around than many lights were seen arranged in order throughout the place where the splendid temple was to be founded. Together they cleft the shadows of the trees and the darkness of night with the clear brilliance of their powerful light.

Then all those standing there, offering praise to the Lord, affirmed that the place ought to be sanctified for the service of him who had filled it with light.

The duke, therefore, not ungrateful for the heavenly kindness, immediately ordered the same valley to be entirely cleared by cutting down the trees and removing the thorns, with the consent of his beloved wife Oda. He had the wooded place, filled with fauns and monsters, cleansed and made suitable for divine praises [Vers. 232.].

After first securing the funds that the work required, he immediately built the walls of a beautiful church, which the splendor of the shining light had marked out.

For this reason the construction of our monastery, begun under the honor of God, was already advancing favorably. Meanwhile, the stones suitable for the building could not at all be found in those places; hence the completion of the temple that had been begun was delayed.

But the abbess Hathumod, hoping in the Lord and believing that through faith she could obtain everything, repeatedly wore herself out with excessive labor, serving God night and day in sacred devotion. Together with many of her associates, she asked that heavenly assistance be brought to her as a consolation, lest the work so well begun should remain unfinished.

Nor was there delay: she perceived that the heavenly mercy she sought was present and ready to show compassion toward her prayers. For while, fasting and devoting herself to sacred prayers, she lay prostrate one day beside the altar, she was commanded by the instructions of a gentle voice to go out and follow a bird which, as she advanced, she would see sitting on the summit of a certain great rock.

Embracing the command in a ready spirit, she went out, believing from her heart the words of the one who commanded her. Taking with her skilled masons, she proceeded quickly wherever the gracious Spirit led her, until she came to the noble temple that had been begun.

There she saw a shining white dove sitting on the lofty summit of the designated rock. At once it flew ahead with outspread wings, moderating its flight in an unfamiliar manner so that it could traverse the furrows of the air in a straight course and allow the young maiden of Christ, walking with her companions, to follow.

When the dove in flight had reached the place which we now know abounds in large stones, it descended and struck the earth with its beak. Many stones lay hidden beneath that mound of earth.

When the most worthy virgin of Christ saw this, she was certain, she ordered her companions to cleanse the place and, by digging, to break through the heavy mass of earth.

When this had been done, through the gracious goodness of heaven a great abundance of large stones was revealed. From these, the walls of the monastery and the temple that had been begun could obtain all their stone material [Vers. 275.].

From then on, with ever greater effort of mind, the builders of the temple to be consecrated under the honor of the Lord pressed on with the work, day and night alike.

But Duke Liudulf, who was its first founder and from whose care the origin of the whole construction proceeded at the prayers of Oda, did not, alas, bring the dutiful work to completion. Touched by the cruel blow of natural death, he was compelled to return his breath to his Maker before the house of the Lord had been entirely completed (in the year 866). In dying, he entrusted the whole burden and care of this unspeakable labor to his dear surviving wife and to his children, the dukes mentioned above, asking them in prayer to complete the entire construction of the monastery.

His venerable body was then suitably committed to the bosom of the earth in the old temple. But after some years his bones were transferred and placed here in this new church.

Perhaps for this reason God removed him from this world while he had scarcely reached middle age [the wording is corrupt; see notes 50–51], so that afterward the mind of the illustrious lady Oda, intent more fully upon God, might attend to heavenly things, entirely free from every carnal affection.

Yet God did not deny her the consolation of assistance; rather, in his accustomed mercy, he continued to provide fresh aid, by which, supported, she might enrich her nuns with all the things that our way of life requires.

Therefore the illustrious Frankish king Ludowicus, by the favor of the eternal and merciful king, chose her daughter, named Liutgard, as his consort in the kingdom and his perpetual companion. He was the son of that Ludowicus, by whose gift Liudulf had first received dominion over his own people.

This woman, made our queen for our prosperity, renders worthy service to her holy mother, providing the assistance of the king, her own lord, and promising many benefits to our monastery.

Meanwhile the blessed virgin of Christ, Hathumod, after she had governed the flock for twice eleven years, passed more swiftly through death in Christ to the stars (in the year 874), entrusting the tender flock to Gerberga to govern.

She had been betrothed to a certain illustrious and exceedingly powerful man named Bernhard. But she had secretly consecrated herself to Christ, truly her heavenly Bridegroom, under the sacred veil, rejecting in her heart a mortal bridegroom altogether.

Yet, to avoid an uprising, she could not immediately put aside her garments glittering with gold; instead, she put on her customary costly attire.

Meanwhile the man whom the bride of God had rejected arrived, seeking to make his intentions known to her through an open conversation. He learned, however, that she had made a vow and wished to preserve her maidenly chastity.

When she delayed and did not wish to proceed quickly, he greatly feared that what he had previously heard might prove true. Impatient at the delay, he appeased Lady Oda with prayers, until she herself ordered her daughter to come forward, beautifully adorned in costly clothing and also in jewels, after the fashion of brides.

When Bernhard saw the woman he desired, he is said to have addressed his beloved in these reproachful words:

“I have often learned, as evil rumor has spread, that you are striving to break our agreement and entirely dissolve the covenant of faith that must be kept.

“But now I am compelled by the command of the king, our lord, to hasten to the war that is about to take place. Therefore this is not now the time to discuss the matter. If I return safely, with health accompanying me, know without doubt that I shall join you to myself and utterly overturn your empty vow.”

He had spoken, and, moved in spirit, raising his right hand, he swore by his sword and by her white neck that what he had declared would be fulfilled in deeds as far as he was able.

Gerberga, therefore, answered in a modest voice:

“I entrust myself wholly, and my life as well, to Christ; and I ask that his will concerning me may be done.”

When this conversation had thus been completed in mutual speech, Bernhard soon departed and quickly experienced his own fate: he learned that no proud man is able to prevail against the Lord. And because he had sinned beyond what was right by speaking vainly, he fell defeated in battle by heavenly power.

The virgin of Christ then immediately joined herself to the love of her heavenly Bridegroom, whom she had always loved chastely.

In the sixth year, if I am not mistaken, of her rule (in the year 880), Duke Brun, eager to defend the holy church, was killed in an attack by savage Hungarians, those wicked enemies of the Lord—alas!—together with two venerable bishops and all the men of his own army.

When he had been killed, his younger brother Oddo became duke of the people by the gift of King Hludowic. He answered in deeds the vow of the holy mother and, agreeing with her in a similar devotion, strove to adorn the new church with worthy services. It was to be consecrated in the second year thereafter [Vers. 369.].

He completed all the walls of our monastery, providing lasting advantages for the maidens who would remain there throughout the ages.

When these things had been properly completed, the very day for the worthy consecration of the temple was chosen (1 November 881), at the request of Lady Oda, in accordance with the command of their mother. This was the day in whose midnight hours, long before, the lamps had shone conspicuously in great numbers on their third appearance.

And because the venerable feast of all the saints, which was celebrated throughout the wide regions of the world, was likewise to be duly celebrated at the beginning of the month of November, the report of the temple’s consecration resounded everywhere.

Immediately very many crowds flocked from every direction, wishing to be present on the solemn day. At the first gleam of dawn, the whole gathered company of our sisters, rejoicing in the reception of the sacred bodies of their pious patrons, proceeded with hymns resounding to the site of the monastery built with the greatest effort.

Then, when everything required for the solemn celebration had been properly prepared, the blessed bishop Wichbert dedicated this beautiful temple to the Lord under the Lord’s honor, for the perpetual praise of all the saints throughout the ages, whose feast was then being worthily celebrated.

On this feast the consecration of the splendid temple took place, after eight hundred and eighty-one years had revolved since the Virgin, with her maidenly chastity unstained, bore the King of the ages and her own Creator.

Then divine songs of praise first began to resound clearly in those wooded places. From that time onward, the community of our company remained there, continually serving the Lord.

And although the abbess Gerberga carefully guarded the newly formed flock and taught it through frequent admonitions to preserve what was appropriate to its way of life and to do nothing profane against its rule, the venerable Lady Oda, living within the monastery’s enclosure with vigilant care, repeatedly examined the conduct, devotion, and manner of life of the sisters joined to her.

She did so lest any one of them, despising the law handed down by her elders, should presume to live wickedly according to her own law, or lest there should be any opportunity for an unlawful act. By her own example she showed what ought to be done.

And just as the gentle love of a prudent mother at one time restrains her daughters from wrongdoing through fear, and at another persuades them through friendly admonitions to desire what is good, so this holy woman instructed her beloved pupils: sometimes by commanding them with the authority of a powerful mistress, sometimes by soothing them with the sweetness of a mother. Thus all, in a common life, might serve the one king whom the stars of heaven acclaim with rejoicing [Vers. 417.].

Moreover, those whom she had truly nurtured through a mother’s devoted love she honored greatly, frequently calling them her own ladies.

For whenever her granddaughters and noble grandsons, whose dignity was elevated by the honor of their high position, gathered to fulfill her service, vying to honor her with splendid gifts as the king’s illustrious mother-in-law and their own forebear, she is said to have addressed them in these words:

“I exhort and admonish you, my dear pledges, to hasten, first of all, to enrich our ladies generously with your fitting gifts. They ought diligently to serve our pious patrons, through whose merits and sacred prayers the success of our desired prosperity and the glory of royal honor have come to us.”

By this approach she had persuaded her entire family to concern itself piously with the service of the monastery.

The estates she had received to possess for her own use through the gift of her son-in-law, King Hludowic, she caused to be transferred to the church of Gandersheim, with his benevolent permission.

Nor did the king himself exalt that place any less, at the pious queen Liutgard’s request. He bestowed many estates upon it, granting them by royal right to Gerberga, our beloved ruler, who was the sister of that illustrious queen.

King Arnulf, the successor of this king, subsequently confirmed the place by a written royal charter, increasing its gifts with vineyards. Thus many prosperous benefits accrued to the monastery, through the gracious merits of the highest pontiffs, under whose honor it is known to have been dedicated.

But lest such prosperity should persuade fragile minds to exalt themselves beyond measure, and so that the happiness of our ruler might be tested, the truly salutary judgment of heaven removed many of those by whose support our monastery had been strengthened from this world.

Therefore, after the pious King Hludowic had died—the first of the kings to assign to our use many estates previously owing service to the crown, and who had also confirmed all the rights of our monastery in charters written under his name —after only a few years had passed, Queen Liutgard, his most worthy consort in the kingdom and the cause of so many benefits for us, departed from this world, alas!, not without great loss to our possessions.

A similar cause of grief followed this loss: The abbess Gerberga, devoted to good works, who, supported by the assistance of the kings mentioned above and joined to the queen by the bond of sisterhood, had often adorned the monastery with splendid gifts and added abundant profit to our resources, after presiding for twenty-two years, fulfilling the office in place of the previous abbess, laid aside the mortal burden of fragile flesh and returned to her Maker the breath she had received from heaven (in the year 896).

She left her flock, deprived of its own ruler, to be administered and holily guarded by her sister Christina.

Following the character of the sisters named above and carefully reflecting on how her life ought to be lived, Christina became like them in the great pattern of virtue, equal to them in the advancement of nobility.

Her mother, whose steadfast mind no change of circumstances could corrupt or weaken so that she became less zealous in the Lord’s service, stirred her by examples and frequent admonitions to watch wisely over herself at all times and to guard carefully the flock entrusted to her.

According to the merit of their various deeds, she was to soothe her subjects at one time with kindly admonitions and at another to terrify them justly with harsh words, lest the sluggishness of her heart allow anyone to violate the observance of divine worship.

Lady Oda herself, praiseworthy for her devotion, shining with the clear rays of wondrous goodness, greatly beloved by God and renowned in the world, always sought, with the customary love of a mother’s piety, to obtain for her adopted daughters whatever she knew the nuns’ needs required.

And the great devotion of the illustrious Duke Oddo, agreeing with the vows of his dear mother, with the assistance of the kings whom he served, gently cherished and lovingly advanced that virgin company of Christ’s servants.

Nor could he be compelled by love of his own life either to harm them by touching them with any loss or to fulfill less completely what his worthy mother commanded.

Thus, throughout the time of life granted to him, with every effort of his fervent mind he strove to provide the monastery of his patrons with the constant protection of his sure assistance. He did not seek to be feared as a terrifying lord, but rather to be loved like a kindly father.

Hence, not undeservedly, the distinguished reputation of his piety has remained in that place to this day.

We too, moved by the sweetness of such great renown, who had not yet then burst forth from our mother’s womb but were truly born only after a long time, burn no less steadfastly with love for him than those who saw him present and were enriched by the gifts of his piety.

This man of such illustrious piety, who bestowed such good things upon our townspeople, preceded our mother and powerful lady in death. He was stripped of limbs woven from the muddy thread of flesh because of the forbidden fruit which the first-created parents tasted. Alas!, he closed his eyes at the bolts of death (in the year 912, November 30), while the company of our sisters surrounded the bed of the dying lord with exceedingly great weeping.

For the funeral rites that were to be celebrated with the greatest effort, our countrymen came together from every direction, weeping, and all alike mourned the bitter death of their beloved lord with excessive lamentation.

But the pitiable wailing of his nuns surpassed the mourning of the nobles and the lamentation of the common people alike. In the weakness of their minds, as is customary among women, they rejected life and desired to die more quickly, wishing to set no limit to their weeping.

For three days they preserved the body of that dear father and gracious lord unburied, as though they hoped that by pouring out their tears they could call back and restore his extinguished breath.

At last, the wise counsel of those who had arrived, judging that this vain hope must be resisted, caused the remains of so great a duke to be placed for honorable keeping in the middle of the church he himself had built, in a tomb swiftly prepared amid sorrow and drenched by the tears of those standing around [Vers. 555.].

There, through the devoted efforts of our sisters, his beloved spirit is continually commended in prayers to the mercy of the One enthroned on high, so that the merciful one may grant him everlasting rest without end.

Eight days and as many nights before this duke’s pitiable death, the famous son Otto was born to Henry, his son and a king-to-be. He was chosen, through the favor of the everlasting King, as the first king of the valiant Saxons after his father, and likewise as Augustus of the powerful Romans.

Six months thereafter, as the swift course of time flew by (in the year 913, May), while this bright glory of so great a lineage had come into being, in whom, without doubt, the joyful promises of Christ’s Baptist are believed first to have been fulfilled—words which, I recall, were spoken at the beginning of this little poem to Oda’s own mother Aeda —Oda, most blessed, our hope and ruler, when she had lived one hundred and seven years, completed her life with a good end and passed to the stars.

In blessed hope she awaits the time when her breath will return and her full body will rise from the dust in the tomb, where it now rests beneath a hard covering beside the graves of her daughters.

Nor did Christina, who alone remained as a consolation to her pupils amid the great grief already upon them, live more than twice three years after her mother. But, giving back her blessed soul when the Maker called her (in the year 919), she was joined in the homeland of light and everlasting peace to her sisters, whose dignity she had inherited and whose holy life she had nobly followed.

Grant, gracious Father, that all of them, united with their mother in heaven, may rejoice with you for ever, may eternally enjoy the reward of that good which through all former ages you have preserved for your beloved ones, so that we may praise you—the sole ruler governing the heavenly powers—with the Son and the Holy Spirit, in a joyous voice of sweet gladness [Vers. 594.].

[Col. 1149]

# Poem on the Deeds of the Emperor Otto I

## Hrotsvit’s Preface to Gerberga, Abbess of Gandersheim

[Col. 1149A]

To Gerberga, illustrious abbess—toward whom, on account of the eminence of her virtue, no less reverent devotion is owed than on account of the distinguished nobility of her royal stock—Hrotsvit of Gandersheim, the least of the least of those serving under the authority of such a person: that which is due from a handmaid to her mistress.

## Textual notes

[Note: 1. Col. 1137; at *suadelis, Ut de gazarum construxisset propriarum Sumptu*. *Sumptu*, “at the expense,” is the reading of 1b; 1 writes *sumtu*, and likewise has *promtus* for *promptus*, “ready,” and other similar spellings.]

[Note: 2. Col. 1137; at *Domino velamine sacro Fine tenus castae possent*. 1 writes *posent* for *possent*, “might be able.”]

[Note: 3. Col. 1137; at *voti Deservire Deo coeperunt protinus ambo. Quis*. 4 has *Queis* for *Quis*, both “to whom.”]

[Note: 4. Col. 1137D; at *locatae, Unde locum celebrem vocitabant Gandeshemensem. Illic*. Compare the *Life of Hathumod*, chapter 4.]

[Note: 5. Col. 1137; at *celebrando Dum locus investigari posset magis aptus*. 3 conjectures *aptus*, “suitable,” masculine to agree with “place”; 1, 1b, and 4 have neuter *aptum*.]

[Note: 6. Col. 1137; at *locus investigari posset magis aptus , Communi*. 3 and 4 read *Communi*, “common”; 1 has *Coram*, “in the presence of,” and 1b has only *Co…*.]

[Note: 7. Col. 1137; at *His habitu similem fieri, sociamque perennem. Utque*. 3 conjectures *Utque*, “and so that”; 1 and 1b have *Atque*, “and.”]

[Note: 8. Col. 1137; at *fieri, sociamque perennem. Utque puellaris rectrix fore*. 1 has *fore rectris*, an altered form and reordered wording for *rectrix fore*, “to be ruler.”]

[Note: 9. Col. 1137; at *Tunc Herifordensem sortita fuit sibi sedem. Tali*. 1 reads neuter *Tale*, “such a thing,” for *Tali*, “with such,” agreeing with “effort.”]

[Note: 10. Col. 1137; at *divinum meditati sunt famulatum Nisu Liudulfus conjux*. 4 spells “spouse” *conjunx*, rather than *conjux*.]

[Note: 11. Col. 1137; at *scriptis senioris, Scilicet almifici regisque pii Hludowici*. 1b and 4 read *Hludowici*, “of Hludowic”; 1 spells it *Ludowici*. The reading of 2 is uncertain. The phrase *de 2. non liquet* reports uncertainty about witness 2; *de* is not a variant reading.]

[Note: 12. Col. 1138D; at *scriptis senioris, Scilicet almifici regisque pii Hludowici*. Liudulf’s charter, published by me, p. 5.]

[Note: 13. Col. 1137; at *comitatu Romam pergebant, sanctique patris visitabant Sedem*. I correct the reading to *Sedem*, “seat.” 1 and 1b have *Eidem*, “to the same.” Leibniz held that this was written for *Aedem*, “church,” and that the reference was to St Peter’s church; Harenberg agreed and adopted *aedem*. But the connection of the sentences seems to show that our author is speaking of the pope. Compare *namque*, “for,” in verse 126, then verses 127 and following, 136, and 137.]

[Note: 14. Col. 1137; at *Juxta velle Dei sese persolvere posse. Hisdem*. 1b and 4 have *Hisdem*; 1 has *Iisdem*: both mean “the same.”]

[Note: 15. Col. 1137; at *venientem, Et perquirendo causam, qua venerat illic*. 1b and 4 have *ille*, “he,” for *illic*, “there.”]

[Note: 16. Col. 1139; at *Exorans dux Liudulfus cum conjuge pronus, Utitur*. Leibniz emended to *Utitur*, “he uses.” 1 has *Utique*, “certainly,” and 1b *Ut igitur*, “so that, therefore.”]

[Note: 17. Col. 1139; at *votis gerimus, factis bene perficiamus. Ac tu*. 1 and 1b read *Ac tu*, “and you.” Leibniz proposes *A te consiliumque*, “and counsel from you,” adopted by 4.]

[Note: 18. Col. 1139; at *constructio possit honori Apte signari, sacris meritisque*. 3 conjectures *meritisque*, “and by merits”; 1 and 1b read *mentisque*, “and of the mind.”]

[Note: 19. Col. 1139; at *solum ditioni Tradimus, ad defendendum pariterque regendum*. 4 has *regundum*, an alternative form of *regendum*, “to be governed.”]

[Note: 20. Col. 1139; at *defendendum pariterque regendum .» Haec dux. Et*. Following Leibniz’s suggestion, 4 has *At*, “but,” for *Et*, “and.”]

[Note: 21. Col. 1139; at *congaudeo vestris, Nec vobis credo fas esse*. 1b reads *fas esse*, “to be lawful.” For 1 the apparatus abbreviates *f. e. c.*, apparently ordering *fas esse credo*, “I believe it to be lawful,” in place of *credo fas esse*. There is no witness 1c and no supplied verb “grant.”]

[Note: 22. Col. 1139; at *Sed quia jure piis concedere debeo votis*. 3 and 4 punctuate after *Amborum*, “of both,” joining that word to the preceding phrase.]

[Note: 23. Col. 1139D; at *jure piis concedere debeo votis , Amborum*. That is, of the bishops.]

[Note: 24. Col. 1139; at *vobis donabo pignora gratis, Corporibus sacris abscisa*. 1, 1b, and 4 spell *abscisa*, “cut off,” as *abcisa*.]

[Note: 25. Col. 1139; at *jam memorati Fine tenus templo vestri munimine*. 1b and 3 have *munimine*, “protection”; 1 has *numine*, “divine power.”]

[Note: 26. Col. 1139; at *et petiistis, Coenobium nostri designamus ditioni, Ut*. 1 and 1b have *Ut quidam t.*, “so that certain …,” with *t.* abbreviating the following *terrenorum*, “of earthly [lords].” The transmitted construction is defective.]

[Note: 27. Col. 1139; at *mox aedificanda. Ut fert multorum sententia vere*. 3 and 4 conjecture *vera*, “true,” agreeing with “account,” for *vere*, “truly.”]

[Note: 28. Col. 1139; at *scientum, Proxima coenobio fuerat tunc silvula, cincta*. 3 emends *cuncta*, “all things,” in 1 and 1b to *cincta*, “surrounded.”]

[Note: 29. Col. 1139; at *quem lux perfuderat ipsum. Qui visu clare*. 3 conjectures adjectival *claro*, “clear,” agreeing with “sight,” for adverbial *clare*, “clearly.”]

[Note: 30. Col. 1139; at *sociatus, Insomnem coepit noctem servare sequentem, Non*. 1b and 4 have *Nunc*, “now,” for *Non*, “not.”]

[Note: 31. Col. 1139; at *Ipso quippe loco, sed prisco quam prius*. *prius*, “earlier,” is the reading of 1b; 1 has *plus*, “more.” Perhaps *prisca*, “former,” should be read: *sed prius quam prisca hora*, “but earlier than the former hour.” This is the editor’s proposed repair of the difficult printed *sed prisco quam prius hora*.]

[Note: 32. Col. 1139; at *si quicquam postea tale Coelitus ostensi monstraret*. 1 has *monstrarit*, “has/may have shown,” for *monstraret*, “might show.”]

[Note: 33. Col. 1141; at *aptum. Hinc, quos poscit opus, prius acquirens*. 4 writes *adquirens* for *acquirens*, “acquiring.”]

[Note: 34. Col. 1141; at *sibi sumptus, Protinus ecclesiae construxit moenia pulchrae*. *pulcre*, “beautifully,” is printed instead of *pulchrae*, “of the beautiful [church].” 1 and 1b contain the statement “Verses are wanting; two lines are missing.” 3 understood this of two verses, adding that nothing is missing from the sense. 4 adds: “In the older manuscript two verses are written less correctly and therefore crossed out. Hence the error arose.” Certainly nothing seems to be missing.]

[Note: 35. Col. 1141; at *lucis designavit rutilantis. Hac igitur causa fuerat*. *fuerat*, “had been,” is absent in 1 but present in 1b; 3 conjectures *nisu*, “with effort.”]

[Note: 36. Col. 1141; at *Domino sperans Hathumoda Impetrare fide credente se*. The word *se*, “herself,” is absent in 1 and 1b but present in 2.]

[Note: 37. Col. 1141; at *mora, coelestem quam quaerebat pietatem Sensit adesse*. 2 reads *adesse*, “to be present”; 1 and 1b have *ad sese*, “to herself.”]

[Note: 38. Col. 1141; at *quaerebat pietatem Sensit adesse suis votis promptam*. 1b has neuter or masculine *promptum*, “ready,” rather than feminine *promptam*, agreeing with “mercy.”]

[Note: 39. Col. 1141; at *die quadam jacuit secus aram, Vocis mansuetae*. 2 has *dulcisonae*, “sweet-sounding,” for *mansuetae*, “gentle.” 1 and 1b have the sequence *Vocis mansuetae die quadam jacuit secus aram*: “of a gentle voice, one day she lay beside the altar.” Leibniz corrected the placement to that of the printed text, where “of a gentle voice” qualifies the commands.]

[Note: 40. Col. 1141; at *monitis exire jubetur Atque sequi volucrem, quam*. 1 has feminine *quam*, “which,” agreeing with “bird”; 1b, 3, and 4 have masculine *quem*.]

[Note: 41. Col. 1141; at *quo duxit Spiritus almus, Donec ad coeptum*. 3 corrects *coeptum* to *incoeptum*: both mean “begun.”]

[Note: 42. Col. 1141; at *Illic candidulam vidit residere columbam In designati*. 2 and 3 read *In designati*, “on [the summit] of the designated [rock]”; 1, 1b, and 4 have *Inde signati*, “from there, of the marked [rock].”]

[Note: 43. Col. 1141; at *suum non sueto more volatum Posset ut*. 1 and 1b read *Posse tunc*, “to be able then,” for *Posset ut*, “so that she might be able.”]

[Note: 44. Col. 1141; at *non sueto more volatum Posset ut aereos*. 4 reads *aethereos*, “heavenly/ethereal,” for *aereos*, “aerial”; the word is absent in 1b.]

[Note: 45. Col. 1141; at *cujus lapides latuerunt aggere plures. Quo certa*. 3 conjectures *certo*, “certainly,” adopted by 4. But *certa*, “certain,” must refer to the virgin, despite the meter.]

[Note: 46. Col. 1141; at *praeceperat ipsum, Tellurisque gravem fodiendo scindere molem*. The poet originally expressed the same meaning thus: “And to cut through the mass of earth by digging around it.”]

[Note: 47. Col. 1141; at *suis natis, ducibus supra memoratis, Totius infandi*. 1 and 1b have *infantis*, “of an infant,” for *infandi*, “unspeakable.” 3 conjectures *ingentis*, “immense,” adopted by 4.]

[Note: 48. Col. 1141; at *sed annorum post decursus aliquorum Sunt hac*. 4 reads *ibi*, “there,” for *hac*, “this,” in “in this church.”]

[Note: 49. Col. 1141; at *ecclesia translata locanda novella. Forsan ad hoc*. 3 conjectures *Forsan ad hoc*, “perhaps for this purpose”; 1 and 1b have *adhuc*, “still/hitherto.”]

[Note: 50. Col. 1141; at *illum mundo Deus abstulit isto, Dum vix*. 1 has the order *aetatis vix*, “of age scarcely,” abbreviated *ae. v.*, rather than *vix aetatis*, “scarcely of age.”]

[Note: 51. Col. 1141; at *Deus abstulit isto, Dum vix aetatis febres*. 3 conjectures *fines … mediocris*, “the limits … of middle [age],” for the difficult *febres … mediocres*, literally “moderate fevers.”]

[Note: 52. Col. 1141; at *post haec ut plenius Odae Mens intenta*. 1b reads *Mens intenta*, “mind intent”; 1 has *intentata*, “unattempted/untried,” in place of that wording.]

[Note: 53. Col. 1141; at *Sed praestabat opem solita pietate recentem, Qua*. 1b reads *Qua*, “by which”; 1 has *Quae*, “which.”]

[Note: 54. Col. 1141; at *quibus indiget usus. Ergo sui natam, Liutgardae*. The name is spelled *lutgardae* in 1 and *luitgarda* in 1b.]

[Note: 55. Col. 1141; at *Francorum rex Ludowicus Regni consortem sibimet sociamque*. 3 conjectures *sociamque*, “and companion”; 1 and 1b have *sacramque*, “and sacred.”]

[Note: 56. Col. 1141D; at *Regni consortem sibimet sociamque perennem, Filius illius*. Louis the German.]

[Note: 57. Col. 1141; at *suae dignum sanctae matri famulatum Praestat, opem*. 3 fills the lacuna with *Praestat, opem*, “renders [service], [providing] assistance.” These words, abbreviated *P. o.*, are absent in 1 and 1b. 4 conjectures *Et nato*, “and to the son.”]

[Note: 58. Col. 1141; at *Praestat, opem regis praebens, proprii senioris, Multaque*. 3 fills the lacuna with *Multaque*, “and many [benefits]”; 4 reads *Plurima*, “very many.”]

[Note: 59. Col. 1141; at *proprii senioris, Multaque coenobio promisit commoda nostro*. 1 and 1b have *nostra*, “our,” in a feminine or neuter form, for *nostro*, agreeing with “monastery.”]

[Note: 60. Col. 1141; at *illustri cuidam nimiumque potenti Desponsata viro, Bernhardo*. 3 corrected the name to *Bernrado* from 2, which, however, also has *Garburgis*. These are forms of the personal names Bernhard and Gerberga; the printed main text has *Bernhardo*.]

[Note: 61. Col. 1143; at *sese Christo clam consecraverat ipsa Coelesti vere*. 3 reads *Coelesti vere*, “truly heavenly”; 1 and 1b have *Coelesti fera*, literally “heavenly wild [one],” an obscure reading.]

[Note: 62. Col. 1143; at *verum fore valde timebat; Impatiensque morae domnam*. 1 and 1b have the uncontracted *dominam*, “lady,” for *domnam*.]

[Note: 63. Col. 1143; at *raro didici, fama procedente sinistra, Quod tu*. 1 and 1b have accusative *te*, “you,” for nominative *tu*.]

[Note: 64. Col. 1143; at *didici, fama procedente sinistra, Quod tu nitaris*. 1b has *nitans*, “striving,” for *nitaris*, “you strive.”]

[Note: 65. Col. 1143; at *cogor, nostri senioris. Hinc tempus quod nunc*. 1 and 1b have the obscure *quodni* for *quod nunc*, “because now”; 3 and 4 conjecture *quoniam*, “because.”]

[Note: 66. Col. 1143; at *His ita colloquiis mutuo sermone peractis, Bernhard*. 2 and 3 spell Bernhard *Bernhrad*.]

[Note: 67. Col. 1143D; at *defendere sanctam, Incursu de saevorum satis Ungariorum*. Northmen, not Hungarians; compare the *Annals of Fulda*, year 880. This is an editorial correction of the identification.]

[Note: 68. Col. 1143; at *legionis. Quo mox occiso, junior frater suus*. 1 has the order *junior suus frater*, “his younger brother,” abbreviated *i. s. f.*, instead of *junior frater suus*; the meaning is unchanged.]

[Note: 69. Col. 1143; at *anno fuerat sacranda secundo. Moenia coenobii perfecit*. 3 conjectures from 2 *perfecit et omnia*, “and completed all [the walls],” abbreviated *p. et o.*]

[Note: 70. Col. 1143; at *parentis Eligitur (an. 881, Nov. 1), domna*. I correct to the contracted *domna*, “lady”; compare verse 410. 1 and 1b have *domina*.]

[Note: 71. Col. 1143; at *In cujus noctis medio quam pluribus illo*. 3 conjectures *illic*, “there,” for *illo*, “that [place/time].”]

[Note: 72. Col. 1143; at *Tertio conspicuae quondam fulsere lucernae, Et quod*. 3 reads *Et quod*, “and because”; 1 and 1b have *quid*, “what,” in place of *quod*.]

[Note: 73. Col. 1143; at *quod cunctorum pariter venerabile festum Sanctorum vasti*. 1 reads *fasti*, “of the calendar,” for *vasti*, “vast.”]

[Note: 74. Col. 1143; at *rite Novembris. Hac fama templi passim resonante*. 1 and 1b read *resonate*, “resound!” for *resonante*, “resounding.”]

[Note: 75. Col. 1143; at *aurorae primo candore micante, Omnis nostrarum collectim*. 3 reads *collectim*, “together”; 1 and 1b have *collectum*, “gathered,” in a masculine or neuter form.]

[Note: 76. Col. 1144D; at *ad cultum rite paratis Festi, Wichbertus praesul*. Bishop of Hildesheim.]

[Note: 77. Col. 1143; at *Quorum nunc festum digne fuerat celebrandum. Hoc*. That is, on this feast.]

[Note: 78. Col. 1143; at *sine sorde pudoris Seclorum regem peperit propriumque*. 3 conjectures masculine *propriumque*, “and her own,” agreeing with “parent”; 1 and 1b have feminine *propriamque*.]

[Note: 79. Col. 1143; at *illis Carmina divinae laudis clare resonare. Exin*. 1 reads *Exin est*, “from then it is”; 1b *Exin et*, “from then also”; 2 *ex tunc*, “from that time.” 4 has the reordered wording abbreviated *E. i. n. est c.*, expanding from the clause as *Exin illius nostri est collectio*, “from then there is the gathering of that company of ours.”]

[Note: 80. Col. 1143; at *licet abbatissa gregem Gerberga recentem Caute servaret*. 3 reads *servaret*, “she guarded/might guard”; 1 and 1b have infinitive *servare*, “to guard.”]

[Note: 81. Col. 1143; at *Gerberga recentem Caute servaret crebris monitisque doceret*. 3 reads *doceret*, “she taught/might teach”; 1 and 1b have infinitive *docere*, “to teach.”]

[Note: 82. Col. 1143; at *crebris monitisque doceret , Conservare suae fuerant*. 1 has singular *fuerat*, “had been,” for plural *fuerant*.]

[Note: 83. Col. 1143; at *nec quid patrare profanum, Domna tamen conversando*. 1 has *conservano*, an altered reading for *conversando*, “by dwelling/living.”]

[Note: 84. Col. 1143; at *mores, vitae quoque cursum, Ne vel, contempta*. 1 and 1b have *concepta*, “conceived,” for *contempta*, “despised.”]

[Note: 85. Col. 1143; at *majorum lege sequenda, Vivere lege sua reprobe*. 3 has adjectival *reprobo*, “wicked,” for adverbial *reprobe*, “wickedly.”]

[Note: 86. Col. 1143; at *praesumeret ulla, Vel locus illiciti foret ullius*. 3 has *ullius*, “of any”; 1 and 1b have *illius*, “of that.”]

[Note: 87. Col. 1143; at *illiciti foret ullius peragendi, Exemploque suo praemonstravit*. 1 abbreviates *praemonstravit*, “showed beforehand,” as *pmonstravit*.]

[Note: 88. Col. 1143; at *Exemploque suo praemonstravit facienda. Et ceu prudentis*. 1 reads *pudentis*, “modest,” for *prudentis*, “prudent.”]

[Note: 89. Col. 1145; at *Nunc etiam matris mulcendo more suavis, Quo*. 1b reads *Quod*, “that/because,” for *Quo*, “so that.”]

[Note: 90. Col. 1145; at *mulcendo more suavis, Quo vita simili cunctae*. 3 conjectures feminine plural *cunctae*, “all [the sisters]”; 1 and 1b have neuter plural *cuncta*, “all things,” or feminine singular “all.”]

[Note: 91. Col. 1145; at *vocitando suas saepissime domnas. Nam quoties neptes*. 1b and 4 spell *neptes*, “granddaughters,” as *neptis*, which can also be the singular “granddaughter.”]

[Note: 92. Col. 1145; at *mea pignora cara, Ut maturetis condignis primulae*. 1b and 4 have *primula*, “first/earliest,” for the difficult *primulae*, used here in the sense “first of all.”]

[Note: 93. Col. 1145; at *pia reginae bonitate precante; Sed tradens illi*. 1 and 1b have *illi*, “to it”; 3 corrects to *illo*, “there.”]

[Note: 94. Col. 1145D; at *precante; Sed tradens illi largitur praedia multa*. 26 January 877; *Origines Guelficae*, IV, p. 377.]

[Note: 95. Col. 1145; at *amandae, Ipsius illustris reginae namque sororis. Quem*. For *Quem*, “which,” referring to the place, 3 conjectures feminine *Quae* or neuter plural “which things”; 4 has *Cui*, “to which.”]

[Note: 96. Col. 1145D; at *amandae, Ipsius illustris reginae namque sororis. Quem*. That is, the place.]

[Note: 97. Col. 1145; at *plus justo fragiles extollere mentes Suaderet talis*. 1b and 4 have plural present *Suadent tales*, “such [successes] persuade,” for singular *Suaderet talis*, “such [success] might persuade.”]

[Note: 98. Col. 1145; at *fultum. Ergo rege pio jam defuncto Hludowico*. 1 spells the name *Ludowico*, rather than *Hludowico*.]

[Note: 99. Col. 1145; at *pio jam defuncto Hludowico , Qui regum*. 1b and 4 have *regem*, “king,” accusative singular, for *regum*, “of kings.”]

[Note: 100. Col. 1146D; at *nomine scriptis Jura monasterii firmaverat omnia nostri*. 26 January 877; *Origines Guelficae*, IV, p. 370 (printed *Cuelf.* in this note).]

[Note: 101. Col. 1145; at *tantorum quae nobis causa bonorum Extitit, e*. 1 has *Exiit e*, “departed from”; 1b *Exstitit in*, “existed in,” where the printed text reads *e mundo discessit*, “departed from the world.”]

[Note: 102. Col. 1145; at *juvamine regum, Necnon reginae germano foedere junctae*. 4 has nominative *juncta*, “joined,” for genitive *junctae*, agreeing with “queen.”]

[Note: 103. Col. 1145; at *annos, Officio vice rectricis perfuncta prioris, Deposito*. 1, 1b, and 4 have feminine *Deposita*, “laid aside,” for masculine/neuter *Deposito*, agreeing with “burden.”]

[Note: 104. Col. 1145; at *Illis fit similis magnae forma probitatis, Quis*. 3 conjectures *Quis*, “to whom”; 1 and 1b have *Qui*, “who”; 4 has *Queis*, “to whom.”]

[Note: 105. Col. 1145; at *magnae forma probitatis, Quis fuit aequalis provectu*. 1 and 1b have *provecta*, “advanced”; 3 has *profectu*, “in advancement,” for *provectu*, also “in advancement.”]

[Note: 106. Col. 1145; at *quoque crebris, Ut sese semper circumspiciens sapienter*. 1, 1b, 3, and 4 have adjectival *sapientem*, “wise,” for adverbial *sapienter*, “wisely.”]

[Note: 107. Col. 1145; at *sibimet servaret ovile, Necnon factorum juxta meritum*. 1b and 4 have *mentem*, “mind,” for *meritum*, “merit.”]

[Note: 108. Col. 1145; at *natis, Quicquid nonnarum deposcere sciverat usum; Oddonisque*. 1 and 2 spell “and of Otto” *Ottonisque*, rather than *Oddonisque*.]

[Note: 109. Col. 1145; at *ducis clari devotio grandis Concordando suae votis*. 3 has *votis*, “with the wishes”; 1 and 1b have *vocis*, “of the voice.”]

[Note: 110. Col. 1145; at *regum, quibus exhibuit famulatum, Ipsum virgineum coetum*. 1 reads *castum*, “chaste,” for *coetum*, “company,” in the phrase “that virgin company.”]

[Note: 111. Col. 1147; at *tutamina certi; Nec vice terribilis metui petiit*. 1b and 4 have *petiit*, “sought”; 1 and 3 have *potuit*, “was able.”]

[Note: 112. Col. 1147; at *dulcedine famae, Necdum maternis quae tunc erupimus*. 3 conjectures *erupimus*, “we burst forth.” 1 has *nunque rumpimus*, an altered phrase, and 1b *nunquam rumpimus*, “we never break forth.”]

[Note: 113. Col. 1147; at *fuimus vere longo post tempore natae, Haut*. 1 has *Hanc*, “this,” accusative feminine, for *Haut*, “not.”]

[Note: 114. Col. 1147; at *natae, Haut minus illius constanter amore flagramus*. 1 has passive infinitive *flagrari*, “to be burned,” for *flagramus*, “we burn.”]

[Note: 115. Col. 1147; at *igitur talis praeclarae vir pietatis, Qui pius*. 1 reads *prius*, “earlier,” for *pius*, “pious.”]

[Note: 116. Col. 1147; at *potentem Praeveniendo prior, vetiti pro crimine pomi*. 1b and 4 have *poni*, “to be placed,” for *pomi*, “of the fruit.”]

[Note: 117. Col. 1147; at *Proh dolor! atque seris clausit sua lumina*. 1b has *lumina*, “eyes”; 1 has *limina*, “thresholds.”]

[Note: 118. Col. 1147C; at *ad exequias summo nisu celebrandas Undique nostrates*. Saxons.]

[Note: 119. Col. 1147; at *summo nisu celebrandas Undique nostrates confluxerunt lacrimantes*. 1 spells *lacrimantes*, “weeping,” as *lacrymantes*.]

[Note: 120. Col. 1147; at *miseranda querela suarum; Quae pro defectu mentis*. 3 has *mentis*, “of mind”; 1 and 1b have *meritis*, “by merits.”]

[Note: 121. Col. 1147; at *Tandem consilium sapiens satis advenientum Decernens vanae*. 3 has *vanae*, “vain”; 1 and 1b have *variae*, “various/changeable.”]

[Note: 122. Col. 1147; at *absque dolore parato, Sed luctu nimio circumstantium*. 4 has *circumstantum* for *circumstantium*, both “of those standing around.”]

[Note: 123. Col. 1147; at *Continuis precibus dilectus spiritus ejus Semper Celsithroni*. 4 has feminine *celsithronae* for masculine *Celsithroni*, “of the One enthroned on high.”]

[Note: 124. Col. 1147; at *ejus Semper Celsithroni commendatur pietati, Quo det*. 3 reads *Quo det*, “so that he may give”; 1 and 1b have *Quod et*, “which also.”]

[Note: 125. Col. 1147; at *(An. 913. Mai.), Dum decus hoc tanti*. 3 has *tanti*, “so great”; 1 and 1b have *hortanti*, “to one exhorting.”]

[Note: 126. Col. 1147; at *exiguae quae mox in vertice Musae Aedae*. 4 has *Aedae*, “to Aeda”; 1 and 1b spell the name *Adae*.]

[Note: 127. Col. 1147; at *quoque vixerat annos, Vitam fine bono consummans*. I correct *consumens*, “consuming,” in 1, 1b, and 4 to *consummans*, “completing.”]

[Note: 128. Col. 1147; at *Alme Pater, tecum praesta gaudere per aevum*. 3 conjectures *tecum*, “with you”; 1 and 1b have *eum*, “him.”]

[Note: 129. Col. 1147; at *tecum praesta gaudere per aevum , Illius*. 3 and 4 read *Illiusque*, “and of that,” for *Illius*, “of that.”]

[Note: 130. Col. 1147; at *Flamine sacro Solum rectorem coelestibus imperitantem Dulci*. 1b and 4 have plural *Dulces*, “sweet,” for singular ablative *Dulci*, “with a sweet [voice].”]

[Note: 131. Col. 1147; at *Solum rectorem coelestibus imperitantem Dulci laetitiae laudemus*. 3 reads *laudemus*, “may we praise”; 1 and 1b have *laudantes*, “praising.”]

[Note: 132. Col. 1149; at *hujusmodi personae dominio militantium, quod famula erae*. *erae* means *herae*, “to the mistress.”]

O my lady, who shines through with the radiant variety of spiritual wisdom, may it not weary you to examine your graciousness [Note: [Col. 1149] 1 reads almie (“of grace”).]—a work completed at your command, as you well know [Note: [Col. 1149] Thus Reuber; 1 reads “your work”; 1 has “if,” while 2 has “not.”]. You have imposed upon me the burden of traversing in verse the deeds of the august Caesar, which I have never been able to gather sufficiently even by hearing. You yourself can conjecture how much difficulty arising from my ignorance has stood in the way during the labor of this undertaking, because I found these matters neither previously written nor was I able to extract them from anyone in an adequately ordered and sufficiently complete account [Col. 1149B]. Rather, it was as though someone ignorant of an unknown region were about to travel across the breadth of a forest, where every path had been covered and concealed by the dense snow, and where, without a guide but led only by the gestures of those pointing the way, he would now wander through bypaths and now unexpectedly encounter the track of the right road, until at last, having traversed half the forest’s thickness, he reached the place of desired rest; and there, fixing his step, he would not dare proceed farther until either someone else arrived to lead him on or he followed the footprints of the one who had gone before. In no other way have I, ordered to enter upon the vast extent of these matters, traversed with the greatest difficulty, wavering and stumbling amid the multitude of royal deeds [Note: [Col. 1149] This appears to be the correct reading: 1 has “you traverse,” 2 “I traverse.”] [Col. 1150A]. Exhausted by these matters, I fall silent, pausing at a suitable point; nor do I presume, without a guide, to undertake the lofty grandeur of imperial excellence. For if I were inspired by the eloquent judgments of the most eloquent writers—judgments which either have recently been written or, I do not doubt, will more readily be written about these matters—I might perhaps find something by which my rusticity could for a while be concealed. But now my whole flank is so much more defenseless because it is supported by no authority whatsoever. Hence I also fear that I may be accused of presumption and fail to avoid the snares of many reproaches, because I have presumed to dishonor, by the uncultivated poverty of my speech, matters that ought to be presented more eloquently in the pomp of graceful urbanity [Note: [Col. 1149] 1 has “pompous”; 2 “in pompous words.”]. Yet if the judgment of a sound mind should be brought to bear—a judgment that knows how to weigh matters correctly—the weaker the sex and the lesser the knowledge, the more readily pardon will be granted [Col. 1150B]; especially since I have begun to spin the thread of this little work not because of my own presumption but because of your command [Note: [Col. 1149] Thus 2; 1 has “if not.”] [Note: [Col. 1149] Thus 1; Reuber has “your.”]. Why, then, do I fear the judgments of others, when I am answerable only to your censure if I have gone astray? Or why should I be unable to avoid reproaches, when I ought to devote myself solely to silence, lest, if I wish a sequence so worthless in itself to be proclaimed when it ought to be shown to no one, I should rightly fall under the criticism of all [Note: [Col. 1149] 1 has “reprehension”]? I leave it to the judgment of yourself and of your most intimate associate, the archbishop William, to whom you have decreed that this rustic work should be presented, however it may have been composed.

## TO THE EMPEROR OTTO I

[Col. 1149]

[Col. 1149C] Otto, powerful ruler of the Caesarian empire,

Who, through the enduring piety of the king that fosters you,

Are illustrious in the scepters of august honor,

And surpass in piety all earlier emperors,

Whom many peoples dwelling everywhere fear,

Whom the Roman and the whole world honor with various gifts:

Do not disdain this small gift of song;

May this offered tribute of praise please you,

Which the least of the flock of Gandersheim pays to you,

Which the sweet devotion of your fathers has gathered,

And which owes you continual diligence in service.

[Col. 1150C] Perhaps many have written of your deeds,

And many will write of these illustrious matters hereafter;

But no one has provided me with an example of this kind,

Nor have written books taught me how to write it beforehand [Note: [Col. 1149] Thus the editors correctly; 1 has “These,” with the letter H in red.];

It is devotion of mind alone that is the cause of this work.

This too urged me to dare an undertaking that ought to be feared;

For I am sufficiently afraid that, in shaping your deeds in verse,

I may carelessly follow what is false instead of unfolding what is true.

But the evil presumption of my mind did not urge this [Note: [Col. 1149] mis, that is, mei, “my”.],

Nor, willingly despising the height of truth, did I go astray;

Rather, those who brought me the material to be written

Told me that matters were exactly as I have written them.

[Col. 1151A] Therefore may august piety not disdain the honor

That the simple devotion of a humble mind has performed.

And although many fitting books praising you

May hereafter be written and rightly judged pleasing,

Let this little book nevertheless not stand last in order,

[Col. 1152A] Since it is known to have been written without any prior example.

And although you hold the glory of Octavian’s empire,

Do not disdain to be called by the name of king,

Until, when the honor of royal life has been written out,

With its order arranged and its language made decorous,

The imperial glory of the second scepter is proclaimed.

## TO THE EMPEROR OTTO II

[Col. 1151]

[Col. 1151A] Otto, shining jewel of the Roman realm,

Flower of the august and venerable Otto, radiant,

To whom the high-throned eternal King, and his everlasting Son,

[Col. 1151B] Granted empire, powerful at the summit of affairs:

Do not disdain the lowly composition of a lowly nun,

Which, if you will remember, you yourself recently ordered

To be presented to your bright eyes,

And, when you see it soiled by frequent blemishes,

Be all the more ready to grant swift pardon [Note: [Col. 1151] “Swift” has been corrected from “sinful” in 1.].

In showing how much more I obey your commands,

If I were not compelled by fear of your dreadful order [Note: [Col. 1151] That is, “of you.”],

There would be no confidence in me so great

That I would dare to place before you for examination

A little book so inadequate in its present rusticity

[Note: [Col. 1151] “To present” has been corrected from “to carry” by the editors.];

You who, with God’s favor, are joined to your father in the palace,

Ready to obey his paternal instructions [Note: [Col. 1151] Thus 2; 1 has “ready to prepare obedience to his instructions.”],

And concordantly retain the equal and expansive glory of empire,

Carrying the royal scepter in your tender right hand.

[Col. 1151C] But because I remember that you are sublimely likened

[Col. 1152A] To Solomon, son of the famous king David,

Who, with his holy father present and commanding,

Received the desired kingdom of his father in peace,

[Col. 1152B] I hope that you will be content to follow his example.

When he sat in the proud citadel while reigning,

Wisely composing decrees of sacred laws

And penetrating the secrets of things with deep understanding,

He nevertheless delighted to relax his mind by investigating small matters;

Nor did he disdain to settle properly the dispute of two women

By the swift judgment of what was right,

Ordering the child to be restored to its true mother.

Therefore I earnestly beseech you, our Solomon:

Although you are occupied with the care of governing the empire,

Deign nevertheless to read in play the recent sequence

Of your own nun,

So that, through its badly composed words, all rusticity may soon fall away,

And the faults of speech [Note: [Col. 1151D] That is, faults removed from the sight of the king.]

Marked by the title of your venerable name

[Col. 1152C] May be protected from the excessive breath of contempt.

## HERE BEGINS THE HISTORY

[Col. 1151]

[Col. 1151C] After the King of kings, who alone reigns forever,

Transferring by his own power the times and kingdoms of all kings,

Commanded the noble kingdom of the Franks to be transferred

To the illustrious people of the Saxons [Note: [Col. 1151] “Saxons” has been corrected from “stones” in 1.] (919),

A people whose name derives from the stone, because of the firm hardness of their mind,

The son of the great and venerable duke Otto,

Namely Henry, first undertook to wield the royal scepters

With a fortunate governance for the people [Note: [Col. 1151] Meibom has “of the people”; 1 has “for the people,” the corrected reading.].

How great was his excellence in the honor of goodness,

With what piety he ruled the peoples subjected to him,

And how he then surpassed all kings of his time

By his exceptional merits, indeed exceeds

The excessively faulty composition of this little poem—

[Col. 1151D] For he was harsh toward the reprobate but gentle toward the just,

[Verse 15] Preserving the laws with the greatest care,

[Col. 1152C] And giving all people rewards sufficiently equal to their merits.

To him Christ, the peaceful King, had granted from heaven

Civil peace throughout the periods of his life.

Under a fortunate omen he held the heights of the kingdom

For, if I am not mistaken, ten years of passing time,

And twice three more, lived through with great good fortune,

With his illustrious wife Mathilda reigning beside him,

To whom no woman now in the kingdom could be compared,

Who could surpass her in supreme merits.

The Trinity, which had granted him three sons,

Now, in its pious ordering of the fortunate people,

So that after the death of Henry, the venerable king,

Criminal men might not wickedly seize the empire of the kingdom,

Had these sons born of royal stock

[Col. 1152D] Rule their paternal kingdom in harmonious peace,

[Verse 31] Although unequal honors were preserved for them,

[Col. 1153A] Namely, two being subject to one ruler.

Among them the first shone like the rising morning star:

Otto, gleaming with the rays of exceedingly bright goodness,

Whom the king’s customary and enduring piety

Rightly foresaw as ruler over a faithful people.

He was older in age and greater also in merits,

And suited to wield the scepters after his father’s death.

There is no need to state in words the sum of his excellence,

Or to praise the laudable merit of so great a boy,

For Christ is now increasing such honor in him

That he possesses proud Rome by powerful right,

Rome, which had always been the stable head of the world,

And, with Christ’s favor, subdues fierce peoples

Who had previously often torn apart the sacred Church.

After him Henry was born in good fortune,

[Col. 1153B] Famous for having received his father’s royal name.

The provident wisdom of the Lord Christ

Deigns to preserve him as a strong leader for the people [Note: [Col. 1153D] That is, “has deigned to preserve him.”],

So that, a vigorous warrior and most skilled in the art of war,

He might strongly fortify the venerable Church,

Like a powerful wall standing against the arrows of the enemy.

After him Brun was born, shepherd of the nourishing Church,

Whom the enduring fullness of pontifical grace

Led to be worthy to bear responsibility for the Catholic people.

Therefore, by divine prompting, his father’s pious care

Caused him to be bound to Christ’s service [Note: [Col. 1153] 1 has “bound” in a variant form.],

Having lovingly withdrawn him from the bosom of his dear nurse,

So that, renouncing the pomp of the kingdom,

He might stand as a soldier in the star-bearing palace

Of the one who reigns forever.

But Christ, the true and everlasting Wisdom of the Father,

With merciful kindness nourishing this, his young recruit,

Gave him gifts of such splendid wisdom

That no one among mortal sages of this fragile world

Was wholly wiser than he [Note: [Col. 1153D] “Was” may have stood here. The present tense above at verse 49 creates uncertainty as to whether Brun, living or already dead, is meant.].

Thus, when these boys had been raised in royal fashion,

Their famous father and king, Henry,

Was pleased to fulfill this proper act:

While he still safely enjoyed the warm air of life,

He arranged for his firstborn son and future king,

Otto, to be betrothed to a suitable bride,

Who could fittingly be joined to his own offspring (929).

He did not wish to seek her in his own kingdom,

But sent prudent ambassadors across the sea

To the sufficiently splendid land of the English,

Instructing them, once the gift had been sent [Note: [Col. 1153] Thus I restore the text; 1 has “common,” 2 “delay.”],

[Col. 1153D] To ask King Edward for his daughter Edith,

Who, after her father’s death [Note: [Col. 1153D] “Edward”; the supplied text reads “her father.”], was then residing at court,

While her brother held the scepter of their paternal kingdom [Note: [Col. 1154D] “Athelstan.”];

[Verse 80] A consort not illustrious as the king’s queen bore him—

[Col. 1154A] The most distinguished mother of this noble lady—

But she was another woman, of considerably lower birth [Note: [Col. 1153] 1 reads milier; [Col. 1154D] Ecgwina; Eadgith’s mother was Aelfleda.].

This daughter of the king, whom I keep writing about in these verses—

This, I say, was well known by reputation to everyone:

Powerful in nobility and likewise eminent in the highest merits,

Born from the highest stock of great kings.

Her face, serene with splendid brightness,

Radiated with the wondrous honor of royal beauty.

And she herself, shining with the rays of perfect goodness,

Earned such praise in her homeland

That, by the judgment of all the people,

She was deemed the best of all the women who then existed.

Nor is it surprising that she shone with outstanding merits,

Since she sprang from a line that produced holy ancestors.

They therefore say that she was born from the blessed stock

[Col. 1154B] Of King Oswald, whose praise the world sings,

Because he submitted himself to death for the name of Christ [Note: [Col. 1154D] Compare Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English People III, 2–9.].

At last, the messengers of our king came

To the brother of the lady, who was then residing in the citadel,

And disclosed to him all the secrets they carried.

These matters pleased him very much once he had learned them,

And immediately he related them to his sister in a sweet voice,

Urging her to obey the faithful king,

Who wished her to be joined to his own offspring.

And as he gently poured into her mind

The sweet love of the royal boy Otto,

He gathered innumerable treasures with the greatest effort.

But when it seemed to him that he had collected enough,

With suitable companions accompanying the aforesaid lady,

He sent her across the sea with the greatest honor,

[Col. 1154C] Presenting her with exceedingly precious treasures.

He also sent with her her sister Adiva [Note: [Col. 1154D] Compare the accounts of William of Malmesbury and Ingulf.],

Who was younger both in age and in merit,

So that by this he might confer a still greater honor

On Otto, the beloved son of the famous king,

By sending him two excellent girls of royal stock,

So that, at first sight, he might join himself in lawful marriage

To whichever bride he wished.

But immediately the venerable Edith pleased him,

Rightly pleasing everyone in her appearance [Note: [Col. 1153] 1 has “of appearance”],

As a person of supreme goodness;

She was suitably judged worthy of the royal son.

She bore him a splendid son,

Liudulf by name, suitable to such parents,

Whom the people rightly loved with tender affection,

Earnestly wishing that his life might be prolonged.

When these matters had thus been arranged, the end at last

[Col. 1154D] Of King Henry drew near, whose death all the people mourned—

The people subjected to his rule and law.

When he had died (936), Otto took up the kingdom,

[Verse 129] The venerable firstborn of that king,

[Col. 1155A] And, with the will of all the people now responding,

He was anointed king, powerful through Christ’s favor.

To him the King of heaven bestowed such gifts of grace

That, deservedly famous among all,

He surpassed all kings in the reputation of his deeds,

Those whom the Ocean now surrounds with its returning waves.

Moreover, the sacred right hand of the Almighty

Protected him from so many ambushes prepared by hidden fraud,

And so often adorned him with magnificent triumphs

That you might believe the faithful King David to be reigning,

Now properly resplendent with ancient triumphs.

He not only governs with the reins of goodness the peoples

Who had previously bowed their necks to his father’s empire,

But he himself claims many more,

Subjugating the territories of the gentiles to Christ’s servants,

[Col. 1155B] So that peace might be established for the sacred Church [Note: [Col. 1155] 1 has an ungrammatical form “to be made.”].

Whenever he himself advanced to war,

There was no people, however proud in valor,

That could harm or overcome him,

Supported as he was by the aid of the heavenly King.

Nor did his army yield to any weapons,

Unless perhaps, scorning his royal commands,

It fought there where the king himself had forbidden it.

At that time Duke Henry, the king’s venerable brother,

Was prince in the peaceful kingdom,

Second after the king and deservedly venerated by all the people.

He fittingly joined himself in lawful marriage

To the noble daughter of the excellent duke Arnulf (938),

Judith by name, radiant in the splendor of her face

And even more brilliant in the radiance of every virtue.

[Col. 1155C] When these matters had thus been arranged, peace everywhere

Lasted for a short time, and less than the peoples desired,

While the savage clamor of wars was silent.

Oh, how peacefully our fortunate commonwealth

Would lead a smiling life,

Ruled as it was by the authority of a wise king,

If the ancient cunning of the enemy

Did not disturb our serenity by secret fraud!

At last, after the weapons of foreigners had been thoroughly defeated,

A powerful discord suddenly arose among our own people,

And civil war wounded the faithful people

More than the frequent structure of various wars had done.

The cause of this evil was a conflict, ultimately,

That was not insignificant and had not been moderated.

Of those involved, one party, with a kindly disposition toward Henry,

[Col. 1155D] Devoted itself to the royal brother’s right of allegiance [Note: [Col. 1155] Thus 2; 1 has “the right of the brother of the king.”],

While another party devoted itself to serving Count Evurhard.

But when each sought the protection of his own lord,

A more serious discord arose among the lords themselves.

At last, as the conflict advanced,

The aforesaid leader, sending his badly assembled forces

[Verse 181] To capture the fortress of Baduliki [Note: [Col. 1155D] Belike, south of the city of Lippstadt.],

[Col. 1156A] Sent them unexpectedly under cover of the dark night,

And led captive the king’s noble brother,

Henry, binding his hands with bloody chains—

His pale hands, more suited to adornments.

He also scattered his innumerable treasures [Note: [Col. 1155] 1 has innumerosos.]

And soon led the household offspring away with him,

So that he might use even the son of his own lord

As a companion.

When the king learned this, grieving secretly in his heart,

He mourned the pitiable deed with profound sadness.

Scarcely able to endure the grievous loss of his dear brother,

He immediately followed the noble example of the patriarch Abraham,

Who, in pity, acted when he rescued Lot from the enemy.

Gathering his soldiers with the greatest effort,

And also a vast host from the whole people,

He advanced with royal pomp to bring relief to his brother,

[Col. 1156B] Under the great anguish and pain of his heart [Note: [Col. 1155] 2 reads “grieving.”].

Without delay, he rescued the brother whom he had come to comfort,

And condemned the perpetrators of so great a crime,

Hanging some upon a tree erected for the condemned,

And ordering others to depart from their beloved homeland.

(939.) After these matters had been wisely arranged

By the command of the wise king,

The ancient fraud of the enemy again brought forth

An invention of crime still worse than the first [Note: [Col. 1155] Thus 2; 1 has “worse.”],

Horrible to all ages and deservedly astonishing [Note: [Col. 1155] Thus 2; 1 has “of the seat.”].

Finally, after the aforesaid Evurhard,

The leader, had returned from exile

And was coming back to his beloved homeland [Note: [Col. 1155] 1 has “was returning.”],

Through this small kindness granted by the king’s benevolence,

He, joined by bonds of affection to Count Gislberht,

Had given counsel that did not please you, O Christ:

That they should seize the just, blessed king of the Lord,

And, what is more, by inflicting unjust force upon the just man,

Should wickedly deprive him of his own kingdom.

With perverse intent they also urged this counsel upon Henry,

the king’s faithful brother,

Excessively soothing him with falsely flattering words,

So that he might be unwilling to restore the harm previously inflicted,

But, obeying their wicked wishes still more,

Might undertake to rule the kingdom after his brother’s removal.

At last, overcome by their evil flattering entreaties,

Alas! he promised that he would be ready to obey their wishes,

And confirmed this with firm words.

But I certainly hope that he did not hold this in his heart,

And that he offered his consent to them only because he was forced by compulsion.

For they, captivated by the comfort of empty hope,

Hoped that they would soon subject to their fragile authority

The king who once ruled over the peoples.

But the King from heaven, the most righteous judge of the world,

Who alone knows the thoughts of all

And is able to destroy the vain things of mortal hearts

[Note: [Col. 1155] I correct the reading thus: 1 has “for this is vain”; 2 “by what means.”],

Broke the plot of so great a crime

By the power of his mighty right hand,

By which he created all created things.

[Verse 233] Namely, the ambushes prepared against Christ’s anointed [Note: [Col. 1155] I correct the reading thus; 1 and the editions have “against the lord of Christ.”]

[Col. 1157A] He deservedly turned against the authors of so great a crime.

Those who had set their malignant snares for their own lord

Were themselves first caught in those very snares.

I do not boast that I possess wisdom beyond what is permitted,

So as to hope to declare fully in words

How often Christ, by the power of heavenly grace,

Made this very blessed king safely pass through

The many deceits and ambushes prepared by the hostile party.

But I do not think it is lawful for a fragile woman,

Placed within the secret quiet of a convent,

To describe a war that she ought not to know.

These matters must be preserved for perfected men.

I say only this, which I can rightly say: he is the beginning

And likewise the end of all kings.

[Col. 1157B] What wisdom of mind gave a toiling woman the power

To recount everything in wisely composed words?

He alone has always powerfully performed wondrous deeds.

He who, so often rescuing faithful King David

From Saul’s treachery, gave him the royal scepter,

Also protected this king,

Following David in piety [Note: [Col. 1157D] “Otto.”],

From dangers by the thousands.

Finally, when he alone, surrounded by very few soldiers,

Was hemmed in on every side by hostile troops,

And, with grieving and deeply sorrowful heart,

Endured the disastrous flight of his own side,

He did not dare place confidence even in the few

Who had not deserted him when the others retreated,

But supposed only that he would soon die a grievous death,

Then, more quickly supported by the strength of heavenly aid,

[Col. 1157C] He marveled that he had already overcome so many

Of the bloodstained crowd, without danger to his own life.

But if, as the unfavorable battle intensified,

He heard that his own companions had been wounded by mortal blows,

He immediately used the words of the aforesaid king,

Which he spoke in grief and felt with a sorrowful heart,

Weeping that the people would perish under the blows of the angelic sword:

“Behold, I am the one who sinned,” he said, “and committed the crime [Note: [Col. 1157D] 2 Samuel 24:17].

Therefore I am ultimately worthy of such vengeance!

What have these men done, that they should suffer such harm?

Now, O Christ, sparing your redeemed, have mercy on your own,

That hostile force may not oppress the innocent beyond what is just!”

Moved by these little prayers,

Divine power spared the king’s accustomed servants,

And, in pity, granted the desired triumph over the enemy,

[Col. 1157D] Destroying the aforesaid companions by a just judgment.

For on the very day when, deceived by empty hope,

They hoped that the king, who deservedly held the royal scepters,

Would be bound in their chains,

The leader Udo suddenly burst forth,

Bringing with him a large army,

[Verse 285] And entered a powerful battle with vigorous struggle.

[Col. 1158A] Without delay, Evurhard was struck down and died by the swords,

And Gislberht, fleeing, was likewise swallowed by the savage waters.

Meanwhile the king did not know of such a mighty battle,

Sitting, indeed, on the far bank of the Rhine [Note: [Col. 1158D] That is, quidem, “indeed.”],

Nor did he then know of the aid and such great relief

Sent to him by God’s mercy through a sudden turn of events.

Finally, when he perceived the dangers of so great a battle,

Not rejoicing at the death of his enemies,

But grieving more deeply in his heart for so many men,

He took up no small lamentation, in the manner of David [Note: [Col. 1157] Thus 2; 1 has “merely.”],

Who piously mourned King Saul after he had been killed.

But when the joyful victors came,

And saw his face wet with flowing tears,

They said that such grief was not suited to so great a triumph,

But that thanks ought to be given to the everlasting King,

[Col. 1158B] Who then, in faithful mercy, fulfilled

What is plainly written in the book of King Solomon:

That the just man is to be delivered from distress,

And that the unjust is soon to be given over in place of the just [Note: [Col. 1158D] Proverbs 11:8.].

With these words of persuasion soothing the king’s mind,

They compelled him to lay aside such great sorrow,

And, rejoicing with the victorious army,

To show himself gracious to his servants after the battle.

Thus, displaying measured joy on his face

But secretly preserving grief beneath his heart,

He gave thanks to Christ from the depths of his heart,

Because at that time he had not handed him over as prey

To his own enemies, but the heavenly right hand had duly protected him.

He attributed the title of so great and illustrious a triumph

Not to himself but to Christ’s piety [Note: [Col. 1157] That is, “to Christ’s pious power.”].

[Col. 1158C] (941.) When these matters had thus been arranged,

The people, wearied by the struggle of civil war,

Rested for a short time.

Yet even so the ancient deceit of the enemy did not end,

For he always tries to pervert fragile minds,

Persuading them, after committing one crime,

To add a worse one.

It is certainly reported that the bile

Of a number of hearts finally penetrated so deeply

With the poison of such pestilence

That they wished to inflict death upon the faithful king

And to place his brother as king over the people.

Nor did they fear to stain the holy day of Easter (April 18),

If it could be done by shedding the blood of the just man.

But the Paschal Lamb, who for our redemption

Gave himself, when dying, as the chosen holocaust to the Father,

Did not consent to a crime so great;

Rather, he soon exposed their plot to everyone,

[Col. 1158D] And thus the blood of the innocent was well preserved.

Those who were found guilty of this criminal conspiracy [Note: [Col. 1157] Thus 1; that is, “those who were found guilty of the criminal conspiracy.”]

Were condemned to bitter punishments according to the measure of their guilt:

Some, indeed, were handed over to capital judgment [Note: [Col. 1157] 2 has “were condemned.”],

Others were driven far from their beloved homeland.

After this, the noble Henry, the king’s brother,

[Verse 337] Touched secretly in his heart by Christ’s grace,

[Col. 1159A] Considered within himself and repeatedly reflected, with the greatest sorrow,

Upon whatever he had ever done against justice.

He also lamented this very thing with frequent and excessive mourning:

That he had yielded to the entreaties of those men’s false flatteries,

Who had corrupted him with deceptive words.

Although he bore such sorrow in his heart,

He nevertheless did not presume to present himself

Before the royal face for a long period of time.

But, absent in body and with a heart flowering in sorrowful devotion,

He wished that the sweet gift of pardon might be granted him.

At last, overcome by strong love,

He immediately cast fear of punishment from his heart,

And, in the deep darkness of night,

He came and entered the royal city (December 25),

In which the pious king began solemnly to celebrate

The everlasting King’s nativity with suitable rites.

After laying aside his precious ornaments,

He took pleasure in the garment of a simple and humble robe,

And entered barefoot the sacred thresholds of the temple

Amid the venerable hymns of the night [Note: [Col. 1159] Thus 2; 1 has “on the way.”].

He did not shudder at the savage cold of raging winter,

But, prostrate before the sacred altar with bowed face,

Joined his noble body to the frozen earth,

Thus, with all the strength of his grieving heart,

Earnestly desiring that the gift of pardon

Be granted to him, the duke [Note: [Col. 1159] I correct the text thus: 1 has “Desiring that the gift of pardon be granted, to him the duke”; Celtes emends it to “Desiring the gift of pardon, sweet to him.”].

When the king learned this, overcome by kindly mercy

And remembering the approaching feast revered by all,

On which the heavenly inhabitants sang peace to the world,

When their joyful King was born from a tender virgin

To save the world, deservedly doomed to perish,

[Col. 1159C] In honor of that day, the bearer of peace,

He grieved in compassion for his brother’s confession of his deeds,

And piously granted him his own favor,

Together with the beloved gift of complete pardon.

Moreover, after a short interval of time (946),

He subjected all the nobles

Of the very famous people of Bavaria

To his authority,

Making him, deservedly, a powerful duke.

After this there was no further discord

Between them, their minds joined in fraternal alliance.

And the Avars [Note: [Col. 1159] Avarosque has been corrected to Avaresque in 1; [Col. 1159D] That is, the Hungarians.], repeatedly defeated by him,

No longer harmed Otto’s extensive royal realm

With their accustomed bloody weapons,

Nor dared to touch the neighboring nations,

So greatly were they shaken by fear of so mighty a duke.

[Col. 1159D] Because he possessed the strength of a prudent mind,

And opposed these monsters of humanity in repeated wars,

He had closed all the roads by which they might come to us.

Moreover, he was the first, secure in Christ’s name [Note: [Col. 1159] “de” has been supplied; 2 reads bene.],

Who boldly, with an army of the subjected people,

Entered the homeland of that criminal people,

[Verse 388] Attacking the nation that had previously been rebellious toward all,

And, after capturing spoils of various things,

Which the enemies had previously gathered for themselves

While ravaging many regions of the world,

He also carried away the wives of nobles

And their beloved offspring.

And thus, with the enemies overthrown, he returned rejoicing.

When these matters had thus been arranged, the appointed sad day
