Had come (January 26), increasing our people’s immense grief,

On which the queen, shining with supreme merits,

Edith departed from the hours of this present life,

Causing the people subject to her rule

Great sadness and grievous anguish of heart

At her departure.

With great and deserved mourning

The whole common people wept for her,

For she had cherished them with the love of a mother

More than she would have broken them by the harsh commands of a ruler.

Although no one who knew the praiseworthy merit of her chaste life

And the gentle disposition that she finally displayed

Could have doubted that Christ would soon grant her

Endless rest and the joy restored to the just of old,

Nevertheless, according to the human custom of grieving,

It is not surprising that the people took up bitter lamentation,

Since such great hope had been so suddenly taken away from them.

And the excessively royal and beloved face of the lady,

Together with the radiant glory of the kingdom she had governed,

Was entrusted to the earth, to be preserved within its broad womb,

Until it should rise again and recover incorrupt,

What the tomb now encloses: that most noble body.

Thus she left the boy Liudulf, whom I mentioned briefly above,

[Col. 1160C] Bitterly bereft,

And also one sweet child of the female sex,

Liudgarda by name, shining with supreme goodness,

In character and appearance like her venerable mother.

Toward these offspring of a beloved line

The whole people was immediately drawn by affection of heart,

In great measure because of the supreme merits of both parents.

But more ardently and justly did it burn with sweet love

Toward the royal boy, Lord Liudulf,

Embracing him in the whole hope of a loving heart.

He, well imitating his natural virtues,

Had become gracious to everyone through the sweetness of his mind,

Gentle, merciful, humble, and exceedingly faithful.

Therefore, through Christ’s kind favor,

He earned and deservedly received such great grace

[Col. 1160D] Among all the peoples bound by his father’s rule,

That whoever heard even a few little words

Of his fame with attentive ears

Was wholly carried away into love of him,

Venerating their absent lord with devoted hearts.

[Verse 439] His excellent father, the venerable senior king,

[Col. 1161A] Seeing him grievously endure the death of his beloved mother,

With paternal affection and kindly piety,

Raised him at once to a worthy honor [Note: [Col. 1161] Thus 2; 1 has “to a marked honor,” probably a scribal error],

Making him properly rule the kingdom subject to him.

Likewise, for the same reason, he honored, advanced, and loved

Liudgarda, venerable in his eyes,

Who was his only hope in the female line,

With a grace equal to that shown to her brother.

He also joined her in bonds of affection

To Conrad, an excellent, vigorous, and exceedingly powerful duke,

Who was plainly worthy of such a gift of honor.

And, in order to make the noble and gracious lords of the Frankish people

Subject to his son Liudulf

With the perfected love of a deeply devoted mind,

And likewise all the leading men of the Swabians,

He ordered Ida, the beautiful daughter of the gracious duke Herimann,

[Col. 1161B] Who had been an illustrious prince in those regions,

To be joined to him in a lawful and most beautiful union.

She too was worthy, by the merits of her own goodness,

To enter into the fellowship of royal offspring,

And was honored with the highest respect in place of a queen [Note: [Col. 1161D] The form is passive in meaning.],

For, by the king’s command and through his customary piety,

The same king did not wish her to dwell in separate places,

Being rightly inflamed with love for his son,

But wished her to pass through the wide kingdom as a queen,

So that his beloved son might always feel

The great and sweet gifts of grace,

While joined with his bride in the palace of the kingdom.

Meanwhile the Italian king Lotharius,

Stricken by a grave illness, departed from this world (950, November 22),

He who had joined to himself in supreme love a queen

Who was the daughter of the great King Rudolf,

Born from the long lineage of great kings.

Her illustrious name, bestowed by the supreme nobility of her parents,

Was Aethelheida.

She too, splendid in the beauty of royal form,

And diligent in deeds suitable to her person,

Responded by her actions to her royal nobility.

Indeed, she had been so radiant in intelligence

That she could have ruled the kingdom left to her with dignity,

If the people themselves had not soon devised bitter treachery.

Finally, after the death of the aforementioned Lotharius,

A certain portion of the people, previously rebellious in mind

And hostile in perverse spirit toward their own lords,

Restored the kingdom to Berengarius’s authority,

[Col. 1161D] A kingdom that, after his grandfather’s death [Note: [Col. 1161D] Avo, “grandfather”; Berengarius I.],

Had once been violently taken from him

And passed, through the hands of the king, to Hugh [Note: [Col. 1161] Thus 2; a word now erased in 1 seems to have been “had given.”] [Note: [Col. 1162D] Namely, the people.].

Certainly raised to the desired honor (December 15),

He revealed whatever envy he had carried

Beneath his sorrowful heart,

While lamenting the loss of his paternal kingdom.

Inflamed with more than justified bitterness of heart,

[Verse 490] He poured out upon the innocent

The rage that had congealed within him,

Inflicting unjust force upon Queen Aethelheida,

Who, while reigning, had done him no harm whatsoever.

Nor did he merely seize for himself the throne of the lofty palace;

After opening the locks of her treasury,

He took everything he found with his greedy right hand:

Gold, gems, treasures of every kind,

And also the most noble crown of the royal brow.

He had not left behind even a single portion of her adornments,

Nor did he fear to strip her of her own servants,

Or of the persons suited to royal service,

Or of royal power—miserable to say.

Finally, he denied her all freedom to go or remain wherever she wished (April 20, 951).

[Col. 1162B] He ordered her to be kept by a certain count who obeyed his commands. This man, ensnared by the orders of a king commanding what was unjust, did not fear to keep his own innocent lady, shut up in the prison-like confines of a chamber, with bands of guards spread around her, as is customary when guilty persons are kept under guard.

But he who rescued Peter from Herod’s bonds, whenever he willed, redeemed her through his gentle mercy.

Certainly, while she was distressed in mind by various cares and had no hope of any assured consolation, Bishop Adelhard [Note: [Col. 1162D] Of Reggio.]—lamenting the pitiable deed and scarcely able to endure the grievous injury done to his beloved lady—sent her at once a secret messenger. Through earnest counsels he urged her to flee and seek a city well fortified by walls,

[Col. 1162C] which was the seat of his own bishopric. There, he promised her the safest place of refuge and service worthy of her.

When these royal messages had struck the ears of the renowned queen [Note: [Col. 1161] Joannis rightly conjectures *mandatelis*; manuscript 1 has *demendat elis*, while the editions have *demandans Elis*, in a sense the editor does not understand.], she was gladdened and desired to be released from her harsh bonds. Yet she did not know what to do, because no door was open through which she could depart during the night hours [Note: [Col. 1161] Thus in witness 2; *ab* in witness 1; cf. v. 548.] while the guards were overcome by deep sleep.

Nor did she possess in the prison caves any person subject to her who might diligently fulfill her commands, except only the girl mentioned above and one presbyter of commendable life.

When she had recounted to them, with continual lamentation, all that she was turning over [Note: [Col. 1161] Thus in witness 2; *volebat* in witness 1.] in her deeply sorrowful heart,

[Col. 1162D] it seemed good to them, by common agreement, that matters might turn out better if, through hidden labor, they dug a secret pit beneath the ground through which they could escape from their hard bonds.

[Vers. 541.] It is altogether certain that this was completed

[Col. 1163A] quickly, with the kindly aid of Christ present.

For, when the pit had been carefully prepared according to plan, a night suitable for renewed freedom arrived (August 20). While sleep was spreading [Note: [Col. 1163] Thus corrected; *proserperet* in witness 1.] through the limbs of the common people, the most devout queen, together with her two companions [Note: [Col. 1163] *bonis* corrected; *binis* in witness 1.], escaped, evading all the guards’ stratagems. She traversed only as much of the road during the night as her tender feet could manage.

But as soon as the murky night yielded to its sundered shadows [Note: [Col. 1163] Thus, rightly, in witness 2; *surua* in witness 1; *surda* could also be read.], and the heavens began to grow pale with the sun’s rays, she concealed herself more carefully in secret caves. Now she wandered through the woods; now she hid in the furrows among the ripe ears of growing Ceres [Note: [Col. 1163] Reuber thus corrected *maturos* in the first edition to *maturas*.], until night returned, clothed once more in its accustomed darkness, and the dark cloud covered the earth again.

[Col. 1163B] Then she undertook again to traverse the road she had begun.

Finally, when the guards did not find her, they tremblingly reported the event to the count [Note: [Col. 1163] *Multum* in the second edition.], who had been entrusted with her keeping.

Struck in the heart by the heavy terror of fear, he went with many companions to search for her. When his efforts failed and he could no longer determine where the illustrious queen had directed her steps, he fearfully reported the matter to King Berengarius.

At once the king, turned to excessive anger, suddenly sent his attendants in every direction, ordering them not to pass over any place but carefully to inspect every hiding-place [Note: [Col. 1163] *Tenebras* in the second edition.], in case the queen might be concealed anywhere.

He himself also followed with a strong troop of soldiers,

[Col. 1163C] like one who wishes to overcome fierce enemies in war, and traversed that same field at a rapid pace. In its winding furrows the lady whom he was seeking then lay hidden, covered beneath the protecting wings of Ceres.

For although he crossed the place from one side to the other [Note: [Col. 1163D] That is, “for although.”], where she lay weighed down by no small terror, and although he tried with all his strength to separate the stalks around her with an extended spear, he nevertheless did not find her, for the grace of Christ had concealed her.

But when he returned in confusion and utterly exhausted, the venerable Bishop Adelhard soon arrived. With joyful heart he led his lady inside the strongly fortified walls of his own city.

There he served her worthily with every honor until, through Christ’s mercy, she received the greater dignity of the kingdom which she had earlier left in grief.

Finally, when certain of our countrymen, who had then learned that the queen had been bereft of her dear lord, began to travel through Italy toward Rome, they frequently recounted to Otto [Note: [Col. 1163] *Ottoni* in the first edition.], then the great king,

[Col. 1164A] now the august ruler of the Roman realm, the manifold kindness of the queen, whose exceedingly sweet charity they had experienced. They said that no other woman was worthy to be brought beneath the royal roof of his bedchamber after the death of the lady Edith, whose loss all had to mourn [Note: [Col. 1163] These two verses are absent from the editions.].

The king, delighted by the sweetness of such a reputation, silently revolved in his heart for a long time how he might join to himself this queen, who had been surrounded by so many plots of the king.

It also came to his mind that the king previously mentioned, who had once been driven from his ancestral fields and had soon been restored through his aid and mercy, would now prove ungrateful for such great gifts of kindness. Therefore he immediately devised a suitable opportunity to bring the Italian kingdom under his own authority.

When Liudulfus, the king’s son, learned of this through his father’s account, true love for his father and hope for his people—not concerning his own interests, but considering his father’s advantage—he secretly gathered a very few companions and set out for Italy. With a strong hand he entered it, urging the people to bow their necks to his father’s authority. Soon he returned, bringing back a splendid triumph without battle.

When Otto [Note: [Col. 1163] *Otto* in the first edition.] learned this from the people’s reports, he rejoiced in his heart over his beloved son, who, for his sake, had now boldly undertaken so great a danger by stirring up a fierce people.

And, so that such a labor of love would not prove fruitless, he himself hastened to visit that same people, accompanied by no small company of his own subjects and adorned with the varied splendor of royal pomp.

[Col. 1164C] He entered the regions girded by the lofty Alps.

When Berengarius learned of this [Note: [Col. 1163] *Compertus* corrected; *compertis* in witness 1.] and was dumbfounded, he did not wage war against the king or come out to meet him. Instead, he immediately withdrew into a suitable fortress situated in secure and strongly defended places.

But our renowned king, proud of his valor, boldly crossed the wholly unfamiliar regions and captured Pavia, the lady-city of the Italian kingdom [Note: [Col. 1163] *Dominam* in witness 1.] (September 23).

Once it had been captured, all the nobles came in a body, seeking the newly arrived king. They vied with one another to submit themselves to his great authority. In accordance with his custom, he received them with a kindly spirit, promising them the gift of his favor

[Col. 1164D] if thereafter they served him with faithful devotion.

With these matters thus arranged, he frequently remembered in his heart the very distinguished queen Aethelheith, desiring one day to see the royal face of one whose goodness he had learned.

Accordingly, through messages secretly conveyed, he sent her a firm pledge of peace and exceedingly sweet love beneath the sign of faithful trust [Note: [Col. 1163] *Mandat: clis* in the first edition; cf. below, verse 651.].

[Vers. 643.] He also urged her through friendly counsels to hasten swiftly to Pavia, the populous city which she had left in bitter sorrow, so that, through the sacred and enduring mercy of the king,

[Col. 1165A] she might now joyfully receive the lofty honor by which she had previously suffered immense grief.

The kindly queen yielded to these messages [Note: [Col. 1163] Witness 1 reads *mandat: clis*; see below, v. 651.]. She went where she had been ordered, accompanied by very many ranks of subject peoples.

When the king learned that she was coming at his command, he ordered her beloved brother Henry to turn back across the banks of the Po to meet her, so that his service might adorn her ladyship [Note: [Col. 1165D] That is, “her mistress.”], elevated by the splendors of the kingdom, and fittingly arrayed for the service of so great a duke [Note: [Col. 1165] Thus the second edition; the first has *d. c.*].

Following the commands of his elder brother with devoted attention,

[Col. 1165B] he went forth with the royal army and joyfully sought the camp of the venerable queen, where she was staying with many companions. He escorted her with the highest honor until he presented her to the royal presence.

She immediately pleased the king greatly, as she deserved, and was chosen as the most worthy partner of his kingdom.

Then [Note: [Col. 1165] The manuscript does not mark a division here.], seeing himself detained by the novelty of the situation, lest the time at hand should bring him back to his ancestral lands, the king decided to send ahead his beloved son Liudulfus, so that the strong Saxon people might hasten to him and the kingdom stand securely beneath so great a protector.

The son, obedient in devoted spirit to his father’s commands, returned to his homeland and undertook responsibility for the kingdom, prudently and exceedingly wisely completing

[Col. 1165C] everything that then had to be done in the country.

Meanwhile Duke Henry, the king’s venerable brother, in Italy devoted himself with the greatest exertion of heart to services appropriate to the king—not merely performing the office of a dear brother, but rather fulfilling, with kindly zeal, the duty of an obedient servant.

For this reason he deservedly pleased the king greatly. He was also joined to the queen by fraternal affection and was loved by her with devoted affection.

Then the king traversed the Italian kingdom in every direction, subjecting its chief men to his authority (951).

When these matters had been completed and settled according to his desire, so that Berengarius would not seize the kingdom for himself again, he ordered the prudent Duke Conradus, together with not a few chosen men from the army, to remain in Pavia.

[Col. 1165D] To him he had given his venerable daughter in marriage.

The king himself immediately returned with his illustrious wife, intending to hasten to his homeland.

The people rejoiced to receive him on his arrival, showering sweet thanks into the heavens above to the Most High,

who, in his accustomed mercy, had compassion on his people and had brought back in peace the one whom he had chosen as their pious king.

[Col. 1166A] When this joy had thus been celebrated with worthy festivities [Note: [Col. 1165] The manuscript does not mark a division here.], Duke Conradus returned in peace, bringing with him the aforementioned Berengarius. He had captured him through his profound skill in such a way that Berengarius came willingly to submit himself to King Otto [Note: [Col. 1165] *Ottoni* in the first edition.].

Then the same king, who always acted wisely, received this king with due honor, restoring to him the height of the kingdom that had been taken from him, but only on this condition:

that thereafter he would not oppose his authority, so greatly to be feared [Note: [Col. 1165] *Mutuendo* in witness 1.], in any matter, but would be obedient to his commands like a devoted subject.

He also decreed, with especially earnest words, that thereafter Berengarius should rule that people more mercifully, whom he had previously chastised [Note: [Col. 1165] The second edition has *contrivit*, “crushed”; the first has *corripuit*, “chastised.”.] too severely with bitter authority.

Pretending to be ready to fulfill the commands, Berengarius quickly departed and joyfully made for his homeland.

But as soon as he possessed the lofty citadel of the kingdom, influenced by the evil counsels of certain men, he soon imposed heavier yokes upon the unfortunate people, with great force for the contempt shown him [Note: [Col. 1165] *Facto* in witness 2.]. He claimed that he had purchased the kingdom at a high price, and that he should not be blamed if he had violated the right of his ancestors; rather, the blame should be charged to Otto [Note: [Col. 1165] *Ottoni* in the first edition.],

[Col. 1166B] who had sold all the leading men of the people to him.

As soon as this matter reached the same king, righteous anger was kindled against Berengarius. Grieving in his heart over the people’s pitiable sufferings, he sought [Note: [Col. 1165] Thus in witness 1; *statuit* in witness 2.] to restore their condition [Note: [Col. 1165] Thus in witness 2; *statuit* in witness 1.] to something better.

He would have done so quickly, supported by Christ’s protection,

[Col. 1166C] if the adverse cause of fortune had not remained.

For while his kingdom was flourishing in every respect, and he rejoiced that he shone amid every success, the renewed plague of the ancient enemy produced a deceitful scheme, grievous to all ages [Note: [Col. 1165] Thus the second edition; the first has *dolentum*, “grieving.”.], already attempting to throw the peaceful kingdom into confusion.

So that the malign enemy might accomplish this as quickly as possible, he first disturbed all the rulers of the kingdom, hoping that the destruction of the people would soon follow.

Finally, when Liudulfus, son of the renowned king (953), learned through sufficiently clear signs of friendship how deeply the faithful queen loved Henry, the king’s brother, and that Henry had submitted himself wholly to her faithful devotion, he was struck by the arrows of inward and secret grief.

[Col. 1166D] He was not burning with anger or wasting away in the gall of hatred, but, because he had lost the love of his dear mother, he drew sighs from the hiding places of his afflicted heart.

Deceived by the evil counsels of many, he feared, in accordance with the weakness of his character, that thereafter he would not receive gifts of fitting honor,

[Vers. 747.] but might perhaps be forced to occupy a secondary position.

[Col. 1167A] Just Christ would never have permitted this to happen if the kingdom had remained peacefully secure under righteous rule.

But when he was repeatedly shown to his sorrowful father with a sad face and no longer cheerful in his accustomed manner, there were some who, deceived by the serpent’s cunning fraud [Note: [Col. 1167] Thus in witness 1; Celtes rightly wrote *deceptum*. This is the end of folio 148. The following quire, which described the events of 953, 954, 955, 956, and 957, has been lost (thus about 388 verses).], [lacuna]

(Very many verses have been lost.)

But so that he might thereby increase his father’s royal honor. [Note: [Col. 1167D] The conclusion of Liudulf’s victorious embassy or letter, sent from Lombardy to his father; its subject can be learned from Otto’s reply.]

When the king learned of these things from the faithful report of his success (957), he rejoiced in his son and, with complete gladness of heart, immediately sent him these words in a letter:

> “May praise remain forever and ever to the Almighty, who has granted you to rejoice amid such great successes.
>
> “Thanks also be given to you, dearest son, whom I know to be wholly faithful. You have indeed given clear signs of your fidelity,
>
> [Col. 1167B] “since, desiring our kingdom to grow through you, you have marked out for us the whole glory of your own labor.
>
> “Therefore, gratefully accepting what you have wisely done, I repay you in fitting exchange. I entrust this same kingdom to you to govern,
>
> “which you have established as subject to our authority.
>
> “And I command you, beloved, by paternal orders, to make the people whom you have overcome with your victorious right hand establish with you, without delay, a treaty to be maintained, founded upon a fear-inspiring oath.”

The venerable Duke Liudulfus read these decrees. Rejoicing at messages of such great kindness, he bound the people to his father’s service with a firm oath, as he had been ordered, and governed them worthily.

When these matters had been properly arranged, burning to earn the face of his absent father under the highest bond of peace, and overcome by sweet love for his dear wife and his two children [Note: [Col. 1167D] Otto and Mahthildis.], who had been left far behind him [Note: [Col. 1167] The first edition has *posterga*.],

[Col. 1167C] he decided to return to his native land, which he had set aside, so that after the excessively heavy burden of harsh exile he might at last obtain rest in his homeland.

And, so that he might accomplish this without delay and no burden might retard his desired journey, he ordered his own treasures to be sent ahead in a group and his entire company to precede him—the force that he had taken there for the sake of war—promising that, with life accompanying him, he himself would reach the borders of his homeland after a short time.

He also conveyed this promise in honey-sweet words, in which he wished suitable hospitality and provisions to be prepared for him in the castles and other places he named.

Moved by this report, our countrymen rejoiced with eager inward affection at what they desired.

[Vers. 1182.] Putting away from their hearts all the weight of grief and every sorrow which they had previously endured because of the absent elder,

[Col. 1168A] they all together considered it the supreme cause for joy if, after the passage of a few days, they might see again the joyful man, in accordance with the announcements of his promise [Note: [Col. 1167] That is, “joyful”; namely, they expected to see Liudulfus again, although he died on September 6 of that year. Hence approximately six leaves, or 290 verses, containing the events of the years 957–962 up to Otto’s Roman coronation, have been lost. Reuber perceived the lacuna here.].

(Very many verses have been lost.)

Equally bearing the scepter and the beautiful diadem of the head (962, February 2) [Note: [Col. 1168D] “Equally with Otto.” [Note: [Col. 1168D] Namely, Aethelheidis, crowned together with Otto at Rome with the imperial crown.]],

and all the royal garments of her rank, she received the adornments of a greater dignity, being immediately blessed together with the supreme Augustus [Note: [Col. 1167] Corrected from *majores* to *majoris* in the first edition.].

Thus far I have sung in measured verse the deeds of the renowned King Otto, although with a slender Muse.

Now the deeds accomplished by that same Augustus, while he held the throne at the summit of affairs, remain to be written.

[Col. 1168B] I fear to touch upon them, since I am restrained by my female sex; nor should they be recounted in an unworthy style:

how, through the hard struggle of unconquered war, he seized the castles built in maritime places (963), which Berengarius and his wife possessed;

how, compelled by an oath after it had been completed, he sent that man into exile together with his wretched wife Willa (964);

how, pierced by the sharp goad of righteous zeal, he deprived the supreme pontiff of the honor of the Apostolic See because he was committing certain perverse acts and did not deign to yield to his repeated warnings, appointing another worthy to bear the title of ruler;

how, when the kingdom rested in tranquil peace, he visited our countrymen and then returned there again (966);

[Col. 1168C] and how, retaining the glory of both empires, he raised to the dignity of the imperial fasces the son who came after him—namely, Otto, the king from the nurse’s breast—on December 25, 967, and caused him to be duly blessed in accordance with his own example.

These matters, therefore, cannot be set forth in our verses; they seek a narrative far nobler than mine.

Therefore I [Note: [Col. 1167] Corrected from *ergo* to *ego* in the first edition.], restrained by the burden of such great events, do not proceed farther. Instead, I wisely set an end, lest after this beginning I should collapse, defeated.

When these things have thus been finished and briefly recapitulated, the king’s everlasting mercy must be earnestly entreated:

may he, in his kindness, grant that our august rulers [Note: [Col. 1167] The editor corrects *augustus* in witness 1 to *augustos*; namely, the Ottos.] pass all the time of their present life happily,

[Col. 1168D] ever supported by every success according to their desires, and preserve them as many years as possible as guardians of the Church,

[Vers. 1517.] giving us solace in his mercy. Amen.

# Appendix to the Works of Hrotsvit

[Col. 1169]

## Life of Saint Hathumoda, First Abbess of Gandersheim

By Agius, a contemporary priest and monk. Appended is Agius’s Dialogue on the Death of Saint Hathumoda.

*(In Pez, Thesaurus Anecdotorum novus I, III, 288.)*

### Prologue

[Col. 1169A]

To the most holy sisters of the monastery of Gandersheim, worthy to be loved with honor and honored with love, Agius, although an unworthy priest through the grace of Christ:

We are wholly unable to say how much we owe to our former spiritual mother, and how much we owe at the same time to your charity. For we cannot express either what sort of affection all of you together have habitually shown us, or what and how many benefits we have received especially from her.

Therefore, because we think this worthy of her holy merits, and because we do not doubt that it will also be pleasing to you, we have judged it fitting to send you a brief transcript of her Life, although written in an unpolished style. Since you can no longer bodily see and possess her, as you desired above all else, you may thus retain a kind of image of her in this Life and may think that you possess her in her examples and deeds.

We hope that we shall not do this improperly, because, as you know, we had learned a considerable part of her life, and we were also present at her falling asleep. Therefore, first of all, we warn the reader to understand that we shall say nothing false or doubtful about her, but shall relate things true, certain, and known to nearly all who were able to know her. For we write nothing other than what the lesser people everywhere proclaim and the greater approve.

If, however, anything concerning the manifestation of her holiness was unable to reach the knowledge of everyone without distinction, we advise that it be entrusted to the faith of the sisters who clung more closely to her, and that their testimony be believed. For her known holiness does not permit us to doubt even matters less widely known.

Touching briefly, therefore, upon each subject, we think that we should speak first of her lineage, so that it may become clear from where she came, for what purpose she came, and how much she spurned, despised, and abandoned for the love of God. For the more anyone abandons for God, the greater will be that person’s merit before God, and the greater the reward that person will receive from God.

### Chapter I. Hathumoda’s Very Noble Birth. Her Distinguished Pursuit of Piety and Learning in Childhood. Her Reception of the Sacred Veil at Herford. Her Transfer Thereafter to the Monastery of Gandersheim, and the Assignment and Acceptance of Its Governance by Hathumoda. The Manner of Life at Herford and Gandersheim.

[Col. 1170A]

To say nothing, finally, of her forebears, all of whom were very illustrious on both her father’s and her mother’s side, the great nobility that this holy and incomparable woman possessed in the world is evident from the following: her brother has the granddaughter of kings as his wife; her sister, worthy of such a husband, has been joined in marriage to a king’s son; the others, throughout the homeland, who were not bound to Christ’s service with lesser glory, obtained most honorable marriages according to the dignity of their birth.

Her father, descended from the most illustrious stock of the Saxons, was duke of the Eastern Saxons. Her mother, likewise descended from the most noble lineage of the Franks, shone even more nobly in her offspring. Hathumoda herself—so called—grew from the good seed of good trees, first a most delightful flower and afterward a most fragrant fruit.

For although, as we have said, she was most noble in the dignity of her birth, the holiness of her mind was nobler still. From earliest childhood she displayed something of her future character and exchanged childish frivolity for Christian seriousness. The games and harmless amusements familiar to that age she mocked as vain with a mature mind, although she possessed a tender body, and she despised them as useful for nothing.

Gold and costly adornment, which children, because they are beautiful, often desire innocently, she neither desired nor wished to possess. Although garments adorned with gold, mitres, ribbons, hair ornaments, earrings, crescent pendants, necklaces, bracelets, armlets, headbands, and scent-boxes were offered freely according to her parents’ means and dignity—objects for which the ambition of many women burns either to possess or to wear them—she refused to accept them. When such things were imposed upon her against her will, she groaned anxiously and wept bitterly.

She rejoiced in attending the churches of Christ as often as she could, since she could not do so continually, and in hearing there something beneficial to herself and devoting herself to prayer. As for letters, which others are compelled to learn by blows, she sought them voluntarily and mastered them through tireless study.

From earliest infancy, integrity of character grew together with her; and as her age increased, she shone daily greater in virtues. As she advanced in age, increasing in wisdom and favor with God and human beings, she preferred the service of Christ to worldly pomp and Christ, the heavenly Bridegroom, to an earthly bridegroom.

Finally, preferring the company of God’s handmaids to the shining halls of her parents, she was consecrated with the sacred veil with her parents’ consent and entrusted for some time to the Herford monastery, then the most renowned place for women dedicated to religion, to be nurtured under regular discipline.

We cannot easily express in words how greatly she afterward loved that place and how worthy of reverence she judged it. For whenever, speaking with her close companions, she mentioned that place, she used to say that she would consider herself fortunate if she deserved to be among them again under the authority of the abbess, and even more fortunate if she were never taken away from there.

She remembered the faces and features of each one and brought the character of all before her eyes. She praised this one’s charity and that one’s humility; she said that one surpassed the others in obedience and another in patience; in one she admired generosity, in another abstinence. In all together she praised modesty, piety, and chastity.

After she had remained there for some time, as we have said, for the sake of instruction, and had given everyone an example of every good quality as far as her age permitted, her father and mother returned from Rome, where they had gone for the sake of prayer, with the apostolic blessing. They had entrusted themselves, together with all their possessions, to Saint Peter and the household of Saint Peter, and had transferred the bodies of Pope Anastasius and Pope Innocent.

She was then recalled to the monastery founded on their own inheritance and dedicated to the Lord and to those same saints. There, with apostolic authority and the blessing of her bishop, she was first elected and established as spiritual mother over a few sisters, and afterward over more.

[Col. 1171D] It is beyond our ability to unfold how chastely in body and how holily in mind she afterward lived with her fellow sisters.

Their life was common to all, their food common, and their clothing similar. It was moderate—neither excessively elegant nor especially humble—and it was not entirely woolen.

None of them ate with parents or with any guests, or spoke with them except by permission. As is customary among many religious women, no one left the monastery for her parents or for dependent properties. Outside the common dining hall and the appointed hour, no one was permitted to eat unless illness had compelled her to do so.

All, established together in one place,

[Col. 1172A] ate together, rested together, gathered together at the hour of prayer for the canonical offices, and, going out together, performed whatever work had to be done.

No one was permitted to have private cells or personal servants within the cloister. They lived outside, in a small village, because at that time their spiritual mother was not yet able to provide them with clothing owing to insufficient resources; she herself supplied the poorer women with what they could not obtain elsewhere.

Their separation from men was so strict that not even presbyters entered their cloister unless the necessity of illness required it or some reasonable matter connected with their official ministry demanded it.

These are the things they shared more or less in common with the others.

### Chapter II. Hathumoda’s Common Life; Her Modesty in Speech, Food, and Clothing. Her Devotion to Prayer, Kindness, Charity, and Other Virtues.

[Col. 1172B]

She not only fulfilled all these practices but even surpassed them.

Thus she shared the common life and food of the others: although she did not deny the others meat on the days and at the times appointed for them, she did not indulge herself in it. She wore similar clothing, but while she prevented those who wished it from wearing linen garments next to the flesh [*cod.*, *lineis*], she herself wore wool.

Moreover, although she did not speak with guests except in church, she would sometimes speak with them at mealtime when courtesy required her presence.

From the time she came there, she never went to her parents or to dependent properties. Outside the monastery she ate with no man—I should rather say, with no one at all. Within the monastery, although it was permitted, she was accustomed to eat nowhere except in the common refectory.

She went to church with the others at the hour of prayer, arriving either first or among the first and leaving last. She slept in the same house as the others, but came to bed last and rose from bed first.

Just as she did not wish to have personal servants within the monastery like the others, so she herself had none. For the holy woman, beloved of God, strove to excel in life just as she excelled in rank; she strove to surpass others in merit just as in name.

Therefore she made it her practice to anticipate the nocturnal chants, remain awake after the morning hymns, and perform many other such duties which seemed arduous to the others but, because of her habit and her immense love of God, exceedingly joyful and entirely easy to her.

She remembered what she was; she remembered what was said. She considered that she had been called a mother; she considered that she was honored by the name of abbess. Therefore she rejoiced more in being useful than in presiding, and desired rather to be loved than feared.

Accordingly, because she considered that she had received not so much an honor as a burden, she never forbade anyone to do something that she herself had done, nor commanded anyone to do something that she herself had not first fulfilled. Thus she urged her subjects to do good more by her own deeds and examples than by discipline.

She was such in speech as in action, and such in action as in speech, because what she taught she did, and what she did she taught.

And because divine Scripture forbids some things in four ways, commands some, permits some, and counsels some,

[Col. 1173A] she herself, as far as human weakness made possible, committed none of the forbidden things. She did whatever was just. From permitted things she made things unlawful for herself. She eagerly seized upon the counseled practices with a view to the greater reward.

She not only refrained in deed from the manifest evils that were prohibited, but also detested them in mind. She strove with all her strength to fulfill the manifest goods that were commanded.

As for things permitted, which according to the manner of their use may be either good or evil—among them the use of the world, the pleasures of marriage, the eating of meat, and the wearing of softer and more elegant clothing—she rejected them with greater caution and avoided them with sounder judgment.

The counseled practices, which, as higher things, could neither be commanded to all nor fulfilled by all—among them renunciation of the world, abstinence from meat, contempt for softer and more elegant clothing, and the observance of virginity—she eagerly embraced and completed with perseverance.

Finally, she despised softer clothing so completely that she also wore rougher garments, not highly ornamented. She abstained from meat so thoroughly that, even along with the other foods and drink necessary for life, she took bread itself only very sparingly.

She renounced the world not only in outward things but also inwardly in her mind and will. She guarded her purpose of virginity so carefully that she gave envious people no opportunity for slander.

There was no boldness or immodest frivolity in her speech. No indecent discourse or shameful word ever came from her mouth. No one ever heard her quarrelling, cursing, swearing, slandering, or lying.

No one saw her angry, turbulent, or laughing excessively and dishonorably. She never injured anyone, brought a charge against anyone, or heaped abuse upon anyone.

She loved all according to their individual qualities, or honored them with reverence. She reproved the faults of her fellow sisters in such a way that she nevertheless loved and venerated them with the greatest affection.

She practiced discipline toward each according to that person’s merits. She loved nature; she hated wickedness. She loved what Christ had made; she hated what the devil had devised.

She wept over the transgressions of her sisters as though they were her own. Whenever one of them was weak in faith or mind, she herself was ill along with her. Whenever one was scandalized, she herself burned with pain.

Yet, with a calm face and serene spirit, even amid mournful and tearful situations, she always displayed serenity.

Moreover, no one was able to possess either purer faith in God or better faith toward human beings. In granting friendships, she appeared extremely cautious and difficult to persuade except in the case of just relationships; in preserving them, she was most steadfast.

### Chapter III. Her Diligence and Skill in Investigating the Divine Scriptures; Her Humility, Patience toward the Needy, Liberality toward the Sick, and Hospitality. Her Foreknowledge in a Night Vision of the Monastery’s Future Condition.

[Cols. 1174A–1174C]

She herself also devoted herself assiduously to the reading of the Scriptures, and greatly loved those who applied themselves to it. Those who were negligent, yet whom she saw might nevertheless make some progress, she compelled to study them by withholding familiarity rather than by discipline. In hearing, reading, and understanding them, scarcely anyone at that time could equal her caution, liveliness of perception, and soundness of understanding. If, as is customary, she had to ask a question, she addressed every point so clearly and thoroughly that in her very questioning she seemed rather to teach than to inquire.

It would take too long if we wished to touch upon all her virtues individually. She possessed extraordinary charity, supreme humility, the greatest patience, incredible generosity, and incomparable piety. How great was the charity with which she loved them all, and how greatly she in turn was loved by them, is shown by the tears of so many people, shed at her falling asleep. Her humility was so great that, although she was born, as we said at the beginning, of a very distinguished family and held the highest position among her fellow sisters, no one appeared readier to bow, humbler in speech, or, in her clothing, almost more modest.

What should I say about her patience, when she never reproved anyone with an insulting reprimand, nor ever returned a harsh word even to one who reviled her? As for her generosity and piety, it is superfluous to say anything, since she treated everyone as though she herself had given birth to them from her own entrails. What poor person, what cleric, ever left her empty-handed? Who was not refreshed by her food? Who did not share in her goods? Sometimes she went without what she could give to others; she herself suffered want so that others might abound; she went hungry so that the poor would not hunger; she thirsted so that her guests would not lack drink. In receiving them, no one could display greater humility, charity, or humaneness.

If their rank warranted it, she would customarily sit with them at the hour of the meal, discuss God, heavenly things, and the divine Scriptures with them, ask them questions or teach them, and thus show them every form of human kindness. She took care that, while the body was being nourished outwardly, the mind should not remain idle within.

[Cols. 1174D–1175C]

It is unnecessary to say how solicitous she was toward the sick. She not only tended those who were present with extraordinary care and varied services, but also visited through messengers those who were ill elsewhere and at a distance, sending whatever foods she thought would please them. Indeed, shortly before her own illness, when most of the sisters were seriously unwell, it cannot be said how anxiously she visited them, how attentively she stood by them, how diligently she hurried between their individual beds, how gently she addressed each one, or by how many remarkable and varied services she attempted to lighten their bodily distress, taking every possible measure to ensure that they lacked neither necessary assistance nor anything they desired.

It was as though that holy woman, beloved of God, already knew that she would soon be departing this world. Yet it is also shown, from certain indications given by the elders, that this had been foretold beforehand not only to her but to others as well. For some of the sisters dreamed that the great sign of the church had fallen and been shattered; many thought they saw the sarcophagus of the saints collapse and be broken into pieces.

Not long before her illness, while speaking with one of her familiar companions, she began, amid their customary conversations, to lament tenderly the precarious condition of her monastery. When he said that it was indeed precarious, but good by God’s grace, she replied that its goodness depended upon God’s power and mercy, but that she was deeply displeased that it had not yet been placed under royal protection.

When he again said that this would soon be remedied if the Lord willed, and that she had both a bishop faithful to them and personally known to her, whose recommendation could accomplish it, as well as parents and other trusted people at court who could and would gladly support her wishes in this matter, she said that she believed so too, but that she herself would not live until it happened. It would, however, happen soon. All these matters, she said, must take place according to the Lord’s will; nevertheless, she was troubled by certain remarkable dreams, unlike any she had previously experienced, and begged him for prayer and blessing concerning them.

For she said that in her dreams she had seen a wheel of extraordinary size, with various figures of animals inserted into its axle. She herself, together with many of her fellow sisters, seemed to be fastened by little chains to the axle above the hub, within the small spaces between the spokes. At the same time she was whirled around with the wheel, which a river running beneath it drove around with extraordinary speed. When, as it seemed to her, she stood terrified, afraid that she might fall into the river flowing beneath, she fell—not into the river, as she feared, but rather onto the adjacent ground. After this, she said, she awoke and lay there, already awake and returned to herself, yet with all her limbs numb and still trembling.

## CHAPTER IV. The time of her death and the place of her burial shown to her in a dream. Saint Martin honored by her with special devotion and seen by her repeatedly.

[Cols. 1175C–1177B]

During those same days she also said that she had often seemed to herself to fly with a light body and, though stripped of her body, to remain bodily present among heavenly and earthly things in a manner ineffable to us. For in those final days she seemed to have been carried up into the air and to have seen all the monastery’s buildings uncovered, with everything that was in them or being done in each one laid open and completely visible to her eyes.

Among these things she seemed to see in the church a great cleft in the earth. When she was deeply distressed by this vision and asked how it had come about or how it might be filled, she heard a voice telling her that it had to be filled because it would be her future dwelling. After this, she said, she heard a multitude of people singing Psalm 140. When they reached the verse, “This is my rest for ever and ever; here I shall dwell, for I have chosen it,” she seemed to be singing it together with them. Then she awoke fully and, while still awake, had the same verse upon her lips.

Although she related this as a dream, and the person to whom she reported it interpreted it in the same way, it seemed quite different to him, and he immediately feared what the outcome of events later revealed. Therefore he did not speak at once, lest she realize that he had understood it in that way. After a short while, however, he thought she should be admonished concerning certain matters that seemed likely to increase her merits and God’s mercies toward her, and he considered it appropriate to pray for these things. She granted this as far as she could at the time, with her customary devotion toward God and kindness toward everyone.

At the same time, when we were also there and already wished to depart, she would not allow us to leave. With a slight smile she said that we did not know how long we would still be permitted to enjoy her company and see her; if it happened that she died soon, we would then regret leaving against her will. She also began earnestly to ask us, both herself and through several of her sisters, that if we heard she had fallen ill, we should not fail to come.

From all this we can not only infer but clearly understand that the time of her falling asleep had been shown to her beforehand. Divine mercy had also chosen to foreshadow it through the illness of the sisters who had fallen sick before her. Thus, while she diligently moved among the sick, she herself fell ill. For a while she resisted the illness and thought she had overcome it—or rather, eluded it. For so long as she could, she remained with the other sisters in the choir for the offices and in the refectory at table, until she was deprived of the ability to walk.

Before the disease grew worse and confined her to bed, however, she dreamed that she saw a great field flourishing with many kinds of flowers. She also thought she saw almost all of her sisters who were blooming in the flower of youth. When she took great delight in its beauty and loveliness, it suddenly seemed to her to burst into flames. Then, moved by immense compassion for them, she began to cry out that the Lord should have mercy and that Christ should come to their aid, lest he allow the wretched women to perish utterly.

Because she had always honored Saint Martin with a special reverence and was accustomed to invoke him in her greatest necessities, she began, as it seemed to her, humbly to pray that through his merits and intervention they might be snatched from the flames. Immediately, someone of astonishing splendor and beauty seemed to stand before her and said that through his merits and intercession the fire would be subdued and they would be saved. When she awoke, she later related the dream to many people and commended Saint Martin, as her particular rescuer, to be celebrated thereafter by them with special veneration and services.

We can confidently believe from her own account and words that she visibly saw Saint Martin even while awake. One day, when several of the sisters were sitting beside her little bed, she suddenly began to cry out that Saint Martin was present and walking on the floor. She urged those who were sitting to rise before the one who was standing, and to rejoice in the one who was walking. She said that those who had described him as deformed, as is written in his Life, were either deceiving others or deceived themselves; she had never seen anything of such beauty.

Although those standing there could see none of this, they could understand from her expression and composure that what she said was true. Turning her face joyfully this way and that around the room, she gave the observers a clear indication that her eyes were following him where she seemed to see him walking on the floor. Although, after taking to her bed, she had never wished to turn onto the other side or to lie on the right side of her body, she then turned herself over spontaneously, without anyone’s assistance, and lay there without any sign of discomfort until the vision had ended.

She also tried to raise with her hands the curtain hanging against the wall and ordered that the wall itself be moved away, so that it would not obstruct God’s saint. Since it was clear from the preceding signs that he was standing on the southern side, she repeatedly urged those present to look at him. Thus it is plainly evident that through his merits she was able to do this despite the violence of her illness: she said that he was visible to her bodily eyes, and she truly saw him with the gaze of her mind.

## CHAPTER V. Hathumoda’s various visions, whose narration she bore with great displeasure to have interrupted by the importunity of others.

[Cols. 1177C–1178C]

At that same time, when no one was present with her in the little room where she lay except her full sisters, who would not allow themselves to be absent from her even for a moment, she lay for some time with her eyes closed as though asleep. After a while she asked who was with her. When they said that they were present, she asked whether they had seen or heard anything.

When they replied that they had neither seen nor heard anything of the kind about which they thought she was asking, she said: “And did you not hear a voice asking whether the dove is ready?” A crystal vessel containing the relics of the saints was hanging beside her bed. Her sister Christina said that she seemed to have seen this so that the crystal’s fastening, which had not been prepared carefully enough, might be corrected. Hathumoda said that this might indeed be so. For even before the fever, and especially during the fever itself, she had the habit that, whenever something interrupted what she intended to say and she tried to turn to another matter, she would not persist in it but would immediately answer, “That may be so.”

What displeased her most in such matters was when she wished to entrust something more secret to someone, and the person whom she had deemed worthy of receiving it thought that someone else should be brought into the conversation. The following episode sufficiently demonstrates this.

One day, while she lay in her little bed and her sister Gerberga, who was especially close to her, stood beside it, she said that she would tell Gerberga a certain vision in secret, with everyone else removed. She had never, she said, seen or heard anything of such beauty, splendor, or sweetness.

When all the others had withdrawn and the two were alone, Hathumoda, helped up from the bed, ordered Gerberga to bring her ear closer to Hathumoda’s mouth. When she had done this, Hathumoda told her to come still closer, lest anyone else hear. But when she had prepared to speak, she began to grow pale and tremble.

Although Gerberga was herself terrified, she nevertheless asked whether she wished the priest Wulffhard, who was standing outside the door, to be summoned so that Hathumoda could tell him what she had intended to reveal. Hathumoda replied that she absolutely did not want this and that she did not wish to tell it to anyone except Gerberga. But when she again prepared to explain what she had intended, she became so violently distressed that she seemed almost about to die.

Gerberga, afraid to remain there alone, immediately summoned the priest. When he came, Hathumoda would tell neither him nor even her sister, complaining bitterly that Gerberga had dared to disclose and publicize the matter against her wish and will. She acted in precisely the same way concerning her mother.

Her mother was not in the monastery when the event just described took place. But after hearing of her daughter’s illness, she came, and after completing what was appropriate for her visit, Hathumoda requested that her mother be summoned to her alone. She said that she would tell her mother a certain utterly astonishing matter in secret.

When everyone had been removed as she requested and mother and daughter stood together alone, Hathumoda began to prepare to speak. But again she began to grow pale, tremble, and become distressed. Seeing her daughter’s failing condition, her mother said that, because of the intimacy between them, she could perhaps tell it instead to her sister Gerberga.

When Hathumoda heard this, she placed a finger to her lips and declared that she would no longer tell it either to Gerberga, to her mother herself, or to any human being. Let whoever can determine why she was not permitted to reveal it. This much is certainly credible: she had seen something great and divine. It could not have been something small and human if she herself had described it as being of such beauty and sweetness, or if she had suspected it with such trembling.

## CHAPTER VI. Hathumoda’s remarkable devotion toward her mother and toward the author, and their love and respect for Hathumoda, especially during her final illness.

[Cols. 1178D–1180B]

It is also plainly evident that she heard or saw several other things. For she often asked those standing nearby what the disturbance or sound was that she heard; often she urged them to listen, or asked what sort of storm there was, or in what agitation, turmoil, and conflict the world was situated.

We might believe that this was merely an impression caused by the severity of her illness, as sometimes happens, if what we have related above did not persuade us otherwise. Yet anyone may find it remarkable that she could conceal from her mother some of the things she had seen, since she always loved and reverenced her above all others. She was always affectionate toward her, as though she were a little child, and obeyed her in everything like a servant.

Whenever she saw her somewhat sad, she tried in various ways and with remarkable attentions to soothe her troubled mind. Since she knew that reading books was especially pleasing to her, she would say that she had found something both pleasant to hear and useful to remember, which she ought to read to her.

Who could adequately describe the joy with which, in her customary devotion toward God, she rejoiced when her mother, having understood her wishes, pretended that she would no longer leave that place, in order to make her daughter happy? She gave thanks to God, caressed her mother with kisses, embraced her with her hands, and repeatedly went over with the sisters what her mother had promised her.

This is less surprising when one considers that, while she was still healthy, she had shown extraordinary affection toward even our utterly unworthy smallness, and, once ill, had desired to see us with immense longing. At the very beginning of her illness she sent us a message, concealing the news of her condition but instructing us to come by every means.

You are witnesses, as is God, who must grant this to her holy soul, with what joy—so far as her illness allowed—she received us when we arrived; with what charity she kept us near her; with what solicitude she continually urged that we be cared for; with what anxiety she searched for us when we had left the room for even a short time; with what persistence she tried to speak with us, repeating our name; and with what sorrow she lamented that we had come so late.

We shall mention a small matter, extraordinary as some may think it, yet one that shows her affection toward us. Whenever she could not otherwise be induced, despite her pain, to taste something, she persuaded herself by this device: if it was said that it had been sent by us or prepared by us, she would take it.

On the very day we arrived, when food had been brought before her, she ordered us to be summoned. She ate as much as she could in our presence, and for our consolation tried in every respect to conduct herself so cheerfully that we conceived the greatest hope that she would escape death.

But when evening came, everything turned in the opposite direction. Our joy was changed into sorrow and our hope into despair. The illness began to grow worse and increase gradually from moment to moment, so that we lost all hope of her recovery and awaited only her death. Yet amid the distress of her sickness, both her affection toward us and your devotion and love for her, most holy sisters, were revealed.

First of all, her venerable aunt, although already advanced in years and worn out by old age, remained beside her tirelessly, as far as her grief allowed her to be present. The monastery’s superior, though burdened with many responsibilities, did not leave her bedside even for a short while. The dean and the keeper of the church came frequently, insofar as the duties entrusted to them permitted, and always wished to be present.

The remaining sisters, who could not remain constantly with her in the room, either devoted themselves in the church to psalms and prayers for her or kept watch outside the room. Above all, however, the devotion toward her that her full sisters had already shown to everyone now shone forth.

They sat beside her bed; they tirelessly attended the one lying there; they arranged the bed; they placed a cushion beneath her head; they supported her with their own bodies when she was raised in bed; they rubbed her hands, warmed her feet, and soothed her stomach. They cooled her as she burned with a fan, wiped away the sweat running down her with a linen cloth, tempered warm water for washing, prepared and set before her food, and anticipated each other in everything that had to be done.

Above all, her admirable mother, concealing her inward grief behind a composed expression, tried to console those who mourned, restrain those who wept, and soothe each one with her words. She wished to console others, although she could not console herself.

With what groans she hurried between the church and her daughter’s bed! How many tears she shed before the tomb of the saints, so that her daughter might not be taken from her; so that she herself might die in her daughter’s place; so that, just as she had entered this light first, she might also depart from it first!

Several times, on her very way to her daughter, she stopped and turned back. Thus that strongest of women almost did not know what she should do: one impulse called her forward, another called her back; one urged her to be present at her daughter’s final moments. What, then, should she do? Affection called her forward; grief called her back. She approached, but she could not bear to see her daughter burning in the agony of death. She withdrew, but she could not bear to be absent from her suffering daughter.

## CHAPTER VII. Her continual psalmody and discourse on divine matters. The author reveals to her the agitation of the absent abbot and brethren at his remaining with her too long.

[Cols. 1180C–1181B]

Her body gradually began to fail, yet her mind, intent upon heaven, remained firm. She often sang with us the same psalms, often others, and often various verses scattered through the Psalter, joined together in such an ordered sequence that it was clear they had been linked by the same spirit in which they had been written and inspired in her holy mind.

Between psalmody and prayers, the Lord was always on her lips and Christ always in her heart. Unless she briefly closed her eyes as though to sleep, she was always either singing psalms or speaking about the salvation of her soul. She continually confessed the sins she had committed in thought, word, and deed, and asked whether she ought to hope for forgiveness for them.

Often, too, she mentioned the division and examination of the good and the wicked on the day of judgment—the sheep on the right and the goats on the left—and asked whether perhaps one saint or good person could then come to the aid and assistance of another.

Finally, commending herself to our faith and hands, she also asked to be commended to the saints whose relics were kept in our monastery, through the service of our lowliness.

Meanwhile, as though she were already present at the very things about which she had previously spoken, as though she were already standing before the tribunal of the Judge, she began to fear and tremble, fixing her eyes upon what she seemed to see.

We can infer that she then heard or saw something concerning the future both from the changing expressions of her face and from other events that she foresaw and foretold. We do not doubt that you who were present then remember that on the night before she died we were there together with you. While we were sitting beside her and you stood near her bed, she seemed to murmur something about our insignificant selves. You thought that she had asked for us in her customary way.

When you told her that we were present, she said that we had incurred guilt on her account and offended our brothers because we were remaining with you longer than usual. When we said that none of this was the case, but that our brothers were pleased for us to do anything that might bring her consolation and comfort, and that we had been sent for this purpose, she replied that it was not so. It would be better if we hurried to leave and depart; what she had said was entirely true.

When we returned to the monastery, we found that this was indeed the case. Our brothers, not yet knowing how serious her illness was, were greatly distressed that we were delaying so long. As we later learned, at almost the same hour of the night when she had said this, our lord abbot spoke about it with some of our brothers.

This also persuades us to believe that she saw something significant at that time, when she cried out so frequently, “Well done! Well done!” and, as though urging those of us who were present to listen, repeatedly exclaimed, “Listen, listen,” because she could no longer say anything more.

## CHAPTER VIII. The holy death of Hathumoda in the presence of Bishop Marquard. The eyes and lips of the dead woman seem to move. Her burial amid the incredible mourning of every order.

[Cols. 1181C–1183A]

At that same time Bishop Marquard was there with the clergy, and he solemnly performed everything that seemed necessary for one about to depart: anointing with the sacred oil, final reconciliation, and participation in the sacrifice. Psalms were continually sung, litanies and prayers were recited, and the Gospel was read. Nothing that ought to be done before the soul’s departure was omitted.

Her limbs gradually became entirely numb, her speech diminished, and her breath slowly began to fail. Yet she devoutly kissed the wood of the holy cross that we had there, fixing her eyes upon it, and from time to time murmured something from the psalms with what strength she could.

We had agreed that, beginning the Psalter at its first verse, we would pay close attention to the psalm or verse at which she died. This accorded fittingly with her holy merits. For when we were reciting, in Psalm 40, the penultimate verse, “But you have upheld me because of my innocence and established me in your presence for ever,” she breathed out her final breath and, as we confidently believe, returned her holy soul to heaven.

Nevertheless, as is customary, we waited to see whether she might perhaps begin breathing again, until we had completed the two following psalms, most appropriate to her departure. At that point the clear signs of her falling asleep became evident, and all the bells of the church rang out to testify to it.

It can scarcely be said how great a crowd flocked to the church, or with what groaning and mourning the company of sisters assembled to commend her holy soul to God. When this had been completed amid many tears, most of the sisters remained there to wash the body according to custom; the others meanwhile devoted themselves in the church to psalms and prayers.

We shall relate something remarkable, yet true according to the testimony of the sisters who were present. When the holy body had been arranged in the room for washing, she seemed to raise her eyes as though she were completely alive and to move her lips as if addressing those standing around her.

After the body had been washed and honorably wrapped in linen, it was carried on the shoulders of priests to the church, with a worthy company of virgins and a choir of singers, preceded by little girls carrying candles.

Who can recall without tears or describe without weeping how great was the groaning, mourning, and lamentation there? Everything was confused; the voices of the singers and the mourners could not be distinguished. The whole church resounded with the voices of those lamenting. Their single cry was that they had lost their excellent lady and most merciful mother; that she was no longer there to love everyone with such great charity and receive them with such humanity, to gather guests with such generosity and assist the poor with such mercy.

Men and women gathered in groups: the women displayed the garments they had received from her, while the men brought forward other gifts bestowed through her generosity. Meanwhile, crowds gathered in groups throughout the entire night and day, until the hour of her burial.

When the time came to bury her, no one had ever heard greater mourning or greater lamentation, nor could it be restrained in any way, although the priests repeatedly asked for this in accordance with their sacred ministry and for God’s sake. Whenever it seemed to be checked for a little while, an even greater outburst arose from the crowds, who continued to stream together in companies, renewed in a certain sense.

This occurred not only on that day and the days immediately following, but until nearly the thirtieth day. The more distinguished people also assembled here and there in small groups. They mourned not so much the one whom they knew was then living more truly for God as they grieved that they had lost such a great good and source of comfort; that the holy congregation had been deprived of such a mother; that so worthy a mother had been deprived of such a daughter; and that our most glorious sister, our lady and queen, had been left desolate by such a sister.

At this, the most glorious mother, with incredible strength of mind, consoled each person and restrained each person’s tears. She fulfilled toward men the duty of a woman and toward strangers the duty of a mother. Although she grieved deeply, though silently, over her loss, she openly rejoiced in their love. She did not think that she had entirely lost the one whom she believed to be living for God and with Christ, and whom she saw living in the memory of human beings.

Yet this great and noble woman, so strong in public, mourned the death of that same daughter beyond measure when she was alone and in private. She gave herself to solitary tears in proportion to how much she seemed to restrain herself before others. She was overcome by grief and by affection, which always tend to abound most greatly in the best people.

Therefore, holy sisters, you ought not so much to grieve that you have lost such a woman as to rejoice that you had—and indeed still have—such a woman. Everything lives for God; therefore do not think her dead to you whom you know to live for God. For if Christ is with you—and indeed he is—she too will be with you, since you do not doubt that she is with Christ. For, truly a virgin, she follows him wherever he goes.

Thus this holy mother of yours lives for you in spirit; she lives in her holy life, in her blameless conduct, in her outstanding character, and in her excellent example.

## CHAPTER IX. The author’s exhortation to the holy women of Gandersheim, whom he commands to imitate the virtues of Saint Hathumoda, especially her devotion to poverty.

[Cols. 1183B–1184B]

We wish to write these things to you so that, since you can no longer see her bodily, you may contemplate in the holiness of her life a kind of image of her, as we said at the beginning of this little work. Do not think that she has entirely departed from you, when each day you can not merely read about an unknown holy way of life, but reread one that you know.

This will be your rule; this will be your mirror. In it you will find what may correct your life and conduct. As long as she was in the flesh, you followed and accompanied her with bodily steps. If you wish to reach the place where we believe she now reigns with Christ, you must follow her with spiritual steps.

She followed Christ, who was poor, as a poor woman herself, and flourished so greatly in this life that at the time of her falling asleep she did not even have the necessities of burial from her own possessions, but was wrapped in someone else’s linen, although she had been born to a high station and placed over a monastery and could have possessed more if she had wished.

Nor should it trouble you, most holy sisters, that a woman of such holiness passed to the Lord by a somewhat more difficult and prolonged departure. The Lord willed this so that no one might say to her in the future, “She was not among human beings, and she was not scourged with human beings.” The Lord willed it so that, if anything still needed to be cleansed from the stains of human weakness in her mind, it might be purified through a more grievous departure.

As for her now, as we pray and believe, she follows Christ her bridegroom as a most chaste bride wherever he goes, singing that new song which no one can sing except the 144,000 who were purchased from among humanity as first fruits for God and the Lamb; and no falsehood was found in their mouths, but they are without blemish before the throne of God.

This holy and incomparable woman died on the third day before the Kalends of December, on a Monday, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 874, in the seventh indiction. She lived in her holy vocation for twenty-two years. All the years of her life were thirty-four, while our Lord Jesus Christ reigned, God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 1183]

[Cols. 1183C–1185B]

# AGIUS’S DIALOGUE ON THE DEATH OF SAINT HATHUMODA, ABBESS

When I, anxious, had perhaps been present at the final moments

Of the holy abbess Hathumoda,

A sufficiently mournful conversation took place

Between me and her holy and worthy sisters.

Yet the great merit of these women compelled me

To say a few things for their consolation.

But since their recent grief perhaps suddenly

Prevented them from hearing such mournful words,

What I then related in tears I now set forth in verse,

Adding several other things as well.

This is because they are known to have asked

That I send them this writing afterward,

So that they might console themselves by it,

And continually behold what I said with the eyes of memory.

Therefore, favoring their just wishes and prayers,

I shall attempt to say a few things according to her merit.

Only now, reader, attend to me as I speak with them,

And share with us in our lamentation.

### AGIUS

I do not doubt that you are saddened by your sister’s death

And that her passing is grievous to you.

For such a woman is rightly mourned,

Since the world now scarcely has another like her:

The best of all whom I have ever seen,

Outstanding in character and pleasing to the Lord.

Let us not mourn her, when the whole world now mourns her

And the elements themselves lament her in various ways.

The conduct of so many people has taught us this;

This barren year has warned us of it:

That this excellent, chaste, and holy mother in every respect

Would soon depart from here to the Lord.

No, I beg you, let us not mourn that she,

Blooming in youthful beauty, died before her time.

Yet this grief must be restrained;

There must be a limit to your tears.

For just as it is natural to grieve,

So reason forbids every excess.

Therefore I ask you, dear and holy sisters,

Now to spare your weeping and tears.

Spare your life; spare your eyes,

Which you ruin altogether by excessive weeping.

For “Nothing in excess” was spoken excellently and aptly by a certain man;

Indeed, through him God himself gives this warning.

### RESPONSE

What you have said is wholly true,

And we know that God forbids all excess.

But we do not at all think this excessive,

Since we know it falls short of her merits.

For we cannot adequately express

How many good things we lack in her alone.

She was our sister, our mother, our nurse, and our teacher;

She was our abbess; she was our lady.

We lived with her, following the same life in every respect,

Though we were very small and insignificant.

There was one will among us all, and one refusal among us all;

Our vows and pursuits were one and the same.

And shall we not weep for her, shall we not grieve for her,

And sigh from the depths of our longing hearts,

For what sweetness and glory of our life has been lost with her,

In whom so many good things were united?

Finally, concerning tears, lamentation, and grief,

We do not believe that we shall ever have enough.

At least let us sate ourselves with tears and lamentation,

if indeed we may not look upon her beloved face.

**AGIUS.**

I do not deny that your grief is now sufficiently just;

I do not deny that your tears likewise are fully justified,

since a limb cannot be torn from limb without groaning,

nor can a body endure its own loss without distress.

And yet this is something he bears which greatly afflicts him,

both in view of nature and in view of God.

For this grief does not merely touch you alone;

it consumes me also, indeed torments me more severely.

For I cannot now adequately say, as would be fitting,

how many benefits I have lost together with you.

You know better how she always cherished me with what love,

with how many devoted services she fostered me when I was well.

You know with what attentive care, when she was already weak,

with what anxiety she longed for my face,

with what yearning she welcomed me when I arrived,

and with what astonishing acts of service she soothed me,

how she deigned to address me in her final speech,

repeating my name continually.

How could I not mourn one who was so devoted to me,

with a devotion I cannot possibly express?

She herself, sharing my sufferings, wept over them as her own,

and likewise rejoiced over my blessings as over her own.

She had made my misfortunes more bearable,

just as, conversely, she made my blessings more splendid.

With her, whatever I strongly desired,

I could speak as freely as with myself.

Wretched me! Unhappy me! Will I ever be able

to relieve this grief by changing it into joy,

since I, miserable survivor, have been deprived at once

of such a great and such a dear friend?

But what am I doing now? Why do I perhaps, by my grief,

make you too weep and groan?

Yet this comes from the frailty of the flesh:

a human being naturally mourns his own dead.

The Lord also wept for Lazarus, and Mary for the Lord;

and all holy and devout people have wept.

But, as I said before, a limit must be placed upon tears,

and mourning must not become excessive.

For this reason the Apostle Paul rightly forbids us,

by these admonitions, to grieve in this way for our loved ones:

“We do not want you to be ignorant, brothers,” he says,
