“about those who have died—indeed, who sleep—

so that you may not be sorrowful like the others,

who are clearly without any hope of life thereafter.

For if we believe that Jesus died,

so that by rising he might conquer dreadful death,

we must also believe that the Lord now raises up with Jesus

those who are proved already to have fallen asleep.”

This is our hope; this is our consolation:

that our dead now live more fully.

In this way, in this way you should lessen your grief;

this should now wipe away your tears;

this should console you, this make you joyful;

this should lift your spirit toward the Lord.

**RESPONSE.**

This alone will certainly console us

in such a funeral and deeply mournful calamity:

that although her body is here covered by the earth,

we believe her soul to be in heaven.

Pure faith urges us to hope for this;

her holy life compels us to believe it.

But because we no longer enjoy her bodily presence,

nor behold her with bodily eyes,

we are held fast by an immense longing for her,

and are afflicted by excessive concern for her.

Thus we groan, thus we mourn, and finally thus we weep;

hence comes our greatest sorrow.

For because we grieve, miserable as we are, to have lost

what alone was supremely dear to us,

nothing other than weeping seems sweet to us,

nothing except mourning, lamenting, and groaning.

But since we can no longer pursue her with bodily steps,

we now pursue her with our tears.

**AGIUS.**

It is, I confess, a sufficiently rare and very difficult thing,

and therefore not at all easy for us:

that a human being, while still carnal,

should not desire to see with bodily eyes

those who were previously close to him in the flesh.

We desire not only to see those whom we knew before;

we also often take pleasure in seeing those whom we did not know.

Thus once the kings of the earth eagerly sought Solomon’s face,

having heard of his wisdom.

But we must remember what the Apostle then sets forth,

wishing to remove us from the appearance of the flesh:

“Now,” he says, “is the time in which we should no longer know anyone

according to the flesh,

although there was once a time when we knew Christ

according to his bodily appearance.

But now we no longer know him according to the flesh,

nor do we seek him according to human appearance,

since Christ has now died for us,

has now cast off the frail garments of the flesh,

and has now placed at the Father’s right hand in heaven

the humanity he had assumed for us.”

Raise your eyes here, here your heart and spirit;

go there in your mind, where it is permitted to behold her.

For it is clear that she should not now be sought in the body,

not as a carnal being, but rather as a heavenly one.

Indeed, while she remained joined to the body in life,

we shall see her to be present outside the body.

Her spirit, therefore, should be loved more than her body:

everlasting, heavenly, living, and light.

For, as the Lord says, “Now the flesh profits nothing;

it is the spirit, rather, that gives life.”

For the body cannot be perpetual and enduring,

and flesh is at once mortal and fragile.

Let it therefore first die, so that afterward it may be able to rise again,

incorruptible and like the spirit.

So also the grain of wheat is first buried in the fields,

so that it may rise with a hundredfold harvest.

Thus every seed in its own manner the earth hides in her womb,

so that afterward it may produce an abundant crop.

Thus winter first strips the leaves of the woods,

which grow green again in the new spring.

Therefore you ought not to lead her away with weeping;

you ought not to pursue her with tears.

For your weeping makes the holy woman sorrowful,

and your tears make her sad.

She should be led in this way into the region of the living;

in this way the holy soul should be commended to God.

Nor is it fitting for you to weep for one over whom heaven rejoices;

it is not fitting to mourn where Christ triumphs,

especially since she cannot be recalled by tears,

nor can weeping help in any way.

**RESPONSE.**

We do not doubt that what you say is true,

nor that we pour out such abundant tears in vain.

Yet we are quite unable to restrain them,

nor can we drive away our continual grief,

whenever we remember that such a woman

has now died by an untimely death,

whenever we remember her manifold devotion,

her pure faith, her lucid speech,

whenever we remember her holy conduct and deeds,

her pleasant countenance and kindly spirit,

when we place her whole life before our eyes

and remember every detail,

what she said when she was well,

and afterward when she was weak,

what she did at various distinguished moments;

when we see with mournful and grieving gaze

the places where she once used to sit and stand;

when our sorrowful heart repeatedly turns all these things over together,

nothing else now gives us pleasure except to weep.

For perhaps in this way the grief of our heart is lightened,

while we seem, as it were, to release a tear for the devout woman.

**AGIUS.**

It does not happen so; grief is not diminished by weeping,

but rather grows and returns, as it were, through weeping.

For just as the body wastes away when the spleen enlarges,

and the spleen weakens the limbs by its own increase,

so these tears, this groaning, this weeping of yours

plainly constitute a kind of nourishment for grief.

For the frequent contemplation of those things

that you say have been placed before your eyes

kindles it.

These are the things that, by wrongly nourishing your laments,

feed them within with sweet poisons,

and do not allow you calmly to endure

what is known to be common to all in every way.

For death is common to all mortals:

to us, to beasts, to kings and commanders,

to slaves and masters, to the poor and the rich,

to the just, the unjust, the rational, and the irrational.

Death neither fears the proud arrogance of kings and nobles,

nor does it distinguish the exalted from the humble.

Who could ever have been more worthy than the first-formed parents,

whom God himself fashioned with his own hands?

And yet this very earth now covers those whom Paradise

once held in exaltation after they had been formed.

Abel, the most righteous offspring of the first father,

perished by the dreadful sword of his brother.

Although he was avenged by the Lord for his brother’s death,

he could in no way escape death himself.

Enoch, who first invoked the name of the Lord,

perished together with his succeeding generations.

Enoch, who together with Elijah has remained alive until now,

was able to continue living; he nevertheless died.

Shem and Japheth, sons not unworthy of their father in merit,

had lived amid the waters; now they lie in tombs.

Why should I now recall Job, for whom, as God himself teaches,

no one then could be equal in goodness?

Why should I likewise recount the holy sons and daughters?

The father died, and the children died.

Melchizedek, whose end is concealed and whose origin is concealed,

succumbed to his end; his beginning remains hidden.

Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, the three patriarchs,

now rest in a tomb joined to the great Adam.

The renowned offspring of the twelvefold line of fathers,

now dead, twice counts its ancestral names:

Judah, Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Issachar, and Zebulun;

Dan, Naphtali, Gad, and Asher have died.

Joseph, Benjamin, Manasseh, and Ephraim—

the earth, their mother, had laid them away.

And Joseph departed; what did he rescue from death for the world,

when famine pressed upon the neighboring fields?

Mount Hor holds the buried limbs of Aaron the prophet,

whom the sacred law had made the first high priest.

Eleazar and Phinehas, prophets of God and brothers to one another,

suffered death one after the other.

The tomb of Moses, who gazed upon the Lord face to face,

is hidden; his death and passing are evident.

The leader Joshua, showing Christ by his deeds and his name,

also made the sun stand still, yet he too set.

Why should I go over Jephthah, Gideon, Lot, and Samson?

The one before whom the lion succumbed was seized by savage death.

King David, from whose line Christ was descended,

struck down Goliath and, laid low by death, died.

King Solomon, than whom no one was ever wiser,

now lies in a worthy mausoleum with his father.

Josiah, whose birth the Lord had foretold,

we later read was laid among the tombs of the kings.

Hezekiah, to whom God added fifteen years,

had postponed death; he had not escaped it altogether.

Kings and commanders, and all the prophets alike,

are dead and lie in tombs.

Who could have been better among the prophets than Samuel?

Who will be greater than Elisha in merit?

The one prophesied; the other, buried, restored life;

yet both brought their final day to a close.

Isaiah, who once caused the sun to turn backward,

himself traveled the common path of death.

Daniel, to whom God disclosed such great mysteries,

from whom nothing then was hidden, is now enclosed by a heavy urn.

The three youths, whom the devouring flame once did not touch,

the hungry earth has now swallowed with its voracious mouth.

For the prophets Ezekiel and Jeremiah,

the one who brought exile did not avert death.

Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum,

and Habakkuk, with his companion Zephaniah,

Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi—

twice six garlands are now covered by the soil.

And Jonah, who once was released from the whale’s belly

and lived beneath the sea, is now pressed beneath the earth.

Judas, Eleazar, Jonathan, Simon, and John,

together with their then-aged father Mattathias,

drove the enemy and the sword from their homeland,

but could not drive death away from themselves.

But lest we remain entirely silent about the female sex,

and say nothing at all about it,

Sarah, Rebecca, Rachel, Deborah, Naomi, Ruth, and Anna,

Huldah, Susanna, Judith, and Esther have all died.

Among these the noble Maccabean woman shines,

glorious in her own achievements,

glorious in her offspring.

But why do I spend so long recounting only the monuments of the ancients,

and not mention the new together with them?

The holy John the Baptist, the Lord’s forerunner,

than whom no one had been greater, was killed here.

Sebaste holds his body, and Alexandria his sacred head,

together with the holy relics of Mark.

Rome rightly holds Peter and Paul,

the first leaders of the Church, the two lights of the world.

It likewise possesses Andrew and Luke,

whose radiant bodies now give splendor to Constantinople.

Bithynia and the province of Syria sent the former; fruitful Achaea bestowed the latter.

Ephesus, the blessed city, honors John,

of whom the Lord said that he would remain until his coming.

Judaea, blessed in its highest ancestral lines,

holds both Jameses, together with Stephen.

Renowned Hierapolis displays the sacred limbs of Philip,

and Ethiopia is adorned by Matthew.

Edessa holds Thomas; India possesses Bartholomew;

Persia stands over the ashes of Judas and Simon.

Matthias and Barnabas, Timothy, Apollos,

Silvanus, Titus, Theophilus, and Gaius,

Joseph, Gamaliel, Nicodemus, and Nathanael—

men of the highest distinction—have died.

It would be altogether too long if I were finally to recount

all the saints throughout the world in metrical verse.

And if I should also pass through the company of women

whom the holy record holds in its sacred books:

the prophetess Anna, Elizabeth, Susanna, Joanna,

and Martha, together with the three Marys, have died.

Christ himself, the salvation and life of the world in every respect,

himself underwent death; himself occupies the tomb.

The very mother of God, the ever-holy virgin Mary,

assumed into heaven, dwells in the blessed heavenly regions.

Who, finally, will think himself able to avoid the death

which he sees life itself undergo before him?

Who would continue to grieve for the dead?

Who would sorrow because his loved ones have died,

when through Christ peace has already been made,

and the world has been reconciled to God through Christ,

and Jesus has been made sin for us

so that he himself might remove all the world’s disgrace?

Therefore do not grieve for one who has completed this short life,

lest something other than what pleases the Lord please you.

No age is fuller, none more perfect,

none more desirable or more advantageous,

than the age which the Lord Christ is shown to have possessed,

according to what the holy Gospel reveals.

For he is remembered as thirty-three years old,

and she likewise completed that same number of years.

At this age it is clear that the first-formed parents were made,

and that the whole human race will rise.

This is what the Apostle Paul says,

when he briefly explains these words:

“Until,” he says, “we meet the Lord in that age

in which it is already clear that we are perfect men—

in that measure of age at which Christ’s life had been completed

when he underwent the cross.”

Who, then, ought rather to rejoice at this:

that she has been transferred so quickly

and now enjoys the Lord,

because she deserved to pass through the world’s dangers

by a shorter route and to find swift rest?

For the just person is taken away

so that an evil will may not change a righteous heart

or deceive the soul.

**RESPONSE.**

We certainly cannot doubt that these things

are supported by sufficiently firm reasoning.

For we know that all mortal things must die;

we know that everything tends toward its setting.

Yet the inborn ardor of love in mortals

does not allow us simply not to weep and groan.

For we grieve, we weep, we mourn, and we groan

not only because of her,

but because her death has left us desolate

and exposed us, miserable as we are, to the wolves’ bites.

For when the mother has been struck down,

the lambs of the flock must either die—

tender and lacking milk—

or wander about seeking another’s milk,

and be exposed to the teeth of the mad wolf.

For, as Scripture relates, “When the shepherd has been killed,

the sheep are scattered and plundered everywhere.”

Anyone who knows the holy Gospel knows well

that this was said or done concerning the Lord’s disciples.

Finally, what hope will there be for the miserable sheep,

if this happened then to so great a flock?

**AGIUS.**

I want you first to know this:

that we possess two affections for our loved ones,

implanted in us from heaven.

One is carnal; the other is considered divine.

One is heavenly; the other earthly.

But carnal love makes us mourn our loved ones,

and makes us weep and groan for the dead.

Divine love, on the other hand, urges us to triumph,

when we are confident of their salvation.

Therefore I shall now warn you again and again

to put aside these excessive tears.

For just as carnal love is pleasing when moderate,

so it becomes harmful when excessive.

Therefore, if this love perhaps urges you to weep,

let faith make you joyful and dance for joy.

For this devotion is shown rather to be impiety

when we love adversity in opposition to the pious Lord.

But because we now believe that your grief has been softened,

and that your groaning has been restrained—

the groaning which in every way tormented your spirit

over the death of your devout and holy sister—

I shall now endeavor to respond to what remains,

although this is certainly difficult enough for me.

For this grief seems sufficiently just to anyone:

the grief by which each person mourns for himself

and grieves for what belongs to him.

And indeed I could now say what the wise have often taught,

a true and devout principle:

that every brave man ought to endure

all the world’s misfortunes with a brave heart.

But this may seem severe for tender women,

and this matter is not at all easy for you.

Yet what shall I do? Shall I say, as a final consolation,

what almost everyone often says:

that what we are entirely unable to correct

we ought to bear well?

I do not want this; I do not want to say this to you.

Rather, I want to say what can rightly console you:

that you will not remain desolate or widowed;

that a most honorable mother will now be present.

The very God who had granted her to you

will preserve, guide, and govern you.

Moreover, your devout mother,

whose constant help she herself continually enjoyed in everything,

will always be present in all that you undertake,

say, or do.

Nor will your queenly sister be lacking to you

wherever royal assistance may perhaps be needed.

Nor will brothers be lacking,

nor so many and such faithful people

as your merit has won far and wide.

Above all, however, the gracious sister, like the best mother,

will protect her little daughters with continual prayers.

For she is now more useful to you,

the closer she is now to the Lord.

Thus once, when the holy Elijah

was being carried back to heaven on a fiery chariot,

his spirit rested doubly upon his disciple Elisha.

And because the Lord can do all things,

he too will be able, if he wishes,

to do this very thing even from the least of these.

Will he not, if he wishes, also be able,

in his mercy, to make daughters of Abraham from these stones?

Only do not be sluggish:

continually implore him for this in your prayer

and with unceasing petition.

As we said earlier, this same holy woman

will be present for you in everything through her merits,

if she wishes and is able to help you.

The Almighty grants to proximity the ability and the will.

For although her spirit has been received into heaven,

she has not therefore departed from us altogether.

Her virtues live; her blessed life also lives;

her devout speech lives, and her life-giving merits.

Since you can no longer see her face,

now place her before your eyes.

If you always loved anything supremely in her,

you possess a most holy life and magnificent merit.

These are the relics; this is the revered little mantle

which, when carried upward, fell from Elijah.

With it Elisha then divided the Jordan;

and you likewise distinguish the true from the false.

**RESPONSE.**

It has now been sufficiently shown to us

that all the tears we shed by weeping are vain:

for they accomplish nothing,

nor, however abundant they may be,

do they bring back any dead person.

Rather, following our own completed course,

we shall go from here as though from a long exile.

Therefore, with our eyes wiped and our tears removed,

with mourning calmed and groaning restrained,

it will now be fitting for us to rejoice with you,

dear sister,

because you have passed through these hardships so quickly.

We weep because we, who have not yet earned

to be with you, are compelled to contend for a long time

in this contest.

We weep because we remain in this valley of tears,

and for so long are kept apart from our homeland.

You, having completed the course and race of faith and life,

now shine with the worthy prize of righteousness.

Our faith, our race—which may perhaps finally reach its end—

remains uncertain.

You now triumph with the Lord,

the enemy having been defeated;

we are still hindered by the ever-present enemy.

You now possess the harbor;

we are still tossed upon the abyss.

The true light holds you;

darkness still holds us.

You, accompanying the virgins wherever the Lamb goes,

gather lilies, violets, and roses.

We, together with our fellow servants,

keep watch beside your tomb,

scattering flowers.

You can now know from there the destinies

of your father and of your brothers and sisters,

and from there you can help us.

Although we believe in the blessings granted by Christ,

we know quite uncertainly what their nature is.

Dear sister, who can both know and help us,

help them with us before the Lord!

We are known to be your part,

just as you too are our part;

dear one, now take your father with you.

Your brothers and sisters, and your parents as well—

what could be more fitting, what sweeter,

than that they should be together there,

not now separated from one another,

sprung from one father and born from one womb?

Dear sister, desire and light of your own,

what is a brief salvation for us is now a long one for you!

Alas, while living with us for so short a time,

how quickly you passed away from us in death!

Now happily placed in the heavenly region,

dear one, often visit us, even through visions.

Let this at least be our consolation in grief:

that you come to us through frequent dreams.

And now, dear one, farewell, our sweetness and our glory,

and help us, dear one, by your worthy merits.

We now humbly ask you, beloved brother:

commend her to the Lord with frequent prayers.

You yourself are her witness, how greatly she always loved you;

now repay her yourself with a fitting return.

We too, her least sisters, according to custom,

now commend her to your hands,

so that you may teach or admonish us in your accustomed manner,

and may always honor us for love of her.

He will give you your reward,

the one whom she served,

whose humble handmaids we also are.

We too shall always honor you with our customary love;

indeed, we honor you more than we have been accustomed to do.

**AGIUS.**

I am very grateful for what you say; indeed,

I ought myself now to have asked this.

But you anticipated me,

both in merit and in the profoundly humble service of this cause.

Therefore, since you know well the love we bear one another,

I love you with this affection, God as my witness.

You have no complete need of my instruction;

the Lord is here, instructing you inwardly.

Whatever may belong to service,

I promise to be ready for it,

and I do not doubt that I shall be so.

You should not now be excessively anxious

about the salvation of your father and brothers who have died.

One sister and three young brothers died;

their youth shows that they were innocent.

Your sister Enda, who had already been joined to a husband,

has in her offspring what she herself possesses only in lesser measure.

Your father himself, although he could not have been without stain,

since he was engaged in worldly office,

nevertheless took care to cleanse his sins

by how many good deeds of his own;

I know that you are well aware of this.

For although he was burdened by innumerable cares of the world,

from which he could not free himself by his own efforts,

he went to Rome, seeking to absolve himself

through the one to whom the power of absolution had been granted.

From there, properly bringing back the worthy ashes of the saints,

he gave a portion of his own estate to the Lord.

Establishing here the sacred bones of the saints,

he there dedicated you five sisters to divine service.

He joined a little son to a monastery of monks,

so that perhaps no portion of his family might be lacking to God.

Finally, redeeming his misdeeds through almsgiving,

and confessing them himself, he died in ashes.

Who would not judge that, through God’s mercy and on account of these things,

he was in every way unworthy of being held guilty of sin?

Do you think he will burn,

whose devout deeds stand almost without end

while the world passes away?

That place of God remains,

which he had entrusted to the handmaids

who continually shed tears on his behalf.

This is the assembly which he had once seen

giving thanks to the holy God for his salvation.

For in a dream he saw you standing very fearfully

on a wall of extraordinary height,

swaying and trembling.

And when it seemed that you were about to fall immediately,

someone suddenly cried out from the side:

“Woe to the wretched one, now about to fall,

now about to perish;

no hope can now be held out for her.”

At this, he, full of faith, said:

“It will not be so;

there will certainly be hope, if God himself so wills.”

Thus, with his foot slipping, he saw you lowered

step by step,

and then standing properly with both feet straight.

At this point he saw a great assembly,

their faces turned toward the east,

immediately offering thanks to the holy God.

He had another vision scarcely different from this one:

he saw himself on a tree of extraordinary height.

And when it seemed that he was about to fall from above,

someone suddenly said to him:

“If he firmly grasps with both hands

the branch that is very small and close to him,

he will suffer no danger at all,

and nothing bad will be able to happen to him.”

Then again he saw an assembly,

as I said, turned toward him,

singing praises to God who was saving him.

He had seen this only a few days earlier,

when he was still completely healthy,

before he became ill.

You can understand well what these things signify,

and that they are not unrelated to one another.

Therefore what is the wall that shines forth

if not the lofty power by which he himself was entirely lifted up?

For the wall is made of many stones,

just as he had been supported by many followers.

But he stood at the summit of the walls,

because he alone had been set as leader over many.

And because he deserved to be saved,

his spirit, falling from there,

came to rest with his feet standing straight.

Therefore your place,

which he founded and initiated,

glorifies the Lord for this salvation.

Nor is what he saw afterward unlike this;

rather, that vision unmistakably explains it.

For the tree that appeared to him sufficiently tall,

with branches standing upright and beautiful with flowers,

is his renowned offspring and lofty progeny,

famous in the world and pleasing to the Lord.

For the fact that it was famous in the world

was signified by the blossom;

but its uprightness shows that it was pleasing to the Lord.

He did not stand at its summit but clung there hanging,

having reached the point he had previously possessed in power.

He was at the top because he had surpassed

all those of his own kind alike in virtue and in honor.

He clung hanging because his power,

now near his own death,

had begun to waver.

The branch was close to him

because Hathumod, gracious through her merits,

helped him as his nearest relation in the flesh.

It was very small because this woman,

in her sex, had not been ambitious for her own fame.

He grasps it with his hands

because he had bestowed very many gifts

upon his daughter and her fellow servants.

This merit, this is what rescued him,

already on the point of falling,

from a twofold downfall.

For what nobility or earthly power had bestowed,

various almsgiving restored.

You, who are his children by the same mother,

together with his worthy wife,

must always remember him.

For she—she is the one—

who urged him to grasp the branch with his hands,

the one who urged him to make his various almsgivings.

You are likewise debtors to both parents,

together with all those whom that place contains.

By giving them to the Lord and to his saints,

they wished them to belong to everyone through the Lord.

You are that holy flock whom the man pleasing to God

saw in his dream giving thanks.

For whatever good you do

will return to those who rightly gave you that place.

Above all, however, it will rightly return to her

who nourished you and instructed you together.

Therefore, although I myself need her prayers more,

I want you to know that I pray for her

as you request:

as long as I remain alive,

I shall keep her in remembrance.

Nor does her dear image ever depart from my heart,

whether I sleep or, rather, whether I am awake.

Indeed, when I am awake,

I either think about her or speak of her;

at night dreams give me her dear face.

For whenever sleep covers my weary eyes,

she immediately appears and soon reminds me of something.

There are many such things,

but I want to mention one of many as an example.

Six nights had already passed, and the seventh had come,

after she had departed and had already been buried,

when, as the light of day was approaching,

I had lain down to sleep.

I saw myself in your monastery.

I saw her speaking with me in the customary way

about various matters that had arisen,

then also about our rule,

and likewise about our whole life

and the condition of our monastery.

When I asked her to give me any book

she might perhaps possess concerning our way of life,

she said that she had indeed possessed one,

but no longer possessed it herself;

she said that you, Gerberga,

had that book.

When it was brought to me,

it appeared small,

but it was well written and well arranged,

and nothing could ever be more pleasing to the heart,

or certainly more beautiful to behold.

After I had awakened happily from sleep,

the vision seemed very welcome to me.

Therefore, as soon as day came,

I explained it to our brothers

and reported what it might signify.

It signified that you, Gerberga,

would be abbess,

and that, as a sister,

you would undertake the governance of your monastery.

For our rule, which you now retain,

and which she herself previously held,

seems to signify this.

It was small because your flock is still small,

but it was well written because of your devout deeds.

And truly, sister, as I said,

I remember never having seen anything more beautiful

or better written.

Therefore, although I grieve and shall grieve

throughout my life that she died so soon,

I nevertheless rejoice that you, a holy woman,

have succeeded a holy woman,

and that you are rightly her companion

in the flesh as well as in merit.

For although it is clear that there are also others among you

who could be placed under this burden,

I knew that you, both in wisdom and in goodness,

were rightly appointed in her place.

For just as you were related to her by the right of the flesh,

so likewise you were close to her in merit.

Finally, we now rejoice that you possess her honor,

for which you were long ago judged a worthy disciple,

and that you are nevertheless now a worthy heir of hers,

whether in the monastery or in devout merit.

Therefore that holy woman is sought in you;

in you that clear affection of her heart is sought.

A kind of image of her discipline is sought,

her virtue, her likeness.

Her life-giving merit is sought,

her revered conduct,

her devout speech,

and her rightly holy life.

She is sought in the matter of lineage,

and likewise in deeds;

in affection as well as in service.

You too, her holy and worthy sisters,

honor this mother of yours as a mistress.

For although you are all known to share one lineage,

she has nevertheless been placed over you

by Christ’s gift.

She is Christ’s chosen one and Christ’s representative;

whatever you do for her, you do for Christ.

If an injury is done to her, it is perhaps done to Christ;

Christ is honored, Christ is worshiped in her.

Moreover, honor your natural mother also

with every kind of service.

This is the Lord’s command;

this is, as you know, your honor;

this, as you know, is to be your glory.

## Volume back matter

### [Col. 1197]

## INDEX OF LATIN IN HROTSVITHA’S WORKS

The reader is referred back to the boldface numerals inserted into the text.

[Note: This index refers only to Hrotsvitha’s works found between columns 0971 and 1196. The citations refer to the boldface numbers inserted into the text, not to Migne’s column numbers.]

### [Col. 1197] A

**Ab aliqua re sermonem facere**, “to speak about something,” instead of *de aliqua re*, 87.

**Abjectionem pati**, “to suffer rejection,” instead of “to be despised or treated with disgrace,” 19.

**Abrenuntiare**, used instead of *renuntiare*, 12.

**Abrogare**, used instead of “to refuse,” 41.

**Abusive**, instead of “by abusing”; *abusus* is commonly used for “corruption,” but is not Latin in this sense, 2.

**Acceptabile munus**, “an acceptable gift,” instead of “an accepted or welcome gift,” also in Lactantius, 40.

**Actum est quid erga me**, “what has been done concerning me,” instead of “something has happened to me,” “has occurred,” 19. See below.

**Adepto consilio**, a passive form, used instead of *accepto consilio*, “having received advice,” 84. This usage also occurs among classical authors.

**Admeruissem**, instead of *meruissem*, 64.

**Admirando deficere**, “to fail through admiration,” instead of “to be unable to admire sufficiently,” 27.

**Adolere**, in passive form, whereas poets use *adolere* in the active form, 15.

**Adonay Emanuel**, “Lord Emmanuel,” 68.

**Ad rectitudinis normam**, “according to the standard of uprightness,” instead of *ad recti normam*, because *rectum* is also used substantivally among the Latins, 4.

**Adusque**, instead of *usque ad*, “up to,” 1, 133.

**Aera et aetherea**, instead of *aerem et aetherem*, “air” and “ether,” also in Virgil and Ovid, etc. For these are Greek accusative forms: *ἀέρα, αἰθέρα* (*aera, aethera*), 35. Among Eastern writers they are also used in the neuter gender and plural number.

“Behold, heaven hangs above you, earth withdraws from you;  
the airs (*aera*) are balanced, the Ocean surges.”

**Aestimo**, instead of *existimo*, “I think,” 48.

**Aeternaliter**, “eternally,” instead of “forever.” Livy used *in aeternum*, 69.

**Aethereum aeterni regis thalamum intrare**, “to enter the heavenly bridal chamber of the eternal king,” instead of “to attain eternal life,” 23.

**Affectus**, “affection,” instead of “love,” 3.

**Agapes**, instead of *Agapae*, 20.

**Agere aliquid erga aliquem**, for example, *quid erga me actum sit*, “what has been done concerning me,” instead of the expression that should be used: “what has happened to me,” “what has occurred to me,” “what has been done to me,” 19.

**Agitatur**, instead of *agit* or *degit*, “he acts” or “he lives,” 16.

**A longe**, instead of *e longinquo*, “from afar,” “at a distance,” 19.

**Aliquantulis**, instead of *aliquibus* or *nonnullis*, “some” or “several,” 70.

**Almificus princeps**, “holy” or “illustrious prince,” 105.

**Almificus consul**, “holy” or “illustrious consul,” 113.

**Almifica vita**, “holy” or “illustrious life,” 115.

**Altithronus**, “high-throned,” Greek *ὑψίθρονος*, 10, 73, 85, 87, 110, 117.

**Alvus virgineus**, “virginal womb,” in the masculine gender, twice, 78.

**Amatrix**, a comic word, also found in Plautus, 2.

**Amniculum**, instead of *amnis*, “river,” 108.

**Amplexaris**, instead of *amplexeris*, “you may embrace,” 33.

**Annullaretur**, instead of “it might be neglected,” 4.

### [Col. 1197]

**Appetere pede**, “to approach on foot,” instead of “to go to,” 108.

**Applicuere sui in propriis Domini**, “they came into the Lord’s own place or estate,” 109.

**Apponere pejora pejoribus**, “to add worse things to worse,” instead of “to increase previous offenses,” 44.

**Apponere**, instead of “to bring” or “to propose,” 44.

**Apponere cor serpentinis lenociniis**, “to set one’s heart on serpent-like allurements,” instead of “to be corrupted by blandishments,” 58.

**Asinum vivere**, “to live like a donkey,” instead of “to live in the manner of a donkey,” 34.

**Asserere**, instead of “to speak” or “to say,” 19.

**Atomum**, neuter, instead of *atomus*, 73.

**Atriolum**, instead of *atrium*, “atrium,” 110, 108, 113.

**Attactu vestri favoris atque petitionis**, “through the touch of your favor and request,” instead of “through your ease and kindness,” 4.

**Auctrix virginitatis**, “leader or originator of virginity,” 33.

**Auctrix criminis**, “author or cause of a crime,” 119.

**Augustalis excellentia**, “the very dignity of the emperor Augustus,” 5.

**Augustalis pietas**, “the emperor’s piety,” 77.

**Aula coelestis patriae**, “the hall of the heavenly homeland,” instead of “the heavenly homeland,” 8.

**Aureola**, “a kind of reward bestowed in return for merit,” 129.

**Aurivagae pennae**, “wings wandering through the air,” 76.

**Aurivagum donum**, “a gift or benefit of the golden spring,” 112.

### B

**Bacchantibus flammis**, “with raging flames,” instead of “with furious flames,” 21.

**Blanditum**, a passive form, “refreshed” or “comforted,” 117.

**Bravium**, instead of *brabeum* or *brabium*, “prize,” 63, 68, 117, 129, 161, 174.

Calceoli, for *calcei* (“shoes”), 110.  
Calumniatum, in the passive form, 20.  
Cantamen, for *cantus* (“song”), 129, 153.  
Capellanus diaboli, “chaplain of the devil,” for “minister of the devil,” 15.  
Captor, for *captator* (“one who seizes” or “one who seeks to capture”), 115.

Cauma, for “the heat of fire” or “intense heat,” 63.  
Causari fertur, “he is said to plead a case,” for “to have accused,” 163.  
Celamentum, for “silence” or “concealment,” 35.  
Celcithronus, for Greek ὑψίθρονος, “high-enthroned,” 89.

Christicola, for “a worshipper of Christ” or “a Christian”; also elsewhere, 10.

[Col. 1198]

Circumflexa, for “wrapped around” or “intertwined,” 26.  
Clancula cordium, “the little secrets of hearts,” for “the hidden or secret thoughts,” 36.  
Claritas ingenuitatis, “the splendor of nobility,” for “nobility of birth,” 58.  
Coaevus, for “the same as coetaneus,” that is, “of the same age,” 38.  
Coarctari, for “to be distressed,” 50.  
Coelicolae, “inhabitants of heaven,” for “heaven-dwellers,” 190.  
Coelitus, for “from heaven,” 80.  
Coeremita, for “a companion of the desert or wilderness,” 32.  
Coinquinatio, for “dirt” or “filth,” 32.  
Collectim, for “together,” e.g. *collectim comitantur*, “they accompany [one another] together,” for *conjunctim comitantur*, “they accompany [one another] together,” 9.  
Colliminare, for “to combine, compose, or unite.” *Unire* (“to unite”) is less respectable usage: Seneca scarcely dares to use it in philosophical writing, and it is found in Gellius only as a corrupt reading, 27.  
Comitata, in the passive form, for “accompanied” or “escorted”; also used in particular by classical poets, 57.  
Comitetur vobiscum, “may he accompany you,” for *nos comitetur*, “may he accompany us,” 67.  
Commansere, for “they remained together,” 93.  
Commissum reato, “entrusted to guilt,” for “a crime,” 57.  
Commodare, for “to be useful” or “to be of advantage,” 32.  
Communicare invicem passionem, “to communicate suffering to one another,” for “to express shared grief” or “to divide sorrows among themselves”; e.g. *communicata invicem compassione*, “with mutual grief expressed,” 23.  
Compar meus, for “my partner, companion, or fellow soldier,” 33.  
*Compar* sometimes means “spouse”; sometimes *compar* refers to those who are compared with one another in relation to a superior master.  
Compassio, for “shared” or “mutual grief,” 73.  
Compatior, for “I grieve with” or “I sympathize,” 16.  
Competit, for “it is fitting,” “it is appropriate,” or “it is proper,” 41.  
Completa oratione, for “with the speech finished,” 68.  
Compunctio, for “sorrow of the soul.” Likewise, *contritio*, “contrition,” means “true inward sorrow of the soul for sins,” and likewise “the sting of conscience,” 38.  
Compunctioni vacare, “to devote oneself to compunction,” for “to pursue repentance or expiation,” 41.  
Compunctionis lacryma, “a tear of compunction,” for “tears prepared for the amendment of the soul,” 48.  
Conamen, the same as *conatus*; it is a poetic expression, 131, 165.  
Concite, for “immediately,” 10.  
Concordari, for “to agree” or “to be in harmony,” in the deponent form. This form is not found in good authors, who use the active form of the verb. Moreover, *concordari mihi* is not found in those authors; rather, they say *concordare cum aliquo*, “to agree with someone.” Thus Terence, *Phormio* IV, scene 3, 36, 68.  
Concordari meum, “my agreeing,” for “my agreement,” 7.  
Concrepare laudes, “to resound with praises,” for “to celebrate,” 85.  
Condescensio, for “gentleness, mildness, or patience,” 41.

Condigne, for “worthily,” 41, 148.  
Condolere alicui, “to grieve with someone,” for “to grieve on someone’s account,” or “to express sorrow arising from something,” 41.  
Condolentes, “grieving with,” for *condoleatis*, “may you grieve with,” 16.  
Conferre injuriam, “to bring an injury,” for “to inflict an injury,” 28.  
Confortare, for “to strengthen,” 65.  
Congaudere dolori, “to rejoice with grief,” for “to rejoice over grief,” 28.  
Congaudere alicui, “to rejoice with someone,” for “to rejoice together over something,” or “to rejoice at something,” 41, 161.  
Congesta, used substantivally, for “collected money” or “valuable furnishings,” 49.  
Conglomerare taedium, “to heap up weariness,” for “to accumulate” or “increase” it, 26.  
Congratulari alicui, for “to give thanks to someone,” 64.  
Congredi ad aliquam, for “to meet with a woman,” 61.  
Connutritae, for “nourished,” 85.  
Consentire aliquid, “to agree to something,” for *in aliquid*, “to agree to something,” 21.  
Consentire nostrum, “our agreeing,” for “our agreement,” 66.  
Consequens est, for “it is proper,” “it is appropriate,” or “it is fitting,” 41.  
Consequentia rerum, for “the outcome of events,” 7.  
Conspectibus nostris, “to our sights,” for *conspectui nostro*, “to our sight”; a plural form used with singular meaning, 10, 18.  
Constat, for “it is,” 147.  
Contraluctor, for “I resist” or “I struggle against,” 12, 18, 41, 43, 57, 66.  
Contrarietas, for “adversity”; also found in Macrobius, 47.  
Conversatio angelica, “angelic association,” for “custom or familiarity with angels,” in a sacred sense, 38.  
Cordetenus, “as far as the heart,” for “from the heart”; *cordicitus* is wholly barbarous, 3, 24, 28, 66, 87.

Crepare, for “to burst”; also in Virgil, 65.  
Cultum deorum, “the worship of the gods,” for *cultu deorum*, “by the worship of the gods”; also in Lactantius, 15, 18.  
Cum, causal, with the indicative mood; e.g. *cum is amens mea deceptus est specie*, “since that madman has been deceived by my appearance,” for *deceptus sit*, “has been deceived,” 25.  
Cum voce affari aliquem, “to address someone with the voice,” for “to speak to someone,” 99.  
Cum felle suffusus, “stained with gall,” for “stained with gall,” 116.  
Cum morte vicisti, “you conquered with death,” for “you conquered by death,” 120.  
Cunctigena bonitas, “goodness of every kind,” for *omnigena*, “of every kind,” 82, 92.  
Curiose, for “entirely” or “carefully,” 10.  
Curiositate frangi, “to be broken by curiosity,” for “to be distressed,” or “to await anxiously,” or “to be in suspense,” 7.  
Cyrographus, -um, Greek χειρόγραφος, “handwritten,” 132, 146.

Elongare, for “to delay,” 28.

Energumenos, for Greek ἐνεργούμενος, “possessed” or “under the influence [of a demon].”  
Enim, for “but” or “indeed,” 65.  
Enim, for “certainly” or “indeed,” in several places, 29.  
Enucleam, for *enucleabo*, “I shall explain clearly,” 25.  
Enucleare secretum, “to lay bare a secret,” for “to disclose” or “declare a hidden matter,” 47.  
Eremicola, for “an inhabitant of the desert or wilderness,” 32.  
Erud re aliquem aliquid, for “to instruct someone in something,” 70.  
Esse simplex, “to be simple,” for “simple essence,” 56.  
Etenim, for “therefore,” 74.  
Etenim, for “entirely,” 48.

[Col. 1200]

Etiam, for “likewise,” 60.  
Evacuare sudores vigiliarum, “to empty out the sweat of vigils,” that is, “to have spent so many vigils in vain.”  
Evacuata virginalis verecundia, “virginal modesty having been emptied,” for “virginal modesty having been cast aside or defeated,” 35, 39.  
Evacuare regularis observantiam conservationis, “to empty out the observance of the rule,” for “to lay it aside,” 39.  
Exagitare caput in aliquem, “to shake the head at someone,” for “to express or indicate indignation against someone by a movement of the head,” 119.  
Exaestuo, for “I burn with desire,” 18.  
Exaestuat mihi quoddam mente agendum, “something to be done burns in my mind,” for “I greatly desire to do something,” 32, 33.  
Exaudibiles preces, for “prayers that are readily heard,” 64.  
Excellentia, “excellence” or “superiority,” 8.  
Excelsus, used substantivally of God, “the Most High,” 12.  
Exoro, for “I pray earnestly,” 65.  
Expassisque palmis, for “with hands spread out,” 110.  
Experior, for “I feel” or “I notice,” 57.  
Exprobratum, in the passive form, 20.  
Expurgare facti, for *expurgare factum*, “to cleanse or clear an act,” 1.  
Exspoliare, for “to strip off” or “to remove,” 20.  
Exuere hominem, “to strip off the human being,” for “to die,” 55.  
Exui hominem, “to strip off the human being,” for “to cast off mortality” or “to die,” 25.  
Exurit me hoc, “this burns me,” for “this torments me,” 25.  
Eya, for *eja*, “come” or “ah,” 143.

## F

Factor, for “author” or “creator,” 47, 60, 77.  
Factor mundi, “maker of the world,” for “creator or producer of the world,” 49, 81, 89.  
Factor orbis, “maker of the universe,” for “creator,” that is, God, 89.  
Factorum coelorum, “of the makers of the heavens,” for “of the creators,” 91.  
Factura, “creation” or “creature,” 152.  
Famella, for *famula*, “servant,” 76, 120.  
Famelli, for *famuli*, “servants,” 131.  
Famen, for “speech” or “word,” 158.  
Famosissimi imperatoris, “of the most famous emperor,” for “of the emperor renowned above all”; more correctly, the expression is used in a bad sense, 14.  
Famulamen, for “servile service” or “attendance,” 154.  
Fastidire honoris, “to disdain of honor,” for “to disdain honor,” 131.  
Fecisse, for “to do,” e.g. *suaserunt mihi votum fecisse*, “they persuaded me to make a vow,” for *facere*, “to make,” 1.  
Fiduciatibus sententiis, “with statements adding confidence,” for “with statements that inspire or give confidence,” 3.  
Fieri, for “to be about to be” or “to wish to become,” e.g. *Fac votum Deo te Christianum fieri velle, vel fore*, “Make a vow to God that you wish, or are going, to become a Christian,” 10.  
Finetenus, for “at last,” “to the end,” or “finally,” 12, 66, 78, 99, 119.  
Fixum memoriae, for “fixed in memory,” 5.  
Fonticulis, for *fons*, “spring” or “source,” 108.  
Foras abjectum, for “cast out,” 26.  
Fore, for *esse*, “to be,” 169, 170.  
Fore potest, for “it can be,” 27.  
Fore adesse, for *adfore*, “to be present,” 93.  
Fragmenta, for “the remains” or “the cast-off fragments of a dead body,” 28.  
Fragmina testis, “fragments of the witness,” for “the martyr’s bones,” 119.

Gaudere, used like the Greek χαίρειν, “to rejoice” or “to greet,” 3.  
Gaudimonium, for “joy,” 42.  
Gentilitas, for “a non-Christian people”; also in Tertullian and other Fathers, 8.  
Gloriari, in the passive form; also in Cicero’s *Tusculan Disputations*, where *glorianda* and *praedicanda* are found, 26.  
Gloriolam tantam, for “such great glory,” 95, 99, 105, 118.  
Gloriolae magnae, for “of great glory,” 111.  
Grates, for “let us give thanks,” 17.  
Gratias illi, for “let us give thanks to him,” or “thanks be to him,” 30.  
Gratis, for “in vain” or “without cause,” 50.

[Col. 1201]

Gratiola, for “grace,” 72, 99.  
Gratiola divina, for “divine grace,” 111.  
Gravidum os, “a heavy mouth,” for “a grave or solemn mouth,” 114.  
Gustamen, for “taste,” 61.

## H

Habita io lutea, printed thus; probably *habitatio lutea*, “a dwelling of clay,” for “the perishable body,” 16.  
Habitus, for “clothing” or “bodily adornment,” 58.  
Hoc et hoc, for “this and that,” 27, 56.  
Homullus, for “a little man,” “a poor fellow,” or “a human being,” 107, 118.  
Homullis, for “wretched human beings,” 98.  
Honorabiliter, for “honorably”; also found in Capitolinus and Cassiodorus, 5.  
Hortamentorum frequentia, “the frequency of exhortations,” for “frequent exhortation,” 9.  
Hortamentum, for “exhortation” or “admonition,” 33.  
Hortari aliquid, for “to exhort to something,” 62.  
Humilitas vestra, “your humility,” for “your lowliness of spirit,” 3.

## I

Illic, for *illuc*, “to that place,” 129.  
Illius amor, “his love,” for “that person’s own love,” 163.  
Illuvies sanguinis, “the filth of blood,” for “the foulness of blood,” 36.  
Immodico, for “in any way” or “anything,” 27 and following.  
Impassibilis, for “free from suffering,” 93.  
In aestimatione aeternae vitae, “in the estimation of eternal life,” for “in comparison with eternal life,” 14.  
Incensum, for “the incense called *thus*,” because it is consumed by fire while it is offered, 74.  
Incensum ponere, “to place incense,” for “to offer incense,” which was consumed by fire, 74.  
Incensum tangere, “to touch incense,” for “to touch the incense,” 74.  
Incircumscriptus, for “infinite”; also in Prudentius, 27.  
Incomparabilis luctus, “incomparable mourning,” for “the most exquisite grief and greatest sorrow,” 34.  
In derisum ferre aliquem, “to bring someone into mockery,” for “to be mocked” or “to be ridiculed by someone.”  
Indignans, for *dedignans*, “despising” or “disdaining,” 158.  
Infantilis, for “belonging to an infant”; also in Justin and Apuleius.  
Infantula, for “a little infant girl”; also in Apuleius, 60.  
Ingenuitas mentis, “nobility of mind,” for “nobility” or “honor,” 9, 17.  
Inhaerere affectu alicujus, “to cling to someone’s affection,” for “to be held by someone’s love,” 34.  
Inhaeream, for “I shall cling,” 41.  
Inhonestas, for “honor” or “distinction,” 18.  
Inlaboratum, for “worked out” or “elaborated,” 70.  
In palam proferre, “to bring into public,” for “to disclose” or “make public,” 4.  
Inquisitus, used substantivally, for “the act of inquiring or investigating,” 36.  
In ruinam fieri alicui, “to become ruin for someone,” for “to overthrow” or “destroy someone,” 25.  
Insensatus, for “deprived of sense,” 25.  
Inserere, for “to be inserted,” 4.  
Insistere aliqua re, for “to persist in something,” 87.  
In soles flere, for “to weep daily” or “to weep every day,” 75.  
Inspirator castitatis, “inspirer of chastity,” for “giver” or “bestower,” used of Christ, 8.  
Intendere, without a governed case, for “to pay attention,” 24.  
Interminabilis, for “not to be ended” or “not to cease”; also in other writers, 56, 69.  
Intermistio, for “mixture,” 4.  
*Intermistio* and *mistum* are barbarous forms, 4.  
Interpretatur, in the passive form, 33.  
Interventu, for “by the decision” or “will,” 34.  
Intrasse, for “to enter,” e.g. *intrasse decrevimus*, “we have decided to enter,” 14.

[Col. 1201]

Intro, for “inside,” 47.  
Ire, added to supine forms; e.g. *sponsam habitum ire*, “to go to have a bride,” for “to have a bride”; likewise *permansum ire in proposito*, “to go to remain in one’s purpose,” for “to remain in it”; likewise *iter acceptum ire*, “to go to undertake a journey,” for “to undertake a journey,” 6.  
Ire mansum, for “to remain,” 55.  
Iri is used incorrectly; e.g. *tecum commoratum iri decrevit*, “he decided that [they] would remain with you,” for “he wished them to remain with you,” 7.  
Irremediabiliter, for “in a way that cannot be remedied,” 40.  
Iturus spiritus, “the spirit about to go,” for “the spirit about to depart” or “be breathed out,” 67.

## J

Jactam pro limine turbam, “a crowd thrown before the threshold,” for “a crowd lying or cast before the threshold,” 117.  
Jam usque, for “until,” 78.  
Jubere alicui aliquid, “to order something to someone,” for “to order someone to do something.” Later writers incorrectly join it with the dative of purpose, 85.  
Jubilatio, for “glory”; e.g. *ipsum decet laus et jubilatio*, “praise and glory befit him,” 13.  
Jucundari, or *jocundari*, for “to rejoice”; also in Lactantius, 69.  
Juvamen, for “help,” e.g. *juvamen coeleste*, “heavenly help.” The same word occurs in a diploma of Charles the Fat, in Freher’s Strasbourg edition, 11, 13, 21, 70, 145.  
Juxta meum posse, “according to my ability,” that is, “to the best of my ability,” 70.

## L

Lactato pectore, “with a breast suckled,” for *lacto*, “with a milk-white breast,” 94.  
Laetificare, for “to console” or “to gladden,” 25.  
Languidulis venis, for “with languid veins,” 116.  
Latrabo, for “I shall say,” “explain,” or “expound,” 105.  
Legalis Dominus, “legal Lord,” for “legitimate Lord,” 113.  
Legalis amor, “legal love,” for “legitimate love,” 116.  
Legalis vir, “legal man,” for “legitimate husband,” 25.  
Levigato timore, “fear having been smoothed,” for “fear having been eased” or “removed,” 55.  
Ligula, for “tongue,” 107, 108, 117, 119.  
Lingula, for “tongue,” 107, 129.  
Liquida vita, “clear life,” for “upright, chaste, or modest life,” 113.  
Litterulae, for “letters,” 117.  
Locellus, for “place,” 94, 107, 110.  
Locellum pictum, “a painted little place,” for “a garden or meadow marked with flowers,” 106.  
Lucifluus thalamus, “a light-flowing chamber,” for “a chamber surrounded by light.” Note: *thalamus* also means “house,” “palace,” or “bedchamber”; e.g. *actum hoc est in thalamo meo*, “this was done in my palace.”  
Luctamen, “struggle”; also in Virgil, 152, 163.

## M

Machina mundi, with neuter gender, for *machinam mundi*, “the mechanism of the world,” 111.  
Magnificare, for “to exalt”; also in Pliny and others, 27.  
Mammona, for “treasure,” 49.  
Mancipatum ire, for “to enslave” or “devote,” 33.  
Mandamen, for “command” or “precept,” 91, 151.  
Mandamina, for “commands,” 95.  
Manibus pedibusque insistere obsequiis alicujus, “to attend to someone’s services with hands and feet,” for “to obey or comply with someone in every possible way,” 5.  
Manifestari, for “to become manifest” or “to appear,” 76.  
Mansiunculae, for “dwellings,” whether in houses or under roofs, 72.  
Mansurni tres, for “three months,” 53.  
Mansurnis binis, for “two months,” 91.

[Col. 1202]

Materiam alicujus rei detegere, “to uncover the material of something,” for “to state or bring forward the cause of something,” 50.  
Materia, for “subject matter” or “argument,” 4.  
Matuta nitescit, “Matuta shines,” for “dawn gleams” or “the sky grows bright,” 40.  
Meatim, for “in my manner,” 53.  
Medietas numeri, “half of a number.” Cicero does mention this word, but nevertheless rejects it; three times, 59.  
Mei, for *meus, mea, meum*, “my,” occurring hundreds of times. The following examples should be included here: *nostri*, for *noster, nostra, nostrum*, “our”; e.g. *nostri congressio*, for *nostra congressio*, “our meeting,” 9. *Sui*, for *sua*, “her” or “his,” 16. *Vestrum*, for *vestra*, “your,” 17. *Meme*, for *me*, “me,” 148.  
Mensurni unius rotatus, “one month’s circuit,” that is, “the space of one month,” or “one month,” 33.  
Mercato, used passively, for “after it had been bought,” 130.  
Mercatum, in the passive form, for “bought” or “acquired,” 116.  
Meruit, for “he obtained” or “secured,” 165.  
Metiri, in the passive form, for “to be completed,” 95.  
Metit, for “he enjoys,” 118.  
Mis, an ancient genitive, for *mei*, “of me,” from *ego*, “I.” Ennius: “A great concern is mine to make equals harmonious.” Conrad Celtes is therefore mistaken in the preface when he uses *mis* for *mihi*, “to me,” 34, 120.  
Mis filia, for “my daughter,” literally “daughter of me”; as it is customarily said, or more correctly *mea filia*, 34.  
Misereri alicui, for *misereri alicujus*, “to pity someone”; e.g. *misereamini furentis nati miseriis*, “have pity on the miseries of the raging child,” for “of the miseries,” 16.

Moestitus, for “sadness”; also in Plautus and Nonius, 38.  
Morula, for “a little delay,” 46.

## N

Nactum, in the passive form, for “received,” 110.  
Namque, used hundreds of times by Hrotsuitha to fill out the verse.

Neophytus, for “newcomer” or “novice,” but ironically in this passage, 37.  
Nequam intentio, for “an evil” or “perverse purpose,” 13, 30.  
Nesciola, for “ignorant,” “inexperienced,” “unskilled,” or “unlearned,” 3.  
Nescita, for “unknown things,” that is, “things that are not known,” 4.  
Nimietas doloris, for “the greatness” or “excess of pain”; also in Columella, Palladius, and Macrobius, though in a physical sense, as in “an excess of wine.” See Vossius, *On the Faults of the Latin Language*, 35.  
Nimium occulte, for “entirely secretly” or “most secretly,” 21, 28.  
Nobiliter, for “praiseworthily,” 129.  
Nocebit me minime, for *nocebit mihi minime*, “it will harm me not at all,” 66.  
Nos huc direxerunt, “they directed us here,” for “they sent us away” or “sent us here.”  
Nudavit illi omnia, “he stripped everything from him,” for “he disclosed everything to him,” 116.  
Nugaces, for “vain” or “foolish,” 46.  
Nugacitas, for “vanity” or “foolishness,” 47.  
Nullatenus, for “in no way,” 2.  
Nullo modo, “in no way,” “by no means,” 21, 28.

Obaudi e, for *obedire*, “to obey,” 27.

Obtemperanter, for “obediently,” 40, 43.

Obtemperare in necem alicujus, “to comply with someone’s death,” for “to consent to someone’s death,” 20.

Odis dulcisonis, “with sweet-sounding songs,” for “with very sweet praises,” 112.  
Offuscationes sordium, “darkenings of filth,” for “filth” or “pollution,” 48.

Pacifice fovere, “to cherish peacefully,” for “to cherish gently,” 56.  
Palliolum candidolum, “a little white cloak,” for “a white cloak,” 109.

Palmula, for “palm,” 117.  
Pangere laudes alicui, “to compose praises for someone,” for “to celebrate someone with praises,” 67.

Parientis te, “of you who are giving birth,” for “of you who have borne [the child],” 114.  
Parte, for “on the part of” or “partly,” 114.  
Passibilis, for “capable of suffering,” 68.  
Passibilitas, for “capacity for suffering”; the word is found in Arnobius and Tertullian, 68.

Patenter, for “openly” or “manifestly,” 95.  
Patronus, for “husband,” 79.  
Paulo, for “I rest,” 63, 93.  
Peccamen, for “sin”; also in Prudentius, 41.  
Pellicula, for “skin,” 114.  
Pendet tuo arbitrio, “it hangs upon your judgment,” for “it depends on your decision,” 10.  
Penetral, the same as *penetrale*, meaning every inner part of a house or temple, even if it is uncovered, as Servius says, 48.  
Percerte, for “entirely,” “certainly,” or “indeed,” 57, 66, 74.  
Peremptor, the same as “killer”; also in Prudentius and others, 156.  
Perfecti scientia, “of perfected knowledge,” for “of cultivated” or “learned” knowledge, 3.  
Pergere patria, “to proceed from one’s homeland,” for “to leave one’s homeland,” 115.

Perventio, for “arrival at a place,” 26.  
Piari, in the deponent form, for “to expiate,” 115.  
Pietas, for “grace”; e.g. *pietatis supernae illustratio*, “the illumination of heavenly grace,” for “the light of heavenly grace.”  
Pietas, for “divine mercy,” 30.  
Pietas, for “mercy” or “grace.”  
Pietates cunctae, plural, “all acts of piety,” 76.  
Pigritari, for “to delay,” 70, 40.  
Piscinula, for “pool,” 112.

In Jeremiah 18 one reads of the potter: “Having turned, he made that vessel another one.” Prosper of Aquitaine writes *replasmavit id in aliud*, “he refashioned it into another,” translating ἀνέπλασε, πάλιν ἐποίησε, “he fashioned it anew; he made it again,” 56.  
Plasmatum, for “refashioned” or “created,” 30.  
Plasma, for Greek πλάσμα, “a fabrication,” or, as poets say, “a creation,” 145.  
Plaudare, for *plaudere*, “to applaud,” 21.  
Plenus homo, “a complete human being,” for “a perfect human being,” 27.  
Plexibilis quaestio, “a pliable question,” for “a perplexing” or “vexed question,” 68.  
Pneumatis almi numen, “the divinity of the nourishing Spirit,” for “the Holy Spirit,” 78.  
Podagro, for “gouty,” 105.  
Poenitudo, for “repentance”; also in Pacuvius, 128.  
Ponere funus in sepulcrum, “to place a corpse in a tomb,” for “to place the lifeless body back in the tomb,” 25.  
Ponere in custodiam, “to place in custody,” for “to throw into prison,” 18.  
Popellus, for “people,” 74, 81, 84, 87, 130.  
Portaret terra consimilem potentem, “the earth would carry a similarly powerful one,” for “it would bring forth [one],”  — [reference not supplied].  
Poscere aliquem, for “to ask” or “pray to someone.”  
Posse, that is, “according to one’s strength,” e.g. *juxta meum posse*, “according to my ability.” Thus Rudolphus Ardens: *pro posse nostro*, “according to our ability,” that is, “with our utmost strength”; likewise *si Deus annuerit posse* in Hrotsuitha, 1, 3, 13.  
Possibilitas, for “ability” or “capacity,” 28.  
Possunt, for *possint*, “they may be able,” 116.  
Praecelsa potestas, “lofty power,” for “high authority,” 164.  
Praecognitor, for “one who knows all things beforehand,” 35.  
Praecordialis amor, “love of the heart,” for “deep” or “sincere love,” 24.  
Praefato opusculo, in the passive form, for “the aforesaid” or “mentioned shortly before”; nevertheless, it is found in Seneca and others, and Arnobius often used this form, 4.  
Praefigurare in facie, “to prefigure in the face,” for “to display or reveal by one’s expression,” 38.  
Praemittere spiritum coelo, “to send the spirit ahead to heaven,” for “to give one’s soul back to heaven,” 56.  
Praepono, for *propono*, “I propose,” 66.  
Praeposita, for “brought forward” or “presented,” 44.  
Praesentare, for “to summon,” “bring,” or “cause someone to be present,” 20, 57.  
Praesicca ligula, “an excessively dry tongue,” for “a very dry tongue,” 108.  
Praesumere, for “to dare,” “arrogate to oneself,” or “attempt,” 36.  
Praesumptio, for “arrogance” or “boldness,” 70.  
Praesumptio, for “light-mindedness,” “wickedness,” or “recklessness,” 48.  
Praesumptuosius, for “more lightly,” “more boldly,” 48.  
Praevalere, for “to be effective,” “to be able,” 61.  
Praevaricatio, for “corruption,” 36.  
Prece, for *precibus*, “by prayers”; also found in good authors, 76.  
Preculae, for “prayers,” 82, 86.  
Pretium vitae, “the price of life,” for “danger to life,” 12.  
Primale, for “immediately,” 112.

[Col. 1204]

Primates parentes, “foremost parents,” for “first parents,” 134.  
Primitus, for “first,” 84.  
Proaulium, for “the front part of a hall,” or “a chamber or house before the hall.” In other medieval writers it also means “hall,” which is likewise called *salutarium*, since those who came to pay their respects were received there, 19.

Pro certo, that is, “certainly,” “surely,” or “indeed,” 25.  
Prolambens arva fonticulis, “washing the fields with little springs,” for “cleansing the fields,” 106.  
Prolambere plantas alicujus, “to lick someone’s soles,” for “to fall at someone’s feet,”  — [reference not supplied].  
Prolixitas, for “length” or “distance,” 67.  
Propalare rerum, with either a genitive or an accusative, for “to disclose something,” 20.  
Properamini, in a deponent sense, that is, “hurry,” 49.  
Propinare mortem alicui, “to drink death to someone,” for “to bring about someone’s death,” 30, 31.  
Proportionatio, for “proportion,” 44.  
Prorumpere in vocem talem coepit, “he began to burst into such a cry,” for “he began to speak as follows,” 166.  
Prosapies, for *prosapia*, “lineage,” 113.  
Prosperor, in the deponent form; e.g. *quo prosperentur exitum pugnae*, “so that they may have a successful outcome in the battle,” for “so that they may prosper,”  — [reference not supplied].  
Protoplastus mundus, “the world first fashioned,” for “the world created first,” 83.  
Protrahis, for “you delay,” “hesitate,” or “doubt,” 5.  
Proximare, for “to approach more closely,” 39.  
Pusioli feminei, for “little girls”; also *pusiolae*, 61.

Qua, for “where,” 37.  
Quadruplicatus exercitus, “a fourfold army,” for “a divided army of four parts,” 13.  
Quadruvium, in later writers *quadrivium*, for the four branches of mathematics: arithmetic, astronomy, geometry, and music, 44.  
Qualitas, for “condition” or “circumstance”; e.g. *ex qualitate rectoris*, “according to the condition of the ruler,” 16.  
Qualiter, for “how,” 41.  
Quandoque, for “sometimes” or “formerly,” 13, 25.  
Quantocius, for “as quickly as possible”; also in Sulpicius Severus, 10, 29.  
Quantum ad me, for “as far as I am concerned,” 6.  
Quantum attulit, for *attulerit*, “how much he has brought,” outside a question, 62.  
Quatenus, for “until,” 8, 66.  
Quatinus, for “so that”; also in Macrobius, 40.  
Qui, for “how,” 33.  
Qui, for “how”; e.g. *qui potest fieri*, “how can it happen,” for “how can it happen”; *qui vocatur*, “how is it called,” for “what is it called,” 46.  
Quia, for “whether,” 84.  
Quid vocaris, for “what are you called?” literally “how are you called?” 46. Likewise *quid pateris*, “how are you suffering?” for “what are you suffering?” 64.  
Quid fieri jubet, for *jubeat*, “what he orders to be done,” 85.  
Quin, with the indicative mood; e.g. *quin estis perventurae*, “that you are about to arrive,” for *quin sitis perventurae*, “that you may be about to arrive,” 9.  
Quivi, for *potui*, “I was able”; this too occurs in good authors.  
Quo, for “which” or “how much,” preceded by *eo*; e.g. *eo magis expaveo, quo meminero nullum evasisse*, “I am the more terrified because I shall remember that no one escaped,” etc.  
Quo, for “where,” preceded by *eo*, 33.  
Quo, for “the more,” preceded by *eo magis*, “the more,” 36.  
Quo meruissemus, for “so that we might deserve,” 63.  
Quoadusque, for “as long as” or “until,” 46.  
Quod, for “so that”; e.g. *spero quod attineat*, “I hope that it concerns,” for *spero ut attineat*, “I hope that it may concern,” 24.

[Col. 1205]

Quo didicisset, for “so that he might learn,” 83.  
Quo vellent desponsare, for “so that they might betroth,” 83.

## R

Receptatrix, for “receiver,” 43.  
Recolo, for “I recall” or “remember,” 68.  
Recompensare, for “to compensate,” 68.  
Recompensatio, for “compensation,” 41.  
Reconcilior, in the deponent form, “I am reconciled,” 9.  
Reformatum, for “corrected” or “amended.”  
Regnat et gloriatur, “he reigns and is glorified,” for “he reigns and is in glory.”  
Regularis conversatio, “regular conduct,” for “to live or conduct oneself according to the rule of one’s sacred order,” 39.  
Repedare patriam, for “to return to one’s homeland,” 79.  
Repedari, for “to return home on foot,” 95.  
Resecare aliquid per tres partes, “to cut something through three parts,” that is, “to divide something into three parts,” 74.  
Retinaculum animarum, “restraint of souls,” that is, “a bond of souls,” 21.  
Retinacula mortis, “restraints of death,” for “bonds of death,” 30.  
Retorquere ingenium in datorem, “to turn one’s ingenuity back upon the giver,” for “to credit the giver with what was received,” 2.  
Retributio, for “reward”; also found in Augustine, 5.  
Retributio aeterna, for “heavenly reward,” 13.  
Retro tempora, for “before the ages,” 68.  
Retro exordium natus, “born before the beginning,” 8.  
Reviviscere, for *revirescere*, “to grow green again,” 68.  
Robur virilis, with *virilis* in the masculine gender, though *virile* has been substituted for it, 2.  
Rostro latrat, “he barks with his snout,” for “he emits from his mouth” or “excludes,”  — [reference not supplied].  
Ruina, used for “damage,” 41.  
Rumpere tristitias, “to break sorrows,” for “to lay aside grief,” 40.  
Rumpere in voces, “to break into cries,” for “to burst into speech.”

## S

Sacelli Gangolphi, “of Gangolphus’s little shrine,” for “of Saint or Blessed Gangolphus,” 109.  
Saeculum, for “the corrupt ways of human beings,” 32.  
Sanum recipere, for “to recover health,” 17.  
Sapere nostrum, for “our wisdom,” 66.  
Satis antiquiorem, for “much older,” 87.  
Scalpsit crimina nudare, “he scratched to uncover crimes,” for “he contrived to expose crimes,” 113.  
Scibilis scientia, “knowable knowledge,” for “knowledge that falls within the grasp of understanding or can be known,” 46.  
Sciscitari aliquem, for “to inquire of someone” or “to question someone.” Here Hrosuitha appears to imitate Suetonius, who likewise uses the accusative, 11.  
Scius, the same as *sciens*, “knowing,” 3, 45.  
Se, for “himself,” 114.  
Secretum habere ad aliquem, “to have a secret with someone,” for “to wish to tell someone something secret,” 19.  
Secus, for “around”; e.g. *undique secus circumdamur*, “we are surrounded all around,” 10.  
Secus me, for “near me” or “beside me,” 35, 47, 53.  
Seducere, for “to lead away from the right course,” 38.  
Sentiscere, for “to feel”; it is also found in Lucretius, 30, 31.  
Sepicolae, for “a little enclosure,” 108.  
Serenitas pulchritudinis, “the serenity of beauty,” for “the excellence of beauty,” 17.  
Serie, for “seriously,” 2.  
Sibi, for “themselves,” 74.  
Sibi fertur, for *ipsi fertur*, “it is reported to him,” 117.  
Sitienter, for “eagerly”; also in Cicero, 149.  
Solatur, in the passive form, for “he is comforted,” 87.  
Solidandi amoris, “of strengthening love,” in a moral sense, for “of confirming love”; in its natural sense it is also found among ancient authors, 7.

[Col. 1205]

Solito, used adverbially, for “in the customary manner,” 42, 45.  
Sollicitare, for “to make anxious,” 37.  
Sonipes, for “horse”; also in Virgil, 37.  
Sonum sapere, “to have a sound,” for “to make good sense,” 50.  
Sospitas, for “safety,” 29.  
Specialiter, for “particularly”; also in Columella and Quintilian.  
Spera, for *sphaera* or *sphera*, “sphere”; here a simple *e* has been changed into the diphthong *ae*, 44, 45.  
Spiritalis, for *spiritualis*, “spiritual”; a word very commonly used by the Christian Fathers, 35, 4.  
Spontanea mente, “with spontaneous mind,” for “spontaneously” or “of one’s own accord,” 41.  
Sputa jacere, “to cast out spittle,” for “to foam,” 16.  
Stabilitas, for “steadfastness”; e.g. *stabilitas fidei*, “steadfastness of faith,” 9.  
Stemma virginitatis, “genealogy of virginity,” for “the author and leader of virgins,” 33.  
Stichus, for “verse,” 70.  
Stringere lacrymas, “to tighten tears,” for “to restrain” or “hold back tears,” 38.  
Strophium heroicum, “heroic band,” for “heroic meter or poem,” 2.  
Sua cura, for *ipsius*, “his or her own,” 73.  
Suadela, for “eloquence,” 88.  
Suam, for *ipsius*, “his or her own,” 114.  
Sua venia, for *ejus venia*, “by his or her permission,” 40.  
Sub spem amatoris, “under the hope of the lover,” for “in the lover’s hope,” unless one should read *sub specie amatoris*, “under the appearance of a lover,” 37.  
Substantia divina, for “the divine Godhead,” 30.  
Substantiola, for “small” or “limited resources,” 74, 145.  
Subtractat sese lucris ab illis, “he withdraws himself from those profits,” for “he withdraws or removes himself from them,” 108.  
Subtraxi faciendis, “I withdrew from things to be done,” for “I withdrew myself from things to be done,” or “I avoided doing them,” 5.  
Successionibus prosperis, for “successful outcomes,” 13, 15.  
Sufficientia, for “abundance” or “what is sufficient”; thus *sufficientia vigoris*, “sufficiency of strength,” for “sufficient strength,” 70.  
Sui causa, for *ipsius causa*, “for his or her own sake,” 112.  
Summotenus, for “summarily,” 40.  
Supercilium montis, “the brow of a mountain,” for “the summit” or “peak of a mountain”; also in Livy and Virgil, 22.  
Superficietenus, for “summarily” or “in general,” 44.  
Supergradieris, for “you will transcend” or “transgress,” 33.  
Superna gratia, for “the grace of God,” 28.  
Superponere equo, for “to place on a horse” or “upon horseback,” 41.  
Suppellex, with double *p*, for *supellex*, “furnishings,” 46.  
Supportare laudem alicujus, “to carry someone’s praise,” for “to bring praise to someone,” 77.  
Suprema sat crimina, “crimes sufficiently supreme,” for “the greatest crimes,” 142.  
Surripere prolixitatem viae, “to steal the length of the road,” for “to undertake a long journey,” 47.  
Susceptio pauperum, “receiving the poor,” for “the relief of the poor” or “mercy toward the poor,” 13.

## T

Taedeo vitae propriae, “I am weary of my own life,” for *taedet me vitae*, “I am weary of life,” 25.  
Talentus, for *talentum*, “talent,” 70.  
Tangaris de mei passione, “may you be touched concerning my suffering,” for “may you be touched by my grief” or “saddened by my torment,” 65.  
Tegmen religionis deponere, “to lay aside the covering of religion,” for “to lay aside the covering of a religious order” or “to remove the religious habit,” 37.  
Temporalium despectio, “contempt of temporal things,” for “contempt for fleeting and perishable things,” 33.

[Col. 1206]

Cicero also uses this word in Nonius; e.g. *alta despectio*, “profound contempt.”  
Tempusculum, for “a short time,” 46.  
Tenebricolarum rex, “king of the inhabitants of darkness,” for “the Devil” or “the enemy of the human race,” 47.  
Tenere stirpem, for “to possess” or “have,” 77.  
Teneritudo, for “a tender body”; also in Varro, 54.  
Teneritudo aetatulae, “the tenderness of a little age,” for “tender youth,” 61.  
Tentamentum, for “temptation”; it is also found in Virgil, *Aeneid* 8.144, 134.  
Tentatrix dextra, “the testing right hand,” that is, “a right hand that touches or feels,” 89.  
Terratenus, for “upon the earth” or “on the ground,” 10.  
Tinnitas responsi, “the ringing of the response,” for “the sound of the reply,” 36.  
Tis, an ancient genitive, for *tui*, “of you”; thus Plautus, *Miles Gloriosus* IV, scene 2, verse 42, 142, 159.  
Triduanae induciae, for “a truce of three days.” *Triduanus* is found in Apuleius and Jerome, 62.  
Turpi udinis locus, printed thus, probably *turpitudinis locus*, “a place of shame,” for “a brothel,” 77.

## U

Undiquessecus, for “everywhere,” “all around,” or “from every side,” 57.  
Universale vitiorum, “the universal of vices,” for “all vices,” 71.  
Usia, for Greek οὐσία, “essence” or “substance”; also in the jurist Ulpian, *Digest* 18.1.9, *On Contracting a Sale*, 43, 74.  
Usque, for “until,” 87.  
Usque solum stratus, “stretched all the way to the ground,” for “stretched or prostrate down to the ground,” 108.  
Usurpasse servituti tuae castella, “to have appropriated castles to your servitude,” for “to appropriate castles for your own use,” 14, 24.  
Ut, causal, with the indicative mood; e.g. *ut non solum gaudent, sed etiam fulgent*, “since they not only rejoice but also shine,” for *gaudeant, fulgeant*, “may they rejoice, may they shine,” 17, 34.  
Ut dedignantur, for *ut dedignentur*, “so that they may disdain,” 57.  
Ut sentit, for *ut sentiat*, “as he may feel,” 117.  
Utquid, for “why” or “to what end,” 50.

## V
To be vacant in some matter, instead of “for some matter,” 13.  
An empty hope, instead of a vain hope, 25.  
The present tense *valere*, used like the Greek **εὗτυγχάνειν**, “to prosper,” 13.  
To serve vanity, instead of “to serve, devote oneself to perishable and empty things,” 35.  
To wish and to be able, instead of “intention,” 28.  
To wish, instead of “intention”; for example, *juxta sui velle*, that is, “according to one’s intention.”  
Your wish, that is, “your intention,” 32.  
To devise an evil intention, that is, “to devise something evil or a crime,” 27.  
Our wish, instead of “our intention,” is a Graecism, 66.  
To offer veneration to metals, instead of “to venerate metals,” or “to honor them with veneration,” 61.  
*Veneratur*, a deponent form, instead of “is affected with veneration,” 83.  
“May my petition come,” instead of “may my petition find a place,” 68.  
*Verbula*, instead of “words,” 113.  
“I fear that not,” instead of “I fear lest,” 66.  
To eat from the fruit, instead of “to eat the fruit,” 94.  
*Veternus*, an adjective, instead of “suffering from lethargy,” “lethargic,” 30.  
To expend a turn on love, instead of “to respond to love,” or “in love,” 24.  
Twenty years, with a distributive used instead of a cardinal numeral, 32.  
“We seem Augustuses,” instead of “Augustuses,” 14.  
An aged virgin, instead of Eve, the mother of the living, 72.  
[Col. 1207] Shaken to the very entrails, instead of “struck in the whole mind,” 48.  
I am disturbed to the very entrails, instead of “I am disturbed from the heart,” “I am wholly disturbed,” 35, 41.  
To embrace to the very entrails, instead of “to embrace wholeheartedly,” 26.  
[Col. 1207] The hiding places of the entrails, instead of “the recesses of the entrails,” 28.  
To utter cries of lamentation aloud, instead of “to raise one’s voice in lamentation,” 34.  
The veins all flutter, instead of “the veins leap for joy,” 106.  
[Col. 1208] *Volutare*, instead of *volutari*; for example, “that you may roll about in the innermost parts of the earth,” instead of “that you may be rolled about,” 33.  
To turn a year, instead of “to pass a year.” Likewise, Olympiads and lustra, 59.

# CONTENTS OF THIS VOLUME

## Wigo, Dean of Phyutwang Monastery

### Letters

9 I.—To Empress Adelheid. He commends himself and his affairs to her with the greatest earnestness. 9  
II.—To Theodoric the Hermit in the Or Forest. He writes how burdened he is with many affairs and cares in administering his monastery, and asks for Brother Adalgoz as his assistant. 9  
III.—To Dietricus. He asks him to send him canonical books, which will be useful to him in the case of a certain cleric badly treated by laymen. 10  
IV.—To Liutold, Bishop of Augsburg. He asks him to provide help amid the severe troubles affecting his monastery. 11  
V.—To Gozpert, Abbot of Tegernsee. He explains to him the difficulty caused by the construction of his new monastery and asks him to send Weicherus to him for consolation and Sigibardus for the sake of study. 11  
VI.—To Liutold, Bishop of Augsburg. He asks him kindly to receive those brothers whom he obtained from Gozpert, Abbot of Tegernsee, for the benefit of his monastery, and to send them to him supplied with the necessities of life. 12  
VII.—Copy of the preceding letter. Wigo commends two young monks to F., the Augsburg schoolmaster, and asks that a copy of Priscian the Elder be made available to him. 12  
VIII.—In the name of his brethren, to Henry, Duke of Bavaria. He asks that fish be sent to him so that Easter may be celebrated with greater festivity. 13  
IX.—To G., archpriest. He asks him to defer for a while the punishment to be inflicted on the priest Ortwine. 13  
X.—To Count E. He wishes him to be the defender of a saltworks recently donated to him and of the entire monastery of Saint Saviour at Phyutwang. 14  
XI.—To Liutold, Bishop of Augsburg. Concerning injuries inflicted on him by the son of Rihhard. 14  
XII.—To the same. He hopes that the extreme shortage of grain may be relieved by his beneficence. 15  
XIII.—Apparently by the same writer, to G. and E. He asks for more frequent letters and their affection. 16
